1. Kāliṅgavaggo

1. The Kāliṅga Division

[301] 1. Cūḷakāliṅgajātakavaṇṇanā

[301] 1. The Commentary on the Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka

Vivarathimāsaṃ [V 3.0001][P 3.0001][M 3.0001] dvāranti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto catunnaṃ paribbājikānaṃ pabbajjaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vesāliyaṃ kira licchavirājūnaṃ satta sahassāni satta satāni satta ca licchavī vasiṃsu. Te sabbepi pucchāpaṭipucchācittakā ahesuṃ. Atheko pañcasu vādasatesu byatto nigaṇṭho vesāliyaṃ sampāpuṇi, te tassa saṅgahaṃ akaṃsu. Aparāpi evarūpā nigaṇṭhī sampāpuṇi[V 3.0002]. Rājāno dvepi jane vādaṃ kāresuṃ, ubhopi sadisāva ahesuṃ. Tato licchavīnaṃ etadahosi “ime dvepi paṭicca uppanno putto byatto bhavissatī”ti. Tesaṃ vivāhaṃ kāretvā dvepi ekato vāsesuṃ. Atha nesaṃ saṃvāsamanvāya paṭipāṭiyā catasso dārikāyo eko ca dārako jāyi. Dārikānaṃ “saccā, lolā, avadhārikā, paṭicchādā”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu, dārakassa “saccako”ti. Te [M 3.0002] pañcapi janā viññutaṃ pattā mātito pañca vādasatāni, pitito pañca vādasatānīti vādasahassaṃ uggaṇhiṃsu. Mātāpitaro dārikānaṃ evaṃ ovadiṃsu “sace koci gihī tumhākaṃ vādaṃ bhindissati, tassa pādaparicārikā bhaveyyātha. Sace pabbajito bhindissati, tassa santike pabbajeyyāthā”ti.

‘Open this gate,’ this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the going forth of four female wanderers. It is said that in Vesālī, seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven Licchavi princes resided. They were all fond of questioning and counter-questioning. Then, a Nigaṇṭha skilled in five hundred doctrines arrived in Vesālī, and they gave him their patronage. Later, a similar female Nigaṇṭha also arrived. The princes had both of them engage in a debate, and both were equally matched. Then the Licchavis thought, ‘A son born from these two will surely be skilled.’ They arranged their marriage and had them live together. Through their cohabitation, in due course, four daughters and one son were born. They named the daughters Saccā, Lolā, Avadhārikā, and Paṭicchādā, and the son they named Saccaka. All five children, having reached maturity, learned five hundred doctrines from their mother and five hundred from their father—thus mastering a thousand doctrines. The parents advised the daughters thus: ‘If any householder defeats you in debate, you should become his handmaidens. If a renunciant defeats you, you should go forth into homelessness in his presence.’

Aparabhāge mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. Tesu kālakatesu saccakanigaṇṭho tattheva vesāliyaṃ licchavīnaṃ sippaṃ sikkhāpento vasi. Bhaginiyo jambusākhaṃ gahetvā vādatthāya [P 3.0002] nagarā nagaraṃ caramānā sāvatthiṃ patvā nagaradvāre sākhaṃ nikhaṇitvā “yo amhākaṃ vādaṃ āropetuṃ sakkoti gihī vā pabbajito vā, so etaṃ paṃsupuñjaṃ pādehi vikiritvā pādeheva sākhaṃ maddatū”ti dārakānaṃ vatvā bhikkhāya nagaraṃ pavisiṃsu. Athāyasmā sāriputto asammaṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā rittaghaṭesu pānīyaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā gilāne ca paṭijaggitvā divātaraṃ sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisanto taṃ sākhaṃ disvā dārake pucchi, dārakā taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhiṃsu. Thero dārakeheva pātāpetvā maddāpetvā “yehi ayaṃ sākhā ṭhapitā, te katabhattakiccāva āgantvā jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake maṃ passantū”ti dārakānaṃ vatvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā katabhattakicco vihāradvārakoṭṭhake aṭṭhāsi. Tāpi paribbājikā bhikkhāya caritvā āgatā sākhaṃ madditaṃ disvā “kenāyaṃ madditā”ti vatvā “sāriputtattherena, sace tumhe vādatthikā, jetavanadvārakoṭṭhakaṃ gacchathā”ti dārakehi vuttā puna nagaraṃ pavisitvā mahājanaṃ sannipātetvā vihāradvārakoṭṭhakaṃ gantvā theraṃ vādasahassaṃ pucchiṃsu. Thero taṃ vissajjetvā “aññaṃ kiñci jānāthā”ti pucchi. “Na jānāma, sāmī”ti. “Ahaṃ pana vo kiñci pucchāmī”ti. “Puccha, sāmi, jānantiyo kathessāmā”ti.

Later, their parents passed away. After their death, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha remained in Vesālī, teaching the Licchavis various arts. His sisters took a rose-apple branch and, traveling from city to city for the sake of debate, arrived at Sāvatthī. At the city gate, they planted the branch and told some children, ‘Whoever—whether a householder or a renunciant—is able to challenge us to a debate, let him scatter this pile of dust with his feet and trample the branch with his feet.’ Then they entered the city for alms. Now, the Venerable Sāriputta, after sweeping the unswept places, filling the empty water pots, and tending to the sick, was entering Sāvatthī for alms later in the day when he saw that branch and asked the children about it. The children explained the matter. The Elder had the children knock down the branch and trample it, and then told them, ‘Let those by whom this branch was planted, after they have finished their meal, come and see me at the gatehouse of Jetavana.’ Having said this to the children, he entered the city, and after finishing his meal, he stood at the monastery gatehouse. Those female wanderers, too, having gone for alms and returned, saw the trampled branch and asked, ‘By whom was this trampled?’ When the children told them, ‘By the Elder Sāriputta. If you desire a debate, go to the gatehouse of Jetavana,’ they re-entered the city, gathered a large crowd, and going to the monastery gatehouse, asked the Elder a thousand questions. The Elder answered them and then asked, ‘Do you know anything else?’ ‘We do not know, sir.’ ‘Then I shall ask you something.’ ‘Ask, sir. If we know, we will answer.’

Thero “ekaṃ nāma ki”nti pucchi. Tā na jāniṃsu. Thero vissajjesi. Tā “amhākaṃ, sāmi, parājayo, tumhākaṃ jayo”ti āhaṃsu. “Idāni kiṃ karissathā”ti? “Amhākaṃ mātāpitūhi ayaṃ ovādo dinno ‘sace vo gihī vādaṃ bhindissati, tassa pajāpatiyo bhaveyyātha. Sace pabbajito, tassa santike pabbajeyyāthā’ti, pabbajjaṃ no dethā”ti. Thero “sādhū”ti vatvā tā uppalavaṇṇāya theriyā santike pabbājesi. Tā sabbāpi na cirasseva arahattaṃ [V 3.0003] pāpuṇiṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ [M 3.0003] bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, sāriputtatthero catunnaṃ paribbājikānaṃ avassayo hutvā sabbā arahattaṃ pāpesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa etāsaṃ avassayo [P 3.0003] ahosi, idāni pana pabbajjābhisekaṃ dāpesi, pubbe rājamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Elder asked, ‘What is “one”?’ They did not know. The Elder answered it. They said, ‘Sir, ours is the defeat; yours is the victory.’ ‘What will you do now?’ ‘Our parents gave us this instruction: “If a householder defeats you in debate, you are to become his wives. If a renunciant defeats you, you are to go forth into homelessness in his presence.” Please grant us the going forth.’ The Elder said, ‘Very well,’ and had them go forth in the presence of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā. Before long, they all attained Arahantship. Then one day, the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: ‘Reverend sirs, the Elder Sāriputta became a refuge for four female wanderers and led them all to Arahantship.’ The Teacher arrived and asked, ‘Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you now gathered together?’ When they told him, ‘For this one,’ he said, ‘Not only now, bhikkhus, was he their refuge, but in the past as well. Now he has given them the consecration of the going forth, but in the past, he established them in the position of chief queen.’ And he related a story of the past.

Atīte kāliṅgaraṭṭhe dantapuranagare kāliṅgarāje rajjaṃ kārente assakaraṭṭhe pāṭalinagare assako nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Kāliṅgo sampannabalavāhano sayampi nāgabalo paṭiyodhaṃ na passati. So yujjhitukāmo hutvā amaccānaṃ ārocesi “ahaṃ yuddhatthiko, paṭiyodhaṃ pana na passāmi, kiṃ karomā”ti. Amaccā “attheko, mahārāja, upāyo, dhītaro te catasso uttamarūpadharā, tā pasādhetvā paṭicchannayāne nisīdāpetvā balaparivutā gāmanigamarājadhāniyo carāpetha. Yo rājā tā attano gehe kātukāmo bhavissati, tena saddhiṃ yuddhaṃ karissāmā”ti vadiṃsu. Rājā tathā kāresi. Tāhi gatagataṭṭhāne rājāno bhayena tāsaṃ nagaraṃ pavisituṃ na denti, paṇṇākāraṃ pesetvā bahinagareyeva vasāpenti. Evaṃ sakalajambudīpaṃ vicaritvā assakaraṭṭhe pāṭalinagaraṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Assakopi nagaradvārāni pidahāpetvā paṇṇākāraṃ pesesi. Tassa nandiseno nāma amacco paṇḍito byatto upāyakusalo. So cintesi “imā kira rājadhītaro sakalajambudīpaṃ vicaritvā paṭiyodhaṃ na labhiṃsu, evaṃ sante jambudīpo tuccho nāma ahosi, ahaṃ kāliṅgena saddhiṃ yujjhissāmī”ti. So nagaradvāraṃ gantvā dovārike āmantetvā tāsaṃ dvāraṃ vivarāpetuṃ paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, while King Kāliṅga was ruling in the city of Dantapura in the kingdom of Kāliṅga, a king named Assaka was ruling in the city of Pāṭali in the kingdom of Assaka. King Kāliṅga, endowed with a powerful army and vehicles, and himself possessing the strength of an elephant, could see no adversary. Desiring to fight, he informed his ministers, 'I am eager for war, but I see no adversary. What should we do?' The ministers replied, 'There is a way, great king. You have four daughters of surpassing beauty. Adorn them, seat them in covered carriages, and, surrounded by an army, have them travel through villages, towns, and royal cities. With whatever king desires to take them into his own house, with him we shall wage war.' The king did so. Wherever they went, the local kings, out of fear, would not allow them to enter their cities; they sent gifts and had them stay outside the city. Thus, having traveled all over Jambudīpa, they arrived at the city of Pāṭali in the kingdom of Assaka. King Assaka also had the city gates closed and sent gifts. His minister, named Nandisena, was wise, accomplished, and skilled in strategy. He thought, 'These royal daughters, it seems, have traveled all over Jambudīpa and found no adversary. If this is so, then Jambudīpa is indeed empty. I shall fight with King Kāliṅga.' Going to the city gate, he addressed the gatekeepers and, in order to have the gate opened for them, spoke the first verse:

1.

1.

“Vivarathimāsaṃ dvāraṃ, nagaraṃ pavisantu aruṇarājassa;

Sīhena susiṭṭhena, surakkhitaṃ nandisenenā”ti.

'Open this gate for them, let them enter the city of King Aruṇa; it is well-guarded by a well-trained lion, well-protected by Nandisena.'

Tattha aruṇarājassāti so hi rajje patiṭṭhitakāle raṭṭhanāmavasena assako nāma jāto, kuladattiyaṃ panassa nāmaṃ aruṇoti[M 3.0004][P 3.0004]. Tenāha “aruṇarājassā”ti. Sīhenāti purisasīhena. Susiṭṭhenāti ācariyehi suṭṭhu anusāsitena. Nandisenenāti mayā nandisenena nāma.

Herein, 'of King Aruṇa' means this: when he was established in the kingdom, he became known as Assaka, according to the name of the country, but his given family name was Aruṇa. Therefore it is said, 'of King Aruṇa.' 'By a lion' means by a lion among men. 'Well-trained' means well-instructed by his teachers. 'By Nandisena' means by me, whose name is Nandisena.

So evaṃ vatvā dvāraṃ vivarāpetvā tā gahetvā assakarañño datvā “tumhe mā bhāyittha, yuddhe sati ahaṃ jinissāmi, imā uttamarūpadharā rājadhītaro mahesiyo karothā”ti tāsaṃ abhisekaṃ dāpetvā tāhi saddhiṃ āgate purise “gacchatha, tumhe rājadhītūnaṃ assakarājena mahesiṭṭhāne [V 3.0004] ṭhapitabhāvaṃ tumhākaṃ rañño ācikkhathā”ti uyyojesi. Te gantvā ārocesuṃ. Kāliṅgo “na hi nūna so mayhaṃ balaṃ jānātī”ti vatvā tāvadeva mahatiyā senāya nikkhami. Nandiseno tassa āgamanaṃ ñatvā “attano kira rajjasīmāyameva hotu, mā amhākaṃ rañño rajjasīmaṃ okkamatu, ubhinnaṃ rajjānaṃ antare yuddhaṃ bhavissatī”ti sāsanaṃ pesesi. So sāsanaṃ sutvā attano rajjapariyanteyeva aṭṭhāsi. Assakopi attano rajjapariyante aṭṭhāsi. Tadā bodhisatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tesaṃ dvinnaṃ rajjānaṃ antare paṇṇasālāyaṃ vasati. Kāliṅgo cintesi “samaṇā nāma kiñci jānissanti, ko jānāti, kiṃ bhavissati, kassa jayo vā parājayo vā bhavissati, tāpasaṃ pucchissāmī”ti aññātakavesena bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “bhante, kāliṅgo ca assako ca yujjhitukāmā attano attano rajjasīmāyameva ṭhitā, etesu kassa jayo bhavissati, kassa parājayo”ti pucchi. Mahāpuñña, ahaṃ “asukassa jayo, asukassa parājayo”ti na jānāmi, sakko pana devarājā idhāgacchati, tamahaṃ pucchitvā kathessāmi, sve āgaccheyyāsīti. Sakko bodhisattassa upaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā [P 3.0005] nisīdi, atha naṃ bodhisatto tamatthaṃ pucchi. Bhante, kāliṅgo jinissati, assako parājissati, idañcidañca pubbanimittaṃ paññāyissatīti.

Having said this, he had the gate opened, took them, and gave them to King Assaka, saying, 'Do not fear; when there is a battle, I will be victorious. These princesses are of supreme beauty; make them your chief queens.' Then, having had them consecrated, he dismissed the men who had come with them, saying, 'Go and inform your king of the fact that the princesses have been placed in the position of chief queens by King Assaka.' They went and reported this. King Kāliṅga said, 'Surely, he does not know my strength,' and immediately set out with a great army. Nandisena, learning of his approach, sent a message: 'Let him remain within his own kingdom's borders; let him not encroach upon our king's territory. The battle shall take place between the two kingdoms.' Hearing the message, he halted at his own kingdom's border. Assaka also halted at his own border. At that time, the Bodhisatta had gone forth as an ascetic and was dwelling in a leaf-hut between the two kingdoms. King Kāliṅga thought, 'Ascetics surely know something. Who knows? What will happen? Whose victory or defeat will it be? I shall ask the ascetic.' In the guise of a stranger, he approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, sat to one side, exchanged pleasantries, and asked, 'Venerable sir, King Kāliṅga and King Assaka wish to fight and are stationed at their own borders. Between them, who will win and who will lose?' 'O man of great merit, I do not know that such a one will win or such a one will lose; however, Sakka, the king of the gods, comes here. I will ask him and then tell you. You should come tomorrow.' Sakka came to attend upon the Bodhisatta and sat down. Then the Bodhisatta asked him about the matter. 'Venerable sir, Kāliṅga will win, Assaka will lose. This and that omen will appear.'

Kāliṅgo punadivase āgantvā pucchi, bodhisattopissa ācikkhi. So “kiṃ nāma pubbanimittaṃ bhavissatī”ti apucchitvāva “ahaṃ kira jinissāmī”ti uṭṭhāya tuṭṭhiyā pakkāmi. Sā kathā vitthārikā ahosi. Taṃ sutvā assako nandisenaṃ pakkosāpetvā “kāliṅgo kira jinissatiṃ[M 3.0005], mayaṃ parājissāma, kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti āha. So “ko etaṃ jānāti mahārāja, kassa jayo vā parājayo vā, tumhe mā cintayitthā”ti rājānaṃ assāsetvā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno “bhante, ko jinissati, ko parājissatī”ti pucchi. “Kāliṅgo jinissati, assako parājissatī”ti? “Bhante, jinantassa pubbanimittaṃ kiṃ bhavissati, kiṃ parājinantassā”ti? “Mahāpuñña, jinantassa ārakkhadevatā sabbaseto usabho bhavissati, itarassa sabbakāḷako, ubhinnampi ārakkhadevatā yujjhitvā jayaparājayaṃ karissantī”ti. Nandiseno taṃ sutvā uṭṭhāya gantvā rañño sahāye sahassamatte mahāyodhe gahetvā avidūre pabbataṃ abhiruyha “ambho, amhākaṃ rañño jīvitaṃ dātuṃ sakkhissathā”ti pucchi. “Āma, sakkhissāmā”ti. “Tena hi imasmiṃ papāte patathā”ti. Te patituṃ ārabhiṃsu. Atha ne vāretvā “alaṃ ettha patanena, amhākaṃ rañño jīvitaṃ dātuṃ suhadayā anivattino hutvā yujjhathā”ti āha. Te sampaṭicchiṃsuṃ.

The next day, King Kāliṅga came and asked, and the Bodhisatta told him. Without even asking, 'What kind of omen will there be?' he departed joyfully, thinking, 'I will surely win.' That report spread. Hearing this, King Assaka summoned Nandisena and said, 'It is said that Kāliṅga will win and we will be defeated. What should we do?' He said, 'Great King, who can know whose victory or whose defeat it will be? Do not worry.' After reassuring the king, he approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, sat to one side, and asked, 'Venerable sir, who will win and who will lose?' 'Kāliṅga will win, and Assaka will lose.' 'Venerable sir, what will be the omen for the one who wins, and what for the one who is defeated?' 'O meritorious donor, the guardian deity of the one who will win will be an entirely white bull; the guardian deity of the one who will be defeated will be an entirely black bull. The guardian deities of both kings will fight and determine the victory and defeat.' Hearing this, Nandisena rose and went to gather about a thousand great warriors who were the king's friends. He climbed a nearby mountain and asked, 'Friends, will you be able to give your lives for our king?' 'Yes, we will,' they said. 'If so, throw yourselves from this precipice.' They prepared to throw themselves off. Then he stopped them, saying, 'Enough of throwing yourselves from this precipice. With hearts full of love for our king and without retreating, go and fight.' They agreed.

Atha [V 3.0005] saṅgāme upaṭṭhite kāliṅgo “ahaṃ kira jinissāmī”ti vosānaṃ āpajji, balakāyāpissa “amhākaṃ kira jayo”ti vosānaṃ āpajjitvā sannāhaṃ akatvā vaggavaggā [P 3.0006] hutvā yathāruci pakkamiṃsu, vīriyakaraṇakāle vīriyaṃ na kariṃsu. Ubhopi rājāno assaṃ abhiruhitvā “yujjhissāmā”ti aññamaññaṃ upasaṅkamanti. Ubhinnaṃ ārakkhadevatā purato gantvā kāliṅgarañño ārakkhadevatā sabbaseto usabho ahosi, itarassa sabbakāḷako. Tā devatāpi aññamaññaṃ yujjhanākāraṃ dassentā upasaṅkamiṃsu. Te pana usabhā ubhinnaṃ rājūnaṃyeva paññāyanti, na aññesaṃ. Nandiseno assakaṃ pucchi “paññāyati te, mahārāja, ārakkhadevatā”ti. “Āma, paññāyatī”ti. “Kenākārenā”ti. “Kāliṅgarañño ārakkhadevatā sabbaseto usabho hutvā paññāyati, amhākaṃ ārakkhadevatā sabbakāḷako kilamanto hutvā tiṭṭhatī”ti. “Mahārāja, tumhe mā bhāyatha, mayaṃ jinissāma, kāliṅgo parājissati, tumhe assapiṭṭhito otaritvā imaṃ sattiṃ gahetvā susikkhitasindhavaṃ udarapasse vāmahatthena uppīḷetvā iminā purisasahassena saddhiṃ vegena gantvā kāliṅgarañño ārakkhadevataṃ sattippahārena pātetha, tato mayaṃ sahassamattā sattisahassena paharissāma[M 3.0006], evaṃ kāliṅgassa ārakkhadevatā nassissati, tato kāliṅgo parājissati, mayaṃ jinissāmā”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti nandisenena dinnasaññāya gantvā sattiyā pahari, sūrayodhasahassāpi amaccā sattisahassena pahariṃsu. Ārakkhadevatā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi, tāvadeva kāliṅgo parājitvā palāyi. Taṃ palāyamānaṃ disvā sahassamattā amaccā “kāliṅgo palāyatī”ti unnadiṃsu. Kāliṅgo maraṇabhayabhīto palāyamāno taṃ tāpasaṃ akkosanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, when the battle began, King Kāliṅga, thinking 'I will surely win,' became slack in his efforts. His army also became slack, thinking 'Victory will be ours.' They did not form their ranks but went about in groups as they pleased; they did not exert effort when effort was required. The two kings, mounted on horses, approached each other to fight. The guardian deities of the two kings went before them. The guardian deity of King Kāliṅga was an entirely white bull; that of King Assaka was an entirely black bull. These deities also approached each other, making the appearance of fighting. Those bulls were visible only to the two kings; they were not visible to others. Nandisena asked King Assaka, 'Great King, is your guardian deity visible to you?' 'Yes, it is,' he replied. 'In what way is it visible?' 'King Kāliṅga's guardian deity is visible as an entirely white bull, while my guardian deity is visible as an entirely black bull and stands there exhausted.' 'Great King, do not be afraid. We shall cause you to win; Kāliṅga will be defeated. Dismount from your horse, take this spear, and while holding your well-trained Sindh horse firmly by the flank with your left hand, go quickly with these thousand warriors and strike King Kāliṅga's guardian deity with the spear to make it fall. After that, we thousand will strike with a thousand spears. When it is thus struck, King Kāliṅga's guardian deity will perish; then King Kāliṅga will be defeated, and we shall win.' Saying 'Very well,' King Assaka went at the signal given by Nandisena and struck with his spear. The thousand ministers, who were brave warriors, also struck with a thousand spears. The guardian deity died right there. At that very moment, King Kāliṅga was defeated and fled. Seeing him fleeing, the thousand ministers shouted so that it echoed, 'Kāliṅga is fleeing!' King Kāliṅga, fleeing in fear of death, wishing to revile the ascetic, spoke the second verse:

2.

2.

“Jayo kaliṅgānamasayhasāhinaṃ, parājayo anayo assakānaṃ;

Icceva [P 3.0007] te bhāsitaṃ brahmacāri, na ujjubhūtā vitathaṃ bhaṇantī”ti.

Victory to the Kāliṅgas, who endure what is difficult to endure; defeat and ruin to the Assakas. Thus you spoke, O ascetic; those who are upright do not speak falsely.

Tattha asayhasāhinanti asayhaṃ dussahaṃ sahituṃ samatthānaṃ. Icceva te bhāsitanti evaṃ tayā kūṭatāpasa lañjaṃ gahetvā parājinakarājānaṃ jinissati, jinanarājānañca parājissatīti bhāsitaṃ. Na ujjubhūtāti ye kāyena vācāya manasā ca ujubhūtā, na te musā bhaṇantīti.

In this verse, 'asayhasāhinaṃ' means those who are able to endure the unendurable, what is difficult to endure. 'Icceva te bhāsitaṃ' means: 'Thus, O deceitful ascetic, having taken a bribe, you said that the king who would be defeated would win, and the king who would win would be defeated.' 'Na ujjubhūtā' means: 'Those who are upright in body, speech, and mind do not speak falsely.'

Evaṃ so tāpasaṃ akkosanto palāyanto attano nagarameva gato, nivattitvā oloketumpi nāsakkhi. Tato katipāhaccayena sakko tāpasassa upaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Tāpaso tena saddhiṃ kathento tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus reviling the ascetic, King Kāliṅga fled and went quickly to his own city; he did not even dare to turn back and look. Then, after two or three days had passed, Sakka came to the ascetic. The ascetic, wishing to speak with Sakka, spoke the third verse:

3.

3.

“Devā [V 3.0006] musāvādamupātivattā, saccaṃ dhanaṃ paramaṃ tesu sakka;

Taṃ te musā bhāsitaṃ devarāja, kiṃ vā paṭicca maghavā mahindā”ti.

Gods have overcome false speech; among them, truth is the supreme wealth, O Sakka. Yet you, King of Gods, spoke that which was false. For what reason, O Maghavā, Great Indra, did you speak a falsehood?

Tattha taṃ te musā bhāsitanti yaṃ tayā mayhaṃ bhāsitaṃ, taṃ atthabhañjanakamusāvādaṃ kathentena tayā musā bhāsitaṃ, tayā kiṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca evaṃ bhāsitanti?

In this verse, 'that you spoke falsely' refers to what you said to me; by telling a lie that destroys the truth, you spoke falsely. Based on what reason did you speak thus?

Taṃ [M 3.0007] sutvā sakko catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Sakka spoke the fourth verse:

4.

4.

“Nanu te sutaṃ brāhmaṇa bhaññamāne, devā na issanti purisaparakkamassa;

Damo samādhi manaso abhejjo, abyaggatā nikkamanañca kāle;

Daḷhañca viriyaṃ purisaparakkamo ca, teneva āsi vijayo assakāna”nti.

Brahmin, have you not heard it said: 'The gods do not overrule human effort'? Restraint, concentration, an unbreakable mind, non-agitation, and timely exertion, firm energy, and human effort—by these alone was the victory of the Assakas.

Tassattho – kiṃ tayā, brāhmaṇa, tattha tattha vacane bhaññamāne idaṃ na sutapubbaṃ, yaṃ devā purisaparakkamassa na issanti na usūyanti, assakarañño [P 3.0008] vīriyakaraṇavasena attadamanasaṅkhāto damo, samaggabhāvena manaso abhejjo, abhejjasamādhi, assakarañño sahāyānaṃ vīriyakaraṇakāle abyaggatā yathā kāliṅgassa manussā vaggavaggā hutvā osakkiṃsu, evaṃ anosakkanaṃ samaggabhāvena abhejjacittānaṃ vīriyañca purisaparakkamo ca thiro ahosi, teneva kāraṇena assakānaṃ jayo ahosīti.

The meaning is this: Brahmin, when various sayings were being spoken there, have you not heard this before, that the gods do not envy or resent human effort? For the Assaka king, self-control, which is defined as the discipline of self, was his exercise of energy. An unbreakable mind through unity was unbreakable concentration. At the time of the exercise of energy by the Assaka king's allies, there was steadfastness; unlike the men of Kalinga who retreated in scattered groups, there was no retreating. The energy and human effort of those with unbreakable minds through unity were firm. For that very reason, the Assakas were victorious.

Palāte ca pana kāliṅge assakarājā vilopaṃ gāhāpetvā attano nagaraṃ gato. Nandiseno kāliṅgassa sāsanaṃ pesesi “imāsaṃ catunnaṃ rājakaññānaṃ dāyajjakoṭṭhāsaṃ pesetu, sace na peseti, kātabbamettha jānissāmī”ti. So taṃ sāsanaṃ sutvā bhītatasito tāhi laddhabbadāyajjaṃ pesesi, tato paṭṭhāya samaggavāsaṃ vasiṃsu.

When the Kalinga king had fled, the Assaka king had the spoils seized and returned to his own city. Nandisena sent a message to the Kalinga king: 'Send the share of inheritance for these four princesses. If you do not send it, I shall know what must be done here.' Hearing that message, the terrified king sent the inheritance that they were to receive. From then on, they lived together in harmony.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā kāliṅgarañño dhītaro imā daharabhikkhuniyo ahesuṃ, nandiseno sāriputto, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the daughters of the Kalinga king were these young bhikkhunīs, Nandisena was Sāriputta, and the ascetic was I myself.'

Cūḷakāliṅgajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka, the first.

[302] 2. Mahāassārohajātakavaṇṇanā

[302] 2. The Commentary on the Mahāassāroha Jātaka

Adeyyesuṃ [V 3.0007][M 3.0008] dadaṃ dānanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ānandattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu heṭṭhā kathitameva. Satthā “porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi attano upakāravaseneva kiriṃsū”ti vatvā idhāpi atītaṃ āhari.

'Giving a gift to those who should not be given to...' This the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder Ānanda. The story of the present has already been told. The Teacher, having said, 'Even the wise of old acted only out of gratitude for service rendered to them,' related a story of the past.

Atīte bodhisatto bārāṇasirājā hutvā dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāreti, dānaṃ deti, sīlaṃ rakkhati. So “paccantaṃ kupitaṃ vūpasamessāmī”ti balavāhanaparivuto gantvā parājito assaṃ abhiruhitvā palāyamāno ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ pāpuṇi. Tattha tiṃsa janā rājasevakā vasanti. Te pātova gāmamajjhe sannipatitvā gāmakiccaṃ karonti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā vammitaṃ assaṃ abhiruhitvā alaṅkatapaṭiyatto gāmadvārena [P 3.0009] antogāmaṃ pāvisi. Te “kiṃ nu kho ida”nti bhītā palāyitvā sakasakagehāni pavisiṃsu. Eko panettha attano gehaṃ agantvā rañño paccuggamanaṃ katvā “rājā kira paccantaṃ gato”ti suyyati, kosi tvaṃ rājapuriso corapurisoti? “Rājapuriso, sammā”ti. “Tena hi ethā”ti rājānaṃ gehaṃ netvā attano pīṭhake nisīdāpetvā “ehi, bhadde, sahāyakassa pāde dhovā”ti bhariyaṃ tassa pāde dhovāpetvā attano balānurūpena āhāraṃ datvā “muhuttaṃ vissamathā”ti sayanaṃ paññāpesi, rājā nipajji. Itaro assassa sannāhaṃ mocetvā caṅkamāpetvā udakaṃ pāyetvā piṭṭhiṃ telena makkhetvā tiṇaṃ adāsi. Evaṃ tayo cattāro divase rājānaṃ paṭijaggitvā “gacchāmahaṃ, sammā”ti vutte puna rañño ca assassa ca kattabbayuttakaṃ sabbamakāsi. Rājā tussitvā gacchanto “ahaṃ, samma, mahāassāroho nāma, nagaramajjhe amhākaṃ gehaṃ, sace kenaci kiccena nagaraṃ āgacchasi, dakkhiṇadvāre ṭhatvā dovārikaṃ ‘mahāassāroho kataragehe vasatī’ti pucchitvā dovārikaṃ gahetvā amhākaṃ gehaṃ āgaccheyyāsī”ti vatvā pakkāmi.

In the past, the Bodhisatta became the king of Benares and ruled with righteousness and justice, gave alms, and observed the precepts. Thinking, 'I will pacify the troubled border region,' he set out surrounded by an army and vehicles, but being defeated, he mounted a horse and fled, reaching a border village. Thirty royal servants lived there. Early in the morning, they gathered in the village center to handle village business. At that moment, the king, riding his armored horse and fully adorned, entered the village through the gate. Frightened, wondering, 'What is this?', they fled and entered their respective homes. However, one man there, without going to his own house, went to welcome the king and asked, 'It is heard that the king has gone to the border; are you a king's man or a robber?' 'A king's man, friend,' he replied. 'In that case, come,' he said, leading the king to his house, seating him on his own stool, and saying to his wife, 'Come, dear, wash the friend's feet.' He had her wash his feet, gave him food according to his own strength, and prepared a bed, saying, 'Rest for a moment.' The king lay down. The other man removed the horse's armor, walked it around, gave it water, rubbed its back with oil, and gave it grass. Thus, having attended to the king for three or four days, when the king said, 'I am going, friend,' he again did all that was proper to do for both the king and the horse. The king, pleased, said as he was leaving, 'Friend, I am a Master of the Horse (Mahāassāroha). Our house is in the middle of the city. If you come to the city for any business, stand at the southern gate, ask the gatekeeper, "In which house does the Master of the Horse live?", take the gatekeeper, and come to our house.' Saying this, he departed.

Balakāyopi rājānaṃ adisvā bahinagare khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā ṭhito rājānaṃ disvā paccuggantvā parivāresi. Rājā nagaraṃ pavisanto dvārantare ṭhatvā [M 3.0009] dovārikaṃ pakkosāpetvā mahājanaṃ paṭikkamāpetvā “tāta, eko paccantagāmavāsī maṃ daṭṭhukāmo āgantvā ‘mahāassārohassa gehaṃ kaha’nti taṃ pucchissati, taṃ tvaṃ hatthe gahetvā ānetvā maṃ dasseyyāsi, tadā tvaṃ sahassaṃ labhissasī”ti āha. So nāgacchati, tasmiṃ anāgacchante rājā tassa vasanagāme baliṃ vaḍḍhāpesi, balimhi vaḍḍhite nāgacchati. Evaṃ dutiyampi tatiyampi [V 3.0008] baliṃ vaḍḍhāpesi, neva āgacchati. Atha naṃ gāmavāsino sannipatitvā āhaṃsu “ayya, tava sahāyassa mahāassārohassa āgatakālato paṭṭhāya [P 3.0010] mayaṃ balinā pīḷiyamānā sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na sakkoma, gaccha tava sahāyassa mahāassārohassa vatvā amhākaṃ baliṃ vissajjāpehī”ti. Sādhu gacchissāmi, na pana sakkā tucchahatthena gantuṃ, mayhaṃ sahāyassa dve dārakā atthi, tesañca bhariyāya cassa sahāyakassa ca me nivāsanapārupanapiḷandhanādīni sajjethāti. “Sādhu sajjissāmā”ti te sabbaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ sajjayiṃsu.

The army, too, not seeing the king, had remained encamped outside the city. Upon seeing the king, they went out to meet and surround him. As the king entered the city, he stood at the gate, summoned the gatekeeper, sent the people away, and said, 'My dear man, a border villager wishing to see me will come and ask you, "Where is the house of the Master of the Horse?" You should take him by the hand, bring him, and show him to me; then you will receive a thousand.' He did not come. Since he did not come, the king increased the tax on his village. Even when the tax was increased, he did not come. He increased the tax a second and third time, but he still did not come. Then the villagers gathered and said, 'Sir, since the time your friend, the Master of the Horse, came, we have been oppressed by taxes and cannot even lift our heads. Go and tell your friend, the Master of the Horse, to have our tax released.' 'Very well, I will go, but it is not proper to go empty-handed. My friend has two children. Prepare garments, robes, ornaments, and so forth for them, for his wife, and for my friend.' 'Very well, we will prepare them,' they said, and they prepared all the gifts.

So tañca attano ghare pakkapūvañca ādāya gantvā dakkhiṇadvāraṃ patvā dovārikaṃ pucchi “kahaṃ, samma, mahāassārohassa geha”nti. So “ehi dassemi te”ti taṃ hatthe gahetvā rājadvāraṃ gantvā “dovāriko ekaṃ paccantagāmavāsiṃ gahetvā āgato”ti paṭivedesi. Rājā taṃ sutvā āsanā uṭṭhāya “mayhaṃ sahāyo ca tena saddhiṃ āgatā ca pavisantū”ti paccuggamanaṃ katvā disvāva naṃ parissajitvā “mayhaṃ sahāyikā ca dārakā ca arogā”ti pucchitvā hatthe gahetvā mahātalaṃ abhiruhitvā setacchattassa heṭṭhā rājāsane nisīdāpetvā aggamahesiṃ pakkosāpetvā “bhadde, sahāyassa me pāde dhovā”ti āha. Sā tassa pāde dhovi, rājā suvaṇṇabhiṅkārena udakaṃ āsiñci. Devīpi pāde dhovitvā gandhatelena makkhesi. Rājā “kiṃ, samma, atthi, kiñci amhākaṃ khādanīya”nti pucchi. So “atthī”ti pasibbakato pūve nīharāpesi. Rājā suvaṇṇataṭṭakena gahetvā tassa saṅgahaṃ karonto “mama sahāyena ānītaṃ khādathā”ti deviyā ca amaccānañca khādāpetvā sayampi khādi. Itaro itarampi paṇṇākāraṃ dassesi. Rājā tassa saṅgahatthaṃ kāsikavatthāni apanetvā tena ābhatavatthayugaṃ nivāsesiṃ[M 3.0010]. Devīpi [P 3.0011] kāsikavatthañceva ābharaṇāni ca apanetvā tena ābhatavatthaṃ nivāsetvā ābharaṇāni piḷandhi.

Taking that gift and the cakes fried in his own house, he went and, arriving at the southern gate, asked the gatekeeper, ‘Friend, where is the house of the great horseman?’ He replied, ‘Come, I will show you.’ Taking him by the hand, he went to the royal gate and had it announced, ‘The gatekeeper has come, bringing a man from a border village.’ The king, hearing this, rose from his seat and said, ‘Let my friend and those who came with him enter.’ Going out to welcome him, he embraced him as soon as he saw him and asked, ‘Are my friend’s wife and children well?’ Taking him by the hand, he ascended to the upper terrace and, under the white parasol, had him seated on the royal throne. Then, having had his chief queen summoned, he said, ‘Lady, wash my friend’s feet.’ She washed his feet, and the king poured water from a golden pitcher. The queen, having washed his feet, also anointed them with fragrant oil. The king asked, ‘Friend, is there anything for us to eat?’ He replied, ‘There is,’ and had the cakes brought out from his bag. The king, taking them on a golden plate and showing him hospitality, said, ‘Eat what my friend has brought.’ He had the queen and the ministers eat, and he himself ate as well. The man also presented the other gift. The king, to honor him, removed his Kāsi garments and put on the pair of clothes that he had brought. The queen, too, having removed her Kāsi garment and jewelry, put on the clothes brought by him and adorned herself with the ornaments.

Atha naṃ rājā rājārahaṃ bhojanaṃ bhojāpetvā ekaṃ amaccaṃ āṇāpesi “gaccha imassa mama karaṇaniyāmeneva massukammaṃ kāretvā gandhodakena nhāpetvā satasahassagghanikaṃ kāsikavatthaṃ nivāsāpetvā rājālaṅkārena alaṅkārāpetvā ānehī”ti. So tathā akāsi. Rājā nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā amacce sannipātāpetvā setacchattassa majjhe jātihiṅgulakasuttaṃ pātetvā upaḍḍharajjaṃ adāsi. Te tato paṭṭhāya ekato bhuñjanti pivanti sayanti, vissāso thiro ahosi kenaci abhejjo. Athassa rājā puttadārepi pakkosāpetvā antonagare nivesanaṃ māpetvā adāsi. Te samaggā sammodamānā rajjaṃ kārenti.

Then the king, having fed him a royal meal, ordered a minister: “Go, have his beard trimmed according to my custom, have him bathed with scented water, have him dressed in Kāsi cloth worth a hundred thousand, have him adorned with royal ornaments, and bring him here.” He did so. The king, having had a drum beaten throughout the city and having assembled his ministers, had a line dyed with genuine vermilion dropped in the middle of the white parasol and gave him half the kingdom. From then on, the two kings ate, drank, and slept together; their intimacy was firm and unbreakable by anyone. Then the king also had the man's wife and children summoned, had a house built for them inside the city, and gave it to them. They ruled the kingdom in harmony and concord.

Atha [V 3.0009] amaccā kujjhitvā rājaputtaṃ āhaṃsu “kumāra, rājā ekassa gahapatikassa upaḍḍharajjaṃ datvā tena saddhiṃ ekato bhuñjati pivati sayati, dārake ca vandāpeti, iminā raññā katakammaṃ na jānāma, kiṃ karoti rājā, mayaṃ lajjāma, tvaṃ rañño kathehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā sabbaṃ taṃ kathaṃ rañño ārocetvā “mā evaṃ karohi, mahārājā”ti āha. “Tāta, ahaṃ yuddhaparājito kahaṃ vasiṃ, api nu jānāthā”ti. “Na jānāma, devā”ti. “Ahaṃ etassa ghare vasanto arogo hutvā āgantvā rajjaṃ kāresiṃ, evaṃ mama upakārino kasmā sampattiṃ na dassāmī”ti evaṃ vatvā ca pana bodhisatto “tāta, yo hi adātabbayuttakassa deti, dātabbayuttakassa na deti, so āpadaṃ patvā kiñci upakāraṃ na labhatī”ti dassento imā gāthā āha –

Then the ministers, becoming angry, said to the prince: “Prince, the king has given half the kingdom to a certain householder, and eats, drinks, and sleeps with him, and even makes his children pay homage to him. We do not understand what the king has done. What is the king doing? We are ashamed. You should speak to the king.” He replied, “Very well,” and having consented, he reported the whole matter to the king and said, “Do not act in this way, great king.” “Dear son, when I was defeated in battle, where did I stay? Do you know?” “We do not know, Your Majesty.” “I stayed in this man's house, and having recovered my health, I returned and ruled the kingdom. Why should I not grant prosperity to one who has been of such service to me?” Having said this, the Bodhisatta, to illustrate that one who gives to the undeserving and not to the deserving finds no help when he falls into misfortune, spoke these verses:

5.

5.

“Adeyyesu [P 3.0012] dadaṃ dānaṃ, deyyesu nappavecchati;

Āpāsu byasanaṃ patto, sahāyaṃ nādhigacchati.

“Giving gifts to the undeserving, and not offering to the deserving; having fallen into trouble and misfortune, one finds no friend.”

6.

6.

“Nādeyyesu dadaṃ dānaṃ, deyyesu yo pavecchati;

Āpāsu byasanaṃ patto, sahāyamadhigacchati.

“Not giving gifts to the undeserving, and offering to the deserving; having fallen into trouble and misfortune, one finds a friend.”

7.

7.

“Saññogasambhogavisesadassanaṃ[M 3.0011], anariyadhammesu saṭhesu nassati;

Katañca ariyesu ca ajjavesu, mahapphalaṃ hoti aṇumpi tādisu.

“The recognition of the special quality of association and fellowship is lost on the ignoble and deceitful; but even a small deed done for the noble and the upright becomes greatly fruitful among such persons.”

8.

8.

“Yo pubbe katakalyāṇo, akā loke sudukkaraṃ;

Pacchā kayirā na vā kayirā, accantaṃ pūjanāraho”ti.

“He who has previously done a good deed, who has performed in the world what is very difficult to do, whether he does so again later or not, is worthy of constant honor.”

Tattha adeyyesūti pubbe akatūpakāresu. Deyyesūti pubbe katūpakāresu. Nappavecchatīti na paveseti na deti. Āpāsūti āpadāsu. Byasananti dukkhaṃ. Saññogasambhogavisesadassananti yo mittena kato saññogo ceva sambhogo ca, tassa visesadassanaṃ guṇadassanaṃ sukataṃ mayhaṃ imināti etaṃ sabbaṃ asuddhadhammattā anariyadhammesu kerāṭikattā saṭhesu nassati. Ariyesūti attano kataguṇajānanena ariyesu parisuddhesu. Ajjavesūti teneva kāraṇena ujukesu akuṭilesu. Aṇumpīti appamattakampi. Tādisūti ye tādisā puggalā honti ariyā ujubhūtā, tesu appampi kataṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahājutikaṃ mahāvipphāraṃ, sukhette vuttabījamiva na nassati[V 3.0010], itarasmiṃ pana pāpe bahumpi kataṃ aggimhi khittabījamiva nassatīti attho. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Therein, 'to the undeserving' (adeyyesu) means to those who have done no service before. 'To the deserving' (deyyesu) means to those who have done a service before. 'Does not offer' (nappavecchati) means does not give. 'In trouble' (āpāsu) means in misfortune. 'Misfortune' (byasanaṃ) means suffering. 'The recognition of the special quality of association and fellowship' (saññogasambhogavisesadassanaṃ) means the association and fellowship provided by a friend; the recognition of its special quality, the recognition of its virtue, thinking, “This was well done for me by this person.” All this is lost on the ignoble and deceitful because of their impure nature and their roguishness. 'Among the noble' (ariyesu) means among the pure who recognize the good done to them. 'Among the upright' (ajjavesu) means, for that very reason, among the straightforward and not crooked. 'Even a small deed' (aṇumpīti) means even a little. 'Among such persons' (tādisū) means among those persons who are noble and upright; even a small deed done for them bears great fruit, is of great radiance and wide influence, and like a seed sown in a fertile field, it is not lost. But for an evil person, even a great deed is lost, like a seed thrown into a fire. This is the meaning. And this is also said:

“Yathāpi bījamaggimhi, ḍayhati na virūhati;

Evaṃ kataṃ asappurise, nassati na virūhati.

“Just as a seed in a fire is burnt and does not sprout;

so a deed done for an unvirtuous person is lost and does not grow.

“Kataññumhi ca posamhi, sīlavante ariyavuttine;

Sukhette viya bījāni, kataṃ tamhi na nassatī”ti. (jā. 1.10.77-78);

“But for a grateful person, virtuous and of noble conduct, a deed done is not lost, like seeds in a fertile field.”

Pubbe katakalyāṇoti paṭhamataraṃ upakāraṃ katvā ṭhito. Akāti akari, ayaṃ loke sudukkaraṃ nāma akāsīti attho. Pacchā kayirāti so pacchā aññaṃ [P 3.0013] kiñci guṇaṃ karotu vā mā vā, teneva paṭhamakatena guṇena accantaṃ pūjanāraho hoti, sabbaṃ sakkārasammānaṃ arahatīti.

‘He who has previously done a good deed’ means one who has already performed a service. ‘He has performed’ means he did; the meaning is that he did what is known in the world as a very difficult thing to do. ‘Whether he does so later’ means whether he does some other good deed later or not, by that first good deed alone he is worthy of constant honor and deserves all honor and respect.

Idaṃ pana sutvā neva amaccā, na rājaputto puna kiñci kathesīti.

But having heard this, neither the ministers nor the prince said anything more.

Satthā [M 3.0012] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā paccantagāmavāsī ānando ahosi, bārāṇasirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the birth, saying: “At that time, the border-villager was Ānanda, and the king of Bārāṇasī was myself.”

Mahāassārohajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Mahāassāroha Jātaka, the second.

[303] 3. Ekarājajātakavaṇṇanā

[303] 3. The Commentary on the Ekarāja Jātaka

Anuttare kāmaguṇe samiddheti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ kosalarājasevakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu heṭṭhā seyyajātake (jā. 1.3.94 ādayo) kathitameva. Idha pana satthā “na tvaññeva anatthena atthaṃ āhari, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi attano anatthena atthaṃ āhariṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Flourishing amidst unsurpassed sensual pleasures”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain courtier of the king of Kosala. The story of the present has already been told previously in the Seyya Jātaka. Here, however, the Teacher said, “It is not only you who has brought about benefit through misfortune; wise men of old also brought about benefit for themselves through misfortune,” and then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasirañño upaṭṭhāko amacco rājantepure dubbhi. Rājā paccakkhatova tassa [V 3.0011] dosaṃ disvā taṃ raṭṭhā pabbājesi. So dubbhisenaṃ nāma kosalarājānaṃ upaṭṭhahantoti sabbaṃ mahāsīlavajātake (jā. 1.1.51) kathitameva. Idha pana dubbhiseno mahātale amaccamajjhe nisinnaṃ bārāṇasirājānaṃ gaṇhāpetvā sikkāya pakkhipāpetvā uttarummāre heṭṭhāsīsakaṃ olambāpesi. Rājā corarājānaṃ ārabbha mettaṃ bhāvetvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā jhānaṃ nibbattesi, bandhanaṃ chijji, tato rājā ākāse pallaṅkena nisīdi. Corarājassa sarīre dāho uppajji, “ḍayhāmi ḍayhāmī”ti bhūmiyaṃ aparāparaṃ parivattati. “Kimeta”nti vutte “mahārāja, tumhe evarūpaṃ dhammikarājānaṃ niraparādhaṃ dvārassa uttarummāre heṭṭhāsīsakaṃ olambāpethā”ti vadiṃsu. Tena hi vegena gantvā mocetha nanti. Purisā gantvā rājānaṃ ākāse pallaṅkena nisinnaṃ [P 3.0014] disvā āgantvā dubbhisenassa ārocesuṃ. So vegena gantvā taṃ vanditvā khamāpetuṃ paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, a courtier of the king of Bārāṇasī committed an offense in the royal palace. The king, seeing his fault with his own eyes, banished him from the kingdom. It has already been told in the Mahāsīlava Jātaka that he then served King Dubbhisena of Kosala. Here, however, Dubbhisena had the king of Bārāṇasī seized while he was sitting in the midst of his ministers on a great dais, had him placed in a net, and hung head-down from the lintel of the northern gate. The king, directed his thoughts toward the robber king, cultivated loving-kindness and, practicing the kasiṇa preparation, developed jhāna. His bonds broke, and then the king sat cross-legged in the sky. A burning sensation arose in the robber king’s body, and he rolled back and forth on the ground, crying, "I am burning, I am burning!" When asked what the matter was, they said, "Great king, you have hung such a righteous and innocent king head-down from the lintel of the northern gate." "In that case, go quickly and release him," he said. The men went and saw the king sitting cross-legged in the sky. They returned and reported this to Dubbhisena. He hurried there, paid homage to the king and, seeking forgiveness, spoke the first verse:

9.

9.

“Anuttare kāmaguṇe samiddhe, bhutvāna pubbe vasi ekarāja;

Sodāni dugge narakamhi khitto, nappajjahe vaṇṇabalaṃ purāṇa”nti.

“Amid unsurpassed and flourishing sensual pleasures, having formerly enjoyed them, you lived, O Ekarāja; though now cast into a difficult place, a pit, you do not relinquish your former complexion and strength.”

Tattha [M 3.0013] vasīti vuttho. Ekarājāti bodhisattaṃ nāmenālapati. Sodānīti so tvaṃ idāni. Duggeti visame. Narakamhīti āvāṭe. Olambitaṭṭhānaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Nappajjahe vaṇṇabalaṃ purāṇanti evarūpe visamaṭṭhāne khittopi porāṇakavaṇṇañca balañca nappajahasīti pucchati.

Therein, 'vasi' means lived. 'Ekarāja' is addressing the Bodhisatta by name. 'Sodāni' means so you now. 'Dugge' means in an uneven place. 'Narakamhi' means in a pit; this is stated with reference to the place where he was hung. 'Nappajjahe vaṇṇabalaṃ purāṇaṃ' means, 'Even when cast into such a difficult place, why do you not abandon your former complexion and strength?' he asks.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto sesagāthā avoca –

Having heard that, the Bodhisatta spoke the remaining verses:

10.

10.

“Pubbeva khantī ca tapo ca mayhaṃ, sampatthitā dubbhisena ahosi;

Taṃdāni laddhāna kathaṃ nu rāja, jahe ahaṃ vaṇṇabalaṃ purāṇaṃ.

“Formerly, O Dubbhisena, patience and austerity were desired by me; now that I have obtained them, O king, why should I abandon my former complexion and strength?

11.

11.

“Sabbā kirevaṃ pariniṭṭhitāni, yasassinaṃ paññavantaṃ visayha;

Yaso ca laddhā purimaṃ uḷāraṃ, nappajjahe vaṇṇabalaṃ purāṇaṃ.

“All my duties have indeed been thus completed, O glorious, wise, and enduring one; and having gained great, unprecedented glory, I do not abandon my former complexion and strength.

12.

12.

“Panujja dukkhena sukhaṃ janinda, sukhena vā dukkhamasayhasāhi;

Ubhayattha santo abhinibbutattā, sukhe ca dukkhe ca bhavanti tulyā”ti.

“Having dispelled happiness by means of suffering, O lord of men, or suffering by means of happiness, O you who endure the unendurable; the peaceful, in both cases, with their nature completely calmed, are equal in happiness and suffering.”

Tattha khantīti adhivāsanakhanti. Tapoti tapacaraṇaṃ. Sampatthitāti icchitā abhikaṅkhitā[V 3.0012]. Dubbhisenāti taṃ nāmenālapati. Taṃdāni laddhānāti taṃ patthanaṃ idānāhaṃ labhitvā. Jaheti kena kāraṇena ahaṃ jaheyyaṃ. Yassa hi dukkhaṃ vā domanassaṃ vā hoti, so taṃ jaheyyāti dīpeti.

Therein, 'patience' means enduring patience. 'Austerity' means the practice of austerity. 'Sampatthitā' means wished for or longed for. 'Dubbhisena' is an address to him by name. 'Now that I have obtained that' means having now obtained that which was desired (the opportunity for patience and austerity). 'Jahe' means for what reason should I abandon it? It is shown that only one who has suffering or sorrow would abandon their appearance.

“Sabbā kirevaṃ pariniṭṭhitānī”ti anussavavasena attano sampattiṃ dassento āha[P 3.0015]. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sabbāneva mama kattabbakiccāni dānasīlabhāvanāuposathakammāni pubbeva niṭṭhitānīti. Yasassinaṃ paññavantaṃ visayhāti parivārasampattiyā yasassi, paññāsampadāya paññavanta, asayhasāhitāya visayha. Evaṃ tīṇipetāni ālapanāneva. Nanti panettha nipāto[M 3.0014]. Byañjanasiliṭṭhatāvasenantakārassa sānunāsikatā katāti paccetabbā. Yaso cāti yasañca, ayameva vā pāṭho. Laddhā purimanti labhitvā purimaṃ pubbe aladdhapubbaṃ. Uḷāranti mahantaṃ. Kilesavikkhambhanamettābhāvanājhānuppattiyo sandhāyevamāha. Nappajjaheti evarūpaṃ yasaṃ laddhā kiṃkāraṇā purāṇavaṇṇabalaṃ jahissāmīti attho.

“All my duties have indeed been thus completed,” he said, showing his own accomplishment by way of renown. The meaning is this: all my necessary duties—deeds of giving, virtue, meditation, and Uposatha observance—were already completed. 'Yasassinaṃ paññavantaṃ visayha': glorious by virtue of the perfection of his retinue, wise by virtue of the perfection of wisdom, and enduring by virtue of his ability to bear the unbearable. Thus, these three are merely vocatives. Herein, 'naṃ' is a particle. It should be understood that the final sound was nasalized for the sake of euphonic smoothness of the consonants. 'Yaso ca' means 'yasañca' (and glory), or this is the reading itself. 'Laddhā purimaṃ' means having obtained something unprecedented, not previously obtained. 'Uḷāraṃ' means great. He spoke thus with reference to the suppression of defilements, the development of loving-kindness, and the arising of jhāna. 'Nappajjahe' means having gained such glory, for what reason would I abandon my former complexion and strength?

Dukkhenāti tayā uppāditena narakamhi khipanadukkhena mama rajjasukhaṃ panuditvā. Sukhena vā dukkhanti jhānasukhena vā taṃ dukkhaṃ panuditvā. Ubhayattha santoti ye santo honti mādisā, te dvīsupi etesu koṭṭhāsesu abhinibbutasabhāvā majjhattā sukhe ca dukkhe ca bhavanti tulyā, ekasadisā nibbikārāva hontīti.

By 'suffering' (dukkhena) he means: “having driven away my royal happiness by the suffering of being cast into a pit caused by you.” By 'or by happiness, suffering' (sukhena vā dukkhaṃ): “or having driven away that suffering by the happiness of jhāna, you endure the unendurable.” 'Peaceful in both': those who are peaceful like me, in both of these conditions, are of a completely calmed nature and impartial; thus they are equal in happiness and suffering, remaining uniform and indeed unperturbed.

Idaṃ sutvā dubbhiseno bodhisattaṃ khamāpetvā “tumhākaṃ rajjaṃ tumheva kāretha, ahaṃ vo core paṭibāhissāmī”ti vatvā tassa duṭṭhāmaccassa rājāṇaṃ kāretvā pakkāmi. Bodhisattopi rajjaṃ amaccānaṃ niyyādetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Hearing this, Dubbhisena asked the Bodhisatta for forgiveness and said, "You should rule your own kingdom; I will ward off your enemies for you." Having said this, he exercised royal authority over that wicked courtier and then departed. The Bodhisatta, too, handed over the kingdom to his ministers, went forth into the life of an ascetic, and was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dubbhiseno ānando ahosi, bārāṇasirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Dubbhisena was Ānanda, but the King of Bārāṇasī was I myself."

Ekarājajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Ekarāja Jātaka, the third.

[304] 4. Daddarajātakavaṇṇanā

[304] 4. The Commentary on the Daddara Jātaka

Imāni manti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kodhanaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu [V 3.0013] heṭṭhā kathitameva. Tadā hi dhammasabhāyaṃ tassa kodhanabhāvakathāya samuṭṭhitāya satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte taṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu kodhanosī”ti vatvā “āma, bhante”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave[P 3.0016], idāneva, pubbepesa kodhanoyeva, kodhanabhāvenevassa porāṇakapaṇḍitā parisuddhā nāgarājabhāve [M 3.0015] ṭhitāpi tīṇi vassāni gūthapūritāya ukkārabhūmiyaṃ vasiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher told this story, which begins with 'Imāni maṃ', while residing in Jetavana, concerning a certain irritable monk. The background story has been told below. At that time, when a discussion about his irritable nature arose in the Dhamma hall, the Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?" When they told him what it was, he had that monk summoned and asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are irritable?" When he replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the Teacher said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past also he was irritable. It was because of his irritable nature that the wise ones of the past, though they were pure and established in the state of a Naga king, had to live for three years on a dung-filled refuse heap in an impure land." So saying, he related the story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese daddarapabbatapāde daddaranāgabhavanaṃ nāma atthi, tattha rajjaṃ kārentassa daddararañño putto mahādaddaro nāma ahosi, kaniṭṭhabhātā panassa cūḷadaddaro nāma. So kodhano pharuso nāgamāṇavake akkosanto paribhāsanto paharanto vicarati. Nāgarājā tassa pharusabhāvaṃ ñatvā nāgabhavanato taṃ nīharāpetuṃ āṇāpesi. Mahādaddaro pana pitaraṃ khamāpetvā nivāresi. Dutiyampi rājā tassa kujjhi, dutiyampi khamāpesi. Tatiyavāre pana “tvaṃ maṃ imaṃ anācāraṃ nīharāpentaṃ nivāresi, gacchatha dvepi janā imamhā nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā bārāṇasiyaṃ ukkārabhūmiyaṃ tīṇi vassāni vasathā”ti nāgabhavanā nikkaḍḍhāpesi. Te tattha gantvā vasiṃsu. Atha ne ukkārabhūmiyaṃ udakapariyante gocaraṃ pariyesamāne gāmadārakā disvā paharantā leḍḍudaṇḍādayo khipantā “ke ime puthulasīsā sūcinaṅguṭṭhā udakadeḍḍubhā maṇḍūkabhakkhā”tiādīni vatvā akkosanti paribhāsanti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as Mahādaddara, the son of King Daddara, who ruled in a Naga realm named Daddara at the foot of Mount Daddara in the Himalayan region. His younger brother was named Cūḷadaddara. The latter was irritable and harsh; he went about abusing, reviling, and striking the young Nagas. Knowing his harsh nature, the Naga king ordered him to be expelled from the Naga realm. Mahādaddara, however, asked his father for forgiveness on his brother's behalf and prevented it. A second time the king grew angry with him, and a second time he asked for forgiveness. But the third time, the king said, "Since you prevented me from expelling this ill-behaved one, both of you must leave this Naga realm and live for three years on the refuse heap in Bārāṇasī." Thus, he had them expelled from the Naga realm. They went there and lived. Then, while they were searching for food at the water's edge on the refuse heap, village boys saw them and began hitting them and throwing clods of earth and sticks at them, saying, "Who are these big-headed, needle-tailed water-snakes, these frog-eaters?" and so on, abusing and reviling them.

Cūḷadaddaro caṇḍapharusatāya tesaṃ taṃ avamānaṃ asahanto “bhātika, ime dārakā amhe paribhavanti, āsīvisabhāvaṃ no na jānanti, ahaṃ tesaṃ avamānaṃ sahituṃ na sakkomi, nāsāvātena te nāsessāmī”ti bhātarā saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Cūḷadaddara, unable to bear their scorn due to his fierce and rough nature, said to his brother, "Brother, these boys disparage us; they do not know our deadly venomous nature. I cannot endure their contempt. I will destroy them with the blast of my breath!" While conversing with his brother, he uttered the first verse:

13.

13.

“Imāni maṃ daddara tāpayanti, vācāduruttāni manussaloke;

Maṇḍūkabhakkhā udakantasevī, āsīvisaṃ maṃ avisā sapantī”ti.

“Daddara, these harsh words spoken in the human world torment me. These frog-eaters, dwelling by the water’s edge, these non-venomous ones, curse me, who am a deadly venomous snake.”

Tattha [P 3.0017] tāpayantīti dukkhāpenti. Maṇḍūkabhakkhā udakantasevīti “maṇḍūkabhakkhā”ti ca “udakantasevī”ti ca vadantā ete avisā gāmadārakā maṃ āsīvisaṃ samānaṃ sapanti akkosantīti.

In this context, 'tāpayanti' means they cause suffering. 'Maṇḍūkabhakkhā udakantasevī' means: saying 'frog-eaters' and 'dwellers by the water’s edge,' these non-venomous village boys revile and insult me, even though I am a deadly venomous snake.

Tassa [V 3.0014] vacanaṃ sutvā mahādaddaro sesagāthā abhāsi –

Hearing his words, Mahādaddara uttered the remaining verses:

14.

14.

“Sakā raṭṭhā pabbājito, aññaṃ janapadaṃ gato;

Mahantaṃ koṭṭhaṃ kayirātha, duruttānaṃ nidhetave.

“One who is driven from his own land and has gone to another country should make a great storehouse for storing away harsh words.

15.

15.

“Yattha [M 3.0016] posaṃ na jānanti, jātiyā vinayena vā;

Na tattha mānaṃ kayirātha, vasamaññātake jane.

“Where people do not know a person by birth or by discipline, there one should not display pride while dwelling among strangers.”

16.

16.

“Videsavāsaṃ vasato, jātavedasamenapi;

Khamitabbaṃ sapaññena, api dāsassa tajjita”nti.

“Living in a foreign land, even if one is like a blazing fire in majesty, a wise person should endure even the intimidation of a slave.”

Tattha duruttānaṃ nidhetaveti yathā dhaññanidhānatthāya mahantaṃ koṭṭhaṃ katvā pūretvā kicce uppanne dhaññaṃ vaḷañjenti, evamevaṃ videsaṃ gato antohadaye paṇḍito poso duruttānaṃ nidhānatthāya mahantaṃ koṭṭhaṃ kayirātha. Tattha tāni duruttāni nidahitvā puna attano pahonakakāle kātabbaṃ karissati. Jātiyā vinayena vāti “ayaṃ khattiyo brāhmaṇo”ti vā “sīlavā bahussuto guṇasampanno”ti vā evaṃ yattha jātiyā vinayena vā na jānantīti attho. Mānanti evarūpaṃ maṃ lāmakavohārena voharanti, na sakkaronti na garuṃ karontīti mānaṃ na kareyya. Vasamaññātake janeti attano jātigottādīni ajānantassa janassa santike vasanto. Vasatoti vasatā, ayameva vā pāṭho.

In this context, 'duruttānaṃ nidhetave' means that just as one builds a large granary to store grain, fills it, and uses the grain when a need arises, so too a wise person who has gone abroad should make a great storehouse in his heart for storing away harsh words. Having stored away those harsh words, he will act appropriately when he has the power to do so. 'Jātiyā vinayena vā' means that they do not know, for instance, 'This one is a noble or a brahmin,' or 'This one is virtuous, learned, and endowed with good qualities.' 'Mānaṃ' means he should not display pride, thinking, 'They address me with contemptuous language; they do not honor or respect me.' 'Vasamaññātake jane' means dwelling in the presence of people who do not know one’s birth, lineage, and so forth. 'Vasato' is used in the sense of 'vasatā', or this is simply the reading.

Evaṃ te tattha tīṇi vassāni vasiṃsu. Atha ne pitā pakkosāpesi. Te tato paṭṭhāya nihatamānā jātā.

Thus, they lived there on the refuse heap in Bārāṇasī for three years. After three years, their father had them summoned. From that point on, they became free of pride.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne kodhano bhikkhu anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā cūḷadaddaro kodhano bhikkhu ahosi, mahādaddaro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the irritable monk was established in the fruit of Non-Returning. He connected the Jātaka thus: “At that time, Cūḷadaddara was the irritable monk, and I myself was Mahādaddara.”

Daddarajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The commentary on the Daddara Jātaka is the fourth.

[305] 5. Sīlavīmaṃsanajātakavaṇṇanā

[305] 5. 5. Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka

Natthi [V 3.0015][P 3.0018] loke raho nāmāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kilesaniggahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu ekādasakanipāte pānīyajātake (jā. 1.11.59 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – pañcasatā bhikkhū antojetavane vasantā majjhimayāmasamanantare kāmavitakkaṃ vitakkayiṃsu. Satthā [M 3.0017] chasupi rattidivākoṭṭhāsesu yathā ekacakkhuko cakkhuṃ, ekaputto puttaṃ, cāmarī vālaṃ appamādena rakkhati, evaṃ niccakālaṃ bhikkhū oloketi. So rattibhāge dibbacakkhunā jetavanaṃ olokento cakkavattirañño attano nivesane uppannacore viya te bhikkhū disvā gandhakuṭiṃ vivaritvā ānandattheraṃ āmantetvā “ānanda, antojetavane koṭisanthāre vasanakabhikkhū sannipātāpetvā gandhakuṭidvāre āsanaṃ paññāpehī”ti āha. So tathā katvā satthu paṭivedesi. Satthā paññattāsane nisīditvā sabbasaṅgāhikavasena āmantetvā “bhikkhave, porāṇakapaṇḍitā ‘pāpakaraṇe raho nāma natthī’ti pāpaṃ na kariṃsū”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“There is no such thing as secrecy in the world”—this the Teacher said while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the restraint of the defilements. The story will appear in the Eleventh Division, in the Pānīya Jātaka. The summary here is as follows: Five hundred monks, dwelling within Jetavana, contemplated thoughts of sensual pleasure during the middle watch of the night. The Teacher, just as a one-eyed man guards his eye, a parent an only son, or a yak its tail, constantly watched over the monks with diligence during the six portions of the day and night. Surveying Jetavana with his divine eye at night, he saw those monks just as a universal monarch would see thieves in his own palace. Opening the door of the Perfumed Chamber and summoning the Venerable Ānanda, he said, “Ānanda, assemble the monks residing in the Koṭisanthāra within Jetavana and prepare a seat for me at the door of the Perfumed Chamber.” He did so and informed the Teacher. Seated on the prepared seat, the Teacher addressed them all, saying, “Monks, the wise of old, saying, ‘There is no such thing as secrecy in doing evil,’ did not commit evil.” Being requested by them, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto tattheva bārāṇasiyaṃ disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike pañcannaṃ māṇavakasatānaṃ jeṭṭhako hutvā sippaṃ uggaṇhāti. Ācariyassa pana vayappattā dhītā atthi. So cintesi “imesaṃ māṇavakānaṃ sīlaṃ vīmaṃsitvā sīlasampannasseva dhītaraṃ dassāmī”ti. So ekadivasaṃ māṇavake āmantetvā “tātā, mayhaṃ dhītā vayappattā, vivāhamassā kāressāmi, vatthālaṅkāraṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, gacchatha tumhe attano attano ñātakānaṃ apassantānaññeva thenetvā vatthālaṅkāre āharatha, kenaci adiṭṭhameva gaṇhāmi, dassetvā ābhataṃ na gaṇhāmī”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tato paṭṭhāya ñātakānaṃ apassantānaṃ thenetvā vatthapiḷandhanādīni āharanti. Ācariyo ābhatābhataṃ visuṃ visuṃ ṭhapesi. Bodhisatto pana na kiñci āhari. Atha naṃ ācariyo āha “tvaṃ [P 3.0019] pana, tāta, na kiñci āharasī”ti. “Āma, ācariyā”ti. “Kasmā, tātā”ti. “Tumhe na kassaci passsantassa ābhataṃ gaṇhatha, ahaṃ pana pāpakaraṇe raho nāma na passāmī”ti dīpento imā dve gāthā āha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. When he came of age, he became the leader of five hundred young men and studied the arts under a world-renowned teacher in Benares itself. Now, the teacher had a daughter who had come of age. He thought, “Having tested the virtue of these young men, I will give my daughter to the one endowed with virtue.” One day, the teacher called the young men and said, “My dears, my daughter has come of age, and I will arrange her marriage. It is necessary to obtain clothes and ornaments. Go and steal clothes and ornaments while your own relatives are not looking, and bring them. I will only accept what is taken unseen by anyone; I will not accept what is brought after being seen.” They agreed, “Very well,” and from then on, they stole clothes, ornaments, and so on while their relatives were not looking and brought them. The teacher set aside each item they brought separately. But the Bodhisatta brought nothing. Then the teacher asked him, “Dear boy, why have you brought nothing?” “Yes, teacher,” he replied. “Why, dear boy?” “You accept only what is brought without anyone seeing, but I see no such thing as secrecy in doing evil,” he explained, and spoke these two verses:

17.

17.

“Natthi loke raho nāma, pāpakammaṃ pakubbato;

Passanti vanabhūtāni, taṃ bālo maññatī raho.

“There is no such thing as secrecy in the world for one who does an evil deed. The spirits of the forest see him, though the fool thinks it is secret.

18.

18.

“Ahaṃ [V 3.0016] raho na passāmi, suññaṃ vāpi na vijjati;

Yattha aññaṃ na passāmi, asuññaṃ hoti taṃ mayā”ti.

“I see no secret place, nor is there any empty place; where I see no other person, that place is not empty of me.”

Tattha [M 3.0018] rahoti paṭicchannaṭṭhānaṃ. Vanabhūtānīti vane nibbattabhūtāni. Taṃ bāloti taṃ pāpakammaṃ raho mayā katanti bālo maññati. Suññaṃ vāpīti yaṃ vā ṭhānaṃ sattehi suññaṃ tucchaṃ bhaveyya, tampi natthīti āha.

Here, ‘raho’ means a concealed place. ‘Vanabhūtāni’ means spirits born in the forest. ‘Taṃ bālo’ means the fool thinks, ‘This evil deed was done by me in secret.’ ‘Suññaṃ vāpi’ means even a place that might be empty or void of beings—even that does not exist, he says.

Ācariyo tassa pasīditvā “tāta, na mayhaṃ gehe dhanaṃ natthi, ahaṃ pana sīlasampannassa dhītaraṃ dātukāmo ime māṇavake vīmaṃsanto evamakāsiṃ, mama dhītā tuyhameva anucchavikā”ti dhītaraṃ alaṅkaritvā bodhisattassa adāsi. Sesamāṇavake “tumhehi ābhatābhataṃ tumhākaṃ gehameva nethā”ti āha.

The teacher, being pleased with him, said: “My dear, it is not that there is no wealth in my house, but I wished to give my daughter to one endowed with virtue; while testing these young men, I acted thus. My daughter is truly suitable for you.” Adorning his daughter, he gave her to the Bodhisatta. To the other young men, he said: “Take back to your own homes whatever you have brought.”

Satthā “iti kho, bhikkhave, te dussīlamāṇavakā attano dussīlatāya taṃ itthiṃ na labhiṃsu, itaro paṇḍitamāṇavo sīlasampannatāya labhī”ti vatvā abhisambuddho hutvā itarā dve gāthā abhāsi –

The Teacher said: “Thus, monks, those immoral young men, owing to their lack of virtue, did not obtain that woman, whereas the other wise young man, owing to his being endowed with virtue, obtained her.” Having said this, as the Fully Awakened One, he uttered these two further verses:

19.

19.

“Dujjacco ca sujacco ca, nando ca sukhavaḍḍhito;

Vajjo ca addhuvasīlo ca, te dhammaṃ jahumatthikā.

“Dujjacca and Sujacca, Nanda and Sukhavaḍḍhita, Vajja and Addhuvasīla—they abandoned the path, being seekers [of the woman].

20.

20.

“Brāhmaṇo ca kathaṃ jahe, sabbadhammāna pāragū;

Yo dhammamanupāleti, dhitimā saccanikkamo”ti.

“How could a Brahmin abandon it—he who has reached the far shore of all things, who upholds the Dhamma, steadfast and resolute in truth?”

Tattha dujjaccotiādayo cha jeṭṭhakamāṇavā, tesaṃ nāmaṃ gaṇhi, avasesānaṃ nāmaṃ aggahetvā sabbasaṅgāhikavaseneva “te dhammaṃ jahumatthikā”ti āha. Tattha teti sabbepi te māṇavā. Dhammanti itthipaṭilābhasabhāvaṃ[P 3.0020]. Jahumatthikāti jahuṃ atthikā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Makāro padabyañjanasandhivasena vutto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sabbepi te māṇavā tāya itthiyā atthikāva hutvā attano dussīlatāya taṃ itthipaṭilābhasabhāvaṃ jahiṃsu.

In those verses, ‘Dujjacco’ and the others were the six leading young men; he mentioned their names, but without mentioning the names of the rest, he spoke inclusively: “They abandoned the path, being seekers.” Here, ‘they’ refers to all those young men. ‘Dhamma’ means the way of obtaining a woman. ‘Jahumatthikā’ means they abandoned (jahuṃ) because they were seekers (atthikā); or this is the reading. The letter ‘m’ is inserted by way of euphonic junction of words. This is what is meant: all those young men, being seekers of that woman, abandoned the way of obtaining a woman due to their own immorality.

Brāhmaṇo cāti itaro pana sīlasampanno brāhmaṇo. Kathaṃ jaheti kena kāraṇena taṃ itthipaṭilābhasabhāvaṃ jahissati. Sabbadhammānanti imasmiṃ ṭhāne lokiyāni pañca sīlāni, dasa [V 3.0017] sīlāni, tīṇi sucaritāni ca, sabbadhammā nāma, tesaṃ so pāraṃ gatoti pāragū. Dhammanti vuttappakārameva [M 3.0019] dhammaṃ yo anupāleti rakkhati. Dhitimāti sīlarakkhanadhitiyā samannāgato. Saccanikkamoti sacce sabhāvabhūte yathāvutte sīladhamme nikkamena samannāgato.

‘And the brahmin’ means the other, the virtuous brahmin. ‘How would he abandon?’ means by what reason will he abandon that nature of obtaining a woman? ‘Of all dhammas’ here refers to the five worldly precepts, the ten precepts, and the three good conducts, which are called ‘all dhammas.’ He has gone to the far shore of them, hence ‘pāragū’ (one who has gone to the far shore). ‘Dhamma’ refers to the dhamma just mentioned, which he upholds and guards. ‘Dhitimā’ means endowed with steadfastness in guarding virtue. ‘Saccanikkamo’ means endowed with striving in the true, inherent dhamma of virtue as described.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne tāni pañca bhikkhusatāni arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsu.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, revealed the Truths and identified the birth story. At the conclusion of the Truths, those five hundred monks were established in Arahantship.

Tadā ācariyo sāriputto ahosi, paṇḍitamāṇavo pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the teacher was Sāriputta, and the wise young man was I myself.

Sīlavīmaṃsanajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The fifth is the explanation of the Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka.

[306] 6. Sujātājātakavaṇṇanā

[306] 6. The Explanation of the Sujātā Jātaka

Kimaṇḍakāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mallikaṃ deviṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasaṃ kira rañño tāya saddhiṃ sirivivādo ahosi, “sayanakalaho”tipi vadantiyeva. Rājā kujjhitvā tassā atthibhāvampi na jānāti. Mallikā devīpi “satthā rañño mayi kuddhabhāvaṃ na jānāti maññe”ti cintesi. Satthāpi ñatvā “imesaṃ samaggabhāvaṃ karissāmī”ti pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya pañcabhikkhusataparivāro sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā rājadvāraṃ agamāsi. Rājā tathāgatassa pattaṃ gahetvā nivesanaṃ pavesetvā paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā yāgukhajjakaṃ āhari. Satthā pattaṃ hatthena pidahitvā “mahārāja, kahaṃ devī”ti āha. “Kiṃ, bhante, tāya attano yasena mattāyā”ti? “Mahārāja, sayameva yasaṃ datvā mātugāmaṃ ukkhipitvā tāya katassa aparādhassa asahanaṃ nāma na yutta”nti. Rājā satthu vacanaṃ sutvā taṃ pakkosāpesi, sā satthāraṃ [P 3.0021] parivisi. Satthā “aññamaññaṃ samaggehi bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sāmaggirasavaṇṇaṃ kathetvā pakkāmi. Tato paṭṭhāya ubho samaggavāsaṃ vasiṃsu. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, satthā ekavacaneneva ubho samagge akāsī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepāhaṃ [M 3.0020] ete ekavādeneva samagge akāsi”nti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this discourse beginning with "Kimaṇḍakā" concerning Queen Mallikā. One day, it is said, the king had a dispute with her—some even say it was a "bed quarrel." The king, in anger, did not even acknowledge her presence. Queen Mallikā thought, "The Teacher, I believe, does not know of the king's anger toward me." The Teacher, knowing this, resolved, "I shall bring about concord between them." In the morning, he dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthi accompanied by five hundred monks. He proceeded to the king's gate. The king took the Tathāgata's bowl, led him into the palace, seated him on the appointed seat, and after offering the water of dedication to the Sangha headed by the Buddha, served rice gruel and other food. The Teacher covered his bowl with his hand and asked, "Great king, where is the queen?" "What of her, venerable sir? She is intoxicated by her own glory." "Great king, having yourself given glory and elevated a woman, it is not fitting to be intolerant of an offense committed by her." Hearing the Teacher's words, the king sent for her, and she attended on the Teacher. The Teacher, stating, "It is fitting for you to live in concord with one another," and having expounded on the benefits of harmony, departed. From then on, the two lived in concord. In the Dhamma hall, the monks raised the discussion: "Friends, the Teacher brought about concord between them with a single word!" The Teacher arrived and asked, "For what reason, monks, are you gathered here now?" When told, he said, "Not just now, monks; in the past too, I brought about concord between them with a single word of advice." Requested by them, he related the past.

Atīte [V 3.0018] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa atthadhammānusāsako amacco ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ rājā vātapānaṃ vivaritvā rājaṅgaṇaṃ olokayamāno aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe ekā paṇṇikadhītā abhirūpā paṭhamavaye ṭhitā sujātā nāma badarapacchiṃ sīse katvā “badarāni gaṇhatha, badarāni gaṇhathā”ti vadamānā rājaṅgaṇena gacchati. Rājā tassā saddaṃ sutvā tāya paṭibaddhacitto hutvā asāmikabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi. Sā rañño piyā ahosi manāpā. Athekadivasaṃ rājā suvaṇṇataṭṭake badarāni khādanto nisīdi. Tadā sujātā devī rājānaṃ badarāni khādantaṃ disvā “mahārāja, kiṃ nāma tumhe khādathā”ti pucchantī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister, advising him on matters of welfare and Dhamma. One day, the king opened a window and stood looking out over the palace courtyard. At that moment, a beautiful greengrocer's daughter named Sujātā, in the prime of her youth, was passing through the palace courtyard with a basket of jujubes on her head, calling out, "Buy jujubes, buy jujubes!" Hearing her voice, the king became captivated by her and, knowing she was unmarried, had her summoned. He installed her in the position of chief queen and bestowed great glory and wealth upon her. She became dear and pleasing to the king. One day, the king was sitting and eating jujubes from a golden dish. Seeing the king eating jujubes, Queen Sujātā asked, "Great king, what kind of fruit are you eating?" and spoke the first verse:

21.

21.

“Kimaṇḍakā ime deva, nikkhittā kaṃsamallake;

Upalohitakā vaggū, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

"What egg-shaped fruits are these, O king, placed in a golden dish? Reddish and beautiful, tell me this when asked."

Tattha kimaṇḍakāti kiṃphalāni nāmetāni, parimaṇḍalavasena pana aṇḍakāti āha. Kaṃsamallaketi suvaṇṇataṭṭake. Upalohitakāti rattavaṇṇā. Vaggūti cokkhā nimmalā.

There, "kimaṇḍakā" means "what fruits?"; but because of their roundness, they are called "aṇḍakā" (egg-shaped). "Kaṃsamallake" means in a golden dish. "Upalohitakā" means red in color. "Vaggū" means pure and stainless.

Rājā kujjhitvā “badaravāṇijake paṇṇikagahapatikassa dhīte attano kulasantakāni badarānipi na jānāsī”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

The king, becoming angry, said, "You jujube-seller, daughter of a greengrocer householder! You do not even recognize the jujubes that belong to your own family!" and spoke two verses:

22.

22.

“Yāni [P 3.0022] pure tuvaṃ devi, bhaṇḍu nantakavāsinī;

Ucchaṅgahatthā pacināsi, tassā te koliyaṃ phalaṃ.

"O queen, those fruits which you formerly gathered, shaven-headed and wearing rags, with your hands in your lap—those are the jujube fruits of your family."

23.

23.

“Uḍḍayhate na ramati, bhogā vippajahanti taṃ;

Tatthevimaṃ paṭinetha, yattha kolaṃ pacissatī”ti.

"She is tormented and finds no joy; the royal pleasures abandon her. Take her back to that very place where she will gather jujubes."

Tattha bhaṇḍūti muṇḍasīsā hutvā. Nantakavāsinīti jiṇṇapilotikanivatthā. Ucchaṅgahatthā pacināsīti aṭaviṃ pavisitvā aṅkusakena sākhaṃ onāmetvā ocitocitaṃ hatthena gahetvā ucchaṅge pakkhipanavasena ucchaṅgahatthā [M 3.0021] hutvā pacināsi ocināsi. Tassā te koliyaṃ phalanti tassā tava evaṃ pacinantiyā ocinantiyā yamahaṃ idāni khādāmi, idaṃ koliyaṃ kuladattiyaṃ phalanti attho.

There, "bhaṇḍu" means having a shaven head. "Nantakavāsinī" means wearing old, worn-out rags. "Ucchaṅgahatthā pacināsi" means that after entering the forest, she bent a branch with a hook and, picking the fruits, took them with her hand and placed them in her lap; thus she gathered them with her hands in her lap. "Tassā te koliyaṃ phalaṃ" means: for you who gathered them in this way, "what I am now eating is the jujube fruit belonging to your family"—this is the meaning.

Uḍḍayhate [V 3.0019] na ramatīti ayaṃ jammī imasmiṃ rājakule vasamānā lohakumbhiyaṃ pakkhittā viya ḍayhati nābhiramati. Bhogāti rājabhogā imaṃ alakkhikaṃ vippajahanti. Yattha kolaṃ pacissatīti yattha gantvā puna badarameva pacinitvā vikkiṇantī jīvikaṃ kappessati, tattheva naṃ nethāti vadati.

"Uḍḍayhate na ramatī" means this wretched woman, while living in this royal palace, burns as if thrown into an iron cauldron and finds no joy. "Bhogā" means the royal pleasures abandon this unlucky woman. "Yattha kolaṃ pacissatī" means: "Take her to the place where she will go and again gather and sell jujubes to make a living"—thus he speaks.

Bodhisatto “ṭhapetvā maṃ añño ime samagge kātuṃ na sakkhissatī”ti rājānaṃ saññāpetvā “imissā anikkaḍḍhanaṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta thought, "Apart from me, no one else will be able to reconcile this king and queen. I will appease the king and ensure she is not expelled," and spoke the fourth verse:

24.

24.

“Honti hete mahārāja, iddhippattāya nāriyā;

Khama deva sujātāya, māssā kujjha rathesabhā”ti.

"These faults of negligence happen, great king, to a woman who has attained glory. Forgive Sujātā, O lord; do not be angry with her, O bull among charioteers."

Tassattho – mahārāja, ete evarūpā pamādadosā yasaṃ pattāya nāriyā hontiyeva, etaṃ evarūpe ucce ṭhāne ṭhapetvā idāni “ettakassa aparādhassa asahanaṃ nāma na yuttaṃ tumhākaṃ, tasmā khama, deva, sujātāya, etissā mā kujjha rathesabha rathajeṭṭhakāti.

The meaning is: Great king, such faults of negligence indeed occur for a woman who has attained fame. Having placed her in such a high position, it is not fitting for you now to be intolerant of such an offense. Therefore, forgive Sujātā, O lord; do not be angry with her, O bull among charioteers, O chief of chariots.

Rājā tassa vacanena deviyā taṃ aparādhaṃ sahitvā yathāṭhāneyeva naṃ ṭhapesi. Tato paṭṭhāya ubho samaggavāsaṃ vasiṃsūti.

The king, by the words of the Bodhisatta, tolerated the queen's offense and kept her in her original position. From then on, the two lived together in harmony.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bārāṇasirājā kosalarājā ahosi, sujātā mallikā, amacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: "At that time, the king of Benares was the king of Kosala, Sujātā was Mallikā, and the minister was I myself."

Sujātājātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Sujātā Jātaka is finished.

[307] 7. Palāsajātakavaṇṇanā

[307] 7. The Commentary on the Palāsa Jātaka

Acetanaṃ [P 3.0023] brāhmaṇa assuṇantanti idaṃ satthā parinibbānamañce nipanno ānandattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sohāyasmā “ajja rattiyā paccūsasamaye satthā parinibbāyissatī”ti ñatvā “ahañcamhi sekkho sakaraṇīyo, satthu ca me parinibbānaṃ bhavissati, pañcavīsati vassāni satthu kataṃ [M 3.0022] upaṭṭhānaṃ nipphalaṃ bhavissatī”ti sokābhibhūto uyyānaovarake kapisīsaṃ ālambitvā parodi. Satthā taṃ apassanto “kahaṃ, bhikkhave, ānando”ti pucchitvā [V 3.0020] tamatthaṃ sutvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “katapuññosi tvaṃ, ānanda, padhānamanuyuñja, khippaṃ hohisi anāsavo, mā cintayi, idāni tayā mama kataṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ kiṃkāraṇā nipphalaṃ bhavissati, yassa te pubbe sarāgādikālepi mama kataṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ nipphalaṃ nāhosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while lying on the couch of his final Nibbāna, spoke this discourse beginning with “Acetanaṃ brāhmaṇa assuṇantaṃ” concerning the Elder Ānanda. That venerable one, knowing that “Today at dawn, the Teacher will attain final Nibbāna,” and thinking, “I am still a trainee with work yet to do; and my Teacher’s final Nibbāna will occur; the twenty-five years of attendance on the Teacher will be fruitless,” was overcome with sorrow, and leaning against the door-post of the garden cell, he wept. The Teacher, not seeing him, asked, “Monks, where is Ānanda?” Having heard the reason, he had him summoned and, wishing to admonish him, said: “You have performed merit, Ānanda. Devote yourself to striving; quickly you will be free from taints. Do not worry. Why should the attendance you have given me now be fruitless? Even in the past, when you were still subject to passion and so on, your attendance on me was not fruitless.” Then he related a past story.
