Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasito avidūre palāsarukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Tadā bārāṇasivāsino manussā devatāmaṅgalikā ahesuṃ niccaṃ balikaraṇādīsu payuttā. Atheko duggatabrāhmaṇo “ahampi ekaṃ devataṃ paṭijaggissāmī”ti ekasmiṃ unnatappadese ṭhitassa mahato palāsarukkhassa mūlaṃ samaṃ nittiṇaṃ katvā parikkhipitvā vālukaṃ okiritvāva sammajjitvā rukkhe gandhapañcaṅgulikāni datvā mālāgandhadhūmehi pūjetvā dīpaṃ jāletvā “sukhaṃ sayā”ti vatvā rukkhaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkamati. Dutiyadivase pātova gantvā sukhaseyyaṃ pucchati. Athekadivasaṃ rukkhadevatā cintesi “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo ativiya maṃ paṭijaggati, imaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vīmaṃsitvā yena kāraṇena maṃ paṭijaggati, taṃ dassāmī”ti. Sā tasmiṃ khaṇe brāhmaṇe āgantvā rukkhamūle sammajjante mahallakabrāhmaṇavesena samīpe ṭhatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a deity in a palāsa tree not far from Bārāṇasī. At that time, the people of Bārāṇasī were devoted to auspicious deities, constantly engaged in making offerings and so forth. Then a poor brahmin thought: “I too will serve a deity.” He cleared the ground around the base of a large palāsa tree standing on an elevated spot, making it level and free of grass, scattering sand and sweeping it clean. He applied scented five-finger marks to the tree, worshipped it with garlands, perfumes, and incense, lit a lamp, and said, “May you sleep well.” Having circumambulated the tree to the right, he departed. The next day, he went early in the morning and asked about its comfortable sleep. One day, the tree deity reflected: “This brahmin serves me with great devotion. I shall test this brahmin to see for what reason he serves me, and then I shall give him that.” At that moment, as the brahmin came and was sweeping the base of the tree, the deity stood nearby in the guise of an elderly brahmin and spoke the first verse:

25.

25.

“Acetanaṃ [P 3.0024] brāhmaṇa assuṇantaṃ, jāno ajānantamimaṃ palāsaṃ;

Āraddhaviriyo dhuvaṃ appamatto, sukhaseyyaṃ pucchasi kissa hetū”ti.

“O brahmin, you, knowing, why do you ask this palāsa tree—which is inanimate, unhearing, and unknowing—about its comfortable sleep? With energy aroused, ever steadfast and heedful, for what reason do you ask?”

Tattha assuṇantanti acetanattāva asuṇantaṃ. Jānoti tuvaṃ jānamāno hutvā dhuvaṃ appamattoti niccaṃ appamatto.

Herein, “unhearing” means not hearing because it is inanimate. “Knowing” means you, being one who knows. “Ever steadfast and heedful” means always heedful.

Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard that, the brahmin spoke the second verse:

26.

26.

“Dūre suto ceva brahā ca rukkho, dese ṭhito bhūtanivāsarūpo;

Tasmā namassāmi imaṃ palāsaṃ, ye cettha bhūtā te dhanassa hetū”ti.

“This tree is famous from afar and is great; standing in this place, it is a dwelling for deities. Therefore, I pay homage to this palāsa tree, for the sake of wealth from the deities who are here.”

Tattha [M 3.0023] dūre sutoti brāhmaṇa ayaṃ rukkho dūre suto vissuto, na āsannaṭṭhāneyeva pākaṭo. Brahā cāti mahanto ca. Dese ṭhitoti unnate same bhūmippadese ṭhito. Bhūtanivāsarūpoti [V 3.0021] devatānivāsasabhāvo, addhā ettha mahesakkhā devatā nivutthā bhavissati. Te dhanassa hetūti imañca rukkhaṃ ye cettha nivutthā bhūtā, te dhanassa hetu namassāmi, na nikkāraṇāti.

Herein, “heard of from afar” means, O brahmin, this tree is heard of from afar and is renowned, not merely known in nearby places. “And great” means large. “Standing in this place” means standing on an elevated, level piece of ground. “Having the nature of a dwelling for beings” means having the nature of a dwelling for deities; indeed, a deity of great power must be dwelling here. “They are the cause of wealth” means I pay homage to this tree and those beings dwelling here for the sake of wealth, not without reason.

Taṃ sutvā rukkhadevatā brāhmaṇassa pasannā “ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, imasmiṃ rukkhe nibbattadevatā, mā bhāyi, dhanaṃ te dassāmī”ti taṃ assāsetvā attano vimānadvāre mahantena devatānubhāvena ākāse ṭhatvā itarā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the tree deity, pleased with the brahmin, reassured him, saying, “O brahmin, I am the deity born in this tree. Do not fear, I will give you wealth.” Then, standing in the sky at the door of his celestial mansion by his great divine power, he spoke the other two verses:

27.

27.

“So te karissāmi yathānubhāvaṃ, kataññutaṃ brāhmaṇa pekkhamāno;

Kathañhi āgamma sataṃ sakāse, moghāni te assu pariphanditāni.

“O brahmin, observing your gratitude, I shall act for you according to my power. For how, having come into the presence of the virtuous, could your exertions be in vain?”

28.

28.

“Yo tindukarukkhassa paro pilakkho, parivārito pubbayañño uḷāro;

Tassesa mūlasmiṃ nidhi nikhāto, adāyādo gaccha taṃ uddharāhī”ti.

“Beyond the tinduka tree is a pilakkha tree, a grand ancient offering. At its root, a treasure is buried, without an heir—go, dig it up!”

Tattha [P 3.0025] yathānubhāvanti yathāsatti yathābalaṃ. Kataññutanti tayā mayhaṃ kataguṇaṃ jānanto taṃ attani vijjamānaṃ kataññutaṃ pekkhamāno. Āgammāti āgantvā. Sataṃ sakāseti sappurisānaṃ santike. Moghāni te assu pariphanditānīti sukhaseyyapucchanavasena vācāphanditāni sammajjanādikaraṇena kāyaphanditāni ca tava kathaṃ aphalāni bhavissanti.

Herein, “according to my power” means according to my ability and strength. “Observing gratitude” means knowing the good deed done by you to me, seeing that gratitude existing in oneself. “Having come” means having arrived. “In the presence of the virtuous” means in the presence of good people. “Could your exertions be in vain?” means how could your verbal exertions, by way of asking about comfortable sleep, and your physical exertions, by way of sweeping and so forth, be fruitless?

Yo tindukarukkhassa paro pilakkhoti yo esa tindukarukkhassa parato pilakkharukkho ṭhitoti vimānadvāre ṭhitāva hatthaṃ pasāretvā dasseti. Parivāritotiādīsu tassa pilakkharukkhassa mūle esa taṃ rukkhamūlaṃ parikkhipitvā nihitatāya parivārito, pubbe yiṭṭhayaññavasena purimasāmikānaṃ uppannatāya pubbayañño, anekanidhikumbhi bhāvena mahantattā [M 3.0024] uḷāro, bhūmiṃ khaṇitvā ṭhapitattā nikhāto, idāni dāyādānaṃ abhāvato adāyādo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – esa taṃ rukkhamūlaṃ parikkhipitvā gīvāya gīvaṃ paharantīnaṃ nidhikumbhīnaṃ vasena mahānidhi nikhāto asāmiko, gaccha taṃ uddharitvā gaṇhāti.

“‘Beyond the tinduka tree is a pilakkha tree’ means that pilakkha tree standing beyond the tinduka tree, which the deity showed by extending a hand while standing at the door of the celestial mansion. In ‘Surrounded’ and so forth, at the root of that pilakkha tree, this treasure is ‘surrounded’ because it was buried encircling that tree root. It is an ‘ancient offering’ because it was offered by previous owners in the past. It is ‘grand’ because of its greatness, being many treasure pots. It is ‘buried’ because it was placed there after digging into the ground. It is ‘without an heir’ because there are no heirs now. This is what is meant: this great, ownerless treasure, consisting of treasure pots striking neck to neck, is buried at the root of that tree, encircling it. Go, dig it up and take it.”

Evañca pana vatvā sā devatā “brāhmaṇa, tvaṃ etaṃ uddharitvā gaṇhanto kilamissasi, gaccha tvaṃ, ahameva taṃ tava gharaṃ netvā asukasmiṃ asukasmiñca ṭhāne nidahissāmi, tvaṃ etaṃ dhanaṃ yāvajīvaṃ paribhuñjanto dānaṃ dehi, sīlaṃ rakkhāhī”ti brāhmaṇassa ovādaṃ datvā taṃ dhanaṃ attano ānubhāvena tassa ghare patiṭṭhāpesi.

Having said this, the deity said, “Brahmin, you will tire yourself digging this up and taking it. Go, I myself will take it to your house and deposit it in such and such places. You, enjoying this wealth throughout your life, should give alms and maintain virtue.” Having given this advice to the brahmin, the deity established that wealth in his house by his own power.

Satthā [V 3.0022] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā brāhmaṇo ānando ahosi, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the brahmin was Ānanda, and the tree deity was I myself.”

Palāsajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Palāsa Jātaka, the Seventh.

[308] 8. Sakuṇajātakavaṇṇanā

[308] 8. The Commentary on the Sakuṇa Jātaka

Akaramhasa te kiccanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattassa akataññutaṃ ārabbha kathesi. “Na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto akataññūyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“We have done for you what was to be done”—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Devadatta’s ingratitude. “Not only now, monks, but also in the past Devadatta was ungrateful,” he said, and related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese rukkhakoṭṭakasakuṇo hutvā [P 3.0026] nibbatti. Athekassa sīhassa maṃsaṃ khādantassa aṭṭhi gale laggi, galo uddhumāyi, gocaraṃ gaṇhituṃ na sakkoti, kharā vedanā pavattati. Atha naṃ so sakuṇo gocarappasuto disvā sākhāya nilīno “kiṃ te, samma, dukkha”nti pucchi. So tamatthaṃ ācikkhi. “Ahaṃ te, samma, etaṃ aṭṭhiṃ apaneyyaṃ, bhayena pana te mukhaṃ pavisituṃ na visahāmi, khādeyyāsipi ma”nti. “Mā bhāyi, samma, nāhaṃ taṃ khādāmi, jīvitaṃ me dehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti taṃ vāmapassena nipajjāpetvā “ko jānāti, kimpesa karissatī”ti cintetvā yathā mukhaṃ pidahituṃ na sakkoti, tathā tassa adharoṭṭhe ca [M 3.0025] uttaroṭṭhe ca daṇḍakaṃ ṭhapetvā mukhaṃ pavisitvā aṭṭhikoṭiṃ tuṇḍena pahari, aṭṭhi patitvā gataṃ. So aṭṭhiṃ pātetvā sīhassa mukhato nikkhamanto daṇḍakaṃ tuṇḍena paharitvā pātentova nikkhamitvā sākhagge nilīyi. Sīho nirogo hutvā ekadivasaṃ ekaṃ vanamahiṃsaṃ vadhitvā khādati. Sakuṇo “vīmaṃsissāmi na”nti tassa uparibhāge sākhāya nilīyitvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a woodpecker in the Himalayan region. One day, as a lion was eating meat, a bone got stuck in his throat. His throat swelled up, he could not take food, and severe pain arose. Then that bird, intent on seeking food, saw him and, perched on a branch, asked: “What troubles you, friend?” He explained the matter to him. The bird said: “Friend, I could remove that bone for you, but I do not dare to enter your mouth for fear that you might eat me.” The lion replied: “Do not be afraid, friend, I will not eat you. Give me my life!” The bird said, “Very well,” and made him lie down on his left side. Thinking, “Who knows what he will do?” he placed a stick between his lower and upper jaws so that the mouth could not be closed. Then he entered the mouth, struck the tip of the bone with his beak, and the bone fell out. After dislodging the bone, as he came out of the lion’s mouth, he struck the stick with his beak, causing it to fall, and perched on the tip of a branch. The lion, now free from illness, one day killed and ate a wild buffalo. The bird thought: “I shall test him,” and perched on a branch above him, and conversing with him, spoke the first verse:

29.

29.

“Akaramhasa te kiccaṃ, yaṃ balaṃ ahuvamhase;

Migarāja namo tyatthu, api kiñci labhāmase”ti.

“We have done for you what was to be done, according to the strength we had. O King of Beasts, homage to you, might we receive something?”

Tattha akaramhasa te kiccanti bho, sīha, mayampi tava ekaṃ kiccaṃ akarimha. Yaṃ balaṃ ahuvamhaseti yaṃ amhākaṃ balaṃ ahosi, tena balena tato kiñci ahāpetvā akarimhayeva.

Herein, “We have done for you what was to be done” means, O lion, we too have done a service for you. “According to the strength we had” means whatever strength was ours, with that strength, without omitting anything, we have indeed done it.

Taṃ [V 3.0023] sutvā sīho dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the lion spoke the second verse:

30.

30.

“Mama lohitabhakkhassa, niccaṃ luddāni kubbato;

Dantantaragato santo, taṃ bahuṃ yampi jīvasī”ti.

“For me, a blood-eater, constantly doing cruel deeds, that you, having been between my teeth, still live—that is much!”

Taṃ sutvā sakuṇo itarā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the bird spoke the other two verses:

31.

31.

“Akataññumakattāraṃ, katassa appaṭikārakaṃ;

Yasmiṃ kataññutā natthi, niratthā tassa sevanā.

“One who is ungrateful, who does not act in return, who does not repay a kindness done; in whom there is no gratitude, association with him is fruitless.”

32.

32.

“Yassa [P 3.0027] sammukhaciṇṇena, mittadhammo na labbhati;

Anusūyamanakkosaṃ, saṇikaṃ tamhā apakkame”nti.

“From whom the way of a friend is not gained, even by deeds done in his presence; without resentment or reproach, one should slowly depart from him.”

Tattha akataññunti kataguṇaṃ ajānantaṃ. Akattāranti yaṃkiñci akarontaṃ. Sammukhaciṇṇenāti sammukhe katena guṇena. Anusūyamanakkosanti taṃ puggalaṃ na usūyanto na akkosanto saṇikaṃ tamhā pāpapuggalā apagaccheyyāti. Evaṃ vatvā so sakuṇo pakkāmi.

Herein, “ungrateful” means not recognizing a good deed done. “One who does not act in return” means one who does nothing whatsoever. “By a deed done in his presence” means by a good deed done in his presence. “‘Without resentment or reproach’ means not resenting or reproaching that person, one should slowly depart from that wicked person.” Having said this, that bird flew away.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sīho devadatto ahosi, sakuṇo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the lion was Devadatta, and the bird was I myself.”

Sakuṇajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Sakuṇa Jātaka, the eighth.

[309] 9. Chavajātakavaṇṇanā

[309] 9. The Commentary on the Chava Jātaka

Sabbamidaṃ [M 3.0026] carimaṃ katanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto chabbaggiye bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu vinaye (pāci. 646) vitthārato āgatameva. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – satthā chabbaggiye pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tumhe, bhikkhave, nīce āsane nisīditvā ucce āsane nisinnassa dhammaṃ desethā”ti pucchitvā “evaṃ, bhante”ti vutte te bhikkhū garahitvā “ayuttaṃ, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ mama dhamme agāravakaraṇaṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitā hi nīce āsane nisīditvā bāhirakamantepi vācente garahiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this discourse concerning the group of six monks, with reference to the verse beginning, 'All this is a base deed.' The incident is fully recounted in the Vinaya (Pācittiya 646). Here is the summary: The Teacher summoned the group of six monks and asked: “Is it true, monks, that you, sitting on low seats, teach the Dhamma to one seated on a high seat?” When they replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” he rebuked them, saying: “Monks, it is improper for you to show disrespect to my Dhamma. Even the wise of old rebuked those who, sitting on low seats, recited even external teachings.” Having said this, he related a past story.

Atīte [V 3.0024] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto caṇḍālakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapesi. Tassa bhariyā ambadohaḷinī hutvā taṃ āha “sāmi, icchāmahaṃ ambaṃ khāditu”nti. “Bhadde, imasmiṃ kāle ambaṃ natthi, aññaṃ kiñci ambilaphalaṃ āharissāmī”ti. “Sāmi, ambaphalaṃ labhamānāva jīvissāmi, alabhamānāya me jīvitaṃ natthī”ti. So tassā paṭibaddhacitto [P 3.0028] “kahaṃ nu kho ambaphalaṃ labhissāmī”ti cintesi. Tena kho pana samayena bārāṇasirañño uyyāne ambo dhuvaphalo hoti. So “tato ambapakkaṃ āharitvā imissā dohaḷaṃ paṭippassambhessāmī”ti rattibhāge uyyānaṃ gantvā ambaṃ abhiruhitvā nilīno sākhāya sākhaṃ ambaṃ olokento vicari. Tassa tathā karontasseva ratti vibhāyi. So cintesi “sace idāni otaritvā gamissāmi, disvā maṃ ‘coro’ti gaṇhissanti, rattibhāge gamissāmī”ti. Athekaṃ viṭapaṃ abhiruhitvā nilīno acchi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of outcastes. When he came of age, he established a household. His wife developed a pregnancy craving for mangoes and said to him, “Husband, I wish to eat a mango.” “My dear,” he replied, “there are no mangoes at this time; I will bring you some other sour fruit.” “Husband,” she insisted, “I shall live only if I get a mango; if I do not get one, I shall not live.” His mind being attached to her, he thought, “Where indeed can I get a mango?” Now, at that time, there was an ever-fruiting mango tree in the king's park in Benares. Thinking, “I will bring a ripe mango from there and allay her craving,” he went to the park at night, climbed the mango tree, and moved from branch to branch, looking for a mango. As he was doing so, the night dawned. He thought, “If I descend and go now, they will see me and seize me as a thief. I will go at night.” Thereupon he climbed onto a thick branch and remained hidden.

Tadā bārāṇasirājā “purohitassa santike mante uggaṇhissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ pavisitvā ambarukkhamūle ucce āsane nisīditvā ācariyaṃ nīce āsane nisīdāpetvā mante uggaṇhi. Bodhisatto upari nilīno cintesi – “yāva adhammiko ayaṃ rājā, yo uccāsane nisīditvā mante uggaṇhāti. Ayaṃ brāhmaṇopi adhammiko, yo nīcāsane nisīditvā mante vāceti. Ahampi adhammiko, yo mātugāmassa vasaṃ gantvā mama jīvitaṃ agaṇetvā ambaṃ āharāmī”ti. So rukkhato otaranto ekaṃ [M 3.0027] olambanasākhaṃ gahetvā tesaṃ ubhinnampi antare patiṭṭhāya “mahārāja, ahaṃ naṭṭho, tvaṃ mūḷho, purohito mato”ti āha. So raññā “kiṃkāraṇā”ti puṭṭho paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king of Benares, thinking, “I will learn the mantras from the royal chaplain,” entered the park. Seating himself on a high seat at the foot of a mango tree, he had his teacher seated on a low seat and began to learn the mantras. The Bodhisatta, hidden above, thought: “How unrighteous this king is, who sits on a high seat while learning mantras. This brahmin is also unrighteous, who sits on a low seat while teaching mantras. And I too am unrighteous, who, having come under the sway of a woman, disregard my own life to steal a mango.” Descending from the tree, he grasped a hanging branch and stood between them both, saying, “Great king, I am ruined, you are deluded, and the royal chaplain is dead.” When asked by the king, “For what reason?” he spoke the first verse:

33.

33.

“Sabbamidaṃ carimaṃ kataṃ, ubho dhammaṃ na passare;

Ubho pakatiyā cutā, yo cāyaṃ mantejjhāpeti;

Yo ca mantaṃ adhīyatī”ti.

“All this is a base deed that has been done; both fail to see the Dhamma. Both have fallen from their proper nature—he who teaches the mantras, and he who learns the mantras.”

Tattha sabbamidaṃ carimaṃ katanti yaṃ amhehi tīhi janehi kataṃ, sabbaṃ idaṃ kiccaṃ lāmakaṃ nimmariyādaṃ adhammikaṃ. Evaṃ attano corabhāvaṃ tesañca mantesu agāravaṃ garahitvā puna itare dveyeva garahanto “ubho [P 3.0029] dhammaṃ na passare”tiādimāha. Tattha ubhoti ime dvepi janā garukārārahaṃ porāṇakadhammaṃ na passanti, tato dhammapakatito cutā. Dhammo hi paṭhamuppattivasena pakati nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Here, “All this is a base deed that has been done” means that all this work done by us three people is base, improper, and unrighteous. Having thus censured his own thievery and their disrespect for the mantras, he then rebuked only the other two, saying, “both fail to see the Dhamma,” and so on. Here, “both” means these two people do not see the ancient Dhamma that is worthy of respect, and thus have fallen from the proper nature of Dhamma. For Dhamma is called “proper nature” because it arose first. As it is said:

“Dhammo [V 3.0025] have pāturahosi pubbe;

Pacchā adhammo udapādi loke”ti. (jā. 1.11.28);

“Indeed, the Dhamma appeared first; afterwards, unrighteousness arose in the world.” (Jā. 1.11.28)

Yo cāyanti yo ca ayaṃ nīcāsane nisīditvā mante ajjhāpeti, yo ca ucce āsane nisīditvā adhīyatīti.

“He who” refers to one who, sitting on a low seat, teaches the mantras, and one who, sitting on a high seat, learns them.

Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard that, the brahmin spoke the second verse:

34.

34.

“Sālīnaṃ odanaṃ bhuñje, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na sevāmi, dhammaṃ isīhi sevita”nti.

“I eat rice of the finest grain, with pure meat sauces; therefore, I do not practice this Dhamma followed by sages.”

Tassattho – ahañhi bho imassa rañño santakaṃ sālīnaṃ odanaṃ suciṃ paṇḍaraṃ nānappakārāya maṃsavikatiyā sittaṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ bhuñjāmi, tasmā udare baddho hutvā etaṃ esitaguṇehi isīhi sevitaṃ dhammaṃ na sevāmīti.

The meaning is: 'For I eat the king's rice from fine grain, pure and white, served with various kinds of meat preparations and meat sauce; therefore, being bound by my belly, I do not cultivate this Dhamma cultivated by seers possessed of sought-after qualities.'

Taṃ sutvā itaro dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the other spoke these two verses:

35.

35.

“Paribbaja mahā loko, pacantaññepi pāṇino;

Mā taṃ adhammo ācarito, asmā kumbhamivābhidā.

“Wander forth! The world is vast; other beings, too, cook for themselves. Let not the unrighteous conduct you have practiced shatter you, as a stone shatters a pot.

36.

36.

“Dhiratthu [M 3.0028] taṃ yasalābhaṃ, dhanalābhañca brāhmaṇa;

Yā vutti vinipātena, adhammacaraṇena vā”ti.

“Shame on that gain of fame and gain of wealth, O brahmin, which is a livelihood gained by downfall or by unrighteous conduct.”

Tattha paribbajāti ito aññattha gaccha. Mahāti ayaṃ loko nāma mahā. Pacantaññepi pāṇinoti imasmiṃ jambudīpe aññepi pāṇino pacanti, nāyameveko rājā. Asmā kumbhamivābhidāti pāsāṇo ghaṭaṃ viya. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ tvaṃ aññattha agantvā idha vasanto adhammaṃ ācarasi, so adhammo evaṃ ācarito pāsāṇo ghaṭaṃ viya mā taṃ bhindi.

Here, 'paribbaja' means 'go elsewhere.' 'Mahā' means 'this world is vast.' 'Pacantaññepi pāṇino' means that in this Jambudīpa, other living beings also cook for themselves; this is not the only king. 'Asmā kumbhamivābhidā' means 'like a stone shatters a pot.' This is what is meant: 'Since you, not going elsewhere, dwell here and practice unrighteousness, let not that unrighteousness, so practiced, shatter you as a stone shatters a pot.'

“Dhiratthū”ti gāthāya ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – brāhmaṇa yo esa evaṃ tava yasalābho ca dhanalābho ca dhiratthu, taṃ garahāma mayaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā ayaṃ tayā [P 3.0030] laddhalābho āyatiṃ apāyesu [V 3.0026] vinipātanahetunā sampati ca adhammacaraṇena jīvitavutti nāma hoti, yā cesā vutti iminā āyatiṃ vinipātena idha adhammacaraṇena vā nippajjati, kiṃ tāya, tena taṃ evaṃ vadāmīti.

The summary meaning of the verse ‘Dhiratthu’ is: “Brahmin, we condemn this gain of fame and wealth of yours. Why? Because this gain you have obtained is a cause for downfall into states of misery in the future, and is presently a livelihood based on unrighteous conduct. And what is the use of a livelihood that is produced by future downfall or by unrighteous conduct in this life? Therefore, I speak to you in this way.”

Athassa dhammakathāya rājā pasīditvā “bho, purisa, kiṃjātikosī”ti pucchi. “Caṇḍālo ahaṃ, devā”ti. Bho “sace tvaṃ jātisampanno abhavissa, rajjaṃ te ahaṃ adassaṃ, ito paṭṭhāya pana ahaṃ divā rājā bhavissāmi, tvaṃ rattiṃ rājā hohī”ti attano kaṇṭhe piḷandhanaṃ pupphadāmaṃ tassa gīvāyaṃ piḷandhāpetvā taṃ nagaraguttikaṃ akāsi. Ayaṃ nagaraguttikānaṃ kaṇṭhe rattapupphadāmapiḷandhanavaṃso. Tato paṭṭhāya pana rājā tassovāde ṭhatvā ācariye gāravaṃ karitvā nīce āsane nisinno mante uggaṇhīti.

Then, pleased by the Dhamma discourse, the king asked, “Friend, man, of what caste are you?” “I am a Caṇḍāla, Your Majesty.” The king said, “If you had been of high birth, I would have given you the kingdom. But from now on, I shall be king by day, and you shall be king by night.” He took the flower garland from his own neck and placed it around the Bodhisatta’s neck, appointing him as the city guardian. This is the origin of the tradition of city guardians wearing a red flower garland around their necks. From then on, the king, abiding by his advice and respecting his teacher, sat on a lower seat and learned the mantras.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, caṇḍālaputto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the Caṇḍāla’s son was none other than myself.”

Chavajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The commentary on the ninth Jātaka, the Chavajātaka, is concluded.

[310] 10. Seyyajātakavaṇṇanā

[310] 10. The Commentary on the Seyya Jātaka

Sasamuddapariyāyanti [M 3.0029] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caranto ekaṃ abhirūpaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ itthiṃ disvā ukkaṇṭhito sāsane nābhirami. Atha bhikkhū bhagavato ārocesuṃ. So bhagavatā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti puṭṭho “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vatvā “ko taṃ ukkaṇṭhāpesī”ti vutte tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Satthā “kasmā tvaṃ evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā ukkaṇṭhitosi, pubbe paṇḍitā purohitaṭṭhānaṃ labhantāpi taṃ paṭikkhipitvā pabbajiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Sasamuddapariyāyaṃ…” This the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a discontented monk. That monk, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, saw a beautiful, well-adorned woman and became discontented, no longer delighting in the Dispensation. Then the monks informed the Blessed One. When asked by the Blessed One, “Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?” he replied, “It is true, venerable sir.” When asked what had caused his discontent, he explained the matter. The Teacher said, “Why, having gone forth in such a liberating Dispensation, are you discontented? In the past, wise men, though obtaining the position of royal priest, rejected it and went forth.” Then he recounted a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto purohitassa brāhmaṇiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhitvā [P 3.0031] rañño puttena saddhiṃ ekadivase vijāyi. Rājā “atthi nu kho koci me puttena saddhiṃ ekadivase jāto”ti amacce pucchi. “Atthi, mahārāja, purohitassa putto”ti. Rājā taṃ āharāpetvā dhātīnaṃ datvā puttena saddhiṃ ekatova paṭijaggāpesi. Ubhinnaṃ ābharaṇāni ceva pānabhojanādīni ca ekasadisāneva ahesuṃ. Te vayappattā [V 3.0027] ekatova takkasilaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā āgamaṃsu. Rājā puttassa oparajjaṃ adāsi, mahāyaso ahosi. Tato paṭṭhāya bodhisatto rājaputtena saddhiṃ ekatova khādati pivati sayati, aññamaññaṃ vissāso thiro ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the royal priest's brahmin wife and was born on the same day as the king’s son. The king asked his ministers, “Is there anyone born on the same day as my son?” “There is, great king, the royal priest’s son,” they replied. The king had him brought and, giving him to wet-nurses, had him cared for together with his son. The ornaments, food and drink, and so on, for both of them were identical. When they came of age, they went together to Takkasilā, learned all the arts, and returned. The king gave his son the viceroyalty, and he became very famous. From then on, the Bodhisatta and the prince ate, drank, and slept together, and their mutual trust was firm.

Aparabhāge rājaputto pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya mahāsampattiṃ anubhavi. Bodhisatto cintesi “mayhaṃ sahāyo rajjamanusāsati, sallakkhitakkhaṇeyeva kho pana mayhaṃ purohitaṭṭhānaṃ dassati, kiṃ me gharāvāsena, pabbajitvā vivekamanubrūhessāmī”ti? So mātāpitaro vanditvā pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetvā mahāsampattiṃ chaḍḍetvā ekakova nikkhamitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā manorame bhūmibhāge paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto vihāsi. Tadā rājā taṃ anussaritvā “mayhaṃ sahāyo na paññāyati, kahaṃ so”ti pucchi. Amaccā tassa pabbajitabhāvaṃ ārocetvā “ramaṇīye kira vanasaṇḍe vasatī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā tassa vasanokāsaṃ [M 3.0030] pucchitvā seyyaṃ nāma amaccaṃ “gaccha sahāyaṃ me gahetvā ehi, purohitaṭṭhānamassa dassāmī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā bārāṇasito nikkhamitvā anupubbena paccantagāmaṃ patvā tattha khandhāvāraṃ ṭhapetvā vanacarakehi saddhiṃ bodhisattassa vasanokāsaṃ gantvā bodhisattaṃ paṇṇasāladvāre suvaṇṇapaṭimaṃ viya nisinnaṃ disvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā katapaṭisanthāro “bhante, rājā tuyhaṃ purohitaṭṭhānaṃ dātukāmo, āgamanaṃ [P 3.0032] te icchatī”ti āha.

Later, the prince, upon his father's death, was established in the kingdom and enjoyed great prosperity. The Bodhisatta thought: "My friend now rules the kingdom; at the very moment he remembers me, he will surely offer me the position of royal priest. But what use is household life to me? I shall go forth and cultivate solitude." So he paid homage to his parents, obtained their permission for renunciation, abandoned his great wealth, and left alone for the Himalayas. There, in a delightful region, he built a leaf hut, undertook the ascetic life, and developed supernormal powers and meditative attainments, dwelling there delighting in the bliss of jhāna. Then the king, remembering him, asked: "My friend is not to be seen; where is he?" The ministers informed him that he had gone forth, saying: "He is said to dwell in a delightful forest grove." The king inquired about his dwelling place and then said to a minister named Seyya: "Go and bring my friend here. I will give him the position of royal priest." He agreed, saying, "Very well," left Bārāṇasī, and in due course reached a border village. There, he set up camp and, accompanied by foresters, went to the Bodhisatta’s dwelling. Seeing the Bodhisatta seated at the door of his leaf hut like a golden statue, he paid homage, sat to one side, exchanged greetings, and said: "Venerable sir, the king wishes to give you the position of royal priest. He desires your return."

Bodhisatto “tiṭṭhatu purohitaṭṭhānaṃ, ahaṃ sakalaṃ kāsikosalajambudīparajjaṃ cakkavattisirimeva vā labhantopi na gacchissāmi, na hi paṇḍitā sakiṃ jahitakilese puna gaṇhanti, sakiṃ jahitañhi niṭṭhubhakheḷasadisaṃ hotī”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

The Bodhisatta said: "Let the position of royal priest be. Even if I were to obtain the entire kingdom of Kāsi and Kosala and the whole of Jambudīpa, or even the glory of a universal monarch, I would not go. For the wise do not take up again the defilements they have once abandoned; what has been abandoned once is like spittle that has been spat out." Having spoken thus, he uttered these verses:

37.

37.

“Sasamuddapariyāyaṃ, mahiṃ sāgarakuṇḍalaṃ;

Na icche saha nindāya, evaṃ seyya vijānahi.

"The earth, with the ocean as its boundary, with the sea as its earring—I would not desire it if it came with blame; know this, Seyya.

38.

38.

“Dhiratthu taṃ yasalābhaṃ, dhanalābhañca brāhmaṇa;

Yā vutti vinipātena, adhammacaraṇena vā.

"Fie upon that gain of fame and gain of wealth, O brahmin, which is a livelihood gained by downfall or by unrighteous conduct.

39.

39.

“Api ce pattamādāya, anagāro paribbaje;

Sāyeva jīvikā seyyo, yā cādhammena esanā.

"Even if, taking a bowl, one were to wander homeless, that very livelihood is superior to any acquisition through unrighteous means.

40.

40.

“Api [V 3.0028] ce pattamādāya, anagāro paribbaje;

Aññaṃ ahiṃsayaṃ loke, api rajjena taṃ vara”nti.

"Even if, taking a bowl, one were to wander homeless, not harming another in the world—that is better even than kingship."

Tattha sasamuddapariyāyanti pariyāyo vuccati parivāro, samuddaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitena cakkavāḷapabbatena saddhiṃ, samuddasaṅkhātena vā parivārena saddhinti attho. Sāgarakuṇḍalanti sāgaramajjhe dīpavasena ṭhitattā tassa kuṇḍalabhūtanti attho. Nindāyāti jhānasukhasampannaṃ pabbajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā issariyaṃ gaṇhīti imāya nindāya. Seyyāti taṃ nāmenālapati. Vijānahīti dhammaṃ vijānāhi. Yā vutti vinipātenāti yā purohitaṭṭhānavasena laddhā yasalābhadhanalābhavutti jhānasukhato attavinipātanasaṅkhātena vinipātena ito gantvā issariyamadamattassa adhammacaraṇena vā hoti, taṃ vuttiṃ dhiratthu.

Here, 'surrounded by the ocean' (sasamuddapariyāyaṃ) means 'with a retinue'; that is, together with the Cakkavāḷa mountains that stand surrounding the ocean, or with the retinue constituted by the ocean. 'With the ocean as its earring' (sāgarakuṇḍalaṃ) means that because it stands in the middle of the ocean in the form of an island, it is like its earring. 'With blame' (nindāya) refers to the blame incurred by abandoning the going forth endowed with the bliss of jhāna and seizing power. 'Seyya' (Seyyā) is addressing him by name. 'Understand' (vijānahi) means 'understand the Dhamma'. 'Which is a livelihood by way of downfall' (yā vutti vinipātena) means: Fie upon that livelihood—the livelihood of gain of fame and gain of wealth obtained through the position of royal priest—which comes about by downfall, understood as casting oneself away from the bliss of jhāna, or by unrighteous conduct due to the intoxication of power.

Pattamādāyāti [M 3.0031] bhikkhābhājanaṃ gahetvā. Anagāroti api ahaṃ agāravirahito parakulesu careyyaṃ. Sāyeva jīvikāti sā eva me jīvikā seyyo varatarā. Yā cādhammena esanāti yā ca adhammena esanā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yā adhammena esanā, tato esāva jīvikā sundaratarāti. Ahiṃsayanti aviheṭhento. Api rajjenāti evaṃ paraṃ aviheṭhento kapālahatthassa mama jīvikakappanaṃ rajjenāpi varaṃ uttamanti.

'Taking a bowl' (pattamādāya) means taking the alms bowl. 'Homeless' (anagāro) means: even if I were without a home, I would wander among other families. 'That very livelihood' (sāyeva jīvikā) means that very livelihood is better and more excellent. 'Seeking by unrighteous means' (yā cādhammena esanā) means that seeking which is by unrighteous means. This is said to mean: 'This livelihood is far more excellent than seeking by unrighteous means.' 'Harming none' (ahiṃsayaṃ) means not harming. 'Even than kingship' (api rajjenāpi) means that my way of life with a bowl in hand, not harming others in this way, is better and supreme even than kingship.

Iti so punappunaṃ yācantampi taṃ paṭikkhipi. Seyyopi tassa manaṃ alabhitvā taṃ vanditvā gantvā tassa anāgamanabhāvaṃ rañño ārocesi.

Thus, he refused him though he repeatedly entreated him. Seyya, unable to win his mind, paid homage to him, departed, and reported to the king his non-return.

Satthā [P 3.0033] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi, aparepi bahū sotāpattiphalādīni sacchikariṃsu.

The Teacher, having brought forth this discourse on the Dhamma, made manifest the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and many others also realized the fruits of stream-entry and so forth.

Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, seyyo sāriputto, purohitaputto pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the king was Ānanda, Seyya was Sāriputta, and the chaplain's son was I myself.

Seyyajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Seyya Jātaka is the tenth.

Kāliṅgavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter: The Kāliṅga Chapter.

2. Pucimandavaggo

2. The Pucimanda Chapter

[311] 1. Pucimandajātakavaṇṇanā

[311] 1. 1. Commentary on the Pucimanda Jātaka

Uṭṭhehi [V 3.0029] corāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. There kira rājagahaṃ upanissāya araññakuṭikāya viharante eko coro nagaradvāragāme ekasmiṃ gehe sandhiṃ chinditvā hatthasāraṃ ādāya palāyitvā therassa kuṭipariveṇaṃ pavisitvā “idha mayhaṃ ārakkho bhavissatī”ti therassa paṇṇasālāya pamukhe nipajji. Thero tassa pamukhe sayitabhāvaṃ ñatvā tasmiṃ āsaṅkaṃ katvā “corasaṃsaggo nāma na vaṭṭatī”ti nikkhamitvā “mā idha sayī”ti nīhari. So coro tato nikkhamitvā padaṃ mohetvā [M 3.0032] palāyi. Manussā ukkaṃ ādāya corassa padānusārena tattha āgantvā tassa āgataṭṭhānaṭhitaṭṭhānanisinnaṭṭhānasayitaṭṭhānādīni disvā “coro ito āgato, idha ṭhito, idha nisinno, iminā ṭhānena apagato, na diṭṭho no”ti ito cito ca pakkhanditvā adisvāva paṭigatā. Punadivase thero pubbaṇhasamayaṃ rājagahe piṇḍāya caritvā piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto veḷuvanaṃ gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ satthu ārocesi. Satthā “na kho, moggallāna, tvaññeva āsaṅkitabbayuttakaṃ āsaṅki, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi āsaṅkiṃsū”ti vatvā therena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Get up, thief!” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. It seems that while the elder was dwelling in a forest hut near Rājagaha, a certain thief, having cut through a wall in a house in a village at the city gate, took valuables and fled. He entered the elder’s dwelling enclosure, thinking, “Here I will find protection,” and lay down in front of the elder’s leaf hut. The elder, knowing that he was lying in front, became apprehensive of him. Thinking, “Association with a thief is not proper,” he went out and drove him away, saying, “Do not lie here!” That thief, leaving that place, confused his tracks and fled. People, taking torches, followed the thief’s footprints and arrived there. Seeing the places where he had come, stood, sat, and lain down, they said, “The thief came from here, stood here, sat here, and departed from this place, but he was not seen by us.” After searching here and there, they returned without finding him. The next day, the elder, having gone for alms in Rājagaha in the forenoon and returned from his alms round, went to the Bamboo Grove and reported that incident to the Teacher. The Teacher said, “Indeed, Moggallāna, it is not only you who have suspected what ought to be suspected; the wise ones of old were also suspicious.” And being requested by the elder, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 3.0034] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto nagarassa susānavane nimbarukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Athekadivasaṃ nagaradvāragāme katakammacoro taṃ susānavanaṃ pāvisi. Tadā ca pana tattha nimbo ca assattho cāti dve jeṭṭhakarukkhā. Coro nimbarukkhamūle bhaṇḍikaṃ ṭhapetvā nipajji. Tasmiṃ pana kāle core gahetvā nimbasūle uttāsenti. Atha sā devatā cintesi “sace manussā āgantvā imaṃ coraṃ gaṇhissanti, imasseva nimbarukkhassa sākhaṃ chinditvā sūlaṃ katvā etaṃ uttāsessanti, evaṃ sante rukkho nassissati, handa naṃ ito nīharissāmī”ti. Sā tena saddhiṃ sallapantī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in a nimba tree in the city's charnel ground. Then one day, a thief who had committed a crime in a village at the city gate entered that charnel ground. At that time, there were two principal trees there: a nimba and an assattha tree. The thief placed his bundle at the root of the nimba tree and lay down. Now, at that time, thieves, having been caught, were impaled on nimba stakes. Then that deity thought: “If people come and seize this thief, they will cut a branch from this very nimba tree, make a stake, and impale him on it. If that happens, the tree will perish. Come, I shall remove him from here.” Desiring to speak with him, she spoke the first verse:

41.

41.

“Uṭṭhehi cora kiṃ sesi, ko attho supanena te;

Mā taṃ gahesuṃ rājāno, gāme kibbisakāraka”nti.

“Get up, thief, why do you sleep? What use is sleep to you? Lest the king's men seize you, the doer of evil in the village.”

Tattha [V 3.0030] rājānoti rājapurise sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kibbisakārakanti dāruṇasāhasikacorakammakārakaṃ.

Here, 'the king’s men' (rājāno) is said with reference to the king's officers. 'Doer of evil' (kibbisakārakaṃ) means one who commits cruel and violent acts of theft.

Iti naṃ vatvā “yāva taṃ rājapurisā na gaṇhanti, tāva aññattha gacchā”ti bhāyāpetvā palāpesi. Tasmiṃ palāte assatthadevatā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this to him, she frightened him, saying, “Go elsewhere before the king’s men catch you,” and made him flee. When he had fled, the assattha deity spoke the second verse:

42.

42.

“Yaṃ nu coraṃ gahessanti, gāme kibbisakārakaṃ;

Kiṃ tattha pucimandassa, vane jātassa tiṭṭhato”ti.

“If they seize the thief, the doer of evil in the village, what is that to the nimba tree, born and standing in the forest?”

Tattha [M 3.0033] vane jātassa tiṭṭhatoti nimbo vane jāto ceva ṭhito ca. Devatā pana tattha nibbattattā rukkhasamudācāreneva samudācari.

Here, 'born and standing in the forest' (vane jātassa tiṭṭhato) means the nimba tree was born and stands in the forest. But the deity, having been reborn there, spoke in the manner of addressing a tree.

Taṃ sutvā nimbadevatā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the nimba deity spoke the third verse:

43.

43.

“Na tvaṃ assattha jānāsi, mama corassa cantaraṃ;

Coraṃ gahetvā rājāno, gāme kibbisakārakaṃ;

Appenti nimbasūlasmiṃ, tasmiṃ me saṅkate mano”ti.

“You, Assattha, do not know the reason for avoiding association between me and the thief. Having caught the thief, the doer of evil in the village, the king's men impale him on a nimba stake—my mind is apprehensive about that.”

Tattha [P 3.0035] assatthāti purimanayeneva tasmiṃ nibbattadevataṃ samudācarati. Mama corassa cantaranti mama ca corassa ca ekato avasanakāraṇaṃ. Appenti nimbasūlasminti imasmiṃ kāle rājāno coraṃ nimbasūle āvuṇanti. Tasmiṃ me saṅkate manoti tasmiṃ kāraṇe mama cittaṃ saṅkati. Sace hi imaṃ sūle āvuṇissanti, vimānaṃ me nassissati, atha sākhāya olambessanti, vimāne me kuṇapagandho bhavissati, tenāhaṃ etaṃ palāpesinti attho.

Here, 'Assattha' refers to the deity born there, whom she addresses in the same manner as before. 'The reason between me and the thief' means the reason for me and the thief not dwelling together. 'They impale him on a nimba stake' means that at that time, the king's men would transfix thieves on nimba stakes. 'My mind is apprehensive about that' means my mind is anxious because of that reason. For if they impale him on a stake, my mansion will be destroyed; or if they hang him from a branch, my mansion will reek of a corpse. That is why I made him flee—such is the meaning.

Evaṃ tāsaṃ devatānaṃ aññamaññaṃ sallapantānaññeva bhaṇḍasāmikā ukkāhatthā padānusārena āgantvā corassa sayitaṭṭhānaṃ disvā “ambho idāneva coro uṭṭhāya palāto, na laddho no coro, sace labhissāma, imasseva naṃ nimbassa sūle vā āvuṇitvā sākhāya vā olambetvā gamissāmā”ti vatvā ito cito ca pakkhanditvā coraṃ adisvāva gatā.

While those deities were thus conversing with each other, the owners of the goods, carrying torches, arrived following the footprints and saw the thief's sleeping place. 'Ah! The thief has just risen and fled—we haven’t caught the thief. If we catch him, we’ll impale him on a stake made from this very nimba tree or hang him from a branch before we go,' they said. Then they rushed here and there but, not seeing the thief, left.

Tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā assatthadevatā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing their words, the assattha deity spoke the fourth verse:

44.

44.

“Saṅkeyya [V 3.0031] saṅkitabbāni, rakkheyyānāgataṃ bhayaṃ;

Anāgatabhayā dhīro, ubho loke avekkhatī”ti.

“One should be suspicious of what is suspect; one should guard against future danger. Out of fear of future danger, the wise one considers both worlds.”

Tattha rakkheyyānāgataṃ bhayanti dve anāgatabhayāni diṭṭhadhammikañceva samparāyikañcāti. Tesu pāpamitte parivajjento diṭṭhadhammikaṃ rakkhati, tīṇi duccaritāni parivajjento samparāyikaṃ rakkhati. Anāgatabhayāti anāgatabhayahetutaṃ bhayaṃ bhāyamāno dhīro paṇḍito puriso pāpamittasaṃsaggaṃ na karoti, tīhipi dvārehi duccaritaṃ na carati. Ubho loketi [M 3.0034] evaṃ bhāyanto hesa idhalokaparalokasaṅkhāte ubho loke avekkhati oloketi, olokayamāno idhalokabhayena pāpamitte vivajjeti, paralokabhayena pāpaṃ na karotīti.

Here, 'one should guard against the future' means two kinds of future dangers: those pertaining to this present life and those pertaining to the life to come. Among these, by avoiding evil friends, one guards against dangers pertaining to this present life; by avoiding the threefold evil conduct, one guards against dangers pertaining to the life to come. 'Future dangers' means that the wise and learned person, fearing the danger that is the cause of future danger, does not associate with evil friends or commit evil conduct through the three doors. 'Both worlds' means that one who thus fears considers and observes both worlds, namely this world and the next world; observing, one avoids evil friends through fear of this world, and does not commit evil through fear of the next world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā assatthadevatā ānando ahosi, nimbadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the Assattha deity was Ānanda, and the Nimba deity was I myself.'

Pucimandajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The commentary on the Pucimanda Jātaka, the first.

[312] 2. Kassapamandiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[312] 2. The Commentary on the Kassapamandiya Jātaka

Api [P 3.0036] kassapa mandiyāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ mahallakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kireko kulaputto kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā satthu santike pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhāne anuyutto na cirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tassa aparabhāge mātā kālamakāsi. So mātu accayena pitarañca kaniṭṭhabhātarañca pabbājetvā jetavane vasitvā vassūpanāyikasamaye cīvarapaccayassa sulabhataṃ sutvā ekaṃ gāmakāvāsaṃ gantvā tayopi tattheva vassaṃ upagantvā vutthavassā jetavanameva āgamaṃsu. Daharabhikkhu jetavanassa āsannaṭṭhāne “sāmaṇera tvaṃ theraṃ vissāmetvā āneyyāsi, ahaṃ puretaraṃ gantvā pariveṇaṃ paṭijaggissāmī”ti jetavanaṃ pāvisi. Mahallakatthero saṇikaṃ āgacchati. Sāmaṇero punappunaṃ sīsena uppīḷento viya “gaccha, bhante, gaccha, bhante”ti taṃ balakkārena neti. Thero “tvaṃ maṃ attano vasaṃ ānesī”ti puna nivattitvā koṭito paṭṭhāya āgacchati. Tesaṃ evaṃ aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ karontānaññeva sūriyo atthaṅgato, andhakāro jāto.

‘Kassapa, even through foolishness’—this the Teacher spoke while residing at Jetavana, concerning an elderly monk. It is said that a certain son of good family in Sāvatthī, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, went forth in the presence of the Teacher and, devoted to his meditation subject, soon attained Arahantship. Later, his mother passed away. After his mother's death, he ordained his father and younger brother and lived at Jetavana. Hearing that robes and other requisites were easily obtainable at the approach of the rainy season, he went to a certain village residence, and all three entered the rains retreat there. Having completed the rains retreat, they returned to Jetavana. When near Jetavana, the young monk said to the novice, ‘Novice, you let the elder rest and then bring him along. I will go ahead and prepare the dwelling.’ Then he entered Jetavana. The elderly elder was coming slowly. The novice, repeatedly urging him on as if pressing him with his head, said, ‘Go, venerable sir, go, venerable sir,’ and led him on by force. The elder, thinking, ‘You are bringing me under your own control,’ turned back and started coming again from the beginning. While they were thus quarreling with each other, the sun set, and darkness fell.

Itaropi pariveṇaṃ sammajjitvā udakaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā tesaṃ āgamanaṃ apassanto ukkaṃ gahetvā [V 3.0032] paccuggamanaṃ katvā te āgacchante disvā “kiṃ cirāyitthā”ti pucchi. Mahallako taṃ kāraṇaṃ kathesi. So te dvepi vissāmetvā saṇikaṃ ānesi. Taṃ divasaṃ buddhupaṭṭhānassa okāsaṃ na labhi. Atha naṃ dutiyadivase buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā vanditvā nisinnaṃ satthā “kadā āgatosī”ti pucchi. “Hiyyo, bhante”ti. “Hiyyo āgantvā ajja buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ [M 3.0035] karosī”ti? So “āma, bhante”ti vatvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ācikkhi. Satthā mahallakaṃ garahitvā “na esa idāneva evarūpaṃ kammaṃ karoti, pubbepi akāsi. Idāni pana tena tvaṃ kilamito, pubbepi paṇḍite kilamesī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The other monk, having swept the dwelling and prepared water, not seeing their arrival, took a torch and went out to meet them. Seeing them coming, he asked, ‘Why were you so late?’ The elder told him the reason. He then had both of them rest and brought them in slowly. That day, he did not get the opportunity to attend upon the Buddha. Then, the next day, having come to attend upon the Buddha, paid homage, and sat down, the Teacher asked him, ‘When did you arrive?’ ‘Yesterday, venerable sir.’ ‘Having arrived yesterday, you are attending upon the Buddha only today?’ ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ he replied and explained the reason. The Teacher rebuked the elder, saying, ‘He does not do such a deed only now; he did it in the past as well. Now you are wearied because of him; in the past, too, he wearied the wise.’ Being requested by the monk, he then related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsinigame brāhmaṇakule nibbatti. Tassa vayappattakāle [P 3.0037] mātā kālamakāsi. So mātu sarīrakiccaṃ katvā māsaddhamāsaccayena ghare vijjamānaṃ dhanaṃ dānaṃ datvā pitarañca kaniṭṭhabhātarañca gahetvā himavantapadese devadattiyaṃ vakkalaṃ gahetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā uñchācariyāya vanamūlaphalāphalehi yāpento ramaṇīye vanasaṇḍe vasi. Himavante pana vassakāle acchinnadhāre deve vassante na sakkā hoti kandamūlaṃ khaṇituṃ, phalāni ca paṇṇāni ca patanti. Tāpasā yebhuyyena himavantato nikkhamitvā manussapathe vasanti. Tadā bodhisatto pitarañca kaniṭṭhabhātarañca gahetvā manussapathe vasitvā puna himavante pupphitaphalite te ubhopi gahetvā himavante attano assamapadaṃ āgacchanto assamassāvidūre sūriye atthaṅgate “tumhe saṇikaṃ āgaccheyyātha, ahaṃ purato gantvā assamaṃ paṭijaggissāmī”ti vatvā te ohāya gato. Khuddakatāpaso pitarā saddhiṃ saṇikaṃ gacchanto taṃ kaṭippadese sīsena uppīḷento viya gaccha gacchāti taṃ balakkārena neti. Mahallako “tvaṃ maṃ attano ruciyā ānesī”ti paṭinivattitvā koṭito paṭṭhāya āgacchati. Evaṃ tesaṃ kalahaṃ karontānaññeva andhakāro ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a market town of Kasi. When he came of age, his mother passed away. After performing the funeral rites for his mother, and after a month and a half had passed, he gave as alms the wealth remaining in the house. Then, taking his father and younger brother, he received bark garments given by a deity in the Himalayan region and went forth as an ascetic. Sustaining himself by gleaning wild roots and fruits, he lived in a pleasant forest grove. During the rainy season in the Himalayas, when the god rains with an unbroken stream, it is not possible to dig for roots, and fruits and leaves fall. Ascetics then mostly leave the Himalayas and dwell in the regions of humankind. At that time, the Bodhisatta, taking his father and younger brother, stayed in a region of humankind. Later, when the Himalayas were in flower and fruit, he took them both and, while returning to his own hermitage in the Himalayas, the sun set when they were not far from the hermitage. He said, ‘You two come along slowly; I will go ahead and prepare the hermitage,’ and leaving them, he went. The younger ascetic, going slowly with his father, led him on by force, as if pressing him in the waist region with his head, saying, ‘Go, go.’ The elder, thinking, ‘You are bringing me according to your own pleasure,’ turned back and started coming again from the beginning. While they were thus quarreling with each other, darkness fell.

Bodhisattopi paṇṇasālaṃ sammajjitvā udakaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā ukkamādāya paṭipathaṃ āgacchanto te disvā “ettakaṃ kālaṃ kiṃ karitthā”ti āha. Khuddakatāpaso pitarā katakāraṇaṃ kathesi. Bodhisatto ubhopi te saṇikaṃ netvā parikkhāraṃ paṭisāmetvā pitaraṃ nhāpetvā pādadhovanapiṭṭhisambāhanādīni katvā aṅgārakapallaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā paṭippassaddhakilamathaṃ pitaraṃ upanisīditvā “tāta, taruṇadārakā nāma mattikābhājanasadisā muhuttaneva bhijjanti[P 3.0038], sakiṃ bhinnakālato paṭṭhāya puna na sakkā honti ghaṭetuṃ, te akkosantāpi paribhāsantāpi mahallakehi adhivāsetabbā”ti vatvā pitaraṃ ovadanto imā gāthā abhāsi –

The Bodhisatta, having swept the leaf-hut and prepared water, took a torch and came along the path to meet them. Seeing them, he said, ‘What were you doing for so long?’ The young ascetic explained what his father had done. The Bodhisatta led them both slowly, put away their requisites, bathed his father, and performed services such as washing his feet and massaging his back. Then, having prepared a charcoal brazier, he sat near his father, whose fatigue had subsided, and advising him, said, ‘Father, young children are like clay vessels—they break in an instant. From the time they are once broken, it is not possible to put them together again. Even if they scold or abuse, they should be endured by the elders.’ While advising his father, he spoke these verses:

45.

45.

“Api [V 3.0033][M 3.0036] kassapa mandiyā, yuvā sapati hanti vā;

Sabbaṃ taṃ khamate dhīro, paṇḍito taṃ titikkhati.

‘Kassapa, even through foolishness, if a youth reviles or strikes, the firm one endures it all; the wise one bears it with patience.

46.

46.

“Sacepi santo vivadanti, khippaṃ santīyare puna;

Bālā pattāva bhijjanti, na te samathamajjhagū.

‘Even if the virtuous dispute, they are quickly reconciled again; but fools shatter like clay pots, for they do not attain calm.

47.

47.

“Ete bhiyyo samāyanti, sandhi tesaṃ na jīrati;

Yo cādhipannaṃ jānāti, yo ca jānāti desanaṃ.

‘They come together even more; their bond does not decay: the one who recognizes the transgression, and the one who knows the confession.

48.

48.

“Eso hi uttaritaro, bhāravaho dhuraddharo;

Yo paresādhipannānaṃ, sayaṃ sandhātumarahatī”ti.

‘He is indeed more excellent, a carrier of the load, a bearer of the burden, who is himself able to reconcile others who have transgressed.’

Tattha kassapāti pitaraṃ nāmenālapati. Mandiyāti mandībhāvena taruṇatāya. Yuvā sapati hanti vāti taruṇadārako akkosatipi paharatipi. Dhīroti dhikkatapāpo, dhī vā vuccati paññā, tāya samannāgatotipi attho. Itaraṃ pana imasseva vevacanaṃ. Ubhayenāpi sabbaṃ taṃ bāladārakehi kataṃ aparādhaṃ mahallako dhīro paṇḍito sahati titikkhatīti dasseti.

Herein, 'Kassapa' is an address to his father by name. 'Mandiyā' means because of dullness, because of youthfulness. 'A youth scolds or strikes' means a young child scolds or strikes. 'Dhīra' means one who has denounced evil; or 'dhī' is called wisdom, so it means one endowed with it. The other word is indeed a synonym of this. By both, it is shown that the elder, the wise one, the learned one, endures and tolerates every offense committed by foolish children.

Sandhīyareti puna mittabhāvena sandhīyanti ghaṭīyanti. Bālā pattāvāti bālakā pana mattikāpattāva bhijjanti. Na te samathamajjhagūti te bālakā appamattakampi vivādaṃ katvā verūpasamanaṃ na vindanti nādhigacchanti. Ete bhiyyoti ete dve janā bhinnāpi puna samāgacchanti. Sandhīti mittasandhi. Tesanti tesaññeva dvinnaṃ sandhi na jīrati. Yo cādhipannanti yo ca attanā adhipannaṃ atikkantaṃ aññasmiṃ katadosaṃ jānāti. Desananti yo ca tena attano dosaṃ jānantena desitaṃ accayadesanaṃ paṭiggaṇhituṃ jānāti.

“They reconcile again” means they are reunited again in friendship, they are joined together. “Fools are like pots” means fools, like clay pots, break. “They do not attain peace” means those fools, having made even a small quarrel, do not find or achieve the appeasement of enmity. “These come together again” means these two people, even having been divided, come together again. “Their bond” means the bond of friendship. “Does not decay” means the bond of these very two does not decay. “One who knows the offense” means one who knows his own offense, having transgressed, a fault committed against another. “And one who knows the confession” means one who knows how to accept the confession of transgression made by the one who knows his own offense.

Yo paresādhipannānanti yo paresaṃ adhipannānaṃ dosena abhibhūtānaṃ aparādhakārakānaṃ. Sayaṃ sandhātumarahatīti tesu akhamāpentesupi “ehi, bhadramukha, uddesaṃ gaṇha, aṭṭhakathaṃ suṇa, bhāvanamanuyuñja, kasmā paribāhiro hosī”ti evaṃ sayaṃ sandhātuṃ arahati mittabhāvaṃ ghaṭeti, eso evarūpo mettāvihārī uttaritaro mittabhārassa mittadhurassa ca vahanato “bhāravaho”ti “dhuraddharo”ti ca saṅkhaṃ gacchatīti.

“Of those others who have offended” means of those who are overcome by fault, who commit offenses. “Is himself able to reconcile” means even when they do not ask for forgiveness, he is able to reconcile them himself, saying, “Come, good sir, take up the recitation, listen to the commentary, apply yourself to meditation; why do you remain outside?” Thus he is able to reconcile them himself, establishing friendship. Such a one, dwelling in loving-kindness, is superior; because he bears the burden of friendship and takes up the yoke of friendship, he is reckoned as a “bearer of burdens” and an “upholder of the yoke.”

Evaṃ [V 3.0034][P 3.0039][M 3.0037] bodhisatto pitu ovādaṃ adāsi, sopi tato pabhuti danto ahosi sudanto.

Thus the Bodhisatta gave advice to his father. And he, from that time onward, became tamed, well-tamed.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā pitā tāpaso mahallako ahosi, khuddakatāpaso sāmaṇero, pitu ovādadāyako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the Jātaka thus: “At that time, the father was the aged ascetic, the young ascetic was the novice, but the one who gave advice to the father was I myself.”

Kassapamandiyajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Kassapamandiya Jātaka is the Second.

[313] 3. Khantivādījātakavaṇṇanā

[313] 3. The Commentary on the Khantivādī Jātaka

Yo te hatthe ca pāde cāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kodhanabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā kathitameva. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ “kasmā, tvaṃ bhikkhu, akkodhanassa buddhassa sāsane pabbajitvā kodhaṃ karosi, porāṇakapaṇḍitā sarīre pahārasahasse patante hatthapādakaṇṇanāsāsu chijjamānāsu parassa kodhaṃ na kariṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

While dwelling in Jetavana, the Teacher told this story, which begins, “He who your hands and feet,” concerning a certain angry monk. The circumstances have been related previously. The Teacher said to that monk: “Why, monk, having gone forth in the teaching of the Buddha who is free from anger, do you become angry? The wise of old, even when a thousand blows were falling on their bodies and their hands, feet, ears, and noses were being cut off, did not become angry with another.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ kalābu nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto asītikoṭivibhave brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā kuṇḍalakumāro nāma māṇavo hutvā vayappatto takkasilaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā mātāpitūnaṃ accayena dhanarāsiṃ oloketvā “imaṃ dhanaṃ uppādetvā mama ñātakā aggahetvāva gatā, mayā panetaṃ gahetvā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sabbaṃ dhanaṃ viceyyadānavasena yo yaṃ āharati, tassa taṃ datvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitvā phalāphalena yāpento ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya manussapathaṃ āgantvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase nagare bhikkhāya caranto senāpatissa nivāsanadvāraṃ sampāpuṇi. Senāpati tassa iriyāpathesu pasīditvā gharaṃ pavesetvā attano paṭiyāditabhojanaṃ [P 3.0040] bhojetvā paṭiññaṃ gahetvā tattheva rājuyyāne vasāpesi.

In the past, a king named Kalābu reigned in Benares. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family possessing a fortune of eighty crores. As a young man named Kuṇḍala Kumāra, he came of age, went to Takkasilā, and mastered all the arts. After establishing a household, upon the death of his parents, he looked upon the mass of wealth and thought, “My relatives who amassed this wealth have departed without taking it; but it is for me to take it and go.” He gave away all his wealth as a discerning gift to all who came for it. Then, he entered the Himalayas, went forth as an ascetic, and lived for a long time sustaining himself on fruits and roots. Later, needing salt and sour seasoning, he came to the region of human habitation. In due course, he reached Benares and dwelt in the royal park. The next day, while wandering for alms in the city, he came to the door of the commander-in-chief’s residence. The commander, pleased with his deportment, invited him into his house, fed him with the food prepared for himself, and, having received his consent, had him take up residence in that same royal park.

Athekadivasaṃ [M 3.0038] kalāburājā surāmadamatto chekanāṭakaparivuto mahantena yasena uyyānaṃ gantvā maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe sayanaṃ attharāpetvā ekissā piyamanāpāya itthiyā aṅke sayi. Gītavāditanaccesu chekā nāṭakitthiyo gītādīni payojesuṃ, sakkassa devarañño viya mahāsampatti ahosi, rājā niddaṃ okkami. Atha tā itthiyo “yassatthāya mayaṃ gītādīni payojayāma, so niddaṃ upagato, kiṃ no gītādīhī”ti vīṇādīni tūriyāni tattha tattheva chaḍḍetvā [V 3.0035] uyyānaṃ pakkantā pupphaphalapallavādīhi palobhiyamānā uyyāne abhiramiṃsu. Tadā bodhisatto tasmiṃ uyyāne supupphitasālamūle pabbajjāsukhena vītināmento mattavaravāraṇo viya nisinno hoti. Atha tā itthiyo uyyāne caramānā taṃ disvā “etha, ayyāyo, etasmiṃ rukkhamūle pabbajito nisinno, yāva rājā na pabujjhati, tāvassa santike kiñci suṇamānā nisīdissāmā”ti gantvā vanditvā parivāretvā nisinnā “amhākaṃ kathetabbayuttakaṃ kiñci kathethā”ti vadiṃsu. Bodhisatto tāsaṃ dhammaṃ kathesi. Atha sā itthī aṅkaṃ cāletvā rājānaṃ pabodhesi. Rājā pabuddho tā apassanto “kahaṃ gatā vasaliyo”ti āha. Etā, mahārāja, gantvā ekaṃ tāpasaṃ parivāretvā nisīdiṃsūti. Rājā kupito khaggaṃ gahetvā “sikkhāpessāmi naṃ kūṭajaṭila”nti vegena agamāsi.

One day, King Kalābu, intoxicated with strong drink and surrounded by skilled dancing women, went to the park with great pomp. He had a couch spread on the auspicious stone slab and lay his head in the lap of a favorite woman. The skilled dancing women performed their songs, music, and dances; the splendor was as great as that of Sakka, king of the gods. The king fell asleep. Then those women thought, “He for whose sake we perform our songs and so on has fallen asleep. What use are our songs to us now?” So they cast aside their lutes and other instruments right where they were and went into the park. Attracted by the flowers, fruits, and new leaves, they amused themselves in the park. At that time, the Bodhisatta was seated at the foot of a fully blossomed sāl tree in that park, passing the time in the bliss of the ascetic life, like a magnificent, noble elephant. As the women were wandering in the park, they saw him and said, “Come, ladies, an ascetic is seated at the foot of this tree. While the king is sleeping, let us sit near him and listen to something.” They went to him, paid homage, and sat down surrounding him. They said, “Please tell us something that is fitting to be told.” The Bodhisatta taught them the Dhamma. Then the woman, by moving her lap, woke the king. The king, upon waking and not seeing the women, said, “Where have the wretches gone?” She replied, “Great king, they have gone and are sitting around an ascetic.” The king became enraged, seized his sword, and went quickly, exclaiming, “I will teach that deceitful, matted-hair ascetic a lesson!”

Atha tā itthiyo rājānaṃ kuddhaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā tāsu vallabhatarā gantvā rañño hatthā asiṃ gahetvā rājānaṃ vūpasamesuṃ. So āgantvā bodhisattassa santike ṭhatvā “kiṃvādī tvaṃ, samaṇā”ti pucchi. “Khantivādī, mahārājā”ti. “Kā esā khanti nāmā”ti? “Akkosantesu paribhāsantesu paharantesu akujjhanabhāvo”ti. Rājā “passissāmi dāni te khantiyā atthibhāva”nti [P 3.0041] coraghātakaṃ pakkosāpesi. So attano cārittena pharasuñca kaṇṭakakasañca ādāya kāsāyanivasano rattamālādharo āgantvā rājānaṃ vanditvā “kiṃ karomi, devā”ti āha. Imaṃ coraṃ duṭṭhatāpasaṃ gahetvā ākaḍḍhitvā bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā kaṇṭakakasaṃ gahetvā purato ca pacchato ca ubhosu passesu cāti catūsupi passesu dvepahārasahassamassa dehīti. So tathā akāsi[M 3.0039]. Bodhisattassa chavi bhijji. Cammaṃ bhijji, maṃsaṃ chijji, lohitaṃ paggharati.

Then those women, seeing the enraged king approaching, those among them who were most favored went and took the sword from the king’s hand and pacified him. He came and stood near the Bodhisatta and asked, “What is your doctrine, ascetic?” “My doctrine is patience, great king.” “And what is this thing called patience?” “It is the state of not being angry when others abuse, revile, or strike one.” The king said, “Now I will see whether this patience of yours exists,” and had the executioner summoned. The executioner, taking his customary axe and thorny whip, dressed in an ochre-colored robe and wearing a red garland, approached, paid homage to the king, and said, “What am I to do, Your Majesty?” “Seize this thief, this wicked ascetic, drag him, throw him to the ground, and with the thorny whip give him two thousand lashes on the four sides—on his front, his back, and both his sides.” He did so. The Bodhisatta’s outer skin was broken, his inner skin was broken, his flesh was cut, and blood flowed forth.

Puna rājā “kiṃvādī tvaṃ bhikkhū”ti āha. “Khantivādī, mahārāja”. “Tvaṃ pana mayhaṃ cammantare khantī”ti maññasi, natthi mayhaṃ cammantare khanti, tayā pana daṭṭhuṃ asakkuṇeyye hadayabbhantare mama khanti patiṭṭhitā. “Mahārājā”ti. Puna coraghātako “kiṃ karomī”ti pucchi. “Imassa kūṭajaṭilassa ubho hatthe chindā”ti. So pharasuṃ gahetvā gaṇḍiyaṃ ṭhapetvā hatthe chindi. Atha naṃ “pāde chindā”ti āha, pādepi chindi. Hatthapādakoṭīhi ghaṭachiddehi lākhāraso viya lohitaṃ paggharati. Puna rājā “kiṃvādīsī”ti pucchi. “Khantivādī, mahārāja”. “Tvaṃ pana mayhaṃ hatthapādakoṭīsu ‘khanti atthī’ti maññasi, natthesā ettha, mayhaṃ khanti gambhīraṭṭhāne patiṭṭhitā”ti. So “kaṇṇanāsamassa chindā”ti āha. Itaro kaṇṇanāsaṃ chindi, sakalasarīre lohitaṃ ahosi. Puna naṃ “kiṃvādī [V 3.0036] nāma tva”nti pucchi. “Mahārāja, khantivādī nāma”. “Mā kho pana tvaṃ ‘kaṇṇanāsikakoṭīsu patiṭṭhitā khantī’ti maññasi, mama khanti gambhīre hadayabbhantare patiṭṭhitā”ti. Rājā “kūṭajaṭila tava khantiṃ tvameva ukkhipitvā nisīdā”ti bodhisattassa hadayaṃ pādena paharitvā pakkāmi.

Again, the king asked, “What is your doctrine, monk?” “Patience, great king.” “Do you think my patience lies within the skin? My patience is not within the skin; rather, my patience is established deep within my heart, where you cannot see it.” “Great king.” Then the executioner asked, “What shall I do?” “Cut off both hands of this deceitful ascetic,” he said. Taking an axe, he placed them on a block and cut off the hands. Then he said, “Cut off his feet,” and he also cut off the feet. From the stumps of his hands and feet, blood flowed like lac-resin from broken vessels. Again, the king asked, “What is your doctrine?” “Patience, great king.” “Do you think there is patience in the stumps of my hands and feet? It is not there. My patience is established in a deep place.” Then he said, “Cut off his ears and nose.” The other cut off his ears and nose, and blood flowed from his entire body. Again, he asked him, “What is your doctrine?” “Great king, my doctrine is patience.” “Do not think that my patience is established in the tips of your ears and nose. My patience is established deep within my heart.” The king said, “Deceitful ascetic, you yourself take up your patience and sit there!” and striking the Bodhisatta on the chest with his foot, he departed.

Tasmiṃ gate senāpati bodhisattassa sarīrato lohitaṃ puñchitvā [P 3.0042] hatthapādakaṇṇanāsakoṭiyo sāṭakakaṇṇe katvā bodhisattaṃ saṇikaṃ nisīdāpetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā “sace, bhante, tumhe kujjhitukāmā, tumhesu katāparādhassa raññova kujjheyyātha, mā aññesa”nti yācanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

When he had departed, the general wiped the blood from the Bodhisatta's body, placed the severed hands, feet, ears, and nose in the fold of his robe, gently helped the Bodhisatta to sit, and after paying homage, sat to one side. Entreating him, he spoke the first verse: “Venerable sir, if you wish to be angry, be angry only with the king who has wronged you, not with others.”

49.

49.

“Yo te hatthe ca pāde ca, kaṇṇanāsañca chedayi;

Tassa kujjha mahāvīra, mā raṭṭhaṃ vinasā ida”nti.

“He who cut off your hands and feet, and your ears and nose—be angry with him, great hero, and let not this kingdom be destroyed.”

Tattha mahāvīrāti mahāvīriya. Mā raṭṭhaṃ vinasā idanti idaṃ niraparādhaṃ kāsiraṭṭhaṃ mā vināsehi.

Herein, ‘mahāvīra’ means one of great energy. ‘Let not this kingdom be destroyed’ means: do not destroy this innocent kingdom of Kāsi.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:

50.

50.

“Yo me hatthe ca pāde ca, kaṇṇanāsañca chedayi;

Ciraṃ jīvatu so rājā, na hi kujjhanti mādisā”ti.

“He who cut off my hands and feet, and my ears and nose—long live that king, for such as I do not become angry.”

Tattha [M 3.0040] mādisāti mama sadisā khantibalena samannāgatā paṇḍitā “ayaṃ maṃ akkosi paribhāsi pahari, chindi bhindī”ti taṃ na kujjhanti.

Herein, ‘mādisā’ means wise ones like myself, endowed with the power of patience, who do not become angry, thinking: ‘He insulted me, reviled me, struck me, cut me, broke me.’

Rañño uyyānā nikkhamantassa bodhisattassa cakkhupathaṃ vijahanakāleyeva ayaṃ catunahutādhikā dviyojanasatasahassabahalā mahāpathavī khalibaddhasāṭako viya phalitā, avīcito jālā nikkhamitvā rājānaṃ kuladattiyena rattakambalena pārupantī viya gaṇhi. So uyyānadvāreyeva pathaviṃ pavisitvā avīcimahāniraye patiṭṭhahi. Bodhisattopi taṃ divasameva kālamakāsi. Rājaparisā ca nāgarā ca gandhamālādhūmahatthā āgantvā bodhisattassa sarīrakiccaṃ akaṃsu. Keci panāhu “bodhisatto puna himavantameva gato”ti, taṃ abhūtaṃ.

As the king was departing from the garden, at the very moment he passed from the Bodhisatta's sight, this great earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, split open like a tattered cloth. Flames issued forth from Avīci and seized the king, as if wrapping him in a red blanket given by his family. Right there at the garden gate, he sank into the earth and was established in the great Avīci hell. The Bodhisatta also passed away that very same day. The king’s retinue and the townspeople, with perfumes, garlands, and incense in hand, came and performed the last rites for the Bodhisatta. Some, however, say that the Bodhisatta returned to the Himalayas, but that is untrue.

51.

51.

“Ahū [V 3.0037][P 3.0043] atītamaddhānaṃ, samaṇo khantidīpano;

Taṃ khantiyāyeva ṭhitaṃ, kāsirājā achedayi.

“In a time long past, there was a monk, an illuminator of patience. While he stood firm in patience, the king of Kāsi had him mutilated.

52.

52.

“Tassa kammapharusassa, vipāko kaṭuko ahu;

Yaṃ kāsirājā vedesi, nirayamhi samappito”ti. –

“The result of his harsh deed was bitter; this the king of Kāsi experienced, being consigned to hell.”

Imā dve abhisambuddhagāthā.

These two are verses of the Fully Enlightened One.

Tattha atītamaddhānanti atīte addhāne. Khantidīpanoti adhivāsanakhantisaṃvaṇṇano. Achedayīti mārāpesi. Ekacce pana “bodhisattassa puna hatthapādakaṇṇanāsā ghaṭitā”ti vadanti, tampi abhūtameva. Samappitoti patiṭṭhito.

Herein, ‘atītamaddhānaṃ’ means ‘in a past time.’ ‘Khantidīpano’ means one who extols patient endurance. ‘Achedayi’ means he caused him to be killed. Some, however, say, “The Bodhisatta's hands, feet, ears, and nose were joined together again,” but that too is untrue. ‘Samappito’ means ‘established.’

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne kodhano bhikkhu anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi, aññe bahū sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇiṃsu.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, identified the characters of the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the teaching on the Truths, the irascible monk was established in the fruit of Non-returning, and many others attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

Tadā kalāburājā devadatto ahosi, senāpati sāriputto, khantivādī tāpaso pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, King Kalābu was Devadatta, the general was Sāriputta, and the ascetic, the teacher of patience, was myself.

Khantivādījātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Khantivādī Jātaka, the Third.

[314] 4. Lohakumbhijātakavaṇṇanā

[314] 4. The Commentary on the Lohakumbhī Jātaka

Dujjīvitamajīvimhāti [M 3.0041] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarājānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā kira kosalarājā rattibhāge catunnaṃ nerayikasattānaṃ saddaṃ suṇi. Eko du-kārameva bhaṇi, eko sa-kāraṃ, eko na-kāraṃ, eko so-kāramevāti. Te kira atītabhave sāvatthiyaṃyeva pāradārikā rājaputtā ahesuṃ. Te paresaṃ rakkhitagopitamātugāmesu aparajjhitvā cittakeḷiṃ kīḷantā bahuṃ pāpakammaṃ katvā maraṇacakkena chinnā sāvatthisāmante catūsu lohakumbhīsu nibbattā saṭṭhi vassasahassāni tattha paccitvā uggatā lohakumbhimukhavaṭṭiṃ disvā “kadā nu kho imamhā dukkhā muccissāmā”ti cattāropi mahantena saddena anupaṭipāṭiyā viraviṃsu. Rājā tesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā maraṇabhayatajjito nisinnakova aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpesi.

“We have lived a wicked life.” The Teacher told this while dwelling in Jetavana concerning the King of Kosala. At that time, it is said, the King of Kosala heard the cries of four beings in hell during the night. One uttered only the syllable ‘du,’ another ‘sa,’ another ‘na,’ and the last only ‘so.’ It seems that in a past life, they were princes in Sāvatthī who were adulterers. They committed offenses with the guarded and protected wives of others, and while engaging in frivolous sport, they performed much evil. Cut down by the wheel of death, they were reborn in four iron cauldrons near Sāvatthī. After being cooked there for sixty thousand years, they rose up, and seeing the rim of the iron cauldron, all four cried out loudly in succession, “When, indeed, shall we be freed from this suffering?” Hearing their cries, the King, terrified by the fear of death, remained seated until dawn.

Aruṇuggamanavelāya [V 3.0038] brāhmaṇā āgantvā rājānaṃ sukhasayitaṃ pucchiṃsu. Rājā “kuto me ācariyā sukhasayitaṃ, ajjāhaṃ evarūpe [P 3.0044] cattāro bhiṃsanakasadde suṇi”nti. Brāhmaṇā hatthe vidhuniṃsu. “Kiṃ ācariyā”ti? “Sāhasikasaddā, mahārājā”ti. “Sapaṭikammā appaṭikammā”ti? “Kāmaṃ appaṭikammā, mayaṃ pana susikkhitā, mahārājā”ti. “Kiṃ katvā paṭibāhissathā”ti? “Mahārāja, paṭikammaṃ mahantaṃ na sakkā kātuṃ, mayaṃ pana sabbacatukkaṃ yaññaṃ yajitvā hāressāmā”ti. “Tena hi khippaṃ cattāro hatthī cattāro asse cattāro usabhe cattāro manusseti laṭukikasakuṇikā ādiṃ katvā cattāro cattāro pāṇe gahetvā sabbacatukkayaññaṃ yajitvā mama sotthibhāvaṃ karothā”ti. “Sādhu, mahārājā”ti sampaṭicchitvā yenattho, taṃ gahetvā yaññāvāṭaṃ paccupaṭṭhapesuṃ, bahupāṇe thūṇūpanīte katvā ṭhapesuṃ. “Bahuṃ macchamaṃsaṃ khādissāma, bahuṃ dhanaṃ labhissāmā”ti ussāhappattā hutvā “idaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, idaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, devā”ti aparāparaṃ caranti.

At the break of dawn, the brahmins came and asked the King if he had slept well. The King replied, “How could I have slept well, teachers? Today I heard four such terrifying sounds.” The brahmins shook their hands. “What is it, teachers?” “Violent sounds, Great King.” “Is there a remedy or no remedy?” “They are indeed irremediable, Great King, but we are well-trained.” “What will you do to ward them off?” “Great King, a great remedy is not possible, but we will avert it by performing a sacrifice of the fourfold.” “Then quickly take four elephants, four horses, four bulls, four men, and so on, starting with quails—taking four of each kind of living being—perform the sacrifice of the fourfold and ensure my well-being.” “Very well, Great King,” they agreed. Taking what was needed, they prepared the sacrificial pit and brought many living beings to the sacrificial posts. Filled with excitement, thinking, “We will eat much fish and meat and get much wealth,” they went to and fro, saying, “This is fit to be obtained, this is fit to be obtained, Your Majesty!”

Mallikā devī rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ nu kho, mahārāja, brāhmaṇā ativiya ussāhayantā vicarantī”ti pucchi. “Devi kiṃ tuyhiminā, tvaṃ attano yaseneva mattā pamattā, dukkhaṃ pana amhākameva na jānāsī”ti? “Kiṃ[M 3.0042], mahārājā”ti. “Devi, ahaṃ evarūpaṃ nāma asotabbaṃ suṇiṃ, tato imesaṃ saddānaṃ sutattā “kiṃ bhavissatī”ti brāhmaṇe pucchiṃ, brāhmaṇā “tumhākaṃ mahārāja rajjassa vā bhogānaṃ vā jīvitassa vā antarāyo paññāyati, sabbacatukkena yaññaṃ yajitvā sotthibhāvaṃ karissāmā”ti vadiṃsu, te mayhaṃ vacanaṃ gahetvā yaññāvāṭaṃ katvā yena yenattho, tassa tassa kāraṇā āgacchantī”ti. “Kiṃ pana deva, imesaṃ saddānaṃ nipphattiṃ sadevake loke aggabrāhmaṇaṃ pucchitthā”ti? “Ko esa devi, sadevake loke aggabrāhmaṇo nāmā”ti? “Mahāgotamo sammāsambuddho”ti. “Devi, sammāsambuddho me na pucchito”ti? “Tena hi gantvā pucchathā”ti.

Queen Mallikā approached the king and asked, "Great king, why are the brahmins bustling about so eagerly?" The king replied, "Queen, what concern is it of yours? You are intoxicated and heedless with your own glory. Do you not know of my suffering?" "What is it, great king?" "Queen, I heard such inauspicious sounds. Hearing these sounds, I asked the brahmins what would happen. They said, 'Great king, a danger to your kingdom, your wealth, or your life is apparent. We will perform a sacrifice of four of every kind to secure your well-being.' Accepting my word, they prepared the sacrificial pit and are now coming for whatever they need." "But sire, have you asked the foremost brahmin in the world with its devas about the origin of these sounds?" "Who is this foremost brahmin in the world with its devas, queen?" "Mahāgotama, the Perfectly Enlightened One." "Queen, I have not asked the Perfectly Enlightened One." "Then go and ask him."

Rājā tassā vacanaṃ gahetvā bhuttapātarāso rathavaramāruyha jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā pucchi “ahaṃ, bhante, rattibhāge cattāro sadde sutvā brāhmaṇe pucchiṃ, te ‘sabbacatukkayaññaṃ [P 3.0045] yajitvā sotthiṃ karissāmā’ti vatvā yaññāvāṭe kammaṃ karonti, tesaṃ saddānaṃ sutattā mayhaṃ kiṃ bhavissatī”ti. “Na kiñci, mahārāja, nerayikasattā dukkhamanubhavantā evaṃ viraviṃsu, na ime saddā idāni tayā eva sutā, porāṇakarājūhipi sutāyeva, tepi brāhmaṇe pucchitvā pasughātayaññaṃ kattukāmā hutvā paṇḍitānaṃ kathaṃ sutvā na kariṃsu, paṇḍitā tesaṃ saddānaṃ antaraṃ kathetvā mahājanaṃ vissajjāpetvā sotthimakaṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The king, accepting her words, finished his morning meal, mounted his excellent chariot, went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and asked: "Venerable sir, during the night I heard four sounds and asked the brahmins about them. They said, 'After performing a sacrifice of four of every kind, we will ensure well-being,' and are now performing the work at the sacrificial pit. What will happen to me from having heard those sounds?" "Nothing at all, great king. Beings in hell, experiencing suffering, cried out thus. These sounds were not heard by you alone now; ancient kings also heard them. They too asked the brahmins and, desiring to perform animal sacrifices, refrained from doing so after hearing the words of the wise. The wise explained the cause of those sounds, released the great multitude of beings, and brought about well-being." Having said this, and being requested by him, he related the past.

Atīte [V 3.0039] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto aññatarasmiṃ kāsigāme brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca uppādetvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto himavante ramaṇīye vanasaṇḍe vasati. Tadā bārāṇasirājā catunnaṃ nerayikānaṃ imeva cattāro sadde sutvā bhītatasito imināva niyāmena brāhmaṇehi “tiṇṇaṃ antarāyānaṃ aññataro bhavissati, sabbacatukkayaññena taṃ vūpasamessāmā”ti vutte sampaṭicchi. Purohito brāhmaṇehi saddhiṃ yaññāvāṭaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpesi, mahājano thūṇūpanīto ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto mettābhāvanaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā dibbacakkhunā lokaṃ olokento imaṃ kāraṇaṃ disvā “ajja, mayā gantuṃ vaṭṭati, mahājanassa sotthi [M 3.0043] bhavissatī”ti iddhibalena vehāsaṃ uppatitvā bārāṇasirañño uyyāne otaritvā maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe kañcanarūpakaṃ viya nisīdi. Tadā purohitassa jeṭṭhantevāsiko ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “nanu, ācariya, amhākaṃ vedesu paraṃ māretvā sotthikaraṇaṃ nāma natthī”ti āha. Purohito “tvaṃ rājadhanaṃ rakkhasi, bahuṃ macchamaṃsaṃ khādissāma, dhanaṃ labhissāma, tuṇhī hohī”ti taṃ paṭibāhi.
