In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a certain Kāsī village. When he came of age, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he renounced them and went forth as a sage. Having developed the supernormal powers and attainments, he dwelt in a delightful forest grove in the Himalayas, enjoying the bliss of jhāna. At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī, hearing these same four sounds of four beings in hell, became terrified and agitated. In this very way, when it was said by the brahmins, 'One of three dangers will occur; we shall pacify it by performing a sacrifice of four of everything,' he consented. The royal priest, together with the brahmins, prepared the sacrificial pit, and a great multitude was brought to the sacrificial post. Then the Bodhisatta, having made the development of loving-kindness his forerunner, surveyed the world with his divine eye and saw this matter. Thinking, 'Today, I must go; there will be well-being for the great multitude,' he rose into the air by his psychic power, descended in the king's park, and sat on the auspicious stone slab like a golden image. At that time, the royal priest's chief pupil approached his teacher and said, 'Teacher, is it not so that in our Vedas there is no such thing as securing well-being by killing another?' The priest rebuked him, saying, 'You are protecting the king's wealth! We shall eat much fish and meat and gain riches. Be silent!'

So “nāhaṃ [P 3.0046] ettha sahāyo bhavissāmī”ti nikkhamitvā rājuyyānaṃ gantvā bodhisattaṃ disvā vanditvā katapaṭisanthāro ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Bodhisatto “kiṃ, māṇava, rājā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretī”ti pucchi. “Bhante, rājā dhammena rajjaṃ kāreti, rattibhāge pana cattāro sadde sutvā brāhmaṇe pucchi. Brāhmaṇā ‘sabbacatukkayaññaṃ yajitvā sotthiṃ karissāmā’”ti vadiṃsu. Rājā pasughātakammaṃ katvā attano sotthiṃ kātukāmo mahājano thūṇūpanīto, “kiṃ nu kho, bhante, tumhādisānaṃ sīlavantānaṃ tesaṃ saddānaṃ nipphattiṃ vatvā mahājanaṃ maraṇamukhā mocetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Māṇava, rājā amhe na jānāti, mayampi taṃ na jānāma, imesaṃ pana saddānaṃ nipphattiṃ jānāma, sace rājā amhe upasaṅkamitvā puccheyya, rājānaṃ nikkaṅkhaṃ katvā kathessāmā”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, muhuttaṃ idheva hotha, ahaṃ rājānaṃ ānessāmī”ti. “Sādhu, māṇavā”ti. So gantvā rañño tamatthaṃ ārocetvā rājānaṃ ānesi.

Thinking, 'I will not be an accomplice in this,' he departed and went to the royal park. Seeing the Bodhisatta, he paid homage, and after exchanging greetings, sat down to one side. The Bodhisatta asked, 'Young man, does the king rule righteously?' 'Venerable sir, the king rules righteously, but in the night he heard four sounds and asked the brahmins. The brahmins said, "We shall bring about well-being by performing a sacrifice of four of everything." The king, wishing to secure his own well-being by performing the act of animal slaughter, has a great multitude brought to the sacrificial post. Venerable sir, is it not fitting for virtuous ones like you to explain the significance of those sounds and free the multitude from the jaws of death?' 'Young man, the king does not know us, nor do we know him, but we do know the significance of these sounds. If the king were to approach and ask us, we would explain it, making the king free from doubt.' 'Then, venerable sir, please remain here for a moment; I will bring the king.' 'Very good, young man.' He went and informed the king of the matter and brought the king.

Atha rājā bodhisattaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno pucchi “saccaṃ kira tumhe mayā sutasaddānaṃ nipphattiṃ jānāthā”ti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Kathetha, bhante”ti. “Mahārāja, ete purimabhave paresaṃ rakkhitagopitesu dāresu cārittaṃ āpajjitvā bārāṇasisāmante catūsu lohakumbhīsu nibbattā pakkuthite khāralohodake pheṇuddehakaṃ paccamānā tiṃsa vassasahassāni adho gantvā kumbhitalaṃ āhacca uddhaṃ ārohantā tiṃsavassasahasseneva kālena kumbhimukhaṃ disvā [V 3.0040] bahi oloketvā cattāro janā catasso gāthā paripuṇṇaṃ katvā vattukāmāpi tathā kātuṃ asakkontā ekekameva akkharaṃ vatvā puna lohakumbhīsuyeva [P 3.0047] nimuggā. Tesu du-kāraṃ vatvā nimuggasatto evaṃ vattukāmo ahosi –

Then the king paid homage to the Bodhisatta and, sitting down to one side, asked, 'Is it true that you know the significance of the sounds I have heard?' 'Yes, great king.' 'Then explain, venerable sir.' 'Great king, in a previous existence, these beings committed misconduct with the guarded and protected wives of others. As a result, they were reborn in four iron cauldrons near Bārāṇasī. Boiling in frothy, caustic, molten metal, they sink for thirty thousand years, and having struck the bottom of the cauldron, they rise for a period of thirty thousand years. Seeing the mouth of the cauldron after that time and looking out, the four persons, though wishing to speak four complete verses, were unable to do so. Uttering only one syllable each, they sank back into the iron cauldrons. Among them, the being who uttered the syllable "du" before sinking wished to say this:'

53.

53.

‘Dujjīvitamajīvimha[M 3.0044], ye sante na dadamhase;

Vijjamānesu bhogesu, dīpaṃ nākamha attano’ti. –

'A wretched life we lived, we who, though things were present, did not give; though wealth was available, we made no refuge for ourselves.'

Taṃ gāthaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhī”ti vatvā bodhisatto attano ñāṇena taṃ gāthaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā kathesi. Sesāsupi eseva nayo.

'He was not able to complete that verse.' Having said this, the Bodhisatta, with his own knowledge, completed the verse and recited it. The same principle applies to the remaining verses.

Tesu sa-kāraṃ vatvā vattukāmassa ayaṃ gāthā –

For the one among them who uttered the syllable 'sa' and wished to speak, this was the verse:

54.

54.

“Saṭṭhi vassasahassāni, paripuṇṇāni sabbaso;

Niraye paccamānānaṃ, kadā anto bhavissatī”ti.

'Sixty thousand years, fully completed in every way; for us who are being cooked in hell, when will there be an end?'

Na-kāraṃ vatvā vattukāmassa ayaṃ gāthā –

For the one who uttered the syllable 'na' and wished to speak, this was the verse:

55.

55.

“Natthi anto kuto anto, na anto paṭidissati;

Tadā hi pakataṃ pāpaṃ, mama tuyhañca mārisā”ti.

'There is no end. From where could there be an end? No end is seen; for then the evil was done, by me and by you, my friends.'

So-kāraṃ vatvā vattukāmassa ayaṃ gāthā –

For the one who uttered the syllable 'so' and wished to speak, this was the verse:

56.

56.

“Sohaṃ nūna ito gantvā, yoniṃ laddhāna mānusiṃ;

Vadaññū sīlasampanno, kāhāmi kusalaṃ bahu”nti.

'Surely I, having gone from here and obtained a human birth, will be generous and accomplished in virtue, and will perform much that is skillful.'

Tattha dujjīvitanti tīṇi duccaritāni caranto dujjīvitaṃ lāmakajīvitaṃ jīvati nāma, sopi tadeva sandhāyāha “dujjīvitamajīvimhā”ti. Ye sante na dadamhaseti ye mayaṃ deyyadhamme ca paṭiggāhake ca saṃvijjamāneyeva na dānaṃ dadimha. Dīpaṃ nākamha attanoti attano patiṭṭhaṃ na karimha. Paripuṇṇānīti anūnāni anadhikāni. Sabbasoti sabbākārena. Paccamānānanti amhākaṃ imasmiṃ niraye paccamānānaṃ.

Here, 'a bad life' (dujjīvitanti) means that one who practices the three types of misconduct lives a bad life, a base life; he said 'we have lived a bad life' with reference to that. 'We who, though things were present, did not give' (ye sante na dadamhase) means that we did not give gifts even when both things to be given and recipients were available. 'We did not make a refuge for ourselves' (dīpaṃ nākamha attano) means that we did not establish a support for ourselves. 'Complete' (paripuṇṇānīti) means without lack or excess. 'In every way' (sabbasoti) means in all respects. 'While being cooked' (paccamānānanti) means while we are being cooked in this hell.

Natthi [V 3.0041] antoti “amhākaṃ asukakāle nāma mokkho bhavissatī”ti evaṃ kālaparicchedo natthi. Kuto antoti kena kāraṇena anto paññāyissati. Na antoti antaṃ daṭṭhukāmānampi no dukkhassa anto na paṭidissati. Tadā hi pakatanti tasmiṃ kāle mārisā mama ca tuyhañca pakataṃ pāpaṃ pakaṭṭhaṃ kataṃ atibahumeva kataṃ. “Tathā hi pakata”ntipi pāṭho, tena kāraṇena kataṃ, yenassa [P 3.0048] anto daṭṭhuṃ na sakkāti attho. Mārisāti mayā sadisā, piyālapanametaṃ etesaṃ. Nūnāti [M 3.0045] ekaṃsatthe nipāto, so ahaṃ ito gantvā yoniṃ mānusiṃ laddhāna vadaññū sīlasampanno hutvā ekaṃseneva bahuṃ kusalaṃ karissāmīti ayamettha attho.

'There is no end' (natthi anto) means there is no such time limit as 'At such and such a time there will be liberation for us.' 'From where is the end?' (kuto anto) means by what reason will an end be discerned? 'No end' (na anto) means that even for those who wish to see an end, the end of suffering does not appear. 'For then it was done' (tadā hi pakataṃ) means that at that time, friend, the evil done by both you and me was done excessively, accumulated to a great extent. 'Thus it was done' (tathā hi pakataṃ) is also a reading; it means it was done for that reason by which its end cannot be seen. 'Friend' (mārisā) means 'like me'; this is an affectionate address for them. 'Surely' (nūna) is a particle indicating certainty. The meaning here is: 'Having gone from here and obtained a human birth, becoming one who knows the words of the wise and being virtuous, I will surely perform much merit.'

Iti bodhisatto ekamekaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā “mahārāja, so nerayikasatto imaṃ gāthaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā vattukāmo attano pāpassa mahantatāya tathā kathetuṃ nāsakkhi, iti so attano kammavipākaṃ anubhavanto viravi. Tumhākaṃ etassa saddassa savanapaccayā antarāyo nāma natthi, tumhe mā bhāyitthā”ti rājānaṃ saññāpesi. Rājā mahājanaṃ vissajjāpetvā suvaṇṇabheriṃ carāpetvā yaññāvāṭaṃ viddhaṃsāpesi. Bodhisatto mahājanassa sotthiṃ katvā katipāhaṃ vasitvā tattheva gantvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke uppajji.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, having recited each verse, said, "Great king, that being in hell, wishing to utter this verse in full, was unable to do so due to the enormity of his own evil deeds. Thus, experiencing the result of his own kamma, he cried out. For you, there is no danger arising from hearing this sound; do not be afraid." He reassured the king. The king dismissed the crowd, had a golden drum beaten through the city, and destroyed the sacrificial enclosure. The Bodhisatta, having ensured the well-being of the people, stayed there for a few days and then, having gone from there with his jhāna undiminished, was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā purohitassa jeṭṭhantevāsikamāṇavo sāriputto ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, revealed the Truths and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the royal priest's chief pupil was Sāriputta, but the ascetic was indeed I myself."

Lohakumbhijātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Lohakumbhi Jātaka: The Fourth.

[315] 5. Sabbamaṃsalābhajātakavaṇṇanā

[315] 5. The Story of Gaining All the Meat.

Pharusā vata te vācāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sāriputtattherena pītavirecanānaṃ dinnarasapiṇḍapātaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā kira jetavane ekacce bhikkhū snehavirecanaṃ piviṃsu. Tesaṃ rasapiṇḍapātena attho hoti, gilānupaṭṭhākā “rasabhattaṃ āharissāmā”ti sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā odanikagharavīthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvāpi rasabhattaṃ alabhitvā nivattiṃsu. Thero divātaraṃ piṇḍāya pavisamāno te bhikkhū disvā “kiṃ, āvuso, atipageva nivattathā”ti pucchi. Te tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Thero “tena hi ethā”ti te gahetvā [P 3.0049] tameva vīthiṃ agamāsi, manussā pūretvā rasabhattaṃ adaṃsu. Gilānupaṭṭhākā rasabhattaṃ āharitvā gilānānaṃ adaṃsu, te paribhuñjiṃsu[V 3.0042]. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, thero kira pītavirecanānaṃ upaṭṭhāke rasabhattaṃ alabhitvā nikkhamante gahetvā odanikagharavīthiyaṃ caritvā bahuṃ rasapiṇḍapātaṃ pesesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā [M 3.0046] “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāni sāriputtova maṃsaṃ labhi, pubbepi muduvācā piyavacanā vattuṃ chekā paṇḍitā labhiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Your words are indeed harsh”: this the Teacher said while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the savory alms-food given by the Venerable Sāriputta to those who had taken purgatives. At that time, it seems, some monks at Jetavana had taken an oily purgative. They needed savory rice, and their attendants, thinking, “We will fetch savory rice,” entered Sāvatthī. They wandered for alms in the street of the cook-shops but, failing to obtain savory rice, turned back. The Elder, entering for alms later in the day, saw those monks and asked, “Why, friends, have you turned back so early?” They explained the matter to him. The Elder said, “Come then,” and taking them, went to that very street. People filled their bowls with savory rice and gave it to them. The attendants brought the savory rice and gave it to the sick monks, who partook of it. Then one day, in the Dhamma hall, the monks started a discussion: “Friends, it is said that the Elder, when the attendants of those who had taken purgatives could not obtain savory rice and were leaving, took them and, wandering in the street of the cook-shops, had much savory alms-food sent to them.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what are you sitting here discussing now?” When they told him, he said, “Not only now, monks, has Sāriputta obtained meat; in the past, too, the wise were skilled at speaking gentle and pleasing words.” And he related a past incident.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto seṭṭhiputto ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ eko migaluddako bahuṃ maṃsaṃ labhitvā yānakaṃ pūretvā “vikkiṇissāmī”ti nagaraṃ āgacchati. Tadā bārāṇasivāsikā cattāro seṭṭhiputtā nagarā nikkhamitvā ekasmiṃ maggasabhāgaṭṭhāne kiñci diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ sallapantā nisīdiṃsu. Etesu eko seṭṭhiputto taṃ maṃsayānakaṃ disvā “etaṃ luddakaṃ maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ āharāpemī”ti āha. “Gaccha āharāpehī”ti. So taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “are, luddaka, dehi me maṃsakhaṇḍa”nti āha. Luddako “mārisa, paraṃ kiñci yācantena nāma piyavacanena bhavitabbaṃ, tayā kathitavācāya anucchavikaṃ maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ labhissasī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was the son of a wealthy merchant. One day, a hunter, having obtained a large amount of meat and filled his cart, thought, “I will sell it,” and came to the city. At that time, four sons of wealthy merchants residing in Benares had left the city and were sitting at a crossroads, chatting about things they had seen or heard. Among them, one merchant’s son, seeing the cart of meat, said, “I will get that hunter to give me a piece of meat.” “Go and get it,” they replied. He approached the hunter and said, “Hey, hunter, give me a piece of meat.” The hunter replied, “Friend, when asking for something from another, one should use pleasant speech. For words such as yours, you will get a befitting piece of meat,” and then he recited the first verse:

57.

57.

“Pharusā vata te vācā, maṃsaṃ yācanako asi;

Kilomasadisī vācā, kilomaṃ samma dammi te”ti.

“Your words are indeed harsh, you who beg for meat; your words are like membrane; here, friend, I give you membrane.”

Tattha kilomasadisīti pharusatāya kilomasadisī. Kilomaṃ samma dammi teti handa gaṇha, idaṃ te vācāya sadisaṃ kilomaṃ dammīti nirasaṃ nimaṃsalohitaṃ kilomakakhaṇḍaṃ ukkhipitvā adāsi.

Here, 'like membrane' (kilomasadisī) means like membrane because of its harshness. And 'Here, friend, I give you membrane' (kilomaṃ samma dammi te) means, 'Here, take this; I give you this membrane, which is like your speech.' Saying this, he lifted up and gave a tasteless, fleshless, and bloodless piece of membrane.

Atha naṃ aparo seṭṭhiputto “kinti vatvā yācasī”ti pucchi. “Are”ti vatvāti. So “ahampi naṃ yācissāmī”ti vatvā gantvā [P 3.0050] “jeṭṭhabhātika, maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ me dehī”ti āha. Itaro “tava vacanassa anucchavikaṃ maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ labhissasī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then another merchant’s son asked him, “How did you ask when you begged?” He replied, “By saying, ‘Hey!’” The other said, “I too will beg him,” and going to him, he said, “Elder brother, give me a piece of meat.” The hunter replied, “You will get a piece of meat befitting your words,” and spoke the second verse:

58.

58.

“Aṅgametaṃ manussānaṃ, bhātā loke pavuccati;

Aṅgassa sadisī vācā, aṅgaṃ samma dadāmi te”ti.

“A brother is called a limb of humans in this world. Your words are like a limb; friend, I give you a limb.”

Tassattho [V 3.0043] – imasmiṃ loke manussānaṃ aṅgasadisattā aṅgametaṃ yadidaṃ bhātā bhaginīti, tasmā tavesā aṅgasadisī vācāti etissā anucchavikaṃ aṅgameva dadāmi teti. Evañca pana vatvā aṅgamaṃsaṃ ukkhipitvā adāsi.

The meaning is: In this world, because a brother or sister is like a limb to people, a brother or sister is called a 'limb'. Therefore, your words are like a limb, and so I give you a limb befitting them. Saying this, he lifted up some flesh from a limb and gave it to him.

Tampi [M 3.0047] aparo seṭṭhiputto “kinti vatvā yācasī”ti pucchi. “Bhātikā”ti vatvāti. So “ahampi naṃ yācissāmī”ti vatvā gantvā “tāta, maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ me dehī”ti āha. Luddako tava vacanānūrūpaṃ lacchasī”ti vatvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then another merchant’s son asked him, “What did you say when you begged?” He replied, “Brother.” The other said, “I also will beg from him,” and going up to him, he said, “Father, give me a piece of meat.” The hunter said, “You will get something befitting your words,” and spoke the third verse:

59.

59.

“Tātāti putto vadamāno, kampeti hadayaṃ pitu;

Hadayassa sadisī vācā, hadayaṃ samma dammi te”ti.

“A son, saying ‘Father,’ moves his father’s heart. Your words are like a heart; friend, I give you a heart.”

Evañca pana vatvā hadayamaṃsena saddhiṃ madhuramaṃsaṃ ukkhipitvā adāsi.

Saying this, he lifted up the heart-meat along with some tasty meat and gave it.

Taṃ catuttho seṭṭhiputto “kinti vatvā yācasī”ti pucchi. So “tātā”ti vatvāti. So “ahampi yācissāmī”ti vatvā gantvā “sahāya maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ me dehī”ti āha. Luddako “tava vacanānurūpaṃ lacchasī”ti vatvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

The fourth merchant’s son asked him, “What did you say when you begged?” He replied, “Father.” The other said, “I’ll beg too,” and going up to him, said, “Friend, give me a piece of meat.” The hunter said, “You will get something befitting your words,” and spoke the fourth verse:

60.

60.

“Yassa gāme sakhā natthi, yathāraññaṃ tatheva taṃ;

Sabbassa sadisī vācā, sabbaṃ samma dadāmi te”ti.

“For one who has no friend in the village, it is just like a forest. Your words are like everything; friend, I give you everything.”

Tassattho – yassa purisassa gāme sukhadukkhesu saha ayanato sahāyasaṅkhāto sakhā natthi, tassa taṃ ṭhānaṃ yathā amanussaṃ araññaṃ tatheva hoti, iti ayaṃ tava vācā sabbassa sadisī, sabbena attano santakena vibhavena sadisī, tasmā sabbameva imaṃ mama santakaṃ maṃsayānakaṃ dadāmi teti.

The meaning is this: For a person who has no friend in the village—a companion so-called for going together through happiness and sorrow—that place is just like a wilderness inhabited by non-humans. Thus, these words of yours are equal to everything, equal to all of one’s own wealth and possessions. Therefore, I give you all of this, my own cart of meat.

Evañca pana vatvā “ehi, samma, sabbameva idaṃ maṃsayānakaṃ tava gehaṃ āharissāmī”ti āha. Seṭṭhiputto tena yānakaṃ [P 3.0051] pājāpento attano gharaṃ gantvā maṃsaṃ otārāpetvā luddakassa sakkārasammānaṃ katvā puttadārampissa pakkosāpetvā luddakammato apanetvā attano kuṭumbamajjhe vasāpento tena saddhiṃ abhejjasahāyo hutvā yāvajīvaṃ samaggavāsaṃ vasi.

Having said this, he continued, “Come, friend, I will bring all this cart of meat to your house.” The merchant’s son, having the hunter drive the cart, went to his own house, had the meat unloaded, and honored the hunter with hospitality. He had the hunter’s wife and children summoned, removed him from the hunter’s trade, and had him dwell in the midst of his own family. He became an inseparable friend to him and they lived together in harmony for the rest of their lives.

Satthā [V 3.0044] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā luddako sāriputto ahosi, sabbamaṃsalābhī seṭṭhiputto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the birth: “At that time, the hunter was Sāriputta, and the merchant’s son who obtained all the meat was none other than myself.”

Sabbamaṃsalābhajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The commentary on the Sabbamaṃsalābhī Jātaka, the fifth.

[316] 6. Sasapaṇḍitajātakavaṇṇanā

[316] 6. The Commentary on the Wise Hare Jātaka

Satta [M 3.0048] me rohitā macchāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira eko kuṭumbiko buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ sajjetvā gharadvāre maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā susajjitamaṇḍape paññattavarāsane nisīdāpetvā nānaggarasaṃ paṇītadānaṃ datvā puna svātanāyāti sattāhaṃ nimantetvā sattame divase buddhappamukhānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ sabbaparikkhāre adāsi. Satthā bhattakiccāvasāne anumodanaṃ karonto “upāsaka, tayā pītisomanassaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, idañhi dānaṃ nāma porāṇakapaṇḍitānaṃ vaṃso, porāṇakapaṇḍitā hi sampattayācakānaṃ jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā attano maṃsampi adaṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Seven red fish”—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the gift of all requisites. It is said that in Sāvatthī a certain householder prepared a gift of all requisites for the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha. Having set up a pavilion at his house door, he invited the Sangha led by the Buddha, seated them on prepared excellent seats in the well-decorated pavilion, and offered them delicious fine food of various flavors. He then invited them again for the next day and for a week. On the seventh day, he presented all the requisites to five hundred monks headed by the Buddha. At the end of the meal, the Teacher, giving thanks, said, “Lay follower, it is fitting for you to experience joy and gladness, for this gift is in the tradition of ancient wise men. For ancient wise men, for the sake of supplicants who had arrived, abandoned their own lives and gave even their own flesh.” Being requested by him, he then related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sasayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā araññe vasi. Tassa pana araññassa ekato pabbatapādo ekato nadī ekato paccantagāmako ahosi. Aparepissa tayo sahāyā ahesuṃ makkaṭo ca siṅgālo ca uddo cāti. Te cattāropi paṇḍitā ekatova vasantā attano attano [P 3.0052] gocaraṭṭhāne gocaraṃ gahetvā sāyanhasamaye ekato sannipatanti. Sasapaṇḍito “dānaṃ dātabbaṃ, sīlaṃ rakkhitabbaṃ, uposathakammaṃ kātabba”nti tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ ovādavasena dhammaṃ deseti. Te tassa ovādaṃ sampaṭicchitvā attano attano nivāsagumbaṃ pavisitvā vasanti. Evaṃ kāle gacchante ekadivasaṃ bodhisatto ākāsaṃ oloketvā candaṃ disvā “sve uposathadivaso”ti ñatvā itare tayo āha “sve uposatho, tumhepi tayo janā sīlaṃ samādiyitvā uposathikā hotha, sīle patiṭṭhāya dinnadānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti, tasmā yācake sampatte tumhehi khāditabbāhārato dānaṃ datvā khādeyyāthā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā attano attano vasanaṭṭhānesu vasiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a hare’s womb and lived in the forest. That forest had a mountain slope on one side, a river on another, and a border village on another. He had three companions: a monkey, a jackal, and an otter. These four wise beings lived together, each foraging in their own territory, and in the evening, they would gather together. The wise hare would teach the Dhamma to the three others, advising them, “Give alms, observe virtue, and perform the Uposatha observance.” Accepting his advice, they would each return to their own dwelling-bushes and stay there. As time passed, one day the Bodhisatta looked up at the sky and, seeing the moon, realized, “Tomorrow is the Uposatha day,” and said to the other three, “Tomorrow is the Uposatha. The three of you, too, should undertake the precepts and be observers of the Uposatha. A gift given while established in virtue is of great fruit. Therefore, when a supplicant arrives, give alms from the food you intend to eat before eating it yourselves.” They replied, “Very well,” accepted his words, and each went to their own dwelling places.

Punadivase tesu uddo pātova “gocaraṃ pariyesissāmī”ti nikkhamitvā gaṅgātīraṃ gato. Atheko bālisiko satta rohitamacche uddharitvā valliyā āvuṇitvā netvā gaṅgātīre vālukaṃ [V 3.0045] viyūhitvā vālikāya [M 3.0049] paṭicchādetvā puna macche gaṇhanto adhogaṅgaṃ gacchi. Uddo macchagandhaṃ ghāyitvā vālukaṃ viyūhitvā macche disvā nīharitvā “atthi nu kho etesaṃ sāmiko”ti tikkhattuṃ ghosetvā sāmikaṃ apassanto vallikoṭiṃ ḍaṃsitvā netvā attano vasanagumbe ṭhapetvā “velāyameva khādissāmī”ti attano sīlaṃ āvajjento nipajji. Siṅgālopi vasanaṭṭhānato nikkhamitvā gocaraṃ pariyesanto ekassa khettagopakassa kuṭiyaṃ dve maṃsasūlāni ekaṃ godhaṃ ekañca dadhivārakaṃ disvā “atthi nu kho etesaṃ sāmiko”ti tikkhattuṃ ghosetvā sāmikaṃ adisvā dadhivārakassa uggahaṇarajjukaṃ gīvāya pavesetvā dve maṃsasūle ca godhañca mukhena ḍaṃsitvā netvā attano vasanagumbe ṭhapetvā “velāyameva khādissāmī”ti attano sīlaṃ [P 3.0053] āvajjento nipajji. Makkaṭopi vasanaṭṭhānato nikkhamitvā vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā ambapiṇḍaṃ āharitvā attano vasanagumbe ṭhapetvā “velāyameva khādissāmī”ti attano sīlaṃ āvajjento nipajji.

The next day, the otter went out early in the morning to search for food and went to the bank of the Ganges. Then a certain fisherman caught seven Rohita fish, strung them on a vine, and after burying them in the sand on the riverbank, went downstream to catch more fish. The otter, smelling the fish, dug up the sand, found the fish, and took them out. He called out three times, 'Is there an owner for these?' Seeing no owner, he bit the end of the vine, carried them away, and placed them in his dwelling-bush. Thinking, 'I will eat them at the proper time,' he lay down reflecting on his virtue. The jackal also left his dwelling place to search for food and in a field-watcher's hut saw two meat skewers, a monitor lizard, and a pot of curds. He called out three times, 'Is there an owner for these?' Seeing no owner, he put the carrying-rope of the curd pot around his neck, took the two meat skewers and the monitor lizard in his mouth, carried them away, and placed them in his dwelling-bush. Thinking, 'I will eat them at the proper time,' he lay down reflecting on his virtue. The monkey also left his dwelling place, entered a forest grove, brought back a cluster of mangoes, placed it in his dwelling-bush, and thinking, 'I will eat it at the proper time,' lay down reflecting on his virtue.

Bodhisatto pana “velāyameva vasanaṭṭhānato nikkhamitvā dabbatiṇāni khādissāmī”ti attano vasanagumbeyeva nipanno cintesi “mama santikaṃ āgatānaṃ yācakānaṃ tiṇāni dātuṃ na sakkā, tilataṇḍulādayopi mayhaṃ natthi, sace me santikaṃ yācako āgacchissati, attano sarīramaṃsaṃ dassāmī”ti. Tassa sīlatejena sakkassa paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So āvajjamāno idaṃ kāraṇaṃ disvā “sasarājānaṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti paṭhamaṃ uddassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā brāhmaṇavesena aṭṭhāsi. “Brāhmaṇa, kimatthaṃ ṭhitosī”ti vutte paṇḍita sace kiñci āhāraṃ labheyyaṃ, uposathiko hutvā vaseyyanti. So “sādhu dassāmi te āhāra”nti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, however, while lying in his own dwelling-bush, thought: 'At the proper time, I will go out from my dwelling place and eat dabba grass. But it is not possible to give grass to those who come to me as supplicants; I have no sesame, rice, or the like. If a supplicant comes to me, I will give my own flesh.' By the power of his virtue, Sakka's Paṇḍukambala stone seat showed signs of heat. Reflecting and seeing this reason, Sakka thought, 'I will test the hare king.' First, he went to the otter's dwelling place and stood there in the guise of a brahmin. When asked, 'Brahmin, why do you stand here?' he replied, 'Wise one, if I could obtain some food, I would observe the Uposatha and stay.' The otter said, 'Very well, I will give you food,' and while conversing with him, spoke the first verse:

61.

61.

“Satta me rohitā macchā, udakā thalamubbhatā;

Idaṃ brāhmaṇa me atthi, etaṃ bhutvā vane vasā”ti.

'Seven Rohita fish I have, lifted from the water onto dry land; this, O brahmin, I possess; eat this and dwell in the forest.'

Tattha thalamubbhatāti udakato thale ṭhapitā, kevaṭṭena vā uddhaṭā. Etaṃ bhutvāti etaṃ mama santakaṃ macchāhāraṃ pacitvā bhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ [M 3.0050] karonto ramaṇīye rukkhamūle nisinno imasmiṃ vane vasāti.

There, 'lifted from the water onto dry land' means placed on the land from the water, or pulled out by a fisherman. 'Eat this' means having cooked and consumed this fish food belonging to me, and then, while practicing the duties of a recluse, sitting at a lovely tree root, dwell in this forest.

Brāhmaṇo “pageva tāva hotu, pacchā jānissāmī”ti siṅgālassa santikaṃ gato. Tenāpi [V 3.0046] “kimatthaṃ ṭhitosī”ti vutto tathevāha. Siṅgālo “sādhu dassāmī”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The brahmin said, 'It is still too early; I will know later,' and went to the jackal. When asked by him, 'Why do you stand here?' he replied the same. The jackal said, 'Very well, I will give it to you,' and while conversing with him, spoke the second verse:

62.

62.

“Dussa [P 3.0054] me khettapālassa, rattibhattaṃ apābhataṃ;

Maṃsasūlā ca dve godhā, ekañca dadhivārakaṃ;

Idaṃ brāhmaṇa me atthi, etaṃ bhutvā vane vasā”ti.

'The night-meal of Dussa the field-guard was brought away by me: two meat skewers, a monitor lizard, and a pot of curds. This, O brahmin, I possess; eat this and dwell in the forest.'

Tattha dussa meti yo esa mama avidūre khettapālo vasati, dussa amussāti attho. Apābhatanti ābhataṃ ānītaṃ. Maṃsasūlā ca dve godhāti aṅgārapakkāni dve maṃsasūlāni ca ekā ca godhā. Dadhivārakanti dadhivārako. Idanti idaṃ ettakaṃ mama atthi, etaṃ sabbampi yathābhirucitena pākena pacitvā paribhuñjitvā uposathiko hutvā ramaṇīye rukkhamūle nisīditvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonto imasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe vasāti attho.

There, 'Dussa me' refers to that field-guard who lives not far from me; 'Dussa' is his name. 'Apābhatanti' means brought or fetched. 'Two meat skewers and a monitor lizard' refers to two meat skewers roasted over charcoal and one monitor lizard. 'Dadhivārakaṃ' means a curd pot. 'Idaṃ' means 'this much I have; having cooked and consumed all this as you like, and having observed the Uposatha, sit at the foot of a pleasant tree and practice the duties of a recluse while dwelling in this forest grove'—this is the meaning.

Brāhmaṇo “pageva tāva hotu, pacchā jānissāmī”ti makkaṭassa santikaṃ gato. Tenāpi “kimatthaṃ ṭhitosī”ti vutto tathevāha. Makkaṭo “sādhu dassāmī”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The brahmin said, 'It is still too early; I will know later,' and went to the monkey. When asked by him, 'Why do you stand here?' he replied the same. The monkey said, 'Very well, I will give it to you,' and while conversing with him, spoke the third verse:

63.

63.

“Ambapakkaṃ dakaṃ sītaṃ, sītacchāyā manoramā;

Idaṃ brāhmaṇa me atthi, etaṃ bhutvā vane vasā”ti.

'Ripe mangoes, cool water, and delightful cool shade; this, O brahmin, I possess; eat this and dwell in the forest.'

Tattha ambapakkanti madhuraambaphalaṃ. Dakaṃ sītanti gaṅgāya udakaṃ sītalaṃ. Etaṃ bhutvā vane vasāti brāhmaṇa etaṃ ambapakkaṃ paribhuñjitvā sītalaṃ udakaṃ pivitvā yathābhirucite ramaṇīye rukkhamūle nisinno samaṇadhammaṃ karonto imasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe vasāti.

Here, 'ripe mango' refers to a sweet mango fruit. 'The water is cool' means the cool water of the Ganges. 'Eat this and dwell in the forest' means, O brahmin, having consumed this ripe mango and drunk the cool water, sitting at the foot of a pleasant tree according to your liking, performing the duties of a recluse, you may dwell in this forest grove.

Brāhmaṇo “pageva tāva hotu, pacchā jānissāmī”ti sasapaṇḍitassa santikaṃ gato. Tenāpi “kimatthaṃ ṭhitosī”ti vutto tathevāha. Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto somanassappatto “brāhmaṇa, suṭṭhu te kataṃ āhāratthāya mama santikaṃ āgacchantena, ajjāhaṃ adinnapubbaṃ dānaṃ dassāmi[M 3.0051]. Tvaṃ pana sīlavā pāṇātipātaṃ na karissasi, gaccha, brāhmaṇa, nānādārūni saṅkaḍḍhitvā aṅgāre katvā mayhaṃ ārocehi, ahaṃ attānaṃ [P 3.0055] pariccajitvā aṅgāramajjhe patissāmi[V 3.0047]. Mama sarīre pakke tvaṃ maṃsaṃ khāditvā samaṇadhammaṃ kareyyāsī”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

The brahmin said, 'It is still too early; I will know later,' and went to the wise hare. When asked by him, 'Why do you stand here?' he replied the same. Hearing this, the Bodhisatta was filled with joy and said, 'Brahmin, you have done well in coming to me for food. Today I will give a gift I have never given before. But you are a virtuous man; you will not take life. Go, brahmin, gather various kinds of wood, make a bed of coals, and tell me. I will sacrifice myself and fall into the midst of the coals. When my body is cooked, you may eat my flesh and practice the duties of a recluse.' While conversing with him, he spoke the fourth verse:

64.

64.

“Na sasassa tilā atthi, na muggā napi taṇḍulā;

Iminā agginā pakkaṃ, mamaṃ bhutvā vane vasā”ti.

'The hare has no sesame, no mung beans, nor rice; eat me, cooked by this fire, and dwell in the forest.'

Tattha mamaṃ bhutvāti yaṃ taṃ ahaṃ aggiṃ karohīti vadāmi, iminā agginā pakkaṃ maṃ bhuñjitvā imasmiṃ vane vasa, ekassa sasassa sarīraṃ nāma ekassa purisassa yāpanamattaṃ hotīti.

Here, 'eat me' means: 'Having eaten me, cooked by this fire that I told you to make, dwell in this forest.' For the body of a single hare is just enough to sustain one person.

Sakko tassa vacanaṃ sutvā attano ānubhāvena ekaṃ aṅgārarāsiṃ māpetvā bodhisattassa ārocesi. So dabbatiṇasayanato uṭṭhāya tattha gantvā “sace me lomantaresu pāṇakā atthi, te mā mariṃsū”ti tikkhattuṃ sarīraṃ vidhunitvā sakalasarīraṃ dānamukhe ṭhapetvā laṅghitvā padumasare rājahaṃso viya pamuditacitto aṅgārarāsimhi pati. So pana aggi bodhisattassa sarīre lomakūpamattampi uṇhaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi, himagabbhaṃ paviṭṭho viya ahosi. Atha sakkaṃ āmantetvā “brāhmaṇa, tayā kato aggi atisītalo, mama sarīre lomakūpamattampi uṇhaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, kiṃ nāmeta”nti āha. “Sasapaṇḍita, nāhaṃ brāhmaṇo, sakkohamasmi, tava vīmaṃsanatthāya āgatomhī”ti. “Sakka, tvaṃ tāva tiṭṭha, sakalopi ce lokasannivāso maṃ dānena vīmaṃseyya, neva me adātukāmataṃ passeyyā”ti bodhisatto sīhanādaṃ nadi. Atha naṃ sakko “sasapaṇḍita, tava guṇo sakalakappaṃ pākaṭo hotū”ti pabbataṃ pīḷetvā pabbatarasaṃ ādāya candamaṇḍale sasalakkhaṇaṃ likhitvā bodhisattaṃ ānetvā tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe tasmiṃyeva vanagumbe taruṇadabbatiṇapiṭṭhe nipajjāpetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva [P 3.0056] gato. Tepi cattāro paṇḍitā samaggā sammodamānā sīlaṃ pūretvā dānaṃ datvā uposathakammaṃ katvā yathākammaṃ gatā.

Having heard his words, Sakka, by his own power, created a heap of burning coals and announced it to the Bodhisatta. Rising from his bed of grass, the Bodhisatta went there and, thinking, 'If there are any small creatures in my fur, may they not die,' shook his body three times. Then, directing his entire body toward the gift of sacrifice, he leaped into the heap of coals like a royal swan diving joyfully into a lotus pond. Yet, the fire could not produce even the slightest warmth in the Bodhisatta’s body—it was as if he had entered a chamber of snow. Then, addressing Sakka, he said, 'Brahmin, the fire you have made is too cold! It cannot produce even the slightest warmth in my body. What is the meaning of this?' 'Wise Hare, I am not a brahmin; I am Sakka. I came to test you.' 'Sakka, let that be. Even if the entire world were to test me in giving, they would not see any reluctance in me to give,' declared the Bodhisatta with a lion’s roar. Then Sakka said, 'Wise Hare, may your virtue be manifest throughout the entire eon!' Pressing the mountain and taking its essence, he inscribed the mark of a hare on the orb of the moon. Then, bringing the Bodhisatta back, he laid him down on that same bed of fresh grass in that very grove and thicket before returning to his own abode. Those four wise ones, united and joyful, fulfilled their moral precepts, gave alms, performed the Uposatha observance, and departed according to their deeds.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne sabbaparikkhāradānadāyako gahapati sotāpattiphale [M 3.0052] patiṭṭhahi.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher revealed the Truths and concluded the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder, the giver of all requisites, was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā uddo ānando ahosi, siṅgālo moggallāno, makkaṭo sāriputto, sakko anuruddho, sasapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the otter was Ānanda, the jackal was Moggallāna, the monkey was Sāriputta, Sakka was Anuruddha, and the wise hare was I myself.

Sasapaṇḍitajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Sixth: The explanation of the Sasapaṇḍita Jātaka.

[317] 7. Matarodanajātakavaṇṇanā

[317] 7. The Explanation of the Matarodana Jātaka.

Mataṃ [V 3.0048] mataṃ eva rodathāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ sāvatthivāsiṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa kira bhātā kālamakāsi. So tassa kālakiriyāya sokābhibhūto na nhāyati na bhuñjati na vilimpati, pātova susānaṃ gantvā sokasamappito rodati. Satthā paccūsasamaye lokaṃ olokento tassa sotāpattiphalūpanissayaṃ disvā “imassa atītakāraṇaṃ āharitvā sokaṃ vūpasametvā sotāpattiphalaṃ dātuṃ ṭhapetvā maṃ añño koci samattho natthi, imassa mayā avassayena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti punadivase pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto pacchāsamaṇaṃ ādāya tassa gharadvāraṃ gantvā “satthā āgato”ti sutvā āsanaṃ paññapetvā “pavesethā”ti kuṭumbikena vutto pavisitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Kuṭumbikopi āgantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha naṃ satthā “kiṃ kuṭumbika cintesī”ti āha. “Āma, bhante, mama bhātu matakālato paṭṭhāya cintemī”ti. “Āvuso, sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, bhijjitabbayuttakaṃ bhijjati, na tattha cintetabbaṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi bhātari matepi ‘bhijjitabbayuttakaṃ bhijjatī’ti na cintayiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

‘You weep for the dead as dead...’ This the Teacher told while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a certain householder from Sāvatthī. It seems his brother had died. Overcome by grief at his death, he did not bathe, eat, or anoint himself, but went early to the cemetery and wept, overwhelmed by sorrow. At dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world, saw that he had the potential for the fruit of stream-entry. Thinking, ‘No one other than me is capable of bringing forth a past event to calm his grief and grant him the fruit of stream-entry; it is right that I should be his refuge,’ the next day, after his meal and returning from his almsround, the Teacher, taking a junior monk with him, went to the householder's door. Hearing that ‘the Teacher has come,’ the householder had a seat prepared and said, ‘Let him enter.’ The Teacher entered and sat on the prepared seat. The householder also came, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat to one side. Then the Teacher asked him, ‘Householder, are you grieving?’ ‘Yes, Venerable Sir, I have been grieving ever since my brother's death,’ he replied. ‘Friend, all conditioned things are impermanent. What is subject to breaking must break. One should not grieve over it. Even the wise of old did not grieve when their brothers died, saying, “What is subject to breaking has broken,”’ said the Teacher. Then, at the householder's request, he recounted the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto asītikoṭivibhave seṭṭhikule nibbatti, tassa vayappattassa mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. Tesu kālakatesu bodhisattassa bhātā kuṭumbaṃ vicāreti, bodhisatto taṃ nissāya [P 3.0057] jīvati. So aparabhāge tathārūpena byādhinā kālamakāsi. Ñātimittā suhajjā sannipatitvā bāhā paggayha kandanti rodanti, ekopi sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi, bodhisatto pana neva kandati na rodati. Manussā “passatha bho, imassa bhātari [M 3.0053] mate mukhasaṅkocanamattampi natthi, ativiya thaddhahadayo, ‘dvepi koṭṭhāse ahameva paribhuñjissāmī’ti bhātu maraṇaṃ icchati maññe”ti bodhisattaṃ garahiṃsu. Ñātakāpi naṃ “tvaṃ bhātari mate na rodasī”ti garahiṃsuyeva. So tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “tumhe attano andhabālabhāvena aṭṭha lokadhamme ajānantā ‘mama bhātā mato’ti rodatha, ahampi marissāmi, tumhepi marissatha, attānampi ‘mayampi marissāmā’ti kasmā na rodatha. Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā hutvā nirujjhanti, teneva sabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ samattho ekasaṅkhāropi natthi. Tumhe andhabālā aññāṇatāya aṭṭha lokadhamme ajānitvā rodatha, ahaṃ kimatthaṃ rodissāmī”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family possessing eighty crores of wealth. When he came of age, his parents died. After their death, the Bodhisatta's brother managed the household, and the Bodhisatta lived depending on him. Later, his brother died of a certain illness. Relatives, friends, and companions gathered, and raising their arms, they wailed and wept; not a single one could remain composed. But the Bodhisatta neither wailed nor wept. The people criticized him, saying, ‘Look, sirs! When his brother died, there is not even a frown on his face. His heart is utterly hardened. Surely, he must be thinking, “Now I alone will enjoy both shares,” and thus desires his brother’s death.’ His relatives also rebuked him, saying, ‘You do not weep for your dead brother!’ Hearing their words, he replied, ‘You, in your blind foolishness, unaware of the eight worldly conditions, weep, saying, “My brother is dead.” But I too will die, and you too will die. Why do you not weep for yourselves, thinking, “We too shall die”? All conditioned things, having arisen, cease; there is not a single conditioned thing capable of remaining in that same state. You, blind fools, weep out of ignorance, not knowing the eight worldly conditions. Why should I weep?’ Having said this, he spoke these verses:

65.

65.

“Mataṃ [V 3.0049] mataṃ eva rodatha, na hi taṃ rodatha yo marissati;

Sabbepi sarīradhārino, anupubbena jahanti jīvitaṃ.

‘You weep for the dead who is dead; but you do not weep for the one who is yet to die. All who bear a body successively abandon life.’

66.

66.

“Devamanussā catuppadā, pakkhigaṇā uragā ca bhogino;

Samhi sarīre anissarā, ramamānāva jahanti jīvitaṃ.

‘Gods and humans, quadrupeds, flocks of birds, and coiled serpents; powerless over their own bodies, even while delighting, they abandon life.’

67.

67.

“Evaṃ calitaṃ asaṇṭhitaṃ, sukhadukkhaṃ manujesvapekkhiya;

Kanditaruditaṃ niratthakaṃ, kiṃ vo sokagaṇābhikīrare.

“Considering that happiness and sorrow among humans are thus wavering and unstable, wailing and weeping are useless. Why do hosts of sorrow overwhelm you?”

68.

68.

“Dhuttā ca soṇḍā akatā, bālā sūrā ayogino;

Dhīraṃ maññanti bāloti, ye dhammassa akovidā”ti.

“The profligate, drunkards, the uncultivated, fools, the reckless, and the undisciplined—those who are unskilled in the nature of the world—consider the wise one a fool.”

Tattha [P 3.0058] mataṃ mataṃ evāti mataṃ mataṃyeva. Anupubbenāti attano attano maraṇavāre sampatte paṭipāṭiyā jahanti jīvitaṃ, na ekatova sabbe maranti, yadi evaṃ mareyyuṃ, lokappavatti ucchijjeyya. Bhoginoti mahantena sarīrabhogena samannāgatā. Ramamānāvāti tattha tattha nibbattā sabbepi ete devādayo sattā attano attano nibbattaṭṭhāne abhiramamānāva anukkaṇṭhitāva jīvitaṃ jahanti. Evaṃ calitanti evaṃ tīsu bhavesu niccalabhāvassa ca saṇṭhitabhāvassa ca abhāvā calitaṃ asaṇṭhitaṃ. Kiṃ vo sokagaṇābhikīrareti kiṃkāraṇā tumhe sokarāsī abhikiranti ajjhottharanti.

There, “mataṃ mataṃ evā” means “each and every one who has died.” “Anupubbenāti” means that as each person’s own turn for death arrives, they give up life in succession, not all at once. If they were to die all at once, the continuity of the world would be cut off. “Bhoginoti” means endowed with great wealth and physical enjoyments. “Ramamānāvāti” means that all these beings, such as devas and others, wherever they are born, delighting in their own places of birth and without dissatisfaction, give up their lives. “Evaṃ calitanti” means thus, in the three realms of existence, due to the absence of permanence and stability, it is wavering and unsettled. “Kiṃ vo sokagaṇābhikīrareti” means for what reason do heaps of sorrow overwhelm and overcome you?

Dhuttā [M 3.0054] ca soṇḍā akatāti itthidhuttā surādhuttā akkhadhuttā ca surāsoṇḍādayo soṇḍā ca akatabuddhino asikkhitakā ca. Bālāti bālyena samannāgatā aviddasuno. Sūrā ayoginoti ayonisomanasikārena sūrā, yogesu ayuttatāya ayogino. “Ayodhino”tipi pāṭho, kilesamārena saddhiṃ yujjhituṃ asamatthāti attho. Dhīraṃ maññanti bāloti, ye dhammassa akovidāti ye evarūpā dhuttādayo aṭṭhavidhassa lokadhammassa akovidā, te appamattakepi dukkhadhamme uppanne attanā kandamānā rodamānā aṭṭha lokadhamme kathato jānitvā ñātimaraṇādīsu akandantaṃ arodantaṃ mādisaṃ dhīraṃ paṇḍitaṃ “bālo ayaṃ na rodatī”ti maññantīti.

“Dhuttā ca soṇḍā akatāti” means those who are profligate with women, liquor, and dice, and those who are drunkards and the like, who are uncultivated in understanding and untrained. “Bālāti” means those endowed with foolishness, the ignorant. “Sūrā ayoginoti” means brave through unwise attention, and undisciplined due to a lack of effort in right practice. There is also a reading “ayodhino,” meaning unable to fight with the Māra of defilements. “Dhīraṃ maññanti bāloti, ye dhammassa akovidāti” means that those profligate ones and the like, who are unversed in the eight worldly conditions, weep and wail themselves when even a slight suffering arises. They consider a wise person like me—who, knowing the eight worldly conditions from discourse, does not weep or wail at the death of relatives and so forth—to be a fool, saying, “This fool does not weep.”

Evaṃ bodhisatto tesaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā sabbepi te nissoke akāsi.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having taught them the Dhamma, made them all free from sorrow.

Satthā [V 3.0050] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne kuṭumbiko sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā mahājanassa dhammaṃ desetvā nissokabhāvakarapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, the householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the wise one who taught the Dhamma to the great assembly and made them free from sorrow was I myself.

Matarodanajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Matarodana Jātaka, the seventh.

[318] 8. Kaṇaverajātakavaṇṇanā

[318] 8. The Commentary on the Kaṇavera Jātaka

Yaṃ taṃ vasanta samayeti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu indriyajātake (jā. 1.8.60 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ “pubbe tvaṃ bhikkhu etaṃ nissāya asinā sīsacchedaṃ paṭilabhī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“That which, in the season of spring…”: this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the enticement by a former wife. The story will be made clear in the Indriya Jātaka. The Teacher said to that monk, “Formerly, monk, on account of this woman, you suffered the severing of your head by a sword,” and being requested by him, he related the past.

Atīte [P 3.0059] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsigāmake ekassa gahapatikassa ghare coranakkhattena jāto vayappatto corakammaṃ katvā jīvikaṃ kappento loke pākaṭo ahosi sūro nāgabalo, koci naṃ gaṇhituṃ nāsakkhi. So ekadivasaṃ ekasmiṃ seṭṭhighare sandhiṃ chinditvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ avahari. Nāgarā rājānaṃ [M 3.0055] upasaṅkamitvā “deva, eko mahācoro nagaraṃ vilumpati, taṃ gaṇhāpethā”ti vadiṃsu. Rājā tassa gahaṇatthāya nagaraguttikaṃ āṇāpesi. So rattibhāge tattha tattha vaggabandhanena manusse ṭhapetvā taṃ sahoḍḍhaṃ gāhāpetvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā “sīsamassa chindā”ti nagaraguttikaññeva āṇāpesi. Nagaraguttiko taṃ pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhāpetvā gīvāyassa rattakaṇavīramālaṃ laggetvā sīse iṭṭhakacuṇṇaṃ okiritvā catukke catukke kasāhi tāḷāpento kharassarena paṇavena āghātanaṃ neti. “Imasmiṃ kira nagare vilopakārako coro gahito”ti sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born in a village of Kasi into the household of a certain householder, under the constellation of thieves. Having come of age, he made his living by thievery and became notorious in the world as a hero with the strength of an elephant, whom no one could capture. One day, breaking into a wealthy merchant’s house, he stole a great amount of wealth. The citizens approached the king and said, “Your Majesty, a great thief is plundering the city; have him captured.” The king ordered the city guard to capture him. At night, the city guard set up men in groups in various places, and having had him caught along with the stolen goods, reported to the king. The king ordered the city guard, “Cut off his head.” The city guard had him bound tightly with his hands behind his back, placed a red oleander garland around his neck, sprinkled brick dust on his head, and, beating him with whips at every crossroads, led him to the execution ground with the harsh sound of a drum. The whole city was in an uproar, saying, “The thief who has been robbing this city has been caught.”

Tadā ca bārāṇasiyaṃ sahassaṃ gaṇhantī sāmā nāma gaṇikā hoti rājavallabhā pañcasatavaṇṇadāsīparivārā. Sā pāsādatale vātapānaṃ vivaritvā ṭhitā taṃ nīyamānaṃ passi. So pana abhirūpo pāsādiko ativiya sobhaggappatto devavaṇṇo sabbesaṃ matthakamatthakena paññāyati. Sāmā taṃ disvā paṭibaddhacittā hutvā “kena nu kho upāyenāhaṃ imaṃ purisaṃ attano sāmikaṃ kareyya”nti cintayantī “attheko upāyo”ti attano atthacarikāya ekissā hatthe nagaraguttikassa sahassaṃ pesesi “ayaṃ coro sāmāya bhātā, aññatra sāmāya añño [V 3.0051] etassa avassayo natthi, tumhe kira idaṃ sahassaṃ gahetvā etaṃ vissajjethā”ti[P 3.0060]. Sā gantvā tathā akāsi. Nagaraguttiko “ayaṃ coro pākaṭo, na sakkā etaṃ vissajjetuṃ, aññaṃ pana manussaṃ labhitvā imaṃ paṭicchannayānake nisīdāpetvā pesetuṃ sakkā”ti āha. Sā gantvā tassā ārocesi.

At that time, in Benares, there was a courtesan named Sāmā, beloved by the king, who received a thousand coins daily and had a retinue of five hundred beautiful slave-girls. She opened a window on the upper floor of her mansion and stood watching as he was being led away. He was handsome, majestic, extremely beautiful, and had the complexion of a god, appearing to stand above the heads of everyone else. Seeing him, Sāmā became deeply infatuated and thought, “By what means can I make this man my husband?” Reflecting, she realized, “There is one way.” She sent a thousand coins to the city guard by the hand of one of her trusted attendants with the message: “This thief is Sāmā’s brother; he has no refuge other than Sāmā. Please take this thousand and release him.” The attendant went and did as instructed. The city guard said, “This thief is notorious; it is not possible to release him. But if another man can be found to take his place, it is possible to seat this one in a covered carriage and send him away.” The attendant returned and reported this to her.

Tadā paneko seṭṭhiputto sāmāya paṭibaddhacitto devasikaṃ sahassaṃ deti. So taṃ divasampi sūriyatthaṅgamanavelāya sahassaṃ gaṇhitvā taṃ gharaṃ agamāsi. Sāmāpi sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ gahetvā ūrūsu ṭhapetvā parodantī nisinnā hoti. “Kiṃ eta”nti ca vuttā “sāmi, ayaṃ coro mama bhātā, ‘ahaṃ nīcakammaṃ karomī’ti mayhaṃ santikaṃ na eti, nagaraguttikassa pahitaṃ ‘sahassaṃ labhamāno vissajjessāmi na’nti sāsanaṃ pesesi. Idāni imaṃ sahassaṃ ādāya nagaraguttikassa santikaṃ gacchantaṃ na labhāmī”ti āha. So tassā paṭibaddhacittatāya “ahaṃ gamissāmī”ti āha. “Tena hi tayā [M 3.0056] ābhatameva gahetvā gacchāhī”ti. So taṃ gahetvā nagaraguttikassa gehaṃ gañchi. So taṃ seṭṭhiputtaṃ paṭicchannaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā coraṃ paṭicchannayānake nisīdāpetvā sāmāya pahiṇitvā “ayaṃ coro raṭṭhe pākaṭo, tamandhakāraṃ tāva hotu, atha naṃ manussānaṃ paṭisallīnavelāya ghātāpessāmī”ti apadesaṃ katvā muhuttaṃ vītināmetvā manussesu paṭisallīnesu seṭṭhiputtaṃ mahantenārakkhena āghātanaṃ netvā asinā sīsaṃ chinditvā sarīraṃ sūle āropetvā nagaraṃ pāvisi.

At that time, a certain merchant’s son, his mind infatuated with Sāmā, gave her a thousand pieces of money daily. On that day too, at the time of sunset, he took a thousand and went to her house. Sāmā, having taken the bundle of a thousand, placed it on her lap and sat weeping. When asked, “What is this?” she replied, “Master, this thief is my brother. Thinking, ‘I do lowly work,’ he does not come near me. The city guard sent a message, saying, ‘If I receive a thousand, I will release him.’ Now I cannot find anyone to take this thousand to the city guard.” Due to his infatuation with her, he said, “I will go.” She replied, “Then take what you yourself have brought and go.” He took it and went to the city guard’s house. The guard hid the merchant’s son in a concealed place, had the thief seated in a covered carriage, and sent him to Sāmā, making the excuse: “This thief is notorious in the land. Let it first become dark, then at the time when people have retired, I will have him executed.” Having waited a moment, when the people had retired, he took the merchant’s son under heavy guard to the execution ground, beheaded him with a sword, impaled his body on a stake, and entered the city.

Tato paṭṭhāya sāmā aññesaṃ hatthato kiñci na gaṇhāti, teneva saddhiṃ abhiramamānā vicarati. So cintesi “sace ayaṃ aññasmiṃ paṭibaddhacittā bhavissati, mampi mārāpetvā tena saddhiṃ abhiramissati, accantaṃ mittadubbhinī esā, mayā idha avasitvā khippaṃ palāyituṃ vaṭṭati, gacchanto ca pana tucchahattho [P 3.0061] agantvā etissā ābharaṇabhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā gacchissāmī”ti cintetvā ekasmiṃ divase taṃ āha – “bhadde, mayaṃ pañjare pakkhittakukkuṭā viya niccaṃ ghareyeva homa, ekadivasaṃ uyyānakīḷaṃ karissāmā”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā khādanīyabhojanīyādiṃ sabbaṃ paṭiyādetvā sabbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍitā tena saddhiṃ paṭicchannayāne nisīditvā uyyānaṃ agamāsi. So tattha tāya saddhiṃ kīḷanto “idāni mayhaṃ palāyituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tāya saddhiṃ kilesaratiyā ramitukāmo viya ekaṃ kaṇavīragacchantaraṃ pavisitvā taṃ āliṅganto viya nippīḷetvā visaññaṃ katvā pātetvā sabbābharaṇāni omuñcitvā tassāyeva uttarāsaṅgena bandhitvā bhaṇḍikaṃ khandhe ṭhapetvā uyyānavatiṃ laṅghitvā pakkāmi.

From then on, Sāmā took nothing from the hand of any other, but lived enjoying herself only with him. He thought, “If she becomes infatuated with someone else, she will have me killed and enjoy herself with him. She is utterly treacherous to friends. It is right for me to flee from here quickly, without staying. And when I go, I will not go empty-handed, but will take her ornaments and go.” Thinking thus, one day he said to her, “Good lady, we are always at home like chickens put in a cage. Let us enjoy a day of sport in the garden.” She agreed, saying, “Very well,” prepared all the food and drink, adorned herself with all her ornaments, and, seated with him in a covered carriage, went to the garden. While playing there with her, he thought, “Now it is time for me to escape.” As if wishing to enjoy sensual pleasure with her, he entered a thicket of oleander bushes, and as if embracing her, he squeezed her until she became unconscious and fell. He stripped off all her ornaments, tied them in her own upper robe, placed the bundle on his shoulder, leaped over the garden fence, and fled.

Sāpi [V 3.0052] paṭiladdhasaññā uṭṭhāya paricārikānaṃ santikaṃ āgantvā “ayyaputto kaha”nti pucchi. “Na jānāma, ayye”ti. “Maṃ matāti saññāya bhāyitvā palāto bhavissatī”ti anattamanā hutvā tatoyeva gehaṃ gantvā “mama piyasāmikassa adiṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāyeva alaṅkatasayane na sayissāmī”ti bhūmiyaṃ nipajji. Tato paṭṭhāya manāpaṃ sāṭakaṃ na nivāseti, dve bhattāni na bhuñjati, gandhamālādīni na paṭisevati, “yena kenaci upāyena ayyaputtaṃ pariyesitvā pakkosāpessāmī”ti naṭe pakkosāpetvā sahassaṃ adāsi. “Kiṃ karoma, ayye”ti vutte [M 3.0057] “tumhākaṃ agamanaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi, tumhe gāmanigamarājadhāniyo carantā samajjaṃ katvā samajjamaṇḍale paṭhamameva imaṃ gītaṃ gāyeyyāthā”ti naṭe sikkhāpentī paṭhamaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā “tumhehi imasmiṃ gītake gīte sace ayyaputto tasmiṃ parisantare bhavissati, tumhehi saddhiṃ kathessati, athassa [P 3.0062] mama arogabhāvaṃ kathetvā taṃ ādāya āgaccheyyātha, no ce āgacchati, sāsanaṃ peseyyāthā”ti paribbayaṃ datvā naṭe uyyojesi. Te bārāṇasito nikkhamitvā tattha tattha samajjaṃ karontā ekaṃ paccantagāmakaṃ agamiṃsu. Sopi coro palāyitvā tattha vasati. Te tattha samajjaṃ karontā paṭhamameva imaṃ gītakaṃ gāyiṃsu –

She, having regained consciousness, arose and went to her attendants, asking, “Where is the young master?” “We do not know, lady,” they replied. Thinking, “He must have fled in fear, under the impression that I was dead,” she became distressed and returned home. She declared, “From the time my beloved master was last seen, I will not sleep on a decorated bed,” and lay down on the floor. From then on, she did not wear pleasing garments, did not eat two meals a day, and did not use perfumes, garlands, and the like. Resolving, “By some means I will search for the young master and have him summoned,” she had actors called and gave them a thousand. When they asked, “What shall we do, lady?” she said, “There is no place to which you do not go. As you travel through villages, towns, and royal cities, holding festivals, you should sing this song first in the assembly circle.” Instructing the actors, she spoke the first verse and said, “If, when you have sung this song, the young master is in that assembly, he will speak with you. Then, tell him of my well-being and bring him with you. If he does not come, send a message.” Giving them their expenses, she sent the actors on their way. They departed from Bārāṇasī and, holding festivals in various places, came to a certain border village. The thief, having fled, was living there. Holding a performance there, they first sang this song:

69.

69.

“Yaṃ taṃ vasantasamaye, kaṇaveresu bhāṇusu;

Sāmaṃ bāhāya pīḷesi, sā taṃ ārogyamabravī”ti.

“She whom you squeezed with your arm in the springtime, among the radiant oleanders—that Sāmā has sent news of her well-being to you.”

Tattha kaṇaveresūti karavīresu. Bhāṇusūti rattavaṇṇānaṃ pupphānaṃ pabhāya sampannesu. Sāmanti evaṃnāmikaṃ. Pīḷesīti kilesaratiyā ramitukāmo viya āliṅganto pīḷesi. Sā tanti sā sāmā arogā, tvaṃ pana “sā matā”ti saññāya bhīto palāyasi, sā attano ārogyaṃ abravi kathesi, ārocesīti attho.

Herein, 'kaṇaveresu' means among oleanders. 'Bhāṇusu' means endowed with the radiance of red-colored flowers. 'Sāmaṃ' refers to the woman of that name. 'Pīḷesi' means: as if wishing to enjoy sensual pleasure, he squeezed her while embracing. 'Sā taṃ... abravī' means: that Sāmā is well, but you, thinking ‘she is dead,’ flee in fear; she spoke of her own well-being, she told, she announced—this is the meaning.

Coro taṃ sutvā naṭaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tvaṃ ‘sāmā jīvatī’ti vadasi, ahaṃ pana na saddahāmī”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard that, the thief approached the actor and, conversing with him, said, “You say that Sāmā lives, but I do not believe it.” Then he spoke the second verse:

70.

70.

“Ambho na kira saddheyyaṃ, yaṃ vāto pabbataṃ vahe;

Pabbatañce vahe vāto, sabbampi pathaviṃ vahe;

Yattha sāmā kālakatā, sā maṃ ārogyamabravī”ti.

“Friend, it is surely unbelievable that the wind could carry away a mountain; if the wind were to carry a mountain, it would carry the whole earth. That Sāmā, who died there, has sent news of her well-being to me [is equally unbelievable].”

Tassattho [V 3.0053] – ambho naṭa, idaṃ kira na saddaheyyaṃ na saddahitabbaṃ. Yaṃ vāto tiṇapaṇṇāni viya pabbataṃ vaheyya, sacepi so pabbataṃ vaheyya, sabbampi pathaviṃ vaheyya, yathā cetaṃ asaddaheyyaṃ, tathā idanti. Yattha sāmā kālakatāti yā nāma sāmā kālakatā, sā maṃ ārogyaṃ abravīti kiṃkāraṇā saddaheyyaṃ. Matā nāma na kassaci sāsanaṃ pesentīti.

The meaning is: 'O actor, this indeed is not to be believed, it should not be believed. Just as it is unbelievable that the wind might carry away a mountain like grass and leaves—and even if it were to carry a mountain, it would carry the whole earth—so too is this. In the phrase "Where Sāmā has died," it means: for what reason should I believe that the one named Sāmā, who is dead, has declared her well-being to me? For the dead do not send messages to anyone.'

Tassa [P 3.0063][M 3.0058] vacanaṃ sutvā naṭo tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Upon hearing his words, the actor spoke the third verse:

71.

71.

“Na ceva sā kālakatā, na ca sā aññamicchati;

Ekabhattikinī sāmā, tameva abhikaṅkhatī”ti.

“Sāmā is not dead, nor does she desire another; she is faithful to you alone and yearns for only you.”

Tattha tameva abhikaṅkhatīti aññaṃ purisaṃ na icchati, taññeva kaṅkhati icchati patthetīti.

In this context, 'tameva abhikaṅkhatī' means: she does not desire another man; she longs for, desires, and yearns for you alone.

Taṃ sutvā coro “sā jīvatu vā mā vā, na tāya mayhaṃ attho”ti vatvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the thief said, “Whether she lives or dies, I have no use for her,” and spoke the fourth verse:

72.

72.

“Asanthutaṃ maṃ cirasanthutena, nimīni sāmā adhuvaṃ dhuvena;

Mayāpi sāmā nimineyya aññaṃ, ito ahaṃ dūrataraṃ gamissa”nti.

“Sāmā exchanged me, the unacquainted, for the one long-acquainted; she traded the unstable for the stable. Sāmā might also exchange me for another; therefore, I will go far away from here.”

Tattha asanthutanti akatasaṃsaggaṃ. Cirasanthutenāti cirakatasaṃsaggena. Nimīnīti parivattesi. Adhuvaṃ dhuvenāti maṃ adhuvaṃ tena dhuvasāmikena parivattetuṃ nagaraguttikassa sahassaṃ datvā maṃ gaṇhīti attho. Mayāpi sāmā nimineyya aññanti sāmā mayāpi aññaṃ sāmikaṃ parivattetvā gaṇheyya. Ito ahaṃ dūrataraṃ gamissanti yattha na sakkā tassā sāsanaṃ vā pavattiṃ vā sotuṃ, tādisaṃ dūrataraṃ ṭhānaṃ gamissaṃ, tasmā mama ito aññattha gatabhāvaṃ tassā ārocethāti vatvā tesaṃ passantānaññeva gāḷhataraṃ nivāsetvā vegena palāyi.

In this context, 'unacquainted' (asanthutaṃ) means not having formed a previous connection. 'By one long-acquainted' (cirasanthutena) means by one with whom she had a long-standing connection. 'She exchanged' (nimīni) means she traded. 'The unstable for the stable' (adhuvaṃ dhuvena) means she gave a thousand coins to the city-guardian to take me, the unstable one, in exchange for that stable husband; this is the meaning. 'Sāmā might also exchange me for another' (mayāpi sāmā nimineyya aññaṃ) means Sāmā might trade me as well for another husband. 'I will go far away from here' (ito ahaṃ dūrataraṃ gamissaṃ) means he would go to such a distant place where it would be impossible to hear news or word of her. Having said, 'Therefore, tell her that I have gone elsewhere,' he tightened his lower garment firmly in their very sight and fled with great speed.

Naṭā gantvā tena katakiriyaṃ tassā kathayiṃsu. Sā vippaṭisārinī hutvā attano pakatiyā eva vītināmesi.

The actors went and told her what the thief had done. She, filled with remorse, lived out her life in her usual state.

Satthā [V 3.0054] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, revealed the Truths and connected the birth story. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā seṭṭhiputto ayaṃ bhikkhu ahosi, sāmā purāṇadutiyikā, coro pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the merchant's son was this monk, Sāmā was the former wife, and the thief was indeed I myself.

Kaṇaverajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kaṇavera Jātaka, the Eighth.

[319] 9. Tittirajātakavaṇṇanā

[319] 9. The Commentary on the Tittira Jātaka.

Susukhaṃ [P 3.0064][M 3.0059] vata jīvāmīti idaṃ satthā kosambiyaṃ nissāya badarikārāme viharanto rāhulattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā tipallatthajātake (jā. 1.1.16) vitthāritameva. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, rāhulo sikkhākāmo kukkuccako ovādakkhamo”ti. Tassāyasmato guṇakathāya samuṭṭhāpitāya satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi rāhulo sikkhākāmo kukkuccako ovādakkhamoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Happy indeed I live.' This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Badarikārāma near Kosambī, concerning the Elder Rāhula. The story has been related in detail previously in the Tipallattha Jātaka (Jā 16). The monks started a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: 'Friends, Rāhula is eager for training, scrupulous, and amenable to advice.' When this talk about the venerable one's virtues arose, the Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered together?' On being told, 'For this one,' he replied, 'Not only now, monks, but in the past too, Rāhula was eager for training, scrupulous, and amenable to advice.' Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā nikkhamma himavantapadese isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto ramaṇīye vanasaṇḍe vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya aññataraṃ paccantagāmakaṃ agamāsi. Tattha naṃ manussā disvā pasannacittā aññatarasmiṃ araññe paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā paccayehi upaṭṭhahantā vāsāpesuṃ. Tadā tasmiṃ gāmake eko sākuṇiko ekaṃ dīpakatittiraṃ gahetvā suṭṭhu sikkhāpetvā pañjare pakkhipitvā paṭijaggati. So taṃ araññaṃ netvā tassa saddena āgatāgate tittire gahetvā vikkiṇitvā jīvikaṃ kappesi. Tittiro “maṃ ekaṃ nissāya bahū mama ñātakā nassanti, mayhametaṃ pāpa”nti nissaddo ahosi. So tassa nissaddabhāvaṃ ñatvā veḷupesikāya naṃ sīse paharati. Tittiro dukkhāturatāya saddaṃ karoti. Evaṃ so sākuṇiko taṃ nissāya tittire gahetvā jīvikaṃ kappesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. When he came of age, he went to Takkasilā, mastered all the arts, and then departed. He took up the ascetic life in the Himalayan region, developed the higher spiritual powers and meditative attainments, and dwelt delighting in the bliss of meditation in a charming forest grove. To obtain salt and sour seasoning, he went to a certain border village. There, the people, seeing him and being filled with faith, built a leaf-hut for him in a forest and supported him with the requisites, inviting him to stay. At that time, a fowler in that village caught a decoy partridge, trained it well, and kept it in a cage. He would take it to the forest and, using its call, catch the partridges that came, selling them to make his living. The partridge thought, 'Because of me alone, many of my kinsfolk are perishing; this is a sin for me,' and became silent. Realizing its silence, the fowler struck it on the head with a bamboo splint. Due to the pain, the partridge would cry out. Thus, the fowler made his living by catching partridges through him.

Atha so tittiro cintesi “ime marantūti mayhaṃ cetanā natthi, paṭiccakammaṃ pana maṃ phusati, mayi saddaṃ akaronte ete nāgacchanti, karonteyeva āgacchanti, āgatāgate ayaṃ gahetvā [V 3.0055] jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpeti, atthi nu kho ettha mayhaṃ pāpaṃ, natthī”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya “ko nu kho me imaṃ kaṅkhaṃ [P 3.0065] chindeyyā”ti tathārūpaṃ paṇḍitaṃ upadhārento carati. Athekadivasaṃ so sākuṇiko bahū tittire gahetvā pacchiṃ [M 3.0060] pūretvā “pānīyaṃ pivissāmī”ti bodhisattassa assamaṃ gantvā taṃ pañjaraṃ bodhisattassa santike ṭhapetvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā vālukātale nipanno niddaṃ okkami. Tittiro tassa niddokkantabhāvaṃ ñatvā “mama kaṅkhaṃ imaṃ tāpasaṃ pucchissāmi, jānanto me kathessatī”ti pañjare nisinnoyeva taṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the partridge thought, 'I have no intention that these should die, but the consequence of the action done in dependence on me affects me. If I do not make a sound, they do not come; but when I do, they come. Each time they come, this man catches them and brings about the destruction of their lives. Is there evil for me in this, or is there not?' From then on, thinking, 'Who can resolve this doubt of mine?' he went about looking for such a wise person. One day, the fowler, having caught many partridges and filled his basket, went to the Bodhisatta's hermitage, thinking, 'I will drink some water.' He placed the cage near the Bodhisatta, drank water, and then lay down on the sandy ground and fell asleep. The partridge, knowing that he had fallen asleep, thought, 'I will ask this ascetic about my doubt; if he knows, he will explain it to me.' Sitting in the cage, he asked his question by reciting the first verse:

73.

73.

“Susukhaṃ vata jīvāmi, labhāmi ceva bhuñjituṃ;

Paripanthe ca tiṭṭhāmi, kā nu bhante gatī mamā”ti.

“Happily indeed I live, and I get food to eat; but I stand in a perilous place. What, venerable sir, will be my destiny?”

Tattha susukhaṃ vata jīvāmīti ahaṃ, bhante, imaṃ sākuṇikaṃ nissāya suṭṭhu sukhaṃ jīvāmi. Labhāmīti yathārucitaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ bhuñjitumpi labhāmi. Paripanthe ca tiṭṭhāmīti apica kho yattha mama ñātakā mama saddena āgatāgatā vinassanti, tasmiṃ paripanthe tiṭṭhāmi. Kā nu, bhante, gatī mamāti kā nu kho, bhante, mama gati, kā nipphatti bhavissatīti pucchi.

Therein, 'Happily indeed I live' means: 'Venerable sir, relying on this fowler, I live very happily.' 'I get to eat' means: 'I get to eat as much as I desire of hard and soft food.' 'But I stand in a perilous place' means: 'Moreover, I stand in that perilous place where my kinsfolk, coming at my call, perish.' By 'What, venerable sir, will be my destiny?' he asked: 'What, venerable sir, will be my fate? What will be my final outcome?'

Tassa pañhaṃ vissajjento bodhisatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Answering his question, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:

74.

74.

“Mano ce te nappaṇamati, pakkhi pāpassa kammuno;

Abyāvaṭassa bhadrassa, na pāpamupalimpatī”ti.

'If your mind, O bird, does not incline to the evil deed, then for the one who is unengaged and virtuous, evil does not stain.'

Tattha pāpassa kammunoti yadi tava mano pāpakammassatthāya na paṇamati, pāpakaraṇe tanninno tappoṇo tappabbhāro na hoti. Abyāvaṭassāti evaṃ sante pāpakammakaraṇatthāya abyāvaṭassa ussukkaṃ anāpannassa tava bhadrassa suddhasseva sato pāpaṃ na upalimpati na allīyatīti.

Therein, 'to the evil deed' means: if your mind does not incline for the sake of an evil deed, and is not intent on, prone to, or directed towards doing evil. 'Of the unengaged' means: this being so, for you who are not engaged in doing an evil deed and who have not exerted effort towards it, being virtuous and pure, evil does not stain or cling.

Taṃ sutvā tittiro tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the partridge spoke the third verse:

75.

75.

“Ñātako [V 3.0056] no nisinnoti, bahu āgacchate jano;

Paṭiccakammaṃ phusati, tasmiṃ me saṅkate mano”ti.

'Thinking, "Our kinsman is sitting there," many birds approach; a deed done in dependence on me affects me; concerning that, my mind is doubtful.'

Tassattho – bhante, sacāhaṃ saddaṃ na kareyyaṃ, ayaṃ tittirajano na āgaccheyya, mayi pana saddaṃ karonte “ñātako no nisinno”ti ayaṃ bahu jano āgacchati[P 3.0066], taṃ āgatāgataṃ luddo gahetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpento maṃ paṭicca nissāya etaṃ pāṇātipātakammaṃ phusati paṭilabhati vindati[M 3.0061], tasmiṃ maṃ paṭicca kate pāpe mama nu kho etaṃ pāpanti evaṃ me mano saṅkate parisaṅkati kukkuccaṃ āpajjatīti.

The meaning is this: 'Venerable sir, if I were not to make a sound, these partridge-folk would not come. But when I make a sound, many birds come, thinking, "Our kinsman is sitting there." As they come, the fowler catches them and brings them to their death. Dependent on me, relying on me, he commits this act of destroying life. Concerning that evil done in dependence on me, I wonder, "Is this evil mine?"—thus my mind is doubtful, anxious, and falls into remorse.'

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the fourth verse:

76.

76.

“Na paṭiccakammaṃ phusati, mano ce nappadussati;

Appossukkassa bhadrassa, na pāpamupalimpatī”ti.

'A deed done in dependence does not affect one whose mind is not corrupted; for the one who is without eagerness and virtuous, evil does not stain.'

Tassattho – yadi tava pāpakiriyāya mano na padussati, tanninno tappono tappabbhāro na hoti, evaṃ sante luddena āyasmantaṃ paṭicca katampi pāpakammaṃ taṃ na phusati na allīyati, pāpakiriyāya hi appossukkassa nirālayassa bhadrassa parisuddhasseva sato tava pāṇātipātacetanāya abhāvā taṃ pāpaṃ na upalimpati, tava cittaṃ na allīyatīti.

The meaning is this: If your mind is not corrupted by the evil action, and is not intent on, prone to, or directed towards it, then this being so, even the evil deed done by the hunter in dependence on you does not touch you or cling to you. Indeed, for you, who are without eagerness for evil action, without attachment, virtuous, and utterly pure, because of the absence of any intention to destroy life, that evil does not stain you or cling to your mind.

Evaṃ mahāsatto tittiraṃ saññāpesi, sopi taṃ nissāya nikkukkucco ahosi. Luddo pabuddho bodhisattaṃ vanditvā pañjaraṃ ādāya pakkāmi.

Thus the Great Being reassured the partridge, and it, relying on him, became free from remorse. The hunter, now awakened, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, took the cage, and departed.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā tittiro rāhulo ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the partridge was Rāhula, and the ascetic was I myself.'

Tittirajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Tittira Jātaka, the Ninth.

[320] 10. Succajajātakavaṇṇanā

[320] 10. The Commentary on the Succaja Jātaka.

Succajaṃ vata naccajīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So [V 3.0057] kira “gāmake uddhāraṃ sādhessāmī”ti bhariyāya saddhiṃ tattha gantvā sādhetvā dhanaṃ āharitvā “pacchā nessāmī”ti ekasmiṃ kule ṭhapetvā puna sāvatthiṃ gacchanto antarāmagge ekaṃ pabbataṃ addasa. Atha naṃ bhariyā āha “sace, sāmi, ayaṃ pabbato suvaṇṇamayo bhaveyya, dadeyyāsi pana me kiñcī”ti. “Kāsi tvaṃ, na kiñci dassāmī”ti. Sā “yāva thaddhahadayo vatāyaṃ, pabbate suvaṇṇamaye jātepi [M 3.0062] mayhaṃ kiñci na dassatī”ti anattamanā ahosi. Te jetavanasamīpaṃ āgantvā “pānīyaṃ pivissāmā”ti vihāraṃ pavisitvā pānīyaṃ piviṃsu. Satthāpi [P 3.0067] paccūsakāleyeva tesaṃ sotāpattiphalassa upanissayaṃ disvā āgamanaṃ olokayamāno gandhakuṭipariveṇe nisīdi chabbaṇṇarasmiyo vissajjento. Tepi pānīyaṃ pivitvā āgantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tehi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kahaṃ gatātthā”ti pucchi. “Amhākaṃ gāmake uddhāraṃ sādhanatthāya, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ, upāsike tava sāmiko tuyhaṃ hitaṃ paṭikaṅkhati, upakāraṃ te karotī”ti. Bhante, ahaṃ imasmiṃ sasinehā, ayaṃ pana mayi nissineho, ajja mayā pabbataṃ disvā “sacāyaṃ pabbato suvaṇṇamayo assa, kiñci me dadeyyāsī”ti vutto “kāsi tvaṃ, na kiñci dassāmī”ti āha, evaṃ thaddhahadayo ayanti. “Upāsike, evaṃ nāmesa vadati, yadā pana tava guṇaṃ sarati, tadā sabbissariyaṃ te detī”ti vatvā “kathetha, bhante”ti tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Regarding the verse beginning, 'What is easy to give up, indeed, he did not give up,' the Teacher spoke this while dwelling in Jetavana concerning a certain householder. It seems that man, intending to recover a debt in a village, went there with his wife, recovered it, and thinking, 'I will take it back later,' left the money with a certain family. While returning to Sāvatthī, on the way he saw a mountain. Then his wife said to him, 'Master, if this mountain were made of gold, would you give me something?' 'Who are you? I will give you nothing,' he replied. She thought, 'How hard-hearted he is! Even if the mountain were made of gold, he would not give me anything,' and became displeased. They arrived near Jetavana and, thinking, 'We will drink water,' entered the monastery and drank. The Teacher, having seen early in the morning the supporting condition for their attainment of the fruit of stream-entry, was sitting in the enclosure of the Gandhakuti, emitting the six-colored rays and watching for their arrival. They too, after drinking water, came, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down. The Teacher exchanged pleasantries with them and asked, 'Where have you been?' 'To our village to recover a debt, venerable sir.' 'Well, upāsikā, does your husband wish for your welfare? Does he help you?' 'Venerable sir, I am affectionate towards him, but he is without affection for me. Today, upon seeing a mountain, when I said to him, "If this mountain were made of gold, would you give me something?" he replied, "Who are you? I will give you nothing." That is how hard-hearted he is.' 'Upāsikā, he speaks thus, but when he remembers your virtues, he gives you all his dominion,' said the Teacher. Then, being requested by them, 'Please tell us, venerable sir,' he brought forth a story from the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa sabbakiccakārako amacco ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ rājā puttaṃ uparājānaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “ayaṃ mama antepure dubbheyyā”ti taṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, yāvāhaṃ jīvāmi, tāva nagare vasituṃ na lacchasi, aññattha vasitvā mamaccayena rajjaṃ kārehī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti pitaraṃ vanditvā jeṭṭhabhariyāya saddhiṃ nagarā nikkhamitvā paccantaṃ gantvā araññaṃ pavisitvā paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā vanamūlaphalāphalehi yāpento vasi. Aparabhāge rājā kālamakāsi. Uparājā nakkhattaṃ olokento tassa kālakatabhāvaṃ ñatvā bārāṇasiṃ āgacchanto antarāmagge ekaṃ pabbataṃ addasa. Atha naṃ bhariyā āha “sace, deva, ayaṃ pabbato suvaṇṇamayo assa, dadeyyāsi me kiñcī”ti. “Kāsi tvaṃ, na kiñci dassāmī”ti. Sā “ahaṃ imasmiṃ sinehaṃ chindituṃ asakkontī araññaṃ pāvisiṃ, ayañca evaṃ vadati, ativiya thaddhahadayo[P 3.0068], rājā hutvāpi esa mayhaṃ kiṃ kalyāṇaṃ karissatī”ti anattamanā ahosi. So āgantvā rajje patiṭṭhito taṃ aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi[M 3.0063], idaṃ yasamattakameva adāsi. Uttari pana sakkārasammāno natthi, tassā atthibhāvampi na jānāti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his minister who conducted all his affairs. One day, the king saw his son, the viceroy, coming to attend upon him and thought, 'This prince might commit a transgression in my inner palace.' Summoning him, he said, 'Dear son, as long as I live, you shall not be able to dwell in the city. Live elsewhere, and after my passing, you may rule the kingdom.' The prince replied, 'Very well,' paid homage to his father, and left the city with his chief wife. He went to the borderlands, entered the forest, built a leaf-hut, and lived there, sustaining himself on forest roots and fruits. Sometime later, the king passed away. The viceroy, observing the stars, learned of his father's passing and set out for Bārāṇasī. Along the way, he saw a mountain. His wife then said to him, 'My lord, if this mountain were made of gold, would you give me a little of it?' He replied, 'Who are you? I will give you nothing.' She thought, 'Unable to sever my affection for this man, I entered the forest, and yet he speaks thus; his heart is exceedingly hard. Even when he becomes king, what good will he do for me?' and she became displeased. Upon arriving, he was established in the kingdom and placed her in the position of chief queen; however, he gave her only that measure of status. Beyond that, there was no special honor or respect; he did not even acknowledge her presence.

Bodhisatto [V 3.0058] “ayaṃ devī imassa rañño upakārikā dukkhaṃ agaṇetvā araññavāsaṃ vasi.
