Ayaṃ panetaṃ agaṇetvā aññāhi saddhiṃ abhiramanto vicarati, yathā esā sabbissariyaṃ labhati, tathā karissāmī”ti cintetvā ekadivasaṃ taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “mahādevi mayaṃ tumhākaṃ santikā piṇḍapātamattampi na labhāma, kasmā amhesu pamajjittha, ativiya thaddhahadayā atthā”ti āha. “Tāta, sacāhaṃ attanā labheyyaṃ, tuyhampi dadeyyaṃ, alabhamānā pana kiṃ dassāmi, rājāpi mayhaṃ idāni kiṃ nāma dassati, so antarāmagge ‘imasmiṃ pabbate suvaṇṇamaye jāte mayhaṃ kiñci dassasī’ti vutto ‘kāsi tvaṃ, na kiñci dassāmī’ti āha, supariccajampi na pariccajī”ti. “Kiṃ pana rañño santike imaṃ kathaṃ kathetuṃ sakkhissathā”ti? “Sakkhissāmi, tātā”ti. “Tena hi ahaṃ rañño santike ṭhito pucchissāmi, tumhe katheyyāthā”ti. “Sādhu, tātā”ti. Bodhisatto deviyā rañño upaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā ṭhitakāle āha “nanu, ayye, mayaṃ tumhākaṃ santikā kiñci na labhāmā”ti? “Tāta, ahaṃ labhamānā tuyhaṃ dadeyyaṃ, ahameva kiñci na labhāmi, alabhamānā tuyhaṃ kiṃ dassāmi, rājāpi idāni mayhaṃ kiṃ nāma dassati, so araññato āgamanakāle ekaṃ pabbataṃ disvā ‘sacāyaṃ pabbato suvaṇṇamayo assa, kiñci me dadeyyāsī’ti vutto ‘kāsi tvaṃ, na kiñci dassāmī’ti vadati, supariccajampi na pariccajī”ti etamatthaṃ [P 3.0069] dīpentī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta thought, 'This queen was of great help to this king; she lived in the forest without regard for hardship. Yet now, he disregards her and roams about enjoying himself with other women. I will act in such a way that she may receive full sovereignty.' Having reflected thus, one day he approached her, paid respects, and said, 'Great queen, we do not receive even a measure of food from you. Why have you become neglectful of us? You have become exceedingly hard-hearted.' She replied, 'Father, if I were to receive anything myself, I would give to you also. But receiving nothing, what can I give? What will the king give me now? On the way here, when he was asked, "If this mountain were to become gold, would you give me something?" he said, "Who are you? I will give you nothing." He did not even grant what was easy to give.' 'But would you be able to speak these words in the king’s presence?' the Bodhisatta asked. 'I would be able, father,' the queen replied. 'Then I will stand in the king’s presence and ask, and you should speak.' 'Very well, father.' At a time when the queen had come to attend upon the king, the Bodhisatta, standing there, said, 'Noble lady, is it not so that we receive nothing from you?' 'Father, if I were receiving anything, I would give it to you. But I myself receive nothing; receiving nothing, what can I give you? What will the king give me now? When we were coming from the forest, upon seeing a mountain, he was asked, "If this mountain were made of gold, would you give me something?" and he replied, "Who are you? I will give you nothing." He did not grant even that which is easy to give.' To explain this matter, she spoke the first verse:

77.

77.

“Succajaṃ vata naccaji, vācāya adadaṃ giriṃ;

Kiñhi tassacajantassa, vācāya adada pabbata”nti.

Indeed, what was easy to give he did not give, not granting the mountain even by word. For that one who does not give, what would he give, he who did not grant the mountain even by word?

Tattha succajaṃ vatāti sukhena cajituṃ sakkuṇeyyampi na caji. Adadanti vacanamattenāpi pabbataṃ adadamāno. Kiñhi tassacajantassāti tassa nāmetassa mayā yācitassa na cajantassa kiñhi cajeyya. Vācāya adada pabbatanti sacāyaṃ mayā yācito mama vacanena suvaṇṇamayampi hontaṃ taṃ pabbataṃ vācāya adada, vacanamattena adassāti attho.

Therein, 'succajaṃ vata' means: he did not give even what could be given up with ease. 'Adadaṃ' means: not giving the mountain even by mere word. 'Kiñhi tassacajantassa' means: what indeed would he give, that person who does not give even when asked by me? 'Vācāya adada pabbataṃ' means: the meaning is that even if that mountain I asked for were to become golden, he did not give it even by word, he did not give it even by a mere utterance.

Taṃ [M 3.0064] sutvā rājā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke the second verse:

78.

78.

“Yañhi kayirā tañhi vade, yaṃ na kayirā na taṃ vade;

Akarontaṃ bhāsamānaṃ, parijānanti paṇḍitā”ti.

What one would do, that one should say; what one would not do, that one should not say. The wise discern one who speaks but does not act.

Tassattho [V 3.0059] – yadeva hi paṇḍito puriso kāyena kareyya, taṃ vācāya vadeyya. Yaṃ na kayirā, na taṃ vadeyya, dātukāmova dammīti vadeyya, na adātukāmoti adhippāyo. Kiṃkāraṇā? Yo hi “dassāmī”ti vatvāpi pacchā na dadāti, taṃ akarontaṃ kevalaṃ musā bhāsamānaṃ parijānanti paṇḍitā. Ayaṃ “dassāmī”ti vacanamattameva bhāsati, na pana deti, yañhi kho pana adinnampi vacanamatteneva dinnaṃ hoti, taṃ puretarameva laddhaṃ nāma bhavissatīti evaṃ tassa musāvādibhāvaṃ parijānanti paṇḍitā, bālā pana vacanamatteneva tussantīti.

Its meaning is: whatever a wise person would do with the body, that they would also say with words. What they would not do, that they would not say. One should say, 'I am giving,' only if one truly intends to give, and not say it if one does not intend to give—this is the point. For what reason? For if someone says, 'I will give,' but later does not give, the wise recognize him as one who does not act but merely speaks falsely. They understand his nature as a liar, thinking: 'This person merely utters the words "I will give," but does not actually give.' For if what is not given were considered given by mere words, it would have been obtained long ago! Thus do the wise recognize his falsehood, while fools are satisfied by mere words.

Taṃ sutvā devī rañño añjaliṃ paggahetvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the queen, raising her joined hands in reverence to the king, spoke the third verse:

79.

79.

“Rājaputta namo tyatthu, sacce dhamme ṭhito casi;

Yassa te byasanaṃ patto, saccasmiṃ ramate mano”ti.

Homage to you, O prince! You stand firm in truth and the Dhamma. Though misfortune has befallen you, your mind delights in truth.

Tattha [P 3.0070] sacce dhammeti vacīsacce ca sabhāvadhamme ca. Byasanaṃ pattoti yassa tava raṭṭhā pabbājanīyasaṅkhātaṃ byasanaṃ pattopi mano saccasmiṃyeva ramati.

There, 'in truth and the Dhamma' refers to truth in speech and the truth of natural reality. 'Though misfortune has befallen you' means: although you have met with the misfortune known as banishment from your country, your mind still delights solely in truth.

Evaṃ rañño guṇakathaṃ kathayamānāya deviyā taṃ sutvā bodhisatto tassā guṇakathaṃ kathento catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, as the queen was speaking of the king's virtues, the Bodhisatta, hearing her, recited the fourth verse to praise her virtues:

80.

80.

“Yā daliddī daliddassa, aḍḍhā aḍḍhassa kittima;

Sā hissa paramā bhariyā, sahiraññassa itthiyo”ti.

She who is poor for the poor man, and rich for the rich man, the renowned one; she indeed is his supreme wife, while other women are merely for the sake of wealth.

Tattha kittimāti kittisampannāti attho. Sā hissa paramāti yā daliddassa sāmikassa daliddakāle sayampi daliddī hutvā taṃ na pariccajati. Aḍḍhassāti aḍḍhakāle aḍḍhā hutvā sāmikameva anuvattati, samānasukhadukkhāva hoti, sā hi tassa paramā uttamā bhariyā nāma. Sahiraññassa pana issariye ṭhitassa itthiyo nāma hontiyeva, anacchariyameva etanti.

In that passage, 'kittimā' means endowed with fame. 'Sā hissa paramā' means she who, when her husband is poor, herself becomes poor and does not abandon him. 'Aḍḍhassa' means that in times of wealth, she becomes wealthy and follows her husband, sharing equal happiness and sorrow; she indeed is his supreme and excellent wife. As for women belonging to a man established in wealth and power, they are always present; this is no wonder.

Evañca [M 3.0065] pana vatvā bodhisatto “ayaṃ, mahārāja, tumhākaṃ dukkhitakāle araññe samānadukkhā hutvā vasi, imissā sammānaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti deviyā guṇaṃ kathesi. Rājā tassa vacanena deviyā guṇaṃ saritvā “paṇḍita, tava kathāyāhaṃ deviyā guṇaṃ anussari”nti vatvā [V 3.0060] tassā sabbissariyamadāsi. “Tayāhaṃ deviyā guṇaṃ sarāpito”ti bodhisattassapi mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ akāsi.

Having said this, the Bodhisatta recounted the queen's virtues, saying: "O great king, this queen lived with you in the forest, sharing your sorrow during your time of hardship. It is fitting to honor her." Hearing his words, the king recalled the queen's virtues and said: "Wise one, because of your words I have remembered the queen's virtues," and he bestowed all sovereignty upon her. Saying, "By you I have been made to remember the queen's virtues," he also bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisatta.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ubho jayampatikā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma and revealed the Truths, the Teacher connected the birth story. At the conclusion of the Truths, both the husband and wife were established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā bārāṇasirājā ayaṃ kuṭumbiko ahosi, devī ayaṃ upāsikā, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī was this householder, the queen was this female lay disciple, and the wise minister was indeed myself.

Succajajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The explanation of the Succaja Jātaka, the tenth.

Pucimandavaggo dutiyo.

The Pucimanda Section is the second.

3. Kuṭidūsakavaggo

3. The Kuṭidūsaka Chapter

[321] 1. Kuṭidūsakajātakavaṇṇanā

[321] 1. The explanation of the Kuṭidūsaka Jātaka

Manussasseva [V 3.0061][P 3.0071] te sīsanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahākassapattherassa paṇṇasālajhāpakaṃ daharabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pana rājagahe samuṭṭhitaṃ. Tadā kira thero rājagahaṃ nissāya araññakuṭiyaṃ viharati, tassa dve daharā upaṭṭhānaṃ karonti. Tesu eko therassa upakārako, eko dubbaco itarena kataṃ attanā katasadisaṃ karoti. Tena mukhodakādīsu upaṭṭhāpitesu therassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā “bhante, udakaṃ ṭhapitaṃ, mukhaṃ dhovathā”tiādīni vadati. Tena kālasseva vuṭṭhāya therassa pariveṇe sammaṭṭhe therassa nikkhamanavelāya ito cito ca paharanto sakalapariveṇaṃ attanā sammaṭṭhaṃ viya karoti. Vattasampanno cintesi “ayaṃ dubbaco mayā kataṃ attanā katasadisaṃ karoti, etassa saṭhakammaṃ pākaṭaṃ karissāmī”ti.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story concerning a young monk who burned down the leaf-hut of the Elder Mahākassapa. The incident, however, arose in Rājagaha. At that time, it is said, the Elder was dwelling in a forest hut near Rājagaha, and two young monks attended to him. One of them was helpful to the Elder, while the other was difficult to speak to; the latter would make whatever the former did appear as if he had done it himself. When the helpful monk prepared the face-water and other things, the difficult one would go to the Elder, pay respects, and say, "Venerable sir, the water is ready, please wash your face," and so on. When the helpful monk rose early and swept the Elder’s enclosure, the other would, at the time of the Elder's departure, strike the broom here and there and make it appear as if he had swept the whole enclosure himself. The monk who was dutiful thought, "This difficult one makes whatever I do appear as if he has done it himself; I will expose his deceitful behavior."

Tasmiṃ [M 3.0066] antogāme bhutvā āgantvā niddāyanteva nhānodakaṃ tāpetvā piṭṭhikoṭṭhake ṭhapetvā aññaṃ aḍḍhanāḷimattaṃ udakaṃ uddhane ṭhapesi. Itaro pabujjhitvāva gantvā usumaṃ uṭṭhahantaṃ disvā “udakaṃ tāpetvā koṭṭhake ṭhapitaṃ bhavissatī”ti therassa santikaṃ gantvā “bhante, nhānakoṭṭhake udakaṃ ṭhapitaṃ, nhāyathā”ti āha. Thero ‘nhāyissāmī”ti tena saddhiṃyeva āgantvā koṭṭhake udakaṃ aditvā “kahaṃ udaka”nti pucchi. So vegena aggisālaṃ gantvā tucchabhājane uḷuṅkaṃ otāresi, uḷuṅko tucchabhājanassa tale paṭihato “tatā”ti saddamakāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya tassa “uḷuṅkasaddako”tveva nāmaṃ jātaṃ.

After returning from his meal in the village, while the other monk was sleeping, the dutiful monk heated bathing water, placed it outside the bathing room, and placed another half-measure of water in a pot on the hearth. The difficult monk woke up, saw the steam rising, and thinking, "The water must have been heated and placed in the room," went to the Elder and said, "Venerable sir, the water is ready in the bathing room; please bathe." The Elder, saying "I will bathe," went with him. Not finding water in the room, he asked, "Where is the water?" The young monk quickly went to the fire-hall and dropped a ladle into an empty vessel. The ladle, striking the bottom of the empty vessel, made the sound "tata." From that time on, his name became "Uḷuṅkasaddaka" (the Ladle-Sound-Maker).

Tasmiṃ khaṇe itaro piṭṭhikoṭṭhakato udakaṃ āharitvā “nhāyatha, bhante”ti āha. Thero nhatvā āvajjento uḷuṅkasaddakassa dubbacabhāvaṃ [P 3.0072] ñatvā taṃ sāyaṃ therupaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ ovadi “āvuso, samaṇena nāma attanā katameva ‘kataṃ me’ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati, aññathā sampajānamusāvādo hoti, ito paṭṭhāya evarūpaṃ mā akāsī”ti. So therassa kujjhitvā punadivase therena saddhiṃ piṇḍāya gāmaṃ na pāvisi. Thero itareneva saddhiṃ pāvisi. Uḷuṅkasaddakopi [V 3.0062] therassa upaṭṭhākakulaṃ gantvā “bhante, thero kaha”nti vutte “aphāsukena vihāreyeva nisinno”ti vatvā “kiṃ, bhante, laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vutte “idañcidañca dethā”ti gahetvā attano rucitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā bhuñjitvā vihāraṃ agamāsi.

At that moment, the other, well-behaved monk brought water from the back of the bath-structure and said, "Please bathe, Venerable sir." The Elder bathed and, reflecting, recognized the unruly nature of Uḷuṅkasaddaka. When Uḷuṅkasaddaka came to attend on the Elder in the evening, the Elder advised him, "Friend, it is proper for a monk to say 'I have done it' only regarding what he has actually done; otherwise, it becomes a deliberate lie. From now on, do not do such a thing." Angered at the Elder, Uḷuṅkasaddaka did not enter the village for alms with the Elder the next day. The Elder went with the other monk instead. Uḷuṅkasaddaka, for his part, went to the Elder’s supporting family. When they asked, "Venerable sir, where is the Elder?" he replied, "He is sitting in the monastery, feeling unwell." When they asked, "Venerable sir, what is suitable to get for him?" he said, "Give this and that," and taking it, he went to a place of his liking, ate, and then returned to the monastery.

Punadivase thero taṃ kulaṃ gantvā nisīdi. Manussehi “kiṃ, bhante, ayyassa aphāsukaṃ, hiyyo kirattha vihāreyeva nisinnā, asukadaharassa hatthe āhāraṃ pesayimha, paribhutto ayyenā”ti vutte thero tuṇhībhūtova bhattakiccaṃ katvā vihāraṃ gantvā sāyaṃ therupaṭṭhānakāle āgataṃ āmantetvā “āvuso, asukagāme nāma asukakule ‘therassa idañcidañca laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti viññāpetvā kira te bhutta”nti vatvā “viññatti nāma na vaṭṭati, mā puna evarūpaṃ anācāraṃ carā”ti āha. So ettakena there āghātaṃ bandhitvā “ayaṃ hiyyopi udakamattaṃ nissāya mayā saddhiṃ kalahaṃ kari, idāni panassa upaṭṭhākānaṃ gehe mayā bhattamuṭṭhi bhuttāti asahanto puna kalahaṃ karoti, jānissāmissa kattabbayuttaka”nti [M 3.0067] punadivase there piṇḍāya paviṭṭhe muggaraṃ gahetvā paribhogabhājanāni bhinditvā paṇṇasālaṃ jhāpetvā palāyi. So jīvamānova manussapeto hutvā sussitvā kālaṃ katvā avīcimahāniraye nibbatti. So tena kato anācāro mahājanassa majjhe pākaṭo jāto.

The next day, the Elder went to that family and sat down. The people said, "Venerable sir, what is the noble one’s illness? Yesterday, it is said you stayed in the monastery, so we sent food in the hands of such-and-such a young monk. Did the noble one partake of it?" The Elder remained silent, finished his meal, and returned to the monastery. In the evening, at the time for attending on the Elder, he called Uḷuṅkasaddaka who had come and said, "Friend, in such-and-such a village, in such-and-such a family, it is said you ate after soliciting by saying, 'This and that is suitable for the Elder to receive.'" Then he added, "Soliciting is not proper. Do not engage in such misconduct again." Nursing a grudge against the Elder for this, he thought, "Yesterday, because of a mere bit of water, he quarreled with me. Now, unable to bear that I ate a handful of rice in his supporters' home, he quarrels again. I will show him what is fit to be done!" The next day, when the Elder had entered the village for alms, he took a club, smashed the utensils, set fire to the leaf hut, and fled. While still alive, he became a human hungry ghost, withered away, died, and was reborn in the Avīci Great Hell. The misconduct he committed became widely known among the people.

Athekacce bhikkhū rājagahā sāvatthiṃ gantvā sabhāgaṭṭhāne pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tehi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kuto āgatatthā”ti pucchi. “Rājagahā, bhante”ti. “Ko tattha ovādadāyako ācariyo”ti. “Mahākassapatthero, bhante”ti. “Sukhaṃ, bhikkhave, kassapassā”ti. “Āma, bhante, therassa sukhaṃ, saddhivihāriko panassa ovāde dinne kujjhitvā therassa paṇṇasālaṃ jhāpetvā [P 3.0073] palāyīti. Taṃ sutvā satthā “bhikkhave, kassapassa evarūpena bālena saddhiṃ caraṇato ekacariyāva seyyo”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammapade gāthamāha –

Then some monks, having gone from Rājagaha to Sāvatthi, after storing their robes and bowls in a congenial place (among fellow monks), approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down. The Teacher exchanged pleasantries with them and asked, "From where have you come?" "From Rājagaha, Venerable Sir." "Who is the teacher giving advice there?" "The Elder Mahākassapa, Venerable Sir." "Monks, is Kassapa well?" "Yes, Venerable Sir, the Elder is well, but his co-resident, having been given advice, became angry, set fire to the Elder's leaf hut, and fled." Hearing this, the Teacher said, "Monks, for Kassapa, living alone is better than associating with such a fool," and spoke this verse from the Dhammapada:

“Carañce nādhigaccheyya, seyyaṃ sadisamattano;

Ekacariyaṃ daḷhaṃ kayirā, natthi bāle sahāyatā”ti. (dha. pa. 61);

"If a traveler cannot find a companion who is better or equal to himself, let him resolutely pursue a solitary course; there is no fellowship with fools."

Idañca pana vatvā puna te bhikkhū āmantetvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva so kuṭidūsako, pubbepi kuṭidūsakoyeva, na ca idāneva ovādadāyakassa kujjhati, pubbepi kujjhiyevā”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Having said this, he then addressed those monks again: "Monks, it is not only now that this hut-destroyer is a hut-destroyer; he was a hut-destroyer in the past as well. And it is not only now that he gets angry at one who gives advice; he got angry in the past as well." Being asked by them, he told a story of the past.

Atīte [V 3.0063] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto siṅgilasakuṇayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto attano manāpaṃ anovassakaṃ kulāvakaṃ katvā himavantapadese vasati. Atheko makkaṭo vassakāle acchinnadhāre deve vassante sītapīḷito dante khādanto bodhisattassa avidūre nisīdi. Bodhisatto taṃ tathā kilamantaṃ disvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a siṅgila bird and, having come of age, lived in the Himalayan region, having made a pleasing, rainproof nest. Then, during the rainy season, a monkey, drenched by the unceasing rain and afflicted by the cold, sat nearby the Bodhisatta, chattering his teeth. Seeing him in such distress, the Bodhisatta spoke to him and first uttered this verse:

81.

81.

“Manussasseva te sīsaṃ, hatthapādā ca vānara;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, agāraṃ te na vijjatī”ti.

"Your head is just like a human's, and your hands and feet, O monkey; for what reason, then, do you have no dwelling?"

Tattha [M 3.0068] vaṇṇenāti kāraṇena. Agāranti tava nivāsagehaṃ kena kāraṇena natthīti pucchi.

Here, `vaṇṇena` means 'by reason'. The question beginning with `agāraṃ...` means he asked: 'For what reason is your dwelling place not present?'

Taṃ sutvā vānaro dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the monkey spoke a second verse:

82.

82.

“Manussasseva me sīsaṃ, hatthapādā ca siṅgila;

Yāhu seṭṭhā manussesu, sā me paññā na vijjatī”ti.

"My head is just like a human's, and your hands and feet, O siṅgila bird; but that wisdom which they call best among humans—that I do not have."

Tattha siṅgilāti taṃ sakuṇaṃ nāmenālapati. Yāhu seṭṭhā manussesūti yā manussesu seṭṭhāti kathenti, sā mama vicāraṇapaññā natthi. Sīsahatthapādakāyabalāni hi loke appamāṇaṃ, vicāraṇapaññāva seṭṭhā, sā mama natthi, tasmā me agāraṃ na vijjatīti.

Here, `siṅgila` is addressing that bird by name. `Yāhu seṭṭhā manussesu` means 'that which they call best among humans'—that discerning wisdom is not mine. For in the world, the strengths of head, hands, feet, and body are beyond measure, but discerning wisdom alone is best; that I do not have; therefore, I have no dwelling.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto itaraṃ gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing that, the Bodhisatta spoke the other two verses:

83.

83.

“Anavaṭṭhitacittassa, lahucittassa dubbhino;

Niccaṃ addhuvasīlassa, sukhabhāvo na vijjati.

"For one with an unsteady mind, a fickle mind, a betrayer of friends, constantly of unstable virtue—happiness is not found."

84.

84.

“So [P 3.0074] karassu ānubhāvaṃ, vītivattassu sīliyaṃ;

Sītavātaparittāṇaṃ, karassu kuṭavaṃ kapī”ti.

"So exert your power, overcome your bad habits; make a hut, O monkey, as protection from the cold wind."

Tattha anavaṭṭhitacittassāti appatiṭṭhitacittassa. Dubbhinoti mittadubbhissa. Addhuvasīlassāti na sabbakālaṃ sīlarakkhakassa. So karassu ānubhāvanti so tvaṃ samma makkaṭa paññāya uppādanatthaṃ ānubhāvaṃ balaṃ upāyaṃ karohi. Vītivattassu sīliyanti attano dussīlabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ [V 3.0064] sīliyaṃ atikkamitvā sīlavā hoti. Kuṭavaṃ kapīti sītavātassa parittāṇasamatthaṃ attano kuṭavaṃ kulāvakaṃ ekaṃ vasanāgārakaṃ karohīti.

Here, `anavaṭṭhitacittassa` means 'one with an unestablished mind'. `Dubbhino` means 'one who betrays friends'. `Addhuvasīlassa` means 'one who does not always protect virtue'. `So karassu ānubhāvaṃ` means: 'You, friend monkey, should exert power, strength, and skillful means for the sake of producing wisdom'. `Vītivattassu sīliyaṃ` means: 'Having overcome one's own conduct characterized by immorality, one becomes virtuous'. `Kuṭavaṃ kapī` means: 'O monkey, make a hut, a nest, a small dwelling, capable of providing protection from the cold wind.'

Makkaṭo cintesi “ayaṃ tāva attano anovassakaṭṭhāne nisinnabhāvena maṃ paribhāsati, na nisīdāpessāmi naṃ imasmiṃ kulāvake”ti. Tato bodhisattaṃ gaṇhitukāmo pakkhandi, bodhisatto uppatitvā aññattha gato. Makkaṭo kulāvakaṃ viddhaṃsetvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

The monkey thought, "This bird, because he sits in a place sheltered from the rain, insults me. I will not let him remain in this nest." Then, desiring to seize the Bodhisatta, he lunged forward, but the Bodhisatta flew up and went elsewhere. The monkey destroyed the nest, reducing it to powder, and then left.

Satthā [M 3.0069] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā makkaṭo kuṭijhāpako ahosi, siṅgilasakuṇo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the birth: "At that time, the monkey was the hut-burner, and the siṅgila bird was none other than myself."

Kuṭidūsakajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kuṭidūsaka Jātaka, the First.

[322] 2. Duddubhajātakavaṇṇanā

[322] 2. Commentary on the Duddubha Jātaka

Duddubhāyati bhaddanteti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññatitthiye ārabbha kathesi. Titthiyā kira jetavanassa samīpe tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne kaṇṭakāpassaye seyyaṃ kappenti, pañcātapaṃ tapenti, nānappakāraṃ micchātapaṃ caranti. Atha sambahulā bhikkhū sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā jetavanaṃ āgacchantā antarāmagge te disvā gantvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “atthi nu kho, bhante, aññatitthiyānaṃ [P 3.0075] vatasamādāne sāro”ti pucchiṃsu. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, tesaṃ vatasamādāne sāro vā viseso vā atthi, tañhi nighaṃsiyamānaṃ upaparikkhiyamānaṃ ukkārabhūmimaggasadisaṃ sasakassa duddubhasadisaṃ hotī”ti vatvā “duddubhasadisabhāvamassa mayaṃ na jānāma, kathetha no, bhante”ti tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Duddubhāyati bhaddante”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning other sectarians. It is said that the sectarians, near Jetavana, arranged their beds on thorny ground in various places, practiced the fivefold mortification, and engaged in various kinds of wrong asceticism. Then, a number of monks, having gone to Sāvatthī for alms and returning to Jetavana, saw them on the way. Approaching the Teacher, they asked, “Venerable sir, is there any substance in the vows and observances of the other sectarians?” The Teacher replied, “No, monks, there is no substance or distinction in their vows and observances; for when scrutinized and investigated, it is like a path to a dung-heap, like the hare's duddubha sound.” When they said, “We do not understand this likeness to the hare's duddubha sound; please tell it to us, Venerable sir,” being thus requested, he told a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sīhayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto araññe paṭivasati. Tadā pana pacchimasamuddasamīpe beluvamissakatālavanaṃ hoti. Tatreko sasako beluvarukkhamūle ekassa tālagacchassa heṭṭhā vasati. So ekadivasaṃ gocaraṃ ādāya āgantvā tālapaṇṇassa heṭṭhā nipanno cintesi “sace ayaṃ pathavī saṃvaṭṭeyya, kahaṃ nu kho gamissāmī”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe ekaṃ beluvapakkaṃ tālapaṇṇassa upari pati. So tassa saddena “addhā pathavī saṃvaṭṭatī”ti uppatitvā pacchato anolokentova palāyi. Taṃ maraṇabhayabhītaṃ [V 3.0065] vegena palāyantaṃ añño sasako disvā pucchi “kiṃ bho, ativiya bhīto palāyasī”ti. “Mā pucchi, bho”ti. So “kiṃ bho, kiṃ bho”ti pacchato dhāvateva. Itaro nivattitvā anolokentova “ettha pathavī saṃvaṭṭatī”ti āha. Sopi tassa pacchato palāyi. Evaṃ tamañño addasa, tamaññoti [M 3.0070] evaṃ sasakasahassaṃ ekato hutvā palāyi. Te ekopi migo disvā ekato hutvā palāyi. Eko sūkaro, eko gokaṇṇo, eko mahiṃso, eko gavayo, eko khaggo, eko byaggho, eko sīho, eko hatthī disvā “kimeta”nti pucchitvā “ettha pathavī saṃvaṭṭatī”ti vutte [P 3.0076] palāyi. Evaṃ anukkamena yojanamattaṃ tiracchānabalaṃ ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a lion and, having come of age, lived in the forest. At that time, near the western ocean, there was a forest of wood-apple and palmyra trees mixed together. There, a hare lived at the foot of a wood-apple tree, beneath a young palmyra tree. One day, after returning from foraging, he lay down beneath a palmyra leaf and thought, “If this earth were to collapse, where would I go?” At that moment, a ripe wood-apple fruit fell onto the palmyra leaf. Hearing its sound, he thought, “Surely, the earth is collapsing!” and leaping up, he fled without looking back. Another hare, seeing him fleeing with great speed in fear of death, asked, “Why, friend, are you fleeing in such terror?” “Do not ask, friend!” But the other kept chasing after him, asking, “What is it, friend? What is it?” The first hare, without turning to look, said, “The earth is collapsing here!” The other also fled after him. In this way, one saw another, and then another, until a thousand hares were fleeing together. A deer saw them and fled together with them, and then a boar, a gokaṇṇa deer, a buffalo, a gayal, a rhinoceros, a tiger, a lion, and an elephant saw them. After asking, “What is this?” and being told, “The earth is collapsing here!” they too fled. Thus, gradually, a host of animals a league long was formed.

Tadā bodhisatto taṃ balaṃ palāyantaṃ disvā “kimeta”nti pucchitvā “ettha pathavī saṃvaṭṭatī”ti sutvā cintesi “pathavīsaṃvaṭṭanaṃ nāma na kadāci atthi, addhā etesaṃ kiñci dussutaṃ bhavissati, mayi kho pana ussukkaṃ anāpajjante sabbe nassissanti, jīvitaṃ nesaṃ dassāmī”ti sīhavegena purato pabbatapādaṃ gantvā tikkhattuṃ sīhanādaṃ nadi. Te sīhabhayatajjitā nivattitvā piṇḍitā aṭṭhaṃsu. Sīho tesaṃ antaraṃ pavisitvā “kimatthaṃ palāyathā”ti pucchi. “Pathavī saṃvaṭṭatī”ti. “Kena saṃvaṭṭamānā diṭṭhā”ti? “Hatthī jānantī”ti. Hatthī pucchi. Te “mayaṃ na jānāma, sīhā jānantī”ti vadiṃsu, sīhāpi “mayaṃ na jānāma, byagghā jānantī”ti, byagghāpi “mayaṃ na jānāma, khaggā jānantī”ti, khaggāpi “gavayā jānantī”ti, gavayāpi “mahiṃsā jānantī”ti, mahiṃsāpi “gokaṇṇā jānantī”ti, gokaṇṇāpi “sūkarā jānantī”ti, sūkarāpi “migā jānantī”ti, migāpi “mayaṃ na jānāma, sasakā jānantī”ti, sasakesu pucchiyamānesu “ayaṃ kathetī”ti taṃ sasakaṃ dassesuṃ. Atha naṃ “evaṃ kira, samma, passasi pathavī saṃvaṭṭatī”ti pucchi. “Āma, sāmi mayā diṭṭhā”ti. “Kattha vasanto passasī”ti? “Pacchimasamuddasamīpe beluvamissakatālavane vasāmi. Ahañhi tattha beluvarukkhamūle tālagacche tālapaṇṇassa heṭṭhā nipanno cintesiṃ “sace pathavī saṃvaṭṭati, kahaṃ gamissāmī”ti, atha taṅkhaṇaññeva pathaviyā saṃvaṭṭanasaddaṃ sutvā palātomhī”ti.

Then the Bodhisatta, seeing that host fleeing, asked, “What is this?” Hearing, “The earth is collapsing here,” he thought, “The collapsing of the earth is something that never happens. Surely they must have misheard something. But if I do not make an effort, they will all perish. I shall give them their lives.” With the speed of a lion, he went ahead to the foot of a mountain and roared a lion’s roar three times. Terrified by the lion’s roar, they turned back and stood huddled together. The lion entered their midst and asked, “Why do you flee?” “The earth is collapsing,” they replied. “By whom was it seen collapsing?” “The elephants know.” He asked the elephants. They said, “We do not know; the lions know.” The lions also said, “We do not know; the tigers know.” The tigers also said, “We do not know; the rhinoceroses know.” The rhinoceroses also said, “The gayals know.” The gayals also said, “The buffaloes know.” The buffaloes also said, “The gokaṇṇas know.” The gokaṇṇas also said, “The boars know.” The boars also said, “The deer know.” The deer also said, “We do not know; the hares know.” When the hares were questioned, they pointed to that hare, saying, “This one told of it.” Then the Bodhisatta asked him, “Is it true, friend, that you saw the earth collapsing?” “Yes, lord, I saw it.” “Where were you living when you saw it?” “I live near the western ocean in a forest of mixed wood-apple and palm trees. There, I was lying at the foot of a wood-apple tree beneath a palm leaf, thinking, ‘If this earth collapses, where shall I go?’ Then, at that very moment, hearing the sound of the earth collapsing, I fled.”

Sīho cintesi “addhā tassa tālapaṇṇassa upari beluvapakkaṃ patitvā duddubhāyanasaddamakāsi, svāyaṃ taṃ saddaṃ sutvā ‘pathavī saṃvaṭṭatī’ti saññaṃ uppādetvā palāyi, tathato [P 3.0077] jānissāmī”ti. So taṃ sasakaṃ gahetvā mahājanaṃ assāsetvā “ahaṃ iminā diṭṭhaṭṭhāne pathaviyā saṃvaṭṭanabhāvaṃ vā asaṃvaṭṭanabhāvaṃ vā tathato jānitvā āgamissāmi, yāva [V 3.0066][M 3.0071] mamāgamanā tumhe ettheva hothā”ti sasakaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ āropetvā sīhavegena pakkhanditvā tālavane sasakaṃ otāretvā “ehi tayā diṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ dassehī”ti āha. “Na visahāmi sāmī”ti. “Ehi mā bhāyī”ti. So beluvarukkhaṃ upasaṅkamituṃ asakkonto avidūre ṭhatvā “idaṃ sāmi duddubhāyanaṭṭhāna”nti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The lion thought, “Surely, a ripe wood-apple fruit must have fallen on that palm leaf, making a ‘duddubha’ sound. Hearing that sound, this one formed the perception that the earth was collapsing and fled. I will ascertain the truth of this.” Taking the hare, he reassured the multitude of animals, saying, “I will go with this one to the place he saw and ascertain the truth of whether the earth is collapsing or not. Until I return, you are to remain right here.” Placing the hare on his back, he dashed off with the speed of a lion to the palm grove and set the hare down. “Come, show me the place you saw,” he said. “I dare not, lord,” the hare replied. “Come, do not be afraid,” the lion urged. Unable to approach the wood-apple tree, the hare stood at a distance and said, “This, lord, is the place of the ‘duddubha’ sound,” and then he spoke the first verse:

85.

85.

“Duddubhāyati bhaddante, yasmiṃ dese vasāmahaṃ;

Ahampetaṃ na jānāmi, kimetaṃ duddubhāyatī”ti.

“A ‘duddubha’ sound is made, venerable sir, in the region where I live; I do not know this thing, what it is that makes this ‘duddubha’ sound.”

Tattha duddubhāyatīti duddubhasaddaṃ karoti. Bhaddanteti bhaddaṃ tava atthu. Kimetanti yasmiṃ padese ahaṃ vasāmi, tattha duddubhāyati, ahampi na jānāmi “kiṃ vā etaṃ duddubhāyati, kena vā kāraṇena duddubhāyati, kevalaṃ duddubhāyanasaddaṃ assosi”nti.

Therein, ‘duddubhāyati’ means it makes a ‘duddubha’ sound. ‘Bhaddante’ means ‘may it be well with you.’ ‘Kimetanti’ means: ‘In the place where I dwell, a ‘duddubha’ sound is made, and I myself do not know what it is that makes this ‘duddubha’ sound, or for what reason it is made; I only heard the sound of the ‘duddubha’.’

Evaṃ vutte sīho beluvarukkhamūlaṃ gantvā tālapaṇṇassa heṭṭhā sasakena nipannaṭṭhānañceva tālapaṇṇamatthake patitaṃ beluvapakkañca disvā pathaviyā asaṃvaṭṭanabhāvaṃ tathato jānitvā sasakaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ āropetvā sīhavegena khippaṃ migasaṅghānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “tumhe mā bhāyathā”ti migagaṇaṃ assāsetvā vissajjesi. Sace hi tadā bodhisatto na bhaveyya, sabbe samuddaṃ pavisitvā nasseyyuṃ. Bodhisattaṃ pana nissāya sabbe jīvitaṃ labhiṃsūti.

When this was said, the lion went to the foot of the wood-apple tree and saw both the place where the hare had lain beneath the palm leaf and the ripe wood-apple fruit that had fallen on top of the palm leaf. Having ascertained the fact that the earth was not collapsing, he placed the hare on his back and swiftly, with the speed of a lion, went to the multitude of animals. There, he related the entire incident and reassured the host of animals, saying, “Do not be afraid,” before dismissing them. For if the Bodhisatta had not been there at that time, they all would have entered the sea and perished. But on account of the Bodhisatta, they all received their lives.

86.

86.

“Beluvaṃ patitaṃ sutvā, duddubhanti saso javi;

Sasassa vacanaṃ sutvā, santattā migavāhinī.

“Hearing a wood-apple fruit fall with a ‘duddubha’ sound, the hare fled; hearing the words of the hare, the animal host was terrified.”

87.

87.

“Appatvā padaviññāṇaṃ, paraghosānusārino;

Panādaparamā bālā, te honti parapattiyā.

“Not having reached an understanding of the cause, following the noise of others; fools for whom clamor is supreme, they are led by others.”

88.

88.

“Ye [P 3.0078] ca sīlena sampannā, paññāyūpasame ratā;

Ārakā viratā dhīrā, na honti parapattiyā”ti. –

“But those who are endowed with virtue, delighting in wisdom and in calm, who are remote from evil, restrained, and wise—they are not led by others.”

Imā tisso abhisambuddhagāthā.

These are the three verses spoken after Enlightenment.

Tattha beluvanti beluvapakkaṃ. Duddubhantīti evaṃ saddaṃ kurumānaṃ. Santattāti utrastā. Migavāhinīti [V 3.0067] anekasahassasaṅkhā migasenā. Padaviññāṇanti viññāṇapadaṃ[M 3.0072], sotaviññāṇakoṭṭhāsaṃ apāpuṇitvāti attho. Te honti parapattiyāti te paraghosānusārino tameva paraghosasaṅkhātaṃ panādaṃ “parama”nti maññamānā bālā andhaputhujjanā viññāṇapadassa appattatāya parapattiyāva honti, paresaṃ vacanaṃ saddahitvā yaṃ vā taṃ vā karonti.

Therein, ‘beluva’ means a ripe beluva fruit. ‘Duddubhanti’ means making such a sound. ‘Santattā’ means terrified. ‘Migavāhinī’ means an animal army numbering many thousands. ‘Padaviññāṇa’ means the basis of consciousness; the meaning is not having reached the sphere of ear-consciousness. ‘Te honti parapattiyā’ means: those followers of the noise of others, those foolish, blind worldlings, considering that very clamor known as the noise of others to be supreme, because of not having attained the basis of consciousness, are indeed led by others; believing the words of others, they do this or that.

Sīlenāti ariyamaggena āgatasīlena samannāgatā. Paññāyūpasame ratāti maggeneva āgatapaññāya kilesūpasame ratā, yathā vā sīlena, evaṃ paññāyapi sampannā, kilesūpasame ratātipi attho. Ārakā viratā dhīrāti pāpakiriyato ārakā viratā paṇḍitā. Na hontīti te evarūpā sotāpannā pāpato oratabhāvena kilesūpasame abhiratabhāvena ca ekavāraṃ maggañāṇena paṭividdhadhammā aññesaṃ kathentānampi na saddahanti na gaṇhanti. Kasmā? Attano paccakkhattāti. Tena vuttaṃ –

‘Endowed with virtue’ means endowed with the virtue that has come by way of the Noble Path. ‘Delighting in wisdom and in calm’ means delighting in the calming of defilements by means of the wisdom that has come by way of the path itself; or, just as they are endowed with virtue, so too are they endowed with wisdom, and the meaning is also ‘delighting in the calming of defilements.’ ‘Aloof, restrained, and wise’ means aloof from and restrained from evil action; the wise. ‘They are not’ means: such ones, stream-enterers, because of their turning away from evil and their delighting in the calming of defilements, having once penetrated the Dhamma with the knowledge of the path, do not believe or accept it even when others speak. Why? Because of their own direct realization. Thus it is said—

“Assaddho akataññū ca, sandhicchedo ca yo naro;

Hatāvakāso vantāso, sa ve uttamaporiso”ti. (dha. pa. 97);

“The man who is without faith, the knower of the uncreated, who has severed connections, who has destroyed all opportunity, and who has disgorged all desires—he is indeed the supreme person.”

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sīho ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth story: “At that time, the lion was I myself.”

Duddubhajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Duddubha Jātaka is finished.

[323] 3. Brahmadattajātakavaṇṇanā

[323] 3. 3. The Brahmadatta Jātaka

Dvayaṃ yācanakoti idaṃ satthā āḷaviṃ nissāya aggāḷave cetiye viharanto kuṭikārasikkhāpadaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pana heṭṭhā maṇikaṇṭhajātake (jā. 1.3.7 ādayo) āgatameva. Idha pana satthā “saccaṃ kira tumhe, bhikkhave, yācanabahulā viññattibahulā viharathā”ti vatvā “āma, bhante”ti vutte te bhikkhū garahitvā “bhikkhave, porāṇakapaṇḍitā pathavissarena raññā pavāritāpi paṇṇacchattañca ekapaṭalikaṃ upāhanayugañca yācitukāmā hirottappabhedanabhayena mahājanamajjhe akathetvā raho kathayiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“A supplicant is twofold”—this the Teacher told while staying at the Aggāḷava Shrine near Āḷavī, concerning the training rule on building huts. The story has been told in the Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka. Here, the Teacher asked, “Is it true, monks, that you live asking and requesting much?” When they said, “Yes, Bhante,” he rebuked them, saying, “Monks, wise men of old, though invited by a king, the lord of the earth, when they wanted to ask for a leaf-umbrella and a pair of single-soled sandals, were afraid of losing their sense of shame and moral dread and did not speak in the midst of the people but spoke in private.” Having said this, he told the story of the past.

Atīte [P 3.0079][M 3.0073] kapilaraṭṭhe uttarapañcālanagare uttarapañcālarāje rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ nigamagāme brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā [V 3.0068] aparabhāge tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavante uñchācariyāya vanamūlaphalāphalena yāpento ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya manussapathaṃ vicaranto uttarapañcālanagaraṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase bhikkhaṃ pariyesamāno nagaraṃ pavisitvā rājadvāraṃ sampāpuṇi. Rājā tassācāre ca vihāre ca pasīditvā mahātale nisīdāpetvā rājārahaṃ paṇītabhojanaṃ bhojetvā paṭiññaṃ gahetvā uyyāneyeva vasāpesi. So nibaddhaṃ rājaghareyeva bhuñjanto vassānassa accayena himavantameva gantukāmo hutvā cintesi “mayhaṃ maggaṃ gacchantassa ekapaṭalikā upāhanā ceva paṇṇacchattañca laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, rājānaṃ yācissāmī”ti. So ekadivasaṃ rājānaṃ uyyānaṃ āgantvā vanditvā nisinnaṃ disvā “upāhanañca chattañca yācissāmī”ti cintetvā puna cintesi “paraṃ ‘imaṃ nāma dehī’ti yācanto rodati nāma, paropi ‘natthī’ti vadanto paṭirodati nāma, ‘mā kho pana maṃ rodantaṃ mahājano addasa, mā rājāna”nti raho paṭicchannaṭṭhāne ubhopi roditvā tuṇhī bhavissāmā”ti. Atha naṃ “mahārāja, raho paccāsīsāmī”ti āha. Rājā taṃ sutvā rājapurise apasakki. Bodhisatto “sace mayi yācante rājā na dassati, metti no bhijjissati, tasmā na yācissāmī”ti taṃ divasaṃ nāmaṃ gahetuṃ asakkonto “gaccha, tāva, mahārāja, punekadivasaṃ jānissāmī”ti āha.

In the past, when King Uttarapañcāla was reigning in the city of Uttarapañcāla in the kingdom of Kapila, the Bodhisatta was born in a brahmin family in a market town. When he came of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā. Later he went forth as an ascetic and lived a long time in the Himalayas, sustaining himself on wild roots and fruits found by gleaning. He came to the world of men for salt and sour things and reached the city of Uttarapañcāla, staying in the royal park. The next day, while seeking alms, he entered the city and reached the palace gate. The king, pleased with his conduct and deportment, invited him to the upper floor, fed him with food fit for a king, and having received his promise, made him stay in the park. He ate regularly at the palace. At the end of the rainy season, wishing to go to the Himalayas, he thought: “For my journey, I should have a pair of single-soled sandals and a leaf-umbrella; I will ask the king.” One day, seeing the king come to the park and sit down after paying homage, he thought: “I will ask for the sandals and umbrella.” Then he thought: “One who asks another for something is said to weep; and the owner who says ‘I have none’ is said to weep in return. Let not the people see me weeping, nor the king. We shall both weep in a private place and then be silent.” Then he said: “Great King, I desire a private word.” The king dismissed the attendants. The Bodhisatta thought: “If the king does not give when I ask, our friendship will be broken. Therefore I will not ask.” Being unable to speak the name of the objects that day, he said: “Go for now, Great King; I will let you know another day.”

Punekadivasaṃ rañño uyyānaṃ āgatakāle tatheva puna tathevāti evaṃ yācituṃ asakkontasseva dvādasa saṃvaccharāni atikkantāni. Tato rājā cintesi “mayhaṃ [P 3.0080] ayyo ‘mahārāja, raho paccāsīsāmī’ti vatvā parisāya apagatāya kiñci vattuṃ na visahati, vattukāmassevassa dvādasa vassāni atikkantāni, ciraṃ kho panassa brahmacariyaṃ carantassa ukkaṇṭhitvā bhoge bhuñjitukāmo rajjaṃ paccāsīsati maññe, rajjassa pana nāmaṃ gahetuṃ asakkonto tuṇhī hoti, ajja dānissāhaṃ rajjaṃ ādiṃ katvā yaṃ icchati, taṃ dassāmī”ti. So uyyānaṃ gantvā vanditvā nisinno bodhisattena “raho [M 3.0074] paccāsīsāmī”ti vutte parisāya apagatāya taṃ kiñci vattuṃ asakkontaṃ āha “tumhe dvādasa vassāni ‘raho paccāsīsāmī’ti vatvā raho laddhāpi kiñci vattuṃ na sakkotha, ahaṃ vo rajjaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ pavāremi, nibbhayā hutvā yaṃ vo ruccati, taṃ yācathā”ti. “Mahārāja, yamahaṃ yācāmi, taṃ dassasī”ti? “Dassāmi, bhante”ti. “Mahārāja, mayhaṃ maggaṃ gacchantassa ekapaṭalikā upāhanā ca paṇṇacchattañca laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Ettakaṃ, bhante, tumhe dvādasa saṃvaccharāni yācituṃ na sakkothā”ti. “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā, bhante, evamakatthā”ti. “Mahārāja, ‘imaṃ nāma me dehī’ti yācanto rodati nāma, ‘natthī’ti vadanto [V 3.0069] paṭirodati nāma. ‘Sace tvaṃ mayā yācito na dadeyyāsi, taṃ no roditapaṭiroditaṃ nāma mahājano mā passatū’ti etadatthaṃ raho paccāsīsāmī”ti vatvā ādito tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Another day when the king came to the park, it was the same, and yet again the same; in this way, twelve years passed without him being able to ask. Then the king thought: “My master says ‘I desire a private word,’ but when the crowd is gone, he dares not say anything. Twelve years have passed for him who wants to speak. Long has he lived the holy life; perhaps he is dissatisfied and desires the kingdom to enjoy pleasures, but being unable to name the kingdom, he remains silent. Today I will offer him everything, beginning with the kingdom.” He went to the park, paid homage, and sat down. When the Bodhisatta said he desired a private word and the crowd was gone, the king said to him: “For twelve years you have said you want a private word, but even when private you cannot speak. I offer you everything, starting with the kingdom; be fearless and ask for whatever you like.” “Great King, will you give me what I ask?” “I will give it, Bhante.” “Great King, for my journey I need a pair of single-soled sandals and a leaf-umbrella.” “Bhante, were you unable to ask for just this for twelve years?” “Yes, Great King.” “Why did you do so, Bhante?” “Great King, one who asks for something is said to weep; he who says ‘I have none’ is said to weep in return. If you did not give when asked, I did not want the people to see us weeping and weeping-in-return. For this reason, I desired a private word.” Having said this, he recited these three verses:

89.

89.

“Dvayaṃ yācanako rāja, brahmadatta nigacchati;

Alābhaṃ dhanalābhaṃ vā, evaṃdhammā hi yācanā.

“A supplicant, O King Brahmadatta, meets with two things: either failure or the gain of wealth; for such is the nature of asking.”

90.

90.

“Yācanaṃ rodanaṃ āhu, pañcālānaṃ rathesabha;

Yo yācanaṃ paccakkhāti, tamāhu paṭirodanaṃ.

“Asking is called weeping, O lord of the charioteers of the Pañcālas; he who refuses the request is said to weep in return.”

91.

91.

“Mā maddasaṃsu rodantaṃ, pañcālā susamāgatā;

Tuvaṃ vā paṭirodantaṃ, tasmā icchāmahaṃ raho”ti.

“May the assembled Pañcālas not see me weeping, nor you weeping in return; therefore, I desire privacy.”

Tattha [P 3.0081] rāja brahmadattāti dvīhipi rājānaṃ ālapati. Nigacchatīti labhati vindati. Evaṃdhammāti evaṃsabhāvā. Āhūti paṇḍitā kathenti. Pañcālānaṃ rathesabhāti pañcālaraṭṭhassa issara rathapavara. Yo yācanaṃ paccakkhātīti yo pana yaṃ yācanakaṃ “natthī”ti paṭikkhipati. Tamāhūti taṃ paṭikkhipanaṃ “paṭirodana”nti vadanti. Mā maddasaṃsūti tava raṭṭhavāsino pañcālā susamāgatā maṃ rodantaṃ mā addasaṃsūti.

Therein, 'O King, Brahmadatta': with both terms he addresses the king. 'Nigacchati' means obtains or finds. 'Evaṃdhammā' means of such a nature. 'Āhu' means the wise say. 'O bull among the charioteers of the Pañcālas' means lord of the Pañcāla country, an excellent chariot-warrior. 'He who refuses a request' means whoever rejects a supplicant, saying, 'There is none.' 'That they call' means that rejection they call 'weeping-in-return.' 'May they not see' means may the well-assembled Pañcālas, the inhabitants of your country, not see me weeping.

Rājā bodhisattassa gāravalakkhaṇe pasīditvā varaṃ dadamāno catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, pleased by the Bodhisatta's mark of respectfulness, offering a boon, spoke the fourth verse:

92.

92.

“Dadāmi te brāhmaṇa rohiṇīnaṃ, gavaṃ sahassaṃ saha puṅgavena;

Ariyo hi ariyassa kathaṃ na dajjā, sutvāna gāthā tava dhammayuttā”ti.

"I give to you, Brahmin, a thousand reddish cows with a bull; for how should a noble one not give to a noble one, having heard your verses that are in accord with the Dhamma?"

Tattha [M 3.0075] rohiṇīnanti rattavaṇṇānaṃ. Ariyoti ācārasampanno. Ariyassāti ācārasampannassa. Kathaṃ na dajjāti kena kāraṇena na dadeyya. Dhammayuttāti kāraṇayuttā.

Therein, 'rohiṇīnaṃ' means of a red color. 'Ariyo' means one accomplished in conduct. 'Ariyassa' means to one accomplished in conduct. 'Kathaṃ na dajjā' means for what reason would he not give? 'Dhammayuttā' means connected with reason.

Bodhisatto pana “nāhaṃ, mahārāja, vatthukāmehi atthiko, yaṃ ahaṃ yācāmi, tadeva me dehī”ti ekapaṭalikā upāhanā ca paṇṇacchattañca gahetvā “mahārāja, appamatto hohi, dānaṃ dehi, sīlaṃ rakkhāhi, uposathakammaṃ karohī”ti rājānaṃ ovaditvā tassa yācantasseva himavantameva [V 3.0070] gato. Tattha abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

But the Bodhisatta said, "Great king, I have no need for objects of sensual pleasure. Give me only what I ask for." Taking the single-soled sandals and the leaf parasol, he advised the king, "Great king, be heedful, give gifts, guard your virtue, and perform the Uposatha observance." Having thus admonished the king while he was still imploring, he went to the Himalayas. There, having produced the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, he was destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having given this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the ascetic was myself.”

Brahmadattajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Brahmadatta Jātaka, the Third.

[324] 4. Cammasāṭakajātakavaṇṇanā

[324] 4. The Commentary on the Cammasāṭaka Jātaka

Kalyāṇarūpo [P 3.0082] vatayanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto cammasāṭakaṃ nāma paribbājakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa kira cammameva nivāsanañca pārupanañca hoti. So ekadivasaṃ paribbājakārāmā nikkhamitvā sāvatthiyaṃ bhikkhāya caranto eḷakānaṃ yujjhanaṭṭhānaṃ sampāpuṇi. Eḷako taṃ disvā paharitukāmo osakki. Paribbājako “esa mayhaṃ apacitiṃ dassetī”ti na paṭikkami. Eḷako vegenāgantvā taṃ ūrumhi paharitvā pātesi. Tassa taṃ asantapaggahaṇakāraṇaṃ bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭaṃ ahosi. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, cammasāṭakaparibbājako asantapaggahaṃ katvā vināsaṃ patto”ti satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa asantapaggahaṃ katvā vināsaṃ pattoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Truly, he is handsome in appearance”—the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this in reference to a wanderer named Cammasāṭaka. It is said that he had only a hide for both his lower garment and upper robe. One day, having left the wanderers’ park, he entered Sāvatthī for alms and reached a place where rams were fighting. A ram, seeing him and wanting to strike him, drew back. The wanderer, thinking, “This one is showing me respect,” did not retreat. The ram swiftly came and struck him on the thigh, knocking him down. This incident of his honouring the unworthy became known among the Sangha of bhikkhus. The bhikkhus started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, the wanderer Cammasāṭaka, by honouring the unworthy, met with destruction.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Bhikkhus, what is the topic of your discussion as you sit together now?” When they replied, “This is the matter,” he said, “Bhikkhus, not only now, but even in the past, he met with destruction by honouring the unworthy.” Then he recounted a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ vāṇijakule nibbattitvā vayappatto vaṇijjaṃ karoti. Tadā eko [M 3.0076] cammasāṭakaparibbājako bārāṇasiyaṃ bhikkhāya caranto eḷakānaṃ yujjhanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā eḷakaṃ osakkantaṃ disvā “apacitiṃ me karotī”ti saññāya apaṭikkamitvā “imesaṃ ettakānaṃ manussānaṃ antare ayaṃ eko eḷako amhākaṃ guṇaṃ jānātī”ti tassa añjaliṃ paggahetvā ṭhitova paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a merchant family and, having come of age, engaged in trade. At that time, a wanderer wearing a hide garment, while wandering for alms in Bārāṇasī, came to a place where rams were fighting. Seeing a ram drawing back, he thought, “It is showing me respect,” and without retreating, he reflected, “Among so many people, this one ram knows our virtue.” Then, standing with hands reverently joined toward it, he spoke the first verse:

93.

93.

“Kalyāṇarūpo vatayaṃ catuppado, subhaddako ceva supesalo ca;

Yo brāhmaṇaṃ jātimantūpapannaṃ, apacāyati meṇḍavaro yasassī”ti.

“Truly, this four-footed one is handsome, auspicious, and very gentle; this glorious, excellent ram reveres the brahmin, endowed with birth and sacred knowledge.”

Tattha [V 3.0071] kalyāṇarūpoti kalyāṇajātiko. Supesaloti suṭṭhu piyasīlo. Jātimantūpapannanti jātiyā ca mantehi ca sampannaṃ. Yasassīti vaṇṇabhaṇanametaṃ.

Here, ‘handsome in appearance’ (kalyāṇarūpo) means of noble birth (kalyāṇajātiko). ‘Very gentle’ (supesalo) means of very pleasing character (suṭṭhu piyasīlo). ‘Endowed with birth and sacred knowledge’ (jātimantūpapannaṃ) means endowed with birth and with sacred texts (mantehi). ‘Glorious’ (yasassī)—this is a term of commendation.

Tasmiṃ [P 3.0083] khaṇe āpaṇe nisinno paṇḍitavāṇijo taṃ paribbājakaṃ nisedhento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

At that moment, the wise merchant sitting in his shop, admonishing that wanderer, spoke the second verse:

94.

94.

“Mā brāhmaṇa ittaradassanena, vissāsamāpajji catuppadassa;

Daḷhappahāraṃ abhikaṅkhamāno, avasakkatī dassati suppahāra”nti.

“O brahmin, do not place trust in a four-footed creature because of a momentary sight; desiring a firm blow, it draws back and will deliver a powerful blow.”

Tattha ittaradassanenāti khaṇikadassanena.

Here, ‘because of a momentary sight’ (ittaradassanena) means by a momentary sight (khaṇikadassanena).

Tassa paṇḍitavāṇijassa kathentasseva so meṇḍako vegenāgantvā ūrumhi paharitvā taṃ tattheva vedanāppattaṃ katvā pātesi. So paridevamāno nipajji. Satthā taṃ kāraṇaṃ pakāsento tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

While the wise merchant was still speaking, that ram swiftly approached and struck him on the thigh, causing him to fall down right there in pain. Lamenting, he lay down. The Teacher, revealing that incident, spoke the third verse:

95.

95.

“Ūruṭṭhi bhaggaṃ vaṭṭito khāribhāro, sabbañca bhaṇḍaṃ brāhmaṇassa bhinnaṃ;

Ubhopi bāhā paggayha kandati, atidhāvatha haññate brahmacārī”ti.

“His thigh-bone is broken, the load of a pole-basket has overturned, and all the brahmin’s goods are shattered; he cries out, raising both arms, ‘Run quickly! The celibate is being killed!’”

Tassattho [M 3.0077] – bhikkhave, tassa paribbājakassa ūruṭṭhikaṃ bhaggaṃ, khāribhāro vaṭṭito pavaṭṭito, tasmiṃ pavaṭṭamāne yaṃ tattha tassa brāhmaṇassa upakaraṇabhaṇḍaṃ, tampi sabbaṃ bhinnaṃ, sopi ubho bāhā ukkhipitvā parivāretvā ṭhitaparisaṃ sandhāya “abhidhāvatha, haññate brahmacārī”ti vadanto kandati rodati paridevatīti.

The meaning is this: Bhikkhus, that wanderer’s thigh-bone was broken, and the load of the pole-basket was overturned and rolled about. As it was rolling about, whatever goods and utensils belonging to that brahmin were there, all of them were shattered. And he, raising both arms and addressing the crowd standing around him, cried out, “Run quickly! The celibate is being killed!” weeping, wailing, and lamenting.

Paribbājako catutthaṃ gāthaṃ āha –

The wanderer spoke the fourth verse:

96.

96.

“Evaṃ so nihato seti, yo apūjaṃ pasaṃsati;

Yathāhamajja pahato, hato meṇḍena dummatī”ti.

“Thus lies he slain who praises the unworthy; as I am struck down today, the fool is slain by the ram.”

Tattha apūjanti apūjanīyaṃ. Yathāhamajjāti yathā ahaṃ ajja asantapaggahaṃ katvā ṭhito meṇḍena daḷhappahārena pahato ettheva mārito[P 3.0084]. Dummatīti duppañño. Evaṃ yo aññopi [V 3.0072] asantapaggahaṃ karissati, sopi ahaṃ viya dukkhaṃ anubhavissatīti so paridevanto tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pattoti.

Here, ‘the unworthy’ (apūjaṃ) means one unworthy of honor (apūjanīyaṃ). ‘As I today’ (yathāhamajja) means as I today, having shown misplaced favor, was struck by the ram with a hard blow and killed right here. ‘The fool’ (dummatī) means the unwise one (duppañño). ‘Thus, whoever else shows misplaced favor will also experience suffering like me’—lamenting thus, he met his end right there.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā cammasāṭako etarahi cammasāṭako ahosi, paṇḍitavāṇijo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having given this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the wanderer with the hide garment was the present wanderer with the hide garment, and the wise merchant was I myself.”

Cammasāṭakajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Cammasāṭaka Jātaka: The Fourth.

[325] 5. Godharājajātakavaṇṇanā

[325] 5. The Commentary on the Godharāja Jātaka

Samaṇaṃ taṃ maññamānoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuhakaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā vitthāritameva. Idhāpi bhikkhū taṃ bhikkhuṃ ānetvā “ayaṃ, bhante, bhikkhu kuhako”ti satthu dassesuṃ. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa kuhakoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Thinking him a recluse”—the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this in reference to a deceitful bhikkhu. The story has been related in detail before. Here too the bhikkhus, bringing that bhikkhu, showed him to the Teacher, saying: “Venerable Sir, this bhikkhu is deceitful.” The Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, not only now, but even in the past, he was deceitful.” Then he recounted a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto godhayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto kāyabalena sampanno araññe vasati[M 3.0078]. Eko dusīlatāpasopi tassa avidūre paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Bodhisatto gocarāya caranto taṃ disvā “sīlavantatāpasassa paṇṇasālā bhavissatī”ti tattha gantvā taṃ vanditvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gacchati. Athekadivasaṃ so kūṭatāpaso upaṭṭhākakule sampāditaṃ madhuramaṃsaṃ labhitvā “kiṃ maṃsaṃ nāmeta”nti pucchitvā “godhamaṃsa”nti sutvā rasataṇhāya abhibhūto “mayhaṃ assamapadaṃ nibaddhaṃ āgacchamānaṃ godhaṃ māretvā yathāruci pacitvā khādissāmī”ti sappidadhikaṭukabhaṇḍādīni gahetvā tattha gantvā muggaraṃ gahetvā kāsāvena paṭicchādetvā bodhisattassa āgamanaṃ olokento paṇṇasāladvāre upasantūpasanto viya nisīdi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a monitor lizard and, having reached maturity, lived in the forest endowed with physical strength. A certain immoral ascetic also built a leaf-hut not far from him and took up residence. The Bodhisatta, while roaming for food, saw it and thought, “This must be the leaf-hut of a virtuous ascetic,” so he went there, paid respects, and then returned to his own dwelling place. One day, that fraudulent ascetic received delicious meat prepared by his supporters and asked, “What kind of meat is this?” Hearing it was monitor lizard meat, overcome by craving for the taste, he thought, “I will kill the monitor lizard that regularly comes to my hermitage, cook it as I please, and eat it.” Taking ghee, curds, and spices, he went there, seized a club, concealed it with his ascetic robe, and sat by the door of the leaf-hut, watching for the Bodhisatta’s arrival, appearing very tranquil.

So āgantvā taṃ paduṭṭhindriyaṃ disvā [P 3.0085] “iminā amhākaṃ sajātikamaṃsaṃ khāditaṃ bhavissati, pariggaṇhissāmi na”nti adhovāte ṭhatvā sarīragandhaṃ ghāyitvā sajātimaṃsassa khāditabhāvaṃ ñatvā tāpasaṃ anupagamma paṭikkamitvā cari. Tāpasopi tassa anāgamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā muggaraṃ khipi, muggaro sarīre apatitvā naṅguṭṭhakoṭiṃ pāpuṇi. Tāpaso “gaccha viraddhosmī”ti āha. Bodhisatto “maṃ tāva viraddhosi, cattāro pana apāye na viraddhosī”ti [V 3.0073] vatvā palāyitvā caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ṭhitaṃ vammikaṃ pavisitvā aññena chiddena sīsaṃ nīharitvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

He arrived and, seeing that one with corrupted faculties, thought, “This one must have eaten the flesh of our own kind. I will investigate.” Standing downwind, he caught the scent and, knowing that the flesh of his own kind had been eaten, did not approach the ascetic but turned back. The ascetic, realizing he was not coming, threw the club. The club missed his body but struck the tip of his tail. The ascetic said, “Go, I have missed you.” The Bodhisatta replied, “You may have missed me, but you have not missed the four states of woe.” Having spoken thus, he fled and entered an anthill that stood at the edge of the walking path. Sticking his head out through another hole, he conversed with the ascetic and uttered two verses:

97.

97.

“Samaṇaṃ taṃ maññamāno, upagacchimasaññataṃ;

So maṃ daṇḍena pāhāsi, yathā assamaṇo tathā.

“Thinking him a recluse, I approached one unrestrained; he struck at me with a stick, just as a non-recluse would.

98.

98.

“Kiṃ te jaṭāhi dummedha, kiṃ te ajinasāṭiyā;

Abbhantaraṃ te gahanaṃ, bāhiraṃ parimajjasī”ti.

“What use are your matted locks, you fool? What use your garment of hide? Your inside is a thicket; you only cleanse the outside.”

Tattha asaññatanti ahaṃ kāyādīhi asaññataṃ assamaṇameva samānaṃ taṃ “samaṇo eso”ti samitapāpatāya samaṇaṃ maññamāno upagacchiṃ. Pāhāsīti pahari. Ajinasāṭiyāti ekaṃsaṃ katvā pārutena ajinacammena tuyhaṃ ko attho. Abbhantaraṃ te gahananti tava sarīrabbhantaraṃ visapūrā viya alābu, gūthapūro viya āvāṭo, āsīvisapūro viya vammiko kilesagahanaṃ. Bāhiranti kevalaṃ bahisarīraṃ parimajjasi[M 3.0079], taṃ antopharusatāya bahimaṭṭhatāya hatthilaṇḍaṃ viya assalaṇḍaṃ viya ca hotīti.

Here, ‘unrestrained’ (asaññataṃ) means: I approached him, thinking, “This is a recluse,” because I thought his evil was calmed, even though he was in fact unrestrained in body and so forth, a non-recluse. ‘He struck’ (pāhāsi) means he hit (pahari). ‘Your garment of hide’ (ajinasāṭiyā) means: what use to you is an antelope hide worn over one shoulder? ‘Your inside is a thicket’ (abbhantaraṃ te gahanaṃ) means: the inside of your body is a thicket of defilements, like a gourd filled with poison, a pit filled with excrement, or an anthill filled with vipers. ‘The outside’ (bāhiraṃ) means: you merely polish the exterior of your body. Because of inner roughness and outer smoothness, it is like elephant dung or horse dung.

Taṃ sutvā tāpaso tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the ascetic spoke the third verse:

99.

99.

“Ehi godha nivattassu, bhuñja sālīnamodanaṃ;

Telaṃ loṇañca me atthi, pahūtaṃ mayha pipphalī”ti.

“Come, monitor lizard, turn back, enjoy a meal of fine rice; I have oil and salt, and plenty of long pepper.”

Tattha [P 3.0086] pahūtaṃ mayha pipphalīti na kevalaṃ sālīnamodanaṃ telaloṇameva, hiṅgujīrakasiṅgiveralasuṇamaricapipphalippabhedaṃ kaṭukabhaṇḍampi mayhaṃ bahu atthi, tenābhisaṅkhataṃ sālīnamodanaṃ bhuñjāhīti.

Here, ‘I have plenty of long pepper’ means: not only fine rice, oil, and salt, but I also have many pungent spices, such as asafoetida, cumin, ginger, garlic, black pepper, and long pepper. Eat this fine rice prepared with them.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Bodhisatta spoke the fourth stanza:

100.

100.

“Esa bhiyyo pavekkhāmi, vammikaṃ sataporisaṃ;

Telaṃ loṇañca kittesi, ahitaṃ mayha pipphalī”ti.

“Now I will enter even further into the anthill, a hundred men deep. You praise oil and salt, but your long pepper is harmful to me.”

Tattha [V 3.0074] pavekkhāmīti pavisissāmi. Ahitanti yaṃ etaṃ tava kaṭukabhaṇḍasaṅkhātaṃ pipphali, etaṃ mayhaṃ ahitaṃ asappāyanti.

Here, ‘I will enter’ (pavekkhāmi) means ‘I will enter’ (pavisissāmi). ‘Harmful’ (ahitaṃ) means: that pungent spice of yours, namely long pepper, is harmful and unsuitable for me.

Evañca pana vatvā “are, kūṭajaṭila, sace idha vasissasi, gocaragāme manusseheva taṃ ‘ayaṃ coro’ti gāhāpetvā vippakāraṃ pāpessāmi, sīghaṃ palāyassū”ti santajjesi. Kūṭajaṭilo tato palāyi.

Having said this, he threatened him, “Hey, false ascetic! If you stay here, I will have the people in the alms-resort village seize you as a thief and bring you to ruin. Flee quickly!” The false ascetic fled from there.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kūṭajaṭilo ayaṃ kuhakabhikkhu ahosi, godharājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the false ascetic was this deceitful monk, and the monitor lizard king was I myself.”

Godharājajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Godharāja Jātaka: The Fifth.

[326] 6. Kakkārujātakavaṇṇanā

[326] 6. The Commentary on the Kakkāru Jātaka

Kāyena yo nāvahareti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa hi saṅghaṃ bhinditvā gatassa aggasāvakehi saddhiṃ parisāya pakkantāya uṇhaṃ lohitaṃ mukhato uggañchi. Atha bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto musāvādaṃ [M 3.0080] katvā saṅghaṃ bhinditvā idāni gilāno hutvā mahādukkhaṃ anubhotī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa musāvādīyeva, na cesa idāneva musāvādaṃ katvā mahādukkhaṃ anubhoti, pubbepi anubhosiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“He who with his body would not take...” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta. For when he had split the Saṅgha and departed, and the assembly had left him along with the chief disciples, hot blood gushed from his mouth. Then the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, Devadatta, having told a lie and split the Saṅgha, is now ill and experiencing great suffering.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered here?” When they told him, he said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past, too, he was a liar. And not only now does he experience great suffering for telling a lie, but he experienced it in the past as well.” Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 3.0087] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tāvatiṃsabhavane aññataro devaputto ahosi. Tena kho pana samayena bārāṇasiyaṃ mahāussavo ahosi. Bahū nāgā ca supaṇṇā ca bhūmaṭṭhakā ca devā āgantvā ussavaṃ olokayiṃsu. Tāvatiṃsabhavanatopi cattāro devaputtā kakkārūni nāma dibbapupphāni tehi katacumbaṭakaṃ piḷandhitvā ussavadassanaṃ āgamiṃsu. Dvādasayojanikaṃ bārāṇasinagaraṃ tesaṃ pupphānaṃ gandhena ekagandhaṃ ahosi. Manussā “imāni pupphāni kena piḷandhitānī”ti upadhārentā vicaranti. Te devaputtā “amhe ete upadhārentī”ti ñatvā rājaṅgaṇe uppatitvā mahantena devānubhāvena ākāse aṭṭhaṃsu. Mahājano sannipati, rājāpi saddhiṃ uparājādīhi agamāsi. Atha ne “kataradevalokato, sāmi, āgacchathā”ti [V 3.0075] pucchiṃsu. “Tāvatiṃsadevalokato āgacchāmā”ti. “Kena kammena āgatatthā”ti. “Ussavadassanatthāyā”ti. “Kiṃpupphāni nāmetānī”ti? “Dibbakakkārupupphāni nāmā”ti. “Sāmi, tumhe devaloke aññāni piḷandheyyātha, imāni amhākaṃ dethā”ti. Devaputtā “dibbakakkārupupphāni mahānubhāvāni devānaññeva anucchavikāni, manussaloke lāmakānaṃ duppaññānaṃ hīnādhimuttikānaṃ dussīlānaṃ nānucchavikāni. Ye pana manussā imehi ca imehi ca guṇehi samannāgatā, tesaṃ etāni anucchavikānī”ti āhaṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a certain deva in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. At that time, a great festival was being held in Bārāṇasī. Many nāgas, supaṇṇas, and earth-dwelling devas came to see the festival. From the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, four devas also came to see the festival, wearing wreaths made of divine flowers called kakkāru. The twelve-yojana city of Bārāṇasī became filled with the fragrance of those flowers. People wandered about wondering, “By whom are these flowers worn?” Those devas, realizing they were being observed, flew up and stood in the air in the royal courtyard by their great divine power. A large crowd gathered, and the king also went there along with the sub-king and others. Then they asked them, “Sirs, from which deva-world have you come?” “We have come from the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world.” “For what purpose have you come?” “To see the festival.” “What is the name of these flowers?” “They are called divine kakkāru flowers.” “Sirs, you may wear other flowers in the deva-world; please give these to us.” The devas said, “Divine kakkāru flowers are of great power and are suitable only for devas. In the human world, they are not suitable for the base, the unwise, those of low intent, and the immoral. But for those humans who are endowed with such and such virtues, these are suitable.”

Evañca pana vatvā tesu jeṭṭhakadevaputto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, the eldest among those devas spoke the first stanza:

101.

101.

“Kāyena yo nāvahare, vācāya na musā bhaṇe;

Yaso laddhā na majjeyya, sa ve kakkārumarahatī”ti.

“He who with his body would not take, nor with his speech speak falsely; who, having gained fame, would not be intoxicated—he is truly worthy of the kakkāru flower.”

Tassattho [P 3.0088] – yo kāyena parassa santakaṃ tiṇasalākampi nāvaharati, vācāya jīvitaṃ pariccajamānopi musāvādaṃ na bhaṇati. Desanāsīsamevetaṃ[M 3.0081], kāyadvāravacīdvāramanodvārehi pana yo dasapi akusalakammapathe na karotīti ayamettha adhippāyo. Yaso laddhāti issariyañca labhitvā yo issariyamadamatto satiṃ vissajjetvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti, sa ve evarūpo imehi guṇehi yutto puggalo imaṃ dibbapupphaṃ arahati. Tasmā yo imehi guṇehi samannāgato, so imāni pupphāni yācituṃ arahati, tassa dassāmīti.

Its meaning is: one who with his body does not take even a blade of grass belonging to another, and even at the cost of his life does not tell a lie with his speech. This is merely the heading of the teaching; the intention here is that one does not commit any of the ten unwholesome courses of action through the doors of body, speech, or mind. ‘Having gained fame’ means: having obtained power, one who, not intoxicated by the pride of power, does not abandon mindfulness and commit evil deeds. Such a person, endowed with these qualities, is truly worthy of this divine flower. Therefore, whoever is endowed with these qualities is worthy to ask for these flowers, and to them I will give them.

Taṃ sutvā purohito cintesi “mayhaṃ imesu guṇesu ekopi natthi, musāvādaṃ pana vatvā etāni pupphāni gahetvā piḷandhissāmi, evaṃ maṃ mahājano ‘guṇasampanno aya’nti jānissatī”ti. So “ahaṃ etehi guṇehi samannāgato”ti vatvā tāni pupphāni āharāpetvā piḷandhitvā dutiyaṃ devaputtaṃ yāci. So dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the chaplain thought, “I do not possess even one of these qualities. But by telling a lie, I will take these flowers and wear them. Then the people will know me as ‘one endowed with virtue.’” So he said, “I am endowed with these qualities,” had the flowers brought, adorned himself with them, and asked the second deva. The second deva spoke the second stanza:

102.

102.

“Dhammena vittameseyya, na nikatyā dhanaṃ hare;

Bhoge laddhā na majjeyya, sa ve kakkārumarahatī”ti.

“One who would seek wealth righteously, not take riches through deceit; having obtained possessions, would not be intoxicated—he is truly worthy of the kakkāru flower.”

Tassattho – dhammena parisuddhājīvena suvaṇṇarajatādivittaṃ pariyeseyya. Na nikatyāti na vañcanāya dhanaṃ hareyya, vatthābharaṇādike bhoge labhitvā pamādaṃ nāpajjeyya, evarūpo imāni pupphāni arahatīti.

Its meaning is: one should seek wealth, such as gold and silver, through a righteous livelihood. ‘Not through deceit’ means one should not take wealth by deception. Having obtained possessions such as clothing and ornaments, one should not fall into negligence. Such a person is worthy of these flowers.

Purohito [V 3.0076] “ahaṃ etehi guṇehi samannāgato”ti vatvā tāni āharāpetvā piḷandhitvā tatiyaṃ devaputtaṃ yāci. So tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The chaplain, saying, “I am endowed with these qualities,” had those flowers brought, adorned himself, and asked the third deva. He spoke the third stanza:

103.

103.

“Yassa cittaṃ ahāliddaṃ, saddhā ca avirāginī;

Eko sāduṃ na bhuñjeyya, sa ve kakkārumarahatī”ti.

“One whose mind is not fickle, and whose faith is unfading; who would not eat delicious food alone—he is truly worthy of the kakkāru flower.”

Tassattho – yassa puggalassa cittaṃ ahāliddaṃ haliddirāgo viya khippaṃ na virajjati, thirameva hoti. Saddhā ca avirāginīti kammaṃ vā vipākaṃ vā okappanīyassa vā puggalassa vacanaṃ saddahitvā appamattakeneva na virajjati na bhijjati. Yo yācake vā aññe vā saṃvibhāgārahe puggale bahi katvā [P 3.0089] ekakova sādurasabhojanaṃ na bhuñjati, nesaṃ saṃvibhajitvā bhuñjati, so imāni pupphāni arahatīti.

Its meaning is: the mind of that person is ‘not fickle’ (ahāliddaṃ), meaning it does not quickly fade like turmeric dye, but is firm. And ‘faith is unfading’ means that having gained confidence in kamma and its result, or believing the words of a person who inspires trust, his faith does not fade or break over a mere trifle. One who does not eat delicious food alone, excluding beggars or others worthy of sharing, but eats after sharing with them—he is worthy of these flowers.

Purohito [M 3.0082] “ahaṃ etehi guṇehi samannāgato”ti vatvā tāni pupphāni āharāpetvā piḷandhitvā catutthaṃ devaputtaṃ yāci. So catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

The chaplain, saying, “I am endowed with these qualities,” had the flowers brought, adorned himself with them, and asked the fourth deva. He spoke the fourth stanza:

104.

104.

“Sammukhā vā tirokkhā vā, yo sante na paribhāsati;

Yathāvādī tathākārī, sa ve kakkārumarahatī”ti.

“Whether face-to-face or behind their back, one who does not disparage the virtuous; who acts as he speaks—he is truly worthy of the kakkāru flower.”

Tassattho – yo puggalo sammukhā vā parammukhā vā sīlādiguṇayutte sante uttamapaṇḍitapurise na akkosati na paribhāsati, yaṃ vācāya vadati, tadeva kāyena karoti, so imāni pupphāni arahatīti.

Its meaning is: A person who, whether face-to-face or behind their back, does not abuse or revile virtuous, excellent, and wise people who are endowed with qualities such as morality, and whose deeds align with his speech—that one indeed deserves these flowers.

Purohito “ahaṃ etehi guṇehi samannāgato”ti vatvā tānipi āharāpetvā piḷandhi. Cattāro devaputtā cattāri pupphacumbaṭakāni purohitassa datvā devalokameva gatā. Tesaṃ gatakāle purohitassa sīse mahatī vedanā uppajji, tikhiṇasikharena nimmathitaṃ viya ca ayapaṭṭena pīḷitaṃ viya ca sīsaṃ ahosi. So vedanāppatto aparāparaṃ parivattamāno mahāsaddena viravi, “kimeta”nti ca vutte “ahaṃ mamabbhantare avijjamāneyeva guṇe ‘atthī’ti musāvādaṃ katvā te devaputte imāni pupphāni yāciṃ, harathetāni mama sīsato”ti āha. Tāni harantāpi harituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, ayapaṭṭena baddhāni viya ahesuṃ. Atha naṃ ukkhipitvā gehaṃ nayiṃsu. Tattha tassa viravantassa satta divasā vītivattā.

The chaplain, saying, "I am endowed with these qualities," had those flowers brought and adorned himself with them. The four divine beings gave four flower wreaths to the chaplain and then departed for the heavenly realm. As they departed, a great pain arose in the chaplain's head; it was as if his head were being churned by a sharp-pointed spike or pressed by an iron band. Overcome by pain, he rolled about incessantly and cried out loudly. When asked, "What is this?" he replied, "I falsely claimed to possess qualities that were not within me, and asked those divine beings for these flowers. Remove these from my head!" But even as they tried to remove them, they could not—they were as if bound by an iron band. So they lifted him up and carried him home. There, he continued to wail for seven days.

Rājā [V 3.0077] amacce āmantetvā “dussīlabrāhmaṇo marissati, kiṃ karomā”ti āha. “Deva, puna ussavaṃ kārema, devaputtā puna āgacchissantī”ti. Rājā puna ussavaṃ [P 3.0090] kāresi. Devaputtā puna āgantvā sakalanagaraṃ pupphagandhena ekagandhaṃ katvā tatheva rājaṅgaṇe aṭṭhaṃsu, mahājano sannipatitvā dussīlabrāhmaṇaṃ ānetvā tesaṃ purato uttānaṃ nipajjāpesi. So “jīvitaṃ me detha, sāmī”ti devaputte yāci. Devaputtā “tuyhaṃ dussīlassa pāpadhammassa ananucchavikānevetāni pupphāni, tvaṃ pana ‘amhe vañcessāmī’ti saññī ahosi, attano musāvādaphalaṃ laddha”nti mahājanamajjhe dussīlabrāhmaṇaṃ garahitvā sīsato pupphacumbaṭakaṃ apanetvā mahājanassa ovādaṃ datvā sakaṭṭhānameva agamaṃsu.

The king summoned his ministers and said, "This immoral brahmin will die; what shall we do?" They replied, "O king, let us hold another festival. The divine beings will surely return." The king arranged another festival. The divine beings returned, making the entire city a single fragrance with the scent of flowers, and stood just as before in the royal courtyard. The great crowd gathered and brought the immoral brahmin, laying him face-up before them. He pleaded with the divine beings, "Lords, give me my life!" But the divine beings rebuked the immoral brahmin in the midst of the crowd, saying, "These flowers are unsuitable for you, an immoral and evil person. You were of the mind, 'I will deceive them,' and now you have received the fruit of your own false speech." Having removed the flower wreath from his head, they gave advice to the great crowd and returned to their own abode.

Satthā [M 3.0083] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā brāhmaṇo devadatto ahosi, tesu devaputtesu eko kassapo, eko moggallāno, eko sāriputto, jeṭṭhakadevaputto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the brahmin was Devadatta, one of those divine beings was Kassapa, one was Moggallāna, one was Sāriputta, but the eldest divine being was myself."

Kakkārujātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The explanation of the Kakkāru Jātaka, the sixth.

[327] 7. Kākavatījātakavaṇṇanā

[327] 7. The explanation of the Kākavatī Jātaka

Vāti cāyaṃ tato gandhoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā taṃ bhikkhuṃ “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchi. “Saccaṃ, bhante”ti. “Kasmā ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti? “Kilesavasena, bhante”ti. “Bhikkhu mātugāmo nāma arakkhiyo, na sakkā rakkhituṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitā pana mātugāmaṃ mahāsamuddamajjhe simbalirukkhavimāne vasāpentāpi rakkhituṃ nāsakkhiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“And this fragrance wafts from there”: The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this regarding a certain discontented monk. At that time, the Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?" "It is true, Venerable Sir." "Why are you discontented?" "Because of the defilements, Venerable Sir." "Monk, women are unguardable; it is not possible to guard them. The wise men of old, even while having a woman dwell in a silk-cotton tree mansion in the middle of the great ocean, were not able to guard her." Having said this, he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchismiṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto pitu accayena rajjaṃ kāresi. Kākavatī nāmassa aggamahesī ahosi abhirūpā devaccharā viya. Ayamettha saṅkhepo[P 3.0091], vitthārato pana atītavatthu kuṇālajātake (jā. 2.21.kuṇālajātaka) āvi bhavissati. Tadā paneko supaṇṇarājā manussavesena āgantvā raññā saha jūtaṃ kīḷanto kākavatiyā aggamahesiyā paṭibaddhacitto taṃ ādāya supaṇṇabhavanaṃ netvā tāya saddhiṃ abhirami. Rājā deviṃ apassanto naṭakuveraṃ nāma [V 3.0078] gandhabbaṃ “tvaṃ vicināhi na”nti āha. So taṃ supaṇṇarājānaṃ pariggahetvā ekasmiṃ sare erakavane nipajjitvā tato supaṇṇassa gamanakāle pattantare nisīditvā supaṇṇabhavanaṃ patvā pattantarato nikkhamitvā tāya saddhiṃ kilesasaṃsaggaṃ katvā puna tasseva pattantare nisinno āgantvā supaṇṇassa raññā saddhiṃ jūtakīḷanakāle attano vīṇaṃ gahetvā jūtamaṇḍalaṃ gantvā rañño santike ṭhito gītavasena paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. When he came of age, he assumed kingship after his father's passing. His chief queen, named Kākavatī, was as beautiful as a celestial nymph. This is the summary here; the detailed past story will be made clear in the Kuṇāla Jātaka. At that time, a garuḍa king, disguised as a human, came and played dice with the king. He became infatuated with the chief queen Kākavatī, took her away to the garuḍa realm, and delighted in her company. The king, not seeing the queen, commanded a gandhabba named Naṭakuvera, "You must search for her." He, having tracked the garuḍa king, lay down in a grove of reeds by a certain lake. Then, when the garuḍa was about to depart, he sat between his wings, reached the garuḍa’s abode, and emerged from the wings. He engaged in carnal intimacy with her, then sat again between those same wings and returned. When the garuḍa king was playing dice with the king, the gandhabba took his lute, went to the gaming circle, stood near the king, and sang this first verse as a song:

105.

105.

“Vāti [M 3.0084] cāyaṃ tato gandho, yattha me vasatī piyā;

Dūre ito hi kākavatī, yattha me nirato mano”ti.

"And this fragrance wafts from there, where my beloved dwells; far from here is Kākavatī, in whom my mind delights."

Tattha gandhoti tassā dibbagandhavilittāya sarīragandho.
