Yattha meti yattha supaṇṇabhavane mama piyā vasati, tato iminā saddhiṃ katakāyasaṃsaggāya tassā imassa kāyena saddhiṃ āgato gandho vāyatīti adhippāyo. Dūre itoti imamhā ṭhānā dūre. Hi-kāro nipātamatto. Kākavatīti kākavatī devī. Yattha meti yassā upari mama mano nirato.

There, 'gandho' means the fragrance of her body, anointed with divine perfumes. 'Yattha me' means where my beloved resides in the garuḍa realm; the intention is that the fragrance of her, who had bodily contact with this one (Naṭakuvera), has come with this one's body and wafts from it. 'Dūre ito' means far from this place. The word 'hi' is a mere particle. 'Kākavatī' refers to Queen Kākavatī. 'Yattha me' means the one upon whom my mind is intent.

Taṃ sutvā supaṇṇo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the garuḍa spoke the second verse:

106.

106.

“Kathaṃ samuddamatarī, kathaṃ atari kepukaṃ;

Kathaṃ satta samuddāni, kathaṃ simbalimāruhī”ti.

"How did you cross the ocean? How did you cross the Kepuka? How did you cross the seven seas? How did you climb the silk-cotton tree?"

Tassattho – tvaṃ imaṃ jambudīpasamuddaṃ tassa parato kepukaṃ nāma nadiṃ pabbatantaresu ṭhitāni satta samuddāni ca kathaṃ atari, kenupāyena tiṇṇo satta samuddāni atikkamitvā ṭhitaṃ amhākaṃ bhavanaṃ simbalirukkhañca kathaṃ āruhīti.

Its meaning is: How did you cross this ocean of Jambudīpa, the river named Kepuka beyond it, and the seven seas situated among the mountains? By what means did you cross them, and having passed beyond the seven seas, how did you climb our abode and the silk-cotton tree?

Taṃ [P 3.0092] sutvā naṭakuvero tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, Naṭakuvera spoke the third verse:

107.

107.

“Tayā samuddamatariṃ, tayā atari kepukaṃ;

Tayā satta samuddāni, tayā simbalimāruhi”nti.

“By you I crossed the ocean; by you I crossed the Kepuka river; by you I crossed the seven seas; by you I climbed the Simbali tree.”

Tattha tayāti tayā karaṇabhūtena tava pattantare nisinno ahaṃ sabbametaṃ akāsinti attho.

There, 'tayā' means: by you as the instrument; sitting in the space between your wings, I did all this—this is the meaning.

Tato [V 3.0079] supaṇṇarājā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Garuḍa king spoke the fourth verse:

108.

108.

“Dhiratthu maṃ mahākāyaṃ, dhiratthu maṃ acetanaṃ;

Yattha jāyāyahaṃ jāraṃ, āvahāmi vahāmi cā”ti.

“Shame on me, having this great body; shame on me, being senseless; for I bring and carry my wife's lover.”

Tattha dhiratthu manti attānaṃ garahanto āha. Acetananti mahāsarīratāya lahubhāvagarubhāvassa ajānanatāya acetanaṃ. Yatthāti yasmā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā ahaṃ attano jāyāya jāraṃ imaṃ gandhabbaṃ [M 3.0085] pattantare nisinnaṃ ānento āvahāmi nento ca vahāmi, tasmā dhiratthu manti. So taṃ ānetvā bārāṇasirañño datvā puna nagaraṃ nāgamāsi.

There, 'Shame on me!' he said, blaming himself. 'Acetananti' means senseless because, due to his large body, he did not perceive the lightness or heaviness of the person he was carrying. 'Yatthāti' means 'yasmā' (because). This is what is meant: 'Because I bring (āvahāmi) and carry (vahāmi) my wife’s lover, this Gandhabba, who is seated between my wings, therefore, shame on me!' Having brought him back and given him to the King of Bārāṇasī, he never returned to that city again.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā naṭakuvero ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu ahosi, rājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Birth Story. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, Naṭakuvera was the dissatisfied monk, but the King was I myself.

Kākavatījātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Seventh, the Commentary on the Kākavatī Jātaka.

[328] 8. Ananusociyajātakavaṇṇanā

[328] 8. The Commentary on the Ananusociya Jātaka

Bahūnaṃ vijjatī bhotīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ matabhariyaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira bhariyāya matāya na nhāyi na pivi na limpi na bhuñji, na kammante payojesi, aññadatthu sokābhibhūto āḷāhanaṃ gantvā paridevamāno vicari. Abbhantare panassa kuṭe padīpo viya sotāpattimaggassa upanissayo jalati. Satthā paccūsasamaye lokaṃ olokento taṃ disvā “imassa maṃ ṭhapetvā añño koci sokaṃ nīharitvā sotāpattimaggassa dāyako natthi, bhavissāmissa avassayo”ti pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto pacchāsamaṇaṃ ādāya tassa gehadvāraṃ gantvā kuṭumbikena sutāgamano [P 3.0093] katapaccuggamanādisakkāro paññattāsane nisinno kuṭumbikaṃ āgantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ “kiṃ, upāsaka, cintesī”ti pucchitvā “āma, bhante, bhariyā me kālakatā, tamahaṃ anusocanto cintemī”ti vutte “upāsaka, bhijjanadhammaṃ nāma bhijjati, tasmiṃ bhinne na yuttaṃ cintetuṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi bhariyāya matāya ‘bhijjanadhammaṃ bhijjatī’ti na cintayiṃsū”ti [V 3.0080] vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari. Atītavatthu dasakanipāte cūḷabodhijātake (jā. 1.10.49 ādayo) āvi bhavissati, ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo.

“For many there is, good lady…”—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a householder whose wife had died. It is said that when his wife died, he neither bathed nor drank nor anointed himself nor ate, nor did he engage in work; overwhelmed by sorrow, he went to the cremation ground and wandered about, lamenting. Yet within him, like a lamp in a jar, the support for the path of stream-entry was shining. At dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world, saw him and thought, 'Except for me, no one else can remove his sorrow and bestow the path of stream-entry; I shall be his refuge.' After the meal, having returned from the almsround, he took a junior monk with him and went to the householder’s door. The householder, hearing of his arrival, went out to meet him and paid respects; when the Teacher was seated on the prepared seat, the householder came, bowed, and sat to one side. The Teacher asked, 'Are you brooding, lay follower?' He replied, 'Yes, Bhante, my wife has died; I am brooding in sorrow for her.' The Teacher said, 'Lay follower, what is subject to dissolution inevitably dissolves. When it has dissolved, it is not fitting to grieve. Even the wise of old did not grieve when their wives died, knowing, “What is subject to dissolution dissolves.”' Having spoken thus, and being entreated by him, he related a past story. The past story will be clear in the Cūḷabodhi Jātaka of the Tenth Book (Dasaka Nipāta). Here is the summary.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā mātāpitūnaṃ [M 3.0086] santikaṃ agamāsi. Imasmiṃ jātake bodhisatto komārabrahmacārī ahosi. Athassa mātāpitaro “tava dārikapariyesanaṃ karomā”ti ārocayiṃsu. Bodhisatto “na mayhaṃ gharāvāsenattho, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ accayena pabbajissāmī”ti vatvā tehi punappunaṃ yācito ekaṃ kañcanarūpakaṃ kāretvā “evarūpaṃ kumārikaṃ labhamāno gaṇhissāmī”ti āha. Tassa mātāpitaro taṃ kañcanarūpakaṃ paṭicchannayāne āropetvā “gacchatha jambudīpatalaṃ vicarantā yattha evarūpaṃ brāhmaṇakumārikaṃ passatha, tattha imaṃ kañcanarūpakaṃ datvā taṃ ānethā”ti mahantena parivārena manusse pesesuṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. Having come of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā and returned to his parents. In this birth, the Bodhisatta was a celibate from his youth. Then his parents said to him, 'We will seek a wife for you.' The Bodhisatta replied, 'I have no need for household life. After your passing, I will go forth.' Though they begged him repeatedly, he had a golden image made and said, 'Only if I find a maiden like this will I marry.' His parents placed the golden image in a covered carriage and sent out a retinue of people, saying, 'Go and travel throughout the land of Jambudīpa. Wherever you see a brahmin maiden like this, give this golden image and bring her back.'

Tasmiṃ pana kāle eko puññavā satto brahmalokato cavitvā kāsiraṭṭheyeva nigamagāme asītikoṭivibhavassa brāhmaṇassa gehe kumārikā hutvā nibbatti, “sammillahāsinī”tissā nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Sā soḷasavassakāle abhirūpā ahosi pāsādikā devaccharappaṭibhāgā sabbaṅgasampannā. Tassāpi kilesavasena cittaṃ nāma na uppannapubbaṃ, accantabrahmacārinī ahosi. Kañcanarūpakaṃ [P 3.0094] ādāya vicarantā manussā taṃ gāmaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tattha manussā taṃ disvā “asukabrāhmaṇassa dhītā sammillahāsinī kiṃkāraṇā idha ṭhitā”ti āhaṃsu. Manussā taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇakulaṃ gantvā sammillahāsiniṃ vāresuṃ. Sā “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ accayena pabbajissāmi, na me gharāvāsenattho”ti mātāpitūnaṃ sāsanaṃ pesesi. Te “kiṃ karosi kumārike”ti vatvā kañcanarūpakaṃ gahetvā taṃ mahantena parivārena pesayiṃsu. Bodhisattassa ca sammillahāsiniyā ca ubhinnampi anicchantānaññeva maṅgalaṃ kariṃsu. Te ekagabbhe vasamānā ekasmiṃ sayane sayantāpi na aññamaññaṃ kilesavasena olokayiṃsu, dve bhikkhū dve brāhmāno viya ca ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasiṃsu.

At that time, a meritorious being, passing away from the Brahma world, was reborn as a girl in the household of a Brahmin with a fortune of eighty crores in a market town in the Kasi kingdom. They named her 'Sammillahāsinī.' When she was sixteen years old, she was extremely beautiful, charming, resembling a celestial nymph, and endowed with all perfections. No thought of defilement had ever arisen in her mind; she was perfectly chaste. The men carrying the golden image reached that village. The people there, seeing it, said, 'Why is Sammillahāsinī, the daughter of such-and-such a Brahmin, standing here?' Hearing this, the men went to the Brahmin's house and asked for Sammillahāsinī. She sent word to her parents: 'After your passing, I will go forth; I have no desire for household life.' They, saying, 'What are you doing, daughter?' took the golden image and sent her off with a great retinue. Although both the Bodhisatta and Sammillahāsinī did not desire it, the marriage ceremony was performed. Living in the same chamber and sleeping on the same bed, they never looked at each other with defiled minds; they lived together like two monks or two Brahmas.

Aparabhāge bodhisattassa mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. So tesaṃ sarīrakiccaṃ katvā sammillahāsiniṃ pakkosāpetvā “bhadde, mama kulasantakā asītikoṭiyo, tava kulasantakā asītikoṭiyoti imaṃ ettakaṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā imaṃ kuṭumbaṃ paṭipajjāhi, ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti āha. “Ayyaputta, tayi pabbajante ahampi pabbajissāmi, na sakkomi taṃ jahitu”nti[M 3.0087]. “Tena hi ehī”ti sabbaṃ dhanaṃ dānamukhe vissajjetvā kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya sampattiṃ [V 3.0081] pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā ubhopi tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vanamūlaphalāhārā tattha ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya himavantā otaritvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasiṃsu.

Subsequently, the Bodhisatta's parents passed away. After performing their funeral rites, he had Sammillahāsinī summoned and said, 'My dear, my family's fortune is eighty crores, and your family's is eighty crores. Take this vast wealth and manage this household. I shall go forth.' 'My lord, if you go forth, I too shall go forth; I cannot bear to leave you,' she replied. 'Very well, then come,' he said. After distributing all the wealth in acts of charity and abandoning his prosperity like a lump of spittle, they both entered the Himalayas, embraced the ascetic life, living there for a long time on roots and fruits from the forest. Later, they descended from the Himalayas to procure salt and sour foods and gradually reached Bārāṇasī, where they took up residence in the royal park.

Tesaṃ tattha vasantānaṃ sukhumālāya paribbājikāya nirojaṃ missakabhattaṃ paribhuñjantiyā lohitapakkhandikābādho uppajji. Sā sappāyabhesajjaṃ alabhamānā dubbalā ahosi. Bodhisatto bhikkhācāravelāya taṃ pariggahetvā nagaradvāraṃ netvā ekissā sālāya phalake nipajjāpetvā sayaṃ bhikkhāya pāvisi. Sā tasmiṃ anikkhanteyeva kālamakāsi. Mahājano paribbājikāya rūpasampattiṃ [P 3.0095] disvā parivāretvā rodati paridevati. Bodhisatto bhikkhaṃ caritvā āgato tassā matabhāvaṃ ñatvā “bhijjanadhammaṃ bhijjati, sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā evaṃgatikāyevā”ti vatvā tāya nipannaphalakeyeva nisīditvā missakabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā mukhaṃ vikkhālesi. Parivāretvā ṭhitamahājano “ayaṃ te, bhante, paribbājikā kiṃ hotī”ti pucchi. “Gihikāle me pādaparicārikā ahosī”ti. “Bhante, mayaṃ tāva na saṇṭhāma rodāma paridevāma, tumhe kasmā na rodathā”ti? Bodhisatto “jīvamānā tāva esā mama kiñci hoti, idāni paralokasamaṅgitāya na kiñci hoti, maraṇavasaṃ gatā, ahaṃ kissa rodāmī”ti mahājanassa dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

While they were living there, the delicate female wanderer, eating unnutritious mixed food, developed dysentery. Unable to obtain suitable medicine, she became weak. The Bodhisatta, at the time of his almsround, took her in his charge and, having taken her to the city gate, laid her on a wooden plank in a hall. Then he entered the city for alms. Before he had even come out, she passed away. The crowd, seeing the beauty of the female wanderer, gathered around weeping and lamenting. The Bodhisatta, having gone for alms and returned, learned of her death. He said, 'What is of a nature to break, breaks; all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, such is their nature.' Then he sat on the very plank where she lay, ate his mixed food, and rinsed his mouth. The crowd standing around asked, 'Venerable sir, what was this female wanderer to you?' He replied, 'In household life, she was my wife.' They said, 'Venerable sir, we cannot bear it—we weep and lament. Why do you not weep?' The Bodhisatta, teaching the Dhamma to the crowd, said, 'While she was alive, she was something to me. Now, destined for another world, she is nothing to me. She has fallen under the power of death—why should I weep?' and spoke these verses:

109.

109.

“Bahūnaṃ vijjatī bhotī, tehi me kiṃ bhavissati;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, piyaṃ sammillahāsiniṃ.

"This lady is now among many; what will she be to me then? Therefore, I do not grieve for her, the beloved Sammillahāsinī."

110.

110.

“Taṃ taṃ ce anusoceyya, yaṃ yaṃ tassa na vijjati;

Attānamanusoceyya, sadā maccuvasaṃ pataṃ.

"If one should grieve for whatever no longer exists for one, then one should grieve for oneself, who is ever falling under the sway of death."

111.

111.

“Na heva ṭhitaṃ nāsīnaṃ, na sayānaṃ na paddhaguṃ;

Yāva byāti nimisati, tatrāpi rasatī vayo.

"Not while standing, nor while sitting, nor while lying down, nor while walking—not even in the time it takes to blink an eye—even then, life wastes away."

112.

112.

“Tatthattani vatappaddhe, vinābhāve asaṃsaye;

Bhūtaṃ sesaṃ dayitabbaṃ, vītaṃ ananusociya”nti.

"When one's self is thus diminished, and separation is without doubt, those who remain and are yet alive should be cherished; what has passed away should not be grieved over."

Tattha [M 3.0088] bahūnaṃ vijjatī bhotīti ayaṃ bhotī amhe chaḍḍetvā idāni aññesaṃ bahūnaṃ matakasattānaṃ [V 3.0082] antare vijjati atthi upalabbhati. Tehi me kiṃ bhavissatīti tehi matakasattehi saddhiṃ vattamānā idānevesā mayhaṃ kiṃ bhavissati[P 3.0096], tehi vā matakasattehi atirekasambandhavasenesā mayhaṃ kiṃ bhavissati, kā nāma bhavissati, kiṃ bhariyā, udāhu bhaginīti? “Tehi meka”ntipi pāṭho, tehi matakehi saddhiṃ idampi me kaḷevaraṃ ekaṃ bhavissatīti attho. Tasmāti yasmā esā matakesu saṅkhaṃ gatā, mayhaṃ sā na kiñci hoti, tasmā etaṃ na socāmi.

Here, 'This lady is now among many' (bahūnaṃ vijjatī bhotī) means: this lady, having abandoned us, now exists among many other dead beings. 'What will she be to me?' (tehi me kiṃ bhavissati) means: existing now with those dead beings, how will she be related to me? Or, by way of a further connection with those dead beings, what will she be to me? What could she be—a wife, or a sister? There is also the reading 'tehi mekaṃ', meaning: 'with those dead ones, this body of mine will also become one'. 'Therefore' (tasmā) means: since she is now reckoned among the dead, she is nothing to me; therefore I do not grieve for her.

Yaṃ yaṃ tassāti yaṃ yaṃ tassa anusocanakassa sattassa na vijjati natthi, mataṃ niruddhaṃ, taṃ taṃ sace anusoceyyāti attho. “Yassā”tipi pāṭho, yaṃ yaṃ yassa na vijjati, taṃ taṃ so anusoceyyāti attho. Maccuvasaṃ patanti evaṃ sante niccaṃ maccuvasaṃ patantaṃ gacchantaṃ attānameva anusoceyya, tenassa asocanakāloyeva na bhaveyyāti attho.

'Whatever does not exist for one' (yaṃ yaṃ tassa na vijjati) means: whatever does not exist for that grieving being—that which is dead and has ceased—if one were to mourn that, such is the meaning. There is also the reading 'yassā': whatever does not exist for someone, that is what they would mourn. 'Falling under the sway of death' (maccuvasaṃ pataṃ) means: if this is so, one should instead mourn for oneself, who is constantly moving under the sway of death. Thus, there would never be a time free from mourning; that is the meaning.

Tatiyagāthāya na heva ṭhitaṃ nāsīnaṃ, na sayānaṃ na paddhagunti kañci sattaṃ āyusaṅkhāro anugacchatīti pāṭhaseso. Tattha paddhagunti parivattetvā caramānaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ime sattā catūsupi iriyāpathesu pamattā viharanti, āyusaṅkhārā pana rattiñca divā ca sabbiriyāpathesu appamattā attano khayagamanakammameva karontīti. Yāva byātīti yāva ummisati. Ayañhi tasmiṃ kāle vohāro. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yāva ummisati ca nimisati ca, tatrāpi evaṃ appamattake kāle imesaṃ sattānaṃ rasatī vayo, tīsu vayesu so so vayo hāyateva na vaḍḍhatīti.

In the third verse, 'Not while standing, nor while sitting, nor while lying down, nor while walking' (na heva ṭhitaṃ nāsīnaṃ, na sayānaṃ na paddhaguṃ) implies that the life-formation does not wait for any being. Here, 'walking' (paddhaguṃ) means moving about. This is what is said: these beings dwell heedlessly in the four postures, but the life-formations, day and night, in all postures, diligently carry out their own work of decay. 'As long as one blinks' (yāva byāti) means as long as one opens the eyes. This was the common expression at that time. This is what is said: as long as one opens and closes the eyes, even in such a brief moment, the life of these beings wastes away; in the three stages of life, each stage only declines and never increases.

Tatthattani vatappaddheti tattha vata attani paddhe. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti tasmiṃ vata evaṃ rasamāne vaye ayaṃ “attā”ti saṅkhyaṃ gato attabhāvo paddho hoti, vayena aḍḍho upaḍḍho aparipuṇṇova hoti[M 3.0089]. Evaṃ tattha imasmiṃ attani paddhe yo cesa tattha tattha nibbattānaṃ sattānaṃ vinābhāvo asaṃsayo, tasmiṃ vinābhāvepi asaṃsaye nissaṃsaye yaṃ bhūtaṃ sesaṃ amataṃ jīvamānaṃ, taṃ jīvamānameva dayitabbaṃ piyāyitabbaṃ mettāyitabbaṃ, “ayaṃ satto arogo hotu abyāpajjo”ti evaṃ tasmiṃ mettābhāvanā [P 3.0097] kātabbā. Yaṃ panetaṃ vītaṃ vigataṃ mataṃ, taṃ ananusociyaṃ na anusocitabbanti.

'When one's self is thus diminished' (tatthattani vatappaddhe) means indeed, in the self that is diminished. This is what is said: as life thus wastes away, this self-existence, reckoned as 'self', becomes diminished (paddho), incomplete by age. Thus, when this self is diminished, and since the separation of beings born here and there is certain—in that certain separation—whatever remains alive should be cherished and treated with loving-kindness, thinking: 'May this being be free from illness and affliction.' In this way, the cultivation of loving-kindness should be practiced towards the living. But as for that which has passed away and died—that should not be lamented; one ought not to grieve over it.

Evaṃ mahāsatto catūhi gāthāhi aniccākāraṃ dīpento dhammaṃ desesi. Mahājano paribbājikāya sarīrakiccaṃ akāsi. Bodhisatto himavantameva pavisitvā jhānābhiññāsamāpattiyo nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus the Great Being, demonstrating the nature of impermanence with four verses, taught the Dhamma. The great multitude performed the funeral rites for the female wanderer. The Bodhisatta entered the Himalayas, developed the meditative absorptions, higher knowledges, and attainments, and was destined for the Brahma realm.

Satthā [V 3.0083] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne kuṭumbiko sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā sammillahāsinī rāhulamātā ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosinti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, Sammillahāsinī was Rāhula's mother, and the ascetic was I myself.

Ananusociyajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The eighth, the Commentary on the Ananusociya Jātaka.

[329] 9. Kāḷabāhujātakavaṇṇanā

[329] 9. The Commentary on the Kāḷabāhu Jātaka

Yaṃ annapānassāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto hatalābhasakkāraṃ devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Devadattena hi tathāgate aṭṭhānakopaṃ bandhitvā dhanuggahesu payojitesu nāḷāgirivissajjanena tassa doso pākaṭo jāto. Athassa paṭṭhapitāni dhuvabhattādīni manussā na kariṃsu, rājāpi naṃ na olokesi. So hatalābhasakkāro kulesu viññāpetvā bhuñjanto vicari. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto ‘lābhasakkāraṃ uppādessāmī’ti uppannampi thiraṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa hatalābhasakkāro ahosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“What food and drink...” – the Teacher spoke this while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta, who had lost his gains and honor. For Devadatta, having conceived groundless anger against the Tathāgata and having employed archers, his fault became manifest through the release of the elephant Nālāgiri. Thereafter, people did not provide him with the regular meals and other offerings that had been established, and even the king did not look upon him. Deprived of gains and honor, he wandered about, eating by requesting from families. The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, Devadatta, though he intended to generate gain and honor, was not even able to make stable what had arisen.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you assembled here now?” When they told him, he said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, he lost his gains and honor,” and he recounted a story of the past.

Atīte [M 3.0090] bārāṇasiyaṃ dhanañjaye rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto rādho nāma suko ahosi mahāsarīro paripuṇṇagatto, kaniṭṭho panassa poṭṭhapādo nāma. Eko luddako te dvepi jane bandhitvā netvā bārāṇasirañño adāsi. Rājā ubhopi te suvaṇṇapañjare pakkhipitvā suvaṇṇataṭṭakena madhulāje khādāpento [P 3.0098] sakkharodakaṃ pāyento paṭijaggi. Sakkāro ca mahā ahosi, lābhaggayasaggappattā ahesuṃ. Atheko vanacarako kāḷabāhuṃ nāmekaṃ mahākāḷamakkaṭaṃ ānetvā bārāṇasirañño adāsi. Tassa pacchā āgatattā mahantataro lābhasakkāro ahosi, sukānaṃ parihāyi. Bodhisatto tādilakkhaṇayogato na kiñci āha, kaniṭṭho panassa tādilakkhaṇābhāvā taṃ makkaṭassa sakkāraṃ asahanto “bhātika, pubbe imasmiṃ rājakule sādhurasakhādanīyādīni amhākameva denti, idāni pana mayaṃ na labhāma, kāḷabāhumakkaṭasseva denti. Mayaṃ dhanañjayarañño santikā lābhasakkāraṃ alabhantā imasmiṃ ṭhāne kiṃ karissāma, ehi araññameva gantvā vasissāmā”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Dhanañjaya was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a parrot named Rādha, large-bodied and perfectly formed, while his younger brother was named Poṭṭhapāda. A hunter captured both of them and presented them to the king of Bārāṇasī. The king placed them both in golden cages, fed them honeyed parched grain from a golden saucer, and gave them sugar water to drink, taking care of them. Their honors were great, and they reached the peak of gain and fame. Then a forest-dweller brought a large black monkey named Kāḷabāhu and presented it to the king of Bārāṇasī. Because it came later, it received greater gain and honor, while that of the parrots diminished. The Bodhisatta, possessing the characteristic of patience, said nothing, but his younger brother, lacking such a characteristic and unable to bear the monkey's honor, said, “Brother, before, in this royal household, they gave fine delicacies and foods to us alone, but now we receive nothing; they give everything to Kāḷabāhu the monkey. Since we are not obtaining gain and honor from King Dhanañjaya, what shall we do in this place? Come, let us go and live in the forest!” Conversing with him, he spoke the first verse:

113.

113.

“Yaṃ [V 3.0084] annapānassa pure labhāma, taṃ dāni sākhamigameva gacchati;

Gacchāma dāni vanameva rādha, asakkatā casma dhanañjayāyā”ti.

“What food and drink we used to receive, that now goes only to the monkey. Let us go now to the forest, Rādha, for we are not honored by Dhanañjaya.”

Tattha yaṃ annapānassāti yaṃ annapānaṃ assa rañño santikā. Upayogatthe vā sāmivacanaṃ. Dhanañjayāyāti karaṇatthe sampadānavacanaṃ, dhanañjayena. Asakkatā casmāti annapānaṃ na labhāma, iminā ca na sakkatamhāti attho.

There, ‘what food and drink’ (yaṃ annapānassa) means the food and drink from the king. Or, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. ‘By Dhanañjaya’ (dhanañjayāya) is the dative case used in the instrumental sense, meaning ‘by Dhanañjaya’ (dhanañjayena). ‘And we are not honored’ (asakkatā casma) means we do not receive food and drink, and thus we are not honored—this is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā rādho dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Rādha spoke the second verse:

114.

114.

“Lābho alābho yaso ayaso ca, nindā pasaṃsā ca sukhañca dukkhaṃ;

Ete aniccā manujesu dhammā, mā soci kiṃ socasi poṭṭhapādā”ti.

“Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, censure and praise, pleasure and pain—these conditions are impermanent among humans. Do not sorrow; why do you sorrow, Poṭṭhapāda?”

Tattha yasoti issariyaparivāro. Ayasoti tassābhāvo. Eteti ete aṭṭha lokadhammā manujesu aniccā, lābhaggayasaggappattā hutvāpi [M 3.0091] aparena samayena appalābhā [P 3.0099] appasakkārā honti, niccalābhino nāma na honti. Yasādīsupi eseva nayo.

There, ‘fame’ (yaso) refers to the retinue of power. ‘Disrepute’ (ayaso) is the absence of that. ‘These’ (ete) means these eight worldly conditions are impermanent among humans; even after reaching the peak of gain and fame, at another time one becomes lacking in gain and honor; they are not permanently endowed with gain. The same principle applies to fame and the rest.

Taṃ sutvā poṭṭhapādo makkaṭe usūyaṃ apanetuṃ asakkonto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, Poṭṭhapāda, unable to dispel his envy for the monkey, spoke the third verse:

115.

115.

“Addhā tuvaṃ paṇḍitakosi rādha, jānāsi atthāni anāgatāni;

Kathaṃ nu sākhāmigaṃ dakkhisāma, niddhāvitaṃ rājakulatova jamma”nti.

“Surely, you are wise, Rādha, you know the matters of things to come; how then shall we see the wretched monkey driven out from the royal household?”

Tattha kathaṃ nūti kena nu kho upāyena. Dakkhisāmāti dakkhissāma. Niddhāvitanti nivuṭṭhāpitaṃ nikkaḍḍhāpitaṃ. Jammanti lāmakaṃ.

There, “how then?” (kathaṃ nu) means “by what means?” “We shall see” (dakkhisāma) means “we will see.” “Driven out” (niddhāvitaṃ) means “expelled, ejected.” “Jamma” means “vile” or “wretched.”

Taṃ sutvā rādho catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard that, Rādha spoke the fourth verse:

116.

116.

“Cāleti kaṇṇaṃ bhakuṭiṃ karoti, muhuṃ muhuṃ bhāyayate kumāre;

Sayameva taṃ kāhati kāḷabāhu, yenārakā ṭhassati annapānā”ti.

“He moves his ears, scowls, and repeatedly frightens the princes; Kāḷabāhu himself will bring that about, whereby he will be far from food and drink.”

Tattha bhāyayate kumāreti rājakumāre utrāseti. Yenārakā ṭhassati annapānāti yena kāraṇena [V 3.0085] imamhā annapānā dūre ṭhassati, sayameva taṃ kāraṇaṃ karissati, mā tvaṃ etassa cintayīti attho.

There, “frightens the princes” (bhāyayate kumāre) means he terrifies the royal princes. “Whereby he will be far from food and drink” means for whatever reason he will be far from this food and drink, he himself will bring about that reason. “Do not worry about this” is the meaning.

Kāḷabāhupi katipāheneva rājakumārānaṃ purato ṭhatvā kaṇṇacalanādīni karonto kumāre bhāyāpesi. Te bhītatasitā vissaramakaṃsu. Rājā “kiṃ eta”nti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “nikkaḍḍhatha na”nti makkaṭaṃ nikkaḍḍhāpesi. Sukānaṃ lābhasakkāro puna pākatiko ahosi.

Kāḷabāhu, in just a few days, stood before the princes and frightened them by moving his ears and such. Terrified and trembling, they cried out. The king, asking, “What is this?” and hearing the matter, ordered, “Drive him out!” and had the monkey driven out. The gain and honor for the parrots returned to normal.

Satthā [P 3.0100] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kāḷabāhu devadatto ahosi, poṭṭhapādo ānando, rādho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka thus: “At that time, Kāḷabāhu was Devadatta, Poṭṭhapāda was Ānanda, and Rādha was indeed myself.”

Kāḷabāhujātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The ninth, the Commentary on the Kāḷabāhu Jātaka.

[330] 10. Sīlavīmaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā

[330] 10. The Commentary on the Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka

Sīlaṃ [M 3.0092] kireva kalyāṇanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sīlavīmaṃsakabrāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Dvepi vatthūni heṭṭhā kathitāneva. Idha pana bodhisatto bārāṇasirañño purohito ahosi. So attano sīlaṃ vīmaṃsanto tīṇi divasāni heraññikaphalakato kahāpaṇaṃ gaṇhi. Taṃ “coro”ti gahetvā rañño dassesuṃ. So rañño santike ṭhito –

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this concerning the brahmin who investigated virtue, beginning with the words, “Virtue, indeed, is good.” Both stories have already been told below. Here, however, the Bodhisatta was the chaplain of the king of Bārāṇasī. Examining his own virtue, for three days he took a kahāpaṇa coin from the money-changer's board. They seized him, saying, “A thief!” and brought him before the king. Standing in the king's presence, he—

117.

117.

“Sīlaṃ kireva kalyāṇaṃ, sīlaṃ loke anuttaraṃ;

Passa ghoraviso nāgo, sīlavāti na haññatī”ti. –

“Virtue indeed is good, virtue is supreme in the world; see the fierce venomous serpent, because it is virtuous, it is not harmed.”

Imāya paṭhamagāthāya sīlaṃ vaṇṇetvā rājānaṃ pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetvā pabbajituṃ gacchati.

By this first verse, having praised virtue and obtained the king's permission for the going forth, he departs to go forth.

Athekasmiṃ divase sūnāpaṇato seno maṃsapesiṃ gahetvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Tamaññe sakuṇā parivāretvā pādanakhatuṇḍakādīhi paharanti. So taṃ dukkhaṃ sahituṃ asakkonto maṃsapesiṃ chaḍḍesi, aparo gaṇhi. Sopi tatheva viheṭhiyamāno chaḍḍesi, athañño gaṇhi. Evaṃ yo yo gaṇhi, taṃ taṃ sakuṇā anubandhiṃsu. Yo yo chaḍḍesi, so so sukhito ahosi. Bodhisatto taṃ disvā “ime kāmā nāma maṃsapesūpamā, ete gaṇhantānaṃyeva dukkhaṃ, vissajjentānaṃ sukha”nti cintetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then one day, a hawk took a piece of meat from a butcher's shop and flew into the sky. Other birds surrounded it and attacked it with their feet, claws, beaks, and so on. Unable to endure that pain, it dropped the piece of meat, and another bird took it. That one too, being harassed in the same way, dropped it, and then another took it. Thus, whichever bird held it, that one was pursued by the other birds. Whichever bird dropped it, that one became happy. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta reflected: “These sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat—they bring suffering only to those who hold them and happiness to those who relinquish them.” Then he spoke the second verse:

118.

118.

“Yāvadevassahū [V 3.0086] kiñci, tāvadeva akhādisuṃ;

Saṅgamma kulalā loke, na hiṃsanti akiñcana”nti.

“Only as long as it had something, so long did they attack it. Having gathered together in the world, the kites do not harm one who has nothing.”

Tassattho [P 3.0101] – yāvadeva assa senassa ahu kiñci mukhena gahitaṃ maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ, tāvadeva naṃ imasmiṃ loke kulalā samāgantvā akhādiṃsu. Tasmiṃ pana vissaṭṭhe tamenaṃ akiñcanaṃ nippalibodhaṃ pakkhiṃ sesapakkhino na hiṃsantīti.

The meaning of this is: As long as that hawk had any piece of meat held in its beak, just that long did the kites, having gathered together in this world, attack it. But when it was released, the other birds did not harm that bird, which was without anything and free from entanglement.

So nagarā nikkhamitvā antarāmagge ekasmiṃ gāme sāyaṃ ekassa gehe nipajji. Tattha pana piṅgalā nāma dāsī “asukavelāya āgaccheyyāsī”ti ekena purisena saddhiṃ saṅketamakāsi. Sā sāmikānaṃ pāde [M 3.0093] dhovitvā tesu nipannesu tassāgamanaṃ olokentī ummāre nisīditvā “idāni āgamissati, idāni āgamissatī”ti paṭhamayāmampi majjhimayāmampi vītināmesi. Paccūsasamaye pana “na so idāni āgamissatī”ti chinnāsā hutvā nipajjitvā niddaṃ okkami. Bodhisatto idaṃ kāraṇaṃ disvā “ayaṃ dāsī ‘so puriso āgamissatī’ti āsāya ettakaṃ kālaṃ nisinnā, idānissa anāgamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā chinnāsā hutvā sukhaṃ supati. Kilesesu hi āsā nāma dukkhaṃ, nirāsabhāvova sukha”nti cintetvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Leaving the city, on the way, he lay down one evening in a house in a certain village. There, a slave woman named Piṅgalā had made an appointment with a man, saying, “Come at such and such a time.” Having washed her masters' feet, when they had lain down, she sat on the threshold watching for his arrival, thinking, “Now he will come, now he will come.” She passed the first watch and the middle watch. At dawn, realizing, “He will not come now,” her hope cut off, she lay down and fell asleep. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta reflected: “This slave woman sat for so long with the hope that ‘that man will come.’ Now, knowing that he is not coming, her hope is cut off, and she sleeps happily. Indeed, hope regarding the defilements is suffering; the state of being without hope is happiness.” Then he spoke the third verse:

119.

119.

“Sukhaṃ nirāsā supati, āsā phalavatī sukhā;

Āsaṃ nirāsaṃ katvāna, sukhaṃ supati piṅgalā”ti.

“One without hope sleeps happily; hope that is fruitful is happiness. Having made hope into hopelessness, Piṅgalā sleeps happily.”

Tattha phalavatīti yassā āsāya phalaṃ laddhaṃ hoti, sā tassa phalassa sukhatāya sukhā nāma. Nirāsaṃ katvānāti anāsaṃ katvā chinditvā pajahitvāti attho. Piṅgalāti esā piṅgaladāsī idāni sukhaṃ supatīti.

Here, “fruitful” means that when the fruit of one's hope has been obtained, that hope is called happiness because of the pleasantness of that fruit. “Having made it without hope” means having made it without hope, having cut it off, having relinquished it. “Piṅgalā” means this slave woman Piṅgalā now sleeps happily.

So punadivase tato gāmā araññaṃ pavisanto araññe ekaṃ tāpasaṃ jhānaṃ appetvā nisinnaṃ disvā “idhaloke ca paraloke ca jhānasukhato uttaritaraṃ sukhaṃ nāma natthī”ti cintetvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

On the following day, as he was entering the forest from that village, he saw an ascetic sitting absorbed in meditation in the forest. Reflecting, “In this world and the next, there is no happiness superior to the bliss of meditation,” he spoke the fourth verse:

120.

120.

“Na samādhiparo atthi, asmiṃ loke paramhi ca;

Na paraṃ nāpi attānaṃ, vihiṃsati samāhito”ti.

“There is nothing superior to concentration, in this world or the next; one who is concentrated harms neither others nor themselves.”

Tattha [V 3.0087][P 3.0102] na samādhiparoti samādhito paro añño sukhadhammo nāma natthīti.

Here, “nothing superior to concentration” means there is no other state of happiness superior to concentration.

So araññaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññā uppādetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Having entered the forest, he went forth as an ascetic, developed the meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, and was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā purohito ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, the chaplain was I myself.”

Sīlavīmaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The explanation of the Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka, the tenth.

Kuṭidūsakavaggo tatiyo.

The Kuṭidūsaka Chapter, the third.

4. Kokilavaggo

4. The Kokila Chapter

[331] 1. Kokilajātakavaṇṇanā

[331] 1. The explanation of the Kokila Jātaka

Yo [V 3.0088][M 3.0094] ve kāle asampatteti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kokālikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu takkāriyajātake vitthāritameva.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this concerning Kokālika, beginning with the words, “He who indeed at the time not reached.” The story is detailed in the Takkāriya Jātaka.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa amacco ovādako ahosi, rājā bahubhāṇī ahosi. Bodhisatto “tassa bahubhāṇitaṃ nisedhessāmī”ti ekaṃ upamaṃ upadhārento vicarati. Athekadivasaṃ rājā uyyānaṃ gato maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe nisīdi, tassupari ambarukkho atthi. Tatrekasmiṃ kākakulāvake kāḷakokilā attano aṇḍakaṃ nikkhipitvā agamāsi. Kākī taṃ kokilaaṇḍakaṃ paṭijaggi, aparabhāge tato kokilapotako nikkhami. Kākī “putto me”ti saññāya mukhatuṇḍakena gocaraṃ āharitvā taṃ paṭijaggi. So avirūḷhapakkho akāleyeva kokilaravaṃ ravi. Kākī “ayaṃ idāneva tāva aññaṃ ravaṃ ravati[P 3.0103], vaḍḍhanto kiṃ karissatī”ti tuṇḍakena koṭṭetvā māretvā kulāvakā pātesi. So rañño pādamūle pati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister and advisor. The king was very talkative. The Bodhisatta, thinking, “I will put a stop to his talkativeness,” went about searching for an analogy. Then one day, the king went to the park and sat on the auspicious stone slab. Above him was a mango tree. There, in a crow's nest, a black cuckoo had laid her egg and departed. The female crow looked after that cuckoo's egg, and later a young cuckoo hatched from it. The female crow, with the perception “This is my son,” brought food in her beak and looked after it. Before its wings were fully grown, it prematurely uttered a cuckoo's call. The female crow thought, “This one is already making a different sound now; what will it do when it grows up?” and pecking it with her beak, she killed it and threw it from the nest. It fell at the king's feet.

Rājā bodhisattaṃ pucchi “kimetaṃ sahāyā”ti? Bodhisatto “ahaṃ rājānaṃ nivāretuṃ ekaṃ upamaṃ pariyesāmi, laddhā dāni me sā”ti cintetvā “mahārāja, atimukharā akāle bahubhāṇino evarūpaṃ labhanti. Ayaṃ mahārāja, kokilapotako kākiyā puṭṭho avirūḷhapakkho akāleyeva kokilaravaṃ ravi. Atha naṃ kākī ‘nāyaṃ mama puttako’ti ñatvā mukhatuṇḍakena koṭṭetvā māretvā kulāvakā pātesi. Manussā vā hontu tiracchānā vā, akāle bahubhāṇino evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ labhantī”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

The king asked the Bodhisatta, "What is this, friend?" The Bodhisatta, thinking, "I have been seeking an analogy to restrain the king, and now I have found it," replied, "Great king, those who are overly talkative and speak much out of season meet with such a fate. This young cuckoo, fostered by the female crow, its wings not yet fully grown, prematurely uttered the cuckoo's call. Then the female crow, realizing 'This is not my offspring,' pecked it with her beak, killed it, and threw it from the nest. Whether humans or animals, those who speak much out of season meet with such suffering." Having said this, he spoke these verses:

121.

121.

“Yo ve kāle asampatte, ativelaṃ pabhāsati;

Evaṃ so nihato seti, kokilāyiva atrajo.

"He who speaks excessively when the time has not yet arrived, lies thus struck down, like the cuckoo's offspring."

122.

122.

“Na [V 3.0089][M 3.0095] hi satthaṃ sunisitaṃ, visaṃ halāhalāmiva;

Evaṃ nikaṭṭhe pāteti, vācā dubbhāsitā yathā.

"For neither a well-honed sword, nor poison like halāhala, strikes down so swiftly as does ill-spoken speech."

123.

123.

“Tasmā kāle akāle vā, vācaṃ rakkheyya paṇḍito;

Nātivelaṃ pabhāseyya, api attasamamhi vā.

"Therefore, whether in season or out of season, a wise person should guard their speech. They should not speak excessively, even to one equal to themselves."

124.

124.

“Yo ca kāle mitaṃ bhāse, matipubbo vicakkhaṇo;

Sabbe amitte ādeti, supaṇṇo uragāmivā”ti.

"But one who speaks in measured terms at the right time, thoughtful and discerning, overcomes all enemies, as a garuḍa overcomes a snake."

Tattha kāle asampatteti attano vacanakāle asampatte. Ativelanti velātikkantaṃ katvā atirekappamāṇaṃ bhāsati. Halāhalāmivāti halāhalaṃ iva. Nikaṭṭheti tasmiṃyeva khaṇe appamattake kāle. Tasmāti yasmā sunisitasatthahalāhalavisatopi khippataraṃ dubbhāsitavacanameva [P 3.0104] pātesi, tasmā. Kāle akāle vāti vattuṃ yuttakāle ca akāle ca vācaṃ rakkheyya, ativelaṃ na bhāseyya api attanā same ninnānākaraṇepi puggaleti attho.

Herein, 'kāle asampatte' means when the time for one's speech has not yet arrived. 'Ativelaṃ' means exceeding the proper limit, speaking beyond measure. 'Halāhalāmiva' means like halāhala poison. 'Nikaṭṭhe' means in that very moment, in a very short time. 'Tasmā' means: because ill-spoken words strike down faster than even a well-honed weapon or halāhala poison, therefore... 'Kāle akāle vā' means one should guard speech whether it is the right time to speak or not, and not speak excessively, even to a person who is one's equal and no different from oneself.

Matipubboti matiṃ purecārikaṃ katvā kathanena matipubbo. Vicakkhaṇoti ñāṇena vicāretvā atthavindanapuggalo vicakkhaṇo nāma. Uragāmivāti uragaṃ iva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā supaṇṇo samuddaṃ khobhetvā mahābhogaṃ uragaṃ ādeti gaṇhāti, ādiyitvā ca taṅkhaṇaññeva naṃ simbaliṃ āropetvā maṃsaṃ khādati, evameva yo matipubbaṅgamo vicakkhaṇo vattuṃ yuttakāle mitaṃ bhāsati, so sabbe amitte ādeti gaṇhāti, attano vase vattetīti.

'Matipubbo' means one who makes thought the precursor to speaking. 'Vicakkhaṇo' refers to a person who investigates with wisdom and finds the meaning. 'Uragāmivā' means like a snake. This is what is meant: Just as a garuḍa stirs the ocean, seizes a large-bodied serpent, and having taken it, immediately carries it to a silk-cotton tree and eats its flesh, even so, one who is led by thought, discerning, and speaks in measured terms at the proper time, seizes all enemies and brings them under his control.

Rājā bodhisattassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā tato paṭṭhāya mitabhāṇī ahosi, yasañcassa vaḍḍhetvā mahantataraṃ adāsi.

Hearing the Bodhisatta's Dhamma discourse, the king from then on became measured in speech; and having increased the Bodhisatta's prosperity, he bestowed much upon him.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kokilapotako kokāliko ahosi, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka thus: 'At that time, the young cuckoo was Kokālika, and the wise minister was myself.'

Kokilajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Explanation of the Cuckoo Jātaka is finished.

[332] 2. Rathalaṭṭhijātakavaṇṇanā

[332] 2. The Explanation of the Chariot-Stick Jātaka

Api [V 3.0090][M 3.0096] hantvā hato brūtīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarañño purohitaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira rathena attano bhogagāmaṃ gacchanto sambādhe magge rathaṃ pājento ekaṃ sakaṭasatthaṃ disvā “tumhākaṃ sakaṭaṃ apanethā”ti gacchanto sakaṭe anapanīyamāne kujjhitvā patodalaṭṭhiyā purimasakaṭe sākaṭikassa rathadhure pahari. Sā rathadhure paṭihatā nivattitvā tasseva nalāṭaṃ pahari. Tāvadevassa nalāṭe gaṇḍo uṭṭhahi. So nivattitvā “sākaṭikehi pahaṭomhī”ti rañño ārocesi. Sākaṭike pakkosāpetvā vinicchinantā tasseva dosaṃ addasaṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, rañño kira [P 3.0105] purohito ‘sākaṭikehi pahaṭomhī’ti aḍḍaṃ karonto sayameva parajjī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa evarūpaṃ akāsiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning the king of Kosala’s chaplain, beginning with 'Even having struck, he says, "I have been struck."' It seems that while traveling by chariot to his own revenue-village, driving his chariot along a narrow road, he saw a caravan of carts. 'Move your carts aside!' he said, but as the carts were not moved, he became angry and struck the pole of the lead cart with his goad-stick. The stick, struck against the pole, recoiled and hit his own forehead. Instantly, a lump arose on his forehead. Returning, he reported to the king, 'I have been struck by the cart-drivers!' The king summoned the cart-drivers and, upon investigating, they saw that the fault lay with the chaplain himself. One day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, it is said that the king’s chaplain, while bringing a lawsuit claiming, "I have been struck by the cart-drivers," was himself defeated.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?' When they told him, he said, 'Monks, not just now—in the past, too, he acted in such a way,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tasseva vinicchayāmacco ahosi. Atha rañño purohito rathena attano bhogagāmaṃ gacchantoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva. Idha pana tena rañño ārocite rājā sayaṃ vinicchaye nisīditvā sākaṭike pakkosāpetvā kammaṃ asodhetvāva “tumhehi mama purohitaṃ koṭṭetvā nalāṭe gaṇḍo uṭṭhāpito”ti vatvā “sabbassaharaṇaṃ tesaṃ karothā”ti āha. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “tumhe, mahārāja, kammaṃ asodhetvāva etesaṃ sabbassaṃ harāpetha, ekacce pana attanāva attānaṃ paharitvāpi ‘parena pahaṭamhā’ti vadanti, tasmā avicinitvā kātuṃ na yuttaṃ, rajjaṃ kārentena nāma nisāmetvā kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister of justice. Now, the king’s chaplain was going to his own revenue-village by chariot, and everything was just as before. But here, when the king was informed by him, the king himself sat in judgment, summoned the cart-drivers, and without investigating the case, said, 'You struck my chaplain and caused a lump to rise on his forehead,' and ordered, 'Confiscate all their property.' Then the Bodhisatta said to him, 'Great king, you order the confiscation of all their property without investigating the case. But some people even strike themselves and then say, “We have been struck by another.” Therefore, it is not right to act without investigation. For one who rules a kingdom, it is proper to act after careful consideration.' Having said this, he spoke these verses:

125.

125.

“Api hantvā hato brūti, jetvā jitoti bhāsati;

Pubbamakkhāyino rāja, aññadatthu na saddahe.

Even after striking, he says, 'I am struck'; having conquered, he says, 'I am conquered.' O king, one should definitely not believe the one who reports first.

126.

126.

“Tasmā paṇḍitajātiyo, suṇeyya itarassapi;

Ubhinnaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, yathā dhammo tathā kare.

Therefore, one of a wise nature should listen to the other party as well; having heard the words of both, one should act according to the truth.

127.

127.

“Alaso [M 3.0097] gihī kāmabhogī na sādhu, asaññato pabbajito na sādhu;

Rājā na sādhu anisammakārī, yo paṇḍito kodhano taṃ na sādhu.

A lazy householder enjoying sensual pleasures is not good; an unrestrained renunciant is not good; a king who acts without consideration is not good; and a wise person who is wrathful is not good.

128.

128.

“Nisamma [V 3.0091][P 3.0106] khattiyo kayirā, nānisamma disampati;

Nisammakārino rāja, yaso kitti ca vaḍḍhatī”ti.

A khattiya should act after careful consideration, not without consideration, O lord of the land. For one who acts after consideration, O king, fame and renown increase.

Tattha api hantvāti api eko attanāva attānaṃ hantvā “parena pahaṭomhī”ti brūti katheti. Jetvā jitoti sayaṃ vā pana paraṃ jitvā “ahaṃ jitomhī”ti bhāsati. Aññadatthūti mahārāja, pubbameva rājakulaṃ gantvā akkhāyantassa pubbamakkhāyino aññadatthu na saddahe, ekaṃsena vacanaṃ na saddaheyya. Tasmāti yasmā paṭhamataraṃ āgantvā kathentassa ekaṃsena vacanaṃ na saddahātabbaṃ, tasmā. Yathā dhammoti yathā vinicchayasabhāvo ṭhito, tathā kareyya.

Herein, ‘api hantvā’ means that one might even strike oneself and then say, ‘I was struck by another.’ ‘Jetvā jito’ means that one might conquer another and then declare, ‘I have been conquered.’ ‘Aññadatthu na saddahe pubbamakkhāyino’ means: O great king, one should by no means believe one who speaks first, having gone to the royal court beforehand to make a report; one should not believe the first person’s statement. ‘Tasmā’ means that because one should not believe the statement of someone who comes first and speaks, for that reason one should listen to the other. ‘Yathā dhammo’ means one should act according to how the legal principle stands.

Asaññatoti kāyādīhi asaññato dussīlo. Taṃ na sādhūti yaṃ tassa paṇḍitassa ñāṇavato puggalassa ādhānaggāhivasena daḷhakopasaṅkhātaṃ kodhanaṃ, taṃ na sādhu. Nānisammāti na anisāmetvā. Disampatīti disānaṃ pati, mahārāja. Yaso kitti cāti issariyaparivāro ceva kittisaddo ca vaḍḍhatīti.

‘Asaññato’ means unrestrained in body and so forth, unvirtuous. ‘Taṃ na sādhu’ means that the anger of that wise and knowledgeable person, which is firmly held through persistent attachment and is reckoned as strong, that is not good. ‘Nānisamma’ means without having examined. ‘Disampati’ means lord of the directions, O great king. ‘Yaso kitti ca’ means both the retinue of sovereignty and the sound of fame increase.

Rājā bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā dhammena vinicchini, dhammena vinicchiyamāne brāhmaṇasseva doso jātoti.

The king, having heard the Bodhisatta’s words, judged according to the Dhamma. When the judgment was made according to the Dhamma, the fault was found to lie with the brahmin alone.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā brāhmaṇo etarahi brāhmaṇova ahosi, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: ‘At that time, the brahmin was the present brahmin, but the wise minister was indeed myself.’

Rathalaṭṭhijātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Rathalaṭṭhi Jātaka: The Second.

[333] 3. Pakkagodhajātakavaṇṇanā

[333] 3. The Commentary on the Pakkagodha Jātaka.

Tadeva [M 3.0098] me tvanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā vitthāritameva. Idha pana tesaṃ uddhāraṃ sādhetvā āgacchantānaṃ antarāmagge luddako “ubhopi khādathā”ti ekaṃ pakkagodhaṃ adāsi. So puriso bhariyaṃ pānīyatthāya pesetvā sabbaṃ godhaṃ khāditvā tassā āgatakāle “bhadde, godhā palātā”ti āha. “Sādhu, sāmi, pakkagodhāya palāyantiyā kiṃ sakkā kātu”nti? Sā jetavane pānīyaṃ [P 3.0107] pivitvā satthu santike [V 3.0092] nisinnā satthārā “kiṃ upāsike, ayaṃ te hitakāmo sasineho upakārako”ti pucchitā “bhante, ahaṃ etassa hitakāmā sasinehā, ayaṃ pana mayi nissineho”ti āha. Satthā “hotu mā cintayi, evaṃ nāmesa karoti. Yadā pana te guṇaṃ sarati, tadā tuyhameva sabbissariyaṃ detī”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

‘Tadeva me tvaṃ’ – This the Teacher told while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a certain householder. The story is detailed below. Here, however, as they were returning after recovering a debt, a hunter on the way gave them a roasted monitor lizard, saying, ‘Both of you eat.’ That man sent his wife to fetch water and ate the entire monitor lizard himself. When she returned, he said, ‘Dear one, the monitor lizard has run away!’ ‘Very well, my lord, what can be done when a roasted monitor lizard runs away?’ she replied. After drinking water in Jetavana, she sat near the Teacher. The Teacher asked, ‘Lay devotee, is this man well-wishing, affectionate, and helpful towards you?’ She answered, ‘Venerable sir, I am well-wishing and affectionate towards him, but he has no affection for me.’ The Teacher said, ‘Let it be, do not worry. This is just his way. But when he remembers your virtues, he will give you all sovereignty.’ Having been requested by them, he brought forth the past.

Atītampi heṭṭhā vuttasadisameva. Idha pana tesaṃ nivattantānaṃ antarāmagge luddako kilantabhāvaṃ disvā “dvepi janā khādathā”ti ekaṃ pakkagodhaṃ adāsi. Rājadhītā taṃ valliyā bandhitvā ādāya maggaṃ paṭipajji. Te ekaṃ saraṃ disvā maggā okkamma assatthamūle nisīdiṃsu. Rājaputto “gaccha bhadde, sarato paduminipattena udakaṃ āhara, maṃsaṃ khādissāmā”ti āha. Sā godhaṃ sākhāya laggetvā pānīyatthāya gatā. Itaro sabbaṃ godhaṃ khāditvā agganaṅguṭṭhaṃ gahetvā parammukho nisīdi. So tāya pānīyaṃ gahetvā āgatāya “bhadde, godhā sākhāya otaritvā vammikaṃ pāvisi, ahaṃ dhāvitvā agganaṅguṭṭhaṃ aggahesiṃ, gahitaṭṭhānaṃ hattheyeva katvā chijjitvā bilaṃ paviṭṭhā”ti āha. “Hotu, deva, pakkagodhāya palāyantiyā kiṃ karissāma, ehi gacchāmā”ti. Te pānīyaṃ pivitvā bārāṇasiṃ agamaṃsu.

The past is just as previously mentioned. Here, however, as they were returning, a hunter, seeing them exhausted on the road, said, ‘You two can eat this,’ and gave them a single roasted monitor lizard. The princess tied it with a vine, took it, and continued on the road. Seeing a lake, they left the road and sat at the foot of an Assattha tree. The prince said, ‘Go, dear one, bring water in a lotus leaf from the lake; we will eat the meat.’ She hung the monitor lizard on a branch and went for water. The other one ate the entire monitor lizard, took the tip of its tail, and sat with his back turned. When she returned with the water, he said, ‘Dear one, the monitor lizard climbed down from the branch and entered an anthill. I ran and grabbed the tip of its tail, but the part I grabbed broke off in my hand, and it entered the hole.’ ‘So be it, my lord, what can we do if a roasted monitor lizard runs away? Come, let us go.’ They drank the water and went to Bārāṇasī.

Rājaputto rajjaṃ patvā taṃ aggamahesiṭṭhānamatte ṭhapesi, sakkārasammāno panassā natthi. Bodhisatto tassā sakkāraṃ kāretukāmo rañño santike ṭhatvā “nanu mayaṃ ayye tumhākaṃ santikā kiñci na labhāma, kiṃ no na olokethā”ti āha. “Tāta, ahameva rañño [M 3.0099] santikā kiñci na labhāmi, tuyhaṃ kiṃ dassāmi, rājāpi mayhaṃ idāni kiṃ dassati, so araññato āgamanakāle pakkagodhaṃ ekakova khādī”ti[P 3.0108]. “Ayye, na devo evarūpaṃ karissati, mā evaṃ avacutthā”ti. Atha naṃ devī “tuyhaṃ taṃ, tāta, na pākaṭaṃ, raññoyeva mayhañca pākaṭa”nti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The prince, upon attaining the kingship, established her merely in the position of chief queen, but she received no honor or respect. The Bodhisatta, wishing to secure honor for her, stood in the king's presence and said to her, ‘Noble lady, do we not receive anything from you? Why do you not look upon us?’ She replied, ‘Dear child, I myself receive nothing from the king. What can I give you? And what will the king give me now? When we were coming from the forest, he ate the roasted monitor lizard all by himself.’ The Bodhisatta said, ‘Noble lady, the king would not do such a thing; do not speak thus.’ Then the queen said, ‘Dear child, that is not known to you, but it is known to the king and to me,’ and she spoke the first verse:

129.

129.

“Tadeva me tvaṃ vidito, vanamajjhe rathesabha;

Yassa te khaggabaddhassa, sannaddhassa tirīṭino;

Assatthadumasākhāya, pakkagodhā palāyathā”ti.

“By that very act you were known to me, O bull among charioteers, in the midst of the forest; for you, with sword girded, clad in armor, and wearing a bark-cloth, a roasted monitor lizard fled from the branch of the Assattha tree.”

Tattha tadevāti tasmiṃyeva kāle “ayaṃ mayhaṃ adāyako”ti evaṃ tvaṃ vidito. Aññe pana tava sabhāvaṃ na jānantīti attho. Khaggabaddhassāti baddhakhaggassa. Tirīṭinoti tirīṭavatthanivatthassa maggāgamanakāle. Pakkagodhāti aṅgārapakkā godhā palāyathāti.

Herein, ‘tadeva’ means: at that very time, you were known thus: ‘This one is ungenerous towards me.’ The meaning is that others do not know your true nature. ‘Khaggabaddhassa’ means one with a sword fastened. ‘Tirīṭino’ means one wearing bark-cloth while traveling on the path. ‘Pakkagodhā palāyatha’ means a monitor lizard roasted on coals fled.

Evaṃ [V 3.0093] raññā katadosaṃ parisamajjhe pākaṭaṃ katvā kathesi. Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto “ayye, devassa appiyakālato pabhuti ubhinnampi aphāsukaṃ katvā kasmā idha vasathā”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Thus she spoke, making manifest in the midst of the assembly the fault committed by the king. Hearing this, the Bodhisatta said, ‘Noble lady, since the time you became displeasing to the king, why do you remain here, causing discomfort for you both?’ and he spoke two verses:

130.

130.

“Name namantassa bhaje bhajantaṃ, kiccānukubbassa kareyya kiccaṃ;

Nānatthakāmassa kareyya atthaṃ, asambhajantampi na sambhajeyya.

“One should bow to one who bows, and attend to one who attends. One should do a service for one who does a service, and promote the welfare of one who does not wish one harm. One should not associate with one who does not associate.”

131.

131.

“Caje cajantaṃ vanathaṃ na kayirā, apetacittena na sambhajeyya;

Dijo dumaṃ khīṇaphalanti ñatvā, aññaṃ samekkheyya mahā hi loko”ti.

“One should abandon one who abandons; one should not create a longing. One should not associate with one whose mind has turned away. A bird, knowing a tree is devoid of fruit, should seek another; for the world is vast.”

Tattha name namantassāti yo attani muducittena namati, tasseva paṭinameyya. Kiccānukubbassāti attano uppannaṃ kiccaṃ anukubbantasseva. Anatthakāmassāti avaḍḍhikāmassa. Vanathaṃ na kayirāti [P 3.0109] tasmiṃ cajante taṇhāsnehaṃ na kareyya. Apetacittenāti apagatacittena virattacittena. Na sambhajeyyāti na samāgaccheyya. Aññaṃ samekkheyyāti aññaṃ [M 3.0100] olokeyya, yathā dijo khīṇaphalaṃ dumaṃ rukkhaṃ ñatvā aññaṃ phalabharitaṃ rukkhaṃ gacchati, tathā khīṇarāgaṃ purisaṃ ñatvā aññaṃ sasinehaṃ upagaccheyyāti adhippāyo.

Herein, 'name namantassa' means: one should bow in return to one who bows to oneself with a gentle heart. 'Kiccānukubbassa' means: one should perform a duty for one who performs a duty for oneself. 'Anatthakāmassa' means one who desires one's non-benefit. 'Vanathaṃ na kayirā' means: when that person abandons you, one should not have any craving or affection for them. 'Apetacittenā' means with a mind that has turned away, with a dispassionate mind. 'Na sambhajeyya' means one should not associate with them. 'Aññaṃ samekkheyya' means one should look for another; the intention is that just as a bird, knowing a tree is devoid of fruit, goes to another tree laden with fruit, so too, knowing a person's affection for you is exhausted, one should approach another who has affection for you.

Rājā bodhisatte kathente eva tassā guṇaṃ saritvā “bhadde, ettakaṃ kālaṃ tava guṇaṃ na sallakkhesiṃ, paṇḍitassayeva kathāya sallakkhesiṃ, mama aparādhaṃ sahantiyā idaṃ sakalarajjaṃ tuyhameva dammī”ti vatvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

While the Bodhisatta was speaking, the king, remembering her virtue, said: “Good lady, for so long I did not recognize your virtue; I have recognized it only through the words of the wise one. To you, who endures my offense, I give this entire kingdom.” Then he spoke the fourth verse:

132.

132.

“So te karissāmi yathānubhāvaṃ, kataññutaṃ khattiye pekkhamāno;

Sabbañca te issariyaṃ dadāmi, yassicchasī tassa tuvaṃ dadāmī”ti.

“I will act for you according to my power, O princess, considering your gratitude. I give you all sovereignty, and you may give it to whomever you wish.”

Tattha soti so ahaṃ. Yathānubhāvanti yathāsatti yathābalaṃ. Yassicchasīti yassa icchasi, tassa idaṃ rajjaṃ ādiṃ katvā yaṃ tvaṃ icchasi, taṃ dadāmīti.

Herein, 'so' means 'I'. 'Yathānubhāvaṃ' means according to one's ability, according to one's strength. 'Yassicchasi' means: to whomever you wish; I give that which you wish, beginning with this kingdom.

Evañca pana vatvā rājā deviyā sabbissariyaṃ adāsi, “imināhaṃ etissā guṇaṃ sarāpito”ti paṇḍitassapi mahantaṃ issariyaṃ adāsi.

Having spoken thus, the king granted the queen full sovereignty. Thinking, “By this wise man I have been reminded of her virtue,” he also bestowed great sovereignty upon the wise man.

Satthā [V 3.0094] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ubho jayampatikā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, both husband and wife were established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā jayampatikā etarahi jayampatikāva ahesuṃ, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the husband and wife were the same husband and wife as now, but the wise minister was none other than myself.

Pakkagodhajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Pakkagodha Jātaka: The Third.

[334] 4. Rājovādajātakavaṇṇanā

[334] 4. The Commentary on the Rājovāda Jātaka.

Gavaṃ [P 3.0110] ce taramānānanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto rājovādaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu tesakuṇajātake (jā. 2.17.1 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Idha pana satthā “mahārāja, porāṇakarājānopi paṇḍitānaṃ kathaṃ sutvā dhammena samena rajjaṃ kārentā saggapuraṃ pūrayamānā gamiṃsū”ti vatvā raññā yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher told this story, beginning with the verse 'If cows are crossing,' while dwelling at Jetavana in connection with advice to a king. The full story will be made clear in the Tesakuṇa Jātaka. Here, however, the Teacher, saying, 'Great king, even the kings of old, having listened to the words of the wise, ruled their kingdoms with Dhamma and equity, and went on to fill the city of the gods,' and being requested by the king, related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 3.0101] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto sikkhitasabbasippo isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā ramaṇīye himavantapadese vanamūlaphalāhāro vihāsi. Atha rājā aguṇapariyesako hutvā “atthi nu kho me koci aguṇaṃ kathento”ti pariyesanto antojane ca bahijane ca antonagare ca bahinagare ca kañci attano avaṇṇavādiṃ adisvā “janapade nu kho katha”nti aññātakavesena janapadaṃ cari. Tatrāpi avaṇṇavādiṃ apassanto attano guṇakathameva sutvā “himavantapadese nu kho katha”nti araññaṃ pavisitvā vicaranto bodhisattassa assamaṃ patvā taṃ abhivādetvā katapaṭisanthāro ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family. Having come of age and mastered all the arts, he went forth into the ascetic life. Developing the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, he dwelt in a delightful region of the Himalayas, sustaining himself on roots and fruits of the forest. Then the king, seeking to find his own faults, searched, thinking, 'Is there anyone who speaks of my faults?' Not seeing anyone who spoke ill of him among the people of his court or the public, within the city or outside the city, he wandered through the countryside in disguise, thinking, 'How is it in the countryside?' Even there, not finding anyone who spoke ill of him and hearing only praise of his own virtues, he entered the forest, thinking, 'How is it in the Himalayan region?' Wandering about, he reached the Bodhisatta's hermitage. After paying homage to him and exchanging pleasantries, he sat down to one side.

Tadā bodhisatto araññato paripakkāni nigrodhaphalāni āharitvā paribhuñji, tāni honti madhurāni ojavantāni sakkharacuṇṇasamarasāni. So rājānampi āmantetvā “imaṃ mahāpuñña, nigrodhapakkaphalaṃ khāditvā pānīyaṃ pivā”ti āha. Rājā tathā katvā bodhisattaṃ pucchi “kiṃ nu kho, bhante, imaṃ nigrodhapakkaṃ ati viya madhura”nti? “Mahāpuñña, nūna rājā dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāreti, tenetaṃ madhuranti. Rañño adhammikakāle [P 3.0111] amadhuraṃ nu kho, bhante, hotī”ti. “Āma, mahāpuñña, rājūsu adhammikesu telamadhuphāṇitādīnipi vanamūlaphalānipi amadhurāni honti nirojāni, na kevalaṃ etāni, sakalampi raṭṭhaṃ nirojaṃ kasaṭaṃ [V 3.0095] hoti. Tesu pana dhammikesu sabbāni tāni madhurāni honti ojavantāni, sakalampi raṭṭhaṃ ojavantameva hotī”ti. Rājā “evaṃ bhavissati, bhante”ti attano rājabhāvaṃ ajānāpetvāva bodhisattaṃ vanditvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā “tāpasassa vacanaṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti adhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā “idāni jānissāmī”ti kiñci kālaṃ vītināmetvā puna tattha gantvā taṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

At that time, the Bodhisatta brought ripe banyan fruits from the forest and ate them; they were sweet, nutritious, and tasted like powdered sugar. He also invited the king, saying, 'Man of great merit, eat this ripe banyan fruit and then drink some water.' The king did so and then asked the Bodhisatta, 'Venerable sir, why is this ripe banyan fruit so exceedingly sweet?' 'Man of great merit, surely the king rules his kingdom with Dhamma and equity; that is why it is sweet.' 'But, venerable sir, when the king is unrighteous, does it become unsweet?' 'Yes, man of great merit. When kings are unrighteous, even oil, honey, and molasses, as well as the roots and fruits of the forest, become unsweet and without nourishment. Not only these, but the entire kingdom becomes insipid and spoiled. But when they are righteous, all those things become sweet and nutritious, and the entire kingdom itself becomes prosperous.' The king said, 'It must be so, venerable sir,' and without revealing that he was the king, he paid homage to the Bodhisatta and went to Benares. Thinking, 'I will test the ascetic's words,' he began to rule unrighteously. After some time had passed, thinking, 'Now I will know,' he went back there, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.

Bodhisattopissa tatheva vatvā nigrodhapakkaṃ adāsi, taṃ tassa tittakarasaṃ ahosi. Rājā “amadhuraṃ nirasa”nti saha kheḷena chaḍḍetvā “tittakaṃ, bhante”ti āha. Bodhisatto “mahāpuñña, nūna rājā adhammiko bhavissati. Rājūnañhi adhammikakāle araññe phalāphalaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ amadhuraṃ nirojaṃ jāta”nti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

The Bodhisatta, speaking to him as before, gave him a ripe banyan fruit, which tasted bitter to him. The king spat it out with his saliva, saying, 'It is unsweet, it is tasteless,' and then said, 'Venerable sir, it is bitter.' The Bodhisatta said, 'Man of great merit, surely the king must be unrighteous. For when kings are unrighteous, everything, beginning with the various fruits in the forest, becomes unsweet and without nourishment.' Having said this, he recited these verses:

133.

133.

“Gave [M 3.0102] ce taramānānaṃ, jimhaṃ gacchati puṅgavo;

Sabbā tā jimhaṃ gacchanti, nette jimhaṃ gate sati.

“If, while the cows are crossing, the lead bull goes crooked, they all go crooked, when their leader has gone crooked.

134.

134.

“Evameva manussesu, yo hoti seṭṭhasammato;

So ce adhammaṃ carati, pageva itarā pajā;

Sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ dukhaṃ seti, rājā ce hoti adhammiko.

“So too among human beings, one who is considered the foremost: if he practices unrighteousness, how much more so the other people? The entire kingdom dwells in misery, if the king is unrighteous.

135.

135.

“Gavaṃ ce taramānānaṃ, ujuṃ gacchati puṅgavo;

Sabbā gāvī ujuṃ yanti, nette ujuṃ gate sati.

“If, while the cows are crossing, the lead bull goes straight, they all go straight, when their leader has gone straight.

136.

136.

“Evameva manussesu, yo hoti seṭṭhasammato;

So sace dhammaṃ carati, pageva itarā pajā;

Sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ sukhaṃ seti, rājā ce hoti dhammiko”ti.

"So too among human beings, one who is considered the foremost: if he practices the Dhamma, how much more so the other people? The entire kingdom dwells in happiness, if the king is righteous."

Tattha [P 3.0112] gavanti gunnaṃ. Taramānānanti nadiṃ otarantānaṃ. Jimhanti kuṭilaṃ vaṅkaṃ. Netteti nāyake gahetvā gacchante gavajeṭṭhake usabhe puṅgave. Pageva itarā pajāti itare sattā puretarameva adhammaṃ carantīti attho. Dukhaṃ setīti na kevalaṃ seti, catūsupi iriyāpathesu dukkhameva vindati. Adhammikoti yadi rājā chandādiagatigamanavasena adhammiko hoti. Sukhaṃ setīti sace [V 3.0096] rājā agatigamanaṃ pahāya dhammiko hoti, sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ catūsu iriyāpathesu sukhappattameva hotīti.

Herein, 'gavaṃ' means 'of cows.' 'Taramānānaṃ' means 'of those crossing a river.' 'Jimhaṃ' means 'crooked, bent.' 'Nette' means the leader, the chief of the cows, the bull, the prime bull that goes at the head. 'Pageva itarā pajā' means the other beings practice unrighteousness even before [the king does]; this is the meaning. 'Dukhaṃ seti' means one does not merely lie down in misery, but experiences misery in all four postures. 'Adhammiko' means if the king is unrighteous by following the wrong courses of action beginning with desire. 'Sukhaṃ seti' means that if the king, having abandoned the wrong courses of action, is righteous, the entire kingdom attains happiness in all four postures.

Rājā bodhisattassa dhammaṃ sutvā attano rājabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā “bhante, pubbe nigrodhapakkaṃ ahameva madhuraṃ katvā tittakaṃ akāsiṃ, idāni puna madhuraṃ karissāmī”ti bodhisattaṃ vanditvā nagaraṃ gantvā dhammena rajjaṃ kārento sabbaṃ paṭipākatikaṃ akāsi.

The king, having heard the Dhamma from the Bodhisatta, revealed that he was the king and said, 'Venerable sir, it was I who previously made the ripe banyan fruit sweet, and then made it bitter. Now I will make it sweet again.' Having paid homage to the Bodhisatta, he returned to the city and, by ruling his kingdom righteously, restored everything to its natural state.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection in the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the ascetic was I myself."

Rājovādajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Rājovāda Jātaka, the fourth.

[335] 5. Jambukajātakavaṇṇanā

[335] 5. The Commentary on the Jambuka Jātaka

Brahā [M 3.0103] pavaḍḍhakāyo soti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa sugatālayakaraṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā vitthāritameva, ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo. Satthārā “sāriputta, devadatto tumhe disvā kiṃ akāsī”ti vutto thero āha “bhante, so tumhākaṃ anukaronto mama hatthe bījaniṃ datvā nipajji. Atha naṃ kokāliko ure jaṇṇunā pahari, iti so tumhākaṃ anukaronto dukkhaṃ anubhavī”ti. Taṃ sutvā satthā “na kho, sāriputta, devadatto idāneva mama anukaronto dukkhaṃ anubhoti, pubbepesa anubhosiyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

This story, beginning with the verse 'He is great, with a well-developed body,' the Teacher told while dwelling at the Bamboo Grove concerning Devadatta's imitation of the Sugata. The full story has been related in detail elsewhere; this is but a summary. When asked by the Teacher, 'Sāriputta, what did Devadatta do when he saw you?' the Elder replied, 'Venerable sir, imitating you, he placed a fan in my hand and lay down. Then Kokālika struck him on the chest with his knee. Thus, by imitating you, he came to grief.' Hearing this, the Teacher said, 'Sāriputta, it is not only now that Devadatta has come to grief by imitating me; he did so in the past as well.' And at his request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sīhayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā himavante guhāyaṃ vasanto [P 3.0113] ekadivasaṃ mahiṃsaṃ vadhitvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā guhaṃ āgacchati. Eko siṅgālo taṃ disvā palāyituṃ asakkonto urena nipajji, “kiṃ jambukā”ti ca vutte “upaṭṭhahissāmi taṃ, bhaddante”ti āha. Sīho “tena hi ehī”ti taṃ attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ netvā divase divase maṃsaṃ āharitvā posesi. Tassa sīhavighāsena thūlasarīrataṃ pattassa ekadivasaṃ māno uppajji. So sīhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āha “ahaṃ, sāmi, niccakālaṃ tumhākaṃ palibodho, tumhe niccaṃ maṃsaṃ āharitvā maṃ posetha, ajja tumhe idheva hotha, ahaṃ ekaṃ vāraṇaṃ vadhitvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā tumhākampi āharissāmī”ti. Sīho “mā te[V 3.0097], jambuka, etaṃ rucci, na tvaṃ vāraṇaṃ vadhitvā maṃsakhādakayoniyaṃ nibbatto, ahaṃ te vāraṇaṃ vadhitvā dassāmi, vāraṇo nāma mahākāyo pavaḍḍhakāyo, mā vāraṇaṃ gaṇhi, mama vacanaṃ karohī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having been reborn as a lion, was dwelling in a cave in the Himalayas. One day, after killing a buffalo, eating its flesh, and drinking water, he returned to his cave. A jackal, seeing him and being unable to flee, lay down on his belly. When asked, 'What is it, jackal?' he replied, 'I will attend upon you, venerable sir.' The lion said, 'Then come,' and taking him to his dwelling place, nourished him by bringing meat day by day. As the jackal grew stout from the lion's leavings, one day pride arose in him. Approaching the lion, he said, 'Master, I am a constant burden to you. You always bring meat to nourish me. Today, you stay here—I will kill an elephant, eat its flesh, and bring some for you too.' The lion replied, 'Jackal, do not let this please you. You were not born into a species that kills elephants and eats their flesh. I will kill an elephant and give it to you. An elephant has a great and well-developed body—do not take on an elephant. Do as I say.' Having said this, he spoke the first verse.

137.

137.

“Brahā pavaḍḍhakāyo so, dīghadāṭho ca jambuka;

Na tvaṃ tattha kule jāto, yattha gaṇhanti kuñjara”nti.

"He is great, with a well-developed body, and long-tusked, O jackal; you were not born in that lineage where they seize elephants."

Tattha brahāti mahanto. Pavaḍḍhakāyoti uddhaṃ uggatakāyo. Dīghadāṭhoti dīghadanto tehi dantehi tumhādise paharitvā jīvitakkhaye [M 3.0104] pāpeti. Yatthāti yasmiṃ sīhakule jātā mattavāraṇaṃ gaṇhanti, tvaṃ na tattha jāto, siṅgālakule pana jātosīti attho.

Here, 'brahā' means 'great.' 'Pavaḍḍhakāyo' means 'having a body that has grown tall.' 'Dīghadāṭho' means 'long-tusked'; with those tusks, by striking the likes of you, he brings one to the end of life. 'Yattha' means: in whichever lion lineage those who are born seize a maddened elephant, you were not born there, but rather you were born in a jackal lineage—this is the meaning.

Siṅgālo sīhena vāritoyeva guhā nikkhamitvā tikkhattuṃ “bukka bukkā”ti siṅgālikaṃ nadaṃ naditvā pabbatakūṭe ṭhito pabbatapādaṃ olokento ekaṃ kāḷavāraṇaṃ pabbatapādena āgacchantaṃ disvā ullaṅghitvā “tassa kumbhe patissāmī”ti parivattitvā pādamūle pati. Vāraṇo purimapādaṃ ukkhipitvā tassa matthake patiṭṭhāpesi, sīsaṃ bhijjitvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ jātaṃ[P 3.0114]. So tattheva anutthunanto sayi, vāraṇo koñcanādaṃ karonto pakkāmi. Bodhisatto gantvā pabbatamatthake ṭhito taṃ vināsappattaṃ disvā “attano mānaṃ nissāya naṭṭho siṅgālo”ti tisso gāthā abhāsi –

The jackal, though prevented by the lion, emerged from the cave and howled the jackal's cry 'bukka bukkā' three times. Standing on the mountain peak and looking down at the mountain's base, he saw a black elephant approaching. Leaping up with the thought, 'I will land on its forehead,' he instead turned over and fell at its feet. The elephant lifted its front foot and placed it on the jackal's head, and his head was smashed to powder. He lay there groaning, while the elephant, making a trumpeting sound, departed. The Bodhisatta went and stood on the mountain peak, and seeing him come to ruin, he thought, 'The jackal is destroyed on account of his pride,' and spoke three verses:

138.

138.

“Asīho sīhamānena, yo attānaṃ vikubbati;

Kotthūva gajamāsajja, seti bhūmyā anutthunaṃ.

"One who, not being a lion, comports himself with the pride of a lion, lies groaning on the ground, like a jackal that has attacked an elephant."

139.

139.

“Yasassino uttamapuggalassa, sañjātakhandhassa mahabbalassa;

Asamekkhiya thāmabalūpapattiṃ, sa seti nāgena hatoyaṃ jambuko.

"Without considering the might, strength, and attainment of that glorious, supreme individual, of well-developed frame and great power, this jackal lies here, slain by the elephant."

140.

140.

“Yo cīdha kammaṃ kurute pamāya, thāmabbalaṃ attani saṃviditvā;

Jappena mantena subhāsitena, parikkhavā so vipulaṃ jinātī”ti.

"But whoever here undertakes an action after assessing it, knowing his own might and strength; through deliberation, counsel, and well-spoken words, being discerning, he wins a great victory."

Tattha vikubbatīti parivatteti. Kotthūvāti siṅgālo viya. Anutthunanti anutthunanto. Idaṃ [V 3.0098] vuttaṃ hoti – yathā ayaṃ kotthu mahantaṃ gajaṃ patvā anutthunanto bhūmiyaṃ seti, evaṃ yo añño dubbalo balavatā viggahaṃ karoti, sopi evarūpova hotīti.

Here, 'vikubbati' means 'transforms himself' or 'modifies himself.' 'Kotthūva' means 'like a jackal.' 'Anutthunaṃ' means 'groaning.' This is what is said: just as this jackal, having encountered a great elephant, lies on the ground groaning, so too whoever else, being weak, enters into conflict with the strong, becomes just like that.

Yasassinoti issariyavato. Uttamapuggalassāti kāyabalena ca ñāṇabalena ca uttamapuggalassa. Sañjātakhandhassāti susaṇṭhitamahākhandhassa. Mahabbalassāti [M 3.0105] mahāthāmassa. Thāmabalūpapattinti evarūpassa sīhassa thāmasaṅkhātaṃ balañceva sīhajātisaṅkhātaṃ upapattiñca ajānitvā, kāyathāmañca ñāṇabalañca sīhaupapattiñca ajānitvāti attho. Sa setīti attānampi sīhena sadisaṃ maññamāno, so ayaṃ jambuko nāgena hato matasayanaṃ seti.

‘Yasassino’ means ‘of one possessing lordship.’ ‘Uttamapuggalassa’ means ‘of the supreme individual,’ supreme in both physical strength and the strength of wisdom. ‘Sañjātakhandhassāti’ means ‘of one with well-proportioned, great shoulders.’ ‘Mahabbalassāti’ means ‘of great might.’ ‘Thāmabalūpapattiṃ’ means: without considering the strength, namely the strength known as might, and the birth known as the lion species of such a lion; the meaning is not knowing its physical might, the strength of its wisdom, and its birth as a lion. ‘Sa seti’ means: he, this jackal, thinking himself equal to a lion, lies dead, slain by the elephant.

Pamāyāti paminitvā upaparikkhitvā. “Pamāṇā”tipi pāṭho, attano pamāṇaṃ gahetvā yo attano pamāṇena kammaṃ kuruteti attho. Thāmabbalanti thāmasaṅkhātaṃ balaṃ, kāyathāmañca ñāṇabalañcātipi attho. Jappenāti japena, ajjhenenāti attho. Mantenāti aññehi paṇḍitehi saddhiṃ mantetvā karaṇena. Subhāsitenāti saccādiguṇayuttena anavajjavacanena. Parikkhavāti [P 3.0115] parikkhāsampanno. So vipulaṃ jinātīti yo evarūpo hoti, yaṃ kiñci kammaṃ kurumāno attano thāmañca balañca ñatvā jappamantavasena paricchinditvā subhāsitaṃ bhāsanto karoti, so vipulaṃ mahantaṃ atthaṃ jināti na parihāyatīti.

‘Pamāya’ means ‘having measured, having examined.’ There is also the reading ‘pamāṇā,’ meaning: one who, taking his own measure, performs an action according to his own measure. ‘Thāmabalaṃ’ means ‘the strength known as might’; the meaning is also ‘physical power and the strength of wisdom.’ ‘Jappena’ means ‘by recitation,’ that is, ‘by study.’ ‘Mantena’ means ‘by the act of taking counsel with other wise people.’ ‘Subhāsitenāti’ means ‘by faultless speech endowed with qualities such as truth.’ ‘Parikkhavā’ means ‘endowed with discernment.’ ‘So vipulaṃ jināti’ means: one who is of such a nature, when performing any action, does so knowing his own might and strength, having determined it by means of recitation and counsel, and speaking well-spoken words—he wins a great and abundant benefit and does not fail.

Evaṃ bodhisatto imāhi tīhi gāthāhi imasmiṃ loke kattabbayuttakaṃ kammaṃ kathesi.

Thus, with these three verses, the Bodhisatta spoke of the action that is fit to be done in this world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siṅgālo devadatto ahosi, sīho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, and the lion was I myself.”

Jambukajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Jambuka Jātaka, the fifth.

[336] 6. Brahāchattajātakavaṇṇanā

[336] 6. The Commentary on the Brahāchatta Jātaka

Tiṇaṃ tiṇanti lapasīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kuhakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu kathitameva.

“‘You mutter, “Grass, grass,”’—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a deceitful monk. The story of the present has already been told.”

Atīte pana bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa atthadhammānusāsako amacco [V 3.0099] ahosi. Bārāṇasirājā mahatiyā senāya kosalarājānaṃ abbhuggantvā sāvatthiṃ patvā yuddhena nagaraṃ pavisitvā rājānaṃ gaṇhi. Kosalarañño pana putto chatto nāma [M 3.0106] kumāro atthi.
