So aññātakavesena nikkhamitvā takkasilaṃ gantvā tayo vede ca aṭṭhārasa sippāni ca uggaṇhitvā takkasilato nikkhamma sabbasamayasippāni sikkhanto ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ pāpuṇi. Taṃ nissāya pañcasatatāpasā araññe paṇṇasālāsu vasanti. Kumāro te upasaṅkamitvā “imesampi santike kiñci sikkhissāmī”ti pabbajitvā yaṃ te jānanti, taṃ sabbaṃ uggaṇhi. So aparabhāge gaṇasatthā jāto.

In the past, however, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister, an advisor on worldly and spiritual matters. The king of Benares, advancing with a great army against the king of Kosala, reached Sāvatthī, entered the city by force of battle, and captured the king. Now, the king of Kosala had a son, a prince named Chatta. He departed in disguise, went to Takkasilā, and learned the three Vedas and the eighteen sciences. Leaving Takkasilā and studying the arts of all schools of thought, he arrived at a border village. Dependent on that village, five hundred ascetics were living in the forest in leaf-huts. The prince approached them, thinking, ‘I will learn something from them as well,’ and went forth as an ascetic, learning everything they knew. In time, he became the teacher of their group.

Athekadivasaṃ isigaṇaṃ āmantetvā “mārisā, kasmā majjhimadesaṃ na gacchathā”ti pucchi. “Mārisa, majjhimadese manussā nāma [P 3.0116] paṇḍitā, te pañhaṃ pucchanti, anumodanaṃ kārāpenti, maṅgalaṃ bhaṇāpenti, asakkonte garahanti, mayaṃ tena bhayena na gacchāmā”ti. “Mā tumhe bhāyatha, ahametaṃ sabbaṃ karissāmī”ti. “Tena hi gacchāmā”ti sabbe attano attano khārivividhamādāya anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ pattā. Bārāṇasirājāpi kosalarajjaṃ attano hatthagataṃ katvā tattha rājayutte ṭhapetvā sayaṃ tattha vijjamānaṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā uyyāne lohacāṭiyo pūrāpetvā nidahitvā tasmiṃ samaye bārāṇasiyameva vasati. Atha te isayo rājuyyāne rattiṃ vasitvā punadivase nagaraṃ bhikkhāya pavisitvā rājadvāraṃ agamaṃsu. Rājā tesaṃ iriyāpathessu pasīditvā pakkosāpetvā mahātale nisīdāpetvā yāgukhajjakaṃ datvā yāva bhattakālā taṃ taṃ pañhaṃ pucchi. Chatto rañño cittaṃ ārādhento sabbapañhe vissajjetvā bhattakiccāvasāne vicitraṃ anumodanaṃ akāsi. Rājā suṭṭhutaraṃ pasanno paṭiññaṃ gahetvā sabbepi te uyyāne vāsāpesi.

One day, he called the group of seers and asked, ‘Sirs, why do you not go to the Middle Country?’ ‘Sir, the people in the Middle Country are wise; they ask questions, have us give a discourse of appreciation, have us recite auspicious verses, and censure us if we are unable. We do not go out of fear of that.’ ‘Do not be afraid, I will handle all of that.’ ‘In that case, let us go.’ Taking their own various requisites, they gradually reached Bārāṇasī. The king of Bārāṇasī, having brought the kingdom of Kosala under his control, placed royal officials there, and taking the wealth available there himself, he went to Bārāṇasī, had bronze pots filled and buried in the park. At that time, he was residing in Bārāṇasī itself. Then those seers, having stayed in the royal park at night, entered the city for alms on the following day and went to the king’s gate. The king, pleased with their deportment, had them summoned, had them seated on the upper floor, gave them rice gruel and snacks, and asked them various questions until mealtime. Chatto, delighting the king’s mind, answered all the questions. At the end of the meal, he gave a varied and splendid discourse of appreciation. The king, exceedingly pleased, took their word and had them all take up residence in the park.

Chatto nidhiuddharaṇamantaṃ jānāti. So tattha vasanto “kahaṃ nu kho iminā mama pitu santakaṃ dhanaṃ nidahita”nti mantaṃ parivattetvā olokento uyyāne nidahitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “idaṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā mama rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā tāpase āmantetvā “mārisā, ahaṃ kosalarañño putto, bārāṇasiraññā amhākaṃ rajje gahite aññātakavesena nikkhamitvā ettakaṃ kālaṃ attano jīvitaṃ anurakkhiṃ, idāni kulasantakaṃ dhanaṃ laddhaṃ, ahaṃ etaṃ ādāya gantvā attano rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmi, tumhe kiṃ karissathā”ti āha. “Mayampi tayāva saddhiṃ gamissāmā”ti[M 3.0107]. So “sādhū”ti mahante mahante cammapasibbake kāretvā rattibhāge bhūmiṃ khaṇitvā dhanacāṭiyo uddharitvā pasibbakesu [P 3.0117] dhanaṃ pakkhipitvā cāṭiyo tiṇassa pūrāpetvā pañca ca isisatāni aññe ca manusse dhanaṃ gāhāpetvā palāyitvā sāvatthiṃ gantvā sabbe rājayutte [V 3.0100] gāhāpetvā rajjaṃ gahetvā pākāraaṭṭālakādipaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ kārāpetvā puna sapattaraññā yuddhena aggahetabbaṃ katvā nagaraṃ ajjhāvasati. Bārāṇasiraññopi “tāpasā uyyānato dhanaṃ gahetvā palātā”ti ārocayiṃsu. So uyyānaṃ gantvā cāṭiyo vivarāpetvā tiṇameva passi, tassa dhanaṃ nissāya mahanto soko uppajji. So nagaraṃ gantvā “tiṇaṃ tiṇa”nti vippalapanto carati, nāssa koci sokaṃ nibbāpetuṃ sakkoti.

Prince Chatto knew the spell for unearthing treasure. While living there, revolving the spell and looking about, he wondered, 'Where could my father's wealth have been buried?' Having discovered that it was buried in the park, he thought, 'I will take this wealth and reclaim my kingdom.' He then addressed the ascetics, saying, 'Sirs, I am the son of the king of Kosala. When our kingdom was seized by the king of Bārāṇasī, I left in disguise and have preserved my life all this time. Now, our ancestral wealth has been found. I will take it and go to reclaim my kingdom. What will you do?' They replied, 'We too will go with you.' Saying, 'Good,' he had large leather bags made. In the night, he dug up the ground, unearthed the pots of treasure, put the treasure into the bags, and had the pots filled with grass. He had the five hundred ascetics and other men carry the treasure, fled to Sāvatthī, had all the royal officials seized, and took the kingdom. He had the walls, watchtowers, and other fortifications repaired, made the city unconquerable in battle by a rival king, and dwelt there. To the king of Bārāṇasī it was reported, 'The ascetics have taken the treasure from the park and fled.' He went to the park, had the pots opened, and saw only grass. Great sorrow arose in him on account of the treasure. He went into the city and wandered about, babbling, 'Grass, grass!' No one was able to extinguish his sorrow.

Bodhisatto cintesi “rañño mahanto soko, vippalapanto carati, ṭhapetvā kho pana maṃ nāssa añño koci sokaṃ vinodetuṃ samattho, nissokaṃ naṃ karissāmī”ti. So ekadivasaṃ tena saddhiṃ sukhanisinno tassa vippalapanakāle paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta thought, 'The king is in great sorrow; he wanders about lamenting. Except for me, no one else is capable of dispelling his sorrow. I will make him free from sorrow.' One day, while sitting comfortably with him at the time of his lamentation, he spoke the first verse:

141.

141.

“Tiṇaṃ tiṇanti lapasi, ko nu te tiṇamāhari;

Kiṃ nu te tiṇakiccatthi, tiṇameva pabhāsasī”ti.

“‘Grass, grass!’ you babble; who now has carried away your grass? What business have you with grass, that you speak only of grass?”

Tattha kiṃ nu te tiṇakiccatthīti kiṃ nu tava tiṇena kiccaṃ kātabbaṃ atthi. Tiṇameva pabhāsasīti tvañhi kevalaṃ “tiṇaṃ tiṇa”nti tiṇameva pabhāsasi, “asukatiṇaṃ nāmā”ti na kathesi, tiṇanāmaṃ tāvassa kathehi “asukatiṇaṃ nāmā”ti, mayaṃ te āharissāma, atha pana te tiṇenattho natthi, nikkāraṇā mā vippalapīti.

Herein, 'What business have you with grass?' means 'What business do you have that must be done with grass?' 'You speak only of grass' means you merely say 'grass, grass,' and speak only of grass, but you do not say, 'It is such-and-such a grass.' First, tell its name, saying, 'It is such-and-such a grass,' and we will bring it to you. But if you have no need for grass, do not babble without reason.

Taṃ sutvā rājā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke the second verse:

142.

142.

“Idhāgamā brahmacārī, brahā chatto bahussuto;

So me sabbaṃ samādāya, tiṇaṃ nikkhippa gacchatī”ti.

“A holy man came here, the tall Chatto, very learned; having taken everything of mine, he departs, leaving grass behind.”

Tattha brahāti dīgho. Chattoti tassa nāmaṃ. Sabbaṃ samādāyāti sabbaṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā. Tiṇaṃ nikkhippa gacchatīti cāṭīsu tiṇaṃ nikkhipitvā gatoti dassento evamāha.

Herein, 'brahā' means tall. 'Chatto' is his name. 'Sabbaṃ samādāya' means having taken all the wealth. 'Tiṇaṃ nikkhippa gacchati' means he spoke thus to show: 'having placed grass in the pots, he departed'.

Taṃ [P 3.0118][M 3.0108] sutvā bodhisatto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:

143.

143.

“Evetaṃ hoti kattabbaṃ, appena bahumicchatā;

Sabbaṃ sakassa ādānaṃ, anādānaṃ tiṇassa cā”ti.

“Thus it should be done by one who desires much from little: taking all that is one's own, and not taking the grass.”

Tassattho [V 3.0101] – appena tiṇena bahudhanaṃ icchatā evaṃ etaṃ kattabbaṃ hoti, yadidaṃ pitu santakattā sakassa dhanassa sabbaṃ ādānaṃ agayhūpagassa tiṇassa ca anādānaṃ. Iti, mahārāja, so brahā chatto gahetabbayuttakaṃ attano pitu santakaṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā aggahetabbayuttakaṃ tiṇaṃ cāṭīsu pakkhipitvā gato, tattha kā paridevanāti.

Its meaning is: by one desiring much wealth by means of little grass, thus should this be done, namely, the taking of all of one's own wealth, because it belonged to his father, and the not taking of the grass, which was not worth taking. Thus, O great king, that tall Chatto took his own father's wealth, which was proper to be taken, and having placed the grass, which was not proper to be taken, into the pots, he departed. What cause for lamentation is there in that?

Taṃ sutvā rājā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke the fourth verse:

144.

144.

“Sīlavanto na kubbanti, bālo sīlāni kubbati;

Aniccasīlaṃ dussīlyaṃ, kiṃ paṇḍiccaṃ karissatī”ti.

“The virtuous do not do such things; a fool practices his own habits. For one of inconstant character, who is immoral, what can his cleverness accomplish?”

Tattha sīlavantoti ye sīlasampannā brahmacārayo, te evarūpaṃ na kubbanti. Bālo sīlāni kubbatīti bālo pana durācāro evarūpāni attano anācārasaṅkhātāni sīlāni karoti. Aniccasīlanti addhuvena dīgharattaṃ appavattena sīlena samannāgataṃ. Dussīlyanti dussīlaṃ. Kiṃ paṇḍiccaṃ karissatīti evarūpaṃ puggalaṃ bāhusaccaparibhāvitaṃ paṇḍiccaṃ kiṃ karissati kiṃ sampādessati, vipattimevassa karissatīti. Taṃ garahanto vatvā so tāya bodhisattassa kathāya nissoko hutvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi.

Herein, 'sīlavanto' means those holy men endowed with virtue; they do not do such a thing. 'Bālo sīlāni kubbati' means a fool, being of bad conduct, performs such actions which are reckoned as his own misconduct. 'Aniccasīlaṃ' means endowed with character that is unstable, not lasting for long. 'Dussīlyaṃ' means immoral. 'Kiṃ paṇḍiccaṃ karissati' means for such a person, what will his cleverness, though cultivated by much learning, do? What will it accomplish? It will only bring him to ruin. Having spoken thus in censure of Prince Chatto, the king became free from sorrow through the Bodhisatta's words and ruled the kingdom righteously.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā brahāchatto kuhakabhikkhu ahosi, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher identified the birth, saying: “At that time, the deceitful monk was the tall Chatto, but the wise minister was I myself.”

Brahāchattajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Brahāchatta Jātaka is finished.

[337] 7. Pīṭhajātakavaṇṇanā

[337] 7. The Commentary on the Pīṭha Jātaka

Na [M 3.0109] te pīṭhamadāyimhāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira janapadato jetavanaṃ gantvā pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā satthāraṃ vanditvā sāmaṇeradahare pucchi “āvuso, sāvatthiyaṃ āgantukabhikkhūnaṃ ke upakārakā”ti[P 3.0119]. “Āvuso, anāthapiṇḍiko nāma mahāseṭṭhi, visākhā nāma mahāupāsikā ete bhikkhusaṅghassa upakārakā mātāpituṭṭhāniyā”ti. So “sādhū”ti punadivase pātova ekabhikkhussapi apaviṭṭhakāle anāthapiṇḍikassa gharadvāraṃ agamāsi. Taṃ avelāya gatattā koci na olokesi[V 3.0102]. So tato kiñci alabhitvā visākhāya gharadvāraṃ gato. Tatrāpi atipātova gatattā kiñci na labhi. So tattha tattha vicaritvā punāgacchanto yāguyā niṭṭhitāya gato, punapi tattha tattha vicaritvā bhatte niṭṭhite gato. So vihāraṃ gantvā “dvepi kulāni assaddhāni appasannāni eva, ime bhikkhū pana ‘saddhāni pasannānī’ti kathentī”ti tāni kulāni paribhavanto carati.

The Teacher told this story while staying at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk, with reference to the words, 'We did not give you a seat.' It is said that this monk, having come from the countryside to Jetavana, put away his bowl and robe, paid homage to the Teacher, and asked the young novices, 'Friends, who are the benefactors of visiting monks in Sāvatthī?' They replied, 'Friend, the great merchant named Anāthapiṇḍika and the great female lay disciple named Visākhā; they are the benefactors of the Saṅgha, standing in the place of parents.' Saying, 'Good,' he went to Anāthapiṇḍika's house very early the next morning, even before any other monk had entered. Because he arrived at such an early hour, no one noticed him. Failing to receive anything there, he went to Visākhā's house. There too, since he arrived too early, he received nothing. Wandering here and there and returning, he arrived when the gruel was finished. Again wandering about and returning, he arrived when the meal was finished. Returning to the monastery, he went about disparaging those families, saying, 'Both these families are faithless and undevoted, yet these monks say they are faithful and devoted!'

Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, asuko kira jānapado bhikkhu atikālasseva kuladvāraṃ gato bhikkhaṃ alabhitvā kulāni paribhavanto caratī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte taṃ bhikkhuṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira bhikkhū”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kasmā tvaṃ bhikkhu kujjhasi, pubbe anuppanne buddhe tāpasāpi tāva kuladvāraṃ gantvā bhikkhaṃ alabhitvā na kujjhiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

One day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, it seems that a certain monk from the countryside goes to the doors of families too early, fails to receive alms, and then goes about disparaging those families.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, what are you gathered here discussing now?' When they told him, he had that monk summoned and asked, 'Is it true, monk?' 'It is true, Venerable Sir,' he replied. The Teacher said, 'Why are you angry, monk? In the past, before the Buddha appeared, even ascetics did not get angry when they went to the doors of families and failed to receive alms.' Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā aparabhāge tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavante ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya bārāṇasiṃ patvā uyyāne vasitvā punadivase nagaraṃ bhikkhāya pāvisi. Tadā bārāṇasiseṭṭhi saddho hoti pasanno. Bodhisatto “kataraṃ kulagharaṃ saddha”nti pucchitvā “seṭṭhighara”nti sutvā [M 3.0110] seṭṭhino gharadvāraṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe seṭṭhi rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gato, manussāpi naṃ na passiṃsu, so nivattitvā gacchati. Atha naṃ seṭṭhi rājakulato nivattanto [P 3.0120] disvā vanditvā bhikkhābhājanaṃ gahetvā gharaṃ netvā nisīdāpetvā pādadhovanatelamakkhanayāgukhajjakādīhi santappetvā antarābhatte kiñci kāraṇaṃ apucchitvā katabhattakiccaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno “bhante, amhākaṃ gharadvāraṃ āgatā nāma yācakā vā dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇā vā sakkārasammānaṃ alabhitvā gatapubbā nāma natthi, tumhe pana ajja amhākaṃ dārakehi adiṭṭhattā āsanaṃ vā pānīyaṃ vā pādadhovanaṃ vā yāgubhattaṃ vā alabhitvāva gatā, ayaṃ amhākaṃ doso, taṃ no khamituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. Having come of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, and later, having embraced the life of an ascetic, he dwelt long in the Himalayas. Then, for the purpose of partaking of salt and sour fare, he came to Bārāṇasī, stayed in a park, and entered the city for alms the next day. At that time, the merchant of Bārāṇasī was faithful and devoted. The Bodhisatta asked, 'Which family is faithful?' and hearing it was the merchant's house, he went to the merchant's door. At that moment, the merchant had gone to attend upon the king, and the people did not see him, so he turned back and left. Then, the merchant, returning from the royal court, saw him, paid homage, took his bowl, led him home, and seated him. He satisfied him with water for washing the feet, oil for anointing, gruel, and solid food, without asking any questions before the meal. When the meal was finished, he paid his respects, sat to one side, and said, 'Venerable sir, no beggars or righteous ascetics and brahmins who have come to our door have ever left without receiving honor and respect. But today, because you were not seen by our people, you went away without receiving a seat, drinking water, water for washing the feet, or gruel and food. This is our fault; it is proper that you should forgive us.' Then he spoke the first verse:

145.

145.

“Na te pīṭhamadāyimhā, na pānaṃ napi bhojanaṃ;

Brahmacāri khamassu me, etaṃ passāmi accaya”nti.

“We did not give you a seat, nor drink, nor food; holy one, forgive me, I see this as a fault.”

Tattha na te pīṭhamadāyimhāti pīṭhampi te na dāpayimha.

In that context, 'We did not give you a seat' means we did not even have a seat given to you.

Taṃ [V 3.0103] sutvā bodhisatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:

146.

146.

“Nevābhisajjāmi na cāpi kuppe, na cāpi me appiyamāsi kiñci;

Athopi me āsi manovitakko, etādiso nūna kulassa dhammo”ti.

“I neither resent nor am I angered, nor was anything displeasing to me; yet this thought occurred to me: ‘Such, indeed, must be the custom of this family.’”

Tattha nevābhisajjāmīti neva laggāmi. Etādisoti “imassa kulassa etādiso nūna sabhāvo, adāyakavaṃso esa bhavissatī”ti evaṃ me manovitakko uppanno.

In that context, 'I neither resent' means I am not stuck or attached. 'Such' means the thought occurred to me: 'Such indeed must be the nature of this family; this must be a non-giving lineage.'

Taṃ sutvā seṭṭhi itarā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the merchant spoke the other two verses:

147.

147.

“Esasmākaṃ kule dhammo, pitupitāmaho sadā;

Āsanaṃ udakaṃ pajjaṃ, sabbetaṃ nipadāmase.

“This is the custom in our family, from our fathers and grandfathers, always; a seat, water, and ointment for the feet—all these we give.

148.

148.

“Esasmākaṃ kule dhammo, pitupitāmaho sadā;

Sakkaccaṃ upatiṭṭhāma, uttamaṃ viya ñātaka”nti.

“This is the custom in our family, from our fathers and grandfathers, always; we respectfully attend to them, as to our highest kinsmen.”

Tattha [P 3.0121][M 3.0111] dhammoti sabhāvo. Pitupitāmahoti pitūnañca pitāmahānañca santako. Udakanti pādadhovanaudakaṃ. Pajjanti pādamakkhanatelaṃ. Sabbetanti sabbaṃ etaṃ. Nipadāmaseti nikārapakārā upasaggā, dāmaseti attho, dadāmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Iminā yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā dāyakavaṃso amhākaṃ vaṃsoti dasseti. Uttamaṃ viya ñātakanti mātaraṃ viya pitaraṃ viya ca mayaṃ dhammikaṃ samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā disvā sakkaccaṃ sahatthena upaṭṭhahāmāti attho.

In those verses, 'dhamma' means nature. 'Pitupitāmaha' means belonging to fathers and grandfathers. 'Udaka' means water for washing the feet. 'Pajja' means oil for anointing the feet. 'Sabbetaṃ' means all of this. In 'Nipadāmase,' 'ni-' and 'pa-' are prefixes; the word is 'dāmase,' which means 'we give.' By this, he shows: 'Our lineage is a line of donors up to the seventh generation.' 'As to our highest kinsmen' means: 'Upon seeing a righteous ascetic or brahmin, we respectfully attend to them with our own hands, as we would our mother or father.'

Bodhisatto pana katipāhaṃ bārāṇasiseṭṭhino dhammaṃ desento tattha vasitvā puna himavantameva gantvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

The Bodhisatta, teaching the Dhamma to the merchant of Bārāṇasī for a few days, dwelt there and then returned to the Himalayas. Having developed the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, he was destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā bārāṇasiseṭṭhi ānando ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this discourse on the Dhamma and revealed the truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the truths, that monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the merchant of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda, and the ascetic was I myself.

Pīṭhajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The seventh, the Pīṭha Jātaka, is finished.

[338] 8. Thusajātakavaṇṇanā

[338] 8. 8. Thusa Jātaka

Verse for the preservation of life

Viditaṃ [V 3.0104] thusanti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ajātasattuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiṃ kira mātukucchigate tassa mātu kosalarājadhītāya bimbisārarañño dakkhiṇajāṇulohitapivanadohaḷo uppajjitvā paṇḍu ahosi. Sā paricārikāhi pucchitā tāsaṃ tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Rājāpi sutvā nemittake pakkosāpetvā “deviyā kira evarūpo dohaḷo uppanno, tassa kā nipphattī”ti pucchi. Nemittakā “deviyā kucchimhi nibbattakasatto tumhe māretvā rajjaṃ gaṇhissatī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā “sace mama putto maṃ māretvā rajjaṃ gaṇhissati, ko ettha doso”ti dakkhiṇajāṇuṃ satthena phālāpetvā lohitaṃ suvaṇṇataṭṭakena gāhāpetvā deviyā pāyesi. Sā cintesi “sace mama kucchiyaṃ [M 3.0112] nibbatto putto pitaraṃ māressati, kiṃ me tenā”ti. Sā gabbhapātanatthaṃ kucchiṃ maddāpesi[P 3.0122].

The Teacher told this story, beginning with 'Known is the husk,' while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Ajātasattu. It is said that when he was conceived in his mother's womb, his mother—the daughter of the King of Kosala and the consort of King Bimbisāra—conceived a pregnancy craving to drink the blood from the king's right knee, and she became pale. When questioned by her attendants, she told them the matter. The king, hearing this, summoned soothsayers and asked: 'The queen has conceived such a craving; what will be the outcome?' The soothsayers said: 'The being conceived in the queen's womb will kill you and seize the kingdom.' The king said: 'If my son kills me and takes the kingdom, what harm is there in that?' He then had his right knee lanced with a blade, had the blood collected in a golden bowl, and gave it to the queen to drink. She thought: 'If the child born in my womb will kill his father, what use is he to me?' and she had her womb massaged to cause a miscarriage.

Rājā ñatvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “bhadde mayhaṃ kira putto maṃ māretvā rajjaṃ gaṇhissati, na kho panāhaṃ ajaro amaro, puttamukhaṃ passituṃ me dehi, mā ito pabhuti evarūpaṃ kammaṃ akāsī”ti āha. Sā tato paṭṭhāya uyyānaṃ gantvā kucchiṃ maddāpesi. Rājā ñatvā tato paṭṭhāya uyyānagamanaṃ nivāresi. Sā paripuṇṇagabbhā puttaṃ vijāyi. Nāmaggahaṇadivase cassa ajātasseva pitu sattubhāvato “ajātasattu”tveva nāmamakaṃsu. Tasmiṃ kumāraparihārena vaḍḍhante satthā ekadivasaṃ pañcasatabhikkhuparivuto rañño nivesanaṃ gantvā nisīdi. Rājā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ paṇītena khādanīyabhojanīyena parivisitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā dhammaṃ suṇanto nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe kumāraṃ maṇḍetvā rañño adaṃsu. Rājā balavasinehena puttaṃ gahetvā ūrumhi nisīdāpetvā puttagatena pemena puttameva mamāyanto na dhammaṃ suṇāti. Satthā tassa pamādabhāvaṃ ñatvā “mahārāja, pubbe rājāno putte āsaṅkamānā paṭicchanne kāretvā ‘amhākaṃ accayena nīharitvā rajje patiṭṭhāpeyyāthā’ti āṇāpesu”nti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The king, learning of this, summoned her and said: 'Dear lady, it is said that my son will kill me and take the kingdom. But I am not ageless or immortal. Let me see my son's face; from now on, do not do such a thing.' From then on, she went to the park to have her womb massaged. The king, discovering this, forbade her from going to the park. When she reached full term, she gave birth to a son. On the naming day, they named him 'Ajātasattu' because he was his father's enemy even before he was born. As the prince was being raised with royal care, one day the Teacher, surrounded by five hundred monks, went to the king's palace and sat down. The king, having served the community of monks headed by the Buddha with choice food, both hard and soft, sat down to listen to the Dhamma after paying homage to the Teacher. At that moment, they adorned the prince and presented him to the king. Out of strong affection, the king took his son and seated him on his lap. Engrossed in love for his son, cherishing him as his own, he could not listen to the Dhamma. The Teacher, perceiving his negligence, said: 'Great King, in the past, kings who suspected their sons had them kept in a hidden place, and commanded: "After our passing, bring him out and establish him in the kingdom."' Being requested by the king, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto takkasilāyaṃ disāpāmokkhaācariyo hutvā bahū rājakumāre ca brāhmaṇakumāre ca sippaṃ vācesi. Bārāṇasiraññopi putto soḷasavassakāle tassa santikaṃ gantvā tayo vede ca sabbasippāni ca uggaṇhitvā paripuṇṇasippo ācariyaṃ āpucchi. Ācariyo aṅgavijjāvasena taṃ olokento “imassa puttaṃ nissāya antarāyo paññāyati, tamahaṃ attano ānubhāvena harissāmī”ti [V 3.0105] cintetvā catasso gāthā bandhitvā rājakumārassa adāsi, evañca pana taṃ vadesi “tāta, paṭhamaṃ gāthaṃ rajje patiṭṭhāya tava puttassa soḷasavassakāle bhattaṃ bhuñjanto vadeyyāsi, dutiyaṃ mahāupaṭṭhānakāle, tatiyaṃ pāsādaṃ abhiruhamāno sopānasīse ṭhatvā, catutthaṃ sayanasirigabbhaṃ [P 3.0123] pavisanto ummāre ṭhatvā”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā [M 3.0113] ācariyaṃ vanditvā gato oparajje patiṭṭhāya pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāsi. Tassa putto soḷasavassakāle rañño uyyānakīḷādīnaṃ atthāya nikkhamantassa sirivibhavaṃ disvā pitaraṃ māretvā rajjaṃ gahetukāmo hutvā attano upaṭṭhākānaṃ kathesi. Te “sādhu deva, mahallakakāle laddhena issariyena ko attho, yena kenaci upāyena rājānaṃ māretvā rajjaṃ gaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vadiṃsu. Kumāro “visaṃ khādāpetvā māressāmī”ti pitarā saddhiṃ sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjanto visaṃ gahetvā nisīdi. Rājā bhattapātiyaṃ bhatte acchupanteyeva paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā and taught the arts to many princes and brahmin youths. The son of the King of Bārāṇasī also went to him at the age of sixteen, mastered the three Vedas and all the arts, and when his education was complete, he took leave of the teacher. The teacher, observing him through the science of physiognomy, thought: 'A danger is foreseen for him on account of his son. I will ward it off by my own power.' He composed four verses and gave them to the prince, saying: 'Dear boy, when you are established in the kingdom and your son is sixteen, recite the first verse while you are eating. Recite the second at the time of the great assembly, the third while ascending to the palace, standing at the head of the stairs, and the fourth when entering the royal bedchamber, standing at the threshold.' He accepted, saying, 'Very well,' paid homage to his teacher, and departed. Having been established as viceroy, he succeeded to the kingdom after his father's passing. When his son was sixteen, seeing the king's splendor and majesty as he went out for sport in the park and so forth, the son desired to kill his father and seize the kingdom, and he spoke to his attendants. They said: 'Good, sire! What use is power gained in old age? It is right to kill the king and take the kingdom by some means.' The prince thought, 'I will kill him by making him eat poison,' and sat down with his father for the evening meal, carrying poison. Just as the king was about to touch the food in the dish, he recited the first verse:

149.

149.

“Viditaṃ thusaṃ undurānaṃ, viditaṃ pana taṇḍulaṃ;

Thusaṃ thusaṃ vivajjetvā, taṇḍulaṃ pana khādare”ti.

Known to the mice is the husk, and known also is the grain; Having rejected every husk, it is the grain that they eat.

Tattha viditanti kāḷavaddalepi andhakāre undurānaṃ thuso thusabhāvena taṇḍulo ca taṇḍulabhāvena vidito pākaṭoyeva. Idha pana liṅgavipallāsavasena “thusaṃ taṇḍula”nti vuttaṃ. Khādareti thusaṃ thusaṃ vajjetvā taṇḍulameva khādanti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tāta kumāra, yathā undurānaṃ andhakārepi thuso thusabhāvena taṇḍulo ca taṇḍulabhāvena pākaṭo, te thusaṃ vajjetvā taṇḍulameva khādanti, evameva mamapi tava visaṃ gahetvā nisinnabhāvo pākaṭoti.

Therein, 'known' means that even in the pitch-black darkness of a cloudy night, the husk is known and manifest to mice as husk, and the grain as grain. Here, however, the words 'thusaṃ' and 'taṇḍulaṃ' are used due to gender transposition. 'They eat' means they reject the husks one by one and eat only the grain. This is the meaning: 'Dear prince, just as the husk is manifest to mice as husk and the grain as grain even in the dark, and they reject the husk to eat only the grain, even so, the fact that you are sitting here with poison is manifest to me.'

Kumāro “ñātomhī”ti bhīto bhattapātiyaṃ visaṃ pātetuṃ avisahitvā uṭṭhāya rājānaṃ vanditvā gato. So tamatthaṃ attano upaṭṭhākānaṃ ārocetvā “ajja tāvamhi ñāto, idāni kathaṃ māressāmī”ti pucchi. Te tato paṭṭhāya uyyāne paṭicchannā hutvā nikaṇṇikavasena mantayamānā “attheko upāyo, khaggaṃ sannayhitvā mahāupaṭṭhānaṃ gatakāle amaccānaṃ antare ṭhatvā rañño pamattabhāvaṃ ñatvā khaggena paharitvā māretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vavatthapesuṃ. Kumāro “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā mahāupaṭṭhānakāle sannaddhakhaggo [P 3.0124] hutvā gantvā ito cito ca rañño paharaṇokāsaṃ upadhāreti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The prince, frightened by the thought, 'I am discovered,' and unable to drop the poison into the food bowl, rose, paid homage to the king, and fled. He then informed his attendants of the matter, asking, 'Today I have been discovered; how shall I kill him now?' From then on, meeting secretly in the garden and conferring in whispers, they resolved on a plan: 'There is one way—gird on your sword, and when you go to the great attendance, stand among the ministers. When you perceive the king to be unguarded, it is right to strike and kill him with your sword.' The prince agreed, saying 'Very well,' and at the time of the great attendance, he went with his sword girt, looking here and there for an opportunity to strike the king. At that moment, the king recited the second verse:

150.

150.

“Yā [M 3.0114] mantanā araññasmiṃ, yā ca gāme nikaṇṇikā;

Yañcetaṃ iti cīti ca, etampi viditaṃ mayā”ti.

The plotting in the forest, the whispering in the village, and this scheming of 'this way and that'—this too is known to me.

Tattha [V 3.0106] araññasminti uyyāne. Nikaṇṇikāti kaṇṇamūle mantanā. Yañcetaṃ iti cīti cāti yañca etaṃ idāni mama paharaṇokāsapariyesanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tāta kumāra, yā esā tava attano upaṭṭhākehi saddhiṃ uyyāne ca gāme ca nikaṇṇikā mantanā, yañcetaṃ idāni mama māraṇatthāya iti cīti ca karaṇaṃ, etampi sabbaṃ mayā ñātanti.

Therein, 'in the forest' means in the garden. 'Whispering' means plotting at the root of the ear. 'And this of "this way and that"' means this present search for an opportunity to strike me. This is what is meant: 'Dear prince, that whispering and plotting with your attendants in the garden and in the village, and this present action of "this way and that" for the purpose of killing me—all of this is known to me.'

Kumāro “jānāti me veribhāvaṃ pitā”ti tato palāyitvā upaṭṭhākānaṃ ārocesi. Te sattaṭṭha divase atikkamitvā “kumāra, na te pitā, veribhāvaṃ jānāti, takkamattena tvaṃ evaṃsaññī ahosi, mārehi na”nti vadiṃsu. So ekadivasaṃ khaggaṃ gahetvā sopānamatthake gabbhadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Rājā sopānamatthake ṭhito tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The prince, thinking, 'My father knows of my enmity,' fled from there and informed his attendants. After seven or eight days had passed, they said, 'Prince, your father does not know of your enmity. You have this perception through mere conjecture. Kill him!' One day, he took a sword and stood at the head of the stairs, at the chamber door. The king, standing at the head of the stairs, recited the third verse:

151.

151.

“Dhammena kira jātassa, pitā puttassa makkaṭo;

Daharasseva santassa, dantehi phalamacchidā”ti.

It is by nature, it seems, that a monkey father tears away with his teeth the 'fruit' of his own son, even while he is still young.

Tattha dhammenāti sabhāvena. Pitā puttassa makkaṭoti pitā makkaṭo puttassa makkaṭapotakassa. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā araññe jāto makkaṭo attano yūthapariharaṇaṃ āsaṅkanto taruṇassa makkaṭapotakassa dantehi phalaṃ chinditvā purisabhāvaṃ nāseti, tathā tava atirajjakāmassa phalāni uppāṭāpetvā purisabhāvaṃ nāsessāmīti.

Therein, 'by nature' means by its intrinsic nature. 'A monkey father of a son' means a monkey father of a young monkey. This is what is meant: 'Just as a monkey born in the forest, fearing for the leadership of his own troop, tears away the "fruit" of a young monkey with his teeth and destroys its manhood, so too, because of your excessive desire for the kingdom, will I have your "fruits" uprooted and destroy your manhood.'

Kumāro “gaṇhāpetukāmo maṃ pitā”ti bhīto palāyitvā “pitarāmhi santajjito”ti upaṭṭhākānaṃ ārocesi. Te aḍḍhamāsamatte vītivatte “kumāra, sace rājā jāneyya, ettakaṃ kālaṃ nādhivāseyya, takkamattena tayā kathitaṃ, mārehi [P 3.0125] na”nti vadiṃsu. So ekadivasaṃ khaggaṃ gahetvā uparipāsāde sirisayanaṃ pavisitvā “āgacchantameva naṃ māressāmī”ti heṭṭhāpallaṅke nisīdi. Rājā bhuttasāyamāso parijanaṃ uyyojetvā “nipajjissāmī”ti sirigabbhaṃ pavisanto ummāre ṭhatvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

The prince, frightened that his father wanted to have him seized, fled and informed his attendants, saying, 'I have been threatened by my father.' When about half a month had passed, they said to him, 'Prince, if the king knew, he would not have tolerated it for so long. What you said is mere conjecture; kill him!' One day, taking a sword, he entered the royal bedchamber upstairs and sat under the couch, thinking, 'I will kill him as soon as he comes.' The king, having finished his evening meal and dismissed his retinue, entered the royal chamber intending to lie down. Standing at the threshold, he recited the fourth stanza:

152.

152.

“Yametaṃ [M 3.0115] parisappasi, ajakāṇova sāsape;

Yopāyaṃ heṭṭhato seti, etampi viditaṃ mayā”ti.

As a one-eyed goat in a mustard field, you creep about; and this one who lies beneath, this too is known by me.

Tattha parisappasīti bhayena ito cito ca sappasi. Sāsapeti sāsapakhette. Yopāyanti yopi ayaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yampi etaṃ tvaṃ sāsapavanaṃ paviṭṭhakāṇaeḷako viya bhayena ito [V 3.0107] cito ca saṃsappasi, paṭhamaṃ visaṃ gahetvā āgatosi, dutiyaṃ khaggena paharitukāmo hutvā āgatosi, tatiyaṃ khaggaṃ ādāya sopānamatthake aṭṭhāsi, idāni maṃ “māressāmī”ti heṭṭhāsayane nipannosi, sabbametaṃ jānāmi, na taṃ idāni vissajjemi, gahetvā rājāṇaṃ kārāpessāmīti. Evaṃ tassa ajānantasseva sā sā gāthā taṃ taṃ atthaṃ dīpeti.

Herein, 'parisappasi' means you creep here and there out of fear. 'Sāsape' refers to a mustard field. 'Yopāyaṃ' means 'and this one who.' This is what is said: 'Just as you, like a one-eyed goat that has entered a mustard field, creep here and there out of fear—first you came having taken poison, second you came intending to strike with a sword, third you stood at the top of the stairs holding a sword, and now you lie under the couch thinking, "I will kill him"—I know all this. I will not release you now; I will have you seized and have the royal punishment inflicted.' Thus, even as the prince did not know, each verse revealed its respective meaning to him.

Kumāro “ñātomhi pitarā, idāni maṃ nāssessatī”ti bhayappatto heṭṭhāsayanā nikkhamitvā khaggaṃ rañño pādamūle chaḍḍetvā “khamāhi me, devā”ti pādamūle urena nipajji. Rājā “na mayhaṃ koci kammaṃ jānātīti tvaṃ cintesī”ti taṃ tajjetvā saṅkhalikabandhanena bandhāpetvā bandhanāgāraṃ pavesāpetvā ārakkhaṃ ṭhapesi. Tadā rājā bodhisattassa guṇaṃ sallakkhesi. So aparabhāge kālamakāsi, tassa sarīrakiccaṃ katvā kumāraṃ bandhanāgārā nīharitvā rajje patiṭṭhāpesuṃ.

The prince, thinking, 'My father knows me; now he will destroy me,' was struck with fear and came out from under the couch. He threw his sword at the king's feet and, saying, 'Forgive me, lord,' prostrated himself with his chest at the king's feet. The king, rebuking him, said, 'You thought, "No one knows my deed,"' and had him bound with chains, put into prison, and placed under guard. At that time, the king reflected on the virtues of the Bodhisatta. Later, the king passed away. After performing the funeral rites for him, they brought the prince out of prison and established him in the kingdom.

Satthā [P 3.0126] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā takkasilāyaṃ disāpāmokkho ācariyo ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher connected the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, I myself was the world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā.'

Thusajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Thusa Jātaka, the Eighth.

[339] 9. Bāverujātakavaṇṇanā

[339] 9. The Commentary on the Bāveru Jātaka.

Adassanena morassāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto hatalābhasakkāre titthiye ārabbha kathesi. Titthiyā hi anuppanne buddhe lābhino ahesuṃ, uppanne pana buddhe hatalābhasakkārā sūriyuggamane khajjopanakā viya jātā. Tesaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārabbha bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi [M 3.0116] kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi yāva guṇavantā na uppajjanti, tāva nigguṇā lābhaggayasaggappattā ahesuṃ, guṇavantesu pana uppannesu nigguṇā hatalābhasakkārā jātā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning the sectarians who had lost their gains and honors: 'Through not seeing the peacock.' For the sectarians had been prosperous before the Buddha arose, but when the Buddha arose, they lost their gains and honors, becoming like fireflies at sunrise. The monks, discussing this matter in the Dhamma hall, raised the topic. The Teacher arrived and asked, 'What is the subject of your discussion now, monks?' When they told him, he said, 'Not only now, monks, but in the past as well, as long as virtuous ones did not appear, those without virtue attained the highest gains and honors. But when virtuous ones arose, those without virtue lost their gains and honors.' Then he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto morayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vuḍḍhimanvāya sobhaggappatto araññe vicari. Tadā ekacce vāṇijā disākākaṃ gahetvā nāvāya bāveruraṭṭhaṃ agamaṃsu. Tasmiṃ kira kāle bāveruraṭṭhe sakuṇā nāma natthi. Āgatāgatā raṭṭhavāsino [V 3.0108] taṃ pañjare nisinnaṃ disvā “passathimassa chavivaṇṇaṃ galapariyosānaṃ mukhatuṇḍakaṃ maṇiguḷasadisāni akkhīnī”ti kākameva pasaṃsitvā te vāṇijake āhaṃsu “imaṃ, ayyā, sakuṇaṃ amhākaṃ detha, amhākaṃ iminā attho, tumhe attano raṭṭhe aññaṃ labhissathā”ti. “Tena hi mūlena gaṇhathā”ti. “Kahāpaṇena no dethā”ti. “Na demā”ti[P 3.0127]. Anupubbena vaḍḍhitvā “satena dethā”ti vutte “amhākaṃ esa bahūpakāro, tumhehi saddhiṃ metti hotū”ti kahāpaṇasataṃ gahetvā adaṃsu. Te taṃ netvā suvaṇṇapañjare pakkhipitvā nānappakārena macchamaṃsena ceva phalāphalena ca paṭijaggiṃsu. Aññesaṃ sakuṇānaṃ avijjamānaṭṭhāne dasahi asaddhammehi samannāgato kāko lābhaggayasaggappatto ahosi.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a peacock. Growing to full size and endowed with great beauty, he wandered in the forest. At that time, some merchants, taking a direction-finding crow, traveled by ship to the land of Bāveru. At that time, it is said, there were no birds in the land of Bāveru. The residents, seeing the crow sitting in a cage as it arrived, exclaimed, "Look at the color of its skin, the beauty of its neck, its beak, and its eyes like jewel-balls!" Praising the crow, they said to the merchants, "Sirs, give us this bird; we have need of it. You can get another in your own land." "Then buy it for a price," they replied. "Give it to us for a kahāpaṇa." "We will not give it for that." Gradually increasing the price, they offered a hundred. The merchants said, "This bird is very useful to us, but let there be friendship with you." Taking a hundred kahāpaṇas, they gave it to them. The people placed it in a golden cage and cared for it with various kinds of fish, meat, and fruits. In a place where no other birds existed, the crow, endowed with the ten bad qualities, attained the highest gains and fame.

Punavāre te vāṇijā ekaṃ morarājānaṃ gahetvā yathā accharasaddena vassati, pāṇippaharaṇasaddena naccati, evaṃ sikkhāpetvā bāveruraṭṭhaṃ agamaṃsu. So mahājane sannipatite nāvāya dhure ṭhatvā pakkhe vidhunitvā madhurassaraṃ nicchāretvā nacci. Manussā taṃ disvā somanassajātā “etaṃ, ayyā, sobhaggappattaṃ susikkhitaṃ sakuṇarājānaṃ amhākaṃ dethā”ti āhaṃsu. Amhehi paṭhamaṃ kāko ānīto, taṃ gaṇhittha, idāni ekaṃ morarājānaṃ ānayimhā, etampi yācatha, tumhākaṃ raṭṭhe sakuṇaṃ nāma gahetvā āgantuṃ na sakkāti. “Hotu, ayyā, attano raṭṭhe aññaṃ labhissatha, imaṃ no dethā”ti mūlaṃ vaḍḍhetvā sahassena gaṇhiṃsu. Atha naṃ sattaratanavicitte pañjare ṭhapetvā macchamaṃsaphalāphalehi ceva madhulājasakkarapānakādīhi ca paṭijaggiṃsu, mayūrarājā lābhaggayasaggappatto jāto, tassāgatakālato paṭṭhāya kākassa lābhasakkāro parihāyi, koci [M 3.0117] naṃ oloketumpi na icchi. Kāko khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ alabhamāno “kākā”ti vassanto gantvā ukkārabhūmiyaṃ otaritvā gocaraṃ gaṇhi.

On a later occasion, those merchants caught a peacock king and, having trained him to cry at the snapping of fingers and dance to the sound of clapping hands, they went to the land of Bāveru. When a great crowd had gathered, the peacock stood on the bow of the ship, flapped his wings, uttered a sweet sound, and danced. Seeing him, the people were filled with joy and said, "Sirs, give us this beautiful, well-trained bird king." The merchants replied, "First we brought a crow and you took it. Now we have brought a peacock king and you ask for him too. It is no longer possible to bring birds to your country!" The people said, "Be that as it may, sirs, you will get another in your own land; give this one to us." Increasing the price, they bought him for a thousand. Then they placed him in a cage adorned with the seven precious gems and cared for him with fish, meat, fruits, honey, parched rice, sugar, drinks, and so on. The peacock king attained the highest gains and fame. From the time of his arrival, the gain and honor of the crow declined; no one even wanted to look at him. Not getting any food, the crow went away crying "Caw! Caw!", alighted on a rubbish heap, and foraged for food.

Satthā dve vatthūni ghaṭetvā sambuddho hutvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

The Teacher, having connected the two stories, being the Fully Enlightened One, spoke these verses:

153.

153.

“Adassanena [P 3.0128] morassa, sikhino mañjubhāṇino;

Kākaṃ tattha apūjesuṃ, maṃsena ca phalena ca.

"Due to not seeing the peacock, the crested one with a sweet voice, they honored the crow there with meat and with fruit.

154.

154.

“Yadā ca sarasampanno, moro bāverumāgamā;

Atha lābho ca sakkāro, vāyasassa ahāyatha.

"But when the sweet-voiced peacock came to Bāveru, then the gain and honor of the crow diminished."

155.

155.

“Yāva [V 3.0109] nuppajjatī buddho, dhammarājā pabhaṅkaro;

Tāva aññe apūjesuṃ, puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe.

"As long as the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, the Light-Maker, does not arise, so long do they honor many other ascetics and brahmins."

156.

156.

“Yadā ca sarasampanno, buddho dhammaṃ adesayi;

Atha lābho ca sakkāro, titthiyānaṃ ahāyathā”ti.

"But when the Buddha, endowed with a sublime voice, taught the Dhamma, then the gain and honor of the sectarians diminished."

Tattha sikhinoti sikhāya samannāgatassa. Mañjubhāṇinoti madhurassarassa. Apūjesunti apūjayiṃsu. Maṃsena ca phalena cāti nānappakārena maṃsena phalāphalena ca. Bāverumāgamāti bāveruraṭṭhaṃ āgato. “Bhāverū”tipi pāṭho. Ahāyathāti parihīno. Dhammarājāti navahi lokuttaradhammehi parisaṃ rañjetīti dhammarājā. Pabhaṅkaroti sattalokaokāsalokasaṅkhāralokesu ālokassa katattā pabhaṅkaro. Sarasampannoti brahmassarena samannāgato. Dhammaṃ adesayīti catusaccadhammaṃ pakāsesīti.

There, 'sikhino' means endowed with a crest. 'Mañjubhāṇino' means having a sweet voice. 'Apūjesuṃ' means they honored. 'Maṃsena ca phalena ca' means with various kinds of meat and various fruits. 'Bāverumāgamā' means he came to the Bāveru country. There is also a reading 'Bhāverū'. 'Ahāyathā' means diminished. 'Dhammarājā' means he delights the assembly with the nine supramundane Dhammas. 'Pabhaṅkaro' means the Light-Maker because of having made light in the world of beings, the world of space, and the world of formations. 'Sarasampanno' means endowed with a voice like that of Brahmā. 'Dhammaṃ adesayī' means he proclaimed the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.

Iti imā catasso gāthā bhāsitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kāko nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto ahosi, morarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having spoken these four verses, he identified the Jātaka by saying: "At that time, the crow was Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, but the peacock king was indeed myself."

Bāverujātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Bāveru Jātaka, the Ninth.

[340] 10. Visayhajātakavaṇṇanā

[340] 10. The Commentary on the Visayha Jātaka.

Adāsi [M 3.0118] dānānīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto anāthapiṇḍikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā khadiraṅgārajātake (jā. 1.1.40) vitthāritameva. Idha pana satthā anāthapiṇḍikaṃ. Āmantetvā “porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi gahapati ‘dānaṃ mā dadāsī’ti ākāse ṭhatvā vārentaṃ sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ paṭibāhitvā dānaṃ adaṃsuyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

"He gave gifts"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Anāthapiṇḍika. The story has been fully told before in the Khadiraṅgāra Jātaka. Here, however, the Teacher, having addressed Anāthapiṇḍika, said, "Even the wise men of old, O householder, rebuffed Sakka, the king of the gods, who stood in the sky preventing them, saying, 'Do not give gifts,' and gave gifts nevertheless." And being asked by him, he related the past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto asītikoṭivibhavo visayho nāma seṭṭhi hutvā [P 3.0129] pañcahi sīlehi samannāgato dānajjhāsayo dānābhirato ahosi. So catūsu nagaradvāresu, nagaramajjhe, attano gharadvāreti chasu ṭhānesu dānasālāyo kāretvā dānaṃ pavattesi, divase divase cha satasahassāni vissajjeti. Bodhisattassa ca vanibbakayācakānañca ekasadisameva bhattaṃ hoti. Tassa jambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ katvā dānaṃ dadato [V 3.0110] dānānubhāvena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi, sakkassa devarañño paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. Sakko “ko nu kho maṃ ṭhānā cāvetukāmo”ti upadhārento mahāseṭṭhiṃ disvā “ayaṃ visayho ativiya pattharitvā sakalajambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ karonto dānaṃ deti, iminā dānena maṃ cāvetvā sayaṃ sakko bhavissati maññe, dhanamassa nāsetvā etaṃ daliddaṃ katvā yathā dānaṃ na deti, tathā karissāmī”ti cintetvā sabbaṃ dhanadhaññaṃ telamadhuphāṇitasakkarādīni antamaso dāsakammakaraporisampi antaradhāpesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a wealthy merchant named Visayha, possessing eighty crores of wealth, endowed with the five precepts, devoted to charity, and delighting in giving. He had alms-halls built in six places—at the four city gates, in the middle of the city, and at his own door—and there he dispensed charity, giving away six hundred thousand each day. The food of the Bodhisatta and of the beggars and solicitors was exactly the same. As he gave gifts, making the whole of Jambudīpa cease its plowing, the power of his giving caused Sakka’s abode to shake. Sakka’s yellow-marble throne showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting, 'Who now wishes to displace me from my position?' saw the great merchant and thought, 'This Visayha is giving gifts with excessive liberality, making the whole of Jambudīpa cease its plowing. By this charity he will displace me and become Sakka himself, I suppose. I will destroy his wealth and reduce him to poverty, so that he will give no more gifts.' And he caused all his money, grain, oil, honey, molasses, sugar, and so forth, even down to his slaves and hired laborers, to disappear.

Tadā dānabyāvaṭā āgantvā “sāmi dānaggaṃ pacchinnaṃ, ṭhapitaṭhapitaṭṭhāne na kiñci passāmā”ti ārocayiṃsu. “Ito paribbayaṃ haratha, mā dānaṃ pacchindathā”ti bhariyaṃ pakkosāpetvā “bhadde, dānaṃ pavattāpehī”ti āha. Sā sakalagehaṃ vicinitvā aḍḍhamāsakamattampi adisvā “ayya, amhākaṃ nivatthavatthaṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ kiñci na passāmi, sakalagehaṃ tuccha”nti āha. Sattaratanagabbhesu dvāraṃ vivarāpetvā na kiñci addasa, seṭṭhiñca bhariyañca ṭhapetvā aññe dāsakammakarāpi na paññāyiṃsu. Puna mahāsatto. Bhariyaṃ [M 3.0119] āmantetvā “bhadde, na sakkā dānaṃ pacchindituṃ, sakalanivesanaṃ vicinitvā kiñci upadhārehī”ti āha. Tasmiṃ khaṇe eko tiṇahārako asitañca kājañca tiṇabandhanarajjuñca dvārantare chaḍḍetvā palāyi. Seṭṭhibhariyā taṃ disvā “sāmi, idaṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ na passāmī”ti [P 3.0130] āharitvā adāsi. Mahāsatto “bhadde, mayā ettakaṃ kālaṃ tiṇaṃ nāma na lāyitapubbaṃ, ajja pana tiṇaṃ lāyitvā āharitvā vikkiṇitvā yathānucchavikaṃ dānaṃ dassāmī”ti dānupacchedabhayena asitañceva kājañca rajjuñca gahetvā nagarā nikkhamitvā tiṇavatthuṃ gantvā tiṇaṃ lāyitvā “eko amhākaṃ bhavissati, ekena dānaṃ dassāmī”ti dve tiṇakalāpe bandhitvā kāje laggetvā ādāya gantvā nagaradvāre vikkiṇitvā māsake gahetvā ekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ yācakānaṃ adāsi. Yācakā bahū, tesaṃ “mayhampi dehi, mayhampi dehī”ti vadantānaṃ itarampi koṭṭhāsaṃ datvā taṃ divasaṃ saddhiṃ bhariyāya anāhāro vītināmesi. Iminā niyāmena cha divasā vītivattā.

Then those engaged in the charity came and reported, 'Master, the alms-giving is interrupted; we see nothing in any of the usual storage places.' 'Take from the household provisions; do not stop the charity,' he said, and summoning his wife, he told her, 'Dear, continue the charity.' She searched the entire house but did not find even half a māsaka. 'Lord, apart from the clothes we are wearing, I see nothing else; the whole house is empty,' she said. They opened the doors of the seven treasure vaults but found nothing. Apart from the merchant and his wife, even the servants and laborers were not to be seen. Again, the Great Being addressed his wife, 'Dear, it is not possible to stop the charity. Search the entire dwelling and look for something.' At that moment, a grass-cutter abandoned a sickle, a carrying pole, and a grass-tying rope between the gates and fled. Seeing this, the merchant's wife said, 'Lord, apart from these, I see nothing else,' and brought them to him. The Great Being said, 'Dear, in all this time, I have never cut grass before. But from today, I will cut grass, bring it, sell it, and give charity according to what I earn.' Fearing the interruption of charity, he took the sickle, the carrying pole, and the rope, went out of the city to a grassy area, and cut grass. He thought, 'One bundle will be for us, and with the other, I will give charity.' He tied two bundles of grass, hung them on the carrying pole, and carried them to the city gate. Selling them, he received māsaka coins and gave one portion to the beggars. There were many beggars, and as they said, 'Give to me too, give to me too!' he gave the other portion as well. That day, he and his wife passed without food. In this manner, six days passed.

Athassa sattame divase tiṇaṃ āharamānassa sattāhaṃ nirāhārassa atisukhumālassa nalāṭe sūriyātapena pahaṭamatte akkhīni bhamiṃsu. So satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkonto tiṇaṃ avattharitvā pati. Sakko tassa kiriyaṃ upadhārayamāno vicarati. So taṅkhaṇaññeva āgantvā ākāse ṭhatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

On the seventh day, as he was carrying grass, having been without food for seven days and being very delicate, as soon as the sun's heat struck his forehead, his eyes spun. Unable to maintain his consciousness, he spread out the grass and fell. Sakka, observing his actions, came at that very moment, stood in the air, and spoke the first verse:

157.

157.

“Adāsi [V 3.0111] dānāni pure visayha, dadato ca te khayadhammo ahosi;

Ito paraṃ ce na dadeyya dānaṃ, tiṭṭheyyuṃ te saṃyamantassa bhogā”ti.

'In the past, O Visayha, you gave gifts, and while you gave, your wealth was subject to depletion. If from now on you were not to give gifts, your wealth would remain for you who restrains yourself.'

Tassattho – ambho visayha tvaṃ ito pubbe tava gehe dhane vijjamāne sakalajambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ karitvā dānāni adāsi. Tassa ca te evaṃ dadato bhogānaṃ khayadhammo khayasabhāvo ahosi, sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ khīṇaṃ, ito paraṃ cepi tvaṃ dānaṃ na dadeyya, kassaci kiñci na dadeyyāsi, tava saṃyamantassa adadantassa bhogā tatheva [P 3.0131] tiṭṭheyyuṃ, “ito paṭṭhāya na dassāmī”ti tvaṃ mayhaṃ paṭiññaṃ dehi, ahaṃ te bhoge dassessāmīti.

The meaning is: 'O Visayha, in the past, when wealth existed in your home, you gave gifts, making the whole of Jambudīpa cease its plowing. And as you gave in this way, your wealth was subject to depletion; all your possessions were exhausted. Even if from now on you do not give gifts and give nothing to anyone, your wealth will remain as it is for you who restrains yourself and does not give. Give me your promise, saying "From now on I will not give," and I will restore your wealth to you.'

Mahāsatto [M 3.0120] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “kosi tva”nti āha. “Sakkohamasmī”ti. Bodhisatto “sakko nāma sayaṃ dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ samādiyitvā uposathakammaṃ katvā satta vattapadāni pūretvā sakkattaṃ patto, tvaṃ pana attano issariyakāraṇaṃ dānaṃ vāresi, anariyaṃ vata karosī”ti vatvā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

The Great Being, hearing his words, said, 'Who are you?' 'I am Sakka,' he replied. The Bodhisatta said, 'Sakka is one who, having given gifts himself, undertaken the precepts, performed the uposatha observance, and fulfilled the seven sacred vows, attained the state of Sakka. But you forbid giving for the sake of your own power; truly, you act ignobly.' Having said this, he spoke three verses:

158.

158.

“Anariyamariyena sahassanetta, suduggatenāpi akiccamāhu;

Mā vo dhanaṃ taṃ ahu devarāja, yaṃ bhogahetu vijahemu saddhaṃ.

'O Thousand-eyed One, the noble call it an ignoble deed, one not to be done even by one in dire straits. May that wealth not be ours, O King of Gods, for the sake of which we would abandon faith.'

159.

159.

“Yena eko ratho yāti, yāti tenaparo ratho;

Porāṇaṃ nihitaṃ vattaṃ, vattataññeva vāsava.

'By the path where one chariot goes, another chariot follows; the ancient established practice continues, O Vāsava.'

160.

160.

“Yadi hessati dassāma, asante kiṃ dadāmase;

Evaṃbhūtāpi dassāma, mā dānaṃ pamadamhase”ti.

'If there is wealth, we will give. When there is nothing, what can we give? Even being in such a state, we will give. Let us not neglect charity.'

Tattha anariyanti lāmakaṃ pāpakammaṃ. Ariyenāti parisuddhācārena ariyena. Suduggatenāpīti sudaliddenāpi. Akiccamāhūti akattabbanti buddhādayo ariyā vadanti, tvaṃ pana maṃ anariyaṃ maggaṃ ārocesīti adhippāyo. Voti nipātamattaṃ. Yaṃ bhogahetūti yassa dhanassa paribhuñjanahetu mayaṃ dānasaddhaṃ vijahemu pariccajeyyāma, taṃ dhanameva mā ahu, na no tena dhanena atthoti dīpeti.

Herein, 'anariya' means a base, evil action. 'Ariya' means noble, by one of pure conduct. 'Even by one in dire straits' means even by one who is very poor. 'They call it unworthy' means the noble ones, such as the Buddha, say it should not be done; but you advised me on a base path—this is the meaning. The word 'vo' is merely a particle. 'For the sake of wealth'—that wealth for the sake of enjoying which we would abandon generosity and faith, let that wealth not exist; we have no need for such wealth—this is what is shown.

Rathoti yaṃkiñci yānaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yena maggena eko ratho yāti, aññopi ratho [V 3.0112] “rathassa gatamaggo eso”ti teneva maggena yāti. Porāṇaṃ nihitaṃ vattanti yaṃ mayā pubbe nihitaṃ vattaṃ, taṃ mayi dharante vattatuyeva, mā tiṭṭhatūti attho. Evaṃbhūtāti evaṃ tiṇahārakabhūtāpi mayaṃ yāva [P 3.0132] jīvāma, tāva dassāmayeva. Kiṃkāraṇā? Mā dānaṃ pamadamhaseti. Adadanto hi dānaṃ pamajjati nāma na sarati na sallakkheti, ahaṃ pana jīvamāno dānaṃ pamussituṃ na icchāmi, tasmā dānaṃ dassāmiyevāti dīpeti.

'Chariot' means any vehicle. This is what is said: by the path one chariot travels, another chariot also goes by that same path, thinking, "This is the path taken by a chariot." 'The ancient established practice' means that the practice laid down by me before continues as long as I uphold it; let it not cease. 'Being of such a nature' means that even being grass-gatherers of this kind, as long as we live, we will continue to give. For what reason? 'Lest we neglect giving.' For one who does not give is said to neglect giving—they neither remember nor consider it. But I, as long as I live, do not wish to forget giving; therefore, I will continue to give—this is what is shown.

Sakko taṃ paṭibāhituṃ asakkonto “kimatthāya dānaṃ dadāsī”ti pucchi. Bodhisatto “neva sakkattaṃ, na brahmattaṃ patthayamāno, sabbaññutaṃ patthento [M 3.0121] panāhaṃ dadāmī”ti āha. Sakko tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tuṭṭho hatthena piṭṭhiṃ parimajji. Bodhisattassa taṅkhaṇaññeva parimajjitamattasseva sakalasarīraṃ paripūri. Sakkānubhāvena cassa sabbo vibhavaparicchedo paṭipākatikova ahosi. Sakko “mahāseṭṭhi, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya divase divase dvādasa satasahassāni vissajjento dānaṃ dadāhī”ti tassa gehe aparimāṇaṃ dhanaṃ katvā taṃ uyyojetvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

Unable to dissuade him, Sakka asked, "For what purpose do you give?" The Bodhisatta replied, "I give, aspiring neither for the state of Sakka nor for the state of Brahmā, but for omniscience." Hearing his words, Sakka was pleased and stroked his back with his hand. At that very moment, as soon as he was stroked, the Bodhisatta's entire body was restored. And by Sakka's power, the full measure of his wealth was restored to its original state. Sakka said, "Great merchant, from now on, give alms, distributing twelve hundred thousand daily," and after creating immeasurable wealth in his house and encouraging him, he went to his own abode.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā seṭṭhibhariyā rāhulamātā ahosi, visayho pana seṭṭhi ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the merchant's wife was Rāhula's mother, and the merchant Visayha was I myself."

Visayhajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Visayha Jātaka, the tenth.

Kokilavaggo catuttho.

The Kokila Chapter, the fourth.

5. Cūḷakuṇālavaggo

5. The Minor Kuṇāla Chapter

[341] 1. Kaṇḍarījātakavaṇṇanā

[341] 1. The Commentary on the Kaṇḍarī Jātaka

Narānamārāmakarāsūti [V 3.0113] imassa jātakassa vitthārakathā kuṇālajātake (jā. 2.21.kuṇālajātaka) āvi bhavissati.

The detailed story of this Jātaka, which begins 'Narānamārāmakarāsu,' will be made clear in the Kuṇāla Jātaka (Jā 546).

Kaṇḍarījātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kaṇḍarī Jātaka, the first.

[342] 2. Vānarajātakavaṇṇanā

[342] 2. The Commentary on the Vānara Jātaka

Asakkhiṃ [P 3.0133] vata attānanti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu (jā. aṭṭha. 2.2.susumārajātakavaṇṇanā) heṭṭhā vitthāritameva.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, spoke this, beginning with 'Asakkhiṃ vata attānaṃ,' in reference to Devadatta's plotting for his murder. The story has been detailed below (in the Susumāra Jātaka, Jā 208).

Atīte pana bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantapadese kapiyoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto gaṅgātīre vasi. Athekā antogaṅgāyaṃ saṃsumārī bodhisattassa hadayamaṃse dohaḷaṃ uppādetvā [M 3.0122] saṃsumārassa kathesi. So “taṃ kapiṃ udake nimujjāpetvā māretvā hadayamaṃsaṃ gahetvā saṃsumāriyā dassāmī”ti cintetvā mahāsattaṃ āha – “ehi, samma, antaradīpake phalāphale khādituṃ gacchāmā”ti. “Kathaṃ, samma, ahaṃ gamissāmī”ti. “Ahaṃ taṃ mama piṭṭhiyaṃ nisīdāpetvā nessāmī”ti. So tassa cittaṃ ajānanto laṅghitvā piṭṭhiyaṃ nisīdi. Saṃsumāro thokaṃ gantvā nimujjituṃ ārabhi. Atha naṃ vānaro “kiṃkāraṇā, bho, maṃ udake nimujjāpesī”ti āha. “Ahaṃ taṃ māretvā tava hadayamaṃsaṃ mama bhariyāya dassāmī”ti. “Dandha tvaṃ mama hadayamaṃsaṃ ure atthīti maññasī”ti? “Atha kahaṃ te ṭhapita”nti? “Etaṃ udumbare olambantaṃ na passasī”ti? “Passāmi, dassasi pana me”ti. “Āma, dassāmī”ti. Saṃsumāro dandhatāya taṃ gahetvā nadītīre udumbaramūlaṃ gato. Bodhisatto tassa piṭṭhito laṅghitvā udumbararukkhe nisinno imā gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a monkey in the Himalayan region. Having reached maturity, he lived on the bank of the Ganges. Then a certain female crocodile in the Ganges developed a craving for the Bodhisatta’s heart-flesh and told the male crocodile. He thought, "I will make that monkey sink in the water, kill him, take his heart-flesh, and give it to my mate." He then said to the Great Being, "Come, friend, let us go to the island in the middle of the river to eat various fruits." "How, friend, shall I go?" "I will have you sit on my back and carry you." Not knowing his intention, the monkey leaped onto his back. The crocodile went a short way and then began to submerge. Then the monkey asked him, "Why, sir, are you making me sink in the water?" "I will kill you and give your heart-flesh to my wife." "You fool, do you think my heart is in my chest?" "Then where have you put it?" "Do you not see it hanging on that fig tree?" "I see it. Will you give it to me?" "Yes, I will give it." Due to his foolishness, the crocodile took him to the foot of the fig tree on the riverbank. The Bodhisatta leaped from his back, sat on the fig tree, and spoke these verses:

161.

161.

“Asakkhiṃ [V 3.0114] vata attānaṃ, uddhātuṃ udakā thalaṃ;

Na dānāhaṃ puna tuyhaṃ, vasaṃ gacchāmi vārija.

“Indeed, I was able to lift myself from the water to the land; now I will not again come under your power, O water-dweller.

162.

162.

“Alametehi ambehi, jambūhi panasehi ca;

Yāni pāraṃ samuddassa, varaṃ mayhaṃ udumbaro.

“Enough of these mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits, which are on the far shore of the ocean; better for me is the fig tree.

163.

163.

“Yo ca uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, na khippamanubujjhati;

Amittavasamanveti, pacchā ca anutappati.

“Whoever does not quickly comprehend a matter that has arisen comes under the power of an enemy and later grieves.

164.

164.

“Yo [P 3.0134] ca uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, khippameva nibodhati;

Muccate sattusambādhā, na ca pacchānutappatī”ti.

“But whoever quickly understands a matter that has arisen is freed from the grip of an enemy and does not later grieve.”

Tattha asakkhiṃ vatāti samattho vata ahosiṃ. Uddhātunti uddharituṃ. Vārijāti saṃsumāraṃ ālapati. Yāni pāraṃ samuddassāti gaṅgaṃ samuddanāmenālapanto “yāni samuddassa pāraṃ gantvā khāditabbāni, alaṃ tehī”ti vadati. Pacchā ca anutappatīti uppannaṃ atthaṃ khippaṃ ajānanto amittavasaṃ gacchati, pacchā ca anutappati.

Herein, 'asakkhiṃ vata' means I was indeed able. 'Uddhātuṃ' means to lift up. 'Vārija' is an address to the crocodile. 'Yāni pāraṃ samuddassa'—addressing the Ganges by the name ‘ocean,’ he says, ‘Enough with those which are to be eaten after going to the far shore of the ocean.’ 'And later grieves' means that one who does not quickly understand a matter that has arisen comes under the power of an enemy and later grieves.

Iti so catūhi gāthāhi lokiyakiccānaṃ nipphattikāraṇaṃ kathetvā vanasaṇḍameva pāvisi.

Thus, having explained in four verses the reason for the accomplishment of worldly affairs, he entered the forest grove.

Satthā [M 3.0123] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā saṃsumāro devadatto ahosi, vānaro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the crocodile was Devadatta, and the monkey was I myself.”

Vānarajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Vānara Jātaka, the second.

[343] 3. Kuntinījātakavaṇṇanā

[343] 3. The Commentary on the Kuntinī Jātaka

Avasimha tavāgāreti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarañño gehe nivutthaṃ kuntinīsakuṇikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā kira rañño dūteyyahārikā ahosi. Dve potakāpissā atthi, rājā taṃ sakuṇikaṃ ekassa rañño paṇṇaṃ gāhāpetvā pesesi. Tassā gatakāle [V 3.0115] rājakule dārakā te sakuṇapotake hatthehi parimaddantā māresuṃ. Sā āgantvā te potake mate passantī “kena me puttakā māritā”ti pucchi. “Asukena ca asukena cā”ti. Tasmiñca kāle rājakule posāvanikabyaggho atthi kakkhaḷo pharuso, bandhanabalena tiṭṭhati. Atha te dārakā taṃ byagghaṃ dassanāya agamaṃsu. Sāpi sakuṇikā tehi saddhiṃ gantvā “yathā imehi mama puttakā māritā, tatheva ne karissāmī”ti te dārake gahetvā byagghassa pādamūle khipi, byaggho murāmurāpetvā khādi. Sā “idāni me manoratho paripuṇṇo”ti uppatitvā himavantameva gatā. Taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutvā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, rājakule kira asukā nāma kuntinī [P 3.0135] sakuṇikā ye hissā potakā māritā, te dārake byagghassa pādamūle khipitvā himavantameva gatā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesā attano potakaghātake dārake gahetvā byagghassa pādamūle khipitvā himavantameva gatā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher spoke this, beginning with the verse 'Avasimha tavāgāre,' while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a female heron named Kuntinī who was living in the house of the king of Kosala. She was, it seems, a messenger for the king. She also had two young ones. The king had her take a letter to another king and sent her off. While she was away, the children in the royal household, crushing those young birds with their hands, killed them. When she returned and saw her young ones dead, she asked, “Who killed my children?” “So-and-so and so-and-so,” they replied. At that time, there was a harsh and savage pet tiger kept in the royal household, held by the strength of its bonds. Then those children went to see the tiger. The heron also went with them and thought, “Just as they killed my children, so shall I do to them.” She seized those children and threw them at the tiger’s feet. The tiger, making a crunching sound, devoured them. She thought, “Now my wish is fulfilled,” and flew straight to the Himalayas. Hearing of this matter, the bhikkhus raised a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: “Friends, in the royal household, it is said a certain heron named Kuntinī, whose young ones were killed, threw those children at the tiger’s feet and went straight to the Himalayas.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now sitting together?” When it was said, “For this one,” he said, “Not only now, monks, but in the past too, she seized those children who killed her young ones, threw them at the tiger’s feet, and went straight to the Himalayas.” Having said this, he related a past incident.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ bodhisatto dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa nivesane ekā kuntinī sakuṇikā dūteyyahārikāti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva. Ayaṃ pana viseso. Ayaṃ kuntinī byagghena dārake mārāpetvā [M 3.0124] cintesi “idāni na sakkā mayā idha vasituṃ, gamissāmi, gacchantī ca pana rañño anārocetvā na gamissāmi, ārocetvāva gamissāmī”ti. Sā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā “sāmi, tumhākaṃ pamādena mama puttake dārakā māresuṃ, ahaṃ kodhavasikā hutvā te dārake paṭimāresiṃ, idāni mayā idha vasituṃ na sakkā”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta ruled the kingdom righteously and justly. In his residence, there was a female heron who was a messenger, and everything was just as in the previous story. This, however, is the difference: This heron, after having the children killed by the tiger, thought: “Now it is not possible for me to dwell here. I will leave, but I will not go without informing the king; I will go only after informing him.” She approached the king, paid homage, stood to one side, and said: “Lord, due to your negligence, the children killed my young ones. Being under the sway of anger, I had those children killed in return. Now it is not possible for me to stay here.” Having said this, she spoke the first verse:

165.

165.

“Avasimha tavāgāre, niccaṃ sakkatapūjitā,

Tvameva dānimakari, handa rāja vajāmaha”nti.

“We lived in your house, always honored and revered. Now you yourself have done this. Well then, O King, I shall go.”

Tattha tvameva dānimakarīti maṃ paṇṇaṃ gāhāpetvā pesetvā attano pamādena mama piyaputtake arakkhanto tvaññeva idāni etaṃ mama domanassakāraṇaṃ akari. Handāti vavassaggatthe nipāto. Rājāti bodhisattaṃ ālapati. Vajāmahanti ahaṃ himavantaṃ gacchāmīti.

Herein, ‘Tvameva dānimakarī’ means: having made me take a letter and sent me off, through your own negligence, by not protecting my beloved young ones, you yourself have now created this cause of my sorrow. ‘Handa’ is a particle in the sense of taking leave or dismissal. ‘Rāja’ is an address to the Bodhisatta. ‘Vajāmaha’ means ‘I will go to the Himalayas.’

Taṃ sutvā rājā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke the second verse:

166.

166.

“Yo [V 3.0116] ve kate paṭikate, kibbise paṭikibbise;

Evaṃ taṃ sammatī veraṃ, vasa kuntini māgamā”ti.

“When a deed is done and repaid, and a wrong is met with a wrong in return; thus that enmity is appeased. Dwell, Kuntinī, do not go.”

Tassattho – yo puggalo parena kate kibbise attano puttamāraṇādike dāruṇe kamme kate puna attano tassa puggalassa paṭikate paṭikibbise “paṭikataṃ [P 3.0136] mayā tassā”ti jānāti. Evaṃ taṃ sammatī veranti ettakena taṃ veraṃ sammati vūpasantaṃ hoti, tasmā vasa kuntini māgamāti.

Its meaning is this: When a person has done a cruel deed, such as killing another's child, and then that person is repaid with a cruel deed in return, one knows: ‘I have retaliated for it.’ ‘Evaṃ taṃ sammatī veraṃ’ means that by this much, that enmity is settled and appeased. Therefore, ‘vasa kuntini māgamā’ means ‘Dwell, Kuntinī, do not go.’

Taṃ sutvā kuntinī tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the heron spoke the third verse:

167.

167.

“Na katassa ca kattā ca, metti sandhīyate puna;

Hadayaṃ nānujānāti, gacchaññeva rathesabhā”ti.

“Between the one oppressed and the doer, friendship is not joined together again; my heart does not consent. I shall indeed go, O bull among charioteers.”

Tattha na katassa ca kattā cāti katassa ca abhibhūtassa upapīḷitassa puggalassa, idāni vibhattivipariṇāmaṃ katvā yo kattā tassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ puna mittabhāvo nāma na sandhīyati na ghaṭīyatīti attho. Hadayaṃ nānujānātīti tena kāraṇena mama hadayaṃ [M 3.0125] idha vāsaṃ nānujānāti. Gacchaññeva rathesabhāti tasmā ahaṃ mahārāja gamissāmiyevāti.

Herein, ‘Na katassa ca kattā ca’ means: for the person who was oppressed and afflicted, and—making a change in the case ending—for the one who was the doer; for these two persons, the state of friendship is not joined together again, it does not come about. ‘Hadayaṃ nānujānāti’ means: for that reason my heart does not consent to dwelling here. ‘Gacchaññeva rathesabhā’ means: ‘Therefore, O great king, I shall indeed go.’

Taṃ sutvā rājā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke the fourth verse:

168.

168.

“Katassa ceva kattā ca, metti sandhīyate puna;

Dhīrānaṃ no ca bālānaṃ, vasa kuntini māgamā”ti.

“Between the one oppressed and the doer, friendship is joined together again; this is so for the wise, but not for the foolish. Dwell, Kuntinī, do not go.”

Tassattho – katassa ceva puggalassa, yo ca kattā tassa metti sandhīyate puna, sā pana dhīrānaṃ, no ca bālānaṃ. Dhīrānañhi metti bhinnāpi puna ghaṭīyati, bālānaṃ pana sakiṃ bhinnā bhinnāva hoti, tasmā vasa kuntini māgamāti.

Its meaning is this: For the person who was oppressed and for the one who was the doer, friendship is joined together again. But this is so for the wise, not for the foolish. For indeed, the friendship of the wise, even if broken, is joined together again; but for the foolish, once broken, it remains broken. Therefore, ‘vasa kuntini māgamā’ means ‘Dwell, Kuntinī, do not go.’

Sakuṇikā “evaṃ santepi na sakkā mayā idha vasituṃ sāmī”ti rājānaṃ vanditvā uppatitvā himavantameva gatā.

The heron said, “Even so, lord, it is not possible for me to live here,” and after paying homage to the king, she flew up and went straight to the Himalayas.

Satthā [V 3.0117] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kuntinīyeva etarahi kuntinī ahosi, bārāṇasirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the birth story: “The heron then was the same heron now, and the king of Bārāṇasī was none other than myself.”

Kuntinījātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Kuntinī Jātaka, the Third.

[344] 4. Ambajātakavaṇṇanā

[344] 4. The Commentary on the Mango Jātaka

Yo [P 3.0137] nīliyaṃ maṇḍayatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ambagopakattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira mahallakakāle pabbajitvā jetavanapaccante ambavane paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā ambe rakkhanto patitāni ambapakkāni khādanto vicarati, attano sambandhamanussānampi deti. Tasmiṃ bhikkhācāraṃ paviṭṭhe ambacorakā ambāni pātetvā khāditvā ca gahetvā ca gacchanti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe catasso seṭṭhidhītaro aciravatiyaṃ nhāyitvā vicarantiyo taṃ ambavanaṃ pavisiṃsu. Mahallako āgantvā tā disvā “tumhehi me ambāni khāditānī”ti āha. “Bhante, mayaṃ idāneva āgatā, na tumhākaṃ ambāni khādāmā”ti. “Tena hi sapathaṃ karothā”ti? “Karoma, bhante”ti sapathaṃ kariṃsu. Mahallako tā sapathaṃ kāretvā lajjāpetvā vissajjesi. Tassa taṃ kiriyaṃ sutvā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ [M 3.0126] samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asuko kira mahallako attano vasanakaṃ ambavanaṃ paviṭṭhā seṭṭhidhītaro sapathaṃ kāretvā lajjāpetvā vissajjesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa ambagopako hutvā catasso seṭṭhidhītaro sapathaṃ kāretvā lajjāpetvā vissajjesī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this, beginning with 'Yo nīliyaṃ maṇḍayati,' concerning an elder who was a mango-guardian. It is said that having gone forth in his old age, he had a leaf-hut built in a mango grove on the outskirts of Jetavana and lived there guarding the mangoes, eating the ripe mangoes that had fallen, and also giving some to his relatives. When he had gone on his alms-round, mango thieves would knock down the mangoes, and after eating some and taking others, they would depart. At that moment, four daughters of a merchant, having bathed in the Aciravatī River, were wandering about and entered that mango grove. The old man arrived, and seeing them, said, 'You have eaten my mangoes!' 'Venerable sir, we have only just arrived; we have not eaten your mangoes.' 'In that case, take an oath.' 'We will, venerable sir,' they said, and took an oath. The old man, having made them take an oath and shaming them, dismissed them. Hearing of his action, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: 'Friends, it seems a certain old man made the daughters of a merchant, who had entered the mango grove where he lived, take an oath, and after shaming them, dismissed them.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now sitting together?' When it was said, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, not only now, but in the past too, this mango-guardian made four daughters of a merchant take an oath, and after shaming them, dismissed them.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sakkattaṃ kāresi. Tadā eko kūṭajaṭilo bārāṇasiṃ upanissāya nadītīre ambavane paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā ambe rakkhanto patitāni ambapakkāni khādanto sambandhamanussānampi dento nānappakārena micchājīvena jīvikaṃ kappento vicarati. Tadā sakko devarājā “ke nu kho loke mātāpitaro upaṭṭhahanti, kule jeṭṭhāpacayanakammaṃ karonti, dānaṃ denti, sīlaṃ rakkhanti, uposathakammaṃ karonti, ke pabbajitā samaṇadhamme yuttapayuttā viharanti, ke anācāraṃ carantī”ti lokaṃ volokento imaṃ ambagopakaṃ [P 3.0138] anācāraṃ kūṭajaṭilaṃ disvā “ayaṃ kūṭajaṭilo kasiṇaparikammādiṃ attano samaṇadhammaṃ pahāya ambavanaṃ [V 3.0118] rakkhanto vicarati, saṃvejessāmi na”nti tassa gāmaṃ bhikkhāya paviṭṭhakāle attano ānubhāvena ambe pātetvā corehi vilumbite viya akāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was Sakka. At that time, a deceitful ascetic, living near Benares, had a leaf-hut built in a mango grove on the riverbank and lived there guarding the mangoes, eating the ripe mangoes that had fallen, giving some to his relatives, and maintaining his livelihood through various forms of wrong livelihood. Then Sakka, king of the devas, was surveying the world, thinking, 'Who in the world attends to their parents? Who performs the duty of respecting the elders in the family? Who gives gifts, keeps the precepts, and observes the Uposatha? Which renunciants are devoted to the duties of a recluse, and who behaves improperly?' Seeing this mango-guardian, this deceitful ascetic, behaving improperly, he thought, 'This deceitful ascetic, having abandoned his own duties as a recluse, such as the preliminary work for kasina meditation, wanders about guarding a mango grove. I shall strike him with terror.' Then, when the ascetic had entered the village for alms, Sakka, by his own power, made the mangoes fall and made it appear as if they had been plundered by thieves.

Tadā bārāṇasito catasso seṭṭhidhītaro taṃ ambavanaṃ pavisiṃsu. Kūṭajaṭilo tā disvā “tumhehi me ambāni khāditānī”ti palibuddhi. “Bhante, mayaṃ idāneva āgatā, na te ambāni khādāmā”ti. “Tena hi sapathaṃ karothā”ti? “Katvā ca pana gantuṃ labhissāmā”ti? “Āma, labhissathā”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti tāsu jeṭṭhikā sapathaṃ karontī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, four daughters of a merchant from Benares entered that mango grove. The deceitful ascetic saw them and accused them, saying, 'You have eaten my mangoes!' 'Venerable sir, we have only just arrived; we have not eaten your mangoes.' 'In that case, take an oath.' 'And after taking it, will we be allowed to go?' 'Yes, you will.' 'Very well, venerable sir.' Among them, the eldest, taking an oath, spoke the first verse:

169.

169.

“Yo nīliyaṃ maṇḍayati, saṇḍāsena vihaññati;

Tassa sā vasamanvetu, yā te ambe avāharī”ti.

'May she who carried off your mangoes come under the power of a man who dyes his hair black and is troubled by tweezers.'

Tassattho – yo puriso palitānaṃ kāḷavaṇṇakaraṇatthāya nīlaphalādīni yojetvā kataṃ nīliyaṃ maṇḍayati, nīlakesantare ca uṭṭhitaṃ [M 3.0127] palitaṃ uddharanto saṇḍāsena vihaññati kilamati, tassa evarūpassa mahallakassa sā vasaṃ anvetu, tathārūpaṃ patiṃ labhatu, yā te ambe avāharīti.

The meaning is: May she who carried off your mangoes come under the power of such an old man and obtain such a husband—a man who dyes his hair black by using indigo dye made from indigo fruits and the like to blacken grey hairs, and who, while plucking out with tweezers the grey hairs that have appeared among the blackened hair, is troubled and weary.

Tāpaso “tvaṃ ekamantaṃ tiṭṭhāhī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ seṭṭhidhītaraṃ sapathaṃ kāresi. Sā sapathaṃ karontī dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The ascetic said, 'Stand to one side,' and made the second merchant’s daughter take an oath. She, while taking the oath, spoke the second verse:

170.

170.

“Vīsaṃ vā pañcavīsaṃ vā, ūnatiṃsaṃva jātiyā;

Tādisā pati mā laddhā, yā te ambe avāharī”ti.

'May she who carried off your mangoes, though she be twenty, or twenty-five, or even twenty-nine years of age, not obtain a husband.'
