Tassattho – nāriyo nāma pannarasasoḷasavassikakāle purisānaṃ piyā honti. Yā pana tava ambāni avāhari, sā evarūpe yobbane patiṃ alabhitvā jātiyā vīsaṃ vā pañcavīsaṃ vā ekena dvīhi ūnatāya ūnatiṃsaṃ vā vassāni patvā tādisā paripakkavayā hutvāpi patiṃ mā laddhāti.

The meaning is: Women are generally dear to men at the age of fifteen or sixteen. But may she who carried off your mangoes, not having obtained a husband in such youth, reach the age of twenty, or twenty-five, or even twenty-nine—that is, thirty years less one or two—and even though she has reached such a mature age, may she still not obtain a husband.

Tāyapi sapathaṃ katvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitāya tatiyā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

When she too had taken the oath and stood to one side, the third daughter spoke the third verse:

171.

171.

“Dīghaṃ [V 3.0119][P 3.0139] gacchatu addhānaṃ, ekikā abhisārikā;

Saṅkete pati mā adda, yā te ambe avāharī”ti.

'May she who carried off your mangoes, as a woman going to meet her lover alone, travel a long distance; and at the appointed place, may she not see her husband.'

Tassattho – yā te ambe avāhari, sā patiṃ patthayamānā tassa santikaṃ abhisaraṇatāya abhisārikā nāma hutvā ekikā adutiyā gāvutadvigāvutamattaṃ dīghaṃ addhānaṃ gacchatu, gantvāpi ca tasmiṃ asukaṭṭhānaṃ nāma āgaccheyyāsīti kate saṅkete taṃ patiṃ mā addasāti.

The meaning is: May she who carried off your mangoes, desiring a husband and thus becoming known as an 'abhisārikā' because she goes to meet him, travel a long distance of one or two leagues alone and without a companion. And even after having gone, may she not see that husband at the appointed place agreed upon with the words, 'You should come to such-and-such a place.'

Tāyapi sapathaṃ katvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitāya catutthā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

When she too had taken the oath and stood to one side, the fourth daughter spoke the fourth verse:

172.

172.

“Alaṅkatā suvasanā, mālinī candanussadā;

Ekikā sayane setu, yā te ambe avāharī”ti. – sā uttānatthāyeva;

'May she who carried off your mangoes, though adorned, well-clothed, wearing garlands, and anointed with sandalwood, lie alone upon her bed.' — The meaning of this is clear.

Tāpaso “tumhehi atibhāriyā sapathā katā, aññehi ambāni khāditāni bhavissanti, gacchatha dāni tumhe”ti tā uyyojesi. Sakko bheravarūpārammaṇaṃ dassetvā kūṭatāpasaṃ tato palāpesi.

The ascetic said, 'You have taken very heavy oaths. The mangoes must have been eaten by others. Now you may go,' and he dismissed them. Sakka then showed a terrifying sight and made the deceitful ascetic flee from that place.

Satthā [M 3.0128] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kūṭajaṭilo ayaṃ ambagopako mahallako ahosi, catasso seṭṭhidhītaro etāyeva, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having presented this Dhamma discourse, connected the birth story: “At that time, the fraudulent ascetic was this old mango-guardian; the four merchant’s daughters were these very same ones; and Sakka was none other than myself.”

Ambajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Mango Jātaka, the Fourth.

[345] 5. Rājakumbhajātakavaṇṇanā

[345] 5. The Commentary on the Rājakumbha Jātaka.

Vanaṃ yadaggi dahatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ alasabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthivāsī kulaputto sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajitvāpi alaso ahosi uddesaparipucchāyonisomanasikāravattapaṭivattādīhi paribāhiro nīvaraṇābhibhūto. Nisinnaṭṭhānādīsu iriyāpathesu tathā eva hoti. Tassa taṃ ālasiyabhāvaṃ ārabbha bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asuko nāma bhikkhu evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā [V 3.0120] ālasiyo kusīto nīvaraṇābhibhūto viharatī”ti[P 3.0140]. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa ālasiyoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“When fire burns the forest...” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain lazy monk. It is said that a certain son of a good family from Sāvatthī, though he had gone forth and dedicated himself to the Dispensation, was lazy, neglectful of recitation, inquiry, wise attention, major and minor duties, and so on, and was overcome by the hindrances. In his postures of sitting, standing, and so forth, he was just the same. Concerning his laziness, the monks started a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma, saying, “Friends, a certain monk, having gone forth in such a liberating Dispensation, lives lazy, indolent, and overcome by the hindrances.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered together?” When they told him, “For such-and-such,” he said, “Not only now, monks, is he lazy; in the past, too, he was lazy,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa amaccaratanaṃ ahosi, bārāṇasirājā ālasiyajātiko ahosi. Bodhisatto “rājānaṃ pabodhessāmī”ti ekaṃ upamaṃ upadhārento vicarati. Athekadivasaṃ rājā uyyānaṃ gantvā amaccagaṇaparivuto tattha vicaranto ekaṃ rājakumbhaṃ nāma ālasiyaṃ passi. Tathārūpā kira ālasiyā sakaladivasaṃ gacchantāpi ekadvaṅgulamattameva gacchanti. Rājā taṃ disvā “vayassa ko nāma so”ti bodhisattaṃ pucchi. Mahāsatto “rājakumbho nāmesa, mahārāja, ālasiyo. Evarūpo hi sakaladivasaṃ gacchantopi ekaṅguladvaṅgulamattameva gacchatī”ti vatvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto “ambho, rājakumbha, tumhākaṃ dandhagamanaṃ imasmiṃ araññe dāvaggimhi uṭṭhite kiṃ karothā”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his jewel of a minister. The king of Benares was of a lazy disposition. The Bodhisatta, thinking, “I will rouse the king,” went about considering a suitable parable. Then one day, the king went to his park and, while wandering there surrounded by his retinue of ministers, he saw a lazy creature called a rājakumbha. Such lazy creatures, it is said, even when moving for a whole day, go only about one or two inches. The king, seeing it, asked the Bodhisatta, “Friend, what is that creature called?” The Great Being replied, “Its name is rājakumbha, Your Majesty; it is a lazy creature. Indeed, such a creature, even when moving for a whole day, goes only about one or two inches.” Then, conversing with it, he said, “Ho, rājakumbha, being so slow-moving, what will you do when a forest fire breaks out in this wilderness?” and he spoke the first verse:

173.

173.

“Vanaṃ [M 3.0129] yadaggi dahati, pāvako kaṇhavattanī;

Kathaṃ karosi pacalaka, evaṃ dandhaparakkamo”ti.

“When fire, the purifier with a black path, burns the forest, what do you do, O Pacalaka, being so slow in your exertion?”

Tattha yadaggīti yadā aggi. Pāvako kaṇhavattanīti aggino vevacanaṃ. Pacalakāti taṃ ālapati. So hi calanto calanto gacchati, niccaṃ vā pacalāyati, tasmā “pacalako”ti vuccati. Dandhaparakkamoti garuvīriyo.

Therein, yadaggi means ‘when fire.’ Pāvako kaṇhavattanī is a synonym for fire. Pacalaka is how he addresses it. For it moves with a waddling motion, or is constantly trembling, therefore it is called ‘pacalaka.’ Dandhaparakkamo means slow in exertion.

Taṃ sutvā rājakumbho dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the rājakumbha spoke the second verse:

174.

174.

“Bahūni rukkhachiddāni, pathabyā vivarāni ca;

Tāni ce nābhisambhoma, hoti no kālapariyāyo”ti.

“There are many hollows in the trees, and crevices in the earth; if we should fail to reach them, for us it is the end of our time.”

Tassattho – paṇḍita, amhākaṃ ito uttarigamanaṃ nāma natthi. Imasmiṃ pana araññe rukkhachiddāni pathaviyaṃ vivarāni ca bahūni. Yadi tāni na pāpuṇāma, hoti no kālapariyāyoti maraṇameva no hotīti.

The meaning is this: O wise one, for us there is no such thing as going any further. But in this forest, there are many hollows in the trees and crevices in the earth. If we do not reach them, it is the end of our time for us—that is, it is death itself for us.

Taṃ [P 3.0141] sutvā bodhisatto itarā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the other two verses:

175.

175.

“Yo [V 3.0121] dandhakāle tarati, taraṇīye ca dandhati;

Sukkhapaṇṇaṃva akkamma, atthaṃ bhañjati attano.

“He who hastens when he should delay, and delays when he should hasten, like one who treads on a dry leaf, destroys his own advantage.

176.

176.

“Yo dandhakāle dandheti, taraṇīye ca tārayi;

Sasīva rattiṃ vibhajaṃ, tassattho paripūratī”ti.

“He who delays when delay is needed, and hastens when haste is needed, like the moon dividing the night, his aim is fully accomplished.”

Tattha dandhakāleti tesaṃ tesaṃ kammānaṃ saṇikaṃ kattabbakāle. Taratīti turitaturito vegena tāni kammāni karoti. Sukkhapaṇṇaṃvāti yathā vātātapasukkhaṃ tālapaṇṇaṃ balavā puriso akkamitvā bhañjeyya, tattheva cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ kareyya, evaṃ so attano atthaṃ vuddhiṃ bhañjati. Dandhetīti dandhayati dandhakātabbāni kammāni dandhameva karoti. Tārayīti turitakātabbāni kammāni turitova karoti. Sasīva rattiṃ vibhajanti yathā cando juṇhapakkhaṃ rattiṃ jotayamāno kāḷapakkharattito rattiṃ vibhajanto divase divase paripūrati, evaṃ tassa purisassa attho paripūratīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Here, 'at a time for delay' refers to the time when certain tasks should be done slowly. 'He hastens' means he performs those tasks swiftly and with haste. 'Like a dry leaf' is like when a strong man steps on a palm leaf dried by wind and sun and breaks it, pulverizing it into tiny fragments—so too does such a person destroy his own advantage and prosperity. 'He delays' means he performs slowly tasks that should be done slowly. 'He acts quickly' means he acts quickly when tasks need to be done quickly. 'Like the moon dividing the night' is like how the moon, illuminating the night in the bright fortnight, distinguishing it from the night of the dark fortnight, grows fuller day by day—so too, it is said, does that man’s purpose become fulfilled.

Rājā [M 3.0130] bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā tato paṭṭhāya analaso jāto.

Hearing the Bodhisatta's words, from that moment the king became diligent.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājakumbho ālasiyabhikkhu ahosi, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka, saying, "At that time, the rājakumbha was the lazy monk, but the wise minister was indeed myself."

Rājakumbhajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Rājakumbha Jātaka, the fifth.

[346] 6. Kesavajātakavaṇṇanā

[346] 6. The Commentary on the Kesava Jātaka

Manussindaṃ jahitvānāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto vissāsabhojanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Anāthapiṇḍikassa kira gehe pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ nibaddhabhattaṃ hoti, gehaṃ niccakālaṃ [P 3.0142] bhikkhusaṅghassa opānabhūtaṃ kāsāvapajjotaṃ isivātapaṭivātaṃ. Athekadivasaṃ rājā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto seṭṭhino nivesane bhikkhusaṅghaṃ disvā “ahampi ariyasaṅghassa nibaddhaṃ bhikkhaṃ dassāmī”ti vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ nibaddhaṃ bhikkhaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Tato paṭṭhāya rājanivesane nibaddhaṃ bhikkhā diyyati, tivassikagandhasālibhojanaṃ paṇītaṃ. Vissāsenapi sinehenapi sahatthā dāyakā natthi, rājayutte dāpesi. Bhikkhū nisīditvā [V 3.0122] bhuñjituṃ na icchanti, nānaggarasabhattaṃ gahetvā attano attano upaṭṭhākakulaṃ gantvā taṃ bhattaṃ tesaṃ datvā tehi dinnaṃ lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā bhuñjanti.

"Having abandoned the lord of men..." This the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke concerning food given out of intimacy. In the house of Anāthapiṇḍika, it is said, there was a perpetual meal for five hundred monks; the house was always like a public well for the Sangha of monks, bright with the glow of saffron robes, wafted by the air of the movement of the ascetics. Then one day, the king, while circumambulating the city, saw the Sangha of monks at the merchant’s residence and thought, "I too shall offer a perpetual meal to the noble Sangha." He went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and established a perpetual meal offering for five hundred monks. From then on, a perpetual meal was given at the king’s residence—excellent food, fragrant sāli rice stored for three years. However, there were no donors giving with their own hands out of intimacy or affection; the king had his royal officials give it. The monks did not wish to sit and eat there; instead, taking the food of various excellent flavors, they went to the homes of their respective supporting families. There, they gave that food to them and ate whatever coarse or fine food was given by those supporters.

Athekadivasaṃ rañño bahuṃ phalāphalaṃ āhariṃsu. Rājā “saṅghassa dethā”ti āha. Manussā bhattaggaṃ gantvā ekabhikkhumpi adisvā “eko bhikkhupi natthī”ti rañño ārocesuṃ. “Nanu velāyeva tāvā”ti? “Āma, velā, bhikkhū pana tumhākaṃ gehe bhattaṃ gahetvā attano attano vissāsikānaṃ upaṭṭhākānaṃ gehaṃ gantvā tesaṃ datvā tehi dinnaṃ lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā bhuñjantī”ti. Rājā “amhākaṃ bhattaṃ paṇītaṃ, kena nu kho kāraṇena abhutvā aññaṃ bhuñjanti, satthāraṃ pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā pucchi. Satthā “mahārāja, bhojanaṃ nāma vissāsaparamaṃ, tumhākaṃ [M 3.0131] gehe vissāsaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā sinehena dāyakānaṃ abhāvā bhikkhū bhattaṃ gahetvā attano attano vissāsikaṭṭhāne paribhuñjanti. Mahārāja, vissāsasadiso añño raso nāma natthi, avissāsikena dinnaṃ catumadhurampi hi vissāsikena dinnaṃ sāmākabhattaṃ na agghati. Porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi roge uppanne raññā pañca vejjakulāni gahetvā bhesajje kāritepi roge avūpasante vissāsikānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā aloṇakaṃ sāmākanīvārayāguñceva udakamattasittaṃ aloṇakapaṇṇañca paribhuñjitvā nirogā jātā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

One day, many assorted fruits were brought to the king. He said, "Give them to the Sangha." The men went to the refectory but, not seeing a single monk, they reported to the king, "There is not even one monk." "Is it not yet the time for the meal?" "Yes, it is the time, but the monks take the food from your palace and go to the homes of their own intimate supporters. They give that food to them and eat whatever coarse or fine food is given by those supporters." The king thought, "Our food is excellent—for what reason do they not eat it but consume other food instead? I shall ask the Teacher." He went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and asked. The Teacher said, "Great king, food is best when given out of intimacy. In your house, because there are no donors who give with affection and establish intimacy, the monks take the meal and consume it in places where they have intimacy. Great king, there is no flavor equal to intimacy. Even the four sweet delicacies given without intimacy are not worth a simple meal of millet given with intimacy. In the past, when ancient wise men fell ill, even though the king had five families of physicians prepare medicine, when the illness did not subside, they went to those they were intimate with. There, they consumed unsalted gruel of sāmā and nīvāra millet, and unsalted leaves boiled in plain water, and they became well." Having said this, being requested by the king, he recounted a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe brāmhaṇakule nibbatti, “kappakumāro”tissa [P 3.0143] nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā aparabhāge isipabbajjaṃ pabbaji. Tadā kesavo nāma tāpaso pañcahi tāpasasatehi parivuto gaṇasatthā hutvā himavante vasati. Bodhisatto tassa santikaṃ gantvā pañcannaṃ antevāsikasatānaṃ jeṭṭhantevāsiko hutvā vihāsi, kesavatāpasassa hitajjhāsayo sasineho ahosi. Te aññamaññaṃ ativiya vissāsikā ahesuṃ. Aparabhāge kesavo te tāpase ādāya loṇambilasevanatthāya manussapathaṃ gantvā bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase nagaraṃ bhikkhāya pavisitvā rājadvāraṃ agamāsi. Rājā isigaṇaṃ disvā pakkosāpetvā antonivesane bhojetvā paṭiññaṃ gahetvā uyyāne vasāpesi. Atha vassāratte atikkante kesavo rājānaṃ āpucchi. Rājā “bhante, tumhe mahallakā, amhe tāva upanissāya vasatha, daharatāpase himavantaṃ pesethā”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti jeṭṭhantevāsikena saddhiṃ te himavantaṃ pesetvā sayaṃ ekakova ohiyi. Kappo himavantaṃ gantvā tāpasehi saddhiṃ vasi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the Kāsī country. They named him Kappakumāra. When he came of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and later went forth as an ascetic. At that time, an ascetic named Kesava, who was a teacher of a group, lived in the Himalayas with a retinue of five hundred ascetics. The Bodhisatta went to him and became the chief disciple among the five hundred pupils. He was well-disposed and affectionate toward the ascetic Kesava. They had very great mutual intimacy. Later, Kesava took those ascetics to the world of men to obtain salt and sour foods. Arriving in Bārāṇasī, they stayed in the royal park. The next day, they entered the city for alms and reached the palace gate. The king, seeing the group of sages, invited them in, fed them in his inner chambers, and, having received their promise to stay, had them dwell in the park. When the rainy season had passed, Kesava took leave of the king. The king said, "Venerable sir, you are elderly. Stay here depending on us, and send only the young ascetics back to the Himalayas." He agreed and sent the young ascetics back to the Himalayas with his chief disciple, remaining behind alone. Kappa went to the Himalayas and lived there with the other ascetics.

Kesavo [V 3.0123] kappena vinā vasanto ukkaṇṭhitvā taṃ daṭṭhukāmo hutvā niddaṃ na labhati, tassa niddaṃ alabhantassa sammā āhāro na pariṇāmaṃ gacchati, lohitapakkhandikā ahosi, bāḷhā vedanā vattanti. Rājā pañca vejjakulāni gahetvā tāpasaṃ paṭijaggi, rogo na vūpasammati. Kesavo rājānaṃ āha “mahārāja, kiṃ mayhaṃ maraṇaṃ icchatha, udāhu arogabhāva”nti[M 3.0132]? “Arogabhāvaṃ, bhante”ti. “Tena hi maṃ himavantaṃ pesethā”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti rājā nāradaṃ nāma amaccaṃ pakkāsāpetvā “nārada, amhākaṃ bhadantaṃ gahetvā vanacarakehi saddhiṃ himavantaṃ yāhī”ti pesesi. Nārado taṃ tattha netvā paccāgamāsi. Kesavassapi kappe diṭṭhamatteyeva cetasikarogo vūpasanto, ukkaṇṭhā paṭippassambhi. Athassa kappo aloṇakena adhūpanena [P 3.0144] udakamattasittapaṇṇena saddhiṃ sāmākanīvārayāguṃ adāsi, tassa taṅkhaṇaññeva lohitapakkhandikā paṭippassambhi.

Kesava, living without Kappa, became dissatisfied and, desiring to see him, could not sleep. Because he could not sleep, his food was not properly digested, and he developed bloody dysentery; intense pains arose. The king brought five families of physicians to treat the ascetic, but the illness did not subside. Kesava asked the king, "Great king, do you wish for my death, or for my health?" "For your health, venerable sir," the king replied. "In that case, send me to the Himalayas." "Very well, venerable sir," said the king, and summoning a minister named Nārada, he sent him, saying, "Nārada, take our venerable teacher and go to the Himalayas with the forest dwellers." Nārada led him there and then returned. For Kesava, as soon as he saw Kappa, his mental distress subsided and his dissatisfaction ceased. Then Kappa gave him unsalted, unsmoked gruel of sāmā and nīvāra millet, along with leaves boiled in plain water. At that very moment, his bloody dysentery was cured.

Puna rājā nāradaṃ pesesi “gaccha kesavassa tāpasassa pavattiṃ jānāhī”ti. So gantvā taṃ arogaṃ disvā “bhante, bārāṇasirājā pañca vejjakulāni gahetvā paṭijagganto tumhe aroge kātuṃ nāsakkhi, kathaṃ te kappo paṭijaggī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Again the king sent Nārada, saying, "Go and learn the news of the ascetic Kesava." He went and, seeing him healthy, said, "Venerable sir, the king of Bārāṇasī, employing five families of physicians to treat you, was not able to make you well. How then did Kappa treat you?" Having said this, he spoke the first verse:

177.

177.

“Manussindaṃ jahitvāna, sabbakāmasamiddhinaṃ;

Kathaṃ nu bhagavā kesī, kappassa ramati assame”ti.

“Having abandoned the lord of men, endowed with the fulfillment of all desires, how now, Blessed Kesī, do you delight in Kappa’s hermitage?”

Tattha manussindanti manussānaṃ indaṃ bārāṇasirājānaṃ. Kathaṃ nu bhagavā kesīti kena nu kho upāyena ayaṃ amhākaṃ bhagavā kesavatāpaso kappassa assame ramatīti.

Here, “lord of men” means the lord of men, the king of Bārāṇasī. “How now, Blessed Kesī?” means by what means does this our Blessed Kesava the ascetic delight in Kappa’s hermitage.

Evaṃ aññehi saddhiṃ sallapanto viya kesavassa abhiratikāraṇaṃ pucchi. Taṃ sutvā kesavo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, as if conversing with others, he asked Kesava about the cause of his delight. Hearing that, Kesava spoke the second verse:

178.

178.

“Sādūni ramaṇīyāni, santi vakkhā manoramā;

Subhāsitāni kappassa, nārada ramayanti ma”nti.

“Pleasant, delightful, and charming trees exist; the well-spoken words of Kappa, O Nārada, delight me.”

Tattha vakkhāti rukkhā. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “rukkhā”tveva likhitaṃ. Subhāsitānīti kappena kathitāni subhāsitāni maṃ ramayantīti attho.

Here, ‘vakkhā’ means trees. In the Pāli text, however, it is written as ‘rukkhā.’ ‘Subhāsitāni’ means ‘the well-spoken words spoken by Kappa delight me’—this is the meaning.

Evañca [V 3.0124] pana vatvā “evaṃ maṃ abhiramāpento kappo aloṇakaṃ adhūpanaṃ udakasittapaṇṇamissaṃ sāmākanīvārayāguṃ pāyesi, tāya me sarīre byādhi vūpasamito, arogo jātomhī”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā nārado tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

And having said this, he added, “Thus delighting me, Kappa gave me a gruel of millet and wild rice mixed with water-sprinkled leaves, without salt or seasoning, to drink. By that, the sickness in my body subsided, and I became healthy.” Hearing this, Nārada spoke the third verse:

179.

179.

“Sālīnaṃ [M 3.0133] odanaṃ bhuñje, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ;

Kathaṃ sāmākanīvāraṃ, aloṇaṃ chādayanti ta”nti.

“I eat the rice of fine paddy, pure, with meat curry; how then do millet and wild rice, unsalted, satisfy you?”

Tattha [P 3.0145] bhuñjeti bhuñjasi, ayameva vā pāṭho. Chādayantīti chādayati pīṇeti toseti. Gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ pana anunāsiko kato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo tvaṃ suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ rājakule rājārahaṃ sālibhattaṃ bhuñjasi, taṃ kathamidaṃ sāmākanīvāraṃ aloṇaṃ pīṇeti toseti, kathaṃ te etaṃ ruccatīti.

Here, ‘bhuñje’ means ‘bhuñjasi’ (you eat), or this is the reading itself. ‘Chādayanti’ means ‘chādayati,’ it pleases, it delights. For the sake of metrical ease, however, the nasal has been added. This is what is said: ‘You who eat fine rice fit for a king with pure meat curry in the royal household—how does this unsalted millet and wild rice please and delight you? How does this appeal to you?’”

Taṃ sutvā kesavo catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, Kesava spoke the fourth verse:

180.

180.

“Sāduṃ vā yadi vāsāduṃ, appaṃ vā yadi vā bahuṃ;

Vissattho yattha bhuñjeyya, vissāsaparamā rasā”ti.

“Whether tasty or not tasty, whether little or much, wherever one might eat with trust—trust is the supreme flavor.”

Tattha yadi vāsādunti yadi vā asāduṃ. Vissatthoti nirāsaṅko vissāsapatto hutvā. Yattha bhuñjeyyāti yasmiṃ nivesane evaṃ bhuñjeyya, tattha evaṃ bhuttaṃ yaṃkiñci bhojanaṃ sādumeva. Kasmā? Yasmā vissāsaparamā rasā, vissāso paramo uttamo etesanti vissāsaparamā rasā. Vissāsasadiso hi añño raso nāma natthi. Avissāsikena hi dinnaṃ catumadhurampi vissāsikena dinnaṃ ambilakañjiyaṃ na agghatīti.

Here, ‘yadi vāsāduṃ’ means ‘or if not tasty.’ ‘Vissattho’ means ‘being without suspicion, having attained confidence.’ ‘Yattha bhuñjeyya’ means ‘in whatever dwelling one might eat in this way, there whatever food is thus eaten is indeed tasty.’ Why? Because ‘vissāsaparamā rasā,’ meaning, ‘trust is supreme, the best, for these flavors.’ Indeed, there is no other flavor equal to trust. For even the four sweets given by one without trust are not worth as much as sour gruel given by one with trust.

Nārado tassa vacanaṃ sutvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “kesavo idaṃ nāma kathesī”ti ācikkhi.

Nārada, having heard his words, went to the king and reported, “Kesava said such and such.”

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, nārado sāriputto, kesavo bakabrahmā, kappo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the king was Ānanda, Nārada was Sāriputta, Kesava was Bakabrahmā, and Kappa was I myself.”

Kesavajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Kesava Jātaka, the Sixth.

[347] 7. Ayakūṭajātakavaṇṇanā

[347] 7. The Commentary on the Ayakūṭa Jātaka

Sabbāyasanti [V 3.0125][M 3.0134] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto lokatthacariyaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu mahākaṇhajātake (jā. 1.12.61 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

“Sabbāyasaṃ”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning conduct for the welfare of the world. The story will become clear in the Mahākaṇha Jātaka (Jā. 1.12.61 ff.).

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbattitvā vayappatto uggahitasabbasippo pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā manussā devamaṅgalikā hutvā bahū ajeḷakādayo [P 3.0146] māretvā devatānaṃ balikammaṃ karonti. Bodhisatto “pāṇo na hantabbo”ti bheriṃ carāpesi. Yakkhā balikammaṃ alabhamānā bodhisattassa kujjhitvā himavante yakkhasamāgamaṃ gantvā bodhisattassa māraṇatthāya ekaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ yakkhaṃ pesesuṃ. So kaṇṇikamattaṃ mahantaṃ ādittaṃ ayakūṭaṃ gahetvā “iminā naṃ paharitvā māressāmī”ti āgantvā majjhimayāmasamanantare bodhisattassa sayanamatthake aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakkassa āsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So āvajjamāno taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā indavajiraṃ ādāya gantvā yakkhassa upari aṭṭhāsi. Bodhisatto yakkhaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho esa maṃ rakkhamāno ṭhito, udāhu māretukāmo”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. Having come of age and mastered all the arts, upon his father’s passing, he was established on the throne and ruled righteously. At that time, people were devoted to divine omens and would kill many goats, sheep, and other animals to make offerings to the deities. The Bodhisatta had a drum beaten, proclaiming, “No living being is to be killed.” The yakkhas, not receiving their offerings, grew angry with the Bodhisatta. They went to a gathering of yakkhas in the Himalayas and sent a fierce yakkha to kill the Bodhisatta. He, taking a great, blazing iron club the size of a roof-finial, came thinking, “With this I will strike and kill him,” and just after the middle watch, he stood at the head of the Bodhisatta's bed. At that moment, Sakka’s throne showed a sign of heat. He, reflecting and knowing the reason, took Indra's thunderbolt, went, and stood above the yakkha. The Bodhisatta, seeing the yakkha, wondered, “Is this one standing here to protect me, or is he intent on killing me?” and, conversing with him, spoke the first verse:

181.

181.

“Sabbāyasaṃ kūṭamatippamāṇaṃ, paggayha yo tiṭṭhasi antalikkhe;

Rakkhāya me tvaṃ vihito nusajja, udāhu me cetayase vadhāyā”ti.

“You who stand in the sky, having raised a club made entirely of iron and of enormous measure; are you appointed today for my protection, or do you intend my death?”

Tattha vihito nusajjāti vihito nu asi ajja.

Here, ‘vihito nusajja’ means ‘are you indeed appointed today?’

Bodhisatto pana yakkhameva passati, na sakkaṃ. Yakkho sakkassa bhayena bodhisattaṃ paharituṃ na sakkoti. So bodhisattassa kathaṃ sutvā “mahārāja, nāhaṃ tava rakkhaṇatthāya ṭhito, iminā pana jalitena ayakūṭena paharitvā taṃ māressāmīti āgatomhi, sakkassa bhayena taṃ paharituṃ na sakkomī”ti etamatthaṃ dīpento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, however, saw only the yakkha, not Sakka. The yakkha, out of fear of Sakka, was unable to strike the Bodhisatta. Having heard the Bodhisatta's words, he said, “Great king, I am not standing here for your protection. Rather, I came to strike you with this blazing iron club and kill you, but out of fear of Sakka, I cannot strike you.” Explaining this matter, he spoke the second verse:

182.

182.

“Dūto [M 3.0135] ahaṃ rājidha rakkhasānaṃ, vadhāya tuyhaṃ pahitohamasmi;

Indo ca taṃ rakkhati devarājā, tenuttamaṅgaṃ na te phālayāmī”ti.

“I am a messenger of the rakkhasas, O king, sent here for your death. And Indra, the king of gods, protects you; for that reason I do not split your head.”

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto itarā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the Bodhisatta spoke the other two verses:

183.

183.

“Sace [V 3.0126] ca maṃ rakkhati devarājā, devānamindo maghavā sujampati;

Kāmaṃ [P 3.0147] pisācā vinadantu sabbe, na santase rakkhasiyā pajāya.

“And if the King of Gods protects me, the lord of gods, Maghavā, Sujampati, let all the pisācas howl as they please; I have no fear of the rakkhasa folk.”

184.

184.

“Kāmaṃ kandantu kumbhaṇḍā, sabbe paṃsupisācakā;

Nālaṃ pisācā yuddhāya, mahatī sā vibhiṃsikā”ti.

“Let the Kumbhaṇḍas wail as they please, and all the dust-pisācas; the pisācas are no match for battle—great is that intimidation!”

Tattha rakkhasiyā pajāyāti rakkhasisaṅkhātāya pajāya, rakkhasasattānanti attho. Kumbhaṇḍāti kumbhamattarahassaṅgā mahodarā yakkhā. Paṃsupisācakāti saṅkāraṭṭhāne pisācā. Nālanti pisācā nāma mayā saddhiṃ yuddhāya na samatthā. Mahatī sā vibhiṃsikāti yaṃ panete yakkhā sannipatitvā vibhiṃsikaṃ dassenti, sā mahatī vibhiṃsikā bhayakāraṇadassanamattameva mayhaṃ, na panāhaṃ bhāyāmīti attho.

Here, ‘rakkhasiyā pajāya’ means ‘of the folk designated as rakkhasas,’ that is, ‘rakkhasa beings.’ ‘Kumbhaṇḍā’ refers to yakkhas with testicles the size of pots and large bellies. ‘Paṃsupisācakā’ means ‘pisācas of the rubbish heaps.’ ‘Nālaṃ’ means ‘these pisācas are not capable of fighting with me.’ ‘Mahatī sā vibhiṃsikā’ means ‘that great intimidation which these yakkhas, having gathered together, display, is for me merely the sight of a cause for fear, but I am not afraid’—this is the meaning.

Sakko yakkhaṃ palāpetvā mahāsattaṃ ovaditvā “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, ito paṭṭhāya tava rakkhā mamāyattā”ti vatvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

Sakka, having made the yakkha flee and having advised the Great Being, said, “Do not fear, great king. From now on, your protection is my responsibility.” Having said this, he returned to his own abode.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sakko anuruddho ahosi, bārāṇasirājā ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, Sakka was Anuruddha, and the king of Bārāṇasī was I myself.”

Ayakūṭajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Ayakūṭa Jātaka, the Seventh.

[348] 8. Araññajātakavaṇṇanā

[348] 8. The Commentary on the Arañña Jātaka

Araññā [M 3.0136] gāmamāgammāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto thullakumārikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu cūḷanāradakassapajātake (jā. 1.13.40 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

“Araññā gāmamāgamma”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk lured by a mature young woman. The story will become clear in the Cūḷanāradakassapa Jātaka (Jā. 1.13.40 ff.). The Teacher then related the story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ uggahitasippo bhariyāya kālakatāya puttaṃ gahetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavante vasanto puttaṃ assamapade ṭhapetvā phalāphalatthāya gacchati. Tadā coresu paccantagāmaṃ paharitvā karamare gahetvā gacchantesu ekā kumārikā palāyitvā taṃ assamapadaṃ patvā tāpasakumāraṃ [P 3.0148] palobhetvā sīlavināsaṃ pāpetvā “ehi gacchāmā”ti āha. “Pitā tāva [V 3.0127] me āgacchatu, taṃ passitvā gamissāmī”ti. “Tena hi disvā āgacchā”ti nikkhamitvā antarāmagge nisīdi. Tāpasakumāro pitari āgate paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. When he came of age, having mastered the arts at Takkasilā, and after his wife had passed away, he took his son and embraced the life of an ascetic. Dwelling in the Himalayas, he left his son at the hermitage while he went out to gather fruits. At that time, robbers raided a border village and took captives as they departed. A young girl among them escaped and reached the hermitage. There, she seduced the young ascetic and caused him to lose his virtue. “Come, let us go,” she said. “First, let my father return. After seeing him, I will go,” he replied. “Then go and see him and come back,” she said, and stepping outside, she waited along the way. When his father arrived, the young ascetic spoke this first verse:

185.

185.

“Araññā gāmamāgamma, kiṃsīlaṃ kiṃvataṃ ahaṃ;

Purisaṃ tāta seveyyaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

“Having come from the forest to the village, what kind of virtue, what kind of observance should I maintain? What kind of person, father, should I associate with? Please tell me this when you are asked.”

Tattha araññā gāmamāgammāti tāta ahaṃ ito araññato manussapathaṃ vasanatthāya gato vasanagāmaṃ patvā kiṃ karomīti.

Herein, 'araññā gāmamāgamma' means: 'Father, having gone from this forest to the world of humans for the purpose of dwelling, and having reached a village to live in, what shall I do?'

Athassa pitā ovādaṃ dadanto tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Then his father, wishing to give him advice, spoke these three verses:

186.

186.

“Yo taṃ vissāsaye tāta, vissāsañca khameyya te;

Sussūsī ca titikkhī ca, taṃ bhajehi ito gato.

“He who would inspire your trust, dear son, and who would welcome your trust; who is eager to listen and is patient—associate with him, having gone from here.

187.

187.

“Yassa kāyena vācāya, manasā natthi dukkaṭaṃ;

Urasīva patiṭṭhāya, taṃ bhajehi ito gato.

“He in whom there is no wrongdoing by body, speech, or mind—associate with him, having gone from here, as if established on the breast.

188.

188.

“Haliddirāgaṃ kapicittaṃ, purisaṃ rāgavirāginaṃ;

Tādisaṃ tāta mā sevi, nimmanussampi ce siyā”ti.

“A person whose attachment is like turmeric dye, whose mind is like a monkey's, who is passionate and then detached—do not associate with such a one, dear son, even if the world were devoid of other humans.”

Tattha [M 3.0137] yo taṃ vissāsayeti yo puriso taṃ vissāseyya na parisaṅkeyya. Vissāsañca khameyya teti yo ca attani kayiramānaṃ tava vissāsaṃ patto nirāsaṅko taṃ khameyya. Sussūsīti yo ca tava vissāsavacanaṃ sotumicchati. Titikkhīti yo ca tayā kataṃ aparādhaṃ khamati. Taṃ bhajehīti taṃ purisaṃ bhajeyyāsi payirupāseyyāsi. Urasīva patiṭṭhāyāti yathā tassa urasi patiṭṭhāya vaḍḍhito orasaputto tvampi tādiso urasi patiṭṭhitaputto viya hutvā evarūpaṃ purisaṃ bhajeyyāsīti attho.

Herein, 'yo taṃ vissāsayeti' means a person who would make you trust him without suspicion. 'Vissāsañca khameyya teti' refers to one who, being trusted by you without doubt, would welcome that trust. 'Sussūsī' means one who wishes to listen to your words of confidence. 'Titikkhī' means one who forgives an offense committed by you. 'Taṃ bhajehī' means you should associate with and attend upon that person. 'Urasīva patiṭṭhāyāti' means: just as an own son grows up established on the breast, so too should you, like a son established on the breast, associate with such a person—this is the meaning.

Haliddirāganti haliddirāgasadisaṃ athiracittaṃ. Kapicittanti lahuparivattitāya makkaṭacittaṃ. Rāgavirāginanti muhutteneva rajjanavirajjanasabhāvaṃ. Nimmanussampi ce siyāti sacepi sakalaṃ jambudīpatalaṃ kāyaduccaritādivirahitassa manussassa abhāvena nimmanussaṃ siyā[V 3.0128], tathāpi, tāta, tādisaṃ lahucittaṃ mā sevi, sabbampi manussapathaṃ vicinitvā heṭṭhā vuttaguṇasampannameva bhajeyyāsīti attho.

“Haliddirāgaṃ” means an unstable mind like turmeric dye. “Kapicittaṃ” refers to a mind that changes quickly like a monkey’s. “Rāgavirāginaṃ” means one whose nature is to be attracted and detached in an instant. “Nimmanussampi ce siyā” means: even if the entire land of Jambudīpa were devoid of people because of the absence of anyone free from bodily misconduct and so on, still, dear son, do not associate with such a fickle-minded person. Having searched the entire human world, you should associate only with one endowed with the previously mentioned virtues—this is the meaning.

Taṃ [P 3.0149] sutvā tāpasakumāro “ahaṃ, tāta, imehi guṇehi samannāgataṃ purisaṃ kattha labhissāmi, na gacchāmi, tumhākaññeva santike vasissāmī”ti vatvā nivatti. Athassa pitā kasiṇaparikammaṃ ācikkhi. Ubhopi aparihīnajjhānā brahmalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Hearing this, the young ascetic said, “Father, where shall I find a person endowed with these qualities? I will not go; I will stay right here with you.” So saying, he turned back from going to the village. Then his father taught him the preliminary work for kasiṇa meditation. Both, with their jhāna unimpaired, were destined for the Brahmā world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā putto ca kumārikā ca eteyeva ahesuṃ, pitā tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the son and the maiden were these very ones, but the ascetic father was I myself.”

Araññajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Arañña Jātaka, the Eighth.

[349] 9. Sandhibhedajātakavaṇṇanā

[349] 9. The Commentary on the Sandhibheda Jātaka

Neva itthīsu sāmaññanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto pesuññasikkhāpadaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiṃ kira samaye satthā “chabbaggiyā bhikkhū pesuññaṃ upasaṃharantī”ti sutvā te pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tumhe, bhikkhave, bhikkhūnaṃ bhaṇḍanajātānaṃ kalahajātānaṃ vivādāpannānaṃ pesuññaṃ upasaṃharatha, tena anuppannāni ceva bhaṇḍanāni uppajjanti, uppannāni ca [M 3.0138] bhiyyobhāvāya saṃvattantī”ti pucchitvā “sacca”nti vutte te bhikkhū garahitvā “bhikkhave, pisuṇā vācā nāma tikhiṇasattipahārasadisā, daḷho vissāsopi tāya khippaṃ bhijjati, tañca pana gahetvā attano mettibhindanakajano sīhausabhasadiso hotī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this discourse beginning with 'Neva itthīsu sāmaññaṃ' concerning the training rule on slander. At one time, the Teacher heard, “The group-of-six monks are carrying slanderous talk,” and summoning them, he asked, “Is it true, monks, that you carry slander among monks who are quarrelsome, contentious, and disputing, thereby causing quarrels to arise where none existed and increasing those that have arisen?” When they admitted it was true, he rebuked those monks, saying, “Monks, slanderous speech is like a blow from a sharp weapon; even long-standing trust is quickly broken by it. And one who takes up that slander and breaks friendship becomes like the lion and the bull.” Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa putto hutvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ uggahitasippo pitu accayena dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā eko gopālako araññe gokulesu gāvo paṭijaggitvā āgacchanto ekaṃ gabbhiniṃ asallakkhetvā pahāya āgato. Tassā ekāya sīhiyā saddhiṃ vissāso uppajji. Tā ubhopi daḷhamittā hutvā ekato vicaranti. Aparabhāge gāvī vacchakaṃ, sīhī sīhapotakaṃ vijāyi. Te ubhopi janā kulena āgatamettiyā daḷhamittā hutvā ekato vicaranti[P 3.0150]. Atheko vanacarako araññaṃ pavisitvā tesaṃ vissāsaṃ disvā araññe uppajjanakabhaṇḍaṃ ādāya bārāṇasiṃ gantvā rañño datvā [V 3.0129] “api te, samma, kiñci araññe acchariyaṃ diṭṭhapubba”nti raññā puṭṭho “deva, aññaṃ kiñci na passāmi, ekaṃ pana sīhañca usabhañca aññamaññaṃ vissāsike ekato vicarante addasa”nti āha. “Etesaṃ tatiye uppanne bhayaṃ bhavissati, yadā tesaṃ tatiyaṃ passati, atha me ācikkheyyāsī”ti. “Sādhu, devā”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born as his son. When he came of age, having learned the arts at Takkasilā, after his father’s passing, he ruled the kingdom righteously. At that time, a cowherd, having tended the cattle in the forest, was returning when he failed to notice a pregnant cow and left her behind. She developed a friendship with a lioness. The two became firm friends and roamed together. Later, the cow gave birth to a calf, and the lioness to a lion cub. Those two, through the friendship inherited from their families, became firm friends and roamed together. Then, a forester entered the forest and, seeing their trust, took some forest products to Benares and presented them to the king. When the king asked, “Friend, have you ever seen anything amazing in the forest?” he replied, “Your Majesty, I have seen nothing else, but I did see a lion and a bull trusting each other and roaming together.” The king said, “When a third companion appears among them, there will be danger. When you see that third one, inform me.” “Very well, Your Majesty,” he replied.

Vanacarake pana bārāṇasiṃ gate eko siṅgālo sīhañca usabhañca upaṭṭhahi. Vanacarako araññaṃ gantvā taṃ disvā “tatiyassa uppannabhāvaṃ rañño kathessāmī”ti nagaraṃ gato. Siṅgālo cintesi “mayā ṭhapetvā sīhamaṃsañca usabhamaṃsañca aññaṃ akhāditapubbaṃ nāma natthi, ime bhinditvā imesaṃ maṃsaṃ khādissāmī”ti. So “ayaṃ taṃ evaṃ vadati, ayaṃ taṃ evaṃ vadatī”ti ubhopi te aññamaññaṃ bhinditvā na cirasseva kalahaṃ kāretvā maraṇākārappatte akāsi. Vanacarakopi gantvā rañño “tesaṃ, deva, tatiyo uppanno”ti āha. “Ko so”ti? “Siṅgālo, devā”ti. Rājā “so ubho mitte bhinditvā mārāpessati, mayaṃ tesaṃ matakāle sampāpuṇissāmā”ti vatvā rathaṃ abhiruyha vanacarakena maggadesakena gacchanto tesu aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ katvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pattesu sampāpuṇi. Siṅgālo pana haṭṭhatuṭṭho ekavāraṃ [M 3.0139] sīhassa maṃsaṃ khādati, ekavāraṃ usabhassa maṃsaṃ khādati. Rājā te ubhopi jīvitakkhayappatte disvā rathe ṭhitova sārathinā saddhiṃ sallapanto imā gāthā abhāsi –

While the forester was in Benares, a jackal began to attend upon both the lion and the bull. The forester, returning to the forest and seeing him, thought, 'I will report the presence of a third party to the king,' and went to the city. The jackal pondered, 'There is no kind of meat I have not eaten before, except for the meat of a lion and a bull. I will set them against each other and eat their flesh.' So, by saying, 'This one says this about you, that one says that about you,' he set the two friends against each other, and before long, he incited a quarrel that brought them to their death. The forester went and told the king, 'Your Majesty, a third companion has appeared among them.' 'Who is it?' 'A jackal, Your Majesty.' The king said, 'He will set the two friends against each other and cause their death. We shall arrive at the time of their demise.' So saying, he mounted his chariot and, with the forester as his guide, arrived just as they, having quarreled with each other, had reached the end of their lives. The jackal, delighted and pleased, ate first the lion's flesh, then the bull's flesh. The king, seeing them both lifeless, standing in his chariot and conversing with his charioteer, spoke these verses:

189.

189.

“Neva [P 3.0151] itthīsu sāmaññaṃ, nāpi bhakkhesu sārathi;

Athassa sandhibhedassa, passa yāva sucintitaṃ.

“There is no commonality between them in women, nor in food, O charioteer. But see how well-conceived was this breaking of a bond.”

190.

190.

“Asi tikkhova maṃsamhi, pesuññaṃ parivattati;

Yatthūsabhañca sīhañca, bhakkhayanti migādhamā.

“Like a sharp sword in the flesh, slander revolves; where the lowest of beasts devour both the bull and the lion.”

191.

191.

“Imaṃ so sayanaṃ seti, yamimaṃ passasi sārathi;

Yo vācaṃ sandhibhedassa, pisuṇassa nibodhati.

“He lies on this bed of death, which you see, O charioteer, who heeds the speech of the slanderer who breaks a friendship.”

192.

192.

“Te janā sukhamedhanti, narā saggagatāriva;

Ye vācaṃ sandhibhedassa, nāvabodhanti sārathī”ti.

“Those people find happiness, like men gone to heaven, who do not heed the speech of the slanderer, O charioteer.”

Tattha neva itthīsūti samma sārathi, imesaṃ dvinnaṃ janānaṃ neva itthīsu sāmaññaṃ atthi na[V 3.0130], bhakkhesupi. Aññameva hi itthiṃ sīho sevati, aññaṃ usabho, aññaṃ bhakkhaṃ sīho khādati, aññaṃ usabhoti attho. Athassāti evaṃ kalahakāraṇe avijjamānepi atha imassa mittasandhibhedakassa duṭṭhasiṅgālassa “ubhinnaṃ maṃsaṃ khādissāmī”ti cintetvā ime mārentassa passa yāva sucintitaṃ, sucintitaṃ jātanti adhippāyo. Yatthāti yasmiṃ pesuññe parivattamāne. Usabhañca sīhañca migādhamā siṅgālā khādanti, taṃ pesuññaṃ maṃsamhi tikhiṇo asi viya mittabhāvaṃ chindantameva parivattatīti dīpeti.

There, ‘neva itthīsu’ means, O good charioteer, there is no commonality between these two regarding females, nor regarding food. For indeed, a lion consorts with one kind of female, a bull with another; a lion eats one kind of food, a bull another—this is the meaning. ‘Athassa’ means, even though there is no cause for a quarrel, yet see how well-conceived—how well-planned—it was by this wicked jackal, the breaker of friendships, who thought, ‘I will devour the flesh of both’ and caused their death. ‘Yattha’ means, where slander revolves. The jackals, the lowest of beasts, devour both the bull and the lion. It shows that slander, like a sharp sword in the flesh, revolves while cutting through the bond of friendship.

Yamimaṃ passasīti samma sārathi, yaṃ imaṃ passasi imesaṃ dvinnaṃ matasayanaṃ, aññopi yo puggalo sandhibhedassa pisuṇassa pisuṇavācaṃ nibodhati gaṇhāti, so imaṃ sayanaṃ seti, evamevaṃ maratīti dasseti. Sukhamedhantīti sukhaṃ vindanti labhanti. Narā saggagatārivāti saggagatā dibbabhogasamaṅgino narā viya te sukhaṃ vindanti. Nāvabodhantīti [P 3.0152] na sārato paccenti, tādisaṃ pana vacanaṃ sutvā codetvā sāretvā mettiṃ abhinditvā pākatikāva hontīti.

‘Yamimaṃ passasi’ means, O good charioteer, this death-bed of these two that you see—any other person who heeds and accepts the slanderous speech of the breaker of friendships lies on this bed, meaning he dies in the same way. ‘Sukhamedhanti’ means they find and obtain happiness. ‘Narā saggagatāriva’ means they find happiness like humans gone to heaven, endowed with divine enjoyments. ‘Nāvabodhanti’ means they do not take it to heart as true; but having heard such words, though urged and reminded, they do not break their friendship and remain as they were.

Rājā [M 3.0140] imā gāthā bhāsitvā sīhassa kesaracammanakhadāṭhā gāhāpetvā nagarameva gato.

Having spoken these verses, the king had the lion’s mane, hide, claws, and fangs taken and returned to the city.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bārāṇasirājā ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth story: “At that time, the king of Benares was I myself.”

Sandhibhedajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The commentary on the Sandhibheda Jātaka is the ninth.

[350] 10. Devatāpañhajātakavaṇṇanā

[350] 10. The Commentary on the Devatāpañha Jātaka

Hanti hatthehi pādehīti ayaṃ devatāpucchā umaṅgajātake (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

“He strikes with hands and feet”—this deity’s question will appear in the Umaṅga Jātaka (Jā. 2.22.590 and following).

Devatāpañhajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The commentary on the Devatāpañha Jātaka is the tenth.

Cūḷakuṇālavaggo pañcamo.

The Cūḷakuṇāla Chapter is the fifth.

Jātakuddānaṃ [V 3.0131] –

The Summary of the Jātakas:

Kāliṅgo assāroho ca, ekarājā ca daddaro;

Sīlavīmaṃsasujātā, palāso sakuṇo chavo;

Seyyoti dasa jātakā.

Kāliṅga, Assāroha, Ekarāja, Daddara, Sīlavīmaṃsa, Sujātā, Palāsa, Sakuṇa, Chava, and Seyya—these are the ten Jātakas.

Pucimando kassapo ca, khantivādī lohakumbhī;

Sabbamaṃsalābhī saso, matārodakaṇaverā;

Tittiro succajo dasa.

Pucimanda, Kassapa, Khantivādī, Lohakumbhī, Sabbamaṃsalābhī, Sasa, Matārodaka, Navera, Tittira, and Succaja—these are ten.

Kuṭidūso duddabhāyo, brahmadattacammasāṭako;

Godharājā ca kakkāru, kākavatī nanu sociyo;

Kāḷabāhu sīlavīmaṃso dasa.

Kuṭidūsa, Daddabha, Brahmadatta, Cammasāṭaka, Godharāja, Kakkāru, Kākavatī, Sociya, Kāḷabāhu, and Sīlavīmaṃsa—these are ten.

Kokāliko [M 3.0141] rathalaṭṭhi, pakkagodharājovādā;

Jambukabrahāchatto ca, pīṭhathusā ca bāveru;

Visayhaseṭṭhi dasadhā.

Kokālika, Rathalaṭṭhi, Pakka-godha, Rājovāda, Jambuka, Brahāchatta, Pīṭha, Thusa, Bāveru, and Visayha-seṭṭhi—these are the ten.

Kinnarīvānarakuntinī, ambahārī gajakumbho;

Kesavāyakūṭāraññaṃ, sandhibhedo devatāpañhā.

Kinnarī, Vānara, Kuntinī, Amba, Gajakumbha, Kesava, Ayakūṭa, Arañña, Sandhibheda, and Devatāpañha.

Vagguddānaṃ –

The Summary of the Chapters:

Kāliṅgo pucimando ca, kuṭidūsakakokilā;

Cūḷakuṇālavaggoti, pañcavaggā catukkamhi;

Honti paññāsa jātakā.

Kāliṅga, Pucimanda, Kuṭidūsaka, Kokila, and Cūḷakuṇāla Chapter—these five chapters in the fourth division make fifty Jātakas.

Catukkanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Book of Fours is concluded.

5. Pañcakanipāto

5. The Book of Fives

1. Maṇikuṇḍalavaggo

1. The Maṇikuṇḍala Chapter

[351] 1. Maṇikuṇḍalajātakavaṇṇanā

[351] 1. The Commentary on the Maṇikuṇḍala Jātaka

Jīno [V 3.0132][P 3.0153][M 3.0142] rathassaṃ maṇikuṇḍale cāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarañño antepure sabbatthasādhakaṃ paduṭṭhāmaccaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā vitthāritameva. Idha pana bodhisatto bārāṇasirājā ahosi. Paduṭṭhāmacco kosalarājānaṃ ānetvā kāsirajjaṃ gāhāpetvā bārāṇasirājānaṃ bandhāpetvā bandhanāgāre pakkhipāpesi. Rājā jhānaṃ uppādetvā ākāse pallaṅkena nisīdi, corarañño sarīre ḍāho uppajji. So bārāṇasirājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

“Jīno rathassaṃ maṇikuṇḍale ca”—this the Teacher related while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a corrupt minister in the inner court of the King of Kosala who was an all-purpose agent. The story has been fully explained previously. Here, however, the Bodhisatta was the King of Benares. The corrupt minister brought the King of Kosala, had the kingdom of Kāsi seized, and had the King of Benares bound and thrown into prison. The King, developing meditative absorption, sat cross-legged in the air, and a burning sensation arose in the body of the robber king. Approaching the King of Benares, he spoke the first verse:

1.

1.

“Jīno rathassaṃ maṇikuṇḍale ca, putte ca dāre ca tatheva jīno;

Sabbesu bhogesu asesakesu, kasmā na santappasi sokakāle”ti.

“You have lost the chariot and horse, and the jeweled earrings; you have lost sons and wives likewise. Having lost all possessions without exception, why do you not grieve in this time of sorrow?”

Tattha jīno rathassaṃ maṇikuṇḍale cāti mahārāja, tvaṃ rathañca assañca maṇikuṇḍalāni ca jīno, “jīno rathasse ca maṇikuṇḍale cā”tipi pāṭho. Asesakesūti nissesakesu.

There, “Jīno rathassaṃ maṇikuṇḍale ca” means: “O great king, you have lost the chariot and horse, and the jeweled earrings.” “Jīno rathasse ca maṇikuṇḍale ca” is also a reading. “Asesakesu” means “without any remainder.”

Taṃ [P 3.0154] sutvā bodhisatto imā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the Bodhisatta spoke these two verses:

2.

2.

“Pubbeva maccaṃ vijahanti bhogā, macco vā te pubbataraṃ jahāti;

Asassatā bhogino kāmakāmi, tasmā na socāmahaṃ sokakāle.

“Possessions abandon a mortal beforehand, or the mortal abandons them even earlier. O desirer of sensual pleasures, the wealthy are impermanent; therefore I do not grieve in a time of sorrow.

3.

3.

“Udeti [V 3.0133][M 3.0143] āpūrati veti cando, atthaṃ tapetvāna paleti sūriyo;

Viditā mayā sattuka lokadhammā, tasmā na socāmahaṃ sokakāle”ti.

“The moon rises, waxes full, and wanes; the sun, having shone, goes to its setting. O foe, the ways of the world are known to me; therefore I do not grieve in a time of sorrow.”

Tattha pubbeva maccanti maccaṃ vā bhogā pubbeva paṭhamataraññeva vijahanti, macco vā te bhoge pubbataraṃ jahāti. Kāmakāmīti corarājānaṃ ālapati. Ambho, kāme kāmayamāna kāmakāmi bhogino nāma loke asassatā, bhogesu vā naṭṭhesu jīvamānāva abhogino honti, bhoge vā pahāya sayaṃ nassanti, tasmā ahaṃ mahājanassa sokakālepi na socāmīti attho. Viditā mayā sattuka lokadhammāti corarājānaṃ ālapati. Ambho, sattuka, mayā lābho alābho yaso ayasotiādayo lokadhammā viditā. Yatheva hi cando udeti ca pūrati ca puna ca khīyati, yathā ca sūriyo andhakāraṃ vidhamanto mahantaṃ ālokaṃ tapetvāna puna sāyaṃ atthaṃ paleti atthaṃ gacchati na dissati, evameva bhogā uppajjanti ca nassanti ca, tattha kiṃ sokena, tasmā na socāmīti attho.

There, ‘pubbeva maccaṃ’ means that wealth abandons a mortal even before death, or the mortal abandons that wealth earlier. ‘Kāmakāmī’—he addresses the robber king. ‘Friend, O one who desires sensual pleasures, the wealthy are indeed impermanent in the world. Either their wealth is lost while they are still alive and they become poor, or they themselves perish after abandoning wealth. Therefore, even in a time of public sorrow, I do not grieve’—this is the meaning. ‘Viditā mayā sattuka lokadhammā’—he addresses the robber king. ‘Friend, O foe, the worldly conditions such as gain and loss, fame and disrepute, and so on, are known to me. Just as the moon rises, waxes full, and then wanes, and just as the sun, dispelling darkness, shines with great light and then sets again in the evening, goes to its setting, and is seen no more, so too wealth arises and perishes. What use is sorrow in that? Therefore, I do not grieve’—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ mahāsatto corarañño dhammaṃ desetvā idāni tameva coraṃ garahanto āha –

Thus, the Great Being, having taught the Dhamma to the robber king, now reproaching that very robber, said:

4.

4.

“Alaso gihī kāmabhogī na sādhu, asaññato pabbajito na sādhu;

Rājā na sādhu anisammakārī, yo paṇḍito kodhano taṃ na sādhu.

“A lazy householder indulging in sensual pleasures is not good; an unrestrained renunciate is not good; a king who acts without consideration is not good; a wise person who is prone to anger is not good.

5.

5.

“Nisamma khattiyo kayirā, nānisamma disampati;

Nisammakārino rāja, yaso kitti ca vaḍḍhatī”ti.

“A noble should act after consideration, not without consideration, O ruler of the land. For one who acts with consideration, O king, glory and renown increase.”

Imā [P 3.0155] pana dve gāthā heṭṭhā vitthāritāyeva. Corarājā bodhisattaṃ khamāpetvā rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā attano janapadameva gato.

These two verses, however, have already been explained in detail previously. The robber king, having sought forgiveness from the Bodhisatta and handed back the kingdom, went back to his own country.

Satthā [M 3.0144] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kosalarājā ānando ahosi, bārāṇasirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, the King of Kosala was Ānanda, and the King of Benares was none other than myself.”

Maṇikuṇḍalajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The commentary on the Maṇikuṇḍala Jātaka is the first.

[352] 2. Sujātajātakavaṇṇanā

[352] 2. The Commentary on the Sujāta Jātaka

Kiṃ [V 3.0134] nu santaramānovāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto matapitikaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira pitari mate paridevamāno vicarati, sokaṃ vinodetuṃ na sakkoti. Atha satthā tassa sotāpattiphalūpanissayaṃ disvā sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchāsamaṇaṃ ādāya tassa gehaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisinno taṃ vanditvā nisinnaṃ “kiṃ, upāsaka, socasī”ti vatvā “āma, bhante”ti vutte “āvuso, porāṇakapaṇḍitā paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā pitari kālakate na sociṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Kiṃ nu santaramāno”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a householder whose father had died. It is said that after his father's death, he wandered about lamenting, unable to dispel his sorrow. Then the Teacher, seeing that he had the supportive conditions for the fruit of stream-entry, went to Sāvatthī for alms and, taking a monk as his attendant, went to the man’s house. Seated on the prepared seat, he addressed the man, who had bowed and sat down: “Why, upāsaka, do you grieve?” When the man replied, “Yes, Venerable Sir,” the Teacher said, “Friend, the wise of old, having heard the words of the wise, did not grieve when their fathers passed away.” Then, being entreated, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kuṭumbikagehe nibbatti, “sujātakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tassa vayappattassa pitāmaho kālamakāsi. Athassa pitā pitu kālakiriyato paṭṭhāya sokasamappito āḷāhanaṃ gantvā āḷāhanato aṭṭhīni āharitvā attano ārāme mattikāthūpaṃ katvā tāni tattha nidahitvā gatagatavelāya thūpaṃ pupphehi pūjetvā cetiyaṃ āvijjhanto paridevati, neva nhāyati na limpati na bhuñjati na kammante vicāreti. Taṃ disvā bodhisatto “pitā me ayyakassa matakālato paṭṭhāya sokābhibhūto carati, ṭhapetvā pana maṃ añño etaṃ saññāpetuṃ na sakkoti, ekena naṃ upāyena nissokaṃ karissāmī”ti bahigāme [P 3.0156] ekaṃ matagoṇaṃ disvā tiṇañca pānīyañca āharitvā tassa purato ṭhapetvā “khāda, khāda, piva, pivā”ti āha. Āgatāgatā naṃ disvā “samma sujāta, kiṃ ummattakosi, matagoṇassa tiṇodakaṃ desī”ti vadanti. So na kiñci paṭivadati. Athassa pitu santikaṃ gantvā “putto te ummattako jāto, matagoṇassa tiṇodakaṃ detī”ti āhaṃsu. Taṃ sutvā kuṭumbikassa [M 3.0145] pitusoko apagato, puttasoko patiṭṭhito. So vegenāgantvā “nanu tvaṃ, tāta sujāta, paṇḍitosi, kiṃkāraṇā matagoṇassa tiṇodakaṃ desī”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a householder's family, and they named him “Sujāta Kumāra.” When he came of age, his grandfather passed away. Then his father, overwhelmed with grief from the time of his father's death, would go to the charnel ground, bring back the bones from there, build a clay stūpa in his own garden, enshrine them there, and at every opportunity would worship the stūpa with flowers, lamenting while circling it as if it were a shrine. He neither bathed, anointed himself, ate, nor attended to his work. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta thought, “My father has been overwhelmed with grief since the death of my grandfather. Except for me, no one else can make him understand. I will free him from sorrow by some stratagem.” Then, seeing a dead ox in the outer village, he brought grass and water and placed them before it, saying, “Eat, eat! Drink, drink!” When people came and saw him, they said, “Friend Sujāta, are you mad? You offer grass and water to a dead ox!” But he did not reply. Then they went to his father and said, “Your son has gone mad—he gives grass and water to a dead ox!” Hearing this, the householder's grief for his father vanished, and grief for his son took its place. He hurried over and said, “Surely, dear Sujāta, you are wise—why then do you offer grass and water to a dead ox?” And he spoke these two verses:

6.

6.

“Kiṃ nu santaramānova, lāyitvā haritaṃ tiṇaṃ;

Khāda khādāti lapasi, gatasattaṃ jaraggavaṃ.

“Why do you act so hastily, having cut green grass? You mutter ‘Eat, eat!’ to a lifeless old ox.”

7.

7.

“Na hi annena pānena, mato goṇo samuṭṭhahe;

Tvañca tucchaṃ vilapasi, yathā taṃ dummatī tathā”ti.

“Indeed, not by food or drink can a dead ox arise; and you lament in vain, just as a fool would.”

Tattha [V 3.0135] santaramānovāti turito viya hutvā. Lāyitvāti lunitvā. Lapasīti vilapasi. Gatasattaṃ jaraggavanti vigatajīvitaṃ jiṇṇagoṇaṃ. Yathā tanti ettha tanti nipātamattaṃ, yathā dummati appapañño vilapeyya, tathā tvaṃ tucchaṃ vilapasīti.

There, `santaramānova` means ‘as if hurried.’ `Lāyitvā` means ‘having cut.’ `Lapasī` means ‘you lament.’ `Gatasattaṃ jaraggavaṃ` means ‘a lifeless, aged ox.’ Here, `taṃ` is merely a particle; just as a foolish, witless person might lament, so you lament in vain.

Tato bodhisatto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the Bodhisatta uttered two verses:

8.

8.

“Tatheva tiṭṭhati sīsaṃ, hatthapādā ca vāladhi;

Sotā tatheva tiṭṭhanti, maññe goṇo samuṭṭhahe.

“Just so remains the head, the limbs, and the tail; just so remain the ears. I think the ox might arise.”

9.

9.

“Nevayyakassa sīsañca, hatthapādā ca dissare;

Rudaṃ mattikathūpasmiṃ, nanu tvaññeva dummatī”ti.

“But the grandfather's head and hands and feet are not seen; weeping at the clay mound, surely you yourself are the fool!”

Tattha tathevāti yathā pubbe ṭhitaṃ, tatheva tiṭṭhati. Maññeti etesaṃ sīsādīnaṃ tatheva ṭhitattā ayaṃ goṇo samuṭṭhaheyyāti maññāmi. Nevayyakassa sīsañcāti ayyakassa pana sīsañca hatthapādā ca na dissanti. “Piṭṭhipādā na dissare”tipi pāṭho. Nanu tvaññeva dummatīti ahaṃ tāva sīsādīni passanto evaṃ karomi, tvaṃ pana na kiñci passasi, jhāpitaṭṭhānato aṭṭhīni āharitvā mattikāthūpaṃ katvā paridevasi. Iti maṃ paṭicca sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena nanu tvaññeva dummati. Bhijjanadhammā nāma saṅkhārā bhijjanti, tattha kā paridevanāti.

There, `tatheva` means: as it stood before, so it remains. `Maññe` means: ‘Since these—the head and so on—remain just as they were, I think this ox might arise.’ `Nevayyakassa sīsañca` means: ‘But the grandfather’s head and hands and feet are not seen.’ There is also a reading: ‘The back and feet are not seen.’ `Nanu tvaññeva dummatī` means: ‘I, at least, seeing the head and so on, act thus; but you see nothing at all, and after bringing bones from the cremation ground and making a mound of clay, you lament. Thus, in comparison to me, by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold, surely you are the foolish one. Formations, being subject to dissolution, do dissolve. What lamentation is there in that?’

Taṃ [P 3.0157] sutvā bodhisattassa pitā “mama putto paṇḍito idhalokaparalokakiccaṃ jānāti, mama saññāpanatthāya etaṃ kammaṃ akāsī”ti cintetvā “tāta sujātapaṇḍita, ‘sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā’ti me ñātā, ito [M 3.0146] paṭṭhāya na socissāmi, pitusokaharaṇakaputtena nāma tādisena bhavitabba”nti vatvā puttassa thutiṃ karonto āha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta’s father thought: ‘My son is wise; he knows the affairs of this world and the next. He has done this deed to make me understand.’ Then, saying, ‘Dear Sujāta the wise, it is known to me that “all conditioned things are impermanent.” From now on, I shall not grieve. A son who removes his father’s sorrow should indeed be like this,’ he praised his son and spoke:

10.

10.

“Ādittaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ, ghatasittaṃva pāvakaṃ;

Vārinā viya osiñcaṃ, sabbaṃ nibbāpaye daraṃ.

“I was burning indeed, like a fire sprinkled with ghee; as if sprinkling me with water, you have extinguished all my anguish.”

11.

11.

“Abbahī vata me sallaṃ, yamāsi hadayassitaṃ;

Yo me sokaparetassa, pitusokaṃ apānudi.

“Indeed, you have drawn out the dart for me, which was lodged in my heart; you who have dispelled my sorrow for my father, while I was overcome by grief.”

12.

12.

“Sohaṃ [V 3.0136] abbūḷhasallosmi, vītasoko anāvilo;

Na socāmi na rodāmi, tava sutvāna māṇava.

“So I am one with the dart drawn out, sorrowless, unperturbed; I do not grieve, nor do I weep, having heard you, young man.”

13.

13.

“Evaṃ karonti sappaññā, ye honti anukampakā;

Vinivattenti sokamhā, sujāto pitaraṃ yathā”ti.

“Thus do the wise act, those who are compassionate; they turn others away from sorrow, as Sujāta did his father.”

Tattha nibbāpayeti nibbāpayi. Daranti sokadarathaṃ. Sujāto pitaraṃ yathāti yathā mama putto sujāto maṃ pitaraṃ samānaṃ attano sappaññatāya sokamhā vinivattayi, evaṃ aññepi sappaññā sokamhā vinivattayantīti.

There, `nibbāpaye` means `nibbāpayi` (extinguished). `Daraṃ` means `sokadarathaṃ` (sorrow and distress). `Sujāto pitaraṃ yathā` means: ‘Just as my son Sujāta, by his own wisdom, turned me, his father, away from sorrow, so too do other wise ones turn others away from sorrow.’

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne kuṭumbiko sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā sujāto ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, Sujāta was none other than myself.

Sujātajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Sujāta Jātaka, the Second.

[353] 3. Venasākhajātakavaṇṇanā

[353] 3. The Commentary on the Venasākha Jātaka

Nayidaṃ niccaṃ bhavitabbanti idaṃ satthā bhaggesu saṃsumāragiraṃ nissāya bhesakaḷāvane viharanto bodhirājakumāraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Bodhirājakumāro nāma udenassa rañño putto tasmiṃ kāle saṃsumāragire vasanto ekaṃ pariyodātasippaṃ vaḍḍhakiṃ pakkosāpetvā aññehi rājūhi asadisaṃ katvā kokanadaṃ nāma pāsādaṃ [P 3.0158] kārāpesi. Kārāpetvā [M 3.0147] ca pana “ayaṃ vaḍḍhakī aññassapi rañño evarūpaṃ pāsādaṃ kareyyā”ti maccharāyanto tassa akkhīni uppāṭāpesi. Tenassa akkhīnaṃ uppāṭitabhāvo bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭo jāto. Tasmā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, bodhirājakumāro kira tathārūpassa vaḍḍhakino akkhīni uppāṭāpesi, aho kakkhaḷo pharuso sāhasiko”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa kakkhaḷo pharuso sāhasikova. Na kevalañca idāneva, pubbepesa khattiyasahassānaṃ akkhīni uppāṭāpetvā māretvā tesaṃ maṃsena balikammaṃ kāresī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“This is not to be permanent”—this the Teacher said, dwelling at Bhesakaḷā Forest near Saṃsumāragiri among the Bhaggas, in reference to Prince Bodhi. Prince Bodhi, the son of King Udena, at that time residing on Saṃsumāragiri, summoned a highly skilled carpenter and had a palace named Kokanada built, unlike any other king’s. But after having it built, out of jealousy, thinking, “This carpenter might build such a palace for another king,” he had his eyes gouged out. Thus the fact that his eyes had been gouged out became known among the community of monks. Therefore, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, it seems Prince Bodhi had the eyes of such a carpenter gouged out—oh, how cruel, harsh, and violent!” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what discussion are you engaged in now, sitting together?” When they replied, “This one,” he said, “Not only now, monks, was he cruel, harsh, and violent; he was so in the past as well. In the past, he had the eyes of a thousand kings gouged out, killed them, and had offerings made with their flesh.” Having said this, he recounted the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto takkasilāyaṃ disāpāmokkho ācariyo [V 3.0137] ahosi. Jambudīpatale khattiyamāṇavā brāhmaṇamāṇavā ca tasseva santike sippaṃ uggaṇhiṃsu. Bārāṇasirañño putto brahmadattakumāro nāma tassa santike tayo vede uggaṇhi. So pana pakatiyāpi kakkhaḷo pharuso sāhasiko ahosi. Bodhisatto aṅgavijjāvasena tassa kakkhaḷapharusasāhasikabhāvaṃ ñatvā “tāta, tvaṃ kakkhaḷo pharuso sāhasiko, pharusena nāma laddhaṃ issariyaṃ aciraṭṭhitikaṃ hoti, so issariye vinaṭṭhe bhinnanāvo viya samudde patiṭṭhaṃ na labhati, tasmā mā evarūpo ahosī”ti taṃ ovadanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a renowned teacher in Takkasilā, foremost in all directions. Young men of the warrior and brahmin castes from all over Jambudīpa came to study skills under him. The son of the king of Benares, Prince Brahmadatta by name, also learned the three Vedas under him. But by nature, he was cruel, harsh, and violent. Knowing his cruel, harsh, and violent nature through the science of physiognomy, the Bodhisatta advised him: “Dear one, you are cruel, harsh, and violent. Power gained through harshness is short-lived. When such power is lost, like a broken ship at sea, one finds no support. Therefore, do not be like this.” While advising him, he spoke these two verses:

14.

14.

“Nayidaṃ niccaṃ bhavitabbaṃ brahmadatta, khemaṃ subhikkhaṃ sukhatā ca kāye;

Atthaccaye mā ahu sampamūḷho, bhinnaplavo sāgarasseva majjhe.

“This is not to be permanent, Brahmadatta: security, prosperity, and ease of body; when misfortune comes, do not be utterly bewildered, like a broken boat in the middle of the ocean.”

15.

15.

“Yāni karoti puriso, tāni attani passati;

Kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ, pāpakārī ca pāpakaṃ;

Yādisaṃ vapate bījaṃ, tādisaṃ harate phala”nti.

“Whatever deeds a person does, those he sees in himself; a doer of good sees good, and a doer of evil, evil; as is the seed that is sown, so is the fruit one reaps.”

Tattha [P 3.0159] sukhatā ca kāyeti tāta brahmadatta, yadetaṃ khemaṃ vā subhikkhaṃ vā yā vā esā sukhatā kāye, idaṃ sabbaṃ imesaṃ sattānaṃ niccaṃ sabbakālameva na bhavati, idaṃ pana aniccaṃ hutvā abhāvadhammaṃ. Atthaccayeti so [M 3.0148] tvaṃ aniccatāvasena issariye vigate attano atthassa accaye yathā nāma bhinnaplavo bhinnanāvo manusso sāgaramajjhe patiṭṭhaṃ alabhanto sampamūḷho hoti, evaṃ mā ahu sampamūḷho. Tāni attani passatīti tesaṃ kammānaṃ vipākaṃ vindanto tāni attani passati nāma.

Therein, ‘and ease of body’ means: ‘Dear Brahmadatta, whatever security or prosperity there is, or whatever ease there is in the body—all this does not exist for these beings permanently at all times, but it is impermanent and subject to cessation.’ ‘At the loss of sovereignty’ means: ‘Thus, due to impermanence, when sovereignty has passed away, at the loss of your own benefit, just as a man with a broken raft or a broken boat in the middle of the ocean, finding no support, is utterly bewildered—do not be thus bewildered.’ ‘Those he sees in himself’ means: ‘Experiencing the result of those actions, he is said to see them in himself.’”

So ācariyaṃ vanditvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā pitu sippaṃ dassetvā oparajje patiṭṭhāya pitu accayena rajjaṃ pāpuṇi. Tassa piṅgiyo nāma purohito ahosi kakkhaḷo pharuso sāhasiko. So yasalobhena cintesi “yaṃnūnāhaṃ iminā raññā sakalajambudīpe sabbe rājāno gāhāpeyyaṃ, evamesa ekarājā bhavissati, ahampi ekapurohito bhavissāmī”ti. So taṃ rājānaṃ attano kathaṃ gāhāpesi. Rājā mahatiyā senāya nagarā nikkhamitvā ekassa rañño nagaraṃ rundhitvā taṃ rājānaṃ gaṇhi. Etenupāyena sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ gahetvā rājasahassaparivuto “takkasilāyaṃ rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti agamāsi. Bodhisatto nagaraṃ paṭisaṅkharitvā parehi appadhaṃsiyaṃ akāsi.

Having paid homage to the teacher, he went to Benares, demonstrated his skill to his father, and after being installed in the viceroyalty, he attained the kingship upon his father’s death. He had a chaplain named Piṅgiya, who was cruel, harsh, and violent. Driven by greed for status and wealth, he thought: ‘What if I have this king capture all the kings in the whole of Jambudīpa? Then he will be the sole emperor, and I will be the sole chaplain.’ He persuaded the king to follow his advice. The king set out from the city with a large army, besieged a king’s city, and captured that king. By this method, having seized the kingdom in all Jambudīpa and surrounded by a thousand kings, he went thinking, ‘I will seize the kingdom in Takkasilā.’ The Bodhisatta fortified the city and made it impregnable to others.”

Bārāṇasirājā [V 3.0138] gaṅgānadītīre mahato nigrodharukkhassa mūle sāṇiṃ parikkhipāpetvā upari vitānaṃ kārāpetvā sayanaṃ paññapetvā nivāsaṃ gaṇhi. So jambudīpatale sahassarājāno gahetvā yujjhamānopi takkasilaṃ gahetuṃ asakkonto attano purohitaṃ pucchi “ācariya, mayaṃ ettakehi rājūhi saddhiṃ āgantvāpi takkasilaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoma, kiṃ nu kho kātabba”nti. “Mahārāja, sahassarājūnaṃ akkhīni uppāṭetvā māretvā kucchiṃ [P 3.0160] phāletvā pañcamadhuramaṃsaṃ ādāya imasmiṃ nigrodhe adhivatthāya devatāya balikammaṃ katvā antavaṭṭīhi rukkhaṃ parikkhipitvā lohitapañcaṅgulikāni karoma, evaṃ no khippameva jayo bhavissatī”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā antosāṇiyaṃ mahābale malle ṭhapetvā ekamekaṃ rājānaṃ pakkosāpetvā nippīḷanena visaññaṃ kāretvā akkhīni uppāṭetvā māretvā maṃsaṃ ādāya kaḷevarāni gaṅgāyaṃ pavāhetvā vuttappakāraṃ balikammaṃ kāretvā balibheriṃ ākoṭāpetvā yuddhāya gato.

The king of Benares, on the bank of the Ganges River, had a screen placed around the roots of a great banyan tree, a canopy spread above, a bed prepared, and took up residence there. Although he had captured a thousand kings in Jambudīpa and was waging war, he was unable to capture Takkasilā. So he asked his chaplain: “Teacher, even after coming with so many kings, we cannot take Takkasilā. What should be done?” “Great king, pluck out the eyes of the thousand kings, kill them, slit open their bellies, take the five choice meats, and offer them as a sacrifice to the deity dwelling in this banyan tree. Then, encircle the tree with the coils of their intestines and make five-finger handprints with their blood. Thus, victory will swiftly be ours.” The king agreed, saying, “Very well.” He placed mighty wrestlers inside the enclosure, summoned each king one by one, made them unconscious by squeezing them, plucked out their eyes, killed them, took the flesh, cast the bodies into the Ganges, performed the sacrifice as described, had the war drum beaten, and went to battle.

Athassa [M 3.0149] aṭṭālakato eko yakkho āgantvā dakkhiṇakkhiṃ uppāṭetvā agamāsi, athassa mahatī vedanā uppajji. So vedanāppatto āgantvā nigrodharukkhamūle paññattāsane uttānako nipajji. Tasmiṃ khaṇe eko gijjho ekaṃ tikhiṇakoṭikaṃ aṭṭhiṃ gahetvā rukkhagge nisinno maṃsaṃ khāditvā aṭṭhiṃ vissajjesi, aṭṭhikoṭi āgantvā rañño vāmakkhimhi ayasūlaṃ viya patitvā akkhiṃ bhindi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sallakkhesi. So “amhākaṃ ācariyo ‘ime sattā bījānurūpaṃ phalaṃ viya kammānurūpaṃ vipākaṃ anubhontī’ti kathento idaṃ disvā kathesi maññe”ti vatvā vilapanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then a yakkha from the watchtower came and tore out his right eye and departed. Then great pain arose in him. Afflicted by pain, he went and lay down on his back on the seat prepared at the foot of the banyan tree. At that moment, a vulture, holding a sharp-pointed bone, sat on the treetop, ate the flesh, and dropped the bone. The tip of the bone, like an iron stake, fell into the king’s left eye and pierced it. At that moment, he remembered the words of the Bodhisatta. Thinking, “Our teacher, when he said that ‘these beings experience results according to their deeds, just as fruits correspond to their seeds,’ must have seen this and spoken,” he lamented and uttered two verses:

16.

16.

“Idaṃ tadācariyavaco, pārāsariyo yadabravi;

‘Mā su tvaṃ akari pāpaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ pacchā kataṃ tape’.

“This is the word of that teacher, which the descendant of Parāsara spoke: ‘Do no evil, lest you later regret what you have done.’”

17.

17.

“Ayameva so piṅgiya venasākho, yamhi ghātayiṃ khattiyānaṃ sahassaṃ;

Alaṅkate candanasārānulitte, tameva dukkhaṃ paccāgataṃ mama”nti.

“This is that very same Venasākha tree, Piṅgiya, where I had a thousand kings slaughtered, who were adorned and smeared with sandalwood paste; that very same suffering has now come back to me.”

Tattha [P 3.0161] idaṃ tadācariyavacoti idaṃ taṃ ācariyassa vacanaṃ. Pārāsariyoti taṃ gottena kitteti. Pacchā katanti yaṃ pāpaṃ tayā kataṃ, pacchā taṃ tapeyya kilameyya, taṃ mā karīti ovādaṃ adāsi, ahaṃ panassa vacanaṃ na karinti. Ayamevāti nigrodharukkhaṃ dassento vilapati. Venasākhoti patthaṭasākho. Yamhi ghātayinti yamhi rukkhe khattiyasahassaṃ māresiṃ. Alaṅkate candanasārānulitteti rājālaṅkārehi alaṅkate lohitacandanasārānulitte te khattiye yatthāhaṃ ghātesiṃ[V 3.0139], ayameva so rukkho idāni mayhaṃ kiñci parittāṇaṃ kātuṃ na sakkotīti dīpeti. Tameva dukkhanti yaṃ mayā paresaṃ akkhiuppāṭanadukkhaṃ kataṃ, idaṃ me tatheva paṭiāgataṃ, idāni no ācariyassa vacanaṃ matthakaṃ pattanti paridevati.

In this context, ‘this is that teacher’s word’ means this is the teacher’s instruction. ‘Pārāsariya’—he mentions him by his clan name. ‘Done afterward’ means: ‘Whatever evil you have done, afterward that will burn or distress you.’ He gave the advice, ‘Do not do it,’ but I did not heed his word. ‘This very one’—pointing to the banyan tree, he laments. ‘Venasākha’ means ‘spreading-branched.’ ‘In which I slaughtered’ means: ‘at which tree I killed a thousand nobles.’ ‘Adorned, anointed with sandalwood essence’ means: ‘those nobles, adorned with royal ornaments and smeared with the essence of red sandalwood, whom I slaughtered there—this very tree now cannot provide even the slightest protection for me,’ he explains. ‘That same suffering’ means: ‘the suffering of plucking out others' eyes that I inflicted, this has now returned to me in the same way. Now, our teacher’s word has reached its fulfillment’—thus he laments.

So [M 3.0150] evaṃ paridevamāno aggamahesiṃ anussaritvā –

Thus lamenting, he remembered the chief queen and said:

18.

18.

“Sāmā ca kho candanalittagattā, laṭṭhīva sobhañjanakassa uggatā;

Adisvā kālaṃ karissāmi ubbariṃ, taṃ me ito dukkhataraṃ bhavissatī”ti. –

“Sāmā, her body anointed with sandalwood, risen like a slender shoot of a drumstick tree; if I die without seeing Ubbarī, that will be even more painful to me than this.”

Gāthamāha –

He spoke the verse:

Tassattho – mama bhariyā suvaṇṇasāmā ubbarī yathā nāma siggurukkhassa uju uggatā sākhā mandamāluteritā kampamānā sobhati, evaṃ itthivilāsaṃ kurumānā sobhati, tamahaṃ idāni akkhīnaṃ bhinnattā ubbariṃ adisvāva kālaṃ karissāmi, taṃ me tassā adassanaṃ ito maraṇadukkhatopi dukkhataraṃ bhavissatīti.

The meaning is: My wife Ubbarī, who is golden-complexioned, is as beautiful as a straight, tall branch of a moringa tree swaying and trembling when struck by a gentle breeze; she is beautiful as she displays her feminine charms. Now, not seeing that Ubbarī because my eyes are destroyed, I shall die. For me, not seeing her will be more painful than even this suffering of death.

So evaṃ vilapantova maritvā niraye nibbatti. Na naṃ issariyaluddho purohito parittāṇaṃ kātuṃ sakkhi, na attano issariyaṃ. Tasmiṃ matamatteyeva balakāyo bhijjitvā palāyi.

Lamenting in this way, he died and was reborn in hell. Neither the chaplain, greedy for power, was able to protect him, nor was his own sovereignty. The moment he died, the army broke up and fled.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bārāṇasirājā bodhirājakumāro ahosi, piṅgiyo devadatto, disāpāmokkhācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the King of Benares was Prince Bodhi, Piṅgiya was Devadatta, but the world-renowned teacher was indeed myself.”

Venasākhajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Venasākha Jātaka, the Third.

[354] 4. Uragajātakavaṇṇanā

[354] 4. The Commentary on the Uraga Jātaka

Uragova [P 3.0162] tacaṃ jiṇṇanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mataputtakaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pana matabhariyamatapitikavatthusadisameva. Idhāpi tatheva satthā tassa nivesanaṃ gantvā taṃ āgantvā vanditvā nisinnaṃ “kiṃ, āvuso, socasī”ti pucchitvā “āma, bhante[V 3.0140], puttassa me matakālato paṭṭhāya socāmī”ti vutte “āvuso, bhijjanadhammaṃ nāma bhijjati, nassanadhammaṃ nāma nassati, tañca kho na ekasmiṃyeva kule, nāpi ekasmiññeva gāme, atha kho aparimāṇesu cakkavāḷesu tīsu bhavesu amaraṇadhammo [M 3.0151] nāma natthi, tabbhāveneva ṭhātuṃ samattho ekasaṅkhāropi sassato nāma natthi, sabbe sattā maraṇadhammā, sabbe saṅkhārā bhijjanadhammā, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi putte mate ‘maraṇadhammaṃ mataṃ, nassanadhammaṃ naṭṭha’nti na sociṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Like a snake its worn-out skin”—this the Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke concerning a householder whose son had died. The story is similar to the story of the one whose wife died and the story of the one whose father died. Here too, the Teacher went to his house and, to the householder who had come, paid homage, and sat down, He asked: “Friend, are you grieving?” When he replied, “Yes, Bhante, I have been grieving since the time of my son’s death,” the Teacher said: “Friend, that which is of a nature to break, breaks; that which is of a nature to perish, perishes. And that happens not only in one family, nor in only one village. Rather, throughout the countless world-systems and the three realms of existence, there is no such thing as being of a non-mortal nature. There is not even a single conditioned thing that is eternal and able to remain in that same state. All beings are subject to death; all conditioned things are subject to breaking. Even the wise of old, when a son died, did not grieve, reflecting: ‘What is subject to death has died; what is subject to perishing has perished.’” Having said this, and being requested by him, He brought forth the past.
