Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ dvāragāmake brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā kasikammena jīvikaṃ kappesi. Tassa putto ca dhītā cāti dve dārakā ahesuṃ. So puttassa vayappattassa samānakulato kumārikaṃ āharitvā adāsi, iti te dāsiyā saddhiṃ cha janā ahesuṃ – bodhisatto, bhariyā, putto, dhītā, suṇisā, dāsīti. Te samaggā sammodamānā piyasaṃvāsā ahesuṃ. Bodhisatto sesānaṃ pañcannaṃ evaṃ ovādaṃ deti “tumhe yathāladdhaniyāmeneva dānaṃ detha, sīlaṃ rakkhatha, uposathakammaṃ karotha, maraṇassatiṃ bhāvetha, tumhākaṃ maraṇabhāvaṃ sallakkhetha, imesañhi sattānaṃ maraṇaṃ dhuvaṃ, jīvitaṃ addhuvaṃ, sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā khayavayadhamminova, rattiñca divā ca appamattā hothā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti ovādaṃ sampaṭicchitvā appamattā maraṇassatiṃ bhāventi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a gate-village of Benares and, having established a household, earned his living by farming. He had two children: a son and a daughter. When the son reached the proper age, he brought a young woman from a family of equal status and gave her to him. Thus there were six people including the female servant: the Bodhisatta, his wife, the son, the daughter, the daughter-in-law, and the servant. They lived in harmony and mutual joy, dwelling in affection. The Bodhisatta gave this advice to the other five: “Give alms according to what you have obtained, keep the precepts, perform the Uposatha duties, cultivate mindfulness of death, and observe your own mortal nature. For the death of these beings is certain, but life is uncertain. All conditioned things are impermanent and subject to decay and dissolution; be heedful both by night and by day.” Saying “Very well,” they accepted the advice and heedfully cultivated mindfulness of death.

Athekadivasaṃ bodhisatto puttena saddhiṃ khettaṃ [P 3.0163] gantvā kasati. Putto kacavaraṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā jhāpeti. Tassāvidūre ekasmiṃ vammike āsīviso atthi. Dhūmo tassa akkhīni pahari. So kuddho nikkhamitvā “imaṃ nissāya mayhaṃ bhaya”nti catasso dāṭhā nimujjāpento taṃ ḍaṃsi, so parivattitvā patito. Bodhisatto parivattitvā taṃ patitaṃ disvā goṇe ṭhapetvā gantvā tassa matabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ ukkhipitvā ekasmiṃ rukkhamūle nipajjāpetvā pārupitvā neva rodi na paridevi – “bhijjanadhammaṃ pana bhinnaṃ, maraṇadhammaṃ mataṃ, sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā maraṇanipphattikā”ti aniccabhāvameva sallakkhetvā kasi. So khettasamīpena gacchantaṃ ekaṃ paṭivissakaṃ purisaṃ disvā “tāta, gehaṃ gacchasī”ti pucchitvā “āmā”ti vutte tena hi amhākampi gharaṃ gantvā brāhmaṇiṃ vadeyyāsi “ajja kira pubbe viya dvinnaṃ bhattaṃ anāharitvā ekassevāhāraṃ āhareyyātha, pubbe ca ekikāva dāsī āhāraṃ āharati, ajja pana cattāropi janā suddhavatthanivatthā gandhapupphahatthā āgaccheyyāthā”ti. So “sādhū”ti gantvā brāhmaṇiyā tatheva kathesi. Kena te, tāta, imaṃ sāsanaṃ dinnanti. Brāhmaṇena[M 3.0152], ayyeti. Sā “putto me mato”ti aññāsi, kampanamattampissā nāhosi. Evaṃ subhāvitacittā suddhavatthanivatthā [V 3.0141] gandhapupphahatthā dāsiṃ pana āhāraṃ āharāpetvā sesehi saddhiṃ khettaṃ agamāsi. Ekassapi roditaṃ vā paridevitaṃ vā nāhosi.

Then one day, the Bodhisatta went to the field with his son and was plowing. The son gathered the rubbish and set it on fire. Near there, in an anthill, lived a venomous snake. The smoke struck its eyes. Being angry, it came out and, thinking “Because of this man there is danger to me,” bit him, sinking in its four fangs. He rolled over and fell. The Bodhisatta, seeing him roll over and fall, stopped the oxen, went to him, and realizing he was dead, lifted him up and laid him at the foot of a tree, covered him, and neither wept nor lamented. Reflecting only on impermanence— “That which is of a nature to break has broken; that which is of a nature to die has died; all conditioned things are impermanent and result in death”—he continued plowing. Seeing a neighbor passing near the field, he asked, “Friend, are you going home?” and when he said “Yes,” he said, “Then go to our house and tell the brahmin woman: ‘Today, instead of bringing food for two as before, bring food for only one; and whereas before only the servant girl brought the food, today let all four of you come, dressed in clean clothes and carrying perfumes and flowers.’” The man said “Very well,” went, and spoke to the brahmin woman exactly as told. She asked, “Friend, who gave you this message?” “The brahmin, lady.” She knew, “My son is dead,” yet not even a tremor arose in her. Thus, with a well-cultivated mind, dressed in clean clothes and carrying perfumes and flowers, she had the servant bring the food and went to the field with the others. Not for even one of them was there weeping or lamentation.

Bodhisatto puttassa nipannachāyāyameva nisīditvā bhuñji. Bhuttāvasāne sabbepi dārūni uddharitvā taṃ citakaṃ āropetvā gandhapupphehi pūjetvā jhāpesuṃ. Ekassa ca ekabindupi assu nāhosi, sabbepi subhāvitamaraṇassatino honti. Tesaṃ sīlatejena sakkassa āsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So “ko nu kho maṃ ṭhānā [P 3.0164] cāvetukāmo”ti upadhārento tesaṃ guṇatejena uṇhabhāvaṃ ñatvā pasannamānaso hutvā “mayā etesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā sīhanādaṃ nadāpetvā sīhanādapariyosāne etesaṃ nivesanaṃ sattaratanaparipuṇṇaṃ katvā āgantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vegena tattha gantvā āḷāhanapasse ṭhito “tāta, kiṃ karothā”ti āha. “Ekaṃ manussaṃ jhāpema, sāmī”ti. “Na tumhe manussaṃ jhāpessatha, ekaṃ pana migaṃ māretvā pacatha maññe”ti. “Natthetaṃ sāmi, manussameva jhāpemā”ti. “Tena hi verimanusso vo bhavissatī”ti. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “orasaputto no sāmi, na veriko”ti āha. “Tena hi vo appiyaputto bhavissatī”ti? “Ativiya piyaputto, sāmī”ti. “Atha kasmā na rodasī”ti? So arodanakāraṇaṃ kathento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta sat down to eat in the very shade where his son was lying. After finishing the meal, they all gathered wood, placed the body on the pyre, honored it with fragrant flowers, and cremated him. Not a single tear fell from any of them, for all were well-practiced in the mindfulness of death. Through the power of their virtue, Sakka's throne grew hot. Wondering, "Who seeks to dislodge me from my seat?" he observed the power of their virtue and, with a joyful heart, thought, "I must go to them, have them utter a lion's roar, and at the conclusion of that lion's roar, fill their dwelling with the seven treasures before returning." Quickly he went there and stood near the cremation site, asking, "Dear ones, what are you doing?" "We are cremating a human, lord." "You are not cremating a human; rather, I think you have killed a deer and are roasting it." "No, lord, we are indeed cremating a human." "Then he must have been your enemy." Then the Bodhisatta replied, "He was my own son, lord, not an enemy." "Then he must have been a son you did not love?" "He was a dearly loved son, lord." "Then why do you not weep?" Explaining the reason for not weeping, the Bodhisatta first spoke this verse:

19.

19.

“Uragova tacaṃ jiṇṇaṃ, hitvā gacchati saṃ tanuṃ;

Evaṃ sarīre nibbhoge, pete kālakate sati.

Just as a snake leaves its worn-out skin and goes its way, so too does one leave his own body; thus when the body is devoid of use and the departed has passed away,

20.

20.

“Ḍayhamāno na jānāti, ñātīnaṃ paridevitaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, gato so tassa yā gatī”ti.

While being cremated, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives; therefore, I do not grieve for him, for he has gone to his own destination.

Tattha saṃ tanunti attano sarīraṃ. Nibbhogeti jīvitindriyassa abhāvena bhogarahite. Peteti paralokaṃ paṭigate. Kālakateti katakāle, mateti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sāmi, mama putto yathā nāma urago jiṇṇatacaṃ nicchinditvā anoloketvā anapekkho chaḍḍetvā [M 3.0153] gaccheyya, evaṃ attano sarīraṃ chaḍḍetvā gacchati, tassa jīvitindriyarahite sarīre evaṃ nibbhoge tasmiñca me putte pete puna paṭigate maraṇakālaṃ katvā ṭhite sati ko kāruññena vā paridevena vā attho. Ayañhi yathā sūlehi vijjhitvā ḍayhamāno sukhadukkhaṃ na jānāti, evaṃ ñātīnaṃ paridevitampi na jānāti, tena kāraṇenāhaṃ etaṃ na socāmi. Yā tassa attano gati, taṃ so gatoti.

There, 'saṃ tanu' means 'his own body.' 'Nibbhoge' means 'devoid of use' because of the absence of the life faculty. 'Pete' means 'gone to the other world.' 'Kālakate' means 'having made his time,' which means 'dead.' This is what was said: 'Lord, just as a snake might shed its old skin, casting it off without looking back and without concern, and go on, so too my son abandons his own body and departs. When his body is thus devoid of use, without the life faculty, and when my son has departed and passed away, having reached his time of death, what purpose is served by compassion or lamentation? For just as one being burned does not feel pleasure or pain, he also does not know the lamentation of his relatives. For this reason, I do not grieve for him. Whatever his own destination was, to that he has gone.'

Sakko [V 3.0142][P 3.0165] bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā brāhmaṇiṃ pucchi “amma, tuyhaṃ so kiṃ hotī”ti? “Dasa māse kucchinā pariharitvā thaññaṃ pāyetvā hatthapāde saṇṭhapetvā vaḍḍhitaputto me, sāmī”ti. “Amma, pitā tāva purisabhāvena mā rodatu, mātu hadayaṃ pana mudukaṃ hoti, tvaṃ kasmā na rodasī”ti? Sā arodanakāraṇaṃ kathentī –

Hearing the Bodhisatta’s words, Sakka asked the brahmin woman, "Mother, what is he to you?" "He is my son, lord, whom I carried in my womb for ten months, nursed, and whose limbs I tended as he grew." "Mother, let the father, being a man, not weep, but a mother’s heart is tender. Why do you not weep?" She, explaining the reason for not weeping, said:

21.

21.

“Anavhito tato āgā, ananuññāto ito gato;

Yathāgato tathā gato, tattha kā paridevanā.

Uncalled he came from there, and without permission he went from here; as he came, so he went—what lamentation can there be in that?

22.

22.

“Ḍayhamāno na jānāti, ñātīnaṃ paridevitaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, gato so tassa yā gatī”ti. – gāthādvayamāha –

While being cremated, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives; therefore, I do not grieve for him, for he has gone to his own destination.

Tattha anavhitoti ayaṃ tāta mayā paralokato anavhito ayācito. Āgāti amhākaṃ gehaṃ āgato. Itoti ito manussalokato gacchantopi mayā ananuññātova gato. Yathāgatoti āgacchantopi yathā attanova ruciyā āgato, gacchantopi tatheva gato. Tatthāti tasmiṃ tassa ito gamane kā paridevanā. Ḍayhamānoti gāthā vuttanayena veditabbā.

Here, 'uncalled' means 'Dear one, he was not summoned or requested by me from the other world.' 'Came' means 'he came to our home.' 'From here' means 'departing from this human world, he went without my permission.' 'As he came' means 'just as he came according to his own preference, so he went.' 'In that' means 'in that departure of his from here, what benefit is there in lamentation?' The verse beginning 'While being cremated' should be understood in the same way as previously explained.

Sakko brāhmaṇiyā kathaṃ sutvā tassa bhaginiṃ pucchi “amma, tuyhaṃ so kiṃ hotī”ti? “Bhātā me, sāmī”ti. “Amma, bhaginiyo nāma bhātūsu sinehā honti, tvaṃ kasmā na rodasī”ti? Sā arodanakāraṇaṃ kathentī –

Hearing the brahmin woman's words, Sakka asked the deceased's sister, "Mother, what was he to you?" "He was my brother, lord." "Mother, sisters are usually affectionate toward their brothers—why do you not weep?" Explaining the reason for not weeping, she said:

23.

23.

“Sace rode kisā assaṃ, tassā me kiṃ phalaṃ siyā;

Ñātimittasuhajjānaṃ, bhiyyo no aratī siyā.

If I were to weep, I would become thin; what benefit would that bring me? It would only increase the unhappiness of our relatives, friends, and well-wishers.

24.

24.

Ḍayhamāno [P 3.0166][M 3.0154] na jānāti, ñātīnaṃ paridevitaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, gato so tassa yā gatī”ti. – gāthādvayamāha –

While being cremated, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives; therefore, I do not grieve for him, for he has gone to his own destination.

Tattha saceti yadi ahaṃ bhātari mate rodeyyaṃ, kisasarīrā assaṃ. Bhātu pana me tappaccayā vuḍḍhi nāma natthīti dasseti. Tassā meti tassā mayhaṃ rodantiyā kiṃ phalaṃ ko ānisaṃso bhaveyya. Mayhaṃ avuddhi pana paññāyatīti dīpeti. Ñātimittasuhajjānanti ñātimittasuhadānaṃ[V 3.0143]. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Bhiyyo noti ye amhākaṃ ñātī ca mittā ca suhadayā ca, tesaṃ adhikatarā arati siyā.

Here, 'if' means 'if I were to weep for my dead brother, I would become thin-bodied.' She shows that no growth or benefit would come to her brother because of that. 'For me in that case' means 'what fruit or advantage would there be for me in weeping?' she indicates that only her own decline would be evident. 'For relatives, friends, and well-wishers' refers to those who are close. 'More for us' means that for those who are our relatives, friends, and dear ones, there would be even greater unhappiness.

Sakko bhaginiyā kathaṃ sutvā bhariyaṃ pucchi “amma, tuyhaṃ so kiṃ hotī”ti? “Pati me, sāmī”ti. “Itthiyo nāma patimhi mate vidhavā honti anāthā, tvaṃ kasmā na rodasī”ti. Sāpissa arodanakāraṇaṃ kathentī –

Hearing the sister’s words, Sakka asked the wife, "Mother, what was he to you?" "He was my husband, lord." "Women, when their husbands die, become widows and helpless—why do you not weep?" She also explained the reason for not weeping:

25.

25.

“Yathāpi dārako candaṃ, gacchantamanurodati;

Evaṃsampadamevetaṃ, yo petamanusocati.

Just as a child cries for the moon as it moves across the sky, so too is it for one who mourns the dead.

26.

26.

“Ḍayhamāno na jānāti, ñātīnaṃ paridevitaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, gato so tassa yā gatī”ti. – gāthādvayamāha –

While being cremated, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives; therefore, I do not grieve for him, for he has gone to his own destination.

Tassattho – yathā nāma yattha katthaci yuttāyuttaṃ labbhanīyālabbhanīyaṃ ajānanto bāladārako mātu ucchaṅge nisinno puṇṇamāsiyaṃ puṇṇaṃ candaṃ ākāse gacchantaṃ disvā “amma, candaṃ me dehi, amma, candaṃ me dehī”ti punappunaṃ rodati, evaṃsampadamevetaṃ, evaṃnipphattikameva etaṃ tassa ruṇṇaṃ hoti, yo petaṃ kālakataṃ anusocati. Itopi ca bālataraṃ. Kiṃkāraṇā? So hi vijjamānacandaṃ anurodati, mayhaṃ pana pati mato etarahi avijjamāno sūlehi vijjhitvā ḍayhamānopi na kiñci jānātīti.

The meaning is this: Just as a foolish child, not knowing what is proper or improper, what can be obtained or what cannot, sits on his mother's lap and, seeing the full moon moving in the sky on a full-moon day, cries again and again, 'Mother, give me the moon! Mother, give me the moon!', of such a nature and result is the weeping of one who mourns for the departed who has passed away. And this is even more foolish. Why? Because that child cries for a moon that actually exists. But my husband is dead and gone; even while being pierced by stakes and burned, he knows nothing.

Sakko [P 3.0167] bhariyāya vacanaṃ sutvā dāsiṃ pucchi “amma, tuyhaṃ so kiṃ hotī”ti? “Ayyo me, sāmī”ti. “Nanu tvaṃ iminā pīḷetvā pothetvā paribhuttā [M 3.0155] bhavissasi, tasmā “sumuttā aha”nti na rodasī”ti. ‘Sāmi, mā evaṃ avaca, na etaṃ etassa anucchavikaṃ, khantimettānuddayasampanno me ayyaputto, ure saṃvaḍḍhitaputto viya ahosī’ti. “Atha kasmā na rodasī”ti? Sāpissa arodanakāraṇaṃ kathentī –

Sakka, having heard the wife’s words, asked the maidservant, "Mother, what is he to you?" "He is my master, lord." "Surely, you must have been oppressed, beaten, and mistreated by him; therefore you do not weep, thinking, 'I am well freed from him.'" "Lord, do not speak thus. That is not fitting to say of him. My young master was endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion; he was like a son nurtured at my breast." "Then why do you not weep?" She then explained the reason for her not weeping:

27.

27.

“Yathāpi udakakumbho, bhinno appaṭisandhiyo;

Evaṃsampadamevetaṃ, yo petamanusocati.

Just as a water pot, once broken, cannot be joined together again, of such a nature is the state of one who mourns the dead.

28.

28.

“Ḍayhamāno [V 3.0144] na jānāti, ñātīnaṃ paridevitaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, gato so tassa yā gatī”ti. – gāthādvayamāha –

While being burned, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives; therefore, I do not grieve for him. He has gone to whatever destination was his.” — She spoke these two verses.

Tassattho – yathā nāma udakakumbho ukkhipiyamāno patitvā sattadhā bhinno puna tāni kapālāni paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapetvā saṃvidahitvā paṭipākatikaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, yo petamanusocati, tassapi etamanusocanaṃ evaṃnipphattikameva hoti, matassa puna jīvāpetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā iddhimato vā iddhānubhāvena bhinnaṃ kumbhaṃ saṃvidahitvā udakassa pūretuṃ sakkā bhaveyya, kālakato pana iddhibalenāpi na sakkā paṭipākatitaṃ kātunti. Itarā gāthā vuttatthāyeva.

The meaning is this: Just as a water pot, when lifted up and dropped, shatters into seven pieces, and even if those shards are arranged in order and carefully reassembled, it cannot be restored to its original condition—so too, the lamentation of one who mourns the dead is likewise fruitless, because it is impossible to bring the dead back to life. While one with psychic power might, by the force of that power, reassemble a broken pot and fill it with water, a person who has passed away cannot be restored to their original state even by psychic power. The other verse has the meaning already stated.

Sakko sabbesaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā pasīditvā “tumhehi appamattehi maraṇassati bhāvitā, tumhe ito paṭṭhāya sahatthena kammaṃ mā karittha, ahaṃ, sakko devarājā, ahaṃ vo gehe satta ratanāni aparimāṇāni karissāmi, tumhe dānaṃ detha[P 3.0168], sīlaṃ rakkhatha, uposathakammaṃ karotha, appamattā hothā”ti tesaṃ ovādaṃ datvā gehaṃ aparimitadhanaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

Having heard the Dhamma discourse from all of them, Sakka was pleased and said, "You have diligently cultivated mindfulness of death. From now on, do not perform labor with your own hands. I, Sakka, king of the gods, will make boundless treasures of the seven kinds appear in your house. Give alms, observe virtue, perform the Uposatha observance, and be diligent." After giving them this advice and filling their home with immeasurable wealth, he departed.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne kuṭumbiko sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā dāsī khujjuttarā ahosi, dhītā uppalavaṇṇā, putto rāhulo, mātā khemā, brāhmaṇo pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, the householder was established in the fruit of stream-entry. He identified the Jātaka thus: 'At that time, the female servant was Khujjuttarā, the daughter was Uppalavaṇṇā, the son was Rāhula, the mother was Khemā, and the brahmin was I myself.'

Uragajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Uraga Jātaka is the fourth.

[355] 5. Ghaṭajātakavaṇṇanā

[355] 5. 5. The Commentary on the Ghaṭa Jātaka

Aññe [M 3.0156] socanti rodantīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarañño ekaṃ amaccaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā kathitasadisameva. Idha pana rājā attano upakārassa amaccassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ datvā paribhedakānaṃ kathaṃ gahetvā taṃ bandhāpetvā bandhanāgāre pavesesi. So tattha nisinnova sotāpattimaggaṃ nibbattesi. Rājā tassa guṇaṃ sallakkhetvā mocāpesi. So gandhamālaṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā nisīdi. Atha naṃ satthā “anattho kira te uppanno”ti pucchitvā “āma, bhante, anatthena pana me attho āgato, sotāpattimaggo nibbatto”ti vutte “na kho, upāsaka, tvaññeva anatthena atthaṃ āhari, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi āhariṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

"Others grieve and weep"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain minister of the King of Kosala. The story is similar to that related before. Here, however, the king, having bestowed great honor upon a minister who had been of service to him, listened to the words of slanderers and had him bound and cast into prison. While sitting there, the minister attained the path of stream-entry. The king, recognizing his virtue, had him released. Taking perfumes and garlands, the minister went to the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down. Then the Teacher asked him, "Is it true that a misfortune befell you?" He replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir, but from that misfortune, a benefit came to me—the path of stream-entry was attained." The Teacher said, "Lay follower, it is not only you who has brought forth benefit from misfortune; the wise of old did so as well," and at his request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 3.0145] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, “ghaṭakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So aparena samayena takkasilāyaṃ uggahitasippo dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa antepure eko amacco dubbhi. So taṃ paccakkhato ñatvā raṭṭhā pabbājesi. Tadā sāvatthiyaṃ dhaṅkarājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi. So tassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ upaṭṭhahitvā heṭṭhā vuttanayena attano vacanaṃ gāhāpetvā bārāṇasirajjaṃ gaṇhāpesi. Sopi rajjaṃ gahetvā bodhisattaṃ saṅkhalikāhi bandhāpetvā bandhanāgāraṃ pavesesi. Bodhisatto jhānaṃ nibbattetvā [P 3.0169] ākāse pallaṅkena nisīdi, dhaṅkassa sarīre ḍāho uppajji. So gantvā bodhisattassa suvaṇṇādāsaphullapadumasassirikaṃ mukhaṃ disvā bodhisattaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. They named him Prince Ghaṭa. In time, having mastered the arts at Takkasilā, he reigned righteously. A certain minister in his court acted treacherously. Knowing this directly, the Bodhisatta banished him from the kingdom. At that time, a king named Dhaṅka was reigning in Sāvatthī. The banished minister went to him, served him, and in the manner previously described, persuaded him to seize the kingdom of Benares. Having seized the kingdom, Dhaṅka had the Bodhisatta bound with chains and cast into prison. The Bodhisatta, having attained jhāna, sat cross-legged in the air. A burning sensation arose in Dhaṅka’s body. He went and, seeing the Bodhisatta’s face, which was as resplendent as a golden mirror or a full-blown lotus, questioned him by speaking the first verse:

29.

29.

“Aññe socanti rodanti, aññe assumukhā janā;

Pasannamukhavaṇṇosi, kasmā ghaṭa na socasī”ti.

"Others grieve and weep, other people have tearful faces; your countenance is serene—why, Ghaṭa, do you not grieve?"

Tattha aññeti taṃ ṭhapetvā sesamanussā.

In this context, 'others' refers to all the remaining people except him.

Athassa bodhisatto asocanakāraṇaṃ kathento catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the Bodhisatta, explaining the reason for his not grieving to King Dhaṅka, uttered four verses:

30.

30.

“Nābbhatītaharo [M 3.0157] soko, nānāgatasukhāvaho;

Tasmā dhaṅka na socāmi, natthi soke dutīyatā.

"Sorrow does not bring back the past, nor does it bring future happiness; therefore, Dhaṅka, I do not grieve—there is no advantage in sorrow."

31.

31.

“Socaṃ paṇḍu kiso hoti, bhattañcassa na ruccati;

Amittā sumanā honti, sallaviddhassa ruppato.

"By grieving, one becomes pale and thin, and food is no longer to one's liking; enemies are gladdened when one suffers, as if pierced by a dart."

32.

32.

“Gāme vā yadi vāraññe, ninne vā yadi vā thale;

Ṭhitaṃ maṃ nāgamissati, evaṃ diṭṭhapado ahaṃ.

"Whether in a village or a forest, in a valley or on high ground, death will come to me wherever I stand; thus have I seen the state of things."

33.

33.

“Yassattā nālamekova, sabbakāmarasāharo;

Sabbāpi pathavī tassa, na sukhaṃ āvahissatī”ti.

"For one for whom his self alone, the provider of the taste of all desires, is not enough, for him even the entire earth will not bring happiness."

Tattha nābbhatītaharoti nābbhatītāhāro, ayameva vā pāṭho. Soko nāma abbhatītaṃ atikkantaṃ niruddhaṃ atthaṅgataṃ puna nāharati. Dutīyatāti sahāyatā. Atītāharaṇena vā anāgatāharaṇena [V 3.0146] vā soko nāma kassaci sahāyo na hoti, tenāpi kāraṇenāhaṃ na socāmīti vadati. Socanti socanto. Sallaviddhassa ruppatoti sokasallena viddhassa teneva ghaṭṭiyamānassa “diṭṭhā vata no paccāmittassa piṭṭhī”ti amittā sumanā hontīti attho.

Herein, 'nābbhatītaharo' means 'nābbhatītāhāro,' or this is the reading itself. Sorrow does not bring back what is past, gone beyond, ceased, or vanished. 'Dutīyatā' means companionship. Sorrow is no companion to anyone, neither by bringing back the past nor by bringing forth the future. For this reason also, he says, 'I do not grieve.' 'Socaṃ' means 'socanto' (grieving). 'Sallaviddhassa ruppato' means of one pierced by the dart of sorrow and afflicted by it; the meaning is that enemies become gladdened, thinking, 'Indeed, we have seen the back of our foe!'

Ṭhitaṃ maṃ nāgamissatīti samma dhaṅkarāja, etesu gāmādīsu yattha katthaci ṭhitaṃ maṃ paṇḍukisabhāvādikaṃ sokamūlakaṃ byasanaṃ na āgamissati. Evaṃ diṭṭhapadoti yathā taṃ byasanaṃ nāgacchati, evaṃ mayā jhānapadaṃ diṭṭhaṃ. “Aṭṭhalokadhammapada”ntipi vadantiyeva[P 3.0170]. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “na mattaṃ nāgamissatī”ti likhitaṃ, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthi. Pariyosānagāthāya icchitapatthitatthena jhānasukhasaṅkhātaṃ sabbakāmarasaṃ āharatīti sabbakāmarasāharo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yassa rañño pahāya aññasahāye attāva eko sabbakāmarasāharo nālaṃ, sabbaṃ jhānasukhasaṅkhātaṃ kāmarasaṃ āharituṃ asamattho, tassa rañño sabbāpi pathavī na sukhaṃ āvahissati. Kāmāturassa hi sukhaṃ nāma natthi, yo pana kilesadaratharahitaṃ jhānasukhaṃ āharituṃ samattho, so rājā sukhī hotīti. Yo panetāya gāthāya “yassatthā nālameko”tipi pāṭho, tassattho na dissati.

'Ṭhitaṃ maṃ nāgamissati' means: 'Friend Dhaṅka, in these villages and other places, wherever I may be, misfortune rooted in sorrow—such as becoming pale and thin—will not come upon me.' 'Evaṃ diṭṭhapado' means: 'Just as that misfortune does not come, so have I seen the path of jhāna.' Some also say it means 'the path of the eight worldly conditions.' In the Pāli canon, however, the reading is 'na mattaṃ nāgamissatī,' but that is not found in this commentary. In the final verse, 'sabbakāmarasāharo' means one who brings the taste of all desires, which is identified with the bliss of jhāna, because that is what is wished for and desired. This is what is meant: For a king for whom his self alone—having abandoned other companions—is not sufficient as the provider of the taste of all desires (that is, he is unable to bring forth the entire taste of desire which is the bliss of jhāna), for such a king, even the whole earth will not bring happiness. For one afflicted by sensual desire, there is no happiness. But a king who is able to bring forth the bliss of jhāna, which is free from the torment of defilements, is happy. As for the variant reading of this verse, 'yassatthā nālameko,' its meaning is not apparent.

Iti [M 3.0158] dhaṅko imā catasso gāthā sutvā bodhisattaṃ khamāpetvā rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā pakkāmi. Bodhisattopi rajjaṃ amaccānaṃ paṭiniyyādetvā himavantapadesaṃ gantvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus Dhaṅka, having heard these four verses, asked forgiveness of the Bodhisatta, restored the kingdom to him, and departed. The Bodhisatta, in turn, handed over the kingdom to his ministers, went to the Himalayan region, and went forth into the ascetic life. With his jhāna undiminished, he was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dhaṅkarājā ānando ahosi, ghaṭarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Dhaṅka was Ānanda, and King Ghaṭa was I myself."

Ghaṭajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Ghaṭa Jātaka is the fifth.

[356] 6. Koraṇḍiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[356] 6. The Commentary on the Koraṇḍiya Jātaka

Eko araññeti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dhammasenāpatiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Thero kira āgatāgatānaṃ dussīlānaṃ migaluddakamacchabandhādīnaṃ diṭṭhadiṭṭhānaññeva “sīlaṃ gaṇhatha, sīlaṃ gaṇhathā”ti sīlaṃ deti. Te there garubhāvena tassa kathaṃ bhindituṃ asakkontā sīlaṃ gaṇhanti, gahetvā ca pana na rakkhanti, attano attano kammameva karonti. Thero saddhivihārike āmantetvā [V 3.0147] “āvuso, ime manussā mama santike sīlaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, gaṇhitvā ca pana na rakkhantī”ti [P 3.0171] āha. “Bhante, tumhe etesaṃ aruciyā sīlaṃ detha, ete tumhākaṃ kathaṃ bhindituṃ asakkontā gaṇhanti, tumhe ito paṭṭhāya evarūpānaṃ sīlaṃ mā adatthā”ti. Thero anattamano ahosi. Taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, sāriputtatthero kira diṭṭhadiṭṭhānaññeva sīlaṃ detī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa diṭṭhadiṭṭhānaṃ ayācantānaññeva sīlaṃ detī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Eko araññeti—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the General of the Dhamma. The Elder, it seems, would give precepts to those who came, to the unvirtuous ones such as hunters and fishers, to whomever he saw, saying, "Take the precepts, take the precepts!" Unable to break his word out of respect for the Elder, they would take the precepts but then not keep them, continuing with their own actions. The Elder called his co-residents and said, "Friends, these people took the precepts in my presence but do not keep them." They replied, "Venerable sir, you give them the precepts against their inclination. Unable to break your word, they take them. From now on, do not give precepts to such people." The Elder was displeased. Hearing of this, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, it seems the Venerable Sāriputta gives precepts to just anyone he sees." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the topic of your discussion now, as you are gathered here?" When told, he said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past too, he gave precepts to those he saw, without their asking." And he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa jeṭṭhantevāsiko koraṇḍiyo nāma ahosi. Tadā so ācariyo diṭṭhadiṭṭhānaṃ kevaṭṭādīnaṃ ayācantānaññeva “sīlaṃ gaṇhatha, sīlaṃ gaṇhathā”ti sīlaṃ deti. Te gahetvāpi na rakkhanti [M 3.0159] ācariyo tamatthaṃ antevāsikānaṃ ārocesi. Antevāsikā “bhante, tumhe etesaṃ aruciyā sīlaṃ detha, tasmā bhindanti, ito dāni paṭṭhāya yācantānaññeva dadeyyātha, mā ayācantāna”nti vadiṃsu. So vippaṭisārī ahosi, evaṃ santepi diṭṭhadiṭṭhānaṃ sīlaṃ detiyeva.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. Coming of age, he became the foremost pupil of the world-renowned teacher at Takkasilā, and was named Koraṇḍiya. At that time, the teacher would give precepts to any fishermen and such he saw, without their asking, saying, "Take the precepts, take the precepts!" They would take them but not keep them. The teacher informed his pupils of this matter. The pupils said, "Venerable sir, you give them precepts against their inclination, so they break them. From now on, you should give precepts only to those who ask, not to those who do not ask." He was remorseful, yet still gave precepts to whomever he saw.

Athekadivasaṃ ekasmā gāmā manussā āgantvā brāhmaṇavācanakatthāya ācariyaṃ nimantayiṃsu. So koraṇḍiyamāṇavaṃ pakkositvā “tāta, ahaṃ na gacchāmi, tvaṃ ime pañcasate māṇave gahetvā tattha gantvā vācanakāni sampaṭicchitvā amhākaṃ dinnakoṭṭhāsaṃ āharā”ti pesesi. So gantvā paṭinivattanto antarāmagge ekaṃ kandaraṃ disvā cintesi “amhākaṃ ācariyo diṭṭhadiṭṭhānaṃ ayācantānaññeva sīlaṃ deti, ito dāni paṭṭhāya yathā yācantānaññeva deti, tathā naṃ karissāmī”ti. So tesu māṇavesu [P 3.0172] sukhanisinnesu uṭṭhāya mahantaṃ mahantaṃ selaṃ ukkhipitvā kandarāyaṃ khipi, punappunaṃ khipiyeva. Atha naṃ te māṇavā uṭṭhāya “ācariya, kiṃ karosī”ti āhaṃsu. So na kiñci kathesi, te vegena gantvā ācariyassa ārocesuṃ. Ācariyo āgantvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

One day, people from a village came and invited the teacher for a Brahminical recitation. He summoned the student Koraṇḍiya and said, 'My son, I will not go. You take these five hundred students and go for the recitation; receive the offerings provided for the recitation and bring back our share.' He sent him off. On his way back, seeing a chasm along the way, he thought, 'Our teacher gives the precepts to anyone he sees, even to those who do not ask. From now on, I will make it so that he gives them only to those who ask.' While those students were sitting comfortably, he stood up, lifted large stones, and threw them into the chasm, again and again. Then those students stood up and asked him, 'Teacher, what are you doing?' He said nothing. They went quickly and reported it to the teacher. The teacher came and, wishing to converse with him, spoke the first verse:

34.

34.

“Eko araññe girikandarāyaṃ, paggayha paggayha silaṃ pavecchasi;

Punappunaṃ santaramānarūpo, koraṇḍiya ko nu tava yidhattho”ti.

'Alone in the forest, in a mountain chasm, you lift up stones and throw them; repeatedly, and with a hurried appearance, Koraṇḍiya, what is your purpose here?'

Tattha ko nu tava yidhatthoti ko nu tava idha kandarāyaṃ silākhipanena attho.

In this context, 'what is your purpose here?' means 'what is your purpose in throwing stones into this chasm?'

So [V 3.0148] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā ācariyaṃ pabodhetukāmo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, wishing to enlighten the teacher, he spoke the second verse:

35.

35.

“Ahañhimaṃ sāgarasevitantaṃ, samaṃ karissāmi yathāpi pāṇi;

Vikiriya sānūni ca pabbatāni ca, tasmā silaṃ dariyā pakkhipāmī”ti.

'I will make this earth, bounded by the oceans, as level as the palm of my hand; having scattered the ridges and the mountains, therefore I throw stones into the chasm.'

Tattha [M 3.0160] ahañhimanti ahañhi imaṃ mahāpathaviṃ. Sāgarasevitantanti sāgarehi sevitaṃ cāturantaṃ. Yathāpi pāṇīti hatthatalaṃ viya samaṃ karissāmi. Vikiriyāti vikiritvā. Sānūni ca pabbatāni cāti paṃsupabbate ca silāpabbate ca.

In this context, 'ahañhi imaṃ' means 'I indeed [shall make] this great earth.' 'Sāgarasevitantaṃ' means 'bounded by the four oceans.' 'Yathāpi pāṇi' means 'I will make it level like the palm of the hand.' 'Vikiriya' means 'having scattered.' 'Sānūni ca pabbatāni ca' means 'both earthen mountains and rocky mountains.'

Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard that, the brahmin spoke the third verse:

36.

36.

“Nayimaṃ mahiṃ arahati pāṇikappaṃ, samaṃ manusso karaṇāya meko;

Maññāmimaññeva dariṃ jigīsaṃ, koraṇḍiya hāhasi jīvaloka”nti.

'It is not fitting for a single man to make this earth level like the palm of a hand; I think that in seeking to fill this very chasm, Koraṇḍiya, you will leave the world of the living.'

Tattha [P 3.0173] karaṇāya mekoti karaṇāya eko kātuṃ na sakkotīti dīpeti. Maññāmimaññeva dariṃ jigīsanti ahaṃ maññāmi tiṭṭhatu pathavī, imaññeva ekaṃ dariṃ jigīsaṃ pūraṇatthāya vāyamanto silā pariyesanto upāyaṃ vicinantova tvaṃ imaṃ jīvalokaṃ hāhasi jahissasi, marissasīti attho.

Here, 'a single person for doing' means 'it shows that a single person is not able to do it.' 'I think that in striving to conquer this very chasm' means 'I think, "Let the earth be"; while you are striving to conquer this single chasm for the purpose of filling it, seeking stones, and searching for a means, you will abandon this world of the living—that is, you will die.' That is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā māṇavo catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the student spoke the fourth verse:

37.

37.

“Sace ayaṃ bhūtadharaṃ na sakkā, samaṃ manusso karaṇāya meko;

Evameva tvaṃ brahme ime manusse, nānādiṭṭhike nānayissasi te”ti.

'If this earth cannot be made level by a single man, so too, O brahmin, you will not lead these men of diverse views.'

Tassattho – sace ayaṃ eko manusso imaṃ bhūtadharaṃ pathaviṃ samaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā na samattho, evameva tvaṃ ime dussīlamanusse nānādiṭṭhike nānayissasi, te evaṃ “sīlaṃ gaṇhatha, sīlaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadanto attano vasaṃ na ānayissasi, paṇḍitapurisāyeva hi pāṇātipātaṃ “akusala”nti garahanti. Saṃsāramocakādayo panettha kusalasaññino, te tvaṃ kathaṃ ānayissasi, tasmā diṭṭhadiṭṭhānaṃ sīlaṃ adatvā yācantānaññeva dehīti.

Its meaning is: If a single man is not able, not capable, of making this earth level, likewise, you will not lead these immoral men of diverse views. By saying to them, 'Take the precepts, take the precepts,' you will not bring them under your control; for indeed, only wise men condemn the destruction of life as 'unwholesome.' But those like the Saṃsāramocakas here perceive it as wholesome; how will you lead them? Therefore, without giving the precepts to anyone you see, give them only to those who ask.

Taṃ [V 3.0149] sutvā ācariyo “yuttaṃ vadati koraṇḍiyo, idāni na evarūpaṃ karissāmī”ti attano viraddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the teacher said, 'Koraṇḍiya speaks what is right; now I will not do such a thing.' Realizing his own error, he spoke the fifth verse:

38.

38.

“Saṃkhittarūpena [M 3.0161] bhavaṃ mamatthaṃ, akkhāsi koraṇḍiya evametaṃ;

Yathā na sakkā pathavī samāyaṃ, kattuṃ manussena tathā manussā”ti.

'In a concise manner, sir, you have explained the matter to me, Koraṇḍiya; it is just so: Just as the earth cannot be made level by a man, so too with humans.'

Tattha samāyanti samaṃ ayaṃ. Evaṃ ācariyo māṇavassa thutiṃ akāsi, sopi naṃ bodhetvā sayaṃ gharaṃ nesi.

In this context, 'samāyaṃ' means 'this level.' Thus the teacher praised the student; and he, having enlightened him, led him home.

Satthā [P 3.0174] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā brāhmaṇo sāriputto ahosi, koraṇḍiyamāṇavo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the brahmin was Sāriputta, and the student Koraṇḍiya was I myself.'

Koraṇḍiyajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Explanation of the Koraṇḍiya Jātaka, the sixth.

[357] 7. Laṭukikajātakavaṇṇanā

[357] 7. The Explanation of the Laṭukika Jātaka

Vandāmi taṃ kuñjara saṭṭhihāyananti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi divase bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto kakkhaḷo pharuso sāhasiko, sattesu karuṇāmattampissa natthī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa nikkaruṇoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'I bow to you, O elephant of sixty years'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, with reference to Devadatta. For one day, in the Dhamma hall, the monks raised a discussion: 'Friends, Devadatta is harsh, rough, and violent; he does not have even a trace of compassion for beings.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now sitting together?' When they said, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, not only now, but in the past also he was merciless,' and he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto hatthiyoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto pāsādiko mahākāyo asītisahassavāraṇaparivāro yūthapati hutvā himavantapadese vihāsi. Tadā ekā laṭukikā sakuṇikā hatthīnaṃ vicaraṇaṭṭhāne aṇḍāni nikkhipi, tāni pariṇatāni bhinditvā sakuṇapotakā nikkhamiṃsu. Tesu aviruḷhapakkhesu uppatituṃ asakkontesuyeva mahāsatto asītisahassavāraṇaparivuto gocarāya caranto taṃ padesaṃ patto. Taṃ disvā laṭukikā cintesi “ayaṃ hatthirājā mama potake madditvā māressati, handa naṃ puttakānaṃ parittāṇatthāya dhammikārakkhaṃ yācāmī”ti. Sā [M 3.0162] ubho pakkhe ekato katvā tassa purato ṭhatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in an elephant's womb. Having reached adulthood, he was pleasing and large-bodied, and having become the leader of a herd surrounded by eighty thousand elephants, he lived in the Himalayan region. At that time, a quail bird laid her eggs in the elephants' roaming ground. When they matured, the shells broke and the young chicks emerged. While their wings were not yet grown and they were unable to fly, the Great Being, surrounded by eighty thousand elephants, arrived at that place while wandering for food. Seeing him, the quail thought, 'This elephant king will crush and kill my young chicks. Now, for the sake of protecting my children, I will beg him for a righteous protection.' She folded both wings together, stood before him, and spoke the first verse:

39.

39.

“Vandāmi [V 3.0150] taṃ kuñjara saṭṭhihāyanaṃ, āraññakaṃ yūthapatiṃ yasassiṃ;

Pakkhehi taṃ pañjalikaṃ karomi, mā me vadhī puttake dubbalāyā”ti.

'I bow to you, O elephant of sixty years, forest-dweller, renowned herd leader; with my wings I make a gesture of reverence to you—do not kill the children of me, a weak one.'

Tattha [P 3.0175] saṭṭhihāyananti saṭṭhivassakāle hāyanabalaṃ. Yasassinti parivārasampannaṃ. Pakkhehi taṃ pañcalikaṃ karomīti ahaṃ pakkhehi taṃ añjalikaṃ karomīti attho.

In this context, 'saṭṭhihāyanaṃ' means the strength that diminishes at the age of sixty years. 'Yasassiṃ' means endowed with a retinue. 'Pakkhehi taṃ pañjalikaṃ karomi' means 'I make a gesture of reverence to you with my wings.'

Mahāsatto “mā cintayi laṭukike, ahaṃ te puttake rakkhissāmī”ti sakuṇapotakānaṃ upari ṭhatvā asītiyā hatthisahassesu gatesu laṭukikaṃ āmantetvā “laṭukike amhākaṃ pacchato eko ekacāriko hatthī āgacchati, so amhākaṃ vacanaṃ na karissati, tasmiṃ āgate tampi yācitvā puttakānaṃ sotthibhāvaṃ kareyyāsī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Sāpi tassa paccuggamanaṃ katvā ubhohi pakkhehi añjaliṃ katvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The Great Being said, 'Do not worry, quail hen, I will protect your young ones.' Standing over the young birds, when the eighty thousand elephants had passed, he called to the quail hen and said, 'Quail hen, a solitary elephant is coming behind us. He will not do our bidding. When he arrives, you should beg him too for the welfare of your young ones.' Having said this, he departed. She, having gone to meet him and having made a gesture of reverence with both wings, spoke the second verse:

40.

40.

“Vandāmi taṃ kuñjara ekacāriṃ, āraññakaṃ pabbatasānugocaraṃ;

Pakkhehi taṃ pañjalikaṃ karomi, mā me vadhī puttake dubbalāyā”ti.

'I bow to you, O elephant, solitary wanderer, forest dweller, frequenting the mountain slopes; with my wings, I make a gesture of reverence to you—do not kill the young of me, a weak one.'

Tattha pabbatasānugocaranti ghanaselapabbatesu ca paṃsupabbatesu ca gocaraṃ gaṇhantaṃ.

Herein, 'pabbatasānugocaraṃ' means one who forages on both solid rock mountains and earthen mountains.

So tassā vacanaṃ sutvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing her words, he spoke the third verse:

41.

41.

“Vadhissāmi te laṭukike puttakāni, kiṃ me tuvaṃ kāhasi dubbalāsi;

Sataṃ sahassānipi tādisīnaṃ, vāmena pādena papothayeyya”nti.

'I will kill your young ones, O quail hen. What will you, a weak one, do to me? Even a hundred thousand such as you, I could crush with my left foot.'

Tattha [M 3.0163] vadhissāmi teti tvaṃ kasmā mama vicaraṇamagge puttakāni ṭhapesi, yasmā ṭhapesi, tasmā vadhissāmi te puttakānīti vadati. Kiṃ me tuvaṃ kāhasīti mayhaṃ mahāthāmassa tvaṃ dubbalā kiṃ karissasi. Papothayeyyanti ahaṃ tādisānaṃ laṭukikānaṃ satasahassampi vāmena pādena sañcuṇṇeyyaṃ, dakkhiṇapādena pana kathāva natthīti.

Herein, 'I will kill your young ones' means he is saying, 'Why did you place your young ones on my path? Because you placed them there, I will kill your young ones.' 'What will you do to me?' means 'What will you, a weak one, do to me who possesses great strength?' 'I could crush' means 'I could pulverize even a hundred thousand such quail hens with my left foot; there is no need to even speak of the right foot.'

Evañca [P 3.0176] pana vatvā so tassā puttake pādena sañcuṇṇetvā muttena pavāhetvā nadantova pakkāmi. Laṭukikā rukkhasākhāya nilīyitvā “idāni tāva vāraṇa nadanto gacchasi, katipāheneva [V 3.0151] me kiriyaṃ passissasi, kāyabalato ñāṇabalassa mahantabhāvaṃ na jānāsi, hotu, jānāpessāmi na”nti taṃ santajjayamānāva catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

And having said this, he crushed her young ones with his foot, washed them away with his urine, and departed roaring. The quail hen, having perched on a tree branch, thought, 'Now, O elephant, you go roaring, but in a few days you will see my deed. You do not know the greatness of the strength of wisdom over the strength of body. So be it, I will make you know it.' Threatening him, she spoke the fourth verse:

42.

42.

“Na heva sabbattha balena kiccaṃ, balañhi bālassa vadhāya hoti;

Karissāmi te nāgarājā anatthaṃ, yo me vadhī puttake dubbalāyā”ti.

'Not in every case is a matter settled by strength, for the strength of a fool leads to his own destruction. I will bring you to ruin, O king of elephants, you who killed the young of me, a weak one.'

Tattha balenāti kāyabalena. Anatthanti avuḍḍhiṃ. Yo meti yo tvaṃ mama dubbalāya puttake vadhī ghātesi.

Herein, 'by strength' means by bodily strength. 'Ruin' means non-prosperity. 'You who killed my young' means 'you who killed the young of me, a weak one.'

Sā evaṃ vatvā katipāhaṃ ekaṃ kākaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā tena tuṭṭhena “kiṃ te karomī”ti vuttā “sāmi, aññaṃ me kātabbaṃ natthi, ekassa pana ekacārikavāraṇassa tuṇḍena paharitvā tumhehi akkhīni bhinnāni paccāsīsāmī”ti āha. Sā tena “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitā ekaṃ nīlamakkhikaṃ upaṭṭhahi. Tāyapi “kiṃ te, karomī”ti vuttā “iminā kākena ekacārikavāraṇassa akkhīsu bhinnesu tumhehi tattha āsāṭikaṃ pātetuṃ icchāmī”ti vatvā tāyapi “sādhū”ti vutte ekaṃ maṇḍūkaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā tena “kiṃ te, karomī”ti vuttā “yadā ekacārikavāraṇo andho hutvā pānīyaṃ pariyesati, tadā pabbatamatthake ṭhito saddaṃ katvā tasmiṃ pabbatamatthakaṃ abhiruhante otaritvā papāte saddaṃ kareyyātha, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ santikā ettakaṃ paccāsīsāmī”ti āha. Sopi tassā vacanaṃ “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi.

Having spoken thus, for some days she attended to a crow. Pleased, the crow asked, "What can I do for you?" She replied, "Master, I have no other task, but I desire that you strike a certain solitary wandering elephant in the eyes with your beak and pierce them." The crow agreed, saying, "Very well." Then she attended to a blue fly. When asked, "What can I do for you?" she said, "When this crow pierces the solitary wandering elephant's eyes, I desire that you drop maggots there." The fly also agreed, saying, "Very well." Next, she attended to a frog. When asked, "What can I do for you?" she said, "When the solitary wandering elephant, now blind, searches for water, you should stand on a mountaintop and make a sound. When he climbs up to that mountaintop, descend and make a sound at the precipice. This much I desire from you." He too agreed to her words, saying, "Very well."

Athekadivasaṃ [M 3.0164] kāko vāraṇassa dvepi [P 3.0177] akkhīni tuṇḍena bhindi, nīlamakkhikā āsāṭikaṃ pātesi. So puḷavehi khajjanto vedanāppatto pipāsābhibhūto pānīyaṃ pariyesamāno vicari. Tasmiṃ kāle maṇḍūko pabbatamatthake ṭhatvā saddamakāsi. Vāraṇo “ettha pānīyaṃ bhavissatī”ti pabbatamatthakaṃ abhiruhi. Atha maṇḍūko otaritvā papāte ṭhatvā saddamakāsi. Vāraṇo “ettha pānīyaṃ bhavissatī”ti papātābhimukho gacchanto parigaḷitvā pabbatapāde patitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Laṭukikā tassa matabhāvaṃ ñatvā “diṭṭhā me paccāmittassa piṭṭhī”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭhā tassa khandhe caṅkamitvā yathākammaṃ gatā.

Then one day, the crow pierced both eyes of the elephant with its beak, and the blue fly dropped maggots there. Being eaten by the maggots, afflicted by pain, and overcome by thirst, he wandered about searching for water. At that time, the frog, standing on a mountaintop, made a sound. The elephant thought, "There must be water here," and climbed to the mountaintop. Then the frog descended and, standing at the precipice, made a sound. The elephant, thinking, "There must be water here," went toward the precipice, slipped, fell to the foot of the mountain, and met his end. The quail, knowing that he was dead, thought, "I have seen the back of my enemy!" and, joyful and glad, she walked to and fro upon his back and then went according to her kamma.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, kenaci saddhiṃ veraṃ nāma kātabbaṃ, evaṃ balasampannampi vāraṇaṃ ime cattāro janā ekato hutvā vāraṇassa jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesu”nti –

The Teacher said, "Monks, one should not harbor enmity toward anyone. Even this elephant, so endowed with strength, was brought to the destruction of life by these four individuals acting together."

43.

43.

“Kākañca [V 3.0152] passa laṭukikaṃ, maṇḍūkaṃ nīlamakkhikaṃ;

Ete nāgaṃ aghātesuṃ, passa verassa verinaṃ;

Tasmā hi veraṃ na kayirātha, appiyenapi kenacī”ti. –

“Behold the crow and the quail, the frog and the blue fly; these slew the elephant. Behold the outcome of enmity for the hostile! Therefore, one should not create enmity, not even with anyone who is disliked.”

Imaṃ abhisambuddhagāthaṃ vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi.

Having spoken this verse of the Perfectly Enlightened One, he made the connection in the Jātaka.

Tattha passāti aniyāmitālapanametaṃ, bhikkhū pana sandhāya vuttattā passatha bhikkhaveti vuttaṃ hoti. Eteti ete cattāro ekato hutvā. Aghātesunti taṃ vadhiṃsu. Passa verassa verinanti passatha verikānaṃ verassa gatinti attho.

Herein, 'passa' (behold) is an indefinite address, but since it was said with reference to the monks, it is said, 'Behold, O monks.' 'Ete' (these) means these four, having come together. 'Aghātesuṃ' (they slew) means they killed him. 'Passa verassa verinaṃ' (Behold the outcome of enmity for the hostile) means, 'Behold the course of enmity for those who harbor it.'

Tadā ekacārikahatthī devadatto ahosi, yūthapati pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the solitary elephant was Devadatta, but the leader of the herd was I myself.

Laṭukikajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Laṭukika Jātaka, the Seventh.

[358] 8. Cūḷadhammapālajātakavaṇṇanā

[358] 8. The Commentary on the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka

Ahameva [M 3.0165] dūsiyā bhūnahatāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Aññesu jātakesu devadatto bodhisattassa tāsamattampi kātuṃ nāsakkhi, imasmiṃ [P 3.0178] pana cūḷadhammapālajātake bodhisattassa sattamāsikakāle hatthapāde ca sīsañca chedāpetvā asimālakaṃ nāma kāresi. Daddarajātake (jā. 1.2.43-44) gīvaṃ gahetvā māretvā uddhane maṃsaṃ pacitvā khādi. Khantīvādījātake (jā. 1.4.49 ādayo) dvīhipi kasāhi pahārasahassehi tāḷāpetvā hatthapāde ca kaṇṇanāsañca chedāpetvā jaṭāsu gahetvā kaḍḍhāpetvā uttānakaṃ nipajjāpetvā ure pādena paharitvā gato. Bodhisatto taṃ divasaṃyeva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Cūḷanandiyajātakepi (jā. 1.2.143-144) mahākapijātakepi (jā. 1.7.83 ādayo) māresiyeva. Evameva so dīgharattaṃ vadhāya parisakkanto buddhakālepi parisakkiyeva. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ – “āvuso, devadatto buddhānaṃ māraṇatthameva upāyaṃ karoti, ‘sammāsambuddhaṃ mārāpessāmī’ti dhanuggahe payojesi, silaṃ pavijjhi, nāḷāgiriṃ vissajjāpesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā ‘kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkiyeva, idāni pana tāsamattampi kātuṃ na sakkoti[V 3.0153], pubbe maṃ cūḷadhammapālakumārakāle attano puttaṃ samānaṃ jīvatakkhayaṃ pāpetvā asimālakaṃ kāresī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, spoke this story, which begins with 'I alone am the guilty one, whose prosperity is destroyed,' concerning Devadatta’s efforts to slay him. In other birth stories, Devadatta was not even able to frighten the Bodhisatta; but in this Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka, when the Bodhisatta was seven months old, he had his hands, feet, and head cut off and made what is called a 'sword-garland.' In the Daddara Jātaka (Jātaka 1.2.43-44), he seized him by the neck, killed him, cooked his flesh on a hearth, and ate it. In the Khantivādī Jātaka (Jātaka 1.4.49 ff.), he had him beaten with a thousand blows from two whips, then had his hands, feet, ears, and nose cut off. He grabbed him by his matted hair, dragged him along, made him lie face-up, struck his chest with his foot, and departed. The Bodhisatta met his demise that very day. Similarly, in the Cūḷanandiya Jātaka (Jātaka 1.2.143-144) and the Mahākapi Jātaka (Jātaka 1.7.83 ff.), he slew him as well. Thus, for a long time, he made repeated attempts to slay him, and even in the time of the Buddha, he continued his efforts. Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, Devadatta is devising ways only to slay the Buddha. He hired archers, thinking, 'I will have the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One slain,' hurled a rock, and set loose Nāḷāgiri." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past also he made repeated attempts to slay me. But now he cannot even frighten me. In the past, when I was Prince Cūḷadhammapāla, though I was his own son, he brought about my demise and had a 'sword-garland' made of me." And so he recounted the past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ mahāpatāpe nāma rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā candādeviyā kucchimhi nibbatti, “dhammapālo”tissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tamenaṃ sattamāsikakāle mātā gandhodakena nhāpetvā alaṅkaritvā kīḷāpayamānā nisīdi. Rājā tassā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Sā puttaṃ kīḷāpayamānā puttasinehena samappitā hutvā rājānaṃ passitvāpi na uṭṭhahi. So cintesi “ayaṃ idāneva tāva puttaṃ nissāya mānaṃ karoti, maṃ kismiñci na maññati, putte pana vaḍḍhante mayi ‘manusso’tipi saññaṃ na karissati, idāneva naṃ ghātessāmī”ti. So nivattitvā rājāsane nisīditvā “attano vidhānena [M 3.0166] āgacchatū”ti coraghātakaṃ pakkosāpesi. So kāsāyavatthanivattho [P 3.0179] rattamālādharo pharasuṃ aṃse ṭhapetvā upadhānaghaṭikaṃ hatthapādaṭhapanadaṇḍakañca ādāya āgantvā rājānaṃ vanditvā “kiṃ karomi, devā”ti aṭṭhāsi. Deviyā sirigabbhaṃ gantvā dhammapālaṃ ānehīti. Devīpi rañño kujjhitvā nivattanabhāvaṃ ñatvā bodhisattaṃ ure nipajjāpetvā rodamānā nisīdi. Coraghātako gantvā taṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ hatthena paharitvā hatthato kumāraṃ acchinditvā ādāya rañño santikaṃ āgantvā “kiṃ karomi, devā”ti āha. Rājā ekaṃ phalakaṃ āharāpetvā purato nikkhipāpetvā “idha naṃ nipajjāpehī”ti āha. So tathā akāsi.

In the past, in Benares, when a king named Mahāpatāpa was reigning, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen, Candādevī. They gave him the name 'Dhammapāla.' When he was seven months old, his mother bathed him with fragrant water, adorned him, and sat playing with him. The king went to her chamber. She, playing with her son and overcome with affection for him, did not rise even upon seeing the king. He thought, "Even now, on account of her son, she acts with pride and does not regard me at all. When the boy grows up, she will not even consider me a human being. I shall slay him right now." He turned back, sat on the royal throne, and had the executioner summoned, saying, "Let him come with his own equipment." The executioner, clad in a dyed garment, wearing a red garland, with an axe on his shoulder, and carrying a chopping block and a board for placing the hands and feet, arrived, paid homage to the king, and stood asking, "What shall I do, Sire?" The king said, "Go to the queen’s inner chamber and bring Dhammapāla." The queen, knowing that the king had turned back in anger, laid the Bodhisatta on her breast and sat weeping. The executioner went, struck her on the back with his hand, snatched the prince from her arms, and, bringing him to the king, asked, "What shall I do, Sire?" The king had a wooden plank brought and placed before him, saying, "Lay him down here." The executioner did so.

Candādevī puttassa pacchatova paridevamānā āgacchi. Puna coraghātako “kiṃ karomī, devā”ti āha. Dhammapālassa hatthe chindāti. Candādevī “mahārāja, mama putto sattamāsiko bālako na kiñci jānāti, natthetassa doso, doso pana honto mayi bhaveyya, tasmā mayhaṃ hatthe chedāpehī”ti imamatthaṃ pakāsentī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Queen Candā came lamenting after her son. Again, the executioner asked, "What shall I do, Sire?" The king said, "Cut off Dhammapāla's hands." Queen Candā, declaring this matter, spoke the first verse, saying, "O great king, my son is a seven-month-old child who knows nothing. There is no fault in him. If there were a fault, it would be in me. Therefore, have my hands cut off instead."

44.

44.

“Ahameva dūsiyā bhūnahatā, rañño mahāpatāpassa;

Etaṃ muñcatu dhammapālaṃ, hatthe me deva chedehī”ti.

“I alone am the guilty one, whose prosperity is destroyed, in relation to King Mahāpatāpa. Let this Dhammapāla be released; cut off my hands, O king.”

Tattha dūsiyāti dūsikā, tumhe disvā anuṭṭhahamānā dosakārikāti attho. “Dūsikā”tipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Bhūnahatāti hatabhūnā, hatavuḍḍhīti attho. Raññoti idaṃ “dūsiyā”ti padena yojetabbaṃ. Ahaṃ rañño mahāpatāpassa aparādhakārikā, nāyaṃ kumāro, tasmā [V 3.0154] niraparādhaṃ etaṃ bālakaṃ muñcatu dhammapālaṃ, sacepi hatthe chedāpetukāmo, dosakārikāya hatthe me, deva, chedehīti ayamettha attho.

Here, 'dūsiyā' means 'dūsikā,' which is to say, 'an offender who, seeing you, does not rise.' The reading 'dūsikā' is also found, with the same meaning. 'Bhūnahatā' means 'hatabhūnā,' which means 'one whose prosperity is destroyed.' The word 'rañño' (of the king) should be connected with the word 'dūsiyā.' 'I am the offender against King Mahāpatāpa, not this prince. Therefore, let this innocent child, Dhammapāla, be released. If you wish to have hands cut off, O king, cut off my hands, the hands of the offender'—this is the meaning here.

Rājā coraghātakaṃ olokesi. “Kiṃ karomi, devā”ti? “Papañcaṃ akatvā hatthe chedā”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe coraghātako tikhiṇapharasuṃ gahetvā kumārassa taruṇavaṃsakaḷīre viya [P 3.0180] dve hatthe chindi. So dvīsu hatthesu chijjamānesu neva rodi na paridevi, khantiñca mettañca purecārikaṃ katvā adhivāsesi. Candā pana devī chinnahatthakoṭiṃ gahetvā ucchaṅge katvā [M 3.0167] lohitalittā paridevamānā vicari. Puna coraghātako “kiṃ karomi, devā”ti pucchi. “Dvepi pāde chindā”ti. Taṃ sutvā candādevī dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The king looked at the executioner. "What shall I do, Sire?" "Without delay, cut off his hands." At that moment, the executioner took a sharp axe and cut off both hands of the prince, as if they were young bamboo shoots. As his two hands were being severed, he neither cried nor lamented, but endured with patience and loving-kindness, making them his priority. Meanwhile, Queen Candā took the severed ends of the hands, placed them in her lap, and wandered about lamenting, smeared with blood. Again, the executioner asked, "What shall I do, Sire?" The king replied, "Cut off both his feet." Hearing this, Queen Candā spoke the second verse:

45.

45.

“Ahameva dūsiyā bhūnahatā, rañño mahāpatāpassa;

Etaṃ muñcatu dhammapālaṃ, pāde me deva chedehī”ti.

“I alone am the guilty one, whose prosperity is destroyed, in relation to King Mahāpatāpa. Let this Dhammapāla be released; cut off my feet, O king!”

Tattha adhippāyo vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

In this context, the intention is to be understood in the same manner as already stated.

Rājāpi puna coraghātakaṃ āṇāpesi. So ubhopi pāde chindi. Candādevī pādakoṭimpi gahetvā ucchaṅge katvā lohitalittā paridevamānā “sāmi mahāpatāpa, chinnahatthapādā nāma dārakā mātarā posetabbā honti, ahaṃ bhatiṃ katvā mama puttakaṃ posessāmi, dehi me eta”nti āha. Coraghātako “kiṃ deva katā rājāṇā, niṭṭhitaṃ mama kicca”nti pucchi. “Na tāva niṭṭhita”nti. “Atha kiṃ karomi, devā”ti? “Sīsamassa chindā”ti. Taṃ sutvā candādevī tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The king again ordered the executioner. He cut off both his feet. Candādevī, taking even the severed tips of the feet and placing them on her lap, covered in blood, lamented, saying, "My lord Mahāpatāpa, children whose hands and feet have been severed must be raised by their mothers. I will work for hire and raise my little son. Give him to me." The executioner asked, "Lord, is the king's command carried out? Is my task finished?" "It is not yet finished," replied the king. "Then what shall I do, lord?" "Cut off his head!" Hearing that, Candādevī spoke a third verse:

46.

46.

“Ahameva dūsiyā bhūnahatā, rañño mahāpatāpassa;

Etaṃ muñcatu dhammapālaṃ, sīsaṃ me deva chedehī”ti.

“I alone am the guilty one, the one who has ruined herself, in relation to King Mahāpatāpa. Let this Dhammapāla be released; cut off my head, O lord!”

Vatvā ca pana attano sīsaṃ upanesi.

Having spoken thus, she then offered her own head.

Puna coraghātako “kiṃ karomi, devā”ti pucchi. “Sīsamassa chindā”ti. So sīsaṃ chinditvā “katā, deva, rājāṇā”ti pucchi. “Na tāva katā”ti. “Atha kiṃ karomi, devā”ti? “Asituṇḍena naṃ sampaṭicchitvā asimālakaṃ nāma karohī”ti. So tassa kaḷevaraṃ [V 3.0155] ākāse khipitvā asituṇḍena sampaṭicchitvā asimālakaṃ nāma katvā mahātale vippakiri. Candādevī bodhisattassa maṃse ucchaṅge katvā mahātale rodamānā paridevamānā imā gāthā abhāsi –

Again, the executioner asked, "What shall I do, lord?" "Cut off his head!" He cut off the head and asked, "Lord, has the king's command been carried out?" "Not yet carried out," was the reply. "Then what shall I do, lord?" "Catch his body with the sword's point and make a 'sword garland'!" He threw the body into the air, caught it with the sword's point, made a 'sword garland,' and scattered it on the palace floor. Candādevī, placing the Bodhisatta's flesh on her lap, weeping and wailing on the palace floor, spoke these verses:

47.

47.

“Na [P 3.0181] hi nūnimassa rañño, mittāmaccā ca vijjare suhadā;

Ye na vadanti rājānaṃ, mā ghātayi orasaṃ puttaṃ.

"Surely, this king has no friends or ministers who are well-meaning, who do not tell the king, 'Do not kill your own legitimate son!'"

48.

48.

“Na hi nūnimassa rañño, ñātī mittā ca vijjare suhadā;

Ye na vadanti rājānaṃ, mā ghātayi atrajaṃ putta”nti.

"Surely, this king has no relatives or friends who are well-meaning, who do not tell the king, 'Do not kill your own son!'"

Tattha [M 3.0168] mittāmaccā ca vijjare suhadāti nūna imassa rañño daḷhamittā vā sabbakiccesu sahabhāvino amaccā vā muduhadayatāya suhadā vā keci na vijjanti. Ye na vadantīti ye adhunā āgantvā “attano piyaputtaṃ mā ghātayī”ti na vadanti, imaṃ rājānaṃ paṭisedhenti, te natthiyevāti maññe. Dutiyagāthāyaṃ ñātīti ñātakā.

Here, 'friends and ministers who are well-meaning' means: Surely, for this king, there exist no steadfast friends, or ministers who are companions in all his affairs, or any who are well-meaning due to their gentle hearts. 'Who do not speak' means: I think that those who would now come and restrain this king by saying, 'Do not kill your own beloved son,' simply do not exist. In the second verse, 'relatives' means kinsmen.

Imā pana dve gāthā vatvā candādevī ubhohi hatthehi hadayamaṃsaṃ dhārayamānā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken these two verses, Candādevī, holding the flesh of her son's heart in both hands, spoke a third verse:

49.

49.

“Candanasārānulittā, bāhā chijjanti dhammapālassa;

Dāyādassa pathabyā, pāṇā me deva rujjhantī”ti.

"The arms of Dhammapāla, the heir to the earth, anointed with sandalwood essence, are being cut off; O king, my life is failing."

Tattha dāyādassa pathabyāti pitusantakāya cāturantāya pathaviyā dāyādassa lohitacandanasārānulittā hatthā chijjanti, pādā chijjanti, sīsañca chijjati, asimālakopi kato, tava vaṃsaṃ pacchinditvā gatosi dānīti evamādīni vilapanti evamāha. Pāṇā me deva rujjhantīti deva, mayhampi imaṃ sokaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkontiyā jīvitaṃ rujjhatīti.

Here, 'of the heir to the earth' means: the hands of the heir to his father's four-continent earth, smeared with the essence of red sandalwood, are being cut off; his feet are being cut off; his head is being cut off; and even a sword-garland has been made. Lamenting such things as, 'Now you are lost, having cut off your lineage,' she spoke thus. 'O king, my life is failing' means: 'O king, for me too, unable to bear this sorrow, life is failing.'

Tassā evaṃ paridevamānāya eva ḍayhamāne veḷuvane veḷu viya hadayaṃ phali, sā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā. Rājāpi pallaṅke ṭhātuṃ asakkonto mahātale pati, padaratalaṃ dvidhā bhijji, so tatopi bhūmiyaṃ pati. Tato catunahutādhikadviyojanasatasahassabahalāpi ghanapathavī tassa [V 3.0156] aguṇaṃ dhāretuṃ asakkontī bhijjitvā vivaramadāsi, avīcito jālā uṭṭhāya kuladattikena kambalena parikkhipantī viya [P 3.0182] taṃ gahetvā avīcimhi khipi. Candāya ca bodhisattassa ca amaccā sarīrakiccaṃ kariṃsu.

While she was lamenting thus, her heart burst like a bamboo in a burning bamboo grove, and right there she met her end. The king, too, unable to remain on his couch, fell to the floor. The floorboards split in two, and from there he fell to the ground. Then, even the solid earth, two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, unable to bear his wickedness, split open and gave a fissure. From Avīci, flames rose up as if encircling him with a traditional red blanket, seized him, and hurled him into Avīci. The ministers performed the funeral rites for Candādevī and the Bodhisatta.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā devadatto ahosi, candādevī mahāpajāpatigotamī, dhammapālakumāro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the Jātaka thus: "At that time, the king was Devadatta, Candādevī was Mahāpajāpati Gotamī, and Prince Dhammapāla was I myself."

Cūḷadhammapālajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka: The Eighth.

[359] 9. Suvaṇṇamigajātakavaṇṇanā

[359] 9. The Commentary on the Suvaṇṇamiga Jātaka

Vikkama [M 3.0169] re haripādāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sāvatthiyaṃ ekaṃ kuladhītaraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā kira sāvatthiyaṃ dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ upaṭṭhākakulassa dhītā saddhā pasannā buddhamāmakā dhammamāmakā saṅghamāmakā ācārasampannā paṇḍitā dānādipuññābhiratā. Taṃ aññaṃ sāvatthiyameva samānajātikaṃ micchādiṭṭhikakulaṃ vāresi. Athassā mātāpitaro “amhākaṃ dhītā saddhā pasannā tīṇi ratanāni mamāyati dānādipuññābhiratā, tumhe micchādiṭṭhikā imissāpi yathāruciyā dānaṃ vā dātuṃ dhammaṃ vā sotuṃ vihāraṃ vā gantuṃ sīlaṃ vā rakkhituṃ uposathakammaṃ vā kātuṃ na dassatha, na mayaṃ tumhākaṃ dema, attanā sadisaṃ micchādiṭṭhikakulāva kumārikaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āhaṃsu. Te tehi paṭikkhittā “tumhākaṃ dhītā amhākaṃ gharaṃ gantvā yathādhippāyena sabbametaṃ karotu, mayaṃ na vāressāma, detha no eta”nti vatvā “tena hi gaṇhathā”ti vuttā bhaddakena nakkhattena maṅgalaṃ katvā taṃ attano gharaṃ nayiṃsu. Sā vattācārasampannā patidevatā ahosi, sassusasurasāmikavattāni katāneva honti.

“Vikkama re haripādā” – this the Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke in Sāvatthī concerning a certain daughter of a good family. She, it seems, was the daughter of a family in Sāvatthī that supported the two chief disciples. She was faithful, devoted, a cherisher of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, virtuous in conduct, wise, and delighted in meritorious deeds such as giving. Another family of the same caste in Sāvatthī sought her hand, a family holding wrong views. Then her parents said, "Our daughter is faithful and devoted, cherishing the Three Jewels, and delighted in meritorious deeds like giving. But you, holding wrong views, will not allow her to give alms as she pleases, to listen to the Dhamma, to visit a monastery, to observe precepts, or to keep the Uposatha. We will not give her to you. Take a girl from a family like your own, holding wrong views." Rejected by them, the family said, "Let your daughter come to our house and do all this as she wishes. We will not prevent her. Give her to us." When told, "Very well, take her," they performed an auspicious ceremony under a favorable constellation and brought her to their home. She, being perfect in customs and conduct, was devoted to her husband as if to a deity. She always fulfilled her duties toward her mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband.

Sā ekadivasaṃ sāmikaṃ āha – “icchāmahaṃ, ayyaputta, amhākaṃ kulūpakattherānaṃ dānaṃ dātu”nti. Sādhu, bhadde, yathājjhāsayena dānaṃ dehīti. Sā there nimantāpetvā mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ katvā paṇītabhojanaṃ bhojetvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā “bhante, imaṃ kulaṃ micchādiṭṭhikaṃ assaddhaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇaṃ na jānāti, sādhu, ayyā, yāva imaṃ kulaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇaṃ jānāti, tāva idheva bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. Therā adhivāsetvā tattha nibaddhaṃ bhuñjanti. Puna sāmikaṃ āha “ayyaputta, therā [P 3.0183] idha nibaddhaṃ āgacchanti, kiṃkāraṇā tumhe na passathā”ti. “Sādhu, passissāmī”ti. Sā punadivase therānaṃ bhattakiccapariyosāne tassa ārocesi[V 3.0157]. So upasaṅkamitvā therehi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Athassa dhammasenāpati dhammakathaṃ kathesi. So therassa dhammakathāya ca iriyāpathesu ca pasīditvā tato paṭṭhāya therānaṃ āsanaṃ paññapeti, pānīyaṃ parissāveti, antarābhatte dhammakathaṃ suṇāti, tassa aparabhāge micchādiṭṭhi bhijji.

One day, she said to her husband, "Dear husband, I wish to give alms to the elders who are the patrons of our family." "Good, my dear, give alms according to your desire," he replied. She invited the elders, showed them great honor, served them excellent food, and then sat to one side. "Venerable sirs, this family holds wrong views, lacks faith, and does not understand the virtues of the Triple Gem. It would be good if the venerable ones accepted alms right here until this family comes to know the virtues of the Triple Gem," she said. The elders consented and began regularly eating there. Later, she said to her husband, "Dear husband, the elders come here regularly. Why do you not see them?" "Very well, I will see them," he replied. The next day, after the elders' meal was finished, she informed him. He approached, exchanged greetings with the elders, and sat to one side. Then, the General of the Dhamma delivered a discourse to him. Pleased by the elder’s discourse and his deportment, from that day onward, he prepared seats for the elders, filtered drinking water for them, and listened to Dhamma talks between meals; in due course, his wrong views were shattered.

Athekadivasaṃ [M 3.0170] thero dvinnampi dhammakathaṃ kathento saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ubhopi jayampatikā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya tassa mātāpitaro ādiṃ katvā antamaso dāsakammakarāpi sabbe micchādiṭṭhiṃ bhinditvā buddhadhammasaṅghamāmakāyeva jātā. Athekadivasaṃ dārikā sāmikaṃ āha – “ayyaputta, kiṃ me gharāvāsena, icchāmahaṃ pabbajitu”nti. So “sādhu bhadde, ahampi pabbajissāmī”ti mahantena parivārena taṃ bhikkhunupassayaṃ netvā pabbājetvā sayampi satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Taṃ satthā pabbājesi. Ubhopi vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā na cirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asukā nāma daharabhikkhunī attano ceva paccayā jātā sāmikassa ca, attanāpi pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patvā tampi pāpesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva tāva esā sāmikaṃ rāgapāsā mocesi, pubbepesā porāṇakapaṇḍite pana maraṇapāsā mocesī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then one day, the elder, while giving a Dhamma talk to both of them, revealed the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the discourse on the truths, both husband and wife became established in the fruit of stream-entry. From that time onward, starting with his parents and extending even to the servants and laborers, all abandoned wrong views and became devoted followers of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha. Then one day, the young woman said to her husband, "Dear husband, what use is household life to me? I wish to go forth." He replied, "Very well, my dear, I too shall go forth." With a large retinue, he led her to the nuns' residence, had her ordained, and then approached the Teacher himself to request ordination. The Teacher ordained him. Both developed insight and before long attained arahantship. Then one day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, such-and-such a young nun brought about her own benefit and that of her husband as well; having gone forth herself and attained arahantship, she then led him to it as well." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing now?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, it is not only now that she freed her husband from the snare of lust. In the past, too, she freed wise ones of old from the snare of death." Having said this, he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto migayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto abhirūpo ahosi pāsādiko dassanīyo suvaṇṇavaṇṇo lākhārasaparikammakatehi [P 3.0184] viya hatthapādehi rajatadāmasadisehi visāṇehi maṇiguḷikapaṭibhāgehi akkhīhi rattakambalageṇḍusadisena mukhena samannāgato. Bhariyāpissa taruṇamigī abhirūpā ahosi dassanīyā. Te samaggavāsaṃ vasiṃsu, asītisahassacitramigā bodhisattaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Tadā luddakā migavīthīsu pāse oḍḍesuṃ. Athekadivasaṃ bodhisatto migānaṃ purato gacchanto pāde pāsena bajjhitvā “chindissāmi na”nti ākaḍḍhi, cammaṃ chijji, puna ākaḍḍhantassa maṃsaṃ chijji, puna nhāru chijji, pāso aṭṭhimāhacca aṭṭhāsi. So pāsaṃ chindituṃ asakkonto maraṇabhayatajjito baddharavaṃ ravi. Taṃ sutvā bhīto migagaṇo palāyi. Bhariyā panassa palāyitvā migānaṃ antare olokentī taṃ adisvā “idaṃ bhayaṃ mayhaṃ piyasāmikassa uppannaṃ bhavissatī”ti vegena tassa santikaṃ gantvā assumukhī rodamānā “sāmi[M 3.0171], tvaṃ mahabbalo, kiṃ [V 3.0158] etaṃ pāsaṃ sandhāretuṃ na sakkhissasi, vegaṃ janetvā chindāhi na”nti tassa ussāhaṃ janentī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a deer. Having reached maturity, he was beautiful, splendid, and lovely to behold, with a golden hue, his feet as if adorned with red lac, his antlers resembling silver garlands, his eyes like jeweled beads, and his mouth like a ball of red wool. His wife, a young doe, was also beautiful and lovely. They lived together in harmony, and eighty thousand dappled deer attended upon the Bodhisatta. At that time, hunters set snares along the deer trails. One day, as the Bodhisatta was going before the deer, his foot was caught in a snare. Thinking, "I will break it!" he pulled, but the skin tore. Pulling again, the flesh tore. Pulling once more, the sinew tore. The snare struck the bone and held fast. Unable to break the snare and terrified by the fear of death, he let out a loud cry. Hearing this, the herd of deer fled in fear. But his wife, after fleeing, looked among the deer and, not seeing him, thought, "This danger must have befallen my beloved husband." Quickly returning to him, her face wet with tears, weeping, she said, "Lord, you are so strong. Are you not able to break this snare? Summon your strength and break it!" Encouraging him, she spoke the first verse:

50.

50.

“Vikkama re haripāda, vikkama re mahāmiga;

Chinda vārattikaṃ pāsaṃ, nāhaṃ ekā vane rame”ti.

“Strive, O golden-footed one, strive, O great deer! Break the leather snare. I will not delight alone in the forest.”

Tattha vikkamāti parakkama, ākaḍḍhāti attho. Reti āmantane nipāto. Haripādāti suvaṇṇapāda. Sakalasarīrampi tassa suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ, ayaṃ pana gāravenevamāha. Nāhaṃ ekāti ahaṃ tayā vinā ekikā vane na ramissāmi, tiṇodakaṃ pana aggahetvā sussitvā marissāmīti dasseti.

In this context, 'strive' (vikkama) means to exert oneself, to pull. 'Re' is a vocative particle. 'Golden-footed' (haripāda) means golden feet. His entire body was golden in color, but she said this out of respect. 'I will not be alone' (nāhaṃ ekā) means 'I will not delight in the forest alone without you; indeed, without taking grass or water, I will wither and die'—this is what is shown.

Taṃ [P 3.0185] sutvā migo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the deer spoke the second verse:

51.

51.

“Vikkamāmi na pāremi, bhūmiṃ sumbhāmi vegasā;

Daḷho vārattiko pāso, pādaṃ me parikantatī”ti.

“I strive, but I cannot succeed; I strike the ground with force. The strong leather snare cuts all around my foot.”

Tattha vikkamāmīti bhadde, ahaṃ vīriyaṃ karomi. Na pāremīti pāsaṃ chindituṃ pana na sakkomīti attho. Bhūmiṃ sumbhāmīti api nāma chijjeyyāti pādenāpi bhūmiṃ paharāmi. Vegasāti vegena. Parikantatīti cammādīni chindanto samantā kantatīti.

In this context, 'I strive' (vikkamāmī) means, 'Good lady, I am making an effort.' 'I cannot succeed' (na pāremi) means, 'I cannot break the snare,' that is, I am unable. 'I strike the ground' (bhūmiṃ sumbhāmi) means 'in the hope that it might break,' so I strike the ground even with my foot. 'With force' (vegasā) means with speed. 'It cuts all around' (parikantati) means it cuts all around, cutting through the skin and so forth.

Atha naṃ migī “mā bhāyi, sāmi, ahaṃ attano balena luddakaṃ yācitvā tava jīvitaṃ āharissāmi. Sace yācanāya na sakkhissāmi, mama jīvitampi datvā tava jīvitaṃ āharissāmī”ti mahāsattaṃ assāsetvā lohitalittaṃ bodhisattaṃ pariggahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Luddakopi asiñca sattiñca gahetvā kappuṭṭhānaggi viya āgacchati. Sā taṃ disvā “sāmi, luddako āgacchati, ahaṃ attano balaṃ karissāmi, tvaṃ mā bhāyī”ti migaṃ assāsetvā luddakassa paṭipathaṃ gantvā paṭikkamitvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā taṃ vanditvā “sāmi, mama sāmiko suvaṇṇavaṇṇo sīlācārasampanno, asītisahassānaṃ migānaṃ rājā”ti bodhisattassa guṇaṃ kathetvā migarāje ṭhiteyeva attano vadhaṃ yācantī tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the doe said to him, “Do not fear, my lord. I will do what I can to beg the hunter for your life. If I cannot succeed by begging, I will give my own life to obtain yours.” Having comforted the Great Being, she stood supporting the blood-stained Bodhisatta against her own body. The hunter, grasping his sword and spear, approached like the fire at the end of an aeon. Seeing him, she said, “My lord, the hunter is coming. I will do my best—do not be afraid.” Comforting the deer, she went to meet the hunter, then stepped back and stood to one side. Bowing to him, she said, “Sir, my husband, who is golden in color, is endowed with virtue and good conduct, and is the king of eighty thousand deer.” Having spoken of the Bodhisatta's virtues, while the deer king stood there, she begged for her own death and spoke the third verse:—

52.

52.

“Attharassu [V 3.0159] palāsāni, asiṃ nibbāha luddaka;

Paṭhamaṃ maṃ vadhitvāna, hana pacchā mahāmiga”nti.

“Spread out the leaves, hunter, draw your sword; First strike me down, then slay the great deer.”

Tattha [M 3.0172] palāsānīti maṃsaṭṭhapanatthaṃ palāsapaṇṇāni attharassu. Asiṃ nibbāhāti asiṃ kosato nīhara.

Here, 'leaves' (palāsāni) means 'spread out palāsa leaves for the purpose of placing the meat.' 'Draw the sword' (asiṃ nibbāha) means 'draw the sword from its sheath.'

Taṃ sutvā luddako “manussabhūtā tāva sāmikassa atthāya attano jīvitaṃ na pariccajanti, ayaṃ tiracchānagatā jīvitaṃ pariccajati, manussabhāsāya ca madhurena sarena [P 3.0186] katheti, ajja imissā ca patino cassā jīvitaṃ dassāmī”ti pasannacitto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the hunter thought: “Even human women do not sacrifice their lives for the sake of their husbands, yet this animal is sacrificing her life. And she speaks in the sweet voice of human speech. Today, I will grant both her and her husband their lives.” With a pleased heart, he spoke the fourth verse:

53.

53.

“Na me sutaṃ vā diṭṭhaṃ vā, bhāsantiṃ mānusiṃ migiṃ;

Tvañca bhadde sukhī hohi, eso cāpi mahāmigo”ti.

“Never have I heard or seen a doe speaking with a human voice; May you be happy, good lady, and this great deer as well.”

Tattha sutaṃ vā diṭṭhaṃ vāti mayā ito pubbe evarūpaṃ diṭṭhaṃ vā sutaṃ vā natthi. Bhāsantiṃ mānusiṃ miginti ahañhi ito pubbe mānusiṃ vācaṃ bhāsantiṃ migiṃ neva addasaṃ na assosiṃ. Yesaṃ pana “na me sutā vā diṭṭhā vā, bhāsantī mānusī migī”ti pāḷi, tesaṃ yathāpāḷimeva attho dissati. Bhaddeti bhaddake paṇḍike upāyakusale. Iti taṃ ālapitvā puna “tvañca eso cāpi mahāmigoti dvepi janā sukhī niddukkhā hothā”ti taṃ samassāsetvā luddako bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā vāsiyā cammapāsaṃ chinditvā pāde laggapāsakaṃ saṇikaṃ nīharitvā nhārunā nhāruṃ, maṃsena maṃsaṃ, cammena cammaṃ paṭipāṭetvā pādaṃ hatthena parimajji.
