Taṅkhaṇaññeva mahāsattassa pūritapāramitānubhāvena luddakassa ca mettacittānubhāvena migiyā ca mettadhammānubhāvena nhārumaṃsacammāni nhārumaṃsacammehi ghaṭayiṃsu. Bodhisatto pana sukhī niddukkho aṭṭhāsi.

Here, 'heard or seen' (sutaṃ vā diṭṭhaṃ vā) means 'before this, I have neither seen nor heard anything of this kind.' 'A doe speaking with a human voice' (bhāsantiṃ mānusiṃ migiṃ) means 'indeed, before this, I have neither seen nor heard a doe speaking human speech.' For those who have the Pāli reading 'na me sutā vā diṭṭhā vā, bhāsantī mānusī migī', the meaning is evident from the text itself. 'Good lady' (bhadde) means 'good one,' 'wise one,' and 'skilled in means.' Having addressed her thus, he then comforted her by saying, “May both of you, you and this great deer, be happy and free from suffering.” The hunter, approaching the Bodhisatta, cut the leather snare with his adze, gently removed the noose clinging to the foot, joined sinew to sinew, flesh to flesh, and skin to skin, and then stroked the foot with his hand. At that very moment, by the power of the Great Being's fulfilled perfections, by the power of the hunter's mind of loving-kindness, and by the power of the doe's nature of guarding her friend, the sinews, flesh, and skin were joined together. The Bodhisatta then stood, happy and free from suffering.

Migī bodhisattaṃ sukhitaṃ disvā somanassajātā luddakassa anumodanaṃ karontī pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing the Bodhisatta happy, the doe, filled with joy, wished to express her gratitude to the hunter and spoke the fifth verse:—

54.

54.

“Evaṃ luddaka nandassu, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Yathāhamajja nandāmi, muttaṃ disvā mahāmiga”nti.

“Thus rejoice, hunter, with all your kin; As I rejoice today, having seen the great deer freed.”

Tattha [V 3.0160] luddakāti dāruṇakammakiriyāya laddhanāmavasena ālapati.

Here, 'hunter' (luddaka) is an address using the name he has acquired through his cruel deeds.

Bodhisatto “ayaṃ luddo mayhaṃ avassayo jāto, mayāpissa avassayeneva bhavituṃ vaṭatī”ti [P 3.0187] gocarabhūmiyaṃ diṭṭhaṃ ekaṃ maṇikkhandhaṃ tassa datvā [M 3.0173] “samma, ito paṭṭhāya pāṇātipātādīni mā kari, iminā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā dārake posento dānasīlādīni puññāni karohī”ti tassovādaṃ datvā araññaṃ pāvisi.

The Bodhisatta thought, “This hunter has become my refuge; it is fitting that I, too, should be his refuge.” Seeing a mass of jewels in the grazing ground, he gave it to him, saying, “Friend, from now on, do not engage in killing living beings and other such acts. With this jewel, establish your family, and while raising your children, perform meritorious deeds such as generosity and observing moral precepts.” Having given him this advice, he entered the forest.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā luddako channo ahosi, migī daharabhikkhunī, migarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the hunter was Channa, the doe was the young bhikkhunī, and the deer-king was indeed myself.”

Suvaṇṇamigajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Suvaṇṇamiga Jātaka, the ninth.

[360] 10. Suyonandījātakavaṇṇanā

[360] 10. The Commentary on the Suyonandī Jātaka

Vāti gandho timirānanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “sacca”nti vutte “kiṃ disvā”ti vatvā “alaṅkatamātugāma”nti vutte “mātugāmo nāmesa bhikkhu na sakkā rakkhituṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitā supaṇṇabhavane katvā rakkhantāpi rakkhituṃ nāsakkhiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“The scent of the Timira trees blows...” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a discontented monk. Indeed, the Teacher asked him, “Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?” When the monk replied, “It is true,” the Teacher asked, “Having seen what?” The monk answered, “An adorned woman.” The Teacher then said, “Monk, a woman is not easy to guard. Even wise men of old, having kept a woman in the realm of the Supaṇṇas and guarding her, were not able to guard her.” Being entreated by him, the Teacher then related a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ tambarājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi. Tassa suyonandī nāma aggamahesī ahosi uttamarūpadharā. Tadā bodhisatto supaṇṇayoniyaṃ nibbatti, tasmiṃ kāle nāgadīpo sedumadīpo nāma ahosi. Bodhisatto tasmiṃ dīpe supaṇṇabhavane vasati. So bārāṇasiṃ gantvā tambarājena saddhiṃ māṇavakavesena jūtaṃ kīḷati. Tassa rūpasampattiṃ disvā paricārikā “amhākaṃ raññā saddhiṃ evarūpo nāma māṇavako jūtaṃ kīḷatī”ti suyonandiyā ārocesuṃ. Sā sutvā taṃ daṭṭhukāmā hutvā ekadivasaṃ alaṅkaritvā jūtamaṇḍalaṃ āgantvā paricārikānaṃ [P 3.0188] antare ṭhitā naṃ olokesi. Sopi deviṃ olokesi. Dvepi aññamaññaṃ paṭibaddhacittā ahesuṃ. Supaṇṇarājā attano ānubhāvena nagare vātaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi, gehapatanabhayena rājanivesanā manussā nikkhamiṃsu. So attano ānubhāvena andhakāraṃ katvā deviṃ [V 3.0161] gahetvā ākāsena āgantvā nāgadīpe attano bhavanaṃ pāvisi [M 3.0174] suyonandiyā gataṭṭhānaṃ jānantā nāma nāhesuṃ. So tāya saddhiṃ abhiramamāno gantvā raññā saddhiṃ jūtaṃ kīḷati.

In the past, in Benares, a king named Tamba ruled the kingdom. His chief queen, named Suyonandī, was of supreme beauty. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a Garuḍa womb; during that time, Nāgadīpa was called Sedumadīpa. The Bodhisatta lived in a Garuḍa palace on that island. He went to Benares and played dice with King Tamba in the guise of a young man. Seeing his splendid appearance, the attendants reported to Queen Suyonandī, "A young man of such appearance plays dice with our king." Hearing this, she desired to see him and, having adorned herself one day, came to the dice hall and stood among the attendants, gazing at him. He too looked at the queen. Both became mutually infatuated. The Garuḍa king, by his power, stirred up a wind in the city, and fearing their houses would collapse, the people fled the royal residence. He then created darkness with his power, took the queen, and flew through the sky to his palace on Nāgadīpa. None knew where Suyonandī had gone. Enjoying himself with her, he would go and play dice with the king.

Rañño pana saggo nāma gandhabbo atthi, so deviyā gataṭṭhānaṃ ajānanto taṃ gandhabbaṃ āmantetvā “gaccha, tāta, gandhabba sabbaṃ thalajalapathaṃ anuvicaritvā deviyā gataṭṭhānaṃ passā”ti uyyojesi. So paribbayaṃ gahetvā dvāragāmato paṭṭhāya vicinanto kurukacchaṃ pāpuṇi. Tadā kurukacchavāṇijā nāvāya suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ gacchanti. So te upasaṅkamitvā “ahaṃ gandhabbo nāvāya vetanaṃ khaṇḍetvā tumhākaṃ gandhabbaṃ karissāmi, mampi nethā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti tampi āropetvā nāvaṃ vissajjesuṃ. Te sukhapayātāya nāvāya taṃ pakkositvā “gandhabbaṃ no karohī”ti āhaṃsu. “Ahaṃ ce gandhabbaṃ kareyyaṃ, mayi pana gandhabbaṃ karonte macchā calissanti, atha vo nāvo bhijjissatī”ti. “Manussamatte gandhabbaṃ karonte macchānaṃ calanaṃ nāma natthi, karohī”ti. “Tena hi mā mayhaṃ kujjhitthā”ti vīṇaṃ mucchitvā tantissarena gītassaraṃ, gītassarena tantissaraṃ anatikkamitvā gandhabbaṃ akāsi. Tena saddena sammattā hutvā macchā caliṃsu.

Now, the king had a musician named Sagga. Not knowing where the queen had gone, he summoned that musician and said, "Go, dear musician, search all land and water routes and find where the queen has gone." Then he sent him off. Taking provisions, he set out from the gate-village and, while searching, reached Kurukaccha. At that time, merchants from Kurukaccha were traveling by ship to Suvaṇṇabhūmi. He approached them and said, "I am a musician. I will play for you in exchange for passage on your ship—take me along." They agreed, "Very well," and took him aboard before setting sail. As the ship sailed smoothly, they called to him and said, "Now, play for us." He replied, "If I play, the fish will stir, and your ship will break apart." They said, "When a mere human plays, the fish do not stir—go ahead." "Then do not be angry with me," he said. Tuning his lute, matching the sound of the song to the sound of the strings and the sound of the strings to the sound of the song without overstepping, he played. At that sound, the fish, enraptured, began to stir.

Atheko makaro uppatitvā nāvāya patanto nāvaṃ bhindi. Saggo phalake nipajjitvā yathāvātaṃ gacchanto nāgadīpe supaṇṇabhavanassa nigrodharukkhassa santikaṃ pāpuṇi. Suyonandīpi devī supaṇṇarājassa jūtaṃ kīḷituṃ gatakāle vimānā otaritvā [P 3.0189] velante vicarantī saggaṃ gandhabbaṃ disvā sañjānitvā “kathaṃ āgatosī”ti pucchi. So sabbaṃ kathesi. “Tena hi mā bhāyī”ti taṃ assāsetvā bāhāhi pariggahetvā vimānaṃ āropetvā sayanapiṭṭhe nipajjāpetvā samassatthakāle dibbabhojanaṃ datvā dibbagandhodakena nhāpetvā dibbavatthehi acchādetvā dibbagandhapupphehi alaṅkaritvā puna dibbasayane nipajjāpesi. Evaṃ divasaṃ pariggahamānā supaṇṇarañño āgamanavelāya paṭicchādetvā gatakāle tena saddhiṃ kilesavasena abhirami. Tato māsaddhamāsaccayena bārāṇasivāsino vāṇijā dārudakagahaṇatthāya tasmiṃ dīpe nigrodharukkhamūlaṃ sampattā. So tehi saddhiṃ nāvaṃ abhiruyha bārāṇasiṃ [M 3.0175] gantvā rājānaṃ disvāva tassa jūtakīḷanavelāya vīṇaṃ gahetvā rañño gandhabbaṃ karonto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then a sea monster leaped up and, falling onto the boat, broke it. Sagga lay down on a plank and, carried by the wind, reached the vicinity of a banyan tree near the Garuḍa’s abode on Nāgadīpa. Meanwhile, Queen Suyonandī, when the Garuḍa king had gone to play dice, descended from her mansion and, wandering along the shore, saw Sagga the musician. Recognizing him, she asked, ‘How did you come here?’ He told her everything. ‘Then do not fear,’ she reassured him, embraced him with her arms, lifted him into the mansion, and had him lie on the bed. When he was rested, she gave him divine food, bathed him with divine scented water, clothed him in divine garments, adorned him with divine flowers, and again had him lie on a divine bed. Thus, she cared for him by day, concealing him when the Garuḍa king was about to arrive; when he had gone, she took her pleasure with him under the influence of defilement. After a month and a half had passed, merchants from Bārāṇasī came to that island to fetch wood and water and arrived at the foot of the banyan tree. He boarded their ship, went to Bārāṇasī, and upon seeing the king, took up a lute during his gambling session. Providing music for the king, he recited the first verse:

55.

55.

“Vāti gandho timirānaṃ, kusamuddo ca ghosavā;

Dūre ito suyonandī, tamba kāmā tudanti ma”nti.

‘The fragrance of the timira trees wafts, and the small ocean roars; far from here is Suyonandī. O Tamba, desires torment me.’

Tattha [V 3.0162] timirānanti timirarukkhapupphānaṃ. Taṃ kira nigrodhaṃ parivāretvā timirarukkhā atthi, te sandhāyevaṃ vadati. Kusamuddoti khuddakasamuddo. Ghosavāti mahāravo. Tasseva nigrodhassa santike samuddaṃ sandhāyevamāha. Itoti imamhā nagarā. Tambāti rājānaṃ ālapati. Atha vā tambakāmāti tambena kāmitakāmā tambakāmā nāma. Te maṃ hadaye vijjhantīti dīpeti.

There, 'timirānaṃ' refers to the flowers of the timira trees. It is said that there are timira trees surrounding that banyan tree; he speaks thus with reference to them. 'Kusamuddo' means a small ocean. 'Ghosavā' means a great sound. He said this referring to the ocean near that very banyan tree. 'Ito' means from this city. 'Tamba' is an address to the king. Alternatively, 'tambakāmā' refers to the objects of desire loved by King Tamba. This explains, 'They pierce my heart.'

Taṃ sutvā supaṇṇo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Garuḍa spoke the second verse:

56.

56.

“Kathaṃ samuddamatari, kathaṃ addakkhi sedumaṃ;

Kathaṃ tassā ca tuyhañca, ahu sagga samāgamo”ti.

‘How did you cross the ocean? How did you see Seduma? How, O Sagga, did a union occur between her and you?’

Tattha sedumanti sedumadīpaṃ.

There, 'sedumaṃ' means Seduma Island.

Tato [P 3.0190] saggo tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Then Sagga recited three verses:

57.

57.

“Kurukacchā payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Makarehi abhidā nāvā, phalakenāhamaplaviṃ.

‘Of the merchants who set out from Kurukaccha seeking wealth, their ship was broken by sea monsters; I floated on a plank.’

58.

58.

“Sā maṃ saṇhena mudunā, niccaṃ candanagandhinī;

Aṅgena uddharī bhaddā, mātā puttaṃva orasaṃ.

‘She, the auspicious one, always fragrant with sandalwood, lifted me up with her smooth and soft limbs, like a mother her own bosom-born son.’

59.

59.

“Sā maṃ annena pānena, vatthena sayanena ca;

Attanāpi ca mandakkhī, evaṃ tamba vijānahī”ti.

‘She provided me with food and drink, with clothing and bedding; and also with herself, the soft-eyed one. Thus, O Tamba, you should know.’

Tattha sā maṃ saṇhena mudunāti evaṃ phalakena tīraṃ uttiṇṇaṃ maṃ samuddatīre vicarantī sā disvā “mā bhāyī”ti saṇhena mudunā vacanena samassāsetvāti attho. Aṅgenāti bāhuyugaḷaṃ idha “aṅgenā”ti vuttaṃ. Bhaddāti dassanīyā pāsādikā. Sā maṃ annenāti sā maṃ etena annādinā [M 3.0176] santappesīti attho. Attanāpi cāti na kevalaṃ annādīheva, attanāpi maṃ abhiramentī santappesīti dīpeti. Mandakkhīti mandadassanī, mudunā ākārena olokanasīlāti [V 3.0163] vuttaṃ hoti. “Mattakkhī”tipi pāṭho, madamattehi viya akkhīhi samannāgatāti attho. Evaṃ tambāti evaṃ tambarāja jānāhīti.

There, 'sā maṃ saṇhena mudunā' means that she, while wandering on the seashore, saw me who had reached the shore by a plank and comforted me with gentle and soft words, saying, 'Do not fear.' 'Aṅgena' (by limb) here refers to the pair of arms. 'Bhaddā' means beautiful and pleasing. 'Sā maṃ annena' means she satisfied me with this food and so forth. 'Attanāpi ca' indicates that she delighted and satisfied me not only with food and the like, but also with her own self. 'Mandakkhī' means one who looks with a gentle gaze, having a soft manner of looking. There is also a reading 'Mattakkhī,' meaning endowed with eyes like those of one intoxicated. 'Evaṃ tamba' means 'Thus, O King Tamba, understand this.'

Supaṇṇo gandhabbassa kathentasseva vippaṭisārī hutvā “ahaṃ supaṇṇabhavane vasantopi rakkhituṃ nāsakkhiṃ, kiṃ me tāya dussīlāyā”ti taṃ ānetvā rañño paṭidatvā pakkāmi, tato paṭṭhāya puna nāgacchīti.

The Garuḍa, feeling remorse even as the Gandhabba was speaking, thought, 'Even though I was dwelling in the Garuḍa abode, I could not protect her. What use is she to me, being immoral?' He then brought her back, handed her over to the king, and departed. From that time onward, he never returned.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, supaṇṇarājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the birth story. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the king was Ānanda, and I myself was the Garuḍa king.

Suyonandījātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Suyonandī Jātaka, the Tenth.

Maṇikuṇḍalavaggo paṭhamo.

The Maṇikuṇḍala Chapter, the First.

2. Vaṇṇārohavaggo

2. The Vaṇṇāroha Chapter

[361] 1. Vaṇṇārohajātakavaṇṇanā

[361] 1. The Commentary on the Vaṇṇāroha Jātaka

Vaṇṇārohenāti [V 3.0164][P 3.0191] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dve aggasāvake ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye ubhopi mahātherā “imaṃ antovassaṃ suññāgāraṃ anubrūhessāmā”ti satthāraṃ āpucchitvā gaṇaṃ pahāya sayameva pattacīvaraṃ ādāya jetavanā nikkhamitvā ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ nissāya araññe vihariṃsu. Aññataropi vighāsādapuriso therānaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ karonto tattheva ekamante vasi. So therānaṃ samaggavāsaṃ disvā “ime ativiya samaggā vasanti, sakkā nu kho ete aññamaññaṃ bhinditu”nti cintetvā sāriputtattheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ nu kho, bhante, ayyena mahāmoggallānattherena saddhiṃ tumhākaṃ kiñci veraṃ atthī”ti pucchi. “Kiṃ panāvuso”ti. Esa, bhante, mama āgatakāle “sāriputto [M 3.0177] nāma jātigottakulapadesehi vā sutaganthapaṭivedhaiddhīhi vā mayā saddhiṃ kiṃ pahotī”ti tumhākaṃ aguṇameva kathesīti. Thero sitaṃ katvā “gaccha tvaṃ āvuso”ti āha.

‘Vaṇṇārohena’—this the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the two chief disciples. At one time, both great elders, thinking, ‘During this rainy season, we will devote ourselves to meditation in an empty dwelling,’ took leave of the Teacher, left their retinue, took only their bowls and robes, and departing from Jetavana, dwelt in a forest near a certain border village. A certain scavenger, attending on the elders, also stayed there in a separate place. Seeing the elders living in harmony, he thought, ‘These two live in great harmony; is it possible to create discord between them?’ So he approached the Elder Sāriputta and asked, ‘Venerable sir, is there any enmity between you and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna?’ ‘Why do you ask, friend?’ ‘Because, venerable sir, when I arrived, he said, “What can Sāriputta accomplish compared to me in terms of birth, lineage, family, learning, scriptural understanding, or psychic power?” He spoke only of your lack of qualities.’ The elder smiled and said, ‘Go now, friend.’

So aparasmimpi divase mahāmoggallānattherampi upasaṅkamitvā tatheva kathesi. Sopi naṃ sitaṃ katvā “gaccha, tvaṃ, āvuso”ti vatvā sāriputtattheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “āvuso, eso vighāsādo tumhākaṃ santike kiñci kathesī”ti pucchi. “Āmāvuso, mayhampi santike kathesi, imaṃ nīharituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Sādhu, āvuso, nīharā”ti vutte thero “mā idha vasī”ti accharaṃ paharitvā taṃ nīhari. Te ubhopi samaggavāsaṃ vasitvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “sukhena vassaṃ vasitthā”ti pucchitvā “bhante, eko vighāsādo amhe bhinditukāmo hutvā bhindituṃ asakkonto palāyī”ti vutte “na kho so, sāriputta, idāneva, pubbepesa tumhe ‘bhindissāmī’ti bhindituṃ asakkonto palāyī”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

On another day, he approached the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and spoke in the same way. He too smiled and dismissed him, saying, ‘Go, friend,’ and then went to the Elder Sāriputta and asked, ‘Friend, has that scavenger said anything to you?’ ‘Yes, friend, he spoke to me as well. It is proper to remove him.’ ‘Good, friend, remove him.’ Thus spoken, the elder, snapping his fingers, said, ‘Do not stay here,’ and drove him away. Both of them, living in harmony, went to the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down. The Teacher exchanged greetings and asked, ‘Did you spend the rains comfortably?’ They replied, ‘Venerable sir, a certain scavenger, wanting to divide us but unable to do so, fled.’ The Teacher said, ‘Sāriputta, it is not only now; in the past also, he intended to divide you, but being unable to do so, he fled.’ Having said this, at their request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto araññe rukkhadevatā ahosi. Tadā sīho ca byaggho [P 3.0192] ca araññe pabbataguhāyaṃ vasanti. Eko siṅgālo te upaṭṭhahanto tesaṃ [V 3.0165] vighāsaṃ khāditvā mahākāyo hutvā ekadivasaṃ cintesi “mayā sīhabyagghānaṃ maṃsaṃ na khāditapubbaṃ, mayā ime dve jane bhindituṃ vaṭṭati, tato nesaṃ kalahaṃ katvā matānaṃ maṃsaṃ khādissāmī”ti. So sīhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ, sāmi, tumhākaṃ byagghena saddhiṃ kiñci veraṃ atthī”ti pucchi. “Kiṃ pana, sammā”ti? Esa, bhante, mamāgatakāle “sīho nāma sarīravaṇṇena vā ārohapariṇāhena vā jātibalavīriyehi vā mama kalabhāgampi na pāpuṇātī”ti tumhākaṃ aguṇameva kathesīti. Atha naṃ sīho “gaccha tvaṃ, na so evaṃ kathessatī”ti āha. Byagghampi upasaṅkamitvā eteneva upāyena kathesi. Taṃ sutvā byagghopi sīhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “samma, tvaṃ kira idañcidañca vadesī”ti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in the forest. At that time, a lion and a tiger lived in a mountain cave in the forest. A jackal attended to them, eating their leftovers, and grew very large. One day he thought, ‘I have never eaten the flesh of a lion or a tiger. I should cause discord between these two; then I will eat the flesh of the lion and tiger when they have died in a quarrel.’ He approached the lion and asked, ‘Master, do you have any enmity with the tiger?’ ‘Why do you ask, friend?’ ‘Because, sir, when I came, he said, “A lion, whether in physical beauty, height and bulk, birth, strength, or prowess, does not equal even a sixteenth part of me,” and he spoke only ill of you.’ Then the lion said, ‘Go, he would not say such a thing.’ The jackal approached the tiger and used the same stratagem. Hearing this, the tiger went to the lion and, asking, ‘Friend, is it true that you said such and such?’ spoke the first verse:

60.

60.

“Vaṇṇārohena jātiyā, balanikkamanena ca;

Subāhu na mayā seyyo, sudāṭha iti bhāsasī”ti.

‘In beauty, lineage, and display of strength, Subāhu is not my superior—is this what you say, Sudāṭha?’

Tattha [M 3.0178] balanikkamanena cāti kāyabalena ceva vīriyabalena ca. Subāhu na mayā seyyoti ayaṃ subāhu nāma byaggho etehi kāraṇehi mayā neva sadiso na uttaritaroti saccaṃ kira tvaṃ sobhanāhi dāṭhāhi samannāgata sudāṭha migarāja, evaṃ vadesīti.

In this verse, ‘by display of strength’ means by physical strength and by the strength of vigor. ‘Subāhu is not superior to me’ means that this tiger named Subāhu, for these reasons, is neither equal to me nor superior. ‘Is it true that you, Sudāṭha, king of beasts, endowed with beautiful fangs, speak thus?’—this is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā sudāṭho sesā catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, Sudāṭha spoke the remaining four verses:

61.

61.

“Vaṇṇārohena jātiyā, balanikkamanena ca;

Sudāṭho na mayā seyyo, subāhu iti bhāsasi.

‘In beauty, lineage, and display of strength, Sudāṭha is not my superior—is this what you say, Subāhu?’

62.

62.

“Evaṃ ce maṃ viharantaṃ, subāhu samma dubbhasi;

Na dānāhaṃ tayā saddhiṃ, saṃvāsamabhirocaye.

‘If, while I live thus, Subāhu, friend, you malign me, then from now on I no longer wish to live together with you.’

63.

63.

“Yo paresaṃ vacanāni, saddaheyya yathātathaṃ;

Khippaṃ bhijjetha mittasmiṃ, verañca pasave bahuṃ.

Whoever believes the words of others as if they were true, quickly breaks with a friend and produces much enmity.

64.

64.

“Na so mitto yo sadā appamatto, bhedāsaṅkī randhamevānupassī;

Yasmiñca [P 3.0193] setī urasīva putto, sa ve mitto yo abhejjo parehī”ti.

He is no friend who is always on guard, apprehensive of dissension, ever watching for flaws; but he in whom one can rest, like a child upon the breast—he is truly a friend who cannot be alienated by others.

Tattha sammāti [V 3.0166] vayassa. Dubbhasīti yadi evaṃ tayā saddhiṃ samaggavāsaṃ vasantaṃ maṃ siṅgālassa kathaṃ gahetvā tvaṃ dubbhasi hanituṃ icchasi, ito dāni paṭṭhāya ahaṃ tayā saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ na abhirocaye. Yathātathanti tathato yathātathaṃ yathātacchaṃ avisaṃvādakena ariyena vuttavacanaṃ saddhātabbaṃ. Evaṃ yo yesaṃ kesañci paresaṃ vacanāni saddahethāti attho. Yo sadā appamattoti yo niccaṃ appamatto hutvā mittassa vissāsaṃ na deti, so mitto nāma na hotīti attho. Bhedāsaṅkīti “ajja bhijjissati, sve bhijjissatī”ti evaṃ mittassa bhedameva āsaṅkati. Randhamevānupassīti chiddaṃ vivarameva passanto. Urasīva puttoti yasmiṃ mitte mātu hadaye putto viya nirāsaṅko nibbhayo seti.

Here, 'samma' means a friend of equal age. 'Dubbhasi' means: if, while living in harmony with you, you, having taken up the jackal's words, act treacherously towards me by wishing to kill me, then from now on I no longer desire to live with you. 'Yathātathaṃ' means as it truly is; the words spoken by a non-deceiving noble one should be believed. Thus, the meaning is: whoever trusts the words of any other person whatsoever as being true. 'Yo sadā appamatto' means: one who is always suspicious and does not give trust to a friend, he is no true friend. 'Bhedāsaṅkī' means: thinking, 'Today it will break, tomorrow it will break,' thus always suspecting a break with the friend. 'Randhamevānupassī' means: always looking for a fault or a flaw. 'Urasīva putto' means: in which friend one rests without suspicion or fear, like a child on its mother's breast.

Iti [M 3.0179] imāhi catūhi gāthāhi sīhena mittaguṇe kathite byaggho “mayhaṃ doso”ti sīhaṃ khamāpesi. Te tattheva samaggavāsaṃ vasiṃsu. Siṅgālo pana palāyitvā aññattha gato.

Thus, when the lion had spoken of the qualities of a friend with these four verses, the tiger, acknowledging 'the fault is mine,' sought forgiveness from the lion. They lived there together in harmony. The jackal, however, fled and went elsewhere.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siṅgālo vighāsādo ahosi, sīho sāriputto, byaggho moggallāno, taṃ kāraṇaṃ paccakkhato diṭṭhā tasmiṃ vane nivuttharukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the jackal was the leftover-eater, the lion was Sāriputta, the tiger was Moggallāna, but the tree deity dwelling in that forest who saw the matter firsthand was none other than myself.'

Vaṇṇārohajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Vaṇṇāroha Jātaka is concluded.

[362] 2. Sīlavīmaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā

[362] 2. 2. Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka: The Commentary on the Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka

Sīlaṃ seyyoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ sīlavīmaṃsakabrāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Taṃ kira rājā “esa sīlasampanno”ti aññehi brāhmaṇehi atirekaṃ katvā passati. So cintesi “kiṃ nu kho maṃ rājā ‘sīlasampanno’ti aññehi atirekaṃ katvā passati, udāhu ‘sutadharayutto’ti, vīmaṃsissāmi tāva sīlassa vā sutassa vā mahantabhāva”nti. So ekadivasaṃ heraññikaphalakato kahāpaṇaṃ gaṇhi. Heraññiko garubhāvena na kiñci āha, dutiyavārepi na kiñci āha. Tatiyavāre pana taṃ “vilopakhādako”ti gāhāpetvā rañño dassetvā “kiṃ iminā kata”nti vutte “kuṭumbaṃ vilumpatī”ti āha. “Saccaṃ kira[P 3.0194], brāhmaṇā”ti? “Na, mahārāja, kuṭumbaṃ vilumpāmi, mayhaṃ pana ‘sīlaṃ nu kho mahantaṃ, sutaṃ nu kho’ti kukkuccaṃ ahosi, svāhaṃ ‘etesu kataraṃ nu kho mahanta’nti vīmaṃsanto tayo vāre kahāpaṇaṃ gaṇhiṃ, taṃ maṃ esa bandhāpetvā tumhākaṃ dasseti. Idāni me sutato [V 3.0167] sīlassa mahantabhāvo ñāto, na me gharāvāsenattho, pabbajissāmaha”nti pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetvā gharadvāraṃ anoloketvāva jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pabbajjaṃ yāci. Tassa satthā pabbajjañca upasampadañca dāpesi. So acirūpasampanno vipassanaṃ vipassitvā aggaphale patiṭṭhahi. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asukabrāhmaṇo attano sīlaṃ vīmaṃsitvā pabbajito [M 3.0180] vipassitvā arahattaṃ patto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāni ayameva, pubbe paṇḍitāpi sīlaṃ vīmaṃsitvā pabbajitvā attano patiṭṭhaṃ kariṃsuyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Virtue is supreme,' said the Teacher while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a certain Brahmin who examined virtue. It seems the king, considering him 'endowed with virtue,' regarded him as superior to other Brahmins. He thought, 'Why does the king regard me as superior to others—is it because I am endowed with virtue or because I am endowed with learning? I will examine which is greater, virtue or learning.' One day, he took a coin from the money-changer's board. The money-changer, out of deference, said nothing the first time, nor the second time. But the third time, he had him seized, calling him a 'plunderer,' and presented him to the king. When asked, 'What has he done?' the money-changer replied, 'He plunders the household.' 'Is it true, Brahmin?' 'No, great king, I do not plunder the household. But a doubt arose in me: Is virtue greater, or is learning greater? To test which was greater, I took a coin three times. This man has had me bound and brought before you. Now I understand the greatness of virtue over learning. I have no need for household life; I will go forth.' Having obtained permission to go forth, without even looking back at his home, he went to Jetavana and requested the going forth from the Teacher. The Teacher granted him both the going forth and the higher ordination. Soon after his higher ordination, he practiced insight and was established in the highest fruit. The monks in the Dhamma hall began a discussion: 'Friends, such-and-such a Brahmin, having examined his own virtue, went forth, practiced insight, and attained arahantship.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?' When told, he said, 'Not only now, monks, but in the past too, the wise examined virtue, went forth, and established themselves.' Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā bārāṇasiṃ āgantvā rājānaṃ passi. Rājā tassa purohitaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. So pañca sīlāni rakkhati. Rājāpi naṃ “sīlavā”ti garuṃ katvā passi. So cintesi “kiṃ nu kho rājā ‘sīlavā’ti maṃ garuṃ katvā passati, udāhu ‘sutadharayutto’”ti. Sabbaṃ paccuppannavatthusadisameva. Idha pana so brāhmaṇo “idāni me sutato sīlassa mahantabhāvo ñāto”ti vatvā imā pañca gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. When he came of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā, returned to Benares, and went to see the king. The king gave him the position of chaplain. He observed the five precepts. The king, too, held him in high esteem, considering him virtuous. He wondered: 'Does the king hold me in high esteem because I am virtuous, or because I am endowed with learning?' The entire story is the same as the present one. Here, however, that Brahmin, saying, 'Now I have understood that virtue is greater than learning,' spoke these five stanzas:

65.

65.

“Sīlaṃ seyyo sutaṃ seyyo, iti me saṃsayo ahu;

Sīlameva sutā seyyo, iti me natthi saṃsayo.

'Is virtue better, or is learning better? Thus was my doubt. Virtue alone is better than learning—of this I have no doubt.'

66.

66.

“Moghā jāti ca vaṇṇo ca, sīlameva kiruttamaṃ;

Sīlena anupetassa, sutenattho na vijjati.

'Birth and appearance are in vain; virtue alone is truly supreme. For one who is not endowed with virtue, learning is of no avail.'

67.

67.

“Khattiyo ca adhammaṭṭho, vesso cādhammanissito;

Te pariccajjubho loke, upapajjanti duggatiṃ.

'A noble who is unrighteous and a merchant who relies on unrighteousness—both, having abandoned the two worlds, are reborn in a woeful state.'

68.

68.

“Khattiyā brāhmaṇā vessā, suddā caṇḍālapukkusā;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, bhavanti tidive samā.

'Nobles, Brahmins, merchants, workers, outcastes, and scavengers—having practiced the Dhamma here, they become equal in the heavenly world.'

69.

69.

“Na [P 3.0195] vedā samparāyāya, na jāti nāpi bandhavā;

Sakañca sīlaṃ saṃsuddhaṃ, samparāyāya sukhāya cā”ti.

'Neither the Vedas, nor birth, nor kin avail for the life to come; but one's own purified virtue is for the life to come and for happiness.'

Tattha [V 3.0168] sīlameva sutā seyyoti sutapariyattito sataguṇena sahassaguṇena sīlameva uttaritaranti. Evañca pana vatvā sīlaṃ nāmetaṃ [M 3.0181] ekavidhaṃ saṃvaravasena, duvidhaṃ cārittavārittavasena, tividhaṃ kāyikavācasikamānasikavasena, catubbidhaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvaraindriyasaṃvaraājīvapārisuddhipaccayasannissitavasenāti mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vitthārento sīlassa vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi.

Herein, "virtue alone is better than learning" means that virtue is a hundred times, a thousand times, superior to the learning of the scriptures. And having said this, he laid down the matrix—that virtue is onefold by way of restraint; twofold by way of performance and avoidance; threefold by way of bodily, verbal, and mental action; and fourfold by way of the restraint of the Pātimokkha, restraint of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, and that which is connected with the requisites—and, elaborating on it, he spoke in praise of virtue.

Moghāti aphalā tucchā. Jātīti khattiyakulādīsu nibbatti. Vaṇṇoti sarīravaṇṇo abhirūpabhāvo. Yā hi yasmā sīlarahitassa jātisampadā vā vaṇṇasampadā vā saggasukhaṃ dātuṃ na sakkoti, tasmā ubhayampi taṃ “mogha”nti āha. Sīlameva kirāti anussavavasena vadati, na pana sayaṃ jānāti. Anupetassāti anupagatassa. Sutenattho na vijjatīti sīlarahitassa sutapariyattimattena idhaloke vā paraloke vā kāci vaḍḍhi nāma natthi.

"Vain" means fruitless and empty. "Birth" means birth in clans such as the warrior clan. "Appearance" means bodily complexion or comeliness. Because for one lacking virtue, neither the accomplishment of birth nor the accomplishment of appearance is able to grant the happiness of heaven, he therefore said both are "vain." "Virtue alone indeed": he speaks thus based on hearsay, but does not know it for himself. "Not endowed with" means not having attained. "Learning is of no avail" means that for one lacking virtue, there is no progress whatsoever in this world or the next merely through the extent of one's scriptural learning.

Tato parā dve gāthā jātiyā moghabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttā. Tattha te pariccajjubho loketi te dussīlā devalokañca manussalokañcāti ubhopi loke pariccajitvā duggatiṃ upapajjanti. Caṇḍālapukkusāti chavachaḍḍakacaṇḍālā ca pupphachaḍḍakapukkusā ca. Bhavanti tidive samāti ete sabbepi sīlānubhāvena devaloke nibbattā samā honti nibbisesā, devātveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti.

The two stanzas that follow were spoken to show the futility of birth. Herein, "both forfeit the two worlds" means that those unvirtuous ones, having abandoned both the deva world and the human world, are reborn in a woeful state. "Caṇḍālas and pukkusas" refers to corpse-discarding caṇḍālas and flower-discarding pukkusas. "They become equal in the heavenly world" means all these, reborn in the deva world through the power of virtue, become equal without distinction; they are reckoned simply as devas.

Pañcamagāthā sabbesampi sutādīnaṃ moghabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttā. Tassattho – mahārāja, ete vedādayo ṭhapetvā idhaloke yasamattadānaṃ samparāye dutiye vā tatiye vā bhave yasaṃ vā sukhaṃ vā dātuṃ nāma na sakkonti, parisuddhaṃ pana attano sīlameva taṃ dātuṃ sakkotīti.

The fifth stanza was spoken to show the futility of all things such as learning. Its meaning is: Great king, these Vedas and so forth, setting aside the granting of a measure of fame in this world, are unable to grant fame or happiness in the life to come, or in a second or third existence; only one’s own purified virtue is able to grant that.

Evaṃ mahāsatto sīlaguṇe thometvā rājānaṃ pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetvā taṃ divasameva himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus the Great Being, having praised the qualities of virtue, obtained the king's permission for the going forth. On that very day, he entered the Himalayas, went forth into the ascetic life, produced the direct knowledges and meditative attainments, and, not having fallen away from his jhāna, was destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sīlaṃ vīmaṃsitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajito ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: "At that time, the one who investigated virtue and went forth into the ascetic life was I myself."

Sīlavīmaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka, the Second.

[363] 3. Hirijātakavaṇṇanā

[363] 3. The Commentary on the Hiri Jātaka

Hiriṃ [V 3.0169][M 3.0182] tarantanti [P 3.0196] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto anāthapiṇḍikassa sahāyaṃ paccantavāsiseṭṭhiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Dvepi vatthūni ekakanipāte navamavaggassa pariyosānajātake vitthāritāneva. Idha pana “paccantavāsiseṭṭhino manussā acchinnasabbasāpateyyā attano santakassa assāmino hutvā palātā”ti bārāṇasiseṭṭhissa ārocite bārāṇasiseṭṭhi “attano santikaṃ āgatānaṃ kattabbaṃ akarontā nāma paṭikārake na labhantiyevā”ti vatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story beginning with "One who crosses over shame," concerning a merchant on the border who was a friend of Anāthapiṇḍika. Both stories have already been set out in detail in the final Jātaka of the ninth chapter in the Book of Ones. Here, however, when it was reported to the merchant of Benares that the people of the border merchant had fled, having been dispossessed of all their property, the merchant of Benares said, "Those who do not do what should be done for those who come to them will indeed not receive a service in return," and spoke these stanzas:

70.

70.

“Hiriṃ tarantaṃ vijigucchamānaṃ, tavāhamasmī iti bhāsamānaṃ;

Seyyāni kammāni anādiyantaṃ, neso mamanti iti naṃ vijaññā.

"One who transgresses shame, loathing [the bond of friendship], who says, 'I am yours,' but does not undertake excellent deeds—know him thus: 'This one is not mine.'"

71.

71.

“Yañhi kayirā tañhi vade, yaṃ na kayirā na taṃ vade;

Akarontaṃ bhāsamānaṃ, parijānanti paṇḍitā.

"One should say what one would do; one should not say what one would not do. The wise discern the one who speaks but does not act."

72.

72.

“Na so mitto yo sadā appamatto, bhedāsaṅkī randhamevānupassī;

Yasmiñca setī urasīva putto, sa ve mitto yo abhejjo parehi.

"He is no friend who is ever watchful, fearing a rift and always looking for a flaw. But he in whom one can rest as a son on the breast—he is truly a friend who is unbreakable by others."

73.

73.

“Pāmojjakaraṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ, pasaṃsāvahanaṃ sukhaṃ;

Phalānisaṃso bhāveti, vahanto porisaṃ dhuraṃ.

"Bearing the manly burden, one who sees the fruit and benefit cultivates the state that causes joy, the happiness that brings praise."

74.

74.

“Pavivekarasaṃ pitvā, rasaṃ upasamassa ca;

Niddaro hoti nippāpo, dhammappītirasaṃ piva”nti.

"Having drunk the taste of seclusion and the taste of peace, one becomes free from distress and free from evil, drinking the taste of Dhamma-rapture."

Tattha hiriṃ tarantanti lajjaṃ atikkantaṃ. Vijigucchamānanti mittabhāvena jigucchayamānaṃ. Tavāhamasmīti “tava ahaṃ mitto”ti kevalaṃ vacanamatteneva bhāsamānaṃ. Seyyāni kammāniti “dassāmi karissāmī”ti vacanassa anurūpāni uttamakammāni. Anādiyantanti akarontaṃ. Neso mamanti evarūpaṃ puggalaṃ “na eso mama mitto”ti vijaññā.

Herein, "one who transgresses shame" means one who has overstepped modesty. "Loathing" means one who loathes the state of friendship. "I am yours" means one who says, "I am your friend," with mere words alone. "Excellent deeds" means supreme actions befitting the words, "I will give, I will do." "Does not undertake" means does not do. "Know him not as mine" means one should know such a person thus: "This is not my friend."

Pāmojjakaraṇaṃ [V 3.0170][P 3.0197][M 3.0183] ṭhānanti dānampi sīlampi bhāvanāpi paṇḍitehi kalyāṇamittehi saddhiṃ mittabhāvopi. Idha pana vuttappakāraṃ mittabhāvameva sandhāyevamāha. Paṇḍitena hi kalyāṇamittena saddhiṃ mittabhāvo pāmojjampi karoti, pasaṃsampi vahati. Idhalokaparalokesu kāyikacetasikasukhahetuto “sukha”ntipi vuccati, tasmā etaṃ phalañca ānisaṃsañca sampassamāno phalānisaṃso kulaputto purisehi vahitabbaṃ dānasīlabhāvanāmittabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ catubbidhampi porisaṃ dhuraṃ vahanto etaṃ mittabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ pāmojjakaraṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ pasaṃsāvahanaṃ sukhaṃ bhāveti vaḍḍheti, na paṇḍitehi mittabhāvaṃ bhindatīti dīpeti.

“A state that causes joy” means generosity, virtue, mental development, and also friendship with wise and good friends. Here, however, it refers specifically to this kind of friendship. For friendship with a wise and good companion both brings joy and carries praise. Because it is the cause of bodily and mental happiness in this world and the next, it is also called “happiness.” Therefore, a son of good family who sees this fruit and benefit, bearing the fourfold manly burden—designated as generosity, virtue, mental development, and friendship—cultivates and increases this state of friendship which causes joy, carries praise, and is happiness. This shows that he does not break friendship with the wise.

Pavivekarasanti kāyacittaupadhivivekānaṃ rasaṃ te viveke nissāya uppannaṃ somanassarasaṃ. Upasamassa cāti kilesūpasamena laddhasomanassassa. Niddaro hoti nippāpoti sabbakilesadarathābhāvena niddaro, kilesābhāvena nippāpo hoti. Dhammappītirasanti dhammapītisaṅkhātaṃ rasaṃ, vimuttipītiṃ pivantoti attho.

“The taste of seclusion” means the taste of the seclusion of body, mind, and acquisitions; the taste of joy born in dependence on that seclusion. “And of peace” refers to the joy attained through the calming of the defilements. “He becomes free from distress and free from evil”: he is free from distress through the absence of all the torments of the defilements, and he is free from evil through the absence of defilements. “The taste of Dhamma-rapture” is the taste known as the rapture of Dhamma; the meaning is “drinking the rapture of liberation.”

Iti mahāsatto pāpamittasaṃsaggato ubbiggo pavivekarasena amatamahānibbānaṃ pāpetvā desanāya kūṭaṃ gaṇhi.

Thus the Great Being, distressed by association with bad friends, led others to the deathless great Nibbāna and reached the climax of the teaching.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā paccantavāsī idāni paccantavāsīyeva, tadā bārāṇasiseṭṭhi ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse and identified the birth: “At that time, the border dweller was the present border dweller, and the Benares merchant was I myself.”

Hirijātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Hiri Jātaka, the Third.

[364] 4. Khajjopanakajātakavaṇṇanā

[364] 4. The Commentary on the Khajjopanaka Jātaka

75-79.

75-79.

Ko nu santamhi pajjoteti ayaṃ khajjopanakapañho mahāumaṅge vitthārato āvi bhavissati.

“Who indeed would light a lamp when there is already light?” This firefly question will be revealed in detail in the Mahā-ummagga Jātaka.

Khajjopanakajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Khajjopanaka Jātaka, the Fourth.

[365] 5. Ahituṇḍikajātakavaṇṇanā

[365] 5. The Commentary on the Ahituṇḍika Jātaka

Dhuttomhīti [V 3.0171][M 3.0184] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ mahallakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā sālūkajātake (jā. 1.3.106 ādayo) vitthāritaṃ. Idhāpi so mahallako ekaṃ gāmadārakaṃ pabbājetvā akkosati paharati. Dārako palāyitvā vibbhami. Dutiyampi naṃ pabbājetvā [P 3.0198] tathevākāsi. Dutiyampi vibbhamitvā puna yāciyamāno oloketumpi na icchi. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asuko nāma mahallako attano sāmaṇerena sahāpi vināpi vattituṃ na sakkoti, itaro tassa dosaṃ disvā puna oloketumpi na icchi, suhadayo kumārako”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa sāmaṇero suhadayova, sakiṃ dosaṃ disvā puna oloketumpi na icchī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this discourse beginning with ‘I am a rogue,’ concerning a certain elderly monk. The story is detailed in the Sālūka Jātaka (Jā. 286) below. Here too, that elder ordained a village boy and then scolded and beat him. The boy ran away and disrobed. A second time, the elder ordained him and acted in the same way. Again the boy disrobed, and when requested once more, he did not want even to look at him. The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: ‘Friends, that elder cannot live either with or without his novice. The other, seeing his fault, did not want even to look at him again—how sensible the youth is!’ The Teacher arrived and asked, ‘Monks, what is the topic of discussion you are gathered here for now?’ When they told him, ‘This is it,’ he said, ‘Monks, not only now, but even in the past this novice was sensible. Having once seen the fault, he did not want to look again.’ And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto dhaññavāṇijakule nibbattitvā vayappatto dhaññavikkayena jīvikaṃ kappesi. Atheko ahituṇḍiko makkaṭaṃ gahetvā sikkhāpetvā ahiṃ kīḷāpento bārāṇasiyaṃ ussave ghuṭṭhe taṃ makkaṭaṃ dhaññavāṇijakassa santike ṭhapetvā ahiṃ kīḷāpento satta divasāni vicari. Sopi vāṇijo makkaṭassa khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ adāsi. Ahituṇḍiko sattame divase ussavakīḷanato āgantvā taṃ makkaṭaṃ veḷupesikāya tikkhattuṃ paharitvā taṃ ādāya uyyānaṃ gantvā bandhitvā niddaṃ okkami. Makkaṭo bandhanaṃ mocetvā ambarukkhaṃ āruyha ambāni khādanto nisīdi. So pabuddho rukkhe makkaṭaṃ disvā “etaṃ mayā upalāpetvā gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of grain merchants. When he came of age, he made his living by selling grain. At that time, a snake charmer, having caught and trained a monkey, arrived in Benares when a festival was proclaimed. He left the monkey with the grain merchant and wandered about for seven days, making his snake perform. The merchant gave the monkey food to eat. On the seventh day, the snake charmer returned from the festival celebrations, struck the monkey three times with a bamboo stick, took it to a park, tied it up, and fell asleep. The monkey freed itself from its bonds, climbed a mango tree, and sat eating mangoes. When the man woke up and saw the monkey in the tree, he thought, ‘I must coax it down and catch it.’ So, speaking to it, he recited the first verse:

80.

80.

“Dhuttomhi samma sumukha, jūte akkhaparājito;

Harehi ambapakkāni, vīriyaṃ te bhakkhayāmase”ti.

“I am a rogue, friend Fair-face, defeated at dice in gambling. Bring ripe mangoes, let us eat the fruit of your effort.”

Tattha akkhaparājitoti akkhehi parājito. Harehīti pātehi. Ayameva vā pāṭho.

Here, ‘akkhaparājito’ means ‘defeated by dice.’ ‘Harehi’ means ‘throw down.’ This is the literal meaning.

Taṃ [M 3.0185] sutvā makkaṭo sesagāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the monkey spoke the remaining verses:

81.

81.

“Alikaṃ [V 3.0172] vata maṃ samma, abhūtena pasaṃsasi;

Ko te suto vā diṭṭho vā, sumukho nāma makkaṭo.

“Truly, friend, you praise me with what is untrue; where has a monkey named Fair-face been heard of, or seen, by you?

82.

82.

“Ajjāpi [P 3.0199] me taṃ manasi, yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ ahituṇḍika;

Dhaññāpaṇaṃ pavisitvā, matto chātaṃ hanāsi maṃ.

“Even today it is in my mind, O snake charmer, how you entered the grain shop and, being drunk, struck me when I was hungry.

83.

83.

“Tāhaṃ saraṃ dukkhaseyyaṃ, api rajjampi kāraye;

Nevāhaṃ yācito dajjaṃ, tathā hi bhayatajjito.

“Remembering that painful lying down, even if you were to make me king, I would not give when begged, for I was so terrified by fear.

84.

84.

“Yañca jaññā kule jātaṃ, gabbhe tittaṃ amacchariṃ;

Tena sakhiñca mittañca, dhīro sandhātumarahatī”ti.

“A wise person is worthy to form companionship and friendship with one whom he knows to be born of a good family, content in the womb, and unselfish.”

Tattha alikaṃ vatāti musā vata. Abhūtenāti avijjamānena. Ko teti kva tayā. Sumukhoti sundaramukho. Ahituṇḍikāti taṃ ālapati. “Ahikoṇḍikā”tipi pāṭho. Chātanti jighacchābhibhūtaṃ dubbalaṃ kapaṇaṃ. Hanāsīti veḷupesikāya tikkhattuṃ paharasi. Tāhanti taṃ ahaṃ. Saranti saranto. Dukkhaseyyanti tasmiṃ āpaṇe dukkhasayanaṃ. Api rajjampi kārayeti sacepi bārāṇasirajjaṃ gahetvā mayhaṃ datvā maṃ rajjaṃ kāreyyāsi, evampi taṃ nevāhaṃ yācito dajjaṃ, taṃ ekampi ambapakkaṃ ahaṃ tayā yācito na dadeyyaṃ. Kiṃkāraṇā? Tathā hi bhayatajjitoti, tathā hi ahaṃ tayā bhayena tajjitoti attho.

Here, ‘alikaṃ vata’ means ‘truly false.’ ‘Abhūtena’ means ‘by what is non-existent.’ ‘Ko te’ means ‘where by you.’ ‘Sumukha’ means ‘fair-faced.’ ‘Ahituṇḍika’ is how he addresses him. There is also a reading ‘Ahikoṇḍikā.’ ‘Chātaṃ’ means ‘overcome by hunger, weak, and wretched.’ ‘Hanāsi’ means ‘you struck three times with a bamboo stick.’ ‘Tāhaṃ’ means ‘that I.’ ‘Saraṃ’ means ‘remembering.’ ‘Dukkhaseyyaṃ’ means the ‘painful lying down’ in that shop. ‘Api rajjampi kāraye’ means ‘even if you were to take the kingdom of Benares and give it to me, making me king, even then I would not give to you when begged; I would not give you even a single ripe mango when begged by you.’ Why? ‘Tathā hi bhayatajjito’ means ‘for I was so terrified by you’.

Gabbhe tittanti subhojanarasena mātukucchiyaṃyeva alaṅkatapaṭiyatte sayanagabbheyeva vā tittaṃ bhogāsāya akapaṇaṃ. Sakhiñca mittañcāti sakhibhāvañca mittabhāvañca tathārūpena kulajātena tittena akapaṇena amaccharinā saddhiṃ paṇḍito sandhātuṃ puna ghaṭetuṃ arahati, tayā pana kapaṇena ahituṇḍikena saddhiṃ ko mittabhāvaṃ puna ghaṭetunti attho. Evañca pana vatvā vānaro vanaṃ sahasā pāvisi.

‘Gabbhe tittaṃ’ means satisfied in the mother’s womb with the taste of delicious food, or satisfied in a well-prepared and adorned bed-chamber, being not wretched with craving for enjoyments. ‘Sakhiñca mittañca’ means companionship and friendship. A wise person is worthy to reconcile and re-establish companionship and friendship with such a person born of a good family, one who is content, not wretched, and unselfish. But who would re-establish friendship with a wretched snake charmer like you? This is the meaning. Having spoken thus, the monkey quickly entered the forest.

Satthā [M 3.0186] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā ahituṇḍiko mahallako ahosi, makkaṭo sāmaṇero, dhaññavāṇijo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the birth story: “At that time, the snake charmer was the old man, the monkey was the novice, and the grain merchant was I myself.”

Ahituṇḍikajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Ahituṇḍika Jātaka, the Fifth.

[366] 6. Gumbiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[366] 6. The Commentary on the Gumbiya Jātaka

Madhuvaṇṇaṃ [V 3.0173][P 3.0200] madhurasanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kiṃ disvā”ti vatvā “alaṅkatamātugāma”nti vutte “bhikkhu ime pañca kāmaguṇā nāma ekena gumbiyena yakkhena halāhalavisaṃ pakkhipitvā magge ṭhapitamadhusadisā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this discourse beginning with ‘Honey-colored, honey-sweet,’ concerning a discontented monk. For the Teacher asked him, ‘Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?’ When he replied, ‘It is true, venerable sir,’ and was asked, ‘Having seen what?’ he answered, ‘An adorned woman.’ The Teacher then said, ‘Monk, these five strands of sensual pleasure are like honey placed on the road by a yakkha named Gumbiya, into which deadly halāhala poison has been mixed.’ Being requested by him, he then related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto satthavāhakule nibbattitvā vayappatto bārāṇasito pañcahi sakaṭasatehi bhaṇḍaṃ ādāya vohāratthāya gacchanto mahāvattaniaṭavidvāraṃ patvā satthake sannipātāpetvā “ambho, imasmiṃ magge visapaṇṇapupphaphalādīni atthi, tumhe kiñci akhāditapubbaṃ khādantā maṃ apucchitvā mā khādittha, amanussāpi visaṃ pakkhipitvā bhattapuṭamadhukaphalāni magge ṭhapenti, tānipi maṃ anāpucchitvā mā khāditthā”ti ovādaṃ datvā maggaṃ paṭipajji. Atheko gumbiyo nāma yakkho aṭaviyā majjhaṭṭhāne magge paṇṇāni attharitvā halāhalavisasaṃyuttāni madhupiṇḍāni ṭhapetvā sayaṃ maggasāmante madhuṃ gaṇhanto viya rukkhe koṭṭento vicarati. Ajānantā “puññatthāya ṭhapitāni bhavissantī”ti khāditvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇanti. Amanussā āgantvā te khādanti. Bodhisattassa satthakamanussāpi tāni disvā ekacce lolajātikā adhivāsetuṃ asakkontā khādiṃsu, paṇḍitajātikā “pucchitvā khādissāmā”ti gahetvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Bodhisatto te disvā hatthagatāni chaḍḍāpesi, yehi paṭhamataraṃ khāditāni, te mariṃsu. Yehi aḍḍhakhāditāni, tesaṃ vamanavirecanaṃ datvā vantakāle catumadhuraṃ [P 3.0201][M 3.0187] adāsi. Iti te tassa ānubhāvena jīvitaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Bodhisatto sotthinā icchitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā bhaṇḍaṃ vissajjetvā attano gehameva agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ kathento satthā imā abhisambuddhagāthā abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a caravan leader's family. When he came of age, he took goods with five hundred carts and set out for trade from Benares. Arriving at the entrance of a road through a great wilderness, he gathered the caravan members and advised them: 'Sirs, on this road there are poisonous leaves, flowers, fruits, and so on. If you wish to eat anything you have not eaten before, do not eat it without asking me. Non-human beings also mix poison into bundles of cooked rice, honey-lumps, and fruits, and leave them on the road. Do not eat those without consulting me either.' Having given this advice, he set out on the road. Now, there was a yakkha named Gumbiya who, in the middle of the forest, spread leaves on the road and placed honey-lumps mixed with deadly poison, while he himself wandered about nearby, tapping on trees as if gathering honey. Those who were unaware, thinking, 'These must have been placed for a meritorious purpose,' ate them and met their death. The non-human beings would then come and devour them. Among the Bodhisatta’s caravan members, some of a greedy nature, unable to restrain themselves, ate them. Those of a wise nature, thinking, 'We will eat only after asking the Bodhisatta,' took them and waited. Seeing them, the Bodhisatta made them discard what was in their hands. Those who had eaten first died. To those who had eaten half, he gave emetics and purgatives, and when they had vomited, he gave them the four sweets. Thus, by the power of the Bodhisatta, they regained their lives. The Bodhisatta safely reached his desired destination, sold his goods, and returned to his own home. Relating this matter, the Teacher, having become fully enlightened, spoke these verses:

85.

85.

“Madhuvaṇṇaṃ madhurasaṃ, madhugandhaṃ visaṃ ahu;

Gumbiyo ghāsamesāno, araññe odahī visaṃ.

Honey-colored, sweet in taste, and with a honey-like scent, it was actually poison. Gumbiya, searching for prey, placed the poison in the forest.

86.

86.

“Madhu iti maññamānā, ye taṃ visamakhādisuṃ;

Tesaṃ taṃ kaṭukaṃ āsi, maraṇaṃ tenupāgamuṃ.

Thinking it was honey, those who ate that poison found it to be bitter in its result, and through it they met their death.

87.

87.

“Ye [V 3.0174] ca kho paṭisaṅkhāya, visaṃ taṃ parivajjayuṃ;

Te āturesu sukhitā, ḍayhamānesu nibbutā.

But those who, upon reflection, avoided that poison, they remained happy among the afflicted, and were at peace among those who were burning.

88.

88.

“Evameva manussesu, visaṃ kāmā samohitā;

Āmisaṃ bandhanañcetaṃ, maccuveso guhāsayo.

Just so, among humans, sensual pleasures are like poison that has been prepared. This is both bait and a bond, the guise of Death dwelling in the cave of the body.

89.

89.

“Evameva ime kāme, āturā paricārike;

Ye sadā parivajjenti, saṅgaṃ loke upaccagu”nti.

Just so, those who always avoid these sensual pleasures—which are afflicting and attended by defilements—have overcome attachment in the world.

Tattha gumbiyoti tasmiṃ vanagumbe vicaraṇena evaṃladdhanāmo yakkho. Ghāsamesānoti “taṃ visaṃ khāditvā mate khādissāmī”ti evaṃ attano ghāsaṃ pariyesanto. Odahīti taṃ madhunā samānavaṇṇagandharasaṃ visaṃ nikkhipi. Kaṭukaṃ āsīti tikhiṇaṃ ahosi. Maraṇaṃ tenupāgamunti tena visena te sattā maraṇaṃ upagatā.

Herein, 'Gumbiya' is the name given to that yakkha because he roamed in that forest grove (gumbe). 'Searching for prey' means searching for his own food, thinking: 'I will eat those who die after eating that poison.' 'Placed' (odahī) means he set down that poison, which had the same color, scent, and taste as honey. 'It was bitter' means it was potent and sharp. 'Through it they came to death' means those beings died because of that poison.

Āturesūti visavegena āsannamaraṇesu. Ḍayhamānesūti visatejeneva ḍayhamānesu. Visaṃ kāmā samohitāti yathā tasmiṃ vattanimahāmagge visaṃ samohitaṃ nikkhittaṃ, evaṃ manussesupi ye ete rūpādayo pañca vatthukāmā tattha tattha samohitā nikkhittā, te “visa”nti veditabbā. Āmisaṃ bandhanañcetanti ete pañca kāmaguṇā nāma evaṃ imassa macchabhūtassa lokassa mārabālisikena pakkhittaṃ āmisañceva[M 3.0188], bhavābhavato nikkhamituṃ appadānena anduādippabhedaṃ nānappakāraṃ bandhanañca. Maccuveso guhāsayoti [P 3.0202] sarīraguhāya vasanako maraṇamaccuveso.

‘Among the afflicted’ means among those near death due to the force of the poison. ‘Among those who were burning’ means among those burning from the very heat of the poison. ‘Sensual pleasures are mixed with poison’ means: just as poison was placed on that great road, so too among humans these five objects of sensual pleasure, such as form and the rest, are placed here and there; these should be understood as ‘poison.’ ‘This is bait and a bond’ means: these five strands of sensual pleasure are both the bait cast by Māra the fisherman for this world, which has become like a fish, and also various kinds of bonds—such as chains and so forth—that prevent escape from the cycle of existence. ‘The guise of Death, dwelling in a cave’ means the attire of Death, which is Death dwelling in the cave of the body.

Evameva ime kāmeti yathā vattanimahāmagge visaṃ nikkhittaṃ, evaṃ tattha tattha nikkhitte ime kāme. Āturāti ekantamaraṇadhammatāya āturā āsannamaraṇā paṇḍitamanussā. Paricāriketi kilesaparicārike kilesabandhake. Ye sadā parivajjentīti ye vuttappakārā paṇḍitapurisā niccaṃ evarūpe kāme vajjenti. Saṅgaṃ loketi loke saṅganaṭṭhena “saṅga”nti laddhanāmaṃ rāgādibhedaṃ kilesajātaṃ. Upaccagunti atītā nāmāti veditabbā, atikkamantīti vā attho.

‘Just so, these sensual pleasures’ means: just as poison is placed on a great highway, so too are these sensual pleasures placed here and there. ‘Afflicting’ means: wise people, being of a nature that is subject to certain death, are afflicted and near death. ‘Attended by defilements’ means serving the defilements, binding with defilements. ‘Those who always avoid them’ means: those wise persons of the kind described always avoid such sensual pleasures. ‘Attachment in the world’ means: in the world, the mass of defilements, differentiated as lust and so on, which has obtained the name ‘attachment’ because it has the characteristic of clinging. ‘Have overcome’ means: they should be understood as ‘having gone beyond,’ or the meaning is ‘they transcend.’

Satthā [V 3.0175] saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā satthavāho ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having proclaimed the truths, connected the birth story. At the conclusion of the truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, I myself was the caravan leader.”

Gumbiyajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Gumbiya Jātaka, the sixth.

[367] 7. Sāḷiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[367] 7. Sāḷiya Jātaka

Yvāyaṃ sāḷiyachāpotīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto “āvuso, devadatto tāsakārakopi bhavituṃ nāsakkhī”ti vacanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa mama tāsakārakopi bhavituṃ nāsakkhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This story beginning “This one is a young myna bird” was told by the Teacher while he was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove with reference to the saying: “Friends, Devadatta was not able even to become a frightener for the Buddha.” For at that time the Teacher said: “Monks, not only now, but in the past too he was unable to frighten me,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto gāmake kuṭumbikakule nibbattitvā taruṇakāle paṃsukīḷakehi dārakehi saddhiṃ gāmadvāre nigrodharukkhamūle kīḷati. Tadā eko dubbalavejjo gāme kiñci alabhitvā nikkhamanto taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā ekaṃ sappaṃ viṭapabbhantarena sīsaṃ nīharitvā niddāyantaṃ disvā “mayā gāme kiñci na laddhaṃ, ime dārake vañcetvā sappena ḍaṃsāpetvā tikicchitvā kiñcideva gaṇhissāmī”ti cintetvā bodhisattaṃ āha “sace sāḷiyachāpaṃ passeyyāsi, gaṇheyyāsī”ti. “Āma, gaṇheyya”nti[P 3.0203]. “Passeso viṭapabbhantare sayito”ti. So [M 3.0189] tassa sappabhāvaṃ ajānanto rukkhaṃ āruyha taṃ gīvāyaṃ gahetvā “sappo”ti ñatvā nivattituṃ adento suggahitaṃ gahetvā vegena khipi. So gantvā vejjassa gīvāyaṃ patito gīvaṃ paliveṭhetvā “kara karā”ti ḍaṃsitvā tattheva naṃ pātetvā palāyi. Manussā parivārayiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a householder's family in a small village. In his youth, he played with other boys who were playing in the dust under a banyan tree at the village gate. At that time, an incompetent physician, having failed to obtain any work in the village, was leaving when he reached that spot. Seeing a snake sleeping with its head sticking out from a hollow between branches, he thought: “I have gained nothing in the village. I will trick these boys, have them bitten by the snake, treat them, and thus get something.” So he said to the Bodhisatta: “My boy, if you see a young myna bird, would you catch it?” “Yes, I would,” he replied. “Look, that young myna is sleeping in the hollow between the branches.” Not knowing it was a snake, the Bodhisatta climbed the tree and grabbed it by the neck. Realizing it was a snake, he did not let it bite him but gripped it firmly and threw it with force. It landed on the physician’s neck, coiled around it, and bit him with a crunching sound, killing the physician right there before it fled. People gathered around.

Mahāsatto sampattaparisāya dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

The Great Being, wishing to teach the Dhamma to the assembled crowd, spoke these verses:

90.

90.

“Yvāyaṃ sāḷiyachāpoti, kaṇhasappaṃ agāhayi;

Tena sappenayaṃ daṭṭho, hato pāpānusāsako.

He who, saying, ‘This is a young myna bird,’ made me seize the black serpent, has been bitten by that very serpent; the instructor in evil is slain.

91.

91.

“Ahantāramahantāraṃ, yo naro hantumicchati;

Evaṃ so nihato seti, yathāyaṃ puriso hato.

The man who wishes to kill one who is harmless and inoffensive lies slain himself, just as this man here lies slain.

92.

92.

“Ahantāramaghātentaṃ[V 3.0176], yo naro hantumicchati;

Evaṃ so nihato seti, yathāyaṃ puriso hato.

The man who wishes to kill one who neither kills nor causes killing lies slain himself, just as this man here lies slain.

93.

93.

“Yathā paṃsumuṭṭhiṃ puriso, paṭivātaṃ paṭikkhipe;

Tameva so rajo hanti, tathāyaṃ puriso hato.

“Just as a man might throw a handful of dust against the wind, and that very dust strikes him; even so is this man slain.”

94.

94.

“Yo appaduṭṭhassa narassa dussati, suddhassa posassa anaṅgaṇassa;

Tameva bālaṃ pacceti pāpaṃ, sukhumo rajo paṭivātaṃva khitto”ti.

“Whoever offends a man who is harmless, a person who is pure and stainless, the evil recoils upon that fool, like fine dust thrown against the wind.”

Tattha yvāyanti yo ayaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Sappenayanti so ayaṃ tena sappena daṭṭho. Pāpānusāsakoti pāpakaṃ anusāsako.

Therein, “yvāyaṃ” means “he who”; or this itself is the reading. “Sappenayaṃ” means: this one was bitten by that serpent. “Pāpānusāsako” means: an instructor in evil.

Ahantāranti apaharantaṃ. Ahantāranti amārentaṃ. Setīti matasayanaṃ sayati. Aghātentanti amārentaṃ. Suddhassāti niraparādhassa. Posassāti sattassa. Anaṅgaṇassāti idampi niraparādhabhāvaññeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Paccetīti kammasarikkhakaṃ hutvā patieti.

“Ahantāraṃ” means one who does not harm. “Ahantāraṃ” also means one who does not kill. “Seti” means he lies down in the sleep of death. “Aghātentaṃ” means one who does not kill. “Suddhassa” means of one who is faultless. “Posassa” means of a being. “Anaṅgaṇassa” is also said with reference to the state of being faultless. “Pacceti” means it returns, becoming a match for the deed.

Satthā [M 3.0190] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dubbalavejjo devadatto ahosi, paṇḍitadārako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the birth story: “At that time, the incompetent physician was Devadatta, but the wise boy was I myself.”

Sāḷiyajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Sāḷiya Jātaka, the seventh.

[368] 8. Tacasārajātakavaṇṇanā

[368] 8. The Commentary on the Tacasāra Jātaka

Amittahatthatthagatāti [P 3.0204] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto paññāpāramiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato paññavā upāyakusaloyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This story beginning “Fallen into the hands of enemies” was told by the Teacher while he was dwelling in Jeta's Grove, with reference to the perfection of wisdom. For at that time the Teacher said: “Not only now, monks, but in the past too the Tathāgata was wise and skilled in means,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto gāmake kuṭumbikakule nibbattitvāti sabbaṃ purimajātakaniyāmeneva kathetabbaṃ. Idha pana vejje mate gāmavāsino manussā “manussamārakā”ti te dārake kudaṇḍakehi bandhitvā “rañño dassessāmā”ti bārāṇasiṃ [V 3.0177] nayiṃsu. Bodhisatto antarāmaggeyeva sesadārakānaṃ ovādaṃ adāsi “tumhe mā bhāyatha, rājānaṃ disvāpi abhītā tuṭṭhindriyā bhaveyyātha, rājā amhehi saddhiṃ paṭhamataraṃ kathessati, tato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ jānissāmī”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tathā kariṃsu. Rājā te abhīte tuṭṭhindriye disvā “ime ‘manussamārakā’ti kudaṇḍakabaddhā ānītā, evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ pattāpi na bhāyanti, tuṭṭhindriyāyeva, kiṃ nu kho etesaṃ asocanakāraṇaṃ, pucchissāmi ne”ti pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a householder’s family in a village—all this should be told in the manner of the previous birth story. Here, however, when the physician died, the villagers, calling the boys “man-killers,” bound them with wooden fetters and took them to Benares, saying, “We will show them to the king.” On the way, the Bodhisatta advised the other boys: “Do not be afraid. Even when you see the king, be fearless and with your senses tranquil. The king will speak with us first, and from that point on, I will know what to do.” They agreed, saying, “Good,” and did as he said. Seeing them fearless and with tranquil senses, the king thought: “These boys, called ‘man-killers,’ have been brought here bound with wooden fetters. Even after experiencing such suffering, they are not afraid but remain with tranquil senses. What could be the reason for their lack of sorrow? I will ask them.” Then, questioning them, he spoke the first verse:

95.

95.

“Amittahatthatthagatā, tacasārasamappitā;

Pasannamukhavaṇṇāttha, kasmā tumhe na socathā”ti.

“Fallen into the hands of enemies, bound with bamboo fetters, you have bright and clear complexions; why do you not grieve?”

Tattha amittahatthatthagatāti kudaṇḍakehi gīvāyaṃ bandhitvā ānentānaṃ amittānaṃ hatthagatā. Tacasārasamappitāti veḷudaṇḍakehi baddhattā evamāha. Kasmāti “evarūpaṃ byasanaṃ pattāpi tumhe kiṃkāraṇā na socathā”ti pucchati.

Therein, “amittahatthatthagatā” means: fallen into the hands of enemies who are bringing you, having bound you by the neck with wooden fetters. “Tacasārasamappitā”: this is said because you are bound with bamboo sticks. “Kasmā”: he asks, “Having met with such a disaster, for what reason do you not grieve?”

Taṃ [M 3.0191] sutvā bodhisatto sesagāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the remaining verses:

96.

96.

“Na socanāya paridevanāya, atthova labbho api appakopi;

Socantamenaṃ dukhitaṃ viditvā, paccatthikā attamanā bhavanti.

“Not by sorrowing or lamenting is any benefit gained, not even the slightest. Seeing that one is sorrowful and afflicted, one's enemies are pleased.

97.

97.

“Yato [P 3.0205] ca kho paṇḍito āpadāsu, na vedhatī atthavinicchayaññū;

Paccatthikāssa dukhitā bhavanti, disvā mukhaṃ avikāraṃ purāṇaṃ.

“But when a wise man in adversity does not waver, being skilled in discerning what is beneficial, his adversaries are troubled, seeing his face unchanged, as it was before.

98.

98.

“Jappena mantena subhāsitena, anuppadānena paveṇiyā vā;

Yathā yathā yattha labhetha atthaṃ, tathā tathā tattha parakkameyya.

“By muttering, by counsel, by well-spoken words, by giving gifts, or by lineage; in whatever way and wherever one may find benefit, in that very way and there one should strive.

99.

99.

“Yato ca jāneyya alabbhaneyyo, mayāva aññena vā esa attho;

Asocamāno adhivāsayeyya, kammaṃ daḷhaṃ kinti karomi dānī”ti.

“And when one knows, ‘This benefit is unattainable, either by me or by another,’ one should endure it without sorrow, thinking, ‘My kamma is strong! What can I do now?’”

Tattha atthoti vuḍḍhi. Paccatthikā attamanāti etaṃ purisaṃ socantaṃ dukkhitaṃ viditvā paccāmittā tuṭṭhacittā honti. Tesaṃ tussanakāraṇaṃ nāma paṇḍitena kātuṃ na vaṭṭatīti dīpeti[V 3.0178]. Yatoti yadā. Na vedhatīti cittutrāsabhayena na kampati. Atthavinicchayaññūti tassa tassa atthassa vinicchayakusalo.

Therein, “attho” means gain. “Paccatthikā attamanā” means: seeing that this person is grieving and suffering, his adversaries become pleased in mind. It is shown that a wise person should not act in a way that causes them to be satisfied. “Yato” means when. “Na vedhati” means one does not tremble out of mental agitation and fear. “Atthavinicchayaññū” means one who is skilled in discerning the benefit in each particular case.

Jappenāti mantaparijappanena. Mantenāti paṇḍitehi saddhiṃ mantaggahaṇena. Subhāsitenāti piyavacanena. Anuppadānenāti lañjadānena. Paveṇiyāti kulavaṃsena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, paṇḍitena nāma āpadāsu uppannāsu na socitabbaṃ na kilamitabbaṃ, imesu pana pañcasu kāraṇesu aññataravasena paccāmittā jinitabbā. Sace hi sakkoti, mantaṃ parijappitvā mukhabandhanaṃ katvāpi te jinitabbā, tathā asakkontena paṇḍitehi [M 3.0192] saddhiṃ mantetvā ekaṃ upāyaṃ sallakkhetvā jinitabbā, piyavacanaṃ vattuṃ sakkontena piyaṃ vatvāpi te jinitabbā, tathā asakkontena vinicchayāmaccānaṃ lañjaṃ datvāpi jinitabbā, tathā asakkontena kulavaṃsaṃ kathetvā “mayaṃ asukapaveṇiyā āgatā, tumhākañca amhākañca ekova pubbapuriso”ti evaṃ vijjamānañātikoṭiṃ ghaṭetvāpi jinitabbā evāti. Yathā yathāti etesu pañcasu kāraṇesu yena yena kāraṇena yattha yattha attano vuḍḍhiṃ labheyya. Tathā tathāti tena tena kāraṇena tattha tattha parakkameyya, parakkamaṃ katvā paccatthike jineyyāti adhippāyo.

“By muttering” means by muttering spells. “By counsel” means by taking counsel with the wise. “By well-spoken words” means by pleasant speech. “By giving” means by giving bribes. “By lineage” means by family line. This is what was said: “O great king, when misfortunes arise a wise person should not grieve or become weary, but should conquer his enemies by one of these five means. If he can, he should conquer them by muttering a spell and imposing a verbal restraint. If unable, he should consult with the wise, devise a stratagem, and conquer them. If he can speak pleasantly, he should conquer them with pleasant words. If unable, he should conquer them by giving bribes to the ministers of justice. If still unable, he should speak of his lineage, saying, ‘We come from such-and-such a lineage, and you and we share the same ancestor,’ thus establishing a connection with existing relatives and conquering them.” “In whatever way” means by whichever of these five means he can achieve his own advancement. “In that same way” means he should exert himself by that means in that situation, and having exerted himself, he should conquer his adversaries—this is the intention.

Yato ca jāneyyāti yadā pana jāneyya, mayā vā aññena vā esa attho alabbhaneyyo nānappakārena vāyamitvāpi [P 3.0206] na sakkā laddhuṃ, tadā paṇḍito puriso asocamāno akilamamāno “mayā pubbe katakammaṃ daḷhaṃ thiraṃ na sakkā paṭibāhituṃ, idāni kiṃ sakkā kātu”nti adhivāsayeyyāti.

“And when one knows” means: when, however, one knows that this objective is unobtainable by oneself or by another, and even after various efforts it cannot be attained, then the wise person, not grieving nor becoming weary, should endure it, thinking, “The kamma I did formerly is strong and firm; it cannot be warded off. What can be done now?”

Rājā bodhisattassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā kammaṃ sodhetvā niddosabhāvaṃ ñatvā kudaṇḍake harāpetvā mahāsattassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ datvā attano atthadhammaanusāsakaṃ amaccaratanaṃ akāsi, sesadārakānampi yasaṃ datvā ṭhānantarāni adāsi.

The king, having heard the Bodhisatta's Dhamma talk, investigated the case, and realizing his innocence, had the wooden stocks removed. He bestowed great honor upon the Great Being and appointed him as his treasured minister and advisor on worldly and spiritual matters. He also bestowed honor upon the other boys and gave them official posts.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā bārāṇasirājā ānando ahosi, dārakā therānutherā, paṇḍitadārako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection in the birth story: “At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda, the boys were the elder and younger monks, but the wise boy was I myself.”

Tacasārajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Tacasāra Jātaka, the Eighth.

[369] 9. Mittavindakajātakavaṇṇanā

[369] 9. The Commentary on the Mittavindaka Jātaka

Kyāhaṃ [V 3.0179] devānamakaranti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ dubbacabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu mahāmittavindakajātake (jā. 1.5.100 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Ayaṃ pana mittavindako samudde khitto atriccho hutvā purato gantvā nerayikasattānaṃ paccanaṭṭhānaṃ ussadanirayaṃ disvā “ekaṃ nagara”nti [M 3.0193] saññāya pavisitvā khuracakkaṃ assādesi. Tadā bodhisatto devaputto hutvā ussadanirayacārikaṃ carati. So taṃ disvā pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

'What have I done to the gods?' This the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was difficult to admonish. The full story will be told in the Mahāmittavindaka Jātaka. This Mittavindaka, having been cast into the ocean, became exceedingly greedy. Going forward, he saw the Ussada hell, the place where hell-beings are tormented, and mistaking it for 'a city,' he entered and experienced the razor-wheel. At that time the Bodhisatta, who had become a deva's son, was touring the Ussada hell. Seeing him, he questioned him, speaking the first verse:

100.

100.

“Kyāhaṃ devānamakaraṃ, kiṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayā;

Yaṃ me sirasmiṃ ohacca, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake”ti.

“What have I done to the gods? What evil have I committed, that a wheel, having descended upon my head, spins on my crown?”

Tattha kyāhaṃ devānamakaranti sāmi devaputta, kiṃ nāma ahaṃ devānaṃ akariṃ, kiṃ maṃ devā pothentīti. Kiṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayāti dukkhamahantatāya vedanāppatto attanā kataṃ pāpaṃ asallakkhento evamāha. Yaṃ meti yena pāpena mama sirasmiṃ ohacca ohanitvā idaṃ khuracakkaṃ mama matthake bhamati, taṃ kiṃ nāmāti?

Therein, 'What have I done to the gods?' means: 'Master, deva's son, what indeed have I done to the gods? Why do the gods strike me?' 'What evil have I committed?' He spoke thus because, afflicted by the greatness of his suffering, he did not notice the evil he himself had done. 'That on my...' means: 'By what evil deed has this razor-wheel descended upon and struck my head and now spins on my crown? What is it?'

Taṃ [P 3.0207] sutvā bodhisatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:

101.

101.

“Atikkamma ramaṇakaṃ, sadāmattañca dūbhakaṃ;

Brahmattarañca pāsādaṃ, kenatthena idhāgato”ti.

“Having passed by Ramaṇaka, Sadāmatta, Dūbhaka, and the Brahmuttara palace, for what reason have you come here?”

Tattha ramaṇakanti phalikapāsādaṃ. Sadāmattanti rajatapāsādaṃ. Dūbhakanti maṇipāsādaṃ. Brahmattarañca pāsādanti suvaṇṇapāsādañca. Kenatthenāti tvaṃ etesu ramaṇakādīsu catasso aṭṭha soḷasa dvattiṃsāti etā devadhītaro pahāya te pāsāde atikkamitvā kena kāraṇena idha āgatoti.

Therein, 'Ramaṇaka' means the crystal palace. 'Sadāmatta' means the silver palace. 'Dūbhaka' means the jewel palace. 'And the Brahmuttara palace' means the golden palace. 'For what reason?' means: 'Having abandoned the four, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two celestial nymphs in those palaces—Ramaṇaka and the others—and having passed by those palaces, for what reason have you come here?'

Tato mittavindako tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Mittavindaka spoke the third verse:

102.

102.

“Ito [V 3.0180] bahutarā bhogā, atra maññe bhavissare;

Iti etāya saññāya, passa maṃ byasanaṃ gata”nti.

“Pleasures far greater than these, I thought, would be here; with such a perception, see me come to ruin.”

Tattha ito bahutarāti imesu catūsu pāsādesu bhogehi atirekatarā bhavissanti.

Therein, 'far greater than these' means: 'Pleasures will be much more abundant than the pleasures in these four palaces.'

Tato bodhisatto sesagāthā abhāsi –

Then the Bodhisatta spoke the remaining verses:

103.

103.

“Catubbhi aṭṭhajjhagamā, aṭṭhāhipi ca soḷasa;

Soḷasāhi ca bāttiṃsa, atricchaṃ cakkamāsado;

Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake.

“From four you came to eight, from eight to sixteen; from sixteen to thirty-two. Through excessive greed you have encountered the wheel. On the head of a person smitten by craving, the wheel spins on his crown.”

104.

104.

“Uparivisālā [M 3.0194] duppūrā, icchā visaṭagāminī;

Ye ca taṃ anugijjhanti, te honti cakkadhārino”ti.

“Vast and hard to fill is craving, which spreads far and wide. Those who are greedy for it become bearers of the wheel.”

Tattha uparivisālāti mittavindaka taṇhā nāmesā āseviyamānā uparivisālā hoti patthaṭā, mahāsamuddo viya duppūrā, rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ icchamānāya icchāya patthaṭāya visaṭagāminī, tasmā ye purisā taṃ evarūpaṃ taṇhaṃ anugijjhanti, punappunaṃ giddhā hutvā gaṇhanti. Te honti cakkadhārinoti te etaṃ khuracakkaṃ dhārentīti vadati.

Therein, 'vast' means: O Mittavindaka, this thing called craving, when indulged in, becomes vast and widespread. It is hard to fill, like the great ocean. It 'spreads far and wide' because of the spreading of desire that seeks this or that object among objects such as forms. Therefore, those persons who are greedy for such craving, being greedy again and again, grasp it. 'They become bearers of the wheel' means he says they bear this razor-wheel.

Mittavindakaṃ pana kathentameva nipisamānaṃ taṃ khuracakkaṃ bhassi, tena so puna kathetuṃ nāsakkhi. Devaputto attano devaṭṭhānameva gato.

But as Mittavindaka was speaking, the razor-wheel, grinding away, whirled, and so he was unable to speak further. The deva's son returned to his own celestial abode.

Satthā [P 3.0208] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mittavindako dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, devaputto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection in the birth story: “At that time, Mittavindaka was the monk who is difficult to admonish, but the deva's son was I myself.”

Mittavindakajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Mittavindaka Jātaka, the Ninth.

[370] 10. Palāsajātakavaṇṇanā

[370] 10. The Commentary on the Palāsa Jātaka

Haṃso palāsamavacāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kilesaniggahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu paññāsajātake [V 3.0181] āvi bhavissati. Idha pana satthā bhikkhū āmantetvā “bhikkhave, kileso nāma āsaṅkitabbova, appamattako samānopi nigrodhagaccho viya vināsaṃ pāpeti, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi āsaṅkitabbaṃ āsaṅkiṃsuyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'The swan spoke to the Palāsa tree.' This the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the subduing of the defilements. The full story will be told in the Paññāsa Jātaka. Here, the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, a defilement is certainly something to be feared. Though it may be tiny, like a banyan sapling, it can lead to destruction. The wise of old also feared what ought to be feared.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto suvaṇṇahaṃsayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto cittakūṭapabbate suvaṇṇaguhāyaṃ vasanto himavantapadese jātassare sayaṃjātasāliṃ khāditvā āgacchati. Tassa gamanāgamanamagge mahāpalāsarukkho ahosi. So gacchantopi tattha vissamitvā gacchati, āgacchantopi tattha vissamitvā āgacchati[M 3.0195]. Athassa tasmiṃ rukkhe nibbattadevatāya saddhiṃ vissāso ahosi. Aparabhāge ekā sakuṇikā ekasmiṃ nigrodharukkhe nigrodhapakkaṃ khāditvā āgantvā tasmiṃ palāsarukkhe nisīditvā viṭapantare vaccaṃ pātesi. Tattha nigrodhagaccho jāto, so caturaṅgulamattakāle rattaṅkurapalāsatāya sobhati.
