Haṃsarājā taṃ disvā rukkhadevataṃ āmantetvā “samma palāsa, nigrodho nāma yamhi rukkhe jāyati, vaḍḍhanto taṃ nāseti, imassa vaḍḍhituṃ mā deti, vimānaṃ te nāsessati, paṭikacceva naṃ uddharitvā chaḍḍehi, āsaṅkitabbayuttakaṃ nāma āsaṅkituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti palāsadevatāya saddhiṃ mantento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a golden goose. When he came of age, he lived in a golden cave on Mount Cittakūṭa, and he would come to the Himalayan region to eat self-grown rice from a natural lake. On his travel route, there was a great Palāsa tree. He would rest there when going and rest there when returning. He became friendly with the deity dwelling in that tree. Later, a certain bird ate a ripe banyan fruit from a banyan tree, came and perched on that Palāsa tree, and dropped its excrement in a fork of the tree. A banyan sapling grew there. When it was about four fingers high, it was beautiful with its red sprouts and leaves. The goose king saw it and addressed the tree deity: 'Friend Palāsa, when a banyan grows on a tree, it destroys that tree as it grows. Do not let this one grow; it will destroy your mansion. Uproot it right away and throw it out. It is proper to fear what ought to be feared.' Conversing thus with the Palāsa deity, he spoke the first verse:

105.

105.

“Haṃso [P 3.0209] palāsamavaca, nigrodho samma jāyati;

Aṅkasmiṃ te nisinnova, so te mammāni checchatī”ti.

“The goose spoke to the Palāsa: ‘Friend, a banyan grows; seated as if in your lap, it will sever your vital parts.’”

Paṭhamapādo panettha abhisambuddhena hutvā satthārā vutto. Palāsanti palāsadevataṃ. Sammāti vayassa. Aṅkasminti viṭabhiyaṃ. So te mammāni checchatīti so te aṅke saṃvaḍḍho sapatto viya jīvitaṃ chindissatīti attho. Jīvitasaṅkhārā hi idha “mammānī”ti vuttā.

The first line of the verse here was spoken by the Teacher after he became fully enlightened. 'To the Palāsa' means to the Palāsa tree-deity. 'Friend' means companion. 'In the lap' means on a forked branch. 'It will sever your vital parts' means: having grown up in your lap, it will cut off your life like an enemy—this is the meaning. For here 'vital parts' refers to the life-formations.

Taṃ sutvā tassa vacanaṃ agaṇhantī palāsadevatā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Palāsa deity, not taking his advice, spoke the second verse:

106.

106.

“Vaḍḍhatāmeva nigrodho, patiṭṭhassa bhavāmahaṃ;

Yathā pitā ca mātā ca, evaṃ me so bhavissatī”ti.

“Let the banyan grow! I will be its support. Just as a father and a mother are, so will it be to me.”

Tassattho – samma, na tvaṃ jānāsi vaḍḍhatameva esa, ahamassa yathā bālakāle puttānaṃ mātāpitaro [V 3.0182] patiṭṭhā honti, tathā bhavissāmi, yathā pana saṃvaḍḍhā puttā pacchā mahallakakāle mātāpitūnaṃ patiṭṭhā honti, mayhampi pacchā mahallakakāle evameva so patiṭṭho bhavissatīti.

The meaning is this: ‘Friend, let this one grow! Just as parents are a support for their children in childhood, so I will be for it. And just as grown children later become a support for their parents in their old age, so too will it be a support for me in my old age.’

Tato haṃso tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the goose spoke the third stanza:

107.

107.

“Yaṃ tvaṃ aṅkasmiṃ vaḍḍhesi, khīrarukkhaṃ bhayānakaṃ;

Āmanta kho taṃ gacchāma, vuḍḍhi massa na ruccatī”ti.

“That which you have raised in your lap, a fearsome milk-tree—we now take leave of you and will go; its growth does not please me.”

Tattha yaṃ tvanti yasmā tvaṃ etañca bhayadāyakattena bhayānakaṃ khīrarukkhaṃ sapattaṃ viya aṅke vaḍḍhesi. Āmanta kho tanti tasmā mayaṃ taṃ āmantetvā [M 3.0196] jānāpetvā gacchāma. Vuḍḍhi massāti assa vuḍḍhi mayhaṃ na ruccatīti.

Herein, 'that which you' means: because you raise this fearsome milk-tree—fearsome because it brings fear—in your lap as if it were a rival. 'We now take leave of you' means: therefore we, having addressed you and informed you, will go. 'Its growth does not please me' means: this one’s growth does not please me.

Evañca pana vatvā haṃsarājā pakkhe pasāretvā cittakūṭapabbatameva gato. Tato paṭṭhāya puna nāgacchi. Aparabhāge nigrodho vaḍḍhiṃ, tasmiṃ ekā rukkhadevatāpi nibbatti. So vaḍḍhanto palāsaṃ bhañji, sākhāhi saddhiṃyeva devatāya vimānaṃ pati. Sā tasmiṃ kāle haṃsarañño vacanaṃ sallakkhetvā “idaṃ anāgatabhayaṃ disvā haṃsarājā kathesi[P 3.0210], ahaṃ panassa vacanaṃ nākāsi”nti paridevamānā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, the goose king spread his wings and went straight to Mount Cittakūṭa. From then on, he never returned. Later, the banyan tree grew, and a tree deity was born in it. As it grew, it broke the Palāsa tree, and the deity's mansion fell along with its branches. At that time, reflecting on the words of the goose king, the deity lamented, “The goose king spoke having foreseen this future danger, but I did not follow his words,” and she uttered the fourth stanza:

108.

108.

“Idāni kho maṃ bhāyeti, mahānerunidassanaṃ;

Haṃsassa anabhiññāya, mahā me bhayamāgata”nti.

“Now it frightens me; through not understanding the goose's advice, which was solid like Great Neru, great fear has come upon me.”

Tattha idāni kho maṃ bhāyetīti ayaṃ nigrodho taruṇakāle tosetvā idāni maṃ bhāyāpeti santāseti. Mahānerunidassananti sinerupabbatasadisaṃ mahantaṃ haṃsarājassa vacanaṃ sutvā ajānitvā taruṇakāleyeva etassa anuddhaṭattā. Mahā me bhayamāgatanti idāni mayhaṃ mahantaṃ bhayaṃ āgatanti paridevi.

Herein, 'now it frightens me' means: this banyan tree, having pleased me when it was young, now frightens and terrifies me. 'Solid like Great Neru' refers to the great words of the goose king which were like Mount Sineru; by not having understood them and failing to uproot the tree in its youth, this fear has come. 'Great fear has come upon me' means: she lamented, ‘Now a great fear has come upon me.’

Nigrodhopi vaḍḍhanto sabbaṃ palāsaṃ bhañjitvā khāṇukamattameva akāsi. Devatāya vimānaṃ sabbaṃ antaradhāyi.

The banyan tree, as it grew, broke the entire palāsa tree and reduced it to a mere stump. The deity’s entire mansion vanished.

109.

109.

“Na [V 3.0183] tassa vuḍḍhi kusalappasatthā, yo vaḍḍhamāno ghasate patiṭṭhaṃ;

Tassūparodhaṃ parisaṅkamāno, patārayī mūlavadhāya dhīro”ti. –

“The growth of one who, while growing, devours his own support is not praised by the wise. The wise one, anticipating obstruction from him, should strive to destroy the root.”

Pañcamā abhisambuddhagāthā.

The fifth is a stanza of perfect enlightenment.

Tattha kusalappasatthāti kusalehi pasatthā. Ghasateti khādati, vināsetīti attho. Patārayīti patarati vāyamati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bhikkhave, yo vaḍḍhamāno attano patiṭṭhaṃ nāseti, tassa vuḍḍhi paṇḍitehi na pasatthā, tassa pana abbhantarassa vā bāhirassa vā parissayassa “ito me uparodho bhavissatī”ti evaṃ uparodhaṃ vināsaṃ parisaṅkamāno vīro ñāṇasampanno mūlavadhāya parakkamatīti.

Herein, 'praised by the wise' means praised by the virtuous. 'Devours' means eats; the meaning is ‘destroys.’ 'Should strive' means one endeavors, one exerts oneself. This is the meaning: ‘Monks, the growth of one who, while growing, destroys his own support is not praised by the wise. But a hero endowed with wisdom, anticipating danger, whether internal or external, and thinking, “Obstruction will come to me from this,” strives for the destruction of its root.’

Satthā [M 3.0197] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne pañcasatā bhikkhū arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tadā suvaṇṇahaṃso ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the truths and made the connection in the birth story. At the conclusion of the teaching on the truths, five hundred monks attained arahantship. ‘At that time, the golden goose was I myself.’

Palāsajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Palāsa Jātaka, the Tenth.

Vaṇṇārohavaggo dutiyo.

The Vaṇṇāroha Chapter, the Second.

3. Aḍḍhavaggo

3. The Half Chapter

[371] 1. Dīghītikosalajātakavaṇṇanā

[371] 1. The Commentary on the Dīghītikosala Jātaka

Evaṃbhūtassa [V 3.0184][P 3.0211] te rājāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosambake bhaṇḍanakārake ārabbha kathesi. Tesañhi jetavanaṃ āgantvā khamāpanakāle satthā te āmantetvā “bhikkhave, tumhe mayhaṃ orasā mukhato jātā puttā nāma, puttehi ca pitarā dinnaṃ ovādaṃ bhindituṃ na vaṭṭati, tumhe pana mama ovādaṃ na karittha, porāṇakapaṇḍitā attano mātāpitaro ghātetvā rajjaṃ gahetvā ṭhitacorepi araññe hatthapathaṃ āgate mātāpitūhi dinnaṃ ovādaṃ na bhindissāmāti na mārayiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this story beginning with the words, “For you, O king, being in such a state,” concerning the quarrelsome monks of Kosambi. When they came to Jetavana to ask for forgiveness, the Teacher addressed them: “Monks, you are my legitimate sons, born from my mouth. It is not proper for sons to break the advice given by their father, yet you did not follow my advice. The wise of old, even when a thief who had killed their own parents and seized their kingdom came into their power in the forest, did not kill him, thinking, ‘We will not break the advice given by our parents.’” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Imasmiṃ pana jātake dvepi vatthūni. Saṅghabhedakakkhandhake vitthārato āvi bhavissanti. So pana dīghāvukumāro araññe attano aṅke nipannaṃ bārāṇasirājānaṃ cūḷāya gahetvā “idāni mayhaṃ mātāpitughātakaṃ coraṃ khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ katvā chindissāmī”ti asiṃ ukkhipanto tasmiṃ khaṇe mātāpitūhi dinnaṃ ovādaṃ saritvā “jīvitaṃ cajantopi tesaṃ ovādaṃ na bhindissāmi, kevalaṃ imaṃ tajjessāmī”ti cintetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In this birth story, there are two accounts, which will be clarified in detail in the Khandhaka on Schism in the Sangha. Prince Dīghāvu, when the king of Bārāṇasī was lying with his head in his lap in the forest, seized him by his top-knot and raised his sword, thinking, “Now I will cut this thief who killed my parents into pieces!” But at that moment, he recalled the advice given by his parents and thought, “Even if I have to give up my life, I will not break their advice. I will only threaten him.” Then he spoke the first stanza:

110.

110.

“Evaṃbhūtassa te rāja, āgatassa vase mama;

Atthi nu koci pariyāyo, yo taṃ dukkhā pamocaye”ti.

“For you, O king, being in such a state, having come into my power, is there any means at all that could release you from this plight?”

Tattha [M 3.0198] vase mamāti mama vasaṃ āgatassa. Pariyāyoti kāraṇaṃ.

Herein, 'into my power' means: of one who has come into my power. 'Means' means: a reason or way.

Tato rājā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the king spoke the second stanza:

111.

111.

“Evaṃbhūtassa me tāta, āgatassa vase tava;

Natthi no koci pariyāyo, yo maṃ dukkhā pamocaye”ti.

“For me, my dear, being in such a state, having come into your power, there is no means at all that could release me from this plight.”

Tattha [V 3.0185][P 3.0212] noti nipātamatthaṃ, natthi koci pariyāyo, yo maṃ etasmā dukkhā pamocayeti attho.

Herein, 'no' (no) is just a particle. The meaning is: ‘There is no means at all that could release me from this plight.’

Tato bodhisatto avasesagāthā abhāsi –

Then the Bodhisatta spoke the remaining stanzas:

112.

112.

“Nāññaṃ sucaritaṃ rāja, nāññaṃ rāja subhāsitaṃ;

Tāyate maraṇakāle, evamevitaraṃ dhanaṃ.

“O king, nothing but good conduct, nothing but well-spoken words protects one at the time of death; and just so is other wealth.

113.

113.

“Akkocchi maṃ avadhi maṃ, ajini maṃ ahāsi me;

Ye ca taṃ upanayhanti, veraṃ tesaṃ na sammati.

“‘He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me’—in those who harbor such thoughts, hatred is not appeased.

114.

114.

“Akkocchi maṃ avadhi maṃ, ajini maṃ ahāsi me;

Ye ca taṃ nupanayhanti, veraṃ tesūpasammati.

“‘He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me’—in those who do not harbor such thoughts, hatred is appeased.

115.

115.

“Na hi verena verāni, sammantīdha kudācanaṃ;

Averena ca sammanti, esa dhammo sanantano”nti.

“For not by hatred are hatreds ever appeased here, but by non-hatred are they appeased; this is an eternal law.”

Tattha nāññaṃ sucaritanti nāññaṃ sucaritā, ayameva vā pāṭho, ṭhapetvā sucaritaṃ aññaṃ na passāmīti attho. Idha “sucarita”ntipi “subhāsita”ntipi mātāpitūhi dinnaṃ ovādaṃyeva sandhāyāha. Evamevāti niratthakameva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, aññatra ovādānusiṭṭhisaṅkhātā sucaritasubhāsitā maraṇakāle tāyituṃ rakkhituṃ samattho nāma añño natthi, yaṃ etaṃ itaraṃ dhanaṃ, taṃ evameva niratthakameva hoti, tvañhi idāni mayhaṃ koṭisatasahassamattampi dhanaṃ dadanto jīvitaṃ na labheyyāsi, tasmā veditabbametaṃ “dhanato sucaritasubhāsitameva uttaritara”nti.

Herein, 'no other good conduct': this can also be read as nāññaṃ sucaritā; the meaning is, ‘I see nothing other than good conduct.’ Here, both ‘good conduct’ and ‘well-spoken words’ refer specifically to the advice given by his parents. 'Just so' (evameva) means simply useless. This is what is said: ‘Great king, apart from good conduct and well-spoken words in the sense of advice and instruction, there is nothing else able to save or protect one at the time of death; as for other wealth, it is just so, simply useless. For even if you were to give me wealth amounting to a hundred thousand crores, you would not get your life back. Therefore, it should be understood that good conduct and well-spoken words are far superior to wealth.’

Sesagāthāsupi ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – mahārāja, ye purisā “ayaṃ maṃ akkosi, ayaṃ maṃ pahari, ayaṃ maṃ ajini, ayaṃ mama santakaṃ ahāsī”ti [M 3.0199] evaṃ veraṃ upanayhanti bandhitvā viya hadaye ṭhapenti, tesaṃ veraṃ na upasammati. Ye ca panetaṃ na upanayhanti hadaye na ṭhapenti, tesaṃ vūpasammati. Verāni hi na kadāci verena sammanti, avereneva pana sammanti. Esa dhammo sanantanoti eso porāṇako dhammo cirakālappavatto sabhāvoti.

This is the summarized meaning of the remaining stanzas: Great king, for those persons who harbor hatred, thinking, ‘He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me of my property,’ keeping it in their hearts as if they have bound it there, their hatred is not appeased. But for those who do not harbor it, who do not keep it in their hearts, for them it is appeased. For hatreds are never appeased by hatred, but they are appeased by non-hatred. 'This is an eternal law' means: this is an ancient law, long-established, the natural state of things.

Evañca [V 3.0186] pana vatvā bodhisatto “ahaṃ, mahārāja, tayi na dubbhāmi, tvaṃ pana maṃ mārehī”ti tassa hatthe asiṃ ṭhapesi. Rājāpi “nāhaṃ tayi dubbhāmī”ti sapathaṃ katvā tena saddhiṃ nagaraṃ gantvā taṃ amaccānaṃ dassetvā “ayaṃ, bhaṇe, kosalarañño putto dīghāvukumāro nāma, iminā mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ [P 3.0213] dinnaṃ, na labbhā imaṃ kiñci kātu”nti vatvā attano dhītaraṃ datvā pitu santake rajje patiṭṭhāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya ubhopi samaggā sammodamānā rajjaṃ kāresuṃ.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta said, “Great king, I bear you no ill will. Will you kill me?” and he placed the sword in the king’s hand. The king too made an oath, saying, “I bear you no ill will,” and went with him to the city. He presented him to his ministers and said, “Sirs, this is Prince Dīghāvu, the son of the king of Kosala. My life has been given to me by him; nothing must be done to him.” Having said this, he gave him his own daughter in marriage and established him in his father’s kingdom. From then on, both kings ruled in harmony and concord.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ, dīghāvukumāro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection in the birth story: “At that time, the parents were the members of the great royal family, but Prince Dīghāvu was I myself.”

Dīghītikosalajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Dīghītikosala Jātaka, the First.

[372] 2. Migapotakajātakavaṇṇanā

[372] 2. The Commentary on the Migapotaka Jātaka

Agārā paccupetassāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ mahallakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kirekaṃ dārakaṃ pabbājesi. Sāmaṇero taṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā aparabhāge aphāsukena kālamakāsi. Tassa kālakiriyāya mahallako sokābhibhūto mahantena saddena paridevanto vicari. Bhikkhū saññāpetuṃ asakkontā dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asuko nāma mahallako sāmaṇerassa kālakiriyāya paridevanto vicarati, maraṇassatibhāvanāya paribāhiro eso bhavissatī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa etasmiṃ mate paridevanto vicarī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This story beginning with 'Having gone forth from the home' was told by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain elderly monk. It is said that he had ordained a young boy. The novice attended to him respectfully, but later he fell ill and passed away. Overcome with grief at his death, the elderly monk wandered about wailing loudly. Unable to console him, the bhikkhus raised a topic of discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: 'Friends, that elderly monk is wandering about lamenting the death of the novice. He must be a stranger to the development of mindfulness of death.' The Teacher came and asked, 'For what discussion are you now sitting together here, bhikkhus?' When they told him what it was, he said, 'Bhikkhus, not only now, but in the past too, he wandered about lamenting when this one died.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 3.0200] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sakkattaṃ kāresi. Tadā eko kāsiraṭṭhavāsī brāhmaṇo himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā phalāphalehi yāpesi. So ekadivasaṃ araññe ekaṃ matamātikaṃ migapotakaṃ disvā assamaṃ ānetvā gocaraṃ datvā posesi. Migapotako vaḍḍhanto abhirūpo ahosi sobhaggappatto. Tāpaso taṃ attano puttakaṃ katvā pariharati. Ekadivasaṃ migapotako bahuṃ tiṇaṃ khāditvā ajīrakena kālamakāsi. Tāpaso “putto me mato”ti paridevanto vicarati. Tadā sakko devarājā lokaṃ pariggaṇhanto [V 3.0187] taṃ tāpasaṃ disvā “saṃvejessāmi [P 3.0214] na”nti āgantvā ākāse ṭhito paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka. At that time, a brahmin from the Kāsi country entered the Himalayas, went forth as an ascetic, and sustained himself on wild fruits and roots. One day in the forest he saw a young deer whose mother had died. He brought it to his hermitage, gave it food, and raised it. The young deer grew up to be handsome and graceful. The ascetic cared for it as if it were his own son. One day, having eaten too much grass, the young deer died of indigestion. The ascetic wandered about lamenting, 'My son is dead!' Then Sakka, king of the devas, surveying the world, saw the ascetic and thought, 'I will stir him.' Coming and standing in the air, he spoke the first verse:

116.

116.

“Agārā paccupetassa, anagārassa te sato;

Samaṇassa na taṃ sādhu, yaṃ petamanusocasī”ti.

“Having gone forth from home to homelessness, for you, an ascetic, it is not good to grieve for one who is dead.”

Taṃ sutvā tāpaso dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the ascetic uttered the second verse:

117.

117.

“Saṃvāsena have sakka, manussassa migassa vā;

Hadaye jāyate pemaṃ, na taṃ sakkā asocitu”nti.

“Through living together, indeed, Sakka, whether with a person or a beast, affection is born in the heart; it is not possible not to grieve for that.”

Tattha na taṃ sakkāti taṃ manussaṃ vā tiracchānaṃ vā na sakkā asocituṃ, socāmiyevāhanti.

Herein, 'na taṃ sakkā' means: it is not possible not to grieve for that person or animal; the meaning is, 'I certainly grieve.'

Tato sakko dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then Sakka spoke two verses:

118.

118.

“Mataṃ marissaṃ rodanti, ye rudanti lapanti ca;

Tasmā tvaṃ isi mā rodi, roditaṃ moghamāhu santo.

“Those who weep and lament weep for the dead and for those who are to die; therefore, sage, do not weep, for the good say that weeping is in vain.”

119.

119.

“Roditena have brahme, mato peto samuṭṭhahe;

Sabbe saṅgamma rodāma, aññamaññassa ñātake”ti.

“If, brahmin, a dead person could arise by weeping, then we would all gather together and weep for each other's relatives.”

Tattha marissanti yo idāni marissati, taṃ. Lapanti cāti vilapanti ca. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ye loke matañca marissantañca rodanti, te rudanti ceva vilapanti ca, tesaṃ assupacchijjanadivaso nāma natthi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Sadāpi matānañca marissantānañca atthitāya. Tasmā tvaṃ isi mā rodi. Kiṃkāraṇā[M 3.0201]? Roditaṃ moghamāhu santoti, buddhādayo pana paṇḍitā roditaṃ “mogha”nti vadanti. Mato petoti yo esa mato petoti vuccati, yadi so roditena samuṭṭhaheyya, evaṃ sante kiṃ nikkammā acchāma, sabbeva samāgamma aññamaññassa ñātake rodāma. Yasmā pana te roditakāraṇā na uṭṭhahanti, tasmā roditassa moghabhāvaṃ sādheti.

Herein, 'for those who are to die' means for one who is now about to die. 'And lament' means and wail. This is the meaning: those in the world who weep for the dead and for those who are to die, they both weep and wail, and for them there is no day when their tears cease. Why is that? Because of the constant existence of the dead and those who are to die. Therefore, sage, do not weep. Why is that? 'For the good say that weeping is in vain': the wise, such as the Buddhas, say that weeping is 'in vain.' 'A dead person': this refers to one who is called 'dead, departed.' If he could rise by weeping, that being so, why should we remain inactive? We would all gather together and weep for each other's relatives. But since they do not rise on account of weeping, he thereby establishes the futility of weeping.

Evaṃ [V 3.0188] sakkassa kathentassa tāpaso “niratthakaṃ rodita”nti sallakkhetvā sakkassa thutiṃ karonto tisso gāthā abhāsi –

When Sakka had spoken thus, the ascetic, realizing that 'weeping is useless,' spoke three verses in praise of Sakka:

120.

120.

“Ādittaṃ [P 3.0215] vata maṃ santaṃ, ghatasittaṃva pāvakaṃ;

Vārinā viya osiñcaṃ, sabbaṃ nibbāpaye daraṃ.

“Indeed, I was burning, like a fire sprinkled with ghee; as if with water you have sprinkled me and extinguished all my grief.”

121.

121.

“Abbahi vata me sallaṃ, yamāsi hadayassitaṃ;

Yo me sokaparetassa, puttasokaṃ apānudi.

“Indeed, you have drawn out the dart that was lodged in my heart—you who have removed the sorrow for my son from me, who was overcome by grief.”

122.

122.

“Sohaṃ abbūḷhasallosmi, vītasoko anāvilo;

Na socāmi na rodāmi, tava sutvāna vāsavā”ti.

“With dart drawn out, I am now sorrow-free and untroubled. I do not grieve, I do not weep, having heard you, O Vāsava.”

Tattha yamāsīti yaṃ me āsi. Hadayassitanti hadaye nissitaṃ. Apānudīti nīhari. Sakko tāpasassa ovādaṃ datvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

Herein, 'yamāsi' means 'which was in me.' 'Hadayassitaṃ' means 'lodged in the heart.' 'Apānudi' means 'he has removed.' Having given this admonition to the ascetic, Sakka went back to his own place.

Satthā idhaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā tāpaso mahallako ahosi, migo sāmaṇero, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: 'At that time, the ascetic was the elderly monk, the deer was the novice, and Sakka was myself.'

Migapotakajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Fawn Jātaka, the second.

[373] 3. Mūsikajātakavaṇṇanā

[373] 3. The Commentary on the Mouse Jātaka

Kuhiṃ gatā kattha gatāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ajātasattuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā thusajātake (jā. 1.4.149 ādayo) vitthāritameva. Idhāpi satthā tatheva rājānaṃ sakiṃ puttena saddhiṃ kīḷamānaṃ sakiṃ dhammaṃ suṇantaṃ disvā “taṃ nissāya rañño bhayaṃ uppajjissatī”ti ñatvā [M 3.0202] “mahārāja, porāṇakarājāno āsaṅkitabbaṃ āsaṅkitvā attano puttaṃ ‘amhākaṃ dhūmakāle rajjaṃ kāretū’ti ekamante akaṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Where has she gone? Where has she gone?' This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove concerning Ajātasattu. The story has been explained in full below in the Thusa Jātaka. Here too, the Teacher, seeing the king at one time playing with his son and at another time listening to the Dhamma, knew, 'On account of him, danger will arise for the king.' He said, 'Great King, the kings of old, being suspicious of what should be suspected, set their sons aside, thinking, "Let them rule the kingdom when we are gone."' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto takkasilāyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā disāpāmokkhācariyo ahosi. Tassa santike bārāṇasirañño putto yavakumāro nāma [V 3.0189] sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā anuyogaṃ datvā gantukāmo taṃ āpucchi. Ācariyo “puttaṃ nissāya tassa antarāyo bhavissatī”ti aṅgavijjāvasena ñatvā “etamassa harissāmī”ti ekaṃ upamaṃ upadhāretuṃ ārabhi. Tadā panassa eko [P 3.0216] asso ahosi, tassa pāde vaṇo uṭṭhahi, taṃ vaṇānurakkhaṇatthaṃ geheyeva kariṃsu. Tassāvidūre eko udapāno atthi. Athekā mūsikā gehā nikkhamitvā assassa pāde vaṇaṃ khādati, asso vāretuṃ na sakkoti. So ekadivasaṃ vedanaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto mūsikaṃ khādituṃ āgataṃ pādena paharitvā māretvā udapāne pātesi. Assagopakā mūsikaṃ apassantā “aññesu divasesu mūsikā āgantvā vaṇaṃ khādati, idāni na paññāyati, kahaṃ nu kho gatā”ti vadiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in Takkasilā and became a world-renowned teacher. The son of the king of Bārāṇasī, Prince Yava, having learned all the arts from him and completed his training, wished to depart and took leave of his teacher. The teacher, knowing by the science of bodily marks that 'danger will come to him from his son,' thought, 'I will avert this for him,' and began to devise a simile. At that time, he had a horse on whose foot a sore had broken out, and to protect the wound, they kept it in a stable. Not far from there was a well. A mouse came out of her hole and would gnaw on the horse’s sore, and the horse could not prevent it. One day, unable to bear the pain, when the mouse came to gnaw, the horse struck it with its hoof, killed it, and dropped it into the well. The horse-grooms, not seeing the mouse, said, 'On other days the mouse comes and gnaws the sore, but now she is not to be seen. Where can she have gone?'

Bodhisatto taṃ kāraṇaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā “aññe ajānantā ‘kahaṃ mūsikā gatā’ti vadanti, mūsikāya pana māretvā udapāne khittabhāvaṃ ahameva jānāmī”ti idameva kāraṇaṃ upamaṃ katvā paṭhamaṃ gāthaṃ bandhitvā rājakumārassa adāsi. So aparaṃ upamaṃ upadhārento tameva assaṃ paruḷhavaṇaṃ nikkhamitvā ekaṃ yavavatthuṃ gantvā “yavaṃ khādissāmī”ti vaticchiddena mukhaṃ pavesentaṃ disvā tameva kāraṇaṃ upamaṃ katvā dutiyaṃ gāthaṃ bandhitvā tassa adāsi. Tatiyagāthaṃ pana attano paññābaleneva bandhitvā tampi tassa datvā “tāta, tvaṃ rajje patiṭṭhāya sāyaṃ nhānapokkharaṇiṃ gacchanto yāva dhurasopānā paṭhamaṃ gāthaṃ sajjhāyanto gaccheyyāsi, tava nivasanapāsādaṃ pavisanto yāva sopānapādamūlā dutiyaṃ gāthaṃ sajjhāyanto gaccheyyāsi, tato yāva sopānamatthakā tatiyaṃ gāthaṃ sajjhāyanto gaccheyyāsī”ti vatvā pesesi.

The Bodhisatta, having witnessed the event, thought, 'Others who do not know say, "Where has Musika gone?" But I alone know that she was killed and thrown into the well.' Taking this very event as a simile, he composed the first verse and gave it to the prince. Then, seeking another simile, he saw that same horse, its wound now healed, go out to a barley field and, intending to eat barley, poke its muzzle through a gap in the fence. Taking this event as a simile, he composed a second verse and gave it to him. He composed the third verse by the power of his own wisdom and gave that to him as well, saying: 'My dear, when you are established in the kingdom, as you go to the bathing pond in the evening, you should recite the first verse until you reach the staircase entrance. When entering your residential palace, you should recite the second verse until you reach the foot of the stairs. Then, you should recite the third verse until you reach the top of the stairs.' Having said this, he sent him away.

So [M 3.0203] kumāro gantvā uparājā hutvā pitu accayena rajjaṃ kāresi, tasseko putto jāyi. So soḷasavassakāle rajjalobhena “pitaraṃ māressāmī”ti cintetvā upaṭṭhāke āha “mayhaṃ pitā taruṇo, ahaṃ etassa dhūmakālaṃ olokento mahallako bhavissāmi jarājiṇṇo, tādise kāle laddhenapi rajjena ko attho”ti. Te āhaṃsu “deva, na sakkā paccantaṃ gantvā corattaṃ kātuṃ, tava pitaraṃ kenaci upāyena māretvā rajjaṃ gaṇhā”ti[P 3.0217]. So “sādhū”ti antonivesane rañño sāyaṃ nhānapokkharaṇīsamīpaṃ gantvā “ettha naṃ māressāmī”ti khaggaṃ gahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Rājā sāyaṃ mūsikaṃ nāma dāsiṃ “gantvā pokkharaṇīpiṭṭhiṃ sodhetvā ehi, nhāyissāmī”ti pesesi. Sā gantvā pokkharaṇīpiṭṭhiṃ sodhentī kumāraṃ passi. Kumāro attano kammassa pākaṭabhāvabhayena taṃ dvidhā chinditvā pokkharaṇiyaṃ pātesi. Rājā nhāyituṃ agamāsi[V 3.0190]. Sesajano “ajjāpi mūsikā dāsī na punāgacchati, kuhiṃ gatā kattha gatā”ti āha. Rājā –

The prince went and became viceroy, and after his father’s passing, he ruled the kingdom. A son was born to him. When his son was sixteen, out of greed for the kingdom, he thought, 'I will kill my father,' and said to his attendants: 'My father is young. If I wait to see his cremation smoke, I will be an old man, worn out by age. What is the use of a kingdom gained at such a time?' They replied: 'Your majesty, it is not possible to go to the border region and become a bandit. Kill your father by some stratagem and take the kingdom.' He agreed, and in the inner palace he went near the king’s evening bathing pond, and thinking, 'I will kill him here,' he stood with a sword. In the evening, the king sent a slave-girl named Mūsikā, saying, 'Go and clean the bank of the pond and come back; I am going to bathe.' She went, and while cleaning the bank of the pond, she saw the prince. Fearing that his deed would be revealed, the prince cut her in two and threw her into the pond. The king went to bathe. The other people said, 'The slave-girl Mūsikā has still not returned. Where has she gone? Where has she gone?' The king—

123.

123.

“Kuhiṃ gatā kattha gatā, iti lālappatī jano;

Ahameveko jānāmi, udapāne mūsikā hatā”ti. –

“Where has she gone? Where has she gone?” Thus the people lament. “I alone know: Musika was killed in the well.”

Paṭhamaṃ gāthaṃ bhaṇanto pokkharaṇītīraṃ agamāsi.

Reciting the first verse, he went to the edge of the pond.

Tattha kuhiṃ gatā kattha gatāti aññamaññavevacanāni. Iti lālappatīti evaṃ vippalapati. Iti ayaṃ gāthā “ajānanto jano mūsikā dāsī kuhiṃ gatāti vippalapati, rājakumārena dvidhā chinditvā mūsikāya pokkharaṇiyaṃ pātitabhāvaṃ ahameva eko jānāmī”ti rañño ajānantasseva imamatthaṃ dīpeti.

Herein, 'Where has she gone? Where has she gone?' are synonymous expressions. 'Thus the people lament' means thus they prattle. This verse, as if from the king who is himself unaware, reveals this meaning: ‘The ignorant people prattle, “Where has the slave-girl Mūsikā gone?” but I alone know that she was cut in two by the prince and thrown into the lotus pond.’

Kumāro “mayā katakammaṃ mayhaṃ pitarā ñāta”nti bhīto palāyitvā tamatthaṃ upaṭṭhākānaṃ ārocesi. Te sattaṭṭhadivasaccayena puna taṃ āhaṃsu “deva, sace rājā jāneyya, na tuṇhī bhaveyya, takkagāhena pana tena taṃ vuttaṃ bhavissati, mārehi na”nti. So punekadivasaṃ khaggahattho sopānapādamūle ṭhatvā rañño āgamanakāle ito cito ca paharaṇokāsaṃ olokesi. Rājā –

The prince, fearing, “My father knows what I have done,” fled and informed his attendants of the matter. After seven or eight days, they told him again: “Sire, if the king knew, he would not remain silent. He must have said that through mere conjecture. Kill him!” One day, standing at the foot of the stairs with a sword in hand, he looked for an opportunity to strike from here and there when the king arrived. The king—

124.

124.

“Yañcetaṃ iti cīti ca, gadrabhova nivattasi;

Udapāne mūsikaṃ hantvā, yavaṃ bhakkhetumicchasī”ti. –

“And as for this ‘here and there,’ you turn about like a donkey. Having killed Musika in the well, you wish to eat the barley.”

Dutiyaṃ [M 3.0204] gāthaṃ sajjhāyanto agamāsi. Ayampi [P 3.0218] gāthā “yasmā tvaṃ iti cīti ca ito cito ca paharaṇokāsaṃ olokento gadrabhova nivattasi, tasmā taṃ jānāmi ‘purimadivase pokkharaṇiyaṃ mūsikaṃ dāsiṃ hantvā ajja maṃ yavarājānaṃ bhakkhetuṃ māretuṃ icchasī’”ti rañño ajānantasseva imamatthaṃ dīpeti.

Reciting the second verse, he went on his way. This verse, too, as if from the king who is himself unaware, reveals this meaning: ‘Because you turn about like a donkey, looking for an opportunity to strike from this way and that, therefore I know it: having killed the slave-girl Mūsikā in the pond on a previous day, today you wish to eat—that is, to kill—me, King Yava, as if I were barley.’

Kumāro “diṭṭhomhi pitarā”ti utrasto palāyi. So puna aḍḍhamāsamattaṃ atikkamitvā “rājānaṃ dabbiyā paharitvā māressāmī”ti ekaṃ dīghadaṇḍakaṃ dabbipaharaṇaṃ gahetvā olumbitvā aṭṭhāsi. Rājā –

The prince, terrified, thinking, “I have been seen by my father,” fled. After about half a month had passed, thinking, “I will strike the king with a ladle and kill him,” he took a long-handled ladle and stood propped up by it. The king—

125.

125.

“Daharo [V 3.0191] cāsi dummedha, paṭhamuppattiko susu;

Dīghañcetaṃ samāsajja, na te dassāmi jīvita”nti. –

“You are young and witless, a fledgling in your first youth. Having taken up this long object, I will not grant you your life.”

Tatiyaṃ gāthaṃ sajjhāyanto sopānapādamatthakaṃ abhiruhi.

Reciting the third verse, he ascended to the top of the staircase.

Tattha paṭhamuppattikoti paṭhamavayena uppattito upeto, paṭhamavaye ṭhitoti attho. Susūti taruṇo. Dīghanti dīghadaṇḍakaṃ dabbipaharaṇaṃ. Samāsajjāti gahetvā, olumbitvā ṭhitosīti attho. Ayampi gāthā “dummedha, attano vayaṃ paribhuñjituṃ na labhissasi, na te dāni nillajjassa jīvitaṃ dassāmi, māretvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ chinditvā sūleyeva āvuṇāpessāmī”ti rañño ajānantasseva kumāraṃ santajjayamānā imamatthaṃ dīpeti.

Herein, 'paṭhamuppattiko' means endowed with birth in the first age; that is, being in the first stage of life. 'Susū' means young. 'Dīghaṃ' refers to the long-handled ladle. 'Samāsajja' means having taken it, that is, standing propped up by it. This verse, too, threatening the prince, reveals this meaning as if from the king who is himself unaware: ‘Witless one, you will not get to enjoy your youth! I will not now grant life to you, shameless as you are. I will kill you, cut you to pieces, and have you impaled on a stake!’

So taṃ divasaṃ palāyituṃ asakkonto “jīvitaṃ me dehi, devā”ti rañño pādamūle nipajji. Rājā taṃ tajjetvā saṅkhalikāhi bandhāpetvā bandhanāgāre kāretvā setacchattassa heṭṭhā alaṅkatarājāsane nisīditvā “amhākaṃ ācariyo disāpāmokkho brāhmaṇo imaṃ mayhaṃ antarāyaṃ disvā imā tisso gāthā abhāsī”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭho udānaṃ udānento sesagāthā abhāsi –

Unable to flee that day, he fell at the king’s feet, pleading, “Grant me my life, sire!” The king rebuked him, had him bound in chains and put in prison. Then, seated on an adorned royal throne beneath the white parasol, joyful and delighted, the king uttered an inspired utterance: “Our teacher, the world-renowned brahmin, foresaw this danger to me and spoke these three verses!” Then he recited the remaining verses:

126.

126.

“Nāntalikkhabhavanena, nāṅgaputtapinena vā;

Puttena hi patthayito, silokehi pamocito.

“Neither by the 'Sky-Mansion' charm, nor by the 'Angaputta-pina' charm was I saved; though targeted by my son, I was delivered by these verses.

127.

127.

“Sabbaṃ [M 3.0205] sutamadhīyetha, hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhimaṃ;

Sabbassa atthaṃ jāneyya, na ca sabbaṃ payojaye;

Hoti tādisako kālo, yattha atthāvahaṃ suta”nti.

“One should learn all that is heard, whether it be low, excellent, or middling. One should know the meaning of all, but not apply it all. There comes a time when what one has learned brings benefit.”

Tattha [P 3.0219] nāntalikkhabhavanenāti antalikkhabhavanaṃ vuccati dibbavimānaṃ, ahaṃ ajja antalikkhabhavanampi na āruḷho, tasmā antalikkhabhavanenāpi ajja maraṇato na pamocitomhi. Nāṅgaputtapinena vāti aṅgasarikkhakena vā puttapinenapi na pamocito. Puttena hi patthayitoti ahaṃ pana attano putteneva ajja māretuṃ patthito. Silokehi pamocitoti sohaṃ ācariyena bandhitvā dinnāhi gāthāhi pamocito.

Herein, 'not by a dwelling in the sky': a celestial mansion is called a dwelling in the sky. I did not ascend to a celestial mansion today, so I was not freed from death today by a dwelling in the sky. 'Nor by affection for a son': I was not freed even by affection for a son who is like my own limb. 'Sought by my son': I, however, was desired to be killed today by my own son. 'Freed by verses': I was freed by the verses that were composed and given to me by my teacher.

Sutanti [V 3.0192] pariyattiṃ. Adhīyethāti gaṇheyya sikkheyya. Hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhimanti hīnaṃ vā hotu uttamaṃ vā majjhimaṃ vā, sabbaṃ adhīyitabbamevāti dīpeti. Na ca sabbaṃ payojayeti hīnaṃ mantaṃ vā sippaṃ vā majjhimaṃ vā na payojaye, uttamameva payojayeyyāti attho. Yattha atthāvahaṃ sutanti yasmiṃ kāle mahosadhapaṇḍitassa kumbhakārakammakaraṇaṃ viya yaṃkiñci sikkhitasippaṃ atthāvahaṃ hoti, tādisopi kālo hotiyevāti attho. Aparabhāge rañño accayena kumāro rajje patiṭṭhāsi.

What is heard means the scriptures. 'One should learn' means one should grasp and train in it. 'Low, excellent, or middling' shows that whether it is inferior, supreme, or middling, all of it should be learned. 'But not apply all' means that one should not make use of an inferior or middling charm or craft, but should use only the supreme; that is the meaning. 'When what one has learned brings benefit' means that just as the craft of a potter was beneficial to the wise Mahosadha, there is indeed a time when any craft one has learned, whatever it may be, brings benefit; that is the meaning. Later, upon the king's demise, the prince was established in the kingdom.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā disāpāmokkho ācariyo ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the birth story: “At that time, the world-renowned teacher was I myself.”

Mūsikajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Mūsika Jātaka, the third, is finished.

[374] 4. Cūḷadhanuggahajātakavaṇṇanā

[374] 4. 4. The Commentary on the Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka

Sabbaṃ bhaṇḍanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tena bhikkhunā “purāṇadutiyikā maṃ, bhante, ukkaṇṭhāpetī”ti vutte satthā “esā bhikkhu, itthī na idāneva tuyhaṃ anatthakārikā, pubbepi te etaṃ nissāya asinā sīsaṃ chinna”nti vatvā bhikkhūhi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ', concerning the enticement by a former wife. When that bhikkhu said, “Venerable sir, my former wife is making me discontented,” the Teacher said: “Bhikkhu, this woman has been harmful to you not only now. In the past, too, on her account your head was cut off with a sword.” And, requested by that bhikkhu, he related the past.

Atīte [M 3.0206] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sakkattaṃ kāresi. Tadā eko bārāṇasivāsī brāhmaṇamāṇavo takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā dhanukamme nipphattiṃ patto cūḷadhanuggahapaṇḍito nāma ahosi. Athassa ācariyo “ayaṃ mayā sadisaṃ sippaṃ uggaṇhī”ti attano dhītaraṃ adāsi. So taṃ gahetvā “bārāṇasiṃ gamissāmī”ti maggaṃ paṭipajji. Antarāmagge eko vāraṇo ekaṃ padesaṃ suññamakāsi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ abhiruhituṃ na koci ussahi. Cūḷadhanuggahapaṇḍito manussānaṃ vārentānaññeva [P 3.0220] bhariyaṃ gahetvā aṭavimukhaṃ abhiruhi. Athassa aṭavimajjhe vāraṇo uṭṭhahi, so taṃ kumbhe sarena vijjhi. Saro vinivijjhitvā pacchābhāgena nikkhami. Vāraṇo tattheva pati, dhanuggahapaṇḍito taṃ ṭhānaṃ khemaṃ katvā purato aññaṃ aṭaviṃ pāpuṇi. Tatthāpi paññāsa corā maggaṃ hananti. Tampi so manussehi vāriyamāno abhiruyha tesaṃ corānaṃ mige vadhitvā maggasamīpe maṃsaṃ pacitvā khādantānaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ pāpuṇi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka. At that time, a young brahmin from Bārāṇasī went to Takkasilā, mastered all the arts, and attained perfection in archery; he became known as the Wise Little Archer. His teacher, thinking, “This one has learned a skill equal to my own,” gave him his daughter. Taking her, he set out on the road to Bārāṇasī. Along the way, an elephant had laid waste to a certain region, and no one dared to pass through it. The Wise Little Archer, though people tried to stop him, took his wife and entered the outskirts of the forest. There, in the middle of the forest, the elephant rose up before him. He shot it in the frontal globe with an arrow. The arrow pierced right through it and came out the back. The elephant fell right there. The wise archer, having made that place safe, went on and came to another forest. There, fifty robbers were infesting the road. Though people warned him, he entered and came to the place where those robbers were standing, having killed a deer and were cooking and eating its flesh beside the road.

Tadā [V 3.0193] taṃ corā alaṅkatapaṭiyattāya bhariyāya saddhiṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā “gaṇhissāma na”nti ussāhaṃ kariṃsu. Corajeṭṭhako purisalakkhaṇakusalo, so taṃ oloketvāva “uttamapuriso aya”nti ñatvā ekassapi uṭṭhahituṃ nādāsi. Dhanuggahapaṇḍito “gaccha ‘amhākampi ekaṃ maṃsasūlaṃ dethā’ti vatvā maṃsaṃ āharā”ti tesaṃ santikaṃ bhariyaṃ pesesi. Sā gantvā “ekaṃ kira maṃsasūlaṃ dethā”ti āha. Corajeṭṭhako “anaggho puriso”ti maṃsasūlaṃ dāpesi. Corā “amhehi kira pakkaṃ khādita”nti apakkamaṃsasūlaṃ adaṃsu. Dhanuggaho attānaṃ sambhāvetvā “mayhaṃ apakkamaṃsasūlaṃ dadantī”ti corānaṃ kujjhi. Corā “kiṃ ayameveko puriso, mayaṃ itthiyo”ti kujjhitvā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Dhanuggaho ekūnapaññāsa jane ekūnapaññāsakaṇḍehi vijjhitvā pātesi. Corajeṭṭhakaṃ vijjhituṃ kaṇḍaṃ nāhosi. Tassa kira kaṇḍanāḷiyaṃ samapaṇṇāsayeva kaṇḍāni. Tesu ekena vāraṇaṃ vijjhi, ekūnapaññāsakaṇḍehi core vijjhitvā corajeṭṭhakaṃ pātetvā tassa ure nisinno “sīsamassa chindissāmī”ti bhariyāya hatthato asiṃ āharāpesi. Sā taṅkhaṇaññeva corajeṭṭhake lobhaṃ katvā corassa [P 3.0221] hatthe tharuṃ, sāmikassa hatthe dhāraṃ [M 3.0207] ṭhapesi. Coro tharudaṇḍaṃ parāmasitvā asiṃ nīharitvā dhanuggahassa sīsaṃ chindi.

Then the robbers, seeing him coming with his finely adorned wife, became eager, thinking, “We will capture them!” But the robber chief, who was skilled in reading the marks of a man, observed him and knew, “This is a superior man,” so he did not allow a single one of them to rise. The wise archer sent his wife to them, saying, “Go and say, ‘Please give us a skewer of meat,’ and bring it back.” She went and said, “Please give us a skewer of meat.” The robber chief, thinking, “This man is invaluable,” had a skewer of meat given to her. The robbers, thinking, “We have eaten the cooked meat ourselves,” gave her a skewer of raw meat. The archer, valuing himself highly, became angry with the robbers, thinking, “They give me raw meat!” The robbers, enraged, rose up, saying, “What is this one man? Are we women?” The archer shot and felled forty-nine of them with forty-nine arrows. He had no arrow left to shoot the robber chief. It seems he had exactly fifty arrows in his quiver: with one he had shot the elephant, and with forty-nine he had shot the robbers. He knocked down the robber chief, sat on his chest, and thinking, “I will cut off his head,” had his wife bring him the sword from her hand. At that very moment, she conceived a desire for the robber chief. She placed the hilt of the sword in the robber’s hand and the blade in her husband’s. The robber, grasping the hilt, drew the sword and cut off the archer’s head.

So taṃ ghātetvā itthiṃ ādāya gacchanto jātigottaṃ pucchi. Sā “takkasilāyaṃ disāpāmokkhācariyassa dhītāmhī”ti āha. “Kathaṃ tvaṃ iminā laddhā”ti. Mayhaṃ pitā “ayaṃ mayā sadisaṃ katvā sippaṃ sikkhī”ti tussitvā imassa maṃ adāsi, sāhaṃ tayi sinehaṃ katvā attano kuladattiyaṃ sāmikaṃ mārāpesinti. Corajeṭṭhako “kuladattiyaṃ tāvesā sāmikaṃ māresi, aññaṃ panekaṃ disvā mampi evamevaṃ karissati, imaṃ chaḍḍetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā gacchanto antarāmagge ekaṃ kunnadiṃ uttānatalaṃ taṅkhaṇodakapūraṃ disvā “bhadde, imissaṃ nadiyaṃ susumārā kakkhaḷā, kiṃ karomā”ti āha. “Sāmi, sabbaṃ ābharaṇabhaṇḍaṃ mama uttarāsaṅgena bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā paratīraṃ netvā puna āgantvā maṃ gahetvā gacchā”ti. So “sādhū”ti sabbaṃ ābharaṇabhaṇḍaṃ ādāya nadiṃ otaritvā taranto viya paratīraṃ patvā taṃ chaḍḍetvā pāyāsi. Sā taṃ disvā “sāmi, kiṃ maṃ chaḍḍetvā viya gacchasi, kasmā evaṃ karosi, ehi mampi ādāya gacchā”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapantī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having killed him and taken the woman, he went on his way, asking about her family and clan. She said, “I am the daughter of a world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā.” “How did you come to be with him?” “My father was pleased that he had learned a craft like his own and gave me to him. But I, having developed affection for you, caused my husband, who was given by my family, to be killed.” The robber chief thought: “She had her husband, given by her family, killed. If she sees another man, she will do the very same to me. It is proper to abandon her.” As he was going, he saw on the way a small river with a shallow bed that was full of water at that moment, and said: “Good lady, there are fierce and cruel crocodiles in this river. What shall we do?” “Master, make a bundle of all the jewelry and goods with my upper robe, carry it to the other shore, then come back, take me, and go.” “Very well,” he said. He took all the jewelry and goods, entered the river, and as if crossing, reached the other shore. Then he abandoned her and departed. Seeing this, she called out: “Master, why do you go on as if abandoning me? Why do you do this? Come, take me too and go!” Conversing with him, she uttered the first verse:

128.

128.

“Sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ samādāya, pāraṃ tiṇṇosi brāhmaṇa;

Paccāgaccha lahuṃ khippaṃ, mampi tārehi dānito”ti.

“Having taken all the goods, you have crossed to the far shore, Brahmin; come back quickly and swiftly, and ferry me across from here now.”

Tattha [V 3.0194] lahuṃ khippanti lahuṃ paccāgaccha, khippaṃ mampi tārehi dāni itoti attho.

Herein, ‘lahuṃ khippaṃ’ means: ‘Come back quickly, and swiftly ferry me across from here now.’ This is the meaning.

Coro taṃ sutvā paratīre ṭhitoyeva dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the robber, standing on the far shore, uttered the second verse:

129.

129.

“Asanthutaṃ maṃ cirasanthutena, nimīni bhotī adhuvaṃ dhuvena;

Mayāpi [P 3.0222] bhotī nimineyya aññaṃ, ito ahaṃ dūrataraṃ gamissa”nti.

“For me, a stranger, you exchanged one long-acquainted; good lady, you traded the constant for the inconstant. You might exchange me, too, for another; therefore, I will go far away from here.”

Sā heṭṭhā vuttatthāyeva –

The meaning of this is just as stated above.

Coro pana “ito ahaṃ dūrataraṃ gamissaṃ, tiṭṭha tva”nti vatvā tassā viravantiyāva ābharaṇabhaṇḍikaṃ ādāya palāto. Tato sā [M 3.0208] bālā atricchatāya evarūpaṃ byasanaṃ pattā anāthā hutvā avidūre ekaṃ eḷagalāgumbaṃ upagantvā rodamānā nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko devarājā lokaṃ olokento taṃ atricchatāhataṃ sāmikā ca jārā ca parihīnaṃ rodamānaṃ disvā “etaṃ niggaṇhitvā lajjāpetvā āgamissāmī”ti mātaliñca pañcasikhañca ādāya tattha gantvā nadītīre ṭhatvā “mātali, tvaṃ maccho bhava, pañcasikha tvaṃ sakuṇo bhava, ahaṃ pana siṅgālo hutvā mukhena maṃsapiṇḍaṃ gahetvā etissā sammukhaṭṭhānaṃ gamissāmi, tvaṃ mayi tattha gate udakato ullaṅghitvā mama purato pata, athāhaṃ mukhena gahitamaṃsapiṇḍaṃ chaḍḍetvā macchaṃ gahetuṃ pakkhandissāmi, tasmiṃ khaṇe tvaṃ, pañcasikha, taṃ maṃsapiṇḍaṃ gahetvā ākāse uppata, tvaṃ mātali, udake patā”ti āṇāpesi. “Sādhu, devā”ti, mātali, maccho ahosi, pañcasikho sakuṇo ahosi. Sakko siṅgālo hutvā maṃsapiṇḍaṃ mukhenādāya tassā sammukhaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Maccho udakā uppatitvā siṅgālassa purato pati. So mukhena gahitamaṃsapiṇḍaṃ chaḍḍetvā macchassatthāya pakkhandi. Maccho uppatitvā udake pati, sakuṇo maṃsapiṇḍaṃ gahetvā ākāse uppati, siṅgālo ubhopi alabhitvā eḷagalāgumbaṃ olokento dummukho nisīdi. Sā taṃ disvā “ayaṃ atricchatāhato neva maṃsaṃ, na macchaṃ labhī”ti kuṭaṃ bhindantī [P 3.0223] viya mahāhasitaṃ hasi. Taṃ sutvā siṅgālo tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The robber, however, said, “I will go much further from here; you stay!” and while she was wailing, he took the bundle of ornaments and fled. Then that foolish woman, having met with such a disaster due to her excessive greed, became helpless. She approached a nearby thicket of eḷagalā plants and sat down weeping. At that moment, Sakka, king of the devas, surveying the world, saw her. Stricken by excessive greed, bereft of both husband and lover, she was weeping. He thought: “I will go and subdue this woman, make her feel ashamed, and then return.” Taking Mātali and Pañcasikha with him, he went there, stood on the riverbank, and gave this command: “Mātali, you become a fish. Pañcasikha, you become a bird. I will become a jackal, and taking a piece of meat in my mouth, I will go before her. When I have gone there, you, Mātali, must leap out of the water and fall in front of me. Then I will drop the piece of meat I am holding in my mouth and pounce to catch the fish. At that moment, you, Pañcasikha, must seize that piece of meat and fly up into the sky. And you, Mātali, must fall back into the water.” “Very well, deva,” they said. Mātali became a fish and Pañcasikha became a bird. Sakka became a jackal, and taking a piece of meat in his mouth, he went to a place in front of her. The fish leaped from the water and fell in front of the jackal. The jackal dropped the piece of meat from his mouth and pounced for the sake of the fish. The fish leaped up and fell back into the water; the bird seized the piece of meat and flew up into the sky. The jackal, having failed to get either, sat with a dejected face, looking at the thicket of eḷagalā plants. Seeing this, the woman thought, “This creature, stricken by excessive greed, got neither the meat nor the fish,” and she laughed a great laugh, as if she were shattering a pot. Hearing this, the jackal uttered the third verse:

130.

130.

“Kāyaṃ eḷagalāgumbe, karoti ahuhāsiyaṃ;

Nayīdha naccagītaṃ vā, tāḷaṃ vā susamāhitaṃ;

Anamhikāle susoṇi, kinnu jagghasi sobhane”ti.

“Who is this in the eḷagalā thicket, laughing such a boisterous laugh? There is no dancing or singing here, nor well-timed music. At this time for weeping, O you of beautiful hips, why, O lovely one, do you laugh?”

Tattha [V 3.0195] kāyanti kā ayaṃ. Eḷagalāgumbeti kambojigumbe. Ahuhāsiyanti dantavidaṃsakaṃ mahāhasitaṃ vuccati, taṃ kā esā etasmiṃ gumbe karotīti pucchati. Nayīdha naccagītaṃ vāti imasmiṃ ṭhāne kassaci naccantassa naccaṃ vā gāyantassa gītaṃ vā hatthe susamāhite katvā vādentassa susamāhitaṃ hatthatāḷaṃ vā natthi, kaṃ disvā tvaṃ haseyyāsīti dīpeti. Anamhikāleti rodanakāle. Susoṇīti sundarasoṇi. Kiṃ nu jagghasīti [M 3.0209] kena kāraṇena tvaṃ rodituṃ yuttakāle arodamānāva mahāhasitaṃ hasasi. Sobhaneti taṃ pasaṃsanto ālapati.

Herein, ‘kāyaṃ’ means ‘Who is this woman?’ ‘Eḷagalāgumbe’ means in a thicket of eḷagalā plants. ‘Ahuhāsiyaṃ’ refers to a great, tooth-baring laugh; he asks, ‘Who is this woman making such a laugh in this thicket?’ By ‘Nayīdha naccagītaṃ vā’, he indicates: ‘In this place there is neither the dancing of a dancer nor the singing of a singer, nor is there well-timed hand-clapping. Seeing what do you laugh?’ ‘Anamhikāle’ means at a time for weeping. ‘Susoṇi’ means one with beautiful hips. ‘Kiṃ nu jagghasi’ means: ‘For what reason do you laugh a great laugh when it is a time appropriate for weeping, not for laughing?’ By ‘sobhane’, he addresses her with praise.

Taṃ sutvā sā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, she uttered the fourth verse:

131.

131.

“Siṅgāla bāla dummedha, appapaññosi jambuka;

Jīno macchañca pesiñca, kapaṇo viya jhāyasī”ti.

“O jackal, you fool, dull-witted, of little wisdom, O jackal! Having lost both the fish and the piece of meat, you brood like a miserable wretch.”

Tattha jīnoti jānippatto hutvā. Pesinti maṃsapesiṃ. Kapaṇo viya jhāyasīti sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ parājito kapaṇo viya jhāyasi socasi cintesi.

Herein, ‘jīno’ means having incurred a loss. ‘Pesiṃ’ means a piece of meat. ‘Kapaṇo viya jhāyasi’ means: you brood, you sorrow, and you ponder like a wretch who has been defeated for a stake of a thousand.

Tato siṅgālo pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the jackal uttered the fifth verse:

132.

132.

“Sudassaṃ vajjamaññesaṃ, attano pana duddasaṃ;

Jīnā patiñca jārañca, maññe tvaññeva jhāyasī”ti.

“Easy to see is the fault of others, but one’s own is hard to see. Having lost both husband and lover, it is you, I think, who truly broods.”

Tattha tvaññeva jhāyasīti pāpadhamme dussīle ahaṃ tāva mama gocaraṃ na labhissāmi, tvaṃ pana atricchatāya hatā taṃmuhuttadiṭṭhake core paṭibaddhacittā hutvā tañca jāraṃ kuladattiyañca patiṃ jīnā, maṃ upādāya sataguṇena sahassaguṇena kapaṇatarā hutvā jhāyasi rodasi paridevasīti lajjāpetvā vippakāraṃ pāpento mahāsatto evamāha.

Herein, by "tvaññeva jhāyasi", the Great Being, shaming her and causing her disgrace, spoke thus: ‘O you of evil ways, immoral one! I, for my part, may not get my food. But you, stricken by excessive greed, having become infatuated with a bandit seen for but a moment, have lost both that lover and your husband given by your family. Compared to me, you have become a hundred times, a thousand times more wretched, and so you brood, weep, and lament.’

Sā [P 3.0224] tassa vacanaṃ sutvā gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, she uttered a verse:

133.

133.

“Evametaṃ migarāja, yathā bhāsasi jambuka;

Sā nūnāhaṃ ito gantvā, bhattu hessaṃ vasānugā”ti.

“So it is, O king of beasts, just as you say, O jackal. Surely, going from here, I will be subservient to my husband.”

Tattha [V 3.0196] nūnāti ekaṃsatthe nipāto. Sā ahaṃ ito gantvā puna aññaṃ bhattāraṃ labhitvā ekaṃseneva tassa bhattu vasānugā vasavattinī bhavissāmīti.

Herein, "nūna" is a particle used in the sense of certainty. The meaning is: ‘I, going from here and getting another husband, will certainly be subservient to that husband, under his authority.’

Athassā anācārāya dussīlāya vacanaṃ sutvā sakko devarājā osānagāthamāha –

Then, hearing the words of that misbehaving, immoral woman, Sakka, king of the devas, uttered the concluding verse:

134.

134.

“Yo hare mattikaṃ thālaṃ, kaṃsathālampi so hare;

Kataṃyeva tayā pāpaṃ, punapevaṃ karissasī”ti.

“One who would steal an earthen bowl, would also steal a bowl of bronze. The evil has been done by you; you will do the same thing again.”

Tassattho [M 3.0210] – anācāre kiṃ kathesi, yo mattikaṃ thālaṃ harati, suvaṇṇathālarajatathālādippabhedaṃ kaṃsathālampi so harateva, idañca tayā pāpaṃ katameva, na sakkā tava saddhātuṃ, sā tvaṃ punapi evaṃ karissasiyevāti. Evaṃ so taṃ lajjāpetvā vippakāraṃ pāpetvā sakaṭṭhānameva agamāsi.

Its meaning is: ‘O misbehaving one, what are you saying? One who steals an earthen bowl will also steal a bronze bowl, and by extension, bowls of gold, silver, and so on. This evil has already been done by you. It is not possible to trust you; you will surely do so again.’ Thus, having shamed her and caused her disgrace, he went back to his own place.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, declared the Truths and identified the birth. At the conclusion of the declaration of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā dhanuggaho ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu ahosi, sā itthī purāṇadutiyikā, sakko devarājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the archer was the dissatisfied monk, the woman was his former wife, and Sakka, king of the devas, was myself.

Cūḷadhanuggahajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka, the Fourth, is concluded.

[375] 5. Kapotajātakavaṇṇanā

[375] 5. Commentary on the Kapota Jātaka

Idāni khomhīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ lolabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Lolavatthu anekaso vitthāritameva. Taṃ pana satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu, lolo”ti pucchitvā “āma, bhante”ti vutte “na kho bhikkhu idāneva, pubbepi tvaṃ lolosi, lolatāya pana jīvitakkhayaṃ patto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story beginning with the words, “Now, indeed,” concerning a greedy monk. The story of the greedy monk has been related in full on many occasions. The Teacher asked him, “Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are greedy?” When he replied, “Yes, venerable sir,” the Teacher said: “Not only now, bhikkhu, are you greedy; in the past, too, you were greedy, and because of your greed you met with the loss of your life.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 3.0225] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto pārāvatayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā bārāṇasiseṭṭhino mahānase nīḷapacchiyaṃ vasati. Atheko kāko macchamaṃsaluddho tena saddhiṃ mettiṃ [V 3.0197] katvā tattheva vasi. So ekadivasaṃ bahuṃ macchamaṃsaṃ disvā “imaṃ khādissāmī”ti nitthunanto nīḷapacchiyaṃyeva nipajjitvā pārāvatena “ehi, samma, gocarāya gamissāmā”ti vuccamānopi “ajīrakena nipannomhi, gaccha tva”nti vatvā tasmiṃ gate “gato me paccāmittakaṇṭako, idāni yathāruci macchamaṃsaṃ khādissāmī”ti cintento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a pigeon and lived in a nest-basket in the kitchen of the Benares merchant. A certain crow, greedy for fish and meat, made friends with him and also lived there. One day, seeing a great deal of fish and meat, the crow thought, “I will eat this!” Groaning, he lay down right in the nest-basket. Even when the pigeon said, “Come, friend, let us go for food,” he replied, “I am lying down with indigestion; you go.” When the pigeon had gone, the crow thought, “The thorn that is my enemy is gone! Now I can eat fish and meat as I please.” Thinking thus, he uttered the first verse:

135.

135.

“Idāni [M 3.0211] khomhi sukhito arogo, nikkaṇṭako nippatito kapoto;

Kāhāmi dānī hadayassa tuṭṭhiṃ, tathā hi maṃ maṃsasākaṃ baletī”ti.

“Now I am happy and healthy, free from thorns, the pigeon has flown away; now I will satisfy my heart, for meat and vegetables make me strong.”

Tattha nippatitoti niggato. Kapototi pārāvato. Kāhāmi dānīti karissāmi dāni. Tathā hi maṃ maṃsasākaṃ baletīti tathā hi maṃsañca avasesaṃ sākañca mayhaṃ balaṃ karoti, uṭṭhehi khādāti vadamānaṃ viya ussāhaṃ mamaṃ karotīti attho.

Herein, "nippatito" means departed. "Kapoto" means a pigeon. "Kāhāmi dāni" means ‘I will do now.’ The words "tathā hi maṃ maṃsasākaṃ baleti" mean: for the meat and the remaining vegetables give me strength; it is as if they give me an impulse, saying, ‘Get up and eat!’ This is the meaning.

So bhattakārake macchamaṃsaṃ pacitvā mahānasā nikkhamma sarīrato sedaṃ pavāhente pacchito nikkhamitvā rasakaroṭiyaṃ nilīyitvā “kiri kirī”ti saddamakāsi. Bhattakārako vegenāgantvā kākaṃ gahetvā sabbapattāni luñjitvā allasiṅgīverañca siddhatthake ca pisitvā lasuṇaṃ pūtitakkena madditvā sakalasarīraṃ makkhetvā ekaṃ kaṭhalaṃ ghaṃsitvā [P 3.0226] vijjhitvā suttakena tassa gīvāyaṃ bandhitvā nīḷapacchiyaṃyeva taṃ pakkhipitvā agamāsi. Pārāvato āgantvā taṃ disvā “kā esā balākā mama sahāyassa pacchiyaṃ nipannā, caṇḍo hi so āgantvā ghāteyyāpi na”nti parihāsaṃ karonto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The cook, having cooked fish and meat, came out of the kitchen with sweat pouring from his body. The crow came out from behind, hid in a sauce pot, and made a ‘kiri kiri’ sound. The cook rushed back, seized the crow, and plucked all its feathers. He then ground up fresh ginger and white mustard seeds, mixed them with garlic and spoiled buttermilk, and smeared this paste all over the crow’s body. He then rubbed a potsherd, pierced it, tied it to the crow’s neck with a string, and placed the crow back in its nest basket before leaving. When the pigeon arrived and saw it, he made a joke, saying, ‘What is this heron lying in my friend’s nest basket? That fierce fellow might come and kill it!’ and then spoke the second stanza:

136.

136.

“Kāyaṃ balākā sikhinī, corī laṅghipitāmahā;

Oraṃ balāke āgaccha, caṇḍo me vāyaso sakhā”ti.

“Who is this crested heron, this thieving grandmother-leaper? Come here, O heron; my friend the crow is fierce.”

Sā heṭṭhā (jā. aṭṭha. 2.3.70) vuttatthāyeva.

Its meaning is just as was stated before (in Ja 247).

Taṃ sutvā kāko tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the crow spoke the third stanza:

137.

137.

“Alañhi te jagghitāye, mamaṃ disvāna edisaṃ;

Vilūnaṃ sūdaputtena, piṭṭhamaṇḍena makkhita”nti.

“Enough of your laughter, seeing me in such a state, plucked by the cook and smeared with flour paste.”

Tattha [V 3.0198] alanti paṭisedhatthe nipāto. Jagghitāyeti hasituṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – idāni maṃ edisaṃ evaṃ dukkhappattaṃ disvā tava alaṃ hasituṃ, mā edise kāle parihāsakeḷiṃ karohīti.

Herein, ‘alaṃ’ is a particle in the sense of prohibition. ‘Jagghitāye’ means ‘for laughing.’ This is what is said: ‘Now, seeing me in such a state, having met with such suffering, enough of your laughter! Do not engage in mockery and sport at such a time.’”

So [M 3.0212] parihāsakeḷiṃ karontova puna catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Continuing his playful jesting, he spoke a fourth stanza:

138.

138.

“Sunhāto suvilittosi, annapānena tappito;

Kaṇṭhe ca te veḷuriyo, agamā nu kajaṅgala”nti.

“You are well-bathed and well-anointed, satisfied with food and drink; and there is a beryl gem on your neck. Did you go to Kajaṅgala?”

Tattha kaṇṭhe ca te veḷuriyoti ayaṃ te veḷuriyamaṇipi kaṇṭhe piḷandho, tvaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ amhākaṃ etaṃ na dassesīti kapālaṃ sandhāyevamāha. Kajaṅgalanti idha bārāṇasīyeva “kajaṅgalā”ti adhippetā. Ito nikkhamitvā kacci antonagaraṃ gatosīti pucchati.

Herein, with the words ‘kaṇṭhe ca te veḷuriyo,’ he speaks referring to the potsherd: ‘This beryl gem is worn on your neck; for so long you did not show it to us!’ By ‘Kajaṅgala,’ Bārāṇasī itself is intended. He asks: ‘Having left here, did you perhaps go into the city?’”

Tato kāko pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the crow spoke the fifth stanza:

139.

139.

“Mā te mitto amitto vā, agamāsi kajaṅgalaṃ;

Piñchāni tattha lāyitvā, kaṇṭhe bandhanti vaṭṭana”nti.

“May no friend or foe of yours go to Kajaṅgala; for there they pluck one’s feathers and tie a ‘vaṭṭana’ around the neck.”

Tattha [P 3.0227] piñchānīti pattāni. Tattha lāyitvāti tasmiṃ bārāṇasinagare luñcitvā. Vaṭṭananti kaṭhalikaṃ.

Herein, ‘piñchāni’ means feathers. ‘Tattha lāyitvā’ means having plucked them in that city of Bārāṇasī. ‘Vaṭṭana’ means a potsherd.

Taṃ sutvā pārāvato osānagāthamāha –

Hearing that, the pigeon spoke the concluding stanza:

140.

140.

“Punapāpajjasī samma, sīlañhi tava tādisaṃ;

Na hi mānusakā bhogā, subhuñjā honti pakkhinā”ti.

“Friend, you will fall into this again, for such is your nature. Human enjoyments are not easily enjoyed by a bird.”

Tattha punapāpajjasīti punapi evarūpaṃ āpajjissasi. Evarūpañhi te sīlanti.

Herein, ‘punapāpajjasi’ means: you will again fall into such a state of misery. For such is your nature.

Iti naṃ so ovaditvā tattha avasitvā pakkhe pasāretvā aññattha agamāsi. Kākopi tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi.

Thus, having advised him, the Bodhisatta did not stay there; spreading his wings, he went elsewhere. The crow, too, met his end right there in that house.

Satthā [V 3.0199] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne lolabhikkhu anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā kāko lolabhikkhu ahosi, kapoto pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the birth story. At the conclusion of the Truths, the fickle monk was established in the fruit of non-returning. “At that time, the crow was the fickle monk, but the pigeon was I myself.”

Kapotajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Kapota Jātaka, the Fifth.

Aḍḍhavaggo tatiyo.

The Half-Chapter, the Third.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

Summary Verse of the Jātakas:

Maṇikuṇḍala [M 3.0213] sujātā, venasākhañca oragaṃ;

Ghaṭaṃ koraṇḍi laṭuki, dhammapālaṃ migaṃ tathā.

Maṇikuṇḍala, Sujātā, Veṇasākha, and Uraga; Ghaṭa, Koraṇḍiya, Laṭukikā, Dhammapāla, and also Miga.

Suyonandī vaṇṇāroha, sīlaṃ hirī khajjopanaṃ;

Ahi gumbiya sāḷiyaṃ, tacasāraṃ mittavindaṃ.

Suyonandī, Vaṇṇāroha, Sīla, Hirī, Khajjopanaka; Ahi, Gumbiya, Sāliya, Tacasāra, Mittavinda.

Palāsañceva dīghiti, migapotaka mūsikaṃ;

Dhanuggaho kapotañca, jātakā pañcavīsati.

Palāsa and Dīghīti, Migapotaka, Mūsika; Dhanuggaha and Kapota: these are the twenty-five Jātakas.

Pañcakanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Book of the Fives is finished.

6. Chakkanipāto

6. The Book of the Sixes

1. Avāriyavaggo

1. The Avāriya Chapter

[376] 1. Avāriyajātakavaṇṇanā

[376] 1. The Commentary on the Avāriya Jātaka

Māsu [V 3.0200][P 3.0228][M 3.0214] kujjha bhūmipatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ titthanāvikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira bālo ahosi aññāṇo, neva so buddhādīnaṃ ratanānaṃ, na aññesaṃ puggalānaṃ guṇaṃ jānāti, caṇḍo pharuso sāhasiko. Atheko jānapado bhikkhu “buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ karissāmī”ti āgacchanto sāyaṃ aciravatītitthaṃ patvā taṃ evamāha “upāsaka, paratīraṃ gamissāmi, nāvaṃ me dehī”ti. “Bhante, idāni akālo, ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasassū”ti. “Upāsaka, idha kuhiṃ vasissāmi, maṃ gaṇhitvā gacchā”ti. So kujjhitvā “ehi re samaṇa, vahāmī”ti theraṃ nāvaṃ āropetvā ujukaṃ agantvā heṭṭhā nāvaṃ netvā ulloḷaṃ katvā tassa pattacīvaraṃ temetvā kilametvā tīraṃ patvā andhakāravelāyaṃ uyyojesi. Atha so vihāraṃ gantvā taṃ divasaṃ buddhupaṭṭhānassa okāsaṃ alabhitvā punadivase satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā satthārā katapaṭisanthāro “kadā āgatosī”ti vutte “hiyyo, bhante”ti vatvā “atha kasmā ajja buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ āgatosī”ti vutte tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā satthā “na kho bhikkhu idāneva, pubbepesa caṇḍo pharuso sāhasiko, idāni pana tena tvaṃ kilamito, pubbepesa paṇḍite kilamesī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher told this story, which begins, “Do not be angry, O lord of the earth,” while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain ferryman. He, it seems, was a foolish and ignorant man who knew neither the qualities of the Three Jewels, such as the Buddha, nor those of other persons; he was fierce, harsh, and reckless. Now a certain monk from the countryside, coming to attend upon the Buddha, arrived at the Aciravatī ferry in the evening and said to him, “Lay follower, I wish to cross to the other shore; give me your boat.” “Venerable sir, now is not the time; stay in some place.” “Lay follower, where can I stay here? Take me across.” Angered, the ferryman said, “Come on, you ascetic, I will carry you.” He got the elder onto the boat, but instead of going straight, he took the boat downstream, rocked it violently, soaked his bowl and robes, and exhausted him. When he reached the shore, he sent him away in the dark. The monk went to the monastery but did not get an opportunity to attend upon the Buddha that day. The next day he approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat to one side. After the Teacher had greeted him and asked, “When did you arrive?” he replied, “Yesterday, venerable sir.” “Then why have you come to attend upon me only today?” The monk related the whole matter. Hearing it, the Teacher said, “Monk, not only now is this man fierce, harsh, and reckless; he was so in the past as well. Now he has exhausted you, but in the past he exhausted the wise.” Then, at the monk’s request, he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ [P 3.0229] sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā dīghamaddhānaṃ himavante phalāphalena yāpetvā loṇambilasevanatthāya bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase nagaraṃ bhikkhāya pāvisi. Atha naṃ rājaṅgaṇappattaṃ rājā disvā tassa iriyāpathe pasīditvā antepuraṃ ānetvā bhojetvā paṭiññaṃ gahetvā [M 3.0215] rājuyyāne vasāpesi, devasikaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ [V 3.0201] agamāsi. Tamenaṃ bodhisatto “raññā nāma, mahārāja, cattāri agatigamanāni vajjetvā appamattena khantimettānuddayasampannena hutvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretabba”nti vatvā devasikaṃ ovadanto –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. When he came of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and then went forth as an ascetic. For a long time he lived in the Himalayas, sustaining himself on wild fruits and roots. Then, for the purpose of obtaining salt and sour seasonings, he journeyed to Bārāṇasī and dwelt in the royal park. The next day, he entered the city for alms. When the king saw him arriving in the royal courtyard, he was pleased with his deportment, brought him into the inner palace, and served him a meal. After receiving a promise from him to stay, the king had him take up residence in the royal park and attended on him daily. The Bodhisatta advised him daily, saying: “Great king, a king should avoid the four wrong courses of action and, being diligent and endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, should rule righteously,” and speaking thus, he uttered these stanzas:

1.

1.

“Māsu kujjha bhūmipati, māsu kujjha rathesabha;

Kuddhaṃ appaṭikujjhanto, rājā raṭṭhassa pūjito.

“Do not be angry, O lord of the earth, do not be angry, O bull among charioteers; a king who does not get angry in return when others are angry is honored by his realm.”

2.

2.

“Gāme vā yadi vāraññe, ninne vā yadi vā thale;

Sabbattha anusāsāmi, māsu kujjha rathesabhā”ti. – dve gāthā abhāsi;

“Whether in a village or in the wilderness, whether in a valley or on high ground, everywhere I give this instruction: do not be angry, O bull among charioteers.”

Tattha raṭṭhassa pūjitoti evarūpo rājā raṭṭhassa pūjanīyo hotīti attho. Sabbattha anusāsāmīti etesu gāmādīsu yattha katthaci vasantopāhaṃ mahārāja, imāya eva anusiṭṭhiyā tamanusāsāmi, etesu vā gāmādīsu yattha katthaci ekasmimpi ekasattepi anusāsāmi. Māsu kujjha rathesabhāti evamevāhaṃ taṃ anusāsāmi, raññā nāma kujjhatuṃ na vaṭṭati. Kiṃkāraṇā? Rājāno nāma vācāvudhā, tesaṃ kuddhānaṃ vacanamatteneva bahū jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇantīti.

Herein, ‘raṭṭhassa pūjito’ means: such a king is worthy of being honored by his realm. ‘Sabbattha anusāsāmi’ means: “Great king, wherever I am dwelling, in a village or some other place, I instruct with this very instruction; or, I instruct even a single being wherever they may be in these places.” ‘Māsu kujjha rathesabha’ means: “Thus I instruct you. It is not proper for a king to be angry.” For what reason? Kings are those who have speech as their weapon; when they are angry, by their mere word many meet with the destruction of their lives.

Evaṃ bodhisatto rañño āgatāgatadivase imā dve gāthā abhāsi. Rājā anusiṭṭhiyā pasannacitto mahāsattassa satasahassuṭṭhānakaṃ ekaṃ gāmavaraṃ adāsi, bodhisatto paṭikkhipi. Iti so tattheva dvādasasaṃvaccharaṃ vasitvā “aticiraṃ nivutthomhi, janapadacārikaṃ tāva caritvā āgamissāmī”ti rañño akathetvāva uyyānapālaṃ āmantetvā “tāta, ukkaṇṭhitarūposmi, janapadaṃ caritvā āgamissāmi, tvaṃ rañño katheyyāsī”ti vatvā pakkanto [P 3.0230] gaṅgāya nāvātitthaṃ pāpuṇi. Tattha avāriyapitā nāma nāviko ahosi. So bālo neva guṇavantānaṃ guṇaṃ jānāti, na attano āyāpāyaṃ jānāti, so gaṅgaṃ taritukāmaṃ janaṃ paṭhamaṃ tāretvā pacchā vetanaṃ yācati, vetanaṃ adentehi saddhiṃ kalahaṃ karonto akkosappahāreyeva bahū labhati, appaṃ lābhaṃ, evarūpo andhabālo. Taṃ sandhāya satthā abhisambuddho hutvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus the Bodhisatta spoke these two verses on each day that the king came. The king, his mind pleased by the instruction, offered the Great Being an excellent village yielding a hundred thousand in revenue, but the Bodhisatta refused it. After living there for twelve years, he thought, ‘I have stayed too long. I will first wander in the countryside and then return.’ Without telling the king, he summoned the park keeper and said, ‘Good man, I have become weary. I will wander in the countryside and return. You should tell the king.’ Having said this, he departed and reached the ferry landing on the Ganges. There was a ferryman there named Avāriyapitā. That fool neither knew the virtue of the virtuous nor understood gain and loss. He would first ferry people who wished to cross the Ganges and then ask for the fare. When they did not pay, he would quarrel with them, receiving much abuse and many blows but little profit. Such was this blind fool. In reference to him, the Teacher, having become perfectly enlightened, spoke the third verse:

3.

3.

“Avāriyapitā [M 3.0216] nāma, ahu gaṅgāya nāviko;

Pubbe janaṃ tāretvāna, pacchā yācati vetanaṃ;

Tenassa bhaṇḍanaṃ hoti, na ca bhogehi vaḍḍhatī”ti.

“There was a ferryman on the Ganges named Avāriyapitā; having first ferried people across, he would afterwards ask for the fare. Because of this he got into quarrels, and he did not prosper in his possessions.”

Tattha [V 3.0202] avāriyapitā nāmāti avāriyā nāma tassa dhītā, tassā vasena avāriyapitā nāma jāto. Tenassa bhaṇḍananti tena kāraṇena, tena vā pacchā yāciyamānena janena saddhiṃ tassa bhaṇḍanaṃ hoti.

Herein, ‘Avāriyapitā nāma’: Avāriyā was the name of his daughter, and on account of her he came to be called Avāriyapitā. ‘Tenassa bhaṇḍanaṃ’: for that reason, he got into quarrels with the people from whom he asked for payment afterwards.

Bodhisatto taṃ nāvikaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “āvuso, paratīraṃ maṃ nehī”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā so āha “samaṇa, kiṃ me nāvāvetanaṃ dassasī”ti? “Āvuso, ahaṃ bhogavaḍḍhiṃ atthavaḍḍhiṃ dhammavaḍḍhiṃ nāma te kathessāmī”ti. Taṃ sutvā nāviko “dhuvaṃ esa mayhaṃ kiñci dassatī”ti taṃ paratīraṃ netvā “dehi me nāvāya vetana”nti āha. So tassa “sādhu, āvuso”ti paṭhamaṃ bhogavaḍḍhiṃ kathento –

The Bodhisatta approached that ferryman and said, ‘Friend, take me to the further shore.’ Hearing this, he said, ‘Ascetic, what will you give me for the boat fare?’ ‘Friend, I will tell you about the increase of possessions, the increase of welfare, and the increase of righteousness.’ Hearing this, the ferryman thought, ‘Surely he will give me something,’ and he took him to the further shore. Then he said, ‘Give me the boat fare.’ The Bodhisatta replied, ‘Very well, friend,’ and first explained the increase of possessions:

4.

4.

“Atiṇṇaṃyeva yācassu, apāraṃ tāta nāvika;

Añño hi tiṇṇassa mano, añño hoti pāresino”ti. – gāthamāha;

“Ask from one who has not yet crossed, while he is not yet on the far shore, dear ferryman. For the mind of one who has crossed is one thing, and the mind of one who seeks to cross is another.” – he spoke this verse.

Tattha apāranti tāta, nāvika paratīraṃ atiṇṇameva janaṃ orimatīre ṭhitaññeva vetanaṃ yācassu, tato laddhañca gahetvā guttaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā pacchā manusse paratīraṃ neyyāsi, evaṃ te bhogavaḍḍhi bhavissati. Añño hi tiṇṇassa manoti tāta nāvika, paratīraṃ gatassa añño mano bhavati, adatvāva gantukāmo hoti. Yo panesa pāresī nāma paratīraṃ esati, paratīraṃ gantukāmo hoti, so atirekampi datvā gantukāmo hoti, iti pāresino añño mano hoti, tasmā tvaṃ atiṇṇameva yāceyyāsi, ayaṃ tāva te bhogānaṃ vaḍḍhi nāmāti.

Herein, ‘apāraṃ’: dear ferryman, you should ask for the fare from a person who has not yet crossed to the further shore, while he is still standing on this shore. Then, having received it and placed it in a safe place, you should afterwards take the people to the further shore. In this way your possessions will increase. ‘Añño hi tiṇṇassa mano’: dear ferryman, the mind of one who has gone to the further shore is different; he wants to leave without paying. But as for the one who seeks to cross, who desires to go to the further shore, he is willing to give even extra to go. Thus the mind of one who seeks to cross is different. Therefore you should ask from one who has not yet crossed. This, for a start, is what is called the increase of your possessions.

Taṃ sutvā nāviko [P 3.0231] cintesi “ayaṃ tāva me ovādo bhavissati, idāni panesa aññaṃ kiñci mayhaṃ dassatī”ti. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “ayaṃ tāva te, āvuso, bhogavaḍḍhi, idāni atthadhammavaḍḍhiṃ suṇāhī”ti vatvā ovadanto –

Hearing that, the ferryman thought, ‘This, for now, is the advice for me; now he will give me something else.’ Then the Bodhisatta said to him, ‘Friend, this for a start is the increase of possessions for you. Now listen to the increase of welfare and righteousness,’ and advising him, he said:

5.

5.

“Gāme [M 3.0217] vā yadi vāraññe, ninne vā yadi vā thale;

Sabbattha anusāsāmi, māsu kujjhittha nāvikā”ti. – gāthamāha;

“Whether in a village or in the wilderness, in a valley or on high ground; everywhere I instruct you: do not be angry, O ferryman.” – he spoke this verse.

Itissa imāya gāthāya atthadhammavaḍḍhiṃ kathetvā “ayaṃ te atthavaḍḍhi ca dhammavaḍḍhi cā”ti āha. So pana dandhapuriso taṃ ovādaṃ na kiñci maññamāno “idaṃ, samaṇa, tayā mayhaṃ dinnaṃ [V 3.0203] nāvāvetana”nti āha. “Āmāvuso”ti. “Mayhaṃ iminā kammaṃ natthi, aññaṃ me dehī”ti. “Āvuso, idaṃ ṭhapetvā mayhaṃ aññaṃ natthī”ti. “Atha tvaṃ kasmā mama nāvaṃ āruḷhosī”ti tāpasaṃ gaṅgātīre pātetvā ure nisīditvā mukhamevassa pothesi.

Thus, with this verse, he explained the increase of welfare and righteousness, saying, ‘This is your increase in welfare and your increase in righteousness.’ But that slow-witted man, thinking nothing of this advice, said, ‘Ascetic, is this the boat fare you have given me?’ ‘Yes, friend.’ ‘I have no use for this. Give me something else.’ ‘Friend, apart from this, I have nothing else.’ ‘Then why did you board my boat?’ And throwing the ascetic down on the bank of the Ganges, he sat on his chest and beat him in the face.

Satthā “iti so, bhikkhave, tāpaso yaṃ ovādaṃ datvā rañño santikā gāmavaraṃ labhi, tameva ovādaṃ andhabālassa nāvikassa kathetvā mukhapothanaṃ pāpuṇi, tasmā ovādaṃ dentena yuttajanasseva dātabbo, na ayuttajanassā”ti vatvā abhisambuddho hutvā tadanantaraṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher said: ‘Thus, monks, that ascetic received an excellent village from the king for giving that advice, but when he told that same advice to the blind and foolish ferryman, he got a beating in the face. Therefore, one who gives advice should give it only to a suitable person, not to an unsuitable one.’ Having said this, as the Perfectly Enlightened One, he then spoke this verse:

6.

6.

“Yāyevānusāsaniyā, rājā gāmavaraṃ adā;

Tāyevānusāsaniyā, nāviko paharī mukha”nti.

“For the very same instruction, the king gave an excellent village; for that very same instruction, the ferryman struck him in the face.”

Tassa taṃ paharantasseva bhariyā bhattaṃ gahetvā āgatā pāpapurisaṃ disvā “sāmi, ayaṃ tāpaso nāma rājakulūpako, mā paharī”ti āha. So kujjhitvā “tvaṃ me imaṃ kūṭatāpasaṃ paharituṃ na desī”ti uṭṭhāya taṃ paharitvā pātesi. Atha bhattapāti patitvā bhijji, tassā ca pana garugabbhāya gabbho bhūmiyaṃ pati. Atha naṃ manussā samparivāretvā “purisaghātakacoro”ti [P 3.0232] gahetvā bandhitvā rañño dassesuṃ. Rājā vinicchinitvā tassa rājāṇaṃ kāresi. Satthā abhisambuddho hutvā tamatthaṃ pakāsento osānagāthamāha –

Just as he was striking him, his wife arrived bringing his meal. Seeing the wicked man, she said, ‘Husband, this ascetic is one who attends on the royal family. Do not strike him.’ He became angry and said, ‘You will not let me strike this fraudulent ascetic?’ and getting up, he struck her and knocked her down. Then the food bowl fell and broke, and as she was heavily pregnant, her fetus fell to the ground. Then people surrounded him, seized him, calling him a ‘murderous thief,’ and after binding him, they showed him to the king. The king investigated and had the royal punishment carried out on him. The Teacher, as the Perfectly Enlightened One, clarifying this matter, spoke the concluding verse:

7.

7.

“Bhattaṃ bhinnaṃ hatā bhariyā, gabbho ca patito chamā;

Migova jātarūpena, na tenatthaṃ abandhi sū”ti.

“The meal was spilt, the wife was struck down, and the fetus fell to the ground. Like a deer with gold, he truly gained no benefit from it.”
