Tattha [M 3.0218] bhattaṃ bhinnanti bhattapāti bhinnā. Hatāti pahatā. Chamāti bhūmiyaṃ. Migova jātarūpenāti yathā migo suvaṇṇaṃ vā hiraññaṃ vā muttāmaṇiādīni vā madditvā gacchantopi attharitvā nipajjantopi tena jātarūpena attano atthaṃ vaḍḍhetuṃ nibbattetuṃ na sakkoti, evameva so andhabālo paṇḍitehi dinnaṃ ovādaṃ sutvāpi attano atthaṃ vaḍḍhetuṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Abandhi sūti ettha abandhi soti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Sa-oiti imesaṃ padānañhi sūti sandhi hoti.

Herein, ‘bhattaṃ bhinnaṃ’ means the food bowl was broken. ‘Hatā’ means struck down. ‘Chamā’ means on the ground. ‘Migova jātarūpena’: just as a deer, though it may walk over or lie down upon gold, silver, pearls, gems, and so on, is unable to produce or increase its own welfare with that gold, so too that blind fool, though he heard the advice given by the wise, was unable to produce or increase his own welfare. This is the meaning. ‘Abandhi sū’: here the meaning should be understood as ‘abandhi so’ (he did not gain). The particle ‘sū’ is a euphonic combination of ‘sa’ and ‘u’.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne [V 3.0204] so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā nāviko idāni nāvikova ahosi, rājā ānando, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths and made the connection in the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, that monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. ‘At that time, the ferryman was the present-day ferryman, the king was Ānanda, but the ascetic was I myself.’

Avāriyajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Avāriya Jātaka, the First.

[377] 2. Setaketujātakavaṇṇanā

[377] 2. The Commentary on the Setaketu Jātaka

Mā tāta kujjhi na hi sādhu kodhoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kuhakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi, paccuppannavatthu uddālajātake (jā. 1.14.62 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

“Dear one, do not be angry, for anger is not good.” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a fraudulent monk. The story of the present will be made clear in the Uddālaka Jātaka (Jā 487).

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ disāpāmokkho ācariyo hutvā pañcasate māṇave mante vācesi. Tesaṃ jeṭṭhako setaketu nāma udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbattamāṇavo, tassa jātiṃ nissāya mahanto māno ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ aññehi māṇavehi saddhiṃ nagarā nikkhamanto nagaraṃ pavisantaṃ ekaṃ caṇḍālaṃ [P 3.0233] disvā “kosi tva”nti pucchitvā “caṇḍālohamasmī”ti vutte tassa sarīraṃ paharitvā āgatavātassa attano sarīre phusanabhayena “nassa, caṇḍāla, kāḷakaṇṇī, adhovātaṃ yāhī”ti vatvā vegena tassa uparivātaṃ agamāsi. Caṇḍālo sīghataraṃ gantvā tassa uparivāte aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ so “nassa kāḷakaṇṇī”ti suṭṭhutaraṃ akkosi paribhāsi. Taṃ sutvā caṇḍālo “tvaṃ kosī”ti pucchi. “Brāhmaṇamāṇavohamasmī”ti[M 3.0219]. “Brāhmaṇo hotu, mayā pana puṭṭhapañhaṃ kathetuṃ sakkhissasī”ti. “Āma, sakkhissāmī”ti. “Sace na sakkosi, pādantarena taṃ gamemī”ti. So attānaṃ takketvā “gamehī”ti āha.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher in Benares who taught the Vedas to five hundred young brahmins. The eldest of them was a young man named Setaketu, born into an Udicca brahmin family, and on account of his birth he was very proud. One day, while leaving the city with the other young brahmins, he saw an outcaste man entering the city. He asked, 'Who are you?' When the man replied, 'I am an outcaste,' Setaketu, fearing that the wind which had struck the outcaste's body and was blowing towards him would touch his own body, said, 'Perish, you wretched outcaste! Go downwind!' and he quickly moved upwind of him. The outcaste, however, moved more quickly and stood upwind of him. Then Setaketu reviled and abused him even more harshly, 'Perish, you wretch!' Hearing this, the outcaste asked, 'Who are you?' 'I am a young brahmin.' 'You may be a brahmin, but will you be able to answer a question I ask?' 'Yes, I will.' 'If you cannot, I will make you pass between my legs.' Considering his own knowledge, Setaketu said, 'Make me pass.'

Caṇḍālaputto tassa kathaṃ parisaṃ gāhāpetvā “māṇava, disā nāma katarā”ti pañhaṃ pucchi. “Disā nāma puratthimādayo catasso disā”ti. Caṇḍālo “nāhaṃ taṃ etaṃ disaṃ pucchāmi, tvaṃ ettakampi ajānanto mama sarīre pahaṭavātaṃ jigucchasī”ti taṃ khandhaṭṭhike gahetvā onametvā attano pādantarena gamesi. Māṇavā taṃ pavattiṃ ācariyassa ācikkhiṃsu. Taṃ sutvā ācariyo “saccaṃ kira, tāta, setaketu caṇḍālenāsi pādantarena gamito”ti? “Āma, ācariya, so maṃ caṇḍāladāsiputto disāmattampi na jānāsī”ti attano pādantarena gamesi, idāni disvā kattabbaṃ assa jānissāmīti kuddho caṇḍālaputtaṃ akkosi paribhāsi. Atha naṃ ācariyo ‘tāta, setaketu mā tassa kujjhi, paṇḍito caṇḍāladāsiputto[V 3.0205], na so taṃ etaṃ disaṃ pucchati, aññaṃ disaṃ pucchi, tayā pana diṭṭhasutaviññātato adiṭṭhāsutāviññātameva bahutara”nti ovadanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

The outcaste's son, having made the assembly take note of his words, asked the young brahmin a question: 'Young man, what is a direction?' 'The directions are the four cardinal directions—east and so forth.' The outcaste said: 'I am not asking you about that kind of direction. You, who do not even know this much, are disgusted by the wind that has struck my body!' Seizing him by the nape of his neck, he bent him down and made him pass between his legs. The young brahmins reported this incident to their teacher. Hearing it, the teacher asked: 'Is it true, dear Setaketu, that you were made to pass between an outcaste's legs?' 'Yes, teacher. That son of an outcaste slave woman made me pass between his legs, saying, "You do not even know what a direction is!" Now I will see him and know what must be done to him!' Angrily, he reviled and abused the outcaste's son. Then the teacher, admonishing him, said: 'Dear Setaketu, do not be angry with him. The outcaste's son is wise. He was not asking you about that kind of direction; he asked about another direction. For what is unseen, unheard, and uncognized by you is far more than what has been seen, heard, and cognized.' Admonishing him, he spoke these two verses:

8.

8.

“Mā tāta kujjhi na hi sādhu kodho, bahumpi te adiṭṭhamassutañca;

Mātā pitā [P 3.0234] disatā setaketu, ācariyamāhu disataṃ pasatthā.

“Do not be angry, dear one, for anger is not good; much is unseen and unheard by you. Mother and father are a direction, Setaketu; the teacher, they say, is the praised direction.

9.

9.

“Agārino annadapānavatthadā, avhāyikā tampi disaṃ vadanti;

Esā disā paramā setaketu, yaṃ patvā dukkhī sukhino bhavantī”ti.

“Householders who give food, drink, and clothing, and those who invite—they too are called a direction. This, Setaketu, is the supreme direction, having reached which the sorrowful become happy.”

Tattha na hi sādhu kodhoti kodho nāma uppajjamāno subhāsitadubbhāsitaṃ atthānatthaṃ hitāhitaṃ jānituṃ na detīti na sādhu na laddhako. Bahumpi te adiṭṭhanti tayā cakkhunā adiṭṭhaṃ sotena ca assutameva bahutaraṃ. Disatāti disā. Mātāpitaro puttānaṃ purimataraṃ [M 3.0220] uppannattā puratthimadisā nāma jātāti vadati. Ācariyamāhu disataṃ pasatthāti ācariyā pana dakkhiṇeyyattā disataṃ pasatthā dakkhiṇā disāti buddhādayo ariyā āhu kathenti dīpenti.

Herein, 'anger is not good': for anger, when it arises, does not allow one to know what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, what is beneficial and harmful, what is advantageous and disadvantageous; thus it is not good, not profitable. 'Much is unseen by you': what is unseen by your eye and unheard by your ear is much more. 'Disatā': a direction. He says that since parents arise before their children, they are called the eastern direction. 'The teacher, they say, is the praised direction': since teachers are worthy of offerings, the noble ones such as the Buddhas say, declare, and clarify that they are the praised direction, the southern direction.

Agārinoti gahaṭṭhā. Annadapānavatthadāti annadā, pānadā, vatthadā ca. Avhāyikāti “etha deyyadhammaṃ paṭiggaṇhathā”ti pakkosanakā. Tampi disaṃ vadantīti tampi buddhādayo ariyā ekaṃ disaṃ vadanti. Iminā catupaccayadāyakā gahaṭṭhā paccaye apadisitvā dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇehi upagantabbattā ekā disā nāmāti dīpeti. Aparo nayo – ye ete agārino annapānavatthadā, tesaṃ chakāmasaggasampattidāyakaṭṭhena uparūpari avhāyanato ye avhāyikā dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇā, tampi disaṃ vadanti, buddhādayo ariyā uparimadisaṃ nāma vadantīti dīpeti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Agārino: householders. Annadapānavatthadā: givers of food, drink, and clothing. Avhāyikā: those who invite, saying, “Come, accept this offering.” They too are called a direction: the noble ones such as the Buddhas also call them a direction. This shows that householders, donors of the four requisites, are called a direction because they are to be approached by righteous ascetics and brahmins for the requisites. Another interpretation: The righteous ascetics and brahmins are the inviters because they repeatedly invite those householders who are givers of food, drink, and clothing, being the means for them to attain the fortune of the six sensual heavens. The noble ones such as the Buddhas call them a direction, that is, the upper direction. And this has been said:

“Mātā pitā disā pubbā, ācariyā dakkhiṇā disā;

Puttadārā disā pacchā, mittāmaccā ca uttarā.

“Mother and father are the eastern direction, teachers are the southern direction; wife and children are the western direction, friends and associates are the northern direction.

“Dāsakammakarā heṭṭhā, uddhaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇā;

Etā disā namasseyya, alamatto kule gihī”ti. (dī. ni. 3.273);

“Servants and workers are the direction below, ascetics and brahmins are the direction above; a clansman who is a householder, being capable, should pay homage to these directions.”

Esā disāti idaṃ pana nibbānaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Jātiādinā hi nānappakārena dukkhena [V 3.0206] dukkhitā sattā yaṃ patvā niddukkhā sukhino bhavanti, esā eva ca sattehi agatapubbā disā nāma. Teneva ca nibbānaṃ “paramā”ti āha. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

'This direction': this is said with reference to Nibbāna. For beings afflicted with various kinds of suffering such as birth, upon reaching which they become free from suffering and happy, this indeed is the direction never before travelled by beings. For that reason he said Nibbāna is supreme. And this has been said:

“Samatittikaṃ [P 3.0235] anavasesakaṃ, telapattaṃ yathā parihareyya;

Evaṃ sacittamanurakkhe, patthayāno disaṃ agatapubba”nti. (jā. 1.1.96);

“As one would carry a bowl of oil filled to the brim, leaving no remainder, so should one guard one’s own mind, aspiring to the direction never travelled before.”

Evaṃ mahāsatto māṇavassa disā kathesi. So pana “caṇḍālenamhi pādantarena gamito”ti tasmiṃ ṭhāne avasitvā takkasilaṃ gantvā [M 3.0221] disāpāmokkhācariyassa santike sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā ācariyena anuññāto takkasilato nikkhamitvā sabbasamayasippaṃ sikkhanto vicari. So ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ patvā taṃ nissāya vasante pañcasate tāpase disvā tesaṃ santike pabbajitvā yaṃ te jānanti sippamantacaraṇaṃ, taṃ uggaṇhitvā gaṇasatthā hutvā tehi parivārito bārāṇasiṃ gantvā punadivase bhikkhaṃ caranto rājaṅgaṇaṃ agamāsi. Rājā tāpasānaṃ iriyāpathe pasīditvā antonivesane bhojetvā te attano uyyāne vasāpesi. So ekadivasaṃ tāpase parivisitvā “ajja sāyanhe uyyānaṃ gantvā ayye vandissāmī”ti āha.

Thus the Great Being spoke to the young man about the directions. But he, thinking, “I was made to pass between an outcaste's legs,” did not stay in that place but went to Takkasilā. There he learned all the arts from the world-renowned teacher. Having been given leave by his teacher, he left Takkasilā and wandered about, learning the arts of every philosophical school. He reached a border village and, seeing five hundred ascetics living in dependence on it, he went forth in their presence. He learned whatever arts, spells, and practices they knew and became the leader of their group. Surrounded by them, he went to Bārāṇasī. The next day, while wandering for alms, he came to the royal courtyard. The king, pleased with the deportment of the ascetics, fed them in the inner palace and had them dwell in his park. One day, after serving the ascetics, he said: “This evening I will go to the park and pay homage to the masters.”

Setaketu uyyānaṃ gantvā tāpase sannipātetvā “mārisā, ajja rājā āgamissati, rājāno ca nāma sakiṃ ārādhetvā yāvatāyukaṃ sukhaṃ jīvituṃ sakkā, ajja ekacce vaggulivataṃ caratha, ekacce kaṇṭakaseyyaṃ kappetha, ekacce pañcātapaṃ tappetha, ekacce ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyuñjatha, ekacce udakorohaṇakammaṃ karotha, ekacce mante sajjhāyathā”ti vicāretvā sayaṃ pakkasāladvāre apassayapīṭhake nisīditvā pañcavaṇṇaraṅgasamujjalavāsanaṃ ekaṃ potthakaṃ vicitravaṇṇe ādhārake ṭhapetvā susikkhitehi catūhi pañcahi māṇavehi pucchite pucchite pañhe kathesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā āgantvā [P 3.0236] te micchātapaṃ karonte disvā tuṭṭho setaketuṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno purohitena saddhiṃ sallapanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Setaketu went to the park, gathered the ascetics, and said: “Sirs, today the king will come. If kings are pleased just once, one can live happily for the rest of one’s life. Today, some of you should practice the bat-vow, some should lie on a bed of thorns, some should practice the five-fire austerity, some should undertake the exertion of squatting, some should perform the act of descending into the water, and some should recite mantras.” Having assigned these tasks, he himself sat on a chair with a backrest at the door of his leaf-hut. Placing a manuscript, radiant with ink of five colors, on a multi-colored stand, he answered the questions asked by four or five well-trained young men. At that moment the king arrived. Seeing them performing their false austerities, he was displeased. He approached Setaketu, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Desiring to speak with his chaplain, he spoke the third verse:

10.

10.

“Kharājinā jaṭilā paṅkadantā, dummakkharūpā yeme jappanti mante;

Kacci nu te mānusake payoge, idaṃ vidū parimuttā apāyā”ti.

“Wearing rough hides with hooves, with matted hair and mud-caked teeth, these of foul appearance who mutter mantras—I wonder, being established in these human endeavors, do they know this world and are they freed from the woeful states?”

Tattha kharājināti sakhurehi ajinacammehi samannāgatā. Paṅkadantāti dantakaṭṭhassa akhādanena malaggahitadantā. Dummakkharūpāti anañjitāmaṇḍitalūkhanivāsanapārupanā mālāgandhavilepanavajjitā[V 3.0207], kiliṭṭharūpāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yeme jappantīti ye ime mante sajjhāyanti. Mānusake payogeti manussehi kattabbapayoge ṭhitā. Idaṃ vidū parimuttā apāyāti imasmiṃ [M 3.0222] payoge ṭhatvā imaṃ lokaṃ viditvā pākaṭaṃ katvā “kacci ete isayo catūhi apāyehi muttā”ti pucchati.

Herein, 'kharājinā' means possessing animal hides with the hooves still attached. 'Paṅkadantā' means having teeth covered in grime from not using a tooth-stick. 'Dummakkharūpā' means unanointed, unadorned, wearing rough clothes, and abstaining from garlands, perfumes, and ointments; that is to say, of soiled appearance. 'Yeme jappanti' refers to those who recite these mantras. 'Mānusake payoge' means established in practices to be performed by humans. 'Idaṃ vidū parimuttā apāyā': he asks, “Established in this practice, having known this world and made it manifest, are these seers freed from the four woeful states?”

Taṃ sutvā purohito catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the chaplain spoke the fourth verse:

11.

11.

“Pāpāni kammāni karitva rāja, bahussuto ce na careyya dhammaṃ;

Sahassavedopi na taṃ paṭicca, dukkhā pamuñce caraṇaṃ apatvā”ti.

“Having done evil deeds, O king, if one who is very learned does not practice the Dhamma; even one who knows a thousand Vedas, on account of that, is not freed from suffering without having attained right conduct.”

Tattha karitvāti katvā. Caraṇanti saha sīlena aṭṭha samāpattiyo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Mahārāja, “ahaṃ bahussutomhī”ti sahassavedopi ce tividhaṃ sucaritadhammaṃ na careyya, pāpāneva kareyya, so tāni pāpāni kammāni katvā taṃ bāhusaccaṃ paṭicca sīlasamāpattisaṅkhātaṃ caraṇaṃ appatvā dukkhā na pamuñce, apāyadukkhato na muccatevāti.

Herein, 'karitvā' means having done. 'Caraṇaṃ' means the eight meditative attainments along with virtue. This is what is meant: Great king, if one who knows a thousand Vedas, thinking, ‘I am very learned,’ does not practice the threefold Dhamma of good conduct but does only evil deeds, then having done those evil deeds, he is not freed from suffering on account of his great learning, as he has not attained the conduct reckoned as virtue and the meditative attainments; that is, he is not released from the suffering of the woeful states.

Taṃ sutvā rājā tāpasesu pasādaṃ hari. Tato setaketu cintesi “imassa rañño tāpasesu pasādo udapādi, taṃ panesa purohito vāsiyā paharitvā viya chindi, mayā etena saddhiṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So tena saddhiṃ kathento pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king lost his confidence in the ascetics. Then Setaketu thought: ‘The king’s confidence in the ascetics had arisen, but this chaplain has cut it off as if by striking with an adze. It is proper for me to speak with this brahmin.’ So, desiring to speak with him, he spoke the fifth verse:

12.

12.

“Sahassavedopi [P 3.0237] na taṃ paṭicca, dukkhā pamuñce caraṇaṃ apatvā;

Maññāmi vedā aphalā bhavanti, sasaṃyamaṃ caraṇameva sacca”nti.

“Even one who knows a thousand Vedas is not, on account of that, freed from suffering without having attained right conduct. I think the Vedas are fruitless; only conduct with self-restraint is the truth.”

Tassattho [V 3.0208][M 3.0223] – sace sahassavedopi taṃ bāhusaccaṃ paṭicca caraṇaṃ appatvā attānaṃ dukkhā na pamuñce, evaṃ sante ahaṃ maññāmi “tayo vedā aphalā honti, sasīlaṃ samāpatticaraṇameva saccaṃ hotī”ti.

Its meaning is: If even one who knows a thousand Vedas does not free himself from suffering on account of that great learning without having attained conduct, this being so, I think: ‘The three Vedas are fruitless; only conduct consisting of virtue and the meditative attainments is the truth.’

Taṃ sutvā purohito chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the chaplain spoke the sixth verse:

13.

13.

“Na heva vedā aphalā bhavanti, sasaṃyamaṃ caraṇameva saccaṃ;

Kittiñhi pappoti adhicca vede, santiṃ puṇeti caraṇena danto”ti.

“The Vedas are certainly not fruitless, and conduct with self-restraint is indeed the truth. For one gains fame by mastering the Vedas, but it is through conduct that the tamed one reaches peace.”

Tassattho – tayo vedā aphalā na bhavanti, sasaṃyamaṃ caraṇameva saccaṃ seyyaṃ uttamaṃ pavaraṃ na heva hoti. Kiṃkāraṇā? Kittiñhi pappoti adhicca vedeti tayo vede adhicca diṭṭhadhamme kittimattaṃ yasamattaṃ lābhamattaṃ labhati, ito paraṃ aññaṃ natthi, tasmā na te aphalā. Santiṃ puṇeti caraṇena dantoti sīle patiṭṭhāya samāpattiyo nibbattetvā samāpattipadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento accantaṃ santaṃ nibbānaṃ nāma taṃ eti pāpuṇāti.

The meaning is: The three Vedas are not fruitless, nor is conduct accompanied by self-restraint alone the truth, the best, the highest, or the supreme. For what reason? ‘Kittiñhi pappoti adhicca vede’ means that by studying the three Vedas, one obtains a measure of fame, honor, and gain in this very life; there is nothing beyond this, therefore they are not fruitless. ‘Santiṃ puṇeti caraṇena danto’ means that, being established in virtuous conduct, one generates the meditative attainments and, developing insight based on those attainments, one reaches and attains that ultimate peace known as Nibbāna.”

Iti purohito setaketuno vādaṃ bhinditvā te sabbe gihī kāretvā phalakāvudhāni gāhāpetvā mahantatarake katvā rañño upaṭṭhāke kāresi. Ayaṃ kira mahantatarakānaṃ vaṃso.

Thus the chaplain refuted Setaketu’s doctrine. He had all the ascetics return to lay life, made them take up shields and weapons, appointed them as court officials (mahantatarake), and made them attendants to the king. This, it is said, was the origin of the Mahantataraka clan.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā setaketu kuhakabhikkhu ahosi, caṇḍālo sāriputto, rājā ānando, purohito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Setaketu was the deceitful bhikkhu, the caṇḍāla was Sāriputta, the king was Ānanda, and the chaplain was I myself.”

Setaketujātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Setaketu Jātaka, the second.

[378] 3. Darīmukhajātakavaṇṇanā

[378] 3. 3. The Commentary on the Darīmukha Jātaka

Paṅko [P 3.0238] ca kāmāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahābhinikkhamanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu heṭṭhā kathitameva.

“Sensual pleasures are a swamp...”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Great Renunciation. The story of the present has already been told.

Atīte rājagahanagare magadharājā nāma rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, brahmadattakumārotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Tassa jātadivaseyeva purohitassapi putto jāyi, tassa mukhaṃ ativiya sobhati, tenassa darīmukhoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Te ubhopi rājakuleyeva saṃvaḍḍhā aññamaññaṃ piyasahāyā hutvā soḷasavassakāle takkasilaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā “sabbasamayasippañca sikkhissāma, desacārittañca jānissāmā”ti gāmanigamādīsu carantā bārāṇasiṃ patvā devakule vasitvā punadivase bārāṇasiṃ bhikkhāya pavisiṃsu. Tattha ekasmiṃ kule “brāhmaṇe bhojetvā [M 3.0224] vācanakaṃ dassāmā”ti pāyāsaṃ pacitvā āsanāni paññattāni honti. Manussā te ubhopi bhikkhāya carante disvā “brāhmaṇā āgatā”ti gehaṃ pavesetvā mahāsattassa āsane suddhavatthaṃ paññāpesuṃ, darīmukhassa āsane rattakambalaṃ. Darīmukho taṃ nimittaṃ disvā “ajja mayhaṃ sahāyo bārāṇasirājā bhavissati, ahaṃ senāpatī”ti aññāsi. Te tattha bhuñjitvā vācanakaṃ gahetvā [V 3.0209] maṅgalaṃ vatvā nikkhamma taṃ rājuyyānaṃ agamaṃsu. Tattha mahāsatto maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe nipajji, darīmukho panassa pāde parimajjanto nisīdi.

In the past, when a king named Magadha was ruling in the city of Rājagaha, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of his chief queen. They named him Prince Brahmadatta. On the very day of his birth, a son was also born to the chaplain. The son's face was exceedingly beautiful, so they named him Darīmukha. The two grew up together in the royal household and became dear friends. At the age of sixteen, they went to Takkasilā and learned all the arts. Resolving, “We will learn all the doctrinal systems and the customs of the regions,” they traveled through villages and towns and eventually arrived at Vārāṇasī. They stayed in a shrine, and the next day they entered Vārāṇasī for alms. In that city, in one household, the people had prepared milk-porridge, intending to feed brahmins and offer a gift of recitation. When the people saw the two wandering for alms, they thought, “The brahmins have arrived,” and invited them into the house. They spread a clean white cloth on the seat for the Great Being and a red woolen blanket for Darīmukha. Seeing this sign, Darīmukha knew: “Today my friend will become the king of Vārāṇasī, and I will be the commander-in-chief.” After eating there, they received their recitation gift, spoke a blessing, and left for the royal park. There, the Great Being lay down on the auspicious stone slab, while Darīmukha sat massaging his feet.

Tadā bārāṇasirañño matassa sattamo divaso hoti. Purohito rañño sarīrakiccaṃ katvā aputtake rajje sattame divase phussarathaṃ vissajjesi. Phussarathavissajjanakiccaṃ mahājanakajātake (jā. 2.22.123 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Phussaratho nagarā nikkhamitvā caturaṅginiyā [P 3.0239] senāya parivuto anekasatehi tūriyehi vajjamānehi uyyānadvāraṃ pāpuṇi. Darīmukho tūriyasaddaṃ sutvā “sahāyassa me phussaratho āgacchati, ajjevesa rājā hutvā mayhaṃ senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ dassati, ko me gharāvāsenattho, nikkhamitvā pabbajissāmī”ti bodhisattaṃ anāmantetvāva ekamantaṃ gantvā paṭicchanne aṭṭhāsi. Purohito uyyānadvāre rathaṃ ṭhapetvā uyyānaṃ paviṭṭho bodhisattaṃ maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe nipannaṃ disvā pādesu lakkhaṇāni oloketvā “ayaṃ puññavā satto dvisahassadīpaparivārānaṃ catunnampi mahādīpānaṃ rajjaṃ kāretuṃ samattho, dhiti panassa kīdisā”ti sabbatūriyāni paggaṇhāpesi. Bodhisatto pabujjhitvā mukhato sāṭakaṃ apanetvā mahājanaṃ oloketvā puna sāṭakena mukhaṃ paṭicchādetvā thokaṃ nipajjitvā passaddhadaratho uṭṭhāya silāpaṭṭe pallaṅkena nisīdi. Purohito jāṇukena patiṭṭhāya “deva, rajjaṃ tumhākaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti āha. “Aputtakaṃ bhaṇe rajja”nti. “Āma, devā”ti. “Tena hi sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Te tassa uyyāneyeva abhisekaṃ akaṃsu. So yasamahantatāya darīmukhaṃ asaritvāva rathaṃ abhiruyha mahājanaparivuto nagaraṃ pavisitvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā rājadvāre ṭhitova amaccānaṃ ṭhānantarāni vicāretvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhi.

At that time, it was the seventh day since the king of Vārāṇasī had died. After performing the king's funeral rites, the chaplain sent forth the Phussa chariot on the seventh day, as the kingdom was without an heir. The procedure for sending forth the Phussa chariot will be explained in the Mahājanaka Jātaka. The Phussa chariot left the city, surrounded by the fourfold army and accompanied by hundreds of musical instruments being played, and arrived at the park gate. Hearing the sound of the instruments, Darīmukha thought: “The Phussa chariot is coming for my friend. Today he will become king and offer me the position of commander-in-chief. What is the use of the household life to me? I will go forth and become a monk.” Without informing the Bodhisatta, he went aside and stood in a hidden place. The chaplain, having stopped the chariot at the park gate, entered the park and saw the Bodhisatta lying on the auspicious stone slab. Observing the marks on his feet, he thought: “This meritorious being is capable of ruling over the four great continents with their two thousand surrounding islands. But what is his fortitude like?” He then ordered all the musical instruments to be played. The Bodhisatta awoke, removed the cloth from his face, looked at the crowd, then covered his face again with the cloth. After lying for a short while until his fatigue was stilled, he arose and sat cross-legged on the stone slab. The chaplain knelt down and said: “Your Majesty, the kingdom comes to you.” “My good man, is the kingdom without an heir?” “Yes, Your Majesty.” “In that case, very well,” he accepted. They performed his consecration right there in the park. Due to his great glory, without remembering Darīmukha, the king mounted the chariot, entered the city surrounded by the crowd, and made a clockwise circumambulation. Standing at the palace gate, he assigned ranks to the ministers and then ascended the palace.

Tasmiṃ [M 3.0225] khaṇe darīmukho “suññaṃ dāni uyyāna”nti āgantvā maṅgalasilāya nisīdi, athassa purato paṇḍupalāsaṃ pati. So tasmiṃyeva paṇḍupalāse khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapetvā tilakkhaṇaṃ sammasitvā pathaviṃ unnādento paccekabodhiṃ nibbattesi. Tassa taṅkhaṇaññeva gihiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyi, iddhimayapattacīvaraṃ ākāsato otaritvā sarīre paṭimuñci. Tāvadeva aṭṭhaparikkhāradharo iriyāpathasampanno vassasaṭṭhikatthero viya hutvā [P 3.0240] iddhiyā ākāse uppatitvā himavantapadese nandamūlakapabbhāraṃ agamāsi. Bodhisattopi dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi, yasamahantatāya pana yasena pamatto hutvā cattālīsa vassāni darīmukhaṃ na sari, cattālīse pana saṃvacchare atīte taṃ saritvā “mayhaṃ sahāyo darīmukho nāma atthi, kahaṃ nu kho so”ti taṃ daṭṭhukāmo ahosi. So tato paṭṭhāya antepurepi parisamajjhepi “kahaṃ nu kho mayhaṃ sahāyo darīmukho[V 3.0210], yo me tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ katheti, mahantamassa yasaṃ dassāmī”ti vadati. Evaṃ tassa punappunaṃ taṃ sarantasseva aññāni dasa saṃvaccharāni atikkantāni.

At that moment, Darīmukha, thinking, “The park is now empty,” returned and sat on the auspicious stone. Then a withered leaf fell before him. Taking that very withered leaf as his object, he established insight into decay and passing away, contemplated the three characteristics, and, making the earth resound, he attained Pacceka-Enlightenment. At that very instant his lay appearance vanished, and a bowl and robes created by psychic power descended from the sky and settled on his body. Instantly, bearing the eight requisites and perfect in deportment, he became like an elder of sixty years’ standing. Rising into the air by psychic power, he went to the Nandamūlaka cave in the Himālayas. The Bodhisatta, for his part, ruled righteously. However, being heedless because of his great glory, he did not remember Darīmukha for forty years. When forty years had passed, he remembered him and thought: “I have a friend named Darīmukha. Where could he be?” Desiring to see him, from then on, both in the inner palace and in the midst of his assembly, he would say: “Where is my friend Darīmukha? To the one who tells me where he is dwelling, I will give great wealth.” As he was repeatedly remembering him in this way, another ten years passed.

Darīmukhapaccekabuddhopi paññāsavassaccayena āvajjento “maṃ kho sahāyo saratī”ti ñatvā “idāni so mahallako puttadhītādīhi vuddhippatto, gantvā dhammaṃ kathetvā pabbājessāmi na”nti iddhiyā ākāsena āgantvā uyyāne otaritvā suvaṇṇapaṭimā viya silāpaṭṭe nisīdi. Uyyānapālo taṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, kuto tumhe ethā”ti pucchi. “Nandamūlakapabbhārato”ti. “Ke nāma tumhe”ti? “Darīmukhapaccekabuddho nāmāhaṃ, āvuso”ti. “Bhante, amhākaṃ rājānaṃ jānāthā”ti? “Āma jānāmi, gihikāle no sahāyo”ti. “Bhante, rājā tumhe daṭṭhukāmo, kathessāmi tassa tumhākaṃ āgatabhāva”nti. “Gaccha kathehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti vatvā turitaturitova gantvā tassa silāpaṭṭe nisinnabhāvaṃ rañño kathesi. Rājā “āgato kira me sahāyo, passissāmi na”nti rathaṃ āruyha mahantena parivārena uyyānaṃ gantvā paccekabuddhaṃ vanditvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha naṃ paccekabuddho “kiṃ, brahmadatta, dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi, agatigamanaṃ na gacchasi, dhanatthāya [M 3.0226] lokaṃ na pīḷesi, dānādīni puññāni karosī”tiādīni [P 3.0241] vadanto paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “brahmadatta, mahallakosi, etarahi kāme pahāya pabbajituṃ te samayo”ti vatvā tassa dhammaṃ desento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Paccekabuddha Darīmukha, at the end of fifty years, adverted and knew, “My friend is remembering me.” He thought: “He is now old and has prospered with sons and daughters. I will go, teach him the Dhamma, and have him go forth.” He traveled through the air by psychic power, descended in the park, and sat on the stone slab like a golden statue. The park keeper saw him, approached, and asked: “Venerable sir, from where have you come?” “From the Nandamūlaka slope.” “What is your name?” “I am the Paccekabuddha named Darīmukha, friend.” “Venerable sir, do you know our king?” “Yes, I know him. He was our friend when we were laymen.” “Venerable sir, the king is desirous of seeing you. I will tell him of your arrival.” “Go and tell him.” Saying, “Very well,” the park keeper went in great haste and told the king that he was sitting on the stone slab. The king thought, “My friend has come, it seems; I will see him.” Mounting his chariot, he went to the park with a large retinue, paid homage to the Paccekabuddha, exchanged friendly greetings, and sat down to one side. Then the Paccekabuddha exchanged friendly greetings with him, saying: “Well, Brahmadatta, do you rule righteously? Do you not follow a wrong course of action? Do you not oppress the people for the sake of wealth? Do you perform meritorious deeds such as giving?” Then he said: “Brahmadatta, you are old. Now is the time for you to abandon sensual pleasures and go forth.” Desiring to teach him the Dhamma, he spoke this first verse:

14.

14.

“Paṅko ca kāmā palipo ca kāmā, bhayañca metaṃ timūlaṃ pavuttaṃ;

Rajo ca dhūmo ca mayā pakāsitā, hitvā tuvaṃ pabbaja brahmadattā”ti.

“Sensual pleasures are a mire, sensual pleasures are a swamp; and this has been called a three-rooted fear. They have been declared by me to be dust and smoke. Having abandoned them, Brahmadatta, go forth!”

Tattha paṅkoti udake jātāni tiṇasevālakumudagacchādīni adhippetāni. Yathā hi udakaṃ tarantaṃ tāni laggāpenti sajjāpenti, tathā saṃsārasāgaraṃ tarantassa yogāvacarassa pañca kāmaguṇā sabbe vā pana vatthukāmakilesakāmā laggāpanavasena paṅko nāma. Imasmiñhi paṅke āsattā visattā devāpi manussāpi tiracchānāpi kilamanti rodanti paridevanti. Palipo ca kāmāti palipo vuccati mahākaddamo, yamhi laggā sūkaramigādayopi sīhāpi vāraṇāpi attānaṃ uddharitvā gantuṃ na sakkonti, vatthukāmakilesakāmāpi taṃsarikkhatāya “palipā”ti vuttā. Paññavantopi hi sattā tesu kāmesu sakiṃ laggakālato paṭṭhāya te kāme padāletvā sīghaṃ uṭṭhāya akiñcanaṃ apalibodhaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ pabbajjaṃ upagantuṃ na sakkonti. Bhayañca metanti bhayañca etaṃ, ma-kāro byañjanasandhivasena vutto. Timūlanti tīhi mūlehi patiṭṭhitaṃ viya [V 3.0211] acalaṃ. Balavabhayassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Pavuttanti mahārāja, ete kāmā nāma diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikassa attānuvādabhayādikassa ceva dvattiṃsakammakaraṇachanavutirogavasappavattassa ca bhayassa paccayaṭṭhena balavabhayanti buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakehi ceva sabbaññubodhisattehi ca pavuttaṃ kathitaṃ, dīpitanti attho. Atha vā bhayañca metanti bhayañca mayā etaṃ timūlaṃ pavuttanti evañcettha attho daṭṭhabboyeva.

Here, 'mire' (paṅko) refers to grass, moss, lotuses, shrubs, and so on, that grow in water. For just as these things entangle and snag one crossing the water, so for the yogi crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, the five cords of sensual pleasure—or indeed all sensual desires, whether for objects or for defilements—are called 'mire' because they cause clinging. Indeed, gods, human beings, and animals, attached and ensnared in this mire, become weary, weep, and lament. And 'swamp' (palipo) refers to a great bog where even boars, deer, lions, and elephants, once stuck, cannot pull themselves out and go on. Similarly, sensual desires—whether for objects or for defilements—are called a 'swamp' because of their resemblance to it. For even wise beings, from the time they are first entangled in these sensual pleasures, cannot quickly break them and rise up to go forth into the homeless life, which is without possessions, without obstructions, and delightful. 'And this is fear' (bhayañca metaṃ): here, the letter 'm' is used for the sake of consonant sandhi. 'Three-rooted' (timūlaṃ) means as if immovable, established on three roots; this is a name for a strong fear. 'It has been declared' (pavuttaṃ): O great king, these sensual pleasures are called a 'strong fear' by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, the Buddha's disciples, and the omniscient Bodhisattas because they are the cause of fear pertaining to this present life and the future life—such as the fear of self-reproach—and of fear that arises by way of the thirty-two kinds of torture and the ninety-six diseases; this is the meaning of 'explained.' Alternatively, 'And this is fear' (bhayañca metaṃ) can be understood to mean: 'And this three-rooted fear has been declared by me.'

Rajo ca dhūmo cāti rajadhūmasadisattā “rajo”ti ca “dhūmo”ti ca mayā pakāsitā. Yathā hi sunhātassa suvilittālaṅkatassa purisassa sarīre sukhumarajaṃ patitaṃ, taṃ sarīraṃ dubbaṇṇaṃ sobhārahitaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ karoti, evameva iddhibalena ākāsena āgantvā cando viya ca sūriyo viya [M 3.0227] ca loke paññātāpi sakiṃ kāmarajassa anto patitakālato paṭṭhāya guṇavaṇṇaguṇasobhāguṇasuddhīnaṃ upahatattā dubbaṇṇā sobhārahitā kiliṭṭhāyeva honti. Yathā ca dhūmena pahaṭakālato paṭṭhāya suparisuddhāpi bhitti kāḷavaṇṇā hoti, evaṃ atiparisuddhaññāṇāpi [P 3.0242] kāmadhūmena pahaṭakālato paṭṭhāya guṇavināsappattiyā mahājanamajjhe kāḷakāva hutvā paññāyanti. Iti rajadhūmasarikkhatāya ete kāmā “rajo ca dhūmo cā”ti mayā tuyhaṃ pakāsitā, tasmā ime kāme hitvā tuvaṃ pabbaja brahmadattāti rājānaṃ pabbajjāya ussāhaṃ janeti.

'Dust and smoke': because of their similarity to dust and smoke, they have been declared by me as 'dust' and 'smoke.' For just as fine dust falling on the body of a well-bathed, well-anointed, and adorned man makes his body discolored, devoid of beauty, and soiled, so too, even those renowned in the world like the moon and the sun, from the moment they fall into the dust of sensual pleasure, become discolored, devoid of beauty, and soiled, because their qualities of virtue, complexion, beauty, and purity have been impaired. And just as even a very clean wall becomes black from the moment it is struck by smoke, so too, even those with exceedingly pure knowledge, from the moment they are struck by the smoke of sensual desire, appear among the great populace as if blackened, having suffered the destruction of their good qualities. Thus, because of their resemblance to dust and smoke, these sensual pleasures have been declared to you by me as 'dust and smoke.' Therefore, Brahmadatta, having abandoned these sensual pleasures, you should go forth; thus he inspires the king with enthusiasm for going forth.

Taṃ sutvā rājā kilesehi attano baddhabhāvaṃ kathento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king, describing his own state of being bound by the defilements, spoke the second verse:

15.

15.

“Gadhito ca ratto ca adhimucchito ca, kāmesvahaṃ brāhmaṇa bhiṃsarūpaṃ;

Taṃ nussahe jīvikattho pahātuṃ, kāhāmi puññāni anappakānī”ti.

“Greedy, impassioned, and deeply infatuated am I, Brahmin, in sensual pleasures of a dreadful nature. Desiring this way of life, I am unable to abandon them. I will perform many meritorious deeds.”

Tattha gadhitoti abhijjhākāyaganthena baddho. Rattoti pakatijahāpanena rāgena ratto. Adhimucchitoti ativiya mucchito. Kāmesvahanti duvidhesupi kāmesu ahaṃ. Brāhmaṇāti darīmukhapaccekabuddhaṃ ālapati. Bhiṃsarūpanti balavarūpaṃ. Taṃ nussaheti taṃ duvidhampi kāmaṃ na ussahāmi na sakkomi. Jīvikattho pahātunti imāya jīvikāya atthiko ahaṃ taṃ kāmaṃ pahātuṃ na sakkomīti vadati. Kāhāmi puññānīti idāni dānasīlauposathakammasaṅkhātāni puññāni anappakāni bahūni karissāmīti.

Here, 'greedy' means bound by the bodily knot of covetousness. 'Impassioned' means dyed by lust, which makes one abandon one’s natural state. 'Deeply infatuated' means utterly infatuated. 'In sensual pleasures, I' means I, in both kinds of sensual pleasures. 'Brahmin' is an address to the Paccekabuddha Darīmukha. 'Dreadfully' means of a powerful form. 'I am unable to abandon them' means: 'I am not able, I cannot, abandon both kinds of sensual pleasure.' 'Being in need of a livelihood, to abandon' means he is saying: 'I, who have need of this livelihood, am unable to abandon those sensual pleasures.' 'I will perform meritorious deeds' means: 'Now I will perform many abundant meritorious deeds, reckoned as giving, moral virtue, and the Uposatha observance.'

Evaṃ kilesakāmo nāmesa sakiṃ allīnakālato paṭṭhāya apanetuṃ na sakkoti, yena saṃkiliṭṭhacitto [V 3.0212] mahāpuriso paccekabuddhena pabbajjāya guṇe kathitepi “pabbajituṃ na sakkomī”ti āha. Yoyaṃ dīpaṅkarapādamūle attani sambhavena ñāṇena buddhakaradhamme vicinanto tatiyaṃ nekkhammapāramiṃ disvā –

Thus, sensual desire is something that one is unable to remove from the time one first becomes attached. Because of this, the great man, with a defiled mind, even when the virtues of going forth were explained by the Paccekabuddha, said, 'I am unable to go forth.' This is the one who, at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, while investigating the qualities that make a Buddha with the knowledge that arose in himself, saw the third perfection of renunciation—

“Imaṃ [M 3.0228] tvaṃ tatiyaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Nekkhammapāramitaṃ gaccha, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

"This third one you should first firmly undertake; fulfill the perfection of renunciation, if you wish to attain enlightenment.

“Yathā andughare puriso, ciravuttho dukhaṭṭito;

Na tattha rāgaṃ janeti, muttiṃyeva gavesati.

"Just as a man in a prison, having dwelt there long, afflicted by suffering, generates no longing for that place but seeks only release;

“Tatheva tvaṃ sabbabhave, passa andughare viya;

Nekkhammābhimukho hutvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti. –

"So too should you see all states of existence as like a prison; having turned your mind to renunciation, you will attain perfect enlightenment."

Evaṃ nekkhamme guṇaṃ parikittesi, so paccekabuddhena pabbajjāya vaṇṇaṃ vatvā “kilese chaḍḍetvā samaṇo hohī”ti vuccamānopi “nāhaṃ kilese chaḍḍetvā samaṇo bhavituṃ sakkomī”ti vadati.

In this way he extolled the virtue of renunciation. Yet that one, even when told by the Paccekabuddha, who had spoken of the excellence of going forth, 'Having abandoned the defilements, become a recluse!', says, 'I am not able to abandon the defilements and become a recluse.'

Imasmiṃ kira loke aṭṭha ummattakā nāma. Tenāhu porāṇā “aṭṭha puggalā ummattakasaññaṃ paṭilabhanti, kāmummattako lobhavasaṃ gato[P 3.0243], kodhummattako dosavasaṃ gato, diṭṭhummattako vipallāsavasaṃ gato, mohummattako aññāṇavasaṃ gato, yakkhummattako yakkhavasaṃ gato, pittummattako pittavasaṃ gato, surummattako pānavasaṃ gato, byasanummattako sokavasaṃ gato”ti. Imesu aṭṭhasu ummattakesu mahāsatto imasmiṃ jātake kāmummattako hutvā lobhavasaṃ gato pabbajjāya guṇaṃ na aññāsi.

It is said that in this world there are eight kinds of mad persons. Thus the ancients have said: 'Eight persons acquire the designation 'mad': the one mad with sensual passion, who has come under the sway of greed; the one mad with anger, who has come under the sway of hatred; the one mad with views, who has come under the sway of distortion; the one mad with delusion, who has come under the sway of ignorance; the one mad from spirits, who has come under the sway of a yakkha; the one mad from bile, who has come under the sway of bile; the one mad from liquor, who has come under the sway of drink; and the one mad from calamity, who has come under the sway of sorrow.' Among these eight kinds of mad persons, the Great Being in this birth became one mad with sensual passion, came under the sway of greed, and did not recognize the virtue of going forth.

Evaṃ anatthakārakaṃ pana imaṃ guṇaparidhaṃsakaṃ lobhajātaṃ kasmā sattā parimuñcituṃ na sakkontīti? Anamatagge saṃsāre anekāni kappakoṭisatasahassāni ekato bandhitabhāvena. Evaṃ santepi taṃ paṇḍitā “appassādā kāmā”tiādīnaṃ anekesaṃ paccavekkhaṇānaṃ vasena pajahanti. Teneva darīmukhapaccekabuddho mahāsattena “pabbajituṃ na sakkomī”ti vuttepi dhuranikkhepaṃ akatvā uttarimpi ovadanto dve gāthā āha.

But why are beings unable to relinquish this greed, which causes harm and destroys virtue? Because of having been bound together in beginningless saṃsāra for many hundreds of thousands of crores of aeons. Even so, the wise abandon it by means of many reflections, such as: 'Sensual pleasures are of little gratification.' Therefore the Paccekabuddha Darīmukha, even when the Great Being said, 'I am unable to go forth,' did not give up his effort but advised him further by speaking two verses:

16.

16.

“Yo [V 3.0213] atthakāmassa hitānukampino, ovajjamāno na karoti sāsanaṃ;

Idameva seyyo iti maññamāno, punappunaṃ gabbhamupeti mando.

“He who, being advised by one who desires his welfare and is compassionate for his benefit, does not follow the teaching, thinking, ‘This alone is better,’ that fool repeatedly enters the womb.”

17.

17.

“So [M 3.0229] ghorarūpaṃ nirayaṃ upeti, subhāsubhaṃ muttakarīsapūraṃ;

Sattā sakāye na jahanti giddhā, ye honti kāmesu avītarāgā”ti.

“He enters a dreadful hell, filled with urine and feces, which the pure regard as impure. Greedy for their own bodies, beings do not abandon them—those who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures.”

Tattha atthakāmassāti vuḍḍhikāmassa. Hitānukampinoti hitena muducittena anukampantassa. Ovajjamānoti ovadiyamāno. Idameva seyyoti yaṃ attanā gahitaṃ aseyyaṃ anuttamampi samānaṃ, taṃ idameva seyyo iti maññamāno. Mandoti so aññāṇapuggalo mātukucchiyaṃ vāsaṃ nātikkamati, punappunaṃ gabbhaṃ upetiyevāti attho.

In that context, 'of one who desires his welfare' means of one who desires his growth. 'Compassionate for his benefit' means of one who is compassionate for his benefit with a gentle mind. 'Being advised' means being admonished. 'Thinking, “This alone is better”' means that although what he has grasped is inferior and not the best, he thinks, 'This alone is better.' 'Fool' refers to that ignorant person who does not transcend dwelling in the mother’s womb; the meaning is that he repeatedly enters the womb.

So ghorarūpanti mahārāja, so mando taṃ mātukucchiṃ upento ghorarūpaṃ dāruṇajātikaṃ nirayaṃ upeti nāma. Mātukucchi hi nirassādaṭṭhena idha “nirayo”ti vutto, “catukuṭṭikanirayo”ti vuccati. “Catukuṭṭikanirayo nāma kataro”ti vutte mātukucchimeva vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Avīcimahāniraye nibbattasattassa hi aparāparaṃ ādhāvanaparidhāvanaṃ hotiyeva, tasmā taṃ “catukuṭṭikanirayo”ti vattuṃ na labbhati, mātukucchiyaṃ pana nava [P 3.0244] vā dasa vā māse catūhipi passehi ito cito ca dhāvituṃ nāma na sakkā, atisambādhe okāse catukoṭena catusaṅkuṭiteneva hutvā acchitabbaṃ, tasmā esa “catukuṭṭikanirayo”ti vuccati.

“He enters a dreadful hell”: O great king, that fool, in entering the mother’s womb, is said to enter a dreadful hell of a cruel nature. For here the mother’s womb is called a 'hell' in the sense of being devoid of gratification; it is called the 'four-cornered hell.' When it is asked, 'What is the four-cornered hell?' it is proper to say it is the mother’s womb itself. For a being reborn in the great Avīci hell, there is indeed running about to and fro, so that cannot be called the 'four-cornered hell.' But in the mother’s womb, for nine or ten months, it is impossible to run about here and there on any of the four sides; in that very confined space, one must remain crouched, contracted on four sides. Therefore, this is called the 'four-cornered hell.'

Subhāsubhanti subhānaṃ asubhaṃ. Subhānañhi saṃsārabhīrukānaṃ yogāvacarakulaputtānaṃ mātukucchi ekantaṃ asubhasammato. Tena vuttaṃ –

'Subhāsubhaṃ' means what is impure to the pure. For to the pure ones—that is, to the sons of good family who are practitioners (yogāvacara) and fearful of saṃsāra—the mother’s womb is considered utterly impure. Therefore it is said:

“Ajaññaṃ jaññasaṅkhātaṃ, asuciṃ sucisammataṃ;

Nānākuṇapaparipūraṃ, jaññarūpaṃ apassato.

"For one who does not see its true nature, what is ignoble is reckoned as noble, what is impure is considered pure, though it is full of various kinds of corpses.

“Dhiratthumaṃ āturaṃ pūtikāyaṃ, jegucchiyaṃ assuciṃ byādhidhammaṃ;

Yatthappamattā adhimucchitā pajā, hāpenti maggaṃ sugatūpapattiyā”ti. (jā. 1.3.128-129);

"Fie on this ailing, putrid body, repulsive, impure, and subject to disease, wherein people, heedless and deeply infatuated, abandon the path to rebirth in a happy destination."

Sattāti āsattā visattā laggā laggitā sakāye na jahantīti taṃ mātukucchiṃ na pariccajanti[V 3.0214]. Giddhāti gadhitā. Ye hontīti ye kāmesu avītarāgā honti, te etaṃ gabbhavāsaṃ na jahantīti.

'Beings': they are attached, ensnared, clinging, stuck. 'Do not abandon their own bodies' means they do not relinquish that mother’s womb. 'Greedy' means they are covetous. 'Those who are': those who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures do not abandon this dwelling in the womb.

Evaṃ [M 3.0230] darīmukhapaccekabuddho gabbhaokkantimūlakañca, parihāramūlakañca dukkhaṃ dassetvā idāni gabbhavuṭṭhānamūlakaṃ dassetuṃ diyaḍḍhagāthamāha.

Thus, the Paccekabuddha Darīmukha, having shown the suffering rooted in conception and in gestation, now speaks a verse and a half to show the suffering rooted in emergence from the womb.

18.

18.

“Mīḷhena littā ruhirena makkhitā, semhena littā upanikkhamanti;

Yaṃ yañhi kāyena phusanti tāvade, sabbaṃ asātaṃ dukhameva kevalaṃ.

“Smeared with filth, stained with blood, smeared with phlegm, they are born. Whatever they touch with their body at that time is all disagreeable, sheer suffering.”

19.

19.

“Disvā vadāmi na hi aññato savaṃ, pubbenivāsaṃ bahukaṃ sarāmī”ti.

“Having seen it myself, I speak, not from hearing it from another; I remember many past lives.”

Tattha mīḷhena littāti mahārāja, ime sattā mātukucchito nikkhamantā na catujjātigandhehi vilimpitvā surabhimālaṃ piḷandhitvā nikkhamanti, purāṇagūthena pana makkhitā palibuddhā hutvā nikkhamanti. Ruhirena makkhitāti rattalohitacandanānulittāpi ca hutvā na nikkhamanti, rattalohitamakkhitā pana hutvā nikkhamanti. Semhena littāti na cāpi setacandanavilittā nikkhamanti, bahalapicchilasemhalittā pana hutvā nikkhamanti. Itthīnañhi [P 3.0245] gabbhavuṭṭhānakāle etā asuciyo nikkhamanti. Tāvadeti tasmiṃ samaye. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, ime sattā tasmiṃ mātukucchito nikkhamanasamaye evaṃ mīḷhādilittā nikkhamantā yaṃ yaṃ nikkhamanamaggapadesaṃ vā hatthaṃ vā pādaṃ vā phusanti, taṃ sabbaṃ asātaṃ amadhuraṃ kevalaṃ asammissaṃ dukkhameva phusanti, sukhaṃ nāma tesaṃ tasmiṃ samaye natthīti.

In that context, 'smeared with filth': O great king, these beings, when emerging from the mother’s womb, do not emerge anointed with the four kinds of perfumes or wearing fragrant garlands; rather, they emerge smeared and entangled with old excrement. 'Stained with blood': They do not emerge anointed with red sandalwood paste; rather, they emerge smeared with red blood. 'Smeared with phlegm': They do not emerge anointed with white sandalwood paste; rather, they emerge smeared with thick, slimy phlegm. For when women give birth, these impurities come out. 'At that time' means at that moment. This is what is meant: O great king, at the moment of emerging from the mother’s womb, these beings, thus smeared with filth and so on, whatever part of the birth canal they touch, or whatever they touch with hand or foot, all that they touch is disagreeable, unpleasant, and purely unmixed suffering. At that time, there is no such thing as happiness for them.

Disvā vadāmi na hi aññato savanti mahārāja, ahaṃ imaṃ ettakaṃ vadanto na aññato savaṃ, aññassa samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā taṃ sutvā na vadāmi, attano pana paccekabodhiñāṇena disvā paṭivijjhitvā paccakkhaṃ katvā vadāmīti attho. Pubbenivāsaṃ bahukanti idaṃ attano ānubhāvaṃ dassento āha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, ahañhi pubbe nivutthakkhandhapaṭipāṭisaṅkhātaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ bahukaṃ sarāmi, satasahassakappādhikāni dve asaṅkhyeyyāni sarāmīti.

“Having seen, I speak, not from hearing it from another”: O great king, in speaking this much, I do not speak from hearsay, nor do I speak having heard it from some other ascetic or brahmin; the meaning is that I speak having seen, penetrated, and personally realized it through my own knowledge of Paccekabodhi. “I remember many past lives”: This he said showing his own spiritual power. This is what is meant: O great king, I remember many past lives, consisting of the sequence of aggregates inhabited in the past; I remember two incalculables and a hundred thousand eons.

Idāni satthā abhisambuddho hutvā “evaṃ so paccekabuddho rājānaṃ subhāsitakathāya saṅgaṇhī”ti vatvā osāne upaḍḍhagāthamāha –

Now the Teacher, having become perfectly enlightened, said, “Thus that Paccekabuddha favored the king with well-spoken speech,” and at the conclusion he spoke this half-verse:

“Citrāhi [V 3.0215][M 3.0231] gāthāhi subhāsitāhi, darīmukho nijjhāpayi sumedha”nti.

“With diverse and well-spoken verses, Darīmukha convinced Sumedha.”

Tattha citrāhīti anekatthasannissitāhi. Subhāsitāhīti sukathitāhi. Darīmukho nijjhāpayi sumedhanti bhikkhave, so darīmukhapaccekabuddho taṃ sumedhaṃ sundarapaññaṃ kāraṇākāraṇajānanasamatthaṃ rājānaṃ nijjhāpesi saññāpesi, attano vacanaṃ gaṇhāpesīti attho.

In that context, 'diverse' means based on various meanings. 'Well-spoken' means well-said. 'Darīmukha convinced Sumedha': Bhikkhus, that Paccekabuddha Darīmukha convinced and persuaded King Sumedha—who was of excellent wisdom and capable of knowing what is a cause and what is not—making him accept his word. This is the meaning.

Evaṃ paccekabuddho kāmesu dosaṃ dassetvā attano vacanaṃ gāhāpetvā “mahārāja, idāni pabbaja vā mā vā, mayā pana tuyhaṃ kāmesu ādīnavo pabbajjāya ca ānisaṃso kathito, tvaṃ appamatto hohī”ti vatvā suvaṇṇarājahaṃso viya ākāse uppatitvā valāhakagabbhaṃ maddanto nandamūlakapabbhārameva gato. Mahāsatto dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ sirasmiṃ ṭhapetvā namassamāno tasmiṃ dassanavisaye [P 3.0246] atīte jeṭṭhaputtaṃ pakkosāpetvā rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā mahājanassa rodantassa paridevantassa kāme pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā na cirasseva abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā āyupariyosāne brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Thus the Paccekabuddha, having shown the danger in sensual pleasures and having made his word accepted, said: “Great king, whether you go forth now or not, I have explained to you the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit of renunciation; remain heedful!” Then, like a golden royal swan, he rose into the sky, passing through the mass of clouds, and went straight to the Nandamūlaka cave. The Great Being, placing his hands in reverential salutation—resplendent with the meeting of his ten fingernails—on his head and paying homage, when the Paccekabuddha had passed beyond his sight, summoned his eldest son and handed over the kingdom. While the great crowd was weeping and lamenting, he abandoned sensual pleasures, entered the Himalayas, built a leaf-hut, went forth into the life of a seer, and before long developed the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Tadā rājā ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, many became stream-enterers and so forth. “At that time, I myself was the king.”

Darīmukhajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The commentary on the Darīmukha Jātaka, the third.

[379] 4. Nerujātakavaṇṇanā

[379] 4. The commentary on the Neru Jātaka.

Kākolā kākasaṅghā cāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ agamāsi. Manussā tassa iriyāpathe pasīditvā taṃ bhojetvā paṭiññaṃ gahetvā araññe paṇṇasālaṃ katvā tattha vasāpesuṃ, ativiya cassa sakkāraṃ kariṃsu. Atheke sassatavādā āgamaṃsu. Te tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā therassa vādaṃ vissajjetvā sassatavādaṃ gahetvā tesaññeva sakkāraṃ kariṃsu. Tato ucchedavādā āgamaṃsu [M 3.0232] te sassatavādaṃ vissajjetvā ucchedavādameva gaṇhiṃsu. Athaññe acelakā āgamiṃsu. Te ucchedavādaṃ vissajjetvā acelakavādaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. So tesaṃ guṇāguṇaṃ ajānantānaṃ [V 3.0216] manussānaṃ santike dukkhena vasitvā vutthavasso pavāretvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā katapaṭisanthāro “kahaṃ vassaṃvutthosī”ti vutte “paccantaṃ nissāya, bhante”ti vatvā “sukhaṃ vutthosī”ti puṭṭho “bhante, guṇāguṇaṃ ajānantānaṃ santike dukkhaṃ vutthosmī”ti āha. Satthā “bhikkhu porāṇakapaṇḍitā tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattāpi guṇāguṇaṃ ajānantehi saddhiṃ ekadivasampi na vasiṃsu, tvaṃ attano guṇāguṇaṃ ajānanaṭṭhāne kasmā vasī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Crows and flocks of crows…” This the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain bhikkhu. It seems that this bhikkhu, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, went to a border village. The people, gaining confidence in his deportment, fed him and, having obtained his consent, built a leaf-hut in the forest and had him dwell there, showing him very great honor. Then some eternalists came. Hearing their words, the people rejected the elder’s teaching and adopted the teaching of eternalism, honoring them instead. Then some annihilationists came, and they rejected the teaching of eternalism and adopted the teaching of annihilation. Then some naked ascetics came, and they rejected the teaching of annihilation and adopted the teaching of the naked ascetics. That bhikkhu, living with difficulty among people who did not know the distinction between virtue and lack of virtue, completed the rains residence and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony. He then went to the Teacher. After an exchange of friendly greetings, he was asked, “Where did you spend the rains?” He replied, “In dependence on a border village, venerable sir.” Asked, “Did you live comfortably?” he said, “Venerable sir, I lived with difficulty among those who do not recognize virtue and lack of virtue.” The Teacher said: “Bhikkhu, the wise of the past, even when reborn in the animal realm, did not live for even a single day with those who do not know the difference between virtue and lack of virtue. Why did you live in a place where your own virtue and lack of virtue were not recognized?” Then, at his request, the Teacher related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto suvaṇṇahaṃsayoniyaṃ nibbatti, kaniṭṭhabhātāpissa [P 3.0247] atthi. Te cittakūṭapabbate vasantā himavantapadese sayaṃjātasāliṃ khādanti. Te ekadivasaṃ tattha caritvā cittakūṭaṃ āgacchantā antarāmagge ekaṃ neruṃ nāma kañcanapabbataṃ disvā tassa matthake nisīdiṃsu. Taṃ pana pabbataṃ nissāya vasantā sakuṇasaṅghā catuppadā ca gocarabhūmiyaṃ nānāvaṇṇā honti, pabbataṃ paviṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya te sabbe tassobhāsena suvaṇṇavaṇṇā honti. Taṃ disvā bodhisattassa kaniṭṭho taṃ kāraṇaṃ ajānitvā “kiṃ nu kho ettha kāraṇa”nti bhātarā saddhiṃ sallapanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a golden goose; he had a younger brother. They lived on Mount Cittakūṭa, eating wild rice in the Himalayan region. One day, while foraging there, on their way back to Cittakūṭa they saw a golden mountain named Neru and alighted on its summit. Now the flocks of birds and the quadrupeds that lived in dependence on that mountain were of various colors in their feeding grounds, but from the time they entered the mountain they all became golden-hued because of its radiance. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta’s younger brother, not knowing the reason, conversed with his brother and spoke two verses:

20.

20.

“Kākolā kākasaṅghā ca, mayañca patataṃ varā;

Sabbeva sadisā homa, imaṃ āgamma pabbataṃ.

“Crows and flocks of crows, and we, the best of those who fly—having come to this mountain, we all become of the same appearance.”

21.

21.

“Idha sīhā ca byagghā ca, siṅgālā ca migādhamā;

Sabbeva sadisā honti, ayaṃ ko nāma pabbato”ti.

“Here lions and tigers, jackals and the lowest of beasts, all become of the same appearance. What, indeed, is the name of this mountain?”

Tattha kākolāti vanakākā. Kākasaṅghāti pakatikākasaṅghā ca. Patataṃ varāti pakkhīnaṃ seṭṭhā. Sadisā homāti sadisavaṇṇā homa.

Herein, crows: forest crows. Flocks of crows: flocks of common crows. The best of those who fly: the best of birds. We become the same: we become of the same color.

Tassa [M 3.0233] vacanaṃ sutvā bodhisatto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his words, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:

22.

22.

“Imaṃ nerūti jānanti, manussā pabbatuttamaṃ;

Idha vaṇṇena sampannā, vasanti sabbapāṇino”ti.

“Humans know this as Neru, the best of mountains; here all beings dwell endowed with its golden color.”

Tattha idha vaṇṇenāti imasmiṃ nerupabbate obhāsena vaṇṇasampannā hutvā.

Herein, endowed with its color: being endowed with color by the radiance of this Mount Neru.

Taṃ [V 3.0217] sutvā kaniṭṭho sesagāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the younger brother spoke the remaining verses:

23.

23.

“Amānanā yattha siyā, antānaṃ vā vimānanā;

Hīnasammānanā vāpi, na tattha visatiṃvase.

“Where there is no respect for the worthy, or contempt for them, or where there is honor for the base, one should not live in such a place.”

24.

24.

“Yatthālaso ca dakkho ca, sūro bhīru ca pūjiyā;

Na tattha santo vasanti, avisesakare nare.

“Where the lazy and the diligent, the brave and the timid are honored alike, the good do not live there among people who make no distinction.”

25.

25.

“Nāyaṃ [P 3.0248] neru vibhajati, hīnaukkaṭṭhamajjhime;

Avisesakaro neru, handa neruṃ jahāmase”ti.

“This Neru does not distinguish between the low, the superior, and the middling. Neru makes no distinction; come, let us abandon Neru!”

Tattha paṭhamagāthāya ayamattho – yattha santānaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ sīlasampannānaṃ mānanassa abhāvena amānanā avamaññanā ca avamānavasena vimānanā vā hīnānaṃ vā dussīlānaṃ sammānanā siyā, tattha nivāse na vaseyya. Pūjiyāti ete ettha ekasadisāya pūjāya pūjanīyā honti, samakaṃ sakkāraṃ labhanti. Hīnaukkaṭṭhamajjhimeti jātigottakulappadesasīlācārañāṇādīhi hīne ca majjhime ca ukkaṭṭhe ca ayaṃ na vibhajati. Handāti vavassaggatthe nipāto. Jahāmaseti pariccajāma. Evañca pana vatvā ubhopi te haṃsā uppatitvā cittakūṭameva gatā.

Herein, this is the meaning of the first verse: One should not live in a place where there is a lack of respect for the good, the wise, and the virtuous, or contempt for them by way of disdain, or where there is honor for the base and the immoral. Are honored alike: Here these are honored with one and the same kind of honor; they receive honor equally. The low, the superior, and the middling: This Neru does not distinguish between those who are low, middling, and superior in terms of birth, clan, family, region, virtue, conduct, knowledge, and so on. Come: This is a particle in the sense of resolve. Let us abandon: We should renounce it. Having said this, both those geese flew up and went right back to Mount Cittakūṭa.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā kaniṭṭhahaṃso ānando ahosi, jeṭṭhakahaṃso pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher delivered this discourse, revealed the Truths, and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the younger goose was Ānanda, and the elder goose was myself.

Nerujātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Neru Jātaka, the fourth.

[380] 5. Āsaṅkajātakavaṇṇanā

[380] 5. The Commentary on the Āsaṅka Jātaka

Āsāvatī [M 3.0234] nāma latāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu indriyajātake (jā. 1.8.60 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Idha pana satthā taṃ bhikkhuṃ “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kena [V 3.0218] ukkaṇṭhāpitosī”ti vatvā “purāṇadutiyikāya, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu esā itthī tuyhaṃ anatthakārikā, pubbepi tvaṃ etaṃ nissāya caturaṅginisenaṃ jahitvā himavantapadese mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavanto tīṇi saṃvaccharāni vasī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“The creeper named Āsāvatī”—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the luring by a former wife. The story will be made clear in the Indriya Jātaka. Here, however, the Teacher asked that bhikkhu, “Is it true that you are discontented?” When he replied, “It is true, venerable sir,” the Teacher asked, “By whom were you made discontented?” and when the bhikkhu said, “By my former wife, venerable sir,” the Teacher said, “Bhikkhu, this woman is harmful to you. In the past, too, on account of her, you left your kingdom with a four-limbed army and endured great suffering in the Himalayan region for three years.” Then he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsigāme brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ [P 3.0249] uggahitasippo isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vanamūlaphalāhāro abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā himavantapadese vasi. Tasmiṃ kāle eko puññasampanno satto tāvatiṃsabhavanato cavitvā tasmiṃ ṭhāne padumasare ekasmiṃ padumagabbhe dārikā hutvā nibbatti, sesapadumesu purāṇabhāvaṃ patvā patantesupi taṃ mahākucchikaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhateva. Tāpaso nahāyituṃ padumasaraṃ gato taṃ disvā “aññesu padumesu patantesupi idaṃ mahākucchikaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti cintetvā udakasāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā otaranto gantvā taṃ padumaṃ vivaritvā taṃ dārikaṃ disvā dhītusaññaṃ uppādetvā paṇṇasālaṃ ānetvā paṭijaggi. Sā aparabhāge soḷasavassikā hutvā abhirūpā ahosi uttamarūpadharā atikkantā mānusakavaṇṇaṃ, apattā devavaṇṇaṃ. Tadā sakko bodhisattassa upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchati, so taṃ dārikaṃ disvā “kuto esā”ti pucchitvā laddhaniyāmaṃ sutvā “imissā kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti pucchi. “Nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ vatthālaṅkārabhojanavidhānaṃ, mārisā”ti. So “sādhu, bhante”ti tassā vasanaṭṭhānassa āsanne phalikapāsādaṃ māpetvā dibbasayanadibbavatthālaṅkāradibbannapānāni māpesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in a village of Kāsi. When he came of age, he mastered the arts at Takkasilā and went forth into the ascetic life. Living on wild roots and fruits, he developed the higher knowledges and meditative attainments and dwelt in the Himalayan region. At that time, a being endowed with merit passed away from the Tāvatiṃsa realm and was reborn in that place as a girl within a lotus in a lotus pond. While the other lotuses grew old and fell, that one remained as a large bud. The ascetic went to the lotus pond to bathe and saw it. He thought: “While the other lotuses are falling, this one remains as a large bud. What could be the reason?” Donning his bathing cloth, he waded in, went to that lotus, opened it, and saw the girl. Arousing the perception of her as a daughter, he brought her to his leaf-hut and looked after her. In time, she reached the age of sixteen. She was lovely, endowed with the highest beauty, surpassing the human complexion but not reaching the divine complexion. Then Sakka came to attend on the Bodhisatta. Seeing the girl, he asked, “Where is she from?” Having heard the story of how she was obtained, he asked, “What is needed for her?” “A dwelling place, clothes, ornaments, and arrangements for food, friend.” “Good, venerable sir,” he said, and near her dwelling place he created a crystal palace and created divine couches, divine clothes and ornaments, and divine food and drink.

So pāsādo tassā abhiruhanakāle otaritvā bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāti, abhiruḷhakāle laṅghitvā ākāse tiṭṭhati. Sā bodhisattassa [M 3.0235] vattapaṭivattaṃ kurumānā pāsāde vasati. Tameko vanacarako disvā “ayaṃ, vo bhante, kiṃ hotī”ti pucchitvā “dhītā me”ti sutvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā “deva, mayā himavantapadese evarūpā nāma ekassa tāpasassa dhītā diṭṭhā”ti rañño ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā so savanasaṃsaggena bajjhitvā vanacarakaṃ maggadesakaṃ katvā caturaṅginiyā senāya taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā khandhāvāraṃ nivāsāpetvā vanacarakaṃ ādāya amaccagaṇaparivuto assamapadaṃ pavisitvā [P 3.0250] mahāsattaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno “bhante, itthiyo nāma brahmacariyassa malaṃ, tumhākaṃ dhītaraṃ ahaṃ paṭijaggissāmī”ti āha. Bodhisatto pana “kiṃ nu kho etasmiṃ padume”ti āsaṅkaṃ katvā udakaṃ otaritvā ānītabhāvena tassā kumārikāya āsaṅkāti nāmaṃ akāsi. So taṃ rājānaṃ “imaṃ gahetvā gacchā”ti ujukaṃ avatvā “mahārāja, imāya kumārikāya nāmaṃ jānanto gaṇhitvā gacchā”ti āha. “Tumhehi [V 3.0219] kathite ñassāmi, bhante”ti. “Ahaṃ te na kathemi, tvaṃ attano paññābalena nāmaṃ jānantova gahetvā yāhī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tato paṭṭhāya amaccehi saddhiṃ “kinnāmā nu kho esā”ti nāmaṃ upadhāreti. So yāni dujjānāni nāmāni, tāni kittetvā “asukā nāma bhavissatī”ti bodhisattena saddhiṃ katheti. Bodhisatto “na evaṃnāmā”ti paṭikkhipati.

When she was about to ascend, the palace would descend and stand on the ground, and when she had ascended, it would leap up and stand in the sky. Residing in the palace, she performed her duties for the Bodhisatta. A certain forest-dweller saw her and asked, “Venerable sir, what is she to you?” Hearing, “She is my daughter,” he went to Bārāṇasī and informed the king: “Your Majesty, in the Himalayan region I have seen such a beautiful daughter of a certain ascetic.” Hearing this, the king became captivated just by the report. He made the forest-dweller his guide and went to that place with his four-limbed army. Having set up camp, he took the forest-dweller and, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, entered the hermitage. He paid homage to the Great Being and, sitting to one side, said: “Venerable sir, women are a defilement to the holy life. I will look after your daughter.” Now, because the Bodhisatta had fetched her after having a suspicion (‘āsaṅka’)—“What can be in this lotus?”—and wading into the water, he had given the girl the name Āsaṅkā. So, without speaking to the king directly, he said: “Great king, if you know this girl’s name, take her and go.” “I will know it when you tell me, venerable sir.” “I will not tell you. You must find out her name by the power of your own wisdom and then take her.” The king agreed, saying, “Good,” and from then on, together with his ministers, he tried to figure out her name, thinking, “What can her name be?” He would recite whatever difficult names he could think of and say to the Bodhisatta, “Her name must be so-and-so.” But the Bodhisatta would reject it, saying, “That is not her name.”

Rañño ca nāmaṃ upadhārentassa saṃvaccharo atīto. Tadā hatthiassamanusse sīhādayo vāḷā gaṇhanti, dīghajātikaparipantho hoti, makkhikaparipantho hoti, sītena kilamitvā bahū manussā maranti. Atha rājā kujjhitvā “kiṃ me etāyā”ti bodhisattassa kathetvā pāyāsi. Āsaṅkā kumārikā taṃ divasaṃ phalikavātapānaṃ vivaritvā attānaṃ dassentī aṭṭhāsi. Rājā taṃ disvā “mayaṃ tava nāmaṃ jānituṃ na sakkoma, tvaṃ himavanteyeva vasa, mayaṃ gamissāmā”ti āha. “Kahaṃ, mahārāja, gacchanto mādisaṃ itthiṃ labhissasi, mama vacanaṃ suṇāhi, tāvatiṃsadevaloke cittalatāvane āsāvatī nāma latā atthi, tassā phalassa abbhantare dibbapānaṃ nibbattaṃ, taṃ ekavāraṃ pivitvā cattāro māse mattā hutvā dibbasayane sayanti, sā pana vassasahassena [P 3.0251] phalati, surāsoṇḍā devaputtā ‘ito phalaṃ labhissāmā’ti dibbapānapipāsaṃ adhivāsetvā vassasahassaṃ [M 3.0236] nibaddhaṃ gantvā taṃ lataṃ ‘arogā nu kho’ti olokenti, tvaṃ pana ekasaṃvacchareneva ukkaṇṭhito, āsāphalavatī nāma sukhā, mā ukkaṇṭhī”ti vatvā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

While the king was trying to figure out her name, a year passed. During that time, lions and other predators seized elephants, horses, and men; danger from snakes arose; danger from flies arose; and many men died, afflicted by the cold. Then the king became angry and said to the Bodhisatta, “What use is she to me?” and set out to leave. That day, the maiden Āsaṅkā opened a crystal window and stood showing herself. Seeing her, the king said: “We are unable to find out your name. You stay here in the Himalayas; we are going.” She replied: “Great king, where will you go and find a woman like me? Listen to my words. In the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, in the Cittalatā Grove, there is a creeper named Āsāvatī. Inside its fruit a divine drink is produced. Having drunk it once, they lie on divine couches, intoxicated for four months. But it bears fruit only once in a thousand years. The devas who are fond of drink, thinking, ‘We will get fruit from this,’ endure their thirst for the divine drink and for a thousand years they constantly go and check on that creeper, wondering, ‘Is it healthy?’ But you have become discontented after only a single year. Fruitful hope is a pleasure; do not be discontented.” Having said this, she recited three verses:

26.

26.

“Āsāvatī nāma latā, jātā cittalatāvane;

Tassā vassasahassena, ekaṃ nibbattate phalaṃ.

“There is a creeper named Āsāvatī, born in the Cittalatā Grove; after a thousand years, a single fruit is produced from it.

27.

27.

“Taṃ devā payirupāsanti, tāva dūraphalaṃ satiṃ;

Āsīseva tuvaṃ rāja, āsā phalavatī sukhā.

“The devas wait upon it, though its fruit is so far off. You too should hope, O king; hope, when fruitful, is happiness.

28.

28.

“Āsīsateva so pakkhī, āsīsateva so dijo;

Tassa cāsā samijjhati, tāva dūragatā satī;

Āsīseva tuvaṃ rāja, āsā phalavatī sukhā”ti.

“That bird still hopes, the twice-born hopes; and its hope, though far-reaching, succeeds. You too should hope, O king; hope, when fruitful, is happiness.”

Tattha āsāvatīti evaṃnāmikā. Sā hi yasmā tassā phale āsā uppajjati, tasmā etaṃ [V 3.0220] nāmaṃ labhati. Cittalatāvaneti evaṃnāmake uyyāne. Tasmiṃ kira uyyāne tiṇarukkhalatādīnaṃ pabhā tattha paviṭṭhapaviṭṭhānaṃ devatānaṃ sarīravaṇṇaṃ cittaṃ karoti, tenassa “cittalatāvana”nti nāmaṃ jātaṃ. Payirupāsantīti punappunaṃ upenti. Āsīsevāti āsīsāhiyeva patthehiyeva, mā āsacchedaṃ karohīti.

Herein, 'Āsāvatī' is so named. Because hope (āsā) arises for its fruit, it receives this name. 'In the Cittalatā Grove' means in the park so named. It is said that in that park, the radiance of the grass, trees, creepers, and so forth makes variegated (citta) the complexions of the devas who enter it; hence it came to be named 'Cittalatāvana' (Variegated Creeper Grove). 'Wait upon it' means they approach it again and again. 'You too should hope' means you should wish, you should desire; do not sever your hope.

Rājā tassā kathāya bajjhitvā puna amacce sannipātāpetvā dasanāmakaṃ kāretvā nāmaṃ gavesanto aparampi saṃvaccharaṃ vasi. Tassā dasanāmakampi nāmaṃ nāhosi, “asukā nāmā”ti vutte bodhisatto paṭikkhipateva. Puna rājā “kiṃ me imāyā”ti turaṅgaṃ āruyha pāyāsi. Sāpi puna vātapāne ṭhatvā attānaṃ dassesi. Rājā “tiṭṭha tvaṃ, mayaṃ gamissāmā”ti [P 3.0252] āha. “Kasmā yāsi, mahārājā”ti? “Tava nāmaṃ jānituṃ na sakkomī”ti. “Mahārāja, kasmā nāmaṃ na jānissasi, āsā nāma asamijjhanakā nāma natthi, eko kira bako pabbatamuddhani ṭhito attanā patthitaṃ labhi, tvaṃ kasmā na labhissasi, adhivāsehi, mahārājā”ti. Eko kira bako ekasmiṃ padumasare gocaraṃ gahetvā uppatitvā pabbatamatthake nilīyi. So taṃ divasaṃ tattheva vasitvā punadivase cintesi “ahaṃ imasmiṃ pabbatamatthake sukhaṃ [M 3.0237] nisinno, sace ito anotaritvā ettheva nisinno gocaraṃ gahetvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā imaṃ divasaṃ vaseyyaṃ, bhadrakaṃ vata assā”ti. Atha taṃ divasameva sakko devarājā asuranimmathanaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsabhavane devissariyaṃ laddhā cintesi ‘mama tāva manoratho matthakaṃ patto, atthi nu kho añño koci aparipuṇṇamanoratho’ti upadhārento taṃ disvā ‘imassa manorathaṃ matthakaṃ pāpessāmī’ti bakassa nisinnaṭṭhānato avidūre ekā nadī atthi, taṃ nadiṃ oghapuṇṇaṃ katvā pabbatamatthakena pesesi. Sopi bako tattheva nisinno macche khāditvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā taṃ divasaṃ tattheva vasi, udakampi bhassitvā gataṃ. “Evaṃ, mahārāja, bakopi tāva attano āsāphalaṃ labhi, kiṃ tvaṃ na labhissasī”ti vatvā “āsīsatevā”tiādimāha.

The king, bound by her speech, again assembled his ministers, had a list of ten names drawn up, and spent another year searching for her name. But none of those ten names was hers; whenever a name was suggested, the Bodhisatta rejected it. Again the king thought, 'What use is this woman to me?' and mounting his horse, he set out. She again stood at the window and showed herself. The king said, 'You stay! We are going.' 'Why are you going, great king?' 'Because I cannot learn your name.' 'Great king, why should you not know my name? There is no such thing as a hope that does not succeed. It is said that a heron, standing on a mountaintop, obtained what it desired. Why should you not obtain yours? Be patient, great king.' It is said that a certain heron, having taken its food in a lotus pond, flew up and alighted on a mountaintop. It stayed there that day, and on the next day it thought, 'I am sitting comfortably on this mountaintop. If, without descending from here, I could remain sitting right here, get my food, drink water, and pass this day, it would be good indeed.' On that very day, Sakka, king of the devas, having crushed the asuras and obtained divine sovereignty in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, reflected, 'My own wish has reached its consummation. Is there anyone else whose wish is unfulfilled?' Surveying, he saw the heron and thought, 'I will bring its wish to fulfillment.' Not far from where the heron was sitting there was a river. Sakka caused that river to become full with a flood and sent it over the mountaintop. The heron, remaining right there, ate fish, drank water, and spent that day right there on the mountaintop. The water then receded and was gone. 'Thus, great king, even a heron obtained the fruit of its hope. Why should you not obtain yours?' So saying, she spoke the verse beginning, 'That bird still hopes...'

Tattha āsīsatevāti āsīsatiyeva patthetiyeva. Pakkhīti pakkhehi yuttatāya pakkhī. Dvikkhattuṃ jātatāya dijo. Tāva dūragatā satīti pabbatamatthakato macchānañca udakassa ca dūrabhāvaṃ passa, evaṃ dūragatā samānā sakkassa ānubhāvena bakassa āsā pūriyevāti.

Herein, 'āsīsateva' means one indeed hopes, one indeed aspires. 'Pakkhī' means 'a winged one', because it is endowed with wings. 'Dijo' (twice-born) means the bird. 'Tāva dūragatā satī' means: see the remoteness of the fish and water from the mountaintop; though they were so far away, by the power of Sakka the heron's hope was indeed fulfilled.

Atha rājā tassā kathaṃ sutvā rūpe bajjhitvā kathāya allīno gantuṃ asakkonto amacce sannipātetvā satanāmaṃ kāresi, satanāmavasena [P 3.0253] nāmaṃ gavesatopissa aññaṃ saṃvaccharaṃ atītaṃ[V 3.0221]. So tiṇṇaṃ saṃvaccharānaṃ accayena bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā satanāmavasena “asukā nāma bhavissatī”ti pucchi. “Na jānāsi, mahārājā”ti. So “gamissāma dāni maya”nti bodhisattaṃ vanditvā pāyāsi. Āsaṅkā kumārikā ca puna phalikavātapānaṃ nissāya ṭhitāva. Rājā taṃ disvā “tvaṃ accha, mayaṃ gamissāmā”ti āha. “Kasmā, mahārājā”ti. “Tvaṃ maṃ vacaneneva santappesi, na ca kāmaratiyā, tava madhuravacanena bajjhitvā vasantassa mama tīṇi saṃvaccharāni atikkantāni, idāni gamissāmī”ti imā gāthā āha –

Then the king, having heard her speech, was bound by her beauty and clung to her conversation, unable to leave. He assembled his ministers and had a list of a hundred names made. While he was searching for her name by means of the hundred names, another year passed. At the end of three years, he approached the Bodhisatta and asked, based on the hundred names, 'Will her name be so-and-so?' The Bodhisatta replied, 'You do not know, great king.' The king said, 'Now I will go,' and after paying homage to the Bodhisatta, he set out. The maiden Āsaṅkā was again standing leaning against the crystal window. Seeing her, the king said, 'You stay! I am going.' 'Why, great king?' 'You have pleased me with words alone, but you have not pleased me with the delight of love. Bound by your sweet words, three years have passed for me while I have been dwelling here. Now I will go.' And he spoke these verses:

29.

29.

“Sampesi kho maṃ vācāya, na ca sampesi kammunā;

Mālā sereyyakasseva, vaṇṇavantā agandhikā.

“You have pleased me with your speech, but you have not pleased me with your deeds; like a garland of sereyyaka flowers, beautiful but without fragrance.

30.

30.

“Aphalaṃ [M 3.0238] madhuraṃ vācaṃ, yo mittesu pakubbati;

Adadaṃ avissajaṃ bhogaṃ, sandhi tenassa jīrati.

“One who offers sweet but fruitless words to friends, not giving, not bestowing wealth—his bond of friendship with them decays.

31.

31.

“Yañhi kayirā tañhi vade, yaṃ na kayirā na taṃ vade;

Akarontaṃ bhāsamānaṃ, parijānanti paṇḍitā.

“What one would do, that one should say; what one would not do, one should not say. The wise recognize one who speaks but does not act.

32.

32.

“Balañca vata me khīṇaṃ, pātheyyañca na vijjati;

Saṅke pāṇūparodhāya, handa dāni vajāmaha”nti.

“Indeed, my strength is exhausted, and my provisions are no more; I fear for the destruction of my life. Come now, I will go!”

Tattha sampesīti santappesi pīṇesi. Sereyyakassāti suvaṇṇakuraṇḍakassa. Desanāsīsamevetaṃ, yaṃkiñci pana suvaṇṇakuraṇḍakajayasumanādikaṃ aññampi pupphaṃ vaṇṇasampannaṃ agandhakaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ sandhāyevamāha. Vaṇṇavantā agandhikāti yathā sereyyakādīnaṃ mālā vaṇṇavantatāya dassanena tappeti, agandhatāya gandhena na tappeti, evaṃ tvampi dassanena piyavacanena ca santappesi, na kammunāti dīpeti. Adadanti bhadde, yo “imaṃ nāma vo bhogaṃ dassāmī”ti madhuravacanena vatvā taṃ bhogaṃ adadanto avissajjento kevalaṃ madhuravacanameva karoti, tena saddhiṃ assa mittassa [P 3.0254] sandhi jīrati, mittasanthavo na ghaṭīyati. Pātheyyañcāti bhadde, mayhaṃ tava madhuravacanena bajjhitvā tīṇi saṃvaccharāni vasantasseva hatthiassarathapattisaṅkhātaṃ balañca khīṇaṃ, manussānaṃ bhattavetanasaṅkhātaṃ pātheyyañca natthi. Saṅke pāṇūparodhāyāti svāhaṃ idheva attano jīvitavināsaṃ āsaṅkāmi, handa dānāhaṃ gacchāmīti.
