Herein, `sampesi` means you have gratified, you have delighted. `Sereyyakassa` means of the golden kurandaka flower. This is just the heading of the teaching. But whatever other flower—golden kurandaka, jayasumana, etc.—is endowed with beauty but is without fragrance, he spoke referring to all of them. `Beautiful but without fragrance`: this shows that just as a garland of sereyyaka and other flowers gratifies by its beauty to the sight, but does not gratify with its fragrance to the smell, so too, 'you gratified me by your appearance and pleasant speech, but not by your deeds.' `Not giving`, good lady: when one, after saying with sweet words, 'I will give you this wealth,' does not give that wealth, does not bestow it, but only offers sweet words, his bond of friendship with that friend decays; the friendly intimacy is not formed. `And my provisions`, good lady: for me, who have dwelt here for three years bound by your sweet words, my strength, consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers, is exhausted, and there are no provisions, consisting of food and wages, for my men. `I fear my life is in danger` means: I myself fear the destruction of my own life right here. Come now, I am going.

Āsaṅkā [V 3.0222] kumārikā rañño vacanaṃ sutvā “mahārāja, tvaṃ mayhaṃ nāmaṃ jānāsi, tayā vuttameva mama nāmaṃ, idaṃ me pitu kathetvā maṃ gaṇhitvā yāhī”ti raññā saddhiṃ sallapantī āha –

The maiden Āsaṅkā, having heard the king's words, said while conversing with him, 'Great king, you say you do not know my name; but my name is precisely what you have spoken. This is my name. Tell this to my father, take me, and go.' Then she spoke:

33.

33.

“Etadeva hi me nāmaṃ, yaṃnāmasmi rathesabha;

Āgamehi mahārāja, pitaraṃ āmantayāmaha”nti.

“This indeed is my name, O bull among charioteers, the very name I bear. Wait, great king, I will take leave of my father.”

Tassattho – yaṃnāmā ahaṃ asmi, taṃ etaṃ āsaṅkātveva mama nāmanti.

The meaning is: The name that I bear, that very name of mine is 'Āsaṅkā' (Expectation/Doubt).

Taṃ [M 3.0239] sutvā rājā bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā “bhante, tumhākaṃ dhītā āsaṅkā nāmā”ti āha. “Nāmaṃ ñātakālato paṭṭhāya taṃ gahetvā gaccha, mahārājā”ti. So mahāsattaṃ vanditvā phalikavimānadvāraṃ āgantvā āha – “bhadde, pitarāpi te mayhaṃ dinnā, ehi dāni gamissāmā”ti. “Āgamehi, mahārāja, pitaraṃ āmantayāmaha”nti pāsādā otaritvā mahāsattaṃ vanditvā roditvā khamāpetvā rañño santikaṃ āgatā. Rājā taṃ gahetvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhanto piyasaṃvāsaṃ vasi. Bodhisatto aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke uppajji.

Hearing this, the king went to the Bodhisatta and said, 'Venerable sir, your daughter is named Āsaṅkā.' 'Since her name is known, great king, take her and go.' The king paid homage to the Great Being, went to the door of the crystal mansion, and said, 'Good lady, you have been given to me by your father. Come now, let us go.' 'Wait, great king, I will take leave of my father,' she said. Descending from the mansion, she paid homage to the Great Being, asked for his forgiveness, and then came to the king. The king took her and went to Benares, where he lived with her in pleasant union, prospering with sons and daughters. The Bodhisatta, with his jhānas undiminished, was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā āsaṅkā kumārikā purāṇadutiyikā ahosi, rājā ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma and explained the Truths, identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the maiden Āsaṅkā was the former wife, the king was the dissatisfied monk, and the ascetic was I myself.

Āsaṅkajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Āsaṅka Jātaka, the Fifth.

[381] 6. Migālopajātakavaṇṇanā

[381] 6. The Commentary on the Migālopa Jātaka

Na [P 3.0255] me ruccīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ dubbacabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Satthā taṃ bhikkhuṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu dubbaco”ti pucchitvā “āma, bhante”ti vutte “na kho bhikkhu idāneva, pubbepi tvaṃ dubbacoyeva, dubbacabhāvañca pana nissāya paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ akaronto verambhavātamukhe byasanaṃ gatosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'It does not please me.' This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was difficult to admonish. The Teacher had that monk summoned and asked: 'Is it true, monk, that you are difficult to admonish?' When he replied, 'Yes, venerable sir,' the Teacher said: 'Not only now, monk, but in the past too you were difficult to admonish. And on account of being difficult to admonish, by not following the words of the wise, you met with disaster in the face of the Verambha winds.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 3.0223] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto gijjhayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā apanandagijjho nāma ahosi. So gijjhagaṇaparivuto gijjhakūṭapabbate vasi. Putto panassa migālopo nāma thāmabalasampanno ahosi, so aññesaṃ gijjhānaṃ sīmaṃ atikkamitvā atiuccaṃ uppati. Gijjhā “putto te atidūraṃ uppatatī”ti gijjharañño ācikkhiṃsu. So taṃ pakkosetvā “tvaṃ kira, tāta, atiuccaṃ [M 3.0240] gacchasi, atiuccaṃ gacchanto jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti vatvā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a vulture and was named Apananda. Surrounded by a flock of vultures, he dwelt on Vulture Peak. His son, named Migālopa, was endowed with great strength and power. He would fly beyond the boundary of the other vultures, soaring very high. The vultures reported to the vulture king: 'Your son flies up too far.' The king summoned him and said: 'Dear son, they say you go up very high. Going up so high, you will come to the destruction of your life.' And he spoke three verses:

34.

34.

“Na me rucci migālopa, yassa te tādisī gatī;

Atuccaṃ tāta patasi, abhūmiṃ tāta sevasi.

“It does not please me, Migālopa, that your flight is such. You fly too high, dear son; you frequent a domain that is not your own, dear son.

35.

35.

“Catukkaṇṇaṃva kedāraṃ, yadā te pathavī siyā;

Tato tāta nivattassu, māssu etto paraṃ gami.

“When the earth appears to you like a four-cornered field, from there, dear son, you should turn back; do not go any further than that.

36.

36.

“Santi aññepi sakuṇā, pattayānā vihaṅgamā;

Akkhittā vātavegena, naṭṭhā te sassatīsamā”ti.

“There are other birds, too, winged creatures that travel through the air; though they deemed themselves eternal, they were tossed by the force of the wind and perished.”

Tattha migālopāti puttaṃ nāmena ālapati. Atuccaṃ tāta patasīti tāta, tvaṃ aññesaṃ gijjhānaṃ sīmaṃ atikkamitvā atiuccaṃ gacchasi. Catukkaṇṇaṃva kedāranti imināssa sīmaṃ ācikkhati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tāta, yadā te ayaṃ mahāpathavī catukkaṇṇaṃ kedāraṃ viya siyā, evaṃ khuddikā [P 3.0256] viya hutvā paññāyetha, atha tvaṃ ettakā ṭhānā nivatteyyāsi, etto paraṃ mā gamīti. Santi aññepīti na kevalaṃ tvameva, aññepi gijjhā evaṃ kariṃsūti dīpeti. Akkhittāti tepi gijjhā amhākaṃ sīmaṃ atikkamitvā gatā vātavegena ākaḍḍhitā nassiṃsu. Sassatīsamāti sassatīhi pathavīpabbatādīhi samaṃ attānaṃ maññamānā attano vassasahassaparimāṇaṃ āyuṃ apūretvāpi antarā naṭṭhāti attho.

Here, he addresses his son by the name Migālopa. "You fly too high, dear son," means, "Dear son, you are going too high, beyond the territory of other vultures." "Like a four-cornered field" indicates his boundary. This means: "Dear son, when this great earth appears to you like a four-cornered field, seeming tiny, then you should turn back from such a place; do not go further than that." "There are others too" indicates that not only you, but other vultures have also done this. "Tossed up" means those vultures, having crossed our boundary, were swept away by the wind and perished. "As if eternal" means they, thinking themselves equal to eternal things like the earth and mountains, perished before completing their lifespan of a thousand years.

Migālopo anovādakattā pitu vacanaṃ akatvā laṅghanto pitarā akkhātaṃ sīmaṃ disvā taṃ atikkamma kālavāte patvā tepi chinditvā uppatito verambhavātamukhaṃ pakkhandi, atha naṃ verambhavātā pahariṃsu. So tehi pahaṭamattova khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ hutvā ākāseyeva antaradhāyi.

Migālopa, being disobedient, disregarded his father’s advice and transgressing the boundary pointed out by his father, reached the seasonal winds and, cutting through them, leapt towards the mouth of the Verambha winds. Then the Verambha winds struck him. Struck by them, he shattered into pieces and vanished in the sky.

37.

37.

“Akatvā [V 3.0224] apanandassa, pitu vuddhassa sāsanaṃ;

Kālavāte atikkamma, verambhānaṃ vasaṃ agā.

“Not heeding the instruction of Apananda, his old father, having crossed the seasonal winds, he went under the sway of the Verambha winds.”

38.

38.

“Tassa puttā ca dārā ca, ye caññe anujīvino;

Sabbe byasanamāpāduṃ, anovādakare dije.

“His sons, his wives, and all his dependents, all met with disaster, due to the unheeding bird.”

39.

39.

“Evampi [M 3.0241] idha vuddhānaṃ, yo vākyaṃ nāvabujjhati;

Atisīmacaro ditto, gijjhovātītasāsano;

Sabbe byasanaṃ papponti, akatvā vuddhasāsana”nti. –

“Thus, whoever here does not comprehend the words of the elders, arrogantly overstepping the bounds, like a vulture who transgressed instruction, they all meet with disaster for not following the elders' teaching.”

Imā tisso abhisambuddhagāthā.

These three verses were spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Tattha anujīvinoti taṃ nissāya jīvanakā. Anovādakare dijeti tasmiṃ migālope gijjhe ovādaṃ agaṇhante sabbepi te tena saddhiṃ atisīmaṃ gantvā vināsaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Evampīti, bhikkhave, yathā so gijjho, evaṃ yo aññopi gahaṭṭho vā pabbajito vā hitānukampakānaṃ vuddhānaṃ vacanaṃ na gaṇhāti, sopi ayaṃ sīmaṃ atikkamitvā caranto ditto gabbito gijjhova byasanaṃ pāpuṇātīti.

Here, 'anujīvino' means those who make a living depending on him. 'Anovādakare dije' means that when Migālopa the vulture did not heed the advice, all of them, going beyond the boundary with him, met destruction. 'Thus' means, 'Monks, just as that vulture, so too any householder or renunciant who does not heed the advice of the elders who are compassionate and wish for their welfare, behaving arrogantly and conceitedly, crossing boundaries, will meet ruin like the vulture.'

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā migālopo dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, apanando pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, revealed the Truths and connected the birth: “At that time, Migālopa was the unruly monk, but Apananda was none other than myself.”

Migālopajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Migālopa Jātaka, the Sixth.

[382] 7. Sirikāḷakaṇṇijātakavaṇṇanā

[382] 7. The Commentary on the Sirikāḷakaṇṇī Jātaka.

Kā [P 3.0257] nu kāḷena vaṇṇenāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto anāthapiṇḍikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya akhaṇḍāni pañca sīlāni rakkhi, bhariyāpissa puttadhītaropi dāsāpi bhatiṃ gahetvā kammaṃ karontā kammakarāpi sabbe rakkhiṃsuyeva. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, anāthapiṇḍiko suciyeva suciparivāro hutvā caratī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya [V 3.0225] sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbe porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi sucīyeva suciparivārā ahesu”nti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Who is this of dark complexion?” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning Anāthapiṇḍika. From the time he was established in the fruit of stream-entry, he maintained the five unbroken precepts. His wife, his sons and daughters, the slaves, and the workers who took wages and performed their duties—all of them maintained the precepts. One day, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, Anāthapiṇḍika is pure and moves about with a pure retinue.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what discussion are you engaged in now?” When they told him, he said, “Not only now, monks, but even the wise of old were pure and had pure retinues.” At their request, he then related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 3.0242] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto seṭṭhi hutvā dānaṃ adāsi, sīlaṃ rakkhi, uposathakammaṃ kari, bhariyāpissa pañca sīlāni rakkhi, puttadhītaropi dāsakammakaraporisāpi pañca sīlāni rakkhiṃsu. So suciparivāraseṭṭhitveva paññāyittha. Athekadivasaṃ so cintesi “sace mayā suciparivārasīlo koci āgamissati, tassa mama nisīdanapallaṅkaṃ vā nipajjanasayanaṃ vā dātuṃ na yuttaṃ, anucchiṭṭhaṃ aparibhuttaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti attano vasanaṭṭhāneyeva ekapasse aparibhuttapallaṅkañca senāsanañca paññāpesi. Tasmiṃ samaye cātumahārājikadevalokato virūpakkhamahārājassa dhītā kāḷakaṇṇī ca nāma dhataraṭṭhamahārājassa dhītā sirī ca nāmāti imā dve bahuṃ gandhamālaṃ ādāya “anotatte kīḷissāmā”ti anotattatitthaṃ āgacchiṃsu. Tasmiṃ pana dahe bahūni titthāni, tesu buddhānaṃ titthe buddhāyeva nhāyanti, paccekabuddhānaṃ titthe paccekabuddhāva nhāyanti, bhikkhūnaṃ [P 3.0258] titthe bhikkhūva nhāyanti, tāpasānaṃ titthe tāpasāva nhāyanti, cātumahārājikādīsu chasu kāmasaggesu devaputtānaṃ titthe devaputtāva nhāyanti, devadhītānaṃ titthe devadhītāva nhāyanti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having become a merchant, gave alms, kept the precepts, and performed the Uposatha observance. His wife also kept the five precepts, as did his sons, daughters, and the slaves, workers, and servants. Thus, he became known as the Merchant with a Pure Retinue. One day, he thought: “If anyone of pure retinue and virtuous conduct like myself should come, it would not be proper to offer them my own seat or bed that has been used. It is fitting to give only what is untouched and unused.” So, on one side of his own dwelling, he had an unused couch and bed prepared. At that time, from the Cātumahārājika deva world, two daughters of the Great Kings—Kāḷakaṇṇī, the daughter of the Great King Virūpakkha, and Sirī, the daughter of the Great King Dhataraṭṭha—taking many perfumes and garlands and thinking, “Let us play in Lake Anotatta,” went to the bathing place of Anotatta. Now, in that lake, there are many bathing places. In the bathing place of the Buddhas, only Buddhas bathe; in that of the Paccekabuddhas, only Paccekabuddhas bathe; in that of the monks, only monks bathe; in that of ascetics, only ascetics bathe; in the bathing places for the devas of the six sense-sphere heavens, beginning with the Cātumahārājika realm, only deva sons bathe in the bathing place of the deva sons, and only deva daughters bathe in that of the deva daughters.

Tatrimā dve āgantvā “ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ nhāyissāmi, ahaṃ paṭhama”nti titthāya kalahaṃ kariṃsu. Kāḷakaṇṇī “ahaṃ lokaṃ pālemi vicāremi, tasmā paṭhamaṃ nāyituṃ yuttāmhī”ti vadati. Sirī “ahaṃ mahājanassa issariyadāyikāya paṭipadāya ṭhitā, tasmā paṭhamaṃ nhāyituṃ yuttāmhī”ti vadati. Tā “amhesu paṭhamaṃ nhāyituṃ yuttarūpaṃ vā ayuttarūpaṃ vā cattāro mahārājāno jānissantī”ti tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “amhesu kā paṭhamaṃ anotattadahe nhāyituṃ yuttarūpā”ti pucchiṃsu. Dhataraṭṭhavirūpakkhā “na sakkā amhehi vinicchinitu”nti virūḷhakavessavaṇānaṃ bhāramakaṃsu. Te “amhepi na sakkhissāma, sakkassa pādamūle pesessāmā”ti tā sakkassa santikaṃ pesesuṃ. Sakko tāsaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā cintesi “imā dvepi mama purisānaññeva dhītaro, na sakkā mayā imaṃ aḍḍaṃ vinicchinitu”nti. Atha tā sakko āha “bārāṇasiyaṃ suciparivāro nāma seṭṭhi atthi, tassa ghare anucchiṭṭhasayanañca paññattaṃ, yā tattha nisīdituṃ vā sayituṃ vā labhati, sā paṭhamaṃ nhāyituṃ yuttarūpā”ti. Taṃ sutvā kāḷakaṇṇī tasmiṃ khaṇeyeva [M 3.0243] nīlavatthaṃ nivāsetvā nīlavilepanaṃ vilimpitvā nīlamaṇipiḷandhanaṃ piḷandhitvā yantapāsāṇo viya devalokato otaritvā majjhimayāmasamanantare seṭṭhino [V 3.0226] pāsādassa upaṭṭhānadvāre sayanassa avidūre ṭhāne nīlarasmiṃ vissajjetvā ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Seṭṭhi oloketvā [P 3.0259] taṃ addasa, sahadassanenevassa sā appiyā ahosi amanāpā. So tāya saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

There, these two arrived and quarreled over the bathing place, saying, “I will bathe first,” “I will bathe first.” Kāḷakaṇṇī said, “I administer and oversee the world; therefore, I am fit to bathe first.” Sirī said, “I am established in the practice of bestowing sovereignty upon the great populace; therefore, I am fit to bathe first.” They thought, “The Four Great Kings will know whether it is fit or unfit for us to bathe first.” So they went to them and asked, “Who among us is fit to bathe first in Lake Anotatta?” Dhataraṭṭha and Virūpakkha said, “We are not able to decide,” and transferred the burden to Virūḷhaka and Vessavaṇa. They too said, “We also will not be able; we will send them to the feet of Sakka.” So they sent them to Sakka. Hearing their words, Sakka thought, “Both of these are the daughters of my own attendants; I am not able to decide this case.” Then Sakka said to them, “In Benares there is a merchant known as the Merchant with a Pure Retinue. In his house, an unused bed is prepared. Whoever is able to sit or lie down there, she is the one fit to bathe first.” Hearing this, Kāḷakaṇṇī immediately dressed in a blue garment, anointed herself with blue unguent, and adorned herself with blue jewels. Like a stone from a catapult, she descended from the deva world and, just after the middle watch, stood in the sky at the entrance to the merchant's mansion, not far from the bed, emitting a blue radiance. The merchant looked and saw her. At the very sight of her, she was unpleasing and disagreeable to him. While conversing with her, he spoke the first verse:

40.

40.

“Kā nu kāḷena vaṇṇena, na cāpi piyadassanā;

Kā vā tvaṃ kassa vā dhītā, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ maya”nti.

“Who are you, of dark appearance, and not pleasing to see? Who are you, whose daughter are you? How may we know you?”

Tattha kāḷenāti nīlena. Vaṇṇenāti sarīravatthābharaṇavaṇṇena. Na cāpi piyadassanāti dhātuso, bhikkhave, sattā saṃsandantīti vuttaṃ, ayañca devadhītā anācārā dussīlā, tasmā sā sahadassanenevassa appiyā jātā, tenevamāha. Kā vā tvanti “kā ca tvaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho.

Herein, 'of dark' means of blue. 'Appearance' refers to the color of the body, garments, and ornaments. As to 'not pleasing to see': it has been said, “Monks, beings associate according to their element,” and this goddess was of bad conduct and immoral; therefore, she became unpleasing to him at the very sight. Thus he spoke. 'Who are you?' means 'Who are you?' or this is an alternative reading.

Taṃ sutvā kāḷakaṇṇī dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, Kāḷakaṇṇī spoke the second verse:

41.

41.

“Mahārājassahaṃ dhītā, virūpakkhassa caṇḍiyā;

Ahaṃ kāḷī alakkhikā, kāḷakaṇṇīti maṃ vidū;

Okāsaṃ yācito dehi, vasemu tava santike”ti.

“I am the fierce daughter of the Great King Virūpakkha. I am Kālī, the unfortunate one; they know me as Kāḷakaṇṇī. Grant me the opportunity I ask for; let us stay near you.”

Tattha caṇḍiyāti kodhanā. Kodhabhāvena hi mayhaṃ caṇḍīti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Alakkhikāti nippaññā. Maṃ vidūti evaṃ maṃ cātumahārājikadevaloke jānanti. Vasemūti mayaṃ ajja ekarattaṃ tava santike vaseyyāma, etasmiṃ me anucchiṭṭhāsanasayane okāsaṃ dehīti.

Herein, 'the fierce one' means irascible. 'Indeed, because of my irascible nature, they gave me the name “Caṇḍī”.' 'The unfortunate one' means unwise. 'They know me' means: 'Thus they know me in the Cātumahārājika deva world.' 'Let us stay' means: 'Let us stay near you for one night today; grant me a place on this untouched seat and bed.'

Tato bodhisatto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:

42.

42.

“Kiṃsīle kiṃsamācāre, purise nivisase tuvaṃ;

Puṭṭhā me kāḷi akkhāhi, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ maya”nti.

“In a person of what virtue, of what conduct, do you dwell? Asked by me, O Kālī, explain, so that we may know you.”

Tattha nivisaseti tava cittena nivisasi patiṭṭhahasīti.

Herein, 'do you dwell' means 'you settle' or 'you are established with your mind'.

Tato [M 3.0244] sā attano guṇaṃ kathentī catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, speaking of her own characteristics, she spoke the fourth verse:

43.

43.

“Makkhī [V 3.0227] paḷāsī sārambhī, issukī maccharī saṭho;

So mayhaṃ puriso kanto, laddhaṃ yassa vinassatī”ti.

“The denigrator, the spiteful, the contentious, the envious, the miserly, and the deceitful—such a person is dear to me, one whose gains are lost.”

Tassattho – yo puriso attano kataguṇaṃ na jānāti, guṇamakkhī hoti, attano kismiñci kāraṇe kathite “kiṃ ahaṃ etaṃ na jānāmī”ti yugaggāhaṃ gaṇhāti[P 3.0260], aññehi kiñci kataṃ disvā sārambhavasena karaṇuttarikaṃ karoti, pare lābhaṃ labhante na tussati, “mayhaṃ issariyaṃ paresaṃ mā hotu, mayhameva hotū”ti sakasampattiṃ gopetvā parassa tiṇaggena telabindumpi na deti, kerāṭikalakkhaṇena samannāgato hutvā attano santakaṃ parassa adatvā tehi tehi upāyehi parasantakameva khādati, yassa laddhaṃ dhaññaṃ vā dhanaṃ vā vinassati na tiṭṭhati, surādhutto akkhadhutto itthidhutto vā hutvā laddhaṃ laddhaṃ vināsetiyeva, ayaṃ etehi guṇehi samannāgato puriso mayhaṃ kanto piyo manāpo, evarūpe ahaṃ cittena patiṭṭhahāmīti.

The meaning is this: a person who does not acknowledge a good deed done for him and is a denigrator of virtue; when any matter concerning himself is mentioned, he becomes obstinate, saying, 'What, do I not know this?'; seeing something done by others, he acts contentiously and tries to outdo them; he is not pleased when others receive gains; thinking, 'Let others not have sovereignty, let it be mine alone,' he guards his own property and does not give another even a drop of oil on the tip of a blade of grass; being endowed with the characteristics of a rogue, he does not give his own property to another but by various means consumes the property of others; whatever grain or wealth he acquires is destroyed and does not last; being a drunkard, a gambler, or a womanizer, he destroys whatever he has gained. Such a person, endowed with these qualities, is dear, beloved, and agreeable to me; in such a one my mind is established.

Sāyeva pañcamachaṭṭhasattamagāthā abhāsi –

She herself spoke the fifth, sixth, and seventh verses:

44.

44.

“Kodhano upanāhī ca, pisuṇo ca vibhedako;

Kaṇḍakavāco pharuso, so me kantataro tato.

“The angry and the grudge-bearing, the slanderer and the divisive, the one of thorny and harsh speech—he is dearer to me than that one.

45.

45.

“Ajja suveti puriso, sadatthaṃ nāvabujjhati;

Ovajjamāno kuppati, seyyaṃ so atimaññati.

“The person who says, ‘Today, tomorrow,’ not understanding his own welfare; when advised, he gets angry, and he despises his superior.

46.

46.

“Davappaluddho puriso, sabbamittehi dhaṃsati;

So mayhaṃ puriso kanto, tasmiṃ homi anāmayā”ti.

“A person addicted to sport falls away from all his friends; that person is dear to me, with him I am free from affliction.”

Tāpi imināva nayena vitthāretabbā. Saṅkhepattho panettha – kodhanoti appamattakenāpi kujjhanako. Upanāhīti parassa aparādhaṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā sucirenapi tassa anatthakārako. Pisuṇoti pisuṇavāco. Vibhedakoti appamattakenapi mittabhindanako. Kaṇḍakavācoti sadosavāco. Pharusoti thaddhavāco. Kantataroti so puriso mayhaṃ purimāpi kantataro piyataro. Ajja suveti “idaṃ kammaṃ ajja kātabbaṃ, idaṃ sve[M 3.0245], idaṃ tatiyadivasādīsū”ti evaṃ so sadatthaṃ attano kiccaṃ nāvabujjhati na jānāti. Ovajjamānoti ovadiyamāno. Seyyaṃ so atimaññatīti jātigottakulappadesasīlācāraguṇehi uttaritaraṃ uttamapuggalaṃ “tvaṃ mayhaṃ [V 3.0228] kiṃ pahosī”ti atikkamitvā maññati. Davappaluddhoti rūpādīsu kāmaguṇesu nirantaradavena paluddho abhibhūto vasaṃ gato. Dhaṃsatīti “tayā mayhaṃ kiṃ kata”ntiādīni vatvā sabbeheva mittehi dhaṃsati parihāyati. Anāmayāti ayaṃ etehi guṇehi samannāgate puggale niddukkhā nissokā homi, taṃ labhitvā aññattha anālayā hutvā vasāmī”ti.

These too should be elaborated in this same way. The meaning in brief here is: ‘Angry’ means one who gets angry even over a trifle. ‘Bearing a grudge’ means one who, having placed another's offense in his heart, causes him harm even after a long time. ‘Slanderous’ means one with slanderous speech. ‘Divisive’ means one who breaks friendships even over a trifle. ‘Thorny speech’ means malicious speech. ‘Harsh’ means rigid speech. ‘Dearer’ means: that person is dearer and more beloved to me than the former one. ‘Today, tomorrow’ means: thinking, 'This work should be done today, this tomorrow, this on the third day, etc.,' he does not understand or know his own welfare, his own duty. ‘When advised’ means when being admonished. ‘He despises his superior’ means: he transgresses and looks down upon a superior person—one more distinguished in birth, clan, family, region, virtue, conduct, or good qualities—thinking, 'What can you do for me?' ‘Obsessed with constant sport’ means overwhelmed and brought under the sway of the constant amusement in sensual pleasures such as forms, etc. ‘Alienates’ means: by saying things like, 'What have you done for me?', he falls away from all his friends. ‘Free from trouble’ means: 'Among people endowed with these qualities I am without suffering, without sorrow. Having found such a one, I dwell there without concern for anything else.'

Atha [P 3.0261] naṃ garahanto mahāsatto aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, rebuking her, spoke the eighth verse:

47.

47.

“Apehi etto tvaṃ kāḷi, netaṃ amhesu vijjati;

Aññaṃ janapadaṃ gaccha, nigame rājadhāniyo”ti.

“Go away from here, O Black One, this is not found among us; go to another country, to market towns and royal cities.”

Tattha apehīti apagaccha. Netaṃ amhesūti etaṃ makkhādikaṃ tava piyabhāvakaraṇaṃ amhesupi na vijjati natthi. Nigame rājadhāniyoti aññe nigamepi aññā rājadhāniyopi gaccha, yattha mayaṃ taṃ na passāma, tattha gacchāti dīpeti.

Herein, ‘go away’ means depart. ‘This is not among us’ means: this cause of your being dear, such as denigration and so on, is not found, does not exist, among us. ‘To market towns and royal cities’ means: go to other market towns and other royal cities; it indicates, 'Go where we will not see you.'

Taṃ sutvā kāḷakaṇṇī additā hutvā anantaragāthamāha –

Hearing that, Kāḷakaṇṇī, being afflicted, spoke the next verse:

48.

48.

“Ahampi kho taṃ jānāmi, netaṃ tumhesu vijjati;

Santi loke alakkhikā, saṅgharanti bahuṃ dhanaṃ;

Ahaṃ devo ca me bhātā, ubho naṃ vidhamāmase”ti.

“I too know this, that this is not found in you. There are unfortunate ones in the world who accumulate much wealth; I and my brother Deva—we both destroy it.”

Tattha netaṃ tumhesūti yaṃ mama piyabhāvakaraṇaṃ makkhādikaṃ yena ahaṃ attanāpi samannāgatā, taṃ tumhesu natthīti ahampi etaṃ jānāmi. Santi loke alakkhikāti aññe pana loke nissīlā nippaññā santi. Saṅgharantīti te nissīlā nippaññāpi samānā etehi makkhādīhi bahuṃ dhanaṃ saṅgharanti piṇḍaṃ karonti. Ubho nanti taṃ pana etehi saṅgharitvā ṭhapitaṃ dhanaṃ ahañca mayhameva bhātā devo ca nāma devaputtoti ubho ekato hutvā vidhamāmase nāsema, amhākaṃ pana devaloke bahū dibbaparibhogā [M 3.0246] atthi dibbāni sayanāni, tvaṃ dadeyyāsi vā no vā, ko me tayā atthoti vatvā pakkāmi.

Herein, ‘this is not in you’ means: that which makes me dear, such as denigration, with which I myself am endowed—that is not in you, this I too know. ‘There are unfortunate ones in the world’ means: there are others in the world who are without virtue and without wisdom. ‘They accumulate’ means: though they are without virtue and without wisdom, by means of this denigration and so on, they accumulate much wealth, they make a heap. ‘We both [destroy] it’ means: but that wealth accumulated and stored by them, both I and my brother, the devaputta named Deva, having come together, we destroy, we annihilate it. But for us in the deva world there are many divine enjoyments and divine couches. 'Whether you give or not, what use have I of you?' Having said this, she departed.

Tassā pakkantakāle sirī devadhītā suvaṇṇavaṇṇehi vatthavilepanehi suvaṇṇālaṅkārena āgantvā [V 3.0229] upaṭṭhānadvāre pītarasmiṃ vissajjetvā samehi pādehi samaṃ pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya sagāravā aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ disvā mahāsatto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At the time of her departure, the devadhītā Sirī, adorned with golden-colored garments, unguents, and golden ornaments, arrived at the door of the attendance hall. Having cast a yellow radiance, she stood respectfully with her feet evenly placed on the ground. Seeing her, the Great Being spoke the first verse:

49.

49.

“Kā nu dibbena vaṇṇena, pathabyā supatiṭṭhitā;

Kā vā tvaṃ kassa vā dhītā, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ maya”nti.

“Who can you be, with divine complexion, so well established on the earth? Who are you, or whose daughter? How may we come to know you?”

Tattha [P 3.0262] dibbenāti visiṭṭhena uttamena.

Herein, ‘divine’ means distinguished, supreme.

Taṃ sutvā sirī dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, Sirī spoke the second verse:

50.

50.

“Mahārājassahaṃ dhītā, dhataraṭṭhassa sirīmato;

Ahaṃ sirī ca lakkhī ca, bhūripaññāti maṃ vidū;

Okāsaṃ yācito dehi, vasemu tava santike”ti.

“I am the daughter of the great king, the glorious Dhataraṭṭha; I am Sirī and also Lakkhī, they know me as Bhūripaññā. Grant the opportunity I request, let me dwell in your presence.”

Tattha sirī ca lakkhī cāti sirīti ca lakkhīti ca ahamevaṃnāmā, na aññā. Bhūripaññāti maṃ vidūti maṃ cātumahārājikadevaloke pathavīsamāya vipulāya paññāya samannāgatāti jānanti. Vasemu tava santiketi tava anucchiṭṭhāsane ceva anucchiṭṭhasayane ca ekarattiṃ vaseyyāma, okāsaṃ me dehīti.

Herein, ‘Sirī and also Lakkhī’ means: I have these names, Sirī and Lakkhī, not another. ‘They know me as Bhūripaññā’ means: in the devaloka of the Four Great Kings they know me as one endowed with vast wisdom equal to the earth. ‘Let me dwell in your presence’ means: let me stay for one night on your unused seat and on your unused bed; give me the opportunity.

Tato paraṃ bodhisatto āha –

Then the Bodhisatta said:

51.

51.

“Kiṃsīle kiṃsamācāre, purise nivisase tuvaṃ;

Puṭṭhā me lakkhi akkhāhi, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ mayaṃ.

“In a person of what virtue, of what conduct, do you, O Lakkhī, make your home? Asked by me, please tell, so that we may know you.”

52.

52.

“Yo cāpi sīte atha vāpi uṇhe, vātātape ḍaṃsasarīsape ca;

Khudhaṃ pipāsaṃ abhibhuyya sabbaṃ, rattindivaṃ yo satataṃ niyutto.

“One who, in cold or in heat, in wind and sun, and among biting flies and reptiles, having overcome all hunger and thirst, is constantly engaged day and night.

53.

53.

“Kālāgatañca [M 3.0247] na hāpeti atthaṃ, so me manāpo nivise ca tamhi;

Akkodhano mittavā cāgavā ca, sīlūpapanno asaṭhojubhūto.

“And does not let a timely opportunity pass—he is agreeable to me, and in him I dwell. One who is not angry, is friendly and generous, endowed with virtue, not deceitful, and upright.

54.

54.

“Saṅgāhako [V 3.0230] sakhilo saṇhavāco, mahattapattopi nivātavutti;

Tasmiṃhaṃ pose vipulā bhavāmi, ūmi samuddassa yathāpi vaṇṇaṃ.

“Hospitable, amiable, and gentle in speech, though having attained greatness, humble in conduct; in such a person I become abundant, as a wave enhances the ocean's splendor.

55.

55.

“Yo cāpi mitte atha vā amitte, seṭṭhe sarikkhe atha vāpi hīne;

Atthaṃ carantaṃ atha vā anatthaṃ, āvī raho saṅgahameva vatte.

“One who, towards friends or foes, superiors, equals, or inferiors, whether they are acting for one's welfare or harm, openly or in secret, treats them only with kindness.

56.

56.

“Vācaṃ [P 3.0263] na vajjā pharusaṃ kadāci, matassa jīvassa ca tassa homi;

Etesaṃ yo aññataraṃ labhitvā, kantā sirī majjati appapañño;

Taṃ dittarūpaṃ visamaṃ carantaṃ, karīsaṭhānaṃva vivajjayāmi.

“I belong to the one who would never speak a harsh word to anyone, living or dead. But the foolish person who, having obtained lovely Sirī, becomes intoxicated—that one, of arrogant appearance and behaving wrongly, I avoid like a dung-pit.

57.

57.

“Attanā kurute lakkhiṃ, alakkhiṃ kurutattanā;

Na hi lakkhiṃ alakkhiṃ vā, añño aññassa kārako”ti.

“By oneself one creates good fortune, by oneself one creates misfortune; for another is not the maker of another's good or bad fortune.”

Seṭṭhissa pucchā hoti, siriyā vissajjanā.

This was the merchant's question and Sirī's answer.

Tattha ḍaṃsasarīsape cāti ḍaṃsā vuccanti piṅgalamakkhikā, sabbāpi vā makkhikājātikā idha “ḍaṃsā”ti adhippetā. Sarīsapāti dīghajātikā. Ḍaṃsā ca sarīsapā ca ḍaṃsasarīsapā, tasmiṃ ḍaṃsasarīsape sati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo mahāseṭṭhi sīte vā uṇhe vā vātātape vā ḍaṃsasarīsape vā sati etehi sītādīhi pīḷiyamānopi etāni ceva sītādīni khudhañca pipāsañcāti sabbampetaṃ parissayaṃ abhibhuyya abhibhavitvā tiṇaṃ viya agaṇetvā rattindivaṃ kasivaṇijjādīsu ceva dānasīlādīsu ca satataṃ attano kammesu niyutto attānaṃ yojetvā vattati.

Herein, regarding ‘and among biting flies and reptiles’: ‘biting flies’ (ḍaṃsā) are said to be tawny flies, or all species of flies are intended here by the term ‘biting flies.’ ‘Reptiles’ (sarīsapā) are long-bodied species. ‘Biting flies and reptiles’ is ḍaṃsasarīsapā; ‘tasmiṃ ḍaṃsasarīsape’ means when biting flies and reptiles are present. This is what is meant: A great merchant, whether in cold or heat, in wind or sun, or when biting flies and reptiles are present, even though oppressed by this cold and so on, overcomes and masters all these hardships—the cold, etc., and hunger and thirst—disregarding them like grass, and day and night remains constantly engaged in his own tasks, such as agriculture and trade, and in giving, virtue, and so on, applying and exerting himself.

Kālāgatañcāti [M 3.0248] kasikālādīsu kasiādīni dhanapariccāgasīlarakkhaṇadhammassavanādikālesu ca dhanapariccajanādippabhedaṃ diṭṭhadhammasamparāye sukhāvahaṃ atthaṃ na hāpeti, yuttappayuttakāle karotiyeva, so mayhaṃ manāpo tasmiñca purise ahaṃ nivisāmīti. Akkodhanoti adhivāsanakhantiyā samannāgato. Mittavāti kalyāṇamittena samannāgato. Cāgavāti dhanapariccāgayutto.

‘And a timely benefit’ means: he does not lose the benefit that brings happiness in this life and the next—such as agriculture during the agricultural season, and the various kinds of welfare such as giving up wealth, protecting virtue, and listening to the Dhamma at the appropriate times. He acts at the proper time. ‘He is agreeable to me, and in him I dwell.’ ‘Not angry’ means endowed with forbearance and patience. ‘Friendly’ means endowed with good friends. ‘Generous’ means devoted to giving up wealth.

Saṅgāhakoti mittasaṅgahaāmisasaṅgahadhammasaṅgahānaṃ kārako. Sakhiloti muduvāco. Saṇhavācoti [V 3.0231] madhuravacano. Mahattapattopi nivātavuttīti mahantaṃ ṭhānaṃ vipulaṃ issariyaṃ pattopi yasena anuddhato nīcavutti paṇḍitānaṃ ovādakaro hoti. Tasmiṃhaṃ poseti tasmiṃ ahaṃ purise. Vipulā bhavāmīti akhuddakā homi. So hi mahatiyā siriyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Ūmi samuddassa yathāpi vaṇṇanti yathā nāma samuddassa vaṇṇaṃ olokentānaṃ uparūpari āgacchamānā ūmi vipulā viya khāyati, evamahaṃ tasmiṃ puggale vipulā homīti dīpeti.

‘A supporter’ is one who practices the four ways of support: through friends, material things, and the Dhamma. ‘Affable’ means soft-spoken. ‘Kindly spoken’ means sweet-spoken. ‘Even having attained greatness, he is of humble conduct’ means: though he has attained a great position and vast authority, he is not puffed up by fame but is of humble conduct and follows the advice of the wise. ‘In that person I’ means in that man. ‘I become abundant’ means I am not small. For he is the foundation for great fortune. ‘Just as the waves of the ocean’ means: just as for those observing the appearance of the ocean, the waves coming one after another appear vast, so too I become abundant in that person—this is what is shown.

Āvī rahoti sammukhā ca parammukhā ca. Saṅgahameva vatteti etasmiṃ mittādibhede puggale catubbidhaṃ saṅgahameva vatteti pavatteti.

‘Openly and in secret’ means both in one's presence and in one's absence. ‘He practices only support’ means: towards various people such as friends and so on, he practices and promotes only the fourfold way of support.

Na vajjāti yo kadāci kismiñci kāle pharusavacanaṃ na vadeyya, madhuravacanova hoti. Matassa jīvassa cāti [P 3.0264] tassāhaṃ puggalassa matassapi jīvantassapi bhattikā homi, idhalokepi paralokepi tādisameva bhajāmīti dasseti. Etesaṃ yoti etesaṃ sītābhibhavanādīnaṃ heṭṭhā vuttaguṇānaṃ yo puggalo ekampi guṇaṃ labhitvā pamajjati pamussati, puna nānuyuñjatīti attho. Kantā sirī, kantasiriṃ, kantaṃ sirinti tayopi pāṭhā, tesaṃ vasena ayaṃ atthayojanā – yo puggalo siriṃ labhitvā “kantā me siri yathāṭhāne ṭhitā”ti etesaṃ aññataraṃ guṇaṃ pamajjati, yo vā puggalo kantasiriṃ piyasiriṃ icchanto etesaṃ guṇānaṃ aññataraṃ labhitvā pamajjati, yo vā puggalo siriṃ labhitvā kantaṃ manāpaṃ siriṃ etesaṃ guṇānaṃ aññataraṃ pamajjati. Appapaññoti nippañño. Taṃ dittarūpaṃ visamaṃ carantanti taṃ ahaṃ dittasabhāvaṃ gabbitasabhāvaṃ [M 3.0249] kāyaduccaritādibhedaṃ visamaṃ carantaṃ sucijātiko manusso gūthakūpaṃ viya dūrato vivajjayāmīti.

‘He would not speak’ means one who would never at any time speak a harsh word, but is only sweet-spoken. ‘For the dead and for the living’ means: I am devoted to such a person whether they are dead or alive; it shows that in this world and the next I associate with such a one. ‘Whoever among these’ refers to the qualities mentioned below, such as overcoming cold and so on; the meaning is a person who, having gained even one of these qualities, becomes heedless and forgets, no longer applying himself. ‘Kantā sirī,’ ‘kantasiriṃ,’ and ‘kantaṃ siriṃ’ are three readings. Based on them, this is the application: a person who, having gained fortune, becomes heedless of one of these qualities, thinking, ‘My fortune is lovely and well-established’; or a person who, desiring a lovely fortune, having gained one of these qualities, becomes heedless of it; or a person who, having gained fortune, becomes heedless of a lovely, pleasing fortune, which is one of these qualities. ‘Of little wisdom’ means without wisdom. ‘Him of arrogant appearance, behaving wickedly’ means: I, a person of pure nature, avoid from afar that one of an arrogant and proud nature who behaves wickedly through bodily misconduct and so on, just as one avoids a cesspool.

Añño aññassa kārakoti evaṃ sante lakkhiṃ vā alakkhiṃ vā añño puriso aññassa kārako nāma natthi, yo koci attanā attano lakkhiṃ vā alakkhiṃ vā karotīti.

‘Another is the doer for another’ means: this being so, there is no such thing as one person being the maker of fortune or misfortune for another; rather, everyone makes his own fortune or misfortune for himself.

Evaṃ mahāsatto deviyā vacanaṃ abhinanditvā “idaṃ anucchiṭṭhaṃ āsanañca sayanañca tuyhaṃyeva anucchavikaṃ, pallaṅke ca sayane ca nisīda ceva nipajja cā”ti āha. Sā tattha vasitvā paccūsakāle nikkhamitvā cātumahārājikadevalokaṃ gantvā anotattadahe paṭhamaṃ nahāyi. Tampi sayanaṃ siridevatāya paribhuttabhāvā sirisayanaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Sirisayanassa ayaṃ vaṃso, iminā kāraṇena yāvajjatanā “sirisayana”nti vuccati.

Thus the Great Being, having delighted in the goddess’s words, said: “This unused seat and bed are indeed suitable for you. Sit and lie down on the couch and bed.” She stayed there and, departing at dawn, went to the heaven of the Four Great Kings and bathed first in Lake Anotatta. That bed, because it had been used by the goddess Sirī, became known as the Sirī-bed. This is the lineage of the Sirī-bed; for this reason, it is called the “Sirī-bed” to this very day.

Satthā [V 3.0232] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siridevī uppalavaṇṇā ahosi, suciparivāraseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: “At that time, the goddess Sirī was Uppalavaṇṇā, and the merchant Suciparivāra was I myself.”

Sirikāḷakaṇṇijātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Seventh Commentary on the Sirikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka is finished.

[383] 8. Kukkuṭajātakavaṇṇanā

[383] 8. Commentary on the Kukkuṭa Jātaka

Sucittapattachadanāti [P 3.0265] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā “kasmā ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “ekaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ itthiṃ disvā kilesavasena, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu itthiyo nāma vañcetvā upalāpetvā attano vasaṃ gatakāle vināsaṃ pāpenti, lolabiḷārī viya hontī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘With brightly colored wings and plumage...’ The Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain discontented monk. The Teacher asked that monk, “Why are you discontented?” When he replied, “Venerable sir, because of the defilements that arose after I saw an adorned and beautifully dressed woman,” the Teacher said: “Bhikkhu, women deceive and coax, and when they have brought a man under their control, they bring him to ruin. They are like a fickle she-cat.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto araññe kukkuṭayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā anekasatakukkuṭaparivāro araññe [M 3.0250] vasati. Tassa avidūre ekā biḷārikāpi vasati. Sā ṭhapetvā bodhisattaṃ avasese kukkuṭe upāyena vañcetvā khādi. Bodhisatto tassā gahaṇaṃ na gacchati. Sā cintesi “ayaṃ kukkuṭo ativiya saṭho amhākañca saṭhabhāvaṃ upāyakusalabhāvañca na jānāti, imaṃ mayā ‘ahaṃ bhariyā te bhavissāmī’ti upalāpetvā attano vasaṃ āgatakāle khādituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Sā tena nisinnarukkhassa mūlaṃ gantvā vaṇṇasambhāsanapubbaṅgamāya vācāya taṃ yācamānā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a cock and lived in the forest with a retinue of many hundreds of cocks. Not far from him lived a certain she-cat. By means of a stratagem, she deceived and ate the other cocks, excluding the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta did not fall into her grasp. She thought: “This cock is extremely crafty; he does not know our craftiness and our skill in stratagems. I should coax him by saying, ‘I will be your wife,’ and when he comes under my control, I will eat him.” Approaching the foot of the tree where he was perched, she addressed him with words preceded by praise, entreating him with the first verse:

58.

58.

“Sucittapattachadana, tambacūḷa vihaṅgama;

Oroha dumasākhāya, mudhā bhariyā bhavāmi te”ti.

“O you with beautifully variegated wings and plumage, O copper-crested bird, come down from the tree branch; I will be your wife for free.”

Tattha sucittapattachadanāti sucittehi pattehi katacchadana. Mudhāti vinā mūlena na kiñci gahetvā ahaṃ bhariyā te bhavāmi.

Here, 'with beautifully variegated wings and plumage' (sucittapattachadana) means having a covering made of well-variegated feathers. 'For free' (mudhā) means without any price, taking nothing, I will be your wife.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto “imāya mama sabbe ñātakā khāditā, idāni maṃ upalāpetvā khāditukāmā ahosi, uyyojessāmi na”nti cintetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta thought: “All my kinsmen have been eaten by her. Now she wants to coax me and eat me. I will dismiss her.” Then he spoke the second verse:

59.

59.

“Catuppadī [V 3.0233] tvaṃ kalyāṇi, dvipadāhaṃ manorame;

Migī pakkhī asaññuttā, aññaṃ pariyesa sāmika”nti.

“You are a quadruped, O lovely one; I am a biped, O charming one. A beast and a bird are incompatible; seek another husband.”

Tattha [P 3.0266] migīti biḷāriṃ sandhāyāha. Asaññuttāti jayampatikā bhavituṃ ayuttā asambandhā, natthi tesaṃ īdiso sambandhoti dīpeti.

Here, 'beast' (migī) refers to the she-cat. 'Incompatible' (asaññuttā) means unsuitable and unrelated to become husband and wife; it indicates that there is no such relationship between them.

Taṃ sutvā tato sā “ayaṃ ativiya saṭho, yena kenaci upāyena vañcetvā naṃ khādissāmī”ti cintetvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, she thought: “This one is extremely crafty. By some stratagem or other, I will deceive him and eat him.” Then she spoke the third verse:

60.

60.

“Komārikā te hessāmi, mañjukā piyabhāṇinī;

Vinda maṃ ariyena vedena, sāvaya maṃ yadicchasī”ti.

“I will be your maiden wife, charming and sweet-spoken. Win me with a noble acquisition; proclaim me if you wish.”

Tattha komārikāti ahaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ aññaṃ purisaṃ na jānāmi, tava komārikā bhariyā bhavissāmīti vadati. Mañjukā piyabhāṇinīti tava madhurakathā piyabhāṇinīyeva bhavissāmi. Vinda manti paṭilabha maṃ. Ariyena vedenāti sundarena paṭilābhena. Ahampi hi ito pubbe purisasamphassaṃ na jānāmi, tvampi itthisamphassaṃ na jānāsi, iti pakatiyā brahmacārī [M 3.0251] brahmacāriniṃ maṃ niddosena lābhena labha. Yadi maṃ icchasi, atha me vacanaṃ na saddahasi, dvādasayojanāya bārāṇasiyā bheriṃ carāpetvā “ayaṃ me dāsī”ti sāvaya, maṃ attano dāsaṃ katvā gaṇhāhīti vadati.

Here, 'maiden' (komārikā) means: she says, “For all this time I have not known another man; I will be your maiden wife.” 'Charming and sweet-spoken' (mañjukā piyabhāṇinī) means: “I will be one who speaks sweetly and pleasantly to you.” 'Win me' (vinda maṃ) means obtain me. 'With a noble acquisition' (ariyena vedenā) means with a fine acquisition. “For I have not known the touch of a man before, and you have not known the touch of a woman. Thus, as a celibate man to a celibate woman, obtain me through a faultless acquisition. If you desire me, but do not trust my word, then have a drum beaten around the twelve-yojana city of Bārāṇasī and proclaim, ‘This is my female slave,’ and take me after making me your slave.”

Tato bodhisatto “imaṃ tajjetvā palāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta, thinking, “It is proper to threaten her and make her flee,” spoke the fourth verse:

61.

61.

“Kuṇapādini lohitape, cori kukkuṭapothini;

Na tvaṃ ariyena vedena, mamaṃ bhattāramicchasī”ti.

“O eater of corpses, blood-drinker, thief, slayer of cocks! You do not desire me as a husband through a noble acquisition.”

Tattha na tvaṃ ariyenāti tvaṃ ariyena brahmacariyavāsalābhena maṃ bhattāraṃ na icchasi, vañcetvā pana maṃ khāditukāmāsi, nassa pāpeti taṃ palāpesi. Sā pana palāyitvāva gatā, na puna oloketumpi visahi.

Here, 'not through a noble one' (na tvaṃ ariyena) means: you do not desire me as a husband by a noble acquisition of a celibate life, but you desire to eat me after deceiving me. “Perish, you evil one!”—saying this, he made her flee. And she, having fled, went away, not daring even to look back again.

62.

62.

“Evampi [V 3.0234] caturā nārī, disvāna sadhanaṃ naraṃ;

Nenti saṇhāhi vācāhi, biḷārī viya kukkuṭaṃ.

“Even so a clever woman, having seen a wealthy man, leads him on with gentle words, like the she-cat did the cock.”

63.

63.

“Yo ca uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, na khippamanubujjhati;

Amittavasamanveti, pacchā ca anutappati.

“One who does not quickly understand a matter that has arisen falls under the power of an enemy and afterwards regrets it.”

64.

64.

“Yo [P 3.0267] ca uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, khippameva nibodhati;

Muccate sattusambādhā, kukkuṭova biḷāriyā”ti. – imā abhisambuddhagāthā;

“But one who quickly understands a matter that has arisen is freed from the oppression of an enemy, like the cock from the she-cat.” These are verses of the Fully Enlightened One.

Tattha caturāti cāturiyena samannāgatā. Nārīti itthiyo. Nentīti attano vasaṃ upanenti. Biḷārī viyāti yathā sā biḷārī taṃ kukkuṭaṃ netuṃ vāyamati, evaṃ aññāpi nāriyo nentiyeva. Uppatitaṃ atthanti uppannaṃ kiñcideva atthaṃ. Na anubujjhatīti yathāsabhāvena na jānāti, pacchā ca anutappati. Kukkuṭovāti yathā so ñāṇasampanno kukkuṭo biḷārito mutto, evaṃ sattusambādhato muccatīti attho.

Here, 'clever' (caturā) means endowed with cleverness. 'Woman' (nārī) refers to females. 'Lead' (nentī) means they bring them under their control. 'Like the she-cat' (biḷārī viya) means: just as that she-cat tried to lead that cock, so other women lead men. 'A matter that has arisen' (uppatitaṃ atthaṃ) means some matter that has come up. 'Does not understand' (na anubujjhati) means one does not know it in its true nature, and afterwards one regrets. 'Like the cock' (kukkuṭova) means: just as that cock endowed with wisdom was freed from the she-cat, so one is freed from the oppression caused by enemies—this is the meaning.

Satthā [M 3.0252] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā kukkuṭarājā ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and explained the Truths, identified the birth. At the conclusion of the explanation of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. “At that time, the cock-king was I myself.”

Kukkuṭajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kukkuṭa Jātaka, the eighth.

[384] 9. Dhammadhajajātakavaṇṇanā

[384] 9. The Commentary on the Dhammadhaja Jātaka

Dhammaṃ caratha ñātayoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuhakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā “na, bhikkhave, ayaṃ idāneva kuhako, pubbepi kuhakoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Practice the Dhamma, kinsfolk”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a deceitful monk. At that time the Teacher, saying, “Monks, this one is not deceitful only now; he was deceitful in the past as well,” told a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sakuṇayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto sakuṇasaṅghaparivuto samuddamajjhe dīpake vasi. Athekacce kāsiraṭṭhavāsino vāṇijā disākākaṃ gahetvā nāvāya samuddaṃ pakkhandiṃsu, samuddamajjhe nāvā bhijji. So disākāko taṃ dīpakaṃ gantvā cintesi “ayaṃ mahāsakuṇasaṅgho, mayā kuhakakammaṃ katvā etesaṃ aṇḍakāni [V 3.0235] ceva chāpake ca varaṃ varaṃ khādituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So otaritvā sakuṇasaṅghassa majjhe mukhaṃ vivaritvā ekena pādena pathaviyaṃ aṭṭhāsi. “Ko nāma tvaṃ, sāmī”ti sakuṇehi puṭṭho “ahaṃ dhammiko nāmā”ti āha. “Kasmā pana ekena pādena ṭhitosī”ti? “Mayā dutiye pāde nikkhitte [P 3.0268] pathavī dhāretuṃ na sakkotī”ti. “Atha kasmā mukhaṃ vivaritvā tiṭṭhasī”ti? “Ahaṃ aññaṃ āhāraṃ na khādāmi, vātameva khādāmī”ti. Evañca pana vatvā te sakuṇe āmantetvā “ovādaṃ vo dassāmi, taṃ suṇāthā”ti tesaṃ ovādavasena paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Varanasi, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the animal kingdom as a bird and, having reached maturity, lived on a small island in the middle of the ocean surrounded by a flock of birds. At that time, some merchants living in the Kasi country, taking a direction-finding crow (disākāka), set out by boat on the ocean. In the middle of the ocean, the boat was wrecked. That direction-finding crow went to that small island and thought, "This flock of birds is large. By performing a deceptive act, I should eat their eggs and their young." Having thought thus, he landed, opened his mouth in the midst of the flock of birds, and stood on only one foot. When asked by the birds, "Sir, what is your name?", he said, "I am named Dhammika." They asked, "Why do you stand on only one foot?" He said, "If I were to put down the second foot, the earth would not be able to bear it." They asked, "Then why do you stand with your mouth open?" He said, "I eat no other food; I only consume the wind." Having spoken thus, he addressed those birds, "I will give you advice; listen to that advice." Then, by way of giving advice, he spoke the first verse:

65.

65.

“Dhammaṃ caratha ñātayo, dhammaṃ caratha bhaddaṃ vo;

Dhammacārī sukhaṃ seti, asmiṃ loke paramhi cā”ti.

“Practice the Dhamma, kinsfolk; practice the Dhamma, may it be a blessing for you. One who practices the Dhamma sleeps happily, in this world and the next.”

Tattha dhammaṃ carathāti kāyasucaritādibhedaṃ dhammaṃ karotha. Ñātayoti te ālapati. Dhammaṃ caratha bhaddaṃ voti ekavāraṃ caritvā mā osakkatha, punappunaṃ caratha, evaṃ bhaddaṃ vo bhavissati. Sukhaṃ setīti desanāsīsametaṃ, dhammacārī pana sukhaṃ tiṭṭhati gacchati nisīdati seti, sabbiriyāpathesu sukhito hotīti dīpeti.

There, 'practice the Dhamma' means perform the Dhamma, which is divided into good bodily conduct and so forth. 'Kinsfolk' is an address to them. 'Practice the Dhamma, may it be a blessing for you' means: having practiced it once, do not retreat; practice it again and again; thus, it will be a blessing for you. 'Sleeps happily' is the main heading of the teaching; however, it shows that one who practices the Dhamma stands happily, walks happily, sits happily, and sleeps happily; one is happy in all postures.

Sakuṇā [M 3.0253] “ayaṃ kāko kohaññena aṇḍakāni khādituṃ evaṃ vadatī”ti ajānitvā taṃ dussīlaṃ vaṇṇentā dutiyaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

The birds, not knowing, "This crow speaks thus in order to eat the eggs by means of deceit," praised that immoral one and spoke the second verse:

66.

66.

“Bhaddako vatayaṃ pakkhī, dijo paramadhammiko;

Ekapādena tiṭṭhanto, dhammamevānusāsatī”ti.

“Excellent indeed is this bird, a twice-born one, supremely righteous; standing on one foot, he instructs only in the Dhamma.”

Tattha dhammamevāti sabhāvameva. Anusāsatīti kathesi.

There, 'only in the Dhamma' means only in the truth. 'Instructs' means he spoke.

Sakuṇā tassa dussīlassa saddahitvā “tvaṃ kira sāmi aññaṃ gocaraṃ na gaṇhasi, vātameva bhakkhasi, tena hi amhākaṃ aṇḍakāni ca chāpake ca olokeyyāsī”ti vatvā gocarāya gacchanti. So pāpo tesaṃ gatakāle aṇḍakāni ca chāpake ca kucchipūraṃ khāditvā tesaṃ āgamanakāle upasantūpasanto hutvā mukhaṃ vivaritvā ekena pādena tiṭṭhati. Sakuṇā āgantvā puttake apassantā “ko nu kho khādatī”ti mahāsaddena viravanti, “ayaṃ kāko dhammiko”ti tasmiṃ āsaṅkāmattampi na karonti. Athekadivasaṃ mahāsatto cintesi “idha pubbe koci [V 3.0236] paripantho natthi, imassa āgatakālato paṭṭhāya jāto, imaṃ pariggaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So sakuṇehi saddhiṃ gocarāya gacchanto viya hutvā nivattitvā paṭicchannaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Kākopi [P 3.0269] “gatā sakuṇā”ti nirāsaṅko hutvā uṭṭhāya gantvā aṇḍakāni ca chāpake ca khāditvā punāgantvā mukhaṃ vivaritvā ekena pādena aṭṭhāsi.

The birds, trusting that immoral crow, said, "Sir, you do not take other food, you eat only the wind. Therefore, please watch over our eggs and our young," and went out for food. When the birds had gone, that wicked one ate the eggs and the young until his belly was full. When it was time for their return, he became very calm, opened his mouth, and stood on one foot. The birds, returning and not seeing their young, cried out with a loud sound, "Who has eaten them?" They did not even have the slightest suspicion, thinking, "This crow is righteous." Then one day, the Great Being thought, "Formerly there was no danger here, but since this crow arrived, it has arisen. It is right to investigate this crow." So, pretending to go out for food with the birds, he turned back and stood in a concealed spot. The crow, being free from suspicion that the birds had gone, went and ate the eggs and the young, then returned, opened his mouth, and stood on one foot.

Sakuṇarājā sakuṇesu āgatesu sabbe sannipātāpetvā “ahaṃ vo ajja puttakānaṃ paripanthaṃ pariggaṇhanto imaṃ pāpakākaṃ khādantaṃ addasaṃ, etha naṃ gaṇhāmā”ti sakuṇasaṅghaṃ āmantetvā parivāretvā “sace palāyati, gaṇheyyātha na”nti vatvā sesagāthā abhāsi –

When the birds had returned, the king of birds had them all assemble and addressed the flock of birds: "Today, while investigating the enemy of your young, I saw this wicked crow eating them. Come, let us seize him!" Having surrounded him, he said, "If he flees, catch him," and spoke the remaining verses:

67.

67.

“Nāssa sīlaṃ vijānātha, anaññāya pasaṃsatha;

Bhutvā aṇḍañca potañca, dhammo dhammoti bhāsati.

“You do not know his virtue, praising him without understanding; having eaten both eggs and young, he speaks of 'Dhamma, Dhamma'.

68.

68.

“Aññaṃ bhaṇati vācāya, aññaṃ kāyena kubbati;

Vācāya no ca kāyena, na taṃ dhammaṃ adhiṭṭhito.

“One thing he says with speech, another he does with the body; by speech but not by body, he is not established in that Dhamma.

69.

69.

“Vācāya [M 3.0254] sakhilo manoviduggo, channo kūpasayova kaṇhasappo;

Dhammadhajo gāmanigamāsu sādhu, dujjāno purisena bālisena.

“Gentle in speech but of a mind difficult to penetrate, like a black snake hidden in a covered pit; bearing the banner of Dhamma, esteemed in villages and towns, he is hard to know by a foolish person.

70.

70.

“Imaṃ tuṇḍehi pakkhehi, pādā cimaṃ viheṭhatha;

Chavañhimaṃ vināsetha, nāyaṃ saṃvāsanāraho”ti.

“With beaks and wings, and with your feet, strike this one; destroy this vile one, he is not worthy of living with us.”

Tattha nāssa sīlanti na assa sīlaṃ. Anaññāyāti ajānitvā. Bhutvāti khāditvā. Vācāya no ca kāyenāti ayañhi vacaneneva dhammaṃ carati, kāyena pana na karoti. Na taṃ dhammaṃ adhiṭṭhitoti tasmā jānitabbo yathāyaṃ dhammaṃ bhaṇati, na taṃ adhiṭṭhito, tasmiṃ dhamme na adhiṭṭhito. Vācāya sakhiloti vacanena mudu. Manoviduggoti manasā viduggo duppaveso visamo. Channoti yasmiṃ bile sayati, tena channo. Kūpasayoti bilāsayo. Dhammadhajoti sucaritadhammaṃ dhajaṃ katvā vicaraṇena dhammaddhajo. Gāmanigamāsu sādhūti gāmesu ca nigamesu ca sādhu bhaddako sambhāvito. Dujjānoti ayaṃ evarūpo dussīlo paṭicchannakammanto bālisena aññāṇena purisena na sakkā jānituṃ. Pādā cimanti attano attano pādena ca imaṃ. Viheṭhathāti paharatha hanatha. Chavanti lāmakaṃ. Nāyanti ayaṃ amhehi saddhiṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne saṃvāsaṃ na arahatīti.

There, 'not his virtue' means 'na assa sīlaṃ'. 'Without understanding' means without knowing. 'Having eaten' means having devoured. 'By speech but not by body' means he practices the Dhamma only by words, but does not do so by body. 'He is not established in that Dhamma' means it should be known that although he speaks of Dhamma, he is not established in it, not committed to that Dhamma. 'Gentle in speech' means soft in words. 'Of a mind difficult to penetrate' means difficult to enter or uneven in mind. 'Hidden' means concealed by the hole in which he lies. 'Lying in a pit' means lying in a hole. 'Bearing the banner of Dhamma' means a banner-bearer of the Dhamma by wandering around making good conduct a banner. 'Esteemed in villages and towns' means well-regarded and good in villages and towns. 'Hard to know' means such an immoral person with concealed actions cannot be known by a foolish, ignorant man. 'And with your feet, this one' means each with your own feet and this one. 'Strike' means hit or kill. 'Vile' (chava) means low or base. 'He is not worthy' means this one is not fit to live in one place together with us.

Evañca [V 3.0237][P 3.0270] pana vatvā sakuṇajeṭṭhako sayameva laṅghitvā tassa sīsaṃ tuṇḍena pahari, avasesā sakuṇā tuṇḍanakhapādapakkhehi pahariṃsu. So tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi.

Having spoken thus, the chief bird himself leaped and struck his head with his beak; the remaining birds struck him with their beaks, claws, feet, and wings. There, he reached the end of his life.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kuhakakāko idāni kuhakabhikkhu ahosi, sakuṇarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the deceitful crow was this deceitful monk, but the king of birds was indeed I myself.”

Dhammadhajajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Dhammadhaja Jātaka Commentary, the ninth.

[385] 10. Nandiyamigarājajātakavaṇṇanā

[385] 10. The Nandiyamigarāja Jātaka Commentary

Sace [M 3.0255] brāhmaṇa gacchesīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ mātuposakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu gihī posesī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kiṃ te hontī”ti vutte “mātāpitaro me, bhante”ti vutte “sādhu sādhu bhikkhu porāṇakapaṇḍitānaṃ vaṃsaṃ pālesi, porāṇakapaṇḍitā hi tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattitvāpi mātāpitūnaṃ jīvitaṃ adaṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“If you go, brahmin”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who supported his mother. For the Teacher asked him, “Is it true, monk, that you support laypeople?” When he replied, “It is true, venerable sir,” and was asked, “Who are they to you?” he answered, “My parents, venerable sir.” The Teacher then said, “Good, good, monk! You maintain the lineage of the ancient wise ones. For the ancient wise ones, even when reborn in the animal realm, sacrificed their lives for their parents.” Having said this, he related a past story.

Atīte kosalaraṭṭhe sākete kosalarāje rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto migayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto nandiyamigo nāma hutvā sīlācārasampanno mātāpitaro posesi. Tadā kosalarājā migavittakova ahosi. So pana manussānaṃ kasikammādīni kātuṃ adatvā mahāparivāro devasikaṃ migavaṃ gacchati. Manussā sannipatitvā “ayyā, ayaṃ rājā amhākaṃ kammacchedaṃ karoti, gharāvāsopi nassati, yaṃnūna mayaṃ ajjunavanaṃ uyyānaṃ parikkhipitvā dvāraṃ yojetvā porakkhaṇiṃ khaṇitvā tiṇāni āropetvā daṇḍamuggarādihatthā araññaṃ pavisitvā gumbe paharantā mige nīharitvā parivāretvā gorūpāni viya vajaṃ uyyānaṃ pavesetvā dvāraṃ pidahitvā rañño ārocetvā attano kammaṃ kareyyāmā”ti mantayiṃsu. “Attheso upāyo”ti sabbe ekacchandā hutvā uyyānaṃ sajjetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā yojanamattaṭṭhānaṃ [P 3.0271] parikkhipiṃsu.

In the past, in the kingdom of Kosala, at Sāketa, while the king of Kosala was ruling, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the deer realm. Having reached maturity, he was named Nandiya the deer, was endowed with virtue and good conduct, and he supported his parents. At that time, the king of Kosala was very fond of hunting. Not allowing the people to attend to their farming and other work, he would go hunting daily with a large retinue. The people gathered and conferred: “Sirs, this king is causing an interruption to our work, and our household life is being ruined. What if we were to enclose the Ajjuna wood as a park, set up a gate, dig a pond, plant grass, and then enter the forest with sticks and clubs in hand? By beating the bushes, we could drive out the deer, surround them, and herd them like cattle into the park as into a pen. Then we could close the gate, inform the king, and attend to our own work.” “This is a good plan,” they said. All being of one mind, they prepared the park, entered the forest, and surrounded an area of about a league.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe nandiyo ekasmiṃ khuddakagumbe mātāpitaro gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ nipanno hoti. Manussā nānāphalakāvudhahatthā bāhunā bāhuṃ pīḷetvā taṃ gumbaṃ parikkhipiṃsu. Athekacce mige olokentā taṃ gumbaṃ pavisiṃsu. Nandiyo te disvā “ajja mayā jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā mātāpitūnaṃ [V 3.0238] jīvitaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā uṭṭhāya mātāpitaro vanditvā “ammatāta, ime manussā imaṃ gumbaṃ pavisitvā amhe tayopi passissanti, tumhe ekena upāyena jīveyyātha, jīvitaṃ vo seyyo, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ jīvitadānaṃ datvā manussehi gumbapariyante ṭhatvā gumbe pahaṭamatteyeva nikkhamissāmi, atha te ‘imasmiṃ khuddakagumbe ekoyeva migo bhavissatī’ti maññamānā gumbaṃ na pavisissanti, tumhe appamattā hothā”ti [M 3.0256] mātāpitaro khamāpetvā gamanasajjo aṭṭhāsi. So manussehi gumbapariyante ṭhatvā unnādetvā gumbe pahaṭamatteyeva tato nikkhami. Te “ekovettha migo bhavissatī”ti gumbaṃ na pavisiṃsu. Atha nandiyo gantvā migānaṃ antaraṃ pāvisi. Manussā parivāretvā sabbe mige uyyānaṃ pavesetvā dvāraṃ thaketvā rañño ārocetvā sakasakaṭṭhānāni agamaṃsu.

At that moment, Nandiya, taking his parents, was lying on the ground in a small thicket. Men armed with various weapons, pressing shoulder to shoulder, surrounded that thicket. Then some, looking for deer, entered the thicket. Seeing them, Nandiya thought, “Today, it is proper for me to sacrifice my life to save my parents' lives.” Rising, he paid homage to his parents and said, “Mother, father, if these men enter this thicket they will see all three of us. You must survive by some means; your lives are more precious. I will give you the gift of life. Standing at the edge of the thicket, I will emerge at the very moment they strike it. Then, thinking, ‘There must be only one deer in this small thicket,’ they will not enter the thicket. Be heedful.” Having asked his parents for forgiveness, he stood ready to go. He stood at the edge of the thicket, made a loud noise, and came out just as the men struck it. Thinking, “There must be only one deer here,” they did not enter the thicket. Then Nandiya went and entered among the deer. The men, having surrounded all the deer, drove them into the park, closed the gate, informed the king, and returned to their respective places.

Tato paṭṭhāya rājā sayameva gantvā ekaṃ migaṃ vijjhitvā taṃ gahetvā ehīti ekaṃ pesetvā āharāpesi. Migā vāraṃ ṭhapayiṃsu, pattavāro migo ekamante tiṭṭhati, taṃ vijjhitvā gaṇhanti. Nandiyo pokkharaṇiyaṃ pānīyaṃ pivati, tiṇāni khādati, vāro panassa na tāva pāpuṇāti. Atha bahūnaṃ divasānaṃ accayena tassa mātāpitaro taṃ daṭṭhukāmā hutvā “amhākaṃ putto nandiyamigarājā nāgabalo thāmasampanno, sace jīvati, avassaṃ vatiṃ laṅghitvā amhākaṃ dassanatthāya āgamissati, sāsanamassa pesessāmā”ti [P 3.0272] cintetvā maggasamīpe ṭhatvā ekaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ disvā “ayya, kahaṃ gacchasī”ti mānusikāya vācāya pucchitvā “sāketa”nti vutte puttassa sāsanaṃ pahiṇantā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

From that time onward, the king himself would go, shoot one deer, and then send a man to bring it back. The deer established a rotation; the deer whose turn it was would stand aside, and they would shoot and take it. Nandiya would drink water at the lotus pond and eat grass, but his turn had not yet come. Then, after many days had passed, his parents, wishing to see him, thought: “Our son, Nandiya the deer king, has the strength of an elephant and is full of power. If he is alive, he will surely leap over the enclosure and come to see us. Let us send him a message.” Standing by the roadside, they saw a brahmin and asked him in a human voice, “Sir, where are you going?” When he replied, “To Sāketa,” they sent a message to their son, reciting the first verse:

71.

71.

“Sace brāhmaṇa gacchesi, sākete ajjunaṃ vanaṃ;

Vajjāsi nandiyaṃ nāma, puttaṃ asmākamorasaṃ;

Mātā pitā ca te vuddhā, te taṃ icchanti passitu”nti.

“If you go, brahmin, to the Ajjuna wood in Sāketa, you should tell Nandiya by name, our own true son: ‘Your mother and father are old; they long to see you.’”

Tassattho – sace, tvaṃ brāhmaṇa, sāketaṃ gacchasi, sākete ajjunavanaṃ nāma uyyānaṃ atthi, tattha amhākaṃ putto nandiyo nāma migo atthi, taṃ vadeyyāsi “mātāpitaro te vuḍḍhā yāva na maranti, tāva taṃ passituṃ icchantī”ti.

The meaning is this: If you, brahmin, go to Sāketa, there is a park in Sāketa called the Ajjuna wood. There our son, a deer named Nandiya, lives. You should tell him, “Your parents are old and wish to see you before they die.”

So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā sāketaṃ gantvā punadivase uyyānaṃ pavisitvā “nandiyamigo nāma kataro”ti pucchi. Migo āgantvā tassa samīpe ṭhatvā “aha”nti āha. Brāhmaṇo tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Nandiyo taṃ sutvā “gaccheyyāmahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, vatiṃ laṅghitvā [V 3.0239] no na gaccheyyaṃ, mayā pana rañño santakaṃ nivāpapānabhojanaṃ bhuttaṃ, taṃ me iṇaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ, imesañca migānaṃ majjhe ciravutthosmi, tassa me rañño ceva [M 3.0257] etesañca sotthibhāvaṃ akatvā attano balaṃ adassetvā gamanaṃ nāma na yuttaṃ, attano vāre pana sampatte ahaṃ etesaṃ sotthibhāvaṃ katvā sukhito āgacchissāmī”ti tamatthaṃ pakāsento dve gāthā abhāsi –

He, saying “Very well,” accepted and went to Sāketa. The next day, he entered the park and asked, “Which one is the deer named Nandiya?” The deer came and stood near him, saying, “I am he.” The brahmin told him the matter. Hearing this, Nandiya said, “Brahmin, I could go by leaping over the fence; it is not that I could not go. But I have eaten the king's provisions of fodder and water, and that stands as a debt for me. Moreover, I have lived long among these deer. For me to go without having ensured the well-being of both the king and these deer, and without having shown my own strength, would not be proper. But when my own turn comes, I will ensure their well-being and then come happily.” Explaining this matter, he spoke two verses:

72.

72.

“Bhuttā mayā nivāpāni, rājino pānabhojanaṃ;

Taṃ rājapiṇḍaṃ avabhottuṃ, nāhaṃ brāhmaṇa mussahe.

“I have eaten the king's provisions, his drink and food; to consume that royal portion improperly, brahmin, I am not able.”

73.

73.

“Odahissāmahaṃ passaṃ, khurappānissa rājino;

Tadāhaṃ sukhito mutto, api passeyya mātara”nti.

“I will offer my flank to the king with the razor-sharp arrow; then, freed and happy, I might even see my mother.”

Tattha nivāpānīti tesu tesu ṭhānesu nivutāni nivāpāni. Pānabhojananti pānīyañca avasesatiṇañca. Taṃ rājapiṇḍanti taṃ rañño santakaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā samodhānakaṭṭhena piṇḍaṃ. Avabhottunti dubbhuttaṃ bhuñjituṃ[P 3.0273]. Rañño hi kiccaṃ anipphādento taṃ avabhuttaṃ bhuñjati nāma, svāhaṃ evaṃ avabhottuṃ na ussahāmīti vadati. Brāhmaṇa mussaheti cettha brāhmaṇāti ālapanaṃ, ma-kāro padasandhivasena vutto.

Therein, 'nivāpāni' means fodder scattered in various places. 'Pānabhojana' means drinkable water and the remaining grass. 'That royal portion' means that which belongs to the king, gathered and combined into a single morsel. 'To consume improperly' means to eat wrongfully. For one who does not accomplish the king's purpose and eats that provision is said to consume it improperly. He says, “I am not able to consume it improperly in such a way.” Here, in 'brāhmaṇa mussahe', 'brāhmaṇa' is a vocative, and the letter 'm' is present due to euphonic combination.

Odahissāmahaṃ passaṃ, khurappānissa rājinoti ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, attano vāre sampatte khurappaṃ sannayhitvā āgatassa rañño migayūthato nikkhamitvā ekamante ṭhatvā “maṃ vijjha, mahārājā”ti vatvā attano mahāphāsukapassaṃ odahissāmi oḍḍessāmi. Sukhito muttoti tadā ahaṃ maraṇabhayā mutto sukhito niddukkho raññā anuññāto api nāma mātaraṃ passeyyanti.

“‘I will offer my flank to the king with the razor-sharp arrow’ means: ‘O brahmin, when my turn comes, when the king has come having prepared his razor-sharp arrow, I will come forth from the herd of deer, stand aside, and saying, “Shoot me, great king,” I will offer, I will expose, my own large flank.’ ‘Freed and happy’ means: then, released from the fear of death, happy, free from sorrow, and permitted by the king, I might even see my mother.”

Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo pakkāmi. Aparabhāge tassa vāradivase rājā mahantena parivārena uyyānaṃ āgacchi. Mahāsatto ekamante aṭṭhāsi. Rājā “migaṃ vijjhissāmī”ti khurappaṃ sannayhi. Mahāsatto yathā aññe maraṇabhayatajjitā palāyanti, evaṃ apalāyitvā nibbhayo hutvā mettaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā mahāphāsukapassaṃ odahitvā niccalova aṭṭhāsi. Rājā tassa mettānubhāvena saraṃ vissajjetuṃ nāsakkhi. Mahāsatto “kiṃ, mahārāja, saraṃ na muccesi, muñcāhī”ti āha. “Na sakkomi, migarājā”ti. “Tena hi guṇavantānaṃ guṇaṃ jāna, mahārājā”ti. Tadā [M 3.0258] rājā bodhisatte pasīditvā dhanuṃ chaḍḍetvā “imaṃ acittakaṃ kaliṅgarakaṇḍampi [V 3.0240] tāva tava guṇaṃ jānāti, ahaṃ sacittako manussabhūtopi tava guṇaṃ na jānāmi, migarāja, mayhaṃ khama, abhayaṃ te dammī”ti āha. “Mahārāja, mayhaṃ tāva abhayaṃ desi, ayaṃ pana uyyāne migagaṇo kiṃ karissatī”ti? “Etassapi abhayaṃ dammī”ti. Evaṃ mahāsatto nigrodhajātake (jā. 1.1.12) vuttanayeneva sabbesaṃ araññe migānaṃ ākāsagatasakuṇānaṃ jalacaramacchānañca abhayaṃ dāpetvā rājānaṃ pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā “mahārāja, raññā nāma agatigamanaṃ pahāya dasa rājadhamme akopentena dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāretuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

Hearing this, the brahmin departed. Later, on his appointed day, the king came to the park with a large retinue. The Great Being stood aside. The king, intending to shoot a deer, prepared a razor-sharp arrow. The Great Being, unlike others who flee, terrified by the fear of death, did not flee but stood fearless, having made loving-kindness his vanguard, and exposing his large flank, stood motionless. The king, under the influence of his loving-kindness, could not release the arrow. The Great Being said, “Why, great king, do you not release the arrow? Release it!” “I cannot, O king of deer.” “Then, great king, recognize the virtue of the virtuous.” Then the king, pleased with the Bodhisatta, laid aside his bow and said, “Even this senseless arrow made of kaliṅgara wood knows your virtue, yet I, a conscious human being, do not know your virtue. O king of deer, forgive me. I grant you safety.” “Great king, you have granted me safety, but what will the herd of deer in this park do?” “I grant them safety too.” Thus, as described in the Nigrodha Jātaka, the Great Being secured safety for all the deer in the forest, the birds in the sky, and the fish in the water, and established the king in the five precepts, saying, “Great king, a king should abandon the paths of partiality and rule righteously and justly, without violating the ten royal virtues.”

“Dānaṃ [P 3.0274] sīlaṃ pariccāgaṃ, ajjavaṃ maddavaṃ tapaṃ;

Akkodhaṃ avihiṃsañca, khantiñca avirodhanaṃ.

“Giving, virtue, relinquishment, honesty, gentleness, austerity; non-anger, non-harming, patience, and non-opposition.”

“Iccete kusale dhamme, ṭhite passāmi attani;

Tato me jāyate pīti, somanassañcanappaka”nti. (jā. 2.21.176-177) –

“When I see these skillful qualities established in myself, then joy and no small gladness arise in me.”

Evaṃ vutte rājadhamme gāthābandheneva desetvā katipāhaṃ rañño santike vasitvā nagare sabbasattānaṃ abhayadānapakāsanatthaṃ suvaṇṇabheriṃ carāpetvā “appamatto hohi, mahārājā”ti vatvā mātāpitūnaṃ dassanatthāya gato.

Thus, having taught the ten royal virtues in verses, he stayed near the king for a few days. Having had a golden drum circulated throughout the city to announce the granting of safety to all beings, he said, “Be heedful, great king,” and departed to see his parents.

74.

74.

“Migarājā pure āsiṃ, kosalassa niketane;

Nandiyo nāma nāmena, abhirūpo catuppado.

“I was once a king of deer, dwelling in the Kosalan king's residence; Nandiya was my name, a handsome quadruped.”

75.

75.

“Taṃ maṃ vadhitumāgacchi, dāyasmiṃ ajjune vane;

Dhanuṃ ārajjaṃ katvāna, usuṃ sannayha kosalo.

“To kill me in the Ajjuna wood, the royal park, the Kosalan king came, having strung his bow and prepared an arrow.”

76.

76.

“Tassāhaṃ odahiṃ passaṃ, khurappānissa rājino;

Tadāhaṃ sukhito mutto, mātaraṃ daṭṭhumāgato”ti. –

“To him, to the king with the razor-sharp arrow, I offered my flank; then, freed and happy, I came to see my mother.”

Imā tisso abhisambuddhagāthā honti.

These are three verses spoken by the Fully Enlightened One.

Tattha [V 3.0241] kosalassa niketaneti kosalassa rañño niketane vasanaṭṭhāne, tassa santike araññasminti attho. Dāyasminti migānaṃ vasanatthāya dinnauyyāne. Ārajjaṃ katvānāti jiyāya saddhiṃ ekato katvā[M 3.0259], āropetvāti attho. Sannayhāti sannayhitvā yojetvā. Odahinti oḍḍesiṃ. Mātaraṃ daṭṭhumāgatoti desanāsīsametaṃ, rañño dhammaṃ desetvā sabbasattānaṃ abhayatthāya suvaṇṇabheriṃ carāpetvā mātāpitaro daṭṭhuṃ āgatosmīti attho.

Here, ‘kosalassa niketane’ means in the dwelling place of the king of Kosala, that is, in the forest near him. ‘Dāyasmiṃ’ means in the park given for the deer to dwell. ‘Ārajjaṃ katvāna’ means having made it one with the bowstring, that is, having strung it. ‘Sannayha’ means having prepared, having notched. ‘Odahiṃ’ means I offered. ‘Mātaraṃ daṭṭhumāgato’ is the climax of the teaching; the meaning is: “After teaching the king the Dhamma and having the golden drum proclaimed for the safety of all beings, I came to see my parents.”

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne mātuposakabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni ahesuṃ, brāhmaṇo sāriputto, rājā ānando, nandiyamigarājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and explained the Truths, identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the parents were the great royal families, the brahmin was Sāriputta, the king was Ānanda, and the deer-king Nandiya was I myself.

Nandiyamigarājajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The tenth commentary on the Nandiyamigarāja Jātaka.

Avāriyavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Section: The Avāriya Vagga.

2. Kharaputtavaggo

2. The Kharaputta Section

[386] 1. Kharaputtajātakavaṇṇanā

[386] 1. The Commentary on the Kharaputta Jātaka

Saccaṃ [V 3.0242][P 3.0275] kirevamāhaṃsūti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “āma, bhante”ti vutte “kena ukkaṇṭhāpitosī”ti vatvā “purāṇadutiyikāyā”ti vutte “bhikkhu ayaṃ te itthī anatthakārikā, pubbepi tvaṃ imaṃ nissāya aggiṃ pavisitvā maranto paṇḍite nissāya jīvitaṃ labhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Saccaṃ kirevamāhaṃsu…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, with reference to the enticement by a former wife. The Teacher asked that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?” When he replied, “Yes, Bhante,” the Teacher asked, “By whom have you been made discontented?” When he said, “By my former wife,” the Teacher said, “Monk, this woman is harmful to you. In the past, too, on account of her, you were about to die by entering a fire, but by relying on the wise, you obtained your life.” And he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ senake nāma raññe rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sakkattaṃ kāresi. Tadā senakassa rañño ekena nāgarājena saddhiṃ mittabhāvo hoti. So kira nāgarājā nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā thale gocaraṃ gaṇhanto carati. Atha naṃ gāmadārakā disvā “sappo aya”nti leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi pahariṃsu. Atha rājā uyyānaṃ kīḷituṃ gacchanto disvā “kiṃ ete dārakā karontī”ti pucchitvā “ekaṃ sappaṃ paharantī”ti sutvā “paharituṃ mā detha, palāpetha ne”ti palāpesi. Nāgarājā jīvitaṃ [M 3.0260] labhitvā nāgabhavanaṃ gantvā bahūni ratanāni ādāya aḍḍharattasamaye rañño sayanagharaṃ pavisitvā tāni ratanāni datvā “mahārāja, mayā tumhe nissāya jīvitaṃ laddha”nti raññā saddhiṃ mittabhāvaṃ katvā punappunaṃ gantvā rājānaṃ passati. So attano nāgamāṇavikāsu ekaṃ kāmesu atittaṃ nāgamāṇavikaṃ rakkhaṇatthāya rañño santike ṭhapetvā “yadā etaṃ na passasi, tadā imaṃ mantaṃ parivatteyyāsī”ti tassa ekaṃ mantaṃ adāsi.

In the past, when a king named Senaka was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was Sakka. At that time, King Senaka had a friendship with a certain Nāga king. It is said that this Nāga king would leave his Nāga abode and roam on land in search of food. Then, some village boys saw him and, thinking, “This is a snake,” struck him with clods, sticks, and so forth. Later, the king, while going to the park for amusement, saw them and asked, “What are these boys doing?” Hearing that they were striking a snake, he said, “Do not let them strike it; drive them away,” and had them driven off. The Nāga king, his life having been saved, returned to his Nāga abode, took many jewels, and at midnight entered the king’s bedchamber. He gave those jewels to the king and said, “Great king, through you my life was saved.” He established a friendship with the king and would go repeatedly to see him. He left one of his Nāga maidens, who was insatiable in sensual pleasures, with the king for her protection, saying, “When you do not see her, you should recite this spell.” He then gave him a spell.

So ekadivasaṃ uyyānaṃ gantvā nāgamāṇavikāya saddhiṃ pokkharaṇiyaṃ udakakīḷaṃ kīḷi. Nāgamāṇavikā ekaṃ udakasappaṃ disvā attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā tena saddhiṃ asaddhammaṃ paṭisevi. Rājā taṃ apassanto “kahaṃ nu [P 3.0276] kho gatā”ti mantaṃ parivattetvā anācāraṃ karontiṃ disvā veḷupesikāya pahari. Sā kujjhitvā tato nāgabhavanaṃ gantvā “kasmā āgatāsī”ti puṭṭhā “tumhākaṃ sahāyo maṃ attano vacanaṃ agaṇhantiṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ paharī”ti pahāraṃ dassesi. Nāgarājā tathato [V 3.0243] ajānitvāva cattāro nāgamāṇavake āmantetvā “gacchatha, senakassa sayanagharaṃ pavisitvā nāsavātena taṃ bhusaṃ viya viddhaṃsethā”ti pesesi. Te gantvā rañño sirisayane nipannakāle gabbhaṃ pavisiṃsu. Tesaṃ pavisanavelāyameva rājā deviṃ āha – “jānāsi nu kho bhadde, nāgamāṇavikāya gataṭṭhāna”nti? “Na jānāmi, devā”ti. “Ajja sā amhākaṃ pokkharaṇiyaṃ kīḷanakāle attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā ekena udakasappena saddhiṃ anācāraṃ akāsi, atha naṃ ahaṃ ‘evaṃ mā karī’ti sikkhāpanatthāya veḷupesikāya pahariṃ, sā ‘nāgabhavanaṃ gantvā sahāyassa me aññaṃ kiñci kathetvā mettiṃ bhindeyyā’ti me bhayaṃ uppajjatī”ti.
