Taṃ sutvā nāgamāṇavakā tatova nivattitvā nāgabhavanaṃ gantvā nāgarājassa tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. So saṃvegappatto hutvā taṅkhaṇaññeva rañño sayanagharaṃ āgantvā tamatthaṃ ācikkhitvā khamāpetvā “idaṃ me daṇḍakamma”nti sabbarutajānanaṃ nāma mantaṃ datvā “ayaṃ, mahārāja, anaggho manto, sace imaṃ mantaṃ aññassa dadeyyāsi, datvāva aggiṃ pavisitvā mareyyāsī”ti āha. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. So tato paṭṭhāya kipillikānampi saddaṃ jānāti.

One day, having gone to the park, he played water sports in the pond with the Nāga maiden. The Nāga maiden, seeing a water snake, abandoned her own form and engaged in misconduct with it. The king, not seeing her, wondered, “Where can she have gone?” and recited the spell. Seeing her behaving improperly, he struck her with a bamboo sliver. Angered, she went to the Nāga abode and, when asked, “Why have you come?” she showed the mark of the blow, saying, “Your friend struck me on the back because I did not heed his word.” The Nāga king, without knowing the truth of the matter, summoned four Nāga youths and sent them, saying, “Go, enter Senaka’s bedchamber and destroy him utterly with your nasal breath, as if he were chaff.” They went and entered the chamber while the king was lying on his royal bed. At the very moment they entered, the king said to the queen, “Do you know, my dear, where the Nāga maiden has gone?” “I do not know, lord.” “Today, while playing in our pond, she abandoned her form and misbehaved with a water snake. Then I struck her with a bamboo sliver to instruct her, saying, ‘Do not do this.’ Now I fear that she may go to the Nāga abode and, by telling my friend something else, break our friendship.” Hearing that, the Nāga youths immediately turned back, went to the Nāga abode, and reported the matter to the Nāga king. Struck with remorse, he immediately went to the king’s bedchamber, explained the matter, begged forgiveness, and said, “This is my penance.” He then gave the king a spell called ‘Knowing All Sounds’ and said, “Great king, this spell is priceless. If you give this spell to another, immediately after giving it, you must enter a fire and die.” The king accepted, saying, “Very well.” From then on, he could understand the sounds of even the ants.

Tassekadivasaṃ [M 3.0261] mahātale nisīditvā madhuphāṇitehi khādanīyaṃ khādantassa ekaṃ madhubindu ca phāṇitabindu ca pūvakhaṇḍañca bhūmiyaṃ pati. Ekā kipillikā taṃ disvā “rañño mahātale madhucāṭi bhinnā, phāṇitasakaṭaṃ pūvasakaṭaṃ [P 3.0277] nikkujjitaṃ, madhuphāṇitañca pūvañca khādathā”ti viravantī vicarati. Atha rājā tassā ravaṃ sutvā hasi. Rañño samīpe ṭhitā devī “kiṃ nu kho disvā rājā hasī”ti cintesi. Tasmiṃ khādanīyaṃ khāditvā nhatvā pallaṅke nisinne ekaṃ makkhikaṃ sāmiko “ehi bhadde, kilesaratiyā ramissāmā”ti āha. Atha naṃ sā “adhivāsehi tāva sāmi, idāni rañño gandhe āharissanti, tassa vilimpantassa pādamūle gandhacuṇṇaṃ patissati, ahaṃ tattha vaṭṭetvā sugandhā bhavissāmi, tato rañño piṭṭhiyaṃ nipajjitvā ramissāmā”ti āha. Rājā tampi saddaṃ sutvā hasi. Devīpi “kiṃ nu kho disvā hasī”ti puna cintesi. Puna rañño sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjantassa ekaṃ bhattasitthaṃ bhūmiyaṃ pati. Kipillikā “rājakule bhattasakaṭaṃ bhaggaṃ, bhattaṃ bhuñjathā”ti viravi. Taṃ sutvā rājā punapi hasi. Devī suvaṇṇakaṭacchuṃ gahetvā rājānaṃ parivisantī “maṃ nu kho disvā rājā hasatī”ti vitakkesi.

One day, while he was sitting on the great terrace and eating sweetmeats with honey and molasses, a drop of honey, a drop of molasses, and a piece of cake fell to the ground. An ant, seeing this, went about crying out, "The king’s honey pot on the great terrace has broken, the molasses cart and the cake cart have overturned—come and eat the honey, molasses, and cake!" Hearing its cry, the king laughed. The queen, standing near the king, thought, "What could the king have seen that made him laugh?" After he had eaten, bathed, and was sitting on his couch, a male fly said to his mate, "Come, my dear, let us enjoy sensual pleasure." But she replied, "Bear with me for a moment, my lord. Soon they will bring the king’s perfumes. When he anoints himself, perfume powder will fall at his feet. I will roll in it and become fragrant. Then we shall lie on the king’s back and enjoy ourselves." Hearing this sound too, the king laughed. The queen again thought, "What did he see that made him laugh?" Later, while the king was eating his evening meal, a morsel of rice fell to the ground. An ant cried out, "The rice cart in the royal court is broken—come and eat the rice!" Hearing this, the king laughed again. The queen, holding a golden ladle and serving the king, wondered, "Is the king laughing at me?"

Sā raññā saddhiṃ sayanaṃ āruyha nipajjanakāle “kiṃkāraṇā deva, hasī”ti pucchi. So “kiṃ te mama hasitakāraṇenā”ti vatvā punappunaṃ nibaddho kathesi. Atha naṃ sā “tumhākaṃ jānanamantaṃ mayhaṃ dethā”ti vatvā “na sakkā dātu”nti paṭikkhittāpi punappunaṃ nibandhi[V 3.0244]. Rājā “sacāhaṃ imaṃ mantaṃ tuyhaṃ dassāmi, marissāmī”ti āha. “Marantopi mayhaṃ dehi, devā”ti. Rājā mātugāmavasiko hutvā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā “imissā mantaṃ datvā aggiṃ pavisissāmī”ti rathena uyyānaṃ pāyāsi.

When she had ascended the bed with the king and was lying down, she asked, "For what reason, my lord, did you laugh?" He replied, "What is the reason for my laughter to you?" But being pressed repeatedly, he spoke. Then she said, "Give me the spell you know," but though he refused, saying, "It cannot be given," she persisted again and again. The king said, "If I give you this spell, I will die." "Even if you die, my lord, give it to me," she insisted. The king, being under the sway of a woman, agreed, saying, "Very well," and thinking, "After giving her the spell, I will enter the fire," he set out for the park by chariot.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko lokaṃ olokento imaṃ kāraṇaṃ disvā “ayaṃ bālarājā mātugāmaṃ nissāya ‘aggiṃ pavisissāmī’ti gacchati, jīvitamassa dassāmī”ti sujaṃ asurakaññaṃ ādāya bārāṇasiṃ āgantvā taṃ ajikaṃ [P 3.0278] katvā attanā ajo hutvā “mahājano mā passatū”ti adhiṭṭhāya rañño rathassa purato ahosi. Taṃ rājā ceva rathe yuttasindhavā ca passanti, añño koci na passati. Ajo kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ rathapurato ajikāya saddhiṃ methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevanto viya [M 3.0262] ahosi. Tameko rathe yuttasindhavo disvā “samma ajarāja, mayaṃ pubbe ‘ajā kira bālā ahirikā’ti assumha, na ca taṃ passimha, tvaṃ pana raho paṭicchannaṭṭhāne kattabbaṃ anācāraṃ amhākaṃ ettakānaṃ passantānaññeva karosi, na lajjasi, taṃ no pubbe sutaṃ iminā diṭṭhena sametī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that moment, Sakka, surveying the world, saw this situation and thought, "This foolish king, on account of a woman, is going to enter the fire. I shall grant him his life." Taking Sujā, the Asura maiden, he came to Bārāṇasī, transformed her into a she-goat and himself into a he-goat. Having resolved, "Let the people not see me," he stood before the king's chariot. Only the king and the thoroughbred horses yoked to the chariot saw them; no one else did. The he-goat, in order to initiate a conversation, appeared to be engaging in sexual intercourse with the she-goat before the chariot. One of the thoroughbreds yoked to the chariot, seeing this, said, "Friend, king of goats, we have previously heard that 'goats are foolish and shameless,' but we had not seen it. Yet you perform an improper act, which ought to be done in a secret, concealed place, right before our very eyes. You feel no shame. What we heard before now matches what we have seen." And so, he spoke the first verse:

77.

77.

“Saccaṃ kirevamāhaṃsu, vastaṃ bāloti paṇḍitā;

Passa bālo rahokammaṃ, āvikubbaṃ na bujjhatī”ti.

"Truly, the wise have spoken thus: 'The goat is a fool'; See the fool, making public a secret act, he does not understand."

Tattha vastanti ajaṃ. Paṇḍitāti ñāṇasampannā taṃ bāloti vadanti, saccaṃ kira vadanti. Passāti ālapanaṃ, passathāhi attho. Na bujjhatīti evaṃ kātuṃ ayuttanti na jānāti.

Therein, 'vasta' means a goat. 'The wise' means those endowed with knowledge; they call him a fool—truly, they speak the truth. 'Passa' (see) is a term of address; the meaning is 'behold!' 'Does not understand' means he does not know that it is improper to act thus.

Taṃ sutvā ajo dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the goat spoke two verses:

78.

78.

“Tvaṃ khopi samma bālosi, kharaputta vijānahi;

Rajjuyā hi parikkhitto, vaṅkoṭṭho ohitomukho.

"You too, friend, are a fool, O son of a donkey, understand this; For you are encircled by a rope, with a crooked lip and a downcast face."

79.

79.

“Aparampi samma te bālyaṃ, yo mutto na palāyasi;

So ca bālataro samma, yaṃ tvaṃ vahati senaka”nti.

"And another foolishness of yours, friend, is that when freed, you do not flee; and even more foolish than that, friend, is the Senaka whom you carry."

Tattha tvaṃ khopi sammāti samma sindhava mayāpi kho tvaṃ bālataro. Kharaputtāti so kira gadrabhassa jātako, tena taṃ evamāha. Vijānahīti ahameva bāloti evaṃ jānāhi. Parikkhittoti [V 3.0245] yugena saddhiṃ gīvāya parikkhitto. Vaṅkoṭṭhoti vaṅkaoṭṭho. Ohitomukhoti mukhabandhanena pihitamukho. Yo mutto na palāyasīti yo tvaṃ rathato mutto samāno muttakāle palāyitvā araññaṃ na pavisasi, taṃ te apalāyanaṃ aparampi bālyaṃ[P 3.0279], so ca bālataroti yaṃ tvaṃ senakaṃ vahasi, so senako tayāpi bālataro.

Therein, 'You too, friend' means: O thoroughbred, you are even more foolish than I. 'Kharaputta' (son of a donkey) means: it is said he was born of a donkey; hence, he addressed him thus. 'Understand this' means: know that you are a fool. 'Enclosed' means: enclosed at the neck together with the yoke. 'Crooked-lipped' means: having a crooked lip. 'With face cast down' means: his face covered by a muzzle. 'Who, being freed, does not flee' means: you, who, when freed from the chariot, do not flee into the forest; that not fleeing of yours is a further foolishness. 'And he is even more foolish' means: King Senaka, whom you carry, is even more foolish than you.

Rājā tesaṃ ubhinnampi kathaṃ jānāti, tasmā taṃ suṇanto saṇikaṃ rathaṃ pesesi. Sindhavopi tassa kathaṃ sutvā puna catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

The king understood the conversation of both of them, so while listening to it, he had the chariot driven slowly. The thoroughbred, upon hearing the goat's words, then spoke the fourth verse:

80.

80.

“Yaṃ nu samma ahaṃ bālo, ajarāja vijānahi;

Atha kena senako bālo, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

“That I am a fool, friend, O king of goats, please understand. But for what reason is Senaka a fool? Explain that to me, as you are asked.”

Tattha [M 3.0263] yanti karaṇatthe paccattavacanaṃ. Nūti anussavatthe nipāto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – samma ajarāja, yena tāva tiracchānagatattena kāraṇena ahaṃ bālo, taṃ tvaṃ kāraṇaṃ jānāhi, sakkā etaṃ tayā ñātuṃ, ahañhi tiracchānagatattāva bālo, tasmā maṃ kharaputtātiādīni vadanto suṭṭhu vadasi, ayaṃ pana senako rājā kena kāraṇena bālo, taṃ me kāraṇaṃ pucchito akkhāhīti.

Herein, 'yaṃ' is a singular term in the instrumental sense. 'Nū' is a particle in the sense of what has been heard. This is what is meant: 'Friend, king of goats, you know the reason why I am a fool, which is my state of being an animal. This is knowable by you. Indeed, it is because of my animal birth that I am a fool. Therefore, in calling me "son of a donkey" and so on, you speak rightly. But this King Senaka, for what reason is he a fool? Since you have been asked, declare that reason to me.'

Taṃ sutvā ajo ācikkhanto pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard that, the goat-king, explaining, spoke the fifth verse:

81.

81.

“Uttamatthaṃ labhitvāna, bhariyāya yo padassati;

Tena jahissatattānaṃ, sā cevassa na hessatī”ti.

“Having attained the highest good, whoever should give it to his wife, by that he will lose his life, and she will not belong to him.”

Tattha uttamatthanti sabbarutajānanamantaṃ. Tenāti tassā mantappadānasaṅkhātena kāraṇena taṃ datvā aggiṃ pavisanto attānañca jahissati, sā cassa bhariyā na bhavissati, tasmā esa tayāpi bālataro, yo laddhaṃ yasaṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkotīti.

Herein, 'the highest good' means the mantra for knowing all sounds. 'By that' means by the cause designated as the giving of that mantra; having given it and entering the fire, he will abandon himself, and she will not be his wife. Therefore, he is even more foolish than you, one who cannot protect the glory he has gained.

Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “ajarāja, amhākaṃ sotthiṃ karontopi tvaññeva karissasi, kathehi tāva no kattabbayuttaka”nti āha. Atha naṃ ajarājā “mahārāja, imesaṃ sattānaṃ attanā añño piyataro nāma natthi, ekaṃ piyabhaṇḍaṃ nissāya [P 3.0280] attānaṃ nāsetuṃ laddhayasaṃ pahātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, hearing his words, said, "O king of goats, if you were to bring about our welfare, you alone would do it. Tell us now what is fitting to be done." Then the king of goats said, "Great king, for these beings there is nothing dearer than themselves. It is not fitting to destroy oneself relying on a beloved object, or to relinquish the glory that has been attained," and he spoke the sixth verse:

82.

82.

“Na [V 3.0246] ve piyammeti janinda tādiso, attaṃ niraṃkatvā piyāni sevati;

Attāva seyyo paramā ca seyyo, labbhā piyā ocitatthena pacchā”ti.

“Indeed, O king, one like you does not pursue beloved things having discarded the self. The self is indeed better, and supremely better; beloved ones may be obtained later by one who has accumulated wealth.”

Tattha piyammeti piyaṃ me, ayameva vā pāṭho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – janinda, tādiso tumhādiso yasamahatte ṭhito puggalo ekaṃ piyabhaṇḍaṃ nissāya “idaṃ piyaṃ me”ti attaṃ niraṃkatvā attānaṃ chaḍḍetvā tāni piyāni na sevateva. Kiṃkāraṇā? Attāva seyyo paramā ca seyyoti, yasmā sataguṇena sahassaguṇena attāva seyyo varo [M 3.0264] uttamo, paramā ca seyyo, paramā uttamāpi aññasmā piyabhaṇḍāti attho. Ettha hi ca-kāro pi-kāratthe nipātoti daṭṭhabbo. Labbhā piyā ocitatthena pacchāti ocitatthena vaḍḍhitatthena yasasampannena purisena pacchā piyā nāma sakkā laddhuṃ, na tassā kāraṇā attā nāsetabboti.

Herein, 'piyammeti' means 'dear to me'; or this is simply the reading. This is what is meant: O king, such a person as you, established in great glory, relying on a single beloved object and thinking 'this is dear to me,' does not pursue those beloved things having discarded and abandoned the self. Why? 'Because the self is indeed better, and supremely better'—meaning, because the self is a hundredfold, a thousandfold better, excellent, and superior. 'And supremely better' means supremely excellent, even more so than any other beloved object. Here, the particle 'ca' should be understood as having the sense of the particle 'pi' (also). 'Beloved ones can be obtained later by one who has accumulated wealth' means that beloved ones can indeed be obtained later by a person endowed with glory that has been accumulated and increased; the self should not be destroyed for that reason.

Evaṃ mahāsatto rañño ovādaṃ adāsi. Rājā tussitvā “ajarāja, kuto āgatosī”ti pucchi. Sakko ahaṃ, mahārāja, tava anukampāya taṃ maraṇā mocetuṃ āgatomhīti. Devarāja, ahaṃ etissā “mantaṃ dassāmī”ti avacaṃ, idāni “kiṃ karomī”ti? “Mahārāja, tumhākaṃ ubhinnampi vināsena kiccaṃ natthi, ‘sippassa upacāro’ti vatvā etaṃ katipaye pahāre paharāpehi, iminā upāyena na gaṇhissatī”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Mahāsatto rañño ovādaṃ datvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Rājā uyyānaṃ gantvā deviṃ pakkosāpetvā āha “gaṇhissasi bhadde, manta”nti? “Āma, devā”ti. “Tena hi upacāraṃ karomī”ti. “Ko upacāro”ti? “Piṭṭhiyaṃ pahārasate [P 3.0281] pavattamāne saddaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti. Sā mantalobhena “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Rājā coraghātake pakkosāpetvā kasā gāhāpetvā ubhosu passesu paharāpesi. Sā dve tayo pahāre adhivāsetvā tato paraṃ “na me mantena attho”ti ravi. Atha naṃ rājā “tvaṃ maṃ māretvā mantaṃ gaṇhitukāmāsī”ti piṭṭhiyaṃ niccammaṃ kāretvā vissajjāpesi. Sā tato paṭṭhāya puna kathetuṃ nāsakkhi.

Thus, the Great Being gave advice to the king. The king, pleased, asked, "O king of goats, where have you come from?" "I am Sakka, O great king; I have come out of compassion for you to free you from the danger of death." "O king of gods, I told her, 'I will give the mantra.' Now, what should I do?" "Great king, there is no need for the destruction of both of you. Saying, 'This is the preliminary rite for the art,' have that queen struck with a few blows. By this means, she will not take it." The king agreed, saying, "Very well." The Great Being, having given advice to the king, returned to his own place. The king went to the park, summoned the queen, and said, "Will you take the mantra, good lady?" "Yes, lord." "Then I will perform the preliminary rite." "What is the preliminary rite?" "While a hundred blows are being inflicted on your back, it is not proper to make a sound." She, greedy for the mantra, agreed, saying, "Very well." The king summoned the executioners, had them take whips, and ordered them to strike her on both sides. She endured two or three blows, then cried out, "I have no need for the mantra!" Then the king, saying, "You wished to kill me and take the mantra," had her back flayed and sent her away. From then on, she was unable to speak of it again.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā rājā ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu ahosi, devī purāṇadutiyikā, asso sāriputto, sakko pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the Jataka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the king was the discontented monk, the queen was the former wife, the horse was Sariputta, and Sakka was I myself.

Kharaputtajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kharaputta Jataka, the First.

[387] 2. Sūcijātakavaṇṇanā

[387] 2. The Commentary on the Suci Jataka

Akakkasaṃ [V 3.0247][M 3.0265] apharusanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto paññāpāramiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu mahāumaṅgajātake (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana satthā bhikkhū āmantetvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato paññavā upāyakusaloyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Not harsh, not rough”—This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Perfection of Wisdom. The story will become clear in the Maha-ummagga Jataka (Ja. 2.22.590 ff.). Then the Teacher addressed the monks, saying, "Not only now, monks, but also in the past the Tathagata was wise and skilled in means." Having said this, he brought forward the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe kammārakule nibbattitvā vayappatto pariyodātasippo ahosi. Mātāpitaro panassa daliddā, tesaṃ gāmato avidūre añño sahassakuṭiko kammāragāmo. Tattha kammārasahassajeṭṭhako kammāro rājavallabho aḍḍho mahaddhano, tassekā dhītā ahosi uttamarūpadharā devaccharāpaṭibhāgā janapadakalyāṇilakkhaṇehi samannāgatā. Sāmantagāmesu manussā vāsipharasuphālapācanādikārāpanatthāya taṃ gāmaṃ gantvā yebhuyyena taṃ kumārikaṃ passanti, te attano attano gāmaṃ gantvā nisinnaṭṭhānādīsu tassā rūpaṃ [P 3.0282] vaṇṇenti. Bodhisatto taṃ sutvā savanasaṃsaggena bajjhitvā “pādaparicārikaṃ naṃ karissāmī”ti uttamajātikaṃ ayaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ sukhumaṃ ghanaṃ sūciṃ katvā pāse vijjhitvā udake uppilāpetvā aparampi tathārūpameva tassā kosakaṃ katvā pāse vijjhi. Iminā niyāmena tassā satta kosake akāsi, “kathaṃ akāsī”ti na vattabbaṃ. Bodhisattānañhi ñāṇamahantatāya karaṇaṃ samijjhatiyeva. So taṃ sūciṃ nāḷikāya pakkhipitvā ovaṭṭikāya katvā taṃ gāmaṃ gantvā kammārajeṭṭhakassa vasanavīthiṃ pucchitvā tattha gantvā dvāre ṭhatvā “ko mama hatthato evarūpaṃ nāma sūciṃ mūlena kiṇituṃ icchatī”ti sūciṃ vaṇṇento jeṭṭhakakammārassa gharadvārasamīpe ṭhatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Varanasi, the Bodhisatta was born into a blacksmith family in the Kasi country. When he came of age, he became consummately skilled in his craft. His parents, however, were poor. Not far from their village was another blacksmith village of a thousand households. There, the chief of the thousand blacksmiths was a favorite of the king, rich and of great wealth. He had a daughter of surpassing beauty, like a celestial nymph, endowed with the marks of a 'beauty of the land.' People from neighboring villages, going to that village to have adzes, axes, ploughshares, goads, and so on made, would usually see that maiden. Returning to their own villages, they would praise her beauty in the places where they sat and so forth. Hearing this, the Bodhisatta was captivated by what he heard and thought, "I will make her my wife." Taking some iron of the highest quality, he fashioned a delicate, solid needle, pierced its eye, and made it float in water. Then he made another similar one for its case and pierced its eye. In this manner, he made seven cases for it—how he made them should not be questioned. For the Bodhisattas, due to the greatness of their wisdom, their endeavors always succeed. He placed that needle in a tube, tucked it into the fold of his garment, and went to that village. Asking for the chief blacksmith's street, he went there, stood at the door and called out, "Who wishes to buy such a needle from my hand for a price?" Praising the needle, he stood near the door of the chief blacksmith's house and spoke the first verse:

83.

83.

“Akakkasaṃ apharusaṃ, kharadhotaṃ supāsiyaṃ;

Sukhumaṃ tikhiṇaggañca, ko sūciṃ ketumicchatī”ti.

“Not rough, not coarse, scoured with stone, with a good eye, fine and sharp-tipped—who wishes to buy a needle?”

Tassattho – mama paṭalassa vā tilakassa vā odhino vā abhāvena akakkasaṃ, sumaṭṭhatāya apharusaṃ, kharena pāsāṇena dhotattā kharadhotaṃ, sundarena suviddhena pāsena samannāgatattā supāsiyaṃ[M 3.0266], saṇhatāya sukhumaṃ, aggassa tikhiṇatāya tikhiṇaggaṃ sūciṃ mama hatthato mūlaṃ datvā ko kiṇituṃ icchatīti.

The meaning is: Not rough due to the absence of any film, blemish, or covering; not coarse due to its smoothness; well-polished because it has been scoured with a hard stone; well-eyed because it is endowed with a beautiful and well-pierced eye; fine due to its delicacy; and sharp-tipped due to the sharpness of its point. Who wishes to buy this needle from my hand by paying the price?

Evañca [V 3.0248] pana vatvā punapi taṃ vaṇṇento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

And having said this, praising it further, he spoke the second verse:

84.

84.

“Sumajjañca supāsañca, anupubbaṃ suvaṭṭitaṃ;

Ghanaghātimaṃ paṭithaddhaṃ, ko sūciṃ ketumicchatī”ti.

“Well-polished and well-eyed, gradually tapered and well-rounded, solidly hammered and firm—who wishes to buy a needle?”

Tattha sumajjañcāti kuruvindakacuṇṇena suṭṭhu majjitaṃ. Supāsañcāti saṇhena pāsavedhakena viddhattā sundarapāsaṃ. Ghanaghātimanti yā ghātiyamānā adhikaraṇiṃ anupavisati, ayaṃ “ghanaghātimā”ti vuccati, tādisinti attho. Paṭithaddhanti thaddhaṃ amudukaṃ.

Therein, 'well-polished' means thoroughly polished with kuruvinda powder. 'Well-eyed' means having a beautiful eye because of being pierced with a fine eye-piercer. 'Solidly hammered' refers to that which, when being hammered, pierces the anvil; such is the meaning. 'Firm' means hard and not soft.

Tasmiṃ [P 3.0283] khaṇe sā kumārikā bhuttapātarāsaṃ pitaraṃ darathapaṭippassambhanatthaṃ cūḷasayane nipannaṃ tālavaṇṭena bījayamānā bodhisattassa madhurasaddaṃ sutvā allamaṃsapiṇḍena hadaye pahaṭā viya ghaṭasahassena nibbāpitadarathā viya hutvā “ko nu kho esa atimadhurena saddena kammārānaṃ vasanagāme sūciṃ vikkiṇāti, kena nu kho kammena āgato, jānissāmi na”nti tālavaṇṭaṃ ṭhapetvā gehā nikkhamma bahiāḷindake ṭhatvā tena saddhiṃ kathesi. Bodhisattānañhi patthitaṃ nāma samijjhati, so hi tassāyevatthāya taṃ gāmaṃ āgato. Sā ca tena saddhiṃ kathentī “māṇava, sakalaraṭṭhavāsino sūciādīnaṃ atthāya imaṃ gāmaṃ āgacchanti, tvaṃ bālatāya kammāragāme sūciṃ vikkiṇituṃ icchasi, sacepi divasaṃ sūciyā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsissasi, na te koci hatthato sūciṃ gaṇhissati, sace tvaṃ mūlaṃ laddhuṃ icchasi, aññaṃ gāmaṃ yāhī”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

At that moment, the young girl, having finished her morning meal, was fanning her father with a palm-leaf fan as he lay on a small bed to relieve his fatigue. Hearing the Bodhisatta’s sweet voice, she felt as if struck in the heart by a lump of fresh meat, and as if her distress were extinguished by a thousand jars of water. Thinking, 'Who is this selling needles in the smiths' village with such an exceedingly sweet voice? For what purpose has he come? I shall find out,' she set down the palm-leaf fan, left the house, and standing on the outer porch, she spoke with him. For the aspirations of Bodhisattas are indeed fulfilled; he had come to that village for her sake alone. Conversing with him, she said: 'Young man, people from the whole country come to this village for needles and such. You, in your folly, wish to sell a needle in the smiths' village! Even if you were to praise the qualities of the needle all day long, no one would buy it from your hand. If you wish to receive a price, go to another village.' Having said this, she spoke two verses:

84.

84.

“Itodāni patāyanti, sūciyo baḷisāni ca;

Koyaṃ kammāragāmasmiṃ, sūciṃ vikketumicchati.

“From here now, needles and fishhooks go out; who is this in the smiths' village who wishes to sell a needle?”

85.

85.

“Ito satthāni gacchanti, kammantā vividhā puthū;

Koyaṃ kammāragāmasmiṃ, sūciṃ vikketumicchatī”ti.

“From here caravans go forth, and various many crafts; who is this in the smiths' village who wishes to sell a needle?”

Tattha itodānīti imasmiṃ raṭṭhe idāni sūciyo ca baḷisāni ca aññāni ca upakaraṇāni imamhā kammāragāmā patāyanti nikkhamanti, taṃ taṃ disaṃ pattharantā niggacchanti. Koyanti evaṃ sante ko ayaṃ imasmiṃ kammāragāme [M 3.0267] sūciṃ vikkiṇituṃ icchati. Satthānīti bārāṇasiṃ [V 3.0249] gacchantāni nānappakārāni satthāni itova gacchanti. Vividhā puthūti nānappakārā bahū kammantāpi sakalaraṭṭhavāsīnaṃ ito gahitaupakaraṇeheva pavattanti.

Therein, 'from here now' means that in this country, at this time, needles, fishhooks, and other implements go out—issue forth—from this smiths' village, spreading in every direction. 'Who is this' means, this being the case, who is this who wishes to sell a needle in this smiths' village? 'Caravans' means various kinds of caravans going to Bārāṇasī go from here. 'Various many' means that many diverse crafts of all the inhabitants of the country proceed by means of the tools obtained from here.

Bodhisatto tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “bhadde, tvaṃ ajānantī aññāṇena evaṃ vadesī”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

The Bodhisatta, hearing her words, said, 'Good lady, you speak thus out of ignorance, not knowing,' and spoke these two verses:

86.

86.

“Sūciṃ [P 3.0284] kammāragāmasmiṃ, vikketabbā pajānatā;

Ācariyāva jānanti, kammaṃ sukatadukkaṭaṃ.

“A needle should be sold in the smiths' village by one who knows; for only the masters know the work, whether well-made or ill-made.”

87.

87.

“Imañce te pitā bhadde, sūciṃ jaññā mayā kataṃ;

Tayā ca maṃ nimanteyya, yañcatthaññaṃ ghare dhana”nti.

“Good lady, if your father knew this needle was made by me, he would invite me with you and whatever other wealth is in the house.”

Tattha sūcinti vibhattivipallāso kato. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sūci nāma pajānatā paṇḍitena purisena kammāragāmasmiṃyeva vikketabbā. Kiṃkāraṇā? Ācariyāva jānanti, kammaṃ sukatadukkaṭanti, tassa tassa sippassa ācariyāva tasmiṃ tasmiṃ sippe sukatadukkaṭakammaṃ jānanti, svāhaṃ kammārakammaṃ ajānantānaṃ gahapatikānaṃ gāmaṃ gantvā mama sūciyā sukatadukkaṭabhāvaṃ kathaṃ jānāpessāmi, imasmiṃ pana gāme mama balaṃ jānāpessāmīti. Evaṃ bodhisatto imāya gāthāya attano balaṃ vaṇṇesi.

Therein, regarding 'sūciṃ', there is an interchange of cases. This is what is said: A needle should be sold by a knowing, wise person in the smiths' village itself. For what reason? 'Only the masters know the work, whether well-made or ill-made'; the masters of each craft know the well-made or ill-made work in that craft. 'If I go to a village of householders who do not know the smith's craft, how shall I make them know whether my needle is well-made or ill-made? But in this village, I shall make my skill known.' Thus, with this verse, the Bodhisatta praised his own skill.

Tayā ca maṃ nimanteyyāti bhadde sace tava pitā imaṃ mayā kataṃ sūciṃ “īdisā vā esā, evaṃ vā katā”ti jāneyya, “imaṃ me dhītaraṃ tava pādaparicārikaṃ dammi, gaṇhāhi na”nti evaṃ tayā ca maṃ nimanteyya. Yañcatthaññaṃ ghare dhananti yañca aññaṃ saviññāṇakaṃ vā aviññāṇakaṃ vā ghare dhanaṃ atthi, tena maṃ nimanteyya. “Yañcassañña”ntipi pāṭho, yañca assa ghare aññaṃ dhanaṃ atthīti attho.

'He would invite me with you' means: Good lady, if your father knew this needle made by me, saying, 'It is of such a kind, or it is made thus,' he would invite me with you, saying, 'I give you this daughter of mine as your attendant; take her.' 'And whatever other wealth is in the house' means he would invite me with whatever other wealth, animate or inanimate, is in the house. There is also a reading 'yañcassaññaṃ', which means 'whatever other wealth he has in the house'.

Kammārajeṭṭhako sabbaṃ tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “ammā”ti dhītaraṃ pakkositvā “kena saddhiṃ sallapasī”ti pucchi. Tāta, eko puriso sūciṃ vikkiṇāti, tena saddhiṃ sallapemīti. “Tena hi pakkosāhi na”nti. Sā gantvā pakkosi. Bodhisatto gehaṃ pavisitvā kammārajeṭṭhakaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ [M 3.0268] aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ so “kataragāmavāsikosī”ti pucchi. “Ahaṃ asukagāmavāsikomhi asukakammārassa putto”ti. “Kasmā idhāgatosī”ti. “Sūcivikkayatthāyā”ti[V 3.0250]. “Āhara, sūciṃ te passāmā”ti[P 3.0285]. Bodhisatto attano guṇaṃ sabbesaṃ majjhe pakāsetukāmo “nanu ekakānaṃ olokitato sabbesaṃ majjhe oloketuṃ varatara”nti āha. So “sādhu, tātā”ti sabbe kammāre sannipātāpetvā tehi parivuto “āhara, tāta, mayaṃ passāma te sūci”nti āha. “Ācariya, ekaṃ adhikaraṇiñca udakapūrañca kaṃsathālaṃ āharāpethā”ti. So āharāpesi. Bodhisatto ovaṭṭikato sūcināḷikaṃ nīharitvā adāsi. Kammārajeṭṭhako tato sūciṃ nīharitvā “tāta, ayaṃ sūcī”ti pucchi. “Nāyaṃ sūci, kosako eso”ti. So upadhārento neva antaṃ, na koṭiṃ addasa. Bodhisatto āharāpetvā nakhena kosakaṃ apanetvā “ayaṃ sūci, ayaṃ kosako”ti mahājanassa dassetvā sūciṃ ācariyassa hatthe, kosakaṃ pādamūle ṭhapesi. Puna tena “ayaṃ maññe sūcī”ti vutto “ayampi sūcikosakoyevā”ti vatvā nakhena paharanto paṭipāṭiyā cha sūcikosake kammārajeṭṭhakassa pādamūle ṭhapetvā “ayaṃ sūcī”ti tassa hatthe ṭhapesi. Kammārasahassāni aṅguliyo phoṭesuṃ, celukkhepā pavattiṃsu.

The chief smith, having heard their entire conversation, called to his daughter, 'My dear,' and asked, 'With whom are you speaking?' 'Father, a man is selling a needle; I am speaking with him.' 'Then call him here.' She went and called him. The Bodhisatta entered the house, paid his respects to the chief smith, and stood to one side. Then the chief smith asked him, 'Of which village are you a resident?' 'I am a resident of such-and-such a village, the son of such-and-such a smith.' 'Why have you come here?' 'For the purpose of selling a needle.' 'Bring it, let us see your needle.' The Bodhisatta, wishing to display his skill in the midst of everyone, said, 'Is it not better to inspect it in the midst of everyone than for individuals to inspect it?' The chief smith said, 'Very well, my dear,' and having gathered all the smiths, surrounded by them he said, 'Bring it, my dear, let us see your needle.' The Bodhisatta said, 'Master, have an anvil and a bronze bowl filled with water brought.' He had them brought. The Bodhisatta took the needle-case from his pouch and gave it to him. The chief smith took a needle from it and asked, 'My dear, is this the needle?' 'That is not the needle; that is its case.' Examining it, he could see neither an end nor a tip. The Bodhisatta had it brought to him, removed the case with his fingernail, and showing it to the great crowd, said, 'This is the needle, this is the case.' He placed the needle in the master's hand and the case at his feet. Again, when the chief smith said, 'This, I think, is the needle,' the Bodhisatta replied, 'This too is just a needle-case,' and striking it with his fingernail, he placed six needle-cases in succession at the chief smith's feet, and saying, 'This is the needle,' he placed it in his hand. The thousands of smiths snapped their fingers, and a waving of cloths ensued.

Atha naṃ kammārajeṭṭhako “tāta, imāya sūciyā kiṃ bala”nti pucchi. “Ācariya balavatā purisena adhikaraṇiṃ ukkhipāpetvā adhikaraṇiyā heṭṭhā udakapātiṃ ṭhapāpetvā adhikaraṇiyā majjhe imaṃ sūciṃ paharathā”ti. So tathā kāretvā adhikaraṇiyā majjhe sūciṃ aggena pahari. Sā adhikaraṇiṃ vinivijjhitvā udakapiṭṭhe kesaggamattampi uddhaṃ vā adho vā ahutvā tiriyaṃ patiṭṭhāsi. Sabbe kammārā “amhehi ettakaṃ kālaṃ ‘kammārā nāma edisā hontī’ti sutivasenapi na sutapubba”nti aṅguliyo phoṭetvā celukkhepasahassaṃ pavattayiṃsu[P 3.0286]. Kammārajeṭṭhako dhītaraṃ pakkositvā tasmiññeva parisamajjhe “ayaṃ kumārikā tuyhameva anucchavikā”ti udakaṃ pātetvā adāsi. So aparabhāge kammārajeṭṭhakassa accayena tasmiṃ gāme kammārajeṭṭhako ahosi.

Then the chief smith asked him, 'Dear one, what is the power of this needle?' 'Master, have a strong man lift an anvil, place a water vessel beneath the anvil, and then strike this needle into the middle of the anvil.' He had this done and struck the needle, point-first, into the middle of the anvil. It pierced through the anvil and, without rising or sinking even a hair’s breadth, stood horizontally on the surface of the water. All the smiths snapped their fingers and waved a thousand cloths, exclaiming, 'For all this time, we have never before heard, even by rumor, that smiths could be of such a kind!' The chief smith called his daughter and, in the midst of that very assembly, poured water and gave her to him, saying, 'This maiden is a suitable match for you.' Later, after the passing of the chief smith, he became the chief smith in that village.

Satthā [M 3.0269] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kammārajeṭṭhakassa dhītā rāhulamātā ahosi, paṇḍitakammāraputto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the birth story: 'At that time, the daughter of the chief smith was Rāhula's mother, and the wise smith's son was none other than myself.'

Sūcijātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The explanation of the Sūci Jātaka, the second.

[388] 3. Tuṇḍilajātakavaṇṇanā

[388] 3. The Explanation of the Tuṇḍila Jātaka

Navachannaketi [V 3.0251] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ maraṇabhīrukaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthivāsī kulaputto buddhasāsane pabbajitvā maraṇabhīruko ahosi, appamattakampi sākhācalanaṃ daṇḍakapatanaṃ sakuṇacatuppadasaddaṃ vā aññaṃ vā tathārūpaṃ sutvā maraṇabhayatajjito hutvā kucchiyaṃ viddhasaso viya kampanto vicari. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asuko kira bhikkhu maraṇabhīruko appamattakampi saddaṃ sutvā vikampamāno palāyati, imesañca sattānaṃ maraṇameva dhuvaṃ, jīvitaṃ addhuvaṃ, nanu tadeva yoniso manasi kātabba”nti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte taṃ bhikkhuṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu maraṇabhīruko”ti vatvā “āma, bhante”ti tena paṭiññāto “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa maraṇabhīrukoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This was told by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who was afraid of death. It seems that this clansman from Sāvatthī had gone forth into the Buddha's dispensation but was terrified of death. Hearing even the slightest movement of a branch, the fall of a stick, the sound of a bird or a four-legged creature, or anything similar, he would wander about trembling, seized by the fear of death, like a hare pierced in the belly. The monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, it seems that a certain monk is so afraid of death that he trembles and flees upon hearing even the slightest sound. Yet for these beings, death is certain and life is uncertain. Should not that very fact be wisely considered?' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'For what discussion are you now gathered here, monks?' When they told him, he had that monk summoned and asked, 'Is it true, monk, that you are afraid of death?' 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' he admitted. The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now; in the past, too, he was afraid of death,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sūkariyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Sūkarī pariṇatagabbhā dve putte vijāyi. Sā ekadivasaṃ te gahetvā ekasmiṃ āvāṭe nipajji. Athekā bārāṇasidvāragāmavāsinī mahallikā kappāsakhettato pacchipuṇṇaṃ kappāsaṃ ādāya [P 3.0287] yaṭṭhiyā bhūmiṃ ākoṭentī āgacchi. Sūkarī taṃ saddaṃ sutvā maraṇabhayena puttake chaḍḍetvā palāyi. Mahallikā sūkarapotake disvā puttasaññaṃ paṭilabhitvā pacchiyaṃ pakkhipitvā gharaṃ netvā jeṭṭhakassa mahātuṇḍilo, kaniṭṭhassa cūḷatuṇḍiloti nāmaṃ karitvā te puttake viya posesi. Te aparabhāge vaḍḍhitvā thūlasarīrā [M 3.0270] ahesuṃ. Mahallikā “ime no mūlena dehī”ti vuccamānāpi “puttā me”ti vatvā kassaci na deti. Athekasmiṃ chaṇakāle dhuttā suraṃ pivantā maṃse khīṇe “kuto nu kho maṃsaṃ labhissāmā”ti vīmaṃsantā mahallikāya gehe sūkarānaṃ atthibhāvaṃ ñatvā mūlaṃ gahetvā tattha gantvā “amma, mūlaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ no sūkaraṃ dehī”ti āhaṃsu. Sā “alaṃ, tātā, puttā me ete, puttaṃ nāma maṃsaṃ khādanatthāya kiṇantānaṃ dadantā nāma natthī”ti paṭikkhipi. Dhuttā “amma, manussānaṃ sūkarā nāma puttā na honti, dehi no”ti punappunaṃ yācantāpi alabhitvā mahallikaṃ suraṃ pāyetvā mattakāle “amma, sūkarehi kiṃ karissasi, mūlaṃ gahetvā paribbayaṃ karohī”ti tassā hatthe kahāpaṇe ṭhapayiṃsu.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of a sow. The sow, her pregnancy at full term, gave birth to two sons. One day, she took them and lay down in a hollow. Then, an old woman who lived in a village at a gate of Bārāṇasī came from a cotton field, carrying a basket full of cotton and striking the ground with her staff. Hearing the sound, the sow, fearing death, abandoned her young and fled. The old woman, seeing the piglets, recognized them as her sons, placed them in her basket, took them home, and named the elder Mahātuṇḍila and the younger Cūḷatuṇḍila. She raised them as if they were her own sons. In time, they grew and became large-bodied. Though people would say, “Give these to us for a price,” the old woman would reply, “They are my sons,” and would not give them to anyone. Then, during a certain festival, some rogues were drinking liquor, and when their meat ran out, they wondered, “Where can we get some meat?” Learning that there were pigs in the old woman’s house, they took some money, went there, and said, “Mother, take this money and give us one of your pigs.” She refused, saying, “Enough, sirs! These are my sons. There is no such thing as giving away a son to those who would buy him for the purpose of eating his meat.” The rogues replied, “Mother, pigs are not the sons of humans. Give them to us.” Though they begged repeatedly, they could not get one. So, they plied her with liquor until she was intoxicated. Then they said, “Mother, what will you do with the pigs? Take the money and use it for your expenses,” and placed the coins in her hand.

Sā kahāpaṇe gahetvā “tātā, mahātuṇḍilaṃ dātuṃ na sakkomi. Cūḷatuṇḍilaṃ pana gaṇhathā”ti [V 3.0252] āha. “Kahaṃ so”ti? “Ayaṃ etasmiṃ gaccheti, saddamassa dehī”ti. “Āhāraṃ na passāmī”ti. Dhuttā mūlena ekaṃ bhattapātiṃ āharāpesuṃ. Mahallikā taṃ gahetvā dvāre ṭhapitaṃ sūkaradoṇiṃ pūretvā doṇisamīpe aṭṭhāsi. Tiṃsamattāpi dhuttā pāsahatthā tattheva aṭṭhaṃsu. Mahallikā “tāta, cūḷatuṇḍila, ehī”ti tassa saddamakāsi. Taṃ sutvā [P 3.0288] mahātuṇḍilo “ettakaṃ kālaṃ mama mātarā cūḷatuṇḍilassa saddo na dinnapubbo, maṃyeva paṭhamaṃ saddāyati, avassaṃ ajja amhākaṃ bhayaṃ uppannaṃ bhavissatī”ti aññāsi. So kaniṭṭhaṃ āmantesi “tāta, mama mātā taṃ pakkosati, gaccha tāva jānāhī”ti. So gacchā nikkhamitvā bhattadoṇisamīpe tesaṃ ṭhitabhāvaṃ disvā “ajja me maraṇaṃ uppanna”nti maraṇabhayatajjito nivattitvā kampamāno bhātu santikaṃ āgantvā thambhituṃ nāsakkhi, kampamāno paribbhami. Mahātuṇḍilo taṃ disvā “tāta, tvaṃ ajja pana pavedhasi paribbhamasi, pavisanaṭṭhānaṃ olokesi, kiṃ nāmetaṃ karosī”ti pucchi. So attanā diṭṭhakāraṇaṃ kathento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

She took the coins and said, “Sirs, I cannot give you Mahātuṇḍila. But you may take Cūḷatuṇḍila.” “Where is he?” they asked. “He is in this thicket; give him a call.” “I see no food [to lure him],” they said. The rogues then had a bowl of rice brought for a price. The old woman took it, filled the pig's trough that was placed at the door, and stood near the trough. About thirty rogues stood right there with snares in their hands. The old woman called out, “Dear Cūḷatuṇḍila, come!” making a call for him. Hearing this, Mahātuṇḍila realized, “For all this time, my mother has never called Cūḷatuṇḍila first; she always calls me first. Surely, today danger has arisen for us.” He addressed his younger brother: “Dear one, our mother is calling you. Go and find out first.” The younger pig went out from the thicket, and seeing them standing near the rice-trough, he thought, “Today, death has come for me.” Overcome by the fear of death, he turned back and went to his brother, trembling. Unable to stand firm, he wandered about, shaking. Seeing him, Mahātuṇḍila asked, “Dear one, why do you tremble and wander about today, looking for a place to hide? What is it that you are doing?” He then related what he had seen and recited the first verse:

88.

88.

“Navachannakedāni diyyati, puṇṇāyaṃ doṇi suvāminī ṭhitā;

Bahuke jane pāsapāṇike, no ca kho me paṭibhāti bhuñjitu”nti.

“A new offering is now given, the trough is full, our mistress stands by; many men with snares in hand, but I have no mind to eat.”

Tattha [M 3.0271] navachannakedāni diyyatīti bhātika, pubbe amhākaṃ kuṇḍakayāgu vā jhāmabhattaṃ vā diyyati, ajja pana navachannakaṃ navākāraṃ dānaṃ diyyati. Puṇṇāyaṃ doṇīti ayaṃ amhākaṃ bhattadoṇi suddhabhattassa puṇṇā. Suvāminī ṭhitāti ayyāpi no tassā santike ṭhitā. Bahuke janeti na kevalañca ayyāva, aññopi bahuko jano pāsapāṇiko ṭhito. No ca kho me paṭibhātīti ayaṃ evaṃ etesaṃ ṭhitabhāvopi idaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjitumpi mayhaṃ na paṭibhāti, na ruccatīti attho.

Herein, ‘a new offering is now given’ means this, brother: previously we were given either rice-bran gruel or burnt rice, but today a new kind of gift is given. ‘The trough is full’ means this food-trough of ours is full of pure rice. ‘Our mistress stands by’ means our lady is also standing near it. ‘Many men’ means not only our lady, but many other men are also standing there with snares in hand. ‘But I have no mind to eat’ means: with them standing there like this, even eating this food does not appeal to me; it is not pleasing—this is the meaning.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “tāta cūḷatuṇḍila, mama kira mātā ettheva sūkare posentī nāma yadatthaṃ poseti, svāssā attho [P 3.0289] ajja matthakaṃ patto, tvaṃ mā cintayī”ti vatvā madhurena sarena buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ desento dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the Great Being said, “Dear Cūḷatuṇḍila, the purpose for which our mother has been raising pigs here—that very purpose has reached its culmination today. Do not worry.” Then, teaching the Dhamma with a sweet voice and with the grace of a Buddha, he spoke two verses:

89.

89.

“Tasasi bhamasi leṇamicchasi, attāṇosi kuhiṃ gamissasi;

Appossukko bhuñja tuṇḍila, maṃsatthāya hi positāmhase.

“You tremble, you roam, you seek a hiding place; you are without protection, where will you go? Eat without anxiety, Tuṇḍila, for we have been raised for the sake of our flesh.

90.

90.

“Ogaha [V 3.0253] rahadaṃ akaddamaṃ, sabbaṃ sedamalaṃ pavāhaya;

Gaṇhāhi navaṃ vilepanaṃ, yassa gandho na kadāci chijjatī”ti.

“Plunge into the mud-free lake, wash away all sweat and grime; take up a fresh anointing, whose fragrance never fades.”

Tattha tasasi bhamasīti maraṇabhayena uttasasi, teneva kilamanto bhamasi. Leṇamicchasīti patiṭṭhaṃ olokesi. Attāṇosīti tāta, pubbe amhākaṃ mātā paṭisaraṇaṃ ahosi, sā ajja pana nirapekkhā amhe chaḍḍesi, idāni kuhiṃ gamissasi. Ogahāti ogāha, ayameva vā pāṭho. Pavāhayāti pavāhehi, hārehīti attho. Na chijjatīti na nassati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tāta, sace maraṇato tasasi, akaddamaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā tava sarīre sabbaṃ sedañca malañca pavāhetvā surabhigandhavilepanaṃ vilimpāti.

Here, ‘you tremble, you wander’ means you are terrified by the fear of death, and being exhausted by that very fear, you wander. ‘You seek a hiding place’ means you look for a support. ‘You are without protection,’ dear one, formerly our mother was our refuge, but today, indifferent, she has abandoned us; where will you go now? ‘Plunge’ (ogahā) means 'plunge in' (ogāha), or this is the reading. ‘Wash away’ (pavāhayā) means 'wash away' (pavāhehi), meaning 'remove'. ‘It is not cut off’ means it does not perish. This is what is said: ‘Dear one, if you are terrified of death, enter a mud-free lotus pond, wash away all the sweat and grime from your body, and anoint yourself with fragrant ointment.’

Tassa dasa pāramiyo āvajjetvā mettāpāramiṃ purecārikaṃ katvā paṭhamaṃ padaṃ udāharantasseva saddo sakalaṃ dvādasayojanikaṃ bārāṇasiṃ ajjhottharitvā gato. Sutasutakkhaṇeyeva rājauparājādayo ādiṃ [M 3.0272] katvā bārāṇasivāsino āgamaṃsu. Anāgatāpi gehe ṭhitāva suṇiṃsu. Rājapurisā gacche chinditvā bhūmiṃ samaṃ katvā vālukaṃ okiriṃsu. Dhuttānaṃ surāmado chijji. Pāse chaḍḍetvā dhammaṃ suṇamānā aṭṭhaṃsu. Mahallikāyapi surāmado chijji. Mahāsatto mahājanamajjhe cūḷatuṇḍilassa dhammadesanaṃ ārabhi. Taṃ [P 3.0290] sutvā cūḷatuṇḍilo “mayhaṃ bhātā evaṃ vadeti, amhākañca vaṃse pokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā nahānaṃ, sarīrato sedamalapavāhanaṃ, purāṇavilepanaṃ hāretvā navavilepanagahaṇañca kismiñci kāle natthi, kiṃ nu kho sandhāya bhātā maṃ eva māhā”ti pucchanto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Reflecting on the ten perfections and putting the perfection of loving-kindness first, the sound of the Bodhisatta as he uttered the first line of the verse pervaded the entire twelve-league city of Bārāṇasī. At the very moment they heard it, the residents of Bārāṇasī, beginning with the king and the sub-king, came. Even those who did not come heard it while staying in their homes. The king's men cleared the bushes, leveled the ground, and scattered sand. The rogues' intoxication with liquor ceased. Leaving their snares behind, they stood listening to the Dhamma. Even the old woman's intoxication with liquor ceased. The Great Being began the Dhamma teaching to Cūḷatuṇḍila in the midst of the crowd. Hearing this, Cūḷatuṇḍila, wishing to ask, 'My brother says this. In our lineage, there is never a time for descending into a lotus pond to bathe, for washing away sweat and grime from the body, or for taking a new ointment after removing the old. To what is my brother referring when he says this to me?' spoke this fourth verse:

91.

91.

“Katamo rahado akaddamo, kiṃsu sedamalanti vuccati;

Katamañca navaṃ vilepanaṃ, yassa gandho na kadāci chijjatī”ti.

“What lake is mud-free? What indeed is called sweat and grime? And what is the new ointment, whose fragrance never fades?”

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto “tena hi kaniṭṭha ohitasoto suṇāhī”ti buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the Great Being, wishing to teach the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, said, “In that case, younger brother Cūḷatuṇḍila, listen with an attentive ear,” and spoke these verses:

92.

92.

“Dhammo rahado akaddamo, pāpaṃ sedamalanti vuccati;

Sīlañca navaṃ vilepanaṃ, tassa gandho na kadāci chijjati.

“The Dhamma is the mud-free lake; evil is called sweat and grime; and virtue is the new ointment, its fragrance never fades.

93.

93.

“Nandanti [V 3.0254] sarīraghātino, na ca nandanti sarīradhārino;

Puṇṇāya ca puṇṇamāsiyā, ramamānāva jahanti jīvita”nti.

“Those who destroy bodies rejoice, but those who bear bodies do not rejoice; on the full moon of the full moon day, they give up life while rejoicing.”

Tattha dhammoti pañcasīlaaṭṭhasīladasasīlāni tīṇi sucaritāni sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammā amatamahānibbānanti sabbopesa dhammo nāma. Akaddamoti rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhikilesakaddamānaṃ abhāvena akaddamo. Iminā sesadhammato vinivattetvā nibbānameva dasseti. “Yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ dhammānaṃ aggamakkhāyati, yadidaṃ madanimmadano pipāsavinayo ālayasamugghāto vaṭṭupacchedo taṇhakkhayo virāgo nirodho nibbāna”nti (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) hi vuttaṃ, tadeva dassento, tāta cūḷatuṇḍila, ahaṃ nibbānataḷākaṃ “rahado”ti kathemi. Jātijarābyādhimaraṇādīni hi tattha natthi, sace maraṇato muñcitukāmo, nibbānagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ gaṇhāti. Upanissayapaccayavasena kira bodhisatto evaṃ kathesi.

In that context, 'Dhamma' refers to the five precepts, the eight precepts, the ten precepts, the three types of good conduct, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the deathless great Nibbāna—all this is called 'Dhamma.' 'Mud-free' means mud-free due to the absence of the mud of defilements such as lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and wrong view. By this, distinguishing it from the rest of the Dhamma, he shows Nibbāna itself. For it is said: “Monks, as far as there are dhammas, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is called the foremost of them, that is, the crushing of pride, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the cycle, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.” Showing that very thing, he said: “Dear Cūḷatuṇḍila, I call the pool of Nibbāna ‘a lake.’ For there, birth, aging, sickness, death, and the like do not exist. If one wishes to be freed from death, one should take up the path leading to Nibbāna.” It is said that the Bodhisatta spoke thus by way of supporting condition.

Pāpaṃ [M 3.0273] sedamalanti [P 3.0291] tāta cūḷatuṇḍila, pāpaṃ sedamalasadisattā “sedamala”nti porāṇakapaṇḍitehi kathitaṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ ekavidhena pāpaṃ yadidaṃ manopadoso, duvidhena pāpaṃ pāpakañca sīlaṃ, pāpikā ca diṭṭhi, tividhena pāpaṃ tīṇi duccaritāni, catubbidhena pāpaṃ cattāri agatigamanāni, pañcavidhena pāpaṃ pañca cetokhilā, chabbidhena pāpaṃ cha agāravā, sattavidhena pāpaṃ satta asaddhammā, aṭṭhavidhena pāpaṃ aṭṭha micchattā, navavidhena pāpaṃ nava āghātavatthūni, dasavidhena pāpaṃ dasa akusalakammapathā, bahuvidhena pāpaṃ rāgo doso mohoti ekakadukatikādivasena vibhattā akusalā dhammā, iti sabbampetaṃ pāpaṃ “sarīranissitasedamalasadisa”nti paṇḍitehi kathitaṃ.

“Evil is sweat and grime” means: Dear Cūḷatuṇḍila, evil is called “sweat and grime” by the ancient sages because it is like sweat and grime. This evil is of one kind: corruption of mind; of two kinds: bad conduct and bad view; of three kinds: the three types of misconduct; of four kinds: the four wrong courses of action; of five kinds: the five mental barrennesses; of six kinds: the six types of disrespect; of seven kinds: the seven ignoble qualities; of eight kinds: the eight wrongnesses; of nine kinds: the nine grounds for resentment; of ten kinds: the ten unwholesome courses of action; of many kinds: greed, hatred, and delusion, unwholesome states classified by way of groups of one, two, three, and so on. Thus, all this evil is said by the wise to be like sweat and grime dependent on the body.

Sīlanti pañcasīlaṃ dasasīlaṃ catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. “Idaṃ, tāta, sīlaṃ catujjātigandhavilepanasadisa”nti vadati. Tassāti tassa silassa gandho tīsu vayesu kadāci na chijjati, sakalalokaṃ pattharitvā gacchati.

“Virtue” means the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the fourfold purification virtue. He says, “This virtue, dear one, is like the ointment of the four-ingredient fragrance.” “Its” means: the fragrance of that virtue never fades during the three stages of life, and it spreads throughout the entire world.

“Na pupphagandho paṭivātameti, na candanaṃ taggaramallikā vā;

Satañca gandho paṭivātameti, sabbā disā sappuriso pavāyati.

“The scent of flowers does not travel against the wind, nor that of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine; but the fragrance of the good travels against the wind; the good person pervades all directions.

“Candanaṃ [V 3.0255] tagaraṃ vāpi, uppalaṃ atha vassikī;

Etesaṃ gandhajātānaṃ, sīlagandho anuttaro.

“Whether sandalwood or tagara, or a lotus, or a jasmine, among all these kinds of fragrances, the fragrance of virtue is supreme.

“Appamatto ayaṃ gandho, yvāyaṃ tagaracandanaṃ;

Yo ca sīlavataṃ gandho, vāti devesu uttamo”ti. (dha. pa. 54-56);

“Faint is this fragrance of tagara and sandalwood, but the fragrance of the virtuous wafts supreme among the gods.” (Dhammapada 54-56);

Nandanti sarīraghātinoti tāta cūḷatuṇḍila, ime aññāṇamanussā “madhuramaṃsaṃ khādissāma, puttadārampi khādāpessāmā”ti pāṇātipātaṃ karontā nandanti tussanti, pāṇātipāto āsevito bhāvito bahulīkato nirayasaṃvattaniko hoti, tiracchānayoni…pe… pettivisayasaṃvattaniko hoti, yo sabbalahuko pāṇātipātassa vipāko, so manussabhūtassa appāyukasaṃvattaniko hotīti imaṃ pāṇātipāte ādīnavaṃ na jānanti. Ajānantā –

Regarding “Those who destroy bodies rejoice”: Dear Cūḷatuṇḍila, these ignorant people, thinking, ‘We will eat delicious meat, and we will also let our children and wives eat it,’ rejoice and are pleased while killing living beings. The killing of living beings, when practiced, developed, and frequently indulged in, leads to hell, the animal realm... [and] the realm of hungry ghosts. The lightest result of the killing of living beings is that it leads to a short life for one who is born as a human. They do not know this danger in the killing of living beings. Not knowing this—

“Madhuvā [M 3.0274] maññati bālo, yāva pāpaṃ na paccati;

Yadā ca paccati pāpaṃ, bālo dukkhaṃ nigacchatī”ti. (dha. pa. 69) –

“The fool thinks it sweet as honey, so long as evil has not ripened. But when evil ripens, the fool comes to suffering.” (Dhammapada 69) –

Madhurasaññino hutvā –

Perceiving it as sweet—

“Caranti bālā dummedhā, amitteneva attanā;

Karontā pāpakaṃ kammaṃ, yaṃ hoti kaṭukapphala”nti. (dha. pa. 66) –

“Fools of poor understanding go about as their own enemies, doing evil deeds that bear bitter fruit.” (Dhammapada 66) –

Ettakampi na jānanti.

They do not know even this much.

“Na taṃ kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu, yaṃ katvā anutappati;

Yassa assumukho rodaṃ, vipākaṃ paṭisevatī”ti. (dha. pa. 67);

“That deed is not well done of which one repents after having done it, and whose result one experiences weeping with a tearful face.” (Dhammapada 67);

Na ca nandanti sarīradhārinoti tāta cūḷatuṇḍila, ye panete sarīradhārino sattā, te attano maraṇe [P 3.0292] āgacchante ṭhapetvā sīhamigarājahatthājānīyaassājānīyakhīṇāsave avasesā bodhisattaṃ ādiṃ katvā abhāyantā nāma natthi.

Regarding “And those who bear bodies do not rejoice”: Dear Cūḷatuṇḍila, as for those beings who bear bodies, when their own death approaches, excluding the lion (the king of beasts), the noble elephant, the noble horse, and those whose cankers are destroyed, there is no one among the rest, beginning with the Bodhisatta, who is not afraid.

“Sabbe [V 3.0256] tasanti daṇḍassa, sabbe bhāyanti maccuno;

Attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā, na haneyya na ghātaye”ti. (dha. pa. 129);

“All tremble at punishment, all fear death. Comparing oneself with others, one should neither kill nor cause to kill.” (Dhammapada 129);

Puṇṇāyāti guṇapuṇṇāya. Puṇṇamāsiyāti puṇṇacandayuttāya, māsaṃ vā pūretvā ṭhitāya. Tadā kira puṇṇamāsī uposathadivaso hoti. Ramamānāva jahanti jīvitanti tāta cūḷatuṇḍila, mā soci mā paridevi, maraṇassa nāma te bhāyanti, yesaṃ abbhantare sīlādiguṇā natthi. Mayaṃ pana sīlācārasampannā puññavanto, tasmā amhādisā sattā ramamānāva jahanti jīvitanti.

“Full”: full of virtues. “On the full moon day”: connected with the full moon, or standing having completed the month. At that time, it was the full moon Uposatha day. “They give up life while rejoicing”: Dear Cūḷatuṇḍila, do not sorrow, do not lament. Those who are afraid of death are those who have no virtues like morality within them. But we are endowed with virtuous conduct and are meritorious; therefore, beings like us give up life while rejoicing.

Evaṃ mahāsatto madhurena sarena buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ desesi. Mahājanakāyā aṅguliyo phoṭesuṃ, celukkhepā ca pavattiṃsu, sādhukārasaddapuṇṇaṃ antalikkhaṃ ahosi. Bārāṇasirājā bodhisattaṃ rajjena pūjetvā mahallikāya yasaṃ datvā ubhopi te gandhodakena nhāpetvā gandhādīhi vilimpāpetvā gīvāsu maṇiratanāni piḷandhāpetvā gharaṃ netvā puttaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā mahantena parivārena paṭijaggi. Bodhisatto rañño [M 3.0275] pañca sīlāni adāsi. Sabbe bārāṇasivāsino ca kāsiraṭṭhavāsino ca pañca sīlāni rakkhiṃsu. Mahāsatto nesaṃ pakkhadivasesu dhammaṃ desesi, vinicchaye nisīditvā aḍḍe tīresi. Tasmiṃ dharamāne kūṭaḍḍakārakā nāma nāhesuṃ. Aparabhāge rājā kālamakāsi. Mahāsatto tassa sarīraparihāraṃ kāretvā vinicchaye potthake likhāpetvā “imaṃ potthakaṃ oloketvā aḍḍaṃ tīreyyāthā”ti vatvā mahājanassa dhammaṃ desetvā appamādena ovādaṃ datvā sabbesaṃ rodantānaṃ paridevantānaññeva saddhiṃ cūḷatuṇḍilena araññaṃ pāvisi. Tadā bodhisattassa ovādo saṭṭhi vassasahassāni pavatti.

Thus, the Great Being, with a sweet voice, taught the Dhamma with the bearing of a Buddha. The great multitude snapped their fingers, threw their garments, and the sky was filled with shouts of approval. The king of Bārāṇasī honored the Bodhisatta with the kingdom, bestowed fortune upon Mahallikā, and after bathing them both with fragrant water, anointing them with perfumes, adorning their necks with jeweled ornaments, he led them to his palace and placed the Bodhisatta in the position of a son. With a great retinue, he attended to him. The Bodhisatta gave the king the five precepts. All the residents of Bārāṇasī and the Kāsi kingdom observed the five precepts. The Great Being taught them the Dhamma on the Uposatha days, and sitting in the hall of judgment, he settled their lawsuits. During his time, there were no fraudulent litigants. Later, the king passed away. The Great Being arranged for his funeral rites, had legal precedents written down in books, and said, "After examining these books, resolve the cases." Then, having taught the Dhamma to the great assembly and exhorted them with heedfulness, he entered the forest with Cūḷatuṇḍila while everyone was weeping and lamenting. At that time, the Bodhisatta’s exhortation remained in effect for sixty thousand years.

Satthā [P 3.0293] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so maraṇabhīruko bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was fearful of death was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, cūḷatuṇḍilo maraṇabhīruko bhikkhu, parisā buddhaparisā, mahātuṇḍilo pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the king was Ānanda, Cūḷatuṇḍila was the monk who feared death, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and Mahātuṇḍila was I myself.

Tuṇḍilajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The third Commentary on the Tuṇḍila Jātaka is finished.

[389] 4. Suvaṇṇakakkaṭakajātakavaṇṇanā

[389] 4. The Commentary on the Suvaṇṇakakkaṭaka Jātaka.

Siṅgīmigoti [V 3.0257] idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ānandattherassa attano atthāya jīvitapariccāgaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu yāva dhanuggahapayojanā khaṇḍahālajātake (jā. 2.22.982 ādayo) dhanapālavissajjanaṃ cūḷahaṃsamahāhaṃsajātake (jā. 1.15.133 ādayo) kathitaṃ. Tadā hi bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, dhammabhaṇḍāgārikaānandatthero sekkhapaṭisambhidāppatto hutvā dhanapālake āgacchante sammāsambuddhassa jīvitaṃ pariccajī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi ānando mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ pariccajiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“The Siṅgī Deer”—this the Teacher related while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning the Elder Ānanda’s sacrifice of his life for his sake. The story up to the archer's mission is told in the Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka, and the release of Dhanapāla is told in the Cūḷahaṃsa and Mahāhaṃsa Jātakas. At that time, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, the Elder Ānanda, keeper of the Dhamma treasury, though being a trainee who has attained the analytical knowledges, sacrificed his life for the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One when Dhanapāla approached.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you sitting together now?” When told, “For such and such,” he said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, Ānanda sacrificed his life for me,” and he related the past.

Atīte rājagahassa pubbapasse sālindiyo nāma brāhmaṇagāmo hoti. Tadā bodhisatto tasmiṃ gāme kassakabrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā [M 3.0276] vayappatto kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā tassa gāmassa pubbuttarāya disāya ekasmiṃ gāmakhette karīsasahassamattaṃ kasiṃ kāresi. So ekadivasaṃ manussehi saddhiṃ khettaṃ gantvā kammakāre “kasathā”ti āṇāpetvā mukhadhovanatthāya khettakoṭiyaṃ mahantaṃ sobbhaṃ upasaṅkami. Tasmiṃ kho pana sobbhe eko suvaṇṇavaṇṇo kakkaṭako paṭivasati abhirūpo pāsādiko. Bodhisatto dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā taṃ sobbhaṃ otari. Tassa mukhadhovanakāle [P 3.0294] kakkaṭako santikaṃ āgamāsi. Atha naṃ so ukkhipitvā attano uttarisāṭakantare nipajjāpetvā gahetvā khette kattabbakiccaṃ katvā gacchanto tattheva naṃ sobbhe pakkhipitvā gehaṃ agamāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya khettaṃ āgacchanto paṭhamaṃ taṃ sobbhaṃ gantvā kakkaṭakaṃ ukkhipitvā uttarisāṭakantare nipajjāpetvā pacchā kammantaṃ vicāresi. Iti tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ vissāso daḷho ahosi.

In the past, to the east of Rājagaha, there was a brahmin village named Sālindiya. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in that village in a farmer-brahmin family. When he came of age, he established a household and had about a thousand karīsas of land cultivated in a field to the northeast of that village. One day, he went to the field with his men and, after ordering the workers to plow, approached a large pool at the edge of the field to wash his face. In that pool lived a golden-colored crab, beautiful and pleasing to behold. The Bodhisatta chewed a tooth-stick and descended into that pool. While he was washing his face, the crab came near him. Then he picked it up, placed it within his upper garment, and after finishing his work in the field, he released it back into the pool before returning home. From then on, whenever he went to the field, he would first go to that pool, pick up the crab, place it within his upper garment, and only then attend to his work. In this way, a strong mutual trust developed between them.

Bodhisatto nibaddhaṃ khettaṃ āgacchati, akkhīsu ca panassa pañca pasādā tīṇi maṇḍalāni visuddhāni hutvā paññāyanti. Athassa khettakoṭiyaṃ ekasmiṃ tāle kākakulāvake kākī akkhīni disvā khāditukāmā hutvā kākaṃ āha – “sāmi, dohaḷo me uppanno”ti. “Kiṃ dohaḷo nāmā”ti? “Etassa brāhmaṇassa akkhīni khāditukāmāmhī”ti. “Duddohaḷo te uppanno, ko etāni āharituṃ sakkhissatī”ti. “Tvaṃ na sakkosī”ti ahampetaṃ jānāmi, yo panesa tālassa avidūre vammiko, ettha kaṇhasappo vasati. “Taṃ upaṭṭhaha, so etaṃ ḍaṃsitvā māressati, athassa akkhīni uppāṭetvā tvaṃ āharissasī”ti[V 3.0258]. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tato paṭṭhāya kaṇhasappaṃ upaṭṭhahi. Bodhisattenapi vāpitasassānaṃ gabbhaggahaṇakāle kakkaṭako mahā ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ sappo kākamāha “samma, tvaṃ nibaddhaṃ maṃ upaṭṭhahasi, kiṃ te karomī”ti. “Sāmi, tumhākaṃ dāsiyā etassa khettasāmikassa akkhīsu dohaḷo uppajji, svāhaṃ tumhākaṃ ānubhāvena tassa akkhīni labhissāmīti tumhe upaṭṭhahāmī”ti. Sappo “hotu, nayidaṃ garukaṃ, labhissasī”ti taṃ assāsetvā puna divase brāhmaṇassa āgamanamagge kedāramariyādaṃ [P 3.0295][M 3.0277] nissāya tiṇehi paṭicchanno hutvā tassāgamanaṃ olokento nipajji.

The Bodhisatta regularly came to the field, and in his eyes, the five sensitivities and the three circles appeared pure and clear. Then, a female crow in a nest on a palm tree at the edge of the field, seeing his eyes and desiring to eat them, said to the male crow, “Master, a craving has arisen in me.” “What kind of craving?” “I wish to eat the eyes of this brahmin.” “A difficult craving has arisen in you; who will be able to bring them?” “Do you mean you cannot?” “I know a way; in the anthill not far from this palm tree lives a black snake. Attend to him. He will bite and kill the man, and then you can pluck out his eyes and bring them to me.” The crow agreed, and from then on, he attended to the black snake. By the time the Bodhisatta's sown crops were bearing grain, the crab had grown large. Then one day the snake said to the crow, “Friend, you constantly attend to me; what can I do for you?” “Master, a craving for the eyes of this field-owner has arisen in your handmaiden. I attend to you so that I might obtain his eyes by your power.” The snake reassured him, saying, “So be it; this is not difficult, you shall obtain them.” Then, on the following day, the snake hid himself among the grass by the embankment on the brahmin’s path and lay in wait, watching for his arrival.

Bodhisatto āgacchanto paṭhamaṃ sobbhaṃ otaritvā mukhaṃ dhovitvā sinehaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā suvaṇṇakakkaṭakaṃ āliṅgetvā uttarisāṭakantare nipajjāpetvā khettaṃ pāvisi. Sappo taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvāva vegena pakkhanditvā piṇḍikamaṃse ḍaṃsitvā tattheva pātetvā vammikaṃ sandhāya palāyi. Bodhisattassa patanañca kakkaṭakassa sāṭakantarato laṅghanañca kākassa āgantvā bodhisattassa ure nilīyanañca apacchāapurimaṃ ahosi. Kāko nilīyitvā akkhīni tuṇḍena pahari. Kakkaṭako “imaṃ kākaṃ nissāya mama sahāyassa bhayaṃ uppannaṃ, etasmiṃ gahite sappo āgacchissatī”ti saṇḍāsena gaṇhanto viya kākaṃ gīvāyaṃ aḷena daḷhaṃ gahetvā kilametvā thokaṃ sithilamakāsi. Kāko “kissa maṃ samma, chaḍḍetvā palāyasi, esa maṃ kakkaṭako bhiyyo viheṭheti, yāva na marāmi, tāva ehī”ti sappaṃ pakkosanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, coming along, first went down into the pool, washed his face, aroused a feeling of affection [for the crab], embraced the golden crab, and having placed it within the folds of his upper robe, entered the field. The snake, seeing him approach, swiftly rushed forward, bit him on the calf, felled him right there, and fled towards the anthill. The Bodhisatta’s fall, the crab’s leap from within the folds of the robe, and the crow’s arrival and perching on the Bodhisatta’s chest all happened almost simultaneously. The crow, having perched, struck his eyes with its beak. The crab thought, “Because of this crow, danger has arisen for my friend. If this one is caught, the snake will come.” So, as if seizing with pincers, it firmly grasped the crow by the neck with its claw, tormented it, and then slightly loosened its grip. The crow, calling to the snake, said, “Friend, why do you abandon me and flee? This crab torments me even more! Come here, before I die!” and spoke the first verse:

94.

94.

“Siṅgīmigo āyatacakkhunetto, aṭṭhittaco vārisayo alomo;

Tenābhibhūto kapaṇaṃ rudāmi, hare sakhā kissa nu maṃ jahāsī”ti.

“The horned creature, with long eyes, bony-skinned, dwelling in water, hairless; overcome by him, I weep miserably. O friend, why do you abandon me?”

Tattha siṅgīmigoti siṅgīsuvaṇṇavaṇṇatāya vā aḷasaṅkhātānaṃ vā siṅgānaṃ atthitāya kakkaṭako vutto. Āyatacakkhunettoti dīghehi cakkhusaṅkhātehi nettehi samannāgato. Aṭṭhimeva taco assāti aṭṭhittaco. Hare sakhāti ālapanametaṃ, ambho sahāyāti attho.

Here, 'horned creature' refers to the crab, either because of its golden color like siṅgī gold, or because of the presence of its claws, which are called 'horns' (siṅga). 'With long eyes' means endowed with long eyes. 'Bony-skinned' means its skin is just bone. 'O friend' is an address, meaning 'O friend!'

Sappo taṃ sutvā mahantaṃ phaṇaṃ katvā kākaṃ assāsento agamāsi. Satthā imamatthaṃ dīpento abhisambuddho hutvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the snake, making a great hood, went to reassure the crow. The Teacher, revealing this meaning, having become fully enlightened, spoke the second verse:

95.

95.

“So [V 3.0259][P 3.0296][M 3.0278] passasanto mahatā phaṇena, bhujaṅgamo kakkaṭamajjhapatto;

Sakhā sakhāraṃ paritāyamāno, bhujaṅgamaṃ kakkaṭako gahesī”ti.

“That serpent, hissing with a great hood, reached the presence of the crab; the friend protecting his friend, the crab seized the serpent.”

Tattha kakkaṭamajjhapattoti kakkaṭakaṃ sampatto. Sakhā sakhāranti sahāyo sahāyaṃ. “Sakaṃ sakhāra”ntipi pāṭho, attano sahāyanti attho. Paritāyamānoti rakkhamāno. Gahesīti dutiyena aḷena gīvāyaṃ daḷhaṃ gahesi.

Here, 'came to the crab' means he reached the crab. 'A friend protecting a friend' means a companion protecting a companion. There is also the reading 'his own friend,' meaning his personal companion. 'Protecting' means guarding. 'Seized' means he firmly grasped its neck with his second claw.

Atha naṃ kilametvā thokaṃ sithilamakāsi. Atha sappo “kakkaṭakā nāma neva kākamaṃsaṃ khādanti, na sappamaṃsaṃ, atha kena nu kho kāraṇena ayaṃ amhe gaṇhī”ti cintetvā taṃ pucchanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, having tormented it, he loosened his grip slightly. Then the snake, thinking, “Crabs do not eat crow’s flesh, nor snake’s flesh. For what reason, then, has this one seized us?” questioned him with the third verse:

96.

96.

“Na vāyasaṃ no pana kaṇhasappaṃ, ghāsatthiko kakkaṭako adeyya;

Pucchāmi taṃ āyatacakkhunetta, atha kissa hetumha ubho gahītā”ti.

“A crab seeking food would not take a crow or a black snake. I ask you, long-eyed one, for what reason have we both been seized?”

Tattha ghāsatthikoti āhāratthiko hutvā. Adeyyātiādiyeyya, na-kārena yojetvā na gaṇhīti attho.

Here, 'seeking food' means being in need of food. 'Adeyya' is explained as 'ādiyeyya' (he would take); connected with the particle 'na', the meaning is 'he would not take'.

Taṃ sutvā kakkaṭako gahaṇakāraṇaṃ kathento dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing that, the crab, explaining the reason for seizing them, spoke two verses:

97.

97.

“Ayaṃ puriso mama atthakāmo, yo maṃ gahetvāna dakāya neti;

Tasmiṃ mate dukkhamanappakaṃ me, ahañca eso ca ubho na homa.

“This man desires my welfare, who takes me and leads me to the water. If he dies, my suffering will be no small thing; both he and I will cease to be.”

98.

98.

“Mamañca disvāna pavaddhakāyaṃ, sabbo jano hiṃsitumeva micche;

Sāduñca thūlañca muduñca maṃsaṃ, kākāpi maṃ disva viheṭhayeyyu”nti.

“And seeing me with a large body, all people would wish to harm me; for my flesh is savory, plump, and tender. Even crows, seeing me, would harass me.”

Tattha [P 3.0297][M 3.0279] ayanti bodhisattaṃ niddisati. Atthakāmoti hitakāmo. Dakāya netīti yo maṃ sampiyāyamāno uttarisāṭakena gahetvāna udakāya neti, attano vasanakasobbhaṃ pāpeti. Tasmiṃ mateti sace so imasmiṃ ṭhāne marissati, etasmiṃ mate mama kāyikaṃ cetasikaṃ mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ bhavissatīti dīpeti. Ubho na homāti dvepi janā na bhavissāma. Mamañca disvānāti gāthāya ayamattho – idañca aparaṃ kāraṇaṃ, imasmiṃ mate anāthaṃ nippaccayaṃ maṃ pavaḍḍhitakāyaṃ [V 3.0260] disvā sabbo jano “imassa kakkaṭakassa sāduñca thūlañca muduñca maṃsa”nti maṃ māretuṃ iccheyya, na kevalañca jano manusso, tiracchānabhūtā kākāpi maṃ disvā viheṭhayeyyuṃ viheseyyuṃ māreyyuṃ.

Here, 'this' refers to the Bodhisatta. 'Desires my welfare' means desires my benefit. 'Leads me to the water' means he who, cherishing me, takes me in his upper robe and leads me to the water, bringing me to his own dwelling pool. 'If he dies' indicates that if he were to die in this place, great physical and mental suffering would arise for me. 'Both will cease to be' means both of us will not exist. The meaning of the verse beginning with 'And seeing me' is this: This is another reason. If he were to die, seeing me unprotected and without support, with a large body, all people would wish to kill me, thinking, “This crab’s flesh is savory, plump, and tender.” Not only human beings, but even animals like crows, upon seeing me, would harass, vex, and kill me.

Taṃ sutvā sappo cintesi “ekenupāyena imaṃ vañcetvā kākañca attānañca mocessāmī”ti. Atha naṃ vañcetukāmo chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the snake thought, “By some stratagem I will deceive him and free both the crow and myself.” Then, wishing to deceive him, he spoke the sixth verse:

99.

99.

“Sacetassa hetumha ubho gahītā, uṭṭhātu pose visamāvamāmi;

Mamañca kākañca pamuñca khippaṃ, pure visaṃ gāḷhamupeti macca”nti.

“If we both have been seized for his sake, let the man arise! I will vomit up [withdraw] the poison. Release me and the crow quickly, before the poison deeply affects the mortal.”

Tattha sacetassa hetūti sace etassa kāraṇā. Uṭṭhātūti nibbiso hotu. Visamāvamāmīti ahamassa visaṃ ākaḍḍhāmi, nibbisaṃ naṃ karomi. Pure visaṃ gāḷhamupeti maccanti imañhi maccaṃ mayā anāvamiyamānaṃ visaṃ gāḷhaṃ balavaṃ hutvā upagaccheyya, taṃ yāva na upagacchati, tāvadeva amhe dvepi jane khippaṃ muñcāti.

Here, 'if for his sake' means if for this reason. 'Let him arise' means let him be free of poison. 'I will draw out the poison' means I will extract his poison, I will make him free of poison. 'Before the poison deeply affects the mortal' means that if the poison were not drawn out from this mortal by me, it would become strong and powerful and overcome him. So, quickly release both of us before it overcomes him.

Taṃ sutvā kakkaṭako cintesi “ayaṃ ekenupāyena maṃ dvepi jane vissajjāpetvā palāyitukāmo, mayhaṃ upāyakosallaṃ na jānāti, ahaṃ dāni yathā sappo sañcarituṃ sakkoti, evaṃ aḷaṃ sithilaṃ karissāmi, kākaṃ pana neva vissajjessāmī”ti evaṃ cintetvā sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the crab thought, “This one wants to deceive me by some stratagem, have us both released, and escape. He does not know my skill in devising plans. Now, I will loosen my claw only so much as the snake is able to move, but I will not release the crow.” Having thought thus, he spoke the seventh verse:

100.

100.

“Sappaṃ [P 3.0298] pamokkhāmi na tāva kākaṃ, paṭibandhako hohiti tāva kāko;

Purisañca disvāna sukhiṃ arogaṃ, kākaṃ pamokkhāmi yatheva sappa”nti.

“I will release the snake, but not yet the crow; the crow will be held as a pledge. Having seen the man happy and healthy, I will release the crow just as I did the snake.”

Tattha [M 3.0280] paṭibandhakoti pāṭibhogo. Yatheva sappanti yathā bhavantaṃ sappaṃ muñcāmi, tathā kākaṃ pamokkhāmi, kevalaṃ tvaṃ imassa brāhmaṇassa sarīrato sīghaṃ visaṃ āvamāhīti.

Here, 'pledge' (paṭibandhako) means 'surety' (pāṭibhogo). 'Just as I did the snake' means just as I release you, the snake, so I will release the crow. You must quickly draw out the poison from this brahmin’s body.”

Evañca pana vatvā tassa sukhasañcāraṇatthaṃ aḷaṃ sithilamakāsi. Sappo visaṃ āvamitvā mahāsattassa sarīraṃ nibbisaṃ akāsi. So niddukkho uṭṭhāya pakativaṇṇeneva aṭṭhāsi. Kakkaṭako “sace ime dvepi janā arogā bhavissanti, mayhaṃ sahāyassa vaḍḍhi nāma na bhavissati, vināsessāmi ne”ti cintetvā kattarikāya uppalamakuḷaṃ viya aḷehi ubhinnampi [V 3.0261] sīsaṃ kappetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Kākīpi tamhā ṭhānā palāyi. Bodhisatto sappassa sarīraṃ daṇḍake veṭhetvā gumbapiṭṭhe khipi. Suvaṇṇakakkaṭakaṃ sobbhe vissajjetvā nhatvā sālindiyagāmameva gato. Tato paṭṭhāya kakkaṭakena saddhiṃ adhikataro vissāso ahosi.

Having said this, he loosened his claw to allow for easy movement. The snake, having drawn out the poison, made the Great Being’s body free of poison. Rising without suffering, he stood there with his natural complexion. The crab thought, “If both these two remain healthy, there will be no benefit for my friend. I will destroy them.” So, with its claws, as if with a pair of scissors, it severed the heads of both of them like lotus buds, bringing them to their death. The female crow also fled from that place. The Bodhisatta wrapped the snake’s body on a stick and threw it onto a thicket. He released the golden crab into the pool, bathed, and went to the village of Sālindiya. From then on, his trust in the crab was even greater.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānento osānagāthamāha –

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, revealed the Truths and, identifying the birth, spoke the concluding verse:

101.

101.

“Kāko tadā devadatto ahosi, māro pana kaṇhasappo ahosi;

Ānandabhaddo kakkaṭako ahosi, ahaṃ tadā brāhmaṇo homi satthā”ti.

“At that time, Devadatta was the crow, and Māra was the black serpent; the venerable Ānanda was the crab, and I, the Teacher, was the brahmin.”

Saccapariyosāne bahū sotāpannādayo ahesuṃ. Kākī pana gāthāya na vuttā, sā ciñcamāṇavikā ahosīti.

At the conclusion of the discourse on the Truths, many became stream-enterers and so on. But Kākī was not mentioned in the verse; she was Ciñcamāṇavikā.

Suvaṇṇakakkaṭakajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Suvaṇṇakakkaṭaka Jātaka, the Fourth.

[390] 5. Mayhakajātakavaṇṇanā

[390] 5. The Explanation of the Mayhaka Jātaka

Sakuṇo [P 3.0299] mayhako nāmāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto āgantukaseṭṭhiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyañhi āgantukaseṭṭhi nāma aḍḍho ahosi mahaddhano. So neva attanā bhoge bhuñji, na paresaṃ adāsi, nānaggarase paṇīte bhojane upanīte taṃ na bhuñjati, bilaṅgadutiyaṃ [M 3.0281] kaṇājakaṃ eva bhuñjati, dhūpitavāsitesu kāsikavatthesu upanītesu tāni hāretvā thūlathūlasāṭake nivāseti, ājānīyayutte maṇikanakavicitte rathe upanīte tampi harāpetvā kattararathakena gacchati, suvaṇṇacchatte dhāriyamāne taṃ apanetvā paṇṇacchattena dhāriyamānena. So yāvajīvaṃ dānādīsu puññesu ekampi akatvā kālaṃ katvā roruvaniraye nibbatti. Tassa aputtakaṃ sāpateyyaṃ rājabalaṃ sattahi rattidivasehi rājakulaṃ pavesesi. Tasmiṃ pavesite rājā bhuttapātarāso jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nisinno “kiṃ, mahārāja, buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ na karosī”ti vutte “bhante, sāvatthiyaṃ āgantukaseṭṭhino nāma kālakatassa assāmikadhane amhākaṃ ghare āhariyamāneyeva satta rattidivasā gatā, so pana etaṃ dhanaṃ labhitvāpi neva attanā paribhuñji, na paresaṃ adāsi, rakkhasapariggahitapokkharaṇī viyassa [V 3.0262] dhanaṃ ahosi, so ekadivasampi paṇītabhojanādīnaṃ rasaṃ ananubhavitvāva maraṇamukhaṃ paviṭṭho, evaṃ maccharī apuññasatto kiṃ katvā ettakaṃ dhanaṃ labhi, kena cassa bhogesu cittaṃ na ramī”ti satthāraṃ pucchi. Satthā “mahārāja, dhanalābho ca, dhanaṃ laddhā aparibhuñjanakāraṇañca teneva kata”nti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“A bird named Mayhaka…”: This the Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke concerning the merchant Āgantuka. In Sāvatthī, there was a merchant named Āgantuka who was wealthy and possessed great riches. Yet he neither enjoyed his wealth himself nor gave it to others. When various exquisite and delicious foods were brought to him, he did not eat them but consumed only broken rice with sour gruel instead. When fine Kāsi garments, perfumed and scented, were offered to him, he had them taken away and wore only coarse robes. When a chariot yoked with thoroughbreds, adorned with jewels and gold, was presented to him, he had it removed and traveled in an old, rickety carriage. When a golden parasol was held over him, he had it taken away and used a leaf parasol instead. Throughout his life, he did not perform even a single meritorious deed such as giving. When he died, he was reborn in the Roruva hell. Because he was childless, his property was taken into the royal treasury by the king’s forces over seven days and nights. When this was done, the king, having finished his morning meal, went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down. When asked, “Great king, why have you not attended upon the Buddha?” the king replied, “Venerable sir, in Sāvatthī, seven days and nights have passed while the ownerless wealth of the deceased merchant Āgantuka was being brought into our palace. Yet, though he obtained this wealth, he neither enjoyed it himself nor gave it to others. His wealth was like a lotus pond guarded by a demon. Without ever tasting the pleasure of fine food or other such things for even a single day, he entered the mouth of death.
