How did such a miserly, meritless being acquire so much wealth, and why did his mind find no delight in his riches?” he asked the Teacher. The Teacher answered, “Great king, the acquisition of wealth and the reason for not enjoying it after obtaining it were both his own doing,” and being requested by the king, he told a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasiseṭṭhi assaddho ahosi maccharī, na kassaci kiñci deti, na kañci saṅgaṇhāti. So ekadivasaṃ rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto tagarasikhiṃ nāma paccekabuddhaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā vanditvā “laddhā, bhante, bhikkhā”ti pucchitvā “nanu carāma mahāseṭṭhī”ti vutte purisaṃ [P 3.0300] āṇāpesi “gaccha, imaṃ amhākaṃ gharaṃ ānetvā mama pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā amhākaṃ paṭiyattabhattassa pattaṃ pūretvā dāpehī”ti. So paccekabuddhaṃ gharaṃ netvā nisīdāpetvā seṭṭhibhariyāya ācikkhi. Sā nānaggarasabhattassa pattaṃ pūretvā tassa adāsi. So bhattaṃ gahetvā seṭṭhinivesanā nikkhamitvā antaravīthiyaṃ paṭipajji. Seṭṭhi rājakulato paccāgacchanto taṃ disvā vanditvā “laddhaṃ, bhante, bhatta”nti pucchi. “Laddhaṃ mahāseṭṭhī”ti. So pattaṃ oloketvā cittaṃ pasādetuṃ nāsakkhi[M 3.0282], “imaṃ me bhattaṃ dāsā vā kammakarā vā bhuñjitvā dukkarampi kammaṃ kareyyuṃ, aho vata me jānī”ti aparacetanaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Dānañhi nāma tisso cetanā paripuṇṇaṃ kātuṃ sakkontasseva mahapphalaṃ hoti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the merchant of Benares was faithless and miserly. He gave nothing to anyone and did not assist anyone. One day, while going to attend on the king, he saw a Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhi walking for alms. He paid homage and asked, “Venerable sir, have you received alms?” When the Paccekabuddha replied, “I am still wandering, great merchant,” he ordered a servant, “Go, bring him to our house, seat him on my couch, fill a bowl with the food prepared for me, and give it to him.” The servant brought the Paccekabuddha to the house, seated him, and informed the merchant's wife. She filled a bowl with various delicious foods and gave it to him. Taking the food, the Paccekabuddha left the merchant's residence and proceeded along the street. The merchant, returning from the palace, saw him, paid homage, and asked, “Venerable sir, have you received food?” “Yes, great merchant,” he replied. The merchant looked at the bowl but could not gladden his heart. He thought, “If my slaves or workers had eaten this food, they would have performed even difficult work. Alas, what a loss for me!” He was unable to fulfill the subsequent intention. For a gift truly bears great fruit only for one who is able to fulfill the threefold intention.

“Pubbeva dānā sumanā bhavāma, dadampi ve attamanā bhavāma;

Datvāpi ve nānutappāma pacchā, tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā namiyyare. (jā. 1.10.95);

“One should be joyful even before giving; while giving, one’s mind should be delighted; and even after giving, one should not regret it later. This is the perfection of merit.”

“Pubbeva dānā sumano, dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādaye;

Datvā attamano hoti, esā yaññassa sampadā”. (a. ni. 6.37; pe. va. 305);

“Before giving, one is joyful; while giving, one makes the mind serene; having given, one is gratified. This is the success of the offering.”

Iti, mahārāja, āgantukaseṭṭhi tagarasikhipaccekabuddhassa dinnapaccayena bahuṃ dhanaṃ labhi, datvā aparacetanaṃ paṇītaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya bhoge bhuñjituṃ nāsakkhīti. “Puttaṃ pana kasmā na labhi, bhante”ti? Satthā “puttassa alabhanakāraṇampi teneva kataṃ, mahārājā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Thus, great king, the merchant Āgantuka, on account of the offering given to the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhi, obtained great wealth. Yet, because he was unable to make his subsequent intention excellent after giving, he could not enjoy that wealth.” “But why, venerable sir, did he not obtain a son?” The Teacher said, “Great king, the reason for not obtaining a son was also his own doing,” and then, being entreated by the king, he recounted the past.

Atīte [V 3.0263] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto asītikoṭivibhave seṭṭhikule nibbattitvā vayappatto mātāpitūnaṃ accayena kaniṭṭhaṃ saṅgaṇhitvā kuṭumbaṃ vicārento gharadvāre dānasālaṃ kāretvā mahādānaṃ pavattento agāraṃ ajjhāvasi. Athassa eko putto jāyi. So tassa padasā gamanakāle kāmesu ādīnavaṃ nekkhamme cānisaṃsaṃ disvā saddhiṃ puttadārena sabbaṃ gharavibhavaṃ [P 3.0301] kaniṭṭhassa niyyātetvā “appamatto dānaṃ pavattehī”ti ovādaṃ datvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā himavantapadese vihāsi. Kaniṭṭhopissa ekaṃ puttaṃ paṭilabhi. So taṃ vaḍḍhantaṃ disvā cintesi “mama bhātu putte jīvante kuṭumbaṃ bhinditvā dvidhā bhavissati, bhātu puttaṃ māressāmī”ti. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ nadiyaṃ opilāpetvā māresi. Tamenaṃ nhatvā āgataṃ bhātu jāyā “kuhiṃ mama putto”ti pucchi. “Nadiyaṃ udakaṃ kīḷi, atha naṃ udake vicinanto nāddasa”nti. Sā roditvā kanditvā tuṇhī ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family possessing a fortune of eighty crores. Upon reaching adulthood, after the passing of his parents, he took care of his younger brother and managed the household wealth. He had an alms hall established at his door and lived at home, distributing great alms. Then, a son was born to him. When his son was able to walk, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation. So, entrusting his wife and son and all the household wealth to his younger brother, he advised, “Be diligent in giving alms,” and then went forth as an ascetic. Developing psychic powers and meditative attainments, he dwelt in the Himalayan region. His younger brother also had a son. Seeing him grow, the brother thought, “While my brother’s son is alive, the family estate will be split into two. I must kill my brother’s son.” One day, he took him to the river and drowned him. When the brother’s wife returned from bathing, she asked him, “Where is my son?” He replied, “He was playing in the river, and then, while searching for him in the water, I could not find him.” She wept and lamented, then fell silent.

Bodhisatto [M 3.0283] taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā “idaṃ kiccaṃ pākaṭaṃ karissāmī”ti ākāsenāgantvā bārāṇasiyaṃ otaritvā sunivattho supāruto tassa gharadvāre ṭhatvā dānasālaṃ adisvā “dānasālāpi iminā asappurisena nāsitā”ti cintesi. Kaniṭṭho tassa āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā āgantvā mahāsattaṃ vanditvā pāsādaṃ āropetvā subhojanaṃ bhojesi. So bhattakiccāvasāne sukhakathāya nisinno “dārako na paññāyati, kahaṃ nu kho”ti pucchi. “Mato, bhante”ti. “Kena kāraṇenā”ti? “Udakakīḷanaṭṭhāne asukakāraṇenāti na jānāmī”ti. “Kiṃ tvaṃ asappurisa na jānissasi, tayā katakiccaṃ mayhaṃ pākaṭaṃ, nanu tvaṃ iminā nāma kāraṇena taṃ māresi, kiṃ nu tvaṃ rājādīnaṃ vasena nassamānaṃ dhanaṃ rakkhituṃ sakkuṇeyyāsi, mayhakasakuṇassa ca tuyhañca kiṃ nānākaraṇa”nti? Athassa mahāsatto buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ desento imā gāthā abhāsi –

The Bodhisatta, knowing of that event, thought, “I will make this matter known,” and came through the air. Descending in Benares, properly dressed and robed, he stood at the door of his house. Not seeing the alms hall, he reflected, “Even the alms hall has been destroyed by this wicked man.” The younger brother, aware of his arrival, came and paid homage to the Great Being. He then led him up to the palace and served him excellent food. After the meal, while sitting for pleasant conversation, the Bodhisatta asked, “The boy is not to be seen—where has he gone?” “He is dead, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “I do not know for what reason while he was playing in the water.” “You wicked man, how could you not know? The deed done by you is clear to me. Did you not kill him for this very reason? Do you think you can protect wealth that is subject to destruction by kings and others? What difference is there between the Mayhaka bird and you?” Then the Great Being, teaching the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, spoke these verses:

102.

102.

“Sakuṇo mayhako nāma, girisānudarīcaro;

Pakkaṃ pipphalimāruyha, ‘mayhaṃ mayha’nti kandati.

“A bird named Mayhaka, roaming the mountain slopes and valleys, having climbed a ripe pipphali tree, cries, ‘Mine, mine!’”

103.

103.

“Tassevaṃ [P 3.0302] vilapantassa, dijasaṅghā samāgatā;

Bhutvāna pipphaliṃ yanti, vilapatveva so dijo.

“While he was thus lamenting, flocks of birds gathered; having eaten the pipphali fruit, they departed, while that bird just lamented.”

104.

104.

“Evameva [V 3.0264] idhekacco, saṅgharitvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ;

Nevattano na ñātīnaṃ, yathodhiṃ paṭipajjati.

“Just so, a certain person here, having amassed much wealth, uses it neither for himself nor for his relatives according to their due portions.”

105.

105.

“Na so acchādanaṃ bhattaṃ, na mālaṃ na vilepanaṃ;

Anubhoti sakiṃ kiñci, na saṅgaṇhāti ñātake.

“He does not enjoy even once any clothing, food, garlands, or perfumes; nor does he support his relatives.”

106.

106.

“Tassevaṃ vilapantassa, mayhaṃ mayhanti rakkhato;

Rājāno atha vā corā, dāyādā yeva appiyā;

Dhanamādāya gacchanti, vilapatveva so naro.

“While he thus laments, guarding his wealth and crying ‘Mine, mine,’ kings, or thieves, or even unloved heirs take his wealth and go, while that man is left only to lament.”

107.

107.

“Dhīro bhoge adhigamma, saṅgaṇhāti ca ñātake;

Tena so kittiṃ pappoti, pecca sagge pamodatī”ti.

“The wise one, having acquired wealth, supports their relatives; through this, they attain renown and rejoice in heaven after death.”

Tattha [M 3.0284] mayhakoti “mayhaṃ mayha”nti viravanavasena evaṃladdhanāmo. Girisānudarīsu caratīti girisānudarīcaro. Pakkaṃ pipphalinti himavantapadese ekaṃ phalabharitaṃ pipphalirukkhaṃ. Kandatīti dijagaṇe taṃ rukkhaṃ parivāretvā pakkāni khādante vāretuṃ “mayhaṃ mayha”nti paridevanto vicarati. Tassevaṃ vilapantassāti tassa vilapantasseva. Bhutvāna vipphaliṃ yantīti taṃ pipphalirukkhaṃ paribhuñjitvā aññaṃ phalasampannaṃ rukkhaṃ gacchanti. Vilapatvevāti so pana dijo vilapatiyeva. Yathodhinti yathākoṭṭhāsaṃ, mātāpitābhātubhaginīputtadhītādīnaṃ upabhogaparibhogavasena yo yo koṭṭhāso dātabbo, taṃ taṃ na detīti attho.

Here, ‘Mayhaka’ means one so-named because of his wailing ‘Mine, mine!’ ‘Roaming the mountain slopes and valleys’ means he wanders on the slopes and in the valleys of the mountains. ‘A ripe pipphali fruit’ refers to a pipphali tree laden with fruit in the Himalayan region. ‘Cries’ means that when flocks of birds surround the tree and eat the ripe fruit, he wanders about lamenting ‘Mine, mine!’ to ward them off. ‘While he was thus lamenting’ means just while he is lamenting. ‘Having eaten the pipphali, they depart’ means having enjoyed the fruit of that pipphali tree, they go to another tree abundant with fruit. ‘Just lamented’ means that bird only keeps lamenting. ‘According to what is due’ means according to the shares; the meaning is that he does not give the portion that should be given for the use and enjoyment of his parents, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, and so on.

Sakinti ekavārampi nānubhoti. “Saka”ntipi pāṭho, attano santakampīti attho. Na saṅgaṇhātīti bhattacchādanabījanaṅgalādidānavasena na saṅgaṇhāti. Vilapatveva so naroti etesu rājādīsu dhanaṃ gahetvā gacchantesu kevalaṃ so puriso vilapatiyeva. Dhīroti paṇḍito. Saṅgaṇhātīti attano santikaṃ āgate dubbalañātake bhattacchādanabījanaṅgalādidānena saṅgaṇhāti. Tenāti so puriso tena ñātisaṅgahena catuparisamajjhe kittiñca attano vaṇṇabhaṇanañca pāpuṇāti, pecca sagge devanagare pamodati.

‘Even once’ means he does not enjoy it even a single time. There is also the reading ‘sakaṃ’, meaning ‘one’s own possession’. ‘Does not support’ means he does not support them by giving food, clothing, seeds, ploughs, and so on. ‘That man is left only to lament’ means when these kings and others take his wealth and go, that man merely laments. ‘The wise one’ means the intelligent person. ‘Supports’ means he supports the poor relatives who come to him by giving food, clothing, seeds, ploughs, and so on. ‘Through this’ means that person, through this support of relatives, gains renown and praise among the four assemblies, and after death, rejoices in heaven, the city of the gods.

Evaṃ [P 3.0303] mahāsatto tassa dhammaṃ desetvā dānaṃ pākatikaṃ kāretvā himavantameva gantvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Thus, the Great Being, having taught him the Dhamma and restored the practice of generosity, returned to the Himalayas, and with his meditation undiminished, he was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā [V 3.0265] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “iti kho, mahārāja, āgantukaseṭṭhi bhātu puttassa māritattā ettakaṃ kālaṃ neva puttaṃ, na dhītaraṃ alabhī”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kaniṭṭho āgantukaseṭṭhi ahosi, jeṭṭhako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, said, “Thus, great king, because the visiting merchant killed his brother’s son, he did not obtain a son or daughter for all this time.” Then he identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the younger brother was the visiting merchant, and the elder brother was I myself.”

Mayhakajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Mayhaka Jātaka, the fifth.

[391] 6. Vijjādharajātakavaṇṇanā

[391] 6. The Commentary on the Vijjādhara Jātaka

Dubbaṇṇarūpanti [M 3.0285] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto lokatthacariyaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu mahākaṇhajātake (jā. 1.12.61 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato lokatthacariyaṃ cariyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Of ugly form…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning his practice for the benefit of the world. The story will become clear in the Mahākaṇha Jātaka. Then the Teacher said, “Monks, not only now, but also in the past the Tathāgata practiced for the benefit of the world,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sakko ahosi. Tadā eko vijjādharo vijjaṃ parivattetvā aḍḍharattasamaye āgantvā bārāṇasirañño aggamahesiyā saddhiṃ aticarati, tassā paricārikāyo sañjāniṃsu. Sā sayameva rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, eko puriso aḍḍharattasamaye sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā maṃ dūsetī”ti āha. “Sakkhissasi pana kiñci saññāṇaṃ kātu”nti? “Sakkomi, devā”ti sā jātihiṅgulikapātiṃ āharāpetvā tassa purisassa rattiṃ āgantvā abhiramitvā gacchantassa piṭṭhiyaṃ pañcaṅgulikaṃ datvā pātova rañño ārocesi. Rājā manusse āṇāpesi “gacchatha, sabbadisāsu oloketvā piṭṭhiyaṃ katajātihiṅgulapañcaṅgulikapurisaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. Vijjādharopi rattiṃ anācāraṃ katvā divā susāne sūriyaṃ namassanto ekapādena tiṭṭhati. Rājapurisā taṃ disvā parivārayiṃsu. So “pākaṭaṃ me kammaṃ jāta”nti [P 3.0304] vijjaṃ parivattetvā ākāsena uppatitvā gato.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was Sakka. At that time, a certain sorcerer, after reciting a spell, would come at midnight and commit misconduct with the chief queen of the king of Benares. Her attendants became aware of this. She herself approached the king and said, “Your Majesty, a man enters the royal bedchamber at midnight and violates me.” “But are you able to make some kind of identifying mark?” “I can, Your Majesty,” she replied. She had a bowl of pure vermilion brought and, when the man came at night, enjoyed himself with her, and was leaving, she placed a five-fingered handprint on his back and reported it to the king early in the morning. The king ordered his men, “Go, search in all directions and arrest the man who has a five-fingered handprint of vermilion on his back.” The sorcerer, having committed misconduct at night, stood during the day in a cemetery worshipping the sun while standing on one foot. The king’s men saw him and surrounded him. Realizing, “My deed has become public,” he recited a spell, flew up into the sky, and escaped.

Rājā taṃ disvā āgatapurise “addasathā”ti pucchi. “Āma, addasāmā”ti. “Ko nāmeso”ti? “Pabbajito, devā”ti. “So hi rattiṃ anācāraṃ katvā divā pabbajitavesena vasati”. Rājā “ime divā samaṇavesena caritvā rattiṃ anācāraṃ karontī”ti pabbajitānaṃ kujjhitvā micchāgahaṇaṃ gahetvā “mayhaṃ vijitā ime sabbe pabbajitā palāyantu, diṭṭhadiṭṭhaṭṭhāne rājāṇaṃ karissantū”ti bheriṃ carāpesi. Tiyojanasatikā kāsiraṭṭhā palāyitvā sabbe pabbajitā aññarājadhāniyo agamiṃsu. Sakalakāsiraṭṭhe manussānaṃ ovādadāyako [V 3.0266] ekopi dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇo nāhosi. Anovādakā manussā pharusā ahesuṃ, dānasīlavimukhā matamatā yebhuyyena apāye nibbattiṃsu, sagge nibbattanakā nāma nāhesuṃ.

The king, seeing those men return, asked, “Did you see him?” “Yes, we saw him.” “What kind of person is he?” “An ascetic, Your Majesty. Indeed, he commits misconduct at night and lives in the guise of an ascetic by day.” The king, becoming angry at the ascetics, thinking, “These men walk about in the guise of recluses by day, but commit misconduct at night,” seized a wrong view and had a drum beaten with the proclamation: “Let all these ascetics flee from my kingdom. Wherever they are seen, the king’s punishment shall be carried out.” All the ascetics fled from the kingdom of Kāsi, which was three hundred yojanas in extent, and went to other royal capitals. In the entire kingdom of Kāsi, there was not even a single righteous recluse or brahmin to give moral instruction to the people. Without guidance, the people became harsh and turned away from generosity and virtue; as they died, they were mostly reborn in the states of loss; there were none who were reborn in heaven.

Sakko [M 3.0286] nave devaputte apassanto “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti āvajjetvā vijjādharaṃ nissāya bārāṇasiraññā kuddhena micchāgahaṇaṃ gahetvā pabbajitānaṃ raṭṭhā pabbājitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ṭhapetvā maṃ añño imassa rañño micchāgahaṇaṃ bhindituṃ samattho nāma natthi, rañño ca raṭṭhavāsīnañca avassayo bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā nandamūlapabbhāre paccekabuddhānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā “bhante, mayhaṃ ekaṃ mahallakaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ detha, kāsiraṭṭhaṃ pasādessāmī”ti āha. So saṅghattherameva labhi, athassa pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā taṃ purato katvā sayaṃ pacchato hutvā sirasmiṃ añjaliṃ ṭhapetvā paccekabuddhaṃ namassanto uttamarūpadharo māṇavako hutvā sakalanagarassa matthakena tikkhattuṃ vicaritvā rājadvāraṃ āgantvā ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Amaccā rañño ārocesuṃ “deva, abhirūpo māṇavako ekaṃ samaṇaṃ ānetvā rājadvāre [P 3.0305] ākāse ṭhito”ti. Rājā āsanā uṭṭhāya sīhapañjare ṭhatvā “māṇavaka, kasmā tvaṃ abhirūpo samāno etassa virūpassa samaṇassa pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā namassamāno ṭhito”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Sakka, not seeing any new devaputtas, reflected, “What could be the cause?” Upon reflecting, he understood that the king of Benares, being angry on account of the sorcerer, had seized a wrong view and banished the ascetics from the kingdom. Sakka thought, “Except for me, there is no one else capable of breaking this king’s wrong view. I will become a refuge for both the king and the inhabitants of the kingdom.” Having thought thus, he went to the Paccekabuddhas at the Nandamūla cave, paid homage, and said, “Venerable sirs, give me one elderly Paccekabuddha; I will bring faith to the kingdom of Kāsi.” He obtained the elder of the community. Then, taking the Paccekabuddha's bowl and robe, he placed the Paccekabuddha in front while he himself followed behind, with his hands reverently folded on his head, paying homage to the Paccekabuddha. Assuming the form of a supremely handsome youth, he circled over the entire city three times, then went to the palace gate and stood in the air. The ministers informed the king, “Your Majesty, a very handsome youth has brought an ascetic and is standing in the air at the palace gate.” The king rose from his seat, stood at the lion-window, and, wishing to converse with Sakka, spoke the first verse:

108.

108.

“Dubbaṇṇarūpaṃ tuvamariyavaṇṇī, purakkhatvā pañjaliko namassasi;

Seyyo nu teso udavā sarikkho, nāmaṃ parassattano cāpi brūhī”ti.

“You, of noble complexion, place this one of ugly form before you and pay homage with joined palms. Is he superior to you, or your equal? Tell me the name of the other, and your own as well.”

Tattha ariyavaṇṇīti sundararūpo. Seyyo nu tesoti eso virūpo pabbajito kiṃ nu tayā uttaritaro, udāhu sarikkho. Nāmaṃ parassattano cāpīti etassa parassa ca attano ca nāmaṃ brūhīti pucchati.

Therein, 'of noble complexion' means one of beautiful form. 'Is he superior to you?' means: Is this deformed ascetic better than you, or is he your equal? 'Tell me the name of the other and your own' means he asks for the names of the other person and himself.

Atha naṃ sakko “mahārāja, samaṇā nāma garuṭṭhāniyā, tena me nāmaṃ lapituṃ na labbhati, mayhaṃ pana te nāmaṃ kathessāmī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Sakka said to him, “Great king, ascetics occupy a position of respect. Therefore, I am not permitted to utter his name. But I will tell you my own name,” and he spoke the second verse:

109.

109.

“Na nāmagottaṃ gaṇhanti rāja, sammaggatānujjugatāna devā;

Ahañca te nāmadheyyaṃ vadāmi, sakkohamasmī tidasānamindo”ti.

“O king, the gods do not take the name and clan of those who are rightly-gone and upright. But I will tell you my name: I am Sakka, the lord of the Thirty-Three.”

Tattha [M 3.0287] sammaggatānujjugatāna devāti mahārāja, sabbasaṅkhāre yathā sabhāvasarasavasena sammasitvā [V 3.0267] aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pattattā sammaggatānaṃ, ujunā ca aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena nibbānaṃ gatattā ujugatānaṃ mahākhīṇāsavānaṃ upapattidevehi uttaritarānaṃ visuddhidevānaṃ upapattidevā nāmagottaṃ na gaṇhanti. Ahañca te nāmadheyyanti apica ahaṃ attano nāmadheyyaṃ tuyhaṃ kathemi.

Therein, 'the gods... of those who are rightly-gone and upright' means: O great king, the gods by rebirth (upapatti-deva) do not take the name and clan of those gods of purity (visuddhi-deva) who are superior to them—those great ones whose taints are destroyed, who are 'rightly-gone' because they have reached the highest fruit of Arahantship by thoroughly comprehending all conditioned things according to their true nature, and who are 'upright' because they have reached Nibbāna via the straight Eightfold Path. 'And I will tell you my name' means: moreover, I tell you my own name.

Taṃ sutvā rājā tatiyagāthāya bhikkhunamassane ānisaṃsaṃ pucchi –

Hearing that, the king asked about the benefit of paying homage to monks with the third verse:

110.

110.

“Yo disvā bhikkhuṃ caraṇūpapannaṃ, purakkhatvā pañjaliko namassati;

Pucchāmi [P 3.0306] taṃ devarājetamatthaṃ, ito cuto kiṃ labhate sukhaṃ so”ti.

“One who, seeing a monk accomplished in conduct, honors him, placing him ahead with joined palms; I ask you, O King of Gods, this matter: what happiness does he gain after passing away from here?”

Sakko catutthagāthāya kathesi –

Sakka spoke with the fourth verse:

111.

111.

“Yo disvā bhikkhuṃ caraṇūpapannaṃ, purakkhatvā pañjaliko namassati;

Diṭṭheva dhamme labhate pasaṃsaṃ, saggañca so yāti sarīrabhedā”ti.

"Whoever, seeing a bhikkhu accomplished in conduct, places him at the front and pays homage with palms joined, in this very life gains praise, and at the breaking up of the body, goes to heaven."

Tattha bhikkhunti bhinnakilesaṃ parisuddhapuggalaṃ. Caraṇūpapannanti sīlacaraṇena upetaṃ. Diṭṭheva dhammeti na kevalaṃ ito cutoyeva, imasmiṃ pana attabhāve so pasaṃsaṃ labhati, pasaṃsāsukhaṃ vindatīti.

Here, 'bhikkhu' means one whose defilements are destroyed, a person utterly pure. 'Accomplished in conduct' means endowed with virtuous conduct. 'In this very life' means not only after passing away from here, but in this very existence, he obtains praise and experiences the happiness of praise.

Rājā sakkassa kathaṃ sutvā attano micchāgahaṇaṃ bhinditvā tuṭṭhamānaso pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard Sakka’s words, the king, dispelling his own wrong view and with a delighted mind, spoke the fifth verse:

112.

112.

“Lakkhī vata me udapādi ajja, yaṃ vāsavaṃ bhūtapatiddasāma;

Bhikkhuñca disvāna tuvañca sakka, kāhāmi puññāni anappakānī”ti.

"Truly, fortune has arisen for me today, in that we have seen Vāsava, the Lord of Beings. And having seen the bhikkhu and you, O Sakka, I shall perform abundant meritorious deeds."

Tattha lakkhīti sirī, paññātipi vadanti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ajja mama tava vacanaṃ suṇantasseva kusalākusalavipākajānanapaññā udapādīti. Yanti nipātamattaṃ. Bhūtapatiddasāmāti bhūtapatiṃ addasāma.

Here, 'fortune' means glory; some also call it wisdom. This means: 'Today, as I listened to your words, the wisdom to know the results of wholesome and unwholesome deeds arose in me.' 'Yaṃ' is merely a particle. 'We saw the Lord of Beings' means we saw the ruler of beings.

Taṃ [M 3.0288] sutvā sakko paṇḍitassa thutiṃ karonto chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Sakka, desiring to praise the wise king, spoke the sixth verse:

113.

113.

“Addhā [V 3.0268] have sevitabbā sapaññā, bahussutā ye bahuṭhānacintino;

Bhikkhuñca disvāna mamañca rāja, karohi puññāni anappakānī”ti.

"Indeed, the wise should be associated with, those who are learned and capable of considering many matters. Seeing both the bhikkhu and me, O king, perform abundant meritorious deeds."

Tattha bahuṭhānacintinoti bahūni kāraṇāni cintanasamatthā.

Here, 'capable of considering many matters' means able to reflect upon many reasons.

Taṃ [P 3.0307] sutvā rājā osānagāthamāha –

Hearing this, the king spoke the final verse:

114.

114.

“Akkodhano niccapasannacitto, sabbātithīyācayogo bhavitvā;

Nihacca mānaṃ abhivādayissaṃ, sutvāna devinda subhāsitānī”ti.

"Free from anger, with a mind ever serene, being devoted to the requests of all guests; having abandoned conceit, I shall pay homage, having heard your well-spoken words, O Lord of gods."

Tattha sabbātithīyācayogo bhavitvāti sabbesaṃ atithīnaṃ āgatānaṃ āgantukānaṃ yaṃ yaṃ te yācanti, tassa tassa yutto anucchaviko bhavitvā, sabbaṃ tehi yācitayācitaṃ dadamānoti attho. Sutvāna devinda subhāsitānīti tava subhāsitāni sutvā ahaṃ evarūpo bhavissāmīti vadati.

Here, 'being devoted to the requests of all guests' means being suitable and appropriate for whatever all the visitors and guests who have arrived might ask, giving everything they repeatedly request. 'Having heard your well-spoken words, O Lord of gods' means: 'Having heard your excellent words, I shall become such a person,' he says.

Evañca pana vatvā pāsādā oruyha paccekabuddhaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Paccekabuddho ākāse pallaṅkena nisīditvā “mahārāja, vijjādharo na samaṇo, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya ‘atuccho loko, atthi dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇā’ti ñatvā dānaṃ dehi, sīlaṃ rakkha, uposathakammaṃ karohī”ti rājānaṃ ovadi. Sakkopi sakkānubhāvena ākāse ṭhatvā “ito paṭṭhāya appamattā hothā”ti nāgarānaṃ ovādaṃ datvā “palātā samaṇabrāhmaṇā āgacchantū”ti bheriṃ carāpesi. Atha te ubhopi sakaṭṭhānameva agamaṃsu. Rājā tassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni akāsi.

Having spoken thus, he descended from the palace, paid homage to the Paccekabuddha, and stood to one side. The Paccekabuddha, seated cross-legged in the air, advised the king: 'Great king, the one who was in your palace at night is a wizard, not a monk. From now on, knowing that "the world is not empty; there are righteous monks and brahmins," give alms, observe moral precepts, and keep the Uposatha.' Sakka, standing in the air by his own power, gave advice to the citizens: 'From now on, be heedful,' and had a drum beaten, announcing: 'Let the monks and brahmins who fled return.' Then both of them returned to their own abodes. The king, abiding by the advice of the Paccekabuddha, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā paccekabuddho parinibbuto, rājā ānando ahosi, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the Paccekabuddha attained final Nibbāna; the king was Ānanda, and Sakka was I myself.'

Vijjādharajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Vijjādhara Jātaka, the sixth.

[392] 7. Siṅghapupphajātakavaṇṇanā

[392] 7. The Siṅghapuppha Jātaka

Yametanti [V 3.0269][M 3.0289] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira jetavanā nikkhamitvā kosalaraṭṭhe aññataraṃ araññaṃ nissāya viharanto ekadivasaṃ padumasaraṃ [P 3.0308] otaritvā supupphitapadumaṃ disvā adhovāte ṭhatvā upasiṅghi. Atha naṃ tasmiṃ vane adhivatthā devatā “mārisa, tvaṃ gandhatheno nāma, idaṃ te ekaṃ theyyaṅga”nti saṃvejesi. So tāya saṃvejito puna jetavanaṃ āgantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nisinno “kahaṃ bhikkhu nivutthosī”ti puṭṭho “asukavanasaṇḍe nāma, tattha ca maṃ devatā evaṃ nāma saṃvejesī”ti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “na kho bhikkhu pupphaṃ upasiṅghanto tvameva devatāya saṃvejito, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi saṃvejitapubbā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, who is the teacher of the world including the gods, spoke this Siṅghapuppha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Yametaṃ', while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk. It is said that this monk, having left Jetavana and dwelling near a certain forest in the Kosala country, one day descended into a lotus pond and, seeing a fully blossomed lotus, stood downwind and sniffed its scent. Then a deity dwelling in that forest startled him: 'Sir, your conduct is the conduct of a fragrance thief.' Stirred by that deity, he returned to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down. When asked, 'Monk, where have you been staying?' he replied, 'In such-and-named forest grove, and there a deity startled me in this way.' Then the Teacher said, 'Monk, it was not only you who were startled by a deity for sniffing a flower; the wise of old were also startled before.' And being requested, he related the past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ kāsikagāme brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ uggahitasippo aparabhāge isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā ekaṃ padumasaraṃ nissāya upavasanto ekadivasaṃ saraṃ otaritvā supupphitapadumaṃ upasiṅghamāno aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ ekā devadhītā rukkhakkhandhavivare ṭhatvā saṃvejayamānā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a village in Kāsi. Having come of age and mastered the arts at Takkasilā, he later went forth into the ascetic life and dwelt near a lotus pond. One day he descended into the pond and stood sniffing a fully blossomed lotus. Then a certain deity, standing in the hollow of a tree trunk and desiring to startle him, spoke the first verse:

115.

115.

“Yametaṃ vārijaṃ pupphaṃ, adinnaṃ upasiṅghasi;

Ekaṅgametaṃ theyyānaṃ, gandhathenosi mārisā”ti.

"This water-born flower which you sniff, though it was not given to you; this is one aspect of theft. You are a fragrance thief, dear sir."

Tattha ekaṅgametanti ekakoṭṭhāso esa.

Here, 'this is one aspect' means this is one part or category of theft.

Tato bodhisatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:

116.

116.

“Na harāmi na bhañjāmi, ārā siṅghāmi vārijaṃ;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, gandhathenoti vuccatī”ti.

"I do not carry it away, I do not break it; from afar I sniff the water-born flower. Then for what reason am I called a fragrance thief?"

Tattha ārā siṅghāmīti dūre ṭhito ghāyāmi. Vaṇṇenāti kāraṇena.

Here, 'from afar I sniff' means I smell it while standing at a distance. 'By what reason' means for what cause.

Tasmiṃ [M 3.0290] khaṇe eko puriso tasmiṃ sare bhisāni ceva khaṇati, puṇḍarīkāni ca bhañjati[V 3.0270]. Bodhisatto taṃ disvā “maṃ ārā ṭhatvā upasiṅghantaṃ ‘coro’ti vadasi, etaṃ purisaṃ [P 3.0309] kasmā na bhaṇasī”ti tāya saddhiṃ sallapanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

At that moment, a certain man was digging up lotus roots and breaking white lotuses in that pond. Seeing that man, the Bodhisatta, wishing to converse with the deity, spoke the third verse: 'You call me a thief for sniffing while standing afar without taking anything; why do you not speak to that man?'

117.

117.

“Yoyaṃ bhisāni khaṇati, puṇḍarīkāni bhañjati;

Evaṃ ākiṇṇakammanto, kasmā eso na vuccatī”ti.

"This man who digs up lotus roots and breaks white lotuses—engaged in such crude actions, why is he not rebuked?"

Tattha ākiṇṇakammantoti kakkhaḷakammanto dāruṇakammanto.

Here, 'engaged in such crude actions' means one whose deeds are harsh and cruel.

Athassa avacanakāraṇaṃ ācikkhantī devatā catutthapañcamagāthā abhāsi –

Then, the deity, wishing to explain the reason for not speaking to that man, spoke the fourth and fifth verses:

118.

118.

“Ākiṇṇaluddo puriso, dhāticelaṃva makkhito;

Tasmiṃ me vacanaṃ natthi, tañcārahāmi vattave.

A man filled with cruelty is like a nurse’s cloth smeared with filth; I have no word for him, but it is you whom I ought to address.

119.

119.

“Anaṅgaṇassa posassa, niccaṃ sucigavesino;

Vālaggamattaṃ pāpassa, abbhāmattaṃva khāyatī”ti.

To a person free from blemish, who is always seeking purity, an evil even the size of a hair’s tip appears as large as a cloud.

Tattha dhāticelaṃvāti kheḷasiṅghāṇikamuttagūthamakkhitaṃ dhātidāsiyā nivatthacelaṃ viya ayaṃ pāpamakkhitoyeva, tena kāraṇena tasmiṃ mama vacanaṃ natthi. Tañcārahāmīti samaṇā pana ovādakkhamā honti piyasīlā, tasmā taṃ appamattakampi ayuttaṃ karontaṃ vattuṃ arahāmi samaṇāti. Anaṅgaṇassāti niddosassa tumhādisassa. Abbhāmattaṃva khāyatīti mahāmeghappamāṇaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti, idāni kasmā evarūpaṃ dosaṃ abbohārikaṃ karosīti.

In this context, 'like a nurse’s cloth' means that just as a nursemaid’s garment is smeared with spit, mucus, urine, and excrement, so is this man smeared with evil; for that reason, I have no word for him. 'But you I ought to address' means that ascetics are receptive to advice and love virtue; therefore, I ought to speak to you, O ascetic, even when you do something slightly improper. 'To one unstained' means to one who is faultless, like yourself. 'Appears as large as a cloud' means it appears as large as a great rain cloud. Why do you now commit such a fault that would be considered negligible for others?

Tāya pana saṃvejito bodhisatto saṃvegappatto chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Stirred by her, the Bodhisatta, filled with a sense of urgency, spoke the sixth verse:

120.

120.

“Addhā maṃ yakkha jānāsi, atho maṃ anukampasi;

Punapi yakkha vajjāsi, yadā passasi edisa”nti.

Truly, O Yakkha, you know me, and you also have compassion for me. Speak to me again, Yakkha, whenever you see such a fault.

Tattha yakkhāti devataṃ ālapati. Vajjāsīti vadeyyāsi. Yadā passasi edisanti yadā mama evarūpaṃ dosaṃ passasi, tadā evaṃ mama vadeyyāsīti vadati.

Here, 'yakkha' is an address to the deity. 'Vajjāsi' means 'you should speak'. 'Whenever you see such a thing' means 'when you see such a fault in me, then you should speak to me thus,' he says.

Athassa [V 3.0271][M 3.0291] sā devadhītā sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then that divine maiden spoke the seventh verse to him:

121.

121.

“Neva taṃ upajīvāmi, napi te bhatakāmhase;

Tvameva bhikkhu jāneyya, yena gaccheyya suggati”nti.

I do not live dependent on you, nor am I your servant. You yourself, O Bhikkhu, should know the way by which one goes to a happy destination.

Tattha [P 3.0310] bhatakāmhaseti tava bhatihatā kammakarāpi na homa. Kiṃkāraṇā taṃ sabbakālaṃ rakkhamānā vicarissāmāti dīpeti. Yena gaccheyyāti bhikkhu yena kammena tvaṃ sugatiṃ gaccheyyāsi, tvameva taṃ jāneyyāsīti.

Here, 'nor are we your hired servants' means 'we are not your hired laborers'. She indicates, 'For what reason should we wander about always protecting you?' 'By what means one may go' means 'O monk, by whatever action you might go to a good destination, you yourself should know that.'

Evaṃ sā tassa ovādaṃ datvā attano vimānameva paviṭṭhā. Bodhisattopi jhānaṃ nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus, having given him that advice, she entered her own celestial mansion. The Bodhisatta, having developed jhāna, became destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, declared the Truths and connected the birth story; at the conclusion of the Truths, that monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā devadhītā uppalavaṇṇā ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the divine maiden was Uppalavaṇṇā, and the ascetic was I myself.

Siṅghapupphajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Sniffing Flower Jātaka, the seventh.

[393] 8. Vighāsādajātakavaṇṇanā

[393] 8. The Commentary on the Vighāsāda Jātaka

Susukhaṃ vata jīvantīti idaṃ satthā pubbārāme viharanto keḷisīlake bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Tesu hi mahāmoggallānattherena pāsādaṃ kampetvā saṃvejitesu dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū tesaṃ aguṇaṃ kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepete keḷisīlakāyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at the Pubbārāma, spoke this, beginning with 'Most happily indeed they live,' concerning some monks who were fond of play. For after the Elder Mahāmoggallāna had shaken the palace and stirred them to spiritual urgency, the monks sat in the Dhamma hall speaking of their faults. The Teacher arrived and asked, 'For what discussion, monks, are you now gathered?' When they replied, 'For such and such,' he said, 'Monks, not only now, but in the past also they were fond of play,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sakko ahosi. Atha aññatarasmiṃ kāsikagāme satta bhātaro kāmesu dosaṃ disvā nikkhamitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā majjhāraññe vasantā yoge yogaṃ akatvā kāyadaḷhībahulā hutvā nānappakāraṃ kīḷaṃ [V 3.0272] kīḷantā [M 3.0292] cariṃsu. Sakko devarājā “ime saṃvejessāmī”ti suko hutvā tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā ekasmiṃ rukkhe nilīyitvā te saṃvejento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka. Then, in a certain village of the Kāsī country, seven brothers, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, went forth and were ordained as ascetics. Dwelling in the middle of the forest, they did not apply themselves to spiritual practice, but became intent on strengthening their bodies and wandered about playing various kinds of games. Sakka, the king of devas, thinking, 'I will stir them to spiritual urgency,' took the form of a parrot, went to their dwelling place, and, perching on a tree, spoke the first verse to stir them:

122.

122.

“Susukhaṃ [P 3.0311] vata jīvanti, ye janā vighāsādino;

Diṭṭheva dhamme pāsaṃsā, samparāye ca suggatī”ti.

Most happily indeed live those people who eat remnants; they are praised in this very life, and in the next, theirs is a happy destination.

Tattha vighāsādinoti bhuttātirekaṃ bhuñjante sandhāyāha. Diṭṭheva dhammeti ye evarūpā, te diṭṭheva dhamme pāsaṃsā, samparāye ca tesaṃ sugati hoti, sagge uppajjantīti adhippāyena vadati.

Here, 'those who eat remnants' is said with reference to those who eat the remainder of a meal. 'In this very life' means that such people are praised in this very life, and in the next, they will have a happy destination; he speaks with the intention that they are reborn in heaven.

Atha tesu eko tassa vacanaṃ sutvā avasese āmantetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then one of them, having heard his words, addressed the others and spoke the second verse:

123.

123.

“Sukassa bhāsamānassa, na nisāmetha paṇḍitā;

Idaṃ suṇātha sodariyā, amhevāyaṃ pasaṃsatī”ti.

O wise ones, do you not hear the parrot speaking? Listen to this, brothers: he is praising none other than us!

Tattha bhāsamānassāti mānusikāya vācāya bhaṇantassa. Na nisāmethāti na suṇātha. Idaṃ suṇāthāti idamassa vacanaṃ suṇātha. Sodariyāti samāne udare vutthabhāvena te ālapanto āha.

Here, 'of one speaking' means of one speaking with human speech. 'Do not listen' means do not hearken. 'Listen to this' means listen to this word of his. 'Brothers' means he addressed them as having dwelt in the same womb.

Atha ne paṭikkhipanto suko tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the parrot, rejecting them, spoke the third verse:

124.

124.

“Nāhaṃ tumhe pasaṃsāmi, kuṇapādā suṇātha me;

Ucchiṭṭhabhojino tumhe, na tumhe vighāsādino”ti.

I do not praise you, O carrion-eaters; listen to me! You are eaters of scraps; you are not eaters of remnants.

Tattha kuṇapādāti kuṇapakhādakāti te ālapati.

Here, 'corpse-eaters' means 'carrion-eaters'; thus he addresses them.

Te tassa vacanaṃ sutvā sabbepi catutthaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

Hearing his words, they all spoke the fourth verse:

125.

125.

“Sattavassā pabbajitā, majjhāraññe sikhaṇḍino;

Vighāseneva yāpentā, mayañce bhoto gārayhā;

Ke nu bhoto pasaṃsiyā”ti.

Having been gone forth for seven years, living as ascetics with topknots in the middle of the forest, we sustain ourselves on remnants. If we are to be censured by you, sir, then who is to be praised by you?

Tattha [V 3.0273] sikhaṇḍinoti cūḷāya samannāgatā. Vighāsenevāti ettakaṃ kālaṃ satta vassāni sīhabyagghavighāseneva yāpentā yadi bhoto gārayhā, atha ke nu te pasaṃsiyāti.

Here, 'with topknots' means endowed with a topknot. 'Sustaining ourselves on remnants' means that if, for such a long time—for seven years—sustaining yourselves on what is left over by lions and tigers, you are to be censured by you, sir, then who indeed is to be praised by you?

Te [M 3.0293] lajjāpento mahāsatto pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

To shame them, the Great Being spoke the fifth verse:

126.

126.

“Tumhe sīhānaṃ byagghānaṃ, vāḷānañcāvasiṭṭhakaṃ;

Ucchiṭṭheneva yāpentā, maññivho vighāsādino”ti.

You sustain yourselves on the leavings of lions, tigers, and other beasts of prey; sustaining yourselves on mere scraps, do you consider yourselves to be 'eaters of remnants'?

Tattha vāḷānañcāvasiṭṭhakanti sesavāḷamigānañca avasiṭṭhakaṃ ucchiṭṭhabhojanaṃ.

Here, 'vāḷānañcāvasiṭṭhakaṃ' means the leftover food of other beasts of prey.

Taṃ [P 3.0312] sutvā tāpasā “sace mayaṃ na vighāsādā, atha ke carahi te vighāsādā”ti? Atha tesaṃ so tamatthaṃ ācikkhanto chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the ascetics said, "If we are not eaters of remnants, then who indeed are those eaters of remnants?" Then, explaining the matter to them, he spoke the sixth verse:

127.

127.

“Ye brāhmaṇassa samaṇassa, aññassa vā vanibbino;

Datvāva sesaṃ bhuñjanti, te janā vighāsādino”ti.

Those people who, having given to a brahmin, an ascetic, or another beggar, eat what remains, are eaters of remnants.

Tattha vanibbinoti taṃ taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ yācanakassa. Evaṃ te lajjāpetvā mahāsatto sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

Here, 'vanibbino' refers to one who begs for various things. Thus, having shamed the ascetics, the Great Being went to his own place in Tāvatiṃsa.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā satta bhātaro ime keḷisīlakā bhikkhū ahesuṃ, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the seven brothers were these monks of frivolous habit, and Sakka was none other than myself.'

Vighāsādajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Vighāsāda Jātaka, the Eighth.

[394] 9. Vaṭṭakajātakavaṇṇanā

[394] 9. Commentary on the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka

Paṇītanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ lolabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu lolo”ti pucchitvā “āma, bhante”ti vutte “na kho bhikkhu idāneva lolo, pubbepi tvaṃ loloyeva, lolatāya pana bārāṇasiyaṃ hatthigavāssapurisakuṇapehi [V 3.0274] atitto ‘ito uttaritaraṃ labhissāmī’ti araññaṃ paviṭṭhosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this discourse beginning with 'Paṇītaṃ' concerning a certain greedy bhikkhu. The Teacher asked him, 'Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are greedy?' When he replied, 'Yes, venerable sir,' the Teacher said, 'Bhikkhu, you are not greedy only now; in the past, too, you were greedy. Due to your greed, being unsatisfied with the corpses of elephants, cattle, and men in Bārāṇasī, thinking, "I will get more than this," you entered the forest.' Thus, he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto vaṭṭakayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā araññe lūkhatiṇabījāhāro vasi. Tadā bārāṇasiyaṃ eko lolakāko hatthikuṇapādīhi atitto “ito uttaritaraṃ labhissāmī”ti araññaṃ pavisitvā phalāphalaṃ khādanto bodhisattaṃ [M 3.0294] disvā “ayaṃ vaṭṭako ativiya thūlasarīro, madhuraṃ gocaraṃ khādati maññe, etassa gocaraṃ pucchitvā taṃ khāditvā ahampi thūlo bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā bodhisattassa uparibhāge sākhāya nilīyitvā bodhisattaṃ pucchi “bho vaṭṭaka, kiṃ nāma paṇītāhāraṃ bhuñjasi, thūlasarīro ahosī”ti? Bodhisatto [P 3.0313] tena pucchito tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karonto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a quail and lived in the forest, feeding on dry grass seeds. At that time, a greedy crow in Bārāṇasī, unsatisfied with elephant carcasses and the like, thinking, 'I will find something even better than this,' entered the forest. While eating various fruits, he saw the Bodhisatta and thought, 'This quail is extremely plump—he must be eating delicious food. If I ask him about his food and eat it, I too will become plump.' So, perching on a branch above the Bodhisatta, he asked, 'O quail, what exquisite food do you eat that you are so plump?' The Bodhisatta, thus questioned, exchanged courtesies with him and then spoke the first verse:

128.

128.

“Paṇītaṃ bhuñjase bhattaṃ, sappitelañca mātula;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, kiso tvamasi vāyasā”ti.

You eat fine food, uncle, with ghee and oil; but by what reason, O crow, are you so thin?

Tattha bhattanti manussānaṃ bhojananiyāmena paṭiyāditabhattaṃ. Mātulāti taṃ piyasamudācārena ālapati. Kisoti appamaṃsalohito.

Here, 'bhattaṃ' refers to a meal prepared according to the customary way of humans. 'Mātula' (uncle) addresses him with affectionate familiarity. 'Kiso' means having little flesh and blood.

Tassa vacanaṃ sutvā kāko tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing his words, the crow spoke these three verses:

129.

129.

“Amittamajjhe vasato, tesu āmisamesato;

Niccaṃ ubbiggahadayassa, kuto kākassa daḷhiyaṃ.

Living amidst enemies, seeking food among them, with a heart ever anxious—how can a crow be stout?

130.

130.

“Niccaṃ ubbegino kākā, dhaṅkā pāpena kammunā;

Laddho piṇḍo na pīṇeti, kiso tenasmi vaṭṭaka.

Crows are always anxious, these raucous birds, because of their evil deeds; the food obtained through theft does not satisfy, and for that reason I am thin, O quail.

131.

131.

“Lūkhāni tiṇabījāni, appasnehāni bhuñjasi;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, thūlo tvamasi vaṭṭakā”ti.

You eat dry grass seeds, lacking in richness; but for what reason, O quail, are you so plump?

Tattha daḷhiyanti evarūpassa mayhaṃ kākassa kuto daḷhībhāvo, kuto thūlanti attho. Ubbeginoti [V 3.0275] ubbegavanto. Dhaṅkāti kākānameva nāmaṃ. Pāpena kammunā laddhoti kākena manussasantakavilumpanasaṅkhātena pāpena kammena laddho piṇḍo. Na pīṇetīti na tappeti. Tenasmīti tena kāraṇenāhaṃ kiso asmi. Appasnehānīti mandojāni. Idaṃ kāko bodhisattaṃ “paṇītabhojanaṃ khādatī”ti saññī hutvāpi vaṭṭakānaṃ gahitagocaraṃ pucchanto āha.

Here, 'daḷhiyaṃ' means: How can there be robustness or stoutness for a crow like me? 'Ubbegino' means full of anxiety. 'Dhaṅkā' is a name for crows. 'Pāpena kammunā laddho' refers to food obtained through evil deeds, such as the crow's act of plundering human food. 'Na pīṇeti' means it does not satisfy or fulfill. 'Tenasmi' means for that reason I am thin. 'Appasnehāni' means lacking in nutritive essence. The crow said this while asking about the quail's food, even though he perceived the Bodhisatta might be eating 'fine food'.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto attano thūlabhāvakāraṇaṃ kathento imā gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta, explaining the reason for his own plumpness, spoke these verses:

132.

132.

“Appicchā [M 3.0295] appacintāya, adūragamanena ca;

Laddhāladdhena yāpento, thūlo tenasmi vāyasa.

With few desires, with little concern, and by not going far; living on whatever is obtained, for that reason I am plump, O crow.

133.

133.

“Appicchassa hi posassa, appacintasukhassa ca;

Susaṅgahitamānassa, vuttī susamudānayā”ti.

For a person of few desires, who has the happiness of little concern, whose measure of food is well-restrained, their livelihood is easily maintained.

Tattha appicchāti āhāresu appicchatāya nittaṇhatāya, kevalaṃ sarīrayāpanavaseneva āhārāharaṇatāyāti attho. Appacintāyāti “ajja kahaṃ āhāraṃ [P 3.0314] labhissāmi, sve kaha”nti evaṃ āhāracintāya abhāvena. Adūragamanena cāti “asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne madhuraṃ labhissāmī”ti cintetvā avidūragamanena ca. Laddhāladdhenāti lūkhaṃ vā hotu paṇītaṃ vā, yaṃ laddhaṃ, teneva. Thūlo tenasmīti tena catubbidhena kāraṇena thūlo asmi. Vāyasāti kākaṃ ālapati. Appacintasukhassāti āhāracintārahitānaṃ appacintānamariyānaṃ sukhaṃ assatthīti appacintasukho, tassa tādisena sukhena samannāgatassa. Susaṅgahitamānassāti “ettakaṃ bhuñjitvā jīrāpetuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti evaṃ suṭṭhu saṅgahitāhāramānassa. Vuttī susamudānayāti evarūpassa puggalassa jīvitavutti sukhena sakkā samudānetuṃ susamudānayā sunibbattiyā.

Here, 'appicchā' means having little desire for food and no craving, taking food only to sustain the body. 'Appacintāya' means the absence of worry such as, 'Where shall I find food today or tomorrow?' 'Adūragamanena ca' means not traveling far with the thought, 'I shall find delicious food in such and such a place.' 'Laddhāladdhena' means with whatever is obtained, whether coarse or refined. 'Thūlo tenasmi' means I am plump due to these four reasons. 'Vāyasa' addresses the crow. 'Appacintasukhassa' refers to one who possesses the happiness of few concerns, a happiness of noble ones free from food-related worry. 'Susaṅgahitamānassa' means one who maintains a well-measured intake, thinking, 'Having eaten this much, I can digest it.' 'Vuttī susamudānayā' means the livelihood of such a person is easily obtained and maintained.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne lolabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher delivered this discourse, revealed the Truths, and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā kāko lolabhikkhu ahosi, vaṭṭako pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the crow was the greedy bhikkhu, and the quail was none other than myself.

Vaṭṭakajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, the Ninth.

[395] 10. Pārāvatajātakavaṇṇanā

[395] 10. Commentary on the Pārāvata Jātaka

Cirassaṃ [V 3.0276] vata passāmīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto lolabhikkhuṃyeva ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this discourse beginning with 'Cirassaṃ vata passāmi' concerning that same greedy bhikkhu. The story of the present occasion is as mentioned above.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto pārāvato hutvā bārāṇasiseṭṭhino mahānase nīḷapacchiyaṃ vasati. Kākopi [M 3.0296] tena saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ katvā tattheva vasatīti sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Bhattakārako kākapattāni luñcitvā piṭṭhena taṃ makkhetvā ekaṃ kapālakhaṇḍaṃ vijjhitvā kaṇṭhe piḷandhitvā pacchiyaṃ pakkhipi. Bodhisatto araññato āgantvā taṃ disvā parihāsaṃ karonto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a pigeon and lived in the kitchen of the treasurer of Bārāṇasī, in a nest-basket. A crow, having established an intimacy with him, lived in that very same place—the details are to be understood in full. The cook plucked the crow’s feathers, smeared him with flour, pierced a piece of a potsherd, hung it around his neck, and placed him back in the basket. When the Bodhisatta returned from the forest and saw him, wishing to mock him, he spoke the first verse:

134.

134.

“Cirassaṃ vata passāmi, sahāyaṃ maṇidhārinaṃ;

Sukatā massukuttiyā, sobhate vata me sakhā”ti.

“Truly, after a long time, I see my friend who wears a jewel! With his beard so well-trimmed, my friend truly looks splendid.”

Tattha massukuttiyāti imāya massukiriyāya.

In this context, 'massukuttiyā' means by this act of grooming the beard.

Taṃ [P 3.0315] sutvā kāko dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the crow spoke the second verse:

135.

135.

“Parūḷhakacchanakhalomo, ahaṃ kammesu byāvaṭo;

Cirassaṃ nhāpitaṃ laddhā, lomaṃ taṃ ajja hārayi”nti.

“With overgrown armpit hair, nails, and body hair, I was occupied with my duties; having found a barber after a long time, I had that hair removed today.”

Tattha ahaṃ kammesu byāvaṭoti ahaṃ samma pārāvata, rājakammesu byāvaṭo okāsaṃ alabhanto parūḷhakacchanakhalomo ahosinti vadati. Ajja hārayinti ajja hāresiṃ.

In this context, 'I was occupied with my duties' means: he says, 'Friend pigeon, being occupied with royal duties and finding no opportunity, I became one with overgrown armpit hair, nails, and body hair.' 'I had it removed today' means I caused it to be removed today.

Tato bodhisatto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:

136.

136.

“Yaṃ nu lomaṃ ahāresi, dullabhaṃ laddha kappakaṃ;

Atha kiñcarahi te samma, kaṇṭhe kiṇikiṇāyatī”ti.

“Since you have had your hair removed, having found a barber who is hard to find; why then, friend, is there a tinkling at your neck?”

Tassattho [V 3.0277] – yaṃ tāva dullabhaṃ kappakaṃ labhitvā lomaṃ harāpesi, taṃ harāpaya, atha kiñcarahi te vayassa idaṃ kaṇṭhe kiṇikiṇāyatīti.

The meaning is: Since you, having found a barber so hard to come by, had your hair removed—let that be—but then, my friend, why is this thing tinkling at your neck?

Tato kāko dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the crow uttered two verses:

137.

137.

“Manussasukhumālānaṃ, maṇi kaṇṭhesu lambati;

Tesāhaṃ anusikkhāmi, mā tvaṃ maññi davā kataṃ.

“Jewels hang from the necks of delicate humans; I am imitating them. Do not think this was done in jest.

138.

138.

“Sacepimaṃ pihayasi, massukuttiṃ sukāritaṃ;

Kārayissāmi te samma, maṇiñcāpi dadāmi te”ti.

“If you, too, desire this well-fashioned grooming, my friend, I will have it done for you, and I will give you a jewel as well.”

Tattha maṇīti evarūpānaṃ manussānaṃ ekaṃ maṇiratanaṃ kaṇṭhesu lambati. Tesāhanti tesaṃ ahaṃ. Mā tvaṃ maññīti tvaṃ pana “etaṃ mayā davā kata”nti [M 3.0297] mā maññi. Sacepimaṃ pihayasīti sace imaṃ mama kataṃ massukuttiṃ tvaṃ icchasi.

In this context, 'maṇi' means that a single precious jewel hangs from the necks of such humans. 'Tesāhaṃ' means I imitate them. 'Mā tvaṃ maññi' means: you, however, do not think, 'This was done by me in jest.' 'Sacepimaṃ pihayasi' means if you desire this grooming of the beard that has been done to me.

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Bodhisatta spoke the sixth verse:

139.

139.

“Tvaññeva maṇinā channo, sukatāya ca massuyā;

Āmanta kho taṃ gacchāmi, piyaṃ me tavadassana”nti.

“You alone are suited for this jewel and for the well-fashioned beard; having taken leave of you, I go, for the sight of you is dear to me.”

Tattha maṇināti maṇino, ayameva vā pāṭho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – samma vāyasa, tvaññeva imassa maṇino anucchaviko imissā ca sukatāya massuyā[P 3.0316], mama pana tava adassanameva piyaṃ, tasmā taṃ āmantayitvā gacchāmīti.

In this context, for 'maṇinā', the reading is 'maṇino'. This is what is meant: 'Friend crow, you alone are worthy of this jewel and this well-fashioned beard; as for me, however, it is precisely not seeing you that is dear. Therefore, having taken leave of you, I go.'

Evañca pana vatvā bodhisatto uppatitvā aññattha gato. Kāko tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ patto.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta flew up and went elsewhere. The crow met his death right there.

Satthā [V 3.0278] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne lolabhikkhu anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā kāko lolabhikkhu ahosi, pārāvato pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having brought forward this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the frivolous monk was established in the fruit of Non-returning. At that time, the crow was the frivolous monk, but the pigeon was I myself.

Pārāvatajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Tenth, the Pārāvata Jātaka.

Kharaputtavaggo dutiyo niṭṭhito.

The Kharaputta Chapter, the second, is finished.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

The Summary of the Jātakas:

Avāriyaṃ setaketu, darīmukhañca neru ca;

Āsaṅkamigālopañca, kāḷakaṇṇī ca kukkuṭaṃ.

Avāriya, Setaketu, Darīmukha, and Neru; Āsaṅka, Miga, and Alopa, Kāḷakaṇṇī, and Kukkuṭa.

Dhammadhajañca nandiyaṃ, kharaputtaṃ sūci ceva;

Tuṇḍilaṃ soṇṇakakkaṭaṃ, mayhakaṃ vijjādharañceva.

Dhammadhaja and Nandiya, Kharaputta and Sūci; Tuṇḍila, Soṇṇakakkaṭa, Mayhaka, and Vijjādhara.

Siṅghapupphaṃ vighāsādaṃ, vaṭṭakañca pārāvataṃ;

Saṅgāyiṃsu mahātherā, chakke vīsati jātake.

Siṅghapuppha, Vighāsāda, Vaṭṭaka, and Pārāvata; the great elders compiled twenty Jātakas in the Book of Sixes.

Chakkanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Book of Sixes is finished.

7. Sattakanipāto

7. The Book of Sevens

1. Kukkuvaggo

1. 1. The Kukku Chapter

[396] 1. Kukkujātakavaṇṇanā

[396] 1. 1. The Kukku Jātaka

Diyaḍḍhakukkūti [V 3.0279][P 3.0317][M 3.0298] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto rājovādaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu tesakuṇajātake (jā. 2.17.1 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

‘Diyaḍḍhakukkū’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning an admonition to a king. The story of the present will be explained in the Tesakuṇa Jātaka (Jā. 2.17.1 ff.).

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa atthadhammānusāsako amacco ahosi. Rājā agatigamane patiṭṭhāya adhammena rajjaṃ kāresi, janapadaṃ pīḷetvā dhanameva saṃhari. Bodhisatto rājānaṃ ovaditukāmo ekaṃ upamaṃ upadhārento vicarati, rañño uyyāne vāsāgāraṃ vippakataṃ hoti aniṭṭhitacchadanaṃ, dārukaṇṇikaṃ āropetvā gopānasiyo pavesitamattā honti. Rājā kīḷanatthāya uyyānaṃ gantvā tattha vicaritvā taṃ gehaṃ pavisitvā ullokento kaṇṇikamaṇḍalaṃ disvā attano uparipatanabhayena nikkhamitvā bahi ṭhito puna oloketvā “kiṃ nu kho nissāya kaṇṇikā ṭhitā, kiṃ nissāya gopānasiyo”ti cintetvā bodhisattaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his minister who advised him on his welfare and the Dhamma. The king, established in the four wrong courses of action, ruled unrighteously, and by oppressing the kingdom, he amassed wealth. The Bodhisatta, desiring to admonish the king, went about looking for a parable. In the king’s park, a garden house was being built, its roof unfinished; the roof-hub had been raised and the rafters had only just been fitted in. The king, having gone to the park for amusement, wandered about and entered that building. Looking up, he saw the circular roof-hub and, fearing it might fall on him, he went out and stood outside. Looking again, he thought, 'What supports the roof-hub? What supports the rafters?' Then, questioning the Bodhisatta, he spoke the first verse:

1.

1.

“Diyaḍḍhakukkū [P 3.0318] udayena kaṇṇikā, vidatthiyo aṭṭha parikkhipanti naṃ;

Sā siṃsapā, sāramayā apheggukā, kuhiṃ ṭhitā upparito na dhaṃsatī”ti.

“One and a half kukkus in height is the roof-hub; eight spans in circumference. It is of siṃsapā wood, made of heartwood and free of sapwood. On what is it supported, that it does not fall from above?”

Tattha diyaḍḍhakukkūti diyaḍḍharatanā. Udayenāti uccattena. Parikkhipanti nanti taṃ panetaṃ aṭṭha vidatthiyo parikkhipanti, parikkhepato aṭṭhavidatthipamāṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kuhiṃ ṭhitāti kattha patiṭṭhitā hutvā. Na dhaṃsatīti na patati.

In this context, 'diyaḍḍhakukkū' means one and a half cubits. 'Udayena' means in height. 'Parikkhipanti naṃ' means eight spans encircle it; it is meant that it is eight spans in circumference. 'Kuhiṃ ṭhitā' means where is it established? 'Na dhaṃsatī' means it does not fall.

Taṃ [V 3.0280][M 3.0299] sutvā bodhisatto “laddhā dāni me rañño ovādatthāya upamā”ti cintetvā imā gāthā āha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta thought, 'Now I have found a simile for advising the king,' and he spoke these verses:

2.

2.

“Yā tiṃsati sāramayā anujjukā, parikiriya gopānasiyo samaṃ ṭhitā;

Tāhi susaṅgahitā balasā pīḷitā, samaṃ ṭhitā upparito na dhaṃsati.

“The thirty rafters, made of heartwood and curved, stand evenly, encircling it. Firmly held by them and pressed by their force, the hub stands evenly and does not fall from above.”

3.

3.

“Evampi mittehi daḷhehi paṇḍito, abhejjarūpehi sucīhi mantibhi;

Susaṅgahīto siriyā na dhaṃsati, gopānasībhāravahāva kaṇṇikā”ti.

“Even so, a wise man, when well-supported by firm friends and by pure, unbreakable advisors, does not fall from his prosperity, just like the roof-hub that bears the weight of the rafters.”

Tattha yā tiṃsati sāramayāti yā etā sārarukkhamayā tiṃsati gopānasiyo. Parikiriyāti parivāretvā. Samaṃ ṭhitāti samabhāgena ṭhitā. Balasā pīḷitāti tāhi tāhi gopānasīhi balena pīḷitā suṭṭhu saṅgahitā ekābaddhā hutvā. Paṇḍitoti ñāṇasampanno rājā. Sucīhīti sucisamācārehi kalyāṇamittehi. Mantibhīti mantakusalehi. Gopānasībhāravahāva kaṇṇikāti yathā gopānasīnaṃ bhāraṃ vahamānā kaṇṇikā na dhaṃsati na patati, evaṃ rājāpi vuttappakārehi mantīhi abhijjahadayehi susaṅgahito sirito na dhaṃsati na patati na parihāyati.

Therein, ‘the thirty made of heartwood’ refers to those thirty rafters made of heartwood. ‘Parikiriya’ means ‘having encircled.’ ‘Samaṃ ṭhitā’ means ‘standing evenly.’ ‘Balasā pīḷitā’ means ‘pressed with force by those various rafters, well-supported, having become bound as one.’ ‘Paṇḍito’ means ‘the king, endowed with wisdom.’ ‘Sucīhi’ means ‘with good friends of pure conduct.’ ‘Mantibhī’ means ‘with those skilled in counsel.’ ‘Like the pinnacle bearing the load of the rafters’ means: just as the pinnacle bearing the load of the rafters does not fall or collapse, so too the king—when well-supported by the aforementioned counselors who have unwavering hearts—does not fall, collapse, or decline from his glory.

Rājā [P 3.0319] bodhisatte kathenteyeva attano kiriyaṃ sallakkhetvā kaṇṇikāya asati gopānasiyo na tiṭṭhanti, gopānasīhi asaṅgahitā kaṇṇikā na tiṭṭhati, gopānasīsu bhijjantīsu kaṇṇikā patati, evameva adhammiko rājā attano mittāmacce ca balakāye ca brāhmaṇagahapatike ca asaṅgaṇhanto tesu bhijjantesu tehi asaṅgahito issariyā dhaṃsati, raññā nāma dhammikena bhavitabbanti. Athassa tasmiṃ khaṇe paṇṇākāratthāya mātuluṅgaṃ āhariṃsu. Rājā “sahāya, imaṃ mātuluṅgaṃ khādā”ti bodhisattaṃ āha. Bodhisatto taṃ gahetvā “mahārāja, imaṃ khādituṃ ajānantā tittakaṃ vā karonti ambilaṃ vā, jānantā [M 3.0300] pana paṇḍitā tittakaṃ hāretvā ambilaṃ anīharitvā mātuluṅgarasaṃ anāsetvāva khādantī”ti rañño imāya upamāya dhanasaṅgharaṇūpāyaṃ dassento dve gāthā abhāsi –

While the Bodhisatta was speaking, the king reflected on his own actions: "Without the pinnacle, the rafters do not stay in place; without the rafters being held together, the pinnacle does not stay; when the rafters break, the pinnacle falls. Similarly, an unrighteous king, failing to support his friends, ministers, army, Brahmins, and householders—when they are divided, being unsupported by them, he falls from his sovereignty. A king must indeed be righteous." At that moment, they brought a citron as a gift. The king said to the Bodhisatta, "Friend, eat this citron." Taking it, the Bodhisatta said, "Great king, those who do not know how to eat this make it either bitter or sour. But the wise, knowing how, remove the bitterness without removing the sourness, and eat the citron without destroying its flavor." Illustrating the means of gathering wealth through this analogy, he spoke these two verses:

4.

4.

“Kharattacaṃ bellaṃ yathāpi satthavā, anāmasantopi karoti tittakaṃ;

Samāharaṃ sāduṃ karoti patthiva, asāduṃ kayirā tanubandhamuddharaṃ.

Just as one with a knife, by not peeling a rough-skinned citron, makes it bitter; so, O king, by preparing it well, one makes it sweet. One would make it unpleasant by removing only the thin skin.

5.

5.

“Evampi [V 3.0281] gāmanigamesu paṇḍito, asāhasaṃ rājadhanāni saṅgharaṃ;

Dhammānuvattī paṭipajjamāno, sa phāti kayirā aviheṭhayaṃ para”nti.

Even so, a wise person in villages and towns, accumulating royal wealth without coercion, following the Dhamma and acting accordingly, would bring about prosperity without harming others.

Tattha kharattacanti thaddhatacaṃ. Bellanti mātuluṅgaṃ. ‘Bela”ntipi pāṭho, ayamevattho. Satthavāti satthakahattho. Anāmasantoti bahitacaṃ tanukampi atacchanto idaṃ phalaṃ tittakaṃ karoti. Samāharanti samāharanto bahitacaṃ tacchanto anto ca ambilaṃ anīharanto taṃ sāduṃ karoti. Patthivāti rājānaṃ ālapati. Tanubandhamuddharanti [P 3.0320] tanukaṃ pana tacaṃ uddharanto sabbaso tittakassa anapanītattā taṃ asādumeva kayirā. Evanti evaṃ paṇḍito rājāpi asāhasaṃ sāhasiyā taṇhāya vasaṃ agacchanto agatigamanaṃ pahāya raṭṭhaṃ apīḷetvā upacikānaṃ vammikavaḍḍhananiyāmena madhukarānaṃ reṇuṃ gahetvā madhukaraṇaniyāmena ca dhanaṃ saṅgharanto –

Here, 'kharattaca' means 'hard-skinned'. 'Bella' refers to the citron fruit. The reading 'Bela' is also found, with the same meaning. 'Satthavā' means 'one with a knife in hand'. 'Anāmasanto' means: by not scraping even the thin outer skin, he makes this fruit bitter. 'Samāharaṃ' means: preparing it by scraping the outer skin and not removing the sourness inside, he makes it sweet. 'Patthiva' is an address to the king. 'Tanubandhamuddharaṃ' means: but by removing only the thin skin, since the bitterness is not completely removed, he would make it unpleasant. Thus, a wise king, not resorting to force, not falling under the control of reckless desire, abandoning wrong courses of action, and without oppressing the kingdom, amasses wealth in the manner of termites building an anthill or of bees gathering pollen to make honey—

“Dānaṃ sīlaṃ pariccāgaṃ, ajjavaṃ maddavaṃ tapaṃ;

Akkodhaṃ avihiṃsañca, khantiñca avirodhana”nti. –

Generosity, virtue, relinquishment, honesty, gentleness, austerity, non-anger, non-harming, patience, and non-opposition.

Iti imesaṃ dasannaṃ rājadhammānaṃ anuvattanena dhammānuvattī hutvā paṭipajjamāno so attano ca paresañca phātiṃ vaḍḍhiṃ kareyya paraṃ aviheṭhentoyevāti.

Thus, by following these ten royal virtues, becoming a follower of the Dhamma and acting accordingly, he would bring about growth and prosperity for himself and others, without harming others at all.

Rājā bodhisattena saddhiṃ mantento pokkharaṇītīraṃ gantvā supupphitaṃ bālasūriyavaṇṇaṃ udakena anupalittaṃ padumaṃ disvā āha – “sahāya, imaṃ [M 3.0301] padumaṃ udake sañjātameva udakena alimpamānaṃ ṭhita”nti. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “mahārāja, raññā nāma evarūpena bhavitabba”nti ovadanto imā gāthā āha –

The king, while consulting with the Bodhisatta, went to the edge of a lotus pond and, seeing a fully bloomed lotus the color of the young sun, unstained by water, said: "Friend, this lotus, though born in the water, stands unstained by water." Then the Bodhisatta, advising him, "Great king, a king should be of such a nature," spoke these verses:

6.

6.

“Odātamūlaṃ sucivārisambhavaṃ, jātaṃ yathā pokkharaṇīsu ambujaṃ;

Padumaṃ yathā agginikāsiphālimaṃ, na kaddamo na rajo na vāri limpati.

"Just as a lotus born in ponds, with a white root, sprung from pure water, and blossomed with a fiery radiance, is not stained by mud, nor dust, nor water.

7.

7.

“Evampi vohārasuciṃ asāhasaṃ, visuddhakammantamapetapāpakaṃ;

Na limpati kammakilesa tādiso, jātaṃ yathā pokkharaṇīsu ambuja”nti.

Even so, such a one who is pure in conduct, without arbitrary force, whose actions are pure and free from evil, is not stained by the defilements of action, just as a lotus born in ponds."

Tattha odātamūlanti paṇḍaramūlaṃ. Ambujanti padumasseva vevacanaṃ. Agginikāsiphālimanti agginikāsinā sūriyena phālitaṃ vikasitanti attho. Na kaddamo na [V 3.0282] rajo na vāri limpatīti neva kaddamo na rajo na udakaṃ limpati, na makkhetīti attho. “Lippati”cceva vā pāṭho, bhummatthe vā etāni paccattavacanāni, etesu kaddamādīsu na lippati, na allīyatīti attho. Vohārasucinti [P 3.0321] porāṇakehi dhammikarājūhi likhāpetvā ṭhapitavinicchayavohāre suciṃ, agatigamanaṃ pahāya dhammena vinicchayakārakanti attho. Asāhasanti dhammikavinicchaye ṭhitattāyeva sāhasikakiriyāya virahitaṃ. Visuddhakammantanti teneva asāhasikaṭṭhena visuddhakammantaṃ saccavādiṃ nikkodhaṃ majjhattaṃ tulābhūtaṃ lokassa. Apetapāpakanti apagatapāpakammaṃ. Na limpati kammakilesa tādisoti taṃ rājānaṃ pāṇātipāto adinnādānaṃ kāmesumicchācāro musāvādoti ayaṃ kammakileso na allīyati. Kiṃkāraṇā? Tādiso jātaṃ yathā pokkharaṇīsu ambujaṃ. Tādiso hi rājā yathā pokkharaṇīsu jātaṃ padumaṃ anupalittaṃ, evaṃ anupalitto nāma hoti.

Here, 'odātamūla' means a white root. 'Ambuja' is a synonym for lotus. 'Agginikāsiphāliṃ' means blossomed or split open by the sun, which resembles fire. 'Na kaddamo na rajo na vāri limpati' means neither mud, nor dust, nor water stains it, that is, does not smear it. Alternatively, the reading may be 'lippati', and these nominative forms are used in a locative sense, meaning it does not stick or adhere to these things, such as mud. 'Vohārasuci' means pure in judicial conduct established by ancient righteous kings, meaning one who judges righteously, having abandoned wrong courses of action. 'Asāhasa' means devoid of violent actions because one is established in righteous judgment. 'Visuddhakammanta' means, by that very non-violence, one whose actions are pure, who is truthful, free from anger, impartial, a balance for the world. 'Apetapāpaka' means one who has abandoned evil actions. 'Na limpati kammakilesa tādiso' means such a king is not tainted by this defilement of action—namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying; it does not cling to him. Why? Because he is like a lotus born in a pond. Indeed, such a king is unstained, just as a lotus born in a pond remains unstained.

Rājā bodhisattassa ovādaṃ sutvā tato paṭṭhāya dhammena rajjaṃ kārento dānādīni puññāni katvā saggaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Having heard the Bodhisatta’s advice, the king, from then on, ruled righteously, performed meritorious deeds such as generosity, and was destined for heaven.

Satthā [M 3.0302] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

After delivering this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the wise minister was none other than myself."

Kukkujātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The first description of the Kukku Jātaka.

[397] 2. Manojajātakavaṇṇanā

[397] 2. Description of the Manoja Jātaka.

Yathā cāpo ninnamatīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto vipakkhasevakaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pana heṭṭhā mahiḷāmukhajātake (jā. 1.1.26) vitthāritameva. Tadā pana satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa vipakkhasevakoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This was told by the Teacher while dwelling at the Bamboo Grove concerning a monk who associated with an opposing faction. The story, however, has been detailed previously in the Mahiḷāmukha Jātaka (Jā. 1.1.26). At that time, the Teacher said, "Not only now, monks, but in the past, too, he associated with an opposing faction," and he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sīho hutvā sīhiyā saddhiṃ saṃvasanto dve potake labhi – puttañca dhītarañca. Puttassa manojoti nāmaṃ ahosi, so vayappatto ekaṃ sīhapotikaṃ gaṇhi. Iti te pañca janā ahesuṃ. Manojo vanamahiṃsādayo vadhitvā maṃsaṃ āharitvā mātāpitaro ca bhaginiñca pajāpatiñca poseti. So [P 3.0322] ekadivasaṃ gocarabhūmiyaṃ giriyaṃ nāma siṅgālaṃ palāyituṃ appahontaṃ urena nipannaṃ disvā “kiṃ, sammā”ti [V 3.0283] pucchitvā “upaṭṭhātukāmomhi, sāmī”ti vutte “sādhu, upaṭṭhahassū”ti taṃ gahetvā attano vasanaguhaṃ ānesi. Bodhisatto taṃ disvā “tāta manoja, siṅgālā nāma dussīlā pāpadhammā akicce niyojenti, mā etaṃ attano santike karī”ti vāretuṃ nāsakkhi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born as a lion and lived with a lioness. They had two cubs—a son and a daughter. The son was named Manoja, and when he came of age, he took a young lioness as his mate. Thus, there were five of them. Manoja would kill wild buffalo and other animals, bring the meat, and support his parents, sister, and mate. One day, while roaming the hunting grounds, he saw a jackal named Giriya lying on its chest, unable to flee. He asked, 'What is it, friend?' When the jackal replied, 'I wish to serve you, master,' Manoja said, 'Very well, serve me,' and he took the jackal to his dwelling cave. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta tried to dissuade him, but being unable, he warned, 'Dear Manoja, jackals are immoral and of wicked nature; they incite one to improper deeds. Do not keep him near you.'

Athekadivasaṃ siṅgālo assamaṃsaṃ khāditukāmo manojaṃ āha – “sāmi, amhehi ṭhapetvā assamaṃsaṃ aññaṃ akhāditapubbaṃ nāma natthi, assaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti. “Kahaṃ pana, samma, assā hontī”ti? “Bārāṇasiyaṃ nadītīre”ti. So tassa vacanaṃ gahetvā tena saddhiṃ assānaṃ nadiyā nhānavelāyaṃ gantvā ekaṃ assaṃ gahetvā piṭṭhiyaṃ āropetvā vegena attano guhādvārameva āgato. Athassa pitā assamaṃsaṃ khāditvā “tāta, assā nāma rājabhogā, rājāno ca nāma anekamāyā kusalehi [M 3.0303] dhanuggahehi vijjhāpenti, assamaṃsakhādanasīhā nāma dīghāyukā na honti, ito paṭṭhāya mā assaṃ gaṇhī”ti āha. So pitu vacanaṃ akatvā gaṇhateva. “Sīho asse gaṇhātī”ti sutvā rājā antonagareyeva assānaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ kārāpesi. Tatopi āgantvā gaṇhiyeva. Rājā assasālaṃ kāretvā antosālāyameva tiṇodakaṃ dāpesi. Sīho pākāramatthakena gantvā antosālātopi gaṇhiyeva.

One day, the jackal, desiring to eat horseflesh, said to Manoja, 'Master, apart from horseflesh, there is no other meat we have not eaten before. Let us catch a horse.' 'But where are horses to be found, friend?' 'On the bank of the river in Benares.' Accepting his advice, Manoja went with him to the river at the time the horses were bathing, seized one, placed it on his back, and swiftly returned to the entrance of his cave. After eating the horseflesh, his father said, 'Son, horses are royal property. Kings have them shot by skilled archers who are clever in many tricks. Lions that eat horseflesh do not live long. From now on, do not take horses.' But he ignored his father’s words and continued to seize them. Hearing that a lion was seizing horses, the king had a pond dug for the horses inside the city. Yet, the lion still came and took them. The king then had a stable built and provided grass and water inside it. Still, the lion went over the top of the wall and took them even from within the stable.

Rājā ekaṃ akkhaṇavedhiṃ dhanuggahaṃ pakkosāpetvā “sakkhissasi tāta, sīhaṃ vijjhitu”nti āha. So “sakkomī”ti vatvā pākāraṃ nissāya sīhassa āgamanamagge aṭṭakaṃ kāretvā aṭṭhāsi. Sīho āgantvā bahisusāne siṅgālaṃ ṭhapetvā assagahaṇatthāya nagaraṃ pakkhandi. Dhanuggaho āgamanakāle “atitikhiṇo vego”ti sīhaṃ avijjhitvā assaṃ gahetvā gamanakāle garubhāratāya olīnavegaṃ sīhaṃ tikhiṇena nārācena pacchābhāge vijjhi. Nārāco purimakāyena nikkhamitvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Sīho [P 3.0323] “viddhosmī”ti viravi. Dhanuggaho taṃ vijjhitvā asani viya jiyaṃ pothesi. Siṅgālo sīhassa ca jiyāya ca saddaṃ sutvā “sahāyo me dhanuggahena vijjhitvā mārito bhavissati, matakena hi saddhiṃ vissāso nāma natthi, idāni mama pakatiyā vasanavanameva gamissāmī”ti attanāva saddhiṃ sallapanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

The king summoned a master archer and asked, 'Dear one, can you shoot the lion?' He replied, 'I can,' and leaning against the city wall, he had a platform built on the lion’s path and stood there. The lion came, left the jackal at the outer cemetery, and entered the city to seize a horse. As the lion was approaching, the archer thought, 'His speed is too fierce,' and did not shoot. But when the lion, having seized a horse, was leaving, his speed slowed by the heavy burden, the archer pierced him in the hindquarters with a sharp arrow. The arrow passed through the front of his body and flew into the sky. The lion roared, 'I am struck!' The archer, having shot him, twanged the bowstring like a thunderbolt. Hearing both the lion’s roar and the sound of the bowstring, the jackal thought, 'My friend must have been shot and killed by the archer. Indeed, there is no fellowship with the dead. Now I shall return to the forest where I normally dwell.' Speaking to himself, he uttered these two verses:

8.

8.

“Yathā cāpo ninnamati, jiyā cāpi nikūjati;

Haññate nūna manojo, migarājā sakhā mama.

As the bow bends and the bowstring resounds; surely Manoja is struck, my friend, the king of beasts.

9.

9.

“Handa [V 3.0284] dāni vanantāni, pakkamāmi yathāsukhaṃ;

Netādisā sakhā honti, labbhā me jīvato sakhā”ti.

Well now, I shall depart for the forest groves as I please; such as these are no longer friends. While I live, other friends can be found.

Tattha yathāti yenākāreneva cāpo ninnamati. Haññate nūnāti nūna haññati. Netādisāti evarūpā matakā sahāyā nāma na honti. Labbhā meti jīvato mama sahāyo nāma sakkā laddhuṃ.

Herein, 'yathā' means: in the very manner that the bow bends. 'Haññate nūna' means: surely he is struck. 'Netādisā' means: such dead companions are not friends. 'Labbhā me' means: for me, while living, it is possible to find a friend.

Sīhopi ekavegena gantvā assaṃ guhādvāre pātetvā sayampi maritvā pati. Athassa ñātakā nikkhamitvā taṃ lohitamakkhitaṃ pahāramukhehi [M 3.0304] paggharitalohitaṃ pāpajanasevitāya jīvitakkhayaṃ pattaṃ addasaṃsu, disvā cassa mātā pitā bhaginī pajāpatīti paṭipāṭiyā catasso gāthā bhāsiṃsu –

The lion, too, with a final burst of speed, dropped the horse at the cave entrance and himself fell down dead. Then his relatives came out and saw him, smeared with blood, with blood flowing from the mouths of his wounds, having reached the end of his life through association with a wicked person. Seeing him, his mother, father, sister, and mate, in that order, spoke these four verses:

10.

10.

“Na pāpajanasaṃsevī, accantaṃ sukhamedhati;

Manojaṃ passa semānaṃ, giriyassānusāsanī.

One who associates with the wicked does not attain lasting happiness; behold Manoja lying here, who followed the advice of Giriya.

11.

11.

“Na pāpasampavaṅkena, mātā puttena nandati;

Manojaṃ passa semānaṃ, acchannaṃ samhi lohite.

A mother does not rejoice in a son who associates with the wicked; behold Manoja lying here, covered in his own blood.

12.

12.

“Evamāpajjate poso, pāpiyo ca nigacchati;

Yo ve hitānaṃ vacanaṃ, na karoti atthadassinaṃ.

Thus does a person come to ruin and fall into a wretched state, who does not follow the word of well-wishers who see what is beneficial.

13.

13.

“Evañca so hoti tato ca pāpiyo, yo uttamo adhamajanūpasevī;

Passuttamaṃ [P 3.0324] adhamajanūpasevitaṃ, migādhipaṃ saravaraveganiddhuta”nti.

And he becomes even more wretched, who, though superior, associates with a base person; behold the superior one, the lord of beasts, who associated with a base person, destroyed by the force of a mighty arrow.

Tattha accantaṃ sukhamedhatīti na ciraṃ sukhaṃ labhati. Giriyassānusāsanīti ayaṃ evarūpā giriyassānusāsanīti garahanto āha. Pāpasampavaṅkenāti pāpesu sampavaṅkena pāpasahāyena. Acchannanti nimuggaṃ. Pāpiyo ca nigacchatīti pāpañca vindati. Hitānanti atthakāmānaṃ. Atthadassinanti anāgataatthaṃ passantānaṃ. Pāpiyoti pāpataro. Adhamajanūpasevīti adhamajanaṃ upasevī. Uttamanti sarīrabalena jeṭṭhakaṃ.

Herein, 'accantaṃ sukhamedhati' means: he does not obtain happiness for long. 'Giriyassānusāsanī' means: speaking in censure, the speaker says, 'This is the kind of instruction given by Giriya.' 'Pāpasampavaṅkena' means: through a wicked companion. 'Acchannaṃ' means: submerged or covered. 'Pāpiyo ca nigacchati' means: he meets with evil. 'Hitānaṃ' means: of those who desire one's welfare. 'Atthadassinaṃ' means: of those who see future benefit. 'Pāpiyo' means: more wretched. 'Adhamajanūpasevī' means: one who associates with a base person. 'Uttamaṃ' means: superior in bodily strength.

Pacchimā [V 3.0285] abhisambuddhagāthā –

The final verse, spoken by the Fully Enlightened One:

14.

14.
