“Nihīyati puriso nihīnasevī, na ca hāyetha kadāci tulyasevī;

Seṭṭhamupagamaṃ udeti khippaṃ, tasmāttanā uttaritaraṃ bhajethā”ti.

A person declines by associating with the inferior; one who associates with equals would never decline. Approaching the superior, one quickly rises; therefore, one should associate with those more excellent than oneself.

Tattha nihīyatīti bhikkhave, nihīnasevī nāma manojo sīho viya nihīyati parihāyati vināsaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tulyasevīti sīlādīhi attanā [M 3.0305] sadisaṃ sevamāno na hāyati, vaḍḍhiyeva panassa hoti. Seṭṭhamupagamanti sīlādīhi uttaritaraṃyeva upagacchanto. Udeti khippanti sīghameva sīlādīhi guṇehi udeti, vuddhiṃ upagacchatīti.

Herein, 'nihīyati,' monks, means: one who associates with the inferior, like the lion Manoja, declines, deteriorates, and comes to ruin. 'Tulyasevī' means: associating with one who is equal to oneself in virtue and so on, one does not decline, but rather experiences growth. 'Seṭṭhamupagamaṃ' means: approaching one who is indeed superior in virtue and so on. 'Udeti khippaṃ' means: one swiftly rises in qualities such as virtue; one attains growth.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne vipakkhasevako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and explained the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who associated with the wicked person was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā siṅgālo devadatto ahosi, manojo vipakkhasevako, bhaginī uppalavaṇṇā, bhariyā khemā bhikkhunī, mātā rāhulamātā, pitā sīharājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, Manoja was the monk who associated with those of the opposite faction, the sister was Uppalavaṇṇā, the wife was the nun Khemā, the mother was Rāhula’s mother, and the father, the lion king, was I myself.

Manojajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The commentary on the Manoja Jātaka, the second.

[398] 3. Sutanujātakavaṇṇanā

[398] 3. The Commentary on the Sutanu Jātaka.

Rājā te bhattanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mātuposakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu sāmajātake (jā. 2.22.296 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

'The king is your food' — this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a monk who supported his mother. The story will become clear in the Sāma Jātaka (Jā. 540).

Atīte [P 3.0325] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto duggatagahapatikule nibbatti, sutanūtissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto bhatiṃ katvā mātāpitaro posetvā pitari kālakate mātaraṃ poseti. Tasmiṃ pana kāle bārāṇasirājā migavittako ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ mahantena parivārena yojanadviyojanamattaṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā “yassa ṭhitaṭṭhānena migo palāyati, so imaṃ nāma jito”ti sabbesaṃ ārocāpesi. Amaccā rañño dhuvamaggaṭṭhāne koṭṭhakaṃ chādetvā adaṃsu. Manussehi migānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānāni parivāretvā unnādentehi uṭṭhāpitesu migesu eko eṇimigo rañño ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ paṭipajji. Rājā “taṃ vijjhissāmī”ti saraṃ khipi[V 3.0286]. Uggahitamāyo migo saraṃ mahāphāsukābhimukhaṃ āgacchantaṃ ñatvā parivattitvā sarena viddho viya hutvā pati. Rājā “migo me viddho”ti gahaṇatthāya dhāvi. Migo uṭṭhāya vātavegena palāyi, amaccādayo rājānaṃ avahasiṃsu. So migaṃ anubandhitvā kilantakāle khaggena dvidhā chinditvā ekasmiṃ daṇḍake laggitvā [M 3.0306] kājaṃ vahanto viya āgacchanto “thokaṃ vissamissāmī”ti maggasamīpe ṭhitaṃ vaṭarukkhaṃ upagantvā nipajjitvā niddaṃ okkami.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor householder’s family, and they named him Sutanu. When he came of age, he worked for wages and supported his parents. After his father passed away, he supported his mother. At that time, the king of Benares was fond of hunting. One day, he entered the forest with a large retinue, covering a distance of one or two yojanas, and had it announced to everyone: 'If a deer flees past the spot where any man stands, that man shall be fined this much.' The ministers assigned a segment for the king at a spot on the regular path of the deer. When the people surrounded the deer’s dwelling places and made a noise to drive them out, a certain antelope headed straight for the king’s position. The king thought, 'I will shoot it,' and let loose an arrow. The clever deer, knowing the arrow was coming directly towards its ribs, turned and fell to the ground as if struck by the arrow. The king, thinking, 'My deer is struck,' rushed to catch it. But the deer sprang up and fled with the speed of the wind, and the ministers and others mocked the king. The king pursued the deer until he was exhausted, cut it in two with his sword, suspended the pieces from a single pole, and, carrying it like a porter's load, he came upon a banyan tree by the roadside. Thinking, 'I will rest a little,' he lay down and fell asleep.

Tasmiṃ pana vaṭarukkhe nibbatto maghadevo nāma yakkho tattha paviṭṭhe vessavaṇassa santikā khādituṃ labhi. So rājānaṃ uṭṭhāya gacchantaṃ “tiṭṭha bhakkhosi me”ti hatthe gaṇhi. “Tvaṃ konāmosī”ti? “Ahaṃ idha nibbattayakkho, imaṃ ṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhake khādituṃ labhāmī”ti. Rājā satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā “kiṃ ajjeva maṃ khādissasi, udāhu nibaddhaṃ khādissasī”ti pucchi. “Labhanto nibaddhaṃ khādissāmī”ti. Rājā “imaṃ ajja migaṃ khāditvā maṃ vissajjehi, ahaṃ te sve paṭṭhāya ekāya bhattapātiyā saddhiṃ ekaṃ manussaṃ pesessāmī”ti. “Tena hi appamatto hohi, apesitadivase taññeva [P 3.0326] khādissāmī”ti. “Ahaṃ bārāṇasirājā, mayhaṃ avijjamānaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Yakkho paṭiññaṃ gahetvā taṃ vissajjesi. So nagaraṃ pavisitvā tamatthaṃ ekassa atthacarakassa amaccassa kathetvā “idāni kiṃ kātabba”nti pucchi. “Divasaparicchedo kato, devā”ti? “Na kato”ti. “Ayuttaṃ vo kataṃ, evaṃ santepi mā cintayittha, bahū bandhanāgāre manussā”ti. “Tena hi tvaṃ etaṃ kammaṃ kara, mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ dehī”ti.

Now, in that banyan tree was born a yakkha named Maghadeva, who had received permission from Vessavaṇa to devour those who entered there. When the king stood up to leave, the yakkha grabbed him by the hand and said, 'Stop! You are my food.' The king asked, 'Who are you?' The yakkha replied, 'I am a yakkha born here. I am permitted to devour anyone who enters this place.' The king, collecting himself, asked, 'Will you eat me just today, or will you eat regularly?' The yakkha answered, 'If I receive it, I will eat regularly.' The king said, 'Today, eat this deer and release me. Starting tomorrow, I will send you one person along with a bowl of food.' The yakkha said, 'Very well, but be heedful. On the day you fail to send someone, I will eat you instead.' The king replied, 'I am the king of Benares. For me, there is nothing that is unavailable.' The yakkha accepted his promise and released him. The king entered the city, related the matter to a minister who looked after his welfare, and asked, 'What is to be done now?' The minister inquired, 'Was a limit set on the number of days, Your Majesty?' 'No, there was not.' 'You have acted wrongly. Even so, do not worry; there are many people in the prison.' The king replied, 'Then you undertake this task; grant me my life.'

Amacco “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā devasikaṃ bandhanāgārato manussaṃ nīharitvā bhattapātiṃ gahetvā kañci ajānāpetvāva yakkhassa pesesi. Yakkho bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā manussaṃ khādati. Aparabhāge bandhanāgārāni nimmanussāni jātāni. Rājā bhattahārakaṃ alabhanto maraṇabhayena kampi. Atha naṃ amacco assāsetvā “deva, jīvitāsāto dhanāsāva balavatarā, hatthikkhandhe sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ ṭhapetvā ‘ko imaṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā yakkhassa bhattaṃ ādāya gamissatī’ti bheriṃ carāpemā”ti vatvā tathā kāresi. Atha taṃ sutvā bodhisatto cintesi “ahaṃ bhatiyā māsakaḍḍhamāsakaṃ saṅgharitvā kicchena mātaraṃ posemi, imaṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā mātu datvā yakkhassa santikaṃ gamissāmi, sace yakkhaṃ dametuṃ sakkhissāmi, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ, no ce sakkhissāmi, mātā me sukhaṃ jīvissatī”ti. So tamatthaṃ mātu ārocetvā “alaṃ tāta, na mama attho dhanenā”ti dve vāre paṭikkhipitvā tatiyavāre taṃ anāpucchitvāva “āharatha, ayya, sahassaṃ, ahaṃ bhattaṃ harissāmī”ti sahassaṃ gahetvā mātu datvā “amma[M 3.0307], mā cintayi[V 3.0287], ahaṃ yakkhaṃ dametvā mahājanassa sotthiṃ karissāmi, ajjeva tava assukilinnamukhaṃ hāsāpentova āgacchissāmī”ti mātaraṃ vanditvā rājapurisehi saddhiṃ rañño santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi.

The minister accepted with 'Very well,' and each day he had a person brought from the prison, and taking a bowl of food, he sent them to the yakkha without letting anyone else know. The yakkha would eat the food and devour the person. After some time, the prisons became empty of people. The king, unable to find a food-carrier, trembled with fear of death. Then the minister consoled him, saying, 'Your Majesty, the desire for wealth is stronger than the desire for life. Let us place a purse of a thousand coins on an elephant’s back and have the drum beaten, proclaiming, "Who will take this wealth and carry the food to the yakkha?"' Having said this, he did so. Hearing this, the Bodhisatta thought, 'By working for wages, I gather a māsaka or half a māsaka with difficulty to support my mother. I will take this wealth, give it to my mother, and go to the yakkha. If I can subdue the yakkha, that will be good. If I cannot, my mother will at least live in comfort.' He told his mother of this matter. 'Enough, my son, I have no need for wealth,' she said, refusing him twice. But the third time, without asking her again, he said, 'Bring the thousand, sirs, I will carry the food.' Taking the thousand, he gave it to his mother, saying, 'Mother, do not worry. I will subdue the yakkha and bring safety to the people. This very day, I will return and make your tear-stained face smile.' Having paid homage to his mother, he went with the king’s men into the king’s presence, bowed, and stood there.

Tato raññā “tāta, tvaṃ bhattaṃ harissasī”ti vutte “āma, devā”ti āha. “Kiṃ te laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Tumhākaṃ [P 3.0327] suvaṇṇapādukā, devā”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? “Deva, so yakkho attano rukkhamūle bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitake khādituṃ labhati, ahaṃ etassa santakabhūmiyaṃ aṭṭhatvā pādukāsu ṭhassāmī”ti. “Aññaṃ kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Tumhākaṃ chattaṃ, devā”ti. “Idaṃ kimatthāyā”ti? “Deva, yakkho attano rukkhacchāyāya ṭhitake khādituṃ labhati, ahaṃ tassa rukkhacchāyāya aṭṭhatvā chattacchāyāya ṭhassāmī”ti. “Aññaṃ kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Tumhākaṃ khaggaṃ, devā”ti. “Iminā ko attho”ti? “Deva, amanussāpi āvudhahatthānaṃ bhāyantiyevā”ti. “Aññaṃ kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Suvaṇṇapātiṃ pūretvā tumhākaṃ bhuñjanakabhattaṃ detha, devā”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā, tātā”ti? “Deva, mādisassa nāma paṇḍitassa purisassa mattikapātiyā lūkhabhojanaṃ harituṃ ananucchavika”nti. “Sādhu, tātā”ti rājā sabbaṃ dāpetvā tassa veyyāvaccakare paṭipādesi.

Then, when the king said, "Dear one, will you carry the food?" he replied, "Yes, Your Majesty." "What is it fitting for you to receive?" he asked. "Your golden sandals, Your Majesty." "For what reason?" "Your Majesty, that yakkha is permitted to eat only those who stand on the ground at the foot of his tree. I will not stand on the ground belonging to him, but will stand on the sandals." "What else is it fitting for you to receive?" "Your parasol, Your Majesty." "What is this for?" "Your Majesty, the yakkha is permitted to eat only those who stand in the shade of his tree. I will not stand in the shade of his tree, but in the shade of the parasol." "What else is it fitting for you to receive?" "Your sword, Your Majesty." "What is the use of this?" "Your Majesty, even non-human beings fear those who carry weapons in their hands." "What else do you desire?" "Fill a golden bowl with the food that you yourself eat and give it to me, Your Majesty." "Why is that, dear one?" "Your Majesty, it is unseemly for a wise man such as I to carry coarse food in an earthen bowl." "Very well, dear one," said the king, and having given everything, he appointed attendants to serve the Bodhisatta.

Bodhisatto “mahārāja, mā bhāyittha, ajjāhaṃ yakkhaṃ dametvā tumhākaṃ sotthiṃ katvā āgamissāmī”ti rājānaṃ vanditvā upakaraṇāni gāhāpetvā tattha gantvā manusse rukkhassāvidūre ṭhapetvā suvaṇṇapādukaṃ āruyha khaggaṃ sannayhitvā setacchattaṃ matthake katvā kañcanapātiyā bhattaṃ gahetvā yakkhassa santikaṃ pāyāsi. Yakkho maggaṃ olokento taṃ disvā “ayaṃ puriso na aññesu divasesu āgamananiyāmena eti, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti cintesi. Bodhisattopi rukkhasamīpaṃ gantvā asituṇḍena bhattapātiṃ antochāyāya karitvā chāyāya pariyante ṭhito paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha.

The Bodhisatta said, "Great king, do not fear. Today I will tame the yakkha and, having ensured your safety, I will return." Having paid homage to the king and having the equipment taken, he went to that place. He stationed the men a short distance from the tree, stepped onto the golden sandals, girded on his sword, held the white parasol over his head, took the food in the golden bowl, and approached the yakkha. The yakkha, watching the path, saw him and thought, "This man does not come in the usual manner as on other days. What could be the reason?" The Bodhisatta, upon reaching the vicinity of the tree, placed the food bowl inside the shade with the tip of his sword and, standing at the edge of the shade, recited the first verse.

15.

15.

“Rājā te bhattaṃ pāhesi, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ;

Maghadevasmiṃ adhivatthe, ehi nikkhamma bhuñjasū”ti.

"The king has sent you food, pure and mixed with meat; O dweller in the Maghadeva tree, come forth and eat."

Tattha [P 3.0328] pāhesīti pahiṇi. Maghadevasmiṃ adhivattheti maghadevoti vaṭarukkho vuccati, tasmiṃ adhivattheti devataṃ ālapati.

In that passage, 'pāhesi' means 'he sent'. 'Maghadevasmiṃ adhivatthe': the banyan tree is called 'Maghadeva'; 'adhivatthe' means 'O dweller therein', addressing the deity.

Taṃ [V 3.0288][M 3.0308] sutvā yakkho “imaṃ purisaṃ vañcetvā antochāyāya paviṭṭhaṃ khādissāmī”ti cintetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the yakkha thought, "I will deceive this man and devour him once he has entered the shade." Then he spoke the second verse:

16.

16.

“Ehi māṇava orena, bhikkhamādāya sūpitaṃ;

Tvañca māṇava bhikkhā ca, ubho bhakkhā bhavissathā”ti.

“Come, young man, come hither, taking the almsfood well-provided with relish; you, young man, and the almsfood, both shall be my food.”

Tattha bhikkhanti mama nibaddhabhikkhaṃ. Sūpitanti sūpasampannaṃ.

In that passage, ‘bhikkhā’ means my regular almsfood. ‘Sūpitaṃ’ means well-provided with relish.

Tato bodhisatto dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the Bodhisatta uttered two stanzas:

17.

17.

“Appakena tuvaṃ yakkha, thullamatthaṃ jahissasi;

Bhikkhaṃ te nāharissanti, janā maraṇasaññino.

“O yakkha, for a trifling matter you will abandon a great benefit; people, perceiving death, will not bring you alms.”

18.

18.

“Laddhāya yakkhā tava niccabhikkhaṃ, suciṃ paṇītaṃ rasasā upetaṃ;

Bhikkhañca te āhariyo naro idha, sudullabho hehiti bhakkhite mayī”ti.

“O yakkha, having obtained your constant alms—pure, excellent, and endowed with flavor—if you eat me, a man who brings you alms here will be very hard to find.”

Tattha thullamatthanti appakena kāraṇena mahantaṃ atthaṃ jahissasīti dasseti. Nāharissantīti ito paṭṭhāya maraṇasaññino hutvā na āharissanti, atha tvaṃ milātasākho viya rukkho nirāhāro dubbalo bhavissasīti. Laddhāyanti laddhaayaṃ laddhāgamanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – samma yakkha, yaṃ ahaṃ ajja āhariṃ, idaṃ tava niccabhikkhaṃ suciṃ paṇītaṃ uttamaṃ rasena upetaṃ laddhāgamanaṃ devasikaṃ te āgacchissati. Āhariyoti āharaṇako. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “sace tvaṃ imaṃ bhikkhaṃ gahetvā āgataṃ maṃ bhakkhasi, athevaṃ mayi bhakkhite bhikkhañca te āharaṇako añño naro idha sudullabho bhavissati. Kiṃkāraṇā? Mādiso hi bārāṇasiyaṃ añño paṇḍitamanusso nāma natthi, mayi pana khādite sutanupi nāma yakkhena khādito, aññassa kassa so lajjissatī”ti bhattāharaṇakaṃ na labhissasi, atha te ito paṭṭhāya bhojanaṃ dullabhaṃ bhavissati, amhākampi rājānaṃ gaṇhituṃ na labhissasi. Kasmā? Rukkhato bahibhāvena. Sace panidaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā maṃ pahiṇissasi, ahaṃ te rañño kathetvā nibaddhaṃ bhattaṃ pesessāmi, attānampi ca te [P 3.0329] khādituṃ [M 3.0309] na dassāmi, ahampi tava santike ṭhāne na ṭhassāmi, pādukāsu ṭhassāmi, rukkhacchāyāyampi te na ṭhassāmi, attano chattacchāyāyameva ṭhassāmi, sace pana mayā saddhiṃ virujjhissasi, khaggena taṃ dvidhā bhindissāmi[V 3.0289], ahañhi ajja etadatthameva sajjo hutvā āgatoti. Evaṃ kira naṃ mahāsatto tajjesi.

In that passage, ‘thullamatthaṃ’ shows that for a small reason, you will lose a great benefit. ‘Nāharissantīti’ means: from now on, being mindful of death, they will not bring it; then you, like a tree with withered branches, will become weak and without food. ‘Laddhāyanti’ means ‘this is obtained’ or ‘the arrival is obtained’. This is what is said: ‘Friend yakkha, what I have brought today is your constant alms—pure, excellent, supreme, and endowed with flavor—this arrival is a regular supply that will reach you daily.’ ‘Āhariyoti’ means ‘one who brings.’ This is what is said: ‘If you eat me, who have come bringing this alms, then with me having been eaten, another man to bring you alms here will be very hard to find.’ For what reason? ‘There is no other wise man like me in Bārāṇasī. If I am eaten, people will think, “Even Sutanu was eaten by the yakkha; for whom else will he feel shame?”’ Thus you will not find a food-bringer, and from now on, food will be hard for you to obtain. Nor will you be able to seize our king. Why? Because he is outside the limits of the tree. But if you eat this food and let me go, I will speak to the king and arrange for regular food to be sent to you, and I will not let you eat me. Nor will I stand in a place that is your property—I will stand on my sandals. I will not stand in the shade of your tree but in the shade of my own parasol. And if you fight with me, I will split you in two with my sword, for today I have come prepared for just this purpose.’ Thus the Great Being intimidated him.

Yakkho “yuttarūpaṃ māṇavo vadatī”ti sallakkhetvā pasannacitto dve gāthā abhāsi –

The yakkha, considering, “The young man speaks what is fitting,” became pleased and uttered two verses:

19.

19.

“Mameva sutano attho, yathā bhāsasi māṇava;

Mayā tvaṃ samanuññāto, sotthiṃ passāhi mātaraṃ.

“The benefit is indeed mine, O Sutanu, just as you say, young man. You are permitted by me; go see your mother in safety.”

20.

20.

“Khaggaṃ chattañca pātiñca, gacchamādāya māṇava;

Sotthiṃ passatu te mātā, tvañca passāhi mātara”nti.

“Take your sword, parasol, and bowl, young man, and go; may your mother see you in safety, and may you see your mother.”

Tattha sutanoti bodhisattaṃ ālapati. Yathā bhāsasīti yathā tvaṃ bhāsasi, tathā yo esa tayā bhāsito attho, eso mamevattho, mayhameva vaḍḍhīti.

In that passage, ‘Sutanu’ is an address to the Bodhisatta. ‘As you speak’ means: just as you speak, so this benefit spoken by you is indeed my own benefit, my own prosperity.

Yakkhassa kathaṃ sutvā bodhisatto “mama kammaṃ nipphannaṃ, damito me yakkho, bahuñca dhanaṃ laddhaṃ, rañño ca vacanaṃ kata”nti tuṭṭhacitto yakkhassa anumodanaṃ karonto osānagāthamāha –

Having heard the yakkha’s words, the Bodhisatta, with a joyful heart, thinking, “My task is accomplished, the yakkha is tamed, much wealth is gained, and the king’s command has been fulfilled,” expressed his appreciation to the yakkha and spoke the concluding verse:

21.

21.

“Evaṃ yakkha sukhī hohi, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Dhanañca me adhigataṃ, rañño ca vacanaṃ kata”nti. –

“Thus, O yakkha, be happy, along with all your relatives; wealth has been obtained by me, and the king’s command has been fulfilled.”

Vatvā ca pana yakkhaṃ āmantetvā “samma, tvaṃ pubbe akusalakammaṃ katvā kakkhaḷo pharuso paresaṃ lohitamaṃsabhakkho yakkho hutvā nibbatto, ito paṭṭhāya pāṇātipātādīni mā karī”ti sīle ca ānisaṃsaṃ, dussīlye ca ādīnavaṃ kathetvā yakkhaṃ pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā “kiṃ te araññavāsena, ehi nagaradvāre taṃ nisīdāpetvā aggabhattalābhiṃ karomī”ti yakkhena saddhiṃ nikkhamitvā khaggādīni yakkhaṃ gāhāpetvā bārāṇasiṃ agamāsi. “Sutanu māṇavo yakkhaṃ gahetvā etī”ti rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā amaccaparivuto bodhisattassa [P 3.0330] paccuggamanaṃ katvā yakkhaṃ nagaradvāre [M 3.0310] nisīdāpetvā aggabhattalābhinaṃ katvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā bheriṃ carāpetvā nāgare sannipātāpetvā bodhisattassa guṇaṃ kathetvā senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. Ayañca bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā saggaparāyaṇo ahosi.

And having spoken, he addressed the yakkha: “Friend, having previously done unwholesome kamma, you were reborn as a harsh, cruel yakkha who feeds on the flesh and blood of others. From now on, do not commit acts such as killing living beings.” He explained the benefits of virtue and the dangers of misconduct, then established the yakkha in the five precepts. “What use is dwelling in the forest for you? Come, I will have you seated at the city gate and make you a recipient of the best almsfood.” Taking the yakkha with him, having the yakkha take hold of the sword and other items, he went to Bārāṇasī. They reported to the king, “The young man Sutanu is coming, having captured the yakkha.” The king, surrounded by his ministers, went out to welcome the Bodhisatta. Having the yakkha seated at the city gate and making him a recipient of the best alms, he entered the city. He had the drum beaten, assembled the citizens, praised the virtues of the Bodhisatta, and gave him the office of commander of the army. And the king, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and was destined for heaven.

Satthā [V 3.0290] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne mātuposakabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā yakkho aṅgulimālo ahosi, rājā ānando, māṇavo pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and revealed the Truths, made the connection for the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the teaching on the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the fruition of stream-entry. At that time, the yakkha was Aṅgulimāla, the king was Ānanda, and the young man was myself.

Sutanujātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Explanation of the Sutanu Jātaka, the Third.

[399] 4. Mātuposakagijjhajātakavaṇṇanā

[399] 4. The Explanation of the Jātaka of the Vulture Who Supported His Mother.

Te kathaṃ nu karissantīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ mātuposakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu sāmajātake (jā. 2.22.296 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

“How will they manage?”—This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who supported his mother. The story will become clear in the Sāma Jātaka (Jā. 2.22.296 ff.).

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto gijjhayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto vuddhe parihīnacakkhuke mātāpitaro gijjhaguhāyaṃ ṭhapetvā gomaṃsādīni āharitvā posesi. Tasmiṃ kāle bārāṇasiyaṃ susāne eko nesādo aniyametvā gijjhānaṃ pāse oḍḍesi. Athekadivasaṃ bodhisatto gomaṃsādiṃ pariyesanto susānaṃ paviṭṭho pādena pāse bajjhitvā attano na cintesi, vuddhe parihīnacakkhuke mātāpitaro anussaritvā “kathaṃ nu kho me mātāpitaro yāpessanti, mama baddhabhāvampi ajānantā anāthā nippaccayā pabbataguhāyameva sussitvā marissanti maññe”ti vilapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a vulture. Having reached maturity, he placed his aged and weak-sighted parents in a vulture’s cave and sustained them by bringing them cow meat and other food. At that time, a hunter in the charnel ground of Bārāṇasī indiscriminately set snares for vultures. One day, the Bodhisatta, searching for cow meat and such, entered the charnel ground and was caught by the foot in a snare. He did not think of himself but, recalling his aged and weak-sighted parents, lamented: “How will my parents survive? Not knowing that I am trapped, helpless and without support, they will surely wither away and die in the mountain cave.” Then he spoke the first verse:

22.

22.

“Te kathaṃ nu karissanti, vuddhā giridarīsayā;

Ahaṃ baddhosmi pāsena, nilīyassa vasaṃ gato”ti.

“How will they manage now, the aged ones dwelling in the mountain cleft? I am bound by a snare; I have fallen under the power of Niliya.”

Tattha nilīyassāti evaṃnāmakassa nesādaputtassa.

Herein, ‘of Niliya’ refers to a hunter’s son of that name.

Atha [M 3.0311] nesādaputto gijjharājassa [P 3.0331] paridevitasaddaṃ sutvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the hunter’s son, hearing the lament of the vulture king, spoke the second verse:

23.

23.

“Kiṃ gijjha paridevasi, kā nu te paridevanā;

Na me suto vā diṭṭho vā, bhāsanto mānusiṃ dijo”ti.

“Why do you lament, O vulture? What is this lamentation of yours? Never before have I heard or seen a bird speaking a human tongue.”

Gijjho āha –

The vulture said:

24.

24.

“Bharāmi [V 3.0291] mātāpitaro, vuddhe giridarīsaye;

Te kathaṃ nu karissanti, ahaṃ vasaṃ gato tavā”ti.

“I support my parents, aged and dwelling in the mountain cleft. How will they manage, now that I have fallen into your power?”

Nesādo āha –

The hunter said:

25.

25.

“Yaṃ nu gijjho yojanasataṃ, kuṇapāni avekkhati;

Kasmā jālañca pāsañca, āsajjāpi na bujjhasī”ti.

“A vulture, it is said, can spot carrion a hundred yojanas away; why then, on approaching a net and a snare, did you not perceive them?”

Gijjharājā āha –

The vulture king said:

26.

26.

“Yadā parābhavo hoti, poso jīvitasaṅkhaye;

Atha jālañca pāsañca, āsajjāpi na bujjhatī”ti.

“When a person’s downfall is due, at the end of their life, then even when approaching a net and a snare, they do not perceive them.”

27.

27.

“Bharassu mātāpitaro, vuddhe giridarīsaye;

Mayā tvaṃ samanuññāto, sotthiṃ passāhi ñātake.

“Support your parents, the aged ones dwelling in the mountain cleft. You are permitted by me; go see your relatives in safety.”

28.

28.

“Evaṃ luddaka nandassu, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Bharissaṃ mātāpitaro, vuddhe giridarīsaye”ti. –

“Thus, hunter, rejoice with all your relatives. I shall support my parents, who are aged and dwell in a mountain cave.”

Nesādaputtena dutiyā, gijjhena tatiyāti imā gāthā paṭipāṭiyā vuttā.

These verses were spoken in order: the second by the hunter’s son, the third by the vulture.

Tattha yaṃ nūti yaṃ nu etaṃ loke kathīyati. Gijjho yojanasataṃ, kuṇapāni avekkhatīti yojanasataṃ atikkamma ṭhitānipi kuṇapāni passati, taṃ yadi tathaṃ, atha kasmā tvaṃ imaṃ jālañca pāsañca āsajjāpi na bujjhasi, santikaṃ āgantvāpi na jānāsīti.

Here, ‘yaṃ nu’ refers to what is commonly spoken of in the world: ‘A vulture can spot carrion a hundred yojanas away’—it sees carrion even when it is a hundred yojanas away. If that is so, then why, even though you came upon this net and snare, did you not perceive it? Even having come near, why did you not know?

Parābhavoti vināso. Bharassūti idaṃ so bodhisattassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā “paṇḍito gijjharājā paridevanto na attano paridevati, mātāpitūnaṃ [M 3.0312] paridevati, nāyaṃ māretuṃ yutto”ti tussitvā āha, vatvā ca pana piyacittena muducittena pāsaṃ mocesi.

‘Parābhavo’ means destruction. Having heard this Dhamma discourse of the Bodhisatta, the hunter, pleased, said, ‘The wise vulture king does not lament for himself but laments for his parents. It is not right to kill him.’ And having spoken thus, with a loving and gentle heart, he released the snare.

Athassa [V 3.0292] bodhisatto maraṇamukhā pamutto sukhito anumodanaṃ karonto osānagāthaṃ vatvā mukhapūraṃ maṃsaṃ ādāya mātāpitūnaṃ adāsi.

Then the Bodhisatta, freed from the jaws of death and happy, expressed his appreciation and, reciting the concluding verse, took a mouthful of meat and gave it to his mother and father.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne mātuposakabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi[P 3.0332].

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his mother was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā nesādaputto channo ahosi, mātāpitaro mahārājakulāni, gijjharājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the hunter’s son was Channa, the parents were of the great royal family, and the vulture king was indeed myself.

Mātuposakagijjhajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Mātuposaka Gijjha Jātaka, the fourth.

[400] 5. Dabbhapupphajātakavaṇṇanā

[400] 5. The Commentary on the Dabbhapuppha Jātaka

Anutīracārī bhaddanteti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto upanandaṃ sakyaputtaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi sāsane pabbajitvā appicchatādiguṇe pahāya mahātaṇho ahosi. Vassūpanāyikāya dve tayo vihāre pariggahetvā ekasmiṃ chattaṃ vā upāhanaṃ vā ekasmiṃ kattarayaṭṭhiṃ vā udakatumbaṃ vā ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ sayaṃ vasati. So ekasmiṃ janapadavihāre vassaṃ upagantvā “bhikkhūhi nāma appicchehi bhavitabba”nti ākāse candaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya bhikkhūnaṃ paccayasantosadīpakaṃ ariyavaṃsapaṭipadaṃ kathesi. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū manāpāni pattacīvarāni chaḍḍetvā mattikāpattāni ceva paṃsukūlacīvarāni ca gaṇhiṃsu. So tāni attano vasanaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā vutthavasso pavāretvā yānakaṃ pūretvā jetavanaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge ekassa araññavihārassa piṭṭhibhāge pāde valliyā palibuddho “addhā ettha kiñci laddhabbaṃ bhavissatī”ti taṃ vihāraṃ pāvisi. Tattha pana dve mahallakā bhikkhū vassaṃ upagacchiṃsu. Te dve ca thūlasāṭake ekañca sukhumakambalaṃ labhitvā bhājetuṃ asakkontā taṃ disvā “thero no bhājetvā dassatī”ti tuṭṭhacittā “mayaṃ, bhante, imaṃ vassāvāsikaṃ bhājetuṃ na sakkoma, imaṃ no nissāya vivādo hoti, idaṃ amhākaṃ bhājetvā dethā”ti āhaṃsu. So [M 3.0313] “sādhu bhājessāmī”ti dve thūlasāṭake dvinnampi bhājetvā “ayaṃ amhākaṃ vinayadharānaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti kambalaṃ gahetvā pakkāmi.

“Anutīracārī bhaddante”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, with reference to Upananda the Sakyan. Having gone forth into the Dispensation, he abandoned such qualities as wanting little and became full of great craving. At the time of the rains retreat, he would take possession of two or three monasteries, leaving an umbrella or sandals in one, a walking staff or water-pot in another, and dwelling in one himself. Once, having entered the rains retreat in a rural monastery, he taught the monks the practice of the Noble Lineage, which illuminates contentment with the requisites, as if raising the moon in the sky, saying, “Monks should indeed be content with little.” Hearing this, the monks discarded their pleasing bowls and robes and took up earthen bowls and rag-robes. He then stored those items in his own dwelling place. After completing the rains retreat and holding the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he filled a small cart and set out for Jetavana. On the way, his foot got caught in a creeper at the back of a forest monastery. Thinking, “Surely, something is to be obtained here,” he entered that monastery. There, two elderly monks had entered the rains retreat. They had received two coarse cloths for robes and one fine woolen blanket but, being unable to divide them, they saw him and, with joyful hearts, thought, “The elder will divide them for us.” They said, “Venerable sir, we are unable to divide this rains-residence gift. Because of this, a dispute has arisen between us. Please divide this for us.” He replied, “Very well, I will divide it.” After dividing the two coarse cloths between the two of them, he took the woolen blanket for himself, saying, “This belongs to us Vinaya experts,” and departed.

Tepi therā kambale sālayā teneva saddhiṃ jetavanaṃ gantvā vinayadharānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tamatthaṃ ārocetvā [V 3.0293] “labbhati nu kho, bhante, vinayadharānaṃ evaṃ vilopaṃ khāditu”nti āhaṃsu. Bhikkhū upanandattherena ābhataṃ pattacīvararāsiṃ disvā “mahāpuññosi tvaṃ āvuso, bahuṃ te pattacīvaraṃ laddha”nti vadiṃsu. So “kuto me āvuso, puññaṃ, iminā me upāyena idaṃ laddha”nti sabbaṃ kathesi. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, upanando sakyaputto mahātaṇho mahālobho”ti. Satthā [P 3.0333] āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, upanandena paṭipadāya anucchavikaṃ kataṃ, parassa paṭipadaṃ kathentena nāma bhikkhunā paṭhamaṃ attano anucchavikaṃ katvā pacchā paro ovaditabbo”ti.

Those elders, still longing for the blanket, went to Jetavana together with him and informed the monks who were experts in the Vinaya, asking, “Venerable sirs, is it permissible for Vinaya experts to enjoy such plunder?” The monks, seeing the heap of bowls and robes brought by Elder Upananda, said, “You are very meritorious, friend; you have obtained many bowls and robes.” He replied, “How can there be merit for me, friends? I obtained this by such a trick,” and he told them the whole story. The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall, saying, “Friends, Upananda the Sakyan is full of great craving and greed.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now sitting together?” When they told him, he said, “Monks, Upananda has not acted in a manner befitting the practice. A monk who instructs others in their practice should first make his own conduct proper and then advise others.”

“Attānameva paṭhamaṃ, patirūpe nivesaye;

Athaññamanusāseyya, na kilisseyya paṇḍito”ti. (dha. pa. 158) –

“One should first establish oneself in what is proper, then instruct others; a wise person who does this will not be defiled.”

Imāya dhammapade gāthāya dhammaṃ desetvā “na, bhikkhave, upanando idāneva, pubbepesa mahātaṇho mahālobhova, na ca pana idāneva, pubbepesa imesaṃ santakaṃ vilumpiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Having taught the Dhamma with this verse from the Dhammapada, he said: “Monks, Upananda is not only like this now; in the past, too, he was full of great craving and greed. And not only now, but in the past, too, he plundered what belonged to these very monks.” Then he related the past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto nadītīre rukkhadevatā ahosi. Tadā eko siṅgālo māyāviṃ nāma bhariyaṃ gahetvā nadītīre ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasi. Athekadivasaṃ siṅgālī siṅgālaṃ āha “dohaḷo me sāmi, uppanno, allarohitamacchaṃ khādituṃ icchāmī”ti. Siṅgālo “appossukkā hohi, āharissāmi te”ti nadītīre caranto valliyā pāde palibujjhitvā anutīrameva agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe gambhīracārī ca anutīracārī cāti dve uddā macche pariyesantā tīre aṭṭhaṃsu. Tesu gambhīracārī mahantaṃ rohitamacchaṃ disvā vegena udake pavisitvā taṃ naṅguṭṭhe gaṇhi. Balavā maccho parikaḍḍhanto yāsi. So gambhīracārī uddo “mahāmaccho ubhinnampi no pahossati, ehi me sahāyo hohī”ti itarena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity on a riverbank. At that time, a jackal lived in a certain place by the river with his wife named Māyāvī. One day, the female jackal said to the jackal, “My lord, a craving has arisen in me; I wish to eat fresh rohita fish.” The jackal replied, “Do not be anxious, I will bring it for you.” While wandering along the riverbank, his foot got caught in a creeper, and he proceeded along the bank. At that moment, two otters—one who frequented deep waters and one who frequented the bank—were searching for fish and stood on the bank. The deep-water otter, seeing a large rohita fish, quickly entered the water and seized it by the tail. The strong fish began to drag him away. That deep-water otter, thinking, “This big fish will be enough for both of us. Come, be my helper!” and speaking to the other, uttered the first verse:

29.

29.

“Anutīracārī [M 3.0314] bhaddante, sahāyamanudhāva maṃ;

Mahā me gahito maccho, so maṃ harati vegasā”ti.

“O good sir, you who frequent the bank, run to my aid, my friend! I have seized a great fish, and it carries me away with speed!”

Tattha [V 3.0294] sahāyamanudhāva manti sahāya anudhāva maṃ, sandhivasena ma-kāro vutto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathāhaṃ iminā macchena na saṃhīrāmi, evaṃ maṃ naṅguṭṭhakhaṇḍe gahetvā tvaṃ anudhāvāti.

There, ‘sahāyamanudhāva maṃ’ means ‘friend, run after me,’ where the ‘ma’ is added for the sake of sandhi. This is what is meant: “So that I am not dragged away by this fish, you should take hold of my tail and run along after me.”

Taṃ [P 3.0334] sutvā itaro dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the other otter spoke the second verse:

30.

30.

“Gambhīracārī bhaddante, daḷhaṃ gaṇhāhi thāmasā;

Ahaṃ taṃ uddharissāmi, supaṇṇo uragāmivā”ti.

“O good sir, you who frequent the deep, grasp it firmly with all your strength; I will pull you out, just as a Supaṇṇa pulls out a serpent.”

Tattha thāmasāti thāmena. Uddharissāmīti nīharissāmi. Supaṇṇo uragāmivāti garuḷo sappaṃ viya.

There, ‘thāmasā’ means ‘by strength.’ ‘Uddharissāmi’ means ‘I will pull it out.’ ‘Supaṇṇo uragāmiva’ means ‘like a garuḍa with a snake.’

Atha dvepi te ekato hutvā rohitamacchaṃ nīharitvā thale ṭhapetvā māretvā “tvaṃ bhājehi, tvaṃ bhājehī”ti kalahaṃ katvā bhājetuṃ asakkontā ṭhapetvā nisīdiṃsu. Tasmiṃ kāle siṅgālo taṃ ṭhānaṃ anuppatto. Te taṃ disvā ubhopi paccuggamanaṃ katvā “ayaṃ, samma, dabbhapupphamaccho amhehi ekato hutvā gahito, taṃ no bhājetuṃ asakkontānaṃ vivādo uppanno, samabhāgaṃ no bhājetvā dehī”ti tatiyaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

Then the two of them, working together, pulled out the rohita fish, placed it on the bank, and killed it. But being unable to divide it, they quarreled, saying, “You divide it!” and “No, you divide it!” Finally, they left it and sat down. At that time, the jackal arrived at that spot. Seeing him, both went to meet him and said, “Friend, this fish was caught by us together. Because we are unable to divide it, a dispute has arisen. Please divide it into equal shares for us,” and they spoke the third verse:

31.

31.

“Vivādo no samuppanno, dabbhapuppha suṇohi me;

Samehi medhagaṃ sammā, vivādo vūpasammata”nti.

“A dispute has arisen for us; Dabbhapuppha, listen to me. Settle the quarrel, friend; let the dispute be calmed.”

Tattha dabbhapupphāti dabbhapupphasamānavaṇṇatāya taṃ ālapanti. Medhaganti kalahaṃ.

Therein, they address him as ‘Dabbhapuppha’ because his complexion is similar to the color of a Dabbha flower. ‘Medhaga’ means a quarrel.

Tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā siṅgālo attano balaṃ dīpento –

Hearing their words, the jackal, displaying his own skill, said:

32.

32.

“Dhammaṭṭhohaṃ pure āsiṃ, bahū aḍḍā me tīritā;

Samemi medhagaṃ sammā, vivādo vūpasammata”nti. –

“I was formerly a judge; many cases were decided by me. I will settle the quarrel, friend; let the dispute be calmed.”

Idaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā bhājento –

Having spoken this verse, as he was about to distribute it, he said:

33.

33.

“Anutīracāri [V 3.0295][M 3.0315] naṅguṭṭhaṃ, sīsaṃ gambhīracārino;

Accāyaṃ majjhimo khaṇḍo, dhammaṭṭhassa bhavissatī”ti. –

“The tail for the bank-runner, the head for the deep-swimmer; as for this middle portion, having surpassed those, it shall belong to the judge.”

Imaṃ gāthamāha –

He spoke this verse:

Tattha paṭhamagāthāya ayamattho – ahaṃ pubbe rājūnaṃ vinicchayāmacco āsiṃ, tena mayā vinicchaye nisīditvā bahū aḍḍā tīritā, tesaṃ tesaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatikādīnaṃ bahū aḍḍā tīritā vinicchitā, svāhaṃ tumhādisānaṃ samajātikānaṃ catuppadānaṃ aḍḍaṃ tīretuṃ kiṃ na sakkhissāmi, ahaṃ vo samemi medhagaṃ, sammā maṃ nissāya tumhākaṃ vivādo vūpasammatūti[P 3.0335].

Therein, this is the meaning of the first verse: ‘Formerly, I was a judging minister for kings. Sitting in judgment, many cases were decided by me; many cases of various brahmins, householders, and others were judged and decided. Why, then, should I not be able to settle a case for quadrupeds of the same species as you? I will settle your quarrel; relying on me, let your dispute be rightly calmed.’

Evañca pana vatvā macchaṃ tayo koṭṭhāse katvā anutīracāri tvaṃ naṅguṭṭhaṃ gaṇha, sīsaṃ gambhīracārino hotu. Accāyaṃ majjhimo khaṇḍoti apica ayaṃ majjhimo koṭṭhāso. Atha vā accāti aticca, ime dve koṭṭhāse atikkamitvā ṭhito ayaṃ majjhimo khaṇḍo dhammaṭṭhassa vinicchayasāmikassa mayhaṃ bhavissatīti.

And having said this, he divided the fish into three portions, saying: ‘You, the bank-runner, take the tail. Let the head be for the deep-swimmer.’ ‘As for this middle portion’ means ‘furthermore, this middle portion.’ Or, ‘acca’ means ‘having surpassed’ (aticca); this middle portion, which remains after surpassing these two parts, shall belong to me, the judge and master of the decision.”

Evaṃ taṃ macchaṃ vibhajitvā “tumhe kalahaṃ akatvā naṅguṭṭhañca sīsañca khādathā”ti vatvā majjhimakhaṇḍaṃ mukhena ḍaṃsitvā tesaṃ passantānaṃyeva palāyi. Te sahassaṃ parājitā viya dummukhā nisīditvā gāthamāhaṃsu –

Having thus divided the fish, he said, “Without quarreling, you two eat the tail and the head.” Then, seizing the middle portion in his mouth, he fled even as they were looking on. They, like men who had lost a lawsuit of a thousand coins, sat with dejected faces and spoke this verse:

34.

34.

“Cirampi bhakkho abhavissa, sace na vivademase;

Asīsakaṃ anaṅguṭṭhaṃ, siṅgālo harati rohita”nti.

“It would have been food for a long time, had we not quarreled. Now the jackal carries off the Rohita fish, headless and tailless.”

Tattha cirampīti dve tayo divase sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Therein, ‘for a long time’ is said with reference to two or three days.

Siṅgālopi “ajja bhariyaṃ rohitamacchaṃ khādāpessāmī”ti tuṭṭhacitto tassā santikaṃ agamāsi. Sā taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā abhinandamānā –

The jackal, with a delighted heart, thinking, “Today I will let my wife eat the Rohita fish,” went to her. Seeing him coming, she, rejoicing, said:

35.

35.

“Yathāpi rājā nandeyya, rajjaṃ laddhāna khattiyo;

Evāhamajja nandāmi, disvā puṇṇamukhaṃ pati”nti. –

“Just as a khattiya king would rejoice upon obtaining a kingdom, so do I rejoice today, seeing my husband with a full mouth.”

Imaṃ [V 3.0296] gāthaṃ vatvā adhigamūpāyaṃ pucchantī –

Having spoken this verse, she spoke the following, wishing to ask how it was obtained:

36.

36.

“Kathaṃ nu thalajo santo, udake macchaṃ parāmasi;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kathaṃ adhigataṃ tayā”ti. –

“How indeed, being a land-dweller, did you seize a fish in the water? Asked by me, dear one, tell me; how was it obtained by you?”

Imaṃ gāthamāha –

She spoke this verse:

Tattha [M 3.0316] kathaṃ nūti “khāda, bhadde”ti macchakhaṇḍe purato ṭhapite “kathaṃ nu tvaṃ thalajo samāno udake macchaṃ gaṇhī”ti pucchi.

Therein, ‘how indeed’: when the piece of fish was placed before her and he said, “Eat, good lady,” she asked, “How indeed did you, being a land-dweller, catch a fish in the water?”

Siṅgālo tassā adhigamūpāyaṃ ācikkhanto anantaragāthamāha –

The jackal, explaining to her how it was obtained, spoke the following verse:

37.

37.

“Vivādena kisā honti, vivādena dhanakkhayā;

Jīnā uddā vivādena, bhuñja māyāvi rohita”nti.

“Through quarrels they become lean; through quarrels wealth is lost. The otters were defeated through a quarrel; eat the Rohita fish, O cunning one!”

Tattha [P 3.0336] vivādena kisā hontīti bhadde, ime sattā vivādaṃ karontā vivādaṃ nissāya kisā appamaṃsalohitā honti. Vivādena dhanakkhayāti hiraññasuvaṇṇādīnaṃ dhanānaṃ khayā vivādeneva honti. Dvīsupi vivadantesu eko parājito parājitattā dhanakkhayaṃ pāpuṇāti, itaro jayabhāgadānena. Jīnā uddāti dve uddāpi vivādeneva imaṃ macchaṃ jīnā, tasmā tvaṃ mayā ābhatassa uppattiṃ mā puccha, kevalaṃ imaṃ bhuñja māyāvi rohitanti.

Therein, ‘through quarrels they become lean’ means: ‘Good lady, these beings, when they quarrel, become lean with little flesh and blood because of that dispute.’ ‘Through quarrels wealth is lost’ means the loss of wealth such as gold and silver occurs precisely through quarrels. When two parties quarrel, one is defeated and suffers the loss of wealth by being defeated, while the other does so by paying the victor’s share. ‘The otters were defeated’ means both otters lost this fish precisely because of their dispute. ‘Therefore, do not ask about the origin of what I have brought; just eat this Rohita fish, O cunning one!’

Itarā abhisambuddhagāthā –

The other is a verse of the Fully Enlightened One:

38.

38.

“Evameva manussesu, vivādo yattha jāyati;

Dhammaṭṭhaṃ paṭidhāvati, so hi nesaṃ vināyako;

Dhanāpi tattha jīyanti, rājakoso pavaḍḍhatī”ti.

“Just so among humans, where a dispute arises, they run to a judge, for he is their guide. Wealth is also lost there, and the royal treasury increases.”

Tattha evamevāti bhikkhave, yathā ete uddā jīnā, evameva manussesupi yasmiṃ ṭhāne vivādo jāyati, tattha te manussā dhammaṭṭhaṃ patidhāvanti, vinicchayasāmikaṃ upasaṅkamanti. Kiṃkāraṇā? So hi nesaṃ vināyako, so tesaṃ vivādāpannānaṃ vivādavūpasamakoti attho. Dhanāpi [V 3.0297] tatthāti tattha te vivādāpannā dhanatopi jīyanti, attano santakā parihāyanti, daṇḍena ceva jayabhāgaggahaṇena ca rājakoso pavaḍḍhatīti.

Therein, ‘just so’ means: ‘Monks, just as these otters were defeated, so too among humans, wherever a dispute arises, those people run to a judge; they approach a master of judgment. For what reason? Because he is their guide, meaning he is the pacifier of the dispute for those in conflict. ‘Wealth is also lost there’ means that those in conflict are deprived of their wealth; their own possessions diminish, and the royal treasury increases through fines and the collection of the victor’s shares.’

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siṅgālo upanando ahosi, uddā dve mahallakā, tassa kāraṇassa paccakkhakārikā rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the jackal was Upananda, the two otters were the two elders, and I myself was the tree deity who witnessed the event.”

Dabbhapupphajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Dabbhapuppha Jātaka is the fifth.

[401] 6. Paṇṇakajātakavaṇṇanā

[401] 6. The Commentary on the Paṇṇaka Jātaka

Paṇṇakaṃ [M 3.0317] tikhiṇadhāranti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhito”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kena ukkaṇṭhāpito”ti vatvā “purāṇadutiyikāyā”ti vutte “bhikkhu ayaṃ itthī tuyhaṃ anatthakārikā, pubbepi tvaṃ imaṃ nissāya cetasikarogena maranto paṇḍite nissāya jīvitaṃ alatthā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“A leaf with a sharp edge…”: This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the enticement by a former wife. For the Teacher asked that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?” When he replied, “It is true, Venerable Sir,” the Teacher asked, “By whom are you made discontented?” and he replied, “By my former wife.” Then the Teacher said, “Monk, this woman works for your harm. In the past, because of her, you were dying of mental distress, but by relying on the wise, you obtained your life.” And he related the story of the past.

Atīte [P 3.0337] bārāṇasiyaṃ maddavamahārāje rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbatti, senakakumārotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā bārāṇasiṃ paccāgantvā maddavarañño atthadhammānusāsako amacco ahosi, “senakapaṇḍito”ti vutte sakalanagare cando viya sūriyo viya ca paññāyi. Tadā rañño purohitaputto rājupaṭṭhānaṃ āgato sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ uttamarūpadharaṃ rañño aggamahesiṃ disvā paṭibaddhacitto hutvā gehaṃ gantvā nirāhāro nipajjitvā sahāyakehi puṭṭho tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Rājāpi “purohitaputto na dissati, kahaṃ nu kho”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “ahaṃ te imaṃ satta divasāni dammi, sattāhaṃ ghare katvā aṭṭhame divase āneyyāsī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā taṃ gehaṃ netvā tāya saddhiṃ abhirami. Te aññamaññaṃ paṭibaddhacittā hutvā kañci ajānāpetvā aggadvārena palāyitvā aññassa rañño vijitaṃ agamasuṃ, koci gataṭṭhānaṃ na jāni, nāvāya gatamaggo viya ahosi. Rājā nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā nānappakārena vicinantopi tassa gataṭṭhānaṃ na aññāsi. Athassa taṃ nissāya balavasoko [V 3.0298] uppajji, hadayaṃ uṇhaṃ hutvā lohitaṃ pagghari. Tato paṭṭhāya cassa kucchito lohitaṃ nikkhami, byādhi mahanto ahosi. Mahantāpi rājavejjā tikicchituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu.

In the past, when King Maddava was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family, and they named him Senaka Kumāra. When he came of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, returned to Bārāṇasī, and became King Maddava’s minister, an advisor on matters of welfare and righteousness. Known as “Senaka the Wise,” he was renowned throughout the city like the moon and the sun. At that time, the chaplain’s son came to attend upon the king. Seeing the king’s chief queen, adorned with all ornaments and of surpassing beauty, he became infatuated. Returning home, he lay down without eating. When questioned by his friends, he revealed the matter. The king, asking, “The chaplain’s son is not to be seen, where can he be?” heard of the matter, had him summoned, and said, “I give her to you for seven days. After keeping her in your house for a week, you must bring her back on the eighth day.” He agreed, saying, “Very well,” took her to his home, and delighted in her company. Their hearts bound to one another, they fled through the main gate without informing anyone and went to another king’s territory. No one knew where they had gone; their path was like that of a ship upon the water. The king had a drum beaten throughout the city and searched in various ways, but could not discover their whereabouts. Then, on account of her, a powerful sorrow arose in him; his heart grew hot, and blood began to flow. From then on, blood issued from his stomach, and his illness became severe. Even the great royal physicians were unable to cure him.

Bodhisatto “imassa rañño byādhi natthi, bhariyaṃ pana apassanto cetasikarogena phuṭṭho, upāyena taṃ tikicchissāmī”ti āyurañca pukkusañcāti dve rañño paṇḍitāmacce āmantetvā “rañño deviyā adassanena [M 3.0318] cetasikaṃ rogaṃ ṭhapetvā añño rogo natthi, bahūpakāro ca kho pana amhākaṃ rājā, tasmā upāyena naṃ tikicchāma, rājaṅgaṇe [P 3.0338] samajjaṃ kāretvā asiṃ gilituṃ jānantena asiṃ gilāpetvā rājānaṃ sīhapañjare katvā samajjaṃ olokāpessāma, rājā asiṃ gilantaṃ disvā ‘atthi nu kho ito aññaṃ dukkaratara’nti pañhaṃ pucchissati. Taṃ samma āyura, tvaṃ ‘asukaṃ nāma dadāmīti vacanaṃ ito dukkaratara’nti byākareyyāsi, tato samma pukkusa, taṃ pucchissati, athassa tvaṃ ‘mahārāja, dadāmīti vatvā adadato sā vācā aphalā hoti, tathārūpaṃ vācaṃ na keci upajīvanti na khādanti na pivanti, ye pana tassa vacanassānucchavikaṃ karonti, yathāpaṭiññātamatthaṃ dentiyeva, idaṃ tato dukkaratara’nti evaṃ byākareyyāsi, ito paraṃ kattabbaṃ ahaṃ jānissāmī”ti vatvā samajjaṃ kāresi.

The Bodhisatta thought, “This king has no physical illness, but he is afflicted by a mental disease from not seeing his queen. I will treat him with a skillful means.” He summoned two of the king’s wise ministers, Āyura and Pukkusa, and said, “The king has no illness other than the mental affliction caused by not seeing the queen. Moreover, the king has been very beneficial to us. Therefore, let us treat him with a skillful means. We will arrange an assembly in the royal courtyard and have someone who knows how to swallow a sword do so. Then, we will place the king in the lion-window and have him observe the assembly. When the king sees the sword-swallower, he will ask, ‘Is there anything more difficult than this?’ Then, friend Āyura, you should answer, ‘To say, “I will give such and such,” is more difficult than this.’ Next, friend Pukkusa, he will ask you, and you should reply, ‘Great king, for one who says, “I will give,” and then does not give, that speech is fruitless. No one lives by such words; they neither eat nor drink them. But those who act in accordance with their words and give precisely what was promised—this is more difficult than that.’ After that, I will know what must be done.” Having said this, he arranged the assembly.

Atha te tayopi paṇḍitā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “mahārāja, rājaṅgaṇe samajjo vattati, taṃ olokentānaṃ dukkhampi na dukkhaṃ hoti, ehi gacchāmā”ti rājānaṃ netvā sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā samajjaṃ olokāpesuṃ. Bahū janā attano attano jānanakasippaṃ dassesuṃ. Eko pana puriso tettiṃsaṅgulaṃ tikhiṇadhāraṃ asiratanaṃ gilati. Rājā taṃ disvā “ayaṃ puriso etaṃ asiṃ gilati, ‘atthi nu kho ito aññaṃ dukkaratara’nti ime paṇḍite pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā āyuraṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then those three wise men went to the king and said, “Great king, an assembly is taking place in the royal courtyard. For those who watch it, even suffering is not suffering. Come, let us go.” They led the king, opened the lion-window, and had him observe the assembly. Many people displayed their own particular skills. One man swallowed a fine, sharp-edged sword, thirty-three finger-breadths long. Seeing this, the king thought, “This man swallows a sword. I will ask these wise men, ‘Is there anything more difficult than this?’” Reflecting thus, he first asked Āyura with this verse:

39.

39.

“Paṇṇakaṃ tikhiṇadhāraṃ, asiṃ sampannapāyinaṃ;

Parisāyaṃ puriso gilati, kiṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Yadaññaṃ dukkaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

“A Paṇṇaka blade, sharp-edged, a sword well-prepared for drinking, a man swallows in the assembly. What is more difficult than that? Tell me, when asked, what other difficult thing there is.”

Tattha paṇṇakanti paṇṇakaraṭṭhe uppannaṃ. Sampannapāyinanti sampannaṃ paralohitapāyinaṃ. Parisāyanti parisamajjhe dhanalobhena ayaṃ puriso gilati. Yadaññanti ito asigilanato yaṃ aññaṃ dukkarataraṃ kāraṇaṃ, taṃ mayā pucchito kathehīti.

Herein, ‘Paṇṇaka’ means produced in the Paṇṇaka country. ‘Well-prepared for drinking’ means well-prepared for drinking the blood of others. ‘In the assembly’ means this man swallows it in the midst of the assembly out of greed for wealth. ‘What other’ means, ‘Tell me, when asked by me, what other action is more difficult than this sword-swallowing’.

Athassa [V 3.0299][P 3.0339][M 3.0319] so taṃ kathento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, explaining that to him, he spoke the second verse:

40.

40.

“Gileyya puriso lobhā, asiṃ sampannapāyinaṃ;

Yo ca vajjā dadāmīti, taṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Sabbaññaṃ sukaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, evaṃ jānāhi maddavā”ti.

“A man might swallow out of greed a sword well-prepared for drinking; but one who would say, ‘I will give’—that is more difficult than that. All other things are easy; thus, know this, O Maddava.”

Tattha vajjāti vadeyya. Taṃ dukkarataranti “dadāmī”ti vacanaṃ tato asigilanato dukkarataraṃ. Sabbaññanti “asukaṃ nāma tava dassāmī”ti vacanaṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ sabbampi kāraṇaṃ sukaraṃ. Maddavāti rājānaṃ gottena ālapati.

Herein, ‘would say’ means ‘should say’. ‘That is more difficult’ means that the statement ‘I will give’ is more difficult than that sword-swallowing. ‘All other things’ means that apart from the statement, ‘I will give you such-and-such,’ every other matter is easy. ‘Maddava’—he addresses the king by his clan name.

Rañño āyurapaṇḍitassa vacanaṃ sutvā “asigilanato kira ‘idaṃ nāma dammī’ti vacanaṃ dukkaraṃ, ahañca ‘purohitaputtassa deviṃ dammī’ti avacaṃ, atidukkaraṃ vata me kata”nti vīmaṃsantasseva hadayasoko thokaṃ tanuttaṃ gato. So tato “parassa imaṃ dammīti vacanato pana aññaṃ dukkarataraṃ atthi nu kho”ti cintetvā pukkusapaṇḍitena saddhiṃ sallapanto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing the words of the wise Āyura, the king reflected, “It is said that saying ‘I will give this’ is more difficult than swallowing a sword, and I said, ‘I will give the queen to the chaplain’s son’—truly, I have done something extremely difficult.” As he pondered this, his heart-sorrow lessened slightly. Then he thought, “But is there anything more difficult than saying ‘I will give this to another’?” Conversing with the wise Pukkusa, he spoke a third verse:

41.

41.

“Byākāsi āyuro pañhaṃ, atthaṃ dhammassa kovido;

Pukkusaṃ dāni pucchāmi, kiṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Yadaññaṃ dukkaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

“Āyura, skilled in the meaning of the Dhamma, has explained the question’s meaning. Now I ask Pukkusa: What is more difficult than that? Tell me, when asked, what other difficult thing there is.”

Tattha pañhaṃ atthanti pañhassa atthaṃ byākāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammassa kovidoti tadatthajotake ganthe kusalo. Tatoti tato vacanato kiṃ dukkarataranti.

Herein, 'the question's meaning' means he explained the meaning of the question. 'Skilled in the Dhamma' means he was skilled in the treatises that illuminate its meaning. 'Than that' means 'What is more difficult than that saying?'

Athassa byākaronto pukkusapaṇḍito catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, while answering him, the wise Pukkusa spoke the fourth verse:

42.

42.

“Na vācamupajīvanti, aphalaṃ giramudīritaṃ;

Yo ca datvā avākayirā, taṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Sabbaññaṃ sukaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, evaṃ jānāhi maddavā”ti.

“They do not live on speech, on fruitless words uttered. But one who, having given, should not be attached—that is more difficult than that. All other things are easy; thus, know this, O Maddava.”

Tattha datvāti “asukaṃ nāma dammī”ti paṭiññaṃ datvā. Avākayirāti taṃ paṭiññātamatthaṃ [V 3.0300] dadanto tasmiṃ lobhaṃ avākareyya chindeyya, taṃ bhaṇḍaṃ [P 3.0340] dadeyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatoti tato asigilanato “asukaṃ nāma te dammī”ti vacanato ca tadeva dukkarataraṃ.

Herein, 'having given' means having made the promise, 'I will give such-and-such.' 'Should not be attached' means that when giving the promised thing, one should remove or cut off greed for it, and should give that item. 'Than that' means this is more difficult than both swallowing the sword and the saying, 'I will give you such-and-such.'

Rañño [M 3.0320] taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “ahaṃ ‘purohitaputtassa deviṃ dammī’ti paṭhamaṃ vatvā vācāya anucchavikaṃ katvā taṃ adāsiṃ, dukkaraṃ vata me kata”nti parivitakkentassa soko tanukataro jāto. Athassa etadahosi “senakapaṇḍitato añño paṇḍitataro nāma natthi, imaṃ pañhaṃ etaṃ pucchissāmī”ti. Tato taṃ pucchanto pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, hearing those words, reflected: 'First I said, "I will give the queen to the chaplain's son," and then, acting in accordance with my word, I gave her; truly, I have done a difficult thing.' As he reflected thus, his sorrow became much lighter. Then it occurred to him: 'There is no one wiser than the wise Senaka; I will ask him this question.' Then, asking him, he spoke the fifth verse:

43.

43.

“Byākāsi pukkuso pañhaṃ, atthaṃ dhammassa kovido;

Senakaṃ dāni pucchāmi, kiṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Yadaññaṃ dukkaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

“Pukkusa, skilled in the Dhamma, has explained the meaning of the question. Now I ask Senaka: What is more difficult than that? Tell me, when asked, what other difficult thing there is.”

Athassa byākaronto senako chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Senaka, while answering him, spoke the sixth verse:

44.

44.

“Dadeyya puriso dānaṃ, appaṃ vā yadi vā bahuṃ;

Yo ca datvā nānutappe, taṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Sabbaññaṃ sukaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, evaṃ jānāhi maddavā”ti.

“A person might give a gift, be it little or much; but one who, having given, does not regret—that is more difficult than that. All other things are easy; thus, know this, O Maddava.”

Tattha nānutappeti attano atikantaṃ atimanāpaṃ piyabhaṇḍaṃ parassa datvā “kimatthaṃ mayā idaṃ dinna”nti evaṃ taṃ piyabhaṇḍaṃ ārabbha yo pacchā na tappati na socati, taṃ asigilanato ca “asukaṃ nāma te dammī”ti vacanato ca tassa dānato ca dukkarataraṃ.

Herein, 'does not regret' means that whoever, having given away one's own exceedingly pleasing and dear item to another, does not later burn with remorse or sorrow concerning that dear item, thinking, 'Why did I give this?' That is more difficult than swallowing a sword, than saying, 'I will give you such-and-such,' and than the act of giving itself.

Iti mahāsatto rājānaṃ saññāpentā kathesi. Dānañhi datvā aparacetanāva dussandhāriyā, tassā sandhāraṇadukkaratā vessantarajātakena dīpitā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Thus the Great Being spoke, instructing the king. For, having given a gift, the subsequent volition is indeed difficult to maintain; the difficulty of maintaining it is shown in the Vessantara Jātaka. For it was said:

“Adu cāpaṃ gahetvāna, khaggaṃ bandhiya vāmato;

Ānessāmi sake putte, puttānañhi vadho dukho.

“Taking up my bow and fastening my sword on my left, I will bring back my own children—for the killing of children is painful.

“Aṭṭhānametaṃ [V 3.0301] dukkharūpaṃ, yaṃ kumārā vihaññare;

Satañca dhammamaññāya, ko datvā anutappatī”ti. (jā. 2.22.2158-2159);

“This is an unbearable form of suffering, that the children should be afflicted. But knowing the Dhamma of the good, who, having given, would regret?”

Rājāpi bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā sallakkhesi “ahaṃ attano maneneva purohitaputtassa deviṃ datvā sakamanaṃ sandhāretuṃ [P 3.0341] na sakkomi, socāmi kilamāmi, na me idaṃ anucchavikaṃ, sace sā mayi sasinehā bhaveyya[M 3.0321], imaṃ issariyaṃ chaḍḍetvā na palāyeyya, mayi pana sinehaṃ akatvā palātāya kiṃ tāya mayha”nti. Tassevaṃ cintentassa padumapatte udakabindu viya sabbasoko nivattitvā gato, taṅkhaṇaññevassa kucchi parisaṇṭhāsi. So nirogo sukhito hutvā bodhisattassa thutiṃ karonto osānagāthamāha –

The king, hearing the Bodhisatta’s words, reflected: 'I, having given the queen to the chaplain's son by my own will, could not control my own mind; I grieved and suffered. This was not fitting for me. If she had affection for me, she would not have abandoned this sovereignty and fled. But since she fled, having no affection for me, what is she to me?' As he pondered thus, all his sorrow vanished and was gone like a drop of water from a lotus leaf, and at that very moment his dysentery ceased. He, being free from illness and happy, praising the Bodhisatta, spoke the concluding verse:

45.

45.

“Byākāsi āyuro pañhaṃ, atho pukkusaporiso;

Sabbe pañhe atibhoti, yathā bhāsati senako”ti.

“Āyura answered the question, as did the man Pukkusa; Senaka overcomes all questions, according to how he speaks.”

Tattha yathā bhāsatīti yathā paṇḍito bhāsati, tathevetaṃ dānaṃ nāma datvā neva anutappitabbanti. Imaṃ panassa thutiṃ katvā tuṭṭho bahuṃ dhanamadāsi.

Herein, 'as he speaks' means as the wise one speaks; in the same way, once a gift has been given, one should indeed not regret it. Having praised him thus, being pleased, he gave him much wealth.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā rājamahesī purāṇadutiyikā ahosi, rājā ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu, āyurapaṇḍito moggallāno, pukkusapaṇḍito sāriputto, senakapaṇḍito ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this discourse on the Dhamma and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the chief queen was the former wife, the king was the discontented monk, the wise Āyura was Moggallāna, the wise Pukkusa was Sāriputta, and the wise Senaka was none other than myself.

Paṇṇakajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Paṇṇaka Jātaka, the sixth.

[402] 7. Sattubhastajātakavaṇṇanā

[402] 7. The Commentary on the Sattubhasta Jātaka.

Vibbhantacittoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto attano paññāpāramiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu umaṅgajātake (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

'Vibbhantacitta'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning his own perfection of wisdom. The present story will become manifest in the Mahā-ummagga Jātaka.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ janako nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbatti[V 3.0302], senakakumārotissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā bārāṇasiṃ paccāgantvā rājānaṃ passi, rājā taṃ amaccaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi, mahantañcassa yasaṃ anuppadāsi[P 3.0342]. So rañño atthañca dhammañca anusāsi, madhurakatho dhammakathiko hutvā rājānaṃ pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā dāne uposathakamme dasasu kusalakammapathesūti imāya kalyāṇapaṭipadāya patiṭṭhāpesi[M 3.0322], sakalaraṭṭhe buddhānaṃ uppannakālo viya ahosi. Pakkhadivasesu rājā ca uparājādayo ca sabbe sannipatitvā dhammasabhaṃ sajjenti. Mahāsatto sajjitadhammasabhāyaṃ ratanapallaṅkavaragato buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ deseti, buddhānaṃ dhammakathāsadisāvassa kathā hoti.

In the past, in Benares, a king named Janaka ruled the kingdom. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family, and they named him Senaka Kumāra. When he came of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and, returning to Benares, visited the king. The king appointed him to a ministerial position and bestowed great honor upon him. He advised the king on both his welfare and the Dhamma; becoming a sweet-spoken preacher of the Dhamma, he established the king in the five precepts, in generosity, in the observance of Uposatha, and in the ten paths of wholesome deeds—thus establishing him in this noble practice. Throughout the entire kingdom, it was as if the time of a Buddha's arising had come. On the fortnightly observance days, the king, the viceroy, and all others would gather and prepare a Dhamma hall. The Great Being, seated on a splendid jeweled throne in the prepared Dhamma hall, taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha. His discourse was like the Dhamma discourses of the Buddhas.

Atha aññataro mahallakabrāhmaṇo dhanabhikkhaṃ caritvā kahāpaṇasahassaṃ labhitvā ekasmiṃ brāhmaṇakule nikkhipitvā puna “bhikkhaṃ carissāmī”ti gato. Tassa gatakāle taṃ kulaṃ kahāpaṇe vaḷañjesi. So āgantvā kahāpaṇe āharāpesi. Brāhmaṇo kahāpaṇe dātuṃ asakkonto attano dhītaraṃ tassa pādaparicārikaṃ katvā adāsi. Brāhmaṇo taṃ gahetvā bārāṇasito avidūre ekasmiṃ brāhmaṇagāme vāsaṃ kappesi. Athassa bhariyā daharatāya kāmesu atittā aññena taruṇabrāhmaṇena saddhiṃ micchācāraṃ cari. Soḷasa hi atappanīyavatthūni nāma. Katamāni soḷasa? Sāgaro sabbasavantīhi na tappati, aggi upādānena na tappati, rājā raṭṭhena na tappati, bālo pāpehi na tappati, itthī methunadhammena alaṅkārena vijāyanenāti imehi tīhi na tappati, brāhmaṇo mantehi na tappati, jhāyī vihārasamāpattiyā na tappati, sekkho apacayena na tappati, appiccho dhutaṅgaguṇena na tappati, āraddhavīriyo vīriyārambhena na tappati, dhammakathiko sākacchāya na tappati, visārado parisāya na tappati, saddho saṅghupaṭṭhānena na tappati, dāyako pariccāgena na tappati, paṇḍito dhammassavanena na tappati, catasso parisā tathāgatadassanena na tappantīti.

Now, a certain elderly brahmin, having wandered begging for wealth and obtained a thousand coins, deposited them in a certain brahmin household and then left again, saying, "I will go begging once more." While he was away, that family spent the coins. He returned and asked for the coins. The brahmin, unable to give the coins, gave his own daughter to serve him as a foot-attendant. The brahmin took her and settled in a brahmin village not far from Benares. But his wife, being young and unsatisfied in sensual pleasures, committed adultery with another young brahmin. There are, indeed, sixteen things that cannot be satisfied. What are these sixteen? The ocean is not satisfied by all the rivers, fire is not satisfied by fuel, a king is not satisfied by his kingdom, a fool is not satisfied by evil deeds, a woman is not satisfied by sexual intercourse, adornments, and childbirth—by these three. A brahmin is not satisfied by mantras, a meditator is not satisfied by abiding in attainments, a trainee is not satisfied by Nibbāna, one of few desires is not satisfied by ascetic qualities, one of aroused energy is not satisfied by energetic striving, a Dhamma preacher is not satisfied by discussion, a confident one is not satisfied by assemblies, a faithful one is not satisfied by attending to the Sangha, a giver is not satisfied by generosity, a wise one is not satisfied by hearing the Dhamma, and the four assemblies are not satisfied by seeing the Tathāgata.

Sāpi brāhmaṇī methunadhammena, atittā [P 3.0343] taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ nīharitvā vissatthā pāpakammaṃ kātukāmā hutvā ekadivasaṃ dummanā nipajjitvā “kiṃ bhotī”ti vuttā “brāhmaṇa, ahaṃ tava gehe kammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkomi, dāsidāsaṃ ānehī”ti āha. “Bhoti dhanaṃ me natthi, kiṃ datvā ānemī”ti. “Bhikkhaṃ caritvā dhanaṃ pariyesitvā ānehī”ti. “Tena hi bhoti pātheyyaṃ me sajjehī”ti. “Sā tassa baddhasattūnañca abaddhasattūnañca cammapasibbakaṃ pūretvā adāsi”. Brāhmaṇo gāmanigamarājadhānīsu [M 3.0323] caranto satta kahāpaṇasatāni labhitvā “alaṃ me ettakaṃ dhanaṃ dāsidāsamūlāyā”ti nivattitvā attano gāmaṃ āgacchanto ekasmiṃ udakaphāsukaṭṭhāne [V 3.0303] pasibbakaṃ muñcitvā sattuṃ khāditvā pasibbakamukhaṃ abandhitvāva pānīyaṃ pivituṃ otiṇṇo. Athekasmiṃ rukkhasusire eko kaṇhasappo sattugandhaṃ ghāyitvā pasibbakaṃ pavisitvā bhogaṃ ābhujitvā sattuṃ khādanto nipajji. Brāhmaṇo āgantvā pasibbakassa abbhantaraṃ anoloketvā pasibbakaṃ bandhitvā aṃse katvā pāyāsi. Antarāmagge ekasmiṃ rukkhe nibbattadevatā khandhaviṭape ṭhatvā “brāhmaṇa, sace antarāmagge vasissasi, sayaṃ marissasi, sace ajja gharaṃ gamissasi, bhariyā te marissatī”ti vatvā antaradhāyi. So olokento devataṃ adisvā bhīto maraṇabhayatajjito rodanto paridevanto bārāṇasinagaradvāraṃ sampāpuṇi.

That brahmin woman, being unsatisfied by sexual intercourse and wanting to get rid of that brahmin so she could confidently commit evil deeds, lay down one day looking dejected. When asked, "What is it, madam?" she replied, "Brahmin, I cannot do the work in your house. Bring me a male or female slave." "But madam, I have no wealth. With what shall I bring one?" "Go begging, seek wealth, and then bring one." "Very well, madam, prepare provisions for my journey." She filled a leather bag for him with both lump and loose parched meal and gave it to him. The brahmin wandered through villages, towns, and royal cities, and obtained seven hundred coins. Thinking, "This much wealth is enough for the price of a male or female slave," he turned back and headed toward his own village. At a certain pleasant watering place, he opened the bag, ate some parched meal, and without tying the bag’s mouth again, went down to drink water. Then, a black snake in a tree hollow, smelling the scent of the parched meal, entered the bag, coiled its body, and lay there eating the meal. The brahmin returned and, without looking inside, tied the bag, placed it on his shoulder, and set off. Along the way, a deity dwelling in a tree stood on a branch and said, "Brahmin, if you stay on the road, you yourself will die. If you go home today, your wife will die." Having spoken thus, the deity vanished. Looking around and not seeing the deity, the brahmin, frightened and terrified by the fear of death, weeping and lamenting, reached the city gate of Bārāṇasī.

Tadā ca pannarasuposatho hoti alaṅkatadhammāsane nisīditvā bodhisattassa dhammakathanadivaso. Mahājano nānāgandhapupphādihattho vaggavaggo hutvā dhammiṃ kathaṃ sotuṃ gacchati. Brāhmaṇo taṃ disvā “kahaṃ gacchathā”ti pucchitvā “brāhmaṇa, ajja senakapaṇḍito madhurassarena buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ deseti, kiṃ tvampi na jānāsī”ti vutte cintesi “paṇḍito kira dhammakathiko, ahañcamhi maraṇabhayatajjito, paṇḍitā kho pana mahantampi [P 3.0344] sokaṃ harituṃ sakkonti, mayāpi tattha gantvā dhammaṃ sotuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So tehi saddhiṃ tattha gantvā mahāsattaṃ parivāretvā nisinnāya sarājikāya parisāya pariyante sattupasibbakena khandhagatena dhammāsanato avidūre maraṇabhayatajjito rodamāno aṭṭhāsi. Mahāsatto ākāsagaṅgaṃ otaranto viya amatavassaṃ vassento viya ca dhammaṃ desesi. Mahājano sañjātasomanasso sādhukāraṃ datvā dhammaṃ assosi.

On that day, it was the fifteenth Uposatha day, the day for the Bodhisatta to deliver a Dhamma talk, seated upon a well-decorated Dhamma seat. A great crowd, with various fragrant flowers and other offerings in hand, went in groups to listen to the Dhamma talk. Seeing them, the brahmin asked, "Where are you going?" Upon being told, "Brahmin, today the wise Senaka is delivering a Dhamma talk with a sweet voice, in the graceful manner of a Buddha. Do you not know?" he thought: "It seems a wise speaker of the Dhamma is teaching. And I am tormented by the fear of death. The wise, however, are able to remove even great sorrow. I, too, should go there and listen to the Dhamma." So he went with them. Having arrived there, at the edge of the assembly which, including the king, was seated surrounding the Great Being, he stood not far from the Dhamma seat with his bag of parched meal on his shoulder, tormented by the fear of death and weeping. The Great Being delivered the Dhamma as if descending from the celestial Ganges, as if showering the rain of the Deathless. The great crowd, filled with joy, gave their acclamation and listened to the Dhamma.

Paṇḍitā ca nāma disācakkhukā honti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahāsatto pasannapañcapasādāni akkhīni ummīletvā samantato parisaṃ olokento taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ disvā cintesi “ettakā parisā somanassajātā sādhukāraṃ datvā dhammaṃ suṇanti, ayaṃ paneko brāhmaṇo domanassappatto rodati, etassa abbhantare assujananasamatthena sokena bhavitabbaṃ, tamassa ambilena [M 3.0324] paharitvā tambamalaṃ viya padumapalāsato udakabinduṃ viya vinivattetvā ettheva naṃ nissokaṃ tuṭṭhamānasaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desessāmī”ti. So taṃ āmantetvā “brāhmaṇa, senakapaṇḍito nāmāhaṃ, idāneva taṃ nissokaṃ karissāmi, vissattho kathehī”ti tena saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The wise are indeed called those with eyes for the directions. At that moment, the Great Being, opening his serene eyes endowed with fivefold clarity, looked around the assembly and, seeing that brahmin, thought: "This great assembly is joyful, giving their acclamation and listening to the Dhamma, yet this one brahmin is overcome with sorrow and weeps. He must have within him a sorrow capable of producing tears. I will dispel it, just as one removes copper dross with acid, or as a drop of water rolls off a lotus leaf. Right here I will make him free from sorrow and joyful of mind, and then I will teach the Dhamma." Calling to him, he said: "Brahmin, I am Senaka the Wise. I will now make you free from sorrow. Speak confidently." Conversing with him, he spoke the first verse:

46.

46.

“Vibbhantacitto kupitindriyosi, nettehi te vārigaṇā savanti;

Kiṃ te naṭṭhaṃ kiṃ pana patthayāno, idhāgamā brahme tadiṅgha brūhī”ti.

Your mind is bewildered, your faculties are agitated, and streams of tears flow from your eyes. What have you lost, or what do you desire, that you have come here? O Brahmin, come, tell me this.

Tattha [V 3.0304] kupitindriyosīti cakkhundriyameva sandhāya “kupitindriyosī”ti āha. Vārigaṇāti assubindūni. Iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto. Tañhi mahāsatto codento evamāha “brāhmaṇa, sattā nāma dvīhi kāraṇehi socanti paridevanti sattasaṅkhāresu kismiñcideva piyajātike naṭṭhe vā, kiñcideva piyajātikaṃ patthetvā alabhantā vā. Tattha kiṃ te naṭṭhaṃ, kiṃ vā pana patthayanto tvaṃ idha āgato, idaṃ me khippaṃ brūhī”ti.

Here, in the phrase 'you are of disturbed faculties' (kupitindriyosī), he spoke referring specifically to the eye faculty. 'Streams of water' (vārigaṇā) means teardrops. 'Iṅgha' is a particle in the sense of urging. Indeed, the Great Being, urging him, spoke thus: 'Brahmin, beings grieve and lament for two reasons: when something dear among the formations of beings (sattasaṅkhāresu) is lost, or when they desire something dear and do not obtain it. In your case, what have you lost, or what do you desire, that you have come here? Tell me this quickly.'

Athassa [P 3.0345] attano sokakāraṇaṃ kathento brāhmaṇo dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, explaining the cause of his own sorrow to the Bodhisatta, the brahmin spoke the second verse:

47.

47.

“Miyyetha bhariyā vajato mamajja, agacchato maraṇamāha yakkho;

Etena dukkhena pavedhitosmi, akkhāhi me senaka etamattha”nti.

A yakkha declared that if I go, my wife would die today; if I do not go, it would be my own death. I am shaken by this sorrow. Senaka, explain this matter to me.

Tattha vajatoti gehaṃ gacchantassa. Agacchatoti agacchantassa. Yakkhoti antarāmagge ekā rukkhadevatā evamāhāti vadati. Sā kira devatā “pasibbake te brāhmaṇa, kaṇhasappo”ti anācikkhantī bodhisattassa ñāṇānubhāvappakāsanatthaṃ nācikkhi. Etena dukkhenāti gacchato bhariyāya maraṇadukkhena, agacchato attano maraṇadukkhena, tenasmi pavedhito ghaṭṭito kampito. Etamatthanti etaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Yena me kāraṇena [M 3.0325] gacchato bhariyāya maraṇaṃ, agacchato attano maraṇaṃ hoti, etaṃ me kāraṇaṃ ācikkhāhīti attho.

Here, 'going' (vajato) means going to his house. 'Not going' (agacchato) means not going. 'A yakkha' means he says that a tree-deity on the path spoke thus. It seems that deity did not announce, 'Brahmin, there is a black snake in your bag,' in order to reveal the power of the Bodhisatta's knowledge. 'By this sorrow' (etena dukkhena) means by the sorrow of his wife’s death if he goes, and by the sorrow of his own death if he does not go—by this he was shaken, struck, and agitated. 'This matter' means this reason. The meaning is: 'Explain to me this reason, why my wife's death occurs if I go, and my own death occurs if I do not go.'

Mahāsatto brāhmaṇassa vacanaṃ sutvā samuddamatthake jālaṃ khipanto viya ñāṇajālaṃ pattharitvā “imesaṃ sattānaṃ bahūni maraṇakāraṇāni. Samudde nimuggāpi maranti, tattha vāḷamacchehi gahitāpi, gaṅgāya patitāpi, tattha susumārehi gahitāpi, rukkhato patitāpi, kaṇṭakena viddhāpi, nānappakārehi āvudhehi pahaṭāpi, visaṃ khāditvāpi, ubbandhitvāpi, papāte patitāpi, atisītādīhi vā nānappakārehi vā rogehi upaddutāpi marantiyeva, evaṃ bahūsu maraṇakāraṇesu katarena nu kho kāraṇena ajjesa brāhmaṇo antarāmagge vasanto sayaṃ marissati, gehamassa vajato bhariyā marissatī”ti cintesi. Cintento eva brāhmaṇassa khandhe pasibbakaṃ disvā “imasmiṃ pasibbake ekena sappena paviṭṭhena bhavitabbaṃ, pavisanto ca paneso imasmiṃ brāhmaṇe pātarāsasamaye sattuṃ khāditvā pasibbakamukhaṃ abandhitvā pānīyaṃ pātuṃ gate sattugandhena sappo paviṭṭho bhavissati. Brāhmaṇopi pānīyaṃ pivitvā āgato sappassa paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ ajānitvā pasibbakaṃ bandhitvā ādāya pakkanto [P 3.0346] bhavissati, sacāyaṃ antarāmagge vasanto sāyaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne “sattuṃ khādissāmī”ti pasibbakaṃ muñcitvā hatthaṃ pavesessati[V 3.0305], atha naṃ sappo hatthe ḍaṃsitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessati, idamassa antarāmagge vasantassa maraṇakāraṇaṃ. Sace pana gehaṃ gaccheyya, pasibbako bhariyāya hatthagato bhavissati, sā ‘antobhaṇḍaṃ olokessāmī”ti pasibbakaṃ muñcitvā hatthaṃ pavesessati, atha naṃ sappo ḍaṃsitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessati, idamassa ajja gehaṃ gatassa bhariyāya maraṇakāraṇa”nti upāyakosallañāṇeneva aññāsi.

The Great Being, hearing the brahmin's words, spread out the net of his knowledge like one casting a net upon the surface of the ocean and reflected: 'These beings have many causes of death. They die even when submerged in the ocean, or because they are seized by fierce fish there; they die even when falling into the Ganges, or because they are caught by crocodiles there; they die falling from trees, pierced by thorns, struck by various weapons, eating poison, hanging themselves, falling into chasms, or being oppressed by various diseases such as extreme cold—indeed, they die. Among these many causes of death, by what cause will this brahmin die today while staying on the road, and why will his wife die if he goes home?' While reflecting thus, he saw the bag on the brahmin’s shoulder and thought: 'A snake must have entered this bag. It must have entered when this brahmin, at breakfast time, having eaten his parched grain meal and gone to drink water without tying the mouth of the bag, a snake entered attracted by the scent of the parched grain meal. The brahmin, having drunk water and returned, unaware that the snake had entered, must have tied the bag and set off with it. If he stays on the road, in the evening at his resting place, he will think, "I will eat some parched grain meal," and upon untying the bag and putting his hand in, the snake will bite his hand and bring about his death. This is the cause of his death while staying on the road. But if he goes home, the bag will come into his wife’s hands. She will think, "I will look at the contents," and upon untying the bag and putting her hand in, the snake will bite her and bring about her death. This is the cause of his wife’s death if he goes home today.' Thus he understood by his knowledge of skillful means.

Athassa etadahosi “iminā kaṇhasappena sūrena nibbhayena bhavitabbaṃ.
