Ayañhi brāhmaṇassa mahāphāsukaṃ paharantopi pasibbake attano calanaṃ vā phandanaṃ vā na dasseti, evarūpāya parisāya majjhepi attano atthibhāvaṃ na dasseti, tasmā iminā kaṇhasappena sūrena nibbhayena bhavitabba”nti. Idampi so upāyakosallañāṇeneva dibbacakkhunā passanto viya aññāsi. Evaṃ sarājikāya parisāya majjhe sappaṃ pasibbakaṃ pavisantaṃ disvā ṭhitapuriso viya mahāsatto upāyakosallañāṇeneva paricchinditvā brāhmaṇassa pañhaṃ kathento tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then it occurred to him: 'This black snake must be brave and fearless. For even though it was struck by the brahmin’s large rib-side, it does not show any movement or wriggling of its own within the bag. Even in the midst of such an assembly, it does not reveal its presence. Therefore, this black snake must be brave and fearless.' This too he understood through his knowledge of skillful means, as if seeing with the divine eye. Thus, like a man who stood and watched the snake entering the bag in the midst of the assembly with the king, the Great Being, having determined it through his knowledge of skillful means, spoke the third verse explaining the brahmin's problem:

48.

48.

“Bahūni [M 3.0326] ṭhānāni vicintayitvā, yamettha vakkhāmi tadeva saccaṃ;

Maññāmi te brāhmaṇa sattubhastaṃ, ajānato kaṇhasappo paviṭṭho”ti.

Having considered many possibilities, what I shall say here is the very truth. I believe, Brahmin, that while you were unaware, a black snake entered your bag of parched grain meal.

Tattha bahūni ṭhānānīti bahūni kāraṇāni. Vicintayitvāti paṭivijjhitvā cintāvasena pavattapaṭivedho hutvā. Yamettha vakkhāmīti yaṃ te ahaṃ etesu kāraṇesu etaṃ kāraṇaṃ vakkhāmi. Tadeva saccanti tadeva tathaṃ dibbacakkhunā disvā kathitasadisaṃ bhavissatīti dīpeti. Maññāmīti sallakkhemi. Sattubhastanti sattupasibbakaṃ. Ajānatoti ajānantasseva eko kaṇhasappo paviṭṭhoti maññāmīti.

Herein, 'many possibilities' (bahūni ṭhānāni) means numerous causes. 'Having considered' (vicintayitvā) means having penetrated it, having a penetration through the power of reflection. 'What I shall declare here' means 'of these causes, I shall declare this cause to you.' 'That alone is true' indicates that it will be just so, similar to what is declared having seen it with the divine eye. 'I believe' (maññāmi) means I perceive. 'Bag of parched grain meal' (sattubhastaṃ) means a bag for parched grain meal. 'Not knowing' means: I perceive that while he was unaware, a black snake entered.

Evañca [P 3.0347] pana vatvā “atthi te brāhmaṇa, etasmiṃ pasibbake sattū”ti pucchi. “Atthi, paṇḍitā”ti. “Ajja pātarāsavelāya sattuṃ khādī”ti? “Āma, paṇḍitā”ti. “Kattha nisīditvā”ti? “Araññe rukkhamūlasmiṃ, paṇḍitā”ti. “Sattuṃ khāditvā pānīyaṃ pātuṃ gacchanto pasibbakamukhaṃ bandhi, na bandhī”ti? “Na bandhiṃ, paṇḍitā”ti. “Pānīyaṃ pivitvā āgato pasibbakaṃ oloketvā bandhī”ti. “Anoloketvāva bandhiṃ, paṇḍitā”ti. “Brāhmaṇa, tava pānīyaṃ pātuṃ gatakāle ajānantasseva te sattugandhena pasibbakaṃ sappo paviṭṭhoti maññāmi, evamettha āgato tvaṃ, tasmā pasibbakaṃ otāretvā parisamajjhe ṭhapetvā pasibbakamukhaṃ [V 3.0306] mocetvā paṭikkamma ṭhito ekaṃ daṇḍakaṃ gahetvā pasibbakaṃ tāva pahara, tato patthaṭaphaṇaṃ susūtisaddaṃ katvā nikkhamantaṃ kaṇhasappaṃ disvā nikkaṅkho bhavissatī”ti catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, he asked, "Brahmin, is there any parched grain in this bag?" "Yes, wise one," he replied. "Did you eat the parched grain this morning at breakfast time?" he asked. "Yes, wise one," he replied. "Where were you sitting while eating?" he asked. "At the root of a tree in the forest, wise one," he replied. "Brahmin, after eating the parched grain and going to drink water, did you tie the mouth of the bag, or not?" he asked. "I did not tie it, wise one," he replied. "After drinking water and returning, did you look into the bag before tying it?" he asked. "I tied it without looking, wise one," he replied. "Brahmin, I think that while you were away drinking water, without your knowing, a snake entered the bag, drawn by the smell of the parched grain. Thus it has come to be here. Therefore, take the bag down, place it in the middle of the assembly, open the mouth of the bag, step back, take a stick, and strike the bag. Then, when you see the black cobra spreading its hood and making a hissing sound as it comes out, you will be free from doubt." Then he spoke the fourth verse:

49.

49.

“Ādāya daṇḍaṃ parisumbha bhastaṃ, passeḷamūgaṃ uragaṃ dujivhaṃ;

Chindajja kaṅkhaṃ vicikicchitāni, bhujaṅgamaṃ passa pamuñca bhasta”nti.

“Taking up the stick, strike the bag! See the spitting, double-tongued serpent. Today, cut off doubt and perplexities! Behold the snake, release the bag!”

Tattha parisumbhāti pahara. Passeḷamūganti eḷaṃ paggharantena mukhena eḷamūgaṃ pasibbakato nikkhamantaṃ dujivhaṃ uragaṃ passa. Chandajja kaṅkhaṃ vicikicchitānīti “atthi nu kho me pasibbake sappo, udāhu natthī”ti kaṅkhameva punappunaṃ uppajjamānāni vicikicchitāni ca ajja chinda, mayhaṃ saddaha, avitathañhi me veyyākaraṇaṃ, idāneva nikkhamantaṃ bhujaṅgamaṃ passa pamuñca bhastanti.

Herein, 'strike' means 'hit'. 'See the spitting one' means: observe the double-tongued serpent emerging from the bag with its mouth dripping spittle. 'Today, cut off doubt and perplexities' means: 'Is there truly a snake in my bag, or is there not?'—today cut off this doubt and these perplexities that repeatedly arise. Believe me, for my declaration is not false. Behold the snake emerging right now—release the bag!

Brāhmaṇo [M 3.0327] mahāsattassa kathaṃ sutvā saṃviggo bhayappatto tathā akāsi. Sappopi sattubhaste daṇḍena pahaṭe pasibbakamukhā nikkhamitvā mahājanaṃ olokento aṭṭhāsi. Tamatthaṃ [P 3.0348] pakāsento satthā pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard the words of the Great Being, the brahmin, agitated and struck with fear, acted accordingly. When the bag of parched grain was struck with the stick, the snake emerged from the mouth of the bag and stood looking at the crowd. Expounding this matter, the Teacher spoke the fifth verse:

50.

50.

“Saṃviggarūpo parisāya majjhe, so brāhmaṇo sattubhastaṃ pamuñci;

Atha nikkhami urago uggatejo, āsīviso sappo phaṇaṃ karitvā”ti.

“In the midst of the assembly, with an agitated form, that brahmin released the bag of parched grain. Then emerged the serpent of fierce energy, a venomous snake with its hood spread.”

Sappassa phaṇaṃ katvā nikkhantakāle “mahāsattassa sabbaññubuddhasseva byākaraṇaṃ ahosī”ti mahājano celukkhepasahassāni pavattesi, aṅguliphoṭanasahassāni paribbhamiṃsu, ghanameghavassaṃ viya sattaratanavassaṃ vassi, sādhukārasahassāni pavattiṃsu, mahāpathavībhijjanasaddo viya ahosi. Idaṃ pana buddhalīḷāya evarūpassa pañhassa kathanaṃ nāma neva jātiyā balaṃ, na gottakulappadesānaṃ balaṃ, kassa panetaṃ balanti? Paññāya balaṃ. Paññavā hi puggalo vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā ariyamaggadvāraṃ vivaritvā amatamahānibbānaṃ pavisati, sāvakapāramimpi paccekabodhimpi sammāsambodhimpi paṭivijjhati. Amatamahānibbānasampāpakesu hi dhammesu paññāva seṭṭhā, avasesā tassā parivārā honti. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ –

When the snake spread its hood and emerged, the great crowd exclaimed, “The Great Being’s declaration was like that of an All-knowing Buddha!” and they flung thousands of cloths aloft. Thousands of fingers were snapped, a rain of the seven precious gems poured down like a dense cloudburst, and thousands of cheers arose, sounding like the great earth splitting apart. Now, the solving of such a problem with Buddha-like grace is not the power of birth, nor the power of lineage or clan. Whose power is it then? It is the power of wisdom. For a wise person, having developed insight and opened the door to the Noble Path, enters the deathless, great Nibbāna. They realize the perfection of a disciple, the enlightenment of a solitary buddha, and supreme, perfect enlightenment. Indeed, among the qualities that lead to the attainment of the deathless, great Nibbāna, wisdom is supreme—the rest are merely its attendants. Thus it is said:

“Paññā [V 3.0307] hi seṭṭhā kusalā vadanti, nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ;

Sīlaṃ sirī cāpi satañca dhammo, anvāyikā paññavato bhavantī”ti. (jā. 2.17.81);

“Indeed, the skillful declare wisdom to be supreme, like the moon, the king of stars, among the constellations. Virtue, prosperity, and the Dhamma of the virtuous—these attend upon the wise.”

Evaṃ kathite ca pana mahāsattena pañhe eko ahituṇḍiko sappassa mukhabandhanaṃ katvā sappaṃ gahetvā araññe vissajjesi. Brāhmaṇo rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā jayāpetvā añjaliṃ paggayha rañño thutiṃ karonto upaḍḍhagāthamāha –

When the Great Being had thus solved the problem, a snake charmer bound the mouth of the snake, took it, and released it in the forest. The brahmin approached the king, acclaimed him with a cry of victory, and with hands reverently joined, praised the king, reciting half a verse:

51.

51.

“Suladdhalābhā janakassa rañño;

Yo passatī senakaṃ sādhupañña”nti.

“Well-gained are the gains of King Janaka, who beholds the wise Senaka.”

Tassattho [M 3.0328] – yo sādhupaññaṃ uttamapaññaṃ senakapaṇḍitaṃ akkhīni ummīletvā icchiticchitakkhaṇe piyacakkhūhi passituṃ labhati, tassa rañño janakassa ete icchiticchitakkhaṇe dassanalābhā suladdhalābhā vata, etena laddhesu sabbalābhesu eteva lābhā suladdhalābhā nāmāti.

Its meaning is: for that King Janaka who, whenever he wishes, gets to see with loving eyes the wise Senaka of supreme wisdom—this opportunity of seeing him is truly a well-gained gain. Among all gains obtained, these alone are called well-gained gains.

Brāhmaṇopi rañño [P 3.0349] thutiṃ katvā puna pasibbakato satta kahāpaṇasatāni gahetvā mahāsattassa thutiṃ katvā tuṭṭhidāyaṃ dātukāmo diyaḍḍhagāthamāha –

The brahmin, having praised the king, then took seven hundred coins from the bag, and wishing to give a gift of appreciation to the Great Being, spoke a verse and a half:

“Vivaṭṭachaddo nusi sabbadassī, ñāṇaṃ nu te brāhmaṇa bhiṃsarūpaṃ.

“Are you one who has drawn back the veil, an all-seeing one? Is your knowledge, O brahmin, awe-inspiring?

52.

52.

“Imāni me sattasatāni atthi, gaṇhāhi sabbāni dadāmi tuyhaṃ;

Tayā hi me jīvitamajja laddhaṃ, athopi bhariyāya makāsi sotthi”nti.

“These seven hundred are mine; take them all, I give them to you. For today my life has been gained through you, and you have also brought well-being to my wife.”

Tattha vivaṭṭachaddo nusi sabbadassīti kiṃ nu kho tvaṃ sabbesu dhammākāresu vivaṭṭachadano vivaṭṭaneyyadhammo sabbaññubuddhoti thutivasena pucchati. Ñāṇaṃ nu te brāhmaṇa bhiṃsarūpanti udāhu asabbaññussapi sato tava ñāṇaṃ ativiya bhiṃsarūpaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ viya balavanti. Tayā hi meti tayā hi dinnattā ajja mayā jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ. Athopi bhariyāya makāsi sotthinti athopi me bhariyāya tvameva sotthiṃ akāsi.

Herein, ‘Are you one who has drawn back the veil, an all-seeing one?’ means: ‘Are you indeed an All-knowing Buddha, who has drawn back the veil of defilements in all states of phenomena?’—thus he asks by way of praise. ‘Is your knowledge, O brahmin, awe-inspiring?’ means: ‘Or, though not being all-knowing, is your knowledge exceedingly awe-inspiring, as powerful as the knowledge of omniscience?’ ‘For today my life has been gained through you’ means: ‘Because of what you have given me, my life has been gained today.’ ‘And you have also brought well-being to my wife’ means: ‘You alone have brought about the safety of my wife.’

Iti [V 3.0308] so vatvā “sacepi satasahassaṃ bhaveyya, dadeyyamevāhaṃ, ettakameva me dhanaṃ, imāni me satta satāni gaṇhā”ti punappunaṃ bodhisattaṃ yāci. Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, he continued, “Even if I had a hundred thousand, I would give it. This is all the wealth I have. Take these seven hundred,” and he repeatedly entreated the Bodhisatta. Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the eighth verse:

53.

53.

“Na paṇḍitā vetanamādiyanti, citrāhi gāthāhi subhāsitāhi;

Itopi te brahme dadantu vittaṃ, ādāya tvaṃ gaccha sakaṃ niketa”nti.

“The wise do not accept a fee for well-spoken verses of beautiful expression. From here, O brahmin, let them give you wealth. Take it and go to your own home.”

Tattha vetananti vettanaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. Itopi te brahmeti brāhmaṇa, ito mama pādamūlatopi tuyhaṃ dhanaṃ dadantu. Vittaṃ ādāya tvaṃ gacchāti [M 3.0329] ito aññāni tīṇi satāni gahetvā sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ ādāya sakanivesanaṃ gaccha.

Herein, ‘fee’ (vetanaṃ) means wages (vettanaṃ); or this is the reading itself. ‘From here, O brahmin’ means: O brahmin, let them give you wealth even from here, from my presence. ‘Take the wealth and go’ means: taking another three hundred from here, and taking the bundle of a thousand coins, go to your own home.

Evañca pana vatvā mahāsatto brāhmaṇassa sahassaṃ pūrāpento kahāpaṇe dāpetvā “brāhmaṇa, kena tvaṃ dhanabhikkhāya pesito”ti pucchi. “Bhariyāya me paṇḍitā”ti. “Bhariyā [P 3.0350] pana te mahallikā, daharā”ti. “Daharā, paṇḍitā”ti. “Tena hi sā aññena saddhiṃ anācāraṃ karontī ‘nibbhayā hutvā karissāmī’ti taṃ pesesi, sace ime kahāpaṇe gharaṃ nessasi, sā te dukkhena laddhakahāpaṇe attano jārassa dassati, tasmā tvaṃ ujukameva gehaṃ agantvā bahigāme rukkhamūle vā yattha katthaci vā kahāpaṇe ṭhapetvā paviseyyāsī”ti vatvā taṃ uyyojesi. So gāmasamīpaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ rukkhamūle kahāpaṇe ṭhapetvā sāyaṃ gehaṃ agamāsi. Bhariyāpissa tasmiṃ khaṇe jārena saddhiṃ nisinnā ahosi. Brāhmaṇo dvāre ṭhatvā “bhotī”ti āha. Sā tassa saddaṃ sallakkhetvā dīpaṃ nibbāpetvā dvāraṃ vivaritvā brāhmaṇe anto paviṭṭhe itaraṃ nīharitvā dvāramūle ṭhapetvā gehaṃ pavisitvā pasibbake kiñci adisvā “brāhmaṇa, kiṃ te bhikkhaṃ caritvā laddha”nti pucchi. “Sahassaṃ me laddha”nti. “Kahaṃ pana ta”nti. “Asukaṭṭhāne nāma ṭhapitaṃ, pātova āharissāmi, mā cintayī”ti. Sā gantvā jārassa ācikkhi. So nikkhamitvā attanā ṭhapitaṃ viya gaṇhi.

Having said this, the Great Being, making up the thousand for the brahmin, had the coins given and asked, “Brahmin, by whom were you sent to beg for money?” “By my wife, wise one,” he replied. “Is your wife old or young?” “Young, wise one.” “In that case, she, committing misconduct with another, sent you thinking, ‘I will act without fear.’ If you take these coins home, she will give the coins obtained through your hardship to her lover. Therefore, do not go straight home, but place the coins outside the village under a tree or somewhere, and then enter.” Having said this, he sent him on his way. He went near the village, placed the coins under a tree, and went home in the evening. At that very moment, his wife was sitting with her lover. The brahmin, standing at the door, called out, “Madam!” Recognizing his voice, she extinguished the lamp, opened the door, and when the brahmin had entered, she led the other man out, placed him at the doorpost, and went back inside. Seeing nothing in his bag, she asked, “Brahmin, what did you get from your alms round?” “I received a thousand,” he replied. “And where is it?” “It is placed in such-and-such a place. I will bring it in the morning, do not worry.” She went and told her lover. He went out and took them, as if he himself had placed them there.

Brāhmaṇo punadivase gantvā kahāpaṇe apassanto bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ, brāhmaṇā”ti vutte “kahāpaṇe na passāmi, paṇḍitā”ti āha. “Bhariyāya te ācikkhī”ti? “Āma, paṇḍitā”ti. Mahāsatto tāya jārassa ācikkhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “atthi pana te brāhmaṇa, bhariyāya kulūpakabrāhmaṇo”ti pucchi. “Atthi, paṇḍitā”ti. “Tuyhampi atthī”ti? “Āma, paṇḍitā”ti. Athassa mahāsatto sattannaṃ divasānaṃ paribbayaṃ dāpetvā [V 3.0309] “gaccha paṭhamadivase tava satta, bhariyāya te sattāti cuddasa brāhmaṇe nimantetvā bhojetha, punadivasato paṭṭhāya ekekaṃ hāpetvā sattame divase tava ekaṃ, bhariyāya te ekanti dve brāhmaṇe nimantetvā bhariyāya te satta divase nimantitabrāhmaṇassa nibaddhaṃ āgamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā mayhaṃ ārocehī”ti [P 3.0351] āha. Brāhmaṇo tathā [M 3.0330] katvā “sallakkhito me paṇḍita, nibaddhaṃ bhuñjanakabrāhmaṇo”ti mahāsattassa ārocesi.

The next day, the brahmin went, and not seeing the coins, he approached the Bodhisatta. When asked, “What is it, brahmin?” he replied, “I do not see the coins, wise one.” “Did you tell your wife?” “Yes, wise one.” The Great Being, knowing that she must have told her lover, asked, “Brahmin, does your wife have a brahmin who is a family intimate?” “Yes, wise one.” “And do you also have one?” “Yes, wise one.” Then the Great Being had him given provisions for seven days and said, “Go, on the first day invite seven of your brahmins and seven of your wife’s—fourteen brahmins in all—and feed them. From the next day onwards, reduce the number by one each day, so that on the seventh day you invite one of yours and one of your wife’s—two brahmins. Having ascertained which of the brahmins invited by your wife attends regularly for the seven days, inform me.” The brahmin did so and reported to the Great Being, “I have identified him, wise one, the brahmin who eats there regularly.”

Bodhisatto tena saddhiṃ purise pesetvā taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ āharāpetvā “asukarukkhamūlato te imassa brāhmaṇassa santakaṃ kahāpaṇasahassaṃ gahita”nti pucchi. “Na gaṇhāmi, paṇḍitā”ti. “Tvaṃ mama senakapaṇḍitabhāvaṃ na jānāsi, āharāpessāmi te kahāpaṇe”ti. So bhīto “gahitā me”ti sampaṭicchi. “Kuhiṃ te ṭhapitā”ti? “Tattheva, paṇḍita, ṭhapitā”ti. Bodhisatto brāhmaṇaṃ pucchi “brāhmaṇa, kiṃ te sāyeva bhariyā hotu, udāhu aññaṃ gaṇhissasī”ti. “Sāyeva me hotu, paṇḍitā”ti. Bodhisatto manusse pesetvā brāhmaṇassa kahāpaṇe ca brāhmaṇiñca āharāpetvā corabrāhmaṇassa hatthato kahāpaṇe brāhmaṇassa dāpetvā itarassa rājāṇaṃ kāretvā nagarā nīharāpetvā brāhmaṇiyāpi rājāṇaṃ kāretvā brāhmaṇassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ datvā attanoyeva santike vasāpesi.

The Bodhisatta sent men with him, had that brahmin brought, and asked, “Did you take the thousand coins belonging to this brahmin from under such-and-such a tree?” “I did not take them, wise one.” “You do not know my nature as Senaka the Wise. I will make you bring forth the coins.” Frightened, he confessed, “I took them.” “Where have you put them?” “They are put in that very same place, wise one.” The Bodhisatta asked the brahmin, “Brahmin, do you want this same wife, or will you take another?” “Let her be my wife, wise one.” The Bodhisatta sent men and had the brahmin’s coins and his wife brought. He had the coins given to the brahmin from the hand of the thief-brahmin, had the latter punished by royal decree and paraded through the city, and had the brahmin woman also punished by royal decree. He bestowed great honor upon the brahmin and had him live in his own presence.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīni sacchikariṃsu. Tadā brāhmaṇo ānando ahosi, rukkhadevatā sāriputto, parisā buddhaparisā, senakapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosinti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher proclaimed the Truths and made the connection of the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the talk on the Truths, many attained the fruit of stream-entry and the other fruits. At that time, the brahmin was Ānanda, the tree-deity was Sāriputta, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and Senaka the Wise was I myself.

Sattubhastajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Seventh, the Commentary on the Sattubhasta Jātaka.

[403] 8. Aṭṭhisenajātakavaṇṇanā

[403] 8. The Commentary on the Aṭṭhisena Jātaka

Yeme ahaṃ na jānāmīti idaṃ satthā āḷaviṃ nissāya aggāḷave cetiye viharanto kuṭikārasikkhāpadaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu heṭṭhā maṇikaṇṭhajātake (jā. 1.3.7 ādayo) kathitameva. Satthā pana te bhikkhū āmantetvā “bhikkhave, porāṇakapaṇḍitā pubbe anuppanne [P 3.0352] buddhe bāhirakapabbajjāya pabbajitvā rājūhi pavāritāpi ‘yācanā nāma paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā’ti na yāciṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Those whom I do not know…” This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling near Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine, with reference to the training rule concerning hut-building. The story of the present has already been told above in the Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka. The Teacher addressed those monks, saying: “Monks, the wise of old, having gone forth into an ascetic life outside the Buddha's dispensation before a Buddha had arisen, did not ask for anything even when invited by kings, thinking, ‘Asking is indeed unloved and displeasing to others.’ Having said this, he related a story of the past.”

Atīte [V 3.0310][M 3.0331] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ nigame brāhmaṇakule nibbatti, aṭṭhisenakumārotissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā aparabhāge kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā gharāvāsato nikkhamitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññāsamāpattiyo nibbattetvā himavantapadese ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya manussapathaṃ otaritvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase bhikkhāya caranto rājaṅgaṇaṃ agamāsi. Rājā tassācāravihāre pasīditvā taṃ nimantāpetvā pāsādatale pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā subhojanaṃ bhojetvā bhojanāvasāne anumodanaṃ sutvā pasanno paṭiññaṃ gahetvā mahāsattaṃ rājuyyāne vasāpesi, divasassa ca dve tayo vāre upaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. So ekadivasaṃ dhammakathāya pasanno rajjaṃ ādiṃ katvā “yena vo attho, taṃ vadeyyāthā”ti pavāresi. Bodhisatto “idaṃ nāma me dehī”ti na vadati. Aññe yācakā “idaṃ dehi, idaṃ dehī”ti icchiticchitaṃ yācanti, rājā asajjamāno detiyeva. So ekadivasaṃ cintesi “aññe yācanakavanibbakā ‘idañcidañca amhākaṃ dehī’ti maṃ yācanti, ayyo pana aṭṭhiseno pavāritakālato paṭṭhāya na kiñci yācati, paññavā kho panesa upāyakusalo, pucchissāmi na”nti. So ekadivasaṃ bhuttapātarāso gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno aññesaṃ yācanakāraṇaṃ tassa ca ayācanakāraṇaṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a certain market town, and they named him the youth Aṭṭhisena. When he came of age, he learned all the arts and sciences at Takkasilā. Later, seeing the peril in sensual pleasures, he went forth from the household life, became an ascetic, and attained the meditative absorptions, higher knowledges, and attainments. After living for a long time in the Himalayan region, he came down to the inhabited areas to seek salt and sour fare. In due course, he reached Benares and stayed in the royal park. The next day, while wandering for alms, he came to the palace courtyard. The king, pleased with his conduct and deportment, invited him in, seated him on a couch on the palace terrace, and served him fine food. After the meal, having heard his words of appreciation, the king was delighted, and after receiving a promise from him, had the Great Being stay in the royal park, attending on him two or three times a day. One day, pleased with a Dhamma talk, the king made an invitation, beginning with his very kingdom, saying, 'Whatever you have need of, please say so.' The Bodhisatta, however, did not say, 'Give me this.' Other beggars would ask for whatever they desired, saying, 'Give me this, give me that,' and the king gave without reservation. One day the king thought: 'Other beggars ask me, "Give us this and that," but the noble Aṭṭhisena has not asked for anything since the time of my invitation. He is indeed wise and skilled in means; I shall ask him.' So one day, after his morning meal, the king went to him, paid his respects, sat to one side, and, wishing to know the reason for others asking and his not asking, spoke the first verse:

54.

54.

“Yeme ahaṃ na jānāmi, aṭṭhisena vanibbake;

Te maṃ saṅgamma yācanti, kasmā maṃ tvaṃ na yācasī”ti.

“These beggars whom I do not know, Aṭṭhisena, they approach me and make their requests; why is it that you do not ask of me?”

Tattha [P 3.0353] vanibbaketi yācanake. Saṅgammāti samāgantvā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ayya, aṭṭhisena, yeme vanibbake ahaṃ nāmagottajātikulappadesena “ime nāmete”tipi na jānāmi, te maṃ samāgantvā icchiticchitaṃ yācanti, tvaṃ pana kasmā maṃ kiñci na yācasīti.

Herein, vanibbake means petitioners. Saṅgamma means having come together. This is what was said: “Venerable Aṭṭhisena, these petitioners whom I do not know by name, clan, birth, family, or region, not even so much as to say ‘these are their names,’ they come and ask for whatever they desire. But why do you not ask me for anything at all?”

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse:

55.

55.

“Yācako appiyo hoti, yācaṃ adadamappiyo;

Tasmāhaṃ taṃ na yācāmi, mā me videssanā ahū”ti.

“A beggar is disliked, and one who does not give is disliked; therefore I do not beg from you, lest aversion arise.”

Tattha [M 3.0332] yācako appiyo hotīti yo hi, mahārāja, puggalo “idaṃ me dehī”ti yācako, so mātāpitūnampi mittāmaccādīnampi appiyo hoti amanāpo. Tassa appiyabhāvo [V 3.0311] maṇikaṇṭhajātakena dīpetabbo. Yācanti yācitabhaṇḍaṃ. Adadanti adadamāno. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yopi yācitaṃ na deti, so mātāpitaro ādiṃ katvā adadamāno puggalo yācakassa appiyo hotīti. Tasmāti yasmā yācakopi dāyakassa, yācitaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ adadantopi yācakassa appiyo hoti, tasmā ahaṃ taṃ na yācāmi. Mā me videssanā ahūti sace hi ahaṃ yāceyyameva, tava videsso bhaveyya, sā me tava santikā uppannā videssanā, sace pana tvaṃ na dadeyyāsi, mama videsso bhaveyyāsi, sā ca mama tayi videssanā, evaṃ sabbathāpi mā me videssanā ahu, mā no ubhinnampi mettā bhijjīti etamatthaṃ sampassanto ahaṃ taṃ na kiñci yācāmīti.

Herein, yācako appiyo hoti: indeed, O great king, a person who is a beggar, saying 'give me this,' is disliked and unpleasing even to his parents, friends, and ministers. This state of being disliked is illustrated in the Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka. Yācaṃ means the thing begged for. Adadaṃ means one who does not give. This is what is said: a person who does not give what is asked, starting with one's parents, is disliked by the beggar. Tasmā: since both the beggar is disliked by the giver, and the one who does not give is disliked by the beggar, therefore 'I do not beg from you.' Mā me videssanā ahū: for if I were to beg, I might become an object of your aversion; that aversion toward me would arise from your side. But if you were not to give, you might become an object of my aversion; and that would be my aversion toward you. Thus, in every way, 'let there not be aversion between us, let not the friendship between us both be broken.' Seeing this reason, I do not beg anything from you.

Athassa vacanaṃ sutvā rājā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Having heard his words, the king spoke three verses:

56.

56.

“Yo ve yācanajīvāno, kāle yācaṃ na yācati;

Parañca puññā dhaṃseti, attanāpi na jīvati.

“One who lives by begging, yet does not beg at the proper time, deprives another of merit and does not live happily himself.

57.

57.

“Yo ca yācanajīvāno, kāle yācañhi yācati;

Parañca puññaṃ labbheti, attanāpi ca jīvati.

“And one who lives by begging, who begs at the right time, enables another to gain merit and lives happily himself.

58.

58.

“Na vedessanti sappaññā, disvā yācakamāgate;

Brahmacāri piyo mesi, vada tvaṃ bhaññamicchasī”ti.

“The wise do not feel aversion upon seeing beggars arrive; O holy one, you are dear to me; tell me what you wish to say.”

Tattha yācanajīvānoti yācanajīvamāno, ayameva vā pāṭho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ayya, aṭṭhisena yo yācanena jīvamāno dhammiko samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā yācitabbayuttapattakāle kiñcideva yācitabbaṃ na yācati, so parañca dāyakaṃ puññā dhaṃseti parihāpeti, attanāpi ca sukhaṃ na jīvati. Puññaṃ labbhetīti [P 3.0354] kāle pana yācitabbaṃ yācanto parañca puññaṃ adhigameti, attanāpi ca sukhaṃ jīvati. Na vedessantīti yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi “mā me videssanā ahū”ti, taṃ kasmā vadasi. Sappaññā hi dānañca [M 3.0333] dānaphalañca jānantā paṇḍitā yācake āgate disvā na dessanti na kujjhanti, aññadatthu pana pamuditāva hontīti dīpeti. Yācakamāgateti ma-kāro byañjanasandhivasena vutto, yācake āgateti attho. Brahmacāri piyo mesīti ayya aṭṭhisena, parisuddhacāri mahāpuñña, tvaṃ mayhaṃ ativiya piyo, tasmā varaṃ tvaṃ maṃ vadehi yācāhiyeva. Bhaññamicchasīti yaṃkiñci vattabbaṃ icchasi, sabbaṃ vada, rajjampi te dassāmiyevāti.

Herein, yācanajīvāno means one who lives by begging; this is also the reading. This is what was said: 'Venerable Aṭṭhisena, a righteous ascetic or brahmin who lives by begging and does not ask for what is appropriate at the right time for asking, he deprives the donor of merit, causing them to lose it, and he himself does not live happily.' Puññaṃ labbhetīti: but one who asks at the right time for what should be asked for enables another to attain merit, and he himself lives happily. Na vedessantīti: as for what you said, 'lest aversion arise,' why do you say that? This explains that the wise, who understand both giving and the fruit of giving, do not feel aversion or anger upon seeing beggars arrive; on the contrary, they are only gladdened. Yācakamāgate: the 'm' is a phonetic insertion for the sake of sandhi; the meaning is 'when beggars have come.' Brahmacāri piyo mesīti: 'Venerable Aṭṭhisena, you of pure conduct and great merit, you are exceedingly dear to me. Therefore, speak to me, indeed, you should ask.' Bhaññamicchasīti: 'Whatever you wish to say, say it all. I will even give you the kingdom.'

Evaṃ [V 3.0312] bodhisatto raññā rajjenāpi pavārito neva kiñci yāci. Rañño pana evaṃ attano ajjhāsaye kathite mahāsattopi pabbajitapaṭipattiṃ dassetuṃ “mahārāja, yācanā hi nāmesā kāmabhogīnaṃ gihīnaṃ āciṇṇā, na pabbajitānaṃ, pabbajitena pana pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya gihīhi asamānaparisuddhājīvena bhavitabba”nti pabbajitapaṭipadaṃ dassento chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, although the king invited the Bodhisatta even with the offer of the kingdom, he did not ask for anything at all. But when the king had thus expressed his own intention, the Great Being, in order to show the practice of one who has gone forth, said: "Great king, this thing called asking is the custom of householders who enjoy sensual pleasures, not of those who have gone forth. One who has gone forth, from the time of going forth, must have a pure livelihood that is unlike that of householders." Showing the path of one who has gone forth, he spoke the sixth verse:

59.

59.

“Na ve yācanti sappaññā, dhīro ca veditumarahati;

Uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhanti, esā ariyāna yācanā”ti.

"Indeed, the wise do not ask; and the wise supporter should understand. The noble ones stand with an objective; this is the asking of the noble ones."

Tattha sappaññāti buddhā ca buddasāvakā ca bodhiyā paṭipannā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitā bodhisattā ca sabbepi sappaññā ca susīlā ca, ete evarūpā sappaññā “amhākaṃ idañcidañca dethā”ti na yācanti. Dhīro ca veditumarahatīti upaṭṭhāko pana dhīro paṇḍito gilānakāle ca agilānakāle ca yena yenattho, taṃ sabbaṃ sayameva vedituṃ jānituṃ arahati. Uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhantīti ariyā pana vācaṃ abhinditvā yenatthikā honti, taṃ uddissa kevalaṃ bhikkhācāravattena tiṭṭhanti, neva kāyaṅgaṃ vā vācaṅgaṃ vā kopenti. Kāyavikāraṃ dassetvā nimittaṃ karonto hi kāyaṅgaṃ kopeti nāma, vacībhedaṃ karonto vācaṅgaṃ kopeti nāma, tadubhayaṃ akatvā buddhādayo ariyā tiṭṭhanti. Esā ariyāna yācanāti esā kāyaṅgavācaṅgaṃ akopetvā bhikkhāya tiṭṭhamānā ariyānaṃ yācanā nāma.

Here, ‘the wise’ refers to the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddha, those practicing for enlightenment, and the Bodhisattas who have gone forth in the sage's going-forth—all of whom are wise and virtuous. Such wise ones do not ask, saying, ‘Give us this and that.’ ‘The wise one should understand’ means the wise and discerning supporter ought to understand and know for himself whatever is needed, whether in times of sickness or health. ‘The noble ones stand with an objective’ means the noble ones, without breaking their silence, stand for the sake of what they need, solely by the practice of the alms-round, without disturbing the body or speech. For one who makes a sign by showing a bodily change is said to disturb the body; one who makes a break in speech is said to disturb the speech. The noble ones, beginning with the Buddha, stand without doing either of these. ‘This is the asking of the noble ones’ means this standing for alms without disturbing the body or speech is called the asking of the noble ones.

Rājā [P 3.0355] bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā “bhante, yadi sappañño upaṭṭhāko attanāva ñatvā kulūpakassa dātabbaṃ deti, ahampi tumhākaṃ idañcidañca dammī”ti vadanto sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing the Bodhisatta’s words, the king said: "Venerable sir, if a wise supporter, knowing for himself, gives what should be given to a monk who visits his family, I too shall give you this and that." Thus speaking, he spoke the seventh verse:

60.

60.

“Dadāmi [M 3.0334] te brāhmaṇa rohiṇīnaṃ, gavaṃ sahassaṃ saha puṅgavena;

Ariyo hi ariyassa kathaṃ na dajjā, sutvāna gāthā tava dhammayuttā”ti.

"I give to you, brahmin, a thousand red cows along with a bull. Indeed, how could a noble one not give to another noble one, having heard your verses which are consistent with the Dhamma?"

Tattha rohiṇīnanti rattavaṇṇānaṃ. Gavaṃ sahassanti khīradadhiādimadhurarasaparibhogatthāya evarūpānaṃ gunnaṃ sahassaṃ tuyhaṃ dammi, taṃ me paṭiggaṇha. Ariyoti ācāraariyo. Ariyassāti ācāraariyassa. Kathaṃ na dajjāti kena kāraṇena na dadeyya.

In that context, ‘of the red cows’ (rohiṇīnaṃ) means those of red color. ‘A thousand cows’ means: ‘I give you a thousand cows of that kind for the enjoyment of the sweet flavors of milk, curds, and so on—accept them from me.’ ‘Noble one’ means one noble in conduct. ‘To a noble one’ means to one noble in conduct. ‘How could he not give?’ means for what reason would he not give?

Evaṃ vutte bodhisatto “ahaṃ mahārāja, akiñcano pabbajito, na me gāvīhi attho”ti [V 3.0313] paṭikkhipi. Rājā tassovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā saggaparāyaṇo ahosi. Sopi aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke uppajji.

When this was said, the Bodhisatta refused, saying: "Great king, I am a renunciant without possessions; I have no need for cows." The king, abiding in his advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and was bound for heaven. The Bodhisatta, too, with his meditative absorption unimpaired, was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne bahū sotāpattiphalādīsu patiṭṭhitā. Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, aṭṭhiseno pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and declared the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, many were established in the fruits of stream-entry and so forth. At that time, the king was Ānanda, and Aṭṭhisena was I myself.

Aṭṭhisenajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Aṭṭhisena Jātaka is finished.

[404] 9. Kapijātakavaṇṇanā

[404] 9. 9. The Commentary on the Kapi Jātaka

Yattha verī nivasatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattassa pathavipavesanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi pathaviṃ paviṭṭhe dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto saha parisāya naṭṭho”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva devadatto saha parisāya naṭṭho, pubbepi nassiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Where an enemy dwells…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Devadatta’s being swallowed by the earth. For when he had entered the earth, they started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, Devadatta has perished along with his following.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered together?” When they said, “For this one,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has perished along with his following—he perished in the past as well.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kapiyoniyaṃ nibbattitvā pañcasatakapiparivāro rājuyyāne [P 3.0356] vasi. Devadattopi kapiyoniyaṃ nibbattitvā pañcasatakapiparivāro tattheva vasi. Athekadivasaṃ purohite uyyānaṃ gantvā nhatvā alaṅkaritvā nikkhamante eko [M 3.0335] lolakapi puretaraṃ gantvā rājuyyānadvāre toraṇamatthake nisīditvā tassa matthake vaccapiṇḍaṃ pātetvā puna uddhaṃ olokentassa mukhe pātesi. So nivattitvā “hotu, jānissāmi tumhākaṃ kattabba”nti makkaṭe santajjetvā puna nhatvā pakkāmi. Tena veraṃ gahetvā makkaṭānaṃ santajjitabhāvaṃ bodhisattassa ārocesuṃ. So “verīnaṃ nivasanaṭṭhāne nāma vasituṃ na vaṭṭati, sabbopi kapigaṇo palāyitvā aññattha gacchatū”ti kapisahassassapi ārocāpesi. Dubbacakapi attano parivāramakkaṭe gahetvā “pacchā jānissāmī”ti tattheva nisīdi. Bodhisatto attano parivāraṃ gahetvā araññaṃ pāvisi. Athekadivasaṃ ekissā vīhikoṭṭikāya dāsiyā ātape pasāritavīhiṃ khādanto eko eḷako ummukkena pahāraṃ labhitvā ādittasarīro palāyanto ekissā hatthisālaṃ nissāya tiṇakuṭiyā kuṭṭe sarīraṃ ghaṃsi[V 3.0314]. So aggi tiṇakuṭikaṃ gaṇhi, tato uṭṭhāya hatthisālaṃ gaṇhi, hatthisālāya hatthīnaṃ piṭṭhi jhāyi, hatthivejjā hatthīnaṃ paṭijagganti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a monkey and lived in the royal park with a retinue of five hundred monkeys. Devadatta was also reborn as a monkey and lived in that same park with a retinue of five hundred monkeys. One day, when the royal priest went to the park, bathed, and adorned himself, a frivolous monkey went ahead as he was leaving, sat on the top of the archway at the royal park gate, and dropped a lump of excrement on the brahmin's head. When the brahmin looked up again, he dropped it in his face. The brahmin turned back and, holding a grudge and threatening the monkeys, said, “So be it; I shall know what to do to you,” then bathed again and departed. The monkeys reported to the Bodhisatta that the brahmin had threatened them. The Bodhisatta sent word to all one thousand monkeys, saying, “It is not proper to live in the dwelling place of enemies. Let the entire troop of monkeys flee and go elsewhere.” The intractable monkey, taking his own retinue, said, “I will see about it later,” and stayed right there. The Bodhisatta, taking his own retinue, entered the forest. One day, a ram was eating rice that a female rice-pounding slave had spread in the sun. Having received a blow with a firebrand, the ram, with its body aflame, fled and rubbed its body against the wall of a grass hut situated near an elephant stable. That fire caught the grass hut, and from there spread to the elephant stable. When the elephant stable was burning, the backs of the elephants were scorched. The elephant doctors were unable to treat the elephants.

Purohitopi makkaṭānaṃ gahaṇūpāyaṃ upadhārento vicarati. Atha naṃ rājupaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā nisinnaṃ rājā āha “ācariya, bahū no hatthī vaṇitā jātā, hatthivejjā paṭijaggituṃ na jānanti, jānāsi nu kho kiñci bhesajja”nti? “Jānāmi, mahārājā”ti. “Kiṃ nāmā”ti? “Makkaṭavasā, mahārājā”ti. “Kahaṃ labhissāmā”ti? “Nanu uyyāne bahū makkaṭā”ti? Rājā “uyyāne makkaṭe māretvā vasaṃ ānethā”ti āha. Dhanuggahā gantvā pañcasatepi makkaṭe vijjhitvā māresuṃ. Eko pana jeṭṭhakamakkaṭo palāyanto sarapahāraṃ labhitvāpi tattheva apatitvā [P 3.0357] bodhisattassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā pati. Vānarā “amhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā mato”ti tassa pahāraṃ laddhā matabhāvaṃ bodhisattassa ārocesuṃ. So gantvā kapigaṇamajjhe nisinno “paṇḍitānaṃ ovādaṃ akatvā veriṭṭhāne vasantā nāma evaṃ vinassantī”ti kapigaṇassa ovādavasena imā gāthā abhāsi –

The royal priest was going about investigating a way to catch the monkeys. Then, when he had come to attend upon the king and was seated, the king said to him, “Teacher, many of our elephants have developed sores, and the elephant doctors do not know how to treat them. Do you know of any remedy?” “I do, great king.” “What is it?” “Monkey fat, great king.” “Where can we obtain it?” “Are there not many monkeys in the park?” The king commanded, “Kill the monkeys in the park and bring their fat.” The archers went and, having shot them, killed all five hundred monkeys. However, one chief monkey, while fleeing, though struck by an arrow, did not fall there but reached the Bodhisatta’s dwelling place and collapsed. The monkeys reported to the Bodhisatta that he, having been wounded, had died upon reaching their dwelling place. The Bodhisatta went and sat amidst the troop of monkeys and, by way of admonishing the troop, spoke these verses: “Those who dwell in the territory of an enemy, not following the advice of the wise, perish in this way.”

61.

61.

“Yattha verī nivasati, na vase tattha paṇḍito;

Ekarattaṃ dvirattaṃ vā, dukkhaṃ vasati verisu.

“Where an enemy dwells, a wise person should not stay; dwelling among enemies, even for one night or two, is suffering.”

62.

62.

“Diso [M 3.0336] ve lahucittassa, posassānuvidhīyato;

Ekassa kapino hetu, yūthassa anayo kato.

“Indeed, for a person who follows one with a fickle mind, an enemy is created; because of one monkey, ruin was brought to the troop.”

63.

63.

“Bālova paṇḍitamānī, yūthassa parihārako;

Sacittassa vasaṃ gantvā, sayethāyaṃ yathā kapi.

“A fool who thinks himself wise, as a leader of a troop, having yielded to his own whims, lies down dead just like this monkey.”

64.

64.

“Na sādhu balavā bālo, yūthassa parihārako;

Ahito bhavati ñātīnaṃ, sakuṇānaṃva cetako.

“A strong fool is not a good leader of a troop; he becomes harmful to his kinsmen, like a decoy bird to other birds.”

65.

65.

“Dhīrova balavā sādhu, yūthassa parihārako;

Hito bhavati ñātīnaṃ, tidasānaṃva vāsavo.

“A wise and strong one is a good leader of a troop; he is beneficial to his kinsmen, like Vāsava among the gods.”

66.

66.

“Yo [V 3.0315] ca sīlañca paññañca, sutañcattani passati;

Ubhinnamatthaṃ carati, attano ca parassa ca.

“And he who sees virtue, wisdom, and learning within himself, works for the welfare of both—his own and others’.”

67.

67.

“Tasmā tuleyya mattānaṃ, sīlapaññāsutāmiva;

Gaṇaṃ vā parihare dhīro, eko vāpi paribbaje”ti.

“Therefore, one should weigh oneself against virtue, wisdom, and learning; the wise one should either lead a troop or wander alone.”

Tattha lahucittassāti lahucitto assa. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo poso lahucittassa mittassa vā ñātino vā anuvidhīyati anuvattati, tassa posassa anuvidhīyato so lahucitto diso hoti, verikiccaṃ karoti. Ekassa kapinoti passatha ekassa lahucittassa andhabālassa kapino hetu ayaṃ sakalassa yūthassa anayo avuḍḍhi mahāvināso katoti. Paṇḍitamānīti yo sayaṃ bālo hutvā “ahaṃ paṇḍito”ti attānaṃ maññamāno paṇḍitānaṃ ovādaṃ akatvā sakassa cittassa vasaṃ gacchati, so sacittassa vasaṃ gantvā yathāyaṃ dubbacakapi matasayanaṃ sayito, evaṃ sayethāti attho.

Herein, lahucittassa means he is one with a fickle mind. This is what is said: whatever person follows and conforms to a friend or relative with a fickle mind, for that person who follows, that fickle-minded one becomes an enemy and acts as an enemy. Regarding ekassa kapino: see how, on account of one fickle-minded, blind, and foolish monkey, this ruin, decline, and great destruction was brought upon the entire troop. Regarding paṇḍitamānī: whoever, being a fool himself, thinks, “I am wise,” and does not follow the advice of the wise but falls under the sway of his own mind—having fallen under the sway of his own mind, just as this intractable monkey is laid on its death-bed, so too would he lie down. This is the meaning.

Na sādhūti bālo nāma balasampanno yūthassa parihārako na sādhu na laddhako. Kiṃkāraṇā? So hi ahito bhavati ñātīnaṃ, vināsameva vahati. Sakuṇānaṃva cetakoti yathā hi tittirasakuṇānaṃ [P 3.0358] dīpakatittiro divasampi vassanto aññe sakuṇe na māreti, ñātakeva māreti, tesaññeva ahito hoti, evanti attho. Hito bhavatīti kāyenapi vācāyapi manasāpi hitakārakoyeva. Ubhinnamatthaṃ caratīti yo idha puggalo ete sīlādayo guṇe attani [M 3.0337] passati, so “mayhaṃ ācārasīlampi atthi, paññāpi sutapariyattipi atthī”ti tathato jānitvā gaṇaṃ pariharanto attano ca paresañca attānaṃ parivāretvā carantānanti ubhinnampi atthameva carati.

Regarding na sādhu: a fool endowed with strength is not a good protector of a troop; he is not excellent, not one who gains. For what reason? Because he is harmful to his kinsmen, bringing only destruction. Regarding sakuṇānaṃva cetako: just as the decoy partridge, calling even during the day, does not bring about the death of other birds but only its own kinsmen, being harmful only to them—this is the meaning. Regarding hito bhavati: he is one who acts for their welfare with body, speech, and mind. Regarding ubhinnamatthaṃ carati: whatever person here sees these qualities of virtue and so on in himself, and, knowing truly, ‘I have virtuous conduct, I have wisdom, I have scriptural learning,’ protects the troop, he works for the welfare of both himself and of the others who move about as his retinue.

Tuleyya mattānanti tuleyya attānaṃ. Tuleyyāti tuletvā. Sīlapaññāsutāmivāti etāni sīlādīni viya. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā sīlādīni attani samanupassanto ubhinnamatthaṃ carati, tasmā paṇḍito etāni sīlādīni viya attānampi tesu tuletvā “patiṭṭhito nu khomhi sīle paññāya sute”ti tīretvā patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā dhīro gaṇaṃ vā parihareyya, catūsu iriyāpathesu eko vā hutvā paribbajeyya vatteyya, parisupaṭṭhākenapi vivekacārināpi imehi tīhi dhammehi samannāgateneva bhavitabbanti. Evaṃ mahāsatto kapirājā hutvāpi vinayapariyattikiccaṃ kathesi.

‘Tuleyya mattānaṃ’ means one should weigh oneself. ‘Tuleyya’ means having weighed. ‘Sīlapaññāsutāmiva’ means like these things: virtue and so on. This is what is meant: since one who perceives virtue and so on in himself works for the welfare of both, therefore a wise person, having weighed himself in these qualities of virtue and so on, and having judged, ‘Am I established in virtue, wisdom, and learning?’ and having directly realized his established state, that wise one should either lead a troop or should live and wander alone in the four postures. Whether one is attended by a retinue or is a solitary wanderer, one must be endowed with these three qualities. In this way, the Great Being, even while being a monkey king, gave a discourse on the scriptural discipline.

Satthā [V 3.0316] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dubbacakapi devadatto ahosi, parisāpissa devadattaparisā, paṇḍitakapirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the birth: “At that time, the intractable monkey was Devadatta, his retinue was Devadatta’s retinue, but the wise monkey king was I myself.”

Kapijātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Kapi Jātaka, the Ninth.

[405] 10. Bakajātakavaṇṇanā

[405] 10. The Commentary on the Baka Jātaka

Dvāsattatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto bakabrahmānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa hi “idaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassataṃ acavanadhammaṃ, ito aññaṃ lokanissaraṇaṃ nibbānaṃ nāma natthī”ti evaṃ diṭṭhi uppajji. Heṭṭhūpapattiko kiresa brahmā pubbe jhānaṃ bhāvetvā vehapphalesu nibbatto, tattha pañcakappasataparimāṇaṃ āyuṃ khepetvā subhakiṇhesu nibbattitvā catusaṭṭhikappaṃ khepetvā tato cuto aṭṭhakappāyukesu ābhassaresu nibbatti, tatrassa esā diṭṭhi uppajji. So hi neva uparibrahmalokato cutiṃ, na tattha upapattiṃ anussari, tadubhayampi apassanto evaṃ diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhi. Bhagavā tassa cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya seyyathāpi [P 3.0359] nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva jetavane antarahito tasmiṃ brahmaloke pāturahosi. Atha [M 3.0338] brahmā bhagavantaṃ disvā “ehi kho, mārisa, svāgataṃ mārisa, cirassaṃ kho, mārisa, imaṃ pariyāyamakāsi, yadidaṃ idhāgamanāya. Idañhi mārisa, niccaṃ idaṃ dhuvaṃ idaṃ sassataṃ idaṃ kevalaṃ idaṃ acavanadhammaṃ, idañhi na ca jāyati na jīyati na mīyati na cavati na upapajjati, ito ca panaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇaṃ natthī”ti āha.

‘Seventy-two’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Brahmā Baka. For the view had arisen in him: ‘This is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to passing away; beyond this, there is no other escape from the world called Nibbāna.’ This Brahmā, it is said, was one who had been reborn from a lower state. Previously, having developed the jhānas, he was reborn among the Vehapphala devas. There, having exhausted a lifespan of five hundred eons, he was reborn among the Subhakiṇha devas, where he exhausted sixty-four eons. After passing away from there, he was reborn among the Ābhassara devas with a lifespan of eight eons. It was there that this view arose in him. For he did not recall his passing away from the higher Brahmā worlds, nor his rebirth there. Not perceiving either of these, he thus grasped this view. The Blessed One, knowing with his mind the thought in the Brahmā’s mind, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend back his outstretched arm, even so did he vanish from Jetavana and reappear in that Brahmā world. Then the Brahmā, seeing the Blessed One, said: ‘Come, good sir! Welcome, good sir! It has been a long time, good sir, since you made this occasion to come here. For this, good sir, is permanent, this is stable, this is eternal, this is complete, this is not subject to passing away. Here one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn. And beyond this, there is no other, higher escape.’

Evaṃ vutte bhagavā bakaṃ brahmānaṃ etadavoca “avijjāgato vata bho bako brahmā, avijjāgato vata bho bako brahmā, yatra hi nāma aniccaññeva samānaṃ niccanti vakkhati…pe… santañca panaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇaṃ, natthaññaṃ uttari nissaraṇanti vakkhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.175). Taṃ sutvā brahmā “tvaṃ evaṃ kathesi, tvaṃ evaṃ kathesi, iti maṃ esa anuyuñjanto anubandhatī”ti cintetvā yathā nāma dubbalo coro katipaye pahāre labhitvā “kiṃ ahameva coro, asukopi coro asukopi coro”ti sabbepi sahāyake ācikkhati, tatheva bhagavato anuyogabhayena bhīto aññepi attano sahāyake ācikkhanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

When this was said, the Blessed One said this to Baka the Brahmā: ‘Brahmā Baka has fallen into ignorance, indeed, Brahmā Baka has fallen into ignorance, in that he says what is impermanent is permanent... and while there is another, higher escape, he says, “There is no other, higher escape.”’ Hearing this, the Brahmā thought: ‘He says this about me, he says this about me; thus he questions and pursues me.’ Just as a weak thief, after receiving a few blows, points out all his companions, saying, ‘Am I the only thief? So-and-so is also a thief, and so-and-so is a thief!’, in the same way, frightened by the Blessed One’s questioning, he pointed out his other companions and spoke the first verse:

68.

68.

“Dvāsattati [V 3.0317] gotama puññakammā, vasavattino jātijaraṃ atītā;

Ayamantimā vedagū brahmapatti, asmābhijappanti janā anekā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.175);

‘Seventy-two, O Gotama, are we of meritorious deeds, wielding power, having transcended birth and aging. This is the final attainment of Brahmā, the state of a master of knowledge; many people aspire to be like us.’

Tattha dvāsattatīti na kevalaṃ bho gotama, ahameva, atha kho imasmiṃ brahmaloke mayaṃ dvāsattati janā puññakammā aññesaṃ upari atthano vasaṃ vattanena vasavattino jātiñca jarañca atītā, ayaṃ no vedehi gatattā vedagū, ayaṃ bho gotama antimā brahmapatti, pacchimakoṭippatti seṭṭhabhāvappatti. Asmābhijappanti janā anekāti amhe aññe bahū janā pañjalikā hutvā – “ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ brahmā mahābrahmā”tiādīni vadantā namassanti patthenti pihayanti, “aho vata mayampi evarūpā bhaveyyāmā”ti icchantīti attho.

Here, ‘seventy-two’ means: Not only I, good Gotama, but in this Brahmā world we are seventy-two persons of meritorious deeds, wielding power by exercising our own authority over others, having transcended birth and aging. This state of ours is that of a master of knowledge (vedagū) because we have arrived through knowledge. This, good Gotama, is the final attainment of Brahmā, the ultimate attainment, the attainment of the supreme state. ‘Many people aspire to be like us’ means that many other people, with hands clasped in reverence, pay homage to us, saying, ‘This is the venerable Brahmā, the Great Brahmā,’ and so on; they aspire and long, wishing, ‘Oh, may we too become like this!’ This is the meaning.

Tassa [P 3.0360][M 3.0339] vacanaṃ sutvā satthā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing those words of the Brahmā, the Teacher spoke the second verse:

69.

69.

“Appaṃ hi etaṃ na hi dīghamāyu, yaṃ tvaṃ baka maññasi dīghamāyuṃ;

Sataṃ sahassāni nirabbudānaṃ, āyuṃ pajānāmi tavāha brahme”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.175);

‘Short indeed is this life, not long, which you, Baka, consider long. I know your lifespan, O Brahmā, to be a hundred thousand nirabbudas.’

Tattha sataṃ sahassāni nirabbudānanti nirabbudasaṅkhātānaṃ gaṇanānaṃ satasahassāni. Vassānañhi dasadasakaṃ sataṃ, dasa satānaṃ sahassaṃ, sataṃ sahassānaṃ satasahassaṃ, sataṃ satasahassānaṃ koṭi nāma, sataṃ koṭisatasahassānaṃ pakoṭi nāma, sataṃ pakoṭisatasahassānaṃ koṭipakoṭi nāma, sataṃ koṭipakoṭisatasahassānaṃ ekaṃ nahutaṃ nāma, sataṃ nahutasatasahassānaṃ ekaṃ ninnahutaṃ nāma. Cheko gaṇako ettakaṃ gaṇetuṃ sakkoti, tato paraṃ gaṇanā nāma buddhānameva visayo. Tattha sataṃ ninnahutasatasahassānaṃ ekaṃ abbudaṃ, vīsati abbudāni ekaṃ nirabbudaṃ, tesaṃ nirabbudasatasahassānaṃ ekaṃ ahahaṃ nāma, ettakaṃ bakassa brahmuno tasmiṃ bhave avasiṭṭhaṃ āyu, taṃ sandhāya bhagavā evamāha.

Here, ‘a hundred thousand nirabbudas’ means a hundred thousand of the number called nirabbuda. For ten tens are a hundred; ten hundreds are a thousand; a hundred thousands are a hundred-thousand; a hundred hundred-thousands are a koṭi; a hundred hundred-thousands of koṭis are a pakoṭi; a hundred hundred-thousands of pakoṭis are a koṭipakoṭi; a hundred hundred-thousands of koṭipakoṭis are one nahuta; and a hundred hundred-thousands of nahutas are one ninnahuta. A skilled calculator can count this far; beyond this, calculation is the domain of the Buddhas alone. Here, a hundred hundred-thousands of ninnahutas are one abbuda; twenty abbudas are one nirabbuda; and a hundred thousand of those nirabbudas are one ahaha. Such was the remaining lifespan of Brahmā Baka in that existence. Referring to this, the Blessed One spoke thus.

Taṃ sutvā bako tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, Baka spoke the third verse:

70.

70.

“Anantadassī [V 3.0318] bhagavāhamasmi, jātijjaraṃ sokamupātivatto;

Kiṃ me purāṇaṃ vatasīlavattaṃ, ācikkha me taṃ yamahaṃ vijañña”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.175);

‘“I am the Blessed One, the Seer of the Infinite, having transcended birth, aging, and sorrow”—so you say. What then was my ancient vow and virtuous conduct? Tell me that, so that I may know it.’

Tattha bhagavāti bhagavā tumhe “āyuṃ pajānāmi tavāha”nti vadantā “ahaṃ anantadassī jātijarañca sokañca upātivattosmī”ti vadatha. Vatasīlavattanti vatasamādānañca sīlavattañca. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadi tumhe sabbaññubuddhā, evaṃ sante kiṃ mayhaṃ purāṇaṃ vatañca sīlavattañca, ācikkha me taṃ, yamahaṃ tayā ācikkhitaṃ yāthāvasarasato vijāneyyanti.

Here, ‘Blessed One’ means: You, O Blessed One, in saying, “I know your lifespan,” are saying, “I am a seer of the infinite, I have overcome birth, aging, and sorrow.” “Vows and virtuous conduct” means the undertaking of vows and virtuous conduct. This is what is said: “If you are an omniscient Buddha, then what was my ancient vow and virtuous conduct? Tell me that, so that I may know it as it truly was, when told by you.”

Athassa [M 3.0340] bhagavā atītāni vatthūni āharitvā ācikkhanto catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the Blessed One, intending to relate past events to Baka Brahmā, spoke these verses:

71.

71.

“Yaṃ tvaṃ apāyesi bahū manusse, pipāsite ghammani samparete;

Taṃ te purāṇaṃ vatasīlavattaṃ, suttappabuddhova anussarāmi.

‘That you gave drink to many people who were thirsty and overcome by the heat—that ancient vow and virtuous conduct of yours, I recall as if just awakened from sleep.’

72.

72.

“Yaṃ [P 3.0361] eṇikūlasmi janaṃ gahītaṃ, amocayī gayhaka nīyamānaṃ;

Taṃ te purāṇaṃ vatasīlavattaṃ, suttappabuddhova anussarāmi.

‘That you freed the people seized on the bank of the Eni as they were being led away by a captor—that ancient vow and virtuous conduct of yours, I recall as if just awakened from sleep.’

73.

73.

“Gaṅgāya sotasmiṃ gahītanāvaṃ, luddena nāgena manussakappā;

Amocayi tvaṃ balasā pasayha, taṃ te purāṇaṃ vatasīlavattaṃ;

Suttappabuddhova anussarāmi.

‘When a boat was seized in the current of the Ganges by a fierce Nāga, you freed the human beings by force, overpowering him. That ancient vow and virtuous conduct of yours, I recall as if just awakened from sleep.’

74.

74.

“Kappo ca te baddhacaro ahosiṃ, sambuddhimantaṃ vatinaṃ amaññaṃ;

Taṃ te purāṇaṃ vatasīlavattaṃ, suttappabuddhova anussarāmī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.175);

‘And I was your attendant named Kappa; I considered you wise and observant of your vows. That ancient vow and virtuous conduct of yours, I recall as if just awakened from sleep.’

Tattha apāyesīti pāyesi. Ghammani sampareteti ghammena samparete ativiya phuṭṭhe ghammakilante. Suttappabuddhovāti paccūsakāle supanto supinaṃ passitvā taṃ supinakaṃ viya anussarāmi. So kira bakabrahmā ekasmiṃ kappe tāpaso hutvā marukantāre vasanto bahūnaṃ kantārapaṭipannānaṃ [V 3.0319] pānīyaṃ āharitvā adāsi. Athekadivasaṃ eko satthavāho pañcahi sakaṭasatehi marukantāraṃ paṭipajji. Manussā disā vavatthapetuṃ asakkontā satta divasāni āhiṇḍitvā khīṇadārudakā nirāhārā uṇhābhibhūtā “idāni no jīvitaṃ natthī”ti sakaṭe parivattetvā goṇe [M 3.0341] mocetvā heṭṭhāsakaṭesu nipajjiṃsu. Tadā tāpaso āvajjento te disvā “mayi passante mā nassiṃsū”ti cintetvā attano iddhānubhāvena gaṅgāsotaṃ ubbattetvā satthavāhābhimukhaṃ akāsi, avidūre ca ekaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ māpesi. Manussā pānīyaṃ pivitvā nhatvā goṇe santappetvā vanasaṇḍato tiṇaṃ lāyitvā dārūni gahetvā disaṃ sallakkhetvā arogā kantāraṃ atikkamiṃsu, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Here, ‘apāyesi’ means ‘pāyesi’ (he gave to drink). ‘Overcome by the heat’ (ghammani samparete) means extremely afflicted and exhausted by the heat. ‘As one awakened from sleep’ (suttappabuddhovā) means: like one who has slept in the early morning and seen a dream, I recall it like that dream. It is said that this Brahmā Baka, in a certain eon, was an ascetic living in the Maru desert. He used to bring water for many people crossing the desert. One day, a caravan leader with five hundred carts entered the desert. The people lost their way and wandered for seven days; their water and firewood were exhausted, and they were overwhelmed by heat. Thinking, “Now we will die,” they turned over their carts, unyoked the oxen, and lay down under the carts. Then the ascetic, reflecting, saw them and thought, “Let them not perish while I am watching.” By his psychic power, he reversed the current of the Ganges and directed it toward the caravan, and nearby he created a forest grove. The people drank, bathed, refreshed the oxen, gathered grass and wood from the grove, discerned their direction, and crossed the desert safely. This verse refers to that event.

Eṇikūlasminti eṇiyā nāma nadiyā kūle. Gayhaka nīyamānanti karamaragāhaṃ gahetvā nīyamānaṃ. So kira tāpaso aparasmiṃ kāle ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ nissāya nadītīre vanasaṇḍe vihāsi. Athekasmiṃ divase pabbatato corā otaritvā taṃ gāmaṃ paharitvā mahājanaṃ gahetvā pabbataṃ āropetvā antarāmagge cārakamanusse ṭhapetvā pabbatabilaṃ pavisitvā āhāraṃ pacāpentā nisīdiṃsu. Tāpaso gomahiṃsādīnañceva dārakadārikādīnañca mahantaṃ aṭṭassaraṃ sutvā “mayi passante mā nassiṃsū”ti iddhānubhāvena attabhāvaṃ jahitvā caturaṅginiyā senāya parivuto rājā hutvā yuddhabheriṃ ākoṭāpento taṃ ṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Cārakamanussā [P 3.0362] taṃ disvā corānaṃ ārocesuṃ. Corā “raññā saddhiṃ viggaho nāma na yutto”ti sabbaṃ gahitagahitaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ chaḍḍetvā bhattaṃ abhuñjitvāva palāyiṃsu. Tāpaso te sabbe ānetvā sakagāmeyeva patiṭṭhāpesi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Eṇikūlasmiṃ: on the bank of the river named Eṇi. Gayhaka nīyamānaṃ: being led away as captives, having been taken as prisoners. It is said that at another time, that ascetic lived in a forest grove on the riverbank near a border village. Then one day, robbers descended from the mountain, raided that village, captured many people, took them up the mountain, stationed scouts along the way, and entered a mountain cave where they sat preparing food. The ascetic, hearing the loud cries of cows, buffaloes, boys, girls, and others, thought, "Let them not perish while I am watching." So, through his psychic power, abandoning his own form, he became a king surrounded by a fourfold army, had the war drum beaten, and went to that place. The scouts, seeing him, reported it to the robbers. The robbers, thinking, "Conflict with a king is indeed not proper," abandoned all the stolen goods and fled without even eating their meal. The ascetic brought all those people back and settled them in their own village. This is what is referred to here.

Gahītanāvanti niggahitanāvaṃ. Luddenāti kakkhaḷena. Manussakappāti manusse vināsetukāmatāya. Balasāti balena. Pasayhāti abhibhavitvā. Aparasmiṃ kāle so tāpaso gaṅgātīre vihāsi. Tadā manussā dve tayo nāvāsaṅghāṭe bandhitvā saṅghāṭamatthake pupphamaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā saṅghāṭe nisīditvā khādantā pivantā sambandhakulaṃ gacchanti. Te pītāvasesaṃ suraṃ bhuttakhāditāvasesāni bhattamacchamaṃsatambulādīni gaṅgāyameva pātenti. Gaṅgeyyo nāgarājā “ime ucchiṭṭhakaṃ mama upari khipantī”ti kujjhitvā “sabbe te jane gahetvā gaṅgāya osīdāpessāmī”ti mahantaṃ ekadoṇikanāvappamāṇaṃ attabhāvaṃ māpetvā udakaṃ bhinditvā [M 3.0342] phaṇaṃ dhārayamāno tesaṃ abhimukho pāyāsi. Te nāgarājānaṃ disvā maraṇabhayatajjitā ekappahāreneva mahāsaddaṃ kariṃsu. Tāpaso tesaṃ paridevitasaddaṃ sutvā nāgarājassa ca kuddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā “mayi passante mā nassiṃsū”ti khippanisantiyā attano ānubhāvena khippaṃ supaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ attānaṃ māpetvā agamāsi[V 3.0320]. Nāgarājā taṃ disvā maraṇabhayatajjito udake nimujji. Manussā sotthibhāvaṃ patvā agamaṃsu, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Gahītanāvaṃ: a boat that has been seized. Luddena: by the cruel one. Manussakappa: with the desire to destroy humans. Balasā: by force. Pasayha: having overpowered. At another time, that ascetic dwelt on the banks of the Ganges. Then, people tied two or three rafts together, made a flower pavilion on top of the raft, sat on the raft, eating and drinking, and traveled to their relatives' families. They threw leftover liquor, food scraps, fish, meat, betel, and other things into the Ganges itself. The Nāga king of the Ganges, thinking, "These people are throwing their leavings upon me," became angry and resolved, "I will seize all these people and drown them in the Ganges." He assumed a massive form the size of a large trough-boat, split the water, raised his hood, and advanced toward them. Seeing the Nāga king, the people, terrified by the fear of death, let out a great cry all at once. The ascetic, hearing their sound of lamentation and knowing the Nāga king’s anger, thought, "Let them not perish while I am watching." Quickly, by his own power through rapid contemplation, he transformed himself into the form of a garuḍa and went there. The Nāga king, seeing him and terrified by the fear of death, plunged into the water. The people, having reached safety, departed. This is what is referred to here.

Baddhacaroti antevāsiko. Sambuddhimantaṃ vatinaṃ amaññanti buddhisampanno ceva vatasampanno ca tāpasoti taṃ maññamāno. Iminā kiṃ dasseti? Mahābrahme ahaṃ atīte tava kesavatāpasakāle kappo nāma antevāsiko veyyāvaccakaro hutvā tuyhaṃ nāradena nāma amaccena bārāṇasito himavantaṃ ānītassa rogaṃ vūpasamesiṃ. Atha naṃ nārado dutiyavāre āgantvā nirogaṃ disvā imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

Baddhacaro: a constant attendant. Sambuddhimantaṃ vatinaṃ amaññanti: they considered him to be an ascetic who was both wise and virtuous. What does this reveal? O Great Brahmā, in the past, during the time you were the ascetic Kesava, I, named Kappa, was a disciple and attendant who performed duties, and I cured your illness when you were brought from Bārāṇasī to the Himalayas by the minister named Nārada. Then Nārada, coming a second time and seeing him free from illness, spoke this verse:

“Manussindaṃ jahitvāna, sabbakāmasamiddhinaṃ;

Kathaṃ nu bhagavā kesi, kappassa ramati assame”ti. (jā. 1.4.181);

"Having abandoned the lord of men, who was endowed with all sensual pleasures, how now, O blessed Kesi, do you delight in Kappa's hermitage?"

Tamenaṃ tvaṃ etadavoca –

Then you said this to him:

“Sādūni ramaṇīyāni, santi vakkhā manoramā;

Subhāsitāni kappassa, nārada ramayanti ma”nti. (jā. 1.4.182);

"Sweet and delightful are the things here, and there are charming words; the well-spoken words of Kappa, Nārada, they delight me."

Itissa bhagavā imaṃ attanā antevāsikena hutvā rogassa vūpasamitabhāvaṃ dīpento evamāha. Tañca pana brahmunā manussaloke katakammaṃ sabbaṃ mahābrahmānaṃ sallakkhāpentova kathesi.

Thus, the Blessed One spoke in this way, pointing out how he himself, as a disciple, had cured the illness. And he recounted all the deeds done by the Brahmā in the human world, making the Great Brahmā take note of them.

So [P 3.0363] satthu vacanena attanā katakammaṃ saritvā tathāgatassa thutiṃ karonto osānagāthamāha –

Remembering his own deeds through the Teacher’s words and praising the Tathāgata, he uttered the concluding verse:

75.

75.

“Addhā pajānāsi mametamāyuṃ, aññampi jānāsi tathā hi buddho;

Tathā hi tāyaṃ jalitānubhāvo, obhāsayaṃ tiṭṭhati brahmaloka”nti.

"Truly, you know this lifespan of mine, and you know others too, for thus you are the Buddha. Indeed, such is your blazing splendor, illuminating the Brahmā-world."

Tattha [M 3.0343] tathā hi buddhoti tathā hi tvaṃ buddho. Buddhānañhi aññātaṃ nāma natthi, sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattāyeva hi te buddhā nāmāti dasseti. Tathā hi tāyanti buddhattāyeva ca pana tava ayaṃ jalito sarīrappabhānubhāvo. Obhāsayaṃ tiṭṭhatīti imaṃ sakalampi brahmalokaṃ obhāsento tiṭṭhati.

There, 'for thus indeed the Buddha' means 'thus indeed you are the Buddha.' For indeed, there is nothing unknown to the Buddhas; it shows that they are called Buddhas precisely because they are awakened to all things. 'Indeed, such is your' refers to the power of the blazing radiance of your body, due to your Buddhahood. 'Illuminating stands' means he stands illuminating this entire Brahmā-world.

Evaṃ [V 3.0321] satthā attano buddhaguṇaṃ jānāpento dhammaṃ desetvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne sampattānaṃ dasamattānaṃ brahmasahassānaṃ anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsu. Iti bhagavā bahūnaṃ brahmānaṃ avassayo hutvā brahmalokā jetavanaṃ āgantvā tattha kathitaniyāmeneva taṃ dhammadesanaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kathetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kesavatāpaso bakabrahmā ahosi, kappamāṇavo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus, the Teacher, making known his own qualities as a Buddha, taught the Dhamma and revealed the truths. At the conclusion of the truths, the minds of about ten thousand brahmās who had arrived were liberated from the taints without clinging. Thus, the Blessed One, having become a refuge for many brahmās, returned from the Brahmā-world to Jetavana. There, in accordance with the manner in which he had spoken in the Brahmā-world, he related that Dhamma discourse to the monks and connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the ascetic Kesava was the Brahmā Baka, and the youth Kappa was none other than myself."

Bakajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The tenth is the commentary on the Baka Jātaka.

Kukkuvaggo paṭhamo.

The first chapter is the Kukkuvagga.

2. Gandhāravaggo

2. The Gandhāra Chapter

[406] 1. Gandhārajātakavaṇṇanā

[406] 1. The Gandhāra Jātaka Commentary.

Hitvā [V 3.0322] gāmasahassānīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto bhesajjasannidhikārasikkhāpadaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pana rājagahe samuṭṭhitaṃ. Āyasmatā hi pilindavacchena ārāmikakulaṃ mocetuṃ rājanivesanaṃ gantvā rañño pāsāde iddhibalena sovaṇṇamaye kate manussā pasīditvā therassa pañca bhesajjāni pahiṇiṃsu. So tāni parisāya vissajjesi. Parisā panassa bāhullikā ahosi, laddhaṃ [P 3.0364] laddhaṃ koḷambepi ghaṭepi pattatthavikāyopi pūretvā paṭisāmesi. Manussā disvā “mahicchā ime samaṇā antokoṭṭhāgārikā”ti ujjhāyiṃsu. Satthā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “yāni kho pana tāni gilānānaṃ bhikkhūna”nti (pārā. 622-623) sikkhāpadaṃ paññapetvā “bhikkhave, porāṇakapaṇḍitā anuppanne buddhe bāhirakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pañcasīlamattakaṃ rakkhantāpi loṇasakkharamattakaṃ punadivasatthāya nidahante [M 3.0344] garahiṃsu, tumhe pana evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā dutiyatatiyadivasatthāya sannidhiṃ karontā ayuttaṃ karothā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This story, beginning with 'Having left behind thousands of villages,' the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the training rule on the hoarding of medicines. The incident, however, arose in Rājagaha. For the Venerable Pilindavaccha, wishing to free a family of monastery attendants, went to the king’s residence. By his psychic power, he made the king's palace golden, and the people, being filled with faith, sent the five medicines to the elder. He distributed them to his following. But his following had many possessions; they filled pots, jars, and alms-bowl bags with whatever they received and stored it away. People, seeing this, complained: 'These ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, are of great desire; they have internal granaries!' Hearing of this matter, the Teacher laid down the training rule: 'Whatever medicines are for sick monks...' (Pārā. 622-623). Then he said: 'Monks, the wise of old, having gone forth in an external dispensation before the Buddha had appeared and observing merely the five precepts, criticized the storing of even a little salt for the next day. But you, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, act improperly by hoarding for a second or third day.' Thus he recounted the past.

Atīte gandhāraraṭṭhe bodhisatto gandhārarañño putto hutvā pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Majjhimapadesepi videharaṭṭhe videho nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Te dvepi rājāno adiṭṭhasahāyā hutvā aññamaññaṃ thiravissāsā ahesuṃ. Tadā manussā dīghāyukā honti, tiṃsa vassasahassāni jīvanti. Athekadā gandhārarājā puṇṇamuposathadivase samādinnasīlo mahātale paññattavarapallaṅkamajjhagato vivaṭena sīhapañjarena pācīnalokadhātuṃ olokento amaccānaṃ dhammatthayuttakathaṃ kathento nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe gaganatalaṃ atilaṅghantamiva paripuṇṇaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ rāhu avatthari, candappabhā antaradhāyi. Amaccā candālokaṃ apassantā candassa rāhunā gahitabhāvaṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā candaṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ cando āgantukaupakkilesena upakkiliṭṭho nippabho jāto, mayhampesa rājaparivāro upakkileso, na kho pana metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yāhaṃ rāhunā gahitacando viya nippabho bhaveyyaṃ, visuddhe gaganatare virocantaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ viya rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajissāmi, kiṃ me parena ovaditena[V 3.0323], kule ca gaṇe ca alaggo hutvā attānameva ovadanto vicarissāmi, idaṃ me patirūpa”nti cintetvā “yaṃ icchatha, taṃ [P 3.0365] rājānaṃ karothā”ti rajjaṃ amaccānaṃ niyyādesi. So rajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā jhānaratisamappito himavantapadese vāsaṃ kappesi.

In the past, in the land of Gandhāra, the Bodhisatta was born as the son of the king of Gandhāra. After his father's passing, he was established in the kingdom and ruled righteously. In the Middle Country, in the land of Videha, a king named Videha also ruled. These two kings, though they were friends who had never met, had mutual and unwavering trust. At that time, human beings were long-lived, living for thirty thousand years. Then one day, on the full moon Uposatha day, the king of Gandhāra, having undertaken the precepts, sat in the middle of a fine couch prepared on the upper storey of his palace. Gazing at the eastern quarter through an open window and discussing matters of Dhamma with his ministers, he sat there. At that moment, Rāhu seized the full orb of the moon as it was traversing the sky, and the moonlight vanished. The ministers, no longer seeing the moonlight, informed the king that the moon had been seized by Rāhu. The king, looking at the moon, thought: 'This moon, defiled by an adventitious blemish, has become bereft of light. For me, this royal retinue is also a blemish. It is not fitting for me to become bereft of light like the moon seized by Rāhu. I shall renounce the kingdom and go forth, to be like the orb of the moon shining in a clear sky. What benefit is there for me in advising others? Being unattached to family and retinue, I shall wander, advising only myself. This is fitting for me.' Having thought thus, he handed the kingdom over to his ministers, saying, 'Make whoever you wish the king.' He abandoned his great kingdom over the two lands of Kasmīra and Gandhāra, went forth as a sage, attained the meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, and, devoted to the bliss of absorption, took up his dwelling in the Himalayan region.

Videharājāpi “sukhaṃ me sahāyassā”ti vāṇije pucchitvā tassa pabbajitabhāvaṃ sutvā “mama sahāye pabbajite ahaṃ rajjena kiṃ karissāmī”ti sattayojanike mithilanagare tiyojanasatike videharaṭṭhe soḷasasu gāmasahassesu pūritāni koṭṭhāgārāni, soḷasasahassā ca nāṭakitthiyo chaḍḍetvā puttadhītaro amanasikatvā himavantapadesaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitvā pavattaphalabhojano hutvā samappavattavāsaṃ vasanto vicari. Te ubhopi samavattacāraṃ carantā aparabhāge samāgacchiṃsu, na pana aññamaññaṃ sañjāniṃsu, sammodamānā ekatova samappavattavāsaṃ vasiṃsu. Tadā videhatāpaso gandhāratāpasassa upaṭṭhānaṃ karoti. Tesaṃ [M 3.0345] ekasmiṃ puṇṇamadivase aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīditvā dhammatthayuttakathaṃ kathentānaṃ gaganatale virocamānaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ rāhu avatthari. Videhatāpaso “kiṃ nu kho candassa pabhā naṭṭhā”ti oloketvā rāhunā gahitaṃ candaṃ disvā “ko nu kho esa ācariya, candaṃ avattharitvā nippabhamakāsī”ti pucchi. Antevāsika ayaṃ rāhu nāma candasseko upakkileso, virocituṃ na deti, ahampi rāhugahitaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ disvā “idaṃ parisuddhassa candamaṇḍalassa āgantukena upakkilesena nippabhaṃ jātaṃ, mayhampi idaṃ rajjaṃ upakkileso, yāva candamaṇḍalaṃ rāhu viya idaṃ nippabhaṃ na karoti, tāva pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā tadeva rāhugahitaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā mahārajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbajitoti. “Ācariya, tvaṃ gandhārarājā”ti[P 3.0366]? “Āma, aha”nti. “Ācariya, ahampi videharaṭṭhe mithilanagare videharājā nāma, nanu mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ adiṭṭhasahāyā”ti. “Kiṃ pana te ārammaṇaṃ ahosī”ti? Ahaṃ “tumhe pabbajitā”ti sutvā “addhā pabbajjāya mahantaṃ guṇaṃ addasā”ti tumheyeva ārammaṇaṃ katvā rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitoti. Te tato paṭṭhāya ativiya samaggā sammodamānā pavattaphalabhojanā hutvā vihariṃsu. Tattha dīgharattaṃ vasitvā ca pana loṇambilasevanatthāya himavantato otaritvā ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu.

The king of Videha also, having asked some merchants, 'Is my friend well?' and hearing of his renunciation, thought, 'If my friend has renounced, what shall I do with the kingdom?' He abandoned the storehouses filled with grain in the sixteen thousand villages of the Videha country, which was three hundred yojanas in extent, and in the city of Mithilā, which was seven yojanas in extent, as well as sixteen thousand dancing women. Paying no heed to his children, he entered the Himalayan region, went forth, and lived on fallen fruits, dwelling in a proper and steady manner. Those two ascetics, living a life of even conduct, eventually met, though they did not recognize each other. Rejoicing together, they dwelt together in a steady manner. Then the Videha ascetic attended upon the Gandhāra ascetic. One full moon day, as they sat at the foot of a certain tree discussing matters of Dhamma, Rāhu seized the orb of the moon shining in the sky. The Videha ascetic, looking up and wondering why the moonlight had vanished, saw the moon seized by Rāhu and asked, 'Teacher, who is this that has seized the moon and made it bereft of light?' 'Disciple, this is one named Rāhu, a blemish of the moon, who does not allow it to shine. I too, upon seeing the orb of the moon seized by Rāhu, thought, "This pure orb of the moon has been made bereft of light by an adventitious blemish. For me, too, this kingdom is a blemish. As long as this blemish does not make me bereft of light, as Rāhu does the moon, I shall go forth." Taking that very moon seized by Rāhu as my object, I abandoned my great kingdom and went forth.' 'Teacher, are you the king of Gandhāra?' 'Yes, I am.' 'Teacher, I was the king named Videha in the city of Mithilā in the land of Videha. Were we not friends who had never seen each other?' 'What then was your object of reflection?' 'Hearing that you had gone forth, I thought, "Surely, he must have seen a great benefit in renunciation." Taking you yourself as my object, I abandoned the kingdom and went forth.' From then on, they lived in great harmony, rejoicing together and subsisting on fallen fruits. Having dwelt there for a long time, they descended from the Himalayas to a border village to obtain salt and sour food.

Manussā tesaṃ iriyāpathe pasīditvā bhikkhaṃ datvā paṭiññaṃ gahetvā araññe rattidivaṭṭhānādīni māpetvā vasāpesuṃ. Antarāmaggepi nesaṃ bhattakiccakaraṇatthāya udakaphāsukaṭṭhāne paṇṇasālaṃ kāresuṃ. Te paccantagāme bhikkhaṃ caritvā tāya paṇṇasālāya nisīditvā [V 3.0324] paribhuñjitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti. Tepi manussā tesaṃ āhāraṃ dadamānā ekadā loṇaṃ patte pakkhipitvā denti, ekadā paṇṇapuṭe bandhitvā denti, ekadā aloṇakāhārameva denti. Te ekadivasaṃ paṇṇapuṭe bahutaraṃ loṇaṃ adaṃsu. Videhatāpaso loṇaṃ ādāya gantvā bodhisattassa bhattakiccakāle pahonakaṃ datvā attanopi pamāṇayuttaṃ gahetvā atirekaṃ paṇṇapuṭe bandhitvā “aloṇakadivase bhavissatī”ti tiṇavaṭṭikaantare ṭhapesi. Athekadivasaṃ aloṇake āhāre laddhe videho gandhārassa bhikkhābhājanaṃ datvā tiṇavaṭṭikaantarato loṇaṃ āharitvā “ācariya, loṇaṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. “Ajja manussehi [M 3.0346] loṇaṃ na dinnaṃ, tvaṃ kuto labhasī”ti? “Ācariya, purimadivase manussā bahuṃ loṇamadaṃsu, athāhaṃ ‘aloṇakadivase bhavissatī’ti atirekaṃ loṇaṃ ṭhapesi”nti. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “moghapurisa, tiyojanasatikaṃ videharaṭṭhaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā akiñcanabhāvaṃ patvā idāni loṇasakkharāya taṇhaṃ janesī”ti tajjetvā ovadanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The people, pleased with the conduct of those ascetics, gave them alms and, having obtained their promise, prepared dwelling places in the forest for night and day use and had them reside there. Along the way, they also built a rest house at a pleasant place near water so that the ascetics could have their meals. After collecting alms in the border village, the ascetics would sit in that rest house, consume their meal, and then return to their own dwelling place. Those people, while giving them food, sometimes put salt in their bowls, sometimes tied it in a leaf packet, and sometimes gave them food without any salt. One day, they gave a large amount of salt in a leaf packet. The Videha ascetic took the salt and, at the time of the Bodhisatta's meal, gave him a sufficient portion. He also took a measured amount for himself and tied the excess in a leaf packet, thinking, 'It will be for days when there is no salt,' and placed it between the layers of the thatch. Then, one day when they received saltless food, the Videhan gave the Gandhāran his alms bowl and fetched the salt from between the thatch, saying, 'Teacher, take some salt.' 'Today, the people gave no salt—where did you get this?' 'Teacher, on a previous day, the people gave much salt, so I set aside the extra, thinking, "It will be for saltless days."' Then the Bodhisatta rebuked him, saying, 'O worthless man! Having renounced the Videha kingdom, three hundred leagues in extent, and gone forth, attaining the state of having nothing—now you stir up craving for a lump of salt!' While admonishing him, he spoke the first verse:

76.

76.

“Hitvā [P 3.0367] gāmasahassāni, paripuṇṇāni soḷasa;

Koṭṭhāgārāni phītāni, sannidhiṃ dāni kubbasī”ti.

"Having left sixteen thousand prosperous villages and full storehouses, do you now make an accumulation?"

Tattha koṭṭhāgārānīti suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttādiratanakoṭṭhāgārāni ceva dussakoṭṭhāgārāni ca dhaññakoṭṭhāgārāni ca. Phītānīti pūrāni. Sannidhiṃ dāni kubbasīti idāni “sve bhavissati, tatiyadivase bhavissatī”ti loṇamattaṃ sannidhiṃ karosīti.

Therein, 'storehouses' (koṭṭhāgārāni) means storehouses for treasure such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls, as well as storehouses for cloth and granaries. 'Prosperous' (phītāni) means full.
