'Do you now make an accumulation?' means: now, thinking, 'It will be for tomorrow, it will be for the third day,' you make an accumulation of even a little salt.

Videho evaṃ garahiyamāno garahaṃ asahanto paṭipakkho hutvā “ācariya, tumhe attano dosaṃ adisvā mayhameva dosaṃ passatha, nanu tumhe ‘kiṃ me parena ovaditena, attānameva ovadissāmī’ti rajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbajitā, tumhe idāni maṃ kasmā ovadathā”ti codento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Videha, being thus reproached and unable to endure the reproach, became hostile and, challenging him, said: "Teacher, you do not see your own fault but only see fault in me. Did you not renounce the kingdom and go forth, thinking, 'What use is it for me to advise others? I will advise only myself'? Why do you now advise me?" Then he spoke the second verse:

77.

77.

“Hitvā gandhāravisayaṃ, pahūtadhanadhāriyaṃ;

Pasāsanato nikkhanto, idha dāni pasāsasī”ti.

"Having abandoned the Gandhāra country, which is abundant with wealth and grain; having gone forth from instructing others, do you now instruct here?"

Tattha pasāsanatoti ovādānusāsanīdānato. Idha dānīti idāni idha araññe kasmā maṃ ovadathāti.

Therein, 'from instructing others' (pasāsanato) means from the giving of advice and instruction. 'Do you now instruct here?' means: why do you now advise me here in the forest?

Taṃ [V 3.0325] sutvā bodhisatto tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta spoke the third verse:

78.

78.

“Dhammaṃ bhaṇāmi vedeha, adhammo me na ruccati;

Dhammaṃ me bhaṇamānassa, na pāpamupalimpatī”ti.

"I speak the Dhamma, Videha; what is not Dhamma does not please me. While I speak the Dhamma, no evil stains me."

Tattha dhammanti sabhāvaṃ, buddhādīhi vaṇṇitaṃ pasatthaṃ kāraṇameva. Adhammo me na ruccatīti adhammo nāma asabhāvo mayhaṃ kadācipi na ruccati. Na pāpamupalimpatīti mama sabhāvameva kāraṇameva bhaṇantassa pāpaṃ nāma hadaye [M 3.0347] na limpati na allīyati. Ovādadānaṃ nāmetaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakabodhisattānaṃ paveṇī. Tehi dinnovādaṃ bālā na gaṇhanti, ovādadāyakassa pana pāpaṃ nāma natthi.

Therein, 'Dhamma' means the true nature, the excellent reason praised by the Buddhas and others. 'What is not Dhamma does not please me' means that which is called Adhamma, the unnatural, is never pleasing to me. 'No evil stains me' means that for me, who speaks only of the true nature and the right reason, evil does not stain or cling to my heart. This giving of advice is the tradition of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, their disciples, and Bodhisattas. Fools do not accept the advice given by them, but for the one who gives advice, there is no evil.

“Nidhīnaṃva pavattāraṃ, yaṃ passe vajjadassinaṃ;

Niggayhavādiṃ medhāviṃ, tādisaṃ paṇḍitaṃ bhaje;

Tādisaṃ bhajamānassa, seyyo hoti na pāpiyo.

"One should regard a wise person who sees one's faults and speaks reprovingly as a revealer of treasure. One should associate with such a sage; for one who associates with such a one, it is better, not worse.

“Ovadeyyānusāseyya, asabbhā ca nivāraye;

Satañhi so piyo hoti, asataṃ hoti appiyo”ti. (dha. pa. 76-77);

"One should advise and instruct, and restrain others from what is unseemly; for such a one is dear to the good, but not dear to the bad.' (Dhp. 76-77);

Videhatāpaso bodhisattassa kathaṃ sutvā “ācariya, atthanissitaṃ kathentenapi paraṃ ghaṭṭetvā rosetvā kathetuṃ na [P 3.0368] vaṭṭati, tvaṃ maṃ kuṇṭhasatthakena muṇḍento viya atipharusaṃ kathesī”ti vatvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

The Videha ascetic, having heard the Bodhisatta's words, said, "Teacher, even when speaking what is based on the truth, it is not proper to speak in a way that offends and angers another. You speak to me extremely harshly, as if shaving me with a blunt razor." Then he spoke the fourth verse:

79.

79.

“Yena kenaci vaṇṇena, paro labhati ruppanaṃ;

Mahatthiyampi ce vācaṃ, na taṃ bhāseyya paṇḍito”ti.

"By whatever way another is vexed, even if it is a speech of great benefit, a wise person should not utter it."

Tattha yena kenacīti dhammayuttenāpi kāraṇena. Labhati ruppananti ghaṭṭanaṃ dussanaṃ kuppanaṃ labhatiyeva. Na taṃ bhāseyyāti tasmā taṃ parapuggalaṃ yāya so vācāya dussati, taṃ mahatthiyaṃ mahantaṃ atthanissitampi vācaṃ na bhāseyyāti attho.

Therein, 'by whatever' means even by a reason connected with the Dhamma. 'Is vexed' means one certainly experiences friction, resentment, and anger. 'Should not utter it' means: therefore, one should not speak those words by which another person becomes upset, even if that speech is of great worth and based on great meaning.

Athassa bodhisatto pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta spoke the fifth verse to him:

80.

80.

“Kāmaṃ [V 3.0326] ruppatu vā mā vā, bhusaṃva vikirīyatu;

Dhammaṃ me bhaṇamānassa, na pāpamupalimpatī”ti.

"Let him certainly be vexed or not, let him be scattered like chaff; while I am speaking the Dhamma, no evil stains me."

Tattha kāmanti ekaṃsena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ayuttakārako puggalo “ayuttaṃ te kata”nti ovadiyamāno ekaṃseneva kujjhatu vā mā vā kujjhatu, atha vā bhusamuṭṭhi viya vikirīyatu, mayhaṃ pana dhammaṃ bhaṇantassa pāpaṃ nāma natthīti.

Therein, 'as he wishes' means certainly. This is what is said: A person who acts improperly, being admonished with 'You have acted improperly,' may certainly get angry or not get angry, or may be scattered like a handful of chaff; but for me, when I speak the Dhamma, there is no evil.

Evañca pana vatvā “na vo ahaṃ, ānanda, tathā parakkamissāmi, yathā kumbhakāro āmake āmakamatte. Niggayha niggayhāhaṃ ānanda, vakkhāmi, yo [M 3.0348] sāro so ṭhassatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.196) imassa sugatovādassa anurūpāya paṭipattiyā ṭhatvā “yathā kumbhakāro bhājanesu punappunaṃ ākoṭetvā ākoṭetvā āmakaṃ aggahetvā supakkameva bhājanaṃ gaṇhāti, evaṃ punappunaṃ ovaditvā niggaṇhitvā pakkabhājanasadiso puggalo gahetabbo”ti dassetuṃ puna taṃ ovadanto –

And having said this, and following the practice befitting this advice of the Well-Farer—'I will not treat you, Ānanda, as a potter does with raw, unfired pots. Having rebuked again and again, Ānanda, I will speak; that which is the essence will remain' (MN 3.196)—and to illustrate that 'Just as a potter, repeatedly tapping the vessels, does not take the unfired ones but only the well-fired vessel, so too, after repeatedly advising and admonishing, a person like a well-fired vessel should be accepted,' he again admonished him—

81.

81.

“No ce assa sakā buddhi, vinayo vā susikkhito;

Vane andhamahiṃsova, careyya bahuko jano.

"If there were no wisdom of one's own, nor well-learned discipline, many people would wander like a blind buffalo in the forest."

82.

82.

“Yasmā ca panidhekacce, āceramhi susikkhitā;

Tasmā vinītavinayā, caranti susamāhitā”ti. – idaṃ gāthādvayamāha;

"But since some here are well-trained by a teacher, therefore, with their discipline perfected, they go about well-composed." – this pair of verses he spoke.

Tassattho [P 3.0369] – samma vedeha, imesañhi sattānaṃ sace attano buddhi vā paṇḍite ovādadāyake nissāya ācārapaṇṇattivinayo vā susikkhito na bhaveyya, evaṃ sante yathā tiṇalatādigahane vane andhamahiṃso gocarāgocaraṃ sāsaṅkanirāsaṅkañca ṭhānaṃ ajānanto carati, tathā tumhādiso bahuko jano careyya. Yasmā pana idha ekacce sakāya buddhiyā rahitā sattā ācariyasantike ācārapaṇṇattisusikkhitā, tasmā ācariyehi attano attano anurūpena vinayena vinītattā vinītavinayā susamāhitā ekaggacittā hutvā carantīti.

The meaning is this: My dear Videha, if these beings did not possess their own wisdom, or if they were not well-trained in the discipline of the rules of conduct by relying on wise advisors, then indeed, many people like you would wander just as a blind water buffalo wanders in a forest thick with grass and creepers, not knowing the safe and unsafe places, the dangerous and secure places. But since some beings here, lacking their own wisdom, are well-trained in the rules of conduct by their teachers, therefore, being disciplined by their teachers with a training suitable for each, they go about well-composed, with one-pointed minds.

Iminā idaṃ dasseti – iminā hi sattena gihinā hutvā attano kulānurūpā, pabbajitena pabbajitānurūpā sikkhā sikkhitabbā. Gihinopi hi attano kulānurūpesu kasigorakkhādīsu sikkhitāva sampannājīvā hutvā susamāhitā caranti, pabbajitāpi pabbajitānurūpesu [V 3.0327] pāsādikesu abhikkantapaṭikkantādīsu adhisīlaadhicittaadhipaññāsikkhāsu sikkhitāva vigatavikkhepā susamāhitā caranti. Lokasmiñhi –

By this, this is shown: indeed, a being, as a householder, should train in the training suitable to their family, and as one who has gone forth, in the training suitable for one who has gone forth. For householders, having trained in the practices appropriate to their families—such as agriculture and cattle-herding—live with a prosperous livelihood, well-composed. Likewise, those who have gone forth, having trained in the practices befitting renunciants—such as refined conduct in going forward and returning, and the higher trainings in virtue, concentration, and wisdom—live free from distraction, well-composed. For in the world—

“Bāhusaccañca sippañca, vinayo ca susikkhito;

Subhāsitā ca yā vācā, etaṃ maṅgalamuttama”nti. (khu. pā. 5.5; su. ni. 264);

"Much learning, skill in crafts, a well-mastered discipline, and well-spoken speech—this is the highest blessing."

Taṃ sutvā vedehatāpaso “ācariya, ito paṭṭhāya maṃ ovadatha anusāsatha, ahaṃ anadhivāsanajātikatāya tumhehi saddhiṃ kathesiṃ, taṃ [M 3.0349] me khamathā”ti vanditvā mahāsattaṃ khamāpesi. Te samaggavāsaṃ vasitvā puna himavantameva agamaṃsu. Tatra bodhisatto vedehatāpasassa kasiṇaparikammaṃ kathesi. So taṃ katvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattesi. Iti te ubhopi aparihīnajjhānā brahmalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Hearing this, the ascetic of Videha said, 'Teacher, from now on, advise and instruct me. It was because of my intolerant nature that I spoke to you; forgive me for that.' Having paid homage, he asked forgiveness of the Great Being. They lived together in harmony and then returned to the Himalayas. There, the Bodhisatta taught the ascetic of Videha the preliminary practice on the kasiṇa. Having done so, he brought forth both the higher knowledges and the attainments. Thus, both of them, without declining from their meditative absorptions, were destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā vedeho ānando ahosi, gandhārarājā pana ahameva ahosī”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka thus: 'At that time, Vedeha was Ānanda, and the king of Gandhāra was I myself.'

Gandhārajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Gandhāra Jātaka, the First.

[407] 2. Mahākapijātakavaṇṇanā

[407] 2. The Commentary on the Mahākapi Jātaka

Attānaṃ saṅkamaṃ katvāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ñātatthacariyaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu bhaddasālajātake (jā. 1.12.13 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, sammāsambuddho ñātakānaṃ atthaṃ caratī”ti. Satthā [P 3.0370] āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato ñātīnaṃ atthaṃ cariyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Having made himself a bridge—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning conduct for the welfare of relatives. The story will be made clear in the Bhaddasāla Jātaka (Jā 1.12.13, etc.). At that time, in the Hall of Dhamma, they raised a discussion: 'Friends, the Perfectly Enlightened One acts for the welfare of his relatives.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'For what discussion, monks, are you now gathered?' When they told him which one, he said, 'Not only now, monks, but in the past too, the Tathāgata acted for the welfare of his relatives,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kapiyoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto ārohapariṇāhasampanno thāmabalūpeto pañcahatthibalaparimāṇo asītisahassakapigaṇaparivuto himavantapadese vasati. Tattha gaṅgātīraṃ nissāya sākhāviṭapasampanno sandacchāyo bahalapatto [V 3.0328] pabbatakūṭaṃ viya samuggato ambarukkho ahosi “nigrodharukkho”tipi vadanti. Tassa madhurāni phalāni dibbagandharasāni mahantāni mahantakumbhappamāṇāni. Tassa ekissā sākhāya phalāni thale patanti, ekissā sākhāya gaṅgājale, dvinnaṃ sākhānaṃ phalāni majjhe rukkhamūle patanti. Bodhisatto kapigaṇaṃ ādāya tattha phalāni khādanto “ekasmiṃ kāle imassa rukkhassa udake patitaṃ phalaṃ nissāya amhākaṃ [M 3.0350] bhayaṃ uppajjissatī”ti udakamatthake sākhāya ekaphalampi anavasesetvā pupphakāle kaḷāyamattakālato paṭṭhāya khādāpeti ceva pātāpeti ca. Evaṃ santepi asītivānarasahassehi adiṭṭhaṃ kipillikapuṭapaṭicchannaṃ ekaṃ pakkaphalaṃ nadiyaṃ patitvā uddhañca adho ca jālaṃ bandhāpetvā udakakīḷaṃ kīḷantassa bārāṇasirañño uddhaṃjāle laggi. Rañño divasaṃ kīḷitvā sāyaṃ gamanasamaye kevaṭṭā jālaṃ ukkhipantā taṃ disvā “asukaphalaṃ nāmā”ti ajānantā rañño dassesuṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a monkey and, upon reaching maturity, was endowed with height and girth, possessed of strength and power equal to five elephants, and lived in the Himalayan region surrounded by a troop of eighty thousand monkeys. There, by the bank of the Ganges, stood a mango tree endowed with branches and boughs, of dense shade and thick foliage, towering like a mountain peak—some also call it a banyan tree. Its fruits were sweet, of divine fragrance and taste, and as large as great water pots. The fruits of one branch fell on the land, of another branch into the water of the Ganges, and the fruits of two branches fell at the base of the tree in the middle. The Bodhisatta, leading his troop of monkeys, ate the fruits there, thinking, 'At some time, danger will arise for us on account of a fruit from this tree falling into the water.' Thus, from the time of flowering, when they were but the size of a pea, he had them eat or knock down every single fruit on the branch over the water, leaving none remaining. Even so, one ripe fruit, unseen by the eighty thousand monkeys and concealed by a nest of ants, fell into the river and was caught in an upstream net of the king of Benares, who was playing in the water after having had nets set both upstream and downstream. When the king had played for the day and it was time to depart in the evening, the fishermen, while lifting the net, saw that fruit and, not knowing what kind of fruit it was, showed it to the king.

Rājā “kiṃphalaṃ nāmeta”nti pucchi. “Na jānāma, devā”ti. “Ke jānissantī”ti? “Vanacarakā, devā”ti. So vanacarake pakkosāpetvā tesaṃ santikā “ambapakka”nti sutvā churikāya chinditvā paṭhamaṃ vanacarake khādāpetvā pacchā attanāpi khādi, itthāgārassāpi [P 3.0371] amaccānampi dāpesi. Rañño ambapakkaraso sakalasarīraṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi. So rasataṇhāya bajjhitvā tassa rukkhassa ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ vanacarake pucchitvā tehi “himavantapadese nadītīre”ti vutte bahū nāvāsaṅghāṭe bandhāpetvā vanacarakehi desitamaggena uddhaṃsotaṃ agamāsi. “Ettakāni divasānī”ti paricchedo na kathito, anupubbena pana taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā “eso deva, rukkho”ti vanacarakā rañño ācikkhiṃsu. Rājā nāvaṃ ṭhapetvā mahājanaparivuto padasā tattha gantvā rukkhamūle sayanaṃ paññapāpetvā ambapakkāni khāditvā nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā nipajji, sabbadisāsu ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā aggiṃ kariṃsu.

The king asked, 'What is the name of this fruit?' 'We do not know, Your Majesty.' 'Who would know?' 'The forest-rangers, Your Majesty.' So he had the forest-rangers summoned and, hearing from them that it was a ripe mango, he had it cut with a knife. First he had the forest-rangers eat some, and afterwards he ate some himself; he also had it given to the women of his court and to his ministers. The taste of the ripe mango pervaded the king’s entire body and lingered. Bound by the craving for that taste, he asked the forest-rangers where the tree was located. When they told him, 'In the Himalayan region, on the riverbank,' he had many rafts bound together and went upstream by the route pointed out by the forest-rangers. The number of days is not stated, but in due course he reached that place, and the forest-rangers told the king, 'This, Your Majesty, is the tree.' The king moored the boat and, surrounded by a great retinue, went there on foot. He had a couch prepared at the foot of the tree, ate ripe mangoes, partook of a meal with various excellent flavors, and lay down. Guards were posted in all directions, and they lit fires.

Mahāsatto manussesu niddaṃ okkantesu aḍḍharattasamaye parisāya saddhiṃ agamāsi. Asītisahassavānarā sākhāya sākhaṃ carantā ambāni khādanti. Rājā pabujjhitvā kapigaṇaṃ disvā manusse uṭṭhāpetvā dhanuggahe pakkosāpetvā “yathā ete phalakhādakā vānarā na palāyanti, tathā te parikkhipitvā vijjhatha, sve ambāni ceva vānaramaṃsañca khādissāmī”ti āha. Dhanuggahā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā rukkhaṃ parivāretvā sare sannayhitvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Te disvā vānarā maraṇabhayabhītā palāyituṃ asakkontā mahāsattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, ‘palāyanamakkaṭe vijjhissāmā’ti rukkhaṃ parivāretvā dhanuggahā ṭhitā, kiṃ karomā”ti pucchitvā kampamānā aṭṭhaṃsu. Bodhisatto “mā bhāyittha, ahaṃ vo jīvitaṃ dassāmī”ti vānaragaṇaṃ [V 3.0329] samassāsetvā ujukaṃ uggatasākhaṃ āruyha gaṅgābhimukhaṃ [M 3.0351] gatasākhaṃ gantvā tassā pariyantato pakkhanditvā dhanusatamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ atikkamma gaṅgātīre ekasmiṃ gumbamatthake patitvā tato oruyha “mamāgataṭṭhānaṃ ettakaṃ bhavissatī”ti ākāsaṃ paricchinditvā [P 3.0372] ekaṃ vettalataṃ mūle chinditvā sodhetvā “ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ rukkhe bajjhissati, ettakaṃ ākāsaṭṭhaṃ bhavissatī”ti imāni dve ṭhānāni vavatthapetvā attano kaṭiyaṃ bandhanaṭṭhānaṃ na sallakkhesi.

When the humans had fallen asleep, the Great Being went with his retinue at midnight. Eighty thousand monkeys, moving from branch to branch, were eating the mangoes. The king awoke, and seeing the troop of monkeys, he roused his men and had the archers summoned, saying, 'Surround these fruit-eating monkeys so that they cannot escape, and shoot them. Tomorrow I shall eat both mangoes and monkey flesh.' The archers replied, 'Very well,' and surrounded the tree, nocked their arrows, and stood ready. Seeing them, the monkeys, terrified with the fear of death and unable to flee, approached the Great Being and, trembling, stood and asked, 'Lord, the archers have surrounded the tree, intending to shoot the fleeing monkeys. What are we to do?' The Bodhisatta comforted the troop of monkeys, saying, 'Do not be afraid; I will give you your lives.' He then climbed a straight, high branch, went along a branch that extended towards the Ganges, and leaping from its very end, he crossed a distance of a hundred bow-lengths and landed on top of a bush on the bank of the Ganges. Descending from it, he measured the space, thinking, 'This is the distance I have come.' He cut a rattan vine at its root, trimmed it, and determined the two lengths, thinking, 'This much will be tied to the tree, and this much will be in the air.' But he failed to take into account the length needed to tie it around his own waist.

So taṃ lataṃ ādāya ekaṃ koṭiṃ gaṅgātīre patiṭṭhitarukkhe bandhitvā ekaṃ attano kaṭiyaṃ bandhitvā vātacchinnavalāhako viya vegena dhanusatamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ laṅghitvā kaṭiyaṃ bandhanaṭṭhānassa asallakkhitattā rukkhaṃ pāpuṇituṃ asakkonto ubhohi hatthehi ambasākhaṃ daḷhaṃ gaṇhitvā vānaragaṇassa saññamadāsi “sīghaṃ mama piṭṭhiṃ maddamānā vettalatāya sotthigamanaṃ gacchathā”ti. Asītisahassavānarā mahāsattaṃ vanditvā khamāpetvā tathā agamaṃsu. Tadā devadattopi makkaṭo hutvā tesaṃ abbhantare hoti. So “ayaṃ me paccāmittassa piṭṭhiṃ passituṃ kālo”ti uccaṃ sākhaṃ āruyha vegaṃ janetvā tassa piṭṭhiyaṃ pati. Mahāsattassa hadayaṃ bhijji, balavavedanā uppajji. Sopi taṃ vedanāppattaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Mahāsatto ekakova ahosi. Rājā aniddāyanto vānarehi ca mahāsattena ca katakiriyaṃ sabbaṃ disvā “ayaṃ tiracchāno hutvā attano jīvitaṃ agaṇetvā parisāya sotthibhāvameva akāsī”ti cintento nipajji.

Then, taking that vine, he tied one end to a tree standing on the bank of the Ganges and the other end to his own waist. Like a cloud torn by the wind, he swiftly leaped across a space of a hundred bow-lengths, but being unable to reach the tree, as he had misjudged the length needed for tying it to his waist, he firmly grasped a mango branch with both hands and gave the troop of monkeys a signal: 'Quickly, treading on my back, cross safely by way of the rattan vine.' The eighty thousand monkeys paid homage to the Great Being, asked for his forgiveness, and did so. At that time, Devadatta, who had become a monkey, was among them. Thinking, 'This is my chance to see the destruction of my enemy,' he climbed a high branch, generated momentum, and landed on the Bodhisatta's back. The Great Being's heart broke, and intense pain arose. Having inflicted such pain, Devadatta departed. The Great Being was left all alone. The king, being sleepless and having seen all that was done by the monkeys and the Great Being, lay reflecting, 'Though an animal, disregarding his own life, he has brought his retinue to safety.'

So pabhātāya rattiyā mahāsattassa tussitvā “na yuttaṃ imaṃ kapirājānaṃ nāsetuṃ, upāyena naṃ otāretvā paṭijaggissāmī”ti antogaṅgāya nāvāsaṅghāṭaṃ ṭhapetvā tattha aṭṭakaṃ bandhāpetvā saṇikaṃ mahāsattaṃ otārāpetvā piṭṭhiyaṃ kāsāvavatthaṃ pattharāpetvā gaṅgodakena nhāpetvā phāṇitodakaṃ pāyetvā parisuddhasarīraṃ sahassapākatelena abbhañjāpetvā sayanapiṭṭhe eḷakacammaṃ santharāpetvā saṇikaṃ tattha nipajjāpetvā attanā nīce āsane nisīditvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

When the night had dawned, the king, being pleased with the Great Being, thought, 'It is not right to destroy this monkey king; I shall bring him down by some means and care for him.' He had a raft of boats placed in the Ganges, had a platform built upon it, and slowly had the Great Being brought down. He had a saffron-dyed cloth spread on the Great Being's back, had him bathed with water from the Ganges, had him drink sugarcane juice, and after his body was cleansed, had him anointed with oil cooked a thousand times. He then had a ram's skin spread on a bed, had him gently laid down there, and seating himself on a low seat, he spoke the first verse:

83.

83.

“Attānaṃ [P 3.0373] saṅkamaṃ katvā, yo sotthiṃ samatārayi;

Kiṃ tvaṃ tesaṃ kime tuyhaṃ, honti ete mahākapī”ti.

“Having made yourself a bridge, you brought them safely across. What are you to them, and what are these great monkeys to you?”

Tassattho [M 3.0352] – ambho mahākapi, yo tvaṃ attānaṃ saṅkamaṃ katvā tulaṃ āropetvā jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā ime vānare sotthiṃ samatārayi, khemena santāresi; kiṃ tvaṃ tesaṃ hosi, kime tuyhaṃ vā kiṃsu ete hontīti?

The meaning is: O great monkey, you who, having made yourself a bridge and having sacrificed your life at great risk, brought these monkeys safely across, causing them to cross in safety; what are you to them, or what are they to you?

Taṃ [V 3.0330] sutvā bodhisatto rājānaṃ ovadanto sesagāthā abhāsi –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta, while instructing the king, spoke the remaining verses:

84.

84.

“Rājāhaṃ issaro tesaṃ, yūthassa parihārako;

Tesaṃ sokaparetānaṃ, bhītānaṃ te arindama.

“I am their king and their lord, the leader of the herd. For them, overcome by sorrow and frightened by you, O subduer of foes,

85.

85.

“Ullaṅghayitvā attānaṃ, vissaṭṭhadhanuno sataṃ;

Tato aparapādesu, daḷhaṃ bandhaṃ latāguṇaṃ.

“I leaped a distance of a hundred bow-lengths, having firmly bound a length of vine to my hind feet.

86.

86.

“Chinnabbhamiva vātena, nuṇṇo rukkhaṃ upāgamiṃ;

Sohaṃ appabhavaṃ tattha, sākhaṃ hatthehi aggahiṃ.

“Like a cloud torn by the wind, propelled, I approached the tree; and as I fell short there, I grasped a branch with my hands.

87.

87.

“Taṃ maṃ viyāyataṃ santaṃ, sākhāya ca latāya ca;

Samanukkamantā pādehi, sotthiṃ sākhāmigā gatā.

“While I was stretched taut between the branch and the vine, the monkeys, treading upon me with their feet, went to safety.

88.

88.

“Taṃ maṃ na tapate bandho, mato me na tapessati;

Sukhamāharitaṃ tesaṃ, yesaṃ rajjamakārayiṃ.

“That bond does not torment me, nor will death torment me; for happiness has been brought to them for whom I exercised kingship.

89.

89.

“Esā te upamā rāja, taṃ suṇohi arindama;

Raññā raṭṭhassa yoggassa, balassa nigamassa ca;

Sabbesaṃ sukhameṭṭhabbaṃ, khattiyena pajānatā”ti.

“This is a lesson for you, O king; listen to it, O subduer of foes. A king, a wise kshatriya, should seek the happiness of all: of the kingdom, of the trained forces, of the army, and of the towns.”

Tattha tesanti tesaṃ asītisahassānaṃ vānarānaṃ. Bhītānaṃ teti tava vijjhanatthāya āṇāpetvā ṭhitassa bhītānaṃ. Arindamāti rājānaṃ ālapati. Rājā hi corādīnaṃ arīnaṃ damanato “arindamo”ti vuccati. Vissaṭṭhadhanuno satanti anāropitadhanusatappamāṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ attānaṃ ākāse ullaṅghayitvā vissajjetvā tato imamhā rukkhā laṅghayitvā gataṭṭhānato. Aparapādesūti pacchāpādesu. Idaṃ kaṭibhāgaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Bodhisatto hi kaṭibhāge taṃ latāguṇaṃ daḷhaṃ bandhitvā pacchimapādehi bhūmiyaṃ akkamitvā vissajjetvā vātavegena ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Nuṇṇo [M 3.0353] rukkhaṃ upāgaminti vātacchinnaṃ abbhamiva attano [P 3.0374] vegajanitena vātena nuṇṇo. Yathā vātacchinnabbhaṃ vātena, evaṃ attano vegena nuṇṇo hutvā imaṃ ambarukkhaṃ upāgamiṃ[V 3.0331]. Appabhavanti so ahaṃ tattha ākāsappadese rukkhaṃ pāpuṇituṃ appahonto tassa rukkhassa sākhaṃ hatthehi aggahesinti attho.

In this context, 'tesaṃ' refers to those eighty thousand monkeys. 'Bhītānaṃ te' means frightened of you, who stood there having given the order to shoot them. 'Arindama' is an address to the king; for a king is called a 'subduer of foes' because he subdues enemies such as thieves. 'Vissaṭṭhadhanuno sataṃ' refers to a distance of a hundred bow-lengths; having leaped through the air and released himself, traveling from this tree to that destination. 'Aparapādesu' means on the hind legs; this is said with reference to the waist. For the Bodhisatta, having firmly tied the vine to his waist, pressed against the ground with his hind feet and released himself, springing into the air with the speed of the wind. 'Nuṇṇo rukkhaṃ upāgamiṃ' means: propelled toward the tree by the wind generated by his own speed, like a cloud torn by the wind. Just as a cloud is driven by the wind, so, propelled by his own momentum, he reached this mango tree. 'Appabhavaṃ' means: 'I, being unable to reach the tree in that region of space, grasped its branch with my hands'; this is the meaning.

Viyāyatanti rukkhasākhāya ca vettalatāya ca vīṇāya bhamaratanti viya vitataṃ ākaḍḍhitasarīraṃ. Samanukkamantāti mayā anuññātā maṃ vanditvā pādehi anukkamantā nirantarameva akkamantā sotthiṃ gatā. Taṃ maṃ na tapate bandhoti taṃ maṃ nāpi so valliyā bandho tapati, nāpi idāni maraṇaṃ tapessati. Kiṃkāraṇā? Sukhamāharitaṃ tesanti yasmā yesaṃ ahaṃ rajjamakārayiṃ, tesaṃ mayā sukhamāharitaṃ. Ete hi “mahārāja, ayaṃ no uppannaṃ dukkhaṃ haritvā sukhaṃ āharissatī”ti maṃ rājānaṃ akaṃsu. Ahampi “tumhākaṃ uppannaṃ dukkhaṃ harissāmi”cceva etesaṃ rājā jāto. Taṃ ajja mayā etesaṃ maraṇadukkhaṃ haritvā jīvitasukhaṃ āhaṭaṃ, tena maṃ nāpi bandho tapati, na maraṇavadho tapessati.

'Viyāyataṃ' means with his body stretched taut between the tree branch and the rattan vine, like a string on a lute. 'Samanukkamantā' means: having been permitted by me, they paid homage to me and, treading upon me with their feet, crossing continuously without interruption, they went to safety. 'Taṃ maṃ na tapate bandho' means: that bond of the vine does not torment me, nor will death torment me now. For what reason? 'Sukhamāharitaṃ tesaṃ' means: because for those over whom I exercised kingship, happiness has been brought by me. For they made me their king thinking, 'This great king will remove our suffering when it arises and bring us happiness.' And I too became their king with the thought, 'I will remove your suffering when it arises.' Today I have removed their suffering of death and brought them the happiness of life; therefore, neither the bond torments me, nor will the fatal blow of death torment me.

Esā te upamāti esā te mahārāja, mayā katakiriyāya upamā. Taṃ suṇohīti tasmā imāya upamāya saṃsandetvā attano diyyamānaṃ ovādaṃ suṇāhi. Raññā raṭṭhassāti mahārāja, raññā nāma ucchuyante ucchuṃ viya raṭṭhaṃ apīḷetvā catubbidhaṃ agatigamanaṃ pahāya catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi saṅgaṇhantena dasasu rājadhammesu patiṭṭhāya mayā viya attano jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā “kintime raṭṭhavāsino vigatabhayā gimhakāle vivaṭadvāre ñātīhi ca parivārakehi ca parivāritā ure putte naccentā sītena vātena bījiyamānā yathāruci attano attano santakaṃ paribhuñjantā kāyikacetasikasukhasamaṅgino bhaveyyu”nti sakalaraṭṭhassa ca rathasakaṭādiyuttavāhanassa yoggassa ca pattisaṅkhātassa balassa ca nigamajanapadasaṅkhātassa nigamassa ca sabbesaṃ sukhameva esitabbaṃ gavesitabbanti attho. Khattiyena pajānatāti khettānaṃ adhipatibhāvena “khattiyo”ti laddhanāmena pana etena avasesasatte atikkamma pajānatā ñāṇasampannena bhavitabbanti.

'Esā te upamā' means: this is a simile for you, O great king, a simile of the deed done by me. 'Taṃ suṇohi' means: therefore, listen to the advice being given to you, connecting it with this simile. Regarding 'Raññā raṭṭhassa,' etc.: O great king, a king should not oppress the kingdom as one presses sugarcane in a press. He should abandon the four wrong courses of prejudice, gather his people with the four bases of sympathy, and establish himself in the ten royal virtues. Like me, he should be willing to sacrifice his own life, thinking: 'How might the inhabitants of my kingdom live free from fear, with open doors in the summer, surrounded by relatives and attendants, with children dancing on their laps, fanned by cool breezes, enjoying their own possessions as they wish, endowed with bodily and mental happiness?' The happiness of all should be sought and pursued: of the entire kingdom, of its trained forces of chariots and other vehicles, of its army of infantry, and of its towns and countryside. This is the meaning. 'Khattiyena pajānatā' means: by a kshatriya, who is so-called for being the lord of the fields (khetta), but who should also be one who knows, being endowed with the wisdom to surpass other beings.

Evaṃ [M 3.0354] mahāsatto rājānaṃ ovadanto anusāsantova kālamakāsi. Rājā amacce pakkosāpetvā “imassa kapirājassa rājūnaṃ viya sarīrakiccaṃ karothā”ti vatvā itthāgārampi āṇāpesi “tumhe rattavatthanivatthā vikiṇṇakesā daṇḍadīpikahatthā kapirājānaṃ parivāretvā āḷāhanaṃ gacchathā”ti. Amaccā [P 3.0375] dārūnaṃ sakaṭasatamattena citakaṃ karitvā rājūnaṃ karaṇaniyāmeneva mahāsattassa sarīrakiccaṃ katvā sīsakapālaṃ gahetvā rañño santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Rājā mahāsattassa āḷāhane cetiyaṃ kāretvā dīpe jālāpetvā gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā [V 3.0332] sīsakapālaṃ suvaṇṇakhacitaṃ kāretvā kuntagge ṭhapetvā purato katvā gandhamālādīhi pūjento bārāṇasiṃ gantvā antorājadvāre ṭhapetvā sakalanagaraṃ sajjāpetvā sattāhaṃ dhātupūjaṃ kāresi. Atha naṃ dhātuṃ gahetvā cetiyaṃ kāretvā yāvajīvaṃ gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā bodhisattassa ovāde patiṭṭhāya dānādīni puññāni karonto dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā saggaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus, the Great Being, while advising and instructing the king, passed away. The king summoned his ministers and said, "Perform the funeral rites for this monkey king as you would for a king." He also commanded the women of the palace, saying, "You, dressed in red garments, with disheveled hair and holding torches, are to surround the monkey king and proceed to the cremation ground." The ministers built a pyre with a hundred cartloads of wood and performed the funeral rites for the Great Being in the manner customary for kings. Then, taking the skull, they went to the king. The king had a shrine built at the cremation site of the Great Being, had lamps lit, and honored it with incense, garlands, and other offerings. He had the skull inlaid with gold, placed it atop a spear, and had it carried before him while worshiping with incense and garlands. He then went to Benares and placed it at the inner palace gate. Having decorated the entire city, he held a week-long relic-worship ceremony. Afterward, taking the relic, he had a stupa built and worshiped it with incense, garlands, and other offerings for the rest of his life. Abiding by the advice of the Bodhisatta, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving, ruled righteously, and was destined for heaven.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, duṭṭhakapi devadatto, parisā buddhaparisā, kapirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma and revealed the Truths, made the connection for the Jātaka, saying: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, the wicked monkey was Devadatta, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and the monkey king was I myself."

Mahākapijātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The second Commentary on the Mahākapijātaka is concluded.

[408] 3. Kumbhakārajātakavaṇṇanā

[408] 3. The Commentary on the Kumbhakārajātaka

Ambāhamaddaṃ vanamantarasminti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kilesaniggahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pānīyajātake (jā. 1.11.59 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana sāvatthiyaṃ pañcasatā sahāyakā pabbajitvā antokoṭisanthāre vasamānā aḍḍharattasamaye kāmavitakkaṃ vitakkayiṃsu. Satthā attano sāvake rattiyā tayo vāre, divasassa tayo vāreti rattindivaṃ cha vāre olokento kikī aṇḍaṃ viya, camarī vāladhiṃ viya, mātā piyaputtaṃ viya, ekacakkhuko puriso cakkhuṃ viya rakkhati, tasmiṃ tasmiṃyeva khaṇe uppannakilesaṃ niggaṇhāti. So taṃ divasaṃ aḍḍharattasamaye jetavanaṃ [M 3.0355] pariggaṇhanto tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vitakkasamudācāraṃ ñatvā “imesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ abbhantare ayaṃ kileso vaḍḍhanto arahattassa hetuṃ bhindissati, idāneva nesaṃ kilesaṃ niggaṇhitvā arahattaṃ dassāmī”ti gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā ānandattheraṃ pakkosāpetvā “ānanda, antokoṭisanthāre [P 3.0376] vasanakabhikkhū sabbe sannipātehī”ti sannipātāpetvā paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīditvā “na, bhikkhave, antopavattakilesānaṃ vase vattituṃ vaṭṭati, kileso hi vaḍḍhamāno paccāmitto viya mahāvināsaṃ pāpeti, bhikkhunā nāma appamattakampi kilesaṃ niggaṇhituṃ vaṭṭati, porāṇakapaṇḍitā appamattakaṃ ārammaṇaṃ disvā abbhantare pavattakilesaṃ niggaṇhitvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Ambāhamaddaṃ vanamantarasminti"—this discourse the Master spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the subjugation of defilements. The story will be made clear in the Pānīya Jātaka. At that time, in Sāvatthī, five hundred friends had gone forth and were dwelling within the precincts of Jetavana. At midnight, they entertained thoughts of sensual desire. The Master, who watches over his disciples six times a day and night—three times by night and three times by day—like a hen her egg, like a yak her tail, like a mother her dear child, like a one-eyed man his eye, restrains defilements the moment they arise. On that day, at midnight, as he surveyed Jetavana, he perceived the arising of thoughts in those monks and thought, "If these defilements grow within these monks, they will destroy the condition for their Arahantship. I must subjugate their defilements now and grant them Arahantship." So he left the Fragrant Chamber, summoned the Elder Ānanda, and said, "Ānanda, gather all the monks dwelling within the monastery precincts." When they were assembled, he sat on the prepared, excellent Buddha-seat and said, "Monks, it is not proper to live under the sway of defilements that arise within. For a growing defilement, like an enemy, brings great ruin. A monk ought to subjugate even a minor defilement. The wise of old, seeing a slight object, subjugated the defilements arising within and attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha." Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasinagarassa dvāragāme kumbhakārakule [V 3.0333] nibbattitvā vayappatto kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā ekaṃ puttañca dhītarañca labhitvā kumbhakārakammaṃ nissāya puttadāraṃ posesi. Tadā kaliṅgaraṭṭhe dantapuranagare karaṇḍako nāma rājā mahantena parivārena uyyānaṃ gacchanto uyyānadvāre phalabhārabharitaṃ madhuraphalaṃ ambarukkhaṃ disvā hatthikkhandhavaragatoyeva hatthaṃ pasāretvā ekaṃ ambapiṇḍaṃ gahetvā uyyānaṃ pavisitvā maṅgalasilāya nisinno dātabbayuttakānaṃ datvā ambaṃ paribhuñji. “Raññā gahitakālato paṭṭhāya sesehi nāma gahetabbamevā”ti amaccāpi brāhmaṇagahapatikādayopi ambāni pātetvā khādiṃsu. Pacchā āgatā rukkhaṃ āruyha muggarehi pothetvā obhaggavibhaggasākhaṃ katvā āmakaphalampi asesetvā khādiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a potter's family in a village at the city gate of Benares. Having come of age, he established a household, had a son and a daughter, and supported his wife and children through his work as a potter. At that time, in the city of Dantapura in the kingdom of Kalinga, a king named Karaṇḍaka, accompanied by a large retinue, was going to a park. At the park gate, he saw a mango tree laden with an abundance of sweet fruit. While still seated on the back of his excellent elephant, he stretched out his hand, took a cluster of mangoes, and entered the park. Seated on the auspicious stone slab, he gave portions to those who were worthy of receiving them and then ate the mangoes. Thinking, "Since the king has taken some, the rest should certainly be taken by others," the ministers, brahmins, householders, and others also made the mangoes fall and ate them. Those who came later climbed the tree, beat it with clubs, leaving its branches broken and shattered, and devoured even the unripe fruit, leaving none behind.

Rājā divasaṃ uyyāne kīḷitvā sāyanhasamaye alaṅkatahatthikkhandhavare nisīditvā gacchanto taṃ rukkhaṃ disvā hatthito otaritvā rukkhamūlaṃ gantvā rukkhaṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ pātova passantānaṃ atittikaro phalabhārabharito sobhamāno aṭṭhāsi, idāni gahitaphalo obhaggavibhaggo asobhamāno ṭhito”ti cintetvā puna aññato olokento aparaṃ nipphalaṃ ambarukkhaṃ disvā “esa rukkho attano nipphalabhāvena muṇḍamaṇipabbato viya sobhamāno ṭhito, ayaṃ [M 3.0356] pana saphalabhāvena imaṃ byasanaṃ [P 3.0377] patto, idaṃ agāramajjhampi phalitarukkhasadisaṃ, pabbajjā nipphalarukkhasadisā, sadhanasseva bhayaṃ atthi, niddhanassa bhayaṃ natthi, mayāpi nipphalarukkhena viya bhavitabba”nti phalarukkhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā rukkhamūle ṭhitakova tīṇi lakkhaṇāni sallakkhetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattetvā “viddhaṃsitā dāni me mātukucchikuṭikā, chinnā tīsu bhavesu paṭisandhi, sodhitā saṃsāraukkārabhūmi, sosito mayā assusamuddo, bhinno aṭṭhipākāro, natthi me puna paṭisandhī”ti āvajjento sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitova aṭṭhāsi.

After spending the day in the park, the king, adorned and seated on his splendid elephant in the evening, was returning when he saw that tree. Descending from the elephant, he went to the foot of the tree and observed it. "This tree, which in the morning stood glorious, laden with fruit, an insatiable delight to those who saw it, now stands with its fruit taken, its branches broken and shattered, bereft of beauty," he reflected. Looking elsewhere, he saw another fruitless mango tree and thought, "That tree, by its very fruitlessness, stands glorious like a bare mountain of jewels, while this one, because it was fruitful, has met with disaster. This household life is like the fruitful tree, while the life of renunciation is like the fruitless tree. The wealthy have fear; the poor have no fear. I too must become like the fruitless tree." Taking the fruitful tree as his object of reflection, standing at the foot of the tree, he discerned the three characteristics, developed insight, and attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. Reflecting, "Now the cottage of my mother’s womb is destroyed, rebirth in the three realms is cut off, the dunghill of saṃsāra is cleansed, the ocean of tears is dried up by me, the wall of bones is broken—there is no more rebirth for me," he stood there, adorned with all his ornaments.

Atha naṃ amaccā āhaṃsu “atibahuṃ ṭhitattha, mahārājā”ti. “Na mayaṃ mahārājāno, paccekabuddhā nāma maya”nti. “Paccekabuddhā nāma tumhādisā na honti, devā”ti. “Atha kīdisā hontī”ti? “Oropitakesamassukāsāvavatthapaṭicchannā kule vā gaṇe vā alaggā vātacchinnavalāhakarāhumuttacandamaṇḍalapaṭibhāgā himavante nandamūlakapabbhāre vasanti, evarūpā deva, paccekabuddhā”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā hatthaṃ ukkhipitvā sīsaṃ parāmasi, tāvadevassa gihiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyi, samaṇaliṅgaṃ pāturahosi.

Then the ministers said to him, "You have stood for a very long time, great king." "I am no longer a great king; I am what is called a Paccekabuddha," he replied. "Paccekabuddhas are not like you, Your Majesty," they said. "Then what are they like?" "They have shaved hair and beards, wear ochre robes, are unattached to family or group, are like a cloud severed by the wind, like the orb of the moon freed from the mouth of Rāhu, and they dwell in the Himalayas on the Nandamūlaka slope. Such, Your Majesty, are Paccekabuddhas." At that moment, the king raised his hand and touched his head; at once his householder's appearance vanished, and the appearance of a renunciant manifested.

“Ticīvarañca [V 3.0334] patto ca, vāsi sūci ca bandhanaṃ;

Parissāvanena aṭṭhete, yuttayogassa bhikkhuno”ti. –

"The three robes and the bowl, the razor, needle, and belt; with the water strainer, these are the eight requisites for a monk devoted to the practice."

Evaṃ vuttā samaṇaparikkhārā kāyapaṭibaddhāva ahesuṃ. So ākāse ṭhatvā mahājanassa ovādaṃ datvā anilapathena uttarahimavante nandamūlakapabbhārameva agamāsi.

The aforementioned requisites of a renunciant appeared upon his body. Standing in the air, he gave counsel to the great assembly and then went by the path of the wind to the Nandamūlaka slope in the northern Himalayas.

Gandhāraraṭṭhepi takkasilanagare naggaji nāma rājā uparipāsāde pallaṅkamajjhagato ekaṃ itthiṃ ekekahatthe ekekaṃ maṇivalayaṃ piḷandhitvā avidūre nisīditvā gandhaṃ pisamānaṃ disvā “etāni valayāni ekekabhāvena na ghaṭṭenti na viravantī”ti olokento nisīdi. Atha sā dakkhiṇahatthato valayaṃ [P 3.0378] vāmahattheyeva piḷandhitvā dakkhiṇahatthena gandhaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā pisituṃ ārabhi, vāmahatthe valayaṃ dutiyaṃ āgamma ghaṭṭiyamānaṃ saddamakāsi. Rājā tāni dve valayāni aññamaññaṃ ghaṭṭentāni viravantāni disvā cintesi “idaṃ valayaṃ ekekakāle na ghaṭṭesi, dutiyaṃ āgamma ghaṭṭeti, saddaṃ karoti, evameva ime sattāpi ekekā [M 3.0357] na ghaṭṭenti na vivadanti, dve tayo hutvā aññamaññaṃ ghaṭṭenti, kalahaṃ karonti. Ahaṃ pana kasmīragandhāresu dvīsu rajjesu raṭṭhavāsino vicāremi, mayāpi ekavalayasadisena hutvā paraṃ avicāretvā attānameva vicārentena vasituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti saṅghaṭṭanavalayaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā yathānisinnova tīṇi lakkhaṇāni sallakkhetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattesi. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

In the kingdom of Gandhāra, in the city of Takkasilā, there was a king named Naggaji. Seated in the middle of a throne in his upper palace, he saw a woman nearby wearing a jewel bracelet on each wrist, grinding perfume. Observing that the bracelets did not strike each other or make a sound when worn singly, he remained watching. Then she took the bracelet from her right wrist and put it on her left, and as she drew in and ground the perfume with her right hand, the jewel bracelet on her left wrist, coming into contact with its companion, made a sound as it struck. Seeing those two bracelets striking each other and making noise, the king reflected: 'This bracelet, when alone, did not strike; but coming to a second, it strikes and makes a sound. In the same way, these beings also do not clash or quarrel when they live alone, but having become two or three, they strike each other and quarrel. But I govern the inhabitants of these two kingdoms, Kasmīra and Gandhāra. It would be fitting for me, having become like a single bracelet, to live without governing others, governing only myself.' Taking the clashing bracelets as his object, just as he was seated, he discerned the three characteristics, developed insight, and generated the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. The rest is similar to the previous account.

Videharaṭṭhe mithilanagare nimi nāma rājā bhuttapātarāso amaccagaṇaparivuto vivaṭasīhapañjarena antaravīthiṃ pekkhamāno aṭṭhāsi. Atheko seno sūnāpaṇato maṃsapesiṃ gahetvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Tamenaṃ ito cito ca gijjhādayo sakuṇā samparivāretvā āhārahetu tuṇḍena vijjhantā pakkhehi paharantā pādehi maddantā agamaṃsu. So attano vadhaṃ asahamāno taṃ maṃsaṃ chaḍḍesi. Añño gaṇhi, sakuṇā imaṃ muñcitvā taṃ anubandhiṃsu. Tenapi vissaṭṭhaṃ añño aggahesi, tampi tatheva viheṭhesuṃ. Rājā te sakuṇe disvā cintesi “yo yo maṃsapesiṃ gaṇhi, tassa tasseva dukkhaṃ, yo yo taṃ vissajjesi, tassa tasseva sukhaṃ, imepi pañca kāmaguṇe yo yo gaṇhāti, tassa tasseva dukkhaṃ, itarassa sukhaṃ, ime hi bahūnaṃ sādhāraṇā, mayhaṃ kho pana soḷasa itthisahassāni, mayā vissaṭṭhamaṃsapiṇḍena viya senena pañca kāmaguṇe pahāya sukhitena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So yoniso manasi karonto yathāṭhitova [V 3.0335][P 3.0379] tīṇi lakkhaṇāni sallakkhetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattesi. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

In the Videha country, in the city of Mithilā, there was a king named Nimi. Having finished his morning meal, surrounded by his ministers, he stood at an open lion-window, looking down the street. Then a hawk, coming from a butcher's shop, seized a piece of meat and flew into the sky. Various birds like vultures surrounded it from all sides, and for the sake of food, they pecked at it with their beaks, struck it with their wings, and trampled it with their feet as they went. Unable to endure the attack, the hawk dropped the piece of meat. Another bird took it, and the birds, releasing the first, pursued the one that took the meat. That one also, harassed in the same way, dropped it, and another took it. The king, seeing these birds, reflected: 'Whoever takes the piece of meat, suffering befalls only them; whoever lets it go, happiness is theirs. Similarly, whoever grasps at these five strands of sensual pleasure, suffering befalls them, while happiness belongs to the one who does not. These pleasures are common to many. But I have sixteen thousand women—like the hawk that dropped the piece of meat, I too should abandon the five strands of sensual pleasure and live happily.' Reflecting wisely, he discerned the three characteristics just as he stood, developed insight, and attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. The rest is similar to the previous account.

Uttarapañcālaraṭṭhe kapilanagare dummukho nāma rājā bhuttapātarāso sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito amaccagaṇaparivuto vivaṭasīhapañjare rājaṅgaṇaṃ olokento aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe gopālakā vajadvāraṃ vivariṃsu, usabhā vajato nikkhamitvā kilesavasena ekaṃ gāviṃ anubandhiṃsu. Tattheko tikhiṇasiṅgo mahāusabho aññaṃ usabhaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā kilesamaccherābhibhūto tikhiṇena siṅgena antarasatthimhi pahari. Tassa pahāramukhena antāni nikkhamiṃsu, so tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Rājā taṃ [M 3.0358] disvā cintesi “ime sattā tiracchānagate ādiṃ katvā kilesavasena dukkhaṃ pāpuṇanti, ayaṃ usabho kilesaṃ nissāya jīvitakkhayaṃ patto, aññepi sattā kileseheva kampanti, mayā imesaṃ sattānaṃ kampanakilese pahātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So ṭhitakova tīṇi lakkhaṇāni sallakkhetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattesi. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

In the Uttarapañcāla country, in the city of Kapila, there was a king named Dummukha. Having finished his morning meal, adorned with all ornaments, and surrounded by his ministers, he stood at an open lion-window, surveying the royal courtyard. At that moment, cowherds opened the gate of the cattle pen, and the bulls, coming out from the pen, pursued a cow out of lust. There, a sharp-horned great bull, seeing another bull approaching, overcome by lust and jealousy, struck him with his sharp horn between the thighs. From the wound caused by the blow, his entrails spilled out, and he died on the spot. The king, seeing this, reflected: 'These beings, beginning from the animals, suffer because of defilements. This bull met his end on account of defilement. Other beings too are agitated by defilements. It is fitting for me to abandon these defilements which cause agitation.' Standing right there, he discerned the three characteristics, developed insight, and attained the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. The rest is similar to the previous account.

Athekadivasaṃ cattāro paccekabuddhā bhikkhācāravelaṃ sallakkhetvā nandamūlakapabbhārā nikkhamma anotattadahe nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā katasarīrapaṭijagganā manosilātale ṭhatvā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya iddhiyā ākāse uppatitvā pañcavaṇṇavalāhake maddamānā gantvā bārāṇasinagaradvāragāmakassa avidūre otaritvā ekasmiṃ phāsukaṭṭhāne cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ gahetvā dvāragāmaṃ pavisitvā piṇḍāya carantā bodhisattassa gehadvāraṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu. Bodhisatto te disvā tuṭṭhacitto hutvā gehaṃ pavesetvā paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena parivisitvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā saṅghattheraṃ vanditvā “bhante, tumhākaṃ pabbajjā ativiya sobhati, vippasannāni vo indriyāni, parisuddho chavivaṇṇo, kiṃ nu kho ārammaṇaṃ disvā [P 3.0380] tumhe imaṃ bhikkhācariyapabbajjaṃ upagatā”ti pucchi. Yathā ca saṅghattheraṃ, evaṃ sesepi upasaṅkamitvā pucchi. Athassa te cattāropi janā “ahaṃ asukanagare asukaraṭṭhe asukarājā nāma hutvā”tiādinā nayena attano attano abhinikkhamanavatthūni kathetvā paṭipāṭiyā ekekaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

One day, four Paccekabuddhas, observing the time for alms, left the Nandamūlaka cave. After chewing the Nāgalatā tooth-stick at Lake Anotatta and attending to their physical needs, they stood on the Manosilā plateau, dressed themselves, took their bowls and robes, and rose into the sky by their psychic power. Treading upon the five-colored clouds, they went and descended not far from the gate-village of the city of Bārāṇasī. In a suitable spot, they draped their robes, took their bowls, and entered the gate-village to seek alms. They arrived at the Bodhisatta’s house door. The Bodhisatta, seeing them, was delighted and invited them inside. He seated them on prepared seats, offered them water, and served them fine food and delicacies. Sitting to one side, he paid respects to the elder of the group and asked, 'Venerable sir, your going forth is exceedingly beautiful. Your faculties are serene, and your complexion is pure. What object did you see that you undertook this alms-mendicant life?' Just as he questioned the elder, so too did he approach and ask the others. Then those four individuals each recounted their own stories of renunciation, saying, 'I was such-and-such a king in such-and-such a city and country,' and so forth. One by one, in order, they each spoke a verse—

90.

90.

“Ambāhamaddaṃ vanamantarasmiṃ, nilobhāsaṃ phalitaṃ saṃvirūḷhaṃ;

Tamaddasaṃ phalahetu vibhaggaṃ, taṃ disvā bhikkhācariyaṃ carāmi.

"I saw a mango tree in the midst of the forest, shining with a dark-green hue, fruiting and flourishing. I saw it broken for the sake of its fruit; seeing that, I wander for alms."

91.

91.

“Selaṃ [V 3.0336] sumaṭṭhaṃ naravīraniṭṭhitaṃ, nārī yugaṃ dhārayi appasaddaṃ;

Dutiyañca āgamma ahosi saddo, taṃ disvā bhikkhācariyaṃ carāmi.

A woman wore a pair of well-polished jewel bracelets, crafted by skilled men, which were silent. But when a second one was added to one hand, a sound arose; seeing that, I wander for alms.

92.

92.

“Dijā [M 3.0359] dijaṃ kuṇapamāharantaṃ, ekaṃ samānaṃ bahukā samecca;

Āhārahetū paripātayiṃsu, taṃ disvā bhikkhācariyaṃ carāmi.

Many birds gathered around a single bird that was carrying a piece of meat. For the sake of food, they attacked it; seeing that, I wander for alms.

93.

93.

“Usabhāhamaddaṃ yūthassa majjhe, calakkakuṃ vaṇṇabalūpapannaṃ;

Tamaddasaṃ kāmahetu vitunnaṃ, taṃ disvā bhikkhācariyaṃ carāmī”ti.

I saw a bull in the midst of the herd, with a moving hump, endowed with beauty and strength. I saw him tormented for the sake of desire; seeing that, I wander for alms.

Tattha ambāhamaddanti ambarukkhaṃ ahaṃ addasaṃ. Vanamantarasminti vanaantare, ambavanamajjheti attho. Saṃvirūḷhanti suvaḍḍhitaṃ. Tamaddasanti taṃ uyyānato nikkhanto phalahetu vibhaggaṃ puna addasaṃ. Taṃ disvāti taṃ phalahetu vibhaggaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaṃvego paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ nibbattetvā imaṃ bhikkhācariyapabbajjaṃ upagatosmi, tasmā bhikkhācariyaṃ carāmīti. Idaṃ so phalahetu vibhaggaṃ ambarukkhaṃ dassanato paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ cittācāraṃ kathesi. Sesānaṃ vissajjanesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ panettha anuttānapadavaṇṇanā – selanti maṇivalayaṃ. Naravīraniṭṭhitanti vīranarehi niṭṭhitaṃ, paṇḍitapurisehi [P 3.0381] katanti attho. Yuganti ekekasmiṃ ekekaṃ katvā ekaṃ valayayugaḷaṃ. Dijā dijanti gahitamaṃsapiṇḍaṃ dijaṃ avasesadijā. Kuṇapamāharantanti maṃsapiṇḍaṃ ādāya āharantaṃ. Sameccāti samāgantvā sannipatitvā. Paripātayiṃsūti koṭṭentā anubandhiṃsu. Usabhāhamaddanti usabhaṃ ahaṃ addasaṃ. Calakkakunti calakkakudhaṃ.

In that context, 'ambāhamaddaṃ' means 'I saw the mango tree.' 'Vanamantarasminti' means 'in the forest,' that is, in the middle of the mango grove. 'Saṃvirūḷhaṃ' means 'well-grown.' 'Tamaddasaṃ' means 'having left the park, I saw it again, destroyed for the sake of its fruit.' 'Taṃ disvā' means 'having seen it destroyed for its fruit, I regained a sense of spiritual urgency, produced the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and undertook this mendicant life; therefore, I wander for alms.' From the time he saw that mango tree destroyed for its fruit, he recounted his entire mental process. The same method applies to the remaining explanations. Here is the explanation of the non-obvious words: 'Sela' means a jewel bracelet. 'Naravīraniṭṭhita' means perfected by heroic men, meaning made by wise men. 'Yuga' means a pair, that is, one on each arm, making a pair of bracelets. 'Dijā dijaṃ' means the remaining birds attacked the bird that had taken the piece of meat. 'Kuṇapamāharanta' means carrying a piece of meat. 'Samecca' means having come together, having assembled. 'Paripātayiṃsu' means pecking and pursuing. 'Usabhāhamadda' means 'I saw a bull.' 'Calakkaku' means one with a moving hump.

Bodhisatto ekekaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā “sādhu, bhante, tumhākameva taṃ ārammaṇaṃ anurūpa”nti ekekassa paccekabuddhassa thutiṃ akāsi. Tañca pana catūhi janehi desitaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā gharāvāse anapekkho hutvā pakkantesu paccekabuddhesu bhuttapātarāso sukhanisinno bhariyaṃ āmantetvā “bhadde, ete cattāro paccekabuddhā rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā akiñcanā apalibodhā pabbajjāsukhena vītināmenti, ahaṃ pana bhatiyā jīvikaṃ kappemi, kiṃ me gharāvāsena, tvaṃ puttake saṅgaṇhantī gehe vasā”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing each verse, the Bodhisatta said, "Excellent, venerable sir, that is indeed a fitting subject for you," and praised each Paccekabuddha individually. Having listened to the Dhamma talk taught by those four individuals, when the Paccekabuddhas had departed, he, unconcerned with household life, having eaten his morning meal, sat comfortably and addressed his wife: "Dear, these four Paccekabuddhas, having renounced kingship, have gone forth and live as those with nothing, without encumbrances, enjoying the bliss of renunciation. But I maintain my livelihood through service—what use is household life to me? You stay home, taking care of the children." Then he spoke these two verses:

94.

94.

“Karaṇḍako [V 3.0337][M 3.0360] kaliṅgānaṃ, gandhārānañca naggaji;

Nimirājā videhānaṃ, pañcālānañca dummukho;

Ete raṭṭhāni hitvāna, pabbajiṃsu akiñcanā.

Karaṇḍaka of the Kalingas, and Naggaji of the Gandharas; King Nimi of the Videhas, and Dummukha of the Pañcālas; these, having abandoned their kingdoms, went forth as those with nothing.

95.

95.

“Sabbepime devasamā samāgatā, aggī yathā pajjalito tathevime;

Ahampi eko carissāmi bhaggavi, hitvāna kāmāni yathodhikānī”ti.

All these, having assembled, are like gods; just as a blazing fire, so are they. I too, O Bhaggavī, will wander alone, having abandoned sensual pleasures as they are defined.

Tāsaṃ attho – bhadde, esa saṅghatthero paccekabuddho dantapure nāma nagare karaṇḍako nāma kaliṅgānaṃ janapadassa rājā, dutiyo takkasilanagare naggaji nāma gandhārānaṃ janapadassa rājā, tatiyo mithilanagare nimi nāma videhānaṃ janapadassa rājā, catuttho kapilanagare dummukho nāma uttarapañcālānaṃ janapadassa rājā, ete evarūpāni raṭṭhāni hitvā akiñcanā hutvā pabbajiṃsu. Sabbepimeti ime pana sabbepi visuddhidevehi purimapaccekabuddhehi samānā ekato samāgatā. Aggī yathāti yathā hi aggi pajjalito obhāsati. Tathevimeti imepi tatheva [P 3.0382] sīlādīhi pañcahi guṇehi obhāsanti. Yathā ete, tathā ahampi pabbajitvā eko carissāmīti attho. Bhaggavīti bhariyaṃ ālapati. Hitvāna kāmānīti rūpādayo vatthukāme hitvā. Yathodhikānīti attano odhivasena ṭhitāni. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – rūpādiodhivasena yathāṭhite kāme pahāya ahampi pabbajitvā eko carissāmīti. “Yatodhikānī”tipi pāṭho, tassattho – yato uparato odhi etesanti yatodhikāni, uparatakoṭṭhāsāni. Pabbajissāmīti cintitakālato paṭṭhāya hi kilesakāmānaṃ eko koṭṭhāso uparato nāma hoti niruddho, tassa vatthubhūto kāmakoṭṭhāsopi uparatova hotīti.

The meaning of these verses is: "Dear one, this Paccekabuddha, the elder of the Saṅgha, was King Karaṇḍaka of the Kalinga country in the city named Dantapura; the second was King Naggaji of the Gandhara country in the city of Takkasila; the third was King Nimi of the Videha country in the city of Mithila; the fourth was King Dummukha of the Uttarapañcala country in the city of Kapila. All these, having abandoned such kingdoms and become possessionless, went forth." "All these" means: these, being equal to pure deities and former Paccekabuddhas, gathered together. "Like fire" means just as a blazing fire shines brightly, so too do these shine with the five virtues such as morality. "As they did, so too shall I, having gone forth, wander alone" is the meaning. "Bhaggavī" is how he addresses his wife. "Having abandoned sensual pleasures" means having given up the object-based sensual pleasures such as forms. "As they are defined" means as they stood according to their own limits. This is what is said: "Having abandoned the sensual pleasures such as forms, which stood according to their own measure, I too shall go forth and wander alone." There is also the reading "yatodhikāni." Its meaning is: "from which the limit has ceased," thus "yatodhikāni" means "the portions where the limit has ceased." From the time of considering going forth, indeed, one portion of the defilements of sensual desire is said to have ceased, to be stopped; and the portion of sensual objects that is its basis also ceases.

Sā tassa kathaṃ sutvā “mayhampi kho sāmi, paccekabuddhānaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutakālato paṭṭhāya agāre cittaṃ na saṇṭhātī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard his words, she said: "Master, since the time I heard the Dhamma talk of the Paccekabuddhas, my mind has not been settled in the household life." Then she spoke this verse:

96.

96.

“Ayameva [M 3.0361] kālo na hi añño atthi, anusāsitā me na bhaveyya pacchā;

Ahampi ekā carissāmi bhaggava, sakuṇīva muttā purisassa hatthā”ti.

This is the time, there is no other; later I might not have an advisor. I too will wander alone, O Bhaggava, like a bird freed from a man's hand.

Tattha anusāsitā me na bhaveyya pacchāti anusāsako ovādako na bhaveyya dullabhattā ovādakānaṃ, tasmā ayameva pabbajituṃ kālo, na hi añño atthīti dasseti. Sakuṇīva muttāti yathā sākuṇikena gahetvā sakuṇapacchiyaṃ khittāsu sakuṇīsu tassa hatthato muttā ekā sakuṇī [V 3.0338] anilapathaṃ laṅghayitvā yathārucitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā ekikāva careyya, tathā ahampi tava hatthato muttā ekikā carissāmīti sayampi pabbajitukāmā hutvā evamāha.

In that context, "later I might not have an advisor" means that an instructor or advisor would not be available, due to the rarity of advisors; therefore, she shows, "This is the time to go forth, for there is no other." "Like a bird freed" means: just as among birds caught by a fowler and thrown into a birdcage, if one bird escaping from his hand were to cross the path of the wind and go to whatever place it pleases, wandering alone, so too, "I, freed from your hand, will wander alone." Thus, being desirous of going forth herself, she spoke.

Bodhisatto tassā kathaṃ sutvā tuṇhī ahosi. Sā pana bodhisattaṃ vañcetvā puretaraṃ pabbajitukāmā “sāmi, pānīyatitthaṃ gamissāmi, dārake olokehī”ti ghaṭaṃ ādāya gacchantī viya palāyitvā nagarasāmante tāpasānaṃ santike gantvā pabbaji. Bodhisatto tassā anāgamanaṃ ñatvā sayaṃ dārake posesi. Aparabhāge tesu thokaṃ vaḍḍhitvā attano ayānayajānanasamatthataṃ sampattesu tesaṃ vīmaṃsanatthaṃ ekadivasaṃ [P 3.0383] bhattaṃ pacanto thokaṃ uttaṇḍulaṃ paci, ekadivasaṃ thokaṃ kilinnaṃ, ekadivasaṃ supakkaṃ, ekadivasaṃ atikilinnaṃ, ekadivasaṃ aloṇakaṃ, ekadivasaṃ atiloṇakaṃ. Dārakā “tāta, ajja bhattaṃ uttaṇḍulaṃ, ajja kilinnaṃ, ajja supakkaṃ, ajja atikilinnaṃ, ajja aloṇakaṃ, ajja atiloṇaka”nti āhaṃsu. Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto “āma, tātā”ti vatvā cintesi “ime dārakā idāni āmapakkaloṇikaatiloṇikāni jānanti, attano dhammatāya jīvituṃ sakkhissanti, mayā pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Atha te dārake ñātakānaṃ datvā paṭicchāpetvā “ammatātā, ime dārake sādhukaṃ posethā”ti vatvā so ñātakānaṃ paridevantānaññeva nagarā nikkhamitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā nagarassa sāmanteyeva vasi.

Hearing her words, the Bodhisatta remained silent. But she, wishing to go forth into the homeless life before him, deceived the Bodhisatta, saying, "Master, I will go to the watering place; watch over the children." Taking a water pot, as if going for water, she fled and went to the presence of female ascetics in the vicinity of the city and went forth. The Bodhisatta, knowing she would not return, raised the children himself. Later, when they had grown a little and had reached an age capable of knowing their own welfare and misfortune, he tested them. One day, while cooking rice, he cooked it slightly undercooked; one day, slightly sodden; one day, well-cooked; one day, over-sodden; one day, without salt; and one day, too salty. The children said, "Father, today the rice is undercooked; today it is sodden; today it is well-cooked; today it is over-sodden; today it is without salt; today it is too salty." Hearing this, the Bodhisatta said, "Yes, children," and thought, "These children now know what is raw, cooked, salty, and unsalted. They will be able to live by their own nature. It is fitting for me to go forth." Then, giving the children to his relatives and entrusting them to their care, he said, "Mothers and fathers, raise these children well." Even as his relatives lamented, he left the city, undertook the ascetic's going-forth, and lived in the vicinity of the city.

Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ bārāṇasiyaṃ bhikkhāya carantaṃ paribbājikā disvā vanditvā “ayya, dārakā te nāsitā maññe”ti āha. Mahāsatto “nāhaṃ dārake nāsemi, tesaṃ attano ayānayajānanakāle pabbajitomhi[M 3.0362], tvaṃ tesaṃ acintetvā pabbajjāya abhiramā”ti vatvā osānagāthamāha –

Then one day, while he was wandering for alms in Bārāṇasī, the female wanderer saw him, paid her respects, and said, "Venerable sir, I think your children are ruined by you." The Great Being replied, "I did not ruin the children; I went forth at the time when they were able to know their own welfare and misfortune. Without worrying about them, you should delight in the life of one who has gone forth." Having said this, he spoke the concluding verse:

97.

97.

“Āmaṃ pakkañca jānanti, atho loṇaṃ aloṇakaṃ;

Tamahaṃ disvāna pabbajiṃ, careva tvaṃ carāmaha”nti.

"They know the raw and the cooked, and also the salty and the unsalted; seeing that, I went forth. You practice the alms-round; I too shall practice."

Tattha tamahanti taṃ ahaṃ dārakānaṃ kiriyaṃ disvā pabbajito. Careva tvaṃ carāmahanti tvampi bhikkhācariyameva cara, ahampi bhikkhācariyameva carissāmīti.

In that verse, 'Tamahaṃ' means 'I, having seen that behavior of the children, went forth.' 'Careva tvaṃ carāmahaṃ' means 'You too should practice the alms-round, and I too shall practice the alms-round.'

Iti so paribbājikaṃ ovaditvā uyyojesi. Sāpi ovādaṃ gahetvā mahāsattaṃ vanditvā [V 3.0339] yathārucitaṃ ṭhānaṃ gatā. Ṭhapetvā kira taṃ divasaṃ na te puna aññamaññaṃ addasaṃsu. Bodhisatto ca jhānābhiññaṃ nibbattetvā brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Having thus advised the female wanderer, he sent her away. She, having accepted the advice, paid homage to the Great Being and went to a place as she pleased. From that day forward, it is said they never saw each other again. The Bodhisatta, having developed meditative absorption and higher knowledge, was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne te pañcasatā bhikkhū arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Tadā dhītā uppalavaṇṇā ahosi, putto rāhulakumāro, paribbājikā rāhulamātā, paribbājako pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, those five hundred monks were established in Arahantship. As for the identification of the Jātaka: 'The daughter at that time was Uppalavaṇṇā, the son was Prince Rāhula, the female wanderer was Rāhula's mother, and the male wanderer was I myself.'

Kumbhakārajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Kumbhakāra Jātaka, the third.

[409] 4. Daḷhadhammajātakavaṇṇanā

[409] 4. 4. Daḷhadhamma Jātaka: The Commentary on the Daḷhadhamma Jātaka

Ahaṃ ce [P 3.0384] daḷhadhammassāti idaṃ satthā kosambiṃ nissāya ghositārāme viharanto udenassa rañño bhaddavatikaṃ hatthiniṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassā pana hatthiniyā laddhavidhānañca udenassa rājavaṃso ca mātaṅgajātake (jā. 1.15.1 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Ekadivasaṃ pana sā hatthinī nagarā nikkhamantī bhagavantaṃ pātova ariyagaṇaparivutaṃ anomāya buddhasiriyā nagaraṃ piṇḍāya pavisantaṃ disvā tathāgatassa pādamūle nipajjitvā “bhagavā sabbaññu sabbalokanittharaṇa udeno vaṃsarājā maṃ taruṇakāle kammaṃ nittharituṃ samatthakāle ‘imaṃ nissāya mayā jīvitañca rajjañca devī ca laddhā’ti piyāyitvā mahantaṃ parihāraṃ adāsi, sabbālaṅkārehi alaṅkaritvā ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ [M 3.0363] gandhena paribhaṇḍaṃ kāretvā matthake suvaṇṇatārakakhacitavitānaṃ bandhāpetvā samantā citrasāṇiṃ parikkhipāpetvā gandhatelena dīpaṃ jālāpetvā dhūmataṭṭakaṃ ṭhapāpetvā karīsachaḍḍanaṭṭhāne suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ patiṭṭhapāpetvā maṃ cittattharaṇapiṭṭhe ṭhapesi, rājārahañca me nānaggarasabhojanaṃ dāpesi. Idāni pana me mahallakakāle kammaṃ nittharituṃ asamatthakāle sabbaṃ taṃ parihāraṃ acchindi, anāthā nippaccayā hutvā araññe ketakāni khādantī jīvāmi, aññaṃ mayhaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, udenaṃ mama guṇaṃ sallakkhāpetvā porāṇakaparihāraṃ me paṭipākatikaṃ kāretha bhagavā”ti paridevamānā tathāgataṃ yāci.

“Ahaṃ ce daḷhadhammassā”ti—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Ghosita's Monastery near Kosambi, concerning King Udena’s she-elephant Bhaddavatika. The story of how that she-elephant was obtained and the royal lineage of King Udena will be revealed in the Mātaṅga Jātaka. One day, as that she-elephant was leaving the city, she saw the Blessed One early in the morning, surrounded by a noble assembly, entering the city for alms with the incomparable splendor of a Buddha. She prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata and, weeping, pleaded with him: “O Blessed One, All-Knowing, Deliverer of all the world—King Udena of the Vatsa lineage, in my youth when I was capable of performing my work, cherished me greatly, saying, ‘Depending on her, I have gained life, kingship, and a queen.’ He granted me great honors, adorned me with all ornaments, had my standing place smeared with perfume, set a golden canopy studded with stars above my head, surrounded the area with colorful screens, lit lamps with fragrant oil, placed incense stands, and set a golden vessel where dung was discarded. He placed me on a decorated rug and provided me with royal meals of various delicious flavors. But now, in my old age, when I am no longer capable of performing my work, he has stripped me of all those honors. Helpless and without support, I live in the forest eating wild grass. I have no other refuge. O Blessed One, may you cause King Udena to recognize my virtues and restore my former honors as they were before!”

Satthā “gaccha tvaṃ, ahaṃ te rañño kathetvā yasaṃ paṭipākatikaṃ kāressāmī”ti vatvā rañño nivesanadvāraṃ agamāsi. Rājā tathāgataṃ antonivesanaṃ pavesetvā buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Satthā bhattakiccapariyosāne anumodanaṃ karonto “mahārāja, bhaddavatikā kaha”nti pucchi. “Na jānāmi, bhante”ti. “Mahārāja, upakārakānaṃ yasaṃ datvā mahallakakāle [V 3.0340] gahetuṃ nāma na vaṭṭati, kataññunā katavedinā bhavituṃ vaṭṭati. Bhaddavatikā idāni mahallikā jarājiṇṇā anāthā hutvā araññe ketakāni khādantī jīvati, taṃ jiṇṇakāle anāthaṃ kātuṃ tumhākaṃ ayutta”nti bhaddavatikāya guṇaṃ kathetvā “sabbaṃ porāṇakaparihāraṃ paṭipākatikaṃ karohī”ti [P 3.0385] vatvā pakkāmi. Rājā tathā akāsi. “Tathāgatena kira bhaddavatikāya guṇaṃ kathetvā porāṇakayaso paṭipākatiko kārito”ti sakalanagaraṃ patthari, bhikkhusaṅghepi sā pavatti pākaṭā jātā. Atha bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, satthārā kira bhaddavatikāya guṇaṃ kathetvā porāṇakayaso paṭipākatiko kārito”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi tathāgato etissā guṇaṃ kathetvā naṭṭhayasaṃ paṭipākatikaṃ kāresiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher said, “You may go. I will speak to the king and have your honors restored.” Having said this, he went to the gate of the king's palace. The king invited the Tathāgata into his inner palace and offered a great alms-meal to the Sangha headed by the Buddha. At the end of the meal, the Teacher, while giving the blessing, asked, “Great king, where is Bhaddavatikā?” “I do not know, venerable sir,” he replied. “Great king, it is not right to give honors to benefactors and then take them away in their old age; one should be grateful and appreciative. Bhaddavatikā is now old, decrepit, and destitute, living in the forest eating ketaka plants. It is not fitting for you to leave her destitute in her old age.” Having spoken of Bhaddavatikā's virtues, he said, “Restore all her former provisions,” and then departed. The king did so. The news that “The Tathāgata spoke of Bhaddavatikā's virtues and had her former honors restored” spread throughout the entire city, and this matter became known among the community of monks as well. Then the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall, “Friends, the Teacher, it is said, spoke of Bhaddavatikā's virtues and had her former honors restored.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered here?” When they replied, “For this one,” he said, “Not only now, monks, but in the past as well the Tathāgata spoke of her virtues and had her lost honors restored,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ daḷhadhammo nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto amaccakule nibbattitvā vayappatto taṃ rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahi. So [M 3.0364] tassa santikā mahantaṃ yasaṃ labhitvā amaccaratanaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Tadā tassa rañño ekā oṭṭhibyādhi hatthinī thāmabalasampannā mahabbalā ahosi. Sā ekadivasaṃ yojanasataṃ gacchati, rañño dūteyyaharaṇakiccaṃ karoti, saṅgāme yuddhaṃ katvā sattu maddanaṃ karoti. Rājā “ayaṃ me bahūpakārā”ti tassā sabbālaṅkāraṃ datvā udenena bhaddavatikāya dinnasadisaṃ sabbaṃ parihāraṃ dāpesi. Athassā jiṇṇadubbalakāle rājā sabbaṃ yasaṃ gaṇhi. Sā tato paṭṭhāya anāthā hutvā araññe tiṇapaṇṇāni khādantī jīvati. Athekadivasaṃ rājakule bhājanesu appahontesu rājā kumbhakāraṃ pakkosāpetvā “bhājanāni kira nappahontī”ti āha. “Gomayāharaṇayānake yojetuṃ goṇe na labhāmi, devā”ti. Rājā tassa kathaṃ sutvā “amhākaṃ oṭṭhibyādhi kaha”nti pucchi. “Attano dhammatāya carati, devā”ti. Rājā “ito paṭṭhāya taṃ yojetvā gomayaṃ āharā”ti taṃ kumbhakārassa adāsi. Kumbhakāro “sādhu, devā”ti tathā akāsi.

In the past, in Benares, a king named Daḷhadhamma ruled the kingdom. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a minister’s family and, having come of age, served that king. He gained great honor from the king and held the position of a jewel among ministers. At that time, the king had a she-elephant named Oṭṭhibyādhi, who was endowed with strength and power, and was of great might. She could travel a hundred leagues in a single day, performed the duty of carrying the king’s messages, and fought in battles, crushing enemies. The king, thinking, “She is of great service to me,” gave her all ornaments and had all provisions given to her, similar to what was given to Bhaddavatikā by Udena. But when she grew old and weak, the king took away all her honors. From then on, she became destitute and lived in the forest, eating grass and leaves. One day, when the vessels in the royal household were insufficient, the king summoned a potter and said, “It seems the vessels are not enough.” The potter replied, “I cannot find oxen to yoke to the cart for fetching cow dung, Your Majesty.” Hearing this, the king asked, “Where is our Oṭṭhibyādhi?” “She roams according to her nature, Your Majesty,” he replied. The king said, “From now on, yoke her and bring cow dung,” and gave her to the potter. The potter agreed, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and did so.

Athekadivasaṃ sā nagarā nikkhamamānā nagaraṃ pavisantaṃ bodhisattaṃ disvā vanditvā tassa pādamūle nipajjitvā paridevamānā “sāmi, rājā maṃ ‘taruṇakāle bahūpakārā’ti sallakkhetvā mahantaṃ yasaṃ datvā [P 3.0386] idāni mahallakakāle sabbaṃ acchinditvā mayi cittampi na karoti, ahaṃ pana anāthā araññe tiṇapaṇṇāni khādantī jīvāmi, evaṃ dukkhappattaṃ maṃ idāni yānake yojetuṃ kumbhakārassa adāsi, ṭhapetvā tumhe aññaṃ mayhaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, mayā rañño [V 3.0341] katūpakāraṃ tumhe jānātha, sādhu idāni me naṭṭhaṃ yasaṃ paṭipākatikaṃ karothā”ti vatvā tisso gāthā abhāsi –

One day, as she was going out of the city, she saw the Bodhisatta entering the city. She paid homage to him, prostrated herself at his feet, and lamented, saying: “Master, the king, recognizing me as ‘of great service in my youth,’ granted me great honor. But now, in my old age, he has taken everything away and pays me no mind. I, a destitute one, live by eating grass and leaves in the forest. Having fallen into such misery, he has now given me to a potter to be yoked to a cart. Except for you, I have no other refuge. You know the service I have rendered to the king. Please, now restore my lost honors.” Then she spoke these three verses:

98.

98.

“Ahaṃ ce daḷhadhammassa, vahantī nābhirādhayiṃ;

Dharantī urasi sallaṃ, yuddhe vikkantacārinī.

“If I, while serving Daḷhadhamma, did not please him, bearing a dart in my chest, advancing valiantly in battle;

99.

99.

“Nūna rājā na jānāti, mama vikkamaporisaṃ;

Saṅgāme sukatantāni, dūtavippahitāni ca.

“Surely the king does not know my valiant prowess, my well-performed deeds in battle, and my missions as a dispatched messenger.

100.

100.

“Sā nūnāhaṃ marissāmi, abandhu aparāyinī;

Tadā hi kumbhakārassa, dinnā chakaṇahārikā”ti.

“Surely, I will die, without kin, without refuge; for I have been given to the potter as a carrier of dung.”

Tattha [M 3.0365] vahantīti dūteyyaharaṇaṃ saṅgāme balakoṭṭhakabhindanaṃ taṃ taṃ kiccaṃ vahantī nittharantī. Dharantī urasi sallanti urasmiṃ baddhaṃ kaṇḍaṃ vā asiṃ vā sattiṃ vā yuddhakāle sattūnaṃ upari abhiharantī. Vikkantacārinīti vikkamaṃ parakkamaṃ katvā parabalavijayena yuddhe vikkantagāminī. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace sāmi, ahaṃ imāni kiccāni karontī rañño daḷhadhammassa cittaṃ nārādhayiṃ na paritosesiṃ, ko dāni añño tassa cittaṃ ārādhayissatīti.

In that context, 'carrying' (vahantī) means delivering messages, breaking strongholds in battle, and carrying out and completing various tasks. 'Bearing a dart in her chest' (dharantī urasi sallaṃ) means carrying an arrow, sword, or spear fixed in her chest, striking at enemies during battle. 'Advancing valiantly' (vikkantacārinī) means one who advances in battle by conquering enemy forces with courage and effort. This is what is meant: 'If, my lord, I, while performing these duties, did not please or satisfy the mind of King Daḷhadhamma, who else now will satisfy his mind?'

Mama vikkamaporisanti mayā kataṃ purisaparakkamaṃ. Sukatantānīti sukatāni. Yathā hi kammāneva kammantāni, vanāneva vanantāni, evamidha sukatāneva “sukatantānī”ti vuttāni. Dūtavippahitāni cāti gale paṇṇaṃ bandhitvā “asukarañño nāma dehī”ti pahitāya mayā ekadivaseneva yojanasataṃ gantvā katāni dūtapesanāni ca. Nūna rājā na jānātīti nūna tumhākaṃ esa rājā etāni mayā katāni kiccāni na jānāti. Aparāyinīti appatiṭṭhā [P 3.0387] appaṭisaraṇā. Tadā hīti tathā hi, ayameva vā pāṭho. Dinnāti ahaṃ raññā chakaṇahārikā katvā kumbhakārassa dinnāti.

‘My valiant prowess’ means the manly effort I have performed. ‘Sukatantāni’ means well-done deeds. Just as the word ‘kammāni’ is the same as ‘kammantāni,’ and ‘vanāni’ the same as ‘vanantāni,’ so here well-done deeds are called ‘sukatantāni.’ And ‘dispatched as a messenger’ (dūtavippahitāni ca) means the messenger missions I performed by traveling a hundred leagues in a single day, after having tied a letter around my neck and being sent with the order, 'Deliver this to such-and-such a king.' ‘Surely the king does not know’ means 'surely this king of yours does not know these tasks I have performed.' ‘Without refuge’ (aparāyinī) means without support, without shelter. ‘For then’ (tadā hi) means 'for thus' (tathā hi), or that is simply the reading. ‘Given’ (dinnā) means 'I was given by the king to the potter as a dung-carrier.'

Bodhisatto tassā kathaṃ sutvā “tvaṃ mā soci, ahaṃ rañño kathetvā tava yasaṃ paṭipākatikaṃ karissāmī”ti taṃ samassāsetvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā bhuttapātarāso rañño santikaṃ gantvā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā “mahārāja, nanu tumhākaṃ asukā nāma oṭṭhibyādhi asukaṭṭhāne ca asukaṭṭhāne [V 3.0342] ca ure sallaṃ bandhitvā saṅgāmaṃ nitthari, asukadivasaṃ nāma gīvāya paṇṇaṃ bandhitvā pesitā yojanasataṃ agamāsi, tumhepissā mahantaṃ yasaṃ adattha, sā idāni kaha”nti pucchi. “Tamahaṃ kumbhakārassa gomayaharaṇatthāya adāsi”nti. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “ayuttaṃ kho, mahārāja, tumhākaṃ taṃ kumbhakārassa yānake yojanatthāya dātu”nti vatvā rañño ovādavasena catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing her story, the Bodhisatta said, "Do not grieve. I will speak to the king and restore your honors." Having consoled her, he entered the city. After finishing his morning meal, he went to the king and, starting a conversation, asked, "Great king, did not that she-elephant named Oṭṭhibyādhi, who, with a dart fixed in her chest, won the battle in such-and-such a place, and on such-and-such a day, sent with a message tied to her neck, traveled a hundred leagues? Did you not give her great honor? Where is she now?" The king replied, "I gave her to a potter to carry dung." Then the Bodhisatta said, "It was indeed improper, Great King, for you to give her to the potter to be yoked to a cart." Having admonished the king, he spoke these four verses—

101.

101.

“Yāvatāsīsatī poso, tāvadeva pavīṇati;

Atthāpāye jahanti naṃ, oṭṭhibyādhiṃva khattiyo.

"As long as a person has hopes, so long does he associate (with another); when benefit is gone, they abandon him, just as the king abandoned the she-elephant Oṭṭhibyādhi."

102.

102.

“Yo [M 3.0366] pubbe katakalyāṇo, katattho nāvabujjhati;

Atthā tassa palujjanti, ye honti abhipatthitā.

"Whoever, for whom a good deed was done and a purpose accomplished in the past, does not recognize it—his desired aims perish."

103.

103.

“Yo pubbe katakalyāṇo, katattho manubujjhati;

Atthā tassa pavaḍḍhanti, ye honti abhipatthikā.

"Whoever, for whom a good deed was done and a purpose accomplished in the past, recognizes it—his desired aims increase."

104.

104.

“Taṃ vo vadāmi bhaddante, yāvantettha samāgatā;

Sabbe kataññuno hotha, ciraṃ saggamhi ṭhassathā”ti.

"I tell you this, good sirs, as many as are assembled here: be all of you grateful, and you will long abide in heaven."
