Tattha paṭhamagāthāya tāva attho – idhekacco aññāṇajātiko poso yāvatāsīsatī, yāva “idaṃ nāma me ayaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissatī”ti paccāsīsati, tāvadeva taṃ purisaṃ pavīṇati bhajati sevati, tassa pana atthāpāye vaḍḍhiyā apagamane parihīnakāle taṃ nānākiccesu patthitaṃ posaṃ ekacce bālā imaṃ oṭṭhibyādhiṃ ayaṃ khattiyo viya jahanti.

Herein, the meaning of the first verse is: in this world, a certain ignorant person, as long as he has hopes, as long as he expects, 'This person will be able to do this for me,' so long does he associate with, resort to, and serve that person. But at the loss of benefit, the departure of prosperity, in times of decline, some fools abandon that person who was sought after for various tasks, just as this king abandoned Oṭṭhibyādhi.

Katakalyāṇoti parena attano katakalyāṇakammo. Katatthoti nipphāditakicco. Nāvabujjhatīti pacchāpi taṃ parena [P 3.0388] kataṃ upakāraṃ tassa jarājiṇṇakāle asamatthakāle na sarati, attanā dinnampi yasaṃ puna gaṇhāti. Palujjantīti bhijjanti nassanti. Ye honti abhipatthitāti ye keci atthā icchitā nāma honti, sabbe nassantīti dīpeti. Mittadubbhipuggalassa hi patthitapatthitaṃ aggimhi pakkhittabījaṃ viya nassati. Katattho manubujjhatīti katattho anubujjhati, ma-kāro byañjanasandhivasena gahito. Taṃ vo vadāmīti tena kāraṇena tumhe vadāmi. Ṭhassathāti kataññuno hutvā cirakālaṃ saggamhi dibbasampattiṃ anubhavantā patiṭṭhahissatha.

Katakalyāṇo means one for whom a good deed has been done by another. Katattho means one whose purpose has been accomplished. Nāvabujjhati means that even later, in that person's old age and infirmity, he does not remember the help given by another, and even takes back the honor he himself had given. Palujjanti means they break up and perish. Ye honti abhipatthitā means whatever desired aims there are—it is shown that they all perish. For indeed, for a person who betrays friends, his desired aims perish like seeds thrown into a fire. Katattho manubujjhati means one whose purpose is fulfilled recognizes it; the letter 'm' is added by way of consonant sandhi. Taṃ vo vadāmi means 'for that reason, I speak to you.' Ṭhassatha means being grateful, you will remain for a long time, experiencing divine prosperity in heaven.

Evaṃ [V 3.0343] mahāsatto rājānaṃ ādiṃ katvā sannipatitānaṃ sabbesaṃ ovādaṃ adāsi. Taṃ sutvā rājā oṭṭhibyādhiyā yasaṃ paṭipākatikaṃ akāsi. Bodhisattassa ca ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā saggaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus the Great Being, beginning with the king, gave advice to all who had assembled. Having heard this, the king restored Oṭṭhibyādhi’s honors to their original state. And abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving and became destined for heaven.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā oṭṭhibyādhi bhaddavatikā ahosi, rājā ānando, amacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the birth: “At that time, the she-elephant Oṭṭhibyādhi was Bhaddavatikā, the king was Ānanda, but the minister was indeed myself.”

Daḷhadhammajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The explanation of the Daḷhadhamma Jātaka is the fourth.

[410] 5. Somadattajātakavaṇṇanā

[410] 5. Explanation of the Somadatta Jātaka

Yo [M 3.0367] maṃ pure paccuḍḍetīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ mahallakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kirekaṃ sāmaṇeraṃ pabbājesi, sāmaṇero tassa upakārako hutvā tathārūpena rogena kālamakāsi. Mahallako tasmiṃ kālakate rodanto paridevanto vicarati. Taṃ disvā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asukamahallako sāmaṇerassa kālakiriyāya rodanto paridevanto vicarati, maraṇassatikammaṭṭhānarahito maññe”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa imasmiṃ mate rodiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“The one who used to greet me”—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain elderly monk. It is said he ordained a novice, and the novice, having been helpful to him, passed away from a certain disease. The elderly monk, when the novice died, wandered about weeping and lamenting. Seeing this, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, such-and-such an elderly monk is wandering about weeping and lamenting over the death of the novice. It seems he is devoid of the meditation on mindfulness of death.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you sitting here now?” When they told him, he said, “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, he wept when this one died,” and he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tāvatiṃsabhavane sakkattaṃ kāresi. Atheko kāsigāmavāsī brāhmaṇamahāsālo kāme pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ [P 3.0389] pabbajitvā uñchācariyāya vanamūlaphalāphalehi yāpento vāsaṃ kappesi. Ekadivasaṃ phalāphalatthāya gato ekaṃ hatthichāpaṃ disvā attano assamaṃ ānetvā puttaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā somadattotissa nāmaṃ katvā tiṇapaṇṇāni khādāpento paṭijaggi. So vayappatto mahāsarīro hutvā ekadivasaṃ bahuṃ bhojanaṃ gahetvā ajīrakena dubbalo ahosi. Tāpaso taṃ assamapade katvā phalāphalatthāya gato, tasmiṃ anāgateyeva hatthipotako kālamakāsi. Tāpaso phalāphalaṃ gahetvā āgacchanto “aññesu divasesu me putto paccuggamanaṃ karoti, ajja na dissati, kahaṃ nu kho gato”ti paridevanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was Sakka in the realm of the Thirty-Three. Then, a wealthy brahmin of a Kāsi village, having abandoned sensual pleasures, entered the Himalayas, became an ascetic, and lived by gleaning and subsisting on forest roots and fruits. One day, while going for fruits, he saw a young elephant, brought it to his hermitage, and treated it as a son. He named it Somadatta and looked after it, feeding it grass and leaves. When it reached maturity and became large-bodied, one day, after eating much food, it became weak from indigestion. The ascetic, leaving it at the hermitage, went for fruits. While he was still away, the young elephant died. The ascetic, returning with fruits, lamented, “On other days my son would come to greet me; today he is not seen. Where can he have gone?” and spoke the first verse:

105.

105.

“Yo [V 3.0344] maṃ pure paccuḍḍeti, araññe dūramāyato;

So na dissati mātaṅgo, somadatto kuhiṃ gato”ti.

“He who used to greet me before, coming from afar in the forest; that elephant is not seen. Where has Somadatta gone?”

Tattha pureti ito pure. Paccuḍḍetīti paccuggacchati. Araññe dūranti imasmiṃ nimmanusse araññe maṃ dūraṃ paccuḍḍeti. Āyatoti āyāmasampanno.

Therein, 'pure' means before this. 'Paccuḍḍeti' means he comes to meet. 'Araññe dūraṃ' means in this uninhabited forest, he meets me from afar. 'Āyato' means endowed with full stature.

Evaṃ [M 3.0368] paridevamāno āgantvā taṃ caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ patitaṃ disvā gale gahetvā paridevamāno dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Lamenting thus, he came and, seeing it fallen at the end of the walking path, embraced its neck and, lamenting, spoke the second verse:

106.

106.

“Ayaṃ vā so mato seti, allasiṅgaṃva vacchito;

Bhūmyā nipatito seti, amarā vata kuñjaro”ti.

“This very one lies dead, like a tender shoot cut off. Fallen to the ground he lies. Alas, the elephant is dead!”

Tattha ayaṃ vāti vibhāvanatthe vā-saddo. Ayameva so, na aññoti taṃ vibhāvento evamāha. Allasiṅganti māluvalatāya aggapavālaṃ. Vacchitoti chinno, gimhakāle majjhanhikasamaye tattavālikāpuline nakhena chinditvā pātito māluvalatāya aṅkuro viyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhūmyāti bhūmiyaṃ. Amarā vatāti mato vata, “amarī”tipi pāṭho.

Here, the word ‘vā’ is used in the sense of clarification. Clarifying it as ‘This very one, not another,’ he spoke thus. ‘Allasiṅga’ refers to the tender, topmost shoot of the māluvā creeper. ‘Vacchito’ means cut off, as when at midday in the hot season, a sprout of the māluvā creeper is cut off with a fingernail on a heated sandy bank and made to fall. ‘Bhūmyā’ means on the ground. ‘Amarā vata’ means ‘indeed dead,’ and there is also the reading ‘amarī’.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko lokaṃ olokento taṃ disvā “ayaṃ tāpaso puttadāraṃ pahāya pabbajito, idāni hatthipotake puttasaññaṃ katvā paridevati, saṃvejetvā naṃ satiṃ paṭilabhāpessāmī”ti tassa assamapadaṃ āgantvā ākāse ṭhitova tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

At that moment, Sakka, surveying the world, saw him and thought: “This ascetic has renounced wife and children to go forth, yet now he laments, having formed the perception of a son toward the young elephant. I will stir him and cause him to regain his mindfulness.” Having arrived at his hermitage, he stood in the air and spoke the third verse:

107.

107.

“Anagāriyupetassa[P 3.0390], vippamuttassa te sato;

Samaṇassa na taṃ sādhu, yaṃ petamanusocasī”ti.

“For you, a recluse, who has gone forth into homelessness and is liberated, it is not proper that you mourn for the dead.”

Athassa vacanaṃ sutvā tāpaso catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, having heard his words, the ascetic spoke the fourth verse:

108.

108.

“Saṃvāsena have sakka, manussassa migassa vā;

Hadaye jāyate pemaṃ, taṃ na sakkā asocitu”nti.

“Through living together, indeed, O Sakka, whether with a human or an animal, affection arises in the heart; it is impossible not to grieve for that.”

Tattha [V 3.0345] migassa vāti imasmiṃ ṭhāne sabbepi tiracchānā “migā”ti vuttā. Tanti piyāyitaṃ sattaṃ.

Here, in this context, by ‘animal’ (migassa), all beasts are meant. ‘That’ (taṃ) refers to a beloved being.

Atha naṃ ovadanto sakko dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then Sakka, admonishing him, spoke two verses:

109.

109.

“Mataṃ marissaṃ rodanti, ye rudanti lapanti ca;

Tasmā tvaṃ isi mā rodi, roditaṃ moghamāhu santo.

“Those who weep and lament, weep for the dead and for one who will die. Therefore, O sage, do not weep; the wise say weeping is in vain.”

110.

110.

“Kanditena have brahme, mato peto samuṭṭhahe;

Sabbe saṅgamma rodāma, aññamaññassa ñātake”ti.

“If, indeed, O brahmin, the departed dead would arise by wailing, then let us all gather together and weep for each other’s relatives.”

Tattha [M 3.0369] ye rudanti lapanti cāti brahme ye sattā rodanti paridevanti ca, sabbe te mataṃ, yo ca marissati, taṃ rodanti, tesaṃyeva evaṃ rodantānaṃ assusukkhanakālo natthi, tasmā tvaṃ isi mā rodi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Roditaṃ moghamāhu santo, paṇḍitā hi “roditaṃ nipphala”nti vadanti. Mato petoti yadi esa petoti saṅkhyaṃ gato mato roditena samuṭṭhaheyya, evaṃ sante sabbepi mayaṃ samāgantvā aññamaññassa ñātake rodāma, kiṃ nikkammā acchāmāti.

Here, ‘those who weep and lament’ means, O brahmin, those beings who weep and lament; all of them weep for the dead and for whoever will die. For those who weep in this way, there is no day when their tears dry up. Therefore, O sage, do not weep. For what reason? The wise say weeping is in vain, for the learned declare, ‘Weeping is fruitless.’ ‘The departed dead’ means: if this one, who is counted as departed, who is dead, could be revived by weeping, then in that case we would all come together and weep for each other’s relatives. Why would we remain inactive?”

Tāpaso sakkassa vacanaṃ sutvā satiṃ paṭilabhitvā vigatasoko assūni puñchitvā sakkassa thutivasena sesagāthā āha –

The ascetic, having heard Sakka’s words, regained his mindfulness, became free from sorrow, wiped away his tears, and spoke the remaining verses in praise of Sakka:

111.

111.

“Ādittaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ, ghatasittaṃva pāvakaṃ;

Vārinā viya osiñcaṃ, sabbaṃ nibbāpaye daraṃ.

“Burning indeed was I, like a fire sprinkled with ghee; as if sprinkling with water, you have extinguished all my distress.”

112.

112.

“Abbahī vata me sallaṃ, yamāsi hadayassitaṃ;

Yo me sokaparetassa, puttasokaṃ apānudi.

“Indeed, you have drawn out my dart, which was lodged in my heart; you who drove away my sorrow for my son, when I was overcome by grief.”

113.

113.

“Sohaṃ [P 3.0391] abbūḷhasallosmi, vītasoko anāvilo;

Na socāmi na rodāmi, tava sutvāna vāsavā”ti.

“I am one from whom the dart is drawn, without sorrow, untroubled. I do not grieve, nor do I weep, having heard you, O Vāsava.”

Tā [V 3.0346] heṭṭhā vuttatthāyeva. Evaṃ sakko tāpasassa ovādaṃ datvā sakaṭṭhānameva gato.

The meaning of these verses is as stated. Thus, having given this admonition to the ascetic, Sakka went to his own abode.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā hatthipotako sāmaṇero ahosi, tāpaso mahallako, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: “At that time, the young elephant was the novice, the ascetic was the elder monk, and Sakka was none other than myself.”

Somadattajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Somadatta Jātaka, the Fifth.

[411] 6. Susīmajātakavaṇṇanā

[411] 6. The Commentary on the Susīma Jātaka

Kāḷāni kesāni pure ahesunti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahābhinikkhamanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi samaye bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ nisīditvā dasabalassa nikkhamanaṃ vaṇṇayiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte [M 3.0370] “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā dāni anekāni kappakoṭisatasahassāni pūritapāraminā mahābhinikkhamanaṃ, pubbepāhaṃ tiyojanasatike kāsiraṭṭhe rajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā nikkhantoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Black were the hairs formerly”—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the great renunciation. At that time, the monks, seated in the Hall of Dhamma, praised the renunciation of the One with Ten Powers. The Teacher arrived and asked, “For what discussion, monks, are you now assembled here?” When they told him what it was, he said, “It is no wonder, monks, that I, having fulfilled the perfections for many hundreds of thousands of crores of eons, have now made the great renunciation. Even in the past, I renounced a kingdom spanning three hundred leagues in the country of Kāsi and went forth.” Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa purohitassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, tassa jātadivaseyeva bārāṇasiraññopi putto jāyi. Tesaṃ nāmaggahaṇadivase mahāsattassa susīmakumāroti nāmaṃ akaṃsu, rājaputtassa brahmadattakumāroti. Bārāṇasirājā “puttena me saddhiṃ ekadivase jāto”ti bodhisattaṃ āṇāpetvā dhātiyo datvā tena saddhiṃ ekato vaḍḍhesi. Te ubhopi vayappattā abhirūpā devakumāravaṇṇino hutvā takkasilāyaṃ [P 3.0392] sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā paccāgamiṃsu. Rājaputto uparājā hutvā bodhisattena saddhiṃ ekato khādanto pivanto nisīdanto sayanto pitu accayena rajjaṃ patvā mahāsattassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ datvā purohitaṭṭhāne taṃ ṭhapetvā ekadivasaṃ nagaraṃ sajjāpetvā sakko devarājā viya alaṅkato alaṅkataerāvaṇapaṭibhāgassa mattavaravāraṇassa khandhe nisīditvā bodhisattaṃ pacchāsane hatthipiṭṭhe nisīdāpetvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ akāsi. Mātāpissa “puttaṃ olokessāmī”ti sīhapañjare ṭhatvā tassa nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā āgacchantassa pacchato nisinnaṃ purohitaṃ disvā paṭibaddhacittā hutvā sayanagabbhaṃ pavisitvā “imaṃ alabhantī ettheva marissāmī”ti āhāraṃ pacchinditvā nipajji.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the chief wife of the chaplain. On the very day of his birth, a son was also born to the king of Benares. On their naming day, they named the great being Prince Susīma, and the king’s son Prince Brahmadatta. The king of Benares, thinking, “He was born on the same day as my son,” had the Bodhisatta brought, provided nurses for him, and had him raised together with his son. Both of them, upon reaching maturity, being handsome with the appearance of divine youths, went to Takkasilā, mastered all the arts, and returned. The king's son became viceroy and, having eaten, drunk, sat, and slept together with the Bodhisatta, upon his father’s death, he attained the throne. He bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisatta and appointed him to the position of chaplain. One day, having had the city decorated, he adorned himself like Sakka, king of the gods, mounted a magnificent, royal, rutting elephant that resembled the adorned Airāvata, seated the Bodhisatta behind him on the elephant’s back, and circumambulated the city. His mother, wishing to see her son, stood in a lion-window and saw the chaplain seated behind him as he was returning from circumambulating the city. She became infatuated and, entering her bedchamber, she refused food and lay down, declaring, “If I cannot have him, I will die right here.”

Rājā [V 3.0347] mātaraṃ apassanto “kuhiṃ me mātā”ti pucchitvā “gilānā”ti sutvā tassā santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā “kiṃ amma, aphāsuka”nti pucchi. Sā lajjāya na kathesi. So gantvā rājapallaṅke nisīditvā attano aggamahesiṃ pakkositvā “gaccha ammāya aphāsukaṃ jānāhī”ti pesesi. Sā gantvā piṭṭhiṃ parimajjantī pucchi, itthiyo nāma itthīnaṃ rahassaṃ na niguhanti, sā tassā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Itarāpi taṃ sutvā gantvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā “hotu, gaccha naṃ samassāsehi, purohitaṃ rājānaṃ katvā tassa taṃ aggamahesiṃ karissāmī”ti āha. Sā āgantvā taṃ samassāsesi. Rājāpi purohitaṃ pakkosāpetvā etamatthaṃ ārocetvā “samma, mātu me jīvitaṃ dehi, tvaṃ rājā bhavissasi, sā aggamahesī, ahaṃ uparājā”ti [M 3.0371] āha. So “na sakkā evaṃ kātu”nti paṭikkhipitvā tena punappunaṃ yāciyamāno sampaṭicchi. Rājā purohitaṃ rājānaṃ, mātaraṃ aggamahesiṃ kāretvā sayaṃ uparājā ahosi.

The king, not seeing his mother, asked, “Where is my mother?” Hearing she was ill, he went to her, paid his respects, and asked, “What is it, mother, are you unwell?” Out of shame, she did not speak. He went and sat on the royal throne, summoned his chief queen, and sent her, saying, “Go and find out what ails my mother.” She went, stroked her back, and asked. Women do not conceal secrets from other women, so she revealed the matter to her. The other, hearing it, went and informed the king. The king said, “Very well, go and comfort her. I will make the chaplain king and her his chief queen.” She returned and comforted her. The king then had the chaplain summoned, explained the matter, and said, “Friend, give my mother her life. You shall be king, she the chief queen, and I the viceroy.” He refused, saying, “This cannot be done,” but being repeatedly entreated by him, he consented. The king had the chaplain made king and his mother the chief queen, while he himself became the viceroy.

Tesaṃ samaggavāsaṃ vasantānaṃ aparabhāge bodhisatto agāramajjhe ukkaṇṭhito kāme pahāya pabbajjāya ninnacitto kilesaratiṃ anallīyanto ekakova tiṭṭhati, ekakova nisīdati, ekakova sayati, bandhanāgāre baddho viya pañjare pakkhittakukkuṭo [P 3.0393] viya ca ahosi. Athassa aggamahesī “ayaṃ rājā mayā saddhiṃ nābhiramati, ekakova tiṭṭhati nisīdati seyyaṃ kappeti, ayaṃ kho pana daharo taruṇo, ahaṃ mahallikā, sīse me palitāni paññāyanti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ ‘sīse te deva, ekaṃ palitaṃ paññāyatī’ti musāvādaṃ katvā ekenupāyena rājānaṃ pattiyāpetvā mayā saddhiṃ abhiramāpeyya”nti cintetvā ekadivasaṃ rañño sīse ūkā vicinantī viya hutvā “deva, mahallakosi jāto, sīse te ekaṃ palitaṃ paññāyatī”ti āha. “Tena hi bhadde, etaṃ palitaṃ luñjitvā mayhaṃ hatthe ṭhapehī”ti. Sā tassa sīsato ekaṃ kesaṃ luñjitvā attano sīse palitaṃ gahetvā “idaṃ te, deva, palita”nti tassa hatthe ṭhapesi. Bodhisattassa taṃ disvāva bhītatasitassa kañcanapaṭṭasadisā nalāṭā sedā mucciṃsu.

While they lived together in harmony, later the Bodhisatta, discontented in the midst of the household, with his mind inclined toward renunciation after having abandoned sensual pleasures, not clinging to the delight of defilements, stood alone, sat alone, and lay down alone; he was like one bound in a prison or like a rooster kept in a cage. Then his chief queen thought, "This king takes no pleasure with me. He stands, sits, and sleeps alone. He is young and tender, while I am old. Gray hairs are appearing on my head. What if I were to tell a lie, saying, 'Your Majesty, a gray hair is appearing on your head,' and by some means win over the king and make him take pleasure with me." So one day, pretending to search for lice on the king's head, she said, "Your Majesty, you have grown old. A gray hair is appearing on your head." "Then, dear lady, pluck out that gray hair and place it in my hand." She plucked a black hair from his head, took a gray hair from her own head, and placing it in his hand, said, "Here, Your Majesty, is your gray hair." Upon seeing it, the Bodhisatta was terrified and alarmed, and sweat broke out on his forehead, which was like a golden plate.

So attānaṃ ovadanto “susīma, tvaṃ daharo hutvā mahallako jāto, ettakaṃ kālaṃ gūthakalale nimuggo gāmasūkaro viya kāmakalale nimujjitvā taṃ kalalaṃ jahituṃ na sakkosi, nanu kāme pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitvā brahmacariyavāsassa te kālo”ti cintetvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Admonishing himself, he thought: "Susīma, you have grown old. For so long you have been submerged in the mire of sensual pleasures, like a village pig submerged in the mire of excrement, and you are unable to abandon that mire. Is it not time for you to abandon sensual pleasures, enter the Himalayas, go forth, and live the holy life?" Having thought thus, he spoke the first verse:

114.

114.

“Kāḷāni [V 3.0348] kesāni pure ahesuṃ, jātāni sīsamhi yathāpadese;

Tānajja setāni susīma disvā, dhammaṃ cara brahmacariyassa kālo”ti.

“The hairs were black formerly, grown on my head in their proper places; seeing them now white, Susīma, practice the Dhamma; it is time for the holy life.”

Tattha yathāpadeseti tava sīse tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kesānaṃ anurūpe padese ito pubbe kāḷāni bhamarapattavaṇṇāni kesāni jātāni ahesunti [M 3.0372] vadati. Dhammaṃ carāti dasakusalakammapathadhammaṃ carāti attānameva āṇāpeti. Brahmacariyassāti methunaviratiyā te kāloti attho.

In those verses, 'in their proper places' (yathāpadese) means he says that in each of those places on your head appropriate for hair, black hairs the color of a bee's wing had previously grown. 'Practice the Dhamma' (dhammaṃ cara) means he enjoins upon himself to practice the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action. 'For the holy life' (brahmacariyassa) means 'it is time for you to abstain from sexual intercourse'.

Evaṃ bodhisattena brahmacariyavāsassa guṇe vaṇṇite itarā “ahaṃ ‘imassa lagganaṃ karissāmī’ti vissajjanameva kari”nti bhītatasitā “idānissa apabbajjanatthāya sarīravaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇayissāmī”ti cintetvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Thus, when the Bodhisatta praised the virtues of living the holy life, the other, terrified and trembling, thought: 'I intended to cause him to be attached, but I have only caused his detachment!' Then, thinking, 'Now I will praise his physical beauty to prevent him from renouncing,' she spoke two verses:

115.

115.

“Mameva [P 3.0394] deva palitaṃ na tuyhaṃ, mameva sīsaṃ mama uttamaṅgaṃ;

‘Atthaṃ karissa’nti musā abhāṇiṃ, ekāparādhaṃ khama rājaseṭṭha.

“The gray hair is mine alone, O king, not yours; it is from my head, my own head. Thinking, ‘I will achieve my aim,’ I spoke falsely. Forgive this one offense, O best of kings.

116.

116.

“Daharo tuvaṃ dassaniyosi rāja, paṭhamuggato hoti yathā kaḷīro;

Rajjañca kārehi mamañca passa, mā kālikaṃ anudhāvī janindā”ti.

“You are young and handsome, O king, like a freshly risen bamboo shoot; rule the kingdom and look upon me; do not pursue what is for a later time, O lord of men.”

Tattha mameva sīsanti mameva sīse sañjātaṃ palitanti dīpeti. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Atthanti attano vuḍḍhiṃ karissāmīti musā kathesiṃ. Ekāparādhanti. Imaṃ mayhaṃ ekaṃ aparādhaṃ. Paṭhamuggatoti paṭhamavayena uggato. Hohīti hosi, paṭhamavaye patiṭṭhitosīti attho. “Hosī”tiyeva vā pāṭho. Yathā kaḷīroti yathā siniddhachavitaruṇakaḷīro mandavāterito ativiya sobhati, evarūposi tvanti dasseti. “Paṭhamuggato hotī”tipi pāṭho, tassattho – yathā paṭhamuggato taruṇakaḷīro dassanīyo hoti, evaṃ tvampi dassanīyoti. Mamañca passāti mamañca olokehi, mā maṃ anāthaṃ vidhavaṃ karohīti attho. Kālikanti brahmacariyacaraṇaṃ nāma dutiye vā tatiye vā attabhāve vipākadānato kālikaṃ nāma, rajjaṃ pana imasmiṃyeva attabhāve kāmaguṇasukhuppādanato akālikaṃ, so tvaṃ imaṃ akālikaṃ pahāya mā kālikaṃ anudhāvīti vadati.

In those verses, 'my head' (mameva sīsaṃ) explains that the gray hair appeared on her head alone. The other term is a synonym for the same. 'Aim' (atthaṃ) means 'I spoke falsely, thinking I would achieve my own prosperity.' 'One offense' (ekāparādhaṃ) means this single offense of mine. 'Freshly risen' (paṭhamuggato) means risen in the first stage of life. 'Hohi' means 'you are,' that is, you are established in the first stage of life. Alternatively, the reading is 'hosi.' 'Like a bamboo shoot' (yathā kaḷīro) shows that 'just as a tender, smooth-skinned young bamboo shoot, gently swayed by the wind, shines exceedingly, so too are you.' There is also a reading 'paṭhamuggato hoti,' meaning just as a freshly risen young bamboo shoot is lovely to see, so too are you lovely. 'And look upon me' (mamañca passa) means 'and look at me; do not make me a helpless widow.' 'For a later time' (kālikaṃ): the practice of the holy life is called 'delayed' because it gives fruit in a second or third existence. But kingship is 'immediate' (akālika) because it produces the pleasure of the cords of sensual desire in this very existence; thus she says, 'Do not abandon this immediate pleasure to pursue that which is delayed.'

Bodhisatto [M 3.0373] tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “bhadde, tvaṃ bhavitabbamevetaṃ kathaṃ kathesi, pariṇamante hi mama vaye imehi kāḷakesehi parivattetvā sāṇavākasadisehi paṇḍarehi bhavitabbaṃ. Ahañhi [V 3.0349] nīluppalādikusumadāmasadisakumārānaṃ kañcanarūpapaṭibhāgānaṃ uttamayobbanavilāsasampattānaṃ khattiyakaññādīnaṃ vaye pariṇamante jaraṃ pattānaṃ vevaṇṇiyañceva sarīrabhaṅgañca passāmi. Evaṃ vipattipariyosānovesa bhadde, jīvaloko”ti vatvā upari buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ desento gāthādvayamāha –

Hearing her words, the Bodhisatta replied, "Good lady, you speak of what must indeed come to be. For as my age advances, these dark hairs of mine must change and become white, like hemp stalks. I see how young men who resemble garlands of blue lotuses and other flowers, who are like golden statues, endowed with the grace and excellence of prime youth, and noble maidens and others, as their age advances, reach decay, experiencing discoloration and the breaking up of the body. Thus, good lady, the world of living beings ends in ruin." Having spoken thus, he then taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, uttering two verses:

117.

117.

“Passāmi [P 3.0395] vohaṃ dahariṃ kumāriṃ, sāmaṭṭhapassaṃ sutanuṃ sumajjhaṃ;

Kāḷappavāḷāva pavellamānā, palobhayantīva naresu gacchati.

“I see a young maiden, a mere girl, / with smooth flanks, a beautiful body, and a fine waist; / swaying like a dark coral vine, / she walks among men as if to entice them.

118.

118.

“Tamena passāmiparena nāriṃ, āsītikaṃ nāvutikaṃva jaccā;

Daṇḍaṃ gahetvāna pavedhamānaṃ, gopānasībhoggasamaṃ caranti”nti.

“Then later I see that same woman, / eighty or ninety years of age, / leaning on a staff, trembling, / walking bent like a curved roof-rafter.”

Tattha voti nipātamattaṃ. Sāmaṭṭhapassanti sammaṭṭhapassaṃ. Ayameva vā pāṭho, sabbapassesu maṭṭhachavivaṇṇanti attho. Sutanunti sundarasarīraṃ. Sumajjhanti susaṇṭhitamajjhaṃ. Kāḷappavāḷāva pavellamānāti yathā nāma taruṇakāle susamuggatā kāḷavallī pavāḷā vā hutvā mandavāteritā ito cito ca pavellati, evaṃ pavellamānā itthivilāsaṃ dassayamānā kumārikā palobhayantīva naresu gacchati. Samīpatthe bhummavacanaṃ, purisānaṃ santike te purise kilesavasena palobhayantī viya gacchati.

Here, 'vo' is merely a particle. 'With smooth flanks' means with well-polished flanks. This is the reading. The meaning is 'of smooth skin and complexion on all sides.' 'With a beautiful body' means having a lovely body. 'With a fine waist' means with a well-proportioned waist. 'Swaying like a dark coral vine' means that just as a dark vine or coral, well-grown in its youth, sways to and fro when stirred by a gentle wind, so this maiden sways, displaying feminine grace, and walks among men as if to entice them. The locative case is used in the sense of proximity, meaning she walks near men, as if enticing those men by way of their defilements.

Tamena passāmiparena nārinti tamenaṃ nāriṃ aparena samayena jaraṃ pattaṃ antarahitarūpasobhaggappattaṃ passāmi. Bodhisatto hi paṭhamagāthāya rūpe assādaṃ kathetvā idāni ādīnavaṃ dassento evamāha. Āsītikaṃ nāvutikaṃva jaccāti asītisaṃvaccharaṃ vā navutisaṃvaccharaṃ vā jātiyā. Gopānasībhoggasamanti gopānasīsamaṃ bhoggaṃ, gopānasīākārena bhaggasarīraṃ onamitvā naṭṭhakākaṇikaṃ pariyesantiṃ viya caramānanti attho. Kāmañca [M 3.0374] bodhisattena daharakāle disvā puna nāvutikakāle diṭṭhapubbā nāma natthi, ñāṇena diṭṭhabhāvaṃ sandhāya panetaṃ vuttaṃ.

'Then later I see that same woman' means 'I see that same woman at a later time, having reached old age, her beauty and charm having disappeared.' The Bodhisatta, having first spoken of the gratification in beauty in the first verse, now reveals its drawback, speaking thus. 'Eighty or ninety years of age' means eighty or ninety years by birth. 'Bent like a curved roof-rafter' means bent like a roof-rafter, her body crooked in the shape of a roof-rafter, walking as if stooped over searching for a lost coin. Although the Bodhisatta had not actually seen a woman in his youth and then again when she was ninety, this was spoken with reference to the state of having been seen with insight.

Iti mahāsatto imāya gāthāya rūpassa ādīnavaṃ dassetvā idāni agāramajjhe attano anabhiratiṃ pakāsento gāthādvayamāha –

Thus the Great Being, having shown the drawback of form with these verses, now declared his own lack of delight in the household life by uttering two verses:

119.

119.

“Sohaṃ [V 3.0350][P 3.0396] tamevānuvicintayanto, eko sayāmi sayanassa majjhe;

‘Ahampi evaṃ’ iti pekkhamāno, na gahe rame brahmacariyassa kālo.

“Reflecting on that very thing, / I behold myself alone in the midst of my bed; / seeing that ‘I, too, will be thus,’ / I find no delight in the home; it is time for the holy life.”

120.

120.

“Rajjuvālambanī cesā, yā gehe vasato rati;

Etampi chetvāna vajanti dhīrā, anapekkhino kāmasukhaṃ pahāyā”ti.

“This delight of one dwelling at home / is a dangling rope. / Having cut even this, the wise go forth, / without longing, having abandoned sensual pleasure.”

Tattha sohanti so ahaṃ. Tamevānuvicintayantoti tameva rūpānaṃ assādañca ādīnavañca cintento. Evaṃ iti pekkhamānoti “yathā esā pariṇatā, ahampi jaraṃ patto bhaggasarīro bhavissāmī”ti pekkhamāno. Na gahe rameti gehe na ramāmi. Brahmacariyassa kāloti bhadde, brahmacariyassa me kālo, tasmā pabbajissāmīti dīpeti.

Therein, 'sohanti' means 'so I am.' 'Tamevānuvicintayanto' means contemplating just that: the gratification and the drawbacks of forms. 'Evaṃ iti pekkhamāno' means observing thus: 'Just as she has aged, I too, having reached old age, will have a broken body.' 'Na gahe rameti' means 'I do not delight in the home (gehe).' 'Brahmacariyassa kāloti' shows: 'Good lady, it is time for my holy life; therefore, I will go forth.'

Rajjuvālambanī cesāti ca-kāro nipātamatto, ālambanarajju viya esāti attho. Katarā? Yā gehe vasato rati, yā gehe vasantassa rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu kāmaratīti attho. Iminā kāmānaṃ appassādataṃ dasseti. Ayaṃ etthādhippāyo – yathā gilānassa manussassa attano balena parivattituṃ asakkontassa “imaṃ ālambitvā parivatteyyāsī”ti ālambanarajjuṃ bandheyyuṃ, tassa taṃ ālambitvā parivattantassa appamattakaṃ kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ bhaveyya, evaṃ kilesāturānaṃ sattānaṃ vivekasukhavasena parivattituṃ asakkontānaṃ agāramajjhe ṭhapitāni kāmaratidāyakāni rūpādīni ārammaṇāni tesaṃ kilesapariḷāhakāle methunadhammapaṭisevanavasena tāni ārabbha parivattamānānaṃ kāyikacetasikasukhasaṅkhātā kāmarati nāma taṃ muhuttaṃ uppajjamānā [M 3.0375] appamattikā hoti, evaṃ appassādā kāmāti. Etampi chetvānāti yasmā pana bahudukkhā kāmā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo, tasmā taṃ ādīnavaṃ sampassamānā paṇḍitā etampi rajjuṃ chetvā gūthakūpe nimuggapuriso taṃ pajahanto viya anapekkhino etaṃ appamattakaṃ bahudukkhaṃ kāmasukhaṃ pahāya vajanti, nikkhamitvā manoramaṃ pabbajjaṃ pabbajantīti.

In 'Rajjuvālambanī cesā,' the word 'ca' is a mere particle; the meaning is 'this is like a supporting rope.' Which one? The delight that comes from living in a home; that is, the sensual delight in objects such as forms for one living at home. By this, he shows the meager gratification of sensual pleasures. The intention here is this: just as for a sick person unable to turn over by their own strength, a supporting rope might be tied for them so that they can 'turn over by holding onto this,' and by relying on it to turn over, they would experience a slight bodily and mental pleasure; so too for beings afflicted by defilements, unable to turn towards the happiness of seclusion, sensual objects such as forms that provide sensual delight are established in the midst of the household. When their defilements burn, by engaging in sexual intercourse, they turn towards those objects, and the sensual delight, known as bodily and mental pleasure, that arises for a moment is meager. Thus, sensual pleasures have little gratification. 'And having cut this too': because sensual pleasures are full of much suffering and much tribulation, and the danger here is greater, therefore the wise, seeing that danger, cut this rope too. Like a man sunk in a cesspit who abandons it without looking back, they, being unconcerned, abandon this slight and very painful sensual pleasure and go forth. Having gone forth, they undertake the delightful life of renunciation.

Evaṃ mahāsatto kāmesu assādañca ādīnavañca dassento buddhalīḷāya dhammaṃ desetvā sahāyaṃ pakkosāpetvā rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā ñātimittasuhajjānaṃ rodantānaṃ paridevantānameva sirivibhavaṃ chaḍḍetvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññaṃ nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus, the great being, showing both the gratification and the danger in sensual pleasures, taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha. Having summoned his companion and had him accept the kingdom, while his relatives, friends, and companions wept and lamented, he abandoned his royal splendor and entered the Himalayas. Taking up the ascetic life of a sage, he developed the meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, and was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā [V 3.0351][P 3.0397] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā bahū jane amatapānaṃ pāyetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā aggamahesī rāhulamātā ahosi, sahāyarājā ānando, susīmarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths, and caused many people to drink the nectar of the deathless, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the chief queen was Rāhula's mother, the companion king was Ānanda, but King Susīma was none other than myself."

Susīmajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Susīma Jātaka, the Sixth.

[412] 7. Koṭasimbalijātakavaṇṇanā

[412] 7. The Commentary on the Koṭasimbali Jātaka

Ahaṃ dasasataṃbyāmanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kilesaniggahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu pana pānīyajātake (jā. 1.11.59 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Idhāpi satthā antokoṭisanthāre kāmavitakkābhibhūte pañcasate bhikkhū disvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā “bhikkhave, āsaṅkitabbayuttakaṃ nāma āsaṅkituṃ vaṭṭati, kilesā nāma vaḍḍhantā vane nigrodhādayo viya rukkhaṃ, purisaṃ bhañjanti, teneva pubbepi koṭasimbaliyaṃ nibbattadevatā ekaṃ sakuṇaṃ nigrodhabījāni khāditvā attano rukkhassa sākhantare vaccaṃ pātentaṃ disvā ‘ito me vimānassa vināso bhavissatī’ti bhayappattā ahosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher told this story, which begins with 'Ahaṃ dasasataṃbyāmaṃ,' concerning the suppression of defilements. The full story will be made clear in the Pānīya Jātaka (Jā 459). Here too, the Teacher, seeing five hundred monks in the inner chamber overcome by sensual thoughts, convened the community of monks and said, 'Monks, it is right to be suspicious of what ought to be suspected. For defilements, as they grow, destroy a person, just as in a forest, trees like the banyan destroy a host tree. Thus, in the past, a deity born in a silk-cotton tree (Koṭasimbali), seeing a bird that had eaten banyan seeds dropping its excrement between the branches of her tree, became fearful, thinking, "From this will come the destruction of my celestial mansion."' So saying, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto koṭasimbaliyaṃ rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Atheko supaṇṇarājā diyaḍḍhayojanasatikaṃ [M 3.0376] attabhāvaṃ māpetvā pakkhavātehi mahāsamudde udakaṃ dvidhā katvā ekaṃ byāmasahassāyāmaṃ nāgarājānaṃ naṅguṭṭhe gahetvā mukhenassa gahitagocaraṃ chaḍḍāpetvā koṭasimbaliṃ sandhāya vanamatthakena pāyāsi. Nāgarājā “olambento attānaṃ mocessāmī”ti nigrodharukkhe bhogaṃ pavesetvā nigrodhaṃ veṭhetvā gaṇhi. Supaṇṇarañño mahābalatāya nāgarājassa ca mahāsarīratāya nigrodharukkho samugghāṭaṃ agamāsi. Nāgarājā neva rukkhaṃ vissajjesi, supaṇṇarājā saddhiṃ nigrodharukkhena nāgarājānaṃ gahetvā koṭasimbaliṃ patvā nāgarājānaṃ khandhapiṭṭhe nipajjāpetvā udaramassa phāletvā [P 3.0398] nāgamedaṃ khāditvā sesakaḷevaraṃ samudde vissajjesi. Tasmiṃ pana nigrodhe ekā sakuṇikā atthi, sā nigrodharukkhe vissaṭṭhe uppatitvā koṭasimbaliyā sākhantare nisīdi. Rukkhadevatā taṃ disvā “ayaṃ sakuṇikā mama rukkhakkhandhe vaccaṃ pātessati, tato nigrodhagaccho vā pilakkhagaccho vā uṭṭhahitvā sakalarukkhaṃ ottharitvā gacchissati, atha me vimānaṃ nassissatī”ti bhītatasitā pavedhi. Tassā pavedhantiyā koṭasimbalīpi yāva mūlā pavedhi. Supaṇṇarājā taṃ pavedhamānaṃ disvā kāraṇaṃ pucchanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree-deity in a silk-cotton tree (Koṭasimbali). Then a king of the Garudas (Supaṇṇas), having created a body one hundred and fifty leagues in size, parted the waters of the great ocean with the wind from his wings. Seizing a Nāga king, a thousand fathoms long, by the tail, he made him disgorge the prey he had caught in his mouth and flew over the top of the forest towards the silk-cotton tree. The Nāga king, thinking, 'I will free myself by hanging down,' thrust his coils into a banyan tree, wrapped himself around it, and held on. Due to the great strength of the Garuda king and the massive body of the Nāga king, the banyan tree was uprooted. The Nāga king did not release the tree, so the Garuda king seized the Nāga king together with the banyan tree. Reaching the silk-cotton tree, he laid the Nāga king on the flat of its trunk, split open his belly, ate the Nāga's fat, and cast the rest of the carcass into the ocean. Now, in that banyan tree there was a small bird. When the banyan tree was released, she flew up and perched between the branches of the silk-cotton tree. The tree-deity saw her and, terrified and afraid, began to tremble, thinking, 'This little bird will drop its excrement on the trunk of my tree. From that, a banyan, a pilakkha, or other such sapling will sprout, grow, and overwhelm my entire tree. Then my celestial mansion will be destroyed.' As she trembled, the silk-cotton tree itself shook to its very roots. The Garuda king, seeing it trembling, asked the reason and spoke two verses:

121.

121.

“Ahaṃ [V 3.0352] dasasataṃbyāmaṃ, uragamādāya āgato;

Tañca mañca mahākāyaṃ, dhārayaṃ nappavedhasi.

'I have come, bringing a serpent a thousand fathoms long; yet bearing both that massive one and me, you do not tremble.'

122.

122.

“Athimaṃ khuddakaṃ pakkhiṃ, appamaṃsataraṃ mayā;

Dhārayaṃ byathasi bhītā, kamatthaṃ koṭasimbalī”ti.

'But holding this tiny bird, with so much less flesh than me, you tremble in fear. For what reason, O Koṭasimbali?'

Tattha dasasataṃbyāmanti sahassabyāmamattāyāmaṃ. Uragamādāya āgatoti evaṃ mahantaṃ uragaṃ ādāya idha āgato. Tañca mañcāti tañca uragaṃ mañca. Dhārayanti dhārayamānā. Byathasīti kampasi. Kamatthanti kiṃ atthaṃ, kena kāraṇenāti pucchati, kaṃ vā atthaṃ sampassamānātipi attho. Koṭasimbalīti rukkhanāmena devaputtaṃ ālapati. So hi simbalirukkho khandhasākhamahantatāya koṭasimbalināmaṃ labhati, tasmiṃ adhivatthadevaputtassapi tadeva nāmaṃ.

Therein, 'dasasataṃbyāmaṃ' means a length of a thousand fathoms. 'Uragamādāya āgato' means having brought such a large serpent here. 'Tañca mañca' means that serpent and me. 'Dhārayaṃ' means holding. 'Byathasi' means you tremble. 'Kamatthaṃ' asks 'For what reason?' or 'For what cause?'; it also means 'Seeing what purpose?' 'Koṭasimbalī' addresses the deity by the name of the tree. For that silk-cotton (simbalī) tree, due to the greatness of its trunk and branches, receives the name 'Koṭasimbali,' and the deity dwelling in it also has that same name.

Athassa [M 3.0377] kāraṇaṃ kathento devaputto catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Then the deity, explaining the reason to him, recited four verses:

123.

123.

“Maṃsabhakkho tuvaṃ rāja, phalabhakkho ayaṃ dijo;

Ayaṃ nigrodhabījāni, pilakkhudumbarāni ca;

Assatthāni ca bhakkhitvā, khandhe me ohadissati.

'O king, you are a flesh-eater, while this bird is a fruit-eater. Having eaten the seeds of the banyan, the pilakkha, the udumbara, and the assattha, it will drop its excrement on my trunk.'

124.

124.

“Te rukkhā saṃvirūhanti, mama passe nivātajā;

Te maṃ pariyonandhissanti, arukkhaṃ maṃ karissare.

'Those trees will sprout, born in the shelter of my branches; they will envelop me and render me no longer a tree.'

125.

125.

“Santi [P 3.0399] aññepi rukkhā se, mūlino khandhino dumā;

Iminā sakuṇajātena, bījamāharitā hatā.

'There are other trees as well, great trees with roots and trunks, that have been destroyed by this kind of bird which brings the seeds.'

126.

126.

“Ajjhārūhābhivaḍḍhanti, brahantampi vanappatiṃ;

Tasmā rāja pavedhāmi, sampassaṃnāgataṃ bhaya”nti.

'Climbing upon and growing over, they overwhelm even a mighty lord of the forest; therefore, O king, I tremble, seeing the danger yet to come.'

Tattha ohadissatīti vaccaṃ pātessati. Te rukkhāti tehi bījehi jātā nigrodhādayo rukkhā. Saṃvirūhantīti saṃviruhissanti vaḍḍhissanti. Mama passeti mama sākhantarādīsu. Nivātajāti mama sākhāhi vātassa nivāritattā nivāte jātā. Te maṃ pariyonandhissantīti ete [V 3.0353] evaṃ vaḍḍhitā maṃ pariyonandhissantīti ayametthādhippāyo. Karissareti athevaṃ pariyonandhitvā maṃ arukkhameva karissanti sabbaso bhañjissanti. Rukkhā seti rukkhā. Mūlino khandhinoti mūlasampannā ceva khandhasampannā ca. Dumāti rukkhavevacanameva. Bījamāharitāti bījaṃ āharitvā. Hatāti aññepi imasmiṃ vane rukkhā vināsitā santi. Ajjhārūhābhivaḍḍhantīti nigrodhādayo rukkhā ajjhārūhā hutvā mahantampi aññaṃ vanappatiṃ atikkamma vaḍḍhantīti dasseti. Ettha pana vane pati, vanassa pati, vanappatīti tayopi pāṭhāyeva. Rājāti supaṇṇaṃ ālapati.

Therein, 'ohadissati' means will drop its excrement. 'Te rukkhā' refers to the trees like the banyan that grow from those seeds. 'Saṃvirūhanti' means they will grow and increase. 'Mama passe' refers to the areas among my branches and so forth. 'Nivātajā' means born in a windless (sheltered) spot because the wind is blocked by my branches. 'Te maṃ pariyonandhissanti' means these, having grown thus, will envelop me; this is the intention here. 'Karissare' means that by enveloping me, they will make me as if I were no longer a tree, utterly breaking me. 'Rukkhā se' means trees. 'Mūlino khandhino' means endowed with roots and a trunk. 'Dumā' is a synonym for trees. 'Bījamāharitā' means having brought the seed. 'Hatā' means other trees in this forest have been destroyed. 'AjjhārūhābhivaḍTargetti' shows that trees like the banyan, having climbed upon others, grow to surpass even a mighty lord of the forest. Here, 'vane pati,' 'vanassa pati,' and 'vanappati'—these three are all variant readings. 'Rājā' addresses the Garuda (Supaṇṇa).

Rukkhadevatāya vacanaṃ sutvā supaṇṇo osānagāthamāha –

Hearing the words of the tree-deity, the Garuda spoke the concluding verse:

127.

127.

“Saṅkeyya saṅkitabbāni, rakkheyyānāgataṃ bhayaṃ;

Anāgatabhayā dhīro, ubho loke avekkhatī”ti.

'One should be wary of what is to be suspected, and guard against future danger. The wise one, seeing future danger, considers both worlds.'

Tattha [M 3.0378] anāgataṃ bhayanti pāṇātipātādīhi viramanto diṭṭhadhammikampi samparāyikampi anāgataṃ bhayaṃ rakkhati nāma, pāpamitte veripuggale ca anupasaṅkamanto anāgatabhayaṃ rakkhati nāma. Evaṃ anāgataṃ bhayaṃ rakkheyya. Anāgatabhayāti anāgatabhayakāraṇā taṃ bhayaṃ passanto dhīro idhalokañca paralokañca avekkhati oloketi nāma.

Therein, regarding 'future danger': one who refrains from killing living beings and so forth is said to protect against future danger, both in this very life and in the life to come. By not associating with evil friends and hostile individuals, one is said to protect against future danger. Thus, one should guard against future danger. 'Because of future danger' [anāgatabhayā] means that the wise person, seeing that danger by reason of future danger, considers and regards both this world and the next.

Evañca pana vatvā supaṇṇo attano ānubhāvena taṃ pakkhiṃ tamhā rukkhā palāpesi.

Having spoken thus, the supaṇṇa, by his own power, drove that bird away from that tree.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “āsaṅkitabbayuttakaṃ āsaṅkituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne [P 3.0400] pañcasatā bhikkhū arahattaphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, saying, "It is fitting to be wary of what should be suspected," and having proclaimed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the teaching on the Truths, five hundred monks were established in the fruit of arahatship.

Tadā supaṇṇarājā sāriputto ahosi, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the supaṇṇa king was Sāriputta, and I myself was the tree deity.

Koṭasimbalijātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Koṭasimbali Jātaka, the seventh.

[413] 8. Dhūmakārijātakavaṇṇanā

[413] 8. The Commentary on the Dhūmakāri Jātaka

Rājā [V 3.0354] apucchi vidhuranti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarañño āgantukasaṅgahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira ekasmiṃ samaye paveṇiāgatānaṃ porāṇakayodhānaṃ saṅgahaṃ akatvā abhinavāgatānaṃ āgantukānaññeva sakkārasammānaṃ akāsi. Athassa paccante kupite yujjhanatthāya gatassa “āgantukā laddhasakkārā yujjhissantī”ti porāṇakayodhā na yujjhiṃsu, “porāṇakayodhā yujjhissantī”ti āgantukāpi na yujjhiṃsu. Corā rājānaṃ jiniṃsu. Rājā parājito āgantukasaṅgahadosena attano parājitabhāvaṃ ñatvā sāvatthiṃ paccāgantvā “kiṃ nu kho ahameva evaṃ karonto parājito, udāhu aññepi rājāno parājitapubbāti dasabalaṃ pucchissāmī”ti bhuttapātarāso jetavanaṃ gantvā sakkāraṃ katvā satthāraṃ vanditvā tamatthaṃ pucchi. Satthā “na kho, mahārāja, tvameveko, porāṇakarājānopi āgantukasaṅgahaṃ katvā parājitā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The king asked Vidhura—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the hospitality given to newcomers by the king of Kosala. It is said that on one occasion he did not honor his veteran warriors who had come in unbroken succession, but showed respect and esteem only to newly arrived newcomers. Then, when his border regions revolted and he went to battle, thinking, "The newcomers, having received honors, will fight," the veteran warriors did not fight. Thinking, "The veteran warriors will fight," the newcomers also did not fight. Bandits defeated the king. The defeated king, realizing his defeat was due to the fault of favoring newcomers, returned to Sāvatthī and thought, "Is it only I who, acting thus, has been defeated, or have other kings also been defeated before?" Resolving to ask the Ten-Powered One, after his morning meal, he went to Jetavana, paid his respects, and asked the Teacher about the matter. The Teacher replied, "Great king, you are not the only one; ancient kings too were defeated by favoring newcomers," and when requested by him, he related a past event.

Atīte [M 3.0379] kururaṭṭhe indapatthanagare yudhiṭṭhilagotto dhanañcayo nāma korabyarājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto tassa purohitakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā indapatthaṃ paccāgantvā pitu accayena purohitaṭṭhānaṃ labhitvā rañño atthadhammānusāsako ahosi, vidhurapaṇḍitotissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tadā dhanañcayarājā porāṇakayodhe agaṇetvā āgantukānaññeva saṅgahaṃ akāsi. Tassa paccante kupite yujjhanatthāya gatassa “āgantukā jānissantī”ti neva porāṇakā yujjhiṃsu, “porāṇakā yujjhissantī”ti na āgantukā yujjhiṃsu. Rājā parājito indapatthameva paccāgantvā “āgantukasaṅgahassa katabhāvena parājitomhī”ti [P 3.0401] cintesi. So ekadivasaṃ “kiṃ nu kho ahameva āgantukasaṅgahaṃ katvā parājito, udāhu aññepi rājāno parājitapubbā atthīti vidhurapaṇḍitaṃ pucchissāmī”ti cintetvā taṃ rājupaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā nisinnaṃ tamatthaṃ pucchi. Athassa taṃ pucchanākāraṃ āvikaronto satthā upaḍḍhaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, in the Kuru country, in the city of Indapatta, King Dhanañjaya of the Yudhiṭṭhila lineage, the Koravya king, ruled the kingdom. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of the royal priest. When he came of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, returned to Indapatta, and after his father’s death, he obtained the position of royal priest. He became the king’s advisor in matters of benefit and righteousness, and they called him Vidhura the Wise. At that time, King Dhanañjaya, disregarding his veteran warriors, favored only newcomers. When the border region revolted and he went to battle, thinking, "The newcomers will know what to do," the veterans did not fight. And thinking, "The veterans will fight," the newcomers did not fight. The king was defeated and returned to Indapatta, reflecting, "I have been defeated because of favoring newcomers." One day, he pondered, "Was it only I who favored newcomers and was defeated, or have other kings also been defeated before?" Resolving to ask Vidhura the Wise, he went to the royal court, where Vidhura was seated, and questioned him on the matter. Then, revealing the manner of his inquiry, the Teacher spoke half a verse:

128.

128.

“Rājā apucchi vidhuraṃ, dhammakāmo yudhiṭṭhilo”ti.

"The king, Yudhiṭṭhila, desirous of Dhamma, asked Vidhura."

Tattha dhammakāmoti sucaritadhammappiyo.

Herein, 'dhammakāmo' means one who is fond of the Dhamma of good conduct.

“Api brāhmaṇa jānāsi, ko eko bahu socatī”ti –

"Brahmin, do you know who it is that alone grieves much?"

Sesaupaḍḍhagāthāya pana ayamattho – api nāma, brāhmaṇa, tvaṃ jānāsi “ko imasmiṃ loke

Regarding the remaining half-verse, the meaning is this: "Brahmin, do you perhaps know who in this world...

Eko [V 3.0355] bahu socati, nānākāraṇena socatī”ti.

...alone grieves much, grieves for various reasons?'"

Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto “mahārāja, kiṃ soko nāma tumhākaṃ soko, pubbe dhūmakārī nāmeko ajapālabrāhmaṇo mahantaṃ ajayūthaṃ gahetvā araññe vajaṃ katvā tattha ajā ṭhapetvā aggiñca dhūmañca katvā ajayūthaṃ paṭijagganto khīrādīni paribhuñjanto vasi. So tattha āgate suvaṇṇavaṇṇe sarabhe disvā tesu sinehaṃ katvā ajā agaṇetvā ajānaṃ sakkāraṃ sarabhānaṃ katvā saradakāle sarabhesu palāyitvā himavantaṃ gatesu ajāsupi naṭṭhāsu sarabhe apassanto sokena paṇḍurogī hutvā jīvitakkhayaṃ patto, ayaṃ āgantukasaṅgahaṃ katvā tumhehi sataguṇena sahassaguṇena socitvā kilamitvā [M 3.0380] vināsaṃ patto”ti idaṃ udāharaṇaṃ ānetvā dassento imā gāthā āha –

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta said, "Great king, what is this grief of yours? Once, there was a brahmin goatherd named Dhūmakārī who, taking a large herd of goats, made a pen in the forest. Having placed the goats there, and making a fire and smoke, he lived tending the herd and enjoying milk and other things. Seeing golden-colored sarabha deer that came there, he became fond of them, neglecting the goats and showing honor to the sarabhas instead. When the autumn season came, the sarabhas fled to the Himalayas. With the goats also lost, and not seeing the sarabhas, he became pale with grief and met his end. This one, having welcomed newcomers, grieved a hundredfold or a thousandfold more than you, suffered, and met with ruin." Bringing forth this example, he spoke these verses:

129.

129.

“Brāhmaṇo ajayūthena, pahūtejo vane vasaṃ;

Dhūmaṃ akāsi vāseṭṭho, rattindivamatandito.

"A brahmin of the Vāseṭṭha clan, with a herd of goats, of great energy, dwelling in the forest, made smoke untiringly, night and day."

130.

130.

“Tassa taṃdhūmagandhena, sarabhā makasaḍḍitā;

Vassāvāsaṃ upagacchuṃ, dhūmakārissa santike.

"By the scent of that smoke, the sarabha deer, harassed by mosquitoes, approached the smoke-maker for their rains-residence."

131.

131.

“Sarabhesu manaṃ katvā, ajā so nāvabujjhatha;

Āgacchantī vajantī vā, tassa tā vinasuṃ ajā.

"Having set his mind on the sarabhas, he paid no heed to the goats; whether coming or going, those goats of his were lost."

132.

132.

“Sarabhā [P 3.0402] sarade kāle, pahīnamakase vane;

Pāvisuṃ giriduggāni, nadīnaṃ pabhavāni ca.

"In the autumn season, when the forest was free from mosquitoes, the sarabha deer entered the mountain fastnesses and the sources of the rivers."

133.

133.

“Sarabhe ca gate disvā, ajā ca vibhavaṃ gatā;

Kiso ca vivaṇṇo cāsi, paṇḍurogī ca brāhmaṇo.

"Seeing that the sarabhas were gone and his goats had come to ruin, the brahmin became thin, pale, and afflicted with jaundice."

134.

134.

“Evaṃ yo saṃ niraṃkatvā, āgantuṃ kurute piyaṃ;

So eko bahu socati, dhūmakārīva brāhmaṇo”ti.

"Thus, he who rejects his own and holds a newcomer dear, grieves much and alone, like the brahmin Dhūmakārī."

Tattha pahūtejoti pahūtaindhano. Dhūmaṃ akāsīti makkhikaparipanthaharaṇatthāya aggiñca dhūmañca akāsi. Vāseṭṭhoti tassa gottaṃ. Atanditoti analaso hutvā. Taṃdhūmagandhenāti tena dhūmagandhena. Sarabhāti sarabhamigā. Makasaḍḍitāti makasehi upaddutā pīḷitā. Sesamakkhikāpi makasaggahaṇeneva [V 3.0356] gahitā. Vassāvāsanti vassārattavāsaṃ vasiṃsu. Manaṃ katvāti sinehaṃ uppādetvā. Nāvabujjhathāti araññato caritvā vajaṃ āgacchantī ceva vajato araññaṃ gacchantī ca “ettakā āgatā, ettakā anāgatā”ti na jānāti. Tassa tā vinasunti tassa tā evaṃ apaccavekkhantassa sīhaparipanthādito arakkhiyamānā ajā sīhaparipanthādīhi vinassiṃsu, sabbāva vinaṭṭhā.

Here, 'pahūtejoti' means having abundant fuel. 'Dhūmaṃ akāsī'—he made fire and smoke to ward off the nuisance of flies. 'Vāseṭṭho' is his clan name. 'Atandito' means being diligent. 'Taṃdhūmagandhena'—by the odor of that smoke. 'Sarabhā' refers to sarabha deer. 'Makasaḍḍitā' means tormented and afflicted by mosquitoes. Other flies are also included by the term 'makasa.' 'Vassāvāsaṃ'—they dwelt during the rainy season. 'Manaṃ katvā' means having developed affection. 'Nāvabujjhatha'—he did not know, when they were coming from the forest to the pen or going from the pen to the forest, “this many have come, this many have not come.” 'Tassa tā vinasuṃ'—thus, his goats, being unguarded by him who was not paying attention in this way, perished due to dangers such as lions; all of them were lost.

Nadīnaṃ pabhavāni cāti pabbateyyānaṃ nadīnaṃ pabhavaṭṭhānāni ca paviṭṭhā. Vibhavanti abhāvaṃ. Ajā ca vināsaṃ pattā disvā jānitvā. Kiso ca vivaṇṇoti khīrādidāyikā ajā pahāya sarabhe saṅgaṇhitvā tepi apassanto ubhato [M 3.0381] parihīno sokābhibhūto kiso ceva dubbaṇṇo ca ahosi. Evaṃ yo saṃ niraṃkatvāti evaṃ mahārāja, yo sakaṃ porāṇaṃ ajjhattikaṃ janaṃ nīharitvā pahāya kismiñci agaṇetvā āgantukaṃ piyaṃ karoti, so tumhādiso eko bahu socati, ayaṃ te mayā dassito dhūmakārī brāhmaṇo viya bahu socatīti.

'Nadīnaṃ pabhavāni ca'—they entered the source-places of mountain rivers. 'Vibhavaṃ' means non-existence. 'Ajā ca vināsaṃ pattā disvā'—having seen and known that the goats had come to ruin. 'Kiso ca vivaṇṇo'—having abandoned the goats that provided milk and other things and having taken up with the sarabhas, but then not seeing them either, he was diminished on both sides, and overcome by sorrow, he became thin and discolored. 'Evaṃ yo saṃ niraṃkatvā'—thus, O great king, whoever, having driven out and abandoned his own old internal people, holding them of no account, makes a newcomer dear, that person, like you, grieves much alone; he grieves much like this brahmin Dhūmakārī shown to you by me.

Evaṃ mahāsatto rājānaṃ saññāpento kathesi. Sopi saññattaṃ gantvā tassa pasīditvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ adāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya ca ajjhattikasaṅgahameva karonto dānādīni puññāni katvā saggaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus, the Great Being spoke, instructing the king. The king, having understood, was pleased with him and gave him much wealth. And from then on, supporting only his own people and performing meritorious deeds such as giving, he became one destined for heaven.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā korabyarājā ānando ahosi, dhūmakārī pasenadikosalo, vidhurapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the birth: "At that time, King Korabya was Ānanda, Dhūmakārī was Pasenadi of Kosala, but the Vidhurapaṇḍita was I myself."

Dhūmakārijātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Dhūmakāri Jātaka, the eighth.

[414] 9. Jāgarajātakavaṇṇanā

[414] 9. The Commentary on the Jāgara Jātaka

Kodha [P 3.0403] jāgarataṃ suttoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ upāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi sotāpanno ariyasāvako sāvatthito sakaṭasatthena saddhiṃ kantāramaggaṃ paṭipajji. Satthavāho tattha ekasmiṃ udakaphāsukaṭṭhāne pañca sakaṭasatāni mocetvā khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ saṃvidahitvā vāsaṃ upagacchi. Te manussā tattha tattha nipajjitvā supiṃsu, upāsako pana satthavāhassa santike ekasmiṃ rukkhamūle caṅkamaṃ adhiṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ satthaṃ vilumpitukāmā [V 3.0357] pañcasatā corā nānāvudhāni gahetvā satthaṃ parivāretvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Te taṃ upāsakaṃ caṅkamantaṃ disvā “imassa niddāyanakāle vilumpissāmā”ti tattha tattha aṭṭhaṃsu, sopi tiyāmarattiṃ caṅkamiyeva. Corā paccūsasamaye gahitagahitā pāsāṇamuggarādayo chaḍḍetvā “bho satthavāha, imaṃ appamādena jaggantaṃ purisaṃ nissāya jīvitaṃ labhitvā tava santakassa sāmiko jāto, etassa sakkāraṃ kareyyāsī”ti vatvā pakkamiṃsu. Manussā [M 3.0382] kālasseva vuṭṭhāya tehi chaḍḍitapāsāṇamuggarādayo disvā “imaṃ nissāya amhehi jīvitaṃ laddha”nti upāsakassa sakkāraṃ akaṃsu. Upāsakopi icchitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā katakicco puna sāvatthiṃ āgantvā jetavanaṃ gantvā tathāgataṃ pūjetvā vanditvā nisinno “kiṃ, upāsaka, na paññāyasī”ti vutte tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Satthā “na kho, upāsaka, tvaṃyeva aniddāyitvā jagganto visesaṃ labhi, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi jaggantā visesaṃ guṇaṃ labhiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

‘Who here is asleep among the wakeful?’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain lay follower. That lay follower, a noble disciple who had attained stream-entry, set out from Sāvatthī with a caravan of carts, traveling along a wilderness road. The caravan leader, having unyoked the five hundred carts at a certain place with convenient water, prepared food and drink, then took up lodging. The people lay down here and there and slept, but the lay follower undertook walking meditation at the foot of a tree near the caravan leader. Then, five hundred robbers, desiring to plunder the caravan, took up various weapons, surrounded the caravan, and stood waiting. Seeing the lay follower walking, they thought, “We will plunder it when this one falls asleep,” and so they waited there. But he continued to walk throughout the three watches of the night. At dawn, the robbers, dropping the stones, clubs, and other things they had taken up, said, “O caravan leader, on account of this man who keeps watch with diligence, you have received your life and become master of your own property. You should pay him honor!” Having said this, they departed. The people, rising early and seeing the stones and clubs they had dropped, said, “On account of him, we have received our lives,” and they paid honor to the lay follower. The lay follower, having gone to his desired destination and completed his business, returned to Sāvatthī. He went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Tathāgata, and sat down. When asked, “What is it, lay follower, why have you not appeared?” he related the matter. The Teacher said, “Lay follower, it is not only you who have gained a distinction by not sleeping and keeping watch; the wise of old also, by keeping watch, gained a special quality.” And, being requested by him, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā paccāgantvā agāramajjhe vasanto aparabhāge nikkhamitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā na cirasseva jhānābhiññaṃ nibbattetvā himavantapadese ṭhānacaṅkamiriyāpatho hutvā vasanto niddaṃ anupagantvā sabbarattiṃ caṅkamati. Athassa caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ nibbattarukkhadevatā [P 3.0404] tussitvā rukkhaviṭape ṭhatvā pañhaṃ pucchantī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. Having come of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā and returned. While living in the house, he later went forth as a seer. Before long, he developed meditative absorptions and higher knowledges. Dwelling in the Himalayan region, he adopted the postures of standing and walking, and not giving in to sleep, he would walk throughout the night. Then a tree deity who had come into being at the end of his walking path was pleased, and standing on a branch of the tree, she asked a question, speaking the first verse:

135.

135.

“Kodha jāgarataṃ sutto, kodha suttesu jāgaro;

Ko mametaṃ vijānāti, ko taṃ paṭibhaṇāti me”ti.

“Who here is asleep among the wakeful? Who here is wakeful among the sleeping? Who understands this of mine? Who will answer it to me?”

Tattha kodhāti ko idha. Ko mametanti ko mama etaṃ pañhaṃ vijānāti. Ko taṃ paṭibhaṇāti meti etaṃ mayā puṭṭhaṃ pañhaṃ mayhaṃ ko paṭibhaṇāti, ko byākarituṃ sakkhissatīti pucchati.

Here, 'Kodhā' means 'who here?' 'Ko mametaṃ' means 'who understands this question of mine?' 'Ko taṃ paṭibhaṇāti me' means 'who will answer this question asked by me? Who will be able to explain it?' she asks.

Bodhisatto tassā vacanaṃ sutvā –

The Bodhisatta, having heard her words, said:

136.

136.

“Ahaṃ jāgarataṃ sutto, ahaṃ suttesu jāgaro;

Ahametaṃ vijānāmi, ahaṃ paṭibhaṇāmi te”ti. –

“I am asleep among the wakeful; I am wakeful among the sleeping. I understand this; I will answer you.”

Imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā puna tāya –

After he spoke this verse, she again asked:

137.

137.

“Kathaṃ [V 3.0358] jāgarataṃ sutto, kathaṃ suttesu jāgaro;

Kathaṃ etaṃ vijānāsi, kathaṃ paṭibhaṇāsi me”ti. –

“How are you asleep among the wakeful? How are you wakeful among the sleeping? How do you understand this? How do you answer me?”

Imaṃ gāthaṃ puṭṭho tamatthaṃ byākaronto –

Being asked this verse, explaining its meaning, he said:

138.

138.

“Ye dhammaṃ nappajānanti, saṃyamoti damoti ca;

Tesu suppamānesu, ahaṃ jaggāmi devate.

“Those who do not know the Dhamma, nor restraint and self-control; among them, who are fast asleep, I am awake, O deity."

139.

139.

“Yesaṃ [M 3.0383] rāgo ca doso ca, avijjā ca virājitā;

Tesu jāgaramānesu, ahaṃ suttosmi devate.

“Those for whom lust, hatred, and ignorance have been dispelled; while they are wakeful, I am asleep, O deity.”

140.

140.

“Evaṃ jāgarataṃ sutto, evaṃ suttesu jāgaro;

Evametaṃ vijānāmi, evaṃ paṭibhaṇāmi te”ti. – imā gāthā āha;

“Thus I am asleep among those who are wakeful; thus I am wakeful among those who are asleep. Thus I understand this; thus I answer you.” – these verses he spoke.

Tattha kathaṃ jāgarataṃ suttoti kathaṃ tvaṃ jāgarataṃ sattānaṃ antare sutto nāma hosi. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ye dhammanti ye sattā navavidhaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ na pajānanti. Saṃyamoti damoti cāti “ayaṃ saṃyamo, ayaṃ damo”ti evañca ye maggena āgataṃ sīlañceva indriyasaṃvarañca na jānanti. Indriyasaṃvaro hi manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ damanato “damo”ti vuccati. Tesu suppamānesūti tesu kilesaniddāvasena supantesu sattesu ahaṃ appamādavasena jaggāmi.

Here, 'Kathaṃ jāgarataṃ sutto' means: how have you become known as 'asleep' among beings who are wakeful? This method applies everywhere. 'Ye dhammaṃ' refers to those beings who do not know the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. 'Saṃyamoti damoti cā' refers to those who do not know 'this is restraint, this is self-control,' and thus do not know the morality and sense-restraint that come by way of the path. For sense-restraint is called 'self-control' (dama) because of the taming of the six senses, with the mind as the sixth. 'Tesu suppamānesū' means: among those beings who are sleeping with the sleep of the defilements, I am awake through diligence.

“Yesaṃ rāgo cā”ti gāthāya yesaṃ mahākhīṇāsavānaṃ padasatena niddiṭṭhadiyaḍḍhasahassataṇhālobhasaṅkhāto rāgo ca navaāghātavatthusamuṭṭhāno doso ca dukkhādīsu aṭṭhasu vatthūsu [P 3.0405] aññāṇabhūtā avijjā cāti ime kilesā virājitā pahīnā, tesu ariyesu sabbākārena jāgaramānesu te upādāya ahaṃ sutto nāma devateti attho. Evaṃ jāgaratanti evaṃ devate ahaṃ iminā kāraṇena jāgarataṃ sutto nāmāti. Esa nayo sabbapadesu.

In the verse 'Yesaṃ rāgo cā': for those great ones whose taints are destroyed, these defilements are dispelled and abandoned: passion (rāga), which is defined as craving and greed, enumerated as one and a half thousand types and indicated by a hundred terms; hatred (dosa), which arises from the nine grounds of resentment; and ignorance (avijjā), which is the state of not knowing the eight subjects beginning with suffering. The meaning is: with reference to those noble ones who are wakeful in every way, I am called 'asleep,' O deity. 'Evaṃ jāgarataṃ' means: thus, O deity, for this reason I am called 'asleep' among the wakeful. This method applies in all instances.

Evaṃ mahāsattena pañhe kathite tuṭṭhā devatā tassa thutiṃ karontī osānagāthamāha –

Thus, when the Great Being had explained the question, the delighted deity, wishing to praise him, uttered this concluding verse:

141.

141.

“Sādhu [V 3.0359] jāgarataṃ sutto, sādhu suttesu jāgaro;

Sādhu metaṃ vijānāsi, sādhu paṭibhaṇāsi me”ti.

“Good it is that you are asleep among the wakeful; good it is that you are awake among the sleeping. Good it is that you understand this; good it is that you answer me.”

Tattha sādhūti bhaddakaṃ katvā tvaṃ imaṃ pañhaṃ kathesi, mayampi naṃ evameva kathemāti. Evaṃ sā bodhisattassa thutiṃ katvā attano vimānameva pāvisi.

Herein, ‘Sādhu’ means: ‘You have explained this question well; we too explain it in this same way.’ Thus, having praised the Bodhisatta, she entered her own celestial mansion.

Satthā [M 3.0384] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā devadhītā uppalavaṇṇā ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, the divine maiden was Uppalavaṇṇā, and the ascetic was indeed myself.”

Jāgarajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The commentary on the Jāgara Jātaka, the ninth.

[415] 10. Kummāsapiṇḍijātakavaṇṇanā

[415] 10. The Commentary on the Kummāsapiṇḍa Jātaka

Na kiratthīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mallikaṃ deviṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā hi sāvatthiyaṃ ekassa mālākārajeṭṭhakassa dhītā uttamarūpadharā mahāpuññā soḷasavassikakāle ekadivasaṃ kumārikāhi saddhiṃ pupphārāmaṃ gacchantī tayo kummāsapiṇḍe gahetvā pupphapacchiyaṃ ṭhapetvā gacchati. Sā nagarato nikkhamanakāle bhagavantaṃ sarīrappabhaṃ vissajjetvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivutaṃ nagaraṃ pavisantaṃ disvā tayo kummāsapiṇḍe upanāmesi. Satthā catumahārājadattiyaṃ pattaṃ upanetvā paṭiggahesi. Sāpi tathāgatassa pāde sirasā vanditvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Satthā taṃ oloketvā sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Āyasmā ānando “ko nu kho, bhante, hetu ko paccayo tathāgatassa sitakaraṇe”ti bhagavantaṃ pucchi. Athassa satthā “ānanda, ayaṃ kumārikā imesaṃ kummāsapiṇḍānaṃ phalena ajjeva kosalarañño aggamahesī bhavissatī”ti sitakāraṇaṃ kathesi.

‘Indeed, there is not...’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Queen Mallikā. She was the daughter of the chief garland-maker in Sāvatthī, endowed with supreme beauty and great merit. At the age of sixteen, one day while going to the flower garden with other maidens, she took three lumps of barley-cake and placed them in her flower basket before setting out. As she was leaving the city, she saw the Blessed One radiating light from his body, surrounded by the community of monks, entering the city. She offered the three lumps of barley-cake to him. The Teacher received them into the bowl given by the Four Great Kings. She then bowed her head at the feet of the Tathāgata, took delight with the Buddha as her object, and stood to one side. The Teacher, looking at her, manifested a smile. The Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One, ‘What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason for the Tathāgata's smile?’ The Teacher explained the reason for his smile: ‘Ānanda, this maiden, as a result of these lumps of barley-cake, will this very day become the chief queen of the king of Kosala.’

Kumārikāpi pupphārāmaṃ gatā[P 3.0406]. Taṃ divasameva kosalarājā ajātasattunā saddhiṃ yujjhanto yuddhaparājito palāyitvā assaṃ abhiruyha āgacchanto tassā gītasaddaṃ sutvā paṭibaddhacitto assaṃ taṃ ārāmābhimukhaṃ pesesi. Puññasampannā kumārikā rājānaṃ disvā apalāyitvāva āgantvā assassa nāsarajjuyā gaṇhi, rājā assapiṭṭhiyaṃ nisinnova “sasāmikāsi, asāmikāsī”ti pucchitvā asāmikabhāvaṃ ñatvā assā oruyha vātātapakilanto tassā aṅke nipanno muhuttaṃ vissamitvā taṃ assapiṭṭhiyaṃ nisīdāpetvā balakāyaparivuto [V 3.0360] nagaraṃ pavisitvā attano kulagharaṃ pesetvā sāyanhasamaye yānaṃ pahiṇitvā [M 3.0385] mahantena sakkārasammānena kulagharato āharāpetvā ratanarāsimhi ṭhapetvā abhisekaṃ datvā aggamahesiṃ akāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya ca sā rañño piyā ahosi manāpā, pubbuṭṭhāyikādīhi pañcahi kalyāṇadhammehi samannāgatā patidevatā, buddhānampi vallabhā ahosi. Tassā satthu tayo kummāsapiṇḍe datvā taṃ sampattiṃ adhigatabhāvo sakalanagaraṃ pattharitvā gato.

The maiden, for her part, went to the flower garden. That very day, the King of Kosala, while fighting with Ajātasattu, was defeated in battle. Fleeing, he came mounted on his horse, and hearing her singing, his heart was captivated, and he directed his horse toward that garden. The maiden, endowed with merit, seeing the king, did not flee, but approached and took hold of the horse's bridle. The king, still seated on the horse, asked, ‘Are you married or unmarried?’ and knowing she was unmarried, he dismounted from the horse. Weary from wind and sun, he lay in her lap and rested for a moment. Then, having seated her on the horse and surrounded by his army, he entered the city, sent her to her family's house, and in the evening, sent a carriage and had her brought with great honor and ceremony from her family's house. He placed her on a heap of jewels, performed the consecration, and made her his chief queen. From then on, she was dear and beloved to the king, a devoted wife endowed with the five excellent qualities beginning with rising early, and she was beloved even of the Buddha. The news that she had attained that prosperity by giving three lumps of barley-cake to the Teacher spread throughout the entire city.

Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, mallikā devī buddhānaṃ tayo kummāsapiṇḍe datvā tesaṃ phalena taṃ divasaññeva abhisekaṃ pattā, aho buddhānaṃ mahāguṇatā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, mallikāya ekassa sabbaññubuddhassa tayo kummāsapiṇḍe datvā kosalarañño aggamahesibhāvādhigamo. Kasmā? Buddhānaṃ guṇamahantatāya. Porāṇakapaṇḍitā pana paccekabuddhānaṃ aloṇakaṃ asnehaṃ aphāṇitaṃ kummāsaṃ datvā tassa phalena dutiye attabhāve tiyojanasatike kāsiraṭṭhe rajjasiriṃ pāpuṇiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then one day in the hall of Dhamma, a discussion arose among the monks: “Sirs, Queen Mallikā, having given three lumps of barley-cake to the Buddha, attained her consecration that very day as its result. Oh, the greatness of the Buddha’s virtues!” The Teacher arrived and asked, “For what discussion, monks, are you now gathered together?” When it was said, “For this one,” he said, “It is not wonderful, monks, that Mallikā, by giving three lumps of barley-cake to one single all-knowing Buddha, attained the state of chief queen to the king of Kosala. Why? Because of the greatness of the Buddha’s virtues. The wise of old, however, by giving unsalted, unoiled, and unsweetened barley-cakes to Paccekabuddhas, attained, as its result, in their next existence, the royal splendor of the kingdom of Kāsī, which was three hundred yojanas in extent.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ daliddakule nibbattitvā vayappatto ekaṃ seṭṭhiṃ nissāya bhatiyā kammaṃ karonto jīvikaṃ kappesi. So ekadivasaṃ “pātarāsatthāya me bhavissatī”ti antarāpaṇato cattāro kummāsapiṇḍe gahetvā kammantaṃ gacchanto cattāro paccekabuddhe bhikkhācāratthāya bārāṇasinagarābhimukhe āgacchante disvā “ime bhikkhaṃ sandhāya bārāṇasiṃ gacchanti[P 3.0407], mayhampime cattāro kummāsapiṇḍā atthi, yaṃnūnāhaṃ ime imesaṃ dadeyya”nti cintetvā te upasaṃkamitvā vanditvā “bhante, ime me hatthe cattāro kummāsapiṇḍā, ahaṃ ime tumhākaṃ dadāmi, sādhu me, bhante, paṭiggaṇhatha, evamidaṃ puññaṃ mayhaṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti vatvā tesaṃ adhivāsanaṃ viditvā vālikaṃ ussāpetvā cattāri āsanāni paññapetvā tesaṃ upari sākhābhaṅgaṃ attharitvā paccekabuddhe paṭipāṭiyā nisīdāpetvā paṇṇapuṭena udakaṃ āharitvā dakkhiṇodakaṃ pātetvā catūsu pattesu cattāro kummāsapiṇḍe patiṭṭhāpetvā vanditvā “bhante, etesaṃ nissandena daliddagehe nibbatti nāma mā hotu, sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭivedhassa paccayo hotū”ti [M 3.0386] āha. Paccekabuddhā paribhuñjiṃsu, paribhogāvasāne anumodanaṃ katvā uppatitvā nandamūlakapabbhārameva agamaṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor family. Having come of age, he made a living by working as a hired laborer for a certain merchant. One day, thinking, 'This will be for my morning meal,' he took four lumps of barley-meal from a shop and was on his way to work when he saw four Paccekabuddhas coming towards the city of Bārāṇasī for alms. He thought, 'These are going to Bārāṇasī for alms. I also have these four lumps of barley-meal. What if I were to give these to them?' Thinking thus, he approached them, paid homage, and said, 'Venerable sirs, in my hands are these four lumps of barley-meal. I give them to you. Please, sirs, accept them from me, so that this merit may be for my long-term welfare and happiness.' Knowing their acceptance, he heaped up sand, prepared four seats, spread broken branches over them, and seated the Paccekabuddhas in order. He brought water in a leaf cup, poured the water of dedication, placed the four lumps of barley-meal into the four bowls, paid homage, and said, 'Venerable sirs, through the fruit of this, let there be no rebirth for me in a poor house, and may it be a cause for the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience.' The Paccekabuddhas partook of the meal, and at the conclusion of their meal, they gave their blessing, rose up, and went to the Nandamūlaka cave.

Bodhisatto añjaliṃ paggayha paccekabuddhagataṃ pītiṃ gahetvā tesu cakkhupathaṃ atītesu attano [V 3.0361] kammantaṃ gantvā yāvatāyukaṃ dānaṃ anussaritvā kālaṃ katvā tassa phalena bārāṇasirañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, brahmadattakumārotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So attano padasā gamanakālato paṭṭhāya “ahaṃ imasmiṃyeva nagare bhatako hutvā kammantaṃ gacchanto paccekabuddhānaṃ cattāro kummāsapiṇḍe datvā tassa dānassa phalena idha nibbatto”ti pasannādāse mukhanimittaṃ viya sabbaṃ purimajātikiriyaṃ jātissarañāṇena pākaṭaṃ katvā passi. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā paccāgantvā sikkhitasippaṃ pitu dassetvā tuṭṭhena pitarā oparajje patiṭṭhāpito, aparabhāge pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāsi. Athassa uttamarūpadharaṃ kosalarañño dhītaraṃ ānetvā aggamahesiṃ akaṃsu, chattamaṅgaladivase panassa sakalanagaraṃ devanagaraṃ viya alaṅkariṃsu.

The Bodhisatta, raising his joined hands in reverence, took with him the joy inspired by the Paccekabuddhas. When they had passed from his sight, he went to his work. For as long as he lived, he recollected that act of giving, and when he died, by the fruit of that merit, he was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of the king of Bārāṇasī. They gave him the name Prince Brahmadatta. From the time he was able to walk, he remembered his former existence through the knowledge of past lives, seeing all his previous actions made manifest as clearly as the reflection of a face in a polished mirror. He thought: 'In this very city, while working as a hired laborer, I gave four lumps of barley-meal to Paccekabuddhas, and as a result of that gift, I have been reborn in this royal family.' When he came of age, he went to Takkasilā, learned all the arts, and returned. Having shown his skills to his father, his father was pleased and appointed him as viceroy. Later, upon his father's death, he succeeded to the throne. Then, they brought the daughter of the king of Kosala, who possessed supreme beauty, and made her his chief queen. On the day of the auspicious umbrella ceremony, the entire city was decorated like a city of the gods.

So nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā alaṅkatapāsādaṃ [P 3.0408] abhiruhitvā mahātalamajjhe samussitasetacchattaṃ pallaṅkaṃ abhiruyha nisinno parivāretvā ṭhite ekato amacce, ekato brāhmaṇagahapatiādayo nānāvibhave sirivilāsasamujjale, ekato nānāvidhapaṇṇākārahatthe nāgaramanusse, ekato alaṅkatadevaccharasaṅghaṃ viya soḷasasahassasaṅkhaṃ nāṭakitthigaṇanti imaṃ atimanoramaṃ sirivibhavaṃ olokento attano pubbakammaṃ anussaritvā “idaṃ suvaṇṇapiṇḍikaṃ kañcanamālaṃ setacchattaṃ, imāni ca anekasahassāni hatthivāhanaassavāhanarathavāhanāni, maṇimuttādipūritā sāragabbhā, nānāvidhadhaññapūritā mahāpathavī, devaccharapaṭibhāgā nāriyo cāti sabbopesa mayhaṃ sirivibhavo na aññassa santako, catunnaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ dinnassa catukummāsapiṇḍadānasseva santako, te nissāya mayā esa laddho”ti paccekabuddhānaṃ guṇaṃ anussaritvā attano kammaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsi. Tassa taṃ anussarantassa sakalasarīraṃ pītiyā pūri. So pītiyā temitahadayo mahājanassa majjhe udānagītaṃ gāyanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

After circumambulating the city, he ascended the decorated palace and sat upon a throne with a white canopy raised over it in the middle of the great hall. Surrounded by ministers on one side, wealthy brahmins and householders shining with the splendor of various riches on another, city dwellers holding various gifts in their hands on another, and a company of sixteen thousand dancing women adorned like a troop of celestial nymphs on yet another, he gazed upon this most delightful display of glory and wealth. Recalling his past merit, he thought: 'This white canopy with its golden knob and golden garlands, these many thousands of elephants, horses, and chariots, these treasure-rooms filled with gems and pearls, this vast earth filled with various grains, and these women resembling celestial nymphs—all this glory of mine belongs to no other. It is the property of the gift of four lumps of barley-meal offered to four Paccekabuddhas. It is because of them that I have attained this.' As he recollected the virtues of the Paccekabuddhas and made his own deed manifest, his entire body was filled with joy. With a heart saturated with delight, wishing to sing a song of joy in the midst of the great assembly, he uttered these two verses:

142.

142.

“Na [M 3.0387] kiratthi anomadassisu, pāricariyā buddhesu appikā;

Sukkhāya aloṇikāya ca, passa phalaṃ kummāsapiṇḍiyā.

"Indeed, no service to the Buddhas of matchless vision is insignificant; behold the fruit of a lump of barley-meal, though it was dry and unsalted."

143.

143.

“Hatthigavāssā cime bahū, dhanadhaññaṃ pathavī ca kevalā;

Nāriyo cimā accharūpamā, passa phalaṃ kummāsapiṇḍiyā”ti.
