"Many are these elephants, cattle, and horses, the wealth and grain, and the entire earth; and these women, like celestial nymphs—behold the fruit of a lump of barley-meal!"

Tattha anomadassisūti anomassa alāmakassa paccekabodhiñāṇassa diṭṭhattā paccekabuddhā anomadassino nāma. Pāricariyāti abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānañjalikammādibhedā sāmīcikiriyāpi, sampatte [V 3.0362] disvā attano santakaṃ appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā deyyadhammaṃ cittaṃ pasādetvā guṇaṃ sallakkhetvā tisso cetanā visodhetvā phalaṃ saddahitvā pariccajanakiriyāpi[P 3.0409]. Buddhesūti paccekabuddhesu. Appikāti mandā parittā nāma natthi kira. Sukkhāyāti nisnehāya. Aloṇikāyāti phāṇitavirahitāya. Nipphāṇitattā hi sā “aloṇikā”ti vuttā. Kummāsapiṇḍiyāti cattāro kummāsapiṇḍe ekato katvā gahitaṃ kummāsaṃ sandhāya evamāha. Guṇavantānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ guṇaṃ sallakkhetvā cittaṃ pasādetvā phaluppattiṃ pāṭikaṅkhamānānaṃ tisso cetanā visodhetvā dinnapadakkhiṇā appikā nāma natthi, nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne mahāsampattimeva detīti vuttaṃ hoti. Hoti cettha –

Therein, 'anomadassisu' (of matchless vision) refers to Paccekabuddhas, who are so called because they have seen the faultless, unblemished knowledge of a Paccekabuddha's enlightenment. 'Pāricariyā' (service) refers to various forms of proper conduct such as paying respects, rising to greet, joining palms in reverence, and so on. It also includes the act of generosity—seeing a worthy recipient, joyfully offering whatever one possesses, be it little or much, coarse or refined, reflecting on their virtues, purifying the threefold intention, and having faith in the fruit of giving. 'Buddhesu' refers to the Paccekabuddhas. 'Appikā' means that no service is meager or insignificant. 'Sukkhāya' means without oiliness. 'Aloṇikāya' means without molasses; because it lacks molasses, it is called 'aloṇikā'. 'Kummāsapiṇḍiyā' (of a lump of sour gruel): he speaks thus with reference to the sour gruel that was made into four lumps. For those who, reflecting on the virtues of virtuous ascetics and brahmins, gladden their minds, aspire for the fruit, and purify the threefold intention, a gift given is not called meager; it is said that in each successive rebirth it bestows great prosperity. Here, it is said:

“Natthi citte pasannamhi, appikā nāma dakkhiṇā;

Tathāgate vā sambuddhe, atha vā tassa sāvake.

"When the heart is serene, no offering is insignificant, whether to the Tathāgata, the Fully Awakened One, or to his disciple."

“Tiṭṭhante nibbute cāpi, same citte samaṃ phalaṃ;

Cetopaṇidhihetu hi, sattā gacchanti suggati”nti. (vi. va. 804, 806);

"Whether they are living or have attained Nibbāna, with an equal mind, the fruit is equal; for it is because of the mind's aspiration that beings go to a happy state."

Imassa panatthassa dīpanatthāya –

To clarify the meaning of this:

“Khīrodanaṃ ahamadāsiṃ, bhikkhuno piṇḍāya carantassa; (Vi. va. 413);

Tassā me passa vimānaṃ, accharā kāmavaṇṇinīhamasmi. (vi. va. 334);

"I gave milk-rice to a monk who was wandering for alms. See my celestial mansion; I am a nymph of desirable form."

“Accharāsahassassāhaṃ[M 3.0388], pavarā passa puññānaṃ vipākaṃ;

Tena metādiso vaṇṇo, tena me idha mijjhati.

"I am the foremost of a thousand celestial nymphs; behold the result of merit! Because of that, such is my complexion; because of that, I prosper here."

“Uppajjanti ca me bhogā, ye keci manaso piyā;

Tenamhi evaṃ jalitānubhāvā, vaṇṇo ca me sabbadisā pabhāsatī”ti. (vi. va. 334-336) –

"And riches arise for me, whatever is pleasing to the mind; because of that, I am of such radiant power, and my complexion shines in all directions."

Evamādīni vimānavatthūni āharitabbāni.

Such stories of celestial mansions should be cited.

Dhanadhaññanti [V 3.0363] muttādidhanañca satta dhaññāni ca. Pathavī ca kevalāti sakalā cesā mahāpathavīti sakalapathaviṃ hatthagataṃ maññamāno vadati. Passa phalaṃ kummāsapiṇḍiyāti attano dānaphalaṃ attanāva dassento evamāha. Dānaphalaṃ kira bodhisattā ca sabbaññubuddhāyeva ca jānanti. Teneva satthā itivuttake suttantaṃ kathento –

'Wealth and grain' means wealth, such as pearls, and the seven kinds of grain. 'The entire earth' means this whole great earth; he speaks thinking the entire earth is in his grasp. 'See the fruit of the lump of sour gruel': he speaks thus, himself showing the fruit of his own gift. Indeed, the fruit of giving is known only by Bodhisattas and Omniscient Buddhas. Therefore the Teacher, while teaching a sutta in the Itivuttaka, said:

“Evañce, bhikkhave, sattā jāneyyuṃ dānasaṃvibhāgassa vipākaṃ, yathāhaṃ jānāmi, na adatvā bhuñjeyyuṃ, na ca nesaṃ maccheramalaṃ cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭheyya. Yopi nesaṃ assa carimo ālopo carimaṃ kabaḷaṃ, tatopi na asaṃvibhajitvā bhuñjeyyuṃ, sace nesaṃ paṭiggāhakā assu. Yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, sattā na evaṃ jānanti dānasaṃvibhāgassa vipākaṃ, yathāhaṃ jānāmi, tasmā adatvā bhuñjanti, maccheramalañca nesaṃ cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī”ti (itivu. 26).

"Monks, if beings knew the result of giving and sharing as I know it, they would not eat without giving, nor would the stain of stinginess possess their minds. Even if it were their last morsel, their last mouthful, they would not eat without sharing it, if there were a recipient. But, monks, because beings do not know the result of giving and sharing as I know it, they eat without giving, and the stain of stinginess possesses their minds."

Bodhisattopi attano chattamaṅgaladivase sañjātapītipāmojjo imāhi dvīhi gāthāhi udānagītaṃ gāyi. Tato paṭṭhāya “rañño piyagīta”nti bodhisattassa nāṭakitthiyo ca sesanāṭakagandhabbādayopi ca antepurajanopi antonagaravāsinopi bahinagaravāsinopi pānāgāresupi amaccamaṇḍalesupi “amhākaṃ rañño piyagīta”nti tadeva [P 3.0410] gītaṃ gāyanti. Evaṃ addhāne gate aggamahesī tassa gītassa atthaṃ jānitukāmā ahosi, mahāsattaṃ pana pucchituṃ na visahati. Athassā ekasmiṃ guṇe pasīditvā ekadivasaṃ rājā “bhadde, varaṃ te dassāmi, varaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti āha. “Sādhu, deva, gaṇhāmī”ti. “Hatthiassādīsu te kiṃ dammī”ti? “Deva, tumhe nissāya mayhaṃ na kiñci natthi, na me etehi attho, sace pana dātukāmāttha, tumhākaṃ gītassa atthaṃ kathetvā dethā”ti. “Bhadde, ko te [M 3.0389] iminā varena attho, aññaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti. “Deva, aññena me attho natthi, etadeva gaṇhāmī”ti. “Sādhu bhadde, kathessāmi, tuyhaṃ pana ekikāya raho na kathessāmi, dvādasayojanikāya bārāṇasiyā bheriṃ carāpetvā rājadvāre ratanamaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā ratanapallaṅkaṃ paññāpetvā amaccabrāhmaṇādīhi ca nāgarehi ceva soḷasahi itthisahassehi ca parivuto tesaṃ majjhe ratanapallaṅke nisīditvā kathessāmī”ti. Sā “sādhu, devā”ti sampaṭicchi.

On the day of his own royal umbrella ceremony, the Bodhisatta, filled with joy and delight, sang an inspired song of exultation with these two verses. From then on, it was known as 'The King's Beloved Song.' The dancing women and other troupes of dancers and musicians, the palace attendants, the city dwellers within and without, those in the taverns, and the circles of ministers—all sang that same song, saying, 'This is our king’s beloved song.' As time passed, the chief queen desired to know the meaning of the song, but she did not dare to ask the Great Being. Then one day, the king, pleased with a certain quality of hers, said, 'Dear lady, I grant you a boon. Choose a boon.' She replied, 'Very well, my lord, I accept.' He asked, 'What shall I give you—elephants, horses, or something else?' She answered, 'My lord, because of you, I lack nothing; I have no need for those. But if you wish to give me something, please explain the meaning of your song.' The king said, 'Dear lady, what use is this boon to you? Choose another.' She replied, 'My lord, I have no need for another; I choose only this.' The king said, 'Very well, dear lady, I will explain it. However, I will not explain it to you alone in private. I will have the drum beaten throughout the twelve-yojana city of Bārāṇasī, have a jeweled pavilion constructed at the palace gate, have a jeweled throne prepared, and then, surrounded by ministers, brahmins, and other citizens, as well as by sixteen thousand women, I will explain it while seated on the jeweled throne in their midst.' She agreed, saying, 'Very well, my lord.'

Rājā tathā kāretvā amaragaṇaparivuto sakko devarājā viya mahājanakāyaparivuto ratanapallaṅke nisīdi. Devīpi sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā kañcanabhaddapīṭhaṃ attharitvā ekamante akkhikoṭiyā oloketvā tathārūpe ṭhāne nisīditvā “deva, tumhākaṃ tussitvā gāyanamaṅgalagītassa [V 3.0364] tāva me atthaṃ gaganatale puṇṇacandaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya pākaṭaṃ katvā kathethā”ti vatvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, having had this arranged, sat upon a jeweled throne surrounded by a great multitude, like Sakka, the king of gods, surrounded by a host of immortals. The queen, adorned with all her ornaments, had a golden auspicious seat spread out and sat in a suitable place. Glancing with the corner of her eye, she said, 'My lord, please first explain to me the meaning of the auspicious song you sing with delight, making it as clear as the full moon rising in the sky,' and she spoke the third verse:

144.

144.

“Abhikkhaṇaṃ rājakuñjara, gāthā bhāsasi kosalādhipa;

Pucchāmi taṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhana, bāḷhaṃ pītimano pabhāsasī”ti.

'O royal elephant, lord of Kosala, you constantly recite verses; I ask you, O increaser of the realm, you speak with a mind exceedingly full of joy.'

Tattha kosalādhipāti na so kosalaraṭṭhādhipo, kusale pana dhamme adhipatiṃ katvā viharati, tena naṃ ālapantī evamāha, kusalādhipa kusalajjhāsayāti [P 3.0411] attho. Bāḷhaṃ pītimano pabhāsasīti ativiya pītiyuttacitto hutvā bhāsasi, tasmā kathetha tāva me etāsaṃ gāthānaṃ atthanti.

Therein, 'lord of Kosala' does not mean he is the ruler of the Kosala country, but that he dwells having made wholesome qualities his mastery; thus, addressing him, she said 'Kosalādhipa,' meaning 'one of wholesome inclination.' 'You speak with a mind exceedingly full of joy' means you speak with a heart intensely filled with joy. 'Therefore, please tell me the meaning of these verses.'

Athassa gāthānamatthaṃ āvi karonto mahāsatto catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Then, making clear the meaning of those verses, the Great Being spoke these four stanzas:

145.

145.

“Imasmiṃyeva nagare, kule aññatare ahuṃ;

Parakammakaro āsiṃ, bhatako sīlasaṃvuto.

'In this very city, I was born into a certain family; I was a worker for others, a hired laborer, restrained in virtue.'

146.

146.

“Kammāya nikkhamantohaṃ, caturo samaṇeddasaṃ;

Ācārasīlasampanne, sītibhūte anāsave.

'As I was setting out for work, I saw four ascetics; endowed with proper conduct and virtue, serene and taintless.'

147.

147.

“Tesu [M 3.0390] cittaṃ pasādetvā, nisīdetvā paṇṇasanthate;

Adaṃ buddhānaṃ kummāsaṃ, pasanno sehi pāṇibhi.

'Having gladdened my heart toward them, and having seated them on a spread of leaves, I gave barley bread to those enlightened ones, with a devout mind, with my own hands.'

148.

148.

“Tassa kammassa kusalassa, idaṃ me edisaṃ phalaṃ;

Anubhomi idaṃ rajjaṃ, phītaṃ dharaṇimuttama”nti.

'Of that wholesome deed, this is such a fruit for me; I enjoy this kingdom, prosperous and supreme on earth.'

Tattha kule aññatareti nāmena vā gottena vā apākaṭe ekasmiṃyeva kule. Ahunti nibbattiṃ. Parakammakaro āsinti tasmiṃ kule jātovāhaṃ daliddatāya parassa kammaṃ katvā jīvikaṃ kappento parakammakaro āsiṃ. Bhatakoti paravetanabhato. Sīlasaṃvutoti pañcasīlasaṃvare ṭhito, bhatiyā jīvantopi dussīlyaṃ pahāya sīlasampannova ahosinti dīpeti. Kammāya nikkhamantohanti taṃ divasaṃ kattabbakiccassa karaṇatthāya nikkhanto ahaṃ. Caturo samaṇeddasanti [V 3.0365] bhadde, ahaṃ nagarā nikkhamma mahāmaggaṃ āruyha attano kammabhūmiṃ gacchanto bhikkhāya bārāṇasinagaraṃ pavisante samitapāpe cattāro pabbajite addasaṃ. Ācārasīlasampanneti ekavīsatiyā anesanāhi jīvikakappanaṃ anācāro nāma, tassa paṭipakkhena ācārena ceva maggaphalehi āgatena sīlena ca samannāgate. Sītibhūteti rāgādipariḷāhavūpasamena ceva ekādasaagginibbāpanena ca sītibhāvappatte. Anāsaveti kāmāsavādivirahite. Nisīdetvāti vālikāsanānaṃ upari santhate paṇṇasanthare nisīdāpetvā. Santharo hi idha santhatoti vutto. Adanti nesaṃ udakaṃ datvā sakkaccaṃ sakehi hatthehi kummāsaṃ adāsiṃ. Kusalassāti ārogyānavajjaṭṭhena kusalassa. Phalanti tassa nissandaphalaṃ. Phītanti sabbasampattiphullitaṃ.

Therein, 'in a certain family' means in a family unknown by name or clan. 'I was' means birth. 'I was a worker for others' means having been born into that family, I lived my life as a servant doing others' work due to poverty. 'A hired laborer' means one who is supported by another's wages. 'Restrained in virtue' means established in the restraint of the five precepts; it shows that even while living on wages, he abandoned immorality and was endowed with virtue. 'As I was setting out for work' means I had gone out to perform the tasks to be done that day. 'I saw four ascetics' means: Dear lady, as I left the city and took the main road to my workplace, I saw four renunciates who had stilled their evil entering the city of Bārāṇasī for alms. 'Endowed with proper conduct and virtue' means: earning a living through the twenty-one types of improper search is called 'misconduct' (anācara); they were endowed with the opposite, which is 'proper conduct' (ācara), and with the virtue that accompanies the paths and fruits. 'Serene' (sītibhūta) means having attained a state of coolness through the calming of the fever of passion and the like, and by the extinguishing of the eleven fires. 'Taintless' means devoid of the taints of sensuality and so on. 'Having seated' means having seated them on a spread of leaves upon sand-seats; for here, the word 'santhata' (spread) is used to mean 'santhara' (a mat). 'I gave' means after giving them water, I respectfully gave them barley bread with my own hands. 'Wholesome' means wholesome in the sense of being healthy and blameless. 'Fruit' means its resulting benefit. 'Prosperous' means flourishing with all successes.

Evañca [P 3.0412] mahāsattassa attano kammaphalaṃ vitthāretvā kathentassa sutvā devī pasannamanā “sace, mahārāja, evaṃ paccakkhato dānaphalaṃ jānātha, ito dāni paṭṭhāya ekaṃ bhattapiṇḍaṃ labhitvā dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ datvāva paribhuñjeyyāthā”ti bodhisattassa thutiṃ karontī –

Thus, having heard the Great Being explain in detail the fruit of his own deed, the queen, with a gladdened heart and wishing to praise the Bodhisatta, said: 'Great king, since you thus know the fruit of giving by direct experience, from this day forward, even if you obtain only a single morsel of food, you should partake of it only after giving to righteous ascetics and brahmins; do not be heedless,' and she spoke this verse:

149.

149.

“Dadaṃ bhuñja mā ca pamādo, cakkaṃ vattaya kosalādhipa;

Mā rāja adhammiko ahu, dhammaṃ pālaya kosalādhipā”ti. – imaṃ gāthamāha;

'Give and enjoy, and do not be heedless; turn the wheel of sovereignty, O lord of Kosala. O king, do not be unrighteous; protect the Dhamma, O lord of Kosala.'

Tattha [M 3.0391] dadaṃ bhuñjāti aññesaṃ datvāva attanā bhuñja. Mā ca pamādoti dānādīsu puññesu mā pamajji. Cakkaṃ vattaya kosalādhipāti kusalajjhāsaya, mahārāja, patirūpadesavāsādikaṃ catubbidhaṃ dhammacakkaṃ pavattehi. Pakatiratho hi dvīhi cakkehi gacchati, ayaṃ pana kāyo imehi catūhi cakkehi devalokaṃ gacchati, tena te “dhammacakka”nti saṅkhyaṃ gatā, taṃ tvaṃ cakkaṃ pavattehi. Adhammikoti yathā aññe chandāgatiṃ gacchantā lokaṃ ucchuyante pīḷetvā viya dhanameva saṃkaḍḍhantā adhammikā honti, tathā tvaṃ mā adhammiko ahu. Dhammaṃ pālayāti –

Therein, 'give and enjoy' means enjoy yourself only after giving to others. 'Do not be heedless' means do not be heedless in meritorious deeds such as giving. 'Turn the wheel, O lord of Kosala' means, O great king of wholesome inclination, set in motion the fourfold Wheel of Dhamma, such as residing in a suitable place. For an ordinary chariot moves with two wheels, but this body goes to the heavenly world with these four wheels; therefore, they are reckoned as the "Wheel of Dhamma." You should set this wheel in motion. 'Do not be unrighteous' means, just as others, swayed by partiality, become unrighteous by oppressing the world and extorting wealth as if squeezing sugarcane, so you too must not be unrighteous. 'Protect the Dhamma' means—

“Dānaṃ sīlaṃ pariccāgaṃ, ajjavaṃ maddavaṃ tapaṃ;

Akkodhaṃ avihiṃsañca, khantiñca avirodhana”nti. (jā. 2.21.176) –

"Generosity, virtue, relinquishment, straightforwardness, gentleness, austerity, non-anger, non-violence, patience, and non-opposition."

Imaṃ pana dasavidhaṃ rājadhammameva pālaya rakkha, mā pariccaji.

Protect and guard this very tenfold royal Dhamma, do not abandon it.

Mahāsatto tassā vacanaṃ sampaṭicchanto –

The Great Being, accepting her words, spoke this verse:

150.

150.

“Sohaṃ tadeva punappunaṃ, vaṭumaṃ ācarissāmi sobhane;

Ariyācaritaṃ sukosale, arahanto me manāpāva passitu”nti. – gāthamāha;

"I shall practice again and again that very path, the conduct of the noble ones, O lovely one. O Sukosalā, Arahants are pleasing for me to behold."

Tattha [V 3.0366] vaṭumanti maggaṃ. Ariyācaritanti ariyehi buddhādīhi āciṇṇaṃ. Sukosaleti sobhane kosalarañño dhīteti attho. Arahantoti kilesehi ārakattā, arānañca arīnañca hatattā, paccayānaṃ arahattā evaṃladdhanāmā paccekabuddhā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bhadde, kosalarājadhīte so ahaṃ “dānaṃ [P 3.0413] me dinna”nti tittiṃ akatvā punappunaṃ tadeva ariyācaritaṃ dānamaggaṃ ācarissāmi. Mayhañhi aggadakkhiṇeyyattā arahanto manāpadassanā, cīvarādīni dātukāmatāya teyeva passituṃ icchāmīti.

Therein, 'vaṭumaṃ' means the path. 'The conduct of the noble ones' means practiced by the noble ones such as the Buddhas. 'Sukosalā' means 'O beautiful one, daughter of the king of Kosala.' 'Arahants' refers to Paccekabuddhas who are so named because they are far from defilements, have destroyed the spokes and the enemies of the cycle of rebirth, and are worthy of requisites. This is what is said: 'O good one, daughter of the king of Kosala, I, not being content with merely thinking "A gift has been given by me," will again and again practice that very noble practice, the path of giving. For in my case, since Arahants are the foremost recipients of offerings, they are pleasing to see, and being desirous of giving robes and other requisites, I desire to see them.'

Evañca pana vatvā rājā deviyā sampattiṃ oloketvā “bhadde, mayā tāva purimabhave attano kusalakammaṃ vitthāretvā kathitaṃ, imāsaṃ pana nārīnaṃ majjhe rūpena vā līḷāvilāsena vā tayā sadisī ekāpi [M 3.0392] natthi, sā tvaṃ kiṃ kammaṃ katvā imaṃ sampattiṃ paṭilabhī”ti pucchanto puna gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, the king, observing the queen’s prosperity, said: "Dear one, I have already described in detail my own wholesome deeds in a past life. But among these women, not even one is equal to you in beauty or grace and charm. What deed did you perform to attain this prosperity?" Asking thus, he spoke another verse:

151.

151.

“Devī viya accharūpamā, majjhe nārigaṇassa sobhasi;

Kiṃ kammamakāsi bhaddakaṃ, kenāsi vaṇṇavatī sukosale”ti.

"Like a goddess, resembling a celestial nymph, you shine amidst this group of women. What wholesome deed did you perform, by which you are so beautiful, O Sukosalā?"

Tassattho – bhadde sukosale kosalarañño sudhīte tvaṃ rūpasampattiyā accharūpamā tidasapure sakkassa devarañño aññatarā devadhītā viya imassa nārīgaṇassa majjhe sobhasi, pubbe kiṃ nāma bhaddakaṃ kalyāṇakammaṃ akāsi, kenāsi kāraṇena evaṃ vaṇṇavatī jātāti.

The meaning is: “O good Sukosalā, good daughter of the Kosala king, by your perfection of form, you shine amidst this group of women like a celestial maiden of Sakka, king of the devas, in the city of the Thirty-Three. What wholesome and auspicious deed did you perform in the past? By what cause have you been born so radiant?”

Athassa sā purimabhave kalyāṇakammaṃ kathentī sesagāthādvayamāha –

Then, recounting her auspicious deeds from a past life, she spoke the remaining two verses:

152.

152.

“Ambaṭṭhakulassa khattiya, dāsyāhaṃ parapesiyā ahuṃ;

Saññatā ca dhammajīvinī, sīlavatī ca apāpadassanā.

"O Khattiya, I was a slave girl in the family of Ambaṭṭha, a servant sent on errands. I was restrained, living righteously, virtuous, and of auspicious appearance."

153.

153.

“Uddhaṭabhattaṃ ahaṃ tadā, caramānassa adāsiṃ bhikkhuno;

Vittā sumanā sayaṃ ahaṃ, tassa kammassa phalaṃ mamedisa”nti.

"At that time, I myself gave a portion of food to a wandering monk. Joyful and glad at heart, this is the fruit of that deed for me."

Sāpi kira jātissarāva ahosi, tasmā attano jātissarañāṇena paricchinditvāva kathesi.

It is said that she too was one who remembered her past lives. Therefore, having ascertained it precisely with her own knowledge of past lives, she spoke.

Tattha [V 3.0367][P 3.0414] ambaṭṭhakulassāti kuṭumbiyakulassa. Dāsyāhanti dāsī ahaṃ, “dāsāha”ntipi pāṭho. Parapesiyāti parehi tassa tassa kiccassa karaṇatthāya pesitabbā pesanakārikā. Saññatāti dāsiyo nāma dussīlā honti, ahaṃ pana tīhi dvārehi saññatā sīlasampannā. Dhammajīvinīti paravañcanādīni akatvā dhammena samena pavattitajīvikā. Sīlavatīti ācārasampannā guṇavatī. Apāpadassanāti kalyāṇadassanā piyadhammā.

Here, “in the household of an Ambaṭṭha” means in the family of a householder. “I am a servant-girl”—some texts read “dāsāha.” “Sent by others” means one who is sent by others to perform various tasks. “Restrained” means that although servant-girls are often immoral, I was restrained in the three doors of action and endowed with virtue. “Living righteously” means she made a living honestly and fairly, without cheating others. “Virtuous” means she was perfect in conduct and endowed with good qualities. “Of faultless appearance” means she was of auspicious appearance and endowed with lovable qualities.

Uddhaṭabhattanti [M 3.0393] attano pattakoṭṭhāsavasena uddharitvā laddhabhāgabhattaṃ. Bhikkhunoti bhinnakilesassa paccekabuddhassa. Vittā sumanāti tuṭṭhā somanassajātā kammaphalaṃ saddahantī. Tassa kammassāti tassa ekabhikkhādānakammassa. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ahaṃ, mahārāja, pubbe sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa kuṭumbiyakulassa dāsī hutvā attano laddhabhāgabhattaṃ ādāya nikkhamantī ekaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā attano taṇhaṃ milāpetvā saññatādiguṇasampannā kammaphalaṃ saddahantī tassa taṃ bhattaṃ adāsiṃ, sāhaṃ yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā kālaṃ katvā tattha sāvatthiyaṃ kosalarañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbattitvā idāni tava pāde paricaramānā evarūpaṃ sampattiṃ anubhavāmi, tassa mama kammassa idamīdisaṃ phalanti. Tattha guṇasampannānaṃ dinnadānassa mahapphalabhāvadassanatthaṃ –

“Uddhaṭabhatta” means the portion of food set aside as one's share. “Bhikkhu” refers to a Paccekabuddha who has destroyed his defilements. “Vittā sumanā” means delighted and filled with joy, believing in the fruit of kamma. “Tassa kammassā” refers to that act of giving alms to a single monk. This is what is meant: “O great king, in the past, I was a slave girl in a certain householder's family in Sāvatthī. Taking the portion of food I had received and going out, I saw a Paccekabuddha wandering for alms. Suppressing my craving and endowed with virtues like restraint, believing in the fruit of kamma, I gave that food to him. After living out my lifespan and passing away, I was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of the Kosala king in that very Sāvatthī. Now, attending at your feet, I experience such prosperity—this is the fruit of that kamma of mine.” Here, to show the great fruitfulness of giving alms to the virtuous, the following is stated:

“Aggato ve pasannāna”nti (itivu. 90) ca.

“Esa devamanussānaṃ, sabbakāmadado nidhī”ti (khu. pā. 8.10) ca. –

“For those who have faith, it is foremost indeed,” (Itivuttaka 90) and “This is a treasure for gods and humans, giver of all desires,” (Khuddakapāṭha 8.10).

Ādigāthā vitthāretabbā.

The initial verses should be explained in detail.

Iti te ubhopi attano purimakammaṃ vitthārato kathetvā tato paṭṭhāya catūsu nagaradvāresu nagaramajjhe nivesanadvāreti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā sakalajambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ katvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā sīlaṃ rakkhitvā uposathakammaṃ katvā jīvitapariyosāne saggaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Thus, both of them recounted their past deeds in detail. From then on, having established six alms halls—at the four city gates, in the middle of the city, and at the palace entrance—and having made the entire Jambudīpa free from the burden of the plow, they dispensed great charity, maintained virtuous conduct, observed the Uposatha, and at the end of their lives, were destined for heaven.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā devī rāhulamātā ahosi, rājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the queen was Rāhula’s mother, and the king was none other than myself.”

Kummāsapiṇḍijātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The commentary on the Kummāsapiṇḍi Jātaka, the tenth.

[416] 11. Parantapajātakavaṇṇanā

[416] 11. The Commentary on the Parantapa Jātaka

Āgamissati [V 3.0368] me pāpanti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto tathāgatassa [P 3.0415] māraṇatthameva parisakkati, dhanuggahe payojesi, silaṃ pavijjhi, nāḷāgiriṃ vissajjāpesi, tathāgatassa [M 3.0394] vināsatthameva upāyaṃ karotī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa mama vadhāya parisakki, tāsamattampi pana kātuṃ asakkonto attanāva dukkhaṃ anubhosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Evil will come to me”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta’s attempt to kill him. At that time, in the Dharma hall, monks started this discussion: “Friends, Devadatta is striving only to kill the Tathāgata—he employed archers, hurled a rock, and released the elephant Nālāgiri, doing everything possible to destroy the Tathāgata.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here now?” When they replied, “This matter,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now; in the past too he tried to kill me, but being unable to cause even a little fear, he himself experienced suffering.” Having said this, he related a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni sikkhi, sabbarutajānanamantaṃ uggaṇhi. So ācariyassa anuyogaṃ datvā bārāṇasiṃ paccāgacchi, pitā taṃ oparajje ṭhapesi. Kiñcāpi oparajje ṭhapeti, mārāpetukāmo pana naṃ hutvā daṭṭhumpi na icchi. Athekā siṅgālī dve potake gahetvā rattiṃ manussesu paṭisallīnesu niddhamanena nagaraṃ pāvisi. Bodhisattassa ca pāsāde sayanagabbhassa avidūre ekā sālā atthi, tattheko addhikamanusso upāhanā omuñcitvā pādamūle bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā ekasmiṃ phalake nipajji, na tāva niddāyati. Tadā siṅgāliyā potakā chātā viraviṃsu. Atha tesaṃ mātā “tātā, mā saddaṃ karittha, etissā sālāya eko manusso upāhanā omuñcitvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā phalake nipanno na tāva niddāyati, etassa niddāyanakāle etā upāhanā āharitvā tumhe khādāpessāmī”ti attano bhāsāya āha. Bodhisatto mantānubhāvena tassā bhāsaṃ jānitvā sayanagabbhā nikkhamma vātapānaṃ vivaritvā “ko etthā”ti āha. “Ahaṃ, deva, addhikamanusso”ti. “Upāhanā te kuhi”nti? “Bhūmiyaṃ, devā”ti. “Ukkhitvā olambetvā ṭhapehī”ti. Taṃ sutvā siṅgālī bodhisattassa kujjhi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. When he came of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā and mastered the mantra for knowing all sounds. Having given his teacher his fee, he returned to Benares, and his father appointed him as viceroy. Although he was made viceroy, his father, wishing to have him killed, did not even wish to see him. At that time, a she-jackal with two cubs entered the city at night through a drain when the people were asleep. Near the palace chamber where the Bodhisatta slept, there was a hall where a traveler had taken off his sandals and placed them on the ground by his feet while lying on a plank, not yet asleep. Then the hungry cubs of the jackal cried out. Their mother said to them in her own language, “Dear ones, do not make a sound. In this hall, a man has taken off his sandals and placed them on the ground while lying on a plank, not yet asleep. When he falls asleep, I will bring those sandals and let you eat them.” The Bodhisatta, through the power of his mantra, understood her speech. He left his chamber, opened the window, and asked, “Who is there?” “It is I, lord, a traveler,” came the reply. “Where are your sandals?” “On the ground, lord.” “Pick them up and hang them up.” Hearing this, the she-jackal became angry at the Bodhisatta.

Puna ekadivasaṃ sā tatheva nagaraṃ pāvisi. Tadā ceko mattamanusso “pānīyaṃ [P 3.0416] pivissāmī”ti pokkharaṇiṃ otaranto patitvā nimuggo nirassāso mari. Nivatthā panassa dve sāṭakā nivāsanantare kahāpaṇasahassaṃ aṅguliyā ca muddikā atthi. Tadāpi sā puttake “chātamhā, ammā”ti viravante “tātā, mā saddaṃ karittha, etissā pokkharaṇiyā manusso mato, tassa idañcidañca atthi, so pana maritvā sopāneyeva nipanno, tumhe etaṃ manussaṃ khādāpessāmī”ti [V 3.0369] āha. Bodhisatto [M 3.0395] taṃ sutvā vātapānaṃ vivaritvā “sālāya ko atthī”ti vatvā ekenuṭṭhāya “ahaṃ, devā”ti vutte “gaccha etissā pokkharaṇiyā matamanussassa sāṭake ca kahāpaṇasahassañca aṅgulimuddikañca gahetvā sarīramassa yathā na uṭṭhahati, evaṃ udake osīdāpehī”ti āha. So tathā akāsi. Sā punapi kujjhitvā “purimadivase tāva me puttakānaṃ upāhanā khādituṃ na adāsi, ajja matamanussaṃ khādituṃ na deti, hotu, ito dāni tatiyadivase eko sapattarājā āgantvā nagaraṃ parikkhipissati. Atha naṃ pitā yuddhatthāya pesessati, tatra te sīsaṃ chindissanti, atha te galalohitaṃ pivitvā veraṃ muñcissāmi. Tvaṃ mayā saddhiṃ veraṃ bandhasi, jānissāmī”ti viravitvā bodhisattaṃ tajjetvā puttake gahetvā nikkhamati.

Again, one day she entered the city in the same manner. At that time, a drunken man, thinking, “I will drink water,” fell into the pond while descending and drowned, dying as his breath ceased. He was wearing two garments, and inside his garments were a thousand coins, and on his finger was a ring. Then, her children cried out, “We are hungry, mother!” She said, “Dear ones, do not make a sound. A man has died in this pond, and he has such and such things. He is dead and lying right on the steps. I will let you eat this man.” Hearing this, the Bodhisatta opened the window and asked, “Who is in the hall?” When a man got up and replied, “It is I, lord,” the Bodhisatta said, “Go to the pond where the dead man is, take his garments, the thousand coins, and his finger ring, and sink his body in the water in such a way that it does not rise.” He did so. Again, the she-jackal became angry and said, “Previously, you did not give my children sandals to eat. Today, you do not let them eat the dead man. So be it! On the third day from now, a rival king will come and besiege the city. Then your father will send you to battle, where they will cut off your head. Then I will drink your throat-blood and settle my grudge. You are making an enemy of me—you shall see!” Shouting thus, she threatened the Bodhisatta, took her children, and left.

Tatiyadivase eko sapattarājā āgantvā nagaraṃ parivāresi. Rājā bodhisattaṃ “gaccha, tāta, tena saddhiṃ yujjhā”ti āha. “Mayā, deva, ekaṃ diṭṭhaṃ atthi, gantuṃ na visahāmi, jīvitantarāyaṃ bhāyāmī”ti. “Mayhaṃ tayi mate vā amate vā kiṃ, gacchāheva tva”nti? So “sādhu, devā”ti mahāsatto parisaṃ gahetvā sapattarañño ṭhitadvārena anikkhamitvā aññaṃ dvāraṃ vivaritvā nikkhami. Tasmiṃ gacchante sakalanagaraṃ tucchaṃ viya ahosi. Sabbe teneva saddhiṃ nikkhamiṃsu. So ekasmiṃ sabhāgaṭṭhāne khandhāvāraṃ nivāsetvā acchi. Rājā cintesi “uparājā nagaraṃ tucchaṃ katvā balaṃ gahetvā palāyi, sapattarājāpi nagaraṃ parivāretvā [P 3.0417] ṭhito, idāni mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ natthī”ti. So “jīvitaṃ rakkhissāmī”ti deviñca purohitañca parantapaṃ nāmekaṃ pādamūlikañca dāsaṃ gahetvā rattibhāge aññātakavesena palāyitvā araññaṃ pāvisi. Bodhisatto tassa palātabhāvaṃ ñatvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā yuddhaṃ katvā sapattaṃ palāpetvā rajjaṃ gaṇhi. Pitāpissa ekasmiṃ nadītīre paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā phalāphalena yāpento vasi. Rājā ca purohito ca phalāphalatthāya gacchanti. Parantapadāso deviyā saddhiṃ paṇṇasālāyameva hoti. Tatrāpi rājānaṃ paṭicca deviyā kucchismiṃ gabbho patiṭṭhāsi. Sā abhiṇhasaṃsaggavasena parantapena saddhiṃ aticari. Sā ekadivasaṃ parantapaṃ āha “raññā ñāte neva tava, na mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ atthi, tasmā mārehi na”nti. “Kathaṃ māremī”ti? Esa taṃ khaggañca nhānasāṭakañca [M 3.0396] gāhāpetvā nhāyituṃ gacchati, tatrassa nhānaṭṭhāne pamādaṃ ñatvā khaggena sīsaṃ chinditvā sarīraṃ khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ katvā bhūmiyaṃ nikhaṇāhīti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi.

On the third day, a rival king arrived and besieged the city. The king said to the Bodhisatta, 'Go, dear son, and fight with him.' 'Sire, I have seen an omen; I dare not go, for I fear for my life.' 'What is it to me whether you live or die? You must go!' 'Very well, sire,' the Great Being replied. Taking his retinue, he did not exit by the gate where the rival king was stationed but opened another gate and departed. As he left, the entire city seemed to become empty. Everyone left with him. He set up camp in a suitable place and stayed there. The king thought, 'The viceroy has emptied the city, taken the army, and fled. The rival king also remains besieging the city. Now my life is as good as gone.' Resolving to save his life, he took the queen, the chaplain, and a personal attendant slave named Parantapa, and fled in disguise during the night into the forest. The Bodhisatta, learning of his father's flight, entered the city, fought the enemy, drove them away, and took the kingdom. His father had a leaf-hut built on a riverbank and lived there, sustained by wild fruits. The king and the chaplain would go out to gather fruits. The slave Parantapa stayed in the leaf-hut with the queen. There, a child was conceived in the queen's womb through the king. Due to constant association, she committed adultery with Parantapa. One day, she said to Parantapa, 'If the king finds out, neither you nor I will live. Therefore, kill him.' 'How should I kill him?' 'He has you carry his sword and bathing cloth and goes to bathe. There, at the bathing place, when you see he is off guard, cut off his head with the sword, chop his body into pieces, and bury it in the ground.' 'Very well,' he agreed.

Athekadivasaṃ purohitoyeva phalāphalatthāya gantvā avidūre rañño nhānatitthasāmante ekaṃ rukkhaṃ [V 3.0370] āruyha phalāphalaṃ gaṇhāti. Rājā “nhāyissāmī”ti parantapaṃ khaggañca nhānasāṭakañca gāhāpetvā nadītīraṃ agamāsi. Tattha naṃ nhānakāle pamādamāpannaṃ “māressāmī”ti parantapo gīvāya gahetvā khaggaṃ ukkhipi. So maraṇabhayena viravi. Purohito taṃ saddaṃ sutvā olokento parantapaṃ rājānaṃ mārentaṃ disvā bhītatasito sākhaṃ vissajjetvā rukkhato oruyha ekaṃ gumbaṃ pavisitvā nilīyi. Parantapo tassa sākhāvissajjanasaddaṃ sutvā rājānaṃ māretvā bhūmiyaṃ khaṇitvā “imasmiṃ ṭhāne sākhāvissajjanasaddo ahosi, ko nu kho etthā”ti vicinanto kañci adisvā nhatvā gato. Tassa gatakāle purohito nisinnaṭṭhānā nikkhamitvā rañño sarīraṃ khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ [P 3.0418] chinditvā āvāṭe nikhātabhāvaṃ ñatvā nhatvā attano vadhabhayena andhavesaṃ gahetvā paṇṇasālaṃ agamāsi. Taṃ disvā parantapo “kiṃ te, brāhmaṇa, kata”nti āha. So ajānanto viya “deva, akkhīni me nāsetvā āgatomhi, ussannāsīvise araññe ekasmiṃ vammikapasse aṭṭhāsiṃ, tatrekena āsīvisena nāsavāto vissaṭṭho me bhavissatī”ti āha. Parantapo “na maṃ sañjānāti, ‘devā’ti vadati, samassāsessāmi na”nti cintetvā “brāhmaṇa, mā cintayi, ahaṃ taṃ paṭijaggissāmī”ti assāsetvā phalāphalaṃ datvā santappesi. Tato paṭṭhāya parantapadāso phalāphalaṃ āhari, devīpi puttaṃ vijāyi. Sā putte vaḍḍhante ekadivasaṃ paccūsasamaye sukhanisinnā saṇikaṃ parantapadāsaṃ etadavoca “tvaṃ rājānaṃ mārento kenaci diṭṭho”ti. “Na maṃ koci addasa, sākhāvissajjanasaddaṃ pana assosiṃ, tassā sākhāya manussena vā tiracchānena vā vissaṭṭhabhāvaṃ na jānāmi, yadā kadāci pana me bhayaṃ āgacchantaṃ sākhāvissaṭṭhaṭṭhānato āgamissatī”ti tāya saddhiṃ sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

One day, the chaplain himself went to gather fruits and climbed a tree near the king's bathing place. The king, intending to bathe, had Parantapa carry his sword and bathing cloth and went to the riverbank. There, as the king was off guard while bathing, Parantapa, intending to kill him, seized him by the neck and raised his sword. The king cried out in fear of death. Hearing the sound, the chaplain looked and saw Parantapa killing the king. Terrified, he let go of the branch he was holding, descended from the tree, and hid in a thicket. Parantapa, hearing the sound of the branch being released, killed the king, dug into the ground, and thinking, 'The sound of a branch being released came from this spot—who could be here?' he searched, but seeing no one, he bathed and left. After he had gone, the chaplain emerged from his hiding place, and knowing that the king's body had been chopped into pieces and buried in a pit, he bathed. Fearing for his own life, he took on the guise of a blind man and went to the leaf-hut. Seeing him, Parantapa asked, 'Brahmin, what has happened to you?' As if not knowing, he replied, 'Sire, I have come here having lost my sight. In the forest abounding with venomous snakes, I stood by an anthill, and a venomous snake there must have blown its breath upon me.' Parantapa thought, 'He does not recognize me; he addresses me as ‘sire.’ I will reassure him.' So he comforted him, saying, 'Brahmin, do not worry, I will take care of you,' and gave him fruits to satisfy him. From then on, the slave Parantapa brought fruits, and the queen gave birth to a son. As the son was growing up, one day at dawn, while sitting comfortably, she quietly said to the slave Parantapa, 'When you were killing the king, were you seen by anyone?' He replied, 'No one saw me, but I heard the sound of a branch being released. I do not know whether that branch was released by a human or an animal. But if ever fear comes to me, it will come from the place where the branch was released.' While conversing with her, he spoke the first verse:

154.

154.

“Āgamissati [M 3.0397] me pāpaṃ, āgamissati me bhayaṃ;

Tadā hi calitā sākhā, manussena migena vā”ti.

"Evil consequence will come to me, fear will come to me; for then the branch was shaken, by a human or by a beast."

Tattha pāpanti lāmakaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ akantaṃ. Bhayanti cittutrāsabhayampi me āgamissati, na sakkā nāgantuṃ. Kiṃkāraṇā? Tadā hi calitā sākhā manussena migena vāti na paññāyati, tasmā tato maṃ bhayaṃ āgamissati.

In that verse, 'pāpaṃ' means that which is base, undesirable, and unpleasant. 'Bhayaṃ' means that even the fear that is mental terror will come upon me; it is not possible for it not to come. For what reason? Because at that time, it was not discernible whether the branch was moved by a human or by a beast; therefore, from that event fear will come to me.

Te “purohito niddāyatī”ti maññiṃsu. So pana aniddāyamānova tesaṃ kathaṃ assosi. Athekadivasaṃ purohito parantapadāse phalāphalatthāya gate attano brāhmaṇiṃ saritvā vilapanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

They thought, 'The chaplain is asleep.' But he, not being asleep, heard their conversation. Then one day, when the slave Parantapa had gone to gather fruits, the chaplain, remembering his brahmin wife and lamenting, spoke the second verse:

155.

155.

“Bhīruyā [V 3.0371][P 3.0419] nūna me kāmo, avidūre vasantiyā;

Karissati kisaṃ paṇḍuṃ, sāva sākhā parantapa”nti.

"My longing for the timid one, who dwells not far away, will surely make me thin and pale—just as that very branch will make Parantapa thin and pale."

Tattha bhīruyāti itthī ca nāma appamattakenāpi bhāyati, tasmā “bhīrū”ti vuccati. Avidūreti nātidūre ito katipayayojanamatthake vasantiyā bhīruyā mayhaṃ brāhmaṇiyā yo mama kāmo uppanno, so nūna maṃ kisañca paṇḍuñca karissatīti dasseti. “Sāva sākhā”ti iminā pana opammaṃ dasseti, yathā sākhā parantapaṃ kisaṃ paṇḍuṃ karoti, evanti attho.

Therein, 'for the timid one' (bhīruyā): a woman, by nature, is afraid even of a trifling matter, therefore she is called 'timid.' 'Not far away' (avidūre) means at a distance not too far, a few leagues from here. He indicates: 'The passion that has arisen in me for the timid one, my brahmin wife who lives there, will surely make me thin and pale.' With 'that very branch,' however, he shows a comparison; the meaning is: just as that branch makes Parantapa thin and pale, so too will this passion.

Iti brāhmaṇo gāthameva vadati, atthaṃ pana na katheti, tasmā imāya gāthāya kiccaṃ deviyā apākaṭaṃ. Atha naṃ “kiṃ kathesi brāhmaṇā”ti āha. Sopi “sallakkhitaṃ me”ti vatvā puna ekadivasaṃ tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, the brahmin spoke only the verse but did not explain its meaning; therefore, the purpose of this verse was not clear to the queen. Then she asked him, 'What did you say, brahmin?' He too replied, 'I have noted it,' and on another day, he spoke a third verse:

156.

156.

“Socayissati maṃ kantā, gāme vasamaninditā;

Karissati kisaṃ paṇḍuṃ, sāva sākhā parantapa”nti.

"My beloved, the blameless one dwelling in the village, will cause me sorrow; she will make me thin and pale—that very branch, O Parantapa."

Tattha socayissatīti sokuppādanena sukkhāpessati. Kantāti iṭṭhabhariyā. Gāme vasanti bārāṇasiyaṃ vasantīti adhippāyo. Aninditāti agarahitā uttamarūpadharā.

Therein, 'will cause me sorrow' (socayissati) means she will cause me to waste away by producing sorrow. 'Beloved' (kantā) means a dear wife. 'Dwelling in the village' means dwelling in Bārāṇasī. 'Blameless' (aninditā) means unreproached, possessing supreme beauty.

Punekadivasaṃ [M 3.0398] catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Again on another day, he spoke the fourth verse:

157.

157.

“Tayā maṃ asitāpaṅgi, sitāni bhaṇitāni ca;

Kisaṃ paṇḍuṃ karissanti, sāva sākhā parantapa”nti.

"O lady with dark-cornered eyes, the smiles and the words spoken by you will make me thin and pale—that very branch, O Parantapa."

Tattha tayā maṃ asitāpaṅgīti tayā maṃ asitā apaṅgi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bhadde, akkhikoṭito añjanasalākāya nīharitvā abhisaṅkhataasitāpaṅgi tayā pavattitāni mandahasitāni ca madhurabhāsitāni ca maṃ sā vissaṭṭhasākhā viravamānā parantapaṃ viya kisaṃ paṇḍuṃ karissatīti. Pa-kārassa va-kāraṃ katvā “vaṅgī”tipi pāṭhoyeva.

Therein, 'tayā maṃ asitāpaṅgī' means: by you, O dark-cornered eyed one. This is what was said: 'Dear lady, you whose dark outer corners of the eyes are well-prepared by being drawn out with a collyrium stick from the corners of the eyes; the gentle smiles and sweet words initiated by you will make me thin and pale, just as that released branch, while making a sound, makes Parantapa thin and pale.' By changing the letter 'p' to the letter 'v', 'vaṅgī' is also a valid reading.

Aparabhāge kumāro vayappatto ahosi soḷasavassuddesiko. Atha naṃ brāhmaṇo yaṭṭhikoṭiṃ gāhāpetvā nhānatitthaṃ gantvā akkhīni ummīletvā olokesi. Kumāro “nanu tvaṃ brāhmaṇa, andho”ti [V 3.0372][P 3.0420] āha. So “nāhaṃ andho, iminā me upāyena jīvitaṃ rakkhāmī”ti vatvā “tava pitaraṃ jānāsī”ti āha. “Ayaṃ me pitā”ti vutte “nāyaṃ tava pitā, pitā pana te bārāṇasirājā, ayaṃ tumhākaṃ dāso, so mātari te vippaṭipajjitvā imasmiṃ ṭhāne tava pitaraṃ māretvā nikhaṇī”ti aṭṭhīni nīharitvā dassesi. Kumārassa balavakodho uppajji. Atha naṃ “idāni kiṃ karomī”ti pucchi. “Yaṃ te ismiṃyeva titthe pitu tena kataṃ, taṃ karohī”ti sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā kumāraṃ katipāhaṃ tharugaṇhanaṃ sikkhāpesi. Athekadivasaṃ kumāro khaggañca nhānasāṭakañca gahetvā “nhāyituṃ gacchāma, tātā”ti āha. Parantapo “sādhū”ti tena saddhiṃ gato. Athassa nhāyituṃ otiṇṇakāle dakkhiṇahatthena asiṃ, vāmahatthena cūḷaṃ gahetvā “tvaṃ kira imasmiṃyeva titthe mama pitaraṃ cūḷāya gahetvā viravantaṃ māresi, ahampi taṃ tatheva karissāmī”ti āha. So maraṇabhayabhīto paridevamāno dve gāthā abhāsi –

Later on, the prince came of age, being about sixteen years old. Then the brahmin had him grasp the end of a staff and, going to the bathing place, he opened his eyes and looked around. The prince said, 'Surely, brahmin, you are not blind?' He replied, 'I am not blind; by this stratagem I protect my life.' Then he asked, 'Do you know your father?' When the prince said, 'This Parantapa is my father,' the brahmin replied, 'This is not your father. Your father was the king of Bārāṇasī. This man is your slave. Having acted wrongly toward your mother, he killed your father in this place and buried him.' Then he took out the bones and showed them. A powerful sorrow arose in the prince. Then he asked the brahmin, 'What shall I do now?' The brahmin said, 'Do to him what was done to your father by him right here at this bathing place.' After explaining the entire matter, he taught the prince how to wield a sword for a few days. Then one day, the prince took his sword and a bathing cloth and said, 'Father, let us go to bathe.' Parantapa agreed and went with the prince. When Parantapa had descended to bathe, the prince seized the sword in his right hand and the topknot in his left, saying, 'It is said that at this very bathing place you seized my father by the topknot and killed him as he cried out. I shall do the same to you.' Terrified by the fear of death, he lamented and spoke these two verses:

158.

158.

“Āgamā nūna so saddo, asaṃsi nūna so tava;

Akkhātaṃ nūna taṃ tena, yo taṃ sākhamakampayi.

"Surely that sound has come to you, surely it has announced to you; surely it has been told by him, who shook that branch."

159.

159.

“Idaṃ [M 3.0399] kho taṃ samāgamma, mama bālassa cintitaṃ;

Tadā hi calitā sākhā, manussena migena vā”ti.

"Indeed, this thought of mine, a fool, has now come to pass with your arrival: 'For at that time the branch was moved, either by a man or by a beast.'"

Tattha āgamāti so sākhasaddo nūna taṃ āgato sampatto. Asaṃsi nūna so tavāti so saddo tava ārocesi maññe. Akkhātaṃ nūna taṃ tenāti yo satto tadā taṃ sākhaṃ akampayi, tena “evaṃ te pitā mārito”ti nūna taṃ kāraṇaṃ akkhātaṃ. Samāgammāti saṅgamma, samāgatanti attho. Yaṃ mama bālassa “tadā calitā sākhā manussena migena vā, tato me bhayaṃ uppajjissatī”ti cintitaṃ parivitakkitaṃ ahosi, idaṃ tayā saddhiṃ samāgatanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Therein, 'āgamā' means: that sound of the branch surely reached and arrived at you. 'asaṃsi nūna so tava' means: that sound, I think, announced it to you. 'akkhātaṃ nūna taṃ tena' means: the creature who shook that branch at that time surely told you the reason, saying, 'Thus was your father killed.' 'Samāgamma' means having come together; the meaning is 'met with.' Whatever was thought and reflected upon by me, a fool—'at that time the branch was shaken by a human or an animal, and from that, fear will arise for me'—this is said to have come to pass with your arrival.

Tato kumāro osānagāthamāha –

Then the prince spoke the concluding verse:

160.

160.

“Tatheva tvaṃ avedesi, avañci pitaraṃ mama;

Hantvā sākhāhi chādento, āgamissati me bhaya”nti.

"Just so you knew, you murdered my father; having slain him and while covering him with branches, you thought, 'Fear will come to me.'"

Tattha [P 3.0421] tatheva tvaṃ avedesīti tatheva tvaṃ aññāsi. Avañci pitaraṃ mamāti tvaṃ mama pitaraṃ [V 3.0373] “nhāyituṃ gacchāmā”ti vissāsetvā nhāyantaṃ māretvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinditvā nikhaṇitvā “sace koci jānissati, mayhampi evarūpaṃ bhayaṃ āgacchissatī”ti vañcesi, idaṃ kho pana maraṇabhayaṃ idāni tavāgatanti.

Therein, 'tatheva tvaṃ avedesi' means 'just so you knew.' 'avañci pitaraṃ mama' (misspelled as avajji/avañci) means you murdered my father. Having gained my father's trust by saying, 'Let us go to bathe,' you killed him while he was bathing, cut him into pieces, buried him, and deceived yourself thinking, 'If anyone finds out, such fear will come upon me too.' This indeed is the fear of death that has now come upon you.

Iti taṃ vatvā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā nikhaṇitvā sākhāhi paṭicchādetvā khaggaṃ dhovitvā nhatvā paṇṇasālaṃ gantvā tassa māritabhāvaṃ purohitassa kathetvā mātaraṃ paribhāsitvā “idha kiṃ karissāmā”ti tayo janā bārāṇasimeva agamaṃsu. Bodhisatto kaniṭṭhassa oparajjaṃ datvā dānādīni puññāni katvā saggapadaṃ pūresi.

Having said this, he brought him to his end right there, buried him, covered him with branches, washed the sword, bathed, and went to the leaf-hut. He told the chaplain that Parantapa had been killed and rebuked his mother. Saying, 'What shall we do here?', the three of them returned to Bārāṇasī. The Bodhisatta gave the viceroyalty to his younger brother, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and peopled the heavenly realm.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā piturājā devadatto ahosi, purohito ānando, puttarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, revealed the Truths and identified the birth-story: "At that time, the father-king was Devadatta, the chaplain was Ānanda, and the son-king was I myself."

Parantapajātakavaṇṇanā ekādasamā.

The Commentary on the Parantapa Jātaka, the Eleventh.

Gandhāravaggo dutiyo.

The Gandhāra Chapter, the Second.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

The Summary of the Jātakas:

Kukku [M 3.0400] manoja sutano, gijjha dabbhapuppha paṇṇako;

Sattubhasta aṭṭhiseno, kapi bakabrahmā dasa.

Kukku, Manoja, Sutano, Gijjha, Dabbhapuppha, Paṇṇaka; Sattubhasta, Aṭṭhisena, Kapi, Baka, Brahmā—these are ten.

Gandhāro mahākapi ca, kumbhakāro daḷhadhammo;

Somadatto susīmo ca, koṭasimbali dhūmakārī;

Jāgaro kummāsapiṇḍo, parantapā ekādasa.

Gandhāra, Mahākapi, Kumbhakāra, Daḷhadhamma; Somadatta, Susīma, Koṭasimbali, Dhūmakārī; Jāgara, Kummāsapiṇḍa, Parantapa—these are eleven.

Sattakanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Book of Sevens is concluded.

8. Aṭṭhakanipāto

8. The Book of Eights

[417] 1. Kaccānijātakavaṇṇanā

[417] 1. The Commentary on the Kaccāni Jātaka

Odātavatthā [V 3.0374][P 3.0422][M 3.0401] suci allakesāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ mātuposakaṃ upāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthiyaṃ kuladārako ācārasampanno pitari kālakate mātudevato hutvā mukhadhovanadantakaṭṭhadānanhāpanapādadhovanādiveyyāvaccakammena ceva yāgubhattādīhi ca mātaraṃ paṭijaggi. Atha naṃ mātā “tāta, tava aññānipi gharāvāsakiccāni atthi, ekaṃ samajātikaṃ kulakumārikaṃ gaṇhāhi, sā maṃ posessati, tvampi attano kammaṃ karissasī”ti āha. “Amma, ahaṃ attano hitasukhaṃ apaccāsīsamāno tumhe upaṭṭhahāmi, ko añño evaṃ upaṭṭhahissatī”ti? “Kulavaḍḍhanakammaṃ nāma tāta, kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Na mayhaṃ gharāvāsena attho, ahaṃ tumhe upaṭṭhahitvā tumhākaṃ dhūmakāle pabbajissāmī”ti. Athassa mātā punappunaṃ yācitvāpi manaṃ alabhamānā tassa chandaṃ aggahetvā samajātikaṃ kulakumārikaṃ ānesi. So mātaraṃ appaṭikkhipitvā tāya saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Sāpi “mayhaṃ sāmiko mahantena ussāhena mātaraṃ upaṭṭhahati, ahampi naṃ upaṭṭhahissāmi, evamassa piyā bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā taṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahi. So “ayaṃ me mātaraṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahī”ti tato paṭṭhāya laddhaladdhāni madhurakhādanīyādīni tassāyeva deti. Sā aparabhāge cintesi “ayaṃ laddhaladdhāni madhurakhādanīyādīni mayhaññeva deti, addhā mātaraṃ nīharitukāmo [P 3.0423] bhavissati, nīharaṇūpāyamassā karissāmī”ti evaṃ ayoniso ummujjitvā ekaṃ divasaṃ āha – “sāmi, tayi bahi nikkhamante tava mātā maṃ akkosatī”ti. So tuṇhī ahosi.

"Clad in white robes, pure, with hair still wet..." This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain lay devotee who supported his mother. It is said that in Sāvatthī, there was a well-behaved young man from a good family. After his father passed away, he regarded his mother as a deity, serving her by providing water for washing the face, tooth-sticks, bathwater, and water for washing the feet, and by performing various other services, as well as by offering her rice porridge and meals. Then his mother said to him, "Dear, you have other household duties. Take a maiden of equal standing from a good family; she will look after me, and you can attend to your own work." "Mother," he replied, "I attend to you without seeking my own welfare and happiness. Who else would attend to you in this way?" "Dear, it is proper to perform the duty of continuing the family line," she said. "I have no need for the household life. After attending to you, I will go forth at the time of your cremation," he answered. Although his mother asked him again and again, she could not win him over. So, without his consent, she brought home a maiden of equal standing from a good family. Not wishing to oppose his mother, he lived with her. She, too, thought, "My husband serves his mother with great effort. I, too, will serve her, and thus I will become dear to him," and so she served her mother-in-law respectfully. Thinking, "She serves my mother respectfully," from then on he gave to her alone whatever sweet foods and delicacies he obtained. Later, she thought, "He gives whatever sweet foods and delicacies he obtains only to me. Surely, he must want to get rid of his mother. I will devise a way to cast her out." With such unwholesome thoughts arising, one day she said, "Husband, when you go out, your mother scolds me." He remained silent.

Sā cintesi – “imaṃ mahallikaṃ ujjhāpetvā puttassa paṭikūlaṃ kāressāmī”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya yāguṃ dadamānā accuṇhaṃ vā atisītalaṃ vā atiloṇaṃ vā aloṇaṃ vā deti. “Amma, accuṇhā”ti vā “atiloṇā”ti vā vutte pūretvā sītodakaṃ pakkhipati. Puna “atisītalā[V 3.0375], aloṇāyevā”ti [M 3.0402] vutte “idāneva ‘accuṇhā, atiloṇā’ti vatvā puna ‘atisītalā, aloṇā’ti vadasi, kā taṃ tosetuṃ sakkhissatī”ti mahāsaddaṃ karoti. Nhānodakampi accuṇhaṃ katvā piṭṭhiyaṃ āsiñcati. “Amma, piṭṭhi me dahatī”ti ca vutte puna pūretvā sītodakaṃ pakkhipati. “Atisītaṃ, ammā”ti vutte “idāneva ‘accuṇha’nti vatvā puna ‘atisīta’nti vadati, kā etissā avamānaṃ sahituṃ sakkhissatī”ti paṭivissakānaṃ kathesi. “Amma, mañcake me bahū maṅgulā”ti ca vuttā mañcakaṃ nīharitvā tassa upari attano mañcakaṃ pothetvā “pothito me”ti atiharitvā paññapeti. Mahāupāsikā diguṇehi maṅgulehi khajjamānā sabbarattiṃ nisinnāva vītināmetvā “amma, sabbarattiṃ maṅgulehi khāditāmhī”ti vadati. Itarā “hiyyo te mañcako pothito, kā imissā kiccaṃ nittharituṃ sakkotī”ti paṭivatvā “idāni naṃ puttena ujjhāpessāmī”ti tattha tattha kheḷasiṅghāṇikādīni vippakiritvā “kā imaṃ sakalagehaṃ asuciṃ karotī”ti vutte “mātā te evarūpaṃ karoti, ‘mā karī’ti vuccamānā kalahaṃ karoti, ahaṃ evarūpāya kāḷakaṇṇiyā saddhiṃ ekagehe vasituṃ na sakkomi, etaṃ vā ghare vasāpehi, maṃ vā”ti āha.

She thought, "I will provoke him against this old woman and make her odious to her son." From then on, when giving gruel, she would give it either too hot or too cold, too salty or without salt. When the old woman said, "Dear, it is too hot," or "It is too salty," she would fill the bowl with cold water. Again, when she said, "It is too cold and has no salt," the daughter-in-law would shout loudly, "Just now you said it was 'too hot and too salty,' and now you say 'too cold and no salt'—who could possibly please you?" She also made the bathwater scalding hot and poured it on the old woman's back. When she said, "Dear, my back is burning," she would then fill the vessel with freezing water. When she said, "It is too cold, dear," the daughter-in-law complained to the neighbors, "Just now she said it was 'too hot,' and now she says it is 'too cold'—who can endure the contempt of this old woman?" When the old woman said, "Dear, there are many bedbugs on my bed," she would take the bed out, beat her own bed over it, and then bring it back and set it up, saying, "I have beaten it." The great laywoman, bitten by twice as many bedbugs, spent the whole night just sitting there. She said, "Dear, I was bitten by bugs all night long." The other retorted, "Your bed was beaten only yesterday—who can ever finish this old woman's business?" Then, thinking, "Now I will make her son find fault with her," she scattered spit, snot, and such like here and there. When the husband asked, "Who is making the whole house filthy?" she replied, "Your mother does such things. When told not to, she starts a quarrel. I cannot live in the same house with such a wretched woman. Either let her stay in the house, or let me."

So tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “bhadde, tvaṃ taruṇā yattha katthaci gantvā jīvituṃ sakkā, mātā pana me jarādubbalā, ahamevassā paṭisaraṇaṃ, tvaṃ nikkhamitvā attano kulagehaṃ gacchāhī”ti āha. Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā bhītā cintesi “na sakkā imaṃ mātu antare bhindituṃ, ekaṃsenassa mātā piyā, sace panāhaṃ kulagharaṃ gamissaṃ, vidhavavāsaṃ vasantī dukkhitā bhavissāmi, purimanayeneva sassuṃ ārādhetvā paṭijaggissāmī”ti[P 3.0424]. Sā tato paṭṭhāya purimasadisameva taṃ paṭijaggi. Athekadivasaṃ so uposako dhammassavanatthāya jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. “Kiṃ, upāsaka, tvaṃ puññakammesu na pamajjasi, mātuupaṭṭhānakammaṃ pūresī”ti ca vutto “āma, bhante, sā pana mama mātā mayhaṃ aruciyāyeva ekaṃ kuladārikaṃ ānesi, sā idañcidañca anācārakammaṃ akāsī”ti sabbaṃ satthu ācikkhitvā “iti bhagavā sā itthī neva maṃ mātu [M 3.0403] antare bhindituṃ sakkhi, idāni naṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahatī”ti āha. Satthā tassa kathaṃ sutvā “idāni tāva tvaṃ upāsaka, tassā vacanaṃ na akāsi, pubbe panetissā vacanena tava mātaraṃ nikkaḍḍhitvā maṃ nissāya puna gehaṃ ānetvā paṭijaggī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Hearing her words, he said, "My dear, you are young and can make a living wherever you go, but my mother is old and frail. I am her only refuge. You must leave and go back to your own family home." Hearing his words, she became frightened and thought, "It is not possible to divide him from his mother. His mother is certainly dear to him. If I go back to my family home, I will be miserable, living like a widow. I will please my mother-in-law and care for her just as before." From then on, she cared for her just as she had initially. One day, that lay devotee went to Jetavana to listen to the Dhamma. He paid homage to the Teacher and sat to one side. The Teacher asked, "Lay follower, are you not heedless in meritorious deeds? Do you fulfill the duty of caring for your mother?" He replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir, but my mother, against my wishes, brought a maiden from a good family. She committed such and such improper acts." He explained everything to the Teacher and said, "Thus, Blessed One, that woman could not divide me from my mother, and now she serves her respectfully." Hearing his account, the Teacher said, "For now, lay follower, you did not act on her words. But in the past, because of her words, you cast out your mother, and then, relying on me, you brought her back home and cared for her." Being requested by him, the Teacher related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente aññatarassa kulassa putto pitari kālakate mātudevato hutvā vuttaniyāmeneva mātaraṃ paṭijaggīti sabbaṃ heṭṭhā kathitanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ[V 3.0376]. “Ahaṃ evarūpāya kāḷakaṇṇiyā saddhiṃ vasituṃ na sakkomi, etaṃ vā ghare vasāpehi, maṃ vā”ti vutte tassā kathaṃ gahetvā “mātuyeva me doso”ti mātaraṃ āha “amma, tvaṃ niccaṃ imasmiṃ ghare kalahaṃ karosi, ito nikkhamitvā aññasmiṃ yathārucite ṭhāne vasāhī”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti rodamānā nikkhamitvā ekaṃ samiddhakulaṃ nissāya bhatiṃ katvā dukkhena jīvikaṃ kappesi. Sassuyā gharā nikkhantakāle suṇisāya gabbho patiṭṭhahi. Sā “tāya kāḷakaṇṇiyā gehe vasamānāya gabbhampi na paṭilabhiṃ, idāni me gabbho laddho”ti patino ca paṭivissakānañca kathentī vicarati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the son of a certain family, after his father had passed away, regarded his mother as a deity and cared for her in the manner already described; all this should be elaborated as explained before. When his wife said, "I cannot live with such an unlucky wretch. Either have her live in this house, or me," he took her words to heart and, thinking, "The fault is indeed my mother's," said to his mother, "Mother, you are always causing quarrels in this house. Leave here and live wherever you please." She replied, "Very well," and weeping, she left. Relying on a prosperous family, she supported herself with difficulty by working for wages. At the time the mother-in-law departed from the house, the daughter-in-law conceived. She went about telling her husband and neighbors, "While that unlucky wretch was living in the house, I could not even conceive. Now I have conceived a child."

Aparabhāge puttaṃ vijāyitvā sāmikaṃ āha “tava mātari gehe vasamānāya puttaṃ na labhiṃ, idāni me laddho, imināpi kāraṇena tassā kāḷakaṇṇibhāvaṃ jānāhī”ti. Itarā “mama kira nikkaḍḍhitakāle puttaṃ labhī”ti sutvā cintesi “addhā imasmiṃ loke dhammo mato bhavissati, sace hi dhammo [P 3.0425] mato na bhaveyya, mātaraṃ pothetvā nikkaḍḍhantā puttaṃ na labheyyuṃ, sukhaṃ na jīveyyuṃ, dhammassa matakabhattaṃ dassāmī”ti. Sā ekadivasaṃ tilapiṭṭhañca taṇḍulañca pacanathāliñca dabbiñca ādāya āmakasusānaṃ gantvā tīhi manussasīsehi uddhanaṃ katvā aggiṃ jāletvā udakaṃ oruyha sasīsaṃ nhatvā sāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā uddhanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā kese mocetvā taṇḍule dhovituṃ ārabhi. Tadā bodhisatto sakko devarājā ahosi. Bodhisattā ca nāma appamattā honti, so tasmiṃ khaṇe lokaṃ olokento taṃ dukkhappattaṃ “dhammo mato”ti saññāya dhammassa matakabhattaṃ dātukāmaṃ disvā “ajja [M 3.0404] mayhaṃ balaṃ dassessāmī”ti brāhmaṇavesena mahāmaggaṃ paṭipanno viya hutvā taṃ disvā maggā okkamma tassā santike ṭhatvā “amma, susāne āhāraṃ pacantā nāma natthi, tvaṃ iminā idha pakkena tilodanena kiṃ karissasī”ti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Later, after giving birth to a son, she said to her husband, "While your mother was living in the house, I did not obtain a child. Now I have obtained one. For this reason too, know her to be an unlucky wretch." The other woman, hearing, "She obtained a child at the time I was driven out," thought, "Surely, in this world, the Dhamma must be dead. For if the Dhamma were not dead, those who beat their mother and drive her out would not obtain a child, nor would they live happily. I will offer a mortuary meal for the Dhamma." One day, taking sesame flour, rice, a cooking pot, and a ladle, she went to a charnel ground for uncremated bodies. There, she made a hearth with three human skulls, lit a fire, went down to the water, bathed from her head down, put on a clean garment, washed her face, returned to the hearth, loosened her hair, and began to wash the rice. At that time, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, the king of the gods. Bodhisattas are ever heedful. Observing the world at that moment, he saw her afflicted with suffering, thinking that "the Dhamma is dead," and wishing to offer a mortuary meal for the Dhamma. Thinking, "Today I will show my power," he took the guise of a brahmin and, appearing like a traveler on the high road, approached her. Stepping off the path, he stood near her and, initiating a conversation, spoke the first verse:

1.

1.

“Odātavatthā suci allakesā, kaccāni kiṃ kumbhimadhissayitvā;

Piṭṭhā tilā dhovasi taṇḍulāni, tilodano hehiti kissahetū”ti.

"Clad in white garments, pure, with hair still wet, O Kaccānī, why, having set this pot upon the hearth, do you wash ground sesame and grains of rice? For what purpose will this sesame-rice be prepared?"

Tattha kaccānīti taṃ gottena ālapati. Kumbhimadhissayitvāti pacanathālikaṃ manussasīsuddhanaṃ āropetvā. Hehitīti ayaṃ tilodano kissa hetu bhavissati, kiṃ attanā bhuñjissasi, udāhu aññaṃ kāraṇamatthīti.

In this context, "Kaccānī" is how he addresses her by her clan name. "Kumbhimadhissayitvā" means having placed the cooking pot upon the hearth made of human skulls. "Hehiti" means: for what reason will this sesame-rice be? Will you eat it yourself, or is there some other purpose?

Athassa sā ācikkhantī dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, explaining the matter to him, she spoke the second verse:

2.

2.

“Na [V 3.0377] kho ayaṃ brāhmaṇa bhojanatthā, tilodano hehiti sādhupakko;

Dhammo mato tassa pahuttamajja, ahaṃ karissāmi susānamajjhe”ti.

"Indeed, brahmin, this well-cooked sesame-rice is not for the purpose of a meal. The Dhamma is dead; today I will make an offering to it in the midst of the charnel ground."

Tattha [P 3.0426] dhammoti jeṭṭhāpacāyanadhammo ceva tividhasucaritadhammo ca. Tassa pahuttamajjāti tassāhaṃ dhammassa idaṃ matakabhattaṃ karissāmīti attho.

In this context, "Dhamma" refers to both the virtue of revering elders and the virtue of threefold wholesome conduct. "Tassa pahuttamajja" means: "I will prepare this mortuary meal for that Dhamma today."

Tato sakko tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Sakka spoke the third verse:

3.

3.

“Anuvicca kaccāni karohi kiccaṃ, dhammo mato ko nu taveva saṃsi;

Sahassanetto atulānubhāvo, na miyyatī dhammavaro kadācī”ti.

"Having investigated, Kaccānī, perform your duty. Is the Dhamma dead? Who indeed told you so? The Thousand-eyed One of incomparable power exists; the excellent Dhamma never dies."

Tattha anuviccāti upaparikkhitvā jānitvā. Ko nu taveva saṃsīti ko nu tava evaṃ ācikkhi. Sahassanettoti attānaṃ dhammavaraṃ uttamadhammaṃ katvā dassento evamāha.

In this context, "anuvicca" means having examined and known. "Ko nu taveva saṃsi" means: who indeed told you so? "Sahassanetto" refers to Sakka himself, and he spoke thus showing himself as the excellent and supreme Dhamma.

Taṃ [M 3.0405] vacanaṃ sutvā itarā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing those words, the other woman spoke two verses:

4.

4.

“Daḷhappamāṇaṃ mama ettha brahme, dhammo mato natthi mamettha kaṅkhā;

Ye yeva dāni pāpā bhavanti, te teva dāni sukhitā bhavanti.

"Firm is my conviction in this matter, O brahmin: the Dhamma is dead; I have no doubt about it. Those who are now evil are the ones who become happy."

5.

5.

“Suṇisā hi mayhaṃ vañjhā ahosi, sā maṃ vadhitvāna vijāyi puttaṃ;

Sā dāni sabbassa kulassa issarā, ahaṃ panamhi apaviddhā ekikā”ti.

"For my daughter-in-law was barren; she beat me and drove me out, and then she bore a son. Now she is the mistress of the entire family, while I am cast out and alone."

Tattha daḷhappamāṇanti daḷhaṃ thiraṃ nissaṃsayaṃ brāhmaṇa ettha mama pamāṇanti vadati. Ye yeti tassa matabhāve kāraṇaṃ dassentī evamāha. Vadhitvānāti pothetvā nikkaḍḍhitvā. Apaviddhāti chaḍḍitā anāthā hutvā ekikā vasāmi.

In this context, "daḷhappamāṇaṃ" means she says, "O brahmin, my conviction in this is firm, certain, and without doubt." "Ye ye" is said as she shows the reason for the Dhamma being dead. "Vadhitvāna" means having beaten and driven out. "Apaviddhā" means abandoned and helpless, living alone.

Tato sakko chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Sakka spoke the sixth verse:

6.

6.

“Jīvāmi vohaṃ na matohamasmi, taveva atthāya idhāgatosmi;

Yā taṃ vadhitvāna vijāyi puttaṃ, sahāva puttena karomi bhasma”nti.

"Indeed, I live, I am not dead; I have come here for your sake. She who beat you and bore a son—her, along with her son, I will reduce to ashes."

Tattha [V 3.0378] voti nipātamattaṃ.

Here, `vo` is merely a particle.

Itarā [P 3.0427] taṃ sutvā “dhī ahaṃ kiṃ kathesiṃ, mama nattu amaraṇakāraṇaṃ karissāmī”ti sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, she thought, "Fie! What have I said? I must ensure that my grandson does not die," and spoke the seventh verse:

7.

7.

“Evañca te ruccati devarāja, mameva atthāya idhāgatosi;

Ahañca putto suṇisā ca nattā, sammodamānā gharamāvasemā”ti.

"If it pleases you, O king of gods, you have come here for my sake; may I, my son, daughter-in-law, and grandson live rejoicing together in our home."

Athassā [M 3.0406] sakko aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Sakka spoke the eighth verse to her:

8.

8.

“Evañca te ruccati kātiyāni, hatāpi santā na jahāsi dhammaṃ;

Tuvañca putto suṇisā ca nattā, sammodamānā gharamāvasethā”ti.

"If it so pleases you, Kātiyānī, for even though driven out, you do not abandon the Dhamma of loving-kindness toward your kin; may you, your son, daughter-in-law, and grandson live rejoicing together in your home."

Tattha hatāpi santāti yadi tvaṃ pothitāpi nikkaḍḍhitāpi samānā tava dārakesu mettadhammaṃ na jahāsi, evaṃ sante yathā tvaṃ icchasi, tathā hotu, ahaṃ te imasmiṃ guṇe pasannoti.

Here, `hatāpi santā` means: if you, even though beaten and driven out, do not abandon the principle of loving-kindness towards your children, in that case, as you wish, so be it. I am pleased with you for this quality.

Evañca pana vatvā alaṅkatapaṭiyatto sakko attano ānubhāvena ākāse ṭhatvā “kaccāni tvaṃ mā bhāyi, putto ca te suṇisā ca mamānubhāvena āgantvā antarāmagge taṃ khamāpetvā ādāya gamissanti, appamattā hohī”ti vatvā attano ṭhānameva gato. Tepi sakkānubhāvena tassā guṇaṃ anussaritvā “kahaṃ no mātā”ti antogāme manusse pucchitvā “susānābhimukhaṃ gatā”ti sutvā “amma, ammā”ti susānamaggaṃ paṭipajjitvā taṃ disvāva pādesu patitvā “amma, amhākaṃ dosaṃ khamāhī”ti taṃ khamāpesuṃ. Sāpi nattāraṃ gaṇhi. Iti te sammodamānā gehaṃ gantvā tato paṭṭhāya samaggavāsaṃ vasiṃsu.

And having spoken thus, Sakka, adorned and prepared, stood in the sky by his own power and said, "Kaccānī, do not be afraid. Your son and daughter-in-law, by my power, will come, ask your forgiveness on the way, and take you with them. Be heedful." Having said this, he returned to his own place. They, by Sakka’s power, recollected her virtue and asked the people in the village, "Where is our mother?" Hearing, "She has gone towards the charnel ground," they took the path to the charnel ground, crying, "Mother, mother!" Upon seeing her, they fell at her feet and had her forgive them, saying, "Mother, forgive us our fault." She also took her grandson. Thus, rejoicing together, they went home and from then on lived together in harmony.

9.

9.

“Sā kātiyānī suṇisāya saddhiṃ, sammodamānā gharamāvasittha;

Putto ca nattā ca upaṭṭhahiṃsu, devānamindena adhiggahītā”ti. –

"That Kātiyānī, together with her daughter-in-law, lived rejoicing in her home; her son and grandson attended to her, supported by the lord of gods."

Ayaṃ abhisambuddhagāthā.

This is the verse spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Tattha [V 3.0379][P 3.0428] sā kātiyānīti bhikkhave, sā kaccānagottā. Devānamindena adhiggahītāti devindena sakkena anuggahitā hutvā tassānubhāvena samaggavāsaṃ vasiṃsūti.

Here, 'sā kātiyānī' means, O monks, she of the Kaccāna clan. 'Devānamindena adhiggahītā' means: having been favored by Sakka, the king of gods, they lived in harmony through his power.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so upāsako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā mātuposako etarahi mātuposako ahosi[M 3.0407], bhariyāpissa tadā bhariyāyeva, sakko pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, that lay devotee was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The one who supported his mother at that time was the one who supports his mother at present; his wife then was also his wife now; and Sakka was none other than myself.

Kaccānijātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kaccānī Jātaka, the First.

[418] 2. Aṭṭhasaddajātakavaṇṇanā

[418] 2. Commentary on the Aṭṭhasadda Jātaka

Idaṃ pure ninnamāhūti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarañño aḍḍharattasamaye sutaṃ bhiṃsanakaṃ avinibbhogasaddaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā lohakumbhijātake (jā. 1.4.53 ādayo) kathitasadisameva. Idha pana satthā “mayhaṃ, bhante, imesaṃ saddānaṃ sutattā kinti bhavissatī”ti vutte “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, na te etesaṃ sutapaccayā koci antarāyo bhavissati, na hi, mahārāja, evarūpaṃ bhayānakaṃ avinibbhogasaddaṃ tvameveko suṇi, pubbepi rājāno evarūpaṃ saddaṃ sutvā brāhmaṇānaṃ kathaṃ gahetvā sabbacatukkayaññaṃ yajitukāmā paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā yaññaharaṇatthāya gahitasatte vissajjetvā nagare māghātabheriṃ carāpesu”nti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

This story, beginning with 'This they called low-lying in the past,' the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a terrifying, indistinct sound heard by the King of Kosala at midnight. The story is similar to that told in the Lohakumbhi Jātaka. Here, when the king said, "Venerable sir, what will be the outcome for me, having heard these sounds?" the Teacher replied, "Do not fear, great king. No harm will come to you because of hearing these sounds. Indeed, great king, you are not the only one who has heard such a frightening, indistinct sound. In the past, kings too, having heard such a sound, took the word of brahmins and desired to perform a complete fourfold sacrifice; but upon hearing the words of the wise, they released the creatures seized for the sacrifice and had the non-slaughter drum paraded throughout the city." Being asked by him, he then related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto asītikoṭivibhave brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ uggahitasippo mātāpitūnaṃ accayena ratanavilokanaṃ katvā sabbaṃ vibhavajātaṃ dānamukhe vissajjetvā kāme pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā aparabhāge loṇambilasevanatthāya manussapathaṃ caranto bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasi. Tadā bārāṇasirājā sirisayane nisinno aḍḍharattasamaye aṭṭha sadde assosi – paṭhamaṃ rājanivesanasāmantā uyyāne eko bako saddamakāsi, dutiyaṃ tasmiṃ sadde anupacchinneyeva hatthisālāya toraṇanivāsinī kākī saddamakāsi, tatiyaṃ [P 3.0429] rājagehe kaṇṇikāyaṃ nivutthaghuṇapāṇako saddamakāsi, catutthaṃ rājagehe posāvaniyakokilo saddamakāsi, pañcamaṃ tattheva posāvaniyamigo saddamakāsi, chaṭṭhaṃ tattheva posāvaniyavānaro saddamakāsi, sattamaṃ tattheva posāvaniyakinnaro [M 3.0408] saddamakāsi, aṭṭhamaṃ tasmiṃ sadde [V 3.0380] anupacchinneyeva rājanivesanamatthakena uyyānaṃ gacchanto paccekabuddho ekaṃ udānaṃ udānento saddamakāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family with a fortune of eighty crores. Having come of age and mastered the arts at Takkasilā, after the passing of his parents, he inspected his treasures and gave away all his wealth in charity. Renouncing sensual pleasures, he entered the Himalayas, embraced the ascetic life, and attained meditative absorptions and higher knowledges. Later, while wandering the paths of humankind in search of salt and sour foods, he arrived in Benares and stayed in the royal garden. At that time, the king of Benares, seated on his royal couch at midnight, heard eight sounds: First, a heron in the garden near the royal residence made a sound. Second, immediately after that sound, a female crow dwelling at the gate of the elephant stable made a sound. Third, a woodworm dwelling in the gable of the royal palace made a sound. Fourth, a reared cuckoo in the royal palace made a sound. Fifth, a reared deer in the same place made a sound. Sixth, a reared monkey in the same place made a sound. Seventh, a reared kinnara in the same place made a sound. Eighth, immediately after that sound, a Paccekabuddha, passing over the top of the royal residence towards the garden, made a sound by uttering an inspired utterance.

Bārāṇasirājā ime aṭṭha sadde sutvā bhītatasito punadivase brāhmaṇe pucchi. Brāhmaṇā “antarāyo te, mahārāja, bhavissati, sabbacatukkayaññaṃ yajissāmā”ti vatvā raññā “yathārucitaṃ karothā”ti anuññātā haṭṭhapahaṭṭhā rājakulato nikkhamitvā yaññakammaṃ ārabhiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ jeṭṭhakassa yaññakārabrāhmaṇassa antevāsī māṇavo paṇḍito byatto ācariyaṃ āha – “ācariya, evarūpaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ pharusaṃ asātaṃ bahūnaṃ sattānaṃ vināsakammaṃ mā karī”ti. “Tāta, tvaṃ kiṃ jānāsi, sacepi aññaṃ kiñci na bhavissati, macchamaṃsaṃ tāva bahuṃ khādituṃ labhissāmā”ti. “Ācariya, kucchiṃ nissāya niraye nibbattanakammaṃ mā karothā”ti. Taṃ sutvā sesabrāhmaṇā “ayaṃ amhākaṃ lābhantarāyaṃ karotī”ti tassa kujjhiṃsu. Māṇavo tesaṃ bhayena “tena hi tumheva macchamaṃsakhādanūpāyaṃ karothā”ti vatvā nikkhamitvā bahinagare rājānaṃ nivāretuṃ samatthaṃ dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇaṃ upadhārento rājuyyānaṃ gantvā bodhisattaṃ disvā vanditvā “bhante, kiṃ tumhākaṃ sattesu anukampā natthi, rājā bahū satte māretvā yaññaṃ yajāpeti, kiṃ vo mahājanassa bandhanamokkhaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti āha. “Māṇava, ettha neva rājā amhe jānāti, na mayaṃ rājānaṃ jānāmā”ti. “Jānātha pana, bhante, raññā sutasaddānaṃ nipphatti”nti? “Āma, jānāmī”ti. “Jānantā rañño [P 3.0430] kasmā na kathethā”ti? “Māṇava kiṃ sakkā ‘ahaṃ jānāmī’ti nalāṭe siṅgaṃ bandhitvā carituṃ, sace idhāgantvā pucchissati, kathessāmī”ti.

The King of Bārāṇasī, hearing these eight sounds, was extremely terrified. The next day, he questioned the brahmins. The brahmins said, 'Great king, there will be danger for you. We shall perform the sacrifice of all groups of four.' Being granted permission by the king with the words, 'Do as you please,' they left the royal household with great joy and began the sacrificial rites. Then, the wise and skilled young pupil of the chief sacrificial brahmin said to his teacher, 'Teacher, do not perform such a harsh, cruel, and unpleasant act that destroys many beings.' 'My dear boy, what do you know? Even if nothing else comes of it, we will at least get to eat plenty of fish and meat.' 'Teacher, do not perform an act for the sake of the belly that leads to rebirth in hell.' Hearing this, the other brahmins were angry with him, saying, 'This one is creating an obstacle to our gain.' Out of fear of them, the young man said, 'Then you yourselves may carry out the means for eating fish and meat,' and left. Seeking a righteous ascetic or brahmin outside the city capable of restraining the king, he went to the royal park and, seeing the Bodhisatta, paid homage and said, 'Venerable sir, do you not have compassion for beings? The king is having many beings killed to perform a sacrifice. Is it not proper for you to bring about the release of the great multitude from bondage?' 'Young man, the king here does not know us, nor do we know the king.' 'But, venerable sir, do you know the origin of the sounds heard by the king?' 'Yes, I know.' 'If you know, why do you not tell the king?' 'Young man, how could one go about with a horn tied to his forehead, proclaiming, "I know"? If he comes here and asks, I will tell him.'

Māṇavo vegena rājakulaṃ gantvā “kiṃ, tātā”ti vutte “mahārāja, tumhehi sutasaddānaṃ nipphattiṃ jānanako eko tāpaso tumhākaṃ uyyāne maṅgalasilāyaṃ nisinno ‘sace maṃ pucchissati, kathessāmī’ti vadati, gantvā taṃ pucchituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Rājā vegena tattha gantvā tāpasaṃ vanditvā katapaṭisanthāro nisīditvā “saccaṃ kira, bhante, tumhe mayā sutasaddānaṃ nipphattiṃ jānāthā”ti pucchi. “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi kathetha taṃ me”ti. “Mahārāja, tesaṃ sutapaccayā tava koci antarāyo natthi[M 3.0409], porāṇuyyāne pana te eko bako atthi, so gocaraṃ alabhanto jighacchāya pareto paṭhamaṃ saddamakāsī”ti tassa kiriyaṃ attano ñāṇena paricchinditvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The young man hurried to the royal palace, and when asked, 'What is it, my dear?' he said, 'Great king, an ascetic who knows the origin of the sounds you heard is sitting on the auspicious stone slab in your park, saying, "If he asks me, I will tell him." It is proper to go and ask him.' The king hurried there, paid homage to the ascetic, and after exchanging greetings, sat down and asked, 'Is it true, venerable sir, that you know the origin of the sounds I heard?' 'Yes, great king.' 'Then please tell it to me.' 'Great king, there is no danger to you on account of those sounds. However, in your old park, there is a heron. Unable to find food and overcome by hunger, it made the first sound.' Discerning its action through his own knowledge, he spoke the first verse:

10.

10.

“Idaṃ [V 3.0381] pure ninnamāhu, bahumacchaṃ mahodakaṃ;

Āvāso bakarājassa, pettikaṃ bhavanaṃ mama;

Tyajja bhekena yāpema, okaṃ na vijahāmase”ti.

'This place, they say, was once a depression, with much water and many fish; it was the dwelling of the heron king, my ancestral home. Today we subsist on frogs, but we do not abandon our home.'
