Tattha idanti maṅgalapokkharaṇiṃ sandhāya vadati. Sā hi pubbe udakatumbena udake pavisante mahodakā bahumacchā, idāni pana udakassa pacchinnattā na mahodakā jātā. Tyajja bhekenāti te mayaṃ ajja macche alabhantā maṇḍūkamattena yāpema. Okanti evaṃ jighacchāya pīḷitāpi vasanaṭṭhānaṃ na vijahāma.

There, 'this' refers to the auspicious lotus pond. For in the past, when water entered through a water-conduit, it had much water and many fish; but now, because the water is cut off, it no longer has much water. 'Today we subsist on frogs' means that today, not finding fish, we survive on mere frogs. 'Home' means that even though oppressed by hunger, we do not abandon our dwelling place.

Iti, mahārāja, so bako jighacchāpīḷito saddamakāsi. Sacepi taṃ jighacchāto mocetukāmo, taṃ uyyānaṃ sodhāpetvā pokkharaṇiṃ udakassa pūrehīti. Rājā tathā kāretuṃ ekaṃ amaccaṃ āṇāpesi.

'Thus, great king, that heron, oppressed by hunger, made the sound. If you wish to free it from hunger, have that park cleaned and fill the pond with water.' The king ordered a minister to have it done accordingly.

“Hatthisālatoraṇe pana te, mahārāja, ekā kākī vasamānā attano puttasokena dutiyaṃ saddamakāsi, tatopi te bhayaṃ natthī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

'And in the archway of your elephant stable, great king, a female crow dwells who made the second sound out of grief for her offspring. From that, too, there is no danger to you.' Having said this, he spoke the second verse:

11.

11.

“Ko dutiyaṃ asīlissa, bandharassakkhi bhecchati;

Ko me putte kulāvakaṃ, mañca sotthiṃ karissatī”ti.

'Who will be my ally and break the eye of the immoral Bandhara? Who will bring safety to my offspring, my nest, and me?'

Vatvā [P 3.0431] ca pana “ko nāma te, mahārāja, hatthisālāya hatthimeṇḍo”ti pucchi. “Bandharo nāma, bhante”ti. “Ekakkhikāṇo so, mahārājā”ti? “Āma, bhante”ti. Mahārāja, hatthisālāya te dvāratoraṇe ekā kākī kulāvakaṃ katvā aṇḍakāni nikkhipi. Tāni pariṇatāni kākapotakā nikkhantā, hatthimeṇḍo hatthiṃ āruyha sālato nikkhamanto ca pavisanto ca aṅkusakena kākimpi puttakepissā paharati, kulāvakampi viddhaṃseti. Sā tena dukkhena pīḷitā tassa akkhibhedanaṃ āyācantī evamāha, sace te kākiyā mettacittaṃ atthi, etaṃ bandharaṃ pakkosāpetvā kulāvakaviddhaṃsanato vārehīti[M 3.0410]. Rājā taṃ pakkosāpetvā paribhāsitvā hāretvā aññassa taṃ hatthiṃ adāsi.

And having spoken, he asked, 'Great king, what is the name of the mahout in your elephant stable?' 'His name is Bandhara, venerable sir.' 'Is he one-eyed, great king?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'Great king, in the gateway arch of your elephant stable, a female crow made a nest and laid eggs. When they matured, the young crows hatched. The mahout, when leaving or entering the stable while riding an elephant, strikes both the crow and her offspring with his goad and destroys the nest. Afflicted by that suffering and praying for the breaking of his eye, she spoke thus. If you have compassion for the crow, have that Bandhara summoned and restrain him from destroying the nest.' The king had him summoned, rebuked him, removed him from his post, and gave that elephant to another.

“Pāsādakaṇṇikāya [V 3.0382] pana te, mahārāja, eko ghuṇapāṇako vasati. So tattha phegguṃ khāditvā tasmiṃ khīṇe sāraṃ khādituṃ nāsakkhi, so bhakkhaṃ alabhitvā nikkhamitumpi asakkonto paridevamāno tatiyaṃ saddamakāsi, tatopi te bhayaṃ natthī”ti vatvā tassa kiriyaṃ attano ñāṇena paricchinditvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

'And in the pinnacle of your palace, great king, a wood-boring insect dwells. Having eaten the sapwood there, when it was exhausted, it was unable to eat the heartwood. Finding no food and unable to get out, it made the third sound while lamenting. From that, too, there is no danger to you.' Having said this and discerning its action through his own knowledge, he spoke the third verse:

12.

12.

“Sabbā parikkhatā pheggu, yāva tassā gatī ahu;

Khīṇabhakkho mahārāja, sāre na ramatī ghuṇo”ti.

'All the sapwood has been consumed, as far as its path went; with its food exhausted, O great king, the wood-boring insect finds no delight in the heartwood.'

Tattha yāva tassā gatī ahūti yāva tassā phegguyā nipphatti ahosi, sā sabbā khāditā. Na ramatīti “mahārāja, so pāṇako tato nikkhamitvā gamanaṭṭhānampi apassanto paridevati, nīharāpehi na”nti āha. Rājā ekaṃ purisaṃ āṇāpetvā upāyena naṃ nīharāpesi.

Therein, 'as far as its path went' means that as far as the extent of that sapwood reached, all of it was eaten. 'Finds no delight' means: 'Great king, that insect, coming out from there and seeing no place to go, laments. Have it removed!' The king commanded a man and had it removed by a clever means.

“Nivesane pana te, mahārāja, ekā posāvaniyā kokilā atthī”ti? “Atthi, bhante”ti. “Mahārāja, sā attanā nivutthapubbaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ saritvā ukkaṇṭhitvā ‘kadā nu kho imamhā pañjarā muccitvā ramaṇīyaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ gacchissāmī’ti catutthaṃ saddamakāsi, tatopi te bhayaṃ natthī”ti vatvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

"Great king, is there a pet cuckoo in your residence?" "There is, venerable sir." "Great king, that cuckoo, remembering the forest grove where she formerly lived and becoming weary, made the fourth sound, crying, 'When, indeed, will I be freed from this cage and go to the delightful forest grove?' From that, too, there is no danger to you." Having said this, he spoke the fourth verse:

13.

13.

“Sā [P 3.0432] nūnāhaṃ ito gantvā, rañño muttā nivesanā;

Attānaṃ ramayissāmi, dumasākhaniketinī”ti.

"Surely, having gone from here, freed from the king's residence, I will delight myself, making my home among the branches of the trees."

Tattha dumasākhaniketinīti supupphitāsu rukkhasākhāsu sakaniketā hutvā. Evañca pana vatvā “ukkaṇṭhitā, mahārāja, sā kokilā, vissajjehi na”nti āha. Rājā tathā kāresi.

Therein, 'making my home among the branches of the trees' means having her own dwelling among the branches of trees in full bloom. And having said this, he then said, 'Great king, that cuckoo is weary; release her.' The king did so.

“Nivesane pana te, mahārāja, eko posāvaniyo migo atthī”ti? “Atthi, bhante”ti. “Mahārāja, so eko yūthapati attano migiṃ anussaritvā kilesavasena ukkaṇṭhito pañcamaṃ saddamakāsi, tatopi te bhayaṃ natthī”ti vatvā pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

"Great king, is there a pet deer in your residence?" "There is, venerable sir." "Great king, that one, a leader of his herd, remembering his doe and weary on account of defilement, made the fifth sound. From that, too, there is no danger to you." Having said this, he spoke the fifth verse:

14.

14.

“So [V 3.0383][M 3.0411] nūnāhaṃ ito gantvā, rañño mutto nivesanā;

Aggodakāni pissāmi, yūthassa purato vaja”nti.

"Surely now, having departed from here, freed from the king’s abode, I will drink the foremost waters, going before the herd."

Tattha aggodakānīti aggaudakāni, aññehi migehi paṭhamataraṃ apītāni anucchiṭṭhodakāni yūthassa purato gacchanto kadā nu kho pivissāmīti.

Therein, 'foremost waters' means the best waters, waters not previously drunk by other deer, undefiled waters. [He thinks:] 'Going before the herd, when, indeed, shall I drink?'

Mahāsatto tampi migaṃ vissajjāpetvā “nivesane pana te, mahārāja, posāvaniyo makkaṭo atthī”ti pucchi. “Atthi, bhante”ti vutte “sopi, mahārāja, himavantapadese yūthapati makkaṭīhi saddhiṃ kāmagiddho hutvā vicaranto bharatena nāma luddena idha ānīto, idāni ukkaṇṭhitvā tattheva gantukāmo chaṭṭhaṃ saddamakāsi, tatopi te bhayaṃ natthī”ti vatvā chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

The Great Being, having had that deer released, asked, 'Great king, is there a pet monkey in your residence?' When it was said, 'Yes, venerable sir,' he continued, 'Great king, that one too, while wandering in the Himalayan region as a troop leader with his female monkeys, infatuated with sensual desire, was brought here by a hunter named Bharata. Now, weary and longing to go back there, he made the sixth sound. From that, too, you have no fear.' Having said this, he spoke the sixth verse:

15.

15.

“Taṃ maṃ kāmehi sammattaṃ, rattaṃ kāmesu mucchitaṃ;

Ānayī bharato luddo, bāhiko bhaddamatthu te”ti.

"Me, crazed with sensual pleasures, attached, infatuated with desires—Bharata the hunter brought me here; good fortune be yours, O Bāhika."

Tattha bāhikoti bāhikaraṭṭhavāsī. Bhaddamatthu teti imamatthaṃ so vānaro āha, tuyhaṃ pana bhaddamatthu, vissajjehi nanti.

Therein, 'Bāhika' means an inhabitant of the Bāhika country. The monkey said, 'May good fortune be yours,' with this meaning: 'May good fortune be yours; now release me.'

Mahāsatto taṃ vānaraṃ vissajjāpetvā “nivesane pana te, mahārāja, posāvaniyo kinnaro atthī”ti pucchitvā “atthī”ti vutte “so, mahārāja, attano kinnariyā kataguṇaṃ anussaritvā [P 3.0433] kilesāturo saddamakāsi. So hi tāya saddhiṃ ekadivasaṃ tuṅgapabbatasikharaṃ āruhi. Te tattha vaṇṇagandharasasampannāni nānāpupphāni ocinantā piḷandhantā sūriyaṃ atthaṅgataṃ na sallakkhesuṃ, atthaṅgate sūriye otarantānaṃ andhakāro ahosi. Tatra naṃ kinnarī ‘sāmi, andhakāro vattati, apakkhalanto appamādena otarāhī’ti vatvā hatthe gahetvā otāresi, so tāya taṃ vacanaṃ anussaritvā saddamakāsi, tatopi te bhayaṃ natthī”ti taṃ kāraṇaṃ attano ñāṇabalena paricchinditvā pākaṭaṃ karonto sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Great Being, having had that monkey released, asked, 'Great king, is there a pet kinnara in your residence?' Upon hearing, 'There is,' he said, 'Great king, that kinnara, recalling the kindness done to him by his kinnarī and being afflicted by passion, made a sound. For he once climbed with her to the peak of a high mountain. There, while gathering and wearing various flowers rich in color, fragrance, and taste, they failed to notice the sun setting. When the sun had set, darkness fell as they were descending. Then the kinnarī said, ‘My lord, darkness prevails; descend heedfully, without stumbling.’ Taking his hand, she led him down. Remembering those words of hers, he made that sound. From that, too, you have no fear.' Discerning this reason through the power of his own knowledge and making it manifest, he spoke the seventh verse:

16.

16.

“Andhakāratimisāyaṃ, tuṅge uparipabbate;

Sā maṃ saṇhena mudunā, mā pādaṃ khali yasmanī”ti.

"In the pitch-black darkness, on the high mountain peak, she, with gentle and soft words, said to me, 'May your foot not slip on the stone.'"

Tattha [V 3.0384][M 3.0412] andhakāratimisāyanti andhabhāvakārake tame. Tuṅgeti tikhiṇe. Saṇhena mudunāti maṭṭhena mudukena vacanena. Mā pādaṃ khali yasmanīti ya-kāro byañjanasandhivasena gahito. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sā maṃ kinnarī saṇhena mudakena vacanena “sāmi, appamatto hohi, mā pādaṃ khali asmani, yathā te upakkhalitvā pādo pāsāṇasmiṃ na khalati, tathā otarā”ti vatvā hatthena gahetvā otāresīti.

Therein, 'in the pitch-black darkness' means in darkness that causes blindness. 'On the high' means on the steep. 'With gentle and soft' means with smooth and soft speech. In 'mā pādaṃ khali y-asmani,' the 'y' is inserted for the sake of consonantal sandhi. This is what is said: That kinnarī, having spoken to me with gentle and soft words, saying, 'My lord, be heedful, may your foot not slip on the stone; descend in such a way that your foot, stumbling, does not strike against the rock,' took me by the hand and led me down.

Iti mahāsatto kinnarena katasaddakāraṇaṃ kathetvā taṃ vissajjāpetvā “mahārāja, aṭṭhamo udānasaddo ahosi. Nandamūlakapabbhārasmiṃ kira eko paccekabuddho attano āyusaṅkhāraparikkhayaṃ ñatvā ‘manussapathaṃ gantvā bārāṇasirañño uyyāne parinibbāyissāmi, tassa me manussā sarīranikkhepaṃ kāretvā sādhukīḷaṃ kīḷitvā dhātupūjaṃ katvā saggapathaṃ pūressantī’ti iddhānubhāvena āgacchanto tava pāsādassa matthakaṃ pattakāle khandhabhāraṃ otāretvā nibbānapurapavesanadīpanaṃ udānaṃ udānesī”ti paccekabuddhena vuttaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus the Great Being, having explained the reason for the sound made by the kinnara and having had him released, said: 'Great king, the eighth sound was an inspired utterance. Indeed, in the Nandamūlaka cave, a certain Paccekabuddha, realizing the exhaustion of his life-formations, thought: “I will go to the world of humans and attain final Nibbāna in the park of the king of Bārāṇasī. There, people will perform the funereal rites for my body, celebrate a festival, worship the relics, and thus fulfill the path to heaven.” Coming by the power of his supernormal ability, at the moment he reached the top of your palace, as if laying down the burden of the aggregates, he uttered an inspired utterance that illuminates the entry into the city of Nibbāna.' He then spoke the verse uttered by the Paccekabuddha:

17.

17.

“Asaṃsayaṃ [P 3.0434] jātikhayantadassī, na gabbhaseyyaṃ punarāvajissaṃ;

Ayamantimā pacchimā gabbhaseyyā, khīṇo me saṃsāro punabbhavāyā”ti.

"Undoubtedly, as one who sees the destruction of birth, I shall not return to lie in a womb again. This is my last, my final lying in a womb; my wandering in saṃsāra is ended, for there is no further becoming."

Tassattho – jātiyā khayantasaṅkhātassa nibbānassa diṭṭhattā jātikhayantadassī ahaṃ asaṃsayaṃ puna gabbhaseyyaṃ na āvajissaṃ, ayaṃ me antimā jāti, pacchimā gabbhaseyyā, khīṇo me punabbhavāya khandhapaṭipāṭisaṅkhāto saṃsāroti.

The meaning is this: Because I have seen Nibbāna, which is called the destruction of birth, I am one who sees the destruction of birth. Undoubtedly, I shall not return to lie in a womb again. This is my last birth, my final lying in a womb. My saṃsāra, reckoned as the succession of aggregates, is ended, for there is no further becoming.

“Idañca pana so udānaṃ vatvā imaṃ uyyānavanaṃ āgamma ekassa supupphitassa sālassa mūle parinibbuto, ehi, mahārāja, sarīrakiccamassa karissāmā”ti mahāsatto rājānaṃ gahetvā paccekabuddhassa parinibbutaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā sarīraṃ dassesi. Rājā tassa sarīraṃ disvā saddhiṃ balakāyena gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā bodhisattassa vacanaṃ nissāya yaññaṃ hāretvā sabbasattānaṃ jīvitadānaṃ datvā nagare māghātabheriṃ carāpetvā sattāhaṃ sādhukīḷaṃ kīḷitvā sabbagandhacitake mahantena sakkārena paccekabuddhassa [M 3.0413] sarīraṃ jhāpetvā dhātuyo catumahāpathe thūpaṃ kāresi. Bodhisattopi rañño dhammaṃ desetvā “appamatto hohī”ti ovaditvā himavantameva pavisitvā brahmavihāresu parikammaṃ katvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Having uttered this inspired utterance, the Paccekabuddha came to this park and attained final Nibbāna at the foot of a fully blossomed sal tree. The Great Being then said to the king, 'Come, great king, let us perform the funeral rites for him.' He took the king to the place where the Paccekabuddha had attained final Nibbāna and showed him the body. Upon seeing the body, the king, together with his retinue, honored it with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings. Following the Bodhisatta's advice, he stopped the sacrifice, granted the gift of life to all beings, and had the drum of non-killing sounded throughout the city. After holding a festival for seven days, he cremated the Paccekabuddha's body with great honor on a pyre made of all kinds of fragrant wood and built a stupa for the relics at the junction of four great highways. The Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma to the king and advised him, 'Be heedful,' entered the Himalayas. There, practicing the divine abidings, he, without falling away from jhāna, was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “mahārāja, tassa saddassa sutakāraṇā tava koci antarāyo [V 3.0385] natthī”ti yaññaṃ harāpetvā “mahājanassa jīvitaṃ dehī”ti jīvitadānaṃ dāpetvā nagare dhammabheriṃ carāpetvā dhammaṃ desetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, māṇavo sāriputto, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said, 'Great king, there is no danger for you on account of hearing that sound.' He had the sacrifice stopped and the gift of life granted, saying, 'Give life to the great multitude.' Having had the drum of Dhamma sounded in the city and taught the Dhamma, he identified the Jātaka: 'At that time the king was Ānanda, the young brahmin was Sāriputta, but the ascetic was I myself.'

Aṭṭhasaddajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Aṭṭhasadda Jātaka, the second.

[419] 3. Sulasājātakavaṇṇanā

[419] 3. The Commentary on the Sulasā Jātaka

Idaṃ [P 3.0435] suvaṇṇakāyūranti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa dāsiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā kira ekasmiṃ ussavadivase dāsigaṇena saddhiṃ uyyānaṃ gacchantī attano sāminiṃ puññalakkhaṇadeviṃ ābharaṇaṃ yāci. Sā tassā satasahassamūlaṃ attano ābharaṇaṃ adāsi. Sā taṃ piḷandhitvā dāsigaṇena saddhiṃ uyyānaṃ pāvisi. Atheko coro tassā ābharaṇe lobhaṃ uppādetvā “imaṃ māretvā ābharaṇaṃ harissāmī”ti tāya saddhiṃ sallapanto uyyānaṃ gantvā tassā macchamaṃsasurādīni adāsi. Sā “kilesavasena deti maññe”ti gahetvā uyyānakīḷaṃ kīḷitvā vīmaṃsanatthāya sāyanhasamaye nipanne dāsigaṇe uṭṭhāya tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. So “bhadde, imaṃ ṭhānaṃ appaṭicchannaṃ, thokaṃ purato gacchāmā”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā itarā “imasmiṃ ṭhāne sakkā rahassakammaṃ kātuṃ, ayaṃ pana nissaṃsayaṃ maṃ māretvā piḷandhanabhaṇḍaṃ haritukāmo bhavissati, hotu, sikkhāpessāmi na”nti cintetvā “sāmi, surāmadena me sukkhaṃ sarīraṃ, pānīyaṃ tāva maṃ pāyehī”ti ekaṃ kūpaṃ netvā “ito me pānīyaṃ osiñcā”ti rajjuñca ghaṭañca [M 3.0414] dassesi. Coro rajjuṃ kūpe otāresi, atha naṃ onamitvā udakaṃ osiñcantaṃ mahabbaladāsī ubhohi hatthehi āṇisadaṃ paharitvā kūpe khipitvā “na tvaṃ ettakena marissasī”ti ekaṃ mahantaṃ iṭṭhakaṃ matthake āsumbhi. So tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ patto. Sāpi nagaraṃ pavisitvā sāminiyā ābharaṇaṃ dadamānā “manamhi ajja imaṃ ābharaṇaṃ nissāya matā”ti sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi, sāpi anāthapiṇḍikassa ārocesi, anāthapiṇḍiko tathāgatassa ārocesi. Satthā “na kho, gahapati, idāneva sā dāsī ṭhānuppattikāya paññāya samannāgatā, pubbepi samannāgatāva, na ca idāneva tāya so mārito, pubbepi naṃ māresiyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'This golden armlet'—this the Teacher told while staying at Jetavana, concerning a slave girl of Anāthapiṇḍika. It is said that on a festival day, as she was going to the park with a group of slave girls, she asked her mistress, the lady Puññalakkhaṇā, for jewelry. Her mistress gave her her own jewelry, worth a hundred thousand. Adorning herself with it, she entered the park with the group of slave girls. Then a thief, conceiving a desire for her jewelry, thought, 'I will kill her and take the jewelry.' Conversing with her, he went to the park and gave her fish, meat, liquor, and other things. She thought, 'I suppose he gives these out of passion.' Having enjoyed the park games, and for the sake of testing him, she rose in the evening when the group of slave girls had lain down and went to him. He said, 'Good lady, this place is not secluded; let us go a little further.' Hearing this, she thought, 'A secret deed could be done in this place, but this man surely wants to kill me and take my ornaments. So be it, I will teach him a lesson.' She said, 'Sir, my body is parched from the intoxication of liquor; first give me some water to drink,' and led him to a well. 'Draw water for me from here,' she said, showing him a rope and a pot. The thief lowered the rope into the well, and as he bent down to draw water, the very strong slave girl pushed him on the hips with both hands, throwing him into the well. Saying, 'You will not die from this alone,' she threw a large brick on his head. He died right there. She returned to the city, gave the jewelry back to her mistress, and reported the whole incident, saying, 'Today, because of this jewelry, I was nearly killed.' Her mistress told Anāthapiṇḍika, and Anāthapiṇḍika told the Tathāgata. The Teacher said, 'Householder, not only now is this slave girl endowed with ready wit; she was endowed with it in the past as well. And not only now did she kill him; she killed him in the past, too.' Requested by him, he then related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente sulasā nāma nagarasobhinī pañcasatavaṇṇadāsiparivārā ahosi, sahassena rattiṃ gacchati. Tasmiṃyeva nagare sattuko nāma [V 3.0386][P 3.0436] coro ahosi nāgabalo, rattibhāge issaragharāni pavisitvā yathāruciṃ vilumpati. Nāgarā sannipatitvā rañño upakkosiṃsu. Rājā nagaraguttikaṃ āṇāpetvā tattha tattha gumbaṃ ṭhapāpetvā coraṃ gaṇhāpetvā “sīsamassa chindathā”ti āha. Taṃ pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā catukke catukke kasāhi tāḷetvā āghātanaṃ nenti. “Coro kira gahito”ti sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhi. Tadā sulasā vātapāne ṭhatvā antaravīthiṃ olokentī taṃ disvā paṭibaddhacittā hutvā “sace imaṃ coroti gahitapurisaṃ mocetuṃ sakkhissāmi, idaṃ kiliṭṭhakammaṃ akatvā imināva saddhiṃ samaggavāsaṃ kappessāmī”ti cintetvā heṭṭhā kaṇaverajātake (jā. 1.4.69 ādayo) vuttanayeneva nagaraguttikassa sahassaṃ pesetvā taṃ mocetvā tena saddhiṃ sammodamānā samaggavāsaṃ vasi. Coro tiṇṇaṃ catunnaṃ māsānaṃ accayena cintesi “ahaṃ imasmiṃyeva ṭhāne vasituṃ na sakkhissāmi, tucchahatthena palāyitumpi na sakkā, sulasāya piḷandhanabhaṇḍaṃ satasahassaṃ agghati, sulasaṃ māretvā idaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ āha – “bhadde, ahaṃ tadā rājapurisehi nīyamāno asukapabbatamatthake rukkhadevatāya balikammaṃ paṭissuṇiṃ, sā maṃ balikammaṃ alabhamānā [M 3.0415] bhāyāpeti, balikammamassā karomā”ti. “Sādhu, sāmi, sajjetvā pesehī”ti. “Bhadde, pesetuṃ na vaṭṭati, mayaṃ ubhopi sabbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍitā mahantena parivārena gantvā dassāmā”ti. “Sādhu, sāmi, tathā karomā”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, there was a courtesan named Sulasā, who was attended by five hundred female slaves; she commanded a thousand coins for a night. In that same city, there was a robber named Sattuka who possessed the strength of an elephant; at night, he would enter the houses of the wealthy and plunder them as he pleased. The citizens gathered and complained to the king. The king ordered the city superintendent, had ambushes set here and there, had the robber caught, and said, 'Cut off his head!' They bound his hands behind his back and, flogging him with whips at every crossroads, led him to the execution ground. Word spread that 'The robber has been caught!' and the whole city was in an uproar. At that time, Sulasā, standing at a window and looking into the street, saw him and her heart became attached to him. She thought, 'If I can free this man who has been caught as a robber, I will abandon this defiled life and live in harmony with him alone.' Following the method described in the Kaṇavera Jātaka, she sent a thousand coins to the city superintendent, had the robber freed, and lived in harmony and joy with him. After three or four months had passed, the robber thought, 'I cannot continue to live in this place, nor can I escape empty-handed. Sulasā’s ornaments are worth a hundred thousand. I will kill Sulasā and take them.' Then one day he said to her, 'Good lady, when I was being led away by the king’s men, I promised an offering to a tree deity on the top of a certain mountain. Not receiving the offering, she is now frightening me. Let us make the offering to her.' 'Very well, my lord, prepare it and have it sent.' 'Good lady, it is not proper to send it. We should both go, adorned with all our ornaments and with a large retinue, and present it.' 'Very well, my lord, let us do as you say.'

Atha naṃ tathā kāretvā pabbatapādaṃ gatakāle āha – “bhadde, mahājanaṃ disvā devatā balikammaṃ na sampaṭicchissati, mayaṃ ubhova abhiruhitvā demā”ti. So tāya “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchito taṃ balipātiṃ ukkhipāpetvā sayaṃ sannaddhapañcāvudho hutvā pabbatamatthakaṃ abhiruhitvā ekaṃ sataporisapapātaṃ [P 3.0437] nissāya jātarukkhamūle balibhājanaṃ ṭhapāpetvā “bhadde, nāhaṃ balikammatthāya āgato, taṃ pana māretvā piḷandhanaṃ te gahetvā gamissāmīti āgatomhi, tava piḷandhanaṃ omuñcitvā uttarasāṭakena bhaṇḍikaṃ karohī”ti āha. “Sāmi, maṃ kasmā māresī”ti? “Dhanakāraṇā”ti. “Sāmi, mayā kataguṇaṃ anussara, ahaṃ taṃ bandhitvā nīyamānaṃ seṭṭhiputtena parivattetvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ datvā jīvitaṃ labhāpesiṃ, devasikaṃ sahassaṃ labhamānāpi aññaṃ purisaṃ na olokemi, evañhi tava upakārikaṃ mā maṃ mārehi, bahuñca te dhanaṃ dassāmi, tava dāsī ca bhavissāmī”ti yācantī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, having arranged it thus, when they arrived at the foot of the mountain, he said: 'Dear, seeing the crowd, the deity will not accept the offering. Let us both climb up alone and give it.' She agreed, saying, 'Very well.' He had her carry the offering vessel and, arming himself with the five weapons, climbed to the mountain top. Near a precipice a hundred persons deep, he had the offering vessel placed at the foot of a tree and said: 'Dear, I have not come for the sake of the offering. I have come to kill you, take your ornaments, and leave. Remove your ornaments and tie them up in your upper garment.' 'Lord, why do you wish to kill me?' she asked. 'For the sake of wealth,' he replied. 'Lord, remember the favor I have done for you. When you were bound and being led away, I substituted a merchant's son for you, gave much wealth, and saved your life. Though receiving a thousand daily, I do not even look at another man. Since I have been so helpful to you, do not kill me. I will give you much wealth and become your slave,' she pleaded, first reciting this stanza:

18.

18.

“Idaṃ suvaṇṇakāyūraṃ, muttā veḷuriyā bahū;

Sabbaṃ harassu bhaddante, mañca dāsīti sāvayā”ti.

'Here is this golden neck-ornament, and many pearls and beryls too; take them all, good sir, and proclaim me as your slave.'

Tattha [V 3.0387] kāyūranti gīvāyaṃ piḷandhanapasādhanaṃ kāyūraṃ. Sāvayāti mahājanamajjhe sāvetvā dāsiṃ katvā gaṇhāti.

In this verse, 'kāyūra' refers to an ornament worn on the neck. 'Sāvayā' means: 'take me as a slave after making it known in the midst of the great multitude.'

Tato sattukena –

Then Sattuka said:

19.

19.

“Oropayassu kalyāṇi, mā bāḷhaṃ paridevasi;

Na cāhaṃ abhijānāmi, ahantvā dhanamābhata”nti. –

'Take off your ornaments, lovely one, do not lament so much; for I do not recall ever having obtained wealth without killing its owner.'

Attano ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ dutiyagāthāya vuttāya sulasā ṭhānuppattikāraṇaṃ paṭilabhitvā “ayaṃ coro mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ na dassati, upāyena naṃ paṭhamataraṃ papāte pātetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessāmī”ti cintetvā gāthādvayamāha –

When the second stanza was spoken in accordance with his own disposition, Sulasā, grasping the situation, thought: 'This thief will not spare my life. By some stratagem, I must first throw him into the precipice and bring about his death.' Thinking thus, she spoke these two stanzas:

20.

20.

“Yato [M 3.0416] sarāmi attānaṃ, yato pattāsmi viññutaṃ;

Na cāhaṃ abhijānāmi, aññaṃ piyataraṃ tayā.

'Since I can remember myself, since I reached the age of reason, I know of no other husband dearer than you.

21.

21.

“Ehi taṃ upagūhissaṃ, karissañca padakkhiṇaṃ;

Na hi dāni puna atthi, mama tuyhañca saṅgamo”ti.

'Come, I will embrace you and circumambulate you in reverence; for there will be no further meeting between you and me.'

Sattuko tassādhippāyaṃ ajānanto “sādhu, bhadde, ehi upagūhassu ma”nti āha. Sulasā taṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā upagūhitvā “idāni taṃ, sāmi, catūsu passesu vandissāmī”ti [P 3.0438] vatvā pādapiṭṭhiyaṃ sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā bāhupasse vanditvā pacchimapassaṃ gantvā vandamānā viya hutvā nāgabalā gaṇikā coraṃ dvīsu pacchāpādesu gahetvā heṭṭhā sīsaṃ katvā sataporise narake khipi. So tattheva cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ patvā mari. Taṃ kiriyaṃ disvā pabbatamatthake nibbattadevatā imā gāthā abhāsi –

Not knowing her intention, Sattuka said, 'Very well, dear, come and embrace me.' Sulasā circumambulated him three times, embraced him, and said, 'Now, lord, I will pay homage to you on all four sides.' Placing her head at his feet and paying homage to his arms, she went to his rear and, as if paying homage, the courtesan, with the strength of an elephant, seized the thief by his two heels. Turning him head downward, she threw him into the abyss a hundred persons deep. There, he was crushed to pieces and died. Seeing this deed, a deity dwelling on the mountaintop spoke these verses:

22.

22.

“Na hi sabbesu ṭhānesu, puriso hoti paṇḍito;

Itthīpi paṇḍitā hoti, tattha tattha vicakkhaṇā.

'Indeed, not in all situations is a man the wise one; a woman too can be wise, being discerning in this and that.

23.

23.

“Na hi sabbesu ṭhānesu, puriso hoti paṇḍito;

Itthīpi paṇḍitā hoti, lahuṃ atthaṃ vicintikā.

'Indeed, not in all situations is a man the wise one; a woman too can be wise, being quick to think of what is beneficial.

24.

24.

“Lahuñca [V 3.0388] vata khippañca, nikaṭṭhe samacetayi;

Migaṃ puṇṇāyateneva, sulasā sattukaṃ vadhi.

'Indeed, she swiftly and quickly devised a plan when at the point of death; as one kills a deer with a fully drawn bow, so Sulasā killed Sattuka.

25.

25.

“Yodha uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, na khippamanubujjhati;

So haññati mandamati, corova girigabbhare.

'He who does not quickly understand a matter that has arisen is destroyed, slow-witted, like the thief in the mountain chasm.

26.

26.

“Yo ca uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, khippameva nibodhati;

Muccate sattusambādhā, sulasā sattukāmivā”ti.

'And he who quickly understands a matter that has arisen is freed from the danger of the enemy, just as Sulasā was freed from Sattuka.'

Tattha paṇḍitā hotīti itthīpi paṇḍitā tattha tattha vicakkhaṇā hoti, atha vā itthī paṇḍitā ceva tattha tattha vicakkhaṇā ca hoti. Lahuṃ atthaṃ vicintikāti lahuṃ khippaṃ atthaṃ vicintikā. Lahuñca vatāti adandhañca vata. Khippañcāti acireneva. Nikaṭṭhe samacetayīti santike ṭhitāva tassa maraṇūpāyaṃ cintesi. Puṇṇāyatenevāti pūritadhanusmiṃ. Idaṃ [M 3.0417] vuttaṃ hoti – yathā cheko migaluddako sakaṇḍapuṇṇadhanusmiṃ khippaṃ migaṃ vadhati, evaṃ sulasā sattukaṃ vadhīti. Yodhāti yo imasmiṃ sattaloke. Nibodhatīti jānāti. Sattukāmivāti sattukā iva, yathā sulasā muttā, evaṃ muccatīti attho.

Here, 'a woman is wise' means a woman is wise and discerning here and there; or, a woman is both wise and discerning here and there. 'Quick to think on the matter' means quickly contemplating the matter. 'Indeed lightly' means indeed without slowness. 'And swiftly' means without delay. 'She devised close at hand' means while standing nearby she contemplated a means for his death. 'With a fully drawn bow' means with a bow fully drawn. This is said to mean: just as a skilled deer-hunter swiftly kills a deer with a bow fully drawn with an arrow, so too did Sulasā slay Sattuka. 'He who here' refers to one in this world of beings. 'Understands' means knows. 'Like from Sattuka' means: just as Sulasā was freed from Sattuka, so too is one freed—this is the meaning.

Iti sulasā coraṃ vadhitvā pabbatā oruyha attano parijanassa santikaṃ gantvā “ayyaputto kaha”nti puṭṭhā “mā taṃ pucchathā”ti vatvā rathaṃ abhiruhitvā nagarameva pāvisi.

Thus, having killed the thief, Sulasā descended from the mountain, went to her attendants, and when asked, 'Where is the master?' she said, 'Do not ask about him.' Then, mounting her chariot, she entered the city.

Satthā [P 3.0439] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā te ubhopi imeyeva ahesuṃ, devatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, those two were these very same individuals, but the deity was I myself.'

Sulasājātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Sulasā Jātaka is the third.

[420] 4. Sumaṅgalajātakavaṇṇanā

[420] 4. The Commentary on the Sumaṅgala Jātaka

Bhusamhi kuddhoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto rājovādasuttaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā pana satthā raññā yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'Bhusamhi kuddho'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Rājovāda Sutta (Discourse on Advice to a King). At that time, the Teacher, being requested by the king, related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 3.0389] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatto vayappatto pitu accayena rajjaṃ kāresi, mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Tassa sumaṅgalo nāma uyyānapālo ahosi. Atheko paccekabuddho nandamūlakapabbhārā nikkhamitvā cārikaṃ caramāno bārāṇasiṃ patvā uyyāne vasitvā punadivase nagaraṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Tamenaṃ rājā disvā pasannacitto vanditvā pāsādaṃ āropetvā rājāsane nisīdāpetvā nānaggarasehi khādanīyabhojanīyehi parivisitvā anumodanaṃ sutvā pasanno attano uyyāne vasanatthāya paṭiññaṃ gāhāpetvā uyyānaṃ pavesetvā sayampi bhuttapātarāso tattha gantvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādīni saṃvidahitvā sumaṅgalaṃ nāma uyyānapālaṃ veyyāvaccakaraṃ katvā nagaraṃ pāvisi. Paccekabuddho tato paṭṭhāya nibaddhaṃ rājagehe bhuñjanto tattha ciraṃ vasi, sumaṅgalopi naṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. Having come of age, he assumed kingship after his father's passing and instituted a great giving. His park-keeper was named Sumaṅgala. Then, a Paccekabuddha, having departed from the Nandamūlaka cave and wandering on tour, arrived in Benares. He stayed in the park and on the next day entered the city for alms. The king, seeing him, with a mind full of faith, paid homage and led him up to the palace. Seating him on the royal throne, he served him with various excellent hard and soft foods of many flavors. Hearing the words of thanksgiving, the king, being pleased, obtained a promise from him to reside in his park. He led him into the park, and after his own morning meal, went there himself, arranged for night and day quarters, and appointed the park-keeper named Sumaṅgala as his attendant before entering the city. From then on, the Paccekabuddha regularly ate in the king's house and stayed there for a long time, and Sumaṅgala attended upon him with great care.

Athekadivasaṃ [M 3.0418] paccekabuddho sumaṅgalaṃ āmantetvā “ahaṃ katipāhaṃ asukagāmaṃ nissāya vasitvā āgacchissāmi, rañño ārocehī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Sumaṅgalopi rañño ārocesi. Paccekabuddho katipāhaṃ tattha vasitvā sāyaṃ sūriye atthaṅgate taṃ uyyānaṃ [P 3.0440] paccāgami. Sumaṅgalo tassa āgatabhāvaṃ ajānanto attano gehaṃ agamāsi. Paccekabuddhopi pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā thokaṃ caṅkamitvā pāsāṇaphalake nisīdi. Taṃ divasaṃ pana uyyānapālassa gharaṃ pāhunakā āgamiṃsu. So tesaṃ sūpabyañjanatthāya “uyyāne abhayaladdhaṃ migaṃ māressāmī”ti dhanuṃ ādāya uyyānaṃ gantvā migaṃ upadhārento paccekabuddhaṃ disvā “mahāmigo bhavissatī”ti saññāya saraṃ sannayhitvā vijjhi. Paccekabuddho sīsaṃ vivaritvā “sumaṅgalā”ti āha. So saṃvegappatto vanditvā “bhante, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ ajānanto ‘migo’ti saññāya vijjhiṃ, khamatha me”ti vatvā “hotu dāni kiṃ karissasi, ehi saraṃ luñcitvā gaṇhāhī”ti vutte vanditvā saraṃ luñci, mahatī vedanā uppajji. Paccekabuddho tattheva parinibbāyi. Uyyānapālo “sace rājā jānissati, nāsessatī”ti puttadāraṃ gahetvā tatova palāyi. Tāvadeva “paccekabuddho parinibbuto”ti devatānubhāvena sakalanagaraṃ ekakolāhalaṃ jātaṃ.

One day, the Paccekabuddha addressed Sumaṅgala and said, 'I will stay near such-and-such a village for a few days and then return. Inform the king.' Having said this, he departed. Sumaṅgala informed the king. The Paccekabuddha stayed there for a few days and returned to that park in the evening after the sun had set. Sumaṅgala, not knowing of his arrival, went to his own home. The Paccekabuddha, having put away his bowl and robe, walked for a short while and sat down on a stone slab. On that day, guests arrived at the park-keeper’s house. To prepare soup and side dishes for them, he thought, 'I will kill a deer in the park that has been granted sanctuary.' Taking his bow, he went to the park and, while searching for a deer, saw the Paccekabuddha. Perceiving him to be a great deer, he readied an arrow and shot. The Paccekabuddha uncovered his head and called out, 'Sumaṅgala!' Stricken with remorse, he paid homage and said, 'Venerable sir, not knowing of your arrival, I shot you, thinking you were a deer. Forgive me.' When he was told, 'Let it be; what can you do now? Come, pull out the arrow and take it,' he paid homage and pulled out the arrow. Great pain arose. The Paccekabuddha attained final Nibbāna right there. The park-keeper, thinking, 'If the king finds out, he will destroy me,' took his wife and children and fled from that very place. At that very moment, by the power of the deities, the entire city broke into a single uproar with the news, 'The Paccekabuddha has attained final Nibbāna!'

Punadivase manussā uyyānaṃ gantvā paccekabuddhaṃ disvā “uyyānapālo paccekabuddhaṃ māretvā palāto”ti rañño kathayiṃsu. Rājā mahantena parivārena uyyānaṃ gantvā sattāhaṃ sarīrapūjaṃ katvā mahantena sakkārena jhāpetvā dhātuyo ādāya cetiyaṃ katvā taṃ pūjento dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Sumaṅgalopi ekasaṃvaccharaṃ vītināmetvā “rañño cittaṃ jānissāmī”ti āgantvā [V 3.0390] ekaṃ amaccaṃ passitvā “mayi rañño cittaṃ jānāhī”ti āha. Amaccopi rañño santikaṃ gantvā tassa guṇaṃ kathesi. Rājā asuṇanto viya ahosi. Puna kiñci avatvā rañño anattamanabhāvaṃ sumaṅgalassa kathesi. So dutiyasaṃvaccharepi āgantvā tatheva rājā tuṇhī ahosi. Tatiyasaṃvacchare āgantvā puttadāraṃ gahetvāva āgami. Amacco rañño cittamudubhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ rājadvāre [P 3.0441] ṭhapetvā tassāgatabhāvaṃ rañño kathesi. Rājā taṃ pakkosāpetvā paṭisanthāraṃ [M 3.0419] katvā “sumaṅgala, kasmā tayā mama puññakkhettaṃ paccekabuddho mārito”ti pucchi. So “nāhaṃ, deva, ‘paccekabuddhaṃ māremī’ti māresiṃ, apica kho iminā nāma kāraṇena idaṃ nāma akāsi”nti taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Atha naṃ rājā “tena hi mā bhāyī”ti samassāsetvā puna uyyānapālameva akāsi.

On the following day, people went to the park, saw the Paccekabuddha, and told the king, 'The park-keeper has killed the Paccekabuddha and fled.' The king went to the park with a large retinue, performed veneration of the body for seven days, had it cremated with great honor, took the relics, built a cetiya, and, while venerating it, ruled righteously. Sumaṅgala, after a year had passed, came thinking, 'I will find out the king’s disposition.' Seeing a certain minister, he said, 'Find out the king’s mind towards me.' The minister went to the king and spoke of Sumaṅgala's virtues. The king acted as if he did not hear. Saying nothing further, the minister reported the king’s displeasure to Sumaṅgala. In the second year, he came again, and likewise the king remained silent. In the third year, he came, bringing his wife and children with him. The minister, knowing that the king's heart had softened, had them stand at the palace gate and informed the king of his arrival. The king had him summoned, gave him a friendly welcome, and asked, 'Sumaṅgala, why did you kill my field of merit, the Paccekabuddha?' He replied, 'Your Majesty, I did not kill him thinking, "I will kill a Paccekabuddha," but for such-and-such a reason, I did this thing,' and he explained the incident. Then the king consoled him, saying, 'In that case, do not be afraid,' and reappointed him as park-keeper.

Atha naṃ so amacco pucchi “deva, kasmā tumhe dve vāre sumaṅgalassa guṇaṃ sutvāpi kiñci na kathayittha, kasmā pana tatiyavāre sutvā taṃ pakkositvā anukampitthā”ti? Rājā “tāta, raññā nāma kuddhena sahasā kiñci kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, tenāhaṃ pubbe tuṇhī hutvā tatiyavāre sumaṅgale mama cittassa mudubhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ pakkosāpesi”nti rājavattaṃ kathento imā gāthā āha –

Then that minister asked him, 'Your Majesty, why after hearing news of Sumaṅgala twice did you say nothing, and why after hearing of him a third time did you summon him and show compassion?' The king said, 'Dear one, it is not fitting for a king to do anything hastily in anger. Therefore, I remained silent at first, and in the third year, knowing the softening of my heart towards Sumaṅgala, I had him summoned,' and speaking on the duty of a king, he uttered these verses:

27.

27.

“Bhusamhi kuddhoti avekkhiyāna, na tāva daṇḍaṃ paṇayeyya issaro;

Aṭṭhānaso appatirūpamattano, parassa dukkhāni bhusaṃ udīraye.

'Having reflected, "I am greatly angered," a ruler should not yet inflict punishment; for he might unreasonably, in a manner unfitting to himself, inflict great suffering upon another.'

28.

28.

“Yato ca jāneyya pasādamattano, atthaṃ niyuñjeyya parassa dukkaṭaṃ;

Tadāyamatthoti sayaṃ avekkhiya, athassa daṇḍaṃ sadisaṃ nivesaye.

“And when he knows his own serenity, he should investigate the facts of another's misdeed. Then, having personally considered, ‘This is the case,’ he should impose a fitting punishment upon him.”

29.

29.

“Na cāpi jhāpeti paraṃ na attanaṃ, amucchito yo nayate nayānayaṃ;

Yo daṇḍadhāro bhavatīdha issaro, sa vaṇṇagutto siriyā na dhaṃsati.

“He burns neither another nor himself, who, being undeluded, discerns what is right and wrong. The ruler who is a wielder of the rod here, protected by his renown, does not fall from glory.”

30.

30.

“Ye khattiyā se anisammakārino, paṇenti daṇḍaṃ sahasā pamucchitā;

Avaṇṇasaṃyutā jahanti jīvitaṃ, ito vimuttāpi ca yanti duggatiṃ.

“Those kings who act without reflection, and in haste and delusion impose punishment, they meet with ill-repute and lose their lives; and once released from here, they go to a state of woe.”

31.

31.

“Dhamme [P 3.0442][M 3.0420] ca ye ariyappavedite ratā, anuttarā te vacasā manasā kammunā ca;

Te santisoraccasamādhisaṇṭhitā, vajanti lokaṃ dubhayaṃ tathāvidhā.

“And those who delight in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones, they are unsurpassed in speech, mind, and action; established in peace, gentleness, and concentration, such as they go to both worlds.”

32.

32.

“Rājāhamasmi [V 3.0391] narapamadānamissaro, sacepi kujjhāmi ṭhapemi attanaṃ;

Nisedhayanto janataṃ tathāvidhaṃ, paṇemi daṇḍaṃ anukampa yoniso”ti.

“I am the king, the lord of men and women; even if I am angry, I restrain myself. Restraining the people from such conduct, I impose punishment with compassion and wise consideration.”

Tattha avekkhiyānāti avekkhitvā jānitvā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tāta, pathavissaro rājā nāma “ahaṃ bhusaṃ kuddho balavakodhābhibhūto”ti ñatvā aṭṭhavatthukādibhedaṃ daṇḍaṃ parassa na paṇayeyya na vatteyya. Kiṃkāraṇā? Kuddho hi aṭṭhavatthukaṃ soḷasavatthukaṃ katvā aṭṭhānena akāraṇena attano rājabhāvassa ananurūpaṃ “imaṃ ettakaṃ nāma āharatha, idañca tassa karothā”ti parassa bhusaṃ dukkhāni balavadukkhāni udīraye.

Therein, ‘avekkhiyāna’ means having considered and known. This is what is said: Dear one, a king, a lord of the earth, knowing, ‘I am greatly angry, overcome by powerful wrath,’ should not initially impose or apply a punishment. For what reason? For one who is angry, making an eightfold matter into a sixteenfold one, and without cause or reason, in a manner unfitting for his own royal status, might say ‘Bring this much to him, and do this to him,’ thus inflicting severe and intense sufferings upon another.

Yatoti yadā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yadā pana rājā parasmiṃ uppannaṃ attano pasādaṃ jāneyya, atha parassa dukkaṭaṃ atthaṃ niyuñjeyya upaparikkheyya, tadā evaṃ niyuñjanto “ayaṃ nāmettha attho, ayaṃ etassa doso”ti sayaṃ attapaccakkhaṃ katvā athassa aparādhakārakassa aṭṭhavatthukahetu aṭṭheva, soḷasavatthukahetu soḷaseva kahāpaṇe gaṇhamāno daṇḍaṃ sadisaṃ katadosānurūpaṃ nivesaye ṭhapeyya pavatteyyāti.

‘Yato’ means ‘when’. This is what is said: When a king knows his own serenity regarding another, then he should investigate and examine the case and the other’s misdeed. At that time, while so investigating, having personally verified, ‘This is the matter here, this is his fault,’ then for the offender, taking just eight kahāpaṇas for an eightfold cause, and just sixteen for a sixteenfold cause, he should establish, impose, or enact a punishment that is fitting and proportionate to the offense committed.

Amucchitoti chandādīhi agatikilesehi amucchito anabhibhūto hutvā yo nayānayaṃ nayate upaparikkhati, so neva paraṃ jhāpeti, na attānaṃ. Chandādivasena hi ahetukaṃ daṇḍaṃ pavattento parampi tena daṇḍena jhāpeti dahati pīḷeti, attānampi tatonidānena pāpena. Ayaṃ pana na paraṃ jhāpeti, na attānaṃ. Yo daṇḍadhāro bhavatīdha issaroti yo idha pathavissaro rājā idha sattaloke dosānucchavikaṃ daṇḍaṃ pavattento daṇḍadhāro hoti. Sa vaṇṇaguttoti guṇavaṇṇena ceva yasavaṇṇena ca gutto rakkhito siriyā na dhaṃsati na parihāyati[M 3.0421]. Avaṇṇasaṃyutā jahantīti adhammikā lolarājāno avaṇṇena yuttā hutvā jīvitaṃ jahanti.

‘Amucchito’ means being undeluded and unovercome by the defilements of the wrong courses, such as partiality. One who discerns and investigates what is right and wrong does not burn another, nor himself. For one who, by the power of partiality and so on, applies an unjust punishment, burns, torments, and oppresses another with that punishment, and also himself with the evil resulting therefrom. But this king burns neither another nor himself. ‘Yo daṇḍadhāro bhavatīdha issaro’ means: whoever, being a king, a lord of the earth, is a wielder of the rod in this world of beings by applying punishment appropriate to the offense. ‘Sa vaṇṇagutto’ means: protected and guarded by the renown of his virtue and the renown of his fame, he does not fall from his glory. ‘Avaṇṇasaṃyutā jahanti’ means: unrighteous and unstable kings, being associated with ill-repute, lose their lives.

Dhamme ca ye ariyappavediteti ye rājāno ācāraariyehi dhammikarājūhi pavedite dasavidhe rājadhamme ratā. Anuttarā teti te vacasā manasā kammunā ca tīhipi etehi anuttarā [P 3.0443] jeṭṭhakā. Te santisoraccasamādhisaṇṭhitāti te agatipahānena kilesasantiyañca susīlyasaṅkhāte soracce ca ekaggatāsamādhimhi ca saṇṭhitā patiṭṭhitā dhammikarājāno. Vajanti lokaṃ dubhayanti dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā manussalokato devalokaṃ, devalokato manussalokanti ubhayalokameva vajanti, nirayādīsu na nibbattanti. Narapamadānanti narānañca nārīnañca. Ṭhapemi attananti kuddhopi kodhavasena agantvā attānaṃ porāṇakarājūhi ṭhapitanayasmiṃyeva dhamme ṭhapemi, vinicchayadhammaṃ na bhindāmīti.

‘Dhamme ca ye ariyappavedite’ means: those kings who are devoted to the tenfold royal duties proclaimed by righteous kings of noble conduct. ‘Anuttarā te’ means: they are unsurpassed, the foremost, in these three: speech, mind, and action. ‘Te santisoraccasamādhisaṇṭhitā’ means: these righteous kings are established through the abandoning of the wrong courses, in the peace from defilements, in gentleness—which is virtuous conduct—and in one-pointed concentration. ‘Vajanti lokaṃ dubhayaṃ’ means: having ruled righteously, they go from the human world to the deva world, and from the deva world to the human world; thus they journey through both worlds and are not reborn in hell and so on. ‘Narapamadānaṃ’ means: of men and of women. ‘Ṭhapemi attanaṃ’ means: even if I am angry, I do not act out of anger but restrain myself in the Dhamma, in the very way established by ancient kings; I do not violate the principles of judgment.

Evaṃ [V 3.0392] chahi gāthāhi raññā attano guṇe kathite sabbāpi rājaparisā tuṭṭhā “ayaṃ sīlācāraguṇasampatti tumhākaññeva anurūpā”ti rañño guṇe kathesuṃ. Sumaṅgalo pana parisāya kathitāvasāne uṭṭhāya rājānaṃ vanditvā añjaliṃ paggayha rañño thutiṃ karonto tisso gāthā abhāsi –

Thus, when the king had spoken of his own virtues in six verses, the entire royal assembly was pleased and, praising the king's virtues, said, “This excellence in virtue and conduct is fitting for you alone.” Then, at the end of the assembly's speech, Sumaṅgala rose, paid homage to the king, and with hands reverently joined, uttered three verses in praise of the king:

33.

33.

“Sirī ca lakkhī ca taveva khattiya, janādhipa mā vijahi kudācanaṃ;

Akkodhano niccapasannacitto, anīgho tuvaṃ vassasatāni pālaya.

“May glory and prosperity be yours alone, O king, lord of the people; may they never abandon you at any time. Free from anger, with a mind ever serene, without affliction, may you rule for a hundred years.”

34.

34.

“Guṇehi etehi upeta khattiya, ṭhitamariyavattī suvaco akodhano;

Sukhī anuppīḷa pasāsa mediniṃ, ito vimuttopi ca yāhi suggatiṃ.

“Endowed with these virtues, O king, steadfast in noble conduct, easy to speak to, and without anger; happy and unoppressing, rule the earth. And once released from here, go to a happy destination.”

35.

35.

“Evaṃ sunītena subhāsitena, dhammena ñāyena upāyaso nayaṃ;

Nibbāpaye saṅkhubhitaṃ mahājanaṃ, mahāva megho salilena medini”nti.

“Thus, guiding with good policy and well-spoken words, with Dhamma, justice, and skillful means, one should pacify the agitated multitude, just as a great cloud cools the earth with rain.”

Tattha [M 3.0422] sirī ca lakkhī cāti parivārasampatti ca paññā ca. Anīghoti niddukkho hutvā. Upeta khattiyāti upeto khattiya, ayameva vā pāṭho. Ṭhitamariyavattīti ṭhitaariyavatti, ariyavatti nāma dasarājadhammasaṅkhātaṃ porāṇarājavattaṃ, tattha patiṭṭhitattā ṭhitarājadhammo hutvāti attho. Anuppīḷa pasāsa medininti anuppīḷaṃ pasāsa mediniñca, ayameva [P 3.0444] vā pāṭho. Sunītenāti sunayena suṭṭhu kāraṇena. Dhammenāti dasakusalakammapathadhammena. Ñāyenāti purimapadasseva vevacanaṃ. Upāyasoti upāyakosallena. Nayanti nayanto rajjaṃ anusāsanto dhammikarājā. Nibbāpayeti imāya paṭipattiyā kāyikacetasikadukkhaṃ darathaṃ apanento kāyikacetasikadukkhasaṅkhubhitampi mahājanaṃ mahāmegho salilena mediniṃ viya nibbāpeyya, tvampi tatheva nibbāpehīti dassento evamāha.

Therein, ‘sirī ca lakkhī ca’ means the fulfillment of a retinue and wisdom. ‘Anīgho’ means being free from suffering. ‘Upeta khattiya’ means ‘endowed, O warrior,’ or this may be the reading. ‘Ṭhitamariyavattī’ means steadfast in noble conduct; ‘noble conduct’ refers to the ancient royal duty known as the ten royal virtues, and being established in that, he is one whose royal virtues are steadfast—this is the meaning. ‘Anuppīḷa pasāsa mediniṃ’ means ‘rule the earth without oppressing,’ or this may be the reading. ‘Sunītena’ means through a good method, through an excellent cause. ‘Dhammena’ means through the Dhamma of the tenfold path of wholesome actions. ‘Ñāyena’ is a synonym of the previous term. ‘Upāyaso’ means through skill in means. ‘Nayaṃ’ means a righteous king, guiding and ruling the kingdom. ‘Nibbāpaye’ means: by removing bodily and mental suffering and distress through this practice, he should pacify the great populace agitated by bodily and mental suffering, just as a great cloud cools the earth with water. Showing ‘you too should pacify them in the same way,’ he spoke thus.

Satthā kosalarañño ovādavasena imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā paccekabuddho parinibbuto, sumaṅgalo ānando ahosi, rājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma discourse by way of advice to the King of Kosala, connected the Jātaka thus: “At that time, the Paccekabuddha had attained final Nibbāna, Sumaṅgala was Ānanda, and the king was indeed myself.”

Sumaṅgalajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Sumaṅgala Jātaka, the fourth.

[421] 5. Gaṅgamālajātakavaṇṇanā

[421] 5. The Commentary on the Gaṅgamāla Jātaka

Aṅgārajātāti [V 3.0393] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto uposathakammaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasañhi satthā uposathike upāsake āmantetvā “upāsakā sādhurūpaṃ vo kataṃ uposathaṃ upavasantehi, dānaṃ dātabbaṃ, sīlaṃ rakkhitabbaṃ, kodho na kātabbo, mettā bhāvetabbā, uposathavāso vasitabbo, porāṇakapaṇḍitā hi ekaṃ upaḍḍhuposathakammaṃ nissāya mahāyasaṃ labhiṃsū”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

‘Aṅgārajātā’—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Uposatha observance. For one day, the Teacher addressed the lay followers observing the Uposatha: ‘Lay followers, it is well done of you to observe the Uposatha. Alms should be given, virtue should be maintained, anger should not be given way to, loving-kindness should be cultivated, and the Uposatha should be observed. For the wise of old, relying on a half-day Uposatha observance, attained great glory.’ Having spoken thus, being requested by them, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tasmiṃ nagare suciparivāro nāma seṭṭhi ahosi asītikoṭidhanavibhavo dānādipuññābhirato. Tassa puttadārāpi parijanopi antamaso tasmiṃ ghare vacchapālakāpi [M 3.0423] sabbe māsassa cha divase uposathaṃ upavasanti. Tadā bodhisatto ekasmiṃ daliddakule nibbattitvā bhatiṃ katvā kicchena jīvati. So “bhatiṃ karissāmī”ti tassa gehaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito “kiṃ āgatosī”ti vutte “tumhākaṃ gehe bhatiyā kammakaraṇattha”nti āha. Seṭṭhi aññesaṃ bhatikānaṃ āgatadivaseyeva “imasmiṃ gehe kammaṃ karontā sīlaṃ rakkhanti, sīlaṃ rakkhituṃ sakkontā kammaṃ karothā”ti vadati, bodhisattassa pana sīlarakkhaṇaācikkhaṇe saññaṃ akatvā “sādhu[P 3.0445], tāta, attano bhatiṃ jānitvā kammaṃ karohī”ti āha. So tato paṭṭhāya suvaco hutvā uraṃ datvā attano kilamathaṃ agaṇetvā tassa sabbakiccāni karoti, pātova kammantaṃ gantvā sāyaṃ āgacchati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, there was a merchant named Suciparivāra in that city, possessing eighty crores of wealth and devoted to meritorious deeds such as giving. His wife, children, and even the household servants, down to the calf-herds, all observed the Uposatha on six days of each month. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor family and, working for wages, lived with difficulty. Thinking, ‘I will work for hire,’ he went to the merchant's house, paid respects, and stood to one side. When asked, ‘Why have you come?’ he replied, ‘To do the work of a wage-earner in your household.’ The merchant would say to other wage-earners on the day they arrived, ‘Those who work in this house keep the precepts; if you can keep the precepts, then you may work here.’ But to the Bodhisatta, he made no mention of keeping the precepts, saying instead, ‘Very well, my dear, know your wages and do your work.’ From then on, the Bodhisatta became obedient, and exerting himself to the utmost, not counting his own exhaustion, he performed all his duties. He would go to work early in the morning and return in the evening.

Athekadivasaṃ nagare chaṇaṃ ghosesuṃ. Mahāseṭṭhi dāsiṃ āmantetvā “ajjuposathadivaso, gehe kammakarānaṃ pātova bhattaṃ pacitvā dehi, kālasseva bhuñjitvā uposathikā bhavissantī”ti āha. Bodhisatto kālasseva uṭṭhāya kammantaṃ agamāsi, “ajjuposathiko bhaveyyāsī”ti tassa koci nārocesi. Sesakammakarā pātova bhuñjitvā uposathikāva ahesuṃ. Seṭṭhipi saputtadāro saparijano uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhahi, sabbepi uposathikā attano attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā sīlaṃ āvajjentā nisīdiṃsu. Bodhisatto sakaladivasaṃ kammaṃ katvā sūriyatthaṅgamanavelāya āgato. Athassa bhattakārikā hatthadhovanaṃ datvā pātiyaṃ bhattaṃ vaḍḍhetvā upanāmesi. Bodhisatto “aññesu divasesu imāya velāya mahāsaddo hoti, ajja kahaṃ gatā”ti pucchi. “Sabbe uposathaṃ samādiyitvā attano attano vasanaṭṭhānāni gatā”ti. Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto cintesi “ettakānaṃ sīlavantānaṃ antare ahaṃ eko dussīlo hutvā na vasissāmi, idāni uposathaṅgesu adhiṭṭhitesu hoti nu kho uposathakammaṃ, no”ti. So gantvā seṭṭhiṃ [V 3.0394] pucchi. Atha naṃ seṭṭhi “tāta pātova anadhiṭṭhitattā sakalaṃ uposathakammaṃ na hoti, upaḍḍhuposathakammaṃ pana hotī”ti āha.

Then one day, they proclaimed a festival in the city. The great merchant summoned a female servant and said, ‘Today is the Uposatha day. Cook food early in the morning for the workers in the house and give it to them, so that having eaten early, they may become observers of the Uposatha.’ The Bodhisatta rose early and went to work, but no one informed him, ‘You should be an observer of the Uposatha today.’ The other workers ate early in the morning and became observers of the Uposatha. The merchant, along with his wife, children, and household, undertook the Uposatha; all the observers went to their respective dwelling places and sat reflecting on their virtue. The Bodhisatta worked the entire day and returned at the time of sunset. Then the cook gave him water to wash his hands, served food in a bowl, and offered it to him. The Bodhisatta asked, ‘On other days, there is much noise at this time. Where has everyone gone today?’ She replied, ‘All have undertaken the Uposatha and gone to their respective dwelling places.’ Hearing this, the Bodhisatta thought, ‘Among so many virtuous people, I alone shall not remain unvirtuous. Is it still possible for the Uposatha observance to be effective now that the factors have been undertaken, or not?’ He went and asked the merchant. The merchant said to him, ‘Dear one, since you did not undertake it this morning, the full Uposatha observance is not possible, but a half-day Uposatha observance is possible.’

So “ettakampi hotū”ti seṭṭhissa santike samādinnasīlo hutvā uposathakammaṃ adhiṭṭhāya attano vasanokāsaṃ pavisitvā sīlaṃ [M 3.0424] āvajjento nipajji. Athassa sakaladivasaṃ nirāhāratāya pacchimayāmasamanantare satthakavātā samuṭṭhahiṃsu. Seṭṭhinā nānāvidhāni bhesajjāni āharitvā “bhuñjā”ti vuccamānopi “uposathaṃ na bhindissāmi, jīvitapariyantikaṃ katvā samādiyi”nti [P 3.0446] āha. Balavavedanā uppajji, aruṇuggamanavelāya satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ “idāni marissatī”ti nīharitvā “osārake nipajjāpesuṃ. Tasmiṃ khaṇe bārāṇasirājā rathavaragato mahantena parivārena nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto taṃ ṭhānaṃ sampāpuṇi. Bodhisatto tassa siriṃ oloketvā tasmiṃ lobhaṃ uppādetvā rajjaṃ patthesi. So cavitvā upaḍḍhuposathakammanissandena tassa aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Sā laddhagabbhaparihārā dasamāsaccayena puttaṃ vijāyi, “udayakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ pāpuṇi, jātissarañāṇena attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā “appakassa kammassa phalaṃ mama ida”nti abhikkhaṇaṃ udānaṃ udānesi. So pitu accayena rajjaṃ patvāpi attano mahantaṃ sirivibhavaṃ oloketvā tadeva udānaṃ udānesi.

“Let it be even that much,” he said. Having undertaken the precepts in the presence of the merchant, he resolved on the Uposatha observance, then entered his dwelling place and lay down, reflecting on his virtue. Then, because he had been without food the entire day, sharp, cutting pains arose in him just after the last watch of the night. Although the merchant brought various medicines and urged him, “Eat,” he replied, “I will not break my Uposatha. I have undertaken it to last even at the cost of my life.” Intense pain arose, and at the time of the rising dawn, he was unable to maintain mindfulness. Then, thinking, “Now he will die,” they took him out and laid him under the eaves of the house. At that moment, the king of Benares, riding in a splendid chariot with a great retinue, arrived at that place while circumambulating the city. The Bodhisatta, seeing his glory, conceived a longing for it and desired the kingship. After passing away, by the result of his half-day Uposatha observance, he took rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of that king. She, receiving the care befitting pregnancy, gave birth to a son after ten months. They named him Prince Udaya. When he came of age, he attained perfection in all the arts. Remembering his past deeds through the knowledge of past lives, he repeatedly uttered this exclamation: “This is the fruit of my small deed!” After his father’s death, having attained the kingship, he uttered the same exclamation upon beholding his own great glory and prosperity.

Athekadivasaṃ nagare chaṇaṃ sajjayiṃsu, mahājano kīḷāpasuto ahosi. Tadā bārāṇasiyā uttaradvāravāsī eko bhatiko udakabhatiṃ katvā laddhaṃ aḍḍhamāsakaṃ pākāriṭṭhakāya antare ṭhapetvā bhatiṃ karonto dakkhiṇadvāraṃ patvā tattha udakabhatimeva katvā jīvamānāya ekāya kapaṇitthiyā saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Sā taṃ āha – “sāmi, nagare chaṇo vattati, sace te kiñci atthi, mayampi kīḷeyyāmā”ti? “Āma, atthī”ti. “Kittakaṃ, sāmī”ti? “Aḍḍhamāsako”ti. “Kahaṃ so”ti? “Uttaradvāre iṭṭhakabbhantare ṭhapitoti ito me dvādasayojanantare nidhānaṃ, tava pana hatthe kiñci atthī”ti? “Āma, atthī”ti. “Kittaka”nti? “Aḍḍhamāsakovā”ti. “Iti tava aḍḍhamāsako, mama aḍḍhamāsakoti māsakova hoti, tato ekena koṭṭhāsena mālaṃ, ekena koṭṭhāsena gandhaṃ, ekena koṭṭhāsena suraṃ gahetvā kīḷissāma, gaccha tayā ṭhapitaṃ aḍḍhamāsakaṃ [P 3.0447] āharā”ti. So “bhariyāya me santikā kathā laddhā”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭho “bhadde, mā cintayi, āharissāmi na”nti vatvā pakkāmi. Nāgabalo bhatiko cha yojanāni atikkamma [M 3.0425] majjhanhikasamaye vītaccikaṅgārasanthataṃ viya uṇhaṃ vālukaṃ maddanto dhanalobhena haṭṭhapahaṭṭho kasāvarattanivāsano kaṇṇe tālapaṇṇaṃ piḷandhitvā ekena āyogavattena gītaṃ gāyanto rājaṅgaṇena pāyāsi.

One day, they prepared a festival in the city, and the people were intent on merrymaking. At that time, a certain laborer living by the northern gate of Benares, having earned half a māsaka by carrying water, placed it between the bricks of the wall. Continuing to work for wages, he reached the southern gate and there lived with a poor woman who also subsisted by carrying water. She said to him, “Master, a festival is going on in the city. If you have anything, we too could enjoy the festival.” “Yes, I have,” he replied. “How much, master?” “Half a māsaka.” “Where is it?” “It is placed within the bricks at the northern gate—my treasure is twelve yojanas from here. But is there anything in your hand?” “Yes, there is,” she said. “How much?” “Just half a māsaka.” “So, with your half-māsaka and my half-māsaka, there is one māsaka. With one part we shall buy a flower, with one part perfume, and with one part liquor, and we shall enjoy the festival. Go and fetch the half-māsaka you placed there.” Thinking, “I have received these words from my wife,” he was overjoyed and said, “My dear, do not worry, I will bring it,” and set off. The laborer, who had the strength of an elephant, crossed six yojanas. At midday, treading on sand as hot as a bed of flameless embers, overjoyed with greed for wealth, wearing a reddish-brown garment and a palm-leaf ornament in his ear, he proceeded through the royal courtyard singing a song while wearing a shoulder-sash.

Udayarājā [V 3.0395] sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā ṭhito taṃ tathā gacchantaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho esa evarūpaṃ vātātapaṃ agaṇetvā haṭṭhatuṭṭho gāyanto gacchati, pucchissāmi na”nti cintetvā pakkosanatthāya ekaṃ purisaṃ pahiṇi. Tena gantvā “rājā taṃ pakkosatī”ti vutte “rājā mayhaṃ kiṃ hoti, nāhaṃ rājānaṃ jānāmī”ti vatvā balakkārena nīto ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ rājā pucchanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

King Udaya, having opened the lion-window and standing there, saw him walking in such a manner and thought, “Why is this man, disregarding the wind and heat, walking so joyfully while singing? I will ask him.” He sent a man to summon him. When the man went and said, “The king summons you,” he replied, “What is the king to me? I do not know the king,” and continued on. Being brought by force, he stood at a respectful distance. Then the king, wishing to question him, spoke two verses:

36.

36.

“Aṅgārajātā pathavī, kukkuḷānugatā mahī;

Atha gāyasi vattāni, na taṃ tapati ātapo.

“The ground is like embers, the earth is filled with hot ashes; yet you sing, wearing your garments—does the heat not burn you?”

37.

37.

“Uddhaṃ tapati ādicco, adho tapati vālukā;

Atha gāyasi vattāni, na taṃ tapati ātapo”ti.

“The sun burns above, the sand burns below; yet you sing, wearing your garments—does the heat not burn you?”

Tattha aṅgārajātāti bho purisa, ayaṃ pathavī vītaccikaṅgārā viya uṇhajātā. Kukkuḷānugatāti ādittachārikasaṅkhātena kukkuḷena viya uṇhavālukāya anugatā. Vattānīti āyogavattāni āropetvā gītaṃ gāyasīti.

In those verses, “The ground is like embers” means, O man, this earth has become hot like flameless embers. “Filled with hot ashes” means followed by hot sand like the ashes of a fire. “Wearing your garments” (vattāni) means that you sing a song after having put on your shoulder-sashes (āyogavattāni).

So rañño kathaṃ sutvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing the king’s words, he spoke the third verse:

38.

38.

“Na maṃ tapati ātapo, ātapā tapayanti maṃ;

Atthā hi vividhā rāja, te tapanti na ātapo”ti.

“The heat does not burn me; the fires of passion burn me. For, O king, various are the desires; they burn me, not the heat.”

Tattha ātapāti vatthukāmakilesakāmā. Purisañhi te abhitapanti, tasmā “ātapā”ti vuttā. Atthā hi vividhāti, mahārāja, mayhaṃ vatthukāmakilesakāme nissāya kattabbā nānākiccasaṅkhātā vividhā atthā atthi, te maṃ tapanti, na ātapoti.

There, “the fires of passion” (ātapā) refers to the heat of sensual objects and the heat of defilements. These indeed torment a person, thus they are called “heats” (ātapā). “Various are the desires” (atthā hi vividhā) means: O great king, I have various matters to attend to, consisting of various tasks to be done based on the desire for sensual objects and defilements. These burn me, not the external heat.

Atha [P 3.0448] naṃ rājā “ko nāma te attho”ti pucchi. So āha “ahaṃ, deva, dakkhiṇadvāre kapaṇitthiyā saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappesiṃ, sā maṃ ‘chaṇaṃ kīḷissāma, atthi te kiñci hatthe’ti pucchi, atha naṃ ahaṃ ‘mama nidhānaṃ uttaradvāre [M 3.0426] pākārantare ṭhapita’nti avacaṃ, sā ‘gaccha taṃ āhara, ubhopi kīḷissāmā’ti maṃ pahiṇi, sā me tassā kathā hadayaṃ na vijahati, taṃ maṃ anussarantaṃ kāmatapo tapati, ayaṃ me, deva, attho”ti. Atha “evarūpaṃ [V 3.0396] vātātapaṃ agaṇetvā kiṃ te tussanakāraṇaṃ, yena gāyanto gacchasī”ti? “Deva, taṃ nidhānaṃ āharitvā ‘tāya saddhiṃ abhiramissāmī’ti iminā kāraṇena tuṭṭho gāyāmī”ti. “Kiṃ pana te, bho purisa, uttaradvāre ṭhapitanidhānaṃ satasahassamattaṃ atthī”ti? “Natthi, devā”ti. Rājā “tena hi paññāsa sahassāni, cattālīsa, tiṃsa, vīsa, dasa, sahassaṃ, pañca satāni, cattāri, tīṇi, dve, ekaṃ, sataṃ, paññāsaṃ, cattālīsaṃ, tiṃsaṃ, vīsaṃ, dasa, pañca, cattāri, tayo, dve, eko kahāpaṇo, aḍḍho, pādo, cattāro māsakā, tayo, dve, eko māsako”ti pucchi. Sabbaṃ paṭikkhipitvā “aḍḍhamāsako”ti vutto “āma, deva, ettakaṃ mayhaṃ dhanaṃ, taṃ āharitvā tāya saddhiṃ abhiramissāmīti gacchāmi, tāya pītiyā tena somanassena na maṃ esa vātātapo tapatī”ti āha.

Then the king asked him, “What is your purpose?” He replied, “Your Majesty, I live together with a poor woman at the southern gate. She asked me, ‘Shall we celebrate the festival? Do you have anything in hand?’ I told her, ‘I have a treasure hidden between the walls at the northern gate.’ She sent me off, saying, ‘Go fetch it, and we will both celebrate.’ Her words never leave my heart. Remembering them, the heat of desire torments me—this is my purpose, Your Majesty.” Then the king asked, “Disregarding such wind and heat, what is the reason for your joy, by which you go singing?” He replied, “Your Majesty, having fetched that treasure, I think, ‘I will delight with her.’ For this reason, I go singing with joy.” The king asked further, “But, my good man, is the treasure you hid at the northern gate worth a hundred thousand?” “No, Your Majesty.” The king then asked, “Then fifty thousand? Forty thousand? Thirty thousand? Twenty thousand? Ten thousand? A thousand? Five hundred? Four hundred? Three hundred? Two hundred? One hundred? Fifty? Forty? Thirty? Twenty? Ten? Five? Four? Three? Two? One kahāpaṇa? Half? A quarter? Four māsakas? Three? Two? One māsaka?” Rejecting all these, when “Half a māsaka” was mentioned, the man said, “Yes, Your Majesty, that is all my wealth. I am going to fetch it and delight with her. Because of that joy and pleasant mental state, this wind and heat does not torment me.”

Atha naṃ rājā “bho purisa, evarūpe ātape tattha mā gami, ahaṃ te aḍḍhamāsakaṃ dassāmī”ti āha. “Deva, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ kathāya ṭhatvā tañca gaṇhissāmi, itarañca dhanaṃ na nāsessāmi, mama gamanaṃ ahāpetvā tampi gahessāmī”ti. “Bho purisa, nivatta, māsakaṃ te dassāmi, dve māsakehi evaṃ vaḍḍhetvā koṭiṃ koṭisataṃ aparimitaṃ dhanaṃ dassāmi, nivattā”ti vuttepi “deva, taṃ gahetvā itarampi gaṇhissāmi”icceva āha. Tato seṭṭhiṭṭhānādīhi ṭhānantarehi palobhito yāva uparajjā tatheva vatvā “upaḍḍharajjaṃ [P 3.0449] te dassāmi, nivattā”ti vutte sampaṭicchi. Rājā “gacchatha mama sahāyassa kesamassuṃ kāretvā nhāpetvā alaṅkaritvā ānetha na”nti amacce āṇāpesi. Amaccā tathā akaṃsu. Rājā rajjaṃ dvidhā bhinditvā tassa upaḍḍharajjaṃ adāsi. “So pana taṃ gahetvāpi aḍḍhamāsakapemena uttarapassaṃ gatoyevā”ti vadanti. So aḍḍhamāsakarājā nāma ahosi. Te samaggā sammodamānā rajjaṃ kārentā ekadivasaṃ uyyānaṃ gamiṃsu. Tattha kīḷitvā udayarājā aḍḍhamāsakarañño aṅke sīsaṃ katvā nipajji. Tasmiṃ niddaṃ okkante parivāramanussā kīḷānubhavanavasena tattha tattha agamaṃsu.

Then the king said to him, “Good man, do not go in such heat. I will give you half a māsaka.” “Your Majesty, I will abide by your word and take that, and I will not lose the other wealth. Without failing in my journey, I will take that too.” “Good man, turn back. I will give you a māsaka, then two māsakas,” and so on, increasing the amount, “I will give you a crore, a hundred crores, immeasurable wealth. Turn back!” Even when told this, he said, “Your Majesty, having taken that, I will still take the other.” Then, tempted by positions such as treasurer and so on, up to the position of viceroy, he spoke in the same way. When told, “I will give you half the kingdom, turn back,” he agreed. The king ordered his ministers, “Go, have my friend’s hair and beard attended to, bathe him, adorn him, and bring him here.” The ministers did so. The king divided the kingdom in two and gave him half. Yet they say that even after taking that, he still went north out of love for the half māsaka. He became known as King Half-Māsaka. Ruling the kingdom in harmony and rejoicing, one day they went to the park. After playing there, King Udaya laid his head on King Half-Māsaka’s lap and fell asleep. While he was sleeping, the attendants went here and there to enjoy the games.

Aḍḍhamāsakarājā [M 3.0427] “kiṃ me niccakālaṃ upaḍḍharajjena, imaṃ māretvā ahameva sakalarajjaṃ kāressāmī”ti khaggaṃ abbāhitvā “paharissāmi na”nti cintetvā puna “ayaṃ rājā maṃ daliddakapaṇaṃ manussaṃ attanā samānaṃ katvā mahante issariye patiṭṭhapesi, evarūpaṃ nāma yasadāyakaṃ māretvā rajjaṃ kāressāmīti mama icchā uppannā, ayuttaṃ vata me kamma”nti satiṃ paṭilabhitvā asiṃ pavesesi. Athassa dutiyampi tatiyampi tatheva cittaṃ uppajji. Tato cintesi “idaṃ cittaṃ punappunaṃ uppajjamānaṃ maṃ pāpakamme niyojeyyā”ti. So asiṃ bhūmiyaṃ khipitvā rājānaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā “khamāhi me, devā”ti pādesu pati. “Nanu samma, tava mamantare [V 3.0397] doso natthī”ti? “Atthi, mahārāja, ahaṃ idaṃ nāma akāsi”nti. “Tena hi samma, khamāmi te, icchanto pana rajjaṃ kārehi, ahaṃ uparājā hutvā taṃ upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti. So “na me, deva, rajjena attho, ayañhi taṇhā maṃ apāyesu nibbattāpessati, tava rajjaṃ tvameva gaṇha, ahaṃ pabbajissāmi, diṭṭhaṃ me kāmassa mūlaṃ, ayañhi saṅkappena vaḍḍhati, na dāni [P 3.0450] naṃ tato paṭṭhāya saṅkappessāmī”ti udānento catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

King Half-Māsaka thought, “What use is half a kingdom to me perpetually? Having killed him, I myself will rule the entire kingdom.” Unsheathing his sword, he considered, “Shall I strike him?” Then he thought again, “This king made me, a poor and wretched man, his equal and established me in great sovereignty. That the desire to kill such a giver of glory and rule the kingdom should arise in me—this is indeed an improper deed for me.” Regaining mindfulness, he sheathed his sword. Then a second and a third time the same thought arose in him. Thereupon he thought, “This thought, repeatedly arising, might engage me in an evil deed.” He threw the sword to the ground, roused the king, and fell at his feet, saying, “Forgive me, Your Majesty.” The king said, “Surely, friend, there is no fault between you and me?” He answered, “There is, great king. I did such and such a thing.” The king said, “Then, friend, I forgive you. If you wish, rule the kingdom. I shall become your viceroy and attend to you.” He replied, “Your Majesty, I have no need for the kingdom. This craving will cause me to be reborn in states of misery. You yourself take your kingdom. I shall go forth. I have seen the root of desire: it grows through thought. From now on, I shall not form such thoughts.” Thus exclaiming his solemn utterance, he spoke the fourth verse:

39.

39.

“Addasaṃ kāma te mūlaṃ, saṅkappā kāma jāyasi;

Na taṃ saṅkappayissāmi, evaṃ kāma na hehisī”ti.

“I have seen your root, O sensual desire; from thought you are born, O sensual desire. I will not form thoughts of you; thus, O sensual desire, you shall not exist.”

Tattha evanti evaṃ mamantare. Na hehisīti na uppajjissasīti.

Here, 'thus' means 'thus, within me.' 'You shall not exist' means 'you will not arise'.

Evañca pana vatvā puna kāmesu anuyuñjantassa mahājanassa dhammaṃ desento pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

And having spoken thus, teaching the Dhamma to the great multitude who were indulging in sensual pleasures, he spoke the fifth verse:

40.

40.

“Appāpi kāmā na alaṃ, bahūhipi na tappati;

Ahahā bālalapanā, parivajjetha jaggato”ti.

“Even few sensual pleasures are not enough, nor is one satisfied by many. Alas, the babbling of fools! The vigilant one should avoid them.”

Tattha ahahāti saṃvegadīpanaṃ. Jaggatoti jagganto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – mahārāja, imassa mahājanassa appakāpi vatthukāmakilesakāmā na alaṃ pariyattāva, bahūhipi ca tehi na tappateva, “aho ime mama rūpā mama saddā”ti lapanato bālalapanā kāmā, ime vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā bodhipakkhiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanānuyogamanuyutto jagganto kulaputto parivajjetha, pariññāpahānābhisamayehi abhisametvā pajaheyyāti.

Here, 'alas' (ahahā) is an expression of spiritual urgency. 'Jaggato' means 'one who is vigilant.' This is what is said: O great king, for this great multitude, even a few sensual pleasures of objects and defilements are not enough or sufficient, and they are not satisfied even by many of them. Sensual pleasures are called 'the babbling of fools' because of their talk, ‘Oh, these forms are mine, these sounds are mine.’ A vigilant son of good family, devoted to developing insight and applying himself to the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment, should avoid these; he should abandon them, having fully understood them through the realizations of full understanding and abandonment.

Evaṃ [M 3.0428] so mahājanassa dhammaṃ desetvā udayarājānaṃ rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā mahājanaṃ assumukhaṃ rodamānaṃ pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitvā jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā vihāsi. Tassa pabbajitakāle rājā taṃ udānaṃ sakalaṃ katvā udānento chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, having taught the Dhamma to the great multitude and having made King Udaya accept the kingdom, he left the great multitude weeping with tearful faces, entered the Himalayas, went forth, and having developed the jhānas and higher knowledges, he dwelt there. At the time of his going forth, the king, making that utterance complete, while inspired, uttered the sixth verse:

41.

41.

“Appassa [V 3.0398] kammassa phalaṃ mamedaṃ, udayo ajjhāgamā mahattapattaṃ;

Suladdhalābho vata māṇavassa, yo pabbajī kāmarāgaṃ pahāyā”ti.

“This is the fruit of my small deed: Udaya has attained greatness. Truly well-gained is the gain of that young man who went forth, having abandoned sensual lust.”

Tattha udayoti attānaṃ sandhāya vadati. Mahattapattanti mahantabhāvappattaṃ vipulaṃ issariyaṃ ajjhāgamā. Māṇavassāti sattassa mayhaṃ sahāyassa suladdhalābho, yo kāmarāgaṃ pahāya pabbajitoti adhippāyenevamāha.

In those verses, ‘Udaya’ (udayo) refers to himself. ‘Attained greatness’ (mahattapattaṃ) means he attained a great state, vast sovereignty. ‘Of the young man’ (māṇavassa) means of that being, my friend, the gain is well-gained, who went forth having abandoned sensual lust; it was with this intention that he spoke.

Imissā [P 3.0451] pana gāthāya na koci atthaṃ jānāti. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ aggamahesī gāthāya atthaṃ pucchi, rājā na kathesi. Eko panassa gaṅgamālo nāma maṅgalanhāpito, so rañño massuṃ karonto paṭhamaṃ khuraparikammaṃ katvā pacchā saṇḍāsena lomāni gaṇhāti, rañño ca khuraparikammakāle sukhaṃ hoti, lomaharaṇakāle dukkhaṃ. So paṭhamaṃ tassa varaṃ dātukāmo hoti, pacchā sīsacchedanamākaṅkhati. Athekadivasaṃ “bhadde, amhākaṃ gaṅgamālakappako bālo”ti deviyā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “ki pana, deva, kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vutte “paṭhamaṃ saṇḍāsena lomāni gahetvā pacchā khuraparikamma”nti āha. Sā taṃ kappakaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, idāni rañño massukaraṇadivase paṭhamaṃ lomāni gahetvā pacchā khuraparikammaṃ kareyyāsi, raññā ca ‘varaṃ gaṇhāhī’ti vutte ‘aññena, deva, me attho natthi, tumhākaṃ udānagāthāya atthaṃ ācikkhathā’ti vadeyyāsi, ahaṃ te bahuṃ dhanaṃ dassāmī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā massukaraṇadivase paṭhamaṃ saṇḍāsaṃ gaṇhi. “Kiṃ, bhaṇe gaṅgamāla, apubbaṃ te karaṇa”nti raññā vutte “deva, kappakā nāma apubbampi karontī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ lomāni gahetvā pacchā khuraparikammaṃ akāsi. Rājā “varaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti āha. “Deva, aññena me [M 3.0429] attho natthi, tumhākaṃ udānagāthāya atthaṃ kathethā”ti. Rājā attano daliddakāle kataṃ kathetuṃ lajjanto “tāta, iminā te varena ko attho, aññaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti āha. “Etameva dehi, devā”ti. So musāvādabhayena “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā kummāsapiṇḍijātake vuttanayeneva sabbaṃ saṃvidahāpetvā ratanapallaṅke nisīditvā “ahaṃ gaṅgamāla, purimabhave imasmiṃyeva nagare”ti sabbaṃ purimakiriyaṃ ācikkhitvā “iminā kāraṇena upaḍḍhagāthaṃ, ‘sahāyo pana me pabbajito, ahaṃ pamatto hutvā rajjameva kāremī’ti iminā kāraṇena [P 3.0452] pacchā upaḍḍhagāthaṃ vadāmī”ti udānassa atthaṃ kathesi.

However, no one understood the meaning of this verse. Then one day the chief queen asked the king the meaning of the verse, but the king did not tell her. Now, there was a royal barber of his named Gaṅgamāla; when he was attending to the king’s beard, he would first do the razor work and afterwards remove the hairs with tweezers. During the razor work, the king felt pleasure, but during the hair removal, he felt pain. At first the king wished to grant him a boon, but afterwards he desired to cut off his head. Then one day the king informed the queen of the matter, saying, ‘Dear, our barber Gaṅgamāla is foolish.’ When she asked, ‘What then, O King, should be done?’, he replied, ‘He should first remove the hairs with tweezers and afterwards do the razor work.’ She summoned the barber and said, ‘My dear, now on the day you attend to the king’s beard, you should first remove the hairs and afterwards do the razor work. And when the king says, “Take a boon,” you should say, “O King, I have no need for any other boon; tell me the meaning of your utterance-verse.” I will give you much wealth.’ He agreed, saying, ‘Very well,’ and on the day of the beard attendance, he first took the tweezers. When the king asked, ‘Why, friend Gaṅgamāla, are you doing something unprecedented?’, he replied, ‘O King, barbers indeed do unprecedented things,’ and having said this, he first removed the hairs and afterwards did the razor work. The king said, ‘Take a boon.’ He replied, ‘O King, I have no need for any other boon; tell me the meaning of your utterance-verse.’ The king, being ashamed to tell what he had done during his time of poverty, said, ‘My dear, what is the use of this boon to you? Take another.’ ‘Give me only this, O King,’ said the barber. Fearing to speak falsely, the king agreed, ‘Very well,’ and having arranged everything in the manner stated in the Kummāsapiṇḍi Jātaka, he sat on a jeweled throne and, saying, ‘O Gaṅgamāla, in a previous life I was in this very city...’ he recounted all his past deeds and explained the meaning of the utterance: ‘For this reason I speak the first half-verse, and for the reason that my friend has gone forth while I, being heedless, rule the kingdom, I speak the latter half-verse.’

Taṃ sutvā kappako “upaḍḍhuposathakammena kira raññā ayaṃ sampatti laddhā, kusalaṃ nāma kātabbameva, yaṃnūnāhaṃ pabbajitvā attano patiṭṭhaṃ kareyya”nti cintetvā ñātibhogaparivaṭṭaṃ pahāya [V 3.0399] rājānaṃ pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetvā himavantaṃ gantvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tilakkhaṇaṃ āropento vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā paccekabodhiṃ patvā iddhiyā nibbattapattacīvaradharo gandhamādanapabbate pañcachabbassāni vasitvā “bārāṇasirājānaṃ olokessāmī”ti ākāsenāgantvā uyyāne maṅgalasilāyaṃ nisīdi. Uyyānapālo sañjānitvā gantvā rañño ārocesi “deva, gaṅgamālo paccekabuddho hutvā ākāsenāgantvā uyyāne nisinno”ti. Rājā taṃ sutvā “paccekabuddhaṃ vandissāmī”ti vegena nikkhami. Rājamātā ca puttena saddhiṃyeva nikkhami. Rājā uyyānaṃ pavisitvā taṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi saddhiṃ parisāya. So raññā saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karonto “kiṃ, brahmadatta, appamattosi, dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi, dānādīni puññāni karosī”ti rājānaṃ kulanāmena ālapitvā paṭisanthāraṃ karoti.
