Taṃ sutvā rañño mātā “ayaṃ hīnajacco malamajjako nhāpitaputto attānaṃ na jānāti, mama puttaṃ pathavissaraṃ jātikhattiyaṃ ‘brahmadattā’ti nāmenālapatī”ti kujjhitvā sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the barber thought, ‘Indeed, the king obtained this prosperity by the merit of an Uposatha observed for only half a day. Merit should certainly be performed. What if I were to go forth and establish my own refuge?’ Having abandoned the wealth and circle of his relatives and having obtained the king's permission to go forth, he went to the Himalayas, entered the life of an ascetic, and applying the three characteristics, he developed insight and attained Paccekabodhi. Possessing a bowl and robes created by psychic power, he dwelt on Mount Gandhamādana for five or six years. Then, thinking, ‘I will go see the King of Bārāṇasī,’ he came through the air and sat on the auspicious stone slab in the park. The park keeper recognized him, went and reported to the king, ‘O King, Gaṅgamāla has become a Paccekabuddha and, having come through the air, is sitting in the park.’ Hearing that, the king set out quickly, thinking, ‘I will pay homage to the Paccekabuddha.’ The queen mother also set out with her son. The king entered the park, paid homage to him, and sat to one side with his retinue. The Paccekabuddha, exchanging pleasantries with the king, addressed him by his clan name, saying, ‘Brahmadatta, are you diligent? Do you rule the kingdom righteously? Do you perform meritorious deeds such as giving?’ Hearing that, the king’s mother became angry, thinking, ‘This low-born, dirt-cleansing son of a barber does not know himself; he addresses my son, the lord of the earth, a khattiya by birth, by the name “Brahmadatta”!’ Enraged, she spoke the seventh verse:

42.

42.

“Tapasā pajahanti pāpakammaṃ, tapasā nhāpitakumbhakārabhāvaṃ;

Tapasā abhibhuyya gaṅgamāla, nāmenālapasajja brahmadattā”ti.

“Through austerity they abandon evil deeds; through austerity they abandon the state of a barber or potter. Having triumphed through austerity, O Gaṅgamāla, do you now address him as Brahmadatta by name?”

Tassattho [M 3.0430] – ime tāva sattā tapasā attanā katena tapoguṇena pāpakammaṃ jahanti, kiṃ panete tapasā nhāpitakumbhakārabhāvampi jahanti, yaṃ tvaṃ gaṅgamāla, attano tapasā abhibhuyya mama puttaṃ brahmadattaṃ nāmenālapasi, patirūpaṃ nu te etanti?

Its meaning is: ‘These beings indeed abandon evil deeds through the quality of austerity they have cultivated. But do they, through austerity, also abandon the state of a barber or potter? That you, Gaṅgamāla, having surpassed others by your own austerity, address my son Brahmadatta by name—is this proper for you?’

Rājā [P 3.0453] mātaraṃ vāretvā paccekabuddhassa guṇaṃ pakāsento aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, restraining his mother and proclaiming the virtues of the Paccekabuddha, spoke the eighth verse:

43.

43.

“Sandiṭṭhikameva amma passatha, khantīsoraccassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Yo sabbajanassa vanditohu, taṃ vandāma sarājikā samaccā”ti.

“Mother, behold the visible result itself: this is the fruit of patience and gentleness. He who is honored by all people—him we honor, along with the royal family and the ministers.”

Tattha khantīsoraccassāti adhivāsanakhantiyā ca soraccassa ca. Taṃ vandāmāti taṃ idāni mayaṃ sarājikā samaccā sabbe vandāma, passatha amma, khantīsoraccānaṃ vipākanti.

Here, 'of patience and gentleness' (khantīsoraccassa) means 'of patient endurance and of gentleness.' 'Him we honor' (taṃ vandāma) means 'him we all, the royal court and ministers, now honor. See, mother, the result of patience and gentleness.'

Raññā mātari vāritāya sesamahājano uṭṭhahitvā “ayuttaṃ vata, deva, evarūpassa hīnajaccassa tumhe nāmenālapana”nti āha. Rājā mahājanampi paṭibāhitvā tassa guṇakathaṃ kathetuṃ osānagāthamāha –

When his mother had been restrained by the king, the rest of the multitude rose up and said, "It is truly improper, O king, for you to address one of such low birth by name." The king, having also restrained the multitude, spoke the concluding verse to speak of the Paccekabuddha's virtues:

44.

44.

“Mā [V 3.0400] kiñci avacuttha gaṅgamālaṃ, muninaṃ monapathesu sikkhamānaṃ;

Eso hi atari aṇṇavaṃ, yaṃ taritvā caranti vītasokā”ti.

"Do not say anything against Gaṅgamāla, who is training in the paths of silence of the sages; for he has crossed the ocean, having crossed which, the sorrowless ones wander."

Tattha muninanti agārikānagārikasekkhāsekkhapaccekamunīsu paccekamuniṃ. Monapathesu sikkhamānanti pubbabhāgapaṭipadābodhipakkhiyadhammasaṅkhātesu monapathesu sikkhamānaṃ. Aṇṇavanti saṃsāramahāsamuddaṃ.

Therein, 'of the sages' refers to the Paccekabuddha among the householder, non-householder, trainee (sekha), non-trainee (asekha), and Pacceka-munis. 'Training in the paths of silence' means training in the paths of silence consisting of the preliminary practice and the factors of enlightenment. 'The ocean' refers to the great ocean of saṃsāra.

Evañca pana vatvā rājā paccekabuddhaṃ vanditvā “bhante, mayhaṃ mātu khamathā”ti āha. “Khamāmi, mahārājā”ti. Rājaparisāpi naṃ khamāpesi. Rājā attānaṃ nissāya vasanatthāya paṭiññaṃ yāci. Paccekabuddho pana paṭiññaṃ adatvā sarājikāya [M 3.0431] parisāya passantiyāva ākāse ṭhatvā rañño ovādaṃ datvā gandhamādanameva gato.

Having spoken thus, the king venerated the Paccekabuddha and said, 'Venerable sir, please forgive my mother.' 'I forgive, great king,' said the Paccekabuddha. The royal assembly also asked him for forgiveness. The king requested a commitment from him to live under his patronage. However, the Paccekabuddha, without giving a commitment, while the assembly including the king was looking on, stood in the sky, gave advice to the king, and then went to Gandhamādana.

Satthā [P 3.0454] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evañca upāsakā uposathavāso nāma vasitabbayuttako”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā paccekabuddho parinibbāyi, aḍḍhamāsakarājā ānando ahosi, rañño mātā mahāmāyā, aggamahesī rāhulamātā, udayarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse and saying, "Thus, lay followers, the observance of the Uposatha should indeed be kept," connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the Paccekabuddha attained final Nibbāna; King Aḍḍhamāsaka was Ānanda; the king’s mother was Mahāmāyā; the chief queen was the mother of Rāhula; and King Udaya was I myself."

Gaṅgamālajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The commentary on the Gaṅgamāla Jātaka, the fifth.

[422] 6. Cetiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[422] 6. The Commentary on the Cetiya Jātaka

Dhammo have hato hantīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devadattassa pathavipavesanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi divase bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, devadatto musāvādaṃ katvā pathaviṃ paviṭṭho avīciparāyaṇo jāto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi pathaviṃ paviṭṭhoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Dhamma, indeed, when destroyed, destroys”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning Devadatta’s sinking into the earth. On that day, the monks in the Dhamma hall raised a discussion: “Friends, Devadatta, having spoken falsely, has sunk into the earth and is destined for the Avīci hell.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?” When they told him, he said, “Not only now, monks, but in the past, too, he sank into the earth,” and he related the past.

Atīte paṭhamakappe mahāsammato nāma rājā asaṅkhyeyyāyuko ahosi. Tassa putto rojo nāma, tassa putto vararojo nāma, tassa putto kalyāṇo nāma, kalyāṇassa putto varakalyāṇo nāma, varakalyāṇassa putto uposatho nāma, uposathassa [V 3.0401] putto varauposatho nāma, varauposathassa putto mandhātā nāma, mandhātussa putto varamandhātā nāma, varamandhātussa putto varo nāma, varassa putto upavaro nāma ahosi, uparivarotipi tasseva nāmaṃ. So cetiyaraṭṭhe sotthiyanagare rajjaṃ kāresi, catūhi rājiddhīhi samannāgato ahosi uparicaro ākāsagāmī, cattāro naṃ devaputtā catūsu disāsu khaggahatthā rakkhanti, kāyato candanagandho vāyati, mukhato uppalagandho. Tassa kapilo nāma brāhmaṇo [M 3.0432] purohito ahosi. Kapilabrāhmaṇassa pana kaniṭṭho korakalambo nāma raññā saddhiṃ ekācariyakule uggahitasippo bālasahāyo. So tassa kumārakāleyeva “ahaṃ rajjaṃ patvā tuyhaṃ [P 3.0455] purohitaṭṭhānaṃ dassāmī”ti paṭijāni. So rajjaṃ patvā pitu purohitaṃ kapilabrāhmaṇaṃ purohitaṭṭhānato cāvetuṃ nāsakkhi. Purohite pana attano upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchante tasmiṃ gāravena apacitākāraṃ dassesi. Brāhmaṇo taṃ sallakkhetvā “rajjaṃ nāma samavayehi saddhiṃ suparihāraṃ hoti, ahaṃ rājānaṃ āpucchitvā pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā “deva, ahaṃ mahallako, gehe kumārako atthi, taṃ purohitaṃ karohi, ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti rājānaṃ anujānāpetvā puttaṃ purohitaṭṭhāne ṭhapāpetvā rājuyyānaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā puttaṃ nissāya tattheva vāsaṃ kappesi.

In the past, in the first eon, there was a king named Mahāsammata whose lifespan was incalculable. His son was named Roja; his son, Vararoja; his son, Kalyāṇa; Kalyāṇa’s son, Varakalyāṇa; Varakalyāṇa’s son, Uposatha; Uposatha’s son, Varauposatha; Varauposatha’s son, Mandhātā; Mandhātā’s son, Varamandhātā; Varamandhātā’s son, Varo; Varo’s son was named Upavaro—Uparivara was also his name. He ruled in the city of Sotthiya in the Cetiya country. He was endowed with four royal powers and was an 'Uparicara' who could travel through the air. Four divine youths, sword in hand, guarded him in the four directions. From his body, the fragrance of sandalwood wafted; from his mouth, the scent of blue lotuses. His chaplain was a brahmin named Kapila. Now, Kapila the brahmin had a younger brother named Korakalamba, who had learned the arts under the same teacher as the king and was his childhood friend. In his youth, the king had promised him, 'When I become king, I will give you the position of chaplain.' When he became king, he was unable to remove his father’s chaplain, Kapila the brahmin, from the post. However, when the chaplain came to attend on him, the king showed him signs of honor and respect. The brahmin, noticing this, thought, 'A kingdom is well-managed with contemporaries. I will ask the king’s permission and go forth.' Reflecting thus, he said to the king, 'Your Majesty, I am old. There is a young man at home—make him your chaplain; I will go forth.' Having obtained the king’s permission, he had his son installed in the position of chaplain, entered the royal park, and went forth as a sage. Developing meditative attainments and higher knowledges, he lived right there in the park, supported by his son.

Korakalambo “ayaṃ pabbajantopi na mayhaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ dāpesī”ti bhātari āghātaṃ bandhitvā ekadivasaṃ sukhakathāya nisinnasamaye raññā “korakalamba kiṃ tvaṃ purohitaṭṭhānaṃ na karosī”ti vutte “āma, deva, na karomi, bhātā me karotī”ti āha. “Nanu te bhātā pabbajito”ti? “Āma pabbajito, ṭhānantaraṃ pana puttassa dāpesī”ti. “Tena hi tvaṃ karohī”ti? “Deva, paveṇiyā āgataṃ ṭhānantaraṃ mama bhātaraṃ apanetvā na sakkā mayā kātu”nti. “Evaṃ sante ahaṃ taṃ mahallakaṃ katvā bhātaraṃ te kaniṭṭhaṃ karissāmī”ti. “Kathaṃ, devā”ti? “Musāvādaṃ katvā”ti. “Kiṃ deva, na jānātha, yadā mama bhātā mahantena abbhutadhammena samannāgato vijjādharo, so abbhutadhammena tumhe vañcessati, cattāro devaputte antarahite viya karissati, kāyato ca mukhato ca sugandhaṃ duggandhaṃ viya karissati, tumhe ākāsā otāretvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhite viya karissati, tumhe pathaviṃ pavisantā viya bhavissatha, tadā tumhākaṃ kathāya patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkhissathā”ti. “Tvaṃ evaṃ saññaṃ mā kari, ahaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissāmī”ti. “Kadā karissatha, devā”ti? “Ito [P 3.0456] sattame divase”ti. Sā kathā sakalanagare pākaṭā ahosi. “Rājā kira musāvādaṃ katvā mahallakaṃ khuddakaṃ, khuddakaṃ mahallakaṃ karissati, ṭhānantaraṃ khuddakassa dāpessati, kīdiso nu kho musāvādo nāma, kiṃ nīlako, udāhu [M 3.0433] pītakādīsu aññataravaṇṇo”ti evaṃ mahājanassa vitakko udapādi[V 3.0402]. Tadā kira lokassa saccavādīkālo, “musāvādo nāma evarūpo”ti na jānanti.

Korakalambo, holding a grudge against his brother, thinking, 'Even though he has gone forth, he did not give the position to me,' one day, while they were sitting in pleasant conversation, was asked by the king, 'Korakalamba, why do you not perform the duties of the chaplain's office?' He replied, 'Indeed, Your Majesty, I do not; my brother performs them.' 'But has your brother not gone forth?' 'Yes, he has gone forth, but he gave the position to his son.' 'Then you perform them.' 'Your Majesty, it is not possible for me to perform the duties by displacing my brother from the position that has come down by lineage.' 'If that is so, I will make you the elder and your brother the younger.' 'How, Your Majesty?' 'By telling a lie.' 'Your Majesty, do you not know? My brother is a master of knowledge, endowed with great and marvelous qualities. He will deceive you with his wonders: he will make the four divine youths seem to disappear; he will make the sweet fragrance from your body and mouth seem like a foul stench; he will make you, who are in the sky, seem to be standing on the ground; you will be as if entering the earth. Then you will not be able to stand by your word.' 'Do not think so. I will be able to do it.' 'When will you do it, Your Majesty?' 'On the seventh day from now.' This news became known throughout the city. 'The king, it is said, will tell a lie to make the elder the younger and the younger the elder, and he will give the position to the younger one. What sort of thing is a lie? Is it blue, or is it some other color like yellow?' Thus a thought arose among the people. For at that time, it was an age of truth-speaking in the world; they did not know, 'A lie is of such a nature.'

Purohitaputtopi taṃ kathaṃ sutvā pitu santikaṃ gantvā kathesi “tāta, rājā kira musāvādaṃ katvā tumhe khuddake katvā amhākaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ mama cūḷapitussa dassatī”ti. “Tāta, rājā musāvādaṃ katvāpi amhākaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ harituṃ na sakkhissati. Kataradivase pana karissatī”ti? “Ito kira sattame divase”ti. “Tena hi tadā mayhaṃ āroceyyāsī”ti. Sattame divase mahājanā “musāvādaṃ passissāmā”ti rājaṅgaṇe sannipatitvā mañcātimañce bandhitvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Kumāro gantvā pitu ārocesi. Rājā alaṅkatapaṭiyatto nikkhamma mahājanamajjhe rājaṅgaṇe ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Tāpaso ākāsenāgantvā rañño purato nisīdanacammaṃ attharitvā ākāse pallaṅkena nisīditvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ mahārāja, musāvādaṃ katvā khuddakaṃ mahallakaṃ katvā tassa ṭhānantaraṃ dātukāmosī”ti? “Āma ācariya, evaṃ me kathita”nti. Atha naṃ so ovadanto “mahārāja, musāvādo nāma bhāriyo guṇaparidhaṃsako catūsu apāyesu nibbattāpeti. Rājā nāma musāvādaṃ karonto dhammaṃ hanati, so dhammaṃ hanitvā sayameva haññatī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The chaplain's son also heard that news and, going to his father, said, 'Father, the king, it is said, will tell a lie to make you the younger and give our position to my younger uncle.' 'Son, even if the king tells a lie, he will not be able to take away our position. But on which day will he do it?' 'It is said it will be on the seventh day from now.' 'Then you should inform me at that time.' On the seventh day, the people, saying, 'We will see the lie,' gathered in the royal courtyard and stood there having arranged tiered benches. The boy went and informed his father. The king, fully adorned and prepared, came out and stood in the air in the middle of the royal courtyard. The ascetic, coming through the air, spread out his sitting-skin in front of the king and sat cross-legged in the air, asking, 'Is it true, Great King, that you wish to tell a lie, making the younger the elder and giving him the position?' 'Yes, teacher, I have said so.' Then, admonishing him, he said, 'Great King, a lie is a heavy matter; it destroys one's virtues and causes rebirth in the four states of misery. A king who tells a lie destroys the Dhamma; by destroying the Dhamma, he is himself destroyed.' Having said this, he spoke the first verse:

45.

45.

“Dhammo have hato hanti, nāhato hanti kiñcanaṃ;

Tasmā hi dhammaṃ na hane, mā tvaṃ dhammo hato hanī”ti.

'Indeed, the Dhamma, when destroyed, destroys; it does not destroy anything when not destroyed. Therefore, do not destroy the Dhamma, lest the Dhamma, being destroyed, destroy you.'

Tattha [P 3.0457] dhammoti jeṭṭhāpacāyanadhammo idhādhippeto.

Herein, 'Dhamma' means the practice of respecting elders.

Atha naṃ uttaripi ovadanto “sace, mahārāja, musāvādaṃ karissasi, catasso iddhiyo antaradhāyissantī”ti vatvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, further admonishing him, he said, 'Great King, if you tell a lie, your four supernatural powers will vanish,' and he spoke the second verse:

46.

46.

“Alikaṃ bhāsamānassa, apakkamanti devatā;

Pūtikañca mukhaṃ vāti, sakaṭṭhānā ca dhaṃsati;

Yo jānaṃ pucchito pañhaṃ, aññathā naṃ viyākare”ti.

'From one who speaks a lie, the deities depart; his mouth emits a foul odor, and he falls from his place—he who, being asked a question, knowingly explains it otherwise.'

Tattha [M 3.0434] apakkamanti devatāti mahārāja, sace alikaṃ bhaṇissasi, cattāro devaputtā ārakkhaṃ [V 3.0403] chaḍḍetvā antaradhāyissantīti adhippāyenetaṃ vadati. Pūtikañca mukhaṃ vātīti mukhañca te kāyo ca ubho pūtigandhaṃ vāyissantīti sandhāyāha. Sakaṭṭhānā ca dhaṃsatīti ākāsato bhassitvā pathaviṃ pavisissasīti dīpento evamāha.

Herein, 'the deities depart' means: 'Great King, if you speak a lie, the four divine youths will abandon their protection and vanish.' 'His mouth emits a foul odor' was said with reference to: 'Both your mouth and your body will emit a foul stench.' 'Falls from his place' means: 'Falling from the sky, you will enter the earth.'

Taṃ sutvā rājā bhīto korakalambaṃ olokesi. Atha naṃ so “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, nanu mayā paṭhamameva tumhākaṃ etaṃ kathita”nti āha. Rājā kapilassa vacanaṃ sutvāpi anādiyitvā attanā kathitameva purato karonto “tvaṃsi, bhante, kaniṭṭho, korakalambo jeṭṭho”ti āha. Athassa saha musāvādena cattāro devaputtā “tādisassa musāvādino ārakkhaṃ na gaṇhissāmā”ti khagge pādamūle chaḍḍetvā antaradhāyiṃsu, mukhaṃ bhinnakukkuṭaṇḍapūti viya, kāyo vivaṭavaccakuṭī viya duggandhaṃ vāyi, ākāsato bhassitvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhahi, catassopi iddhiyo parihāyiṃsu. Atha naṃ mahāpurohito “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, sace saccaṃ bhaṇissasi, sabbaṃ te pākatikaṃ karissāmī”ti vatvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king, terrified, looked at Korakalamba. Then Korakalamba said to him, 'Do not fear, Great King, did I not tell you this earlier?' Even though the king heard Kapila's words, he did not take them to heart, and putting forward only what he himself had said, he declared, 'You, venerable sir, are the younger, and Korakalamba is the elder.' Simultaneously with that lie, the four divine youths, saying, 'We will not provide protection for such a liar,' threw down their swords at his feet and vanished. His mouth became foul like a broken rotten egg, his body emitted a stench like an open latrine, he fell from the sky and stood on the ground, and all four supernatural powers vanished. Then the chief chaplain, wishing to say, 'Do not fear, Great King; if you speak the truth, I will make everything normal for you again,' spoke the third verse:

47.

47.

“Sace hi saccaṃ bhaṇasi, hohi rāja yathā pure;

Musā ce bhāsase rāja, bhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭha cetiyā”ti.

'If you speak the truth, O King, be as you were before; but if you speak a lie, O Cetiya, stand upon the ground.'

Tattha [P 3.0458] bhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭhāti bhūmiyaṃyeva patiṭṭha, puna ākāsaṃ laṅghituṃ na sakkhissasīti attho.

Herein, 'stand upon the ground' means 'remain established on the ground; you will not be able to rise into the air again.'

So “passa, mahārāja, paṭhamaṃ musāvādeneva te catasso iddhiyo antarahitā, sallakkhehi, idānipi sakkā pākatikaṃ kātu”nti vuttopi “evaṃ vatvā tumhe maṃ vañcetukāmā”ti dutiyampi musāvādaṃ bhaṇitvā yāva gopphakā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Atha naṃ punapi brāhmaṇo “sallakkhehi, mahārāja, idānipi sakkā pākatikaṃ kātu”nti vatvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

The brahmin said, “See, great king, by your first lie alone your four psychic powers vanished. Reflect—even now it is possible to restore things to normal.” But though he was told this, the king said, “You desire to deceive me by saying this,” and lying a second time, he sank into the earth up to his ankles. Then the brahmin said again, “Reflect, great king, even now it is possible to restore things to normal,” and he spoke the fourth verse:

48.

48.

“Akāle vassatī tassa, kāle tassa na vassati;

Yo jānaṃ pucchito pañhaṃ, aññathā naṃ viyākare”ti.

“For one who, when asked a question, knowingly answers it otherwise, it rains out of season, and in season it does not rain.”

Tattha [M 3.0435] tassāti yo jānanto pucchitaṃ pañhaṃ musāvādaṃ katvā aññathā byākaroti, tassa rañño vijite devo yuttakāle avassitvā akāle vassatīti attho.

Herein, by “for him” is meant that for the king who, knowing the question asked, speaks falsehood and answers otherwise, in his realm the rain god will not rain in due season but will rain out of season.

Atha [V 3.0404] naṃ punapi musāvādaphalena yāva jaṅghā pathaviṃ paviṭṭhaṃ “sallakkhehi, mahārājā”ti vatvā pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, as a consequence of his lie, he sank up to his shins in the earth. The brahmin said again, “Reflect, great king,” and spoke the fifth verse:

49.

49.

“Sace hi saccaṃ bhaṇasi, hohi rāja yathā pure;

Musā ce bhāsase rāja, bhūmiṃ pavisa cetiyā”ti.

“If you speak the truth, O king, be as you were before; but if you speak a lie, O King Cetiya, enter the earth.”

So tatiyampi “tvaṃsi, bhante, kaniṭṭho, jeṭṭho korakalambo”ti musāvādameva katvā yāva jāṇukā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Atha naṃ punapi “sallakkhehi, mahārājā”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

He, for the third time, spoke the same lie, saying, “You, venerable sir, are the younger, and Korakalamba is the elder,” and sank into the earth up to his knees. Then the brahmin said to him again, “Reflect, great king,” and spoke two verses:

50.

50.

“Jivhā tassa dvidhā hoti, uragasseva disampati;

Yo jānaṃ pucchito pañhaṃ, aññathā naṃ viyākare.

“The tongue of one who, when asked a question, knowingly answers it otherwise, becomes forked like a snake's, O lord of the realm.”

51.

51.

“Sace hi saccaṃ bhaṇasi, hohi rāja yathā pure;

Musā ce bhāsase rāja, bhiyyo pavisa cetiyā”ti.

“If you speak the truth, O king, be as you were before; but if you speak a lie, O King Cetiya, sink even further.”

Imā dve gāthā vatvā “idāni sakkā pākatikaṃ kātu”nti āha. Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvāpi anādiyitvā “tvaṃsi, bhante, kaniṭṭho, jeṭṭho korakalambo”ti catutthampi musāvādaṃ katvā [P 3.0459] yāva kaṭito pathaviṃ pāvisi. Atha naṃ brāhmaṇo “sallakkhehi, mahārājā”ti vatvā puna dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having spoken these two verses, the brahmin said, “Even now it is possible to restore things to normal.” The king, however, disregarding his words, spoke the fourth lie, saying, “You, venerable sir, are the younger, and Korakalamba is the elder,” and sank into the earth up to his waist. Then the brahmin said to him, “Reflect, great king,” and spoke two more verses:

52.

52.

“Jivhā tassa na bhavati, macchasseva disampati;

Yo jānaṃ pucchito pañhaṃ, aññathā naṃ viyākare.

“One who, when asked a question, knowingly answers it otherwise, has no tongue, like a fish, O lord of the realm.”

53.

53.

“Sace hi saccaṃ bhaṇasi, hohi rāja yathā pure;

Musā ce bhāsase rāja, bhiyyo pavisa cetiyā”ti.

“If you speak the truth, O king, be as you were before; but if you speak a lie, O King Cetiya, sink even further.”

Tattha macchassevāti nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne musāvādino macchassa viya kathanasamatthā jivhā na hoti, mūgova hotīti attho.

Herein, 'like a fish' means that for a liar, in every place of rebirth, there is no tongue capable of speaking, just like a fish; he becomes mute—this is the meaning.

So [V 3.0405] pañcamampi “tvaṃsi kaniṭṭho, jeṭṭho korakalambo”ti musāvādaṃ katvā yāva nābhito pathaviṃ pāvisi. Atha naṃ brāhmaṇo punapi “sallakkhehi, mahārājā”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

For the fifth time, he spoke the lie, “You are the younger, and Korakalamba is the elder,” and sank into the earth up to his navel. Then the brahmin said to him again, “Reflect, great king,” and spoke two verses:

54.

54.

“Thiyova [M 3.0436] tassa jāyanti, na pumā jāyare kule;

Yo jānaṃ pucchito pañhaṃ, aññathā naṃ viyākare.

“In the family of one who, when asked a question, knowingly answers it otherwise, only women are born; no men are born.”

55.

55.

“Sace hi saccaṃ bhaṇasi, hohi rāja yathā pure;

Musā ce bhāsase rāja, bhiyyo pavisa cetiyā”ti.

“If you speak the truth, O king, be as you were before; but if you speak a lie, O King Cetiya, sink even further.”

Tattha thiyovāti nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne musāvādissa dhītarova jāyanti, puttā na jāyantīti attho.

Herein, by 'only women' is meant that for one who speaks falsely, in birth after birth only daughters are born, not sons.

Rājā tassa vacanaṃ anādiyitvā chaṭṭhampi tatheva musāvādaṃ bhaṇitvā yāva thanā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Atha naṃ punapi brāhmaṇo “sallakkhehi, mahārājā”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

The king, disregarding his words, spoke the same lie for the sixth time and sank into the earth up to his chest. Then the brahmin spoke to him again, saying, “Reflect, great king,” and recited two verses:

56.

56.

“Puttā tassa na bhavanti, pakkamanti disodisaṃ;

Yo jānaṃ pucchito pañhaṃ, aññathā naṃ viyākare.

“He has no sons, or they depart in all directions, for him who, when asked a question, knowing the answer, explains it otherwise.”

57.

57.

“Sace hi saccaṃ bhaṇasi, hohi rāja yathā pure;

Musā ce bhāsase rāja, bhiyyo pavisa cetiyā”ti.

“If you speak the truth, be as you were before, O king; but if you speak a lie, O King Cetiya, sink even further.”

Tattha pakkamantīti sace musāvādissa puttā bhavanti, mātāpitūnaṃ anupakārā hutvā palāyantīti attho.

Here, 'pakkamanti' means that if a liar has sons, they become unhelpful to their parents and run away—this is the meaning.

So pāpamittasaṃsaggadosena tassa vacanaṃ anādiyitvā sattamampi tatheva musāvādaṃ akāsi. Athassa pathavī vivaraṃ adāsi, avīcito jālā uṭṭhahitvā gaṇhi.

Due to the fault of associating with bad friends, he disregarded the teacher's words and lied for the seventh time as well. Then the earth split open, and flames from Avīci rose up and seized him.

58.

58.

“Sa [P 3.0460] rājā isinā satto, antalikkhacaro pure;

Pāvekkhi pathaviṃ cecco, hīnatto patva pariyāyaṃ.

That king, cursed by the sage, who once roamed the sky; Cetiya entered the earth, having become inferior and reached his end.

59.

59.

Tasmā [V 3.0406] hi chandāgamanaṃ, nappasaṃsanti paṇḍitā;

Aduṭṭhacitto bhāseyya, giraṃ saccūpasaṃhita”nti. –

Therefore, the wise do not praise partiality. One should speak with a mind free from corruption, words connected with truth.

Imā dve abhisambuddhagāthā honti.

These are two verses spoken after his enlightenment.

Tattha sa rājāti bhikkhave, so rājā cetiyo pubbe antalikkhacaro hutvā pacchā isinā abhisatto parihīnasabhāvo hutvā. Patva pariyāyanti attano kālapariyāyaṃ patvā pathaviṃ pāvisīti attho. Tasmāti [M 3.0437] yasmā cetiyarājā chandāgamanena avīciparāyaṇo jāto, tasmā. Aduṭṭhacittoti chandādīhi adūsitacitto hutvā saccameva bhāseyya.

Here, 'that king' means, monks, that King Cetiya, who formerly traveled in the sky, later, having been cursed by a sage, was ruined in nature. 'Having reached his end' means that having reached his time, he entered the earth—this is the meaning. 'Therefore' means: because King Cetiya, due to acting on partiality, was destined for Avīci, therefore. 'With an uncorrupted mind' means that with a mind undefiled by desire and so on, one should speak only the truth.

Mahājano “cetiyarājā isiṃ akkositvā musāvādaṃ katvā avīciṃ paviṭṭho”ti bhayappatto ahosi. Rañño pañca puttā āgantvā brāhmaṇassa pādesu patitvā “amhākaṃ avassayo hohī”ti vadiṃsu. Brāhmaṇo “tātā, tumhākaṃ pitā dhammaṃ nāsetvā musāvādaṃ katvā isiṃ akkositvā avīciṃ upapanno, dhammo nāmesa hato hanati, tumhehi na sakkā idha vasitu”nti vatvā tesu sabbajeṭṭhakaṃ “ehi tvaṃ, tāta, pācīnadvārena nikkhamitvā ujukaṃ gacchanto sabbasetaṃ sattapatiṭṭhaṃ hatthiratanaṃ passissasi, tāya saññāya tattha nagaraṃ māpetvā vasa, taṃ nagaraṃ hatthipuraṃ nāma bhavissatī”ti āha. Dutiyaṃ āmantetvā “tvaṃ, tāta, dakkhiṇadvārena nikkhamitvā ujukameva gacchanto sabbasetaṃ assaratanaṃ passissasi, tāya saññāya tattha nagaraṃ māpetvā vasa, taṃ nagaraṃ assapuraṃ nāma bhavissatī”ti āha. Tatiyaṃ āmantetvā “tvaṃ, tāta, pacchimadvārena nikkhamitvā ujukameva gacchanto kesarasīhaṃ passissasi, tāya saññāya tattha nagaraṃ māpetvā vasa, taṃ nagaraṃ sīhapuraṃ nāma bhavissatī”ti āha. Catutthaṃ āmantetvā “tvaṃ, tāta, uttaradvārena nikkhamitvā ujukameva gacchanto sabbaratanamayaṃ cakkapañjaraṃ passissasi, tāya saññāya tattha [P 3.0461] nagaraṃ māpetvā vasa, taṃ nagaraṃ uttarapañcālaṃ nāma bhavissatī”ti āha. Pañcamaṃ āmantetvā “tāta, tayā imasmiṃ ṭhāne vasituṃ na sakkā, imasmiṃ nagare mahāthūpaṃ katvā nikkhamitvā pacchimuttarāya disāya ujukameva gacchanto dve pabbate aññamaññaṃ paharitvā paharitvā daddarasaddaṃ karonte passissasi, tāya saññāya tattha nagaraṃ māpetvā vasa, taṃ nagaraṃ daddarapuraṃ nāma bhavissatī”ti āha. Te pañcapi janā tāya tāya saññāya gantvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne nagarāni māpetvā vasiṃsu.

The great populace became fearful, thinking, 'King Cetiya, having reviled the sage and spoken falsely, has entered Avīci.' The king’s five sons came and fell at the brahmin’s feet, saying, 'Be our refuge!' The brahmin said, 'Dear ones, your father, having destroyed the Dhamma, spoken falsely, and reviled the sage, was reborn in Avīci. For the Dhamma, when destroyed, destroys in turn. You cannot stay here.' Then, addressing the eldest, he said, 'Come, dear one, depart by the eastern gate and go straight ahead. You will see an all-white elephant treasure of the sevenfold firm stance. By that sign, build a city there and dwell. That city will be named Hatthipura.' Addressing the second, he said, 'You, dear one, depart by the southern gate and go straight ahead. You will see an all-white horse treasure. By that sign, build a city there and dwell. That city will be named Assapura.' Addressing the third, he said, 'You, dear one, depart by the western gate and go straight ahead. You will see a maned lion. By that sign, build a city there and dwell. That city will be named Sīhapura.' Addressing the fourth, he said, 'You, dear one, depart by the northern gate and go straight ahead. You will see a wheel-frame made entirely of jewels. By that sign, build a city there and dwell. That city will be named Uttarapañcāla.' Addressing the fifth, he said, 'Dear one, you cannot stay in this place. Having built a great stupa in this city, depart and go straight to the northwest. You will see two mountains striking against each other and making a rumbling sound. By that sign, build a city there and dwell. That city will be named Daddarapura.' All five men went according to their respective signs, built cities in those places, and dwelt there.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto musāvādaṃ katvā [V 3.0407] pathaviṃ paviṭṭho”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā cetiyarājā devadatto ahosi, kapilabrāhmaṇo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher said, "Not only now, monks, but in the past too, Devadatta, having spoken falsely, was swallowed by the earth." Then he connected the Jātaka: "At that time, King Cetiya was Devadatta, but the brahmin Kapila was none other than myself."

Cetiyajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Cetiya Jātaka, the Sixth.

[423] 7. Indriyajātakavaṇṇanā

[423] 7. The Commentary on the Indriya Jātaka

Yo [M 3.0438] indriyānanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kireko kulaputto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā “na sakkā agāramajjhe vasantena ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ ekantaparisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carituṃ, niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmī”ti ghare vibhavaṃ puttadārassa niyyādetvā nikkhamitvā satthāraṃ pabbajjaṃ yāci. Satthāpissa pabbajjaṃ dāpesi. Tassa ācariyupajjhāyehi saddhiṃ piṇḍāya carato navakattā ceva bhikkhūnaṃ bahubhāvena ca kulaghare vā āsanasālāya vā āsanaṃ na pāpuṇāti, saṅghanavakānaṃ koṭiyaṃ pīṭhakaṃ vā phalakaṃ vā pāpuṇāti. Āhāropi uḷuṅkapiṭṭhena ghaṭṭitā bhinnasitthakayāgu vā pūtisukkhakhajjakaṃ vā jhāmasukkhakūro vā pāpuṇāti, yāpanapamāṇaṃ na hoti. So attanā [P 3.0462] laddhaṃ gahetvā purāṇadutiyikāya santikaṃ gacchati. Athassa sā pattaṃ gahetvā vanditvā pattato bhattaṃ nīharitvā susampāditāni yāgubhattasūpabyañjanāni deti. Mahallako rasataṇhāya bajjhitvā purāṇadutiyikaṃ jahituṃ na sakkoti. Sā cintesi “baddho nu kho, noti vīmaṃsissāmi na”nti.

'Yo indriyānanti'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the luring by a former wife. In Sāvatthī, it is said, a certain clansman, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, thought, 'It is not possible, while living in a household, to lead the perfectly complete, perfectly pure holy life. I will go forth in the teaching that leads to deliverance and make an end of suffering.' Having handed over his wealth at home to his wife and children, he went forth and requested the going-forth from the Teacher. The Teacher had him ordained. While wandering for alms with his teachers and preceptors, due to being new and the large number of monks, he did not obtain a seat either in the homes of the laity or in the assembly hall; he only obtained a stool or a plank at the end of the row of new monks. As for food, he received gruel with broken rice grains stirred with the back of a ladle, or putrid dry food, or burnt dry rice—it was not enough to sustain him. Taking what he had received, he went to his former wife. Then she, taking his bowl and paying homage, removed the food from the bowl and gave him well-prepared rice gruel, rice, soups, and curries. The elder, bound by craving for flavors, was not able to abandon his former wife. She thought, 'Is he attached or not? I will test him.'

Athekadivasaṃ janapadamanussaṃ setamattikāya nhāpetvā gehe nisīdāpetvā aññepissa katipaye parivāramanusse āṇāpetvā thokathokaṃ pānabhojanaṃ dāpesi. Te khādantā bhuñjantā nisīdiṃsu. Gehadvāre ca cakkesu goṇe bandhāpetvā ekaṃ sakaṭampi ṭhapāpesi, sayaṃ pana piṭṭhigabbhe nisīditvā pūve paci. Mahallako āgantvā dvāre aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ disvā eko mahallakapuriso “ayye, eko thero dvāre ṭhito”ti āha. “Vanditvā aticchāpehī”ti. So “aticchatha, bhante”ti punappunaṃ kathetvāpi taṃ agacchantaṃ disvā “ayye, thero na gacchatī”ti āha. Sā āgantvā sāṇiṃ ukkhipitvā oloketvā “ambho ayaṃ mama dārakapitā”ti vatvā nikkhamitvā pattaṃ gahetvā gehaṃ pavesetvā parivisitvā bhojanapariyosāne vanditvā “bhante, tumhe idheva parinibbāyatha, mayaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ aññaṃ kulaṃ na gaṇhimha, asāmike pana ghare gharāvāso na saṇṭhāti, mayaṃ aññaṃ kulaṃ gaṇhāma, dūraṃ janapadaṃ [V 3.0408] gacchissāma, tumhe appamattā hotha, sace me doso atthi, khamathā”ti āha. Mahallakassa hadayaphālanakālo viya ahosi. Atha naṃ “ahaṃ [M 3.0439] taṃ jahituṃ na sakkomi, mā gaccha, vibbhamissāmi, asukaṭṭhāne me sāṭakaṃ pesehi, pattacīvaraṃ paṭicchāpetvā āgacchissāmī”ti āha. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Mahallako vihāraṃ gantvā ācariyupajjhāye pattacīvaraṃ paṭicchāpento “kasmā, āvuso, evaṃ karosī”ti vutto “purāṇadutiyikaṃ jahituṃ na sakkomi vibbhamissāmī”ti āha. Atha naṃ te anicchantaññeva satthu santikaṃ netvā “kiṃ, bhikkhave, imaṃ anicchantaññeva ānayitthā”ti vutte “bhante, ayaṃ ukkaṇṭhitvā vibbhamitukāmo”ti vadiṃsu. Atha naṃ satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchi. “Saccaṃ, bhante”ti. “Ko taṃ ukkaṇṭhāpesī”ti? “Purāṇadutiyikā bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu na idāneva sā itthī tuyhaṃ anatthakārikā, pubbepi tvaṃ taṃ nissāya catūhi jhānehi parihīno mahādukkhaṃ patvā maṃ nissāya tamhā dukkhā muccitvā naṭṭhajjhānaṃ paṭilabhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

One day, she had a man from the countryside bathed with white clay, made him sit in the house, and ordered that a few of his attendants be given a little food and drink. They sat eating and munching. At the house door, she had oxen yoked to the wheels of carts and placed a cart there; she herself sat in the back room and baked cakes. An elderly monk arrived and stood at the door. Seeing him, an old man of the household said, 'Madam, an elder is standing at the door.' 'Pay respects and tell him to pass on,' she replied. He repeatedly said, 'Please pass on, venerable sir,' but seeing that he did not go, he reported, 'Madam, the elder is not going.' She came, lifted the curtain, looked, and said, 'Oh, this is the father of my child!' Then she went out, took his bowl, led him into the house, served him, and at the end of the meal, she bowed and said, 'Venerable sir, may you attain final Nibbāna right here. For all this time, we have not taken another family. But in a house without a master, a household life cannot be maintained. We will take another family and go to a distant region. Be heedful. If I have any fault, please forgive me.' It was as if the elderly monk's heart would break. Then he said to her, 'I cannot abandon you. Do not go. I will return to the lay life. Send me a lay garment at such-and-such a place. I will hand over my bowl and robes and return.' She agreed, 'Very well.' The elderly monk went to the monastery and, while handing over his bowl and robes to his teacher and preceptor, when asked, 'Friend, why are you doing this?' he replied, 'I cannot abandon my former wife. I will return to the lay life.' Though he was unwilling, they took him to the Teacher. The Teacher asked, 'Monks, why have you brought him against his will?' They replied, 'Venerable sir, this one is discontented and wants to return to the lay life.' The Teacher then asked him, 'Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'Who has made you discontented?' 'My former wife, venerable sir.' The Teacher said, 'Monk, this woman is not only now doing what is harmful to you; in the past too, because of her, you fell away from the four jhānas and reached great misery, but through me, you were freed from that suffering and regained the lost jhānas.' Then he recounted the past.

Atīte [P 3.0463] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa purohitaṃ paṭicca tassa brāhmaṇiyā kucchimhi nibbatti. Jātadivase cassa sakalanagare āvudhāni pajjaliṃsu, tenassa “jotipālakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā rañño sippaṃ dassetvā issariyaṃ pahāya kañci ajānāpetvā aggadvārena nikkhamitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā sakkadattiye kaviṭṭhakaassame isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññāyo nibbattesi. Taṃ tattha vasantaṃ anekāni isisatāni parivāresuṃ, mahāsamāgamo ahosi. So sarabhaṅgasatthā nāma ahosi, tassa satta antevāsikajeṭṭhakā ahesuṃ. Tesu sālissaro nāma isi kaviṭṭhakaassamā nikkhamitvā suraṭṭhajanapade puratthimajanapade sātodikāya nāma nadiyā tīre anekasahassaisiparivāro vasi. Meṇḍissaro nāma isi pajjotakapañcālarañño vijite kalabbacūḷakaṃ nāma nigamaṃ nissāya anekasahassaisiparivāro vasi. Pabbato nāma isi ekaṃ aṭavijanapadaṃ nissāya anekasahassaisiparivāro vasi. Kāḷadevilo nāma isi avantidakkhiṇāpathe ekagghanaselaṃ nissāya anekasahassaisiparivāro vasi. Kisavaccho nāma isi ekakova daṇḍakirañño kumbhavatīnagaraṃ nissāya uyyāne vasi. Anupiyatāpaso pana bodhisattassa upaṭṭhāko tassa santike [M 3.0440] vasi. Nārado nāma isi kāḷadevilassa kaniṭṭho majjhimadese ārañjaragirimhi pabbatajālantare ekakova ekasmiṃ guhāleṇe vasi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the wife of the royal chaplain. On the day of his birth, weapons blazed throughout the entire city, so they named him 'Prince Jotipāla.' When he came of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā, demonstrated his skills to the king, renounced his high position, and left without informing anyone. Departing through the main gate, he entered the forest and went forth as an ascetic in the Kaviṭṭhaka hermitage given by Sakka. There, he developed the meditative absorptions and supernormal knowledges. Many hundreds of ascetics gathered around him, and there was a great assembly. He became known as the teacher Sarabhaṅga, with seven chief senior disciples. Among them, the ascetic named Sālissara left the Kaviṭṭhaka hermitage and settled on the banks of the Sātodikā River in the Suraṭṭha country and the eastern region, surrounded by many thousands of ascetics. The ascetic Meṇḍissara lived near the town of Kalabbacūḷaka in the kingdom of King Pajjota of Pañcāla, attended by many thousands of ascetics. The ascetic Pabbata resided in a certain forest region, likewise surrounded by many thousands of ascetics. The ascetic Kāḷadevila dwelled near a massive rock in Avanti in the southern region, accompanied by many thousands of ascetics. The ascetic Kisavaccha lived alone in a park near the city of Kumbhavatī in the kingdom of Daṇḍaki. The ascetic Anupiya, however, stayed close to the Bodhisatta as his attendant. The ascetic Nārada, the younger brother of Kāḷadevila, lived alone in a cave within a mountain range at Ārañjara in the Middle Country.

Ārañjaragirino nāma avidūre eko ākiṇṇamanusso nigamo atthi, tesaṃ antare mahatī [V 3.0409] nadī atthi, taṃ nadiṃ bahū manussā otaranti. Uttamarūpadharā vaṇṇadāsiyopi purise palobhayamānā tassā nadiyā tīre nisīdanti. Nāradatāpaso tāsu ekaṃ disvā paṭibaddhacitto hutvā jhānaṃ antaradhāpetvā nirāhāro parisussanto [P 3.0464] kilesavasaṃ gantvā sattāhaṃ vasitvā nipajji. Athassa bhātā kāḷadevilo āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā ākāsenāgantvā leṇaṃ pāvisi. Nārado taṃ disvā “kasmā bhavaṃ āgatosī”ti āha. “Bhavaṃ ‘akallako’ti bhavantaṃ paṭijaggituṃ āgatomhī”ti. Atha naṃ so “abhūtaṃ kathaṃ kathesi, alikaṃ tucchaṃ kathesī”ti musāvādena niggaṇhi. So “netaṃ pahātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sālissaraṃ ānesi, meṇḍissaraṃ ānesi, pabbatampi ānesi. Itaropi te tayo musāvādena niggaṇhi. Kāḷadevilo “sarabhaṅgasatthāraṃ ānessāmī”ti ākāsenāgantvā taṃ ānesi. So āgantvā taṃ disvā “indriyavasaṃ gato”ti ñatvā “kacci nārada, indriyānaṃ vasaṃ gato”ti pucchi. Itarena taṃ sutvāva uṭṭhāya vanditvā “āma, ācariyā”ti vutte “nārada, indriyavasaṃ gatā nāma imasmiṃ attabhāve sussantā dukkhaṃ anubhavitvā dutiye attabhāve niraye nibbattantī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Not far from the mountain called Ārañjaragiri, there was a market town crowded with people. Between the mountain and the town, there was a great river which many people crossed. Courtesans of excellent beauty, enticing men, would also sit on the bank of that river. The ascetic Nārada, seeing one of them, became infatuated; his meditative absorption vanished, and, going without food and withering away, he fell under the sway of defilements and lay down for seven days. Then his brother, Kāḷadevila, reflecting on the matter and knowing the reason, came through the sky and entered the cave. Seeing him, Nārada asked, 'Why have you come, sir?' 'Thinking you were unwell, sir, I have come to look after you,' he replied. But Nārada rebuked him with false speech, saying, 'You speak what is not true; you speak what is false and empty.' Thinking, 'It is not right to abandon him,' Kāḷadevila brought the ascetic Sālissara, then Meṇḍissara, and also Pabbata. But Nārada rebuked those three as well with false speech. Kāḷadevila then thought, 'I will bring the teacher Sarabhaṅga,' and, going through the sky, he brought him. When the teacher arrived and saw him, he knew, 'He has fallen under the sway of his faculties,' and asked, 'Nārada, have you perhaps fallen under the sway of your faculties?' As soon as he heard this, Nārada rose, paid homage, and said, 'Yes, teacher.' When he said this, the teacher said, 'Nārada, those who fall under the sway of their faculties wither away in this very life and, having experienced suffering, are reborn in hell in the next life.' He then spoke this first verse:

60.

60.

“Yo indriyānaṃ kāmena, vasaṃ nārada gacchati;

So pariccajjubho loke, jīvantova visussatī”ti.

'Whoever, Nārada, through sensual desire, falls under the sway of the senses, abandons both worlds and withers away even while living.'

Tattha yo indriyānanti nārada, yo puriso rūpādīsu subhākāraṃ gahetvā kilesakāmavasena channaṃ indriyānaṃ vasaṃ gacchati. Pariccajjubho loketi so manussalokañca devalokañcāti ubholoke pariccajitvā nirayādīsu nibbattantīti attho. Jīvantova visussatīti jīvantoyeva attanā icchitaṃ kilesavatthuṃ alabhanto sokena visussati, mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇātīti.

Herein, 'Whoever... of the senses' means: Nārada, any person who, grasping the sign of beauty in forms and so on, falls under the sway of the six senses through the power of sensual defilements. 'Abandons both worlds' means that, having abandoned both the human world and the celestial world, one is reborn in states of woe such as hell. 'Withers away while still alive' means that even while living, not obtaining the desired object of defilement, one withers away with sorrow and reaches great suffering.

Taṃ sutvā nārado “ācariya, kāmasevanaṃ nāma sukhaṃ, evarūpaṃ sukhaṃ kiṃ sandhāya dukkhanti vadasī”ti pucchi. Athassa sarabhaṅgo “tena hi suṇāhī”ti dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having heard that, Nārada asked, 'Teacher, the pursuit of sensual pleasures is happiness. With what in mind do you say that such happiness is suffering?' Then Sarabhaṅga said to him, 'In that case, listen,' and spoke the second verse:

61.

61.

“Sukhassānantaraṃ [M 3.0441] dukkhaṃ, dukkhassānantaraṃ sukhaṃ;

Sosi patto sukhā dukkhaṃ, pāṭikaṅkha varaṃ sukha”nti.

'After happiness, suffering; after suffering, happiness. You have reached suffering from happiness; aspire to the supreme happiness.'

Tattha [P 3.0465] sukhassānantaranti kāmasukhassa anantaraṃ nirayadukkhaṃ. Dukkhassāti sīlarakkhaṇadukkhassa [V 3.0410] anantaraṃ dibbamānusakasukhañceva nibbānasukhañca. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – nārada, ime hi sattā kāmasevanasamaye kālaṃ katvā ekantadukkhe niraye nibbattanti, sīlaṃ rakkhantā vipassanāya kammaṃ karontā ca pana kilamanti, te dukkhena sīlaṃ rakkhitvā sīlabalena vuttappakāraṃ sukhaṃ labhanti, idaṃ dukkhaṃ sandhāyāhaṃ evaṃ vadāmīti. Sosi pattoti so tvaṃ nārada, idāni jhānasukhaṃ nāsetvā tato sukhā mahantaṃ kāmanissitaṃ cetasikadukkhaṃ patto. Pāṭikaṅkhāti idaṃ kilesadukkhaṃ chaḍḍetvā puna tadeva varaṃ uttamaṃ jhānasukhaṃ iccha patthehīti.

Here, 'immediately after happiness' means the suffering of hell that follows sensual pleasure. 'After suffering' means both divine and human happiness and the bliss of Nibbāna that follow the hardship of guarding virtue. This is what is meant: 'Nārada, these beings, at the time of indulging in sensual pleasures, pass away and are reborn in the hell of absolute suffering. But those who guard virtue and perform the work of insight indeed toil, and having guarded virtue with difficulty, they obtain the aforementioned happiness through the power of virtue. It is with reference to this hardship that I speak thus.' 'You have reached' means that you, Nārada, having now destroyed the bliss of meditative absorption, have reached from that happiness the great mental suffering dependent on sensual desire. 'Aspire to' means that, having discarded this suffering of defilements, you should again desire and long for that same supreme and noble bliss of meditative absorption.

Nārado “idaṃ ācariya, dukkhaṃ dussahaṃ, na taṃ adhivāsetuṃ sakkomī”ti āha. Atha naṃ mahāsatto “nārada, dukkhaṃ nāma uppannaṃ adhivāsetabbamevā”ti vatvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Nārada said, 'Teacher, this suffering is hard to bear; I am not able to endure it.' Then the Great Being, saying, 'Nārada, any suffering that has arisen must indeed be endured,' spoke the third verse:

62.

62.

“Kicchakāle kicchasaho, yo kicchaṃ nātivattati;

Sa kicchantaṃ sukhaṃ dhīro, yogaṃ samadhigacchatī”ti.

'The wise one who endures hardship in a time of hardship, and does not yield to hardship, attains the happiness that is the end of hardship and achieves spiritual application.'

Tattha nātivattatīti nānuvattati, ayameva vā pāṭho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – nārada, yo kāyikacetasikadukkhasaṅkhātassa kicchassa uppannakāle appamatto tassa kicchassa haraṇūpāyaṃ karonto kicchasaho hutvā taṃ kicchaṃ nānuvattati, tassa vase avattitvā tehi tehi upāyehi taṃ kicchaṃ abhibhavati vināseti, so dhīro kicchassa antimasaṅkhātaṃ nirāmisasukhasaṅkhātaṃ jhānasukhaṃ adhigacchati, taṃ vā kicchantaṃ yogasukhaṃ adhigacchati, akilamantova pāpuṇātīti.

There, 'does not yield to' (nātivattati) means does not follow along with (nānuvattati); or this is simply the reading. This is what is meant: 'Nārada, when hardship—consisting of bodily and mental suffering—arises, one who is heedful and employs the means to remove that hardship, becoming an endurer of hardship, does not yield to it. Without falling under its control, he overcomes and destroys that hardship by various means. That wise one attains the bliss of meditative absorption, which is known as the end of hardship and as happiness free from sensual stimuli; or he reaches that happiness of spiritual application (yoga) which is the end of hardship, attaining it without weariness.'

So “ācariya, kāmasukhaṃ nāma uttamasukhaṃ, na taṃ jahituṃ sakkomī”ti āha. Atha naṃ mahāsatto “nārada, dhammo nāma na kenaci kāraṇena nāsetabbo”ti vatvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

He said, 'Teacher, sensual pleasure is the supreme pleasure; I cannot give it up.' Then the Great Being, saying, 'Nārada, the Dhamma should not be destroyed for any reason whatsoever,' spoke the fourth verse:

63.

63.

“Na [P 3.0466] heva kāmāna kāmā, nānatthā nātthakāraṇā;

Na katañca niraṅkatvā, dhammā cavitumarahasī”ti.

'Neither for the love of sensual pleasures, nor for what is harmful, nor for the sake of benefit, and not even by disregarding what has been accomplished, should you fall away from the Dhamma.'

Tattha [M 3.0442] kāmāna kāmāti kāmānaṃ kāmā, vatthukāmānaṃ patthanāyāti attho. Nānatthā nātthakāraṇāti na anatthato na atthakāraṇā. Na katañca niraṅkatvāti katañca nipphāditaṃ jhānaṃ [V 3.0411] niraṃkatvā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – nārada, na heva vatthukāmapatthanāya dhammā cavitumarahasi, ekasmiṃ anatthe uppanne taṃ paṭihanitukāmo nānatthā na atthenapi kāraṇabhūtena dhammā cavitumarahasi, “asuko nāma me attho uppajjissatī”ti evampi atthakāraṇāpi na dhammā cavitumarahasi, kataṃ pana nipphāditaṃ jhānasukhaṃ niraṃkatvā vināsetvā neva dhammā cavitumarahasīsi.

There, 'kāmāna kāmā' means 'for the desires of sensual pleasures', that is, for the longing for sensual objects. 'Nānatthā nātthakāraṇā' means not due to harm, and not for the sake of a benefit. 'Na katañca niraṅkatvā' means having discarded the jhāna that has been produced and accomplished. This is what is meant: Nārada, you should not fall away from the Dhamma due to a longing for sensual objects. When harm (anattha) arises and you desire to counteract it, you should not fall away from the Dhamma for that reason, nor even for the sake of some benefit. Even thinking, 'Such and such a benefit will arise for me,' you should not fall away from the Dhamma for the sake of benefit. Moreover, having discarded and destroyed the jhāna happiness that has been produced and accomplished, you should certainly not fall away from the Dhamma.

Evaṃ sarabhaṅgena catūhi gāthāhi dhamme desite kāḷadevilo attano kaniṭṭhaṃ ovadanto pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, when Sarabhaṅga had taught the Dhamma with four verses, Kāḷadevila, advising his younger brother, spoke the fifth verse:

64.

64.

“Dakkhaṃ gahapatī sādhu, saṃvibhajjañca bhojanaṃ;

Ahāso atthalābhesu, atthabyāpatti abyatho”ti.

Good is skill for a householder, and the sharing of food; not being elated at the attainment of gain, and being undisturbed at the failure of gain.

Tattha dakkhaṃ gahapatīti nārada gharāvāsaṃ vasantānaṃ gahapatīnaṃ bhoguppādanatthāya analasyachekakusalabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ dakkhaṃ nāma sādhu, dakkhabhāvo bhaddako. Saṃvibhajjañca bhojananti dukkhena uppāditabhogānaṃ dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇehi saddhiṃ saṃvibhajitvā paribhogakaraṇaṃ dutiyaṃ sādhu. Ahāso atthalābhesūti mahante issariye uppanne appamādavasena ahāso anuppilāvitattaṃ tatiyaṃ sādhu. Atthabyāpattīti yadā pana attano atthabyāpatti yasavināso hoti, tadā abyatho akilamanaṃ catutthaṃ sādhu, tasmā tvaṃ, nārada, “jhānaṃ me antarahita”nti mā soci, sace indriyānaṃ vasaṃ na gamissasi, naṭṭhampi te jhānaṃ puna pākatikameva bhavissatīti.

Here, 'skill, householder' means, Nārada, for householders living in the home life, that skill—defined as being proficient, capable, and free from laziness for the purpose of generating wealth—is good; the state of being skilled is excellent. 'And the sharing of food' means that sharing wealth, obtained with difficulty, with righteous ascetics and brahmins, and then partaking of it, is the second good. 'Not being elated at the attainment of gain' means when great power or wealth arises, not being elated and not being overjoyed by means of heedfulness, is the third good. 'At the failure of gain' means when one’s own loss of benefit and destruction of reputation occurs, then being undisturbed and not weary is the fourth good. Therefore, Nārada, do not grieve thinking, 'My jhāna has disappeared.' If you do not come under the sway of the senses, even if your jhāna is lost, it will be restored to its natural state.

Taṃ puna kāḷadevilena nāradassa ovaditabhāvaṃ ñatvā satthā abhisambuddho hutvā chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, knowing that Kāḷadevila had advised Nārada, the Teacher, having become perfectly enlightened, spoke the sixth verse:

65.

65.

“Ettāvatetaṃ paṇḍiccaṃ, api so devilo bravi;

Na yito kiñci pāpiyo, yo indriyānaṃ vasaṃ vaje”ti.

This is the extent of wisdom, as even Devila said: 'There is no one more wicked than he who comes under the sway of the senses.'

Tassattho [P 3.0467] – bhikkhave, ettakaṃ etaṃ paṇḍiccaṃ soyaṃ devilo abravi. Yo pana kilesavasena indriyānaṃ vasaṃ vajati, ito añño pāpiyo natthīti.

Its meaning is: Monks, this is the extent of the wisdom that Devila spoke: 'But there is no one more wicked than he who, on account of defilements, comes under the sway of the senses.'

Atha [V 3.0412][M 3.0443] naṃ sarabhaṅgo āmantetvā “nārada, idaṃ tāva suṇa, yo hi paṭhamameva kattabbayuttakaṃ na karoti, so araññaṃ paviṭṭhamāṇavako viya socati paridevatī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then Sarabhaṅga addressed him: "Nārada, listen now to this: one who does not do at the very first what ought to be done, grieves and laments like a young man who has entered the forest." Having said this, he recounted the past.

Atīte ekasmiṃ kāsinigame eko brāhmaṇamāṇavo abhirūpo ahosi thāmasampanno nāgabalo. So cintesi – “kiṃ me kasikammādīni katvā mātāpitūhi puṭṭhehi, kiṃ puttadārena, kiṃ dānādīhi puññehi katehi, kañci aposetvā kiñci puññaṃ akatvā araññaṃ pavisitvā mige māretvā attānaṃyeva posessāmī”ti? So pañcāvudhasannaddho himavantaṃ gantvā nānāmige vadhitvā khādanto antohimavante vidhavāya nāma nadiyā tīre giriparikkhittaṃ mahantaṃ pabbatajālaṃ patvā tattha mige vadhitvā aṅgāre pakkamaṃsaṃ khādanto vāsaṃ kappesi. So cintesi “ahaṃ sabbadā thāmasampanno na bhavissāmi, dubbalakāle araññe carituṃ na sakkhissāmi, idāneva nānāvaṇṇe mige pabbatajālaṃ pavesetvā dvāraṃ yojetvā araññaṃ anāhiṇḍantova yathāruciyā mige vadhitvā khādissāmī”ti tathā akāsi. Athassa kāle atikkante taṃ kammaṃ matthakappattaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ jātaṃ, attano hatthapādehi na labhi gantuṃ, aparāparaṃ parivattetuṃ nāsakkhi, neva kiñci khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ, na pānīyaṃ passi, sarīraṃ milāyi, manussapeto ahosi, gimhakāle pathavī viya sarīraṃ bhijjitvā rājiyo dassesi, so durūpo dussaṇṭhito mahādukkhaṃ anubhavi.

In the past, in a certain village in Kasi, there was a handsome young brahmin, endowed with strength and mighty as an elephant. He thought: "What use is it for me to engage in farming and the like to support my parents? What use are children and a wife? What use are meritorious deeds like giving? Without supporting anyone or doing any merit, I will enter the forest, kill animals, and sustain only myself." Armed with five weapons, he went to the Himalayas, killed various animals and ate them. In the inner Himalayas, on the banks of the river named Vidhavā, he reached a great mountain range surrounded by hills. There he killed animals, ate the meat roasted on coals, and took up residence. He thought: "I will not always be strong. When I become weak, I will not be able to roam the forest. Right now, I will drive animals of various kinds into this mountain range, close the entrance, and without wandering the forest, I will kill and eat animals as I please." And so he did. Then, as time passed, that deed came to fruition, becoming experienceable in this very life. He was not able to move with his own hands and feet, nor could he turn himself over. He saw nothing to eat or drink. His body withered; he became a human ghost. Like the earth in the hot season, his body cracked, showing fissures. He became ugly and deformed, and experienced great misery.

Evaṃ addhāne gate siviraṭṭhe sivirājā nāma “araññe aṅgārapakkamaṃsaṃ khādissāmī”ti amaccānaṃ rajjaṃ niyyādetvā pañcāvudhasannaddho araññaṃ pavisitvā mige vadhitvā maṃsaṃ khādamāno anupubbena taṃ padesaṃ patvā taṃ purisaṃ disvā bhītopi satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā “kosi tvaṃ ambho purisā”ti pucchi. “Sāmi, manussapeto ahaṃ, attano katakammassa phalaṃ anubhomi, tvaṃ pana kosī”ti? “Sivirājāhamasmī”ti. “Atha kasmā idhāgatosī”ti? “Migamaṃsaṃ [P 3.0468] khādanatthāyā”ti. Athassa so “ahampi mahārāja, imināva kāraṇena āgantvā manussapeto jāto”ti sabbaṃ vitthārena kathetvā attano dukkhitabhāvaṃ rañño ācikkhanto sesagāthā āha –

Thus, when a long time had passed, in the kingdom of Sivi, a king named Sivirājā thought, "I will eat meat roasted on coals in the forest." Having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, armed with the five weapons, he entered the forest. After killing game and eating the meat, he gradually reached that place and saw that man. Though frightened, he established mindfulness and asked, "Who are you, good sir?" "Lord, I am a human ghost, experiencing the fruit of my own deeds. But who are you?" "I am King Sivi." "Then why have you come here?" "To eat game meat." Then that man said to him, "Great king, I too came for this very reason and became a human ghost." Explaining everything in detail and revealing his suffering to the king, he spoke the remaining verses:

66.

66.

“Amittānaṃva [M 3.0444] hatthatthaṃ, sivi pappoti māmiva;

Kammaṃ vijjañca dakkheyyaṃ, vivāhaṃ sīlamaddavaṃ;

Ete ca yase hāpetvā, nibbatto sehi kammehi.

Like being at the mercy of foes, O Sivi, one meets ruin as I have. Labor, knowledge, skill, marriage, virtue, and gentleness—having lost these along with my reputation, I am reborn by my own deeds.

67.

67.

“Sohaṃ [V 3.0413] sahassajīnova, abandhu aparāyaṇo;

Ariyadhammā apakkanto, yathā peto tathevahaṃ.

I, who am like one who has lost a thousand pieces of wealth, am without kin and without refuge; having strayed from the Noble Dhamma, I am just like a ghost.

68.

68.

“Sukhakāme dukkhāpetvā, āpannosmi padaṃ imaṃ;

So sukhaṃ nādhigacchāmi, ṭhito bhāṇumatāmivā”ti.

Having tormented those who desire pleasure, I have reached this state. I do not attain happiness, like one standing amidst glowing embers.

Tattha amittānaṃva hatthatthanti amittānaṃ hatthe atthaṃ vināsaṃ viya. Sivīti rājānaṃ ālapati. Pappoti māmivāti mādiso pāpakammena pāpuṇāti, attanova kammena vināsaṃ pāpuṇātīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kammanti kasikammādibhedaṃ ājīvasādhakaṃ kiccaṃ. Vijjanti nānappakārakaṃ hatthisippādikaṃ sippaṃ. Dakkheyyanti nānappakārena bhoguppādanakosallaṃ. Vivāhanti āvāhavivāhasambandhaṃ. Sīlamaddavanti pañcavidhasīlañceva muduvacanaṃ hitakāmaṃ pāpanivāraṇaṃ kalyāṇamittatañca. So hi idha maddavoti adhippeto. Ete ca yase hāpetvāti ete ettake yasadāyake dhamme hāpetvā ca. Nibbatto sehi kammehīti attano kammehi nibbatto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ahaṃ, mahārāja, imasmiṃ loke issariyadāyakaṃ kattabbayuttakaṃ kammaṃ akatvā sippaṃ asikkhitvā upāyena bhoge anuppādetvā āvāhavivāhaṃ akatvā sīlaṃ arakkhitvā maṃ akiccaṃ karontaṃ pāpanivāraṇasamatthe kalyāṇamitte abhajitvā ime ettake yasadāyakattā “yase”ti saṅkhyaṃ gate lokappavattidhamme hāpetvā chaḍḍetvā imaṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā sayaṃ katehi pāpakammehi idāni manussapeto hutvā nibbattosmīti.

Here, 'like ruin in the hands of enemies' (hatthatthaṃ) means as if destruction (vināsaṃ) is in the hands of foes. 'Sivi' is how he addresses the king. 'One meets it, as I have' (pappoti māmiva) means 'one like me attains it through an evil deed'; it means that one attains destruction through one's own action. 'Work' (kamma) refers to duties that accomplish a livelihood, such as farming. 'Knowledge' (vijjā) refers to various kinds of crafts, such as the art of elephant training. 'Skill' (dakkheyya) means proficiency in generating wealth in various ways. 'Marriage' (vivāha) refers to the bond of marriage and unions. 'Virtue and gentleness' (sīlamaddava) means the fivefold virtue, as well as gentle speech and the association with a good friend who desires one's welfare and prevents evil. Indeed, that is what 'gentleness' (maddava) is intended to mean here. 'Having abandoned these sources of honor' (yase) means having abandoned these qualities that bestow honor. 'Reborn by his own deeds' means produced by his own actions. This is what is meant: 'O great king, in this world, without performing the work that is proper to be done and which bestows sovereignty, without learning a craft, without generating wealth through skillful means, without entering into marriage, without guarding virtue, and without associating with good friends who are capable of preventing me from improper conduct—having abandoned and discarded these many worldly ways which, because they bestow honor, are reckoned as "honors" (yase)—I entered this forest and, by my own evil deeds, have now been reborn as a human ghost (manussapeta).'

Sahassajīnovāti sahassajīnapuriso viyāti attho. Svāhaṃ sammā paṭipajjitvā bhoge uppādeyyaṃ, tehi anekasahassehi bhogehi jitotipi attho. Aparāyaṇoti asaraṇo, nippatiṭṭhoti attho. Ariyadhammāti sappurisadhammato. Yathā [P 3.0469] petoti yathā mato peto hutvā uppajjeyya, jīvamānoyeva tathā [M 3.0445] manussapeto jātosmīti attho. Sukhakāme dukkhāpetvāti sukhakāme satte dukkhāpetvā. “Sukhakāmo”tipi pāṭho, sayaṃ sukhakāmo paraṃ dukkhāpetvāti attho. Āpannosmi padaṃ imanti evarūpaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ pattosmi. Pathantipi pāṭho, idaṃ dukkhassa pathabhūtaṃ attabhāvaṃ pattosmīti attho. Ṭhito bhāṇumatāmivāti bhāṇumā vuccati aggi, vītaccikaṅgārehi samantā parikiṇṇo viya sarīre uṭṭhitena mahādāhena dayhanto kāyikacetasikasukhaṃ na vindāmīti vadati.

'Sahassajīnova' means like a man who is a thousand-fold victor. The meaning is: if I had practiced rightly, I could have generated wealth, and with those many thousands of riches, I would have been victorious. 'Aparāyaṇo' means without a refuge, that is, without support. 'Ariyadhammā' means from the Dhamma of good people. 'Yathā peto' means as if one were to die and arise as a ghost; the meaning is that even while living, I have become a human ghost. 'Sukhakāme dukkhāpetvā' means having tormented beings who desire happiness. There is also the reading 'Sukhakāmo,' meaning I myself, desiring pleasure, tormented another. 'Āpannosmi padaṃ imaṃ' means I have attained such a state. There is also the reading 'pathaṃ,' meaning I have attained this existence, which has become a path to suffering. 'Ṭhito bhāṇumatāmiva' means: 'bhāṇumā' is said of fire; it means like one surrounded by flameless coals, burning with a great fever that has arisen in the body, I do not find physical or mental happiness—thus he speaks.

Evañca pana vatvā “ahaṃ, mahārāja, sukhakāmo paraṃ dukkhāpetvā diṭṭheva dhamme manussapeto [V 3.0414] jāto, tasmā tvaṃ pāpaṃ mā kari, attano nagaraṃ gantvā dānādīni puññāni karohī”ti āha. Rājā tathā katvā saggapuraṃ pūresi. Sarabhaṅgasatthā imaṃ kāraṇaṃ āharitvā tāpasaṃ saññāpesi. So tassa dhammakathāya saṃvegaṃ paṭilabhitvā taṃ vanditvā khamāpetvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā naṭṭhaṃ jhānaṃ paṭipākatikaṃ akāsi. Sarabhaṅgo tassa tattha vasituṃ adatvā taṃ ādāya attano assamaṃ gato.

Having spoken thus, he said, "O great king, I, desiring happiness, caused suffering to others and became a human ghost (manussapeta) in this very life. Therefore, do not perform evil; go to your own city and perform meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna)." The king did so and filled the heavenly city. The teacher Sarabhaṅga, relating this account, admonished the ascetic. Gaining a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) from that Dhamma talk, the ascetic paid homage to him, asked for forgiveness, performed the kasiṇa preliminary exercises, and restored the jhāna he had lost. Sarabhaṅga, not allowing him to stay there, took him back to his own hermitage.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā nārado ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu ahosi, nagarasobhiṇī purāṇadutiyikā, sālissaro sāriputto, meṇḍissaro kassapo, pabbato anuruddho, kāḷadevilo kaccāyano, anupiyo ānando, kisavaccho mahāmoggallāno, sarabhaṅgo pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, Nārada was the dissatisfied monk, the courtesan (Nagarasobhiṇī) was the former wife, Sālissara was Sāriputta, Meṇḍissara was Kassapa, Pabbata was Anuruddha, Kāḷadevila was Kaccāyana, Anupiya was Ānanda, Kisavaccha was Mahāmoggallāna, and Sarabhaṅga was I myself.

Indriyajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The seventh, the description of the Indriya Jātaka, is finished.

[424] 8. Ādittajātakavaṇṇanā

[424] 8. 8. The Commentary on the Āditta Jātaka

Ādittasminti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto asadisadānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Asadisadānaṃ mahāgovindasuttavaṇṇanāto (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.296) vitthāretvā kathetabbaṃ. Tassa pana dinnadivasato dutiyadivase dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, kosalarājā vicinitvāva[P 3.0470], puññakkhettaṃ ñatvā buddhappamukhassa [M 3.0446] ariyasaṅghassa asadisadānaṃ adāsī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, rañño vicinitvā anuttare puññakkhette dānapatiṭṭhāpanaṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitāpi vicinitvāva mahādānaṃ adaṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this discourse beginning with 'Ādittasmiṃ' concerning the incomparable gift (asadisadāna). The story of the incomparable gift is to be told in detail as found in the commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.296). On the second day after the gift was given, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, the King of Kosala, having carefully investigated and recognized the field of merit, gave the incomparable gift to the Noble Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?' and when they replied, 'For such and such a discussion,' he said, 'It is no wonder, monks, that the king established a gift in the unsurpassed field of merit after careful investigation; the wise of old also gave great gifts only after careful investigation.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte siviraṭṭhe roruvanagare roruvamahārājā nāma dasa rājadhamme akopetvā catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi janaṃ saṅgaṇhanto mahājanassa mātāpituṭṭhāne ṭhatvā kapaṇaddhikavanibbakayācakādīnaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Tassa samuddavijayā nāma aggamahesī ahosi paṇḍitā ñāṇasampannā. So ekadivasaṃ dānaggaṃ olokento “mayhaṃ dānaṃ dussīlā lolasattā bhuñjanti, taṃ maṃ na hāseti, ahaṃ kho pana sīlavantānaṃ aggadakkhiṇeyyānaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ dātukāmo, te ca himavantapadese [V 3.0415] vasanti, ko nu kho te nimantetvā ānessati, kaṃ pesessāmī”ti cintetvā tamatthaṃ deviyā ārocesi. Atha naṃ sā āha “mahārāja, mā cintayittha, amhākaṃ dātabbadānabalena sīlabalena saccabalena pupphāni pesetvā paccekabuddhe nimantetvā tesaṃ āgatakāle sabbaparikkhārasampannadānaṃ dassāmā”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā “sakalanagaravāsino sīlaṃ samādiyantū”ti nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā sayampi saparijano uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya mahādānaṃ pavattetvā sumanapupphapuṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇasamuggaṃ gāhāpetvā pāsādā oruyha rājaṅgaṇe ṭhatvā pañcaṅgāni pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā pācīnadisābhimukho vanditvā “pācīnadisāya arahante vandāmi, sace amhākaṃ koci guṇo atthi, amhesu anukampaṃ katvā amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vatvā satta pupphamuṭṭhiyo khipi. Pācīnadisāya paccekabuddhānaṃ abhāvena punadivase nāgamiṃsu. Dutiyadivase dakkhiṇadisaṃ namassi, tatopi nāgatā. Tatiyadivase pacchimadisaṃ [P 3.0471] namassi, tatopi nāgatā. Catutthadivase uttaradisaṃ namassi, namassitvā ca pana “uttarahimavantapadesavāsino paccekabuddhā amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhantū”ti satta pupphamuṭṭhiyo vissajjesi. Pupphāni gantvā nandamūlakapabbhāre pañcannaṃ paccekabuddhasatānaṃ upari patiṃsu.

In the past, in the Sivi kingdom, in the city of Roruva, there was a great king named Roruva. Without violating the ten royal duties, he supported the people with the four bases of sympathy and, standing in the place of parents for the multitude, he provided great alms to the poor, wayfarers, beggars, and petitioners. His chief queen was named Samuddavijayā, who was wise and endowed with knowledge. One day, while inspecting the alms-hall, he thought: 'My alms are enjoyed by the immoral and the greedy, which does not gladden me. I wish to give to the virtuous, the foremost worthy of offerings—the Paccekabuddhas. But they dwell in the Himalayan region. Who will invite them and bring them here? Whom shall I send?' Reflecting thus, he informed the queen of this matter. Then she said to him: 'Great king, do not worry. By the power of our giving, the power of our virtue, and the power of our truth, let us send flowers to invite the Paccekabuddhas. When they arrive, we will offer them alms complete with all requisites.' The king, approving with "Excellent," had a drum beaten throughout the city, urging all residents to undertake morality. He himself, along with his retinue, undertook the Uposatha precepts and arranged a great alms-giving. Having had a golden casket filled with jasmine flowers brought, he descended from the palace, stood in the royal courtyard, prostrated with his five limbs on the ground, and facing the eastern direction, paid homage, saying: 'I pay homage to the Arahants in the eastern direction. If we possess any virtue, may you, out of compassion for us, accept our alms-food.' Having spoken thus, he threw seven handfuls of flowers. As there were no Paccekabuddhas in the eastern direction, they did not come the next day. On the second day, he paid homage to the southern direction, but they did not come from there either. On the third day, he paid homage to the western direction, but they did not come from there either. On the fourth day, he paid homage to the northern direction, and having paid homage, he said: 'May the Paccekabuddhas dwelling in the northern Himalayan region accept our alms-food,' and released seven handfuls of flowers. The flowers traveled and fell upon five hundred Paccekabuddhas in the Nandamūlaka Grotto.

Te [M 3.0447] āvajjamānā raññā attano nimantitabhāvaṃ ñatvā punadivase satta paccekabuddhe āmantetvā “mārisā, rājā vo nimanteti, tassa saṅgahaṃ karothā”ti vadiṃsu. Satta paccekabuddhā ākāsenāgantvā rājadvāre otariṃsu. Te disvā rājā somanassajāto vanditvā pāsādaṃ āropetvā mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ katvā dānaṃ datvā bhattakiccapariyosāne punadivasatthāya punadivasatthāyāti evaṃ cha divase nimantetvā sattame divase sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ sajjetvā sattaratanakhacitāni mañcapīṭhādīni paññapetvā ticīvarādike sabbasamaṇaparibhoge sattannaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ santike ṭhapetvā “mayaṃ ime parikkhāre tumhākaṃ demā”ti vatvā tesaṃ bhattakiccapariyosāne rājā ca devī ca ubhopi namassamānā aṭṭhaṃsu. Atha nesaṃ anumodanaṃ karonto saṅghatthero dve gāthā abhāsi –

They, reflecting and knowing that they had been invited by the king, the next day addressed seven Paccekabuddhas, saying, 'Sirs, the king invites you; please accept his support.' The seven Paccekabuddhas came through the sky and descended at the king's gate. Seeing them, the king was filled with joy. He paid homage, led them up to the palace, showed them great honor, and gave alms. At the end of the meal, he invited them for the next day, and so on for six days. On the seventh day, he prepared a gift of all requisites—having couches and seats adorned with the seven precious gems spread out, and having the three robes and all other requisites for ascetics placed near the seven Paccekabuddhas—and said, 'We give these requisites to you.' At the end of their meal, both the king and the queen stood paying homage. Then, the elder of the group, expressing his appreciation, spoke two verses—

69.

69.

“Ādittasmiṃ agārasmiṃ, yaṃ nīharati bhājanaṃ;

Taṃ tassa hoti atthāya, no ca yaṃ tattha ḍayhati.

When a house is on fire, whatever vessel one carries out, that is of use to him, not what is burnt therein.

70.

70.

“Evamādīpito loko, jarāya maraṇena ca;

Nīharetheva dānena, dinnaṃ hoti sunīhata”nti.

Even so, the world is ablaze with aging and death. One should carry out [one's wealth] by giving; what is given is well carried out.

Tattha [V 3.0416] ādittasminti taṅkhaṇe pajjalite. Bhājananti upakaraṇaṃ. No ca yaṃ tattha ḍayhatīti yaṃ pana tattha ḍayhati, antamaso tiṇasanthāropi, sabbaṃ tassa anupakaraṇameva hoti. Jarāya maraṇena cāti desanāsīsametaṃ, atthato panesa ekādasahi aggīhi ādīpito nāma. Nīharethevāti [P 3.0472] tato ekādasati aggīhi pajjalitalokā dasavidhadānavatthubhedaṃ taṃ taṃ parikkhāradānaṃ cetanāya nikkaḍḍhetheva. Dinnaṃ hotīti appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā yaṃ dinnaṃ, tadeva sunīhataṃ nāma hotīti.

Herein, 'ādittasmiṃ' means blazing at that very moment. 'Bhājanaṃ' means equipment. As for 'no ca yaṃ tattha ḍayhati', whatever burns there, even a mere grass mat, all of that is of no use to him. 'Jarāya maraṇena ca' is the heading of the teaching; but in meaning, this world is said to be ablaze with the eleven fires. As for 'nīharetheva', it means: from that world blazing with the eleven fires, one should indeed draw out by intention the gift of various requisites, which are divided into the ten kinds of bases for giving. As for 'dinnaṃ hoti', whatever is given, whether little or much, that indeed is called 'well carried out'.

Evaṃ saṅghatthero anumodanaṃ katvā “appamatto hohi, mahārājā”ti rañño ovādaṃ datvā ākāse uppatitvā pāsādakaṇṇikaṃ dvidhā katvā gantvā nandamūlakapabbhāreyeva otari. Tassa dinnaparikkhāropi teneva saddhiṃ uppatitvā nandamūlakapabbhāreyeva otari. Rañño ca deviyā ca sakalasarīraṃ pītiyā puṇṇaṃ ahosi. Evaṃ tasmiṃ gate avasesāpi –

Thus, the elder of the group, having expressed his appreciation, gave the king the advice, 'Be diligent, great king,' rose into the sky, split the pinnacle of the palace in two, and departed, descending right in the Nandamūlaka Grotto. The requisites given to him also rose up with him and descended right in the Nandamūlaka Grotto. The entire bodies of the king and queen were filled with joy. When he had thus departed, the remaining ones also spoke:

71.

71.

“Yo [M 3.0448] dhammaladdhassa dadāti dānaṃ, uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatassa jantu;

Atikkamma so vetaraṇiṃ yamassa, dibbāni ṭhānāni upeti macco.

Whatever person gives a gift from wealth righteously obtained, acquired through the energy of exertion; that mortal, having crossed beyond Yama's river Vetaraṇī, reaches heavenly abodes.

72.

72.

“Dānañca yuddhañca samānamāhu, appāpi santā bahuke jinanti;

Appampi ce saddahāno dadāti, teneva so hoti sukhī parattha.

They say giving and battle are alike: even a few who are good may conquer many. If, with faith, one gives even a little, by that alone one is happy hereafter.

73.

73.

“Viceyya dānaṃ sugatappasatthaṃ, ye dakkhiṇeyyā idha jīvaloke;

Etesu dinnāni mahapphalāni, bījāni vuttāni yathā sukhette.

A gift given with discernment is praised by the Sugata. To those in this living world who are worthy of offerings—gifts given to them are of great fruit, like seeds sown in a good field.

74.

74.

“Yo pāṇabhūtāni aheṭhayaṃ caraṃ, parūpavādā na karoti pāpaṃ;

Bhīruṃ pasaṃsanti na tattha sūraṃ, bhayā hi santo na karonti pāpaṃ.

One who lives without harming living beings, and does no evil from fear of others' blame; they praise the one who fears [sin], not the bold [who sins]; for out of fear, the virtuous do no evil.

75.

75.

“Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati;

Majjhimena ca devattaṃ, uttamena visujjhati.

By an inferior holy life, one is reborn among the Khattiyas; by a middling one, one attains the state of a deva; by the highest, one is purified.

76.

76.

“Addhā hi dānaṃ bahudhā pasatthaṃ, dānā ca kho dhammapadaṃva seyyo;

Pubbeva [P 3.0473] hi pubbatareva santo, nibbānamevajjhagamuṃ sapaññā”ti. –

Truly, giving is praised in many ways, but the path of Dhamma is even better than giving. Indeed, long ago, even earlier, the wise and virtuous attained Nibbāna itself.

Evamekekāya gāthāya anumodanaṃ katvā tatheva agamiṃsu saddhiṃ parikkhārehi.

Thus, having expressed their appreciation with one verse each, they departed in that very same way, together with their requisites.

Tattha [V 3.0417] dhammaladdhassāti khīṇāsavaṃ ādiṃ katvā yāva sukkhavipassakayogāvacaro puggalo dhammassa laddhattā dhammaladdho nāma. Sveva uṭṭhānavīriyena tassa dhammassa adhigatattā uṭṭhānavīriyādhigato nāma. Tassa puggalassa yo jantu dadāti dānanti attho, dhammena laddhassa uṭṭhānasaṅkhātena vīriyena [M 3.0449] adhigatassa deyyadhammassa aggaṃ gahetvā yo jantu sīlavantesu dānaṃ dadātītipi attho. Upayogatthe vā sāmivacanaṃ katvāpettha attho veditabbo. Vetaraṇinti desanāsīsametaṃ, aṭṭha mahāniraye soḷasa ca ussade atikkamitvāti attho. Dibbāni ṭhānāni upetīti devaloke uppajjati.

Herein, 'dhammaladdhassa' (to one who has acquired the Dhamma) means: from one who has destroyed the taints down to a practitioner of dry-insight meditation, a person is called 'one who has acquired the Dhamma' because the Dhamma has been acquired by them. That very person is called 'uṭṭhānavīriyādhigata' (one who has achieved through energetic exertion) because of having achieved that Dhamma through the energy of exertion. The meaning is: 'whatever living being gives a gift to such a person.' Or, the meaning is also: 'whatever living being, having taken the best of a gift-item that was righteously acquired and obtained through the energy known as exertion, gives a gift to the virtuous.' The genitive case here should be understood as having the sense of the accusative. 'Vetaraṇi' is a representative term; the meaning is 'having crossed beyond the eight great hells and the sixteen subsidiary hells.' 'Dibbāni ṭhānāni upeti' means one is reborn in the world of the devas.

Samānamāhūti sadisaṃ vadanti. Khayabhīrukassa hi dānaṃ natthi, bhayabhīrukassa yuddhaṃ natthi. Jīvite ālayaṃ vijahitvā yujjantova yujjhituṃ sakkoti, bhogesu ālayaṃ vijahitvā dāyako dātuṃ sakkoti, teneva taṃ ubhayaṃ “samāna”nti vadanti. Appāpi santāti thokāpi samānā pariccattajīvitā bahuke jinanti, evameva appāpi muñcacetanā bahumpi maccheracittaṃ lobhādiṃ vā kilesagahanaṃ jināti. Appampi ceti thokampi ce deyyadhammaṃ kammañca phalañca saddahanto deti. Teneva soti tena parittadeyyadhammavatthukena parittakenāpi cāgena so parattha sukhī hoti, mahārājāti.

They call it 'equal' because they speak of similarity. For one who fears decline, there is no gift; for one who fears danger, there is no battle. Only by abandoning attachment to life can one truly fight; only by abandoning attachment to possessions can a giver truly give. Thus, they call both 'equal.' 'Appāpi santā' means even a few, having relinquished their lives, conquer many. Just so, even a small generous intention (muñcacetanā) conquers many defilements like stinginess and greed. 'Appampi ce' means if one gives even a little of the things to be given, believing in the deed and its result.
