Therefore, O great king, through that small act of generosity, one becomes happy in the next world.

Viceyya dānanti dakkhiṇañca dakkhiṇeyyañca vicinitvā dinnadānaṃ. Tattha yaṃ vā taṃ vā adatvā aggaṃ paṇītaṃ deyyadhammaṃ vicinitvā dadanto dakkhiṇaṃ vicināti nāma, yesaṃ tesaṃ vā adatvā sīlādiguṇasampanne vicinitvā tesaṃ dadanto dakkhiṇeyyaṃ vicināti nāma. Sugatappasatthanti evarūpaṃ dānaṃ buddhehi pasatthaṃ. Tattha dakkhiṇeyyavicinanaṃ dassetuṃ “ye dakkhiṇeyyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha dakkhiṇeyyāti dakkhiṇāya anucchavikā buddhādayo.

'Giving with discernment' means a gift given after having discerned both the offering and the worthy recipient. Here, not giving just anything, but discerning the best and most excellent offering before giving is called discerning the offering. Not giving to just anyone, but discerning those endowed with virtues like morality before giving to them is called discerning the worthy recipient. 'Praised by the Sugata' means such giving is praised by the Buddhas. In this context, to show the discernment of worthy recipients, it is said, 'Those who are worthy of offerings,' etc. Here, 'worthy of offerings' means those such as the Buddhas who are suitable for offerings.

Pāṇabhūtānīti pāṇasaṅkhātāni bhūtāni. Aheṭhayaṃ caranti kāruññena aviheṭhayanto caramāno. Parūpavādāti parūpavādabhayena pāpaṃ na karoti. Bhīrunti upavādabhīrukaṃ. Na tattha sūranti yo pana ayonisomanasikārena tasmiṃ upavāde sūro hoti, taṃ paṇḍitā nappasaṃsanti. Bhayā hīti upavādabhayena hi paṇḍitā pāpaṃ na karonti.

'Pāṇabhūtāni' means beings so-called because of life. 'Aheṭhayaṃ caraṃ' means walking without harming, with compassion. 'Parūpavādā' means he does no evil for fear of others' blame. 'Bhīruṃ' means one who is fearful of blame. As for 'na tattha sūraṃ,' one who, through unwise attention, becomes bold in the face of that blame—this the wise do not praise. As for 'bhayā hi,' the wise do no evil because of fear of blame.

Hīnena brahmacariyenāti bāhiratitthāyatane tāva methunaviratisīlamattakaṃ [P 3.0474] hīnaṃ brahmacariyaṃ nāma, tena khattiyakule uppajjati. Jhānassa upacāramattaṃ majjhimaṃ, tena devaloke uppajjati. Aṭṭha samāpattiyo uttamaṃ, tena [M 3.0450] brahmaloke uppajjanto visujjhati nāma. Sāsane pana [V 3.0418] sīlavantasseva ekaṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ hīnaṃ nāma, parisuddhasīlasseva samāpattinibbattanaṃ majjhimaṃ nāma, parisuddhasīle ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattuppatti uttamaṃ nāma.

By 'inferior holy life' is meant, in external sectarian practices, the mere virtue of abstinence from sexual intercourse; by this one is born in a noble family. The intermediate is the mere access concentration of jhāna; by this one is born in the heavenly realms. The eight attainments are the highest; by this one is born in the Brahma world and is said to be completely purified. In the Dispensation, however, for a virtuous person who aspires to rebirth in a single heavenly realm, the holy life is called inferior. For one with perfectly pure virtue, the generation of the meditative attainments is called intermediate. For one established in perfectly pure virtue and developing insight, the arising of arahantship is called the highest.

Osānagāthāya ayamattho – mahārāja, kiñcāpi ekaṃseneva dānaṃ bahudhā pasatthaṃ vaṇṇitaṃ, dānato pana samathavipassanāsaṅkhātaṃ nibbānasaṅkhātañca dhammakoṭṭhāsabhūtaṃ dhammapadameva uttaritaraṃ. Kiṃkāraṇā? Pubbeva hi imasmiṃ kappe kassapadasabalādayo pubbatareva vessabhūdasabalādayo santo sappurisā sapaññā samathavipassanaṃ bhāvetvā nibbānameva ajjhagamuṃ adhigatāti.

The meaning of the concluding verse is this: Great king, although giving has been praised and extolled in many ways, the Dhamma-path itself, which is reckoned as serenity and insight and as Nibbāna, being a constituent of the Dhamma, is even superior. Why? Because, previously in this aeon, virtuous and wise persons like Kassapa the Ten-Powered One and others, and earlier still, like Vessabhū the Ten-Powered One and others, having cultivated serenity and insight, attained Nibbāna itself.

Evaṃ satta paccekabuddhā anumodanāya rañño amatamahānibbānaṃ vaṇṇetvā rājānaṃ appamādena ovaditvā vuttanayeneva attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gatā. Rājāpi saddhiṃ aggamahesiyā dānaṃ datvā yāvajīvaṃ ṭhatvā tato cavitvā saggapuraṃ pūresi.

Thus, the seven Paccekabuddhas, having expressed their appreciation and extolled the deathless great Nibbāna to the king, advised him to be heedful and then departed to their own dwelling places in the manner stated. The king, too, having given alms together with his chief queen, remained thus for life and after passing away, filled the heavenly city.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ pubbepi paṇḍitā viceyya dānaṃ adaṃsū”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā paccekabuddhā parinibbāyiṃsu, samuddavijayā rāhulamātā ahosi, roruvamahārājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said, "Thus, even in the past, the wise, having investigated, gave alms," and he connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the Paccekabuddhas attained final Nibbāna; Samuddavijayā was Rāhula’s mother; and King Roruva was indeed myself."

Ādittajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The explanation of the Āditta Jātaka is the eighth.

[425] 9. Aṭṭhānajātakavaṇṇanā

[425] 9. The Explanation of the Aṭṭhāna Jātaka

Gaṅgā kumudinīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kiṃkāraṇā”ti vatvā “kilesavasenā”ti vutte “bhikkhu mātugāmo nāma akataññū mittadubbhī avissāsanīyo. Atīte paṇḍitā devasikaṃ sahassaṃ dentāpi mātugāmaṃ tosetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Sā ekadivasamattaṃ sahassaṃ alabhitvāva [M 3.0451] te gīvāyaṃ gāhāpetvā nīharāpesi[P 3.0475], evaṃ akataññū mātugāmo, mā tassa kāraṇā kilesavasaṃ gacchā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"The Ganges with water lilies..." While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher told this story concerning a discontented monk. He asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?" When the monk replied, "Yes, venerable sir," the Teacher asked, "For what reason?" When the monk said, "Because of defilements," the Teacher then said, "Monk, women are ungrateful, betrayers of friends, and untrustworthy. In the past, even wise men, giving a thousand daily, could not satisfy a woman. She, not having received a thousand for even a single day, had him seized by the neck and thrown out. Such is the ungrateful nature of women; do not fall under the sway of defilements because of her." Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 3.0419] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tassa ca putto brahmadattakumāro, bārāṇasiseṭṭhino ca putto mahādhanakumāro nāma. Te ubhopi sahapaṃsukīḷakā sahāyakā ahesuṃ, ekācariyakuleyeva sippaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Rājakumāro pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāsi, seṭṭhiputtopissa santikeyeva ahosi. Bārāṇasiyañca ekā nagarasobhiṇī vaṇṇadāsī abhirūpā ahosi sobhaggappattā. Seṭṭhiputto devasikaṃ sahassaṃ datvā niccakāle tāyeva saddhiṃ abhiramanto pitu accayena seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ labhitvāpi na taṃ vijahi, tatheva devasikaṃ sahassaṃ datvā abhirami. Seṭṭhiputto divasassa tayo vāre rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati. Athassa ekadivasaṃ rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gatassa raññā saddhiṃ samullapantasseva sūriyo atthaṅgami, andhakāraṃ jātaṃ. So rājakulā nikkhamitvā “idāni gehaṃ gantvā āgamanavelā natthi, nagarasobhiṇiyāyeva gehaṃ gamissāmī”ti upaṭṭhāke uyyojetvā ekakova tassā gehaṃ pāvisi. Atha naṃ sā disvā “ayyaputta, sahassaṃ ābhata”nti āha. “Bhadde, ahaṃ ajjeva ativikālo jāto, tasmā gehaṃ agantvā manusse uyyojetvā ekakova paviṭṭhosmi, sve pana te dve sahassāni dassāmī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, his son was named Prince Brahmadatta, and the son of the Benares merchant was named Mahādhana. These two were childhood friends who had played in the dirt together and learned their skills in the same teacher’s household. The prince, upon his father’s death, was established on the throne, and the merchant’s son remained in his service. In Benares, there was a beautiful courtesan, a city-beautifier, who was exceedingly lovely and had reached the height of charm. The merchant’s son, giving a thousand coins daily, constantly enjoyed himself with her. Even after inheriting the position of merchant upon his father's death, he did not abandon her but continued giving a thousand daily. The merchant’s son visited the king’s court three times a day. One day, while he was conversing with the king during a court visit, the sun set and darkness fell. Leaving the palace, he thought, 'Now there is no time to go home and return; I will go to the courtesan’s house.' Dismissing his attendants, he entered her house alone. Seeing him, she asked, 'Young master, have you brought the thousand?' He replied, 'Dear lady, I am very late today; therefore, I dismissed my people without going home and have come alone. Tomorrow, however, I will give you two thousand.'

Sā cintesi “sacāhaṃ ajja okāsaṃ karissāmi, aññesupi divasesu tucchahatthakova āgamissati, evaṃ me dhanaṃ parihāyissati, na dānissa okāsaṃ karissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ evamāha “sāmi, mayaṃ vaṇṇadāsiyo nāma, amhākaṃ sahassaṃ adatvā keḷi nāma natthī”ti. “Bhadde, sve diguṇaṃ āharissāmī”ti punappunaṃ [P 3.0476] yāci. Nagarasobhiṇī dāsiyo āṇāpesi “etassa idha ṭhatvā maṃ oloketuṃ mā adattha, gīvāyaṃ taṃ gahetvā nīharitvā dvāraṃ pidahathā”ti. Taṃ sutvā dāsiyo tathā kariṃsu. Atha so cintesi “ahaṃ imāya saddhiṃ asītikoṭidhanaṃ khādiṃ, sā maṃ ekadivasaṃ tucchahatthaṃ disvā gīvāyaṃ gahetvā nīharāpesi, aho mātugāmo nāma pāpo nillajjo akataññū mittadubbhī”ti. So mātugāmassa aguṇaṃ anussarantova virajji, paṭikūlasaññaṃ paṭilabhi, gharāvāsepi ukkaṇṭhito [M 3.0452] “kiṃ me gharāvāsena, ajjeva nikkhamitvā pabbajissāmī”ti puna gehaṃ agantvā rājānampi adisvāva nagarā nikkhamitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā gaṅgātīre assamaṃ māpetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññāyo uppādetvā vanamūlaphalāhāro tattha vāsaṃ kappesi.

She thought, 'If I grant him an opportunity today, he will come empty-handed on other days as well. Thus my wealth will diminish. I will not grant him an opportunity now.' Then she said to him, 'Master, we are courtesans; for us, without receiving a thousand, there is no such thing as dalliance.' 'Good lady, tomorrow I will bring double,' he begged again and again. The city-beautifier ordered her maids, 'Do not let him stand here and look at me. Seize him by the neck, cast him out, and shut the door.' Hearing this, the maids did as she ordered. Then he reflected, 'I have spent eighty crores of wealth with this woman. Yet, seeing me empty-handed for just one day, she had me seized by the neck and cast out. Alas, womankind is wicked, shameless, ungrateful, and treacherous to friends.' As he recalled the faults of womankind, he became dispassionate. He acquired the perception of foulness and grew weary of household life. 'What use is household life to me? This very day I shall go forth and renounce.' Without returning home or even seeing the king, he left the city and entered the forest. On the banks of the Ganges, he built a hermitage, undertook the renunciation of a sage, developed the meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, and lived there, sustaining himself on wild roots and fruits.

Rājā taṃ apassanto “kahaṃ mama sahāyo”ti pucchi. Nagarasobhiṇiyāpi katakammaṃ sakalanagare pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ. Athassa tamatthaṃ ācikkhitvā “iti te deva, sahāyo lajjāya gharampi agantvā araññaṃ pavisitvā pabbajito bhavissatī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā taṃ sutvā nagarasobhiṇiṃ [V 3.0420] pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ ekadivasaṃ sahassaṃ alabhitvā mama sahāyaṃ gīvāyaṃ gāhāpetvā nīharāpesī”ti pucchi. “Saccaṃ, devā”ti. “Pāpe jammī, sīghaṃ mama sahāyassa gataṭṭhānaṃ gantvā taṃ ānehi, no ce ānessasi, jīvitaṃ te natthī”ti. Sā rañño vacanaṃ sutvā bhītā rathaṃ āruyha mahantena parivārena nagarā nikkhamitvā tassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pariyesantī sutavasena taṃ ṭhānaṃ sutvā tattha gantvā vanditvā “ayya, mayā andhabālabhāvena kataṃ dosaṃ khamatha, ahaṃ na punevaṃ karissāmī”ti yācitvā “sādhu, khamāmi te, natthi me tayi āghāto”ti vutte “sace me khamatha, mayā saddhiṃ rathaṃ abhiruhatha, nagaraṃ gacchissāma, gatakāle [P 3.0477] yaṃ mama ghare dhanaṃ atthi, sabbaṃ dassāmī”ti āha. So tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “bhadde, idāni tayā saddhiṃ gantuṃ na sakkā, yadā pana imasmiṃ loke yena na bhavitabbaṃ, taṃ bhavissati, api nāma tadā gaccheyya”nti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, not seeing him, asked, 'Where is my friend?' The deed done by the city-beautifier became known throughout the entire city. Then they explained the matter to him, saying, 'Thus, Your Majesty, your friend, out of shame, did not return home but entered the forest and must have renounced.' Hearing this, the king had the city-beautifier summoned and asked, 'Is it true that you, not having received a thousand for one day, had my friend seized by the neck and cast out?' 'It is true, Your Majesty.' 'You wicked, wretched woman! Quickly go to the place where my friend has gone and bring him back. If you do not bring him, your life is forfeit.' Hearing the king's words, she was terrified. Mounting a chariot with a large retinue, she left the city and, seeking his dwelling place, learned of it by hearsay and went there. Having arrived, she paid homage and pleaded, 'Sir, forgive the fault I committed in my blind folly. I will not do such a thing again.' When he said, 'Very well, I forgive you; I bear no ill will towards you,' she said, 'If you forgive me, please mount the chariot with me; let us go to the city. When we return, whatever wealth is in my house, I will give it all to you.' Hearing her words, he replied, 'Good lady, it is not possible for me to go with you now. But when that which should not be in this world comes to pass, then perhaps I might go.' And he spoke the first verse:

77.

77.

“Gaṅgā kumudinī santā, saṅkhavaṇṇā ca kokilā;

Jambū tālaphalaṃ dajjā, atha nūna tadā siyā”ti.

“When the Ganges is still and covered in lilies, and cuckoos are the color of conch shells; when the rose-apple tree bears palm fruits, then indeed might that be.”

Tassattho – bhadde, yathā hi kumudasarā kumudehi sañchannā tiṭṭhanti, tatheva sace sakalāpi mahāgaṅgā kumudinī sīghasotaṃ pahāya santā upasantā siyā, sabbe kokilā ca saṅkhavaṇṇā bhaveyyuṃ, sabbo jamburukkho ca tālaphalaṃ dadeyya. Atha nūna tadā siyāti atha tādise kāle amhākampi samāgamo nūna siyā, bhaveyya nāmāti vuttaṃ hoti.

The meaning is: Good lady, just as ponds of water-lilies stand covered with lilies, so too if the entire great Ganges, abandoning its swift current, were to become calm, tranquil, and lily-covered, and all cuckoos were to become the color of conch shells, and every rose-apple tree were to bear palm fruits—‘then indeed might that be’ means that at such a time our meeting might possibly come to pass.

Evañca [M 3.0453] vatvā punapi tāya “ehi, ayya, gacchāmā”ti vutte “gacchissāmā”ti vatvā “kasmiṃ kāle”ti vutte “asukasmiñca asukasmiñcā”ti vatvā sesagāthā abhāsi –

Having said this, when she again said, 'Come, sir, let us go,' he replied, 'I will go.' And when she asked, 'At what time?' he said, 'At such and such a time,' and spoke the remaining verses:

78.

78.

“Yadā kacchapalomānaṃ, pāvāro tividho siyā;

Hemantikaṃ pāvuraṇaṃ, atha nūna tadā siyā.

“When from the hair of tortoises, a three-ply cloak is made, a covering for the winter season, then indeed might that be.”

79.

79.

“Yadā makasapādānaṃ, aṭṭālo sukato siyā;

Daḷho ca avikampī ca, atha nūna tadā siyā.

“When from the feet of mosquitoes, a watchtower is well-made, strong and unshakeable, then indeed might that be.”

80.

80.

“Yadā sasavisāṇānaṃ, nisseṇī sukatā siyā;

Saggassārohaṇatthāya, atha nūna tadā siyā.

“When from the horns of rabbits, a stairway is well-made for the purpose of ascending to heaven, then indeed might that be.”

81.

81.

“Yadā [V 3.0421] nisseṇimāruyha, candaṃ khādeyyu mūsikā;

Rāhuñca paripāteyyuṃ, atha nūna tadā siyā.

“When mice, having climbed a ladder, might devour the moon and cast down Rāhu, then indeed might that be.

82.

82.

“Yadā surāghaṭaṃ pitvā, makkhikā gaṇacāriṇī;

Aṅgāre vāsaṃ kappeyyuṃ, atha nūna tadā siyā.

“When flies, roaming in a swarm, having drunk from a pot of liquor, might then make their dwelling on hot coals, then indeed might that be.

83.

83.

“Yadā bimboṭṭhasampanno, gadrabho sumukho siyā;

Kusalo naccagītassa, atha nūna tadā siyā.

“When a donkey might be endowed with lips like bimba fruit, have a beautiful face, and be skilled in dance and song, then indeed might that be.

84.

84.

“Yadā kākā ulūkā ca, mantayeyyuṃ rahogatā;

Aññamaññaṃ pihayyeyyuṃ, atha nūna tadā siyā.

“When crows and owls confer in secret and feel affection for one another, then indeed might that be.

85.

85.

“Yadā [P 3.0478] muḷālapattānaṃ, chattaṃ thirataraṃ siyā;

Vassassa paṭighātāya, atha nūna tadā siyā.

“When a parasol made of lotus-stalk leaves might be firm enough to ward off the rain, then indeed might that be.

86.

86.

“Yadā kulako sakuṇo, pabbataṃ gandhamādanaṃ;

Tuṇḍenādāya gaccheyya, atha nūna tadā siyā.

“When a tiny bird might take up Mount Gandhamādana with its beak and fly away, then indeed might that be.

87.

87.

“Yadā sāmuddikaṃ nāvaṃ, sayantaṃ savaṭākaraṃ;

Ceṭo ādāya gaccheyya, atha nūna tadā siyā”ti.

“When a young boy might take an ocean-going ship, lying with its rigging, and carry it away, then indeed might that be.”

Tattha [M 3.0454] tividhoti eko kacchapalomamayena pupphena, eko tūlena, eko ubhayenāti evaṃ tippakāro. Hemantikaṃ pāvuraṇanti himapātasamaye pāvuraṇāya bhavituṃ samattho. Atha nūna tadā siyāti atha tasmiṃ kāle mama tayā saddhiṃ ekaṃseneva saṃsaggo siyā. Evaṃ sabbattha pacchimapadaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Aṭṭālo sukatoti abhiruhitvā yujjhantaṃ purisasataṃ dhāretuṃ yathā sakkoti, evaṃ sukato. Paripāteyyunti palāpeyyuṃ. Aṅgāreti vītaccikaṅgārasanthare. Vāsaṃ kappeyyunti ekekaṃ surāghaṭaṃ pivitvā mattā vaseyyuṃ. Bimboṭṭhasampannoti bimbaphalasadisehi oṭṭhehi samannāgato. Sumukhoti suvaṇṇaādāsasadiso mukho. Pihayeyyunti aññamaññassa sampattiṃ icchantā pihayeyyuṃ pattheyyuṃ. Muḷālapattānanti saṇhānaṃ muḷālagacchapattānaṃ. Kulakoti eko khuddakasakuṇo. Sāmuddikanti samuddapakkhandanamahānāvaṃ. Sayantaṃ savaṭākaranti yantena ceva vaṭākarena [V 3.0422] ca saddhiṃ sabbasambhārayuttaṃ. Ceṭo ādāyāti yadā evarūpaṃ nāvaṃ khuddako gāmadārako hatthena gahetvā gaccheyyāti attho.

Herein, ‘threefold’ means: one made from tortoise-hair fiber, one from cotton, and one from both—thus of three kinds. ‘A covering for the winter season’ means capable of being used as a covering during the time of frost. ‘Then indeed might that be’ means: then, at that time, our union would certainly be. Thus, the last line should be connected in every case. ‘A watchtower well-made’ means so well-constructed that it could support a hundred men fighting after they have climbed it. ‘They would cast down’ means they would drive them away. ‘On coals’ means on a bed of flameless embers. ‘Might make their dwelling’ means that, having each drunk a pot of liquor, they would dwell there intoxicated. ‘Endowed with lips like bimba fruit’ means endowed with lips resembling ripe bimba fruits. ‘Beautiful face’ means a face like a golden mirror. ‘They might feel affection’ means, desiring each other’s success, they would feel affection and longing. ‘Of lotus-stalk leaves’ means of the smooth leaves of the lotus plant. ‘A kulaka’ is a small bird. ‘Ocean-going’ refers to a great ship for crossing the ocean. ‘Lying with its rigging’ means furnished with all its gear, including machinery and sails. ‘A young boy taking it’ means: when a small village boy could take such a ship in his hand and go away with it.

Iti mahāsatto iminā aṭṭhānaparikappena ekādasa gāthā abhāsi. Taṃ sutvā nagarasobhiṇī mahāsattaṃ khamāpetvā nagaraṃ gantvā rañño taṃ kāraṇaṃ ārocetvā attano jīvitaṃ yācitvā gaṇhi.

Thus the Great Being spoke these eleven verses on the theme of impossibility. Hearing them, the city-beauty asked forgiveness of the Great Being, went to the city, reported the matter to the king, and begged for and received her life.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ bhikkhu mātugāmo nāma akataññū mittadubbhī”ti vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma discourse, said, “Thus, monks, womankind is ungrateful and treacherous to friends.” Then, having proclaimed the Truths, he connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the ascetic was I myself.

Aṭṭhānajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Aṭṭhāna Jātaka, the Ninth.

[426] 10. Dīpijātakavaṇṇanā

[426] 10. The Commentary on the Dīpi Jātaka

Khamanīyaṃ [P 3.0479][M 3.0455] yāpanīyanti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ekaṃ eḷikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye mahāmoggallānatthero giriparikkhitte ekadvāre giribbajasenāsane vihāsi. Dvārasamīpeyevassa caṅkamo ahosi. Tadā eḷakapālakā “eḷakā ettha carantū”ti giribbajaṃ pavesetvā kīḷantā viharanti. Tesu ekadivasaṃ sāyaṃ āgantvā eḷake gahetvā gacchantesu ekā eḷikā dūre caramānā eḷake nikkhamante adisvā ohīyi. Taṃ pacchā nikkhamantiṃ eko dīpiko disvā “khādissāmi na”nti giribbajadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Sāpi ito cito ca olokentī taṃ disvā “esa maṃ māretvā khāditukāmatāya ṭhito, sace nivattitvā palāyissāmi, jīvitaṃ me natthi, ajja mayā purisakāraṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā siṅgāni ukkhipitvā tassa abhimukhaṃ vegena pakkhanditvā dīpikassa “ito gaṇhissāmi, ito gaṇhissāmī”ti vipphandatova gahaṇaṃ anupagantvā vegena palāyitvā eḷakānaṃ antaraṃ pāvisi. Atha thero taṃ tesaṃ kiriyaṃ disvā punadivase gantvā tathāgatassa ārocetvā “evaṃ bhante, sā eḷikā attano upāyakusalatāya parakkamaṃ katvā dīpikato muccī”ti āha. Satthā “moggallāna, idāni tāva so dīpiko taṃ gahetuṃ nāsakkhi, pubbe pana naṃ viravantiṃ māretvā khādī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Is it tolerable? Is it maintainable?”—this the Teacher told while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning a certain female goat. On one occasion, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was staying in the single-gated mountain-enclosed dwelling of Giribbaja. His walking path was right near the gate. At that time, goatherds would let their goats graze there, driving them into the mountain enclosure and amusing themselves. One day, when they returned in the evening to take the goats away, a female goat, grazing far off, did not see the others leaving and was left behind. A leopard saw her as she was coming out later and stood at the gate, thinking, “I shall devour her.” She, looking here and there, saw him and thought, “This one stands there wanting to kill and eat me. If I turn back and flee, my life is gone; today I must act with a man’s courage.” Raising her horns, she charged towards the leopard. While he was struggling, thinking, “I’ll catch her here! I’ll catch her there!” she escaped his grasp, fled swiftly, and rejoined the other goats. The Elder, seeing their actions, went the next day and told the Tathāgata, saying, “Venerable sir, that female goat, through her skill in means and effort, escaped from the leopard.” The Teacher said, “Moggallāna, just as that leopard could not catch her now, in the past he killed and ate her while she was bleating,” and being requested, he related the past story.

Atīte [V 3.0423] magadharaṭṭhe bodhisatto ekasmiṃ gāme mahābhogakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññāyo nibbattetvā ciraṃ himavante vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya rājagahaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃyeva giribbaje paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Tadā imināva niyāmena eḷakapālakesu eḷake carantesu ekadivasaṃ evameva ekaṃ eḷikaṃ pacchā nikkhamantiṃ disvā eko dīpiko “khādissāmi na”nti dvāre aṭṭhāsi. Sāpi taṃ disvā “ajja mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ natthi, ekenupāyena iminā saddhiṃ madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ katvā hadayamassa mudukaṃ janetvā [P 3.0480] jīvitaṃ rakkhissāmī”ti cintetvā dūratova tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karontī āgacchamānā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of great wealth in a village in the kingdom of Magadha. When he came of age, he renounced sensual pleasures, became an ascetic, developed the meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, and lived for a long time in the Himalayas. He then went to Rājagaha for the sake of salt and sour fare, and built a leaf hut in that same mountain-enclosed place to live in. At that time, in the same way, as the goatherds were grazing their goats, one day a leopard saw a female goat coming out late and stood at the entrance, thinking, “I shall devour her.” Seeing him, she thought, “Today my life is gone; I must truly strive for the sake of my life. By some stratagem, I will make friendly conversation with this leopard, soften his heart, and save my life.” Thinking thus, she approached him while making friendly conversation from afar and spoke the first verse:

88.

88.

“Khamanīyaṃ [M 3.0456] yāpanīyaṃ, kacci mātula te sukhaṃ;

Sukhaṃ te ammā avaca, sukhakāmāva te maya”nti.

“Is it tolerable, is it maintainable? I hope you are well, uncle? My mother spoke of your well-being; we too desire your happiness.”

Tattha sukhaṃ te ammāti mayhaṃ mātāpi “tumhākaṃ sukhaṃ puccheyyāsī”ti ajja maṃ avacāti attho. Mayanti mātula mayampi tumhākaṃ sukhaṃ eva icchāmāti.

Therein, 'Is it well with you, mother?' means: 'My mother also said to me today, “You should ask after their well-being.”' 'We' means: 'Uncle, we too desire only your happiness.'

Taṃ sutvā dīpiko “ayaṃ dhuttikā maṃ mātulavādena vañcetukāmā, na me kakkhaḷabhāvaṃ jānātī”ti cintetvā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the leopard thought, 'This cunning creature desires to deceive me by calling me "uncle"; she does not know my harsh nature,' and he spoke the second verse:

89.

89.

“Naṅguṭṭhaṃ me avakkamma, heṭhayitvāna eḷike;

Sājja mātulavādena, muñcitabbā nu maññasī”ti.

'Having stepped upon my tail and harassed me, O goat, do you think that today you shall be released by calling me "uncle"?'

Tassattho – tvaṃ mama naṅguṭṭhamaṇḍalaṃ akkamitvā heṭhayitvā āgacchasi, sā tvaṃ “ajja mātulavādena muñcitabbāhamasmī”ti maññasi nu, evaṃ maññasi maññeti.

The meaning is: 'You approach having stepped upon and harassed the circle of my tail. Do you think, "Today I should be released by calling him uncle"?' So you think, it seems.

Taṃ sutvā itarā “mātula, mā evaṃ karī”ti vatvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the other said, 'Uncle, do not speak so,' and spoke the third verse:

90.

90.

“Puratthāmukho nisinnosi, ahaṃ te mukhamāgatā;

Pacchato tuyhaṃ naṅguṭṭhaṃ, kathaṃ khvāhaṃ avakkami”nti.

'You are seated facing the east, and I have come before your face. Your tail is behind you; how then could I have stepped upon it?'

Tattha [V 3.0424] mukhanti abhimukhaṃ. Kathaṃ khvāhaṃ avakkaminti tava pacchato ṭhitaṃ ahaṃ kathaṃ avakkaminti attho.

Therein, 'face' means 'facing'. 'How then could I have stepped upon it?' means: 'How could I have stepped upon that which was situated behind you?'

Atha naṃ so “kiṃ kathesi eḷike, mama naṅguṭṭhassa aṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthī”ti vatvā catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then he said to her, 'What are you saying, goat? There is no place where my tail does not reach,' and spoke the fourth verse:

91.

91.

“Yāvatā [P 3.0481] caturo dīpā, sasamuddā sapabbatā;

Tāvatā mayhaṃ naṅguṭṭhaṃ, kathaṃ kho taṃ vivajjayī”ti.

'As far as the four continents extend, with their seas and mountains, so far extends my tail. How then could you have avoided it?'

Tattha tāvatāti ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ mama naṅguṭṭhaṃ parikkhipitvā gatanti vadati.

Therein, 'so far' means: 'My tail has gone encircling this much space,' he says.

Taṃ sutvā eḷikā “ayaṃ pāpo madhurakathāya na allīyati, paṭisattu hutvā tassa kathessāmī”ti vatvā pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the female goat thought, 'This wicked one is not won over by sweet words. I will become his adversary and speak to him,' and she spoke the fifth verse:

92.

92.

“Pubbeva [M 3.0457] metamakkhiṃsu, mātā pitā ca bhātaro;

Dīghaṃ duṭṭhassa naṅguṭṭhaṃ, sāmhi vehāyasāgatā”ti.

'My mother, father, and brothers told me this before: “Long is the tail of the wicked one!” Therefore, I came through the sky.'

Tattha akkhiṃsūti pubbeva me etaṃ mātā ca pitā ca bhātaro ca ācikkhiṃsu. Sāmhīti sā ahaṃ ñātakānaṃ santikā tava naṅguṭṭhassa dīghabhāvaṃ sutvā tava naṅguṭṭhaṃ pariharantī vehāyasā ākāsena āgatāti.

Therein, 'they told' means: 'My mother, father, and brothers told me this before.' 'I came' means: 'I, having heard from my relatives about the length of your tail, came through the air, through the sky, avoiding your tail.'

Atha naṃ so “jānāmi te ahaṃ ākāsena āgatabhāvaṃ, evaṃ āgacchantī pana mayhaṃ bhakkhe nāsetvā āgatāsī”ti vatvā chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Then he said to her, 'I know that you came through the sky. But in coming thus, you have come having destroyed my food,' and he spoke the sixth verse:

93.

93.

“Tañca disvāna āyantiṃ, antalikkhasmi eḷike;

Migasaṅgho palāyittha, bhakkho me nāsito tayā”ti.

'Seeing you coming through the sky, O goat, the herd of deer fled. My food has been destroyed by you.'

Taṃ sutvā itarā maraṇabhayabhītā aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ āharituṃ asakkontī “mātula, mā evarūpaṃ kakkhaḷakammaṃ kari, jīvitaṃ me dehī”ti vilapi. Itaropi naṃ vilapantiññeva khandhe gahetvā māretvā khādi.

Hearing this, the other, terrified by the fear of death and unable to bring forward any other reason, lamented, 'Uncle, do not do such a cruel deed! Give me my life!' But the other, even as she was lamenting, seized her by the neck, killed, and devoured her.

94.

94.

“Iccevaṃ [V 3.0425] vilapantiyā, eḷakiyā ruhagghaso;

Galakaṃ anvāvamaddi, natthi duṭṭhe subhāsitaṃ.

'Even as the goat lamented thus, the flesh-eater crushed her neck; for the wicked, there is no well-spoken word.'

95.

95.

“Neva duṭṭhe nayo atthi, na dhammo na subhāsitaṃ;

Nikkamaṃ duṭṭhe yuñjetha, so ca sabbhiṃ na rañjatī”ti. –

'In the wicked, there is neither reason, nor righteousness, nor well-spoken word; one should apply effort against the wicked, for such a one does not delight in what is well-spoken.'

Imā dve abhisambuddhagāthā –

These two are verses of the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Tattha [P 3.0482] ruhagghasoti ruhirabhakkho lohitapāyī sāhasikadīpiko. Galakaṃ anvāvamaddīti gīvaṃ maddi, ḍaṃsitvā phālesīti attho. Nayoti kāraṇaṃ. Dhammoti sabhāvo. Subhāsitanti sukathitavacanaṃ, sabbametaṃ duṭṭhe natthīti attho. Nikkamaṃ duṭṭhe yuñjethāti bhikkhave, duṭṭhapuggale parakkamameva yuñjeyya. So ca sabbhiṃ na rañjatīti so pana puggalo sabbhiṃ sundaraṃ subhāsitaṃ na rañjati, na piyāyatīti attho. Tāpaso tesaṃ kiriyaṃ sabbaṃ addasa.

Therein, ‘flesh-eater’ means a blood-eater, a blood-drinker, a violent leopard. ‘Crushed her neck’ means he crushed the neck; the meaning is that, having bitten it, he tore it apart. ‘Reason’ means cause. ‘Righteousness’ means nature. ‘Well-spoken word’ means a well-said utterance; the meaning is that all these are absent in the wicked. ‘One should apply effort against the wicked’ means: 'Bhikkhus, one should apply only exertion against a wicked person.' ‘For such a one does not delight in what is well-spoken’ means that person does not delight in, nor find pleasing, what is beautiful and well-spoken. The ascetic saw all their actions.

Satthā [M 3.0458] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā eḷikāva etarahi eḷikā ahosi, dīpikopi etarahi dīpikova, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka thus: “At that time the female goat was the present female goat, the leopard was the present leopard, but the ascetic was I myself.”

Dīpijātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Dīpi Jātaka, the Tenth.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

The Summary of the Jātakas:

Kaccānī aṭṭhasaddañca, sulasā ca sumaṅgalaṃ;

Gaṅgamālañca cetiyaṃ, indriyañceva ādittaṃ;

Aṭṭhānañceva dīpi ca, dasa aṭṭhanipātake.

Kaccānī and Aṭṭhasadda, Sulasā and Sumaṅgala; Gaṅgamāla and Cetiya, Indriya and Āditta; Aṭṭhāna and Dīpi also—these ten are in the Book of Eights.

Aṭṭhakanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Book of Eights is concluded.

9. Navakanipāto

9. The Book of Nines

[427] 1. Gijjhajātakavaṇṇanā

[427] 1. The Commentary on the Gijjha Jātaka

Parisaṅkupatho [V 3.0426][P 3.0483][M 3.0459] nāmāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ dubbacabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira eko kulaputto niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvāpi atthakāmehi ācariyupajjhāyehi ceva sabrahmacārīhi ca “evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ paṭikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ ālokitabbaṃ, evaṃ vilokitabbaṃ, evaṃ samiñjitabbaṃ, evaṃ pasāritabbaṃ, evaṃ nivāsetabbaṃ, evaṃ pārupitabbaṃ, evaṃ patto gahetabbo, yāpanamattaṃ bhattaṃ gahetvā paccavekkhitvāva paribhuñjitabbaṃ, indriyesu guttadvārena bhojane mattaññunā jāgariyamanuyuttena bhavitabbaṃ, idaṃ āgantukavattaṃ nāma jānitabbaṃ, idaṃ gamikavattaṃ nāma, imāni cuddasa khandhakavattāni, asīti mahāvattāni. Tattha te sammā vattitabbaṃ, ime terasa dhutaṅgaguṇā nāma, ete samādāya vattitabba”nti ovadiyamāno dubbaco ahosi akkhamo appadakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsaniṃ. “Ahaṃ tumhe na vadāmi, tumhe pana maṃ kasmā vadatha, ahameva attano atthaṃ vā anatthaṃ vā jānissāmī”ti attānaṃ avacanīyaṃ akāsi. Athassa dubbacabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ aguṇakathaṃ kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte taṃ bhikkhuṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu dubbacosī”ti pucchitvā “sacca”nti vutte “kasmā bhikkhu evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā [P 3.0484] atthakāmānaṃ vacanaṃ na karosi, pubbepi tvaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ akatvā verambhavātamukhe cuṇṇavicuṇṇo jāto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘Parisaṅkupatho’ is its name. This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain recalcitrant bhikkhu. It seems that a certain son of good family, having gone forth in the dispensation leading to deliverance, was recalcitrant, impatient, and resistant to advice when being advised by teachers, preceptors, and fellow bhikkhus with these words: ‘You should go forward like this, you should go back like this, you should look ahead like this, you should look around like this, you should bend your limbs like this, you should stretch them like this, you should wear the lower robe like this, you should wear the upper robe like this, you should hold the bowl like this; you should take only enough food to sustain life, and having reflected upon it, you should consume it; you should be one who guards the doors of the senses, be moderate in eating, and be devoted to wakefulness; you should know this as the duty for newcomers, this as the duty for travelers; these are the fourteen duties from the Khandhakas, and these are the eighty major duties. You should conduct yourself properly in these. These are the thirteen ascetic qualities; you should undertake and practice them.’ When thus advised, he was recalcitrant, saying, ‘I do not speak to you, so why do you speak to me? I alone will know what is for my own benefit or harm,’ making himself one who is not to be spoken to. Then, knowing his recalcitrant nature, the bhikkhus sat in the Dhamma hall discussing his lack of good qualities. The Teacher arrived and asked, ‘Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you now assembled?’ When they told him, he had that bhikkhu summoned and asked, ‘Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are recalcitrant?’ When he replied, ‘It is true,’ the Teacher said, ‘Why, bhikkhu, having gone forth in such a dispensation leading to deliverance, do you not heed the words of those who wish for your welfare? In the past, too, because you did not heed the words of the wise, you were reduced to powder at the mouth of the Verambha wind.’ And he related a past event.

Atīte gijjhakūṭe pabbate bodhisatto gijjhayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Putto panassa supatto nāma gijjharājā anekasahassagijjhaparivāro thāmasampanno ahosi. So mātāpitaro posesi, thāmasampannattā pana atidūraṃ uppatati. Atha naṃ pitā “tāta, ettakaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ atikkamitvā na gantabba”nti ovadi. So “sādhū”ti vatvāpi ekadivasaṃ pana [M 3.0460] vuṭṭhe deve gijjhehi [V 3.0427] saddhiṃ uppatitvā sese ohāya atibhūmiṃ gantvā verambhavātamukhaṃ patvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇabhāvaṃ pāpuṇi. Satthā tamatthaṃ dassento abhisambuddho hutvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

In the past, on the Vulture Peak mountain, the Bodhisatta was born in the womb of a vulture. His son, named Supatta, was a vulture king who had a following of many thousands of vultures and was endowed with great strength. He supported his parents, and due to his strength, he would fly very far. Then his father advised him, ‘Dear son, you should not go beyond such and such a place.’ Though he replied, ‘Very well,’ one day, after it had rained, he flew up with the vultures. Leaving the others behind, he went beyond the proper limit and, reaching the mouth of the Verambha wind, was reduced to powder. The Teacher, revealing this meaning, after becoming fully enlightened, uttered these verses:

1.

1.

“Parisaṅkupatho nāma, gijjhapantho sanantano;

Tatrāsi mātāpitaro, gijjho posesi jiṇṇake;

Tesaṃ ajagaramedaṃ, accahāsi bahuttaso.

“‘Parisaṅkupatho’ is the name, the ancient path of vultures. There was a vulture who supported his aged mother and father. To them he brought much python fat.”

2.

2.

“Pitā ca puttaṃ avaca, jānaṃ uccaṃ papātinaṃ;

Supattaṃ thāmasampannaṃ, tejassiṃ dūragāminaṃ.

“And the father spoke to his son, knowing him to be one who flies high—Supatta, endowed with strength, mighty, and far-ranging.”

3.

3.

“Pariplavantaṃ pathaviṃ, yadā tāta vijānahi;

Sāgarena parikkhittaṃ, cakkaṃva parimaṇḍalaṃ;

Tato tāta nivattassu, māssu etto paraṃ gami.

“‘When, dear son, you perceive the earth floating, encircled by the ocean and perfectly round like a wheel; then, dear son, turn back; do not go beyond that.’”

4.

4.

“Udapattosi vegena, balī pakkhī dijuttamo;

Olokayanto vakkaṅgo, pabbatāni vanāni ca.

“He rose up with speed, the mighty bird, the best of winged creatures; looking down with curved neck at mountains and forests.”

5.

5.

“Addassa pathaviṃ gijjho, yathāsāsi pitussutaṃ;

Sāgarena parikkhittaṃ, cakkaṃva parimaṇḍalaṃ.

“The vulture saw the earth just as he had heard from his father—encircled by the ocean and perfectly round like a wheel.”

6.

6.

“Tañca so samatikkamma, paramevaccavattatha;

Tañca vātasikhā tikkhā, accahāsi baliṃ dijaṃ.

“But having gone beyond that, he went even further; and sharp wind-crests swept away that mighty bird.”

7.

7.

“Nāsakkhātigato poso, punadeva nivattituṃ;

Dijo byasanamāpādi, verambhānaṃ vasaṃ gato.

“Having gone too far, the creature was unable to turn back again; the bird met with ruin, having come under the sway of the Verambha winds.”

8.

8.

“Tassa [P 3.0485] puttā ca dārā ca, ye caññe anujīvino;

Sabbe byasanamāpāduṃ, anovādakare dije.

“His sons, his wives, and whatever other dependents there were—all met with ruin because of the bird who did not heed advice.”

9.

9.

“Evampi [V 3.0428] idha vuḍḍhānaṃ, yo vākyaṃ nāvabujjhati;

Atisīmacaro ditto, gijjhovātītasāsano;

Sa ve byasanaṃ pappoti, akatvā vuḍḍhasāsana”nti.

“Even so, here, whoever does not understand the words of the elders, but wanders beyond the limit, conceited like the vulture who transgressed the instruction; he indeed meets with ruin, not having followed the instruction of the elders.”

Tattha parisaṅkupathoti saṅkupatho. Manussā hiraññasuvaṇṇatthāya gacchantā tasmiṃ padese khāṇuke koṭṭetvā tesu rajjuyo bandhitvā gacchanti, tena so gijjhapabbate jaṅghamaggo “saṅkupatho”ti vuccati. Gijjhapanthoti [M 3.0461] gijjhapabbatamatthake mahāmaggo. Sanantanoti porāṇo. Tatrāsīti tasmiṃ gijjhapabbatamatthake saṅkupathe eko gijjho āsi, so jiṇṇake mātāpitaro posesi. Ajagaramedanti ajagarānaṃ medaṃ. Accahāsīti ativiya āhari. Bahuttasoti bahuso. Jānaṃ uccaṃ papātinanti “putto te atiuccaṃ ṭhānaṃ laṅghatī”ti sutvā “ucce papātī aya”nti jānanto. Tejassinti purisatejasampannaṃ. Dūragāminanti teneva tejena dūragāmiṃ. Pariplavantanti uppalapattaṃ viya udake uplavamānaṃ. Vijānahīti vijānāsi. Cakkaṃva parimaṇḍalanti yasmiṃ te padese ṭhitassa samuddena paricchinno jambudīpo cakkamaṇḍalaṃva paññāyati, tato tāta nivattāhīti ovadanto evamāha.

There, ‘parisaṅkupatho’ means a path with stakes. People traveling for the sake of gold and bullion would drive stakes into the ground in that region, tie ropes to them, and proceed; therefore, that foot-path on the Vulture Peak is called ‘saṅkupatho’ (the path with stakes). ‘Gijjhapantho’ refers to the great road at the summit of the Vulture Peak mountain. ‘Sanantano’ means ancient. ‘Tatrāsi’ means: on that path with stakes at the summit of the Vulture Peak mountain, there was a vulture; he supported his aged parents. ‘Ajagarameda’ means the fat of pythons. ‘Accahāsi’ means he brought an exceeding amount. ‘Bahuttaso’ means many times. ‘Jānaṃ uccaṃ papātinaṃ’ means, having heard ‘your son is crossing beyond a very high place,’ and thus knowing ‘this one flies very high.’ ‘Tejassiṃ’ means endowed with manly power. ‘Dūragāminaṃ’ means one who goes far due to that very power. ‘Pariplavantaṃ’ means floating on the water like a lotus leaf. ‘Vijānahī’ means ‘you understand.’ ‘Cakkaṃva parimaṇဍalaṃ’ means the place where, as you stand, Jambudīpa, bounded by the ocean, appears like the circle of a wheel. Advising him, ‘Turn back from there, dear one,’ he spoke thus.

Udapattosīti pitu ovādaṃ akatvā ekadivasaṃ gijjhehi saddhiṃ uppatito te ohāya pitarā kathitaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Olokayantoti taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā heṭṭhā olokento. Vakkaṅgoti vaṅkagīvo. Yathāsāsi pitussutanti yathāssa pitu santikā sutaṃ āsi, tatheva addasa, “yathāssāsī”tipi pāṭho. Paramevaccavattathāti pitarā akkhātaṭṭhānato paraṃ ativattova. Tañca vātasikhā tikkhāti taṃ anovādakaṃ balimpi samānaṃ dijaṃ tikhiṇaverambhavātasikhā accahāsi atihari, cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ akāsi. Nāsakkhātigatoti nāsakkhi atigato. Posoti satto. Anovādakareti tasmiṃ dije paṇḍitānaṃ ovādaṃ akaronte sabbepi te mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Akatvā vuḍḍhasāsananti vuḍḍhānaṃ hitakāmānaṃ vacanaṃ akatvā evameva byasanaṃ mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā [P 3.0486] tvaṃ bhikkhu mā gijjhasadiso bhava, atthakāmānaṃ vacanaṃ karohīti. So satthārā evaṃ ovadito tato paṭṭhāya suvaco ahosi.

‘Udapattosīti’ means, not heeding his father’s advice, one day he flew up with the vultures, then leaving them behind, he went to the place his father had mentioned. ‘Olokayanto’ means, having reached that place, looking below. ‘Vakkaṅgo’ means with a bent neck. ‘Yathāsāsi pitussutanti’ means, just as he had heard from his father, so he saw; ‘yathāssāsī’ is also a reading. ‘Paramevaccavattathāti’ means he went beyond the place his father had described. ‘Tañca vātasikhā tikkhāti’ means the sharp Verambha wind-blades swept away that disobedient bird, though strong, and reduced it to dust. ‘Nāsakkhātigato’ means he was not able, having gone too far. ‘Poso’ means a being. ‘Anovādakare’ means, because that bird did not heed the counsel of the wise, all of them met with great suffering. ‘Akatvā vuḍḍhasāsananti’ means, by not heeding the words of the elders who wished him well, he met with ruin and great suffering. Therefore, bhikkhu, do not be like the vulture; heed the words of those who wish you well. Thus admonished by the Teacher, from then on he became compliant.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dubbacagijjho etarahi dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, gijjhapitā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time the stubborn vulture was the stubborn bhikkhu of the present, and the vulture-father was I myself.”

Gijjhajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Vulture Jātaka, the First.

[428] 2. Kosambiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[428] 2. The Commentary on the Kosambiya Jātaka

Puthusaddoti [V 3.0429][M 3.0462] idaṃ satthā kosambiṃ nissāya ghositārāme viharanto kosambiyaṃ bhaṇḍanakārake bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu kosambakakkhandhake (mahāva. 451 ādayo) āgatameva, ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo. Tadā kira dve bhikkhū ekasmiṃ āvāse vasiṃsu vinayadharo ca suttantiko ca. Tesu suttantiko ekadivasaṃ sarīravalañjaṃ katvā udakakoṭṭhake ācamanaudakāvasesaṃ bhājane ṭhapetvā nikkhami. Pacchā vinayadharo tattha paviṭṭho taṃ udakaṃ disvā nikkhamitvā itaraṃ pucchi “āvuso, tayā udakaṃ ṭhapita”nti. “Āmāvuso”ti. “Kiṃ panettha āpattibhāvaṃ na jānāsī”ti? “Āmāvuso na jānāmī”ti. “Hoti, āvuso, ettha āpattī”ti? “Tena hi paṭikarissāmi na”nti. “Sace pana te, āvuso, asañcicca asatiyā kataṃ, natthi āpattī”ti. So tassā āpattiyā anāpattidiṭṭhi ahosi. Vinayadharopi attano nissitakānaṃ “ayaṃ suttantiko āpattiṃ āpajjamānopi na jānātī”ti ārocesi. Te tassa nissitake disvā “tumhākaṃ upajjhāyo āpattiṃ āpajjitvāpi āpattibhāvaṃ na jānātī”ti āhaṃsu. Te gantvā attano upajjhāyassa ārocesuṃ. So evamāha – “ayaṃ vinayadharo pubbe ‘anāpattī’ti vatvā idāni ‘āpattī’ti vadati, musāvādī eso”ti. Te gantvā “tumhākaṃ upajjhāyo musāvādī”ti evaṃ aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ vaḍḍhayiṃsu. Tato vinayadharo okāsaṃ labhitvā tassa āpattiyā adassanena ukkhepanīyakammaṃ akāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya tesaṃ paccayadāyakā upāsakāpi dve koṭṭhāsā ahesuṃ. Ovādapaṭiggāhikā bhikkhuniyopi ārakkhadevatāpi dve koṭṭhāsā ahesuṃ. Tāsaṃ sandiṭṭhasambhattā ākāsaṭṭhadevatāpi yāva [P 3.0487] brahmalokā sabbe puthujjanā dve pakkhā ahesuṃ. Yāva akaniṭṭhabhavanā pana idaṃ kolāhalaṃ agamāsi.

The Teacher related this story concerning 'The Uproar' while dwelling at Ghositārāma in Kosambi, regarding the quarrelsome bhikkhus of Kosambi. The incident is detailed in the Kosambaka Khandhaka (Mahāvagga 451 onwards); here, however, is a summary. At that time, two bhikkhus lived in the same monastery: one a Vinaya-holder, and the other a Sutta-holder. One day, the Sutta-holder, having attended to his bodily needs, left the remaining rinsing water in a vessel in the washroom and departed. Later, the Vinaya-holder entered there, saw the water, and going out, asked the other, 'Friend, did you leave this water?' 'Yes, friend.' 'Do you not know that this is an offense?' 'No, friend, I do not know.' 'There is an offense here, friend.' 'Then I will make amends.' 'But if, friend, you did it unintentionally and without mindfulness, there is no offense.' He held the view that it was not an offense. The Vinaya-holder, for his part, announced to his own dependents, 'This Sutta-holder commits an offense and does not even know it.' They, seeing his dependents, said, 'Your preceptor commits an offense and does not know the nature of an offense.' They went and reported it to their preceptor, who said, 'This Vinaya-holder, having first said 'no offense,' now says 'it is an offense'; he is a liar.' They went and said, 'Your preceptor is a liar,' and in this way they increased the quarrel among themselves. Then the Vinaya-holder, finding an opportunity, performed an act of suspension against him for not seeing the offense. From that time onwards, even the lay followers who provided them with requisites became two factions. Even the bhikkhunīs who received their instructions and the guardian deities became two factions. Even the sky-dwelling deities who were their friends and companions, and all worldlings up to the Brahma world, became two factions. This uproar, moreover, extended as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm.

Atheko bhikkhu tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā ukkhepakānaṃ “dhammikeneva kammena ayaṃ ukkhitto, ukkhittānuvattakānaṃ adhammikena kammena ukkhitto”ti laddhiṃ, ukkhepakehi vāriyamānānampi tesaṃ taṃ anuparivāretvā caraṇabhāvañca satthu ārocesi. Bhagavā “samaggā kira hontū”ti dve vāre pesetvā “na icchanti bhante samaggā bhavitu”nti sutvā [M 3.0463] tatiyavāre “bhinno bhikkhusaṅgho”ti tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā ukkhepakānaṃ ukkhepane, itaresañca asañcicca āpattiyā adassane ādīnavaṃ vatvā pakkāmi. Puna tesaṃ tattheva ekasīmāyaṃ uposathādīni kāretvā bhattaggādīsu bhaṇḍanajātānaṃ “āsanantarikāya nisīditabba”nti bhattagge vattaṃ paññāpetvā “idānipi bhaṇḍanajātā viharantī”ti sutvā tattha gantvā “alaṃ, bhikkhave, mā bhaṇḍana”ntiādīni [V 3.0430] vatvā aññatarena bhikkhunā dhammavādinā bhagavato vihesaṃ anicchantena “āgametu, bhante, bhagavā dhammasāmi, appossukko bhante, bhagavā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ anuyutto viharatu, mayaṃ tena bhaṇḍanena kalahena viggahena vivādena paññāyissāmā”ti vutte –

Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Tathāgata and reported the view of the suspenders: 'This one has been suspended by a lawful act,' and the view of the followers of the suspended one: 'He has been suspended by an unlawful act.' He also reported to the Teacher that his followers, though forbidden by the suspenders, continued to attend upon him. The Blessed One, having sent messengers twice saying, 'May they indeed be harmonious,' and hearing 'Venerable sir, they do not wish to be harmonious,' went to them himself on the third occasion, as the Saṅgha of bhikkhus was divided. He then explained to the suspenders the danger in their act of suspension, and to the others the danger in not seeing an offense committed unintentionally, before departing. Again, having made them perform Uposatha and other acts within the same boundary, and having laid down a rule in the refectory for those who were quarrelsome at meal-times and so forth, that 'one should sit without leaving gaps,' and hearing that 'they are still dwelling in quarrel,' he went there and, having said 'Enough, bhikkhus, do not quarrel!' and so on, was addressed by a certain Dhamma-speaking bhikkhu who did not wish to trouble the Blessed One: 'Let the Blessed One, the Master of the Dhamma, forbear. Let the Blessed One dwell unconcerned, devoted to a pleasant abiding in this very life. We shall be known by this quarrel, dispute, contention, and controversy.'

Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto nāma kāsirājā ahosīti brahmadattena dīghītissa kosalarañño rajjaṃ acchanditvā aññātakavesena vasantassa māritabhāvañceva dīghāvukumārena attano jīvite dinne tato paṭṭhāya tesaṃ samaggabhāvañca kathetvā “tesañhi nāma, bhikkhave, rājūnaṃ ādinnadaṇḍānaṃ ādinnasatthānaṃ evarūpaṃ khantisoraccaṃ bhavissati. Idha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, sobhetha, yaṃ tumhe evaṃ svākkhāte dhammavinaye pabbajitā samānā khamā ca bhaveyyātha soratā cā”ti ovaditvā dutiyampi tatiyampi “alaṃ, bhikkhave, mā bhaṇḍana”nti vāretvā anoramante disvā “pariyādiṇṇarūpā kho ime moghapurisā, na yime sukarā saññāpetu”nti pakkamitvā punadivase piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto gandhakuṭiyā thokaṃ vissamitvā senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā attano pattacīvaramādāya saṅghamajjhe ākāse ṭhatvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

Once in the past, bhikkhus, there was a king of Kasi named Brahmadatta in Bārāṇasī. Having related how Brahmadatta, having seized the kingdom of Dīghīti, king of Kosala, had him killed while he was living in disguise, and how, after Prince Dīghāvu spared his life, they were in harmony from that time onwards, he said: 'If, bhikkhus, such forbearance and gentleness could exist for those kings who had taken up weapons and instruments of punishment, how much more should it be fitting for you, bhikkhus, who have gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Discipline, to be forbearing and gentle!' Thus advising them, and restraining them a second and a third time, saying, 'Enough, bhikkhus, do not quarrel!' Seeing that they did not desist, he thought: 'These foolish men are indeed obsessed; they are not easy to persuade.' Then he departed. On the following day, after returning from his alms-round, resting a little in the Perfumed Chamber, setting his dwelling in order, taking his bowl and robe, he stood in the air in the midst of the Saṅgha and uttered these verses:

10.

10.

“Puthusaddo [P 3.0488] samajano, na bālo koci maññatha;

Saṅghasmiṃ bhijjamānasmiṃ, nāññaṃ bhiyyo amaññaruṃ.

The people are in a mass uproar; no one considers himself a fool. While the Saṅgha is being split, they do not think of any other reason.

11.

11.

“Parimuṭṭhā paṇḍitābhāsā, vācāgocarabhāṇino;

Yāvicchanti mukhāyāmaṃ, yena nītā na taṃ vidū.

They are forgetful, masquerading as wise, speaking only as far as words reach. They talk as much as they wish, but do not know that by which they are led.

12.

12.

“Akkocchi maṃ avadhi maṃ, ajini maṃ ahāsi me;

Ye ca taṃ upanayhanti, veraṃ tesaṃ na sammati.

‘He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me’—in those who harbor such thoughts, hatred is not appeased.

13.

13.

“Akkocchi [M 3.0464] maṃ avadhi maṃ, ajini maṃ ahāsi me;

Ye ca taṃ nupanayhanti, veraṃ tesūpasammati.

‘He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me’—in those who do not harbor such thoughts, hatred is appeased.

14.

14.

“Na hi verena verāni, sammantīdha kudācanaṃ;

Averena ca sammanti, esa dhammo sanantano.

For never in this world is hatred appeased by hatred; it is appeased by non-hatred. This is an eternal law.

15.

15.

“Pare [V 3.0431] ca na vijānanti, mayamettha yamāmase;

Ye ca tattha vijānanti, tato sammanti medhagā.

Others do not realize that here we are all heading towards death; but for those who do realize this, their quarrels are thereby stilled.

16.

16.

“Aṭṭhicchinnā pāṇaharā, gavāssadhanahārino;

Raṭṭhaṃ vilumpamānānaṃ, tesampi hoti saṅgati;

Kasmā tumhāka no siyā.

Even for those who have had bones broken, lives taken, cattle, horses, and wealth stolen, and their kingdom plundered—even for them there was concord. Why should there not be for you?

17.

17.

“Sace labhetha nipakaṃ sahāyaṃ, saddhiṃcaraṃ sādhuvihāridhīraṃ;

Abhibhuyya sabbāni parissayāni, careyya tenattamano satīmā.

If one should find a prudent companion, a fellow traveler who is virtuous and wise, then, overcoming all dangers, one should wander with him, gratified and mindful.

18.

18.

“No ce labhetha nipakaṃ sahāyaṃ, saddhiṃcaraṃ sādhuvihāridhīraṃ;

Rājāva raṭṭhaṃ vijitaṃ pahāya, eko care mātaṅgaraññeva nāgo.

If one should not find a prudent companion, a fellow traveler who is virtuous and wise, then like a king who leaves behind his conquered kingdom, one should wander alone like a Matanga elephant in the forest.

19.

19.

“Ekassa caritaṃ seyyo, natthi bāle sahāyatā;

Eko care na pāpāni kayirā, appossukko mātaṅgaraññeva nāgo”ti.

It is better to wander alone; there is no companionship with a fool. Wandering alone, one does no evil and is free from care, like a Matanga elephant in the forest.

Tattha puthu mahāsaddo assāti puthusaddo. Samajanoti samāno ekasadiso jano, sabbovāyaṃ bhaṇḍanakārakajano samantato saddanicchāraṇena puthusaddo ceva sadiso cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Na bālo koci maññathāti tattha koci ekopi “ahaṃ bālo”ti [M 3.0465] na maññittha, sabbe paṇḍitamānino, sabbovāyaṃ bhaṇḍanakārako janoyeva. Nāññaṃ bhiyyo amaññarunti koci ekopi “ahaṃ bālo”ti na maññittha, bhiyyo ca saṅghasmiṃ bhijjamāne aññampi ekaṃ “mayhaṃ kāraṇā saṅgho bhijjatī”ti idaṃ kāraṇaṃ na maññitthāti attho.

Herein, 'puthusaddo' means a great noise. 'Samajano' means people who are alike; that is, all these quarrelsome people, by making a noise all around, are both a mass noise and similar to one another. 'Na bālo koci maññatha' means that not a single person there thought, 'I am a fool.' All were conceited about their wisdom; all these people were simply quarrelsome. 'Nāññaṃ bhiyyo amaññaruṃ' means that not a single one thought, 'I am a fool,' and further, while the Saṅgha was splitting, they did not consider this other reason: 'The Saṅgha is splitting because of me'—this is the meaning.

Parimuṭṭhāti muṭṭhassatino. Paṇḍitābhāsāti attano paṇḍitamānena [P 3.0489] paṇḍitasadisā. Vācāgocarabhāṇinoti rā-kārassa rassādeso kato, vācāgocarā ca na satipaṭṭhānādiariyadhammagocarā, bhāṇino ca. Kathaṃ bhāṇino? Yāvicchanti mukhāyāmanti, yāva mukhaṃ pasāretuṃ icchanti, tāva pasāretvā aggapādehi ṭhatvā bhāṇino, ekopi saṅghagāravena mukhasaṅkocanaṃ na karotīti attho. Yena nītāti yena bhaṇḍanena imaṃ nillajjabhāvaṃ nītā. Na taṃ vidūti evaṃ “ādīnavaṃ ida”nti taṃ na jānanti.

'Parimuṭṭhā' means forgetful. 'Paṇḍitābhāsā' means appearing wise due to their own conceit of wisdom. 'Vācāgocarabhāṇino' (with the long 'ā' shortened) means their range is speech, not the noble Dhamma such as the foundations of mindfulness, and they are talkers. How are they talkers? 'Yāvicchanti mukhāyāmaṃ' means they open their mouths as much as they wish, standing on their tiptoes to speak. Not even one, out of respect for the Sangha, restrains his mouth—this is the meaning. 'Yena nītā' means 'by which quarrel they are led to this shamelessness.' 'Na taṃ vidū' means they do not know it, saying 'this is a danger.'

Ye [V 3.0432] ca taṃ upanayhantīti taṃ “akkocchi ma”ntiādikaṃ ākāraṃ ye upanayhanti. Sanantanoti porāṇo. Pareti paṇḍite ṭhapetvā tato aññe bhaṇḍanakārakā pare nāma. Te ettha saṅghamajjhe kolāhalaṃ karontā “mayaṃ yamāmase upayamāma nassāma, satataṃ samitaṃ maccusantikaṃ gacchāmā”ti na jānanti. Ye ca tattha vijānantīti ye tattha paṇḍitā “mayaṃ maccusamīpaṃ gacchāmā”ti vijānanti. Tato sammanti medhagāti bhikkhave, evañhi te jānantā yonisomanasikāraṃ uppādetvā medhagānaṃ kalahānaṃ vūpasamāya paṭipajjanti.

'Ye ca taṃ upanayhanti' means those who harbor that attitude of 'He abused me,' and so on. 'Sanantano' means ancient. 'Pare' refers to the quarrelsome ones, excluding the wise. They, making a commotion in the midst of the Sangha, do not know: 'We are going to the realm of Yama, we are perishing, we are being destroyed, we are constantly going to the presence of death.' 'Ye ca tattha vijānanti' means the wise ones there who know: 'We are going near death.' 'Tato sammanti medhagā' means: 'Bhikkhus, knowing this, they develop wise attention and practice for the cessation of disputes and quarrels.'

Aṭṭhicchinnāti ayaṃ gāthā brahmadattañca dīghāvukumārañca sandhāya vuttā. Tesampi hoti saṅgati. Kasmā tumhākaṃ na hoti? Yesaṃ vo neva mātāpitūnaṃ aṭṭhīni chinnāni, na pāṇā haṭā, na gavāssadhanāni haṭāni. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bhikkhave, tesañhi nāma ādinnadaṇḍānaṃ ādinnasatthānaṃ rājūnaṃ evarūpā saṅgati samāgamo āvāhavivāhasambandhaṃ katvā ekato pānabhojanaṃ hoti, tumhe evarūpe sāsane pabbajitvā attano veramattampi jahituṃ na sakkotha, ko tumhākaṃ bhikkhubhāvoti.

“Bones broken”—this verse was spoken with reference to Brahmadatta and Prince Dīghāvu. Even for them, there was concord. Why should there not be for you? For you, neither have your parents’ bones been broken, nor lives taken, nor cattle, horses, and wealth stolen. This was said: ‘Bhikkhus, for those kings who have taken up weapons and instruments of punishment, such concord and coming together occurs, establishing marriage alliances and sharing food and drink together. But you, having gone forth in such a teaching, cannot even abandon your own small enmities—what then is your state of being a monk?’

Sace [M 3.0466] labhethātiādigāthāyo paṇḍitasahāyassa ca bālasahāyassa ca vaṇṇāvaṇṇadīpanatthaṃ vuttā. Abhibhuyya sabbāni parissayānīti sabbe pākaṭaparissaye ca paṭicchannaparissaye ca abhibhavitvā tena saddhiṃ attamano satimā careyya. Rājāva raṭṭhaṃ vijitaṃ pahāyāti yathā attano vijitaṃ raṭṭhaṃ mahājanakarājā ca arindamarājā ca pahāya ekakova cariṃsu, evaṃ careyyāti attho. Mātaṅgaraññeva nāgoti mātaṅgo araññe nāgova. Mātaṅgoti hatthī vuccati, nāgoti mahantādhivacanametaṃ. Yathā hi mātuposako mātaṅganāgo araññe ekako cari, na ca pāpāni akāsi, yathā ca sīlavahatthināgo. Yathā ca pālileyyako, evaṃ eko care, na ca pāpāni kayirāti vuttaṃ hoti.

“If one should find,” etc.—these verses were spoken to illustrate the praise and blame of wise and foolish companions. “Having overcome all perils”—having overcome all manifest and hidden perils, one should live mindfully and joyfully with him. “Like a king abandoning a conquered kingdom”—just as King Mahājanaka and King Arindama abandoned their conquered kingdoms and wandered alone, so should one live—this is the meaning. “Like a mātaṅga elephant in the forest.” Here, ‘mātaṅga’ means elephant, and ‘nāga’ is a term for greatness. Just as the mother-supporting Mātaṅga elephant wandered alone in the forest and did no evil, like the virtuous Sīlavā elephant and like the Pālileyyaka elephant, so should one wander alone and do no evil—this is the meaning.

Satthā evaṃ kathetvāpi te bhikkhū samagge kātuṃ asakkonto bālakaloṇakagāmaṃ gantvā bhaguttherassa ekībhāve ānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā tato tiṇṇaṃ kulaputtānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā tesaṃ sāmaggivāse ānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā tato pālileyyakavanasaṇḍaṃ gantvā tattha [P 3.0490] temāsaṃ vasitvā puna kosambiṃ agantvā sāvatthimeva agamāsi. Kosambivāsinopi upāsakā “ime kho ayyā, kosambakā bhikkhū bahuno amhākaṃ anatthassa kārakā, imehi ubbāḷho bhagavā pakkanto, imesaṃ neva abhivādanādīni karissāma, na upagatānaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ dassāma, evaṃ ime [V 3.0433] pakkamissanti vā veraṃ viramissanti vā bhagavantaṃ vā pasādessantī”ti sammantayitvā tatheva akaṃsu. Te tena daṇḍakammena pīḷitā sāvatthiṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ khamāpesuṃ.

The Teacher, having spoken thus, was unable to reconcile those monks. He went to the village of Bālakaloṇaka and spoke to the venerable Bhagu about the benefits of solitude. From there, he went to the dwelling place of three clansmen and spoke to them about the benefits of living in harmony. Then, he went to the Pālileyyaka forest grove and stayed there for three months. Instead of returning to Kosambī, he went straight to Sāvatthī. The lay followers of Kosambī also consulted among themselves: “These venerable Kosambī monks have caused us much harm. Harassed by them, the Blessed One has departed. We shall neither pay homage to them nor perform other duties, nor shall we give them alms when they approach. In this way, they will either leave, cease their quarreling, or reconcile with the Blessed One.” Having agreed thus, they acted accordingly. Those monks, oppressed by that punishment, went to Sāvatthī and asked the Blessed One for forgiveness.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “pitā suddhodanamahārājā ahosi, mātā mahāmāyā, dīghāvukumāro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, King Suddhodana was the father, Mahāmāyā was the mother, and I myself was Prince Dīghāvu.”

Kosambiyajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The second commentary on the Kosambiya Jātaka is finished.

[429] 3. Mahāsuvajātakavaṇṇanā

[429] 3. The Commentary on the Mahāsuva Jātaka

Dumo [M 3.0467] yadā hotīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā kosalajanapade aññataraṃ paccantagāmaṃ upanissāya araññe vihāsi. Manussā tassa rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni sampādetvā gamanāgamanasampanne ṭhāne senāsanaṃ katvā sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Tassa vassūpagatassa paṭhamamāseyeva so gāmo jhāyi, manussānaṃ bījamattampi avasiṭṭhaṃ nāhosi. Te tassa paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ dātuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. So sappāyasenāsanepi piṇḍapātena kilamanto maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ temāsaccayena satthāraṃ vandituṃ āgataṃ satthā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kacci bhikkhu piṇḍapātena na kilamantosi, senāsanasappāyañca ahosī”ti pucchi. So tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Satthā “tassa senāsanaṃ sappāya”nti ñatvā “bhikkhu samaṇena nāma senāsanasappāye sati loluppacāraṃ pahāya kiñcideva yathāladdhaṃ paribhuñjitvā santuṭṭhena samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Porāṇakapaṇḍitā tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā attano nivāsasukkharukkhe cuṇṇaṃ [P 3.0491] khādantāpi loluppacāraṃ pahāya santuṭṭhā mittadhammaṃ abhinditvā aññattha na gamiṃsu, tvaṃ pana kasmā ‘piṇḍapāto paritto lūkho’ti sappāyasenāsanaṃ pariccajī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“When a tree is,” etc.—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk. That monk, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, lived in the forest near a border village in the Kosala country. The people, having prepared places for his day and night residence and built a dwelling in a place convenient for travel, attended on him respectfully. In the very first month of his Rains retreat, that village burned down, and not even a seed was left for the people. They were unable to give him choice almsfood. Though his dwelling was suitable, he was weary from the lack of almsfood and could not produce the path or the fruit. After three months, when he came to pay homage to the Teacher, the Teacher greeted him and asked: “Monk, I hope you are not weary from lack of almsfood, and that your dwelling was suitable?” He told him that matter. The Teacher, knowing the dwelling was suitable, said: “Monk, when a recluse has a suitable dwelling, he should give up greedy conduct, use whatever is received, and practice the recluse’s duties with contentment. Wise ones of old, even though reborn in animal wombs, did not break the law of friendship and go elsewhere even when their dwelling-tree became dry and they had to eat its wood-dust, giving up greedy conduct and remaining content. But why did you abandon a suitable dwelling, saying ‘the almsfood is scant and coarse’?” Having said this, and being requested by him, he brought forward the past.

Atīte himavante gaṅgātīre ekasmiṃ udumbaravane anekasatasahassā sukā vasiṃsu. Tatra eko suvarājā attano nivāsarukkhassa phalesu khīṇesu yadeva avasiṭṭhaṃ hoti aṅkuro vā pattaṃ vā taco vā papaṭikā vā, taṃ khāditvā gaṅgāya pānīyaṃ pivitvā paramappicchasantuṭṭho hutvā aññattha na gacchati. Tassa appicchasantuṭṭhabhāvaguṇena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi. Sakko āvajjamāno taṃ disvā tassa vīmaṃsanatthaṃ attano ānubhāvena taṃ rukkhaṃ sukkhāpesi. Rukkho [V 3.0434] khāṇukamatto hutvā chiddāvachiddo vāte paharante ākoṭiyamāno viya aṭṭhāsi. Tassa chiddehi cuṇṇāni nikkhamanti. Suvarājā tāni cuṇṇāni khāditvā gaṅgāya pānīyaṃ pivitvā aññattha agantvā vātātapaṃ agaṇetvā udumbarakhāṇuke nisīdi. Sakko tassa paramappicchabhāvaṃ ñatvā “mittadhammaguṇaṃ kathāpetvā varamassa datvā udumbaraṃ [M 3.0468] amataphalaṃ karitvā āgamissāmī”ti eko haṃsarājā hutvā sujaṃ asurakaññaṃ purato katvā taṃ udumbaravanaṃ gantvā avidūre ekarukkhassa sākhāya nisīditvā tena saddhiṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, on the bank of the Ganges in the Himalayas, hundreds of thousands of parrots lived in a fig-tree grove. Among them, one parrot king, when the fruits of his dwelling-tree were exhausted, ate whatever remained—whether sprouts, leaves, bark, or flakes of wood—drank water from the Ganges, and being supremely content with few wishes, did not go elsewhere. Due to his virtue of fewness of wishes and contentment, Sakka’s abode trembled. Sakka, reflecting and seeing him, in order to test him, dried up that tree by his power. The tree became a mere stump, full of holes, and when the wind blew, it stood as if whistling. Wood-dust came out of its holes. The parrot king, eating that dust and drinking water from the Ganges, not going elsewhere and disregarding the wind and sun, sat on that fig-tree stump. Sakka, knowing his supreme fewness of wishes, thought: “I will make him speak on the virtue of friendship, give him a boon, and make the fig-tree bear ambrosial fruit.” Taking the form of a king of geese, with the Asura maiden Sujā in front, he went to that fig-tree grove and, perched on the branch of a tree nearby, initiated a conversation with him and spoke the first verse:

20.

20.

“Dumo yadā hoti phalūpapanno, bhuñjanti naṃ vihaṅgamā sampatantā;

Khīṇanti ñatvāna dumaṃ phalaccaye, disodisaṃ yanti tato vihaṅgamā”ti.

“When a tree is laden with fruit, birds come flying and feast upon it; knowing the tree is exhausted when its fruit is gone, the birds then fly from it in all directions.”

Tassattho – suvarāja, rukkho nāma yadā phalasampanno hoti, tadā taṃ sākhato sākhaṃ sampatantāva vihaṅgamā bhuñjanti, taṃ pana khīṇaṃ ñatvā phalānaṃ accayena tato rukkhato disodisaṃ vihaṅgamā gacchantīti.

The meaning is: O parrot king, when a tree is indeed full of fruit, birds eat from it, flying from branch to branch. But knowing it is exhausted by the passing of the fruits, birds go from that tree in all directions.

Evañca [P 3.0492] pana vatvā tato naṃ uyyojetuṃ dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, to urge him to depart, he then uttered a second verse:

21.

21.

“Cara cārikaṃ lohitatuṇḍa mā mari, kiṃ tvaṃ suva sukkhadumamhi jhāyasi;

Tadiṅgha maṃ brūhi vasantasannibha, kasmā suva sukkhadumaṃ na riñcasī”ti.

"Wander, O red-beaked one, do not die. Why, O parrot, do you brood over a withered tree? Come now, tell me, you who resemble spring, why, O parrot, do you not abandon the withered tree?"

Tattha [M 3.0469] jhāyasīti kiṃkāraṇā sukkhakhāṇumatthake jhāyanto pajjhāyanto tiṭṭhasi. Iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto. Vasantasannibhāti vasantakāle vanasaṇḍo suvagaṇasamokiṇṇo viya nīlobhāso hoti, tena taṃ “vasantasannibhā”ti ālapati. Na riñcasīti na chaḍḍesi.

Here, 'jhāyasi' means: for what reason do you stand meditating and pondering on the dry stump? 'Iṅgha' is a particle used in the sense of urging. 'Vasantasannibha' means 'resembling spring': in springtime, a forest grove strewn with a flock of parrots has a blue-green luster; therefore, he addresses him as 'resembling spring.' 'Na riñcasi' means 'you do not abandon'.

Atha naṃ suvarājā “ahaṃ haṃsa attano kataññukataveditāya imaṃ rukkhaṃ na jahāmī”ti vatvā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the parrot king said to him, "O goose, I do not abandon this tree out of gratitude and thankfulness for what has been done," and spoke two verses:

22.

22.

“Ye ve sakhīnaṃ sakhāro bhavanti, pāṇaccaye dukkhasukhesu haṃsa;

Khīṇaṃ akhīṇampi na taṃ jahanti, santo sataṃ dhammamanussarantā.

"Those who are friends to their friends, O goose, in suffering and in happiness, even at the cost of their lives; the good do not forsake them, whether diminished or undiminished, remembering the Dhamma of the good."

23.

23.

“Sohaṃ [V 3.0435] sataṃ aññatarosmi haṃsa, ñātī ca me hoti sakhā ca rukkho;

Taṃ nussahe jīvikattho pahātuṃ, khīṇanti ñatvāna na hesa dhammo”ti.

"I am one of those good ones, O goose; this tree is both my kinsman and my friend. I cannot bring myself to abandon it for the sake of my livelihood; for to abandon one who is depleted, knowing it to be so, is not the Dhamma."

Tattha ye ve sakhīnaṃ sakhāro bhavantīti ye sahāyānaṃ sahāyā honti. Khīṇaṃ akhīṇampīti paṇḍitā nāma attano sahāyaṃ bhogaparikkhayena khīṇampi akhīṇampi na jahanti. Sataṃ dhammamanussarantāti paṇḍitānaṃ paveṇiṃ anussaramānā. Ñātī ca meti haṃsarāja, ayaṃ rukkho sampiyāyanatthena mayhaṃ ñāti ca samāciṇṇacaraṇatāya sakhā ca. Jīvikatthoti tamahaṃ jīvikāya atthiko hutvā pahātuṃ na sakkomi.

Here, 'ye ve sakhīnaṃ sakhāro bhavanti' means those who are companions to their companions. 'Khīṇaṃ akhīṇampi' means the wise do not abandon their friend, whether diminished by loss of possessions or not diminished. 'Sataṃ dhammamanussarantā' means recalling the tradition of the wise. 'Ñātī ca me' means: O king of geese, this tree is both my kinsman through affection and my friend through long association. 'Jīvikattho' means: I, being in need of a livelihood, am unable to abandon it.

Sakko tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tuṭṭho pasaṃsitvā varaṃ dātukāmo dve gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing his words, Sakka was pleased, and praising him, wishing to grant a boon, he spoke two verses:

24.

24.

“Sādhu [P 3.0493] sakkhi kataṃ hoti, metti saṃsati santhavo;

Sacetaṃ dhammaṃ rocesi, pāsaṃsosi vijānataṃ.

"Well done! Friendship, loving-kindness, association, and intimacy have been demonstrated. If you approve of this Dhamma, you are praised by the wise."

25.

25.

“So te suva varaṃ dammi, pattayāna vihaṅgama;

Varaṃ varassu vakkaṅga, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasī”ti.

"Therefore, O parrot, I grant you a boon, O bird that goes by wing. Choose a boon, O crooked-limbed one, whatever you desire in your mind."

Tattha sādhūti sampahaṃsanaṃ. Sakkhi kataṃ hoti, metti saṃsati santhavoti sakhibhāvo ca metti ca parisamajjhe santhavo cāti tayā mittaṃ kataṃ sādhu hoti laddhakaṃ bhaddakameva. Sacetaṃ dhammanti sace etaṃ mittadhammaṃ. Vijānatanti evaṃ sante viññūnaṃ pasaṃsitabbayuttakosīti attho. So teti so ahaṃ tuyhaṃ. Varassūti icchassu. Yaṃ kiñci manasicchasīti yaṃ kiñci manasā icchasi, sabbaṃ taṃ varaṃ dadāmi teti.

Here, 'sādhu' is an expression of approval. 'Sakkhi kataṃ hoti, metti saṃsati santhavo' means: this friendship made by you—that is, companionship, loving-kindness, and intimacy in the midst of an assembly—is indeed good, acquired, and auspicious. 'Sace taṃ dhammaṃ' means: if this Dhamma of friendship. 'Vijānataṃ' means: this being so, you are worthy of praise by the wise; this is the meaning. 'So te' means: so I to you. 'Varassu' means: choose. 'Yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi' means: whatever you desire in your mind, I give that entire boon to you.

Taṃ sutvā suvarājā varaṃ gaṇhanto sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the parrot king, accepting the boon, spoke the seventh verse:

26.

26.

“Varañca me haṃsa bhavaṃ dadeyya, ayañca rukkho punarāyuṃ labhetha;

So sākhavā phalimā saṃvirūḷho, madhutthiko tiṭṭhatu sobhamāno”ti.

"If you, my lord goose, would grant me a boon, may this tree regain its life; may it stand, possessed of branches, laden with fruit, well-grown, rich in sweetness, and shining beautifully."

Tattha sākhavāti sākhasampanno. Phalimāti phalena upeto. Saṃvirūḷhoti samantato virūḷhapatto [V 3.0436] taruṇapattasampanno hutvā. Madhutthikoti saṃvijjamānamadhuraphalesu pakkhittamadhu viya madhuraphalo hutvāti attho.

Here, 'sākhavā' means possessed of branches. 'Phalimā' means endowed with fruit. 'Saṃvirūḷho' means having grown leaves all around, being possessed of young leaves. 'Madhutthiko' means having fruit as sweet as honey placed in existing sweet fruits; this is the meaning.

Athassa [M 3.0470] sakko varaṃ dadamāno aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Sakka, granting him a boon, spoke the eighth verse:

27.

27.

“Taṃ passa samma phalimaṃ uḷāraṃ, sahāva te hotu udumbarena;

So sākhavā phalimā saṃvirūḷho, madhutthiko tiṭṭhatu sobhamāno”ti.

"Behold, friend, that splendid, fruit-laden tree. May you be together with this fig tree. May it stand, possessed of branches, laden with fruit, well-grown, rich in sweetness, and shining beautifully."

Tattha sahāva te hotu udumbarenāti tava udumbarena saddhiṃ saha ekatova vāso hotu.

Here, 'sahāva te hotu udumbarena' means: may your dwelling be together with the udumbara tree, as one.

Evañca [P 3.0494] pana vatvā sakko taṃ attabhāvaṃ vijahitvā attano ca sujāya ca ānubhāvaṃ dassetvā gaṅgāto hatthena udakaṃ gahetvā udumbarakhāṇukaṃ pahari. Tāvadeva sākhāviṭapasacchanno madhuraphalo rukkho uṭṭhahitvā muṇḍamaṇipabbato viya vilāsasampanno aṭṭhāsi. Suvarājā taṃ disvā somanassappatto sakkassa thutiṃ karonto navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken thus, Sakka abandoned that form, and displaying his own power and that of Sujā, he took water from the Ganges with his hand and struck the udumbara stump. Instantly, a tree covered with branches and boughs and laden with sweet fruits arose, standing splendid like a polished jeweled mountain. Seeing this, the parrot king, filled with joy, praised Sakka, uttering the ninth verse:

28.

28.

“Evaṃ sakka sukhī hohi, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Yathāhamajja sukhito, disvāna saphalaṃ duma”nti.

"Thus, Sakka, may you be happy, along with all your kinsmen; just as I am happy today, seeing the fruitful tree."

Sakkopi tassa varaṃ datvā udumbaraṃ amataphalaṃ katvā saddhiṃ sujāya attano ṭhānameva gato. Tamatthaṃ dīpayamānā osāne abhisambuddhagāthā ṭhapitā –

Sakka, having granted him the boon and having made the udumbara bear ambrosial fruit, returned with Sujā to his own abode. To illuminate this matter, the verse of the Fully Awakened One was placed at the end:

29.

29.

“Suvassa ca varaṃ datvā, katvāna saphalaṃ dumaṃ;

Pakkāmi saha bhariyāya, devānaṃ nandanaṃ vana”nti.

"Having given a boon to the parrot, and having made the tree fruitful, he departed with his wife to the devas' Nandana Grove."

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ bhikkhu porāṇakapaṇḍitā tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattāpi aloluppacārā ahesuṃ. Tvaṃ pana kasmā evarūpe sāsane pabbajitvā loluppacāraṃ carasi, gaccha tattheva vasāhī”ti kammaṭṭhānamassa kathetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi. So bhikkhu tattha gantvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tadā sakko anuruddho ahosi, suvarājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said, 'Thus, Bhikkhu, the wise of old, though born in the animal realm, were of non-covetous conduct. But you—why, having gone forth in such a dispensation, do you behave greedily? Go and dwell right there!' After giving him a meditation subject, he connected the Jātaka. That bhikkhu, going there and developing insight, attained arahantship. At that time, Sakka was Anuruddha, and the parrot king was myself.

Mahāsuvajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Mahāsuva Jātaka, the third.

[430] 4. Cūḷasuvajātakavaṇṇanā

[430] 4. 4. The Commentary on the Cūḷasuva Jātaka

Santi [V 3.0437][M 3.0471] rukkhāti idaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ jetavane viharanto verañjakaṇḍaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Satthari verañjāyaṃ vassaṃ vasitvā anupubbena sāvatthiṃ anuppatte bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, tathāgato khattiyasukhumālo buddhasukhumālo mahantena iddhānubhāvena samannāgatopi verañjabrāhmaṇena nimantito temāsaṃ vasanto mārāvaṭṭanavasena tassa santikā ekadivasampi bhikkhaṃ alabhitvā loluppacāraṃ pahāya temāsaṃ patthapulakapiṭṭhodakena yāpento aññattha na agamāsi, aho tathāgatānaṃ [P 3.0495] appicchasantuṭṭhabhāvo”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgatassa idāni loluppacārappahānaṃ, pubbepi tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattopi loluppacāraṃ pahāsi”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari. Sabbampi vatthu purimanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ.

‘There are trees.’ The Teacher, while residing in Jetavana at Sāvatthi, spoke this concerning the Verañja section. Having spent the rains retreat in Verañja and gradually arriving at Sāvatthi, the monks initiated a discussion in the Dhamma hall: ‘Friends, though the Tathāgata is of delicate khattiya birth, of delicate Buddha birth, and endowed with great psychic power, when invited by the Verañja brahmin, he stayed for three months. Yet, due to Māra’s interference, he did not receive alms from the brahmin even for a single day. Abandoning any tendency toward greed, he sustained himself for three months with water mixed with ground barley and did not go elsewhere. Ah, how few are the wants and how great the contentment of the Tathāgatas!’ The Teacher approached and asked, ‘Monks, what discussion are you engaged in now?’ When they replied, ‘This one,’ he said, ‘It is no wonder, monks, that the Tathāgata has now abandoned greedy conduct. Even in the past, when reborn in the animal realm, he gave up greedy conduct.’ Having said this, he recounted the past. The entire story should be elaborated in the same manner as before.

30.

30.

“Santi rukkhā haripattā, dumā nekaphalā bahū;

Kasmā nu sukkhe koḷāpe, suvassa nirato mano.

‘There are trees with green leaves, many trees with abundant fruit; why then is the parrot’s mind intent on a dry, hollow fig tree that rattles in the wind?’

31.

31.

“Phalassa upabhuñjimhā, nekavassagaṇe bahū;

Aphalampi viditvāna, sāva metti yathā pure.

‘We have enjoyed its fruit for many long years; even knowing it is now fruitless, our friendship remains as it was before.’

32.

32.

“Sukkhañca rukkhaṃ koḷāpaṃ, opattamaphalaṃ dumaṃ;

Ohāya sakuṇā yanti, kiṃ dosaṃ passase dija.

‘The birds abandon and fly away from a dry, hollow tree, stripped of its leaves and fruit. What fault do you see in this, O twice-born bird?’

33.

33.

“Ye phalatthā sambhajanti, aphaloti jahanti naṃ;

Attatthapaññā dummedhā, te honti pakkhapātino.

‘Those who associate with a tree only for its fruit and abandon it when it is fruitless are fools who seek only their own gain; they are merely fair-weather friends.’

34.

34.

“Sādhu sakkhi kataṃ hoti, metti saṃsati santhavo;

Sacetaṃ dhammaṃ rocesi, pāsaṃsosi vijānataṃ.

‘Good is a friendship formed through kindness, association, and intimacy. If you delight in this principle, you are truly praised by the wise.’

35.

35.

“So te suva varaṃ dammi, pattayāna vihaṅgama;
