Varaṃ varassu vakkaṅga, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

‘I grant you a boon, O parrot, O winged traveler of the sky; choose a boon, O crooked-necked one, whatever you desire in your heart.’

36.

36.

“Api [V 3.0438][M 3.0472] nāma naṃ passeyyaṃ, sapattaṃ saphalaṃ dumaṃ;

Daliddova nidhiṃ laddhā, nandeyyāhaṃ punappunaṃ.

‘If I could see that tree with leaves and fruit again, I would rejoice over it repeatedly, like a poor man who has found a treasure.’

37.

37.

“Tato amatamādāya, abhisiñci mahīruhaṃ;

Tassa sākhā virūhiṃsu, sītacchāyā manoramā.

‘Then, taking the water of immortality, Sakka sprinkled the tree. Its branches sprouted forth, becoming delightful with cool shade.’

38.

38.

“Evaṃ sakka sukhī hohi, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Yathāhamajja sukhito, disvāna saphalaṃ dumaṃ.

‘May you, Sakka, be happy along with all your kinsmen, just as I am happy today, seeing this fruitful tree.’

39.

39.

“Suvassa ca varaṃ datvā, katvāna saphalaṃ dumaṃ;

Pakkāmi saha bhariyāya, devānaṃ nandanaṃ vana”nti. –

‘Having given the boon to the parrot and made the tree fruitful, Sakka departed with his wife to the Nandana Grove of the devas.’

Pañhapaṭipañhāpi atthopi purimanayeneva veditabbā, anuttānapadameva pana vaṇṇayissāma.

The questions and counter-questions, as well as the meanings, should be understood in the same way as before. However, we will now explain only the obscure words.

Haripattāti nīlapattasacchannā. Koḷāpeti vāte paharante ākoṭitasaddaṃ [P 3.0496] viya muñcamāne nissāre. Suvassāti āyasmato suvarājassa kasmā evarūpe rukkhe mano nirato. Phalassāti phalaṃ assa rukkhassa. Nekavassagaṇeti anekavassagaṇe. Bahūti samānepi anekasate na dve tayo, atha kho bahūva. Viditvānāti haṃsarāja idāni amhākaṃ imaṃ rukkhaṃ aphalaṃ viditvāpi yathā pure etena saddhiṃ metti, sāva metti, tañhi mayaṃ na bhindāma, mettiṃ bhindantā hi anariyā asappurisā nāma hontīti pakāsento evamāha.

“Haripattā” means covered with green leaves. “Koḷāpe” means on the sapless tree, which emits a sound as if being beaten when struck by the wind. “Suvassa” means: why is the mind of the venerable Parrot King intent on such a tree? “Phalassa” means the fruit of this tree. “Nekavassagaṇe” means for many multitudes of years. “Bahū” means not just two or three, but indeed many, even many hundreds of similar trees. “Viditvāna” means the king of swans, declaring thus: “Even knowing now that this tree of ours is fruitless, our friendship remains the same as before; we do not break that friendship. For those who break a friendship are called ignoble and unworthy persons.”

Opattanti avapattaṃ nippattaṃ patitapattaṃ. Kiṃ dosaṃ passaseti aññe sakuṇā etaṃ ohāya aññattha gacchanti, tvaṃ evaṃ gamane kiṃ nāma dosaṃ passasi. Ye phalatthāti ye pakkhino phalatthāya phalakāraṇā sambhajanti upagacchanti, aphaloti ñatvā etaṃ jahanti. Attatthapaññāti attano atthāya paññā, paraṃ anoloketvā attaniyeva vā ṭhitā etesaṃ paññāti attatthapaññā. Pakkhapātinoti te attanoyeva vuḍḍhiṃ paccāsīsamānā mittapakkhaṃ pātenti nāsentīti pakkhapātino nāma honti. Attapakkheyeva vā patantīti pakkhapātino.

“Opattanti” means having shed its leaves, leafless, with fallen leaves. “Kiṃ dosaṃ passase” means: other birds abandon this and go elsewhere; what fault do you see in so doing? “Ye phalatthā” means: those birds who associate with or approach for the sake of fruit, for the reason of fruit, abandon it upon knowing it is fruitless. “Attatthapaññā” means wisdom for one's own benefit; their wisdom, not considering others, is established in themselves alone—this is “attatthapaññā”. “Pakkhapātino” means: they, hoping for their own growth, cause the side of their friends to fall, they destroy it, thus they are called “pakkhapātino”. Or, they fall only on their own side, thus they are “pakkhapātino”.

Api [M 3.0473] nāma nanti haṃsarāja, sace me manoratho nipphajjeyya, tayā dinno varo sampajjeyya, api nāma ahaṃ imaṃ rukkhaṃ sapattaṃ saphalaṃ puna passeyyaṃ, tato daliddo nidhiṃ [V 3.0439] labhitvāva punappunaṃ etaṃ abhinandeyyaṃ, taṃ disvāva pamodeyyaṃ. Amatamādāyāti attano ānubhāvena ṭhito gaṅgodakaṃ gahetvā abhisiñcayīti attho. Imasmiṃ jātake imāya saddhiṃ dve abhisambuddhagāthā honti.

“Api nāma nanti” means: O king of swans, if my wish were to be accomplished, if the boon given by you were to succeed, would that I might see this tree again with leaves and fruit. Then, just like a poor man having found a treasure, I would rejoice in it again and again; just seeing it, I would be delighted. “Amatamādāya” means: standing by his own power, he took water from the Ganges and sprinkled it; this is the meaning. In this Jataka, together with this one, there are two verses of the Fully Enlightened One.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā sakko anuruddho ahosi, suvarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jataka: "At that time, Sakka was Anuruddha, and the parrot king was indeed myself."

Cūḷasuvajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷasuva Jātaka, the fourth.

[431] 5. Haritacajātakavaṇṇanā

[431] 5. Commentary on the Haritaca Jātaka

Sutaṃ metaṃ mahābrahmeti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhikkhuṃ ekaṃ alaṅkatamātugāmaṃ disvā ukkaṇṭhitaṃ dīghakesanakhalomaṃ vibbhamitukāmaṃ ācariyupajjhāyehi aruciyā ānītaṃ. Satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kiṃkāraṇā”ti vatvā “alaṅkatamātugāmaṃ disvā kilesavasena, bhante”ti [P 3.0497] vutte “bhikkhu kileso nāma guṇaviddhaṃsako appassādo niraye nibbattāpeti, esa pana kileso kiṃkāraṇā taṃ na kilamessati? Na hi sineruṃ paharitvā paharaṇavāto purāṇapaṇṇassa lajjati, imañhi kilesaṃ nissāya bodhiñāṇassa anupadaṃ caramānā pañcaabhiññaaṭṭhasamāpattilābhino visuddhamahāpurisāpi satiṃ upaṭṭhapetuṃ asakkontā jhānaṃ antaradhāpesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘I have heard this, O Great Brahma.’ The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning a discontented monk. That monk, after seeing an adorned woman, became discontented. With long hair, nails, and body hair, and wishing to leave the monkhood, he was brought by his teachers and preceptors against his will. The Teacher asked him, ‘Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?’ When he replied, ‘It is true, Bhante,’ the Teacher asked, ‘For what reason?’ The monk said, ‘Bhante, it is due to the power of defilement after seeing an adorned woman.’ The Teacher then said, ‘Monk, defilement destroys virtue, brings little satisfaction, and leads to rebirth in hell. How could this defilement not affect you? A great wind that could strike down Mount Sineru has no shame in blowing away a withered leaf. Indeed, on account of this defilement, even pure and great men who had attained the five higher knowledges and the eight meditative attainments—who were following the path to enlightenment—were unable to maintain mindfulness and lost their meditative states.’ Having said this, he recounted the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ nigame asītikoṭivibhave brāhmaṇakule nibbatti, kañcanachavitāya panassa “haritacakumāro”ti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vayappatto takkasilaṃ gantvā uggahitasippo kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā mātāpitūnaṃ accayena dhanavilokanaṃ katvā “dhanameva paññāyati, dhanassa uppādakā na paññāyanti, mayāpi maraṇamukhe cuṇṇavicuṇṇena bhavitabba”nti maraṇabhayabhīto mahādānaṃ datvā [M 3.0474] himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā sattame divase abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā tattha ciraṃ vanamūlaphalāhāro yāpetvā loṇambilasevanatthāya pabbatā otaritvā anupubbena bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase bārāṇasiyaṃ bhikkhāya caranto rājadvāraṃ sampāpuṇi. Rājā taṃ disvā pasannacitto pakkosāpetvā samussitasetacchatte rājapallaṅke nisīdāpetvā [V 3.0440] nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhojetvā anumodanāvasāne atirekataraṃ pasīditvā “kahaṃ, bhante, gacchathā”ti vatvā “vassāvāsaṭṭhānaṃ upadhārema, mahārājā”ti vutte “sādhu, bhante”ti bhuttapātarāso taṃ ādāya uyyānaṃ gantvā tattha rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādīni kārāpetvā uyyānapālaṃ paricārakaṃ katvā datvā vanditvā nikkhami. Mahāsatto tato paṭṭhāya nibaddhaṃ rañño gehe bhuñjanto dvādasa vassāni tattha vasi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in a certain market town, possessing eighty crores of wealth. Because of his golden complexion, they named him ‘Haritacakumāra.’ When he came of age, he went to Takkasilā, mastered the arts, and established a household. After his parents passed away, he examined his wealth and thought, ‘Only the wealth remains; those who produced it are gone. I too will be crushed in the jaws of death.’ Fearing death, he gave great alms, entered the Himalayas, and went forth as an ascetic. On the seventh day, he attained the higher knowledges and meditative attainments. Living there for a long time, sustaining himself on forest roots and fruits, he eventually descended from the mountains to seek salt and sour food. Gradually reaching Benares, he stayed in the royal garden. The next day, while wandering for alms in Benares, he arrived at the king’s gate. The king, seeing him and being pleased, had him summoned and seated on the royal throne under a white parasol. He offered him various exquisite foods. At the conclusion of the meal, being exceedingly pleased, the king asked, ‘Where are you going, Bhante?’ The Bodhisatta replied, ‘We are seeking a place for the rains-residence, Great King.’ The king said, ‘Very well, Bhante.’ After eating his morning meal, the king took him to the garden, had dwellings for night and day prepared, appointed a gardener as his attendant, and after paying his respects, departed. From then on, the Great Being regularly ate in the king’s palace and lived there for twelve years.

Athekadivasaṃ rājā paccantaṃ kupitaṃ vūpasametuṃ gacchanto [P 3.0498] “amhākaṃ puññakkhettaṃ mā pamajjī”ti mahāsattaṃ deviyā niyyādetvā agamāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya sā mahāsattaṃ sahatthā parivisati. Athekadivasaṃ sā bhojanaṃ sampādetvā tasmiṃ cirāyamāne gandhodakena nhatvā saṇhaṃ maṭṭhasāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā sīhapañjaraṃ vivarāpetvā sarīre vātaṃ paharāpentī khuddakamañcake nipajji. Mahāsattopi divātaraṃ sunivattho supāruto bhikkhābhājanaṃ ādāya ākāsenāgantvā sīhapañjaraṃ pāpuṇi. Deviyā tassa vākacirasaddaṃ sutvā vegena uṭṭhahantiyā maṭṭhasāṭako bhassi, mahāsattassa visabhāgārammaṇaṃ cakkhuṃ paṭihaññi. Athassa anekavassakoṭisatasahassakāle abbhantare nivutthakileso karaṇḍake sayitaāsīviso viya uṭṭhahitvā jhānaṃ antaradhāpesi. So satiṃ upaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkonto gantvā deviṃ hatthe gaṇhi, tāvadeva sāṇiṃ parikkhipiṃsu. So tāya saddhiṃ lokadhammaṃ sevitvā bhuñjitvā uyyānaṃ gantvā tato paṭṭhāya devasikaṃ tatheva akāsi. Tassa tāya saddhiṃ lokadhammapaṭisevanaṃ sakalanagare pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ. Amaccā “haritacatāpaso evamakāsī”ti rañño paṇṇaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Rājā “maṃ bhinditukāmā evaṃ vadantī”ti asaddahitvā paccantaṃ vūpasametvā bārāṇasiṃ paccāgantvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā deviyā santikaṃ gantvā “saccaṃ, kira mama ayyo [M 3.0475] haritacatāpaso tayā saddhiṃ lokadhammaṃ paṭisevatī”ti pucchi. “Saccaṃ, devā”ti. So tassāpi asaddahitvā “tameva paṭipucchissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā taṃ pucchanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

One day, as the king was departing to pacify a rebellion in the border region, he entrusted the Great Being to the queen, saying, 'Do not neglect our field of merit.' From then on, the queen served the Great Being with her own hands. One day, after preparing the meal, as the Great Being was late in arriving, she bathed in perfumed water, dressed in a smooth and fine cloth, opened the lion-window, and lay down on a small couch, letting the breeze blow upon her body. The Great Being, well-dressed and properly covered, took his alms bowl and, traveling through the air late in the day, arrived at the lion-window. Hearing the sound of his bark-cloth robe, the queen rose quickly, and her fine cloth slipped off. An unsuitable object of sight struck the Great Being's eyes. At that moment, the defilement that had been lying dormant within him for many hundreds of thousands of crores of years arose like a poisonous snake sleeping in a basket and caused his meditative absorption to vanish. Unable to maintain mindfulness, he went and took the queen by the hand; immediately, they drew a curtain around them. Having indulged in the worldly way with the queen and eaten his meal, he went to the garden and continued to do the same every day thereafter. His practice of the worldly way with the queen became known throughout the entire city. The ministers sent a message to the king, saying, 'The Haritaca ascetic has acted thus.' The king, not believing it and thinking, 'They speak thus wishing to cause a division,' pacified the border region and returned to Benares. After circumambulating the city, he went to the queen and asked, 'Is it true, as they say, that my noble Haritaca ascetic indulges in the worldly way with you?' 'It is true, Your Majesty,' she replied. Still not believing even her, he thought, 'I will question the ascetic himself,' and went to the garden. After paying homage and sitting to one side, wishing to question him, he spoke the first verse:

40.

40.

“Sutaṃ metaṃ mahābrahme, kāme bhuñjati hārito;

Kaccetaṃ vacanaṃ tucchaṃ, kacci suddho iriyyasī”ti.

I have heard this, O Great Brahma, that Harita enjoys sensual pleasures. Is this saying perchance empty? Do you conduct yourself in purity?

Tattha kaccetanti kacci etaṃ “hārito kāme paribhuñjatī”ti amhehi sutaṃ vacanaṃ tucchaṃ abhūtaṃ, kacci tvaṃ suddho iriyyasi viharasīti.

In that verse, 'kaccetaṃ' means: Is this saying we have heard, 'Harita partakes of sensual pleasures,' empty and untrue? 'Kacci suddho iriyyasi' means: Do you conduct yourself and dwell in purity?

So [V 3.0441][P 3.0499] cintesi – “ayaṃ rājā ‘nāhaṃ paribhuñjāmī’ti vuttepi mama saddahissateva, imasmiṃ loke saccasadisī patiṭṭhā nāma natthi. Ujjhitasaccā hi bodhimūle nisīditvā bodhiṃ pāpuṇituṃ na sakkonti, mayā saccameva kathetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Bodhisattassa hi ekaccesu ṭhānesu pāṇātipātopi adinnādānampi kāmesumicchācāropi surāmerayamajjapānampi hotiyeva, atthabhedakavisaṃvādanaṃ purakkhatvā musāvādo nāma na hoti, tasmā so saccameva kathento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

He thought: 'This king would believe me even if I said, "I do not partake," but there is no refuge in this world like the truth. Those who have abandoned the truth cannot attain enlightenment even if they sit at the foot of the Bodhi tree. It is proper for me to speak only the truth.' For a Bodhisatta, in certain circumstances, there may be the taking of life, the taking of what is not given, sexual misconduct, and the drinking of intoxicants; but there is no telling of a lie with the primary intention of being deceptive and destroying welfare. Therefore, speaking only the truth, he uttered the second verse:

41.

41.

“Evametaṃ mahārāja, yathā te vacanaṃ sutaṃ;

Kummaggaṃ paṭipannosmi, mohaneyyesu mucchito”ti.

It is so, great king, just as you have heard. I have entered upon a wrong path, infatuated by things that cause delusion.

Tattha mohaneyyesūti kāmaguṇesu. Kāmaguṇesu hi loko muyhati, te ca lokaṃ mohayanti, tasmā te “mohaneyyā”ti vuccantīti.

In that verse, 'mohaneyyesu' refers to the strands of sensual pleasure. For the world is deluded by the strands of sensual pleasure, and they delude the world; therefore they are called 'mohaneyyā' (things that cause delusion).

Taṃ sutvā rājā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke the third verse:

42.

42.

“Adu paññā kimatthiyā, nipuṇā sādhucintinī;

Yāya uppatitaṃ rāgaṃ, kiṃ mano na vinodaye”ti.

Then of what use is that subtle wisdom which reflects on what is good? Why, with it, did your mind not dispel the lust that had arisen?

Tattha adūti nipāto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bhante, gilānassa nāma bhesajjaṃ, pipāsitassa pānīyaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ, tumhākaṃ panesā nipuṇā sādhūnaṃ atthānaṃ cintinī paññā kimatthiyā, yāya puna uppatitaṃ rāgaṃ kiṃ mano na vinodaye, kiṃ cittaṃ vinodetuṃ nāsakkhīti.

In that verse, 'adū' is a particle. This is what is said: 'Venerable sir, medicine is a refuge for the sick, and water for the thirsty; but of what use is this subtle wisdom of yours, which reflects on the welfare of the good? Why was your mind unable to dispel the lust that had arisen?'

Athassa [M 3.0476] kilesabalaṃ dassento hārito catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, showing the king the power of the defilements, Harita spoke the fourth verse:

43.

43.

“Cattārome mahārāja, loke atibalā bhusā;

Rāgo doso mado moho, yattha paññā na gādhatī”ti.

These four, great king, are exceedingly mighty and strong in the world: lust, hatred, intoxication, and delusion, wherein wisdom finds no footing.

Tattha [P 3.0500] yatthāti yesu pariyuṭṭhānaṃ pattesu mahoghe patitā viya paññā gādhaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ na labhati.

In that verse, 'yattha' (wherein) means: when these have arisen and overwhelmed the mind, wisdom finds no footing or firm standing, like one fallen into a great flood.

Taṃ [V 3.0442] sutvā rājā pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the king spoke the fifth verse:

44.

44.

“Arahā sīlasampanno, suddho carati hārito;

Medhāvī paṇḍito ceva, iti no sammato bhava”nti.

'A worthy one, accomplished in virtue, Harita conducts himself purely; intelligent and wise'—thus were you regarded by us.

Tattha iti no sammatoti evaṃ amhākaṃ sammato sambhāvito bhavaṃ.

In that verse, 'iti no sammato' means: thus were you esteemed and honored by us.

Tato hārito chaṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Haritaca the ascetic spoke the sixth verse:

45.

45.

“Medhāvīnampi hiṃsanti, isiṃ dhammaguṇe rataṃ;

Vitakkā pāpakā rāja, subhā rāgūpasaṃhitā”ti.

They harm even the wise, O king, the sage who delights in the qualities of the Dhamma—evil thoughts, appearing beautiful, associated with lust.

Tattha subhāti subhanimittaggahaṇena pavattāti.

In that verse, 'subhā' means that they arise from grasping the sign of beauty.

Atha naṃ kilesappahāne ussāhaṃ kārento rājā sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, encouraging him to make an effort to abandon the defilements, the king spoke the seventh verse:

46.

46.

“Uppannāyaṃ sarīrajo, rāgo vaṇṇavidūsano tava;

Taṃ pajaha bhaddamatthu te, bahunnāsi medhāvisammato”ti.

This lust has arisen, born of the body, the defiler of your beauty. Abandon it! May it be well with you. You were once regarded as wise by many.

Tattha vaṇṇavidūsano tavāti tava sarīravaṇṇassa ca guṇavaṇṇassa ca vidūsano. Bahunnāsīti bahūnaṃ āsi medhāvīti sammato.

Herein, vaṇṇavidūsano tava means the defiler of both your physical beauty and the beauty of your virtue. Bahunnāsi means: you were esteemed as wise by many.

Tato mahāsatto satiṃ labhitvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ sallakkhetvā aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, having regained mindfulness and perceived the danger in sensual pleasures, spoke the eighth verse:

47.

47.

“Te andhakārake kāme, bahudukkhe mahāvise;

Tesaṃ mūlaṃ gavesissaṃ, checchaṃ rāgaṃ sabandhana”nti.

These sensual pleasures that bring darkness, are full of suffering, and are a great poison—I will search for their root; I will cut off lust with its fetters.

Tattha [M 3.0477] andhakāraketi paññācakkhuvināsanato andhabhāvakare. Bahudukkheti ettha “appassādā kāmā”tiādīni (ma. ni. 1.234; pāci. 417; cūḷava. 65) suttāni haritvā tesaṃ bahudukkhatā dassetabbā. Mahāviseti sampayuttakilesavisassa ceva vipākavisassa [V 3.0443] ca mahantatāya mahāvise. Tesaṃ mūlanti te vuttappakāre kāme pahātuṃ tesaṃ mūlaṃ [P 3.0501] gavesissaṃ pariyesissāmi. Kiṃ pana tesaṃ mūlanti? Ayonisomanasikāro. Checchaṃ rāgaṃ sabandhananti mahārāja, idāneva paññākhaggena paharitvā subhanimittabandhanena sabandhanaṃ rāgaṃ chindissāmīti.

In this context, 'blinding' means causing the state of blindness by destroying the eye of wisdom. As for 'full of suffering,' by citing such suttas as 'Sensual pleasures give little satisfaction' (MN 1.234; Pāc. 417; Cūḷava. 65), the abundance of suffering in them should be demonstrated. 'Great poison' means they are a great poison because of the magnitude of both the associated defilement-poison and the result-poison. 'Their root' means I will seek and search for the root of these sensual pleasures described above in order to abandon them. And what is their root? Unwise attention. 'I will cut off passion along with its bonds' means, 'O king, I will now strike with the sword of wisdom and sever passion along with its bond, which is the sign of beauty.'

Idañca pana vatvā “mahārāja, okāsaṃ tāva me karohī”ti okāsaṃ kāretvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ oloketvā puna naṭṭhajjhānaṃ uppādetvā paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā ākāse pallaṅkena nisīditvā rañño dhammaṃ desetvā “mahārāja, ahaṃ aṭṭhāne vutthakāraṇā mahājanamajjhe garahappatto, appamatto hohi, puna dāni ahaṃ anitthigandhavanasaṇḍameva gamissāmī”ti rañño rodantassa paridevantassa himavantameva gantvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokūpago ahosi.

Having said this, he then requested, 'Great king, please grant me leave.' After receiving permission, he entered the leaf hut, gazed at the kasiṇa circle, and re-attained the lost jhāna. Emerging from the leaf hut, he sat cross-legged in the air and taught the Dhamma to the king, saying, 'Great king, because I dwelt in an unsuitable place, I have met with reproach in the midst of the multitude. Be diligent; now I shall return to a forest grove where there is no scent of women.' Then, while the king was weeping and lamenting, he went to the Himalayas, and with his jhānas intact, he was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā –

The Teacher, knowing that circumstance—

48.

48.

“Idaṃ vatvāna hārito, isi saccaparakkamo;

Kāmarāgaṃ virājetvā, brahmalokūpago ahū”ti. –

“Having said this, Harita the sage, striving in truth, having dispelled sensual passion, was reborn in the Brahma world.”

Abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhahi.

Having become fully enlightened, he spoke this verse, revealed the Truths, and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of Arahantship.

Tadā rājā ānando ahosi, haritacatāpaso pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the ascetic Harita was I myself.

Haritacajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The commentary on the Haritaca Jātaka, the fifth, is finished.

[432] 6. Padakusalamāṇavajātakavaṇṇanā

[432] 6. Commentary on the Padakusalamāṇava Jātaka

Bahussutanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ dārakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthiyaṃ kuṭumbikaputto sattavassakāleyeva padakusalo ahosi. Athassa pitā “imaṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti tassa ajānantasseva [M 3.0478] mittagharaṃ agamāsi. So pitu gataṭṭhānaṃ apucchitvāva tassa padānusārena gantvā pitu santike aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ pitā ekadivasaṃ pucchi [V 3.0444] “tāta, tvaṃ mayi taṃ ajānāpetvā gatepi mama gataṭṭhānaṃ kiṃ jānāsī”ti? “Tāta[P 3.0502], padaṃ te sañjānāmi, padakusalo aha”nti. Athassa vīmaṃsanatthāya pitā bhuttapātarāso gharā nikkhamitvā anantaraṃ paṭivissakagharaṃ gantvā tato dutiyaṃ, tato tatiyaṃ gharaṃ pavisitvā tatiyagharā nikkhamitvā puna attano gharaṃ āgantvā tato uttaradvārena nikkhamitvā nagaraṃ vāmaṃ karonto jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā dhammaṃ suṇanto nisīdi. Dārako “kahaṃ me pitā”ti pucchitvā “na jānāmā”ti vutte tassa padānusārena anantarapaṭivissakassa gharaṃ ādiṃ katvā pitu gatamaggeneva jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā pitu santike aṭṭhāsi. Pitarā ca “kathaṃ tāta, mama idhāgatabhāvaṃ aññāsī”ti puṭṭho “padaṃ te sañjānitvā padānusārena āgatomhī”ti āha. Satthā “kiṃ kathesi upāsakā”ti pucchitvā “bhante, ayaṃ dārako padakusalo, ahaṃ imaṃ vīmaṃsanto iminā nāma upāyena āgato, ayampi maṃ gehe adisvā mama padānusārena āgato”ti vutte “anacchariyaṃ, upāsaka, bhūmiyaṃ padasañjānanaṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitā ākāse padaṃ sañjāniṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Regarding 'Very learned,' the Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke concerning a certain boy. It is said that in Sāvatthī, the son of a householder was skilled in recognizing footprints at the age of only seven. Then his father, thinking, 'I will test him,' went to a friend's house without the boy's knowledge. The boy, without even asking where his father had gone, followed his footprints and stood in his presence. One day, his father asked him, 'Dear son, how do you know my location even when I go without letting you know?' He replied, 'Father, I recognize your footprints; I am skilled in footprints.' Then, to test him further, the father, after having had his breakfast, left the house, went to a neighbor's house, from there to a second, and then to a third. After leaving the third house, he returned home, then left by the north gate, and keeping the city on his left, went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat listening to the Dhamma. The boy asked, 'Where is my father?' and being told, 'We do not know,' he followed the footprints starting from the neighbor's house, following the same path his father took, and reached Jetavana. There he paid homage to the Teacher and stood near his father. When asked by his father, 'How, dear son, did you know I came here?' he said, 'I recognized your footprints and followed them here.' The Teacher asked, 'What are you discussing, lay devotee?' The lay devotee said, 'Venerable sir, this boy is skilled in footprints. I came here by such and such a way to test him, and he, not seeing me at home, followed my footprints and came here.' The Teacher said, 'Lay devotee, it is not surprising to recognize footprints on the ground; the wise of old recognized footprints even in the sky.' Being requested by him, he then related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tassa aggamahesī aticaritvā raññā pucchitā “sace ahaṃ tumhe aticarāmi, assamukhī yakkhinī homī”ti sapathaṃ katvā tato kālaṃ katvā ekasmiṃ pabbatapāde assamukhī yakkhinī hutvā leṇaguhāyaṃ vasamānā mahāaṭaviyaṃ pubbantato aparantaṃ gamanamagge anusañcarante manusse gahetvā khādati. Sā kira tīṇi vassāni vessavaṇaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā āyāmato tiṃsayojane vitthārato pañcayojane ṭhāne manusse khādituṃ labhi. Athekadivasaṃ eko aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo abhirūpo brāhmaṇo bahūhi manussehi parivuto taṃ maggaṃ abhiruhi. Taṃ disvā yakkhinī tussitvā pakkhandi, taṃ disvā parivāramanussā palāyiṃsu. Sā vātavegena gantvā brāhmaṇaṃ gahetvā piṭṭhiyā [P 3.0503] nipajjāpetvā guhaṃ gacchantī purisasamphassaṃ paṭilabhitvā kilesavasena tasmiṃ sinehaṃ uppādetvā taṃ akhāditvā attano sāmikaṃ akāsi. Te ubhopi samaggasaṃvāsaṃ vasiṃsu [M 3.0479] tato paṭṭhāya yakkhinī manusse gaṇhantī vatthataṇḍulatelādīnipi gahetvā tassa nānaggarasabhojanaṃ upanetvā attanā manussamaṃsaṃ khādati. Gamanakāle tassa palāyanabhayena mahatiyā silāya guhādvāraṃ pidahitvā gacchati. Evaṃ tesu sammodamānesu vasantesu bodhisatto nibbattaṭṭhānā cavitvā brāhmaṇaṃ paṭicca tassā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Sā dasamāsaccayena puttaṃ vijāyitvā putte ca brāhmaṇe ca balavasinehā hutvā ubhopi posesi. Sā aparabhāge putte vuḍḍhippatte puttampi pitarā saddhiṃ antoguhāyaṃ pavesetvā dvāraṃ pidahi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, his chief queen, having committed adultery, was questioned by the king. She swore an oath, saying, 'If I am unfaithful to you, may I become a yakkhinī with the face of a horse.' After making this vow, she died and was reborn as a yakkhinī with the face of a horse, dwelling in a cave at the foot of a mountain. Roaming the great forest from the eastern end to the western end along the path where people traveled, she would seize and devour them. It is said that for three years she served Vessavaṇa and was granted permission to eat humans within a space thirty yojanas long and five yojanas wide. One day, a wealthy brahmin, possessing great riches and abundance, handsome and surrounded by many attendants, took that same road. Seeing him, the yakkhinī, delighted, rushed forward. Upon seeing her, the attendants fled. Moving swiftly as the wind, she seized the brahmin, laid him on her back, and, while carrying him to her cave, having experienced the touch of a man, she developed affection for him due to defilements and, instead of eating him, made him her husband. The two lived together harmoniously. From then on, whenever the yakkhinī captured people, she would also take cloth, rice, oil, and other things and offer various excellent foods to him, while she herself ate human flesh. When she left, fearing he might escape, she would block the cave entrance with a large rock. While they lived thus enjoying themselves, the Bodhisatta, having passed away from his previous existence, was conceived in her womb dependent on the brahmin. After ten months, she gave birth to a son and, filled with deep love for both the child and the brahmin, she raised them both. Later, when the son had grown up, she also put the son, along with his father, inside the cave and sealed the entrance.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 3.0445] bodhisatto tassā gatakālaṃ ñatvā silaṃ apanetvā pitaraṃ bahi akāsi. Sā āgantvā “kena silā apanītā”ti vatvā “amma, mayā apanītā, andhakāre nisīdituṃ na sakkomī”ti vutte puttasinehena na kiñci avoca. Athekadivasaṃ bodhisatto pitaraṃ pucchi “tāta, mayhaṃ mātu mukhaṃ aññādisaṃ, tumhākaṃ mukhaṃ aññādisaṃ, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti? “Tāta, tava mātā manussamaṃsakhādikā yakkhinī, mayaṃ ubho manussā”ti. “Tāta, yadi evaṃ, idha kasmā vasāma, ehi manussapathaṃ gacchāmā”ti. “Tāta, sace mayaṃ palāyissāma, ubhopi amhe tava mātā khādissatī”ti. Bodhisatto “mā bhāyi, tāta, tava manussapathasampāpanaṃ mama bhāro”ti pitaraṃ samassāsetvā punadivase mātari gatāya pitaraṃ gahetvā palāyi. Yakkhinī āgantvā te adisvā vātavegena pakkhanditvā te gahetvā “brāhmaṇa, kiṃ palāyasi, kiṃ te idha natthī”ti vatvā “bhadde, mā mayhaṃ kujjhi, putto te maṃ [P 3.0504] gahetvā palāyatī”ti vutte puttasinehena kiñci avatvā te assāsetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaññeva te gahetvā gantvā evaṃ punapi katipaye divase palāyante ānesi.

One day, the Bodhisatta, knowing the time of her departure, removed the stone and brought his father outside. When she returned and asked, 'Who removed the stone?' he replied, 'Mother, I removed it—I cannot sit in the dark.' Out of love for her son, she said nothing. Another day, the Bodhisatta asked his father, 'Father, my mother’s face is different, and your face is different—what is the reason?' 'Son, your mother is a yakkhinī who eats human flesh; we are both humans.' 'Father, if that is the case, why do we stay here? Come, let us go to the human world.' 'Son, if we flee, your mother will devour us both.' The Bodhisatta reassured him, 'Do not fear, Father, taking you to the human world is my responsibility.' The next day, when his mother had gone, he took his father and fled. The yakkhinī returned, and not seeing them, rushed after them with the speed of the wind. Catching them, she said, 'Brahmin, why do you flee? Is there nothing for you here?' He replied, 'Good lady, do not be angry with me—your son is taking me away.' Out of love for her son, she said nothing, consoled them, and took them back to her dwelling place. Thus, when they fled again after a few days, she brought them back.

Bodhisatto cintesi “mayhaṃ mātu paricchinnena okāsena bhavitabbaṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imissā āṇāpavattiṭṭhānasīmaṃ puccheyyaṃ, atha naṃ atikkamitvā palāyissāmā”ti. So ekadivasaṃ mātaraṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisinno “amma, mātusantakaṃ nāma puttānaṃ pāpuṇāti, akkhāhi tāva me attano santakāya bhūmiyā pariccheda”nti āha. Sā sabbadisāsu pabbatanadīnimittādīni kathetvā āyāmato tiṃsayojanaṃ, vitthārato pañcayojanaṃ puttassa kathetvā “idaṃ ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ sallakkhehi puttā”ti āha. So [M 3.0480] dve tayo divase atikkamitvā mātu aṭavigatakāle pitaraṃ khandhaṃ āropetvā tassā dinnasaññāya vātavegena pakkhando paricchedanadītīraṃ sampāpuṇi. Sāpi āgantvā te apassantī anubandhi. Bodhisatto pitaraṃ gahetvā nadīmajjhaṃ agamāsi. Sā āgantvā nadītīre ṭhatvā attano paricchedaṃ atikkantabhāvaṃ ñatvā tattheva ṭhatvā “tāta, pitaraṃ gahetvā ehi, ko mayhaṃ doso, tumhākaṃ maṃ nissāya kiṃ nāma na sampajjati, nivatta, sāmī”ti puttañca patiñca yāci. Atha brāhmaṇo nadiṃ uttari. Sā puttameva yācantī “tāta, mā evaṃ kari, nivattāhī”ti āha. “Amma, mayaṃ manussā, tvaṃ yakkhinī, na sakkā sabbakālaṃ tava santike vasitu”nti. “Neva nivattissasi, tātā”ti. “Āma, ammā”ti. “Tāta, yadi na nivattissasi, manussaloke jīvitaṃ nāma dukkhaṃ, sippaṃ ajānantā jīvituṃ na sakkonti, ahaṃ ekaṃ cintāmaṇiṃ nāma vijjaṃ jānāmi, tassānubhāvena dvādasasaṃvaccharamatthake haṭabhaṇḍampi padānupadaṃ gantvā [V 3.0446] sakkā jānituṃ. Ayaṃ te jīvikā bhavissati, uggaṇha, tāta, anagghaṃ manta”nti tathārūpena dukkhena abhibhūtāpi puttasinehena mantaṃ [P 3.0505] adāsi.

The Bodhisatta thought, 'My mother must have a defined domain. I should ask her the boundary of her authority, and then we can escape by crossing it.' One day, taking his mother aside, he sat down and said, 'Mother, a mother’s property rightly passes to her sons. Pray, tell me the extent of your own territory.' She described landmarks such as mountains and rivers in all directions, telling her son that it was thirty yojanas in length and five yojanas in width. 'Son, mark well this extent of land,' she said. After two or three days had passed, when his mother had gone to the forest, he placed his father on his shoulders and, by the sign she had given, fled with the speed of the wind and reached the river that was the boundary. She too, upon returning and not seeing them, pursued them. The Bodhisatta, carrying his father, went into the middle of the river. She arrived and stood on the riverbank, and realizing that her boundary had been crossed, she stood right there and pleaded, 'Son, come back with your father. What is my fault? What can you not accomplish by relying on me? Return, my lord!' She begged both her son and her husband. Then the brahmin crossed the river. Still pleading with her son, she said, 'Son, do not do this—turn back!' 'Mother, we are humans, and you are a yakkhinī; we cannot live with you forever.' 'Will you not return, son?' 'No, mother.' 'Son, if you will not return, know that life in the human world is difficult. Those who know no skill cannot survive. I know a certain magical spell called the Cintāmaṇi, by whose power it is possible to trace, step by step, even stolen goods up to twelve years after they were taken. This will be your livelihood. Learn this priceless spell, son!' Overcome with such sorrow, yet moved by love for her son, she gave him the spell.

Bodhisatto nadiyā ṭhitakova mātaraṃ vanditvā atisakkaccaṃ sutaṃ katvā mantaṃ gahetvā mātaraṃ vanditvā “gacchatha, ammā”ti āha. “Tāta, tumhesu anivattantesu mayhaṃ jīvitaṃ natthī”ti vatvā –

The Bodhisatta, while still standing in the river, paid homage to his mother. Having listened with great care and learned the mantra, he bowed to his mother again and said, 'Mother, you may go.' She said, 'My son, if you do not return, I shall have no life,' and spoke this verse:

“Ehi putta nivattassu, mā anāthaṃ karohi me;

Ajja puttaṃ apassantī, yakkhinī maraṇaṃ gatā”ti.

'Come, my son, return; do not leave me without refuge. Today, failing to see her son, the yakkhinī will meet her death.'

Yakkhinī uraṃ pahari, tāvadevassā puttasokena hadayaṃ phali. Sā maritvā tattheva patitā. Tadā bodhisatto tassā matabhāvaṃ ñatvā pitaraṃ pakkositvā mātu santikaṃ gantvā citakaṃ katvā jhāpetvā āḷāhanaṃ nibbāpetvā nānāvaṇṇehi pupphehi pūjetvā vanditvā roditvā paridevitvā pitaraṃ ādāya bārāṇasiṃ gantvā rājadvāre ṭhatvā “padakusalo māṇavo dvāre ṭhito”ti rañño paṭivedetvā “tena hi āgacchatū”ti vutte pavisitvā rājānaṃ vanditvā “tāta, kiṃ sippaṃ jānāsī”ti vutte “deva, dvādasasaṃvaccharamatthake haṭabhaṇḍaṃ padānupadaṃ gantvā gaṇhituṃ [M 3.0481] jānāmī”ti āha. “Tena hi maṃ upaṭṭhāhī”ti. “Deva, devasikaṃ sahassaṃ labhanto upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti. “Sādhu tāta, upaṭṭhahā”ti. Rājā devasikaṃ sahassaṃ dāpesi.

The yakkhinī struck her chest, and at that very moment her heart broke from grief for her son. She died and fell right there. Then the Bodhisatta, realizing she was dead, called his father. He went to his mother, prepared a funeral pyre, cremated her, and after extinguishing the fire, honored her with flowers of various colors, paid his respects, wept, and lamented. Taking his father, he went to Bārāṇasī and stood at the king’s gate. Word was brought to the king: 'A young man skilled in tracking is standing at the gate.' When the king said, 'Then let him come,' he entered, paid homage to the king, and was asked, 'My boy, what skill do you know?' He replied, 'Your Majesty, I know how to follow tracks and recover stolen goods, even after twelve years.' The king said, 'Then serve me.' 'Your Majesty, I will serve you if I receive a thousand daily.' 'Very well, my boy, serve me.' The king had a thousand given to him daily.

Athekadivasaṃ purohito rājānaṃ āha – “mahārāja, mayaṃ tassa māṇavassa sippānubhāvena kassaci kammassa akatattā ‘sippaṃ atthi vā natthi vā’ti na jānāma, vīmaṃsissāma tāva na”nti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā ubhopi janā nānāratanagopakānaṃ saññaṃ datvā ratanasārabhaṇḍikaṃ gahetvā pāsādā oruyha rājanivesanantare tikkhattuṃ āvijjhitvā nisseṇiṃ attharitvā pākāramatthakena bahi otaritvā vinicchayasālaṃ pavisitvā tattha nisīditvā puna gantvā nisseṇiṃ attharitvā pākāramatthakena otaritvā antepure pokkharaṇiyā tīraṃ gantvā pokkharaṇiṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā otaritvā antopokkharaṇiyaṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ ṭhapetvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhiṃsu. Punadivase “rājanivesanato [P 3.0506] kira ratanaṃ hariṃsū”ti ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi. Rājā ajānanto viya hutvā bodhisattaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, rājanivesanato bahuratanabhaṇḍaṃ haṭaṃ, handa naṃ anuvicinituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha[V 3.0447]. “Mahārāja, dvādasasaṃvaccharamatthake haṭabhaṇḍaṃ corānaṃ padānupadaṃ gantvā āharaṇasamatthassa mama anacchariyaṃ ajja rattiṃ haṭabhaṇḍaṃ āharituṃ, āharissāmi taṃ, mā cintayitthā”ti. “Tena hi āharā”ti. So “sādhu, devā”ti vatvā mātaraṃ vanditvā mantaṃ parivattetvā mahātale ṭhitova “mahārāja, dvinnaṃ corānaṃ padaṃ paññāyatī”ti vatvā rañño ca purohitassa ca padānusārena sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā tato nikkhamitvā pāsādā oruyha rājanivesanantare tikkhattuṃ parigantvā padānusāreneva pākārasamīpaṃ gantvā pākāre ṭhatvā “mahārāja, imasmiṃ ṭhāne pākārato muccitvā ākāse padaṃ paññāyati, nisseṇiṃ attharāpetvā dethā”ti nisseṇiṃ pākāramatthakena otaritvā padānusāreneva vinicchayasālaṃ gantvā puna rājanivesanaṃ āgantvā nisseṇiṃ attharāpetvā pākāramatthakena oruyha pokkharaṇiṃ gantvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā “mahārāja, corā imaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ otiṇṇā”ti vatvā attanā ṭhapitaṃ viya bhaṇḍikaṃ nīharitvā [M 3.0482] rañño datvā “mahārāja, ime dve corā abhiññātamahācorā iminā maggena rājanivesanaṃ abhiruḷhā”ti āha. Mahājanā tuṭṭhapahaṭṭhā aṅguliyo phoṭesuṃ, celukkhepā pavattiṃsu.

One day, the chaplain said to the king, 'Great king, because we have not yet performed any task using that young man’s skill, we do not know if he truly possesses it or not. Let us test him first.' The king agreed, and both of them, having given a sign to the jewel-guards, took a casket of precious gems and descended from the palace. They circled within the palace grounds three times, set up a ladder, climbed over the wall to the outside, and entered the judgment hall. After sitting there, they went again, set up the ladder, climbed over the wall, went to the edge of the lotus pond in the inner palace, circumambulated the pond three times, and then, having descended into the water, placed the casket inside. They then returned to the palace. The next day, a great uproar arose: 'Jewels have been stolen from the royal residence!' The king, pretending to be unaware, summoned the Bodhisatta and said, 'My boy, a great treasure has been stolen from the palace. It is right that you should investigate it.' The Bodhisatta replied, 'Great king, for one like me who is capable of following the tracks of thieves and recovering goods stolen twelve years ago, it is no wonder that I can retrieve goods stolen last night. I will bring them back; do not worry.' The king said, 'Then bring them.' Saying, 'Very well, Your Majesty,' he paid homage to his mother, recited the mantra, and standing on the upper terrace, said, 'Great king, the tracks of two thieves are visible.' Following the tracks of the king and the chaplain, he entered the royal chamber, came out, descended from the palace, circled the palace grounds three times, and following the tracks to the wall, stood there and said, 'Great king, at this spot the tracks leave the wall and appear in the sky. Have a ladder set up for me.' He descended from the wall by the ladder, followed the tracks to the judgment hall, returned to the palace, had the ladder set up again, descended from the wall, went to the lotus pond, and circumambulated it three times. 'Great king, the thieves entered this pond,' he said, and taking out the casket as if he had placed it there himself, gave it to the king. He added, 'Great king, these two thieves are well-known great thieves; they entered the palace by this path.' The people, delighted and overjoyed, snapped their fingers and waved their cloths.

Rājā cintesi – “ayaṃ māṇavo padānusārena gantvā corehi ṭhapitabhaṇḍaṭṭhānameva maññe jānāti, core pana gaṇhituṃ na sakkotī”ti. Atha naṃ āha “corehi haṭabhaṇḍaṃ tāva no tayā āhaṭaṃ, corā pana na āhaṭā”ti. “Mahārāja, idheva corā, na dūre”ti. “Ko [P 3.0507] ca ko cā”ti. “Yo mahārāja, icchati, sova coro hoti, tato tumhākaṃ bhaṇḍikassa laddhakālato paṭṭhāya corehi ko attho, mā pucchitthā”ti. “Tāta, ahaṃ tuyhaṃ devasikaṃ sahassaṃ dammi, core me gahetvā dehī”ti. “Mahārāja, dhane laddhe kiṃ corehī”ti. “Dhanatopi no, tāta, core laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Tena hi, mahārāja, ‘ime nāma corā’ti tumhākaṃ na kathessāmi, atīte pavattakāraṇaṃ pana te āharissāmi, sace tumhe paññavanto, taṃ kāraṇaṃ jānāthā”ti so evaṃ vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The king thought, 'This young man, by following the tracks, seems only to know where the thieves placed the goods, but he is unable to catch the thieves.' Then he said to him, 'You have brought back the goods stolen by the thieves, but the thieves themselves have not been brought.' 'Great king, the thieves are right here, not far away.' 'Who are they?' 'Great king, whoever desires it, he is the thief. Since you have recovered your goods, what use is there for the thieves? Do not ask.' 'My boy, I give you a thousand daily; seize the thieves and give them to me.' 'Great king, when the wealth is recovered, what is the use of the thieves?' 'My boy, it is better for us to get the thieves even than the wealth.' 'In that case, great king, I will not tell you, "These are the thieves," but I will bring forth a past incident for you. If you are wise, you will understand the meaning.' Having said this, he related a past incident.

Atīte bārāṇasito avidūre nadītīragāmake pāṭali nāma eko naṭo vasati. So ekasmiṃ ussavadivase bhariyamādāya bārāṇasiṃ pavisitvā naccitvā vīṇaṃ vāditvā gāyitvā dhanaṃ labhitvā ussavapariyosāne bahuṃ surābhattaṃ gāhāpetvā attano gāmaṃ gacchanto nadītīraṃ patvā navodakaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā bhattaṃ bhuñjanto suraṃ pivanto nisīditvā matto hutvā attano balaṃ ajānanto “mahāvīṇaṃ gīvāya bandhitvā nadiṃ uttaritvā gamissāmī”ti bhariyaṃ hatthe gahetvā nadiṃ otari. Vīṇāchiddehi udakaṃ pāvisi. Atha naṃ sā vīṇā udake osīdāpesi[V 3.0448]. Bhariyā panassa osīdanabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ vissajjetvā uttaritvā tīre aṭṭhāsi. Naṭapāṭali sakiṃ ummujjati, sakiṃ nimujjati, udakaṃ pavisitvā uddhumātaudaro ahosi. Athassa bhariyā cintesi “mayhaṃ sāmiko idāni marissati, ekaṃ naṃ gītakaṃ yācitvā parisamajjhe taṃ gāyantī jīvikaṃ kappessāmī”ti cintetvā “sāmi, tvaṃ udake nimujjasi, ekaṃ me gītakaṃ dehi, tena jīvikaṃ kappessāmī”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

In the past, not far from Bārāṇasī, in a riverside village, there lived a dancer named Pāṭali. On a festival day, he took his wife and entered Bārāṇasī. After dancing, playing the lute, and singing, he earned money. At the end of the festival, he had much liquor and food brought and set off for his village. Reaching the riverbank, he saw the new water rising. While eating and drinking liquor, he sat down, became intoxicated, and unaware of his own strength, he said, 'I will tie the great lute around my neck and cross the river.' Taking his wife by the hand, he entered the river. Water entered through the lute's holes. Then the weight of that lute caused him to sink in the water. His wife, realizing he was sinking, let go of him, came out of the river, and stood on the bank. The dancer Pāṭali surfaced once and submerged once; his belly was swollen with the water he had swallowed. Then his wife thought, 'My husband will now die. I will request a song from him and, singing it in the midst of an assembly, I will make a living.' Thinking thus, she said, 'Master, you are sinking in the water. Give me one song, and with it I will make a living.' Then she spoke this verse:

49.

49.

“Bahussutaṃ [M 3.0483] cittakathiṃ, gaṅgā vahati pāṭaliṃ;

Vuyhamānaka bhaddante, ekaṃ me dehi gāthaka”nti.

The Gaṅgā carries away Pāṭali, the learned and eloquent speaker; O you who are being carried away, good sir, give me one short verse.

Tattha gāthakanti khuddakaṃ gāthaṃ.

Here, 'gāthaka' means a short verse.

Atha [P 3.0508] naṃ naṭapāṭali “bhadde, kathaṃ tava gītakaṃ dassāmi, idāni mahājanassa paṭisaraṇabhūtaṃ udakaṃ maṃ māretī”ti vatvā gāthamāha –

Then the dancer Pāṭali said to her, 'Good lady, how can I give you a song? Now the water, which is a refuge for the multitude, is killing me.' And he spoke this verse:

50.

50.

“Yena siñcanti dukkhitaṃ, yena siñcanti āturaṃ;

Tassa majjhe marissāmi, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

That with which they sprinkle the afflicted, that with which they sprinkle the sick, in the midst of that very thing I shall die; fear has arisen from my refuge.

Bodhisatto imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā “mahārāja, yathā udakaṃ mahājanassa paṭisaraṇaṃ, tathā rājānopi, tesaṃ santikā bhaye uppanne taṃ bhayaṃ ko paṭibāhissatī”ti vatvā “mahārāja, idaṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicchannaṃ, mayā pana paṇḍitavedanīyaṃ katvā kathitaṃ, jānāhi, mahārājā”ti āha. “Tāta ahaṃ evarūpaṃ paṭicchannakathaṃ na jānāmi, core me gahetvā dehī”ti. Athassa mahāsatto “tena hi, mahārāja, idaṃ sutvā jānāhī”ti aparampi kāraṇaṃ āhari. Deva, pubbe imissāva bārāṇasiyā dvāragāme eko kumbhakāro bhājanatthāya mattikaṃ āharanto ekasmiṃyeva ṭhāne nibaddhaṃ gaṇhitvā antopabbhāraṃ mahantaṃ āvāṭaṃ khaṇi. Athekadivasaṃ tassa mattikaṃ gaṇhantassa akālamahāmegho uṭṭhahitvā mahāvuṭṭhiṃ pātesi. Udakaṃ avattharamānaṃ āvāṭaṃ pātesi, tenassa matthako bhijji. So paridevanto gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, having spoken this verse, said, 'Great king, just as water is a refuge for the multitude, so too are kings. When fear arises from them, who will ward off that fear?' Having said this, he continued, 'Great king, this matter is concealed, but I have spoken it making it understandable to the wise; understand it, great king.' 'Dear son, I do not understand such hidden talk. Seize the thieves for me and bring them,' replied the king. Then the Great Being said, 'Very well, great king, listen to this and understand,' and he presented another example. 'Your Majesty, in the past, in a village at the gates of this very city of Bārāṇasī, there was a potter who, while gathering clay for pots, continually dug in one spot and excavated a large pit with a hollow inside. One day, as he was collecting clay, an untimely great cloud arose and poured down heavy rain. The spreading water caused the pit to collapse, and his head was crushed by it. Wailing, he spoke this verse:'

51.

51.

“Yattha bījāni rūhanti, sattā yattha patiṭṭhitā;

Sā me sīsaṃ nipīḷeti, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

Where seeds sprout, where beings are established, that very ground now crushes my head; fear has arisen from my refuge.

Tattha [V 3.0449] nipīḷetīti nipatitvā pīḷeti bhindati.

Here, 'nipīḷeti' means 'it crushes by falling upon, it breaks'.

Yathā hi deva, mahājanassa paṭisaraṇabhūtā mahāpathavī kumbhakārassa sīsaṃ bhindi, evameva mahāpathavīsame sabbalokassa paṭisaraṇe narinde uṭṭhāya corakammaṃ karonte ko bāhissati, sakkhissasi, mahārāja, evaṃ paṭicchādetvā [P 3.0509] kathitaṃ coraṃ jānitunti. Tāta, mayhaṃ paṭicchannena kāraṇaṃ natthi, ayaṃ coroti evaṃ me coraṃ gahetvā dehīti. So rājānaṃ rakkhanto “tvaṃ coro”ti avatvā aparampi udāharaṇaṃ āhari. Mahārāja, pubbe imasmiṃyeva nagare ekassa purisassa gehaṃ ādittaṃ. So [M 3.0484] “anto pavisitvā bhaṇḍakaṃ nīharā”ti aññaṃ āṇāpesi. Tasmiṃ pavisitvā nīharante gehadvāraṃ pidahi. So dhūmandho hutvā nikkhamanamaggaṃ alabhanto uppannaḍāhadukkho hutvā anto ṭhitova paridevanto gāthamāha –

Just as, Your Majesty, the great earth, which is a refuge for the multitude, broke the potter’s head, so too, when the king, who is like the great earth and a refuge for the whole world, rises up to commit thievery, who will restrain him? Will you be able, great king, to identify the thief thus spoken of in a concealed way?' 'My dear man, there is no reason for me to speak in riddles. Tell me, "This is the thief," seize him, and bring him to me.' That man, wishing to protect the king, did not say, 'You are the thief,' but brought forth another example: 'Great king, formerly in this very city, a man’s house caught fire. He ordered another, “Go inside and bring out the goods.” As that man entered and was bringing them out, the house door shut. Blinded by smoke and unable to find a way out, suffering the agony of being burned, he stood inside and lamented with this verse:'

52.

52.

“Yena bhattāni paccanti, sītaṃ yena vihaññati;

So maṃ ḍahati gattāni, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

That by which meals are cooked, by which the cold is dispelled, that very thing now burns my limbs; fear has arisen from my refuge.

Tattha so maṃ ḍahatīti so me ḍahati, ayameva vā pāṭho.

Herein, 'so maṃ ḍahati' means 'that burns me,' or this is the alternative reading.

“Mahārāja, aggi viya mahājanassa paṭisaraṇabhūto eko manusso ratanabhaṇḍikaṃ hari, mā maṃ coraṃ pucchā”ti. “Tāta, mayhaṃ coraṃ dehiyevā”ti. So rājānaṃ “tvaṃ coro”ti avatvā aparampi udāharaṇaṃ āhari. Deva, pubbe imasmiṃyeva nagare eko puriso atibahuṃ bhuñjitvā jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto vedanāppatto hutvā paridevanto gāthamāha –

'Great king, one man, who is a refuge for the multitude like fire, stole a bundle of jewels. Do not ask me about the thief.' 'My dear man, you must give me the thief.' Without telling the king, 'You are the thief,' he gave another example. 'Your Majesty, formerly in this very city, a man ate too much and, unable to digest it, was afflicted with pain. Lamenting, he uttered this verse:'

53.

53.

“Yena bhuttena yāpanti, puthū brāhmaṇakhattiyā;

So maṃ bhutto byāpādeti, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

The food by which many brahmins and nobles are sustained, that very food, having been eaten, now kills me; fear has arisen from my refuge.

Tattha so maṃ bhutto byāpādetīti so odano bhutto maṃ byāpādeti māreti.

Herein, 'so maṃ bhutto byāpādeti' means 'that food, having been eaten, kills me—it causes my death.'

“Mahārāja, bhattaṃ viya mahājanassa paṭisaraṇabhūto eko bhaṇḍaṃ hari, tasmiṃ laddhe kiṃ coraṃ pucchasī”ti? “Tāta, sakkonto coraṃ me dehī”ti. So tassa saññāpanatthaṃ aparampi udāharaṇaṃ āhari. Mahārāja[P 3.0510], pubbepi imasmiṃyeva nagare ekassa vāto uṭṭhahitvā gattāni bhañji. So paridevanto gāthamāha –

'Great king, one person, who is a refuge for the multitude like food, stole the goods. When the goods are recovered, why do you ask about the thief?' 'My dear man, if you are able, give me the thief.' To make him understand, he gave another example: 'Great king, once before in this very city, a wind arose in a man's body and broke his limbs. Lamenting, he spoke this verse:'

54.

54.

“Gimhānaṃ [V 3.0450] pacchime māse, vātamicchanti paṇḍitā;

So maṃ bhañjati gattāni, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

In the last month of summer, the wise desire the wind; yet it now shatters my limbs—fear has arisen from my refuge.

Iti mahārāja, saraṇato bhayaṃ uppannaṃ, jānāhi taṃ kāraṇanti. Tāta, coraṃ me dehīti. So tassa saññāpanatthaṃ aparampi udāharaṇaṃ āhari. Deva, atīte himavantapadese sākhāviṭapasampanno mahārukkho ahosi pupphaphalasampanno anekasahassānaṃ sakuṇānaṃ nivāso [M 3.0485] tassa dve sākhā aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭṭesuṃ, tato dhūmo uppajji, aggicuṇṇāni patiṃsu. Taṃ disvā sakuṇajeṭṭhako gāthamāha –

‘Thus, O great king, fear has arisen from refuge; know that to be the cause.’ ‘My dear man, give me the thief,’ said the king. To make him understand, he offered another example. ‘Your Majesty, in the past, in the Himalayan region, there was a great tree, abundant with branches and foliage, rich with flowers and fruits, a dwelling place for many thousands of birds. Two of its branches rubbed against each other, from which smoke arose, and sparks fell. Seeing this, the chief of the birds spoke this verse:’

55.

55.

“Yaṃ nissitā jagatiruhaṃ, svāyaṃ aggiṃ pamuñcati;

Disā bhajatha vakkaṅgā, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

‘The very tree upon which we depend now emits fire; take to the various quarters, O birds! Fear has arisen from our refuge.’

Tattha jagatiruhanti mahīruhaṃ.

In this verse, ‘jagatiruhaṃ’ means ‘mahīruhaṃ,’ a tree.

Yathā hi, deva, rukkho pakkhīnaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ, evaṃ rājā mahājanassa paṭisaraṇaṃ, tasmiṃ corikaṃ karonte ko paṭibāhissati, sallakkhehi, devāti. Tāta, mayhaṃ corameva dehīti. Athassa so aparampi udāharaṇaṃ āhari. Mahārāja, ekasmiṃ kāsigāme aññatarassa kulagharassa pacchimabhāge kakkhaḷā susumāranadī atthi, tassa ca kulassa ekova putto. So pitari kālakate mātaraṃ paṭijaggi. Tassa mātā anicchamānasseva ekaṃ kuladhītaraṃ ānesi. Sā pubbabhāge sassuṃ sampiyāyitvā pacchā puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhamānā taṃ nīharitukāmā ahosi. Tassā pana mātāpi tasmiṃyeva ghare vasati. Sā sāmikassa santike sassuyā nānappakāraṃ dosaṃ vatvā paribhinditvā “ahaṃ te mātaraṃ posetuṃ na sakkomi, mārehi na”nti vatvā “manussamāraṇaṃ nāma [P 3.0511] bhāriyaṃ, kathaṃ naṃ māremī”ti vutte “niddokkamanakāle naṃ mañcakeneva saddhiṃ gahetvā susumāranadiyaṃ khipissāma, atha naṃ susamārā khādissantī”ti āha. “Tuyhaṃ pana mātā kaha”nti? “Tassāyeva santike supatī”ti. “Tena hi gaccha, tassā nipannamañcake rajjuṃ bandhitvā saññaṃ karohī”ti. Sā tathā katvā “katā me saññā”ti āha. Itaro “thokaṃ adhivāsehi, manussā tāva niddāyantū”ti niddāyanto viya nipajjitvā gantvā taṃ rajjukaṃ bhariyāya mātu mañcake bandhitvā bhariyaṃ pabodhetvā ubhopi gantvā taṃ mañcakeneva saddhiṃ ukkhipitvā nadiyaṃ khipiṃsu. Tattha naṃ niddāyamānaṃ susumārā viddhaṃsetvā khādiṃsu.

‘Just as, Your Majesty, a tree is a refuge for birds, so is a king a refuge for the multitude. When he commits theft, who will prevent it? Consider this, Your Majesty.’ ‘My dear man, just give me the thief,’ said the king. Then he provided another example. ‘Great king, in a certain village of Kāsi, behind a certain family's house, there was a river full of fierce crocodiles. That family had an only son. After his father died, he supported his mother. Though he was unwilling, his mother brought a young woman to be his wife. At first, the daughter-in-law was fond of her mother-in-law, but later, when she had children of her own, she wished to drive her out. Now, the daughter-in-law's own mother also lived in that same house. The daughter-in-law spoke various faults of the mother-in-law to the husband, slandering her, and said, "I cannot support your mother. Kill her!" When he replied, "Killing a human is a grave matter; how can I kill her?" she said, "When she is fast asleep, we will take her, bed and all, and throw her into the crocodile-infested river; then the crocodiles will devour her." "Where is your mother?" he asked. "She sleeps right beside her," she replied. "In that case, go and tie a rope to her bed as a marker." She did so and said, "The marker is made." He said, "Wait a little, let the people fall asleep." Then, pretending to sleep, he went and tied that rope to his wife's mother's bed. Waking his wife, they both went, lifted the bed, and threw it into the river. There, as she slept, the crocodiles tore her apart and devoured her.’

Sā [V 3.0451] punadivase mātu parivattitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “sāmi, mama mātāva māritā, idāni tava mātaraṃ mārehī”ti vatvā “tena hi sādhū”ti vutte “susāne citakaṃ katvā aggimhi naṃ pakkhipitvā māressāmā”ti āha. Atha naṃ niddāyamānaṃ ubhopi susānaṃ netvā ṭhapayiṃsu. Tattha sāmiko [M 3.0486] bhariyaṃ āha “aggi te ābhato”ti? “Pamuṭṭhāsmi, sāmī”ti. “Tena hi gantvā ānehī”ti. “Na sakkomi sāmi, gantuṃ, tayi gatepi ṭhātuṃ na sakkhissāmi, ubhopi mayaṃ gacchissāmā”ti. Tesu gatesu mahallikā sītavātena pabodhitā susānabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ime maṃ māretukāmā aggiatthāya gatā”ti ca upadhāretvā “na me balaṃ jānantī”ti ekaṃ matakaḷevaraṃ gahetvā mañcake nipajjāpetvā upari pilotikāya paṭicchādetvā sayaṃ palāyitvā tattheva leṇaguhaṃ pāvisi. Itare aggiṃ āharitvā “mahallikā”ti saññāya kaḷevaraṃ jhāpetvā pakkamiṃsu. Ekena corena tasmiṃ guhāleṇe pubbe bhaṇḍikā ṭhapitā, so “taṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti āgantvā mahallikaṃ disvā “ekā yakkhinī bhavissati, bhaṇḍikā me amanussapariggahitā”ti ekaṃ bhūtavejjaṃ ānesi. Vejjo mantaṃ karonto guhaṃ pāvisi.

The next day, realizing that her own mother had been switched, she said, ‘Master, my mother has been killed; now kill your mother.’ When he agreed, she said, ‘Let us make a funeral pyre in the cemetery, throw her into the fire, and kill her.’ So while she was sleeping, they both took her to the cemetery and laid her there. There, the husband asked his wife, ‘Did you bring the fire?’ ‘I forgot, master,’ she said. ‘Then go and fetch it.’ ‘I cannot go, master; nor can I stay here if you go. Let us both go.’ When they had gone, the old woman, awakened by the cold wind, realized she was in a cemetery. Deducing, ‘These two wish to kill me and have gone for fire,’ and thinking, ‘They do not know my resourcefulness,’ she took a corpse, laid it on the bed, covered it with a cloth, and fled, entering a nearby cave. The couple returned with fire and, thinking it was the old woman, cremated the corpse and left. A thief had previously hidden a bundle of goods in that cave. Coming to retrieve it, he saw the old woman and thought, ‘This must be a yakkhiṇī; a non-human has taken possession of my goods.’ He then fetched an exorcist. The exorcist, chanting spells, entered the cave.

Atha naṃ sā āha “nāhaṃ yakkhinī, ehi ubhopi imaṃ dhanaṃ bhājessāmā”ti. “Kathaṃ saddahitabba”nti? “Tava jivhaṃ mama jivhāya ṭhapehī”ti. So tathā akāsi. Athassa sā jivhaṃ ḍaṃsitvā chinditvā pātesi. Bhūtavejjo “addhā esā yakkhinī”ti jivhāya lohitaṃ paggharantiyā viravamāno [P 3.0512] palāyi. Mahallikā punadivase maṭṭhasāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā nānāratanabhaṇḍikaṃ gahetvā gharaṃ agamāsi. Suṇisā taṃ disvā “kahaṃ te, amma, idaṃ laddha”nti pucchi. “Amma, etasmiṃ susāne dārucitakāya jhāpitā evarūpaṃ labhantī”ti. “Amma, mayāpi sakkā laddhu”nti. “Mādisī hutvā labhissasī”ti. Sā laddhabhaṇḍikalobhena sāmikassa kathetvā tattha attānaṃ jhāpesi. Atha naṃ punadivase sāmiko apassanto “amma, imāyapi velāya tvaṃ āgatā, suṇisā te nāgacchatī”ti āha. Sā taṃ sutvā “are pāpapurisa, kiṃ matā nāma āgacchantī”ti taṃ tajjetvā gāthamāha –

Then she said to him, ‘I am not a yakkhiṇī; come, let us both divide this wealth.’ ‘How can I trust you?’ he asked. ‘Place your tongue upon mine,’ she replied. He did so. Then she bit his tongue, severing it. The exorcist, crying out ‘Surely this is a yakkhiṇī!’ as blood poured from his tongue, fled. The next day, the old woman, dressed in a fine robe and carrying the bundle of various jewels, went home. The daughter-in-law, seeing her, asked, ‘Mother, where did you get this?’ ‘My dear, those who are cremated on a wooden pyre in that cemetery obtain such as this.’ ‘Mother, can I also obtain it?’ ‘If you are like me, you will obtain it.’ Driven by greed for the goods, the daughter-in-law spoke to her husband and had herself cremated there. The next day, when the husband did not see her, he said, ‘Mother, you have come back at this time, but your daughter-in-law does not come.’ Hearing this, she scolded him, ‘You wicked man! Why would one who is dead return?’ and rebuking him, she spoke this verse:

56.

56.

“Yamānayiṃ somanassaṃ, māliniṃ candanussadaṃ;

Sā maṃ gharā nicchubhati, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

‘She whom I brought with joy, wearing garlands and anointed with sandalwood, now drives me from my home; fear has arisen from my refuge.’

Tattha somanassanti somanassaṃ uppādetvā. “Somanassā”tipi pāṭho, somanassavatī hutvāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yamahaṃ “imaṃ [M 3.0487] me nissāya putto puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhissati, mañca [V 3.0452] mahallikakāle posessatī”ti māliniṃ candanussadaṃ katvā alaṅkaritvā somanassajātā ānesiṃ. Sā maṃ ajja gharā nīharati, saraṇatoyeva me bhayaṃ uppannanti.

Therein, ‘somanassaṃ’ means having generated joy. Another reading is ‘somanassā,’ meaning being joyful. This is what is said: ‘She whom I, having become joyful, brought—having adorned her with garlands and anointed her with sandalwood, thinking, “Depending on this one, my son will prosper with sons and daughters, and she will support me in my old age”—that same one today drives me from the house; from my very refuge has fear arisen for me.”

“Mahārāja, suṇisā viya sassuyā mahājanassa rājā paṭisaraṇaṃ, tato bhaye uppanne kiṃ sakkā kātuṃ, sallakkhehi, devā”ti. Taṃ sutvā rājā “tāta, nāhaṃ tayā ānītakāraṇāni jānāmi, corameva me dehī”ti āha. So “rājānaṃ rakkhissāmī”ti aparampi udāharaṇaṃ āhari. Deva, pubbe imasmiṃyeva nagare eko puriso patthanaṃ katvā puttaṃ labhi. So puttajātakāle “putto me laddho”ti somanassajāto taṃ posetvā vayappattakāle dārena saṃyojetvā aparabhāge jaraṃ patvā kammaṃ adhiṭṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ putto “tvaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkosi, ito nikkhamā”ti gehato nīhari[P 3.0513]. So kicchena kasirena jīvikaṃ kappento paridevamāno gāthamāha –

“Great king, just as a daughter-in-law is a refuge for a mother-in-law, so is the king a refuge for the great populace. When fear arises from that very refuge, what can be done? Consider this, O king.” Hearing this, the king said, “My dear man, I do not understand the reasons you bring forth. Just give me the thief.” Thinking, “I will protect the king,” he brought forth another example. “O king, formerly in this very city, a certain man made a wish and obtained a son. At the time of the son’s birth, he became overjoyed, thinking, ‘A son has been born to me.’ He raised him, and when he came of age, united him with a wife. In later life, having reached old age, he was unable to carry out his work. Then his son expelled him from the house, saying, ‘You cannot work, get out of here.’ Eking out a living with hardship and difficulty, he lamented, uttering this verse:”

57.

57.

“Yena jātena nandissaṃ, yassa ca bhavamicchisaṃ;

So maṃ gharā nicchubhati, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

“He at whose birth I rejoiced, and for whose prosperity I wished, that very one drives me from my home; fear has arisen from my refuge.”

Tattha so manti so putto maṃ gharato nicchubhati nīharati. Svāhaṃ bhikkhaṃ caritvā dukkhena jīvāmi, saraṇatoyeva me bhayaṃ uppannanti.

Therein, ‘so maṃ’ means ‘that son’ drives me out, expels me from the house. I wander for alms and live in suffering; from my very refuge has fear arisen for me.

“Mahārāja, yathā pitā nāma mahallako paṭibalena puttena rakkhitabbo, evaṃ sabbopi janapado raññā rakkhitabbo, idañca bhayaṃ uppajjamānaṃ sabbasatte rakkhantassa rañño santikā uppannaṃ, iminā kāraṇena ‘asuko nāma coro’ti jānāhi, devā”ti. “Tāta, nāhaṃ kāraṇaṃ vā akāraṇaṃ vā jānāmi, coraṃ vā me dehi, tvaññeva vā coro hohī”ti evaṃ rājā punappunaṃ māṇavaṃ anuyuñji. Atha naṃ so evamāha “kiṃ pana, mahārāja, ekaṃsena coragahaṇaṃ rocethā”ti? “Āma, tātā”ti. Tena hi “asuko ca asuko ca coro”ti parisamajjhe pakāsemīti. “Evaṃ karohi, tātā”ti. So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ rājā attānaṃ rakkhituṃ na deti, gaṇhissāmi dāni cora”nti sannipatite mahājane āmantetvā imā gāthā āha –

“Great king, just as an elderly father ought to be protected by a capable son, so ought the entire country to be protected by the king. And this fear that is arising has arisen from the presence of the king, the protector of all beings. For this reason, know, O king, who the thief is.” “My dear man, I know neither reason nor lack of reason. Either give me the thief, or you yourself shall be the thief.” Thus the king repeatedly pressed the young man. Then he said to him, “But, great king, do you approve of seizing the thief without exception?” “Yes, my dear man.” “In that case, shall I declare in the midst of the assembly that ‘So-and-so and so-and-so are the thieves’?” “Do so, my dear man.” Hearing his words, he thought, “This king does not allow himself to be protected; now I will seize the thief.” Having called together the great populace, he addressed them and spoke these verses:

58.

58.

“Suṇantu [M 3.0488] me jānapadā, negamā ca samāgatā;

Yatodakaṃ tadādittaṃ, yato khemaṃ tato bhayaṃ.

“Let the country folk and the assembled townsfolk listen to me: from where there is water, there is fire; from where there is safety, there is fear.”

59.

59.

“Rājā [V 3.0453] vilumpate raṭṭhaṃ, brāhmaṇo ca purohito;

Attaguttā viharatha, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

“The king plunders the kingdom, and the brahmin, the royal chaplain. Live on your guard; fear has arisen from your refuge.”

Tattha yatodakaṃ tadādittanti yaṃ udakaṃ tadeva ādittaṃ. Yato khemanti yato rājato khemena bhavitabbaṃ, tatova bhayaṃ uppannaṃ. Atthaguttā viharathāti tumhe idāni anāthā jātā, attānaṃ mā vināsetha, attanāva [P 3.0514] guttā hutvā attano santakaṃ dhanadhaññaṃ rakkhatha, rājā nāma mahājanassa paṭisaraṇaṃ, tato tumhākaṃ bhayaṃ uppannaṃ, rājā ca purohito ca vilopakhādakacorā, sace core gaṇhitukāmattha, ime dve gahetvā kammakaraṇaṃ karothāti.

Therein, ‘from where there is water, there is fire’ means that the very water is aflame. ‘From where there is safety’ means that from the very place safety should come, that is, from the king, fear has arisen. ‘Live on your guard’ means: now you have become protectorless; do not destroy yourselves. Guarding yourselves, protect your own wealth and grain. A king is supposed to be the refuge of the great populace, yet from him your fear has arisen. The king and the royal chaplain are plundering, consuming thieves. If you wish to seize the thieves, seize these two and put them to punishment.

Te tassa kathaṃ sutvā cintayiṃsu “ayaṃ rājā rakkhaṇārahopi samāno idāni aññassa upari dosaṃ āropetvā attano bhaṇḍikaṃ sayameva pokkharaṇiyaṃ ṭhapetvā coraṃ pariyesāpeti, ito dāni paṭṭhāya puna corakammassa akaraṇatthāya mārema naṃ pāparājāna”nti. Te daṇḍamuggarādihatthā uṭṭhāya tattheva rājānañca purohitañca pothetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā mahāsattaṃ abhisiñcitvā rajje patiṭṭhapesuṃ.

Hearing his speech, they thought: “This king, though he ought to be protected, now casts blame on another while he himself, having placed his own goods in the lotus pond, has a search made for the thief. From now on, in order to prevent the act of thievery from happening again, let us kill this wicked king.” Armed with sticks, clubs, and other weapons, they rose up and right there beat the king and the royal chaplain, causing the destruction of their lives. Then, having anointed the Great Being, they established him in the kingdom.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “anacchariyaṃ, upāsaka, pathaviyaṃ padasañjānanaṃ, porāṇakapaṇḍitā evaṃ ākāse padaṃ sañjāniṃsū”ti vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne upāsako ca putto ca sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitā. Tadā pitā kassapo ahosi, padakusalamāṇavo pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, “It is no wonder, lay follower, to recognize footprints on the earth; the wise of old recognized a footprint even in the sky.” Then, having declared the Truths, he made the connection in the birth story. At the conclusion of the declaration of the Truths, both the lay follower and his son were established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the father was Kassapa, and the youth skilled in footprints was I myself.

Padakusalamāṇavajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Explanation of the Jātaka of the Youth Skilled in Footprints, the Sixth.

[433] 7. Lomasakassapajātakavaṇṇanā

[433] 7. The Explanation of the Lomasakassapa Jātaka

Assa indasamo rājāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “sacca”nti vutte “bhikkhu sinerukampanavāto kiṃ [M 3.0489] purāṇapaṇṇāni na kampessati, yasasamaṅginopi sappurisā āyasakyaṃ pāpuṇanti, kilesā nāmete parisuddhasattepi saṃkiliṭṭhe karonti, pageva tādisa”nti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“A king like Indra…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a discontented monk. The Teacher questioned that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?” When he replied, “It is true,” the Teacher said, “Monk, will not the wind that shakes Sineru also shake old leaves? Even virtuous men endowed with glory attain misfortune. These defilements indeed stain even pure-minded beings—how much more so one such as you?” Then, having been requested by him, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 3.0454] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente brahmadattassa putto brahmadattakumāro nāma purohitaputto ca kassapo nāma dve sahāyakā [P 3.0515] hutvā ekācariyakule sabbasippāni uggaṇhiṃsu. Aparabhāge brahmadattakumāro pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāsi. Kassapo cintesi “mayhaṃ sahāyo rājā jāto, idāni me mahantaṃ issariyaṃ dassati, kiṃ me issariyena, ahaṃ mātāpitaro ca rājānañca āpucchitvā pabbajissāmī”ti. So rājānañca mātāpitaro ca āpucchitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā sattame divase abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā uñchācariyāya yāpento vihāsi. Pabbajitaṃ pana naṃ “lomasakassapo”ti sañjāniṃsu. So paramajitindriyo ghoratapo tāpaso ahosi. Tassa tejena sakkassa bhavanaṃ kampi. Sakko āvajjento taṃ disvā cintesi “ayaṃ tāpaso ativiya uggatejo sakkabhāvāpi maṃ cāveyya, bārāṇasiraññā saddhiṃ ekato hutvā tapamassa bhindissāmī”ti. So sakkānubhāvena aḍḍharattasamaye bārāṇasirañño sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā sakalagabbhaṃ sarīrappabhāya obhāsetvā rañño santike ākāse ṭhito “uṭṭhehi, mahārājā”ti rājānaṃ pabodhesi. “Kosi tva”nti vutte “sakkohamasmī”ti āha. “Kimatthaṃ āgatosī”ti? “Mahārāja, sakalajambudīpe ekarajjaṃ icchasi, na icchasī”ti? “Kissa na icchāmī”ti? Atha naṃ sakko “tena hi lomasakassapaṃ ānetvā pasughātayaññaṃ yajāpehi, sakkasamo ajarāmaro hutvā sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ kāressasī”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, his son, Prince Brahmadatta, and the son of the chaplain, named Kassapa, were friends and learned all the arts from the same teacher. Later, when his father passed away, Prince Brahmadatta was established on the throne. Kassapa thought: 'My friend has become king; now he will give me great wealth. What use have I for wealth? I will take leave of my parents and the king and go forth.' Having taken leave of the king and his parents, he entered the Himalayas and went forth as an ascetic. On the seventh day, he attained the five direct knowledges and the eight meditative attainments. He lived sustaining himself by gleaning. He became known as the ascetic 'Lomasakassapa.' He had calmed his faculties and practiced fierce austerities. By the power of those austerities, Sakka’s abode trembled. Sakka, reflecting, saw him and thought: 'This ascetic has exceedingly fierce austerities; he might even dislodge me from the state of Sakka. I will join with the King of Benares and break his virtue.' By his divine power, at midnight, Sakka entered the King of Benares’s royal bedchamber, illuminating the entire chamber with his bodily radiance. Standing in the air near the king, he roused him, saying, 'Arise, great king.' When asked, 'Who are you?' he replied, 'I am Sakka.' When asked, 'For what purpose have you come?' he said, 'Great king, do you desire sole sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa, or not?' When the king replied, 'Why should I not desire it?' Sakka said to him: 'In that case, bring Lomasakassapa and have him perform a sacrifice by slaughtering four-footed animals. You will become like Sakka, ageless and deathless, and you will rule over all Jambudīpa.' Having said this, he spoke the first verse:

60.

60.

“Assa indasamo rāja, accantaṃ ajarāmaro;

Sace tvaṃ yaññaṃ yājeyya, isiṃ lomasakassapa”nti.

“O King, you would be like Indra, eternally ageless and immortal, if you would have the sage Lomasakassapa perform the sacrifice.”

Tattha assāti bhavissasi. Yājeyyāti sace tvaṃ araññāyatanato isiṃ lomasakassapaṃ ānetvā yaññaṃ yajeyyāsīti.

Herein, 'assa' means 'you would be.' 'Yājeyya' means: if you, having brought the sage Lomasakassapa from his forest abode, were to have him perform the sacrifice.

Tassa [M 3.0490] vacanaṃ sutvā rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Sakko “tena hi mā papañcaṃ karī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Rājā punadivase [P 3.0516] seyyaṃ nāma amaccaṃ pakkosāpetvā “samma, mayhaṃ piyasahāyakassa lomasakassapassa santikaṃ gantvā mama vacanena evaṃ vadehi ‘rājā kira tumhehi pasughātayaññaṃ yajāpetvā sakalajambudīpe ekarājā bhavissati, tumhākampi yattakaṃ padesaṃ icchatha, tattakaṃ dassati, mayā saddhiṃ yaññaṃ yajituṃ āgacchathā’”ti āha. So “sādhu, devā”ti tāpasassa vasanokāsajānanatthaṃ nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā ekena vanacarakena “ahaṃ [V 3.0455] jānāmī”ti vutte taṃ purato katvā mahantena parivārena tattha gantvā isiṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno taṃ sāsanaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ so “seyya kiṃ nāmetaṃ kathesī”ti vatvā paṭikkhipanto catasso gāthā abhāsi –

Hearing his words, the king agreed, saying, 'Very well.' Sakka said, 'In that case, do not delay,' and departed. The next day, the king summoned a minister named Seyya and said: 'Friend, go to my dear friend Lomasakassapa and, in my name, say this: "The king, it is said, by having you perform a sacrifice of slaughtered four-footed animals, will become the sole ruler of all Jambudīpa. He will also grant you any place you desire. Come to perform the sacrifice with me."' Seyya replied, 'Very well, your majesty,' and to find out the ascetic’s dwelling place, he had a drum beaten throughout the city. When a hunter said, 'I know it,' he put the hunter in front and went there with a large retinue. He paid homage to the sage and, sitting to one side, delivered the message. Then the sage, rejecting him, said, 'Seyya, what is this you say?' and uttered four verses:

61.

61.

“Sasamuddapariyāyaṃ, mahiṃ sāgarakuṇḍalaṃ;

Na icche saha nindāya, evaṃ seyya vijānahi.

“The earth bounded by the sea, adorned with the ocean as its earring, I would not desire if it came with censure; thus, Seyya, understand this.

62.

62.

“Dhiratthu taṃ yasalābhaṃ, dhanalābhañca brāhmaṇa;

Yā vutti vinipātena, adhammacaraṇena vā.

“Cursed be that gain of fame and wealth, O brahmin, which is a livelihood gained through downfall or through unrighteous conduct.

63.

63.

“Api ce pattamādāya, anagāro paribbaje;

Sāyeva jīvikā seyyo, yā cādhammena esanā.

“Even if one should wander as a homeless one, carrying an alms bowl, that very livelihood is better than seeking wealth through unrighteousness.

64.

64.

“Api ce pattamādāya, anagāro paribbaje;

Aññaṃ ahiṃsayaṃ loke, api rajjena taṃ vara”nti.

“Even if one should wander as a homeless one, carrying an alms bowl, harming no one in the world—that is better even than kingship.”

Tattha sasamuddapariyāyanti sasamuddaparikkhepaṃ. Sāgarakuṇḍalanti cattāro dīpe parikkhipitvā ṭhitasāgarehi kaṇṇavaliyā ṭhapitakuṇḍalehi viya samannāgataṃ. Saha nindāyāti “iminā pasughātakammaṃ kata”nti imāya nindāya saha cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ mahāpathaviṃ na icchāmīti vadati. Yā vutti vinipātenāti narake vinipātakammena yā ca jīvitavutti hoti, taṃ dhiratthu, garahāmi taṃ vuttinti dīpeti. Sāyeva jīvikāti pabbajitassa mattikāpattaṃ ādāya paragharāni upasaṅkamitvā āhārapariyesanajīvikāva yasadhanalābhato sataguṇena sahassaguṇena varatarāti attho [M 3.0491] api rajjena taṃ varanti taṃ anagārassa sato aññaṃ avihiṃsantassa paribbajanaṃ sakalajambudīparajjenapi varanti attho.

In this context, 'sasamuddapariyāyaṃ' means encircled by the sea. 'Sāgarakuṇḍalaṃ' means endowed, as if with earrings placed on the earlobes, by the oceans that stand encircling the four continents. 'Saha nindāya' means he says, 'I do not desire the great earth up to the edge of the world-system along with this censure: "This man has performed the slaughter of animals."' 'Yā vutti vinipātena': he explains, 'Cursed be that livelihood which results from an act leading to a downfall in hell; I despise that livelihood.' 'Sāyeva jīvikā': the meaning is that for one who has gone forth, the livelihood of seeking food by approaching the houses of others, carrying a clay alms bowl, is a hundred times, a thousand times better than the gain of fame and wealth. 'Api rajjena taṃ varaṃ': the meaning is that for a homeless one, that wandering about without harming another is better even than kingship over all of Jambudīpa.

Amacco tassa kathaṃ sutvā gantvā rañño ārocesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā “anāgacchante kiṃ sakkā kātu”nti tuṇhī ahosi. Puna sakko aḍḍharattasamaye [P 3.0517] āgantvā ākāse ṭhatvā “kiṃ, mahārāja, lomasakassapaṃ ānetvā yaññaṃ na yajāpesī”ti āha. “Mayā pesitopi nāgacchatī”ti. “Tena hi, mahārāja, attano dhītaraṃ candavatiṃ kumārikaṃ alaṅkaritvā seyyaṃ tatheva pesetvā ‘sace kira āgantvā yaññaṃ yajissasi, rājā te imaṃ kumārikaṃ [V 3.0456] dassatī’ti vadāpehi, addhā so kumārikāya paṭibaddhacitto hutvā āgacchissatī”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā punadivase seyyassa hatthe dhītaraṃ adāsi. So rājadhītaraṃ gahetvā tattha gantvā isiṃ vanditvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā devaccharapaṭibhāgaṃ rājadhītaraṃ tassa dassetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha isi indriyāni bhinditvā taṃ olokesi, saha olokaneneva paṭibaddhacitto hutvā jhānā parihāyi. Amacco tassa paṭibaddhacittabhāvaṃ ñatvā “bhante, sace kira yaññaṃ yajissatha, rājā te imaṃ dārikaṃ pādaparicārikaṃ katvā dassatī”ti āha. So kilesavasena kampanto “imaṃ kira me dassatī”ti āha. “Āma, yaññaṃ yajantassa te dassatī”ti. So “sādhu imaṃ labhanto yajissāmī”ti vatvā taṃ gahetvā saheva jaṭāhi alaṅkatarathaṃ abhiruyha bārāṇasiṃ agamāsi. Rājāpi “āgacchati kirā”ti sutvā yaññāvāṭe kammaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Atha naṃ āgataṃ disvā “sve yaññaṃ yajāhi, ahaṃ indasamo bhavissāmi, yaññapariyosāne te dhītaraṃ dassāmī”ti āha. Kassapo “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Atha naṃ rājā punadivase taṃ ādāya candavatiyā saddhiṃyeva yaññāvāṭaṃ gato. Tattha hatthiassausabhādisabbacatuppadā paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitāva ahesuṃ. Kassapo te sabbe hanitvāva ghātetvā yaññaṃ yajituṃ ārabhi. Atha naṃ tattha sannipatito mahājano disvā “idaṃ te [P 3.0518] lomasakassapa ayuttaṃ appatirūpaṃ, kiṃ nāmetaṃ karosī”ti vatvā paridevanto dve gāthā abhāsi –

The minister, hearing his words, went and reported to the king. On hearing this, the king remained silent, thinking, “What can be done if he does not come?” Again at midnight, Sakka came and, standing in the sky, said, “Great king, why do you not bring Lomasakassapa and have the sacrifice performed?” “Though I sent for him, he does not come.” “In that case, great king, adorn your daughter, the maiden Candavatī, and send the minister Seyya as before, having him say: ‘If you come and perform the sacrifice, the king will give you this maiden.’ Surely, with his heart captivated by the maiden, he will come.” The king agreed, saying, “Very well,” and the next day he placed his daughter in Seyya’s hands. Taking the king’s daughter, he went there, paid homage to the sage, exchanged courteous greetings, and presented the king’s daughter, who was like a celestial nymph, to him and stood to one side. Then the sage, breaking his control over his faculties, gazed at her. As soon as he looked at her, his heart was captivated, and he fell from his meditative absorption.
