The minister, knowing his heart was captivated, said, “Venerable sir, if you perform the sacrifice, the king will give you this girl to be your personal attendant.” Shaken by the power of defilement, he asked, “Will he really give her to me?” “Yes, he will give her to you if you perform the sacrifice.” He said, “Very well, if I obtain her, I will perform the sacrifice.” Having said this, he took her and, with his matted locks still on him, mounted an adorned chariot and went to Benares. The king, hearing he was coming, had the work started on the sacrificial enclosure. Seeing him arrive, he said, “Tomorrow, perform the sacrifice. I will become like Indra, and at the end of the sacrifice, I will give you my daughter.” Kassapa agreed, saying, “Very well.” On the next day, the king took him and went to the sacrificial enclosure together with Candavatī. There, all kinds of quadrupeds such as elephants, horses, and bulls were arranged in rows. Kassapa began to perform the sacrifice by striking and killing them all. Then the great crowd gathered there saw this and lamented, saying, “This is improper and unfitting for you, Lomasakassapa. What is this you are doing?” and uttered two verses:

65.

65.

“Balaṃ [M 3.0492] cando balaṃ suriyo, balaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇā;

Balaṃ velā samuddassa, balātibalamitthiyo.

“A power is the moon, a power the sun, a power are ascetics and brahmins; a power is the ocean’s shore, but women are a power beyond power.”

66.

66.

“Yathā uggatapaṃ santaṃ, isiṃ lomasakassapaṃ;

Pitu atthā candavatī, vājapeyyaṃ ayājayī”ti.

“Since Candavatī, for her father’s sake, made the sage Lomasakassapa, though of fierce austerities and peaceful, perform the Vājapeyya sacrifice.”

Tattha balaṃ cando balaṃ suriyoti mahandhakāravidhamane aññaṃ balaṃ nāma natthi, candimasūriyāvettha balavantoti attho. Samaṇabrāhmaṇāti iṭṭhāniṭṭhavisayavegasahane khantibalañāṇabalena samannāgatā samitapāpabāhitapāpā samaṇabrāhmaṇā. Balaṃ velā samuddassāti mahāsamuddassa uttarituṃ adatvā udakaṃ āvaritvā vināsetuṃ samatthatāya velā balaṃ nāma. Balātibalamitthiyoti itthiyo pana visadañāṇepi avītarāge attano vasaṃ ānetvā vināsetuṃ samatthatāya tehi sabbehi balehipi atibalā nāma, sabbabalehi itthibalameva mahantanti attho. Yathāti yasmā. Pitu atthāti pitu vuḍḍhiatthāya. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā imaṃ uggatapaṃ samānaṃ [V 3.0457] sīlādiguṇānaṃ esitattā isiṃ ayaṃ candavatī nissīlaṃ katvā pitu vuḍḍhiatthāya vājapeyyaṃ yaññaṃ yājeti, tasmā jānitabbametaṃ “balātibalamitthiyo”ti.

Herein, ‘balaṃ cando balaṃ suriyo’ means in dispelling great darkness there is no other power; the meaning is that the moon and sun are powerful in this. ‘Samaṇabrāhmaṇā’ refers to ascetics and brahmins who have stilled evil and banished evil, endowed with the power of patience and the power of knowledge in enduring the force of agreeable and disagreeable sense objects. ‘Balaṃ velā samuddassa’ means because of its ability to hold back the water of the great ocean and prevent it from transgressing, the shore is a power. ‘Balātibalamitthiyo’ means but women, because of their ability to bring under their control and ruin even those of clear knowledge who are not free from lust, are a power beyond all those other powers. The meaning is that of all powers, the power of women is the greatest. ‘Yathā’ means ‘since.’ ‘Pitu atthā’ means for the sake of the father’s prosperity. This is what is said: since this Candavatī, for the sake of her father’s prosperity, made this sage—who was of fierce austerities and a seeker of such virtues as moral conduct—immoral and had him perform the Vājapeyya sacrifice, therefore it should be known that ‘women are a power beyond power.’

Tasmiṃ samaye kassapo yaññaṃ yajanatthāya “maṅgalahatthiṃ gīvāyaṃ paharissāmī”ti khaggaratanaṃ ukkhipi. Hatthī taṃ disvā maraṇabhayatajjito mahāravaṃ ravi. Tassa ravaṃ sutvā sesāpi hatthiassausabhādayo maraṇabhayatajjitā bhayena viraviṃsu. Mahājanopi viravi. Kassapo taṃ mahāviravaṃ sutvā saṃvegappatto hutvā attano jaṭādīni olokesi. Athassa jaṭāmassukacchalomāni pākaṭāni ahesuṃ. So vippaṭisārī hutvā “ananurūpaṃ vata me pāpakammaṃ kata”nti saṃvegaṃ pakāsento aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, Kassapa, intending to perform the sacrifice, raised the sword-jewel, thinking, “I will strike the auspicious elephant on the neck.” Seeing him raise the sword, the elephant, terrified by the fear of death, let out a great cry. Hearing its cry, the other elephants, horses, bulls, and so on, also terrified by the fear of death, cried out in fear. The great crowd also cried out. Hearing that great uproar, Kassapa was overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency and looked at his own matted hair and so on. Then his matted hair, beard, and the hair of his armpits became evident to him. Filled with remorse, he declared his sense of spiritual urgency, saying, “Indeed, I have done an unsuitable, evil deed,” and spoke the eighth verse:

67.

67.

“Taṃ [P 3.0519] lobhapakataṃ kammaṃ, kaṭukaṃ kāmahetukaṃ;

Tassa mūlaṃ gavesissaṃ, checchaṃ rāgaṃ sabandhana”nti.

“That deed done out of greed, bitter, caused by sensual desire; I will seek out its root, and cut off passion with its fetter.”

Tassattho – mahārāja, yaṃ etaṃ mayā candavatiyā lobhaṃ uppādetvā tena lobhena pakataṃ kāmahetukaṃ pāpakaṃ, taṃ kaṭukaṃ tikhiṇavipākaṃ. Tassāhaṃ ayonisomanasikārasaṅkhātaṃ mūlaṃ gavesissaṃ, alaṃ [M 3.0493] me iminā khaggena, paññākhaggaṃ nīharitvā subhanimittabandhanena saddhiṃ sabandhanaṃ rāgaṃ chindissāmīti.

Its meaning is: Great king, this evil deed that I have done—having aroused greed for Candavatī, and acting out of that greed and because of sensual desire—is bitter, with sharp consequences. I will seek out its root, known as unwise attention. Enough of this sword for me! Drawing the sword of wisdom, I will cut off passion with its fetter, together with the fetter of the sign of beauty.

Atha naṃ rājā “mā bhāyi samma, idāni te candavatiṃ kumāriñca raṭṭhañca sattaratanarāsiñca dassāmi, yajāhi yañña”nti āha. Taṃ sutvā kassapo “na me, mahārāja, iminā kilesena attho”ti vatvā osānagāthamāha –

Then the king said to him, “Do not fear, friend. Now I will give you Princess Candavatī, the kingdom, and the heap of the seven treasures. Perform the sacrifice!” Hearing that, Kassapa said, “Great king, I have no need for this defilement,” and then spoke the concluding verse:

68.

68.

“Dhiratthu kāme subahūpi loke, tapova seyyo kāmaguṇehi rāja;

Tapo karissāmi pahāya kāme, taveva raṭṭhaṃ candavatī ca hotū”ti.

“Fie on sensual pleasures, though abundant in the world; austerity is better than the strands of sensual pleasure, O king. I will practice austerity, having abandoned sensual pleasures; let the kingdom and Candavatī be yours alone.”

Tattha subahūpīti atibahukepi. Tapo karissāmīti sīlasaṃyamatapameva karissāmi.

Therein, ‘subahūpi’ means ‘even though very many.’ ‘I will practice austerity’ means: I will practice only the austerity of moral virtue and restraint.

So evaṃ vatvā kasiṇaṃ samannāharitvā naṭṭhaṃ visesaṃ uppādetvā ākāse pallaṅkena nisīditvā rañño dhammaṃ desetvā “appamatto hohī”ti ovaditvā yaññāvāṭaṃ viddhaṃsāpetvā mahājanassa [V 3.0458] abhayadānaṃ dāpetvā rañño yācantasseva uppatitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gantvā yāvajīvaṃ ṭhatvā āyupariyosāne brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Having spoken thus, he adverted to the kasiᅀa, produced the lost special attainment, sat cross-legged in the sky, taught the Dhamma to the king, and advised him, saying, ‘Be heedful.’ He had the sacrificial pit destroyed, the gift of fearlessness given to the great crowd, and even while the king was beseeching him, he rose up and went to his own dwelling place. He remained there for the rest of his life, and at its end, he was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā seyyo mahāamacco sāriputto ahosi, lomasakassapo pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the minister Seyya was Sāriputta, but Lomasakassapa was I myself.’

Lomasakassapajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Lomasakassapa Jātaka, the Seventh.

[434] 8. Cakkavākajātakavaṇṇanā

[434] 8. The Commentary on the Cakkavāka Jātaka

Kāsāyavattheti [P 3.0520] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ lolabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira lolo ahosi paccayaluddho, ācariyupajjhāyavattādīni chaḍḍetvā pātova sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā visākhāya [M 3.0494] gehe anekakhādanīyaparivāraṃ yāguṃ pivitvā nānaggarasasālimaṃsodanaṃ bhuñjitvāpi tena atitto tato cūḷaanāthapiṇḍikassa mahāanāthapiṇḍikassa kosalaraññoti tesaṃ tesaṃ nivesanāni sandhāya vicari. Athekadivasaṃ tassa lolabhāvaṃ ārabbha dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte taṃ bhikkhuṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu lolo”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhu kasmā lolosi, pubbepi tvaṃ lolabhāvena bārāṇasiyaṃ hatthikuṇapādīni khāditvā vicaranto tehi atitto tato nikkhamitvā gaṅgātīre vicaranto himavantaṃ pavaṭṭho”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher spoke this discourse beginning ‘Birds in russet plumage,’ while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain greedy monk. It is said he was greedy and avaricious for requisites. Having abandoned his duties toward his teachers and preceptors, he would enter Sāvatthĩ early in the morning. At Visākhā’s house, he would drink gruel accompanied by various edibles, and even after eating fine sāli rice with various choice flavors and meat, he would remain unsatisfied. Then he would wander about, visiting the residences of Cũᄷa-Anāthapiᅆᄱika, Mahā-Anāthapiᅆᄱika, and the king of Kosala. One day, a talk arose in the hall of Dhamma concerning his greediness. The Teacher came and asked, ‘For what discussion, monks, are you now gathered together?’ When they replied, ‘For this one,’ he had that monk summoned and asked, ‘Is it true, monk, that you are greedy?’ When the monk replied, ‘It is true, Blessed One,’ the Teacher said, ‘Monk, why are you greedy? In the past, too, because of your greed, you wandered about in Bārāᅆasĩ eating the carcasses of elephants and so on, but you were still not satisfied. Leaving there, you wandered along the bank of the Ganges and entered the Himalayas.’ And he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente eko lolakāko bārāṇasiyaṃ hatthikuṇapādīni khāditvā vicaranto tehi atitto “gaṅgākūle macchamataṃ khādissāmī”ti gantvā tattha matamacche khādanto katipāhaṃ vasitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā nānāphalāphalāni khādanto bahumacchakacchapaṃ mahantaṃ padumasaraṃ patvā tattha suvaṇṇavaṇṇe dve cakkavāke sevālaṃ khāditvā vasante disvā “ime ativiya vaṇṇasampannā sobhaggappattā, imesaṃ bhojanaṃ manāpaṃ bhavissati, imesaṃ bhojanaṃ pucchitvā ahampi tadeva bhuñjitvā suvaṇṇavaṇṇo bhavissāmī”ti cintetvā tesaṃ santikaṃ gantvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekasmiṃ sākhapariyante nisīditvā tesaṃ pasaṃsanapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ kathento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāᅆasĩ, a greedy crow was wandering about Bārāᅆasĩ eating the carcasses of elephants and so on. Still unsatisfied, he thought, ‘I will go and eat dead fish on the bank of the Ganges.’ He went there, ate dead fish, and after staying for a few days, he entered the Himalayas. While eating various kinds of fruits, he came upon a great lotus lake teeming with fish and turtles. There he saw two golden-hued ruddy geese living on algae. He thought: ‘These are extremely beautiful and have attained great splendor; their food must be delicious. I will ask about their food, eat the same, and I too will become golden-hued.’ He approached them, exchanged friendly greetings, sat down on the end of a branch, and, engaging in a conversation of praise for them, he spoke the first verse:

69.

69.

“Kāsāyavatthe [V 3.0459] sakuṇe vadāmi, duve duve nandamane carante;

Kaṃ aṇḍajaṃ aṇḍajā mānusesu, jātiṃ pasaṃsanti tadiṅgha brūthā”ti.

‘I speak to you birds in russet robes, who wander in pairs, rejoicing. What egg-born species, O egg-born ones, do people praise among humans? Pray, tell me this.’

Tattha [P 3.0521] kāsāyavattheti suvaṇṇavaṇṇe kāsāyavatthe viya. Duve duveti dve dve hutvā. Nandamaneti tuṭṭhacitte. Kaṃ aṇḍajaṃ aṇḍajā mānusesu jātiṃ pasaṃsantīti ambho aṇḍajā tumhe manussesu pasaṃsantā kaṃ aṇḍajaṃ jātiṃ kataraṃ nāma aṇḍajanti vatvā pasaṃsanti, kaṃ sakuṇaṃ [M 3.0495] nāmāti vatvā tumhe manussānaṃ antare vaṇṇentīti attho. “Kaṃ aṇḍajaṃ aṇḍajamānusesū”tipi pāṭho. Tassattho – tumhe aṇḍajesu ca mānusesu ca kataraṃ aṇḍajanti vatvā pasaṃsantīti.

Therein, kāsāyavatthe means like golden-hued saffron robes. Duve duve means in pairs. Nandamane means with delighted minds. The line Kaᅃ aᅆᄱajaᅃ aᅆᄱajā mānusesu jātiᅃ pasaᅃsanti means: ‘O egg-born ones, what egg-born species do people praise among humans? What bird by name do they extol among people?’ That is the meaning. There is also the reading Kaᅃ aᅆᄱajaᅃ aᅆᄱajamānusesũ’ti. Its meaning is: ‘Among the egg-born and among humans, which egg-born one do they praise?’

Taṃ sutvā cakkavāko dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the ruddy goose spoke the second verse:

70.

70.

“Amhe manussesu manussahiṃsa, anubbate cakkavāke vadanti;

Kalyāṇabhāvamhe dijesu sammatā, abhirūpā vicarāma aṇṇave”ti.

‘O human-harmer, among people they call us, who live in concord, ruddy geese. Among the twice-born we are esteemed for our good nature; beautiful, we wander on the lake.’

Tattha manussahiṃsāti kāko manusse hiṃsati viheṭheti, tena naṃ evaṃ ālapati. Anubbateti aññamaññaṃ anugate sammodamāne viyasaṃvāse. Cakkavāketi cakkavākā nāma sā aṇḍajajātīti pasaṃsanti vaṇṇenti kathenti. Dijesūti yattakā pakkhino nāma, tesu mayaṃ “kalyāṇabhāvā”tipi manussesu sammatā. Dutiye atthavikappe manussesu amhe “cakkavākā”tipi vadanti, dijesu pana mayaṃ “kalyāṇabhāvā”ti sammatā, “kalyāṇabhāvā”ti no dijā vadantīti attho. Aṇṇaveti imasmiṃ ṭhāne saro “aṇṇavo”ti vutto, imasmiṃ padumasare mayameva dve janā paresaṃ ahiṃsanato abhirūpā vicarāmāti attho. Imissāya pana gāthāya catutthapadaṃ “na ghāsahetūpi karoma pāpa”nti paṭhanti. Tassattho – yasmā mayaṃ ghāsahetūpi pāpaṃ na karoma, tasmā “kalyāṇabhāvā”ti amhe manussesu ca dijesu ca sammatā.

Therein, manussahiᅃsa: the crow harms and harasses humans, therefore the goose addresses it thus. Anubbate: in a dwelling where they live in concord, following one another and rejoicing together. Cakkavāke: they praise, extol, and speak of that egg-born species named ruddy geese. Dijesu: among all birds so named, we are esteemed by humans as being ‘of good nature.’ In a second interpretation: among humans they call us ‘ruddy geese,’ but among the twice-born we are esteemed as being ‘of good nature’; that is, the twice-born call us ‘of good nature.’ Aᅆᅆave: in this context the lake is called aᅆᅆavo; the meaning is that in this lotus lake we two alone wander, beautiful because we do not harm others. But for this verse, some recite the fourth line as: Na ghāsahetũpi karoma pāpaᅃ (‘Not even for the sake of food do we do evil’). Its meaning is: because we do not do evil even for the sake of food, we are esteemed as ‘of good nature’ among both humans and the twice-born.

Taṃ sutvā kāko tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the crow spoke the third verse:

71.

71.

“Kiṃ aṇṇave kāni phalāni bhuñje, maṃsaṃ kuto khādatha cakkavākā;

Kiṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjatha vo anomā, balañca vaṇṇo ca anapparūpā”ti.

‘What fruits do you eat on the lake? From where do you eat meat, O ruddy geese? What food do you eat, O excellent ones, that your strength and beauty are so abundant?’

Tattha [V 3.0460] kinti pucchāvasena ālapanaṃ, kiṃ bho cakkavākāti vuttaṃ hoti. Aṇṇaveti imasmiṃ sare. Bhuñjeti bhuñjatha, kiṃ bhuñjathāti attho [M 3.0496] maṃsaṃ kuto khādathāti katarapāṇānaṃ sarīrato maṃsaṃ khādatha. Bhuñjatha voti [P 3.0522] vokāro nipātamattaṃ, parapadena vāssa sambandho “balañca vā vaṇṇo ca anapparūpā”ti.

Therein, kiṃ is a term of address in the form of a question; it means ‘What, friend cakkavāka?’ Aṇṇave means ‘in this lake.’ Bhuñje is the same as bhuñjatha; the meaning is ‘what do you eat?’ Maṃsaṃ kuto khādatha means ‘from the body of what living being do you eat meat?’ In bhuñjatha vo, the particle vo is a mere expletive, or it is connected with the following word thus: ‘balañca vā vaṇṇo ca anapparūpā’ (‘your strength and beauty are abundant’).

Tato cakkavāko catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the ruddy goose spoke the fourth verse:

72.

72.

“Na aṇṇave santi phalāni dhaṅka, maṃsaṃ kuto khādituṃ cakkavāke;

Sevālabhakkhamha apāṇabhojanā, na ghāsahetūpi karoma pāpa”nti.

“There are no fruits on the lake, O crow; where would one get meat to eat for a ruddy goose? We eat algae, a food without living beings; not even for the sake of sustenance do we do evil.”

Tattha cakkavāketi cakkavākassa. Apāṇabhojanāti pāṇakarahitaudakabhojanā. Amhākañhi sevālañceva udakañca bhojananti dasseti. Na ghāsahetūti tumhādisā viya mayaṃ ghāsahetu pāpaṃ na karomāti.

Therein, cakkavāke means ‘for a ruddy goose.’ Apāṇabhojanā means our food is devoid of living beings. It shows that our food is just algae and water. Na ghāsahetu means: unlike the likes of you, we do not do evil for the sake of sustenance.

Tato kāko dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the crow spoke two verses:

73.

73.

“Na me idaṃ ruccati cakkavāka, asmiṃ bhave bhojanasannikāso;

Ahosi pubbe tato me aññathā, icceva me vimati ettha jātā.

“This does not please me, O cakkavāka, in this existence, this resemblance between the food and the existence. Previously it was otherwise for me; thus a doubt has arisen in me here.”

74.

74.

“Ahampi maṃsāni phalāni bhuñje, annāni ca loṇiyateliyāni;

Rasaṃ manussesu labhāmi bhottuṃ, sūrova saṅgāmamukhaṃ vijetvā;

Na ca me tādiso vaṇṇo, cakkavāka yathā tavā”ti.

“I too eat meat and fruit, and foods seasoned with salt and oil; I get to enjoy the delicious tastes among humans, like a hero victorious at the battlefront; yet my complexion is not like yours, O cakkavāka.”

Tattha idanti idaṃ tumhākaṃ bhuñjanabhojanaṃ mayhaṃ na ruccati. Asmiṃ bhave bhojanasannikāsoti imasmiṃ bhave bhojanasannikāso yaṃ imasmiṃ cakkavākabhave bhojanaṃ, tvaṃ tena sannikāso taṃsadiso tadanurūpo ahosi, ativiya pasannasarīrosīti attho. Tato me aññathāti [M 3.0497] yaṃ mayhaṃ pubbe tumhe disvāva ete ettha nānāvidhāni phalāni ceva macchamaṃsañca khādanti, tena evaṃ sobhaggappattāti ahosi, idāni me tato aññathā hotīti attho. Icceva meti eteneva me kāraṇena ettha tumhākaṃ sarīravaṇṇe [P 3.0523] vimati jātā “kathaṃ nu kho ete evarūpaṃ lūkhabhojanaṃ bhuñjantā vaṇṇavanto jātā”ti. Ahampīti ahañhi, ayameva vā pāṭho[V 3.0461]. Bhuñjeti bhuñjāmi. Annāni cāti bhojanāni ca. Loṇiyateliyānīti loṇatelayuttāni. Rasanti manussesu paribhogaṃ paṇītarasaṃ. Vijetvāti yathā sūro vīrayodho saṅgāmamukhaṃ vijetvā vilumpitvā paribhuñjati, tathā vilumpitvā paribhuñjāmīti attho. Yathā tavāti evaṃ paṇītaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjantassapi mama tādiso vaṇṇo natthi, yādiso tava vaṇṇo, tena tava vacanaṃ na saddahāmīti dīpeti.

Here, ‘idaṃ’ means: this food you are eating does not please me. ‘Asmiṃ bhave bhojanasannikāso’ means: in this existence, you resemble the food; that is, the food in this cakkavāka-existence. You are similar to it, like it, conforming to it, being of very clear complexion; this is the meaning. ‘Tato me aññathā’ means: ‘Previously, when I saw you, I thought you were eating various kinds of fruit, fish, and meat here, and it was because of that you had attained such beauty, but now it is otherwise for me’; this is the meaning. ‘Icceva me’ means: for this very reason, a doubt has arisen in me concerning your physical complexion: ‘How indeed have these beings become so beautiful while eating such coarse food?’ ‘Ahampi’ means ‘I indeed,’ or this is the reading. ‘Bhuñje’ means ‘I eat.’ ‘Annāni ca’ means ‘and foods.’ ‘Loṇiyateliyāni’ means ‘endowed with salt and oil.’ ‘Rasaṃ’ means: the exquisite taste for human enjoyment. ‘Vijetvā’ means: just as a heroic warrior, having conquered the battlefront, plunders and enjoys, so do I plunder and enjoy; this is the meaning. ‘Yathā tava’ shows: ‘Even though I eat such exquisite food, my complexion is not like yours; therefore I do not believe your words.’

Athassa vaṇṇasampattiyā abhāvakāraṇaṃ attano ca bhāvakāraṇaṃ kathento cakkavāko sesagāthā abhāsi –

Then, explaining the reason for the crow's lack of beauty and the reason for his own, the cakkavāka spoke the remaining verses:

75.

75.

“Asuddhabhakkhosi khaṇānupātī, kicchena te labbhati annapānaṃ;

Na tussasī rukkhaphalehi dhaṅka, maṃsāni vā yāni susānamajjhe.

“You feed on what is impure, you are an opportunist; with difficulty you obtain food and drink. You are not content with tree-fruits, O crow, nor with the flesh that is in the middle of a charnel ground.”

76.

76.

“Yo sāhasena adhigamma bhoge, paribhuñjati dhaṅka khaṇānupātī;

Tato upakkosati naṃ sabhāvo, upakkuṭṭho vaṇṇabalaṃ jahāti.

“Whoever acquires wealth through violence and enjoys it, O crow, you opportunist—his own nature then rebukes him; being rebuked, he loses his beauty and strength.”

77.

77.

“Appampi ce nibbutiṃ bhuñjatī yadi, asāhasena aparūpaghātī;

Balañca vaṇṇo ca tadassa hoti, na hi sabbo āhāramayena vaṇṇo”ti.

“But if one, without violence, without harming others, enjoys even a little peaceful food, then he will have strength and beauty; for not all beauty is made from food alone.”

Tattha asuddhabhakkhosīti tvaṃ thenetvā vañcetvā bhakkhanato asuddhabhakkho asi. Khaṇānupātīti pamādakkhaṇe anupatanasīlo. Kicchena [M 3.0498] teti tayā dukkhena annapānaṃ labbhati. Maṃsāni vā yānīti yāni vā susānamajjhe maṃsāni, tehi na tussasi. Tatoti pacchā. Upakkosati naṃ sabhāvoti attāva taṃ puggalaṃ garahi. Upakkuṭṭhoti attanāpi parehipi upakkuṭṭho garahito vippaṭisāritāya vaṇṇañca balañca jahāsi. Nibbutiṃ bhuñjatī yadīti yadi pana paraṃ aviheṭhetvā appakampi dhammaladdhaṃ nibbutibhojanaṃ bhuñjati. Tadassa hotīti tadā assa paṇḍitassa sarīre balañca [P 3.0524] vaṇṇo ca hoti. Āhāramayenāti nānappakārena āhāreneva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bho kāka, vaṇṇo nāmesa catusamuṭṭhāno, so na āhāramatteneva hoti, utucittakammehipi hotiyevāti.

Here, ‘asuddhabhakkho si’ means: you are an eater of the impure because you eat by stealing and deceiving. ‘Khaṇānupātī’ means: one who has the nature of pouncing in a moment of heedlessness. ‘Kicchena te’ means: food and drink is obtained by you with difficulty. ‘Maṃsāni vā yāni’ means: you are not satisfied even with the meats that are in the middle of the charnel ground. ‘Tato’ means: afterwards. ‘Upakkosati naṃ sabhāvo’ means: one's own self censures that person. ‘Upakkuṭṭho’ means: being rebuked and censured by oneself and by others, because of remorse you lose your beauty and strength. ‘Yadi nibbutiṃ bhuñjati’ means: if, without harassing others, one eats even a little peaceful food obtained righteously. ‘Tadassa hoti’ means: then that wise person has strength and beauty in his body. ‘Āhāramayena’ means: just by food of various kinds. This is what is said: ‘O crow, beauty is of fourfold origin; it does not come about by food alone, but also by climate, mind, and kamma.’

Evaṃ cakkavāko anekapariyāyena kākaṃ garahi. Kāko harāyitvā “na mayhaṃ tava vaṇṇena attho, kā kā”ti vassanto palāyi.

Thus the cakkavāka censured the crow in many ways. The crow, being ashamed, crying ‘Caw, caw!’ as if saying ‘I have no use for your beauty,’ fled away.

Satthā [V 3.0462] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne lolabhikkhu anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā kāko lolabhikkhu ahosi, cakkavākī rāhulamātā, cakkavāko pana ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having given this Dhamma discourse, declared the Truths and identified the birth. At the conclusion of the talk on the Truths, the greedy bhikkhu was established in the fruit of non-returning. At that time, the crow was the greedy bhikkhu, the female cakkavāka was Rāhula’s mother, and the male cakkavāka was I myself.

Cakkavākajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Cakkavāka Jātaka is the eighth.

[435] 9. Haliddirāgajātakavaṇṇanā

[435] 9. The Commentary on the Haliddirāga Jātaka

Sutitikkhanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto thullakumārikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu terasakanipāte cūḷanāradajātake (jā. 1.13.40 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Atītavatthumhi pana sā kumārikā tassa tāpasakumārassa sīlaṃ bhinditvā attano vase ṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “imaṃ vañcetvā manussapathaṃ nessāmī”ti cintetvā “rūpādikāmaguṇavirahite araññe rakkhitasīlaṃ nāma na mahapphalaṃ hoti, manussapathe rūpādīnaṃ paccupaṭṭhāne mahapphalaṃ hoti, ehi mayā saddhiṃ tattha gantvā sīlaṃ rakkhāhi, kiṃ te araññenā”ti vatvā paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this, beginning with ‘Sutitikkhaṃ,’ concerning a monk who was seduced by a mature maiden. The story will become clear in the Cūḷanārada Jātaka in the Thirteenth Book. In the story of the past, that maiden, having broken the young ascetic's virtue and realizing he was under her control, thought, 'I will deceive this young ascetic and lead him to the world of men.' She said: “Guarding virtue in the forest, which is devoid of forms and other sense-pleasures, is not of great fruit. In the world of men, where forms and so on are present, guarding virtue is of great fruit. Come, go with me to the world of men and guard your virtue. What use is the forest to you?” and spoke the first verse:

78.

78.

“Sutitikkhaṃ [M 3.0499] araññamhi, pantamhi sayanāsane;

Ye ca gāme titikkhanti, te uḷāratarā tayā”ti.

“It is easy to endure in the forest, in a remote lodging; but those who endure in the village—they are far more noble than you.”

Tattha sutitikkhanti suṭṭhu adhivāsanaṃ. Titikkhantīti sītādīni adhivāsenti.

There, ‘sutitikkhaṃ’ means easy to endure. ‘Titikkhanti’ means: they endure cold and so on.

Taṃ sutvā tāpasakumāro “pitā me araññaṃ gato, tasmiṃ āgate taṃ āpucchitvā gamissāmī”ti āha. Sā cintesi “pitā kirassa [P 3.0525] atthi, sace maṃ so passissati, kājakoṭiyā maṃ pothetvā vināsaṃ pāpessati, mayā paṭhamameva gantabba”nti. Atha naṃ sā “tena hi ahaṃ maggasaññaṃ kurumānā paṭhamataraṃ gamissāmi, tvaṃ pacchā āgacchāhī”ti vatvā agamāsi. So tassā gatakāle neva dārūni āhari, na pānīyaṃ, na paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpesi, kevalaṃ pajjhāyantova nisīdi, pitu āgamanakāle paccuggamanaṃ nākāsi. Atha naṃ pitā “itthīnaṃ vasaṃ gato eso”ti ñatvāpi “kasmā tāta, neva dārūni āhari, na pānīyaṃ, na paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpesi, pajjhāyantoyeva pana nisinnosī”ti āha. Atha naṃ tāpasakumāro “tāta, araññe kira rakkhitasīlaṃ nāma na mahapphalaṃ hoti, manussapathe mahapphalaṃ[V 3.0463], ahaṃ tattha gantvā sīlaṃ rakkhissāmi, sahāyo me maṃ ‘āgaccheyyāsī’ti vatvā purato gato, ahaṃ teneva saddhiṃ gamissāmi, tattha pana vasantena mayā kataro puriso sevitabbo”ti pucchanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the young ascetic said: “My father has gone into the forest. When he returns, I will take my leave of him and go.” She thought: “So he has a father! If he sees me, he will beat me with the end of a carrying pole and kill me. I must go first.” Then she said to him: “Well then, I will go on ahead, marking the path. You come along afterwards,” and she left. After she had gone, the young ascetic did not fetch firewood or prepare drinking or usable water, but just sat there moping. When his father returned, he did not go out to meet him. Although the father knew, “He has followed the will of a woman,” he asked: “Why, my dear, have you not fetched firewood or prepared drinking or usable water, but just sit there moping?” Then the young ascetic replied: “Father, they say that guarding virtue in the forest is not of great fruit, but in the world of men it is of great fruit. I will go to the world of men and guard my virtue. A companion of mine told me to come and has gone on ahead. I will go with that companion. But while living in the world of men, what kind of person should I associate with?” Asking this, he spoke the second verse:

79.

79.

“Araññā gāmamāgamma, kiṃsīlaṃ kiṃvataṃ ahaṃ;

Purisaṃ tāta seveyyaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti.

“Having come from the forest to a village, what kind of virtue, what observance should I have? What kind of person, father, should I associate with? Tell me this, since you have been asked.”

Athassa pitā kathento sesagāthā abhāsi –

Then his father, wishing to inform him, spoke the remaining verses:

80.

80.

“Yo te vissāsaye tāta, vissāsañca khameyya te;

Sussūsī ca titikkhī ca, taṃ bhajehi ito gato.

“One who would be intimate with you, my dear, and who would welcome your intimacy, one who is eager to listen and is patient—associate with him when you have gone from here.

81.

81.

“Yassa kāyena vācāya, manasā natthi dukkaṭaṃ;

Urasīva patiṭṭhāya, taṃ bhajehi ito gato.

“One for whom there is no wrongdoing by body, speech, or mind—associate with him when you have gone from here, relying on him as if established on a mother’s breast.

82.

82.

“Yo ca dhammena carati, carantopi na maññati;

Visuddhakāriṃ sappaññaṃ, taṃ bhajehi ito gato.

“One who lives righteously, and in so living is not conceited, a wise person who acts with purity—associate with him when you have gone from here.

83.

83.

“Haliddirāgaṃ [M 3.0500] kapicittaṃ, purisaṃ rāgavirāginaṃ;

Tādisaṃ tāta mā sevi, nimmanussampi ce siyā.

“A person whose affection is like turmeric dye, whose mind is like a monkey’s, who loves and loathes in an instant—do not associate with such a one, my dear, even if the earth were empty of other men.

84.

84.

“Āsīvisaṃva kupitaṃ, mīḷhalittaṃ mahāpathaṃ;

Ārakā parivajjehi, yānīva visamaṃ pathaṃ.

“Avoid him from afar, like an angered venomous snake, like a highway smeared with filth, just as a traveler in a vehicle avoids a treacherous road.

85.

85.

“Anatthā [P 3.0526] tāta vaḍḍhanti, bālaṃ accupasevato;

Māssu bālena saṃgacchi, amitteneva sabbadā.

“Misfortunes grow, my dear, for one who associates excessively with a fool. Do not keep company with a fool; he is always like an enemy.

86.

86.

“Taṃ tāhaṃ tāta yācāmi, karassu vacanaṃ mama;

Māssu bālena saṃgacchi, dukkho bālehi saṅgamo”ti.

“Therefore I implore you, my dear, do what I say: do not keep company with a fool, for association with fools is painful.”

Tattha [V 3.0464] yo te vissāsayeti yo tava vissāseyya. Khameyya teti yo ca tava attani tayā kataṃ vissāsaṃ khameyya. Sussūsī ca titikkhī cāti tava vacanaṃ sussūsāya ceva vacanādhivāsanena ca samannāgato bhaveyyāti attho. Urasīva patiṭṭhāyāti yathā mātu urasi putto patiṭṭhāti, evaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā attano mātaraṃ viya maññamāno taṃ bhajeyyāsīti vadati. Yo ca dhammena caratīti yo tividhena sucaritena dhammena iriyati. Na maññatīti tathā carantopi “ahaṃ dhammaṃ carāmī”ti mānaṃ na karoti. Visuddhakārinti visuddhānaṃ dasakusalakammapathānaṃ kārakaṃ.

There, ‘yo te vissāsaye’ means one who would be intimate with you. ‘Khameyya te’ means one who would be pleased with the intimacy you have established in him. ‘Sussūsī ca titikkhī ca’ means he would be endowed with an eagerness to listen to your words and with patience toward them; this is the meaning. ‘Urasīva patiṭṭhāya’ means just as a son is established on his mother's breast, so you should associate with him, relying on him and regarding him like your own mother. ‘Yo ca dhammena carati’ means one who conducts oneself by the Dhamma of threefold good conduct. ‘Na maññati’ means even while living so, one does not generate the conceit, “I alone am living righteously.” ‘Visuddhakāriṃ’ means a doer of the pure ten wholesome courses of action.

Rāgavirāginanti rāginañca virāginañca rajjitvā taṃkhaṇaññeva virajjanasabhāvaṃ. Nimmanussampi ce siyāti sacepi sakalajambudīpatalaṃ nimmanussaṃ hoti, soyeva eko manusso tiṭṭhati, tathāpi tādisaṃ mā sevi. Mahāpathanti gūthamakkhitaṃ maggaṃ viya. Yānīvāti yānena gacchanto viya. Visamanti ninnaunnatakhāṇupāsāṇādivisamaṃ. Bālaṃ accupasevatoti bālaṃ appaññaṃ atisevantassa. Sabbadāti tāta, bālena saha saṃvāso nāma amittasaṃvāso viya sabbadā niccakālameva dukkho. Taṃ tāhanti tena kāraṇena taṃ ahaṃ.

‘Who loves and loathes’ (rāgavirāginaṃ) means one who has the nature of being passionate and then immediately dispassionate. ‘Even if the land were empty of other humans’ means even if the whole surface of Jambudīpa were devoid of humans, and only that one person remained, still one should not associate with such a person. ‘A great path’ is like a road smeared with excrement. ‘As if by vehicle’ means like one traveling by a vehicle. ‘Uneven’ means uneven with depressions, elevations, stumps, stones, and the like. ‘Associating excessively with a fool’ means associating with a fool of little wisdom. ‘Always’ means: dear one, association with a fool is like association with an enemy—always, perpetually painful. ‘Therefore I’ means: for that reason, I...

So evaṃ pitarā ovadito “tāta, ahaṃ manussapathaṃ gantvā tumhādise paṇḍite na labhissāmi, tattha gantuṃ bhāyāmi, idheva tumhākaṃ santike vasissāmī”ti āha. Athassa bhiyyopi ovādaṃ datvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ [M 3.0501] ācikkhi. So na cirasseva abhiññāsamāpattiyo nibbattetvā saddhiṃ pitarā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus advised by his father, the young ascetic said: “Father, if I go to the world of men, I will not find wise persons like you. I am afraid to go there; I will stay right here in your presence.” Then, having given him further advice, his father taught him the preliminary kasiṇa meditation. Before long, he produced the direct knowledges and meditative attainments and, together with his father, reached the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, explained the truths, and identified the birth. At the conclusion of the truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā tāpasakumāro ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu ahosi, kumārikā thullakumārikāva, pitā tāpaso pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the ascetic youth was the discontented bhikkhu, the young woman was the old maid, and the ascetic father was I myself.

Haliddirāgajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Haliddirāga Jātaka, the Ninth.

[436] 10. Samuggajātakavaṇṇanā

[436] 10. The Commentary on the Samugga Jātaka

Kuto [V 3.0465][P 3.0527] nu āgacchathāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “kasmā bhikkhu mātugāmaṃ patthesi, mātugāmo nāmesa asabbho akataññū, pubbe dānavarakkhasā gilitvā kucchinā pariharantāpi mātugāmaṃ rakkhituṃ ekapurisanissitaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, tvaṃ kathaṃ sakkhissasī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'From where have you come?' This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jeta's Grove, concerning a discontented bhikkhu. The Teacher asked him: 'Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are discontented?' When he replied, 'It is true, Bhante,' the Teacher said: 'Why, bhikkhu, do you long for a woman? A woman, you know, is unworthy of association and ungrateful. In the past, even demonic ogres who swallowed a woman and carried her in their belly were unable to protect her and keep her faithful to one man. How then will you be able to?' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāme pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā phalāphalena yāpento vihāsi. Tassa paṇṇasālāya avidūre eko dānavarakkhaso vasati. So antarantarā mahāsattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ suṇāti, aṭaviyaṃ pana manussānaṃ sañcaraṇamagge ṭhatvā āgatāgate manusse gahetvā khādati. Tasmiṃ kāle ekā kāsiraṭṭhe kuladhītā uttamarūpadharā aññatarasmiṃ paccantagāme nivutthā hoti. Tassā ekadivasaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ dassanatthāya gantvā paccāgamanakāle parivāramanusse disvā so dānavo bheravarūpena pakkhandi. Manussā bhītā gahitagahitāvudhāni chaḍḍetvā palāyiṃsu. Dānavo yāne nisinnaṃ abhirūpaṃ mātugāmaṃ disvā paṭibaddhacitto hutvā taṃ attano guhaṃ netvā bhariyaṃ akāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya sappitelataṇḍulamacchamaṃsādīni ceva madhuraphalāphalāni ca āharitvā taṃ posesi, vatthālaṅkārehi ca naṃ alaṅkaritvā rakkhaṇatthāya ekasmiṃ karaṇḍake pakkhipitvā [M 3.0502] karaṇḍakaṃ gilitvā kucchinā pariharati. So ekadivasaṃ nhāyitukāmatāya ekaṃ saraṃ gantvā karaṇḍakaṃ uggilitvā taṃ tato nīharitvā nhāpetvā vilimpetvā alaṅkāretvā “thokaṃ tava sarīraṃ utuṃ gaṇhāpehī”ti taṃ karaṇḍakasamīpe ṭhapetvā sayaṃ nhānatitthaṃ otaritvā taṃ anāsaṅkamāno thokaṃ dūraṃ gantvā [P 3.0528] nhāyi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta renounced sensual pleasures, entered the Himalayas, and went forth as an ascetic. Having produced the direct knowledges and meditative attainments, he dwelt there, sustaining himself on wild fruits and roots. Not far from his leaf-hut lived a demonic ogre. From time to time, he would approach the Great Being and listen to the Dhamma. But he would also stand on the path that humans used to travel through the forest, seize those who came along, and devour them. At that time, a daughter of a good family in the Kāsī country, who was of supreme beauty, was living in a certain border village. One day, after going to see her parents, she was on her way back. Seeing her retinue, the demon rushed at them in a terrifying form. The people were frightened, dropped whatever weapons they had seized, and fled. Seeing the beautiful woman seated in the carriage, the demon became infatuated with her. He took her to his cave and made her his wife. From then on, he brought her ghee, oil, rice, fish, meat, and sweet wild fruits to nourish her. He adorned her with clothes and ornaments and, in order to protect her, he placed her in a casket, swallowed the casket, and carried her around in his belly. One day, wanting to bathe, he went to a lake, disgorged the casket, took her out, bathed her, anointed her, and adorned her. He said, 'Let your body get some fresh air for a while.' He placed her near the casket, went down to the bathing spot, and, not suspecting her of anything, went a short distance away to bathe.

Tasmiṃ samaye vāyussaputto nāma vijjādharo sannaddhakhaggo ākāsena gacchati. Sā taṃ disvā “ehī”ti hatthamuddaṃ akāsi, vijjādharo khippaṃ otari. Atha naṃ sā karaṇḍake pakkhipitvā dānavassa āgamanaṃ olokentī karaṇḍakūpari nisīditvā taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā tassa attānaṃ dassetvā tasmiṃ karaṇḍakasamīpaṃ asampatteyeva karaṇḍakaṃ vivaritvā anto pavisitvā vijjādharassa upari nipajjitvā attano sāṭakaṃ pārupi. Dānavo āgantvā karaṇḍakaṃ asodhetvā “mātugāmoyeva me”ti saññāya karaṇḍakaṃ gilitvā attano guhaṃ gacchanto [V 3.0466] antarāmagge cintesi “tāpaso me ciraṃ diṭṭho, ajja tāva naṃ gantvā vandissāmī”ti. So tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Tāpasopi naṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā dvinnaṃ janānaṃ kucchigatabhāvaṃ ñatvā sallapanto paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, a sorcerer named Vāyussaputta, girt with a sword, was traveling through the sky. Seeing him, she made a hand signal to him, saying, 'Come!' and the sorcerer quickly descended. Then she put him in the casket and, watching for the demon's return, sat on top of it. When she saw him coming, she showed herself to him. Before he reached the casket, she opened it, got inside, lay down on top of the sorcerer, and covered herself with her outer robe. The demon came, and without checking the casket, thinking, 'It is just my woman,' he swallowed it. While going back to his cave, he thought on the way: 'It has been a long time since I have seen the ascetic. Today I will go and pay homage to him.' So he went to the ascetic. Seeing him coming from afar and knowing that there were two people in his belly, the ascetic spoke, reciting the first verse:

87.

87.

“Kuto nu āgacchatha bho tayo janā, svāgatā etha nisīdathāsane;

Kaccittha, bhonto kusalaṃ anāmayaṃ, cirassamabbhāgamanañhi vo idhā”ti.

'From where, sirs, do you three people come? Welcome! Come, take a seat. I trust, sirs, that you are well and healthy? For it has been a long time since you have come here.'

Tattha bhoti ālapanaṃ. Kaccitthāti kacci hotha bhavatha vijjatha. Bhontoti puna ālapanto āha. Kusalaṃ anāmayanti kacci tumhākaṃ kusalaṃ ārogyaṃ. Cirassamabbhāgamanañhi vo idhāti ajja tumhākaṃ idha abbhāgamanañca ciraṃ jātaṃ.

Herein, 'bho' is a term of address. 'Kaccittha' means: I trust you are, you exist, you are present. With 'bhonto' he addresses them again. 'Kusalaṃ anāmayaṃ' means: I trust you have well-being and health. 'Cirassamabbhāgamanañhi vo idhā' means: your arrival here today has occurred after a long time.

Taṃ sutvā dānavo “ahaṃ imassa tāpasassa santikaṃ ekakova āgato, ayañca tāpaso ‘tayo janā’ti vadati, kiṃ nāmesa katheti, kiṃ nu kho sabhāvaṃ ñatvā katheti, udāhu ummattako hutvā vilapatī”ti cintetvā tāpasaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the demon thought: 'I have come to this ascetic all alone, yet this ascetic says, "three people." What on earth is he saying? Is he speaking because he knows the real situation, or is he raving because he has gone mad?' Having thought thus, he approached the ascetic, paid homage, sat down to one side, and while conversing with him, spoke the second verse:

88.

88.

“Ahameva [P 3.0529][M 3.0503] eko idha majja patto, na cāpi me dutiyo koci vijjati;

Kimeva sandhāya te bhāsitaṃ ise, kuto nu āgacchatha bho tayo janā”ti.

'I alone have arrived here today, and there is no second person with me. In reference to what, O sage, did you say: "From where, sirs, do you three people come?"'

Tattha idha majjāti idha ajja. Kimeva sandhāya te bhāsitaṃ iseti bhante, isi kiṃ nāmetaṃ sandhāya tayā bhāsitaṃ, pākaṭaṃ tāva me katvā kathehīti.

Herein, 'idha majja' means 'idha ajja' (here today). The phrase 'Kimeva sandhāya te bhāsitaṃ ise' means: 'Venerable sage, in reference to what did you say this? First make it plain to me, and then speak.'

Tāpaso “ekaṃsenevāvuso sotukāmosī”ti pucchitvā “āma, bhante”ti vutte “tena hi suṇāhī”ti vatvā tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

The ascetic asked, 'Friend, do you definitely wish to hear?' When he replied, 'Yes, venerable sir,' the ascetic said, 'Well then, listen,' and recited the third verse.

89.

89.

“Tuvañca eko bhariyā ca te piyā, samuggapakkhittanikiṇṇamantare;

Sā rakkhitā kucchigatāva te sadā, vāyussaputtena sahā tahiṃ ratā”ti.

'You are one, and your dear wife is another, placed in a casket and swallowed, inside you. Though always protected by you, being in your belly, she delights there together with Vāyussaputta.'

Tattha tuvañca ekoti paṭhamaṃ tāva tvaṃ eko jano. Pakkhittanikiṇṇamantareti pakkhittānikiṇṇaantare taṃ tattha bhariyaṃ rakkhitukāmena sadā tayā samugge pakkhittā saddhiṃ samuggena [V 3.0467] nikiṇṇā antare, antokucchiyaṃ ṭhapitāti attho. Vāyussaputtena sahāti evaṃnāmakena vijjādharena saddhiṃ. Tahiṃ ratāti tattha tava antokucchiyaññeva kilesaratiyā ratā. So dāni tvaṃ mātugāmaṃ “ekaṃ purisanissitaṃ karissāmī”ti kucchināpi pariharanto tassā jāraṃ ukkhipitvā carasīti.

Herein, 'tuvañca eko' means: first, you are one person. 'Pakkhittanikiṇṇamantareti' means: 'pakkhittānikiṇṇa-antare' is she who was swallowed along with the casket and kept inside by you, who always wished to protect your wife there; the meaning is, she was placed inside your belly. 'Vāyussaputtena sahā' means: together with the sorcerer of that name. 'Tahiṃ ratā' means: she delights right there inside your very belly in sensual pleasure. So now you, thinking, 'I will make this woman faithful to only one man,' carry her in your belly and yet you go about carrying her lover too.

Taṃ sutvā dānavo “vijjādharā nāma bahumāyā honti, sacassa khaggo hatthagato bhavissati, kucchiṃ me phāletvāpi palāyissatī”ti bhītatasito hutvā khippaṃ karaṇḍakaṃ uggilitvā purato ṭhapesi. Satthā abhisambuddho hutvā taṃ pavattiṃ pakāsento catutthaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the demon thought: 'Sorcerers possess many illusions. If his sword comes into his hand, he might even split open my belly and escape.' Frightened and trembling, he quickly disgorged the casket and placed it in front of him. The Teacher, as the Perfectly Enlightened One, clarifying this matter, spoke the fourth verse:

90.

90.

“Saṃviggarūpo [M 3.0504] isinā viyākato, so dānavo tattha samuggamuggili;

Addakkhi [P 3.0530] bhariyaṃ sucimāladhāriniṃ, vāyussaputtena sahā tahiṃ rata”nti.

'Agitated by what the sage had explained, that demon there disgorged the casket. He saw his wife, wearing a pure garland, delighting there together with Vāyussaputta.'

Tattha addakkhīti so karaṇḍakaṃ vivaritvā addasa.

Herein, 'addakkhi' means: he opened the casket and saw.

Karaṇḍake pana vivaṭamatteyeva vijjādharo vijjaṃ jappitvā khaggaṃ gahetvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Taṃ disvā dānavo mahāsattassa tussitvā thutipubbaṅgamā sesagāthā abhāsi –

But as soon as the casket was opened, the sorcerer muttered a charm, seized his sword, and leapt into the sky. Seeing this, the demon was pleased with the Great Being and, beginning with praise, spoke the remaining verses:

91.

91.

“Sudiṭṭharūpamuggatapānuvattinā, hīnā narā ye pamadāvasaṃ gatā;

Yathā have pāṇarivettha rakkhitā, duṭṭhā mayī aññamabhippamodayi.

'This true nature has been well seen by you, follower of the ascetic path. Base are the men who fall under the power of women. Though protected by me here as my very life, she, treacherous towards me, delighted in another.'

92.

92.

“Divā ca ratto ca mayā upaṭṭhitā, tapassinā jotirivā vane vasaṃ;

Sā dhammamukkamma adhammamācari, akiriyarūpo pamadāhi santhavo.

'I, dwelling in the forest, attended on her day and night as an ascetic attends a fire. But she, transgressing what is right, practiced what is wrong. Intimacy with women is an improper thing.'

93.

93.

“Sarīramajjhamhi ṭhitāti maññahaṃ, mayhaṃ ayanti asatiṃ asaññataṃ;

Sā dhammamukkamma adhammamācari, akiriyarūpo pamadāhi santhavo.

'I regarded this unmindful and unrestrained one as standing in the midst of my body, thinking, "She is mine." She transgressed the Dhamma and practiced what is not the Dhamma. Intimacy with women is an unseemly thing.'

94.

94.

“Surakkhitaṃ meti kathaṃ nu vissase, anekacittāsu na hatthi rakkhaṇā;

Etā hi pātālapapātasannibhā, etthappamatto byasanaṃ nigacchati.

'How can one trust that she is well protected by me? There is no protecting those of fickle minds. For they are like a chasm, a precipice; herein a heedless person meets with disaster.'

95.

95.

“Tasmā [V 3.0468] hi te sukhino vītasokā, ye mātugāmehi caranti nissaṭā;

Etaṃ sivaṃ uttamamābhipatthayaṃ, na mātugāmehi kareyya santhava”nti.

'Therefore, happy are they, free from sorrow, who live detached from women. Aspiring to this supreme security, one should not cultivate intimacy with women.'

Tattha [P 3.0531][M 3.0505] sudiṭṭharūpamuggatapānuvattināti bhante, isi uggatapānuvattinā tayā sudiṭṭharūpaṃ idaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Hīnāti nīcā. Yathā have pāṇarivettha rakkhitāti ayaṃ mayā attano pāṇā viya ettha antokucchiyaṃ pariharantena rakkhitā. Duṭṭhā mayīti idāni mayi mittadubbhikammaṃ katvā duṭṭhā aññaṃ purisaṃ abhippamodati. Jotirivā vane vasanti vane vasantena tapassinā aggi viya mayā upaṭṭhitā paricaritā. Sā dhammamukkammāti sā esā dhammaṃ okkamitvā atikkamitvā. Akiriyarūpoti akattabbarūpo. Sarīramajjhamhi ṭhitāti maññahaṃ, mayhaṃ ayanti asatiṃ asaññatanti imaṃ asatiṃ asappurisadhammasamannāgataṃ asaññataṃ dussīlaṃ “mayhaṃ sarīramajjhamhi ṭhitā”ti ca “mayhaṃ aya”nti ca maññāmi.

Therein, 'sudiṭṭharūpamuggatapānuvattinā' means: 'Venerable sir, O seer, this reason has been clearly seen by you who follow the ascetic path.' 'Hīnā' means base. 'Yathā have pāṇarivettha rakkhitā' means: she was protected by me, carrying her here inside my belly, as if she were my own life. 'Duṭṭhā mayī' means: now, having committed an act of treachery against me, she is corrupted and delights in another man. 'Jotirivā vane vasaṃ' means: she was attended and served by me like a fire is by an ascetic dwelling in the forest. 'Sā dhammamukkamma' means: this one, having departed from and transgressed the Dhamma. 'Akiriyarūpo' means: of a nature that should not be done. 'Sarīramajjhamhi ṭhitāti maññahaṃ, mayhaṃ ayanti asatiṃ asaññatanti' means: I think of this unmindful, unrestrained, immoral one, who possesses the qualities of an unworthy person, 'She stands in the middle of my body' and 'This one is mine.'

Surakkhitaṃ meti kathaṃ nu vissaseti ayaṃ mayā surakkhitāti kathaṃ paṇḍito vissāseyya, yatra hi nāma mādisopi antokucchiyaṃ rakkhanto rakkhituṃ nāsakkhi. Pātālapapātasannibhāti lokassādena duppūraṇīyattā mahāsamudde pātālasaṅkhātena papātena sadisā. Etthappamattoti etāsu evarūpāsu nigguṇāsu pamatto puriso mahābyasanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā hīti yasmā mātugāmavasaṃ gatā mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇanti, tasmā ye mātugāmehi nissaṭā hutvā caranti, te sukhino. Etaṃ sivanti yadetaṃ mātugāmato nissaṭānaṃ visaṃsaṭṭhānaṃ caraṇaṃ, etaṃ jhānasukhameva sivaṃ khemaṃ uttamaṃ abhipatthetabbaṃ, etaṃ patthayamāno mātugāmehi saddhiṃ santhavaṃ na kareyyāti.

'Surakkhitaṃ meti kathaṃ nu vissase' means: how could a wise person trust, 'She is well protected by me,' when even one like me, while protecting her inside my belly, was unable to protect her? 'Pātālapapātasannibhā' means: because they are difficult to satisfy with worldly tastes, they are similar to the precipice in the great ocean known as the abyss. 'Etthappamatto' means: a heedless man among such worthless women as these comes to great disaster. 'Tasmā hi' means: since those who fall under the sway of women meet with great destruction, therefore those who live detached from women are happy. 'Etaṃ sivaṃ' means: this living detached and disassociated from women—this very bliss of jhāna—is the security, the safety, the supreme state that should be aspired to. Aspiring to this, one should not form an intimacy with women.

Evañca pana vatvā dānavo mahāsattassa pādesu nipatitvā “bhante, tumhe nissāya mayā jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ, ahaṃ imāya pāpadhammāya vijjādharena mārāpito”ti mahāsattaṃ abhitthavi. Sopissa dhammaṃ desetvā “imissā mā kiñci pāpaṃ akāsi, sīlāni gaṇhāhī”ti taṃ pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi. Dānavo “ahaṃ kucchinā pariharantopi taṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkomi, añño ko rakkhissatī”ti taṃ uyyojetvā attano araññameva agamāsi.

Having spoken thus, the demon fell at the Great Being's feet, praised him, and said: 'Venerable sir, because of you I have received my life. I was almost killed by this wicked woman and the sorcerer.' The Great Being taught him the Dhamma, saying: 'Do no harm to her. Undertake the precepts,' and he established him in the five precepts. The demon, thinking, 'If even I, carrying her in my belly, am unable to protect her, who else will protect her?' sent her away and went back to his own forest.

Satthā [M 3.0506] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tadā dibbacakkhukatāpaso ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and proclaimed the Truths, identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the ascetic with the divine eye was myself.

Samuggajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Samugga Jātaka: The Tenth.

[437] 11. Pūtimaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā

[437] 11. The Commentary on the Pūtimaṃsa Jātaka

Na [V 3.0469][P 3.0532] kho me ruccatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto indriyaasaṃvaraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye bahū bhikkhū indriyesu aguttadvārā ahesuṃ. Satthā “ime bhikkhū ovadituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ānandattherassa vatvā aniyamavasena bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā alaṅkatapallaṅkavaramajjhagato bhikkhū āmantetvā “na, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā nāma rūpādīsu subhanimittavasena nimittaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati, sace hi tasmiṃ samaye kālaṃ karoti, nirayādīsu nibbattati, tasmā rūpādīsu subhanimittaṃ mā gaṇhatha. Bhikkhunā nāma rūpādigocarena na bhavitabbaṃ, rūpādigocarā hi diṭṭheva dhamme mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇanti, tasmā varaṃ, bhikkhave, tattāya ayosalākāya ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya cakkhundriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭha”nti vitthāretvā “tumhākaṃ rūpaṃ olokanakālopi atthi anolokanakālopi. Olokanakāle subhavasena anoloketvā asubhavaseneva olokeyyātha, evaṃ attano gocarā na parihāyissatha. Ko pana tumhākaṃ gocaroti? Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, nava lokuttaradhammā. Etasmiñhi vo gocare carantānaṃ na lacchati māro otāraṃ, sace pana kilesavasikā hutvā subhanimittavasena olokessatha, pūtimaṃsasiṅgālo viya attano gocarā parihāyissathā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“It does not please me...” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana regarding non-restraint of the senses. At one time, many monks were unguarded in their sense-doors. The Teacher, thinking, “These monks should be admonished,” spoke to the Elder Ānanda and, without making any special distinction, had the Saṅgha of monks assembled. Seated in the middle of a splendid decorated couch, he addressed the monks: “Monks, it is not proper for a monk to grasp at a sign through the power of the beautiful in forms and so on. If he were to die at that time, he would be reborn in hell or the like. Therefore, do not grasp at the sign of beauty in forms and so on. A monk should not make forms and so on his pasture. Those whose pasture is forms and so on meet with great ruin in this very life. Therefore, monks, it would be better for the eye faculty to be seared with a red-hot iron stake, blazing, flaming, and glowing.” He elaborated, saying: “For you, there is a time to look and a time not to look. When it is time to look, do not look with an idea of beauty, but look with an idea of foulness. In this way, you will not fall away from your own pasture. And what is your pasture? The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases of spiritual power, the Noble Eightfold Path, and the nine supramundane states. If you dwell within this pasture, Māra will find no opportunity. But if, overcome by defilements, you look with an idea of beauty, you will fall away from your pasture like the jackal Pūtimaṃsa.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente himavantapadese araññāyatane pabbataguhāyaṃ anekasatā eḷakā vasanti. Tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānato avidūre ekissā guhāya pūtimaṃso nāma siṅgālo veṇiyā nāma bhariyāya saddhiṃ vasati. So ekadivasaṃ bhariyāya saddhiṃ vicaranto [M 3.0507] te eḷake disvā “ekena upāyena imesaṃ maṃsaṃ khādituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā upāyena ekekaṃ eḷakaṃ māresi. Te ubhopi eḷakamaṃsaṃ khādantā thāmasampannā thūlasarīrā ahesuṃ. Anupubbena eḷakā parikkhayaṃ agamaṃsu. Tesaṃ antare meṇḍamātā [P 3.0533] nāma ekā eḷikā byattā ahosi upāyakusalā. Siṅgālo taṃ māretuṃ asakkonto ekadivasaṃ bhariyāya saddhiṃ sammantento “bhadde, eḷakā khīṇā, imaṃ eḷikaṃ ekena upāyena khādituṃ vaṭṭati, ayaṃ panettha upāyo, tvaṃ ekikāva gantvā etāya saddhiṃ sakhī hohi, atha te tāya saddhiṃ vissāse uppanne ahaṃ matālayaṃ karitvā nipajjissāmi, tvaṃ etaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ‘eḷike sāmiko me mato, ahañca anāthā, ṭhapetvā taṃ añño me ñātako natthi, ehi roditvā kanditvā tassa sarīrakiccaṃ karissāmā’ti vatvā taṃ gahetvā āgaccheyyāsi, atha naṃ ahaṃ uppatitvā gīvāya ḍaṃsitvā māressāmī”ti āha.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, in a forest region of the Himalayas, many hundreds of goats lived in a mountain cave. Not far from their dwelling place, in another cave, lived a jackal named Pūtimaṃsa with his wife named Veṇī. One day, while wandering with his wife, he saw those goats and thought, 'By some means, it would be good to eat their meat.' So, by a trick, he killed the goats one by one. Both of them ate the goat meat and became strong and stout. Gradually, the goats dwindled in number. Among them was an astute and clever she-goat named Meṇḍamātā. Unable to kill her, one day the jackal consulted with his wife: 'My dear, the goats are gone. We must eat this she-goat by some stratagem. Here is the plan: you go alone and befriend her. Then, when you have gained her trust, I will make a pretense of being dead and lie down. You should approach her and say, “Friend she-goat, my husband is dead, and I am helpless. Apart from you, I have no other kinsman. Come, let us weep and wail, and perform his funeral rites.” Then bring her here, and I will spring up, bite her on the neck, and kill her.'

Sā [V 3.0470] “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tāya saddhiṃ sakhibhāvaṃ katvā vissāse uppanne eḷikaṃ tathā avoca. Eḷikā “āḷi siṅgāli tava sāmikena sabbe mama ñātakā khāditā, bhāyāmi na sakkomi gantu”nti āha. “Āḷi, mā bhāyi, matako kiṃ karissatī”ti? “Kharamanto te sāmiko, bhāyāmevāha”nti sā evaṃ vatvāpi tāya punappunaṃ yāciyamānā “addhā mato bhavissatī”ti sampaṭicchitvā tāya saddhiṃ pāyāsi. Gacchantī pana “ko jānāti, kiṃ bhavissatī”ti tasmiṃ āsaṅkāya siṅgāliṃ purato katvā siṅgālaṃ pariggaṇhantīyeva gacchati. Siṅgālo tāsaṃ padasaddaṃ sutvā “āgatā nu kho eḷikā”ti sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā akkhīni parivattetvā olokesi. Eḷikā taṃ tathā karontaṃ disvā “ayaṃ pāpadhammo maṃ vañcetvā māretukāmo matālayaṃ dassetvā nipanno”ti nivattitvā palāyantī siṅgāliyā “kasmā palāyasī”ti vutte taṃ kāraṇaṃ kathentī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

She agreed, saying, 'Good,' and after befriending her and gaining her trust, she spoke to the she-goat as planned. The she-goat said, 'Friend she-jackal, your husband has eaten all my kinsmen. I am afraid and cannot go.' 'Friend, do not be afraid. What can a dead one do?' 'Your husband is of sharp counsel; I am still afraid.' Although she said this, being repeatedly implored by the she-jackal, she finally thought, 'He must surely be dead,' and agreed to go with her. But as she went, thinking, 'Who knows what will happen?' she became suspicious and made the she-jackal walk in front, keeping a close watch on the jackal. Hearing their footsteps, the jackal thought, 'Has the she-goat come?' and lifted his head, turning his eyes to look. Seeing him do this, the she-goat realized, 'This wicked one wants to deceive and kill me; he is lying down feigning death.' Turning back to flee, she was asked by the she-jackal, 'Why are you fleeing?' Explaining the reason, she spoke the first verse:

96.

96.

“Na [P 3.0534] kho me ruccati āḷi, pūtimaṃsassa pekkhanā;

Etādisā sakhārasmā, ārakā parivajjaye”ti.

“Indeed, friend, the sight of Pūtimaṃsa does not please me. From such a friend as this, one should keep far away.”

Tattha [M 3.0508] āḷīti ālapanaṃ, sakhi sahāyiketi attho. Etādisā sakhārasmāti evarūpā sahāyakā apakkamitvā taṃ sahāyakaṃ ārakā parivajjeyyāti attho.

Therein, 'āḷi' is a term of address; the meaning is 'friend,' 'companion.' 'From such a friend as this' means: one should withdraw from such a companion and avoid that companion from afar.

Evañca pana vatvā sā nivattitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gatā. Siṅgālī taṃ nivattetuṃ asakkontī tassā kujjhitvā attano sāmikasseva santikaṃ gantvā pajjhāyamānā nisīdi. Atha naṃ siṅgālo garahanto dutiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Having said this, she turned back and went to her own dwelling place. The she-jackal, unable to make her return, became angry with her, went to her own husband, and sat down sulking. Then the jackal, rebuking her, spoke the second verse:

97.

97.

“Ummattikā ayaṃ veṇī, vaṇṇeti patino sakhiṃ;

Pajjhāyi paṭigacchantiṃ, āgataṃ meṇḍamātara”nti.

“This Veṇī is mad! She praises her friend to her husband, and sulks over Meṇḍamātā, who came and is now returning.”

Tattha veṇīti tassā nāmaṃ. Vaṇṇeti patino sakhinti paṭhamameva attano sakhiṃ eḷikaṃ “mayi sinehā vissāsikā āgamissati no santikaṃ, matālayaṃ karohī”ti patino santike vaṇṇeti. Atha naṃ sā idāni āgataṃ mama santikaṃ anāgantvāva paṭigacchantiṃ meṇḍamātaraṃ pajjhāyati anusocatīti.

Herein, Veṇī is her name. 'She praises her friend to her husband' means: first, she praised her own friend, the she-goat, to her husband, saying: ‘Out of affection and trust for me, she will come into our presence. Make a pretense of death!’ Then, when the she-goat had come near but was turning back without approaching, she sulks and grieves for Meṇḍamātā.

Taṃ sutvā siṅgālī tatiyaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the she-jackal spoke the third verse:

98.

98.

“Tvaṃ [V 3.0471] khosi samma ummatto, dummedho avicakkhaṇo;

Yo tvaṃ matālayaṃ katvā, akālena vipekkhasī”ti.

“Friend, you are surely mad, dull-witted, and undiscerning, you who, having feigned death, look out at the wrong time.”

Tattha avicakkhaṇoti vicāraṇapaññārahito. Akālena vipekkhasīti eḷikāya attano santikaṃ anāgatāyeva olokesīti attho.

Herein, 'undiscerning' means devoid of investigative wisdom. 'You look out at the wrong time' means: you looked out when the ewe had not yet come into your presence; this is the meaning.

99.

99.

“Na akāle vipekkhayya, kāle pekkheyya paṇḍito;

Pūtimaṃsova pajjhāyi, yo akāle vipekkhatī”ti. – ayaṃ abhisambuddhagāthā;

“A wise person would not look out at the wrong time; one should look out at the right time. Like the Putrid Flesh jackal, one who looks out at the wrong time grieves.” This is a verse of the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Tattha akāleti kāmaguṇe ārabbha subhavasena cittuppādakāle. Ayañhi bhikkhuno rūpaṃ oloketuṃ akālo nāma. Kāleti asubhavasena anussativasena kasiṇavasena vā rūpaggahaṇakāle. Ayañhi [M 3.0509] bhikkhuno rūpaṃ oloketuṃ kālo nāma. Tattha akāle sārattakāle rūpaṃ olokentā mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇantīti haritacajātakalomasakassapajātakādīhi dīpetabbaṃ. Kāle asubhavasena olokentā arahatte patiṭṭhahantīti asubhakammikatissattheravatthunā kathetabbaṃ. Pūtimaṃsova pajjhāyīti bhikkhave, yathā pūtimaṃsasiṅgālo akāle eḷikaṃ oloketvā attano [P 3.0535] gocarā parihīno pajjhāyati, evaṃ bhikkhu akāle subhavasena rūpaṃ oloketvā satipaṭṭhānādigocarā parihīno diṭṭhadhamme samparāyepi socati pajjhāyati kilamatīti.

Herein, 'at the wrong time' means at the time when a mind arises based on sensual pleasures, by way of the perception of beauty. This, indeed, is the wrong time for a monk to look at a form. 'At the right time' means at the time of grasping a form by way of the perception of foulness, by way of recollection, or by way of a kasiṇa. This, indeed, is the right time for a monk to look at a form. Herein, it should be illustrated by the Haritaca Jātaka, the Lomasakassapa Jātaka, and so on, that those who look at a form at the wrong time—the time of lust—meet with great destruction. It should be told through the story of the Elder Tissa, the practitioner of meditation on foulness, that those who look at the right time with the perception of foulness become established in arahantship. 'Like the Putrid Flesh jackal, one grieves' means: monks, just as the Putrid Flesh jackal, having looked for the ewe at the wrong time and thus been deprived of his feeding ground, grieves; so too a monk, having looked at a form at the wrong time with the perception of beauty and thus been deprived of his feeding ground of the foundations of mindfulness and so on, sorrows, grieves, and is tormented both in this present life and in the future.

Veṇīpi kho siṅgālī pūtimaṃsaṃ assāsetvā “sāmi, mā cintesi, ahaṃ taṃ punapi upāyena ānessāmi, tvaṃ āgatakāle appamatto gaṇheyyāsī”ti vatvā tassā santikaṃ gantvā “āḷi, tava āgatakāleyeva no attho jāto, tava āgatakālasmiṃyeva hi me sāmiko satiṃ paṭilabhi, idāni jīvati, ehi tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karohī”ti vatvā pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the she-jackal Veṇī, having comforted Pūtimaṃsa, said: ‘Master, do not worry. I will bring her back again by a stratagem. When she comes, you must be heedful and seize her.’ Then, going to the ewe’s presence, she said: ‘Friend, just when you arrived, our purpose was served. For it was just at the time of your arrival that my master regained his senses and is now alive. Come, exchange friendly greetings with him.’ Having said this, she spoke the fifth verse:

100.

100.

“Piyaṃ kho āḷi me hotu, puṇṇapattaṃ dadāhi me;

Pati sañjīvito mayhaṃ, eyyāsi piyapucchikā”ti.

‘Friend, may what is pleasing be mine! Give me a full bowl. My husband has been revived; come, you who inquire after my beloved.’

Tattha puṇṇapattaṃ dadāhi meti piyakkhānaṃ akkhāyikā mayhaṃ tuṭṭhidānaṃ dehi. Pati sañjīvito mayhanti mama sāmiko sañjīvito uṭṭhito arogoti attho. Eyyāsīti mayā saddhiṃ āgaccha.

Here, ‘Give me a full bowl’ means: ‘Give me, the announcer of good news, a gift of satisfaction.’ ‘My husband has been revived’ means: my master has returned to life, has stood up, and is healthy. ‘Come’ means: come with me.

Eḷikā [V 3.0472] “ayaṃ pāpadhammā maṃ vañcetukāmā, ayuttaṃ kho pana paṭipakkhakaraṇaṃ, upāyeneva naṃ vañcessāmī”ti cintetvā chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

The ewe thought: ‘This wicked one desires to deceive me. But it is improper to act as an opponent; I will deceive her by a stratagem.’ Then she spoke the sixth verse:

101.

101.

“Piyaṃ kho āḷi te hotu, puṇṇapattaṃ dadāmi te;

Mahatā parivārena, essaṃ kayirāhi bhojana”nti.

‘Friend, may what is pleasing be yours! I give you a full bowl. I will come with a great retinue; prepare a meal for them!’

Tattha essanti āgamissāmi. Āgacchamānā ca attano ārakkhaṃ katvā mahantena parivārena āgamissāmīti.

Here, ‘I will come’ means: I will arrive. And it means: ‘While coming, having arranged for my own protection, I will come with a large retinue.’

Atha [M 3.0510] naṃ siṅgālī parivāraṃ pucchantī sattamaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the she-jackal, asking her about the retinue, spoke the seventh verse:

102.

102.

“Kīdiso tuyhaṃ parivāro, yesaṃ kāhāmi bhojanaṃ;

Kiṃ nāmakā ca te sabbe, te me akkhāhi pucchitā”ti.

‘What is your retinue like, for whom I shall prepare a meal? And what are all their names? Tell them to me, as you are asked.’

Sā ācikkhantī aṭṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

She, explaining it, spoke the eighth verse:

103.

103.

“Māliyo caturakkho ca, piṅgiyo atha jambuko;

Ediso mayhaṃ parivāro, tesaṃ kayirāhi bhojana”nti.

‘Māliya and Caturakkha, Piṅgiya and then Jambuka; such is my retinue, prepare a meal for them.’

Tattha [P 3.0536] te meti te parivāre mayhaṃ ācikkhi. Māliyotiādīni catunnaṃ sunakhānaṃ nāmāni. “Tattha ekekassa pañca pañca sunakhasatāni parivārenti, evaṃ dvīhi sunakhasahassehi parivāritā āgamissāmī”ti vatvā “sace te bhojanaṃ na labhissanti, tumhe dvepi jane māretvā khādissantī”ti āha.

Here, ‘Tell them to me’ means: tell me about that retinue. Māliya and so on are the names of four dogs. She said: ‘Each of them is attended by five hundred dogs; thus I will come surrounded by two thousand dogs.’ Then she added: ‘If they do not get a meal, they will kill and devour both of you.’

Taṃ sutvā siṅgālī bhītā “alaṃ imissā tattha gamanena, upāyenassā anāgamanameva karissāmī”ti cintetvā navamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the she-jackal was frightened and thought: ‘Enough of her coming here! By a stratagem I will ensure she does not come.’ Then she spoke the ninth verse:

104.

104.

“Nikkhantāya agārasmā, bhaṇḍakampi vinassati;

Ārogyaṃ āḷino vajjaṃ, idheva vasa māgamā”ti.

‘When you have left your house, your property will be ruined. I will tell your friend of your good health. Dwell right here, do not come!’

Tassattho [V 3.0473] – āḷi, tava gehe bahubhaṇḍakaṃ atthi, taṃ te nikkhantāya agārasmā anārakkhaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ vinassati, ahameva te āḷino sahāyakassa ārogyaṃ vajjaṃ vadissāmi, tvaṃ idheva vasa māgamāti.

The meaning is this: Friend, there is much property in your house; when you leave the house, that unguarded property of yours will be ruined. I myself will tell your friend and companion of your good health. You dwell right here, do not come.

Evañca pana vatvā maraṇabhayabhītā vegena sāmikassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ gahetvā palāyi. Te puna taṃ ṭhānaṃ āgantuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu.

And having said this, terrified by the fear of death, she quickly went to her master's side, took him, and fled. They did not dare to come to that place again.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā ahaṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne vanajeṭṭhakarukkhe nibbattadevatā ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the birth story: ‘At that time, I was the deity born in the chief tree of the forest in that place.’

Pūtimaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā ekādasamā.

The Commentary on the Pūtimaṃsa Jātaka, the eleventh.

[438] 12. Daddarajātakavaṇṇanā

[438] 12. The Commentary on the Tittira Jātaka

Yo [M 3.0511] te puttaketi idaṃ satthā gijjhakūṭe viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi samaye dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “aho āvuso devadatto nillajjo anariyo evaṃ uttamaguṇadharassa sammāsambuddhassa ajātasattunā saddhiṃ ekato hutvā dhanuggahapayojanasilāpavijjhananāḷāgirivissajjanehi vadhāya upāyaṃ karotī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti [P 3.0537] vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi devadatto mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakki, idāni pana me tāsamattampi kātuṃ nāsakkhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher spoke this, beginning with ‘Yo te puttaketi,’ while dwelling at the Vulture Peak, concerning Devadatta's striving to kill him. At that time, in the Hall of Dhamma, the monks raised a discussion: ‘Friends, Devadatta is shameless and ignoble; having joined with Ajātasattu, he contrives means to kill the Perfectly Enlightened One, who possesses supreme virtues, by employing archers, hurling a rock, and releasing the Nāḷāgiri elephant.’ The Teacher arrived and asked, ‘For what discussion are you now gathered here, monks?’ When they replied, ‘For this one,’ he said: ‘Not only now, monks, but in the past too Devadatta strove to kill me. But now he was not able to cause me even a particle of alarm.’ Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente eko disāpāmokkho ācariyo pañcasatānaṃ māṇavakānaṃ sippaṃ vācento ekadivasaṃ cintesi “mayhaṃ idha vasantassa palibodho hoti, māṇavakānampi sippaṃ na niṭṭhāti, himavantapadese araññāyatanaṃ pavisitvā tattha vasanto vācessāmī”ti. So māṇavakānaṃ kathetvā tilataṇḍulatelavatthādīni gāhāpetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā maggato avidūre ṭhāne paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā nivāsaṃ kappesi, māṇavāpi attano paṇṇasālaṃ kariṃsu. Māṇavakānaṃ ñātakā telataṇḍulādīni pesenti. Raṭṭhavāsinopi “disāpāmokkho ācariyo kira araññe asukaṭṭhāne nāma vasanto sippaṃ uggaṇhāpetī”ti tassa taṇḍulādīni abhiharanti, kantārappaṭipannāpi denti, aññataropi puriso khīrapānatthāya savacchaṃ [V 3.0474] dhenuṃ adāsi. Ācariyassa paṇṇasālāya santike dvīhi potakehi saddhiṃ ekā godhā vasati, sīhabyagghāpissa upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchanti. Eko tittiropi tattha nibaddhavāso ahosi. So ācariyassa māṇavānaṃ mante vācentassa saddaṃ sutvā tayopi vede uggaṇhi. Māṇavā tena saddhiṃ ativissāsikā ahesuṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a world-renowned teacher was teaching the arts to five hundred young brahmins. One day he thought: ‘Living here is an obstruction for me, and the students’ training is not being completed. I will enter a forest haunt in the Himalayan region and teach while living there.’ He told the students, had them gather sesame, rice, oil, cloth, and so on, and entered the forest. In a place not far from the path, he had a leaf-hut built and took up residence. The students also made their own leaf-huts. The students’ relatives sent them oil, rice, and so on. The country-folk too, hearing, ‘A world-renowned teacher, they say, is living in the forest in such-and-such a place and teaching the arts,’ brought him rice and other provisions. Travelers on the wilderness path also gave things. A certain man gave a cow with its calf for the purpose of drinking milk. Near the teacher’s leaf-hut lived an iguana with her two young. Lions and tigers also came to attend on him. A partridge, too, lived there regularly. Hearing the sound of the teacher reciting the mantras to the students, it learned the three Vedas. The students became very intimate with it.

Aparabhāge māṇavesu nipphattiṃ appattesuyeva ācariyo kālamakāsi. Māṇavā tassa sarīraṃ jhāpetvā vālukāya thūpaṃ katvā nānāpupphehi pūjetvā rodanti paridevanti. Atha ne tittiro “kasmā [M 3.0512] rodathā”ti āha. “Ācariyo no sippe aniṭṭhiteyeva kālakato, tasmā rodāmā”ti. “Evaṃ sante mā socittha, ahaṃ vo sippaṃ vācessāmī”ti. “Tvaṃ kathaṃ jānāsī”ti? “Ahaṃ ācariye tumhākaṃ vācente saddaṃ sutvā tayo vede paguṇe akāsinti. Tena hi attano paguṇabhāvaṃ amhe jānāpehī”ti. Tittiro [P 3.0538] “tena hi suṇāthā”ti tesaṃ gaṇṭhiṭṭhānameva pabbatamatthakā nadiṃ otaranto viya osāresi. Māṇavā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā hutvā tittirapaṇḍitassa santike sippaṃ paṭṭhapesuṃ. Sopi disāpāmokkhācariyassa ṭhāne ṭhatvā tesaṃ sippaṃ vācesi. Māṇavā tassa suvaṇṇapañjaraṃ karitvā upari vitānaṃ bandhitvā suvaṇṇataṭṭake madhulājādīni upaharantā nānāvaṇṇehi pupphehi pūjentā mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ kariṃsu. “Tittiro kira araññāyatane pañcasate māṇavake mantaṃ vācetī”ti sakalajambudīpe pākaṭo ahosi.

Later, while the young men had not yet completed their training, their teacher passed away. The young men cremated his body, built a stūpa of sand, honored it with various flowers, and wept and lamented. Then the partridge asked them, "Why are you weeping?" "Our teacher passed away before our training was complete, so we weep." "If that is so, do not grieve. I will teach you the arts." "How do you know them?" "While your teacher was teaching you, I listened to the sound and became proficient in the three Vedas." "Then let us know of your proficiency." The partridge said, "Very well, listen," and he recited the difficult passages as if they were water descending from a mountaintop to a river. Delighted and joyful, the young men began their training under the wise partridge. He, standing in the place of the world-renowned teacher, taught the arts to them. The young men made a golden cage for him, fastened a canopy above, offered honey, parched grain, and other things on golden plates, honored him with flowers of various colors, and showed him great respect. The news, "A partridge is reciting the mantras to five hundred young men in a forest abode," became known throughout all of Jambudīpa.

Tadā jambudīpe giraggasamajjasadisaṃ mahantaṃ chaṇaṃ ghosayiṃsu. Māṇavānaṃ mātāpitaro “chaṇadassanatthāya āgacchantū”ti pesesuṃ. Māṇavā tittirassa ārocetvā tittirapaṇḍitaṃ sabbañca assamapadaṃ godhaṃ paṭicchāpetvā attano attano nagarameva agamiṃsu. Tadā eko nikkāruṇiko duṭṭhatāpaso tattha tattha vicaranto taṃ ṭhānaṃ sampāpuṇi. Godhā taṃ disvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “asukaṭṭhāne taṇḍulā, asukaṭṭhāne telādīni atthi, bhattaṃ pacitvā bhuñjāhī”ti vatvā gocaratthāya gatā. Tāpaso pātova bhattaṃ pacitvā dve godhāputtake māretvā khādi, divā tittirapaṇḍitañca vacchakañca māretvā khādi, sāyaṃ dhenuṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā tampi māretvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā rukkhamūle nipajjitvā ghurughurāyanto niddaṃ okkami. Godhā sāyaṃ āgantvā puttake apassantī upadhārayamānā vicari. Rukkhadevatā godhaṃ puttake adisvā kampamānaṃ oloketvā khandhaviṭapabbhantare dibbānubhāvena ṭhatvā “godhe mā kampi, iminā pāpapurisena tava puttakā ca tittiro ca vaccho ca dhenu ca māritā, gīvāya naṃ ḍaṃsitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpehī”ti sallapantī paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, a great festival like a mountain-top fair was proclaimed in Jambudīpa. The parents of the young men sent a message, saying: "Come to see the festival." The young men informed the partridge, entrusted the wise partridge and the entire hermitage to the iguana, and each went to his own city. Then a merciless, wicked ascetic, wandering here and there, arrived at that place. The iguana saw him, gave him a friendly greeting, and said, "There are rice grains in such-and-such a place, and oil and other things in another place. Cook a meal and eat." Then she went out to forage. Early in the morning, the ascetic cooked a meal, killed and ate the two young iguanas. At midday, he killed and ate the wise partridge and the calf. In the evening, seeing the cow returning, he killed her too, ate the flesh, lay down at the foot of a tree, and fell asleep, snoring loudly. When the iguana returned in the evening, she did not see her young and wandered about searching. A tree-deity, seeing the iguana trembling at not finding her young, stood within the trunk and branches by divine power and, addressing her, spoke the first stanza: "O iguana, do not tremble. Your young, the partridge, the calf, and the cow have been killed by this evil man. Bite him on the neck and bring him to the destruction of his life."

105.

105.

“Yo [V 3.0475][P 3.0539] te puttake akhādi, dinnabhatto adūsake;

Tasmiṃ dāṭhaṃ nipātehi, mā te muccittha jīvato”ti.

"On him who ate your harmless young, though you had given him a meal, unleash your fangs; may he not escape from you alive."

Tattha [M 3.0513] dinnabhattoti bhattaṃ pacitvā bhuñjāhīti tayā dinnabhatto. Adūsaketi niddose niraparādhe. Tasmiṃ dāṭhaṃ nipātehīti tasmiṃ pāpapurise catassopi dāṭhā nipātehīti adhippāyo. Mā te muccittha jīvatoti jīvanto sajīvo hutvā tava hatthato eso pāpadhammo mā muccittha, mokkhaṃ mā labhatu, jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpehīti attho.

Herein, 'given a meal' means: he was given a meal by you with the words, 'Cook a meal and eat.' 'Harmless' means: the faultless, blameless ones. 'Unleash your fangs on him' means: the intention is, 'Unleash all four fangs on that evil man.' 'May he not escape from you alive' means: let not this evil one escape from your hand alive, as a living being; let him not gain release; bring him to the destruction of his life.

Tato godhā dve gāthā abhāsi –

Then the iguana recited two stanzas:

106.

106.

“Ākiṇṇaluddo puriso, dhāticelaṃva makkhito;

Padesaṃ taṃ na passāmi, yattha dāṭhaṃ nipātaye.

"A man intensely cruel, smeared over like a nurse's cloth; I do not see a single spot on him where I could set my fang."

107.

107.

“Akataññussa posassa, niccaṃ vivaradassino;

Sabbaṃ ce pathaviṃ dajjā, neva naṃ abhirādhaye”ti.

"To an ungrateful person, always looking for a flaw, even if one were to give the whole earth, one could never please him."

Tattha ākiṇṇaluddoti gāḷhaluddo. Vivaradassinoti chiddaṃ otāraṃ pariyesantassa. Neva naṃ abhirādhayeti evarūpaṃ puggalaṃ sakalapathaviṃ dentopi tosetuṃ na sakkuṇeyya, kimaṅgaṃ panāhaṃ bhattamattadāyikāti dasseti.

Herein, 'intensely cruel' means extremely cruel. 'Looking for a flaw' means seeking a fault or an opening. 'One could never please him' shows: "Even by giving the entire earth one would not be able to please such a person; how much less I, who am a giver of just a meal?"

Godhā evaṃ vatvā “ayaṃ pabujjhitvā mampi khādeyyā”ti attano jīvitaṃ rakkhamānā palāyi. Tepi pana sīhabyagghā tittirassa sahāyakāva, kadāci te āgantvā tittiraṃ passanti, kadāci so gantvā tesaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā āgacchati, tasmiṃ pana divase sīho byagghaṃ āha – “samma, ciraṃ diṭṭho no tittiro, ajja sattaṭṭhadivasā honti, gaccha, tāvassa pavattiṃ ñatvā ehī”ti. Byaggho “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā godhāya palāyanakāle taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā taṃ pāpapurisaṃ niddāyantaṃ passi. Tassa jaṭantare tittirapaṇḍitassa lomāni [P 3.0540] paññāyanti, dhenuyā ca vacchakassa ca aṭṭhīni paññāyanti. Byaggharājā taṃ sabbaṃ disvā suvaṇṇapañjare ca tittirapaṇḍitaṃ adisvā “iminā pāpapurisena ete māritā bhavissantī”ti taṃ pādena paharitvā uṭṭhāpesi. Sopi taṃ disvā bhītatasito ahosi. Atha naṃ byaggho “tvaṃ ete māretvā khādasī”ti pucchi. “Neva māremi, na khādāmī”ti. “Pāpadhamma tayi amārente añño [V 3.0476] ko māressati, kathehi tāva kāraṇaṃ, akathentassa jīvitaṃ te natthī”ti. So maraṇabhayabhīto “āma, sāmi, godhāputtake ca vacchakañca dhenuñca māretvā khādāmi, tittiraṃ pana [M 3.0514] na māremī”tiāha. So tassa bahuṃ kathentassapi asaddahitvā “tvaṃ kuto āgatosī”ti pucchitvā “sāmi, kaliṅgaraṭṭhato vāṇijakānaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ vahanto jīvikahetu idañcidañca kammaṃ katvā idānimhi idhāgato”ti tena sabbasmiṃ attanā katakamme kathite “pāpadhamma tayi tittiraṃ amārente añño ko māressati, ehi sīhassa migarañño santikaṃ taṃ nessāmī”ti taṃ purato katvā tāsento agamāsi. Sīharājā taṃ ānentaṃ byagghaṃ pucchanto catutthaṃ gāthamāha –
