The iguana, having said this, fled to protect her life, thinking, "If this man wakes up, he might eat me too." Now, that lion and tiger were friends of the partridge. Sometimes the lion and tiger would come to visit the partridge; sometimes the partridge would go to them, preach the Dhamma, and return. On that day, however, the lion said to the tiger, "Friend, it has been a long time since we saw the wise partridge—it has been seven or eight days now. Go, find out what has happened to him and return." The tiger agreed, saying, "Very well," and arrived at that place at the time the iguana was fleeing. There he saw that wicked man sleeping. In the man's matted hair, the feathers of the wise partridge were visible; the bones of a cow and a calf were also visible. Seeing all this, and not finding the wise partridge in the golden cage, the tiger king thought, "This wicked man must have killed these creatures." He struck the man with his paw to wake him. The deceitful ascetic, seeing the tiger, was terrified. Then the tiger asked him, "You wicked man, did you kill and eat those creatures?" "Lord, I did not eat them," replied the deceitful ascetic. The tiger said, "You man of evil conduct, if you did not kill them, who else did? If you do not speak the truth, you shall not live." Fearing death, the deceitful ascetic said, "Lord, I killed and ate the offspring of the iguana, the calf, and the cow. But I did not kill the partridge." Although he spoke much, the tiger did not believe him and asked, "Where have you come from?" The deceitful ascetic replied, "I came from the Kalinga country, carrying goods for merchants for my livelihood. I have done this and that work, and now I have arrived here." When the deceitful ascetic had thus recounted all his deeds, the tiger said, "You man of evil conduct, if you did not kill the partridge, who else would? Come, I will take you to my friend, the king of beasts." Then, putting the man in front and threatening him, the tiger went to the lion. The lion king, wishing to question the tiger who was bringing the deceitful ascetic, spoke the fourth stanza:

108.

108.

“Kiṃ nu subāhu taramānarūpo, paccāgatosi saha māṇavena;

Kiṃ kiccamatthaṃ idhamatthi tuyhaṃ, akkhāhi me pucchito etamattha”nti.

"Why, O Strong-Arm, do you return in such a hurry together with this young man? What business or purpose do you have here? Being asked, explain this matter to me."

Tattha subāhūti byagghaṃ nāmenālapati. Byagghassa hi purimakāyo manāpo hoti, tena taṃ evamāha. Kiṃ kiccamatthaṃ idhamatthi tuyhanti kiṃ karaṇīyaṃ atthasaññitaṃ iminā māṇavena idha atthi. “Tuyhaṃ kiṃ kiccamattha”ntipi pāṭho, ayamevattho.

In this context, 'Subāhu' (Strong-Arm) is the name he uses to address the tiger. This is because the forebody of a tiger is pleasing. 'What business or purpose do you have here?' means: what task, designated as a purpose, is there here with this young man? There is also the reading 'Tuyhaṃ kiṃ kiccamatthaṃ,' which has the same meaning. The lion asks the tiger to explain the reason after being questioned.

Taṃ [P 3.0541] sutvā byaggho pañcamaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the tiger recited the fifth stanza:

109.

109.

“Yo te sakhā daddaro sādhurūpo, tassa vadhaṃ parisaṅkāmi ajja;

Purisassa kammāyatanāni sutvā, nāhaṃ sukhiṃ daddaraṃ ajja maññe”ti.

"Your friend Daddara, of such excellent character—I suspect his death today. Having heard this man's occupations, I do not think Daddara is safe and well today."

Tattha daddaroti tittiro. Tassa vadhanti tassa tittirapaṇḍitassa imamhā purisamhā ajja vadhaṃ parisaṅkāmi. Nāhaṃ sukhinti ahaṃ ajja daddaraṃ sukhiṃ arogaṃ na maññāmi.

In this context, 'Daddara' refers to the partridge. 'I suspect his death' means: I suspect the slaying of that wise partridge today because of this man. 'I do not think him well' means: I do not consider Daddara to be well and healthy today.

Atha naṃ sīho chaṭṭhaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the lion recited the sixth stanza to the tiger:

110.

110.

“Kānissa kammāyatanāni assu, purisassa vuttisamodhānatāya;

Kaṃ vā paṭiññaṃ purisassa sutvā, parisaṅkasi daddaraṃ māṇavenā”ti.

"What were the occupations of this man in the course of his livelihood that you heard? Or having heard what admission from him do you suspect Daddara was killed by this young man?"

Tattha [M 3.0515] assūti assosi. Vuttisamodhānatāyāti jīvitavuttisamodhānatāya, kāni nāma iminā [V 3.0477] attano kammāni tuyhaṃ kathitānīti attho. Māṇavenāti kiṃ sutvā iminā māṇavena māritaṃ parisaṅkasi.

In this context, 'assu' means 'assosi' (you heard). 'In the course of his livelihood' means in the sum of his means of sustaining life; the meaning is: 'What deeds of his were related to you?' 'By the young man' means: 'Having heard what, do you suspect that he killed Daddara?'

Athassa kathento byaggharājā sesagāthā abhāsi –

Then the tiger king, explaining to the lion king, recited these stanzas:

111.

111.

“Ciṇṇā kaliṅgā caritā vaṇijjā, vettācaro saṅkupathopi ciṇṇo;

Naṭehi ciṇṇaṃ saha vākurehi, daṇḍena yuddhampi samajjamajjhe.

"He has traversed the Kalinga country and practiced trade. He has travelled the path of canes and the path of spikes. He has associated with actors and with trappers. He has even fought with a staff in the midst of an assembly."

112.

112.

“Baddhā kulīkā mitamāḷakena, akkhā jitā saṃyamo abbhatīto;

Abbāhitaṃ pubbakaṃ aḍḍharattaṃ, hatthā daḍḍhā piṇḍapaṭiggahena.

"Birds were bound by him; he worked with false measures; he won at dice; he transgressed all restraint. He drew off the blood of the wounded at midnight; his hands were burnt by accepting hot food."

113.

113.

“Tānissa [P 3.0542] kammāyatanāni assu, purisassa vuttisamodhānatāya;

Yathā ayaṃ dissati lomapiṇḍo, gāvo hatā kiṃ pana daddarassā”ti.

"Those were the spheres of work of this man in the pursuit of his livelihood that I heard. Since this mass of feathers is visible in his hair—he who killed the cows, how could he not have killed the partridge?"

Tattha ciṇṇā kaliṅgāti vāṇijakānaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ vahantena kira tena kaliṅgaraṭṭhe ciṇṇā. Caritā vaṇijjāti vaṇijjāpi tena katā. Vettācaroti vettehi sañcaritabbo. Saṅkupathopi ciṇṇoti khāṇukamaggopi valañjito. Naṭehīti jīvikahetuyeva naṭehipi saddhiṃ. Ciṇṇaṃ saha vākurehīti vākuraṃ vahantena vākurehi saddhiṃ caritaṃ. Daṇḍena yuddhanti daṇḍena yuddhampi kira tena yujjhitaṃ.

Here, 'traversed Kalinga' means: it is said he traversed the Kalinga country while carrying the goods of merchants. 'Engaged in trade' means: he also engaged in trade. 'Wandered the cane-brake' means: to be traversed with canes. 'Trodden the staked path' means: even a path with stakes was frequented. 'With actors' means: solely for the sake of livelihood, even with actors. 'Associated with trappers' means: while carrying a trap, he associated with trappers. 'Fought with a stick' means: it is said he even fought with a stick.

Baddhā kulīkāti sakuṇikāpi kira tena baddhā. Mitamāḷakenāti dhaññamāpakakammampi kira tena kataṃ. Akkhā jitāti akkhadhuttānaṃ veyyāvaccaṃ karontena [M 3.0516] akkhā haṭā. Saṃyamo abbhatītoti jīvitavuttiṃ nissāya pabbajanteneva sīlasaṃyamo atikkanto. Abbāhitanti apaggharaṇaṃ kataṃ. Pubbakanti lohitaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – iminā kira jīvikaṃ nissāya rājāparādhikānaṃ hatthapāde chinditvā te ānetvā sālāya nipajjāpetvā vaṇamukhehi paggharantaṃ lohitaṃ aḍḍharattasamaye tattha gantvā kuṇḍakadhūmaṃ datvā ṭhapitanti. Hatthā daḍḍhāti ājīvikapabbajjaṃ pabbajitakāle uṇhapiṇḍapātapaṭiggahaṇe hatthāpi kirassa daḍḍhā.

'A bird was bound' means: it is said that even a quail was bound by him. 'With a measuring basket' means: it is said that even the work of measuring grain was done by him. 'The dice were won' means: while performing services for gamblers, the dice were taken. 'Restraint was transgressed' means: because he had gone forth depending on a livelihood, moral restraint was transgressed. 'Not drawn out' means: it was made to ooze. 'The former thing' means: blood. This is what is said: it is said that, depending on this for his livelihood, after cutting off the hands and feet of royal offenders, he brought them and laid them down in a hall; then, going there at midnight and applying bran-smoke, he collected the blood oozing from the mouths of the wounds. 'Hands were burnt' means: it is said that when he went forth as a livelihood-ascetic, his hands were also burnt in receiving hot almsfood.

Tānissa kammāyatanānīti tāni assa kammāni. Assūti assosiṃ. Yathā ayanti yathā esa etassa jaṭantare tittiralomapiṇḍopi dissati, iminā kāraṇena veditabbametaṃ “eteneva [V 3.0478] so mārito”ti. Gāvo hatā kiṃ pana daddarassāti gāvopi etena hatā, daddarassa pana kiṃ na hanitabbaṃ, kasmā esa taṃ na māressatīti.

'Those were his spheres of work' means those were his deeds. 'Assu' means 'I heard.' 'Just as this one' means just as this mass of partridge feathers is seen within his matted hair; for this reason, it should be known that 'he was killed by this very man.' 'Cows were killed, why then would he not kill Daddara?' means since even cows were killed by him, why would the partridge not be killed? Why would he spare him?

Sīho taṃ purisaṃ pucchi “mārito te tittirapaṇḍito”ti? “Āma, sāmī”ti. Athassa saccavacanaṃ sutvā sīho taṃ vissajjetukāmo ahosi. Byaggharājā pana “māretabbayuttako eso”ti vatvā tattheva naṃ dāṭhāhi paharitvā māretvā āvāṭaṃ khaṇitvā [P 3.0543] pakkhipi. Māṇavā āgantvā tittirapaṇḍikaṃ adisvā roditvā paridevitvā nivattiṃsu.

The lion asked the man, "Did you kill the wise partridge?" "Yes, lord," he replied. Then, having heard his truthful admission, the lion wished to release him. But the tiger king, saying, "This man deserves to be killed," struck him right there with his fangs, killed him, and buried him in a pit. The young men came, and not seeing the wise partridge, they wept and returned.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, devadatto pubbepi mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkī”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kūṭajaṭilo devadatto ahosi, godhā uppalavaṇṇā, byaggho moggallāno, sīho sāriputto, disāpāmokkho ācariyo mahākassapo, tittirapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having presented this Dhamma discourse, said: "Bhikkhus, in this way Devadatta strove to kill me in the past also." Then he identified the birth story: "At that time, the deceitful ascetic was Devadatta, the iguana was Uppalavaṇṇā, the tiger was Moggallāna, the lion was Sāriputta, the world-renowned teacher was Mahākassapa, and the wise partridge was I myself."

Daddarajātakavaṇṇanā dvādasamā.

The Commentary on the Daddara Jātaka, the Twelfth.

Jātakuddānaṃ –

The Summary of the Jātakas –

Gijjhakosambī [M 3.0517] suvañca, cūḷasūvaṃ harittacaṃ;

Kusalaṃ lomakassapaṃ, cakkavākaṃ haliddi ca.

The Gijjha, Kosambī, and Suva, Cūḷasūva, Harittaca; Kusala, Lomakassapa, Cakkavāka, and Haliddi.

Samuggaṃ pūtimaṃsañca, daddarañceva dvādasa;

Jātake navanipāte, gīyiṃsu gītikārakā.

Samugga, Pūtimaṃsa, and Daddara make twelve Jātakas in the Book of Nine that the composers sang.

Navakanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Book of Nines is finished.

(Tatiyo bhāgo niṭṭhito.)

(The Third Part is finished.)
